SUMMARY

In recent weeks, an unlikely coalition has assembled around a simple idea: Artificial intelligence companies should be held legally responsible when their systems go rogue. In a series of escalating attacks reported since July, A.I. models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others have hacked companies and even meddled with government websites, all without the knowledge of their creators. Common sense might indicate A.I. companies would also be held liable for their runaway technology.

ARTICLE

A.I. Is Going Rogue. Who Should Be Held Responsible?
Many think artificial intelligence companies should be held liable for their runaway technology. But legal scholars say applying existing law could be messy
By David McCabe
Published 2026-10-01 15:25 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/technology/ai-rogue-agents-liability.html

In recent weeks, an unlikely coalition has assembled around a simple idea: Artificial intelligence companies should be held legally responsible when their systems go rogue.

In a series of escalating attacks reported since July, A.I. models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others have hacked companies and even meddled with government websites, all without the knowledge of their creators.

Since then, Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive; David Sacks, the venture capitalist and a top White House adviser; and Lina Khan, the Federal Trade Commission chair under the Biden administration, have all endorsed the idea that A.I. companies are liable.

“Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products,” Ms. Khan said in a post to X last month, adding there’s “no A.I. exemption from laws already on the books.”

Companies have long been held accountable for everything from faulty toys to plane crashes under consumer protection laws. Courts can hold companies legally responsible for damage caused by negligence or a defective product. And they can assign additional blame to other people or organizations that were involved.

Common sense might indicate A.I. companies would also be held liable for their runaway technology. But the problem is so new that courts have largely yet to confront it, according to legal experts.

There are some cases where A.I. companies would clearly be held responsible, the experts said — for example, if executives understand predicted risks posed by their models. But other claims will push the justice system's application of laws that hinge on human intent and knowledge.

Some legal test cases are emerging. Florida’s Republican attorney general asked a state court on Monday to temporarily block OpenAI from developing new A.I. models without safety measures approved by an outside group, an attempt to prevent A.I. from going rogue.

On Tuesday, a nonprofit in California sued OpenAI under a state unfair competition law for the hacking of the start-up Hugging Face. On Wednesday, an investigation by the F.T.C. into potential liability for harm to consumers became public. And on Thursday, California’s attorney general said the state had served a subpoena to OpenAI as part of a “broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models.”

Given the relative lack of safeguards around A.I., the legal drumbeat is likely to continue, said Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University who studies technology law.

“Worst-case scenario, they have massive liability on both the criminal and civil side, just depending on the facts of the individual case,” he said. “We haven’t seen the firm-busting case yet. But I could envision it.”

A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment. A spokeswoman for OpenAI did not comment. (The New York Times has sued OpenAI and its partner, Microsoft, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. OpenAI and Microsoft have denied those claims.)

Since ChatGPT was publicly launched in 2022, A.I. companies have built increasingly sophisticated models capable of writing code, operating a computer and engaging in daily interactions. A.I. companies have also built tools referred to as “agents,” able to traverse the internet to accomplish tasks ranging from sending an email to booking a reservation — or scraping vast amounts of data.

The debate over liability exploded after companies ran tests in which agents broke out of testing environments and breached other companies. In the July incident, OpenAI disclosed that its A.I. had hacked Hugging Face, another tech firm, without its knowledge. Last month, OpenAI said its product had penetrated an Australian government system.

OpenAI apologized for the Australian incident on Tuesday and said it was “working to do better in the future.” One Australian official said that in such cases, “liability has to be traced back to the intent of a person or a company that created or directed the agent.”

The incidents have incited calls for more regulation of A.I. systems. But the U.S. government has largely taken a hands-off approach to the technology, citing fierce competition with China in a global A.I. race.

On Tuesday, a group of companies including OpenAI and Anthropic met with President Trump and signed a voluntary pledge to add safety measures. States have also tried to fill the gap, issuing rules that require A.I. companies to take safety measures.

Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, said at a congressional hearing on Wednesday that lawmakers might need to clarify that A.I. agents should be held liable like individuals and companies for consumer harms.

“We don’t have to invent an entirely new system,” he said, adding, “American law has worked beautifully when it comes to other products for literally centuries now.”

The most prominent early lawsuits over A.I. harms have claimed chatbots advised teenagers to commit self-harm, ending in death by suicide. Parents have filed lawsuits against OpenAI and Character AI, a start-up, arguing the companies should be held responsible.

In those cases, the companies have tried to use classic tech legal defenses: that speech is protected under the First Amendment and Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. The latter shields online platforms from liability for content posted by users.

In the Character AI case, the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida ruled last year that the company’s A.I. models did not produce speech protected by the First Amendment. Section 230’s applicability in a second case remains an open question.

When it comes to corporate liability involving humans, the law is more established. There are many ways that cybersecurity breaches can violate the law, according to legal experts. Hacking is a crime. Consumers can sue when their information is exposed in a breach. Regulators can bring lawsuits if a company’s management releases a defective product.

But in many of the A.I. cases, the companies’ agents have gone rogue, disobeying or ignoring humans who set up security guardrails.

Some of those cases may still be clear-cut, legal experts said. If an A.I. agent hacks another company during testing, the company that developed the agent could be held liable, they said. The A.I. company also may have used the product directly or through an outside testing firm, leaving little question about whether another entity, like a cavalier customer, might be responsible.

The companies could also have known the potential for their products to carry out a hack, which can increase liability, the legal experts said. Employees at OpenAI, for example, have raised concerns about the company’s security practices when testing models, which were ignored, The Times reported.

In those situations, a court could hold the A.I developer negligent if damage or harm was associated with a hack, the experts said.

Liability becomes less clear in cases involving open-source A.I. models, the experts said, in which the developer of an A.I. product shares its underlying code and people can change it.

Many legal liability concepts could be easily applied to A.I., said Catherine Sharkey, a law professor at New York University who is an expert in liability. If an A.I.-powered physical system, such as a medical device, causes harm, that could be an easy case.

But judges will need to grapple with the implications of rapidly advancing systems that can do more and more on their own, she added.

“With fully agentic A.I., it starts to really press the boundaries of a lot of doctrines that will have to adapt in a more significant way,” she said.

Adding to the uncertainty: A.I. is inherently unpredictable.

Courts find companies liable for negligence when they foresee that their products can cause harm. But building that case could be challenging if an A.I. model exhibited harmful behavior for the first time, said Ryan Calo, a law professor at the University of Washington who studies autonomous systems.

It may also be difficult to show that an A.I. company intended to do harm, which can be essential to some criminal prosecutions, he added.

“You have the possibility of victims without perpetrators,” Mr. Calo said.

Kate Conger and Cecilia Kang contributed reporting.

Parents Are Charged After Toddler Pulls Out Loaded Gun at Day Care
No one was hurt in what the police described as a shocking episode that was captured on video inside a day care center in Canton, Mich., on Monday.
By Michael Levenson

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/child-gun-daycare-michigan-parents-misdemeanor.html

The parents of a 3-year-old were charged with misdemeanors on Thursday after the child pulled a loaded handgun out of a backpack at a day care center in Michigan, where it was passed around to other children, the authorities said.

No one was injured in what the police described as a shocking episode that was captured on video cameras inside the Childrens World Early Learning Center in Canton, Mich., on Monday. The authorities have not said who brought the backpack into the center but said the gun, a Glock pistol, was registered to the child’s mother.

A teacher at the center quickly intervened, taking the gun, which was in a holster, away from the children, prosecutors said.

“It is very unsettling to think about what may have happened in this case,” Kym L. Worthy, the Wayne County prosecutor, said in a statement on Thursday. “We are thankful that there was no loss of life at this day care center.”

The father, Brandon John Ely, 28, a Detroit police officer, was charged with one count of fourth-degree child abuse, a misdemeanor punishable by a year in jail. The mother, Rabab Ibrahim Al Zayad, 27, was charged with one count of unsafe storage of a firearm, a misdemeanor punishable by up to 93 days in jail.

Both parents were arraigned on Thursday morning, and pleaded not guilty. They were expected back in court for a pretrial conference on Oct. 30. Their lawyer, Ryan E. Hill, declined to comment on the charges.

Ms. Worthy’s office said that the child had found the gun in a backpack that had been stored in a classroom.

The Canton police chief, Joseph Bialy, said that video cameras recorded “the unsecured firearm being retrieved by a toddler, which is something that was hard for me to be able to watch, even though I know the outcome.”

Chief Bialy praised the center’s staff members for their “swift and responsible actions” in response to the gun.

“I’ve seen what their staff did, and they were prepared and ready to be able to remove this firearm and keep all the kids safe there,” he said at a news conference on Monday. “And I commend them for their actions.”

The chief added that he did not believe that there was “any ill intent” by anyone involved.

“I think it really falls back on safe security of a firearm, making sure that we know where our firearms are located, and they are not accessible to anyone,” he said.

Childrens World Early Learning Center said in a statement that it was working closely with the police and had introduced new security measures, including backpack checks.

“At Childrens World, there is nothing we take more seriously than the safety, security and well-being of the children entrusted to our care,” it said. “We understand the concerns this event has caused our families, and as educators and parents ourselves, we fully share those feelings.”

The Detroit Police Department said in a statement that Mr. Ely had been placed on administrative duty, without access to his gun, while it reviewed the episode. “If it is determined that the officer violated department policy or the law, that individual will be held accountable,” it said.

In 2023, a 6-year-old boy shot a teacher at an elementary school in Newport News, Va., with a 9-millimeter handgun he said he had taken from his mother’s purse. The boy’s mother, Deja Taylor, was sentenced in December 2023 to two years in prison after she pleaded guilty to felony child neglect. Prosecutors did not charge the boy, and a jury later awarded $10 million to Abigail Zwerner, the first-grade teacher who was shot.

SUMMARY

Christa Pike, a Tennessee woman who was set to be executed on Wednesday, survived two doses of a lethal drug that had been administered, according to her lawyers. Ms. Pike, who was convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate, is the only woman on death row in Tennessee. Reporters who witnessed the execution attempt described Ms. Pike as somewhat alert.

ARTICLE

What to Know About the Attempted Execution of Christa Pike
Ms. Pike, 50, survived two doses of a lethal injection in Tennessee. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of a classmate.
By Yan Zhuang
Published 2026-10-01 05:16 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/christa-pike-alive-tennessee-execution-halted.html

Christa Pike, a Tennessee woman who was set to be executed on Wednesday, survived two doses of a lethal drug that had been administered, according to her lawyers.

Ms. Pike, who was convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate, is the only woman on death row in Tennessee. Before the failed attempt to put her to death, she was set to become the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years.

Ms. Pike was in “critical condition, receiving life-saving care” on Thursday afternoon, one of her lawyers said.

Here’s what to know:

The Case

In 1996, a jury found Ms. Pike guilty of torturing and murdering a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in an attack that she carried out with her boyfriend and a friend. They slashed Ms. Slemmer with a box cutter, carved a pentagram into her chest and removed a piece of her skull.

Ms. Pike, who was 18 at the time of the killing, received the death penalty. Her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 at the time of the crime and was sentenced to life in prison, as he was too young to be eligible for capital punishment in Tennessee.

Ms. Pike, now 50, does not deny her guilt.

“I run through this execution every day in my heart,” she told The New York Times in September. “Whatever happens on Sept. 30, this will not be my hell anymore.”

Some experts have questioned whether Ms. Pike would receive the same sentence if she were to be tried today. Her lawyers argued that Ms. Pike’s initial legal defense did not adequately present her history of child sexual abuse and neglect.

She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, which her lawyers said contributed to her mental state during the murder.

“Christa Pike would likely not be sentenced to death if she were tried today,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. “A lot has changed.”

The Victim

Ms. Slemmer, 19, was living hundreds of miles from her family home in Florida when she was killed, having enrolled in a Job Corps educational program in Knoxville, Tenn., to pursue an interest in computers.

She had volunteered at the Special Olympics and loved bowling and computer games, according to her mother, May Martinez.

On the night she was killed, Ms. Slemmer tried to call her mother. The call quickly ended because of a shaky phone signal. When Ms. Martinez called back, her daughter “was already gone,” she said.

Ms. Slemmer’s family has remained firmly in support of Ms. Pike’s sentence, and Ms. Slemmer’s mother is adamant that Ms. Pike could not atone for the murder and should be executed.

“Nobody could ever, ever convince me she’s changed,” Ms. Martinez told The Times.

The Legal Battle

Ms. Pike’s lawyers have tried to stop the execution in recent weeks, arguing that she could support other women in prison and that her crime could not be separated from her traumatic childhood.

They also questioned whether lethal drugs could be administered without causing her excessive pain. In an appeal to the Supreme Court to pause the execution, Ms. Pike’s lawyers argued that the execution was causing her “unnecessary agony” and that it violated the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

Gov. Bill Lee of Tennessee, a Republican, said on Monday that he would not intervene to allow Ms. Pike to serve the remainder of her life in prison.

On Wednesday, a federal appeals court briefly paused the execution and said more time was needed to consider the case. After a delay of about nine hours, the Supreme Court allowed the execution to proceed, and the state raced to go ahead with it before the day ended and to avoid having to reschedule.

The court’s three liberal justices dissented from the order allowing the execution. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote that the majority “unnecessarily prevents” the appeals court from fully considering Ms. Pike’s argument.

The Botched Execution

It was not immediately clear what went wrong with the administration of the lethal drug on Wednesday night.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers said that while two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered, she did not lose consciousness. She still had a heartbeat, they said, and was audibly snoring.

Reporters who witnessed the execution attempt described Ms. Pike as somewhat alert. Although the curtains separating the execution chamber from the witnesses were closed for nearly an hour after the attempt, reporters said they could still hear breathing and steady snoring.

The Tennessee Department of Correction later said Ms. Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.

This was the second time this year that Tennessee had struggled to administer a lethal injection. In May, the state called off an execution because staff members could not find a vein to administer lethal drugs.

The Fallout

After the bungled attempt to execute Ms. Pike, Governor Lee paused capital punishment in Tennessee and called for a review of the state’s policies on how it puts people to death.

It was the second time in five years that Mr. Lee, a Republican, has paused executions because of questions over the effectiveness of the state’s lethal injections. In 2022, he ordered a review after prison officials failed to properly test the drugs before an execution.

In at least one instance, a botched execution has led, effectively, to a reduced punishment.

In Alabama in 2018, an execution team struggled for nearly three hours to locate a vein in Doyle Hamm, injuring several of his organs before giving up. The state then entered into a confidential legal settlement, leaving Mr. Hamm in prison without parole. Mr. Hamm died of cancer three years later.

However, states are far more likely to use administrative holds, revise their methods, or proceed through courts before trying again to execute.

Emily Cochrane, Ann E. Marimow and Adeel Hassan contributed reporting.

Gavin Newsom and President Trump weren’t at the debate for California governor on Wednesday night, but they were repeatedly invoked by the two actual candidates as proxies for the choice that voters will make in November. ARTICLE

5 Takeaways From the Debate for California Governor
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Steve Hilton, a Republican, sparred over President Trump, taxes and immigration in their only scheduled meeting.
By Laurel Rosenhall and Soumya Karlamangla
Published 2026-10-01 04:27 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/politics/california-governor-debate-takeaways.html

Gov. Gavin Newsom and President Trump weren’t at the debate for California governor on Wednesday night, but they were repeatedly invoked by the two actual candidates as proxies for the choice that voters will make in November.

Xavier Becerra, the Democratic front-runner, often tried to cast his Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, as a stand-in for Mr. Trump during the hourlong event on CNN. Mr. Hilton, a former Fox talk show host, told voters that Mr. Becerra represented more of the same that they were getting from Mr. Newsom and Democratic lawmakers.

Unlike the chaotic open primary debates this spring, which featured stages crowded with candidates for governor who could barely get a word in edgewise, the face-off on Wednesday in CNN’s studio in Burbank, Calif., was a head-to-head clash that offered a clear contrast in philosophies.

It was the only scheduled fall debate between Mr. Becerra and Mr. Hilton, and the moderators Dana Bash and Jake Tapper rattled through about a dozen topics, from education to health care. In California, a heavily Democratic state, Mr. Becerra has enjoyed a sizable lead in every major poll this cycle, and it was up to Mr. Hilton to convince voters to move in his direction on Wednesday.

Here are five takeaways from the debate.

‘Trump, Trump, Trump.’

No matter the topic, Mr. Becerra had an attack line at the ready that boiled down to linking Mr. Hilton with President Trump. It was a logical strategy, given that the president had endorsed Mr. Hilton and is deeply unpopular in California.

In the first 20 minutes of the debate, Mr. Becerra answered questions about taxes, artificial intelligence and immigration enforcement by saying Mr. Hilton’s positions were aligned with Mr. Trump.

Finally, it seemed that Mr. Hilton had had enough.

“All you ever say is ‘Trump, Trump, Trump,’” Mr. Hilton said. “That’s nothing but an insult to every Californian who is desperate for something to change in this state.”

Mr. Becerra seemed to revel in the opportunity to reiterate his point.

“Your words, ‘Trump, Trump, Trump,’ because he is your supporter,” Mr. Becerra said. “You chased his endorsement.”

Mr. Newsom, who cannot run again because of term limits, has found Mr. Trump a valuable foil throughout his eight years in office, even fending off a recall in 2021 by casting his opponent as a Trump acolyte. Mr. Becerra is using the same playbook and likely will find Mr. Trump just as useful politically over the next two years if he is elected governor this fall.

Hilton as the change candidate.

Mr. Hilton began with a dig, thanking CNN for hosting the debate and “for bringing Xavier out of hiding.” He kept up the attacks, repeatedly criticizing Mr. Newsom and other Democrats in the state and blaming the party for California’s problems, including homelessness and a high cost of living.

Mr. Hilton positioned himself as an antidote to years of Democratic rule in California. He said that after 16 years of Democratic governorship, California’s problems had not been solved. He added that Mr. Becerra assumed that he would win in November simply because of the “D” next to his name.

“They think that they can just do whatever they want, get whatever bad results, the highest taxes in the country for the worst results,” he said. “That’s why he hasn’t been campaigning in this election. They take you for granted.”

“And I just want to ask every Californian: Aren’t you tired of that?” he added. “It’s time to try something different instead of the same thing over and over again.”

A.I. is top of mind.

The moderators asked the candidates about another contentious topic: artificial intelligence.

The day before the debate, President Trump invited tech leaders to the White House in response to growing concerns about a potential existential threat posed by the technology. But instead of mandating formal regulation, Mr. Trump had the tech leaders sign an agreement to police themselves.

Mr. Hilton said he would watch the A.I. companies carefully to see if they kept their promises to adopt safety policies. He said he would not shy away from regulations if necessary and that he already supported a ban on A.I. in classrooms.

“Here in this state, we lead this industry, and I think we need to lead the regulation of this industry as well,” Mr. Hilton said.

Mr. Becerra and Mr. Hilton then traded barbs, with Mr. Becerra challenging Mr. Hilton’s willingness to regulate the companies and criticizing what he called Mr. Trump’s “pinky promise” with them.

Neither mentioned Mr. Hilton had moved to the United States for his wife’s career in Silicon Valley. She has held high-level positions at Google and other tech companies and now works for an A.I. start-up.

Tensions flare on immigration.

One comment from Mr. Becerra seemed to particularly strike a particular nerve with Mr. Hilton, an immigrant from Britain.

As the candidates were debating immigration, Mr. Hilton said that California had been flouting its own laws on cooperating with federal authorities in cases involving dangerous criminals. He said that political posturing had gotten in the way of compliance and that his goal was to lower the temperature on the issue by depoliticizing it.

“I’m an immigrant,” he said. “My parents were immigrants, from Hungary to England, so I want to make sure that we protect our legal immigrant communities and we enforce the law.”

In response, Mr. Becerra accused Mr. Hilton of only wanting some immigrants to be allowed to stay in the state.

“Here’s the problem I have with your policies: You seem to welcome immigrants who look like you, but deport immigrants who look like me,” said Mr. Becerra, whose parents immigrated from Mexico.

Mr. Hilton seemed taken aback and said Mr. Becerra’s comment was an example of how California leaders have politicized immigration.

“Your party isn’t enforcing California law as it is now,” he said. “And what a disgraceful remark that was. I don’t think people want to hear that kind of remark in a debate like this.”

Becerra lacks Newsom’s sizzle.

As the debate unfolded on television, Mr. Newsom announced that he had signed his final bill as governor — while standing at the tippy-top of the Golden Gate Bridge.

Even for a flashy politician known for his indulgent photo ops, this one was next level. Literally. The bill signing, 746 feet above the Pacific Ocean, with sweeping vistas of the San Francisco skyline, was emblematic of Mr. Newsom’s attention-grabbing, risk-taking approach to politics.

Mr. Becerra, if elected, would likely be a very different kind of leader. His vibe is low-key. His m.o. has been to play it safe. He’s a Stanford-trained lawyer, and his style throughout Wednesday night’s debate was measured and deliberative.

Mr. Becerra brags about shopping at Costco. Mr. Newsom declared on his taxes that he had given away $45,000 worth of Armani suits.

Debate moderators did not ask the candidates if they would emulate Mr. Newsom by hosting a podcast with right-wing influencers, spilling their family tea in a memoir or staging a photo op at the top of a bridge. They really didn’t have to.

ARTICLE

Should Democrats Spend in Deep-Red Texas? A Battle Could Echo in 2028.
Allies of Gina Hinojosa want a Democratic group to support her bid for Texas governor — putting pressure on its chairman, Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, who is weighing a run for president.
By Reid J. Epstein
Published 2026-10-01 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/politics/gina-hinojosa-andy-beshear-democratic-governors-association.html

As polls suggest that Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, is competitive in her campaign to become the first Latina governor of the usually reliably Republican state of Texas, a growing number of prominent Latino officials are angry that she is not getting more help from the party.

Now there are veiled threats that if the Democratic Governors Association fails to invest in her bid, some Latino leaders could withhold their support from the group’s chairman, Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, should he, as expected, run for president in 2028.

“We are asking you to invest in a competitive race with the largest Latino electorate in the country following an election cycle where Republicans made alarming inroads with Latinos,” read a letter more than 70 Latino officials sent Wednesday to Mr. Beshear at the D.G.A.

Ms. Hinojosa’s allies have recruited a cadre of officials, including some from the early-voting states of Nevada and New Mexico, to push Mr. Beshear to direct the group to spend $10 million on her campaign against Gov. Greg Abbott, the incumbent Republican who is seeking a fourth term.

“All Democrats would do better when and if we help Gina Hinojosa win Texas,” said one of the Democrats who signed the letter, Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona, who like Mr. Beshear is considering a 2028 run. “No matter who you are, no matter if you’re running for president, you want Gina Hinojosa to be the governor of Texas.”

Last week, the D.G.A. allocated $650,000 to help the Democratic candidate for governor in Alaska. Texas has been a back-burner race for the D.G.A., which has so far invested in backing Democratic candidates in Arizona, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio, and Wisconsin. It has not yet spent or directed money on advertising in Texas.

“Gina Hinojosa is a great candidate and running a great campaign,” Mr. Beshear said in a statement to The New York Times on Wednesday. “The D.G.A. is currently investing by paying expenses and providing staff, with more to come. My goal as chair of the D.G.A. this year is to win as many races as we can and that’s exactly what we’re doing by going on offense and expanding the map.”

When asked about Ms. Hinojosa’s race in an interview published last week by USA Today, Mr. Beshear said he would not allow his own presidential aspirations to color how he directs D.G.A. resources this year.

“I, as the DGA chair, can’t be motivated by pleasing or not pleasing anyone when it comes to ’28,” Mr. Beshear said. “I made a commitment to win as many races as I can in ’26.”

The pleas for more aid come as polls show Ms. Hinojosa competitive with Mr. Abbott, whose campaign has spent $68 million in advertising so far, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm, while she has spent just $8.7 million.

Mr. Beshear’s PAC, In This Together, sent $25,000 to Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign and he has been making fund-raising calls to donors on her behalf, a D.G.A. official said. Mr. Beshear and Ms. Hinojosa spoke by phone on Tuesday, according to two people briefed on the exchange.

Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham of New Mexico, the nation’s lone sitting Latina governor, has been phoning donors to help Ms. Hinojosa raise money, she said. She said she has also worked with Mr. Beshear to direct resources to Hispanic communities. “We should all be focused on supporting Gina,” said Ms. Lujan Grisham, whose state will be early in the 2028 primary calendar.

The fund-raising disparity in Texas illustrates a longstanding problem in Democratic politics: Their donors are far more inclined to invest in candidates running for Congress or president than they are in those running for state office.

“It is extremely challenging for us to get national donors to pay attention to governor’s races outside of their states,” said Peter O’Keefe, a former Democratic Governors Association treasurer who remains involved in the group’s fund-raising.

Texas has been a reliably Republican state for decades. President Trump won it by 14 points in 2024. The state’s last Democratic governor was Ann Richards, who lost her 1994 re-election bid to George W. Bush.

But Ms. Hinojosa’s allies are trying to pressure Mr. Beshear with a host of polls that show her within shouting distance of Mr. Abbott. Staying out of Texas, they say, would damage Mr. Beshear’s chances in Nevada and New Mexico, Latino-heavy states that Democrats have put at the front of their presidential nominating calendar in 2028.

“I don’t think it’s helpful for his politics at all,” said Sergio Gonzales, a veteran of Democratic Latino politics who was a senior aide to Vice President Kamala Harris, and who helped organize the letter. “It hurts his politics now, it certainly would hurt any future aspirations that he has for higher office because Latinos are all over this country.”

The letter was a follow-up to another sent last month, which made the initial $10 million request.

Asked about the $10 million request from her allies, Ms. Hinojosa said in a text message Wednesday: “That would be great!”

Republicans in Congress this week spent their last hours in the Capitol before the midterm elections pushing a series of meant-to-fail votes that they hoped could signal to voters that they were at least trying to address widespread concerns about the high cost of living. It was a familiar pre-election exercise made more urgent this year because those Republicans are battling stiff headwinds, including economic concerns and President Trump’s sagging approval ratings, in their battle to maintain control of Congress.

But they emerged with no meaningful progress on a long list of issues weighing on their constituents, leaving some wondering — if not openly doubting — whether they had done enough to persuade voters to keep them in power.

“If you can’t pay the bills, you know, no matter how much you love us as Republicans, we’re in control,” said Senator Jim Justice, Republican of West Virginia. “And if you can’t pay the bills, you’ve got a real problem with us.”

Though polls have shown voters to be concerned with the economy, the cost of living, the war in Iran and government corruption, the Senate spent most of its final two weeks of floor time debating an expansive college sports bill that few thought would have much resonance on the campaign trail.

Republicans’ marquee legislative achievements have been a sweeping tax cut and domestic policy bill that was so unpopular they tried to rename it; a tranche of funding for federal immigration enforcement efforts of which Americans are increasingly wary; and a substantial housing law that the president refused to sign and is unlikely to have an immediate impact on housing costs.

G.O.P. leaders who have spent most of their party’s two-year governing trifecta deferring to Mr. Trump had little choice but to project optimism that it would all be enough to overcome the growing dismay over the cost of food, fuel and other consumer goods. “If you vote for Democrats, what you’re going to get is higher taxes, more spending, bigger government and open borders,” said Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader. “I mean, that’s the choice in front of the American people. So irrespective of where things are today and what the price of diesel is today, if you want a better future for your family as you look at this election, the choices in front of you, to me, it’s a no-brainer.”

Still, Mr. Thune is not on the ballot. With a growing number of races seen by both parties as tossups, some in the party conceded that control of the Senate may rest on how successful individual Republicans are in distancing themselves from Mr. Trump and the G.O.P. brand.

“You’ve got to be pitch perfect,” said Senator Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican who decided not to run for re-election. “Be who you are, and be focused on the priorities of your constituents. Forget the national mood. Forget the national agenda. Focus on your state.”

Though Republicans entered the midterms with a map that favored them, they have found themselves on the defensive in reliably red states in the face of an unpopular war in Iran, continued inflation and the president’s low approval ratings.

In an indication of how the party’s fortunes have changed, Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, the chairman of Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, told reporters on Wednesday that Kansas, once seen as reliably red, had become more competitive than he had hoped.

Mr. Husted has faced a flurry of attack ads accusing him of supporting data centers.

“We gave everybody a chance to do something about affordability, and the Democrats blocked it,” Mr. Husted said. “So we’ll go campaign on it, and we’ll talk about it.”

Such messaging votes have become a routine for Congress in the weeks before the election, and Mr. Schumer himself brought a number of them before the 2024 election in which Democrats lost control of Congress.

Senator John Cornyn, the Texas Republican who will leave office next year after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, said those doomed-to-fail procedural votes could matter.

“I think it is important to show we are trying, even if we are not successful,” he said. “It is up to the candidates to get the message through.”

ARTICLE

John Roberts and His Island
After decades of potlucks and paddle-boarding on Maine’s midcoast, rising anger and protests have left the Supreme Court’s chief justice more isolated than ever.

To many people on this remote stretch of Maine coastline, where every day looks like a fresh painting made of light and water, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. is just “John.”

John, who has spent over 20 summers on Hupper Island, a refuge about 90 miles northeast of Portland with no cars and barely two dozen homes. John, who swaps favors with neighbors and endures jokes about his boating skills from more experienced operators. John, who has spent many mornings on the dock in Port Clyde, the postage-stamp-sized town across the water from the island, nursing a half-caff and a cinnamon bun.

For a long time, the chief justice’s life here was a story of potluck dinners and easy friendships, according to a summer of interviews with more than two dozen residents. Neighbors reveled in his position but kept exchanges with him about it brief or light. At a long-ago annual summer party, he used to participate in touch football, then call dinner to order by proclaiming: “Oyez, oyez, oyez, the lobsters are ready.”

But in recent years, as the Supreme Court has reshaped American life and handed more power to President Trump, a very personal form of anger has been rising here at the chief justice, transforming his getaways.

His summer retreats, long a well-known fact, are now a source of debate. Neighbors have taken to the water to protest him. Calling themselves “kayak-tivists,” they form flotillas facing his island home, holding waterproof signs conveying their disappointment. A local newspaper columnist recommended that people in town give him the finger.

Even some longtime friends who would not dream of joining the kayakers said they have been drawing back socially because of their distress over his decisions, notably the court’s 2024 decision granting the president broad immunity from prosecution.

He is now ringed by far more security than in the past, residents say, adding to the distance.

The chief justice’s narrowing world in Maine shows how the court’s controversial decisions and languishing public trust, along with increasing peril for public officials, have reshaped the lives of the justices, leaving them more isolated than ever before.

In Washington and beyond, ever-present security threats as well as protests are separating and shielding the justices from the people whose lives will be affected by their decisions. They are less likely to spontaneously interact with people who disagree with their work, and their exposure to the texture and mess of everyday life is diminishing. Being just John, even here, has grown much harder.

“From what I see, the barrier runs both ways,” said Mary Anne Mason, a friend and former law partner of the chief justice who lives in Port Clyde. “It’s harder for him to feel comfortable approaching people — and vice versa.”

The protests have split Port Clyde and the nearby villages on this peninsula, as people here have debated how best to convey displeasure with a justice, if at all. Is it better to ensure their famous neighbor hears from those who disagree or to leave him alone, because his job is to be impervious to pressure?

For the demonstrators, the hour is too dire, the threat to democracy too serious for niceties. They argue that citizens have no other way to hold justices, with their lifetime appointments, accountable.

“Maine is not here as your happy place, your wind-down from all of your hard work destroying my civil liberties and democracy,” wrote Becca Shaw Glaser in her column for the local newspaper, shortly after the Supreme Court eliminated the federal right to abortion in 2022. “No. May you never feel welcome here again.”

But others argue that disturbing the chief justice and his family at home is invasive, scary, and out of line with Maine’s tradition of maintaining respectful distance. They also worry such actions could be counterproductive, alienating the justice.

“John is a credit to the community and an asset to all of us whether you agree with him or not,” Kevin Lipson, his closest friend and chief defender here, wrote as neighbors debated the protests on Facebook. “Civility should be our guiding principle.”

The chief justice used to preside over a Supreme Court whose members were afforded more privacy and freedom than many other public officials. Once, years ago, Mr. Lipson and the chief justice found themselves up the peninsula from Port Clyde without a car, Mr. Lipson recalled in an interview. So he stuck out his thumb by the side of the road and a pickup truck pulled over. He and the nation’s top jurist hopped in the back and hitchhiked back to town.

Now, Mr. Lipson said, he is cautious about introducing his friend to strangers. This year, on an outing to nearby Monhegan Island, people recognized the chief justice as he walked by a brewery and started to chant: You should be ashamed.

Pride and Deference

Chief Justice Roberts purchased his gray-shingled waterside home on Hupper Island in 2006, the year after he ascended to the court. He generally does not give interviews about the law, let alone his vacation plans, and declined to provide comment for this article.

But the location of his retreat clearly says, Get Me Away From Washington. An hour and a half north of Portland, out on a green, rock-ringed finger of land jutting into the sea, lies the town of Port Clyde. Across the water is the island, accessible only by private boat. There is no ferry or bridge.

The spot is secluded, but also a place where the nation’s highest judge, his wife and their two children could become part of a tight-knit community where people live and vacation for generations. Each year during the court’s break, from early July to the start of October, the chief justice could enter a different world. His circle included well-heeled “summah people” like him, but also year-rounders like lobstermen and a local kayak outfitter, Democrats and Republicans alike.

Hupper Island has no municipal trash pickup, and friends remember the chief justice jumping up from a dockside chat and exclaiming in a panicked tone: “I’ve got to get to the dump!”

Mr. Lipson, a former law partner of the chief justice who has been vacationing in the area for 40 years, introduced him to the island and made a project of settling him in. Mr. Lipson located the Roberts home, negotiated the deal, assigned him the lobster-dinner-announcement shtick, and integrated the Roberts family into what he described as an unusually cohesive place.

“This is a community where people actually rely on each other,” Mr. Lipson said. “You live on the ocean. Things happen on the water. Sometimes your boat breaks down. Sometimes you need assistance. This is the kind of community where you can depend upon your neighbors.”

Plenty of news stories documented the court leader’s presence, and local pride in him was so great that the boat service to another local island started pointing out his house to passengers. (Friends requested the announcements end.) At fund-raisers, yard sales and parties, “a chat or a seat near the justice was a social chit,” said Joline Godfrey, a financial educator who lives a few miles up the road.

But there was also an unspoken deference, a rule against initiating conversation with him about the court, numerous residents said in interviews. If a stranger asked what he did for work, his standard response was to say he was a judge, without elaborating.

Residents had strong reactions to some of his decisions, from dismantling campaign spending limits to saving President Barack Obama’s health care plan, but saw him overall as “a defender of the Constitution, a trustworthy, reasonable man,” she said.

In person, the chief justice came across to his summer friends as affable, very conservative and confident in his views. With double Harvard degrees, and days spent in hushed chambers, he struck them as a little removed from real life, but also eager to connect.

During the pandemic, when the summer crowd gathered on Zoom, John and Jane Roberts appeared in a little box onscreen, just like everyone else.

‘Yell, Boo, Whisper’

The first visible crack between the chief justice and his Maine community came soon after the abortion decision, with the publication of Ms. Shaw Glaser’s column in the now-defunct Free Press in 2022. “We Need to Talk about Chief Justice John Roberts Blissfully Summering Off Port Clyde,” read the headline.

Ms. Shaw Glaser had spent most of her life in midcoast Maine, living year-round in Port Clyde as a child and as an adult in nearby Rockport, where she was a professional gardener and activist and then a newspaper columnist as well.

She wrote that she could no longer bear watching her state welcome a jurist who had gutted the Voting Rights Act, voted against declaring a constitutional right to same-sex marriage, and just that summer, had overseen Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which eliminated the federal right to abortion. She called her neighbors to action.

“Should you see Chief Justice John Roberts duck into Squid Ink coffee or the Port Clyde General Store this summer, consider letting him know exactly what you think of him and his illegitimate, ultraconservative court,” she wrote. “Yell, boo, whisper, weep audibly, give him the thumbs down or the finger, hand him a note, refuse to serve him.”

She urged residents to speak with the chief justice, but also to organize boat protests in front of his home. “He might see you,” she wrote.

The chief justice’s position in the Dobbs case had in fact been nuanced: He had taken a lonely, losing stand in favor of keeping the constitutional right to abortions before 15 weeks. But he had voted with the majority, he was the court’s leader, and Ms. Shaw Glaser saw him as responsible for its decisions. Plus he was right there in the community.

In letters to the editor, some cheered Ms. Shaw Glaser, but many said she had gone too far.

“Our children and grandchildren will learn nothing from this type of printed vitriol other than a complete disrespect for public servants at any level,” wrote one person.

“I believe she is inciting violence,” wrote another, adding: “If people go out and destroy Chief Justice Roberts’s home or property, it’ll be on you.”

Ms. Shaw Glaser was soon fired from her columnist gig, and the newspaper published an apology to the chief justice. Her attempt at rousing others looked like a bust.

But then, others slowly started to follow her instructions.

The newspaper received a new round of infuriated letters, this time expressing anger over how Ms. Shaw Glaser had been treated. Bumper stickers started to pop up on cars all over the peninsula opposing the abortion decision: “Roe, Roe, Roe Your Vote,” they read.

Two years later, the court awarded Mr. Trump sweeping immunity from prosecution for actions he took in his official role ahead of the Jan. 6, 2021, storming of the Capitol. The chief wrote the majority opinion. As Mr. Trump was re-elected and pushed constitutional boundaries, the court approved many of his policies, decisions that were technically temporary but allowed him to reshape the federal government.

No one on the outside knew the chief justice’s actual voting record, because many of those cases were handled on the secretive emergency or “shadow” docket, in which the court publishes orders without vote counts and sometimes without reasoning. But he had long favored expanding presidential power. Maine had voted twice against Mr. Trump. Now many of the chief justice’s neighbors felt he was maddeningly hesitant about confronting the president or defending the rule of law.

A Dockside Encounter

The waterborne protests began last year and have now become regular parts of the landscape. Twice each summer, two rows of demonstrators face his island home. The first group sits on kayaks, linking oars, just a few hundred yards from his house. Behind them, others stand on the Port Clyde dock.

The number of participants, on land and sea, has never been more than a few dozen. But their message has spread throughout the peninsula and beyond. A local artist started making and displaying cardboard sculptures of kangaroos, as in “kangaroo court,” and named them after the conservative justices. Signs have proliferated, including on major roads, where the chief justice seems sure to see them.

“Roberts Benched the Constitution,” reads one popular one.

“Mainers Against the Roberts Agenda,” reads another.

One day in September last year, residents of Port Clyde woke up to an instant piece of graphic art. Across an intersection leading into town, someone had chalked in bold, bright letters “Equal Justice Under Law,” the same words carved into the Supreme Court’s facade.

The chief justice did not respond. As a lawyer, he had been regarded as one of the most talented courtroom advocates of his generation, with a gift for explaining concepts simply. He still has flawless aim with toasts and eulogies, winning over room after room, friends say.

But as the court’s leader, he has gained a reputation for silence, declining to give interviews, delivering few public remarks and preferring for the most part to speak through his written opinions. To those incensed with his rulings, he has appeared distant and aloof.

But the protesters did encounter another member of his household. After an August 2025 protest, Ms. Shaw Glaser and other demonstrators were standing near the Port Clyde dock when a young woman approached them with a serious look on her face. She asked them: What did they hope to accomplish? Had they considered how their actions affected the chief justice’s wife and children?

Only then did she identify herself. She said she was Josephine Roberts, the chief’s daughter, then 25, according to Ms. Shaw Glaser, who wrote about it in her journal. Another protester also wrote about the scene in a message to a friend afterward.

Her father wasn’t even home, Ms. Roberts told them. He respected that she had her own left-leaning political views, she said, according to the protesters’ written accounts. And he was a wonderful father, she added.

Ms. Roberts did not respond to The New York Times’s inquiries about the encounter. That night, when Ms. Shaw Glaser wrote about it in her journal, she noted she was still horrified by the court’s decisions.

But, she wrote, “I am now left with this feeling of empathy for her as a person.”

The Cigar Club and the Picnic

In May, at the start of the summer season, Jane Roberts sent an email to fellow members of the Port Clyde Cigar Club, a loose social organization. “Look forward to seeing you all this summer,” she wrote.

But all season, the state pulsed with controversy, over a U.S. Senate race and the July killing of a 25-year-old Colombian delivery driver by immigration agents just south of Portland. The Supreme Court’s approval rating dropped to a historic low of 33 percent in a Gallup poll. More anti-Roberts signs sprang up. The activists added small weekly vigils to their monthly protests. Local factions supporting and opposing the protests dueled in person and on social media.

At a July protest on the Port Clyde dock, Mr. Lipson, the chief justice’s close friend, approached Ellen Koches, a retired museum educator from Washington, Maine, who was mounting a sign along the railing showing the American flag imprinted with some of the court’s most conservative decisions.

“I’m going to take a picture of your license plate, look up where you live, and stand in front of your house and protest,” Mr. Lipson said, according to both him and Ms. Koches.

“Is that a threat?” she responded.

“It’s a promise,” he replied.

The law seemed unlikely to settle their dispute. A federal statute prohibits picketing outside judges’ homes, but few people have been prosecuted. Timothy Zick, an expert on the subject at William & Mary Law School, said that a water protest facing a justice’s home was a novel question, and that he was stumped by how the rules might apply.

Longtime neighbors and friends said the chief justice drew back. With rising violent threats against public officials, including a 2022 attempt on Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s life, security has been tightened. The chief justice took walks and briefly dropped in on a concert this summer, but his detail stayed close around him. On Sundays after church, he used to hang out on the dock. Now, with the protesters, he stayed away all day.

The shift has been “hard to watch,” said Tamara Cody, the owner of Port Clyde Kayaks and a longtime friend of the chief justice’s.

The chief justice and his wife did attend cigar club gatherings, friends said, but some former members said in interviews that they sent their own regrets, in part because they were not interested in socializing with the Robertses.

He was also busy. In contrast with his early years in Maine, the court was no longer really on vacation over the summer. The justices issued emergency orders on several Trump administration policies, standing up to Mr. Trump on some issues, including nixing his attempt to change mail-in ballot rules. In August, the chief justice made a strong statement against the president’s renovation of the White House ballroom, writing a rare, passionate dissent against the court’s decision to let it go ahead.

One event that the chief justice did attend was the annual Hupper Island Independence Day picnic. On July 4, he gathered with 60 or so neighbors on a lawn overlooking the water to hear a patriotic benediction from a rabbi, a reading of the entire Declaration of Independence and a performance of “God Bless America.”

Wendy Schlotterbeck, a neighbor who had been summering on Hupper Island since the days when it had no docks or electricity, grew upset at the sight of the chief justice’s celebrating. He and his colleagues had just narrowed protections for trans athletes and minors and allowed Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown to proceed. Three of Ms. Schlotterbeck’s relatives were transgender. Immigrant friends of hers had been arrested.

She fantasized about having a real conversation with the court’s leader, looking into his eyes. “Do you realize what your decisions are doing to my family and my community?” she wanted to ask.

Instead, she left the picnic. The next morning, she protested her neighbor for the first time, grabbing a sign that said “Justice for All” and paddling back and forth in front of his home, hoping he would see.

Julie Tate contributed research.

ARTICLE

Tennessee Pauses a Planned Execution After a Failed Attempt
Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, ordered a review of the state’s lethal injection process after the botched attempt to put Christa Pike to death. She was hospitalized Wednesday.
By Emily Cochrane
Published 2026-10-01 12:51 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/tennessee-executions-christa-pike-lee-review.html

Tennessee has called off another planned execution in 2026 and will review the way it puts prisoners to death after an inmate, Christa Pike, survived two doses of a lethal drug in the state’s second botched attempt at capital punishment this year.

It is the second time in five years that Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, has paused executions because of questions over the effectiveness of the state’s lethal injections. In 2022, he ordered a review after prison officials failed to properly test the drugs before an execution.

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the state’s most serious responsibilities,” he said in a statement after the attempted execution of Ms. Pike. “The people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective.”

Mr. Lee also ordered a third-party review of what happened during the execution attempt, during which Ms. Pike remained alive, breathing and snoring for nearly an hour before she was taken to a hospital.

The remaining execution for this year, for a man convicted of murdering a friend, had been scheduled for December. This year, Mr. Lee issued a reprieve for another death-row inmate whose execution was canceled after medical staff members failed to find a vein.

Out of four planned executions this year in Tennessee, only one took place without incident.

Ms. Pike, 50, was hospitalized Wednesday evening after it was clear she was still conscious after two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbital. It was not immediately clear Thursday morning what her condition was, or what had gone wrong.

Ms. Pike, convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate, had been on death row for more than three decades. She would have been the first woman executed in the state in more than 200 years.

Her lawyers had raised concerns about whether the procedure could be carried out, given the first failed execution attempt this year. They also warned that Ms. Pike’s pain could be exacerbated by her history of sexual trauma, along with other medical issues.

The Wednesday execution was already delayed after a flurry of last-minute legal challenges. But after the Supreme Court cleared the way, Tennessee officials moved ahead.

Only a few people were allowed to witness the attempt to end Ms. Pike’s life. While the curtains separating the witness space from the execution chamber were drawn for much of the time, reporters said they could hear Ms. Pike breathing and snoring for nearly an hour.

At one point, they said, she described a burning pain in her arm.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement it “had followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general’s office.”

“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective,” the department said.

Who Is the FlyDubai Pilot Being Hailed as a Hero?

On his professional profile listing his decade of experience as a commercial pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar emphasized his “strong focus on safety.”

That was needed on Wednesday, when he found himself at the center of a cockpit drama high in the skies. Officials say his co-pilot attacked him and repeatedly stabbed him, with the apparent intention of crashing a plane with more than 170 passengers onboard, traveling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv.

Praise for his lifesaving actions came from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, who called Mr. Machchhar a “hero.”

After the passengers and crew members subdued the assailant, the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

“In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others,” Mr. Modi said.

The captain’s family lives in Ghatkopar East, a suburb of Mumbai, according to Parag Shah, the local legislator from the area. Mr. Shah said by telephone that the captain’s parents were flown to Saudi Arabia early Thursday.

On his LinkedIn profile, Mr. Machchhar lists 13 years of commercial aviation experience. He spent the early part of his career at India’s SpiceJet, in Mumbai, where he worked as a senior commander and a line training captain. He joined FlyDubai in 2022.

He had initially planned to join the family’s textile business, he said on a podcast last year. It was while studying for a management degree, with the aim of helping grow the business, that he came across an aviation seminar.

“That is where the aviation bug bit me,” he said on the podcast.

He said his mother had been reluctant to accept his career; but as India’s aviation industry grew rapidly over the past decade, it helped ease his choice.

“The aviation now and 15 to 17 years ago was completely different,” he said. “You didn’t hear a lot of people becoming pilots, no one had any idea how to do it. So first of all, that was something that scared my mom — and of course, the flying bit.”

ARTICLE

Japan Raises Residency Fees 2,000 Percent Amid ‘Anxiety’ Over Foreigners
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is making it harder for immigrants to stay in the country. Critics say she is hurting Japan’s ability to address labor shortages.
By Javier C. Hernández and Hisako Ueno
Published 2026-10-01 04:39 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/world/asia/japan-raises-residency-fees-2000-percent-amid-anxiety-over-foreigners.html

The Japanese government increased fees for permanent residency by 2,000 percent on Thursday as part of a bid by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to make it harder for foreigners to stay in the country.

The authorities raised the application fee to $1,271 from $64, the largest increase in Japan’s history, and put in place stringent requirements regarding income, pensions and proficiency in the Japanese language.

Ms. Takaichi, a hard-line conservative, said the policies were necessary to quell rising concerns among Japanese citizens about a recent influx of foreigners; both immigration and tourism have risen since the pandemic thanks to a weak yen and companies bringing in staff from overseas to stem labor shortages.

“There are citizens who feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness,” Ms. Takaichi wrote on X in announcing the measures.

She said the policies, which include a minimum income requirement of $36,428 per year, were meant to ensure that “both citizens and foreigners can live safely and securely.” Previously there were no detailed guidelines around income, pension levels or language for permanent residents.

Ms. Takaichi has rolled out several measures recently to more strictly regulate immigration and tourism. In July, the government raised the price of some tourist visas by more than 400 percent. Ms. Takaichi has also led a crackdown on business manager visas, requiring small businesses to have $188,000 in capital, up from $31,000 previously. That has led to an exodus of some longtime residents of Japan, including restaurant owners.

Critics say the measures risk stoking xenophobia and hurting Japan’s efforts to deal with severe labor shortages. Japan’s population is rapidly declining — it fell by more than three million people between 2020 and 2025 — and experts say that the country must recruit millions more foreign workers to offset demographic decline and galvanize the economy.

Taku Yamazoe, a Japanese lawmaker who represents the Communist Party, said Ms. Takaichi was exploiting fears in Japanese society. In a social media post, he said that the government was asserting “foreigners themselves threaten ‘safety and peace of mind,’” without providing evidence.

While the increases are most substantial for foreigners seeking permanent residency, the government is also raising fees for other types of visas. A five-year residence permit, for example, will now cost $475, up from $38, an increase of almost 1,300 percent.

Leny Tolentino, a coordinator at the Kalakasan Migrant Women Empowerment Center, which assists Filipino women living and working in Japan, wrote in an email that the increases would “add burdens for migrants especially those with dependents.”

The number of foreign workers in Japan, while still relatively small, has reached record highs, while tourism has surged since the coronavirus pandemic. Foreigners now make up about 3.4 percent of Japan’s population of 119 million — the largest proportion ever. As of last year, there were 947,125 permanent residents, compared with 807,517 in 2020, an increase of about 17 percent.

Right-wing groups, pushing a “Japan First” mantra, have called for even tougher immigration policies, portraying foreigners as troublemakers who are diluting Japanese culture. They also say foreigners are exploiting Japan’s visa rules to stay in the country indefinitely.

Under the new rules, which are known as the “Comprehensive Measures for Acceptance and Coexistence of Foreign Nationals,” permanent residents will be required to have an income at or above the average for Japanese households, and projected pension benefits in line with what an employee might receive after 30 years of service.

The government will, for the first time, evaluate applicants for permanent residency based on Japanese language abilities and understanding of Japanese rules and customs. Under the rules, the government can revoke permanent residency if an immigrant fails to pay their pension contributions, health insurance and taxes or if they violate immigration law or the penal code.

The Mainichi Shimbun, one of Japan’s major liberal newspapers, said in an editorial this month that the rules “disregard human rights and should be withdrawn.”

“Many foreign nationals who have chosen to live in Japan and want to spend the rest of their lives here will be robbed of that hope,” the newspaper wrote.

Foreigners said they were concerned about the tougher policies and the increasingly negative portrayal of immigrants in Japan.

Dennis McAdams, a teacher from the United States who has lived in Japan for 13 years and whose wife is from Japan, said his application for permanent residency was recently rejected; he said immigration officials told him he was one day late for a pension payment. He posted about his experience on X this week and received a flood of comments from people telling him to leave the country.

Mr. McAdams said in an interview that he worries he will not be able to qualify if he reapplies under the new rules.

“Even a model foreigner might not meet the requirements now,” he said. “The tide is shifting, and not in a productive way.”

ARTICLE

Forget Quiet Luxury. In Ancient Rome, the Fashion Was Loud.
An exhibition in Copenhagen reveals how imperial expansion delivered the vivid dyes, exotic fabrics and real-hair wigs that Romans used to broadcast their status.
By Nicolas Liney
Published 2026-10-02 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/arts/ancient-rome-fashion-glyptotek-museum-copenhagen.html

Copenhagen built its reputation as the capital of Scandinavian quiet luxury on a palette of beige and gray. But inside the city’s Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek museum, a new exhibition reveals that the power players of ancient Rome preferred a far louder aesthetic: garish garments, vibrant dyes and unapologetic display.

The show, “The Power of Fashion in the Roman Empire” running through March 29, assembles sculptures from the era to examine how imperial expansion delivered the raw materials and styles that Romans used to assert themselves in a hypercompetitive social world.

“The exhibition explores fashion as a means of expressing status and power,” said Cecilie Broens, a senior researcher at the Glyptotek who curated the show. “It also helps us understand how Roman fashion drew on the resources of its empire to express these forms of power.”

As Rome consolidated its control over the Mediterranean and beyond in the early centuries of the first millennium, a thriving trade network fueled an increasingly consumerist society. Fashion trends and materials, like silk, pearls and dyes, flowed in from encounters with other cultures and helped demarcate social hierarchies in Rome.

The more exotic or rarefied your outfit was, the more clout you carried.

Textiles decay easily, and hard evidence for Roman fashion is vanishingly rare. But Roman portrait sculpture can tell us a lot about clothing, hairstyles and jewelry — even what perfumes people used. And because these statues broadcast idealized versions of their subjects, they reveal even more about how people wanted to be seen.

Perhaps predictably, many sculptures in the exhibition feature a subject wearing a toga or a stola, a sort of pinafore for women. These garments, which telegraphed Roman citizenship, remained remarkably unchanged over the centuries. But ornaments, hairstyles and dyes offered a way of standing out.

Many of the statues were originally painted in vibrant pigments, although barely any trace is left today. The Glyptotek, a major center for research on the use of color in ancient sculpture, has used paint residue analysis to produce digital reconstructions displayed on screens in the show.

Dyes for garments were sourced from around the empire. Purple — the most prestigious — was traditionally restricted to the garments of the elite. The best purples came from the glands of Murex sea snails from the eastern Mediterranean, an exploitative practice that nearly drove the species to extinction. “The word sustainability wouldn’t make any sense to Romans,” Broens said.

Plant-based imitations provided an access point for the less affluent — “much like fake handbags of today,” Broens explained. (A discerning eye could tell the difference: In his “Epistles,” the poet Horace pities the know-nothing who can’t tell one from the other.) The exhibition displays a rare fragment of a tunic with a woad or indigo border from Egypt, on loan from the British Museum, to compare with a remnant of Murex purple from the Glyptotek’s archives.

Purple was a versatile color for Romans, covering a wide spectrum from pink to blue. Shifting trends favored different shades, and adopting new hues could give an edge. As Eve D’Ambra, an art history professor at Vassar College, writes in the exhibition catalog, “The quest to acquire the most prestigious dyes was akin to striking a moving target.”

Other dyes from imperial provinces were equally valuable and signified wealth, like kermes, a vermilion derived from insects, or saffron. These dyes were used for the clothes of wealthy citizens outside the Roman elite, including freed slaves, who were not allowed to wear purple.

The show includes a portrait sculpture of the ex-slave and actor Caius Fundilius in a toga and dress shoes like a member of the elite. His toga, however, was originally painted orange, perhaps suggesting that it was colored with saffron — an expensive dye, but still not purple.

Other fashion trends, like hairstyles, could reflect Roman conquests. When Rome was struggling to subdue Germanic territories in the first century, elite women often wore wigs made from the blonde hair of Germanic captives or tried to imitate the color with dye. In this case, Broens said, “Women’s beauty was quite literally constructed from subjugated peoples.”

Yet not all foreign influences were harvested by force. As Rome’s elite diversified, hairstyles were borrowed for cosmopolitan cachet. Julia Domna, the wife of the emperor Septimius Severus, came from a powerful Syrian family, and her distinctive coiffure appears to have been a popular style in that region. A portrait bust in the exhibition displays the look, which was widely copied.

We also know that perfume styles tracked the empire’s expansion, with popular varieties including “Egyptian” and “Assyrian.” Recent research shows that statues of the elite would even be regularly anointed with scents. Some recipes for scents survive, but we’ll never know what they really smelled like. Instead, the Glyptotek invited the Danish cosmetics brand Karmameju to create its own interpretations — bringing a touch of Scandinavian elegance to the imperial glitz.
