ARTICLE

In Alabama, Trump Relives His Glory Days (This Time With Some Empty Seats)
The Deep South was the birthplace of the mega MAGA rally. How do people on the Gulf feel about President Trump now?
By Shawn McCreesh
Published 2026-10-03 02:29 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/politics/alabama-trump-rally-glory-days.html

On Friday night, President Trump turned up in Mobile, Ala., to give a campaign rally five weeks ahead of the midterm elections.

What on earth was he doing all the way down there?

“I’m really here because, sometimes,” he said, “you’ve got to pay respect to the people that loved you right from the beginning.”

The indoor arena at the University of South Alabama purred.

As Republican prospects for November have darkened, Mr. Trump has started to really throw himself into the campaign trail. So far, that trail has led him to some interesting destinations. A Republican president, campaigning in ruby-red Alabama? Texas? Oklahoma? What’s next, Nebraska? Yes, actually, that is where he will be on Monday.

Mobile occupies a mythic place in Trump lore, though. This is, in some sense, the birthplace of the MAGA rally, that traveling roadshow of Mr. Trump’s that would come to define the next decade of national political life in America.

“I don’t know if you know. It sort of all began here,” Mr. Trump reminded his audience as soon as he took the stage Friday.

When he came here in August 2015, his rise had only just begun. It was shortly after the first Republican primary debate. He was still duking it out against Marco Rubio, Jeb Bush and Ted Cruz, and still being treated by much of the news media as little more than a tulip craze.

Mr. Trump’s campaign apparatus at the time was small and scrappy and run out of his tower on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. His campaign made the potentially embarrassing move of staging his event in Mobile at a massive, open-air football stadium. They were vindicated when some 30,000 people showed up, much to the shock of the establishment and the candidate himself.

“It was a big friggin’ deal,” recalled Michael Glassner, a political operative who was there working for Mr. Trump that day.

“I’ve either been on presidential campaigns, or been around them, since 1988, and there never really had been something on that scale for a primary candidate, in modern American politics, to my knowledge,” Mr. Glassner said.

It was the moment he realized that the Trump phenomenon “was going to break all of the rules” of politics, he added.

One aide who traveled with Mr. Trump to Mobile that day was Corey Lewandowski. “I was in his vehicle,” Mr. Lewandowski recalled. “We passed a number of homes that were in communities that weren’t affluent at all, and there were people outside sitting in their chairs, holding handmade signs, waving, supporting. It was very, very humbling.”

The significance of that moment, he said, was that “at a venue in the Deep South, with a candidate who many chastised or criticized for being married three times, and said didn’t quote unquote uphold traditional Republican values, that clearly was not on the minds of the people of Alabama. They turned out in record numbers.” This was a sign of much to come.

The president relived those glorious days from the stage Friday night.

“We packed the stadium and the rest was history,” he said, “right here in Mobile.”

But that was then.

These days, Mr. Trump is in political trouble, even with members of his famously loyal base. The indoor arena that he spoke at on Friday was a fraction of the size of the football stadium he once spoke in — security concerns are such that he rarely speaks in outdoor venues anymore — and still the place was not full. Some upper sections were almost completely empty.

Mr. Trump’s poll numbers have been falling for months. On Friday, The New York Times reported that he personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency.

A day before the rally in Mobile, this reporter took a circuitous drive along the Gulf Coast and detected signs along the way that Donald Trump’s decade-long love affair with the Deep South may be wilting.

“I’m very disheartened right now,” a 76-year-old, three-time Trump-voting woman named Kris Rouse said while grocery shopping at a supersized Walmart in the Mississippi town of Pass Christian.

“Most of the things that he said were going to happen have not happened,” she said as she pushed her cart around the produce aisle. “The gas has gone up, the groceries have gone up, and my taxes on my property have gone up. I’m a senior citizen on a fixed income, and it’s hard right now.”

She retired after 33 years of working in a local bank branch, but has since picked up a part-time job as a door hostess at Waffle House because, she said, “it’s necessary.”

She is done with Mr. Trump, she said, and won’t be voting for anyone this November. Some of her friends are sticking with the president, but there are lots of “others who are just like me,” she explained.

But what about the president’s promise that he is going to send everybody a check for $5,000?

“Nope,” she answered. “I don’t think we’re going to get anything else from Trump.”

(On Friday, in Mobile, Mr. Trump said again that he was going to send out checks for $5,000, and reminded his audience that he sent a check for $1,776 to members of the military. The $5,000 giveaway would cost more than $1 trillion and likely require congressional approval, for which there seems to be very little.)

Asked what she made of the big ballroom project the president is hard at work on back in Washington, Ms. Rouse laughed bitterly and gave a one-word reply.

“Ridiculous.”

Over in the bread aisle, there was a little more sympathy and jingoism to be found.

“He has made some mistakes, like they all have,” said Skip King, a 75-year-old retired construction worker. He allowed that gas and groceries had gotten more expensive, but said that was a price worth paying if it meant toppling the Iranian regime. He only wished Mr. Trump would hurry up.

“We need to quit playing handsies,” the old construction worker said as he tossed a box of Jiffy corn muffin mix into his cart. “We are the most powerful nation on this planet, and we need to prove it, and show it, and show no mercy.”

“I’d still vote for him,” he concluded.

A few miles up the coastline, in the town of Ocean Springs, Ala., at the corner of Government Street and Washington Street, a man and a woman wearing red MAGA hats were stopping people at random to talk about “the importance of voting in the midterms,” as the man put it.

His name was Adam Francisco. He was 43 years old. The woman said her name on the internet was “Freedom and Whiskey,” and that she could not give her actual name for “safety” reasons. She was 30 years old. Both were MAGA influencers. Each held a camera and a foam-topped microphone on a grip. They were on a mission, driving around the entirety of “the Gulf of America” to warn about Democratic socialism, to remind people why they loved Mr. Trump in the first place, and to hopefully get some good viral content, of course.

They stopped two elderly women on the corner. A friendly chat ensued. Then the women strolled on. “Pro-choice Democrats,” Mr. Francisco said.

He acknowledged that gas prices are a huge liability for the president. “If he doesn’t get them down by between now and Nov. 3, I’m going to say that I’m a little concerned about the Republicans’ chances,” he said. “I’m not in denial about it.”

The last town in Mississippi before the Louisiana state line is a small and swampy one called Pearlington. It’s the sort of place where alligators swim in the bayou behind the local dive bar — and the bartender swims with them, or so she says.

The road out of town leads to a broken-down bridge that used to be the way to New Orleans. Beside the bridge is a gas station with three pumps. The two women working behind the counter there Wednesday morning shook their heads slowly at the mention of Mr. Trump. One said it had never cost her this much to fill up her truck. Asked how many people around these parts had turned on the president, she estimated half.

ARTICLE

Agency Diverted $1.4 Billion in Science Funds Mandated by Congress
The move, affecting about one-fifth of the National Science Foundation’s primary research budget, is the latest sign of how the White House is asserting more control over grants.
By Adam Sella, Christopher Flavelle and Irena Hwang
Published 2026-10-02 18:41 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/politics/national-science-foundation-research-funds.html

The National Science Foundation, one of the biggest sources of federal research funding, withheld $1.4 billion that Congress had intended for research over the course of the past year, according to internal data reviewed by The New York Times.

The extraordinary move — holding back about one-fifth of the N.S.F.’s primary research budget — is the latest sign of how the Trump administration is finding creative ways to work around Congress. Lawmakers from both parties have consistently opposed White House-led proposals to cut funding to major science agencies, including the N.S.F. and the National Institutes of Health.

Since the N.S.F. was founded over 75 years ago, the agency has spent nearly all of its budget on so-called basic research from a wide range of scientific fields, which has led to major advances in technology such as M.R.I.s, semiconductors and the internet.

The White House wants to redirect the money to a limited set of administration priorities, including artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to two people with knowledge of the administration’s plans.

Congress appropriates money to the N.S.F. on two-year cycles, so the agency could still spend the held-over money in the new fiscal year, which began on Thursday.

But Democratic lawmakers see the strategy as more of a political power grab by the White House.

“The money should be granted as Congress intended, and essentially, they’re ignoring what Congress did,” said Representative Zoe Lofgren of California, the top Democrat on the Science, Space and Technology Committee. “It’s a dramatic attack on the science enterprise that has served us very well since World War II, when this whole system was set up,” Ms. Lofgren added.

The White House and the N.S.F. said that diverting the money was allowed under Congress’s two-year appropriation.

Mike England, a spokesman for the science foundation, said in a statement that the agency had “carried over funds to invest in agency priorities that are aligned with broader administration initiatives.”

Mr. England said the agency “remains committed to investing in meritorious foundational research across the sciences and engineering that advances American scientific leadership.”

The Trump administration’s efforts to gain more power over grants have played out across the government, where funding decisions have historically been led by experts.

Last month, the N.I.H. signed an agreement to collaborate with the Defense Department, drawing criticism from Democrats on Capitol Hill who warned that the plan could allow the Pentagon to go around Congress and gain access to billions of dollars meant for infectious disease research. The administration previously fired the N.S.F.’s independent oversight board. And it has canceled or delayed thousands of grants across both agencies as part of its quest to punish elite universities and eliminate spending President Trump and his aides view as “woke.”

Mr. Trump’s science adviser, Michael Kratsios, has criticized the agency’s system for deciding which grants to fund. In a report released in July, Mr. Kratsios wrote that the science foundation, under the Biden administration, awarded too many grants that focused on diversity and equity. He also argued the N.S.F. should issue more “fast grants,” in ways “that bypass external review panels.”

The plan to divert N.S.F. funding was reported earlier by Nature, a science journal.

Several people with knowledge of the situation described confusion inside the agency as the staff complied with White House guidance to carry over money as funding deadlines neared. Some divisions had to pull back research proposals that were recommended for funding after peer review, these officials said.

Altogether, the $1.4 billion carried over after the last fiscal year ended on Wednesday amounted to 19 percent of the N.S.F.’s primary research budget allocated by Congress. That is a far higher percentage than in either of the two prior fiscal years, when less than $175 million went unspent, according to internal data from the agency.

At an agency town hall this week, leaders stood by the plan to divert money to administration priorities while offering assurances that the N.S.F. would also remain true to its roots, according to a recording reviewed by The Times.

When an employee raised concerns about whether the N.S.F. would continue supporting basic research, an official responded that “we’re transitioning.” Still, the official said, the agency would continue to “focus on our mission of foundational research.”

ARTICLE

Trump Directed Use of Taxpayer Money for Ads Praising His Presidency
The government-funded ads show just how much President Trump has been able to use federal money for his own aims.
By Maggie Haberman, Hamed Aleaziz, Shane Goldmacher and Jonathan Swan
Published 2026-10-02 19:36 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/politics/trump-ads.html

President Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency, setting in motion a $20 million contract that used funds from the Department of Homeland Security, according to people familiar with the matter.

The ads have run across cable and network television — on Fox News, CNN and MS Now, with football games on Fox and with national newscasts on CBS, ABC and NBC, including “Meet the Press,” which Mr. Trump is known to watch.

Mr. Trump was eager to see the laudatory ads on the air and told Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to come up with the money from within the government, the people said. Mark Paoletta, the budget office’s counsel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel, both said it would be legal to use D.H.S. funds. The president and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, both spoke with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, about the ads.

On Sept. 20, U.S. Customs and Border Protection — which falls under D.H.S. — awarded the contract to LMD, a Maryland marketing firm, federal records show.

This article is based on interviews with 12 people familiar with the president’s interest in the ads and how they came to be. They spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the president’s demand.

The taxpayer-funded ads have been criticized by Democrats and even some Republicans as a possible violation of federal laws against using taxpayer dollars for “publicity or propaganda purposes.” And they come as the president is also directing spending from his super PAC — MAGA Inc., which entered the fall with $400 million — for which he has been raising money since he won re-election in 2024.

It was not clear why taxpayer funds, and not money from the super PAC, were used for the spots.

The White House has called the ads public service announcements and said they are appropriate because there is no “call to action” to vote for any candidate. Some of his aides also noted that Mr. Trump is not running for office now, in an attempt to blunt criticism of the ads as violating federal laws about the use of public money.

When pressed by a reporter on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said: “If somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money.”

“But these are ads for the country,” he added. “You have to understand. I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

At least four spots have run so far, at a cost of about $5.5 million, and that is expected to grow, according to the media tracker AdImpact and people familiar with the spending. One played images of Mr. Trump to the song “Love Me” by Christian Berishaj, who performs as JMSN. (The artist has protested the use of his song.)

Another was identical to a Trump campaign video from 2024 that condemns “villains” whom the president perceives as enemies. The use of material originally made during Mr. Trump’s political campaign has given fuel to critics who reject the White House claim that the ads are simply public service announcements.

A third ad, about the Iran war, features remarks from both Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Such public service spots typically say which agency paid for them. In this case, all of the ads had an unusual tagline: “Paid for by the U.S. government.”

‘Love Me’

On Aug. 7, Mr. Trump was in the Oval Office with a group of Republican strategists working with his team, along with James Blair, his top political adviser, and Ms. Wiles. Natalie Harp, his ever-present assistant and provider of positive news about himself, was there as well.

At the time, Mr. Trump’s advisers were waiting for him to sign off, finally, on spending from his super PAC for midterm candidates, after months of anxiety from Republican candidates about whether he would help them financially in tight races.

But during that meeting, the president was much more interested in looking at videos of himself.

He turned to Ms. Harp and asked her to show the group the type of imagery he favors.

Ms. Harp pulled up a series of videos made by the White House digital team on her tablet: Mr. Trump standing in front of vast crowds; Mr. Trump beside Marine One; Mr. Trump with fighter jets streaking overhead.

One video showed Dana White, the U.F.C. president, at the 2024 Republican convention, calling Mr. Trump “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met.” Mr. Trump has talked with delight about that quote repeatedly ever since.

Mr. Trump made clear he planned to travel to support candidates in the midterms, but also that his presidency needed to be promoted, front and center, in the commercials his advisers were making.

Later that month, The Atlantic reported that MAGA Inc. was planning a blitz of midterm ads, with Trump as the centerpiece.

Instead, a Trump-linked nonprofit called Securing American Greatness aired a spot featuring the Dana White quote, spending just under $60,000, according to AdImpact. The ad primarily aired over Sept. 2 and Sept. 3 around Washington, where Mr. Trump was sure to see them.

But then, weeks later, several ads glorifying Mr. Trump began appearing across the country — this time paid for by taxpayers, by way of Customs and Border Protection.

The ads included the “Love Me” spot, in which Mr. Trump says in a voice-over that “America will never be a communist country.”

As the taxpayer-funded spots began running, MAGA Inc. has spent directly to help out in one specific race, putting more than $20 million into the Texas Senate campaign. Two other new groups linked to MAGA Inc. — No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC — were recently created and have spent and reserved more than $163 million on spots in races across the country.

But those ads feature Mr. Trump only sparingly.

Asked to comment for this story, the White House press office sent an unsigned statement saying, “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders and abroad.”

The White House has said there is precedent for using taxpayer money for the ads. “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, posted on X on Sept. 27.

His office sent out an email stating that “presidential public service announcements are nothing new,” comparing the spots to efforts to promote health care policy in past administrations, or President Woodrow Wilson’s World War I propaganda campaign.

The Government Accountability Office has found likely or confirmed violations of the anti-propaganda rule before, including during the tenures of both President Barack Obama and President George W. Bush. Those cases concerned publicity campaigns related to policies, not ads focused on the presidents themselves.

‘This Is My Money’

The money for the ads was freed up on Sept. 19, when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events.

The next day, C.B.P. awarded a $20 million contract to LMD, a marketing firm based in Columbia, Md., that federal records show had past work as a government contractor. The actual purchase of the airtime was made by a second firm, LMO, according to a person familiar with the events, who wasn’t authorized to discuss them publicly.

A spokeswoman for the Office of Management and Budget declined to comment on the reporting for this story. A spokesperson for the Homeland Security Department would only say, “D.H.S. follows all applicable rules for contracting decisions and keeps all decision makers informed. All contracting decisions are made in accordance with applicable law.” Officials with LMD and LMO did not respond to requests for comment.

The spots started out airing narrowly but soon ran in heavy rotation not just on cable channels, but on broadcast networks as well. They ran heavily on the network morning programs like “Good Morning America” and “CBS Mornings,” according AdImpact, and appeared in entertainment shows including “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and “The Amazing Race.” One aired repeatedly during weekend football broadcasts on the Fox network.

The ads are not the first costly television campaign under Mr. Trump, nor are they the first controversial ones. In 2025, Kristi Noem, the homeland security secretary at the time, appeared in a $200 million-plus government ad campaign. The ads, which showed Ms. Noem on a horse at Mount Rushmore, ultimately drew the president’s disapproval, and became the justification for replacing Ms. Noem.

The latest ads promoting Mr. Trump come as his standing with the public has dropped. His approval rating sits at around 37 percent, a number that has been low and steady for months, according to a polling tracker by The New York Times. Republicans are increasingly fearful of a Democratic sweep of both House and Senate, and losses in state legislatures.

Mr. Trump has remained a prodigious fund-raiser for his various construction projects around Washington and at the White House, as well as his future presidential library. Last month, he promised to spend “probably” $400 million to $500 million on midterm election races, but he made clear who holds the purse strings to his super PAC.

“This is my money that I control,” Mr. Trump said.

Reporting was contributed by Jim Rutenberg in New York and Luke Broadwater in Washington.

ARTICLE

Truckers Are ‘Just Trying to Hang On’ When a Fill-Up Tops $1,000
Truckers are among the hardest hit by the soaring cost of diesel fuel. High prices are forcing some to stay on the road for months and others to park their rigs.
By Audra D. S. Burch
Published 2026-10-02 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/truckers-diesel-costs.html

When Sean Howarth started his independent trucking business last year, he made sure to reserve one week a month for his family — a girlfriend and her two children — at home in Miami between three weeks on the road.

Then came the war in Iran, which sent the price of diesel fuel skyrocketing and turned a fill-up into an $1,000-a-tank ordeal. For now, the only way to make ends meet, Mr. Howarth said, is to get on the road and stay there. He has not been home since mid-August. He sleeps in his truck and has missed birthdays, volleyball games and date nights salsa dancing at a local club. He does not plan to return home until the holidays unless diesel prices fall sharply.

“I am just trying to hang on,” he said.

Diesel prices are averaging $6.39 a gallon nationally, up from $3.71 a year ago, according to AAA. The high cost of fuel is battering owner-operator truck drivers, who help deliver food, construction materials, medical supplies, electronics and other goods across the country.

Independent truckers, already dealing with stagnant freight rates, rising expenses, and wafer-thin profit margins, are doing all they can to stay afloat. Some have turned to crowdfunding to raise money for gas and maintenance. Others have simply parked their rigs as they hope for a reprieve.

“This is crushing to our industry,” said Lewie Pugh, executive vice president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association, which represents more than 135,000 members. “When fuel goes up a dollar a gallon at the pump, that’s another $400 per week that they have to spend. That’s a huge, huge hit to a small business trucker.”

Last week, Mr. Howarth said, he hauled a load of construction equipment from Rogers, Minn., to Johnstown, N.Y. With about 800 miles to go, he began the dreaded search for cheap diesel fuel, tapping on a mobile app to identify the best prices in real time. The final cost: $626 to top off for a load that grossed about $1,000. The profit was a fraction of the $5,300 he owes on his monthly truck payment and insurance.

Mr. Howarth often tries to match load drop-offs with nearby pickups to avoid empty miles and increase profits, but each jump in diesel price has felt like a gut punch, he said. He can make the numbers work with enough good-paying loads, but any more fuel spikes could wipe him out. For now, he is limiting jobs to the East Coast and Midwest, avoiding California, where the average cost of diesel is $8.38 a gallon.

“When I started, it cost me $500 to fill my tank, and now it’s $950 or $1,100-plus, depending on where I am in the country,” said Mr. Howarth, 36, who worked for a trucking company before starting his own business. “Right when things are starting to seem a little easier and go in the right direction, the fuel costs go through the roof.”

For many Americans, the rising price of regular gasoline is a grim reminder of the painfully expensive cost of living. But diesel prices reverberate beyond the gas tank to consumer goods trucked from ports and factories, agricultural products harvested by diesel-powered machinery, even the mail. Fuel supplies were disrupted not only by the war in Iran but by Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries in response to Russia’s missile strikes on its cities.

Republicans, particularly those in close midterm races, are looking for ways to tamp down bubbling voter anger by calling for an end to the war and a ban on diesel exports. On Tuesday, Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia, who would like another Republican, Rick Jackson, to succeed him when he retires this year, became the latest state leader to suspend gas taxes temporarily.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said President Trump met with refiners at the White House to try to find ways to expand refining capacity to bring prices down. She added, “As the U.S. continues to maintain full control of the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices will fall back to pre-conflict levels.”

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said this week on Fox News Channel that he intends to ask European countries to release strategic diesel reserves to draw down prices.

“There’s a very good chance we have hit peak prices,” he said. “We are almost surely going to see diesel prices decline.”

For truckers, a price drop cannot come fast enough. Mr. Pugh, who has been driving trucks for more than 25 years, said that about 90 percent of all trucking companies are small businesses and that many are forced to float costs until they get paid 30 to 90 days later. Most negotiate with a broker on the pay for each run, working “load to load.” They can’t raise their rates when fuel spikes in the same way their larger competitors can, he said.

The situation has set social media ablaze. Truckers have posted videos from gas stations and truck stops as fill-ups top $1,000. In one TikTok clip, an exasperated trucker standing next to his rig said the high cost effectively “takes food out of the mouths of your children.”

For about two years, Renardo Harmon has subcontracted with a small Alabama-based carrier to haul dry goods to stores such as Dollar General, Big Lots and Roses Discount Stores across the Southeast.

Mr. Harmon makes a flat rate of around $2.40 a mile and covers his own expenses, including diesel fuel, maintenance and insurance. It now costs him $900 to $1,000 to fill his tank, double the pre-Iran war price.

“These high diesel costs are trickling down to my house expenses, my rent, my groceries,” said Mr. Harmon, 40, of Atlanta. “If I am not making a profit, than I am not going to be able to afford my rent or make payments on my car.”

“At $3 to $4 a gallon, you can survive,” he continued. “But if the prices don’t drop, a lot of us might be forced to suspend operations until things get better,” he said, adding that he is not sure whether to blame “the government or the oil refineries.”

“What I know for sure, is that it doesn’t have to be this way,” he said. “We should be able to make a decent living.”

Kirsten Noyes and Alain Delaqueriere contributed research.

ARTICLE

Extreme Heat in Los Angeles Area Expected to Last at Least a Week
Forecasters say a dangerous heat wave is descending across much of Southern California, which is likely to bring triple-digit temperatures.
By Livia Albeck-Ripka and Amy Graff
Published 2026-10-02 21:12 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/weather/extreme-heat-wave-california.html

The seasonal pools are closed. Many playground fountains have been turned off. Along Southern California’s beaches, some lifeguard towers are no longer staffed.

Summer is over.

But extreme heat is not. Forecasters say a dangerous heat wave is descending across much of Southern California, which is likely to bring triple-digit temperatures that will last at least a week.

Hot weather is not unusual in Southern California in October, but typically it lasts two or three days. The extended stretch of extreme heat makes this episode particularly dangerous, experts say.

October also tends to be one of the months when the risk of wildfires in Southern California is high because the vegetation has dried out after the summer and winds can grow stronger.

The wildfire risk will be elevated, particularly in inland valleys and mountains, but it is not expected to be so extreme as to prompt red-flag warnings.

Extreme heat warnings have been issued from Santa Barbara to San Diego, lasting through at least next Friday. Temperatures in downtown Los Angeles could reach 100 or higher on Saturday and Sunday, according to the National Weather Service. A few miles from downtown, the Dodgers are set to open a playoff series on Saturday in the middle of the day.

Temperatures will be even more extreme across the region’s inland valleys and deserts. Over the weekend, Death Valley National Park could reach 109 degrees, forecaster predict.

While the highest temperatures are likely to be recorded over the weekend, the weather next week is could feel equally stifling.

“We’re not going to see a pronounced peak in temperatures this weekend. It’s pretty much going to be hot through the entire week,” said Devin Black, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in Oxnard, Calif.

Across the region, counties and cities were making preparations.

Officials were urging the public not to leave pets and children in vehicles. Crews were on alert for power outages. The Los Angeles County Fire Department has increased staffing and positioned units in some of the most high-risk places, said Jonathan Torres, a spokesman for the department.

County health officials also urged residents to stay hydrated and avoid going outdoors during the hottest hours. Those without air-conditioning, officials said, should take cool showers or baths, avoid using stoves and ovens, and seek shelter in a library, cooling center or mall.

Daniela Simunovic, the chief heat officer for the City of Los Angeles, said those at greatest risk were children, seniors and pregnant people, as well as people living in homes without air-conditioning or cooling. “This week is particularly dangerous,” she said.

Mr. Torres said high-risk heat conditions have become the norm.

“It used to be a season; now it’s year-round,” Mr. Torres said. “That’s just the reality that we have to live with here in Southern California.”

The expected heat wave is the first since the region suffered through scorching temperatures for two days in September, during which the temperature in downtown Los Angeles soared to 105, the highest recorded there so far this year.

Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Oxnard, warned that heat events lasting six or seven days — and including high temperatures at night — could overwhelm the body’s natural cooling system, since there is no time for recovery.

Above normal temperatures in the Pacific Ocean have fueled tropical storms that have sent big waves to the Southern California coast. The increased storm activity is in part driven by the weather pattern known as El Niño that is particularly powerful this year and expected to affect winter weather around the globe. But Ms. Schoenfeld said she and her colleagues are not aware of a direct correlation between the coming heat wave and El Niño.

The heat will be accompanied by the winds that blow dry, warm air from inland areas toward the coast, while simultaneously, the sea breeze that pushes cool air off the ocean toward the coast will weaken, she said.

“That wind pattern is critical to what our temperatures will end up being,” said Ms. Schoenfeld.

While Southern California was wrapped in hot, sticky air much of the summer, relative humidity levels during this event are not expected to be high. The offshore winds pulling in dry air will help prevent muggy weather, but a hurricane churning far offshore could send moisture to the region as early as Saturday.

“It could be a little muggy, but not like it was during a lot of the summer,” said Ms. Schoenfeld.

The hurricane could also cause high surf and rip currents. In a social media post, the Weather Service warned beachgoers seeking relief from the heat not to go into dangerous waters.

Lifeguards in Los Angeles County said last month that over the summer they rescued more than 10,000 people from the ocean.

ARTICLE

The Headaches Disrupted Her Life
The woman’s severe pain seemed to ease only when she was lying down. What would cause such a thing?
By Lisa Sanders, M.D.
Published 2026-10-02 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/well/headaches-brain-sag-spinal-fluid-leak.html

In the early morning light of her home in Dover, Ohio, the 62-year-old woman carefully swung her legs over the side of the bed and stood. And there it was: A clamp tightened around the right side of her head. The pain was over her right ear, in her face and down the right side of her neck. She took a deep breath. Another day. Another headache.

She hadn’t been a headache person for most of her life. But that changed early in 2025 with these headaches that hit as soon as she got up in the morning. It was a pressure-like pain, always on the right side, and ibuprofen and acetaminophen barely touched it.

Given the severity of her pain, the nurse practitioner who was the woman’s primary care provider wondered if these were migraines. She prescribed a medication meant to stop this type of headache when taken as soon as the pain starts. But because it is unusual to start getting headaches at this age, and because the patient’s mother had suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm, she sent her for a head CT. It was a relief for the patient to hear that the CT was normal, but she needed to know the cause of her pain. She went to her eye doctor to find out if she needed a new glasses prescription. She did, but that didn’t help. Her boss installed a shade over her desk to cut the glare from the fluorescent light. She was grateful, but the headaches were unrelenting.

Her P.C.P., still wondering if this could be an aneurysm, referred her to a local neurosurgeon. Hearing her story, the physician assistant in the neurosurgery practice agreed that these probably were migraines and prescribed an additional medication, propranolol, to be taken daily. But the possibility of an aneurysm remained, so she also ordered an M.R.I. of her brain and a CT scan of the blood vessels in her brain. The woman had the two studies a couple of weeks later. There was no aneurysm. Her vessels were normal. Her brain, however, was not.

A Worrisome Explanation

When the patient saw the M.R.I. result, she was alarmed. She had, the report said, something called brain sag. She wasn’t sure what that was, but it sounded bad. She left a message for the P.A., and when she didn’t hear back, she got scared. She called her P.C.P. and was referred to another neurosurgeon, this time at the Cleveland Clinic.

The patient’s first thought when she saw Dr. Mohammed Abdulrazzak at the Cleveland Clinic branch in Canton, Ohio, was that he was too young to be a doctor, much less a neurosurgeon. He introduced himself, then sat in the chair across from hers. “I hear you have a headache,” he said. She felt a sense of real interest from him as she told her story. She explained how terrible her headaches were when she was upright, when she laughed or even spoke. When she sneezed, the pain was unbelievable. And recently the headaches seemed to be affecting her memory as well. She had to write things down to keep herself from forgetting. The migraine medications did help, but the only thing that made her headaches almost completely subside was lying down. When she said this, she thought she saw just a hint of excitement in the young doctor’s eyes.

Brain sag, Abdulrazzak explained, was usually caused by the loss of some of the spinal fluid that cushions and supports the brain. When standing, gravity pulls the already-depleted fluid farther downward, stretching the pain-sensitive membranes and structures around the brain. Lying down eases that stretch immediately. The woman’s story was classic for the diagnosis: a headache that responds to posture almost like a light switch, in a way that tension headaches and migraines rarely do.

Abdulrazzak pointed to the black and white curves of her brain on the M.R.I. Even when she was lying down, her cerebellum was so low that it was almost touching the skull near the foramen magnum, the hole through which the spinal column emerged. That’s why her brain appeared to be sagging. He asked the patient if she had had any recent surgery or trauma. She hadn’t. Abdulrazzak wasn’t surprised. Many of these leaks are spontaneous, the cause never discovered.

The hardest part of this disease was finding the leak. In the necessary test, called a myelogram, contrast is injected into the space around the spinal column and a CT scan captures where it leaks out.

The test was awful. The increased pressure caused by the injection of the contrast made her whole head ache. She waited anxiously for the results. No leak was seen. But Abdulrazzak was sure there was one. There was another study, he told her, only recently available, that would give them a better image. They could give her general anesthesia so she wouldn’t feel the pressure from the injected contrast. The woman considered this possibility then shook her head. The headaches were manageable with the medications, she said. She asked if she could just wait and see what happened. Abdulrazzak assured her she could, and told her to come back in a few months.

Another Test

She felt OK for awhile. But just over a year after the headaches started, the medications suddenly stopped working. Getting out of bed in the morning was almost torture, and some days she had to call in sick and spend the entire day in bed.

Her best friend was distressed to see the woman suffer so much. On weekends, the women and their husbands often went to listen to music in the local bars. But the last time they went out, the woman had to leave. The music, the crowd — it was all just too much for her. These days her friend couldn’t help noticing how tired she looked. She was pale. She had dark circles under her eyes. And she was so forgetful. The way she repeated herself reminded the friend of her own grandmother who had Alzheimer’s.

“You’ve got to go back to that doctor and see what he can do,” the friend exclaimed one evening when the woman was in the grips of a really bad headache.

Her friend went with her a few weeks later to see Abdulrazzak, who arranged the second test. In it, the patient lay on her right side. Once she was sedated, a catheter was inserted into the base of the sac containing the spinal cord, and contrast was injected. Then the table was tilted so that the contrast could flow upward, highlighting the entire spinal column. And there it was — the leak. A thin trickle of contrast filled one of the tiny veins leading away from the sac at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra, just above the bottom of the rib cage.

Two weeks later, Abdulrazzak inserted a tiny catheter into the woman’s thigh. He slowly threaded it up the vein, carefully navigating toward the tiny vessel the spinal fluid was leaking into. He guided his way using a viewable X-ray called a fluoroscope to find the exact spot. Once he was at the site of the leak, he injected a material to completely seal off the vein.

When the patient woke up, Abdulrazzak told her that she would have a headache for a week or so. Her body had increased the amount of spinal fluid it made trying to compensate for the leak. Now that the leak was sealed, her body would have to reduce its spinal fluid output, and that would take a little time.

She went home the next day, and she did have a headache. But as promised, over the next couple of weeks, the pain gradually disappeared. Her memory started to improve. The real test, she knew, would come when she and her friend and their husbands went out. So, some six weeks after her procedure, the two couples struck out for one of their favorite places. She hadn’t had a headache for weeks, and worried the thunderous music would bring it all back. They found a seat as far from the speakers as they could get. Finally the band came out and picked up their instruments. The woman’s heart raced. But once the lead guitarist struck his first chord, quickly followed by bass, drums and keyboard, she sensed that her headaches were gone for good and life could finally return to normal.

SUMMARY

As China’s government pushes its citizens to embrace artificial intelligence, it is confronting a problem partly of its own making: overreliance on the technology. These cases and others have raised concerns in China that as it rushes to catch up with the United States in A.I., it is running into adverse side effects created by the new technology, which is accused of undermining human relationships and depriving people of their better judgment.

ARTICLE

China’s Push into A.I. Has Led to a Problem: Too Much Usage
As citizens embrace the technology for entertainment, relationships and even farming advice, the government is stepping up efforts to set limits.
By Yan Zhuang
Published 2026-10-02 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/world/asia/china-ai-overuse.html

As China’s government pushes its citizens to embrace artificial intelligence, it is confronting a problem partly of its own making: overreliance on the technology.

State media reports have featured stories that serve as cautionary tales: a farmer who lost 25 acres of seedlings after asking an A.I. for advice, children who have become so attached to chatbots that they want their parents to speak like them and A.I.-generated micro dramas with characters that look like carbon copies of one another.

These cases and others have raised concerns in China that as it rushes to catch up with the United States in A.I., it is running into adverse side effects created by the new technology, which is accused of undermining human relationships and depriving people of their better judgment. The government, seeking to direct how people use the technology, has responded by imposing new regulations and judicial guidelines on its use — and misuse.

The response reflects how the ruling Communist Party is trying to balance its ambitions to promote the widespread use of A.I. with a desire to avoid anything that might undermine social order, say analysts.

The party is “recognizing that the more they develop the technology, the more there’s going to be social challenges that they have to deal with,” said Scott Singer, a fellow and co-director of the China A.I. Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “Where the party is sensitive is any area where they feel like the technology is getting better in a way that fundamentally could disrupt social stability.”

Mr. Singer said the party is particularly sensitive to disruptions caused not only to human relationships but also the job market as A.I. threatens to replace workers.

Concerns about overuse are shared among China’s citizens, who say they see the spread of the technology as inevitable even as they question its benefits and tire of its ubiquity.

Xie Tong, a graphic designer in Beijing, uses A.I. in her own work at a consulting agency and can no longer imagine her life without it. But she despairs at encountering A.I. all around her — in the subway ads that she sees on her commute and in the work of contractors at her job who obviously relied on A.I.

“It’s like a marriage where you curse your partner but you can’t leave them,” she said.

Limits on Virtual Friends

For a time, China’s A.I. push created a boom in virtual companion apps, including ones offering romantic partners, personal tutors and A.I. avatars of family members.

In a country already struggling with a shrinking population and a historically low birthrate, the proliferation has led to concerns from Beijing about A.I. replacing human relationships. State media quoted experts saying people could soon find it hard to navigate real interactions. Reports cited a 2025 survey by the China Youth and Children Research Center of more than 8,500 minors that showed more than 20 percent “only wanted to chat with A.I. and did not want to talk with real people.”

That mirrored the concerns of some parents like Vivian Lyu, a stay-at-home mother in Hangzhou who two years ago introduced her 5-year-old daughter, Polly, to Doubao, an A.I. assistant created by ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok.

Soon, the child was chatting with the A.I. and a personalized companion on the app nearly every day. At first, Ms. Lyu thought the A.I. was good at keeping Polly entertained when the mother had to take care of household tasks. “When you feel like you don’t have a choice, you use Doubao,” she said.

Over time, though, Polly started asking for Doubao instead of seeking out activities that used to interest her, like playing with other children or drawing pictures. Ms. Lyu said she worried that the chatbot was warping her daughter’s understanding of how relationships worked, saying that Polly sometimes talked to Doubao in a “very self-centered, doing-whatever-she-wants kind of way.”

In July, the government imposed limits on A.I. companions that require platforms to step in if users exhibited unhealthy dependencies. Under the new rules, platforms must intervene if users show signs of self-harm.

The rules also banned virtual relationships between chatbots and minors, which forced ByteDance to shut down the feature on Doubao that allowed users to create companions.

Polly can no longer access her personalized A.I. companion, but she is still talking to Doubao’s A.I. chatbot, Ms. Lyu said. The mother considered banning her daughter from using chatbots but concluded that such a step could make it harder for Polly to adjust to the technology as she grows older. Instead, Ms. Lyu has limited Polly’s chatbot time to one hour a day.

“My hope is for her to understand from a young age that these electronic products, or all of these things related to A.I., are just tools,” Ms. Lyu said.

Real World Problems

Just as in many countries, China is struggling with so-called A.I. literacy — understanding how the technology works and its limits. In recent months, the media has documented a growing number of A.I. mishaps involving people who blindly believed in the technology.

There was the case of a hiker who became stranded atop a mountain in August after A.I.-generated instructions left him improperly equipped. In several separate cases earlier in the summer, people fell ill after eating poisonous mushrooms that were misidentified by A.I., including a 9-year-old boy who spent eight days in a hospital.

One of the most widely covered cases involved a farmer in the eastern province of Anhui who lost 25 acres of sesame seedlings in July after following a pesticide regimen drawn up by an A.I. assistant.

The 67-year-old farmer, whom the reports identified only by his last name, Wu, lost 150,000 yuan, or about $22,000, worth of crops after the A.I. recommended an herbicide that turned out to be unsuitable, the reports said.

The Communist Party’s mouthpiece, People’s Daily, argued in a commentary that A.I. in sectors like agriculture should use only information that comes from authoritative sources.

It also called for farmers to be trained in “critical thinking about A.I. suggestions, helping farmers transform from passive implementers of technology into active participants who can control the tools.”

A Backlash Against Cheap A.I. Fodder

A.I. has also become ubiquitous in micro dramas, the wildly popular short-form, soapy shows that are made for mobile viewing. In the first eight months of the year, more than 90 percent of the 430,000 micro dramas released in China were generated by A.I., the government said in late September.

These dramas can be churned out cheaply in minutes with no cameras, production crews or human performers. But they have come under fire for their low quality and for taking the jobs of humans.

An article in August in Beijing Youth Daily, the official publication of the Communist Youth League, complained that production companies were churning out A.I.-created micro dramas with boring, interchangeable characters.

Some influential voices have gone as far as to say they will boycott micro dramas generated entirely by A.I.

Hu Xijin, the former editor of the state-run Global Times, told his 25 million followers on the social media platform Weibo recently that he would not watch such dramas to avoid “filling up our recreational time with cheap A.I. fodder like pig feed.”

Siyi Zhao contributed research.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Ignore the Profanity. Could Michael Douglas Actually Be Mellowing?
At 82, the famously roguish leading man has written a memoir, “One Helluva Ride,” that’s as candid and intimate as it is feisty.
By Elisabeth Egan
Published 2026-10-03 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/books/review/michael-douglas-memoir-one-helluva-ride-interview.html

His hair is more salt than pepper. His forehead has deep furrows. His brows have a mind of their own.

But Michael Douglas’s eyes are as they always were, close set and blue, with the piercing gaze he brought to his most famous line, “Greed is good,” as Gordon Gekko in “Wall Street.”

Once a poster boy for ’80s excess, Douglas, 82, has returned to his hippie roots, at least ideologically.

“Obsessions aren’t healthy. We have to rekindle a philosophy about trying to help each other,” he said, leaning forward as if to emphasize the point. “Train yourself to help others.”

We were at Estiatorio Milos, a cavernous Greek restaurant in Midtown Manhattan, to discuss Douglas’s sprawling memoir, “One Helluva Ride,” coming out from Grand Central on Oct. 6. The place wasn’t yet open to the lunch rush, but members of the wait staff bustled around, refilling our water glasses at attentive intervals, and Douglas was polite, almost courtly, with each one. This might seem like a low bar, but it says something about a person.

“I’ve been working my ass off for 55 years,” Douglas said, glancing proudly at his 496-page book, which had a seat of its own at our table. “This is sort of a culmination.”

Some celebrity memoirs skate over the good stuff, offering a highlight reel more than an in-depth feature. “One Helluva Ride” is a blockbuster — intimate and uncensored, worthy of a bucket of popcorn with extra butter.

Aside from Clint Eastwood, Robert Redford and maybe George Clooney in a decade or two, few actor-producers have had Douglas’s staying power.

His memoir covers it all: six decades of filmmaking (including Oscars for “Wall Street” and “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest,” which he produced with Saul Zaentz); two generations of Hollywood royalty (Douglas’s father, Kirk, paved the way); two marriages (one turbulent, the second, to Catherine Zeta-Jones, “a joy and a comfort,” he said); many, many romantic dalliances (with Brenda Vaccaro, Jeanne Tripplehorn, Kathleen Turner, the Times opinion writer Maureen Dowd, an Israeli soldier he met on the side of the road, the list goes on); lots of drugs (including suitcases of “grass” that Douglas sold to pay for his last two years at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and a memorable bender after which he woke up with a cocaine straw still up his nose); and parenthood, recounted with refreshing candor.

Douglas’s older son, Cameron, spent seven years in prison on drug charges, including two in solitary confinement. Douglas’s descriptions of that time — and of Cameron’s battles with heroin addiction — are among the most powerful in the book, which is as much a family story as it is a time capsule of a certain era.

“I wasn’t around a lot, so I have my own guilt with Cameron,” Douglas said, referring to the difficult years when he and his first wife, Diandra Luker, lived on opposite coasts.

A few minutes later, he answered a FaceTime call from his 23-year-old daughter, Carys Zeta Douglas, who was filming a movie in the Canary Islands. Their exchange was quick and endearing — “Angel? Hi, sweetheart,” Douglas said, his face alight with a blindingly white smile. But after he hung up with a promise to call back later, he briskly returned to the subject at hand: a 34-year-old tabloid rumor that, in 1992, he went to rehab for sex addiction. In fact, he was at Sierra Tucson in Arizona to kick a drug habit and he still resents being sold out by fellow patients, whom he spoke of with contempt. Ditto the paparazzi who followed his children to school when he had cancer.

“I was really pissed off,” Douglas said.

There’s a lot of that in “One Helluva Ride” — Douglas gets irritated with Oliver Stone on the set of “Wall Street”; with Steven Soderbergh, when he almost loses his part in “Traffic” to Harrison Ford; with Kathleen Turner, when she hires Roy Cohn to represent her in a lawsuit over “The Jewel of the Nile”; and so forth.

The book contains 22 F-bombs and an impressive tally of lesser expletives. It’s not bashful about sex, either — no surprise, when you consider that Douglas starred opposite Sharon Stone in the erotic thriller “Basic Instinct.” (And let’s not forget “Fatal Attraction,” with its elevator scene and its kitchen-table-to-countertop-to-bedroom scene.) There’s plenty of nudity in the memoir, too, both onscreen and off; apparently Douglas did without clothing while living in a commune during college. His father, visiting at the peak of his fame, was amused to learn that the place had no toilet.

In person, Douglas appeared more polished than he has in recent Instagram videos, where his hair often has a mad scientist vibe à la Doc Brown in “Back to the Future.” He wore a meticulously pressed blue shirt and his hair was combed back in a way that can only be described as power broker chic. Thanks to a walnut-size tumor he had removed from his tongue 16 years ago, his voice is slightly altered — it’s as gravelly as ever, but now sounds as though he’s talking around a wad of Bubble Yum.

Douglas’s Stage 4 throat cancer diagnosis led to a reckoning with mortality — “I wondered if my luck had run out,” he writes — and a new appreciation for the friends who stuck around.

“There’s something about cancer, it makes people not want to be near you,” he said. “I was surprised by how few people checked in. They don’t know what to say.”

One person he heard from regularly was Shane Salerno, a screenwriter he met in the early 2000s, who fired off a series of missives ribbing Douglas about being an unserious television actor and living in his father’s shadow, both charges that had dogged him early in his career.

“I tried to remind Michael that every time someone had told him he couldn’t do something he had proven them wrong,” Salerno said in an interview.

After a few months of these irreverent notes, Douglas finally fired back: “Keep ’em coming, motherfucker!!!!”

He said: “I was really touched. It meant a lot.”

When Salerno first broached the idea of collaborating on a memoir a decade ago, Douglas declined. He was busy; the time wasn’t right. But his father had written a memoir, as had his mother and his son Cameron — so maybe it was a family tradition? Then, after playing Benjamin Franklin in the Apple TV+ series “Franklin” in 2024, Douglas took a break from acting and started to think about his legacy.

When asked how he sees that legacy taking shape, he gave a self-aware shrug.

“Pretty good batting average,” Douglas said. “A reflection of my times. A reflection of what was going on.”

He and Salerno teamed up with Michael Fleming Jr., a writer for Deadline and Variety who had interviewed Douglas on the eve of a Hollywood Reporter story that included allegations from Susan Braudy, a former employee who said that Douglas had mistreated her and subjected her to sexual harassment decades earlier. Douglas acknowledged using raunchy language in front of Braudy but denied her claims that he had masturbated in front of her and blackballed her in the industry. He does not address the issue in his memoir.

In our interview, Douglas said that Fleming’s article helped him “get out in front of it.”

The three worked on the memoir in hotel rooms, on the phone and on hundreds of Zoom calls. Salerno and Fleming conducted more than 40 interviews, with Zeta-Jones, Douglas’s children, Danny DeVito, Glenn Close and a bevy of other sources. They selected 10 movies they wanted to focus on alongside Douglas’s evolution from son of a star to a leading man in his own right, with plenty of struggle along the way.

He had “four or five turkeys” before he really got started as an actor. After a college production of “Much Ado About Nothing,” he recalls in the book, his father said: “Son, you were terrible. Absolutely terrible.”

In those days, Douglas suffered from debilitating stage fright. He said he’d been told early on: “The camera can tell when you’re lying. So there was a whole period of method acting, of just trying to rip the skin off my face and get down to the truth. Then one day it dawned on me: Acting is all about lying. You become a better liar to convince an audience. Once I realized that, it changed the whole picture.”

“One Helluva Ride” is packed with vintage grudges and escapades — the time Douglas passed over his father for the lead in “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest,” a decision that took years to smooth over; the time Luker walked in on Douglas with an unnamed paramour in a room at the Beverly Wilshire; the time he snorted cocaine through a rolled-up dollar bill with O.J. Simpson at a “Saturday Night Live” after-after-party; the time he insulted Julia Roberts in lewd terms at a Golden Globes party; the time Debra Winger bit his arm, costing herself the lead in “Romancing the Stone.”

The role went to Kathleen Turner, with whom Douglas had an on-set romance.

“There will be some intimate relationships revealed here for the first time,” Douglas writes in the prologue to his memoir. “I called each woman involved and asked for their permission to share our story.”

DeVito, who also appeared in “Romancing the Stone” and its sequel, “The Jewel of the Nile,” said in an interview that he hadn’t noticed the fireworks between Turner and Douglas at the time, but said there was no denying Douglas’s star power.

“He had a mystique,” DeVito said. “He was a babe magnet. But he was also a big softy and a sweet guy.”

DeVito fondly recalled their days of “chasing windmills” and behaving “like a couple of wackos.”

During our interview, Douglas was more a romantic than a rogue, repeatedly steering the conversation back to his family, to whom the memoir is dedicated.

“I started realizing how important family really is,” he said. “This is what holds us together.”

He spoke lovingly of his mother, Diana Dill, a Bermudian actor who completed the Sunday Times crossword puzzle in ink, and of his father.

“My love for him grew as we both aged,” Douglas said. “Between Dad and I, we had 80 years in the business, 160 movies. He’d say, ‘Michael, if I knew how successful you were going to be I would have been nicer.’”

But Douglas got misty-eyed when he spoke of Bill Darrid, who became his stepfather when Douglas was 12.

“He was the first person who listened,” Douglas said. “I remember the shock that he was actually listening to what I had to say.”

Douglas talked about the rage he inherited from his father: “I used to count on anger as a false sense of energy. Anger gives you energy,” he said. But age and success and a lasting marriage have tempered all that: “I have really found much more joy and peace with Catherine all these years we’ve been together and less involved in the business.”

He’s dismayed about the state of the world — our fractured politics, our sense of disconnection from the public good that was an organizing principle for him in the ’60s, even as a child of privilege.

“This is the most difficult time I can remember in my lifetime,” Douglas said, sounding more like a worried grandfather than a guy who used to party with Jack Nicholson and Jann Wenner. “I’m an optimist and I really try to be hopeful, but I’m deeply scared.”

He mentioned the Jewish concept of tikkun olam, or “repairing the world.”

He said: “Something’s got to give. There’s too much focus on money.”

Many years ago, Douglas was asked to consider a run for California governor — he’s played several politicians onscreen, including the president — but he declined.

“In terms of skeletons in the closet,” he said, “particularly the drug areas going back 20 years, it probably was not a good idea.”

Nevertheless, Douglas has strong opinions: “We should be taking a fraction of these military budgets and using them for positive good. Trying to bring back the Peace Corps. Trying to improve inequality in terms of affordability and education.”

Then he seemed to catch himself.

“I love this country,” Douglas said. “I feel very patriotic. But we’ve got to wake up. We just have to wake up. This is not good. And I guess I’m speaking like a cancer survivor. But beautiful weather anyway, huh?”

ARTICLE

‘Digger,’ Warner Bros.’ Last Release Before Merger, Is a Major Flop
The film, starring Tom Cruise, grossed an estimated $8 million in its opening weekend. That could put the movie on track to lose at least $125 million.
By Nicole Sperling
Published 2026-10-03 21:22 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/business/media/digger-tom-cruise-box-office.html

On paper, it all sounded great. The superstar Tom Cruise meets the auteur Alejandro G. Iñárritu and together they construct a satire lampooning the power-hungry billionaire class. Warner Bros., the filmmaker-friendly studio under the guidance of Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca, believe in Mr. Iñárritu, who had made two very different films, “Birdman” and “The Revenant,” into back-to-back best picture nominees.

But that was over a decade ago.

Whether audiences were rejecting the idea of their never-aging action star Mr. Cruise in a quirky dramatic role playing a gray-haired older man or they were following the dismal reviews of the film, “Digger” is on track in its opening weekend to be a resounding flop. Audiences gave the film a C, according to the marketing research company CinemaScore.

Opening in over 3,000 locations, the R-rated movie grossed an estimated $8 million for the weekend. The studio has said the film cost $125 million but others put the total closer to $150 million because of a delay in production after a cast member, John Goodman, fell on the set and had to recover before shooting could continue. With nearly $100 million more spent on marketing — Mr. Cruise only flies private — the studio could lose $125 million to $150 million in total, making it one of the biggest flops of the year.

It is an extraordinary capper for a year that has been marred by misfires. None of Warner Bros.’ 2026 films has grossed more than $100 million, and “Supergirl” and “The Bride” both produced big losses for the studio.

Now, “Digger” will be the final movie Warner Bros. will release as a stand-alone studio before it is scooped up by Paramount. (The deal is set to close on Tuesday.) That is quite a different fate from a year ago, when the studio was riding high on its box office successes with “Sinners” and “Weapons” and its big Oscar winner, “One Battle After Another.”

Warner Bros. executives declined to comment on the film’s performance but industry watchers are calling it the end of an era.

“This was an eccentric story, and WB deserves credit for taking the risk,” said David A. Gross, a film consultant who publishes a newsletter on box office numbers. “But ‘Digger’ is not working, and Paramount, headed by David Ellison, Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, will soon decide what kind of movies they want from WB. Paramount does not have a recent history of making big, auteur-driven films like this.”

In contrast, Amazon MGM released “Verity,” the fourth adaptation of a Colleen Hoover novel in the past two years, to an estimated $33 million. That put the psychological thriller in first place for the weekend and in the middle of the four adaptations, based on gross.

Directed by Michael Showalter, “Verity” received weak reviews, though it was not the worst reviewed of the four Hoover projects. That title belongs to “Regretting You,” from October 2025. It’s also not the best performing one either. That was “It Ends with Us,” which earned $351 million worldwide. “Verity” will still be a sizable hit for the streamer. Earning an additional estimated $30 million overseas, on a production budget of $40 million, it doesn’t have to do much more to become profitable.

The movie was also Anne Hathaway’s fifth theatrical movie of the year, and with “Verity” hitting No. 1, it will mark the actress’s third first-place finisher this year. Ms Hathaway, who is also a producer on the film, plays Verity Crawford, a famous novelist who has been left in a catatonic state after a car accident. Dakota Johnson plays the struggling writer brought in to finish the novel Verity has left but all does not appear as it seems.

The film has been embraced by audiences, primarily women, who turned the novel into a best seller.

Chris Rock Has Been Thinking About Forgiveness
The comedian and filmmaker on what real friendship looks like, what keeps him up at night and his new movie, “Misty Green.”
By David Marchese
