Chris Rock is inarguably one of the greatest stand-up comedians of all time. From specials like his 1996 breakout, “Bring the Pain,” to his most recent, “Selective Outrage” in 2023, he has established himself as not only scabrously funny but also fearless and insightful when tackling race, politics, relationships — you name it. Rock’s movie career, though, has been more variable. He’s been in plenty of hits, often alongside his friend Adam Sandler (two “Grown Ups” films; 2005’s “The Longest Yard”). And I’d point to the cult-classic hip-hop satire “CB4” (1993) as well as “Top Five” (2014), about a superstar comedian at a career crossroads, as film work that ably translated Rock’s intelligence and wit to the big screen. But there hasn’t quite been a cinematic statement on par with his stand-up. Until now. “Misty Green,” which opens Oct. 9, is an indisputable leap forward.

The film, the fourth that Rock has written, directed and acted in, is about a midcareer Hollywood actress named Misty, played in a riveting performance by Rosalind Eleazar (best known for the Apple TV show “Slow Horses”). Misty is at a moment of peak personal and professional crisis, and her story allows Rock to examine serious questions about social inequality, getting older in show business and compromise. I wanted to ask him about those subjects as well as his thoughts on comedy today, forgiveness and what his future holds.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

One of the themes of “Misty Green” is status: who has it and who loses it when it comes to success, money, relationships. I want to know: When do you feel insecure about your status? I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the last few years, post-Covid, and a lot of it is about not feeling insecure. A lot of it is about “you’re enough.” But I don’t ever really feel insecure about my “status,” per se. Occasionally I’ll meet people that are obviously working harder than me and that’ll make me feel insecure. Adam Sandler, Rick Rubin. You’re like, “How many things are you doing right now?” And some people are better with their kids than me. I think I’m a good dad.

You kept them off the pole. I kept them off the pole, but they’re on OnlyFans!

The movie makes Hollywood very appealing, because of the talent there and the love that people have for doing what they do, but it also makes Hollywood seem awful: racist, sexist, chipping away at your soul. Has that been your experience? You’re not going to get a “how bad Hollywood is” soliloquy from me. I always say every generation laughs at their children’s racism. So my kids are like, “This is racist,” and I’m like [Rolls eyes]. And what I would call racist, my mother would laugh at. Are there bad parts about Hollywood? Yes. But it’s still better than a normal job by a ton. I used to work at Red Lobster. I used to work at a home for severely autistic adults. I had the night shift, and sometimes you had to change the diaper of a grown man. So what if I can’t get a sketch on? So what if somebody doesn’t respond to my script? I used to wipe people’s asses!

But the question of compromises comes up throughout the film. There’s compromises in everything, man.

So what are the compromises that you’ve had to make in your career? I came up in cable television. I could say what I wanted. Honestly I don’t know if I could do “Bring the Pain” today. I’d have to compromise. But in ’96, I did pretty much whatever I wanted. Dude, I made “Pootie Tang.” I did a documentary about hair. So I’m the last guy to complain.

A second ago you said you didn’t know if you’d be able to make “Bring the Pain” today. That’s a sentiment I see a lot: comedians saying, “I don’t know if I’d be able to make that today.” But do you really think that’s true? You’re right. I’d be able to make it. As a matter of fact, I’ll go even further, “Bring the Pain” would be bigger today. You know why? Because you wouldn’t be able to report on it. The New York Times wouldn’t be able to say it was great. It wouldn’t be on Netflix. It would be like the Shane Gillis thing, which would actually elevate it. You know, The New York Times has got a weird thing with comedy.

What’s the weird thing? The Times, The Journal — they ignore the nuance. So it’s like, This is the manosphere-conservative thing, or, This is the wokey-woke thing. And all the people in the middle they kind of ignore. I remember five, 10 years ago, Bill Burr sold out Madison Square Garden. At that point, maybe eight comedians had sold out Madison Square Garden. I wake up the next day and I want to read the review. There’s no review, because Bill Burr is this guy that walks a crazy line. Is he conservative? Maybe. Wait a minute, he’s got a Black wife. Oh, he’s sexist. Wait a minute, there’s a lot of women here. You guys are not [expletive] with that middle. So anyway, “Bring the Pain” would be bigger today because it would be less lauded.

I think something has happened in comedy since Trump was first elected, where it seems like comedians feel as if they have to subtly or overtly signal their politics. Audiences are looking for that, and comedians are giving it to them. Maybe. I mean, I’m trying to decide if I’m gonna go back out now. Do I want to?

Why wouldn’t you? Do I want to jump in this bed? I don’t know. I am loving directing. Maybe I should do a run of pictures.

I have a question about Rosalind Eleazar and “Misty Green.” What did she bring to the part that wasn’t in the script initially? When I’m directing, I say, “It’s my movie, it’s your part.” And it was hers, man. Put it this way: I only met Rosalind about a month ago. For the months we were shooting, there was only Misty. She was Misty in the audition. She was Misty through the whole filming process. She never asked me one question that didn’t have to do with the character.

There’s a scene in the film where her character performs at a nightclub, and we see that she’s also an incredible singer. When I saw that, I was thinking about the amount of talent that’s out there — even people who are not household names. It’s staggering. Do you understand who makes it and who doesn’t? Talent must have so little to do with it. There’s a lot that goes into it. Right place, right time. What kind of friend are you? That goes a long, long way. Even now if I look over my career, probably half of my gigs are just somebody going, “Oh, he’s cool.” You have to be considerate. You have to ask people how they’re doing. A lot of artists, we’re so self-centered. So to answer your question, yes, there’s a lot of talent out there, and a lot is just right time, right place. Sometimes you’re on the subway and you see a guy playing the violin, and you’re like, They should be at the Met. Like, what the [expletive]?

Who’s someone you’ve worked with that you thought was incredibly talented, but they were self-destructive or they just never got a break? Ooh, I can’t say that. I wish I could. I’d say that off-camera. There’s a bunch of people. That self-destructive thing is a really sad thing. A self-destructive person is basically a person that makes six bad decisions a year. That’s 359 days of being fine. But those six bad decisions a year will [expletive] up your whole life.

How many bad decisions a year do you make? I don’t know. Show business is like the Olympics. And in the Olympics, the difference between first and last can be less than a second sometimes.

I want to ask another question about the movie. Were there ideas that you’d had about men and women that you then had to examine in order to credibly create the character of Misty? Because in a lot of your comedy, you make distinctions between men and women, but the distinctions are coming from the male point of view, and “Misty Green” is so much about a woman’s story. Did it take any excavation to be able to do what you wanted to do with her character? Saying there are stark differences between men and women is a perfect device for comedy. It doesn’t work in a drama. I’ll say this: Part of all this therapy is developing empathy and really being able to get inside of another character. So the last four or five years, I’m a way more empathetic person. It also helps that my daughters are like grown-ups, so I really watch women around my house. My daughters don’t forgive my sins, but they give me an education that I wouldn’t normally have.

I want to go back to directing. It was 12 years between you directing “Top Five” and “Misty Green.” What took so long? Life, Covid, I got divorced, which meant I had to make real money. Maybe I had some other scripts that the market didn’t respond to. It’s not like I was sitting around. But Covid was a time to be like, OK, what am I doing with my life? And other [expletive] I don’t feel like talking about. I had a lot of stuff going on the last 12 years.

Did you come up with answers to “What should I be doing with my life?” I should be directing small movies, character-driven pieces. Maybe I’m not in the movie as much as I used to be. So I’ve been writing a lot more. I’m actually working on a book of essays. We’ll see where that goes.

Could we talk about those things you don’t feel like talking about? I mean, I’m a big boy. I can answer stuff coolly, or not answer. Whatever. What do you want to know?

Is there more to say about the slap than what you said in your last special? I’m good, man. That was so long ago.

Not that long ago. I wish everyone well. I’ve moved on with my life.

Do you forgive what happened? I’m not going to get into clickbait things. I don’t think I’m in a beef. I’m done, dude. I’m done.

Let’s return to the movie. I was slightly surprised to hear that you don’t have anything that bad to say about Hollywood, given the content of the film, which to me was about how hard and hurtful to an artist’s soul Hollywood can be. So what were the themes that you were interested in exploring in “Misty Green?” I’m really into expiration dates. Everybody tells you that you can do art forever, and that’s just not true. In show business, you’ve got to reach certain plateaus by a certain time or else you’re going to be in trouble. So Misty is turning 40, and it’s a little bit of an expiration date happening. But, yeah, I wanted to do a movie about Hollywood. I wanted to do a movie about L.A. It’s this tale of two cities. Sunshine and palm trees, but we’re constantly walking over homeless people — the most liberal people in the world. Rodeo Drive and Skid Row are in the same city, probably eight, 10 miles apart. In a lot of ways, America’s like that: very rich, very poor. We live in a world where either you order [expletive] or you deliver [expletive], and you really don’t want to deliver [expletive], you know?

What should your response to that disparity be? So, the running title of the book that I’m writing right now is “When the Homeless Know Your Name.” Because when the homeless know your name, you feel that. Somebody asks you for money on the street, they just ask you for the money. When they ask me, they say, “Yo, Chris!” I don’t know what I should do. First of all, who the hell carries cash anymore? You give what you can.

I want to dig into that feeling a bit more. When the homeless know your name, what do you feel? Put it this way: I get up around 7. I get coffee by about 7:15. I go to my supermarket, get some fruit, and inevitably there’s always a bunch of guys setting up for the day. Did you ever see “12 Years a Slave” or any slave movie with a free slave? The slaves look at Chiwetel [Ejiofor]. He’s dressed all cool and he got his hat and they’re just looking at him like: “How the [expletive] did this happen? We’re the same.” That’s me at the supermarket in the morning. They’re looking at me, not even as a famous person, just like, “Who’s this brother buying mango at 7:25 in the morning?” Because there are no Black dudes living in SoHo. Am I answering your question?

Yeah. You’ve seen behind the veil. Yeah, and it’s like, they’re looking at me, and I’m looking at them, because I know I could be that. I know if I don’t walk into a comedy club in ’84 or ’83, I’d probably have a normal job. I’d have a lovely life, by the way. I’m not one of these guys who thinks that if I didn’t find comedy, I’d be in jail. No, I’d work for Amazon and I’d have a wife and some kids and I’d be OK. I’d be the funny guy on the Amazon route.

It’s interesting that you’re writing a book because I remember, before the pandemic, there was an announcement that you were working on a book about interracial relationships. What happened there? The book never showed up. I’m not trying to be like a gangster or anything. When you’re writing something about race, especially in this era of everybody taking everything out of context — I just didn’t feel like everything I was saying to the publisher, they were listening. I was like, I don’t trust these people. So I gave the money back.

How much was it that you gave back? It was a significant sum. More than I’m making today.

I’ll make a check out to you later. Do you think that taking things out of context is an ongoing problem for artists and comedians? There’s so much discussion about whether somebody said something offensive or who’s allowed to say what, and I never know how real that is. I hate to say, it’s just B.S. It’s just nerd bullies. Do you know how easy it is to go, “What did you mean by that?” before you elect to be angry at something? It is so easy to ask somebody: “Hey, man, could you not say that thing? I just felt a certain way when you said that.” Then if you’re ignored, yes, reply with anger. But it is so easy to pause and just go, “Hey, what did you mean?” I don’t know who I was having this argument with, but they said, “People are so sensitive.” I’m like: “No, they’re not sensitive. They’re mean. And they can’t stop being mean.”

You think it’s all about meanness? I’m just saying, meanness is the new kale. It’s on the platter, OK? It’s like, “Oh, do you got any mean here?”

When is offense justified? People are entitled to their feelings. Don’t get me wrong. We’re all entitled to be offended. Don’t take me out of context. Context does matter, though. A lot of people are ignoring context because it prevents them from being mean.

This morning when you came in, you said, “I don’t think I’ve been here since I filmed ‘Top Five’ with the canceled all-stars, Scott Rudin and Charlie Rose.” And I listened to a podcast interview you did with David Spade and Dana Carvey earlier this year, and you also used the phrase “the canceled all-stars” to talk about Louis C.K. and Kanye. How do you think about questions of forgiveness and who gets forgiven and why? Hey, man, I’m Black. When you’re Black, white people believe every accusation is a conviction. I grew up at 619 Decatur Street, between Howard and Saratoga. A guy named Roger Logan, who I grew up with and was one of my best friends’ brothers, went to jail for years for a murder he didn’t commit. And here’s the weird thing: His brother used to plead with me to pay for a lawyer for Roger, and I never did it. I always had a no-lawyer thing. I’ll pay your mortgage; there’s a bunch I’ve paid for — education and all sorts of [expletive]. I always stay out of lawyers because it’s so open-ended. And it still [expletives] with me. I had the means to help him and I didn’t. I don’t know if we could’ve got him out or not, but still. So all that to say, Black men get accused of [expletive] they didn’t do all the time, every day. We let Black men out of jail and go: “Whoops! That Black guy just did 30 years — too bad.” So to answer your question, hopefully I don’t get accused of anything, but it’s real when people get accused of things, and you better be real sure they did it. Am I making sense?

You’re making sense. I think you’re describing a kind of lived empathy that —— I’ll go even further. My grandfather, Allen Rock, killed a man. Legend has it, he thought the guy was sleeping with my grandmother. The guy lived next door. He told the guy, “If you take another step in my yard, I’m going to shoot you.” The guy took one step and my grandfather blew him away. My grandfather went to jail. He was a preacher. He gets out of jail on a Wednesday, and by Friday he was picking us up from school. Within a year or two, he was the reverend of that church again. My brother Charles shot a guy. I say all that to say, my grandfather went to jail. He did his time. So a) if you’re going to accuse somebody, make sure they did it. And b) when people do things, there’s a time limit in the real world. In your world, you just shun people. But in the real world, we have to live with each other. It’s up to the victims to forgive, and two things can be true: My brother shot a guy. I love my brother. Because I love my brother, does that mean I think the person should have gotten shot? No. The last thing I’ll say: When I was a kid, I was in police lineups two, three times. Stay away from Howard Avenue. Howard and Decatur.

In Bed-Stuy? In Bed-Stuy, and you’re minding your business and you get swooped up. And now you’re in a police lineup. And you’ve seen enough cop movies to know that behind that window is a person — could be a man, but probably a woman — and if she points at you, your whole life’s over. If she points at me, she’s wrong, but she’s not lying. She’s traumatized, and when you’re traumatized you try to wrap [expletive] up. My dad drove a newspaper truck, and I’ve been reading the paper since I was a kid. The news has taken all the nuance out of it. Everything’s black and white.

I want to go back to what you said about becoming a more empathetic person. How does one consciously learn to be more empathetic? And is being more empathetic good for a comedian? It better be, or I’m in trouble. I don’t know if I’ve learned to be empathetic. A friend of mine told me I had Asperger’s a few years back, and I got it checked out. It wasn’t Asperger’s, but it was a thing called NVLD, nonverbal learning disorder. It requires its own level of therapy.

What are the effects of that? The effects are that I’m really bad at reading nonverbal signals. I catastrophize, I have black-and-white thinking — both things that are great for being a comedian but bad in personal life and real relationships. So I’ve been learning. I have to see a woman once a week. “Misty Green” would be the first piece of art that I’ve done since my diagnosis.

You said earlier that part of what you were talking about in therapy is feeling like you’re “enough.” When do you have self-esteem questions? All artists have self-esteem questions, especially the good ones. An artist is an egomaniac with an inferiority complex. I would absolutely fall into that. “I am great. I hope they notice.” So, yeah, I can feel that way. Eddie Murphy makes me feel like that. In the presence of Eddie Murphy, I can get a little insecure.

Of course. Also, not to name-drop, but one of my biggest regrets in life is I could never relax around Prince. He wanted to be friends. Hanging out, I couldn’t not be like, “Oh [expletive], Prince is drinking ice tea!”

Did you and he ever get to a place where he was normal? I mean, a normal rock star. Those degrees of normal are so different than yours. I remember, I was at Prince’s house. I’m in Minneapolis. I’d just done some shows, and he had a party for me at Paisley Park. I am literally in the vault, and he’s playing me new music, and there’s lots of people there, and his wife called. I think he was married to Mayte at the time. And he was like: “Everybody be quiet! Be quiet!” It’s like 200 people. Mayte called, he’s picking up the phone, and he goes: “Hey. Nothing. Nah, I’m just chillin’. Yeah, I’ll probably go to bed in a couple of hours. Love you, too.” And then the party started again. [Sings] “Gett Off”! Right away!

Even Prince has to take that call. Even Prince had the check-in.

You said that you want to direct more films, but you also talked about the idea of an expiration date, and it can be hard for comedians to get older. It can definitely be hard for comedians to get older.

It’s hard to stay edgy. Well, nobody stays edgy. You become the establishment. Early in your career, it’s your performance, but it’s also the promise of who you are. So the public is investing in this thing, this stock. But later on you’re like LeBron. It’s all results and we’ll give you a one-year deal — as long as you play like LeBron. I mean, I’ve seen careers and people change. Steve Martin’s the king of reinvention.

If you listen to a Steve Martin album, because of the style of comedy he’s doing — absurdist and whimsical — you’re never asking yourself, Does he really believe that? But now audiences are asking, Does the comedian believe what they’re saying? So when you’re telling jokes about real-life things, are we supposed to understand that you believe what you’re saying, or that you’re just saying what you need to say to make the bit work? Jokes tend to work better when there’s some truth in them, when you’re not just making up stuff. I think the audience can tell who’s fake. They can tell if you’re married, they can tell if you’ve got kids, they can tell if you worked. You can’t fake anything. The thing about comedians is, there’s no mystique. There’s no Ziggy Stardust of comedians. You are who you are, and they’re rolling with you or not.

Do you think you are who you are in your film work? I think “Misty” is a good barometer of me right now. I’m like every character in the movie on some level.

Hopefully not the Adam Driver character, a guy who procures prostitutes for Saudi princes. There is nothing different between the Adam Driver character in my movie and the Jack Lemmon character in “The Apartment.” It’s just an outfit and some hairstyle.

And the drugs. Alcohol is the biggest drug in the world. What are you talking about? See, you are leaving out your nuance. You literally are making my point in front of me. You conveniently made yourself stupid to make a point.

I never conveniently make myself stupid. You’re so much smarter than that!

If people are like, David left out the nuance of what drug Jack Lemmon was using in “The Apartment”! — I’ll die on that hill. It hurt you that Jack Lemmon was basically the same character. And you have this love for “The Apartment,” which is deserved. It’s one of the best movies ever. But that’s what he was. He was a pimp.

I guess you’re right. I don’t know where to go from that. Jack Lemmon is a pimp. In “The Apartment” he’s a lovable pimp, but a pimp nonetheless.

In so many ways, we all are. Or hoes! Mostly hoes.

You know, before we spoke initially, I had asked if you could send over the names of some films that were influential on “Misty Green.” You sent a list that included Bob Fosse’s “Cabaret,” “Bad Lieutenant,” “Klute.” Can you tell me how they helped shape your vision for your movie? There’s a great line in “Husbands and Wives,” the Woody Allen film. He’s playing a professor, and the line is something to do with, You can’t teach people to write; all you can do is expose them to great writing and hope they pick up on it. It’s kind of the same thing with film. You can’t teach a person really to make a good movie. You just gotta show them some good movies and hope that they run with it. All of those movies, especially the Fosse stuff — there’s a lot of “Lenny” in “Misty Green.” I love those movies. My mother would always say, “If you feed a kid long enough, he starts to look like you.” If you love movies hard enough, you’ll eventually make that kind of movie.

Wait, did Fosse also direct “Star 80”? Yeah! “Star 80” is my go-to. How could I forget “Star 80”? “Misty Green” is so “Star 80.” The Fosse stuff more than anything has been an influence.

There’s a line in your movie that I wanted to ask about. The character that you play in the film says to Misty, “True love starts at forgiveness.” Is that your experience of forgiveness? Yeah. You don’t really realize if you love somebody until you have to forgive them. I can enjoy myself with just about anybody. It’s when somebody tests you, when somebody betrays you, when somebody lets you down and you still want to be around them — that’s love. I have a friend that’s going to be nameless that might have gotten canceled. Another friend of mine was like, “How can you be friends with that person?” I was like, “If you’re only friends with your friends when they’re good, they’re not your friends.” If you’ve got a bunch of people that are only going to be there when you’re good, you have no friends. That doesn’t mean condoning abusive behavior; you can reprimand your friends. That’s also part of friendship.

But we all have a line, right? You and I live in different worlds. I’ve got friends that are in jail. I’ve got friends that are drugged out. I don’t live like you.

You don’t know that. I can tell.

I mean, you happen to be right. And by the way, I’m not being dismissive of you. I’m just saying that my friends have tested me more than yours, and maybe I’ve tested them. I’m not religious, but I’m a Christian, and God forgives. That’s what it’s all about. The problem with quote, unquote, wokeness — and don’t get me wrong, it is great that marginalized people have a voice; it is great to advocate for anybody that feels marginalized — but the problem is we’re in the Old Testament right now, and the Old Testament has no forgiveness. The Old Testament didn’t work, so they had to write a remix called the New Testament.

There’s been discussion lately about how the Woke 1.0 era, which refers to the immediate post-George Floyd era, was “crazy.” Do you see that moment in time as just “crazy?” Was there anything redeeming about it? I think I just answered. Again, it’s great to help those that need help. We need more of that. The problem is when you institutionalize it. My half a joke: The Salem witch hunts — I’m sure the first three witches they caught were actually witches. But then you open up a witch office, and now you gotta start lying because you got overhead. You gotta justify the witch hunters’ pensions and [expletive]. I’m glad that all of this stuff happened, it needed to happen, and because it happened, maybe I’ve heard some voices that I probably wouldn’t have heard otherwise.

Let me switch gears and ask a comedy question. Sure — but before you do, because I keep saying how bad my friends are: I have some genius friends who are unproblematic, the most progressive. Some of the greatest artists that have ever lived, some that you know of and some that you don’t, are my friends.

All right, so on the record: Chris Rock’s friends are perfectly fine people. One thing I always wanted to ask a great comedian is, Do you understand what the purpose of laughter is? Why do we laugh? I never thought about it that hard. Here’s what I do know: The greatest feelings in life are sex and laughter. We break up with people that we have great sex with all the time. We don’t break up with anybody that makes us laugh. And the ability to laugh at oneself is probably the highest form of intelligence. The inability to laugh at oneself is a sure sign you’re dealing with an idiot.

Chris, professionally or personally, what keeps you up at night? I don’t worry about anything.

Everyone worries about something. I’m not worried about nothing, dude. I’m worried about my kids, but the world? The world is the world. The world is exactly what it wants to be. It’s sad where it’s sad, it’s happy where it’s happy. But this is what people want.

What do you mean “this is what people want”? People have the America they want. If they want to change it, we’ll see.

Is it the America you want? I’ve been here a while. I have a long sample size. Martin Luther King was shot in 1968. Black people pretty much live where Black people lived in 1968, especially in New York City. Maybe a neighborhood or two is gentrified that wasn’t. Maybe Beyoncé has more points on her deal than Aretha Franklin did. People are nicer. Blatant disrespect in the streets doesn’t happen like it did in 1968. But the distribution of wealth, the access to education, the access to health care is pretty much where it was when Dr. King got shot. And I could say that about other places in the world, too. Somehow I got out of it. But Louis Armstrong was the most famous singer in the world in the ’30s and ’40s, so Black entertainers have always gotten off the Titanic before everybody else.

Let me try to end with something more hopeful. Hey, “Misty Green!” Oct. 9! Sexy movie! A24! Those guys are great. No oppression there.

I asked what keeps you up at night. But what gets you up in the morning? You know what’s weird? I’m excited every morning. It’s my favorite time to get up and take my walk and get my fruit, listen to the news a little bit. ’Cause every day can be great. Even when you know what’s going to happen, you don’t know what’s going to happen. So I wake up pretty happy, man. And I’m very fortunate. I’m not going to sit here and act like my experience is everybody’s.

I appreciate you taking the time to speak with me. I especially enjoyed it when you pushed back. Oh, man, that’s always where the good stuff is. I’ll leave you with this: A friend of mine called me up, she was working on her special, and she said, “I’ve had a hard time writing material.” I said: “Well, you have this podcast. What I need you to do is go to your podcast, and every hard episode, that is where the material is. Every one you thought was a hard time, that’s where the good [expletive] is.” So if I’ve given you a hard time, this is the good [expletive].

This interview has been edited and condensed from two conversations. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

ARTICLE

The Luxury of Looking a Mess
You live long enough and the music and the clothes of your youth get repackaged and sold back to you. But skinny jeans and white belts? Really?
By Lizzy Goodman
Published 2026-10-03 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/opinion/culture/the-luxury-of-looking-a-mess.html

I’ve been obsessing over this year’s return to relevance of a fashion brand that I wore 20 years ago: 7 for All Mankind. It’s once again selling the low-rise jeans that made it famous, now alongside the rest of the 2006 uniform: hip-hugger belts, tiny jackets with princess shoulders and giant, comically impractical platform heels. In a runway show during New York Fashion Week last month, it doubled down on hyping a self-consciously 2006 tousled party girl.

These deliberately messy clothes feel deeply familiar to me. I wore them all the first time around. My friends and I mixed vintage with repurposed clothing: shrunken leather jackets off the racks at Buffalo Exchange, plus a skinny scarf stolen from rail-thin rock boys who bought their jeans from the Gap’s girls department. So it’s been equal parts hilarious and destabilizing to watch the look of my early 20s reappear, to rapturous praise, on the Instagram feeds of very stylish friends who are actually in their early 20s.

I understand this is an established-to-the-point-of-cliché pattern. Isn’t there some adage about living long enough to see the music and the clothes of your youth repackaged and sold back to you? Fine. But skinny jeans and white belts? Really?

In an era when even teenagers are plumping, smoothing, nipping and tucking their way into uniformity, it suddenly feels luxurious to look undone, to be able to afford that kind of recklessness, sartorially and emotionally. Quiet luxury, the dominant fashion philosophy of the past few years, was never about restraint so much as erasure: the expensive, exhausting work of looking as if you have no visible seams, no history, no night before.

When I was 22 and living on the Lower East Side, my roommate, Sarah, and I scoured Rainbow on Canal Street for Day-Glo clothes in fabrics that felt (and probably were) flammable. We wore them with thrifted ’50s lingerie and vintage rock T-shirts Sarah cut apart and safety-pinned back together, dressing from an ever-shifting pile of shared clothes on the floor, then painting our lips with drugstore Wet n Wild red lipstick.

Nobody wanted to look bad, obviously. We were as vain and as preening as any other set of young people. But it was possible to look terrible and still be cool. Joe Strummer famously said about punk that “if you were ugly, you were in.” Karen O once put it this way: “Every photo you’d see would be basically the most unattractive, ugly moment of every show, but it’s pretty awesome that that’s what they wanted to showcase. The real. The gritty, visceral — bleh — real.” Beauty had value in the early 2000s, as it always does and always will. It just wasn’t the only currency. And more to the point, it would have seemed gauche to have beauty and not spend it: not live in it, not see how far it could get you.

Is that what is missing today? We live in an era of mass market Botox and filler (and now on-demand GLP-1s) and wellness coaches and self-improvement book clubs and ketamine shamans, and all the other self-management products that are meant to fix our faces, bodies and souls are merely the market responding to our need to curate ourselves, 24/7, for life online. In the end, what are we really getting out of that? Where is the carnal payoff?

When I asked one of my 20-something friends why she loves 7 she sent me multiple screenshots of Ashton Kutcher in cargo shorts, part of a trove of Y2K inspiration she apparently keeps handy on her phone. Looking at these, I was reminded that the 2000s were not, by any reasonable measure, a great fashion era. Message T-shirts, trucker hats, asymmetrical striped dresses from Forever 21 that look like dish towels. So much of what we wore was so very bad. And yet, in those images she’d collected of the era’s celebrities, with their disheveled frosted-tip fashion sense, I could see an appealing idea of early 2000s life. It was an experience of youth that was messier, smaller, more D.I.Y., more insouciant and private — and that now feels mostly unavailable, even to people who are actually young.

Look again at my friend’s Y2K party pic collection and you’ll see people who were completely absorbed in the actual living of their actual lives — even the Olsen twins, even the C-listers with the bad self-tans that, in hindsight, my friend pointed out, just made everyone look young.

It’s appropriate that the 7 relaunch would be fronted by Chloë Sevigny, who at 51 remains the reigning archetype of the girl the brand is appealing to, and who has, for years, been lamenting the blandification of fashion and culture. Two years ago, asked where she would never want to live, Ms. Sevigny landed on Los Angeles, drolly rattling off a list of critiques that included the hard water and “monotonous” sunshine, before more thoughtfully describing the as a place that makes her feel “self-conscious” and “uncomfortable” because it’s so specifically constructed around the entertainment business. So many places feel like that now — virtually every street corner on every city block is just another anonymous stage for influencers with indistinguishable faces and bodies shooting indistinguishable content to sell products that will make us look more like them.

These new 7 clothes feel like an attempt to sell you a different option. Instead of looking like someone styled for a repressive fantasy of perfection, perhaps you might like to look like someone caught in the middle of her imperfect life. There’s a risk associated with this approach: that you’ll look bad, wear the wrong thing, say the wrong thing, be seen as unfinished. But for the cost of a moment of messiness, you can reclaim a little lived-in disorder. That may be why wearing a pair of cheap-looking but not actually cheap low-rise jeans can suddenly feel like a deliberate act of freedom.

Back in the day I owned a pair of 7s. They were probably the most expensive thing in my wardrobe then. Stiff, dusty blue with a little stretch — novel, at the time — something like a denim scuba suit, with a crease built permanently into the fade. They were great. They were ridiculous. They’ve been in storage for the last 20 years. This fall, they’re going back into rotation.

Lizzy Goodman, a contributing writer at The New York Times Magazine, is the author of “Meet Me in the Bathroom: Rebirth and Rock and Roll in New York City 2001-2011.”

ARTICLE

‘What Authoritarian Governments Do to Promote Their Leaders’
The president shows his contempt for us. Again.
By Jamelle Bouie
Published 2026-10-03 15:27 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/opinion/trump-ad-love-me-painter.html

Have you seen this?

It’s one in a slew of pro-Trump ads that has been airing since last Wednesday. Set to the song “Love Me” by the singer-songwriter JMSN, the roughly 30-second spot shows a rapid progression of pictures and video of President Trump, as he touts his accomplishments and denounces “communism, socialism and Marxism.” As it ends, you are informed that it was “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

Trump is deeply unpopular and running strange, propagandistic advertisements is not likely to change that fact. But the wisdom of the campaign notwithstanding, the real problem with this is more legal than political. It is against the law to use taxpayer dollars for propaganda and explicitly partisan purposes.

“This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, a Democrat, wrote on social media. “It is a Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it. It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns.”

In a news release, The White House wrote that the ad is a public service announcement, “a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad.” For his part, President Trump — who personally directed the chief of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, to use taxpayer funds for the ad campaign — says “these are ads for the country.” “I’m not promoting a candidate,” he added. “I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

But unlike a public service announcement, this ad — and others like it — aren’t promoting a government program or service. They exist to glorify President Trump: to love him, as the song suggests.

Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer who served under President George W. Bush, gave The Associated Press a blunt assessment of the advertising campaign. “You watch all three ads, they’re sheer propaganda,” he said, adding that “This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders.”

Compared with the money used to build the president’s ballroom, this is not an expensive campaign. So far, the White House has spent about $5.5 million of a $20 million contract to produce and promote its pro-Trump propaganda. But again, it is less the cost than the fact that the president is showing his deep contempt for a fundamental norm of American democracy: We don’t use government to glorify our political leaders, at least not while they’re alive.

If future Americans want to vote to memorialize or otherwise praise past leaders, that is up to them. But it is not the place of the president to issue propaganda on his behalf, with money taken from the public till.

It is not clear that Democrats have the appetite to impeach Trump for a third time. Even if they did, there is almost no chance that they would have the votes to convict and remove him from office. And yet, this is exactly the type of offense that demands a response from the legislature. A president that shows this much contempt for the republican character of the American system — who seeks, at every opportunity, to set himself up as a strongman over the entire nation — is a president who must be sanctioned by the people’s representatives.

There are any number of strategic reasons to do this as well. With both chambers of Congress, should they win them, Democrats could orchestrate a long investigation and drawn-out trial that consumes the administration and implicates key figures beyond the president. But to be honest, I care less about the politics here than I do the principle. If this propaganda campaign — among many other offenses — isn’t worthy of an article of impeachment, then nothing is.

It does not receive as much attention as Trump’s assault on American cities or his draconian program of deportations and removals, but the president and his administration have been waging an all-out war on Congress’s once-sacrosanct power of the purse.

Now Eating: Taverna Salad

We’re still getting good summer produce here in Virginia, and so I used a recent haul from the market to make this salad. It is a perfect accompaniment to a meal of grilled meat or fish. It also works on its own as a nice, light lunch. Be sure to use your best olive oil and red wine vinegar. And feel free to adjust the recipe to your liking. I prefer to make this, for instance, with feta cheese. I also go easy on the capers, or omit them entirely. Recipe comes from NYT Cooking.

Ingredients

- ⅓ cup plus 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
- 2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
- 1 teaspoon minced garlic (1 small clove)
- ½ teaspoon dried oregano
- Salt and pepper
- 3 medium tomatoes, cored, seeded and diced into ½-inch pieces (or 1 cup halved cherry tomatoes)
- 1 (15-ounce) can chickpeas, rinsed
- 1 orange or yellow bell pepper, halved, seeded and diced into ½-inch pieces
- ½ large English cucumber, halved, seeded and diced into ½-inch pieces
- ½ cup pitted Kalamata olives
- ¼ cup chopped fresh parsley
- ¼ cup minced red onion or shallot
- 2 tablespoons (drained) capers, coarsely chopped
- 2 scallions, thinly sliced
- 1 (6-inch) pita
- 1 (8-ounce) block halloumi cheese, patted dry and cut into ¾-inch-thick slices

Directions

In a small bowl, combine ⅓ cup olive oil with the vinegar, garlic and oregano. Whisk vigorously to combine then season to taste with salt and pepper.

In a large bowl, combine the tomatoes, chickpeas, bell pepper, cucumber, olives, parsley, red onion, capers and scallions. Pour the dressing over the salad and toss well.

Chop the pita into 1-inch pieces and place them in a small bowl. Drizzle with 1 tablespoon olive oil, sprinkle with salt and toss to coat. Heat an 8-inch skillet over medium. Add the pita pieces and cook, tossing often, until toasted and golden brown, about 5 minutes. Return to the small bowl to cool, reserving the skillet.

Place the halloumi slices on a small plate and drizzle with 1 tablespoon olive oil. Heat the same skillet over medium-high heat, and cook the halloumi until golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Transfer to a cutting board and cut the slices into bite-size cubes.

Add the pita and halloumi to the salad, toss well and serve.

SUMMARY

In early March, nine days after starting his war with Iran, President Trump held a news conference to crow about his “military success, the likes of which people haven’t seen.” Peter Navarro, a White House senior counselor, wrote an essay in March explaining why: “Iran War Will Lower Energy Prices.” Instead, Trump’s Iran war should be taught for decades as a model of how not to conduct either war or foreign policy.

ARTICLE

Why Iran Could Choose to Escalate the War
Threats to withdraw from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty are growing in Tehran.
By Nicholas Kristof
Published 2026-10-03 11:32 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/opinion/trump-empowers-iranian-extremists.html

In early March, nine days after starting his war with Iran, President Trump held a news conference to crow about his “military success, the likes of which people haven’t seen.”

“We’re winning very decisively,” he claimed, and “the result will be lower oil prices.”

Peter Navarro, a White House senior counselor, wrote an essay in March explaining why: “Iran War Will Lower Energy Prices.” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in April announced “a historic and overwhelming victory” that had rendered Iran “combat-ineffective for years to come.”

Instead, Trump’s Iran war should be taught for decades as a model of how not to conduct either war or foreign policy. It’s an example of how hubris can swamp a presidency and lead it to military solutions for difficult global problems — and, in the process, make everything worse.

Now Trump finds himself stuck in the Sartre play “No Exit.”

“The unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over,” Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group writes in a Foreign Affairs essay titled “The New Forever War.”

Still, the Trumpian myopia persists, with the administration continuing to claim that its pressure on Iran is a smashing success. “The blockade is working; it’s working like nothing we’ve ever seen,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News in September.

Hmm. Diesel prices at a few places in California have hit $9.99 a gallon, the maximum price those pumps can display. The United States has already spent more than $43 billion on the war, by a lowball Pentagon estimate — more than enough to provide free college education for a year to every American family earning less than $125,000 annually. Higher prices caused by the war have cost the typical American family about $1,000, according to the economist Mark Zandi. More broadly, we’ve depleted our arsenal, cost American and Iranian lives, possibly committed war crimes, exposed American vulnerabilities, effectively lost access to some bases and weakened American military credibility as far away as East Asia.

Against that, the Trump administration believes it has the upper hand because of the economic pressure the blockade is creating for Iran.

Well, maybe. It’s true that the Iranian economy is a catastrophe and that ordinary Iranians — the people we are supposed to be helping — are suffering greatly. The exchange rate is now more than 2.5 million rials to the dollar, one-tenth of the rial’s value in 2021.

Yet Washington doesn’t seem to understand that instead of surrendering, Iran may choose to escalate. “They’ve come to the conclusion that the only way they survive is to shoot their way out,” Vali Nasr, an Iran expert at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, told me. He suggested that Iran could increase attacks on shipping and, especially if it is attacked, strike oil infrastructure around the Gulf.

I fear that Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, an Iran watcher at a British think tank, is right when he says: “Iran did not wage a scorched earth campaign — but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long. That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.”

It’s difficult to see a deal being reached, partly because both Trump and Iran have a history of overreaching. It doesn’t help that Trump’s chief negotiators, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are real estate investors chosen for their closeness to Trump rather than for, er, their diplomatic savvy.

Iranian leaders also seem cocky. Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, boasted in August that Iran had brought the United States “to its knees.” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told “Meet the Press” that Iran was fully prepared for a new round of fighting, “even if it comes to a doomsday war.”

One rare issue on which I agree with Trump is the paramount importance of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. In Trump’s speech to the United Nations — the one in which he mused about whether he should “annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly” — he insisted that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

That’s easy to say. But Trump’s war may have actually increased the likelihood of Iran’s making a drive toward a nuclear weapon.

Trump’s war began by killing the previous supreme leader, who had issued a fatwa saying that Iran would not develop nuclear weapons. The new supreme leader, his son, does not inherit that fatwa and has not issued his own, so now “there’s a serious conversation in Iran” about pursuing nuclear weapons, Nasr told me.

A new measure before the Iranian Parliament proposes withdrawing from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, and 32 Iranian figures have called on the country to do so. That would be a cataclysm.

“Any other country but Iran would have pulled out of the N.P.T. if treated the same way,” Araghchi told reporters.

We should take these warnings seriously.

One reason professors will teach Trump’s war as an example of military malpractice is that it fits neatly into a larger pattern of counterproductive American policies toward Iran. I deplore the brutality, corruption and economic incompetence of Iran’s rulers — so it’s infuriating that America has repeatedly empowered Iranian extremists.

First, the United States helped topple a democratically elected prime minister in 1953, energizing nationalists and souring Iranians on the West. Then in the 1960s and 70s, the United States gave Iran a nuclear reactor, backed an increasingly autocratic shah and overstepped in ways that helped allow Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to become a national force by denouncing American imperialism.

President George W. Bush’s 2003 Iraq war toppled Saddam Hussein, an enemy of Iran, and empowered Shiite militias that support Iran. In 2018, President Trump announced his withdrawal from the Obama nuclear pact with Iran. The capstone in this “march of folly,” to borrow a phrase from the historian Barbara Tuchman, was Trump’s war on Iran this year, which has bolstered military hard-liners in Tehran and enabled them to project greater power over the Persian Gulf and global oil markets.

That’s what I find particularly worth studying: How is it that for three-quarters of a century, we Americans have so bungled our foreign policy that we have systematically empowered Iranian extremists? They call us the “Great Satan,” but in truth our ineptitude has made us their benefactors.

ARTICLE

Mamdani’s Surprisingly Persuasive Solution to a World on Fire
The New York City mayor has an antidote to globe-spanning distemper.
By Lydia Polgreen
Published 2026-10-03 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/opinion/zohran-mamdani-united-nations.html

A few days before the leaders of the world streamed into the cavernous, marble-lined General Assembly Hall to deliver their speeches on the grave crises convulsing our combustible world, Mayor Zohran Mamdani offered his own, somewhat surprising solution to the problem of rising authoritarianism: filling potholes.

“If politics cannot deliver on the block where you live, why would you trust it to deliver anywhere?” Mamdani asked a gathering of mayors from big cities across the world, explaining his obsession with potholes, more than 200,000 of which have been filled across the city since he took office. “If you are making a New Yorker’s life a little smoother, so too you are making their journey to believe in government’s ability to deliver for them.”

It is commonplace to lament the ineffectual talking shop that the United Nations General Assembly has become, with its blustering speeches and endless unread communiqués. Wars of aggression are raging in Ukraine and Iran; Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza; climate catastrophes impoverish and kill. In the face of these calamities, the organization appears powerless.

Today, the body’s soaring aims — to create a more peaceful, humane world that respects the sovereignty of each nation and the dignity of each human being — seem like a fantasy from another dimension. Citizens the world over are dissatisfied with their governments and in many places are souring on democracy itself. Can it be any surprise that this supranational body comes in for such contempt?

And yet Mamdani sensed an opportunity to reclaim some of its founding spirit. Racing across the city last week, he seemed to be offering an antidote to globe-spanning distemper. To restore faith in institutions, you must begin from the bottom up, starting with things as simple as potholes. Politics, as he put it, “has to translate to the pavement.”

New York City has long held a singular spot on the international stage, and its mayors have become global figures. But Mamdani, by dint of his youth, his improbable rise and his unusual background, brings a vivid symbolism to the role. African by birth, South Asian by heritage, American by choice, Mamdani in many ways embodies the cosmopolitan ideal at the heart of the United Nations’ founding.

World leaders lined up to spend time with him. He went to Queens with Ireland’s prime minister for a bingo game at an Irish American community center. He met with Brazil’s octogenarian leftist president and breakfasted with Spain’s dashing left-wing prime minister. Norway’s prime minister tagged along with him to visit a New York City classroom and talk about artificial intelligence in education.

Even President Trump couldn’t resist some time with the mayor. Last Monday he dropped by Gracie Mansion, spending about an hour behind closed doors with Mamdani — an eternity in presidential scheduling. Trump seemed in no rush to leave as the two took questions from reporters, beaming as he declared, “I want him to be a great mayor, and he’s certainly got potential, got great potential.”

Mamdani’s agenda, as befits a mayor, was mostly municipal. He visited a wastewater treatment facility with his counterparts from Helsinki, Rome and Barcelona; welcomed families moving into public housing with the mayors of Paris, Amsterdam and Greater Manchester; and handed out fliers to delivery workers explaining their rights with Mexico City’s mayor.

When he wasn’t hanging out with his fellow mayors, he celebrated the city’s victory in court against the delivery service DoorDash, wresting over $131 million from the company in a settlement for underpaying or not paying its workers. He also announced a new initiative to give out 70,000 free tickets to the Metropolitan Opera House, part of his push to make the city’s most exclusive cultural offerings accessible to everyday New Yorkers.

Mamdani’s many critics have tried to portray him as fixated on distant hobbyhorses, like arresting Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for war crimes in Gaza. But if anything, it was Netanyahu who seemed obsessed with the mayor. In his thundering speech at the United Nations last week, he called Mamdani an antisemite with “Hamas buddies.” He darkly name-checked the leftist streamer Hasan Piker and even castigated Mamdani’s wife for her likes on social media.

When I caught up with Mamdani by phone late last week, I asked him what he had hoped to get out of his first General Assembly. “We are a city that is home to hundreds of nationalities and even more languages,” Mamdani told me. “If any city is an illustration of what the United Nations principles hope to achieve, it is ours.”

But no matter how admirable those principles, the weakness of institutions like the United Nations in the face of the world’s spiraling chaos is an invitation to ask deeper questions, Mamdani said: “In a moment of a rising far right and the questioning of institutions that have otherwise been durable over many decades, it is also an opportunity to rethink what has been at the heart of those institutions, and the question of who they can serve and who they seek to serve.”

I heard an echo of Mamdani’s words in a speech the next day by a young world leader from South Asia, Prime Minister Balendra Shah of Nepal. “The United Nations was born from humanity’s experience of horrific world wars,” he said. “Its promise was that sovereignty would matter. International law would matter. The dignity of every human being would matter. Today, that international system is under strain. Too often, military and economic power determines whose voice is heard.”

In August, a glacier on Nepal’s border with Tibet collapsed, sending a deadly torrent of water and debris hurtling through a gorge. At least 1,300 people died and thousands more are missing in the villages and towns buried under the torrent. Scientists have concluded that rising temperatures caused by fossil fuel emissions played a critical role in destabilizing the Himalayan glacier. The disaster was merely the latest blow to Nepal: It faces soaring prices for fuel and fertilizer caused by the Iran war.

Besides South Asian roots and a history as a rapper, Shah has another thing in common with Mamdani. Before he was elected prime minister earlier this year, Shah was the mayor of Kathmandu, Nepal’s biggest city and its capital. Like Mamdani’s, his victory was driven by young voters, fed up with the country’s self-serving ruling elite. Along with Britain’s Andy Burnham, another former mayor turned prime minister, he shows how successful stewardship of a city can translate into national power.

Mamdani, of course, will never be president of the United States — the Constitution forbids the office to those not born in America. For Mamdani, this may be a blessing. The minute the midterms are over, the news media and the political world will shift their focus to the 2028 presidential race, as if the most important political question on earth is who will replace Trump.

But Mamdani seems to be asking a different question: How can we renew faith in politics and close the gap between citizens and their representatives? The answer, he suggests, lies in the city itself. If cities gave birth to democracy, perhaps they are the best place to midwife its rebirth. After all, more than half the world’s population lives in urban areas, and if current trends hold, by 2050 that figure will rise to almost 70 percent.

That’s a lot of trust to build — and a lot of potholes to fill.

SUMMARY

On paper, the Democrats’ path to winning the Senate in November is daunting. ARTICLE

Democrats May Have Found the Recipe for Flipping Red-State Senate Seats
Five new Times/Siena polls continue a run of strong results for the party in states that President Trump won easily in 2024.
By Nate Cohn
Published 2026-10-03 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/upshot/polls-midterms-senate-times-siena.html

On paper, the Democrats’ path to winning the Senate in November is daunting. They need to flip at least two seats that President Trump won by 11 percentage points or more — no party has pulled off a similar feat since 2008.

But in polls over the last month, the party’s path to the Senate hasn’t seemed daunting at all. Since Labor Day, Democrats have been tied or ahead in nearly every nonpartisan poll of not just two but five states that voted for Mr. Trump by between 11 and 16 points: Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

Today’s latest New York Times/Siena polls continue the streak. They find Democrats ahead in Texas, Alaska and Ohio; tied in Kansas; and down by only one point in Iowa. If the polls were to be exactly right — they won’t be — Democrats would take the Senate with room to spare.

This is an extraordinary run of polls for Democrats, most of all in Texas and Alaska. The Times/Siena polls — and others over the last month — show Democrats building a consistent and potentially meaningful lead in both states. If Democrats won Texas and Alaska, held their own seats and added North Carolina, as expected, they would need to win only one more Republican-held state, whether in Maine, Ohio, Iowa or Kansas, or elsewhere.

Of course, leading polls in September is not the same thing as winning in November — especially in Republican-leaning states, where polls have often overestimated Democrats. And even if they’re not overestimating them this time, Republicans need only to win back reliably Republican voters over the next month to prevail. This is harder than it sounds in this political environment, but it would not be a surprise if they did so. Republicans will have the financial resources they need to make their case.

Nonetheless, just about everything has gone right for the Democrats so far. They enter the final month of the campaign in a better position than anyone would have imagined when the year began. While the story varies somewhat by state, Democrats are cooking with the same recipe across all five contests: At a time when Mr. Trump is very unpopular, Democrats have nominated popular, relatively moderate candidates against surprisingly unpopular Republicans.

Ingredient No. 1: Trump

By now, it’s hard to be surprised by bad poll results for Mr. Trump. Still, these results from such Republican-leaning states — which gave Mr. Trump an average of 56 percent of the vote in 2024 — are striking.

Across the five states, the president’s approval rating was just 40 percent, while 57 percent had an unfavorable view. That’s not much better than Mr. Trump’s ratings in recent national polls. The results also represent a significant decline in his support since our last polls in four of these states in June. Since then, his ratings have fallen by five points.

There are two basic possible explanations for how Mr. Trump’s numbers are this bad in these states. One is that his ratings have continued to slide everywhere, not just in these states, since our last Times/Siena poll, which wouldn’t necessarily be hard to explain with gas prices and mortgage rates rising.

Another possibility is that Mr. Trump is suffering disproportionate losses in these five Republican-leaning states. Demographics, alone, would not be a sufficient explanation. It would take something more, like greater exposure to high diesel prices in the Farm Belt. Or there could even be a break in Mr. Trump’s support among the traditional Republicans who never loved Mr. Trump’s conduct or his policies on issues like tariffs or immigration, but nonetheless consistently backed him in every general election.

Interestingly, all five of these states voted against Mr. Trump in the 2016 Republican presidential primary.

Ingredient No. 2: Candidate quality

In all five states, Democrats have something more going for them, even beyond Mr. Trump’s extraordinary unpopularity: a significant advantage in candidate quality.

Let’s take the simplest measure: favorability. In all five states, more voters view the Democrat favorably than unfavorably, while more voters view the Republican candidate unfavorably than favorably.

This is a real triumph for Democrats in such reliably Republican states. They’ve managed to find candidates who are both personally appealing and ideologically acceptable to red-state voters.

In all five states, voters say that the phrase “has good character” describes the Democratic candidate better than the Republican.

In four of the five states (in the fifth, Ohio, it’s essentially even), a greater share of voters say the Republican is “too far to the right” than say the Democrat is “too far to the left.”

In contrast, a majority of voters in all five states said the Democratic Party was “too far” to the left, and did not say the Republican Party was “too far” to the right. That’s to be expected in Republican-leaning states, and yet it didn’t translate to the candidates themselves.

Let’s look at some of the results by state.

Perfect storm in Texas

Of all the polls, none capture the Republican challenge better than Texas, where the Democrat James Talarico is leading the Republican Ken Paxton by six points.

If Democrats are cooking with the same recipe in all five of these states, Texas is the one where Republicans have contributed the finest ingredients. The president’s approval rating has fallen to just 38 percent among likely voters there — the same as in our last national poll — and Mr. Paxton is the least popular of all 10 Senate candidates tested in these polls. And all of this is occurring in a state where Hispanic voters, who are swinging hard toward the Democrats, represent a large share of the electorate.

While the G.O.P. is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to try to bring down Mr. Talarico, so far his candidacy appears essentially undamaged. His favorable ratings actually ticked up since the last Times/Siena poll in June. Only 40 percent say he’s “too far to the left,” barely changed from 39 percent in June — and less than the 47 percent who say Mr. Paxton is “too far to the right.”

If there’s a “glass half full” interpretation for Republicans, it’s that the poll found a very favorable electorate for Democrats. If the poll is right about who will show up to vote, then many Trump voters — especially Hispanic and young Trump voters — will stay home. At the same time, an influx of new Democratic-leaning voters would enter the electorate. Together, the electorate jolts to the left.

If the 2024 electorate showed up, the race would be a dead heat.

Alaska primaries and ranked choice

Can a seven-point lead for a Democrat in Alaska be unsurprising? If there ever were a case, this might be it.

Unlike most states, Alaska holds a top-four primary — all candidates from every party compete on the same ballot, and the top four candidates advance. In this year’s primary, the Democrat Mary Peltola finished eight points ahead of the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan — quite similar to the result of the poll.

One twist on the ballot — and in our poll — is the other Dan Sullivan. Yes, two people named Dan Sullivan are running for Senate in Alaska, and the other Dan Sullivan will indeed appear on the ballot in November.

This was an unexpected issue back in our June poll, when we didn’t specify which Dan Sullivan we were talking about — and may have gotten a handful of confused, serious or trolling responses. To avoid it this time, we asked voters about Dan Sullivan “the incumbent” (as he is described on the ballot).

A.I. in Ohio

As I wrote after our last national poll, artificial intelligence hasn’t quite emerged as a top-tier issue in electoral politics. For now, it’s a third-tier issue like climate change — something that activists care about and that might matter in a race under certain circumstances, but that doesn’t yet shape national electoral outcomes.

That story basically held in our state polls, with one exception: Ohio, where the Democrat Sherrod Brown led the Republican Jon Husted by three points.

In Ohio, 3 percent of voters said A.I. was the most important issue to their vote, compared with about 0.3 percent of voters in the other states. That may not sound like a big difference, but that puts A.I. alongside issues that regularly affect the outcome of national elections and the partisan leanings of a broader share of the electorate, like abortion or health care.

Ohio has been an epicenter of the backlash over data centers, and Mr. Brown was an early mover in trying to capitalize on the issue against the incumbent, Mr. Husted. As my colleague Shane Goldmacher reported in August, a memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that “more than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

The Times/Siena poll found that voters preferred Mr. Brown on A.I. and data centers by 10 points — a bigger lead on A.I. than any candidate had in any of the polls. It was Mr. Brown’s biggest lead on any question.

Can Hamilton gain in Kansas?

Kansas? If you’re not the kind of person who follows the latest polls (and we have a great new page tracking the latest polls, if you would like to do so), you might be surprised that we’re polling Kansas at all. But it has been on the edge of the radar for a while, and over the last month a string of nonpartisan, Democratic and Republican polls have all shown an extremely close race. Our poll shows a tie.

How are Democrats so competitive in Kansas? There are a lot of factors, but what might get them over the top is the appeal of their candidate, Adam Hamilton. He is the senior pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, and he’s a first-time candidate who says he’s running against socialism and health care cuts.

Mr. Hamilton has the highest net favorability rating of any of the candidates tested in these polls, and he may have more room to grow. Overall, 28 percent of likely voters said they hadn’t heard of him. The danger for Republicans is obvious: If more voters learn that he’s no ordinary Democrat, Mr. Hamilton might gain more support.

Mr. Hamilton is actually performing worse than the Democratic Party on the generic congressional ballot among the voters who haven’t heard of him. Among the voters who do have an opinion of him, he’s running 12 points ahead of the generic ballot — which would be enough for him to win.
