SUMMARY

The Digital Revolution was born in 1843, when Ada Lovelace produced a 20,000-word set of notes about a calculating machine invented by her friend, Charles Babbage. Now, as we face a choice about the role of humans in an era of artificial intelligence, Lovelace’s approach to human-machine partnership remains the right one. Humans would “originate” the ideas and intentions, the machines would become the “executive right hand,” Lovelace wrote, and the iterative back and forth would deepen human understanding.

ARTICLE

Ada Lovelace Already Answered the Big Questions About A.I.
What Ada Lovelace can teach us as we develop artificial intelligence.
By Walter Isaacson
Published 2026-10-05 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/opinion/ada-lovelace-ai.html

The Digital Revolution was born in 1843, when Ada Lovelace produced a 20,000-word set of notes about a calculating machine invented by her friend, Charles Babbage. She showed how humans and digital technology could work together to produce beautiful results. Now, as we face a choice about the role of humans in an era of artificial intelligence, Lovelace’s approach to human-machine partnership remains the right one.

The only legitimate child of the romantic poet Lord Byron, Lovelace had inherited her father’s rebellious artistic spirit, a trait that her mother, Anne Isabella Milbanke, tried to temper by having her tutored mainly in math. Lovelace came to realize that math was poetic: it’s a lovely language that describes the harmonies of the universe. Despite her mother’s efforts, she remained her father’s daughter, with a sensibility that allowed her to view an equation as a brushstroke that painted an aspect of nature’s splendor. The combination produced in Lovelace a passion for what she took to calling “poetical science,” which linked her artistic imagination to her enchantment with numbers.

Her father was a Luddite, literally. In his maiden speech in the House of Lords, Byron defended the followers of the folkloric Ned Ludd who were rampaging against the mechanical weaving machines that were being deployed in England at the time. The Luddites believed automation would reduce the number of human jobs. They were wrong — just as modern Luddites are wrong about other new technologies. By the end of the 19th century, there were roughly 10 times more workers in textile industries than before.

Unlike her father, Lovelace saw the power and the potential of automated technology. When her mother took her on a trip through the British industrial Midlands, she was particularly impressed by the new looms, known as Jacquard looms, that used punch cards to direct the creation of the desired fabric patterns.

In her notes about Babbage’s computational machine, which he called the “Analytical Engine,” Lovelace explained how the use of punch cards, with their rows of places that were either punched or unpunched, could store and convey information. “The Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves,” she wrote. Its operations, she realized, did not need to be limited to math and numbers. The punch cards could store, manipulate, process and act upon anything that could be expressed in symbols: words and logic and music and pictures and “the most complicated patterns in the fabrication of brocaded stuffs.” The calculating machine could become a general-purpose computer.

Lovelace’s insight would become the core concept of the digital age: Any piece of content or information — music, text, pictures, numbers, symbols, sounds, video — could be expressed in digital form and manipulated by machines. She even wrote some step-by-step procedures a calculating machine could execute, which became the first published computer programs.

There was another significant concept that she introduced in her notes: artificial intelligence. Can machines think?

She believed not. A machine such as Babbage’s could perform operations as instructed, she asserted, but it could not come up with ideas or intentions of its own. “The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything,” she wrote. “It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform. It can follow analysis, but it has no power of anticipating any analytical relations or truths.”

Just over a century later, in his seminal 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence,” the computer pioneer Alan Turing called this assertion “Lady Lovelace’s Objection” and argued that she was wrong.

The Digital Revolution ended up featuring two schools of thought, which can be called the Turing camp and the Lovelace camp.

On the Turing side are those who believe that artificial general intelligence will surpass all aspects of human intelligence, resulting in A.I. systems that can design themselves. That could lead to a “singularity” when the machines will turn themselves into a superintelligent successor species that no longer needs us.

On the other side is the Lovelace camp, which holds that there will always be a role for human creativity, intention, agency and empathy. Human creativity involves values, aesthetic judgments, emotions, personal consciousness and a moral sense. We humans possess an imagination that, as Lovelace said, “brings together things, facts, ideas, conceptions in new, original, endless, ever-varying combinations.” We appreciate beauty. We weave information into narratives. We are storytelling and social animals. Those are what the arts and humanities teach us and are what humans are distinctively able to do.

The greatest gains, according to this camp, will not come from machines working alone, but from a symbiosis that tightly connects machine processing power with human creativity in a mutually beneficial way. Humans would “originate” the ideas and intentions, the machines would become the “executive right hand,” Lovelace wrote, and the iterative back and forth would deepen human understanding.

The modern pioneer of this approach was Joseph Carl Robnett Licklider, a psychologist and computer scientist. In 1960, he published one of the most influential yet least-known papers in the history of postwar technology, “Man-Computer Symbiosis.” While other researchers, such as Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy, were pursuing the Turing vision of artificial intelligence, Mr. Licklider believed that the goal should be augmented intelligence, a system in which humans and machines “cooperate in making decisions.” Mr. Licklider wrote: “The resulting partnership will think as no human brain has ever thought and process data in a way not approached by the information-handling machines we know today.”

The personal computer revolution that began in the 1970s pursued this goal of augmenting rather than replacing human intelligence. Beginning with humanistic engineers such as Douglas Engelbart, who in 1962 wrote a book-length manifesto called “Augmenting Human Intellect,” personal-computer pioneers emphasized the importance of the human-computer interface: the ways that humans interact with their machines and communicate back and forth with them. Some of the most transformative advances came from breakthroughs that made it simpler and more intuitive for humans to interact with machines, such as the mouse and point-and-click graphical user interfaces.

Mr. Engelbart’s disciples, such as Alan Kay and Steve Jobs, had an intuitive, humanistic feel for user-friendly interfaces. At his product introductions, Jobs would often conclude with a slide of street signs showing the intersection of the Liberal Arts and Technology. At his last such appearance, for the iPad 2 in 2011, he stood in front of that image and declared, “It’s in Apple’s D.N.A. that technology alone is not enough — that it’s technology married with liberal arts, married with the humanities, that yields us the result that makes our heart sing.”

Humans now face a technology revolution that could be fundamentally different. Many artificial intelligence systems are being designed to accomplish objectives while minimizing — perhaps eliminating — the need for human involvement. We have only a very short period to decide whether we want our A.I. systems to remain tightly tethered to human oversight, human values and human agency.

That will involve thousands of very specific decisions: How much power should we give to each of our software agents, drones, robots and other autonomous devices, virtual and physical, to act without humans in the loop?

Making these decisions requires answering a more fundamental question: Why should we insist that we humans remain in the loop?

One argument is that, as Lovelace and Mr. Licklider implied, symbiosis is a force multiplier: The combination of machine processing power and human creativity will accomplish things that are cooler than what machines alone can produce.

Ah, yes! Wouldn’t it be pretty to think so? But in many realms, that is no longer the case. Self-driving cars are becoming safer than those operated by humans. A military drone that must partner with a human is probably less effective in war than a purely autonomous one. Our moral instincts may want to keep humans in the loop, but our competitive instincts won’t.

Suppose we get to a level of A.I. where machines totally surpass us? Suppose that the novels and poetry and code and movies and military actions and policing decisions and legal judgments are better without our involvement, the way that self-driving cars are becoming?

That leads to the most essential question: Why are we building these systems? The answer should be the obvious one: to make life better for humans.

Human flourishing involves more than consumption. We derive meaning from creating and discovering things, exercising judgment and solving problems, caring for people and having some influence over the world around us. A society in which machines do everything for us would provide abundance while depriving us of agency and meaning.

We should continue to hew closely to Lovelace’s vision of building systems that encourage a partnership between humans and machines. The responsibility rests with the engineers and tech companies that are building large language models and robots — and with all of us, in the decisions we make and the way we use our technologies every day. We should try to work in tight partnership, in a hands-on way, with the technologies we choose to use.

That means taking the time to understand how they work and requiring them to accurately display their reasoning and sources, delegating less to autonomous agents and choosing tools that invite our participation. Following the path set by Ada Lovelace, we can help assure a flourishing human future by favoring services and devices that have human-computer interfaces in the tradition of J.C.R. Licklider, Douglas Engelbart, Alan Kay and Steve Jobs: ones that are user-friendly, intuitive and interactive and that seek to include humans in every step rather than to seduce their users into letting them handle things without us.

Walter Isaacson is the author of “The Innovators: How a Group of Hackers, Geniuses and Geeks Created the Digital Revolution” and the host of the video podcast “The Builders.”

SUMMARY

What’s more, Israel has lost even many American Jews. There remains, however, an opportunity for AIPAC to play a positive and, no less important, honest role in American politics. Were AIPAC to commit itself to the battle against this fusion of old-fashioned right-wing antisemitism with its new, virulent anti-Zionism, it could serve the interests of Israel, American Jews and the United States simultaneously.

ARTICLE

How AIPAC Failed — and How It Can Recover
There remains an opportunity for the group to play a positive and honest role in American politics.
By Eric Alterman
Published 2026-10-05 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/opinion/aipac-israel-lobby-netanyahu-gaza.html

In December 2018, Representative Nancy Pelosi made a pledge to a largely Jewish audience: If the U.S. Capitol “crumbled to the ground, the one thing that would remain is our commitment to our aid — and I don’t even call it aid — our cooperation — with Israel. That’s fundamental.” That commitment apparently faltered in mid-July, when Ms. Pelosi voted with over a hundred of her colleagues to slash U.S. aid to the Jewish state.

Unconditional support for Israel was once as common in Congress as the flag pin on a senator’s lapel, largely thanks to the bipartisan efforts of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Today, in the aftermath of Israel’s bloody war on Gaza, launched in reaction to Hamas’s brutal attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, Israel has reached near-pariah status globally and domestically. “The condemnation of what Bibi Netanyahu is doing is almost universal” within the Democratic Party, California Governor Gavin Newsom told PBS News in September, speaking of Israel’s actions in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank. Furthermore, he said, these days the party has a “pretty overwhelming opposition to accepting money from AIPAC.”

The age of AIPAC’s unmatched political power and influence is at an end. Rejection may be the most bipartisan act the group inspires. In the U.S. Senate race in Michigan, allies of the Republican candidate Mike Rogers reportedly asked AIPAC not to advertise on his behalf. AIPAC and affiliated groups invested nearly $30 million in advertising during the summer’s Democratic primaries to help Representative Haley Stevens in her bid for the Senate nomination in Michigan. During that race, her opponent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed bragged, “AIPAC has called me the single most dangerous candidate in this race.” Dr. El-Sayed, of course, won.

Despite the profound transformation in how the world sees AIPAC’s sole client, and its increasing marginalization in American politics, the group not only hasn’t acknowledged the change, but it operates as though Israel were as popular as it was in 1991, when the Jewish state enjoyed a nearly 80 percent favorable rating among Americans. According to a 2026 NBC News poll, just 32 percent of American voters now view Israel positively; among Democrats, that number falls to just 13 percent.

What’s more, Israel has lost even many American Jews. According to a 2025 Washington Post poll, 61 percent of American Jews said they believe Israel committed war crimes in Gaza and some 40 percent believe Israel has committed genocide. Another recent poll found nearly half of American Jews under the age of 35 believing that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict should be solved by creating a single, binational state, an idea considered to be fringe since the Palestinian American scholar Edward Said advocated it in 1999.

Support for Israel is now a millstone around the neck of Democratic politicians and a source of profound inner conflict for American Jews who seek to balance their Zionism with their liberalism. Many of the Jews who continue to define their identities via their support for Israel are, today, most likely calculating the cost of nursing homes and retirement communities. Younger Jews, like most young Americans of virtually all religions and ethnicities, increasingly express negative views about the Jewish state.

The question facing AIPAC is not simply whether it can find a way to adjust to this new political world but, more fundamentally, whether it can even see the changes demanded by these new circumstances?

AIPAC was founded by I.L. “Si” Kenen, a former lobbyist for the Israeli foreign ministry, in the wake of a 1953 Israeli military massacre of 69 Palestinians in a village called Qibya. Mr. Kenen suggested to friends and colleagues that they create a new organization, initially called the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, to make Israel’s case whenever circumstances made it necessary. The U.S. State Department consistently tried to pressure Israel to take a more generous attitude toward the roughly 750,000 Palestinians it had expelled before and during its war of independence — what Palestinians call the Nakba, or “catastrophe”— but were stymied in part by the political opposition AIPAC’s predecessor helped engender.

AIPAC’s goal in those early years was to promote the interests of an Israel then understood to be a young and scrappy David surrounded by a Goliath of hostile Arab nations. Its message was straightforward and bipartisan: As a democracy in the Middle East, Israel was morally deserving of generous American financial, military and diplomatic support.

For the United States, that support could be expected to pay strategic dividends, both in the region, where America would gain a reliable ally, and in domestic politics, where Israel was extremely popular with voters, pretty much regardless of religion. By 1963, Senator J. William Fulbright, then the chair of the powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called AIPAC “the most powerful and efficient foreign policy lobby in American politics.”

In the early 1980s, AIPAC’s executive director Thomas Dine, a former aide to Ted Kennedy, set out to expand the lobby into a coast-to-coast operation comparable to the National Rifle Association or the AARP, with a national membership made up of wealthy funders as well as American Jews who increasingly defined their religious and political identities through support for Israel. Both groups could be relied upon to call, write and, if necessary, threaten senators and representatives. Relying on a mix of the extremely wealthy and the extremely committed, Mr. Dine increased AIPAC’s annual budget to $15 million from some $1.7 million. By the end of the century, it was $50 million, with nine regional offices and 10 satellite offices. At the same time, U.S. public spending on military aid to Israel roughly doubled.

AIPAC also began to woo candidates and congressional staff and provided each with language for legislation and talking points. It funded luxury junkets and met frequently with reporters and editors to try to shape the narratives about Israel and the Middle East that reached the public. Rabbis were offered ready-to-use pro-Israel sermons.

Still, for many years, AIPAC did not endorse specific candidates or dispense funds directly to them. Instead, it merely made sure that certain candidates it approved of, from either party, were well-funded, and that those it did not were not.

AIPAC’s role started to shift in 1993 with the resignation of Mr. Dine and his replacement by a more conservative set of board members and top executives. When former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin attempted to make peace with the Palestinians in the early 1990s, AIPAC only grudgingly supported the cause. While its leaders did not openly undermine the peace process, they did independently lobby for legislation that complicated the negotiations, such as a bill calling on the Clinton administration to move the American embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem.

After the 1995 assassination of Rabin and the subsequent collapse of the peace process, AIPAC resumed its steady march rightward. The lobby also began to embrace the support of far-right Christian Zionists. At a public interview in 2021, Ron Dermer, a former Israeli ambassador to the U.S. and a close ally of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said “the backbone of Israel’s support in the United States is the evangelical Christians” rather than American Jews, who he said were “disproportionately among [Israel’s] critics.” AIPAC followed suit.

The specific challenges the organization faces today can be traced to Mr. Netanyahu’s decision to appear before Congress in March 2015 at the invitation of Representative John Boehner, then the Republican speaker of the House. In an unusual move for a foreign ally, Mr. Netanyahu publicly aligned himself with the Republican Party’s attempts to undermine President Obama, a Democrat and a leader who happened to be supported by a majority of American Jews. In his address, Mr. Netanyahu denounced the Obama administration’s diplomatic efforts toward the nuclear disarmament in Iran, better known as the Iran deal. AIPAC and an affiliate spent nearly $30 million on a failed campaign to prevent the deal’s passage.

AIPAC’s increasing identification with both the methods and the goals of the Republican Party has become ever more evident over the past decade. In early 2020, it produced a Facebook ad accusing “radicals in the Democratic Party” of “pushing their antisemitic and anti-Israel policies down the throats of the American people.”

AIPAC’s annual conference was once a way station for all presidential hopefuls, but in 2019 Senators Elizabeth Warren and Kamala Harris, as well as former Representative Beto O’Rourke, among others, all declined to attend, a decision that would have been hard to imagine just four years earlier.

In December 2021, AIPAC created a super PAC that also swung right. The group immediately amassed an enormous war chest and announced endorsements of over a hundred Republicans, many of whom had voted against certifying the results of the 2020 presidential election. By 2022, its high-profile donors included conservative Republican billionaires such as the Home Depot founder Bernie Marcus and the hedge fund manager Paul Singer.

Using right-wing Republican money to defeat liberal candidates in Democratic primaries exposed AIPAC to considerable anger on the part of progressives, and further alienated the lobby from the mainstream opinions of American Jews. This was especially true of young American Jews whose views of Israel had been shaped by an ever more oppressive occupation of the West Bank and Gaza well before Oct. 7, and the mass killing of Palestinians that followed in its wake.

As a result, the group’s electoral strategy has begun to backfire. In February, AIPAC’s super PAC dropped $2.3 million into a New Jersey special primary election to try to defeat former Representative Tom Malinowski for what it saw as his wobbly support for Israel. Mr. Malinowski lost — but not to the more pro-Israel candidate. He was ousted by a candidate to his left: Analilia Mejia, a former aide to Bernie Sanders who has indicated she believes that Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

In Illinois, AIPAC-aligned super PACs invested more than $5 million in an effort to thwart Daniel Biss in his Democratic primary race for Congress in Illinois. Mr. Bliss is the grandson of Holocaust survivors, and his mother is Israeli — but he supports limiting arms sales to Israel and recognizing a Palestinian state. When Mr. Biss won his race, he boasted about his willingness to call “AIPAC out clearly and repeatedly.”

Even establishment Democrats such as Cory Booker and Ruben Gallego have sworn off AIPAC money, no doubt cognizant that public association with the lobby these days can turn a campaign radioactive. Many Democrats who support Israel feel compelled to resist Mr. Netanyahu and publicly criticize his government’s behavior — and to vocally and unequivocally reject the lobby’s support. AIPAC’s influence in future Democratic Party politics will likely be limited to the role of either boogeyman or secret spoiler.

By sticking to its long-held, inflexible, “Israel right or wrong” line and allying itself with a party whose views on race, immigration, economics — and, these days, democracy — are anathema to most American Jews, AIPAC has effectively forfeited the role it enjoyed in the days when Israel was a genuinely bipartisan cause. As America heads into the midterms, it is clear the lobby has all but lost the Democrats and may be skating on ever thinner ice with Republicans as well.

There remains, however, an opportunity for AIPAC to play a positive and, no less important, honest role in American politics.

While no doubt a traditional flavor of antisemitism occasionally attaches to pro-Palestinian arguments on the left, more recently it has been the right’s increasing tolerance of widespread antisemitism among its most influential voices — from Tucker Carlson to Candace Owens to Nick Fuentes — that has morphed into a particularly fervent form of anti-Zionism. MAGA anger over Iran (and Israel’s role in the war) has hardened that space.

Were AIPAC to commit itself to the battle against this fusion of old-fashioned right-wing antisemitism with its new, virulent anti-Zionism, it could serve the interests of Israel, American Jews and the United States simultaneously. It might also rescue its own reputation in the process.

Eric Alterman is a CUNY distinguished professor at Brooklyn College and the author, most recently, of “We Are Not One: A History of America’s Fight Over Israel.”

SUMMARY

On Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign website is a low-res video game called “Salmon Run,” in which you can play the part of a fish trying to avoid being caught by commercial trawlers. Though a Democrat, Ms. Peltola in 2010 helped Ms. Murkowski’s improbable and successful write-in re-election campaign after Ms. Murkowski lost her party’s primary. Ms. Peltola has used this space to campaign as a normal person who has normal views.

ARTICLE

She Could Flip the Senate. All She Wants to Talk About Are Fish and Diesel.
Inside the weird campaign that could flip the Senate to the Democrats.
By Stephen Stromberg
Published 2026-10-05 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/opinion/mary-peltola-alaska-campaign-senate.html

Politics in Alaska are different.

On Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign website is a low-res video game called “Salmon Run,” in which you can play the part of a fish trying to avoid being caught by commercial trawlers. As you navigate around nets and menacing ocean predators, messages pop up about Dan Sullivan, the state’s Republican senator seeking re-election. “Dan Sullivan took hundreds of thousands of dollars from the trawling lobby,” one reads. If you clear the run without being caught, you are congratulated for avoiding Mr. Sullivan’s nets.

Ms. Peltola’s kelp-roots campaign, in which trawlers are a big issue, is taglined “fish, family and freedom.” Her pitch can seem parochial, even incomprehensible beyond Alaska’s frigid waters.

Yet it is a blaring statement to the activists trying to reshape her party: In today’s hyper-online, partisan, siloed politics, the real outsider Democratic candidate isn’t the leftmost one. It’s the one who has actually spent time, well, outside.

Alaska is, if not ruby-red, at least salmon pink. In her effort to beat the political odds, Ms. Peltola, 53, offers a contrast, in age, demeanor and substance, to Washington’s aging Democratic establishment and to the faction trying to replace it — an ascendant, increasingly organized and aggressive left wing.

“We really do need people in these positions who are normal people,” Ms. Peltola told me. There aren’t many of those left in Congress, from which the constant need to raise campaign money and navigate impossible factional purity tests repels all but the most committed powerseekers.

Ms. Peltola differentiates herself from a noxious Democratic brand by building a practical personal one rather than adopting a trendy ideological one. The logic of her approach: In the tough races that make or break Democratic majorities, сandidates who read off the progressive left's script will underperform.

Sure, even with her own lines, she might lose. Her lack of polish is one potential problem.

Voters often fall for politicians who act authentic — think Bill Clinton and his studied sentimentality or George W. Bush and his cowboy cosplay. Ms. Peltola is authentic. Hers is not a calculated, polished, flannel-shirt-sleeves-rolled-up-to-just-the-right-length sort of authenticity. Ms. Peltola’s is rawer.

Listening to her, one must regularly confront a question: Was it a gaffe?

“When I served in the 117th and 118th Congresses, there were six senators in the middle, out of a hundred,” she said in September to a small crowd in Valdez, a town of 4,000 on Prince William Sound. “Now there are three senators in the middle, out of a hundred. I would like to be the fourth.”

Who are the three Senate pragmatists, I asked her after the event? “Lisa Murkowski,” she said immediately. “Angus King,” she offered with less self-assurance, her intonation rising as if she were asking a question. Then a pause. “Who’s the other one?” she said. Eventually, a campaign aide mentioned Susan Collins. “Yea, Susan Collins,” Ms. Peltola said.

National Democrats might wish that she had just moved on. Ms. Peltola made common cause with their top target, Ms. Collins, Maine’s sitting Republican senator, and undercut Troy Jackson, the Democrat running to unseat her.

In both campaign events I attended, Ms. Peltola paused awkwardly as she tried to remember what she wanted to say to her audience. The Times also reported last month that her temperament — including the purported use of slurs with staff members — made her congressional office chaotic and her campaign a mess.

Still, observers in Anchorage doubt that these reports or her plain manner will matter much — they might even help her with Alaska’s many hardscrabble independents. Having to stop for a bit to remember what to say? Forgetting senators? Not exactly senatorial. But definitely relatable.

The truth is that Ms. Peltola, in her unprepossessing way, would probably work more comfortably with Susan Collins than with Elizabeth Warren.

“I don’t have anything in common with any other candidate,” she said when I asked her about what she and Democrats in other midterm races share. This seems unlikely. But purposefully or not, the statement bolstered the claim, per one of her campaign spokesmen, that she has been one of the “least loyal Democrats.”

Her call for pragmatism is an agenda in itself, reflecting a theory of politics that getting things done by building weird, sometimes uncomfortable political coalitions is better than ideological purity. Her message is for oil-industry workers and small-time fishermen, suburbanites around Anchorage and off-the-grid libertarians, Native and non-Native Alaskans. Her career has been a test case in the proposition that practicality is a common denominator that makes her approachable.

Alaskans “build coalitions based on people who are easy to work with,” she said. They must in their rugged, remote, sparsely inhabited state — population just shy of 750,000.

Ms. Peltola is a lifelong subsistence fisherman from Bethel, an outpost in far west Alaska that is accessible only by plane or boat. An Alaska Native of the Yup’ik people, she captained her own fishing boat at age 14.

Her parents worked on the first congressional campaign of Don Young, a Republican who went on to represent Alaska in the House for decades. Ms. Peltola boasts that, in Alaska’s statehouse, she worked with Ms. Murkowski, a Republican, before Ms. Murkowski rose to the U.S. Senate in 2002. Though a Democrat, Ms. Peltola in 2010 helped Ms. Murkowski’s improbable and successful write-in re-election campaign after Ms. Murkowski lost her party’s primary. Ms. Murkowski returned the favor by endorsing Ms. Peltola when she ran for Congress in 2022. (Ms. Murkowski gave Mr. Sullivan, her follow Republican, a lukewarm endorsement this year but has also defended Ms. Peltola.)

Ms. Peltola won her 2022 race, a special election to replace Mr. Young, who died in office that year. She hired Mr. Young’s chief of staff to run her own office and, by her telling, went “toe-to-toe with the Biden administration.” She pushed President Joe Biden to approve ConocoPhillips’s Willow project, an oil drilling venture in Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve. She also favors oil exploration in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, though her pro-oil position isn’t unqualified: She declined to support a bill that would have threatened nearby fisheries.

In her Senate campaign, she typically doesn’t attack “Republican” but rather “D.C.” policies from the past two years in which the G.O.P. has controlled Washington. Ms. Peltola often mentions broadly unpopular Medicaid cuts. The Department of Government Efficiency’s federal employee firings are vulnerable to criticism in Alaska, which has one of the highest concentrations of federal civilian employees in the country — and where accurate weather reports and ocean monitoring are life-or-death matters. So is Republicans’ defunding of public radio, an information lifeline in remote environs.

President Trump’s Iran war has enabled Ms. Peltola to blame him for raising Alaska’s high cost of living. She constantly mentions the price of diesel fuel, which Alaskans use at high rates to fuel small generators and heat homes. And she derides Republicans’ rescinding of Biden-era renewable energy subsidies — not necessarily on behalf of the climate, but because Alaskans want cheaper energy and technologies that enable them to live off-grid.

Ms. Peltola hardly mentions culture wars, which some supporters seem to appreciate. “Different sexual orientations … I don’t care.” said Leila Dengel, 73-year-old nonpartisan voter who said Ms. Peltola won her over at the Valdez event. But, even as she emphasized that she is not “socialistic,” Ms. Dengel said she likes that Ms. Peltola is for average people, and she is furious about the direction of the country, the Iran war and corporations pushing new technologies, such as her insurance company, which she resents for trying to make her go paperless.

The big exception to Ms. Peltola’s de-emphasis on cultural issues is abortion. Championing reproductive choice helps put the “freedom” in her “fish, family, freedom” mantra.

The Peltola agenda might seem like an assortment of positions chosen opportunistically to appeal to Alaskans. “I really wish I had something better to say,” she said after I asked her what a national agenda for center-left pragmatists might look like. She explained that she’s too “Alaska-centric” to think much about partisan politics.

But she has a program, in effect if not in intent.

Ms. Peltola’s pro-oil, pro-fishery stand reflects a concept of environmental stewardship that sees conserving nature as essential to preserving it for human use. Similarly, she emphasizes that building renewables could diversify energy sources in a state addicted to diesel. As Alaska politicians have from time immemorial, she favors spending on basic infrastructure — and gun rights.

In keeping with the times, she indulges in some populist flair, lambasting “millionaires and billionaires” and “corporate greed.” But she isn’t mounting a class revolution. Her objection to wealthy people focuses on their degree of influence in Washington, and she centers on an anti-corruption message backed by proposals to limit political spending and conflicts of interest among members of Congress.

Ms. Peltola campaigns on enhancing Obamacare rather than enacting Medicare for all, which also gives a sense of what she would be like in the Senate. She would be the critical swing vote on tough deals that get Obamacare subsidies and renewables tax credits restored, the debt limit raised or a gratuitous government shutdown ended.

People aren’t out in the streets calling for cooperation and moderation. Then again, activists aren’t the only ones who vote. Particularly in many Mountain West states — which have big natural resource issues, lots of federal land, affection for guns and gas, an outdoorsy culture of self-reliance, relatively little racial polarization and few successful Democratic candidates — a Peltola-like combination of deep-rooted identity and practical outlook has a chance of working.

Even if she loses but overperforms in her state, which has backed Mr. Trump in three elections straight, the result would suggest her strategy worked.

Native Alaskans are politically swingy — Sealaska, a major Native Alaska group, endorsed both Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan — but her background should help her. She might appeal to voters who backed the president but aren’t happy. Mr. Trump in 2024 carried Alaska 54 percent to 41 percent, but his approval ratings in the state now hover in the mid-40s.

And, critically, Alaska Democrats aren’t at war with one another over their direction. They appear to have taken the right lesson from national Democrats’ struggles: Don’t scare the middle. Ms. Peltola has used this space to campaign as a normal person who has normal views. Focusing on persuadable voters with a practical persona built by relentless focus on local issues shouldn’t be a bold strategy. But it makes her a true outsider candidate.

Even as the Republican Party has devolved, the Democrats have lost huge swaths of the country. To get them back, the party needs to leave plenty of room for pragmatists who want to run offbeat campaigns about fish.

SUMMARY

It’s no wonder, then, that when Canada legalized medical assistance in dying a decade ago, it quickly became a major topic of conversation in our clinics. Canada’s medical assistance in dying program started in 2016 as an option only for patients with a “reasonably foreseeable” natural death. Cases like this are not arguments against assisted dying, and we do not seek to dissuade patients from going forward with the procedure.

ARTICLE

‘Death Must Not Become the Only Kind of Relief People Can Imagine’
Assisted dying accounts for more than 5 percent of deaths in Canada.
By Gary Rodin and Madeline Li
Published 2026-10-05 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/opinion/medical-assistance-in-dying-counseling.html

We are psychiatrists who work with patients with advanced cancer. It’s no wonder, then, that when Canada legalized medical assistance in dying a decade ago, it quickly became a major topic of conversation in our clinics. We’ve counseled patients about the procedure and assessed whether they were eligible. One of us has administered the drugs to end patients’ lives. We’ve also researched what leads people to choose this option. And together, we created an institutional framework that determined how one of Canada’s largest medical centers would respond to requests for assisted death.

We know that medical assistance in dying can be dignified and profoundly meaningful for everyone involved. We remember a man in his 30s in our palliative care unit who, thanks to the procedure, was able to choose to die before he became even sicker and potentially lost the ability to communicate. He said a final goodbye to everyone he loved, including his 5-year-old son, and died with his wife beside him and a music therapist singing Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah.”

But Canada’s system for assisted death is no longer an option of last resort. Too many people are receiving the procedure without the opportunity for careful reflection about it with a health provider. In some cases, patients are being approved who should not be. Reports have emerged of people seeking assisted death in the context of poverty or loneliness, raising concerns that they may feel they have no other options. In other cases, including for many of our cancer patients, medical assistance in dying may be the right choice eventually, but there’s a risk of rushing into it and shortening what can be a meaningful period in patients’ lives.

Canada’s medical assistance in dying program started in 2016 as an option only for patients with a “reasonably foreseeable” natural death. In 2021, Parliament removed the foreseeable death requirement. Today, Canada’s system is one of the most permissive in the world, allowing assisted dying for almost any form of subjectively intolerable suffering that has a medical basis, or even for medically unexplained physical symptoms. This latitude may contribute to Canada having the fastest growth rate of assisted dying in the world, increasing 16-fold in the eight years since legalization. The procedure now accounts for over 5 percent of all deaths in the country.

How did we get here? Within the Canadian system, medical assistance in dying is the result of a decades-long campaign aimed at enshrining it as a human right — often in the face of strong pressure from groups who opposed the procedure on religious or other grounds. Activists who support the procedure are still understandably wary of anything that could make it harder to get, often warning of unnecessary “gatekeeping” that might interfere with a patient’s autonomy. These activists helped shape the laws that govern the procedure and were instrumental in supporting the first medical networks that emerged to administer it.

Perhaps as a result of this influence, many doctors have come to see their primary role to be making sure their patients meet the legal eligibility requirements to qualify for assisted dying. They must, for instance, be experiencing intolerable suffering and have the mental capacity for informed consent. The problem is that there has become far more focus on whether patients can get an assisted death and not enough on whether they should.

A study published earlier this year looked at how Canadian physicians involved in medical assistance in dying understood their role. One provider described being “just a conduit really for someone’s desires and someone’s choices.” In a separate but similar study, another provider professed to have no role in evaluating suffering — though one of the legal requirements to receive the procedure is that a clinician must confirm that the patient is experiencing intolerable suffering. Determining that degree of suffering “is entirely up to the patient — 100 percent,” that provider said.

While it is critical that patients are able to make decisions about their bodies, doctors have an important role in guiding those decisions. There is an old saying about surgeons that is apt here: Good ones know how to operate, better ones know when to operate and the best know when not to.

Our research shows that the suffering of patients with an advanced disease arises from a complex interplay of physical and psychological distress, family strain and a slow erosion of identity and meaning. In this context, the loss of the will to live is not a fixed state. It fluctuates. It can be treated. And it can be misread.

Here’s how Canada’s medical assistance in dying program works: Two clinicians (either physicians or nurse practitioners) are required to approve an assisted dying request. The vast majority of cases are what is known as Track 1, in which the patient must have an illness that will lead to a “reasonably foreseeable death” (although no time frame is specified in the law). In these cases, they can request the procedure and get it quickly — sometimes even on the same day. Track 2 cases, in which the person does not have a life-threatening illness, are much less common. In these cases, patients are required to wait 90 days before receiving the procedure.

The law, however, does not require clinicians to engage in deeper conversations that explore the complex meaning of the request. We’ve seen cases where people request medical aid in dying in the face of a new cancer diagnosis or flare-up of an existing illness and get the procedure within a matter of days. There is no requirement in either track that patients attempt treatment to relieve their suffering. Nor does the law specify adequate safeguards to protect vulnerable individuals whose decision may be affected by social disadvantage.

We wonder whether inadequate consideration of such factors helps explain why in 2024, 98 percent of people assessed for medical assistance in dying in Canada were found to meet the criterion of “intolerable suffering” and over 92 percent were approved for the procedure.

In contrast, in the Netherlands, which legalized medical assistance in dying nearly 25 years ago, it’s common for cases to be rejected because a doctor judged that the patient’s suffering was not unbearable or that they did not pursue alternate treatment options.

We’ve seen how beneficial it is to pause and reflect with our own patients. One of them, a woman in her 70s, was the matriarch of her family, the one who made Sunday dinners. She sought and received approval for assisted dying after she lost the ability to cook. She felt she had lost her value to her family. Through counseling, she came to understand that her family valued who she was, not what she did for them. She decided not to go through with ending her life, at least for now. That Christmas, her family gathered and she sat proudly at the table, while others did the cooking and serving.

Another patient, a man in his 80s, refused a new treatment that might extend his life and instead requested and was approved for assisted dying. He survived the Holocaust as a child and viewed the freedom to choose the timing of his own death as a way of reclaiming what Hitler had taken away from his parents. However, his living family’s grief mattered to him, too, and they had concerns about him giving up too soon. With counseling, he chose to delay. Months later, he had adapted to his illness and continued to find meaning in his life. Eventually he got sicker and Dr. Li told him he was at risk of losing capacity to consent to assisted dying. This time, he chose the procedure, fully supported and surrounded by his family.

Cases like this are not arguments against assisted dying, and we do not seek to dissuade patients from going forward with the procedure. We are arguing instead that medical providers pause, that they help their patients (in both Track 1 and Track 2) consider and truly understand alternatives that might relieve their suffering and allow them the possibility of more time to live meaningfully.

What form should that pause take? We do not believe patients requesting assisted dying need to be assessed for a psychiatric disorder as a matter of course. We do, however, find that most benefit from counseling and reflective conversations. Unfortunately, psychological care of this kind for patients requesting assisted dying is not routinely offered by doctors or other health care providers, nor is it routinely covered by insurance. It should be the standard of care and fully funded.

We have developed and demonstrated the effectiveness of one such approach, which we have called Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully, or CALM. This approach helps patients with advanced cancer sustain engagement in life, while approaching and preparing for the end of life.

Physicians are expected to explore what is driving a patient’s stated preference, whether it might change and what alternatives exist. This is called shared decision-making. It is standard practice in medicine — except for assisted dying in Canada.

A society that permits assisted dying should also ask whether it has done enough to help people sustain their sense of dignity and meaning in life. Death must not become the only kind of relief people can imagine.

Madeline Li and Gary Rodin are professors of psychiatry at the University of Toronto.

SUMMARY

Many people who have experienced significant mental illness collect diagnoses over time, like stamps on a passport. More than half of people who qualify for one diagnosis also qualify for another during their lifetime. Moreover, research shows that genetic risks associated with brain disorders aren’t confined to specific types: If your biological parents have, say, depression, you not only have an increased risk of developing depression, but you may also be more likely to receive a diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, autism or schizophrenia.

ARTICLE

I Was Labeled Bipolar, Depressed, O.C.D. Here’s Why.
More than half of people who qualify for one diagnosis also qualify for another during their lifetime.
By Maia Szalavitz
Published 2026-10-05 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/opinion/mental-health-diagnosis-labels.html

Many people who have experienced significant mental illness collect diagnoses over time, like stamps on a passport. I have had at least six. As a toddler, I was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or A.D.H.D., because even though I was reading at 3, I was overwhelmed by noises, lights and preschool. In my 20s, the diagnosis was cocaine and heroin use disorder, which landed me in rehab. There, in a five-minute psychiatrist visit, I was labeled bipolar. Later, I picked up labels of depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

After reading a 2004 article in The Times about autism, I realized that this diagnosis seemed to fit better than any of the others. Sensory overload? Check. Intense intellectual obsessions, social difficulties, desire for sameness, self-soothing behaviors? Check, check, check, check. My other diagnoses seemed to result, in large part, from attempts to cope with these aspects of my neurology.

I am far from alone in having a long, strange diagnostic journey. More than half of people who qualify for one diagnosis also qualify for another during their lifetime. The earlier in life someone develops a disorder, the more likely he or she is to experience multiple conditions. Moreover, research shows that genetic risks associated with brain disorders aren’t confined to specific types: If your biological parents have, say, depression, you not only have an increased risk of developing depression, but you may also be more likely to receive a diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, autism or schizophrenia. And sometimes, a diagnosis is just wrong.

This high prevalence of overlapping diagnoses — known as comorbidity — in mental health care suggests that the labels psychiatrists assign using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders aren’t like those in most of medicine. That is to say: Mental health diagnoses often do not define distinct, specific pathologies. The former director of the National Institute of Mental Health, Thomas Insel, analogized psychiatric diagnosis to diagnosing someone with “chest pain disorder,” whether that pain is caused by a heart attack or heartburn. We need a better system than that.

As leaders in psychiatry embark on a revision of the D.S.M. that they aim to publish in the next few years, improving diagnosis is taking center stage.

One way to address this problem is to focus on commonalities between disorders, rather than distinctions. Some researchers have gone so far as to claim that there is an underlying, shared factor (or, more likely, factors) that causes a majority of mental illness. Avshalom Caspi, a professor of psychology at Duke University, has called it the “p factor,” for psychopathology.

So what is “p”? One candidate is childhood trauma, which strongly raises the risk for nearly all psychiatric conditions, ranging from anxiety and depression to schizophrenia and personality disorders.

Another possible “p” is found in the genes that affect brain development. For example, a 2023 study in the journal Nature Medicine found that people who had genes associated with excess connections in the frontal regions of the brain — which regulate emotional responses and behavior — also had a higher risk for many types of mental disorders. This is especially striking because during adolescence and early adulthood (when 75 percent of mental illnesses start to show), the brain undergoes a process of pruning redundant or little-used connections.

In some cases, “p” may be less about a shared cause of mental illness and more about the way symptoms of one illness can lead to additional mental distress. Indeed, my diagnoses often reinforced one another. My oversensitivity and difficulty making friends led to me being bullied, which contributed to depression. Depression, isolation and a feeling of being overwhelmed by experiences led me to become addicted to drugs. Perhaps all of that was a response to having a hyperconnected brain, which some evidence links to both autistic abilities, like systematic thinking, and autistic disabilities, like extreme social struggles.

While some researchers are debating how to rewrite the D.S.M., others are developing alternatives to it that better take into account how symptoms overlap. One, known as the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, or HiTOP, classifies disorders based on shared symptom clusters and common underlying features, known as spectra. For instance, the “internalizing” spectrum encompasses symptoms related to emotional distress, anxiety, depression and mood difficulties. The “externalizing” one is related to impulsivity and risk-taking behavior.

HiTOP also recognizes that a mental illness is not an on-off switch but that symptoms exist on a continuum: A person might be a bit compulsive, but not to a disabling degree, or she may have severe obsessions and compulsions, perhaps in the context of anorexia or autism. Under HiTOP, that wouldn’t require multiple diagnoses. This makes the system more flexible, because it assumes that people and their symptoms will vary over time and that underlying issues can take different forms as people mature.

Efforts like HiTOP will not replace the D.S.M. any time soon — but, ideally, they will improve understanding of the causes of symptoms and how these symptoms interact.

In psychiatry, diagnoses aren’t just labels to help clinicians treat patients; they are also ways that people come to understand themselves. Even though “schizophrenia” and “depression” may not be as clearly defined as “Covid-19,” knowing that your problems tend to take a particular shape and can be managed with relevant treatment can be crucial for healing.

For me, learning that I was on the autism spectrum was an enormous relief, and I wish it had happened earlier. Finally, my oddities made sense. For many people, being diagnosed allows them to stop blaming themselves for their temperaments and address traits that are dysfunctional, while embracing those that are harmless or positive. In a recent paper, the psychiatrist Awais Aftab and the religion scholar Alan Levinovitz termed this experience the “Rumpelstiltskin effect,” after the fairy tale in which naming the bad guy takes away his power.

Others, however, see labels as life sentences that preclude recovery or high quality of life. Whether it’s the D.S.M., HiTOP or any other approach, improving diagnosis will require reckoning with the complex ways people respond to their temperaments and experiences — including the fact that the same psychiatric label and accompanying treatment can be a poison, a panacea or a placebo, depending on how wisely we apply them to ourselves or others.

Maia Szalavitz is a contributing Opinion writer who covers addiction, mental health and public policy.

One human who has deep thoughts on that mystery is Daniel Lieberman, an evolutionary biologist at Harvard. Dr. Lieberman is one of 100 scientists to whom the writers and editors on The Times’s Science desk recently posed a query of their own: “What is a big unanswered question in your field?” Imagine them, perhaps, as a road map for the future of science — charting long journeys of human exploration that will be well worth the trip, even if we never see the destination.

ARTICLE

What Are the Biggest Questions in Science Today? 100 Scientists Weigh In.
We asked 100 scientists about unsolved problems in their fields. They sent back provocations — on the origins of life, the possibilities for human progress and much more.
By Bill Wasik
Published 2026-10-05 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/science/100-unanswered-questions-science.html

Are you proud of your chin?

You should be. In fact, give it an appreciative rub right now, or admire it in the mirror: That bony protuberance jutting out past your teeth is a trait that distinguishes you from the rest of the animal kingdom. Even your extinct hominin cousins — those enigmatic Neanderthals and Denisovans who strode bipedally like humans and even sometimes mated with them — never belonged to the chin club.

But why just us? One human who has deep thoughts on that mystery is Daniel Lieberman, an evolutionary biologist at Harvard. It’s a question he loves to ponder in part because his students love to ponder it, too. When he poses it to them in class, he says, “it always gets them on the edge of their seat, even though it’s completely unimportant.”

Dr. Lieberman is one of 100 scientists to whom the writers and editors on The Times’s Science desk recently posed a query of their own: “What is a big unanswered question in your field?” Responses poured in from biochemists, quantum physicists, archaeologists, oceanographers, Nobel Prize-winning biologists, geoscientists, entomologists, you name it.

Scroll down and you can read the 100 questions they sent back — a list that demonstrates the fascinating range of the scientific mission and mind-set. Some questions aim at concrete, day-to-day mysteries (“How do ants work together to produce the collective behavior of colonies?” asks Deborah Gordon, a biologist). Others interrogate first principles: “What determines the laws of physics as they exist in our universe?” Katie Mack, an astrophysicist, wonders. Still others express an urgency about human problems that want solving — like “Can we make the wildlife trade sustainable?” and “Can the human aging process be safely reversed?”

And some, like Dr. Lieberman’s, express a pure curiosity for its own sake. Various hypotheses have tried to explain why chins might have helped our ancestors survive, he notes, but none really make sense. The only one left is sexual selection: Maybe chins made some hominins more attractive to the opposite sex, and the trait won out over time. But the theory is impossible to prove; testing it would entail “showing pictures of people without chins and asking if you would sleep with them,” which, Dr. Lieberman notes, is “a terrible experiment.”

In that regard, it’s one of the many big questions below that are most likely impossible to answer, at least not in our lifetimes. Still, we hope you’ll spend some time pondering them yourself. Imagine them, perhaps, as a road map for the future of science — charting long journeys of human exploration that will be well worth the trip, even if we never see the destination.

K. R. Callaway, Stella Raine Chu, Carolyn Y. Johnson, Carl Zimmer, Katrina Miller, Amber Williams, Alan Burdick and Alexandra Sifferlin contributed reporting.

consciousness-brain-babies.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 34  Words: 1792/1812

SUMMARY

Even if we can’t say when babies gain consciousness, Dr. Austin said, “one thing we can be certain of is that they will become conscious.” Some experiments have failed to find certain other markers of consciousness in babies. But what if consciousness has more dimensions, more ways of being?

ARTICLE

Are Babies Conscious?
By pinpointing when it begins in young humans, scientists hope to better understand what consciousness is, and how it arises, in all of us.
By Carl Zimmer
Published 2026-10-05 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/science/consciousness-brain-babies.html

Imagine that a scientist sits you in a device that can detect changes in the activity of your brain, and then plays a cycle of sounds. Over and over you hear three low tones, followed by a high one. Then your hear something different: four low tones in a row.

The scientist doesn’t have to ask you if you were aware of the change. That’s because our brains typically respond to an oddball sound with a brief, distinctive blip.

That blip turns out to be a surprisingly reliable marker of consciousness — that complex, mysterious state of being aware of one’s own thoughts and one’s existence in the world, which may also be present to some degree in other animals. People in a coma don’t produce this blip when they hear oddball sounds. Nor do people who are asleep.

Now imagine that the parents of a newborn bring their baby into the same lab for the same test. The tones play. Will there be a blip? Is that squirming, gurgling infant conscious? As humans, they are potentially conscious; we know that much. But in the moment, with their semi-developed brains and cognitive limitations — they can’t yet speak, focus their eyes, respond to instructions — they don’t seem to be conscious, at least not in the way adults are. Indeed, there’s an active scientific debate over whether newborns possess consciousness. Resolving it could help solve one of science’s most stubborn mysteries: what consciousness is, how it emerges and how we can know if another being possesses it.

Ask any researcher who studies consciousness, and they probably have a rough but useful definition. “Consciousness is a process of being receptive to the outside world and mixing that with our own internal world, to create the feeling of who we are and where we are,” said Dr. Topun Austin, a neonatologist at the University of Cambridge.

But Dr. Austin is well aware that this definition doesn’t speak to how that process plays out: where in the brain consciousness arises from the activity of neurons, or how their symphony of signals creates that feeling of being ourselves in the world.

Scientists have developed many detailed theories to address those questions. But there’s little accord on which is right, with no resolution in sight. “There’s not a consensus that we all agree on,” said Joel Frohlich, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Tübingen in Germany.

The stakes have only grown in recent years. Researchers have implanted millions of functional human brain cells in mice, for instance, prompting speculation that the work might someday endow mice with consciousness. Philosophers and theologians are musing about whether A.I. will become conscious, and how we can know for sure.

Amid all the uncertainty, there’s one fact that everyone can agree on. In each of our lives, there was a time when our brains were still too rudimentary to support consciousness, and there was a time when that changed. Even if we can’t say when babies gain consciousness, Dr. Austin said, “one thing we can be certain of is that they will become conscious.”

In recent years, Dr. Austin and other researchers have zeroed in on that transition. They are using new kinds of brain-scanning technology to study the brains of babies as never before, giving infants not only the blip tests, but even investigating what babies experience before birth. By determining when consciousness fully blooms, perhaps they can advance our understanding of how it works, and what it does, in all of us.

“I really see it as a frontier area in consciousness science,” Dr. Frohlich said.

Darwin’s babies

When Charles Darwin became a father in 1839, he opened a notebook. Observing his children, he believed, could help him understand a question that fascinated him: “How does consciousness commence?”

By the time his first son, William, was born, Darwin had come to embrace the idea of evolution: The human mind, endowed with consciousness, had evolved over many generations from simpler instincts. Darwin also believed that all children followed a similar path in their early lives, as their brains developed from simple structures into complex vessels of thought. And so, starting with William and continuing with his subsequent children, he kept careful notes about how young humans changed over the first months of life.

At first Darwin recorded “instinctive actions” such as “sneezing, hickuping, yawning, stretching, and of course sucking and screaming.” Only when his children grew older did any mention of sophisticated behavior start to appear in his notebook: His children learned to recognize themselves in mirrors, spoke simple words, reached for objects. Before then, he declared, “There is no trace of consciousness in very young children.”.

Darwin was hardly an outlier in this belief. Doctors of the time also assumed babies were not conscious, and that assumption shaped their care of babies for generations. During surgery on newborns, for example, it was common not to use anesthesia; the drugs might damage a young brain — if babies weren’t conscious, what was the value of making them unconscious? As recently as the 1980s, doctors routinely withheld anesthesia from newborns, seeing no benefits that might offset the risks.

Doctors have since reversed this practice, as the study of babies has matured. More recent research has found, for instance, that newborns process pain signals in many regions of the brain, suggesting that their experience is similar to that of older children and adults.

Other studies have found signs that babies are capable of surprisingly complex forms of thought long before they can speak. They can recognize that a face is more than the sum of its parts; they can carry out simple forms of math in their heads. Findings like these made scientists rethink Darwin’s conclusion; perhaps consciousness emerges earlier than previously believed.

To explore that possibility, researchers have borrowed some of the methods used to gauge consciousness in adults, like playing those oddball sounds. In an experiment in Germany, scientists placed newborns in a special crib lined with sensors that could detect tiny magnetic fluctuations, then outfitted the babies with earphones. When the researchers played combinations of low and high tones, the brains of the babies produced distinct blips in response.

“It shows that the newborn brain is already performing very close to what we find in an adult brain,” said Claudia Passos-Ferreira, a philosopher at New York University.

But Dr. Passos-Ferreira and other researchers don’t consider that one finding conclusive. Some experiments have failed to find certain other markers of consciousness in babies. So researchers are running many different tests, to perhaps identify a cluster of markers of consciousness.

“If we see a lot of markers appearing at the same time, that’s highly suggestive that this is when consciousness begins,” Dr. Frohlich said.

Some of the most promising recent results have come from a major effort in London called the Developing Connectome Project. To carry it out, scientists had to modify a functional magnetic resonance imaging device. Normally, adult subjects lie on a table that slides into a large cylinder. Instead, engineers built a small cradle with a plastic head-cap at one end, to detect activity in a baby’s brain.

The project team ran brain scans on hundreds of babies, including newborns. They drew maps of the infant brains and recorded electrical activity that arose spontaneously during the 15-minute-long scans.

Lorina Naci, a neuroscientist at Trinity College Dublin, and her colleagues have been busy analyzing those recordings. One hallmark of consciousness in adults is the way different parts of the brain become active in a coordinated fashion. Those connections can evaporate when adults are asleep, or are under anesthesia. In recent studies, Dr. Naci’s team has discovered that regions of baby brains become active together in networks that are similar to those of waking adults, offering another early marker of consciousness.

In the meantime, new technology is speeding up data collection: Instead of putting babies in scanners, researchers can fit caps on their heads that monitor the brain with ultrasound or light.

Mapping the birth of consciousness

As more markers of consciousness turn up in newborns, scientists have begun wondering what’s happening in the fetal brain, before birth.

Dr. Naci and her colleagues have found that some babies born prematurely also display networks of active brain regions that hint at conscious experiences. Dr. Frohlich and his colleague are studying fetuses that are still in utero, by having pregnant volunteers lean their bellies on a device that can detect the faint magnetic fields produced by fetal brains.

For now, consciousness before birth is an even bigger mystery than consciousness in newborns. Scientists generally agree that consciousness cannot emerge before the fetal brain has matured enough to receive signals from the senses, and then integrate them into a unified experience. Before about 26 weeks of gestation, those neural connections don’t exist.

How soon afterward these connections develop, scientists can only guess at. In a survey of experts by Dr. Passos-Ferreira, most estimated that infants have some consciousness by the time they are born.

“There are still some skeptics about infant consciousness who think that it emerges later,” Dr. Passos-Ferreira said. “It’s a minority, but they’re still there.”

As scientists map the birth of consciousness, they hope to gain a better understanding of how it evolved in humans in the first place. For children and adults, consciousness is vital for communicating through language, and for carrying out complex forms of thought. But if babies turn out to be conscious at birth, and long before they can talk or make plans for the future, then it must serve some additional purposes.

Perhaps, Dr. Naci said, consciousness allows babies to start making sense of the world as soon as they enter it, “to help them really hit the ground running in terms learning and development as soon they are born.”

But, she added, understanding consciousness in babies may demand a change in how we typically think of consciousness in general. By counting all the ways that the regions of a baby’s brain interact with each other from second to second, Dr. Naci and her colleagues have found that the baby brain actually exhibits more complexity than a waking adult’s. We tend to think of consciousness along a single line, on a gradient from unconscious to fully conscious. It’s the road we travel each day as we wake, and sleep. But what if consciousness has more dimensions, more ways of being?

Dr. Naci speculates that babies may be conscious at birth, but in a way that is perhaps more open to the world. “The idea is that they have this capacity to perceive more of the environment in much richer and more diverse ways,” she said. “They could have a very different experience than we have as grown adults.”

ARTICLE

This High-Profile Campaign May Be the Ugliest in the Country
The candidates for Ohio governor have significant policy differences, but the campaign ads have been strikingly personal, with exaggerated portrayals of one candidate as a con artist and the other as a drunk.
By Campbell Robertson
Published 2026-10-05 17:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/elections/ohio-governor-election.html

Of all the mudslinging and smear campaigning across the country in this fraught election year, few races are as nasty as the one for governor of Ohio.

Dr. Amy Acton, a Democrat who was once the state’s chief public health officer, holds a narrow lead against Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican who made a mint in pharmaceutical start-ups, according to a New York Times and Siena University poll released on Sunday.

The two candidates differ significantly on policy matters, but their campaign advertisements, mailers and social media have not all been about substance.

Instead, voters might think one candidate is a con artist; the other is a drunk.

“It’s definitely ugly,” said Christopher Gagin, the former chairman of the Belmont County Republican Party. In past races, he and others said, even hard-hitting attack ads were mostly based on issues or a candidate’s past performance in office. “This,” Mr. Gagin said, “is all very, very personal.”

As is often the case, the campaign attacks in Ohio might be based on actual events, but the sound bites are hardly the full stories. Voters might actually be tuning out all the toxicity.

Dr. Acton, who has faced an onslaught of attacks maligning her as a violent pill popper, is viewed more favorably than unfavorably by voters, according to the Times/Siena poll. Mr. Ramaswamy, who has been accused of making millions by swindling everyday Ohioans, is viewed more unfavorably than favorably, but by a narrow margin not much different from surveys taken months ago.

And there are few signs that the specific nature of the attacks is undermining traditional partisan loyalties.

Despite being painted as an out-of-touch billionaire, Mr. Ramaswamy has a healthy lead among Ohioans without college degrees, as would be expected for any Republican these days. Dr. Acton, painted as scandalously underqualified, has an even larger lead among Ohioans with college degrees, a reliable Democratic constituency.

Still, even if the voters are ignoring them, the ads are unquestionably nasty, especially the ones launched by groups backing Mr. Ramaswamy that aim at Dr. Acton.

“Ohio is not new to negative advertising, but typically that revolves around issues or maybe tying candidates to unpopular national figures,” said Robert Alexander, a professor at Bowling Green State University in northwest Ohio who directs a statewide poll. “But the personal nature, particularly of those anti-Acton ads, have been somewhat alarming.”

Ramaswamy backers are outspending the Acton camp on advertising by a more than three-to-one margin, and many of their ads have inflated the events of a single night in the Columbus suburbs in late August 2019.

A daughter of Dr. Acton’s called 911 to say that her stepfather and her mother were fighting and that her mother had been “drinking and throwing things.” In an incident report, a police officer who came to the house wrote that Dr. Acton and her husband had been arguing about her long work hours and that in the course of the argument she “grabbed hold of a mirror on the wall and pulled it down,” breaking the glass. The officer wrote that the two had been drinking and that she had taken medication.

The police left and nothing came of it — until it was reported by NBC News this past April. Dr. Acton’s husband, Eric Acton, said in a statement that his wife had a single drink that night and that the argument, which he said he had started, was over before the police showed up. The Acton campaign said the prescription medications were for migraines and high blood pressure. As for the mirror, she bumped into it, knocking it off the wall, the campaign said.

But the incident has become something of a foundational text for a vicious oeuvre of attacks. The state Republican Party has described Dr. Acton as “violent,” and “unstable,” posting computer-generated images of her jeep with a license plate that reads “Drunk Mom” or staring into a broken mirror on which is written, in blood-red lettering, “Mom has been drinking.”

“Amy Acton: Drinking. Drugs. Disaster. Disqualified,” said one ad among many, showing a spilled wine glass, an empty pill bottle and a woman passed out on a couch.

Candidates typically turn negative when they are down in the polls, and the Times/Siena poll has been among several recent surveys showing Mr. Ramaswamy narrowly behind. But, Professor Alexander said, the main problem facing Republicans this year is a discouraged electorate, and it’s unclear that this strategy would fix that.

“Are you really inspiring people with those kinds of attacks?” he asked.

Jai Chabria, chief strategist for the Ramaswamy campaign, pointed out that these ads were from outside spending groups, not the campaign itself, but he defended their content.

“The instances that are described in those ads are factual, and they point to a person who doesn’t have the capability to take on a chief executive role,” he said. “I think it’s completely fair.”

The Acton campaign cited the “baseless lies about her and her family” as the reason Dr. Acton was not going to debate Mr. Ramaswamy.

The Democrats’ counteroffensive has not been as intensely personal, directing its fire instead at Mr. Ramaswamy’s business history and ample wealth. But the hits have been nasty all the same.

Ads have called Mr. Ramaswamy a “con man” and a “swindler,” emphasizing the millions he made pitching his pharmaceutical start-ups and suggesting criminality that authorities have not alleged. One prominent ad features a widower whose wife had suffered from Alzheimer’s disease, accusing Mr. Ramaswamy of making “hundreds of millions of dollars scamming people like me.”

(The ad is not dissimilar to an ad from the Ramaswamy campaign, in which a woman says she would never forgive Dr. Acton for the fact that her mother died alone during Covid lockdowns. But an obituary surfaced by a progressive Ohio outlet showed that the woman’s mother died in Kentucky, six weeks after Dr. Acton had left state government in Ohio.)

While the anti-Ramaswamy ad does not make clear precisely how the man believes he was scammed, it is referring to Axovant, one of Mr. Ramaswamy’s pharmaceutical companies.

Axovant, which employed eight people, including Mr. Ramaswamy’s mother and brother, both physicians, was founded to bring to market an Alzheimer’s drug that the pharmaceutical giant GlaxoSmithKline had given up on after four failed clinical trials.

Mr. Ramaswamy talked up the drug, intepirdine, wherever he could, portraying it as a potential breakthrough that “could help millions” of people. Then, six months after buying the drug, he took Axovant public in a debut that sent the company’s market value soaring to nearly $3 billion.

In late 2015, Mr. Ramaswamy sold off a portion of Axovant’s parent company, Roivant, claiming more than $37 million in capital gains on his tax return that year. In August 2017, he secured another big payday for Roivant when the Japanese conglomerate SoftBank led an investment of $1.1 billion in Roivant, which had a broad portfolio of pharmaceuticals. A few weeks later, intepirdine failed in a clinical trial and Axovant stock plunged.

The Acton camp has framed these events as a classic “pump and dump” that made Mr. Ramaswamy hugely rich while fleecing regular folks in the form of pension funds and retirement investments.

Mr. Ramaswamy has strongly denied such claims, saying if he had held onto the Roivant shares he sold, he would have made money. In an interview with The Times during his failed presidential campaign in 2023, he said criticism of his actions “grates on me a little bit.”

But in the ugly Ohio race, that criticism has taken center stage.

“Vivek Ramaswamy is a billionaire scam artist who pumped up an Alzheimer's drug that he knew didn’t work, gave false hope to millions of impacted families, and cashed out days before the drug failed,” Addie Bullock, a spokeswoman for the Acton campaign, wrote in an email. “Now, he’s running a disgusting smear campaign riddled with ads that have been condemned as ‘defamatory’ and ‘vile’.”
