glacier-archaeology-melting-alps.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 30  Words: 1200/1200
================================================================================

SUMMARY

The Alps are losing ice faster than almost anywhere on the planet. Secrets like an enigmatic, 2,500-year-old ski that melted not long ago out of a strip of dying Swiss ice. It would be the latest in a growing trove of tools, garments and human remains that archaeologists have recovered from the Alps’ shriveling ice.

ARTICLE

A 2,500-Year-Old Ski? The Melting Alps Release Ancient Secrets.
Archaeologists are scouring mountain passes as artifacts from a bygone world all but tumble out of Switzerland’s shrinking ice.
By Raymond Zhong, Giacomo d’Orlando and Mira Rojanasakul
Published 2026-10-06 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/climate/glacier-archaeology-melting-alps.html

The Alps are losing ice faster than almost anywhere on the planet. And, as the glaciers and ice patches disappear, they are releasing secrets that had been locked away for millenniums.

Secrets like an enigmatic, 2,500-year-old ski that melted not long ago out of a strip of dying Swiss ice.

On a bright recent morning, Romain Andenmatten, a 42-year-old archaeologist, peered down at his discovery. Exploring the paltry remains of the ice at a mountain pass called Col de Barberine, he spotted a three-foot-long slat of grayish wood, nestled between rocks at the ice’s edge.

Three years ago at this same pass, elevation 7,500 feet, Dr. Andenmatten found a similar plank, also with a tapered end suggesting a ski or snowshoe. Carbon dating revealed it to be from roughly the fifth century B.C., when, on a certain day in the Iron Age, its owner might have been crossing the Alps and lost his footing.

Now Dr. Andenmatten wondered whether he’d found the second in the pair. It would be the latest in a growing trove of tools, garments and human remains that archaeologists have recovered from the Alps’ shriveling ice.

Between a winter of little snow and a summer of broiling heat waves, this year has been another devastating one for Switzerland’s glaciers. They have shed nearly 20 percent of their volume over the past five years, scientists said this month. At the current pace of global warming, 97 percent of today’s glaciers across the Alps could be gone by century’s end, posing big challenges for the tens of millions of Europeans for whom the ice is a vital reserve of water in dry years.

In much of the world, it’s mostly stone, metal and pottery that survive from ancient times. Not in the Alps, where the ice has preserved organic materials — leather, wood, textiles, body parts — that can tell a richer, more human story about the past.

“The Stone Age was not really a stone age,” said Regula Gubler, an archaeologist for the Swiss canton of Bern. “Most of what people used and wore was made out of organic materials,” she said. To find the leather shoes that protected their feet, the baskets of woven lime bark they carried into the mountains, “that’s just really special,” Ms. Gubler said.

The objects that have welled up out of Switzerland’s ice span the ordinary to the beguiling.

A fragment of an elm wood bowl from the fifth millennium B.C., long before the pyramids of Egypt and Stonehenge. A birch bark quiver with two flint arrowheads tucked inside, from around 2800 B.C. A two-foot-long statuette sculpted from larch, with a human figure at one end and a sharpened point at the other, from the last two centuries B.C., its purpose unknown.

Such discoveries are challenging old ideas about how early societies interacted with the alpine environment. Far from being forbidding, off-limits zones, the icy mountain passes apparently bustled with traffic: hunters, herdsmen, traders bearing barrels of wine on mules.

“The Alps were always used; it wasn’t an empty space,” Ms. Gubler said.

Nor, evidently, did early populations limit themselves to the gentlest routes. Their preferred paths between valleys seem to have been the shortest ones, never mind the steepness or the elevation.

There’s an urgency to the archaeologists’ work. Once organic materials are defrosted and exposed, they decompose quickly, or are snatched up by private treasure hunters. In 2024, the police and the archaeological authorities in the canton of Valais seized a collection of 11,000 artifacts, including coins, tools and decorative objects from as far back as the Bronze Age, and questioned a man for using a metal detector to scavenge them without permission.

With so many small glaciers and ice patches disappearing each year, some relics are probably doomed never to be found, to be consigned to oblivion simply because no one was in the right place, at the right moment, to spot it.

“An archive of human existence in the Alps is being lost,” said Marcel Cornelissen, an independent archaeologist based near Bern.

Archaeologists in Valais are maximizing their eyes on the ground with an app they developed, IceWatcher. Anyone — hikers, shepherds, crystal collectors — can use it to report potential finds in the mountains.

It was through IceWatcher that Dr. Andenmatten, an archaeologist for Valais’s cantonal government, heard in 2024 about some fragments of wood in an ice patch. He hiked up to a crossing called Restipass and collected some pieces that he later dated to the Bronze Age, making them perhaps 3,000 years old. Some might have been stakes in the ice that marked paths for travelers and warned of crevasses. Others might have been pieces of a sled or scraps of firewood.

Now, he and a colleague, David Gucker, were going back to see what this year’s sweltering temperatures had uncovered.

They drove up switch-backed roads and hiked for two hours through steepening alpine meadows. Finally, they clambered up to the pass and got a shock: The ice was all but gone. When Dr. Andenmatten was here two years ago, it had carpeted the slope where they stood. Now it was barely an icy area rug, leaking streams of water.

Sometimes, the ice in these passes can shrink noticeably over the course of a single day of fieldwork, Dr. Andenmatten said. “In the past, climate change might have unfolded over several generations, or over a lifetime,” he said. “Today, we experience it almost day to day.”

He and Mr. Gucker scoured the gravel and stones. They were well above the tree line, so any wood here had to have been brought by humans. The question was when: five years ago, or 5,000?

Dr. Andenmatten was in his element. He leaped from rock to rock like a mountain goat, flashing an impish, gaptoothed grin.

Something caught his eye: two slender pieces of wood, with smooth, squared-off edges. Delicate tree rings ran through them like flaky layers of mille-feuille pastry.

Dr. Andenmatten rotated the pieces this way and that. It wasn’t obvious they’d fit together. But miraculously, they did, and with that they transformed from lifeless fragments into an implement, something crafted by human hands.

“Really nice, this piece,” Dr. Andenmatten declared, before tucking it into a plastic bag.

Using satellite images and topographic maps, Swiss archaeologists are working with environmental scientists to predict where the next discoveries might emerge.

It would be “amazing” to find something atop a mountain peak, not just in the passes below, said Albert Hafner, an emeritus professor of archaeology at the University of Bern. Prehistoric people crossed the Alps, but we don’t know whether they scaled them, or, if they did, why. “We know that mountains were sacred in many cultures,” Dr. Hafner said. A religious object on a peak might reveal something about early people’s curiosities, their beliefs, their inner lives.

The next morning, Dr. Andenmatten hiked into the mountains again, to Col de Barberine. There, he found the possible second ski.

A ski might not tell us much about inner lives. But “the thing that is for me more spectacular is that it’s conserved,” Dr. Andenmatten said — that an accident of nature has allowed this modest object to speak across the ages.

gender-identity-gap-voting-polarization.html

SUMMARY

The traditional gender gap is losing ground as a key factor in politics to intragender gaps that have emerged among Republican and Democratic voters along the fault lines of masculinity and femininity. This recent development involves differences within each gender, as opposed to the gender gap between men and women, which came to the forefront in the aftermath of the 1980 election between Ronald Reagan and Jimmy Carter, The gap between the two is just as significant if not more significant than the gender gap.

ARTICLE

The Gender Gap Has Taken a Strange Turn
Republican and Democratic voters are seeing masculinity and femininity very differently.
By Thomas B. Edsall
Published 2026-10-06 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/opinion/gender-identity-gap-voting-polarization.html

The traditional gender gap is losing ground as a key factor in politics to intragender gaps that have emerged among Republican and Democratic voters along the fault lines of masculinity and femininity.

This recent development involves differences within each gender, as opposed to the gender gap between men and women, which came to the forefront in the aftermath of the 1980 election between Ronald Reagan and Jimmy Carter,

Men — specifically white men — who see themselves as extremely masculine tend to support President Trump, while those who are weaker in their assessment of their masculinity — or in how they think about masculinity — are far less likely to support Trump. The gap between the two is just as significant if not more significant than the gender gap.

A similar, but more complex spread has emerged among women, although it is smaller and lends itself to competing interpretations.

While the invocation of intragender gaps instead of a “gender gap” may sound like an intellectual exercise relevant only in ivory towers, the size of these gaps provides insight into the distinct Republican and Democratic policy agendas that have emerged in recent years.

The Republican Party, long the champion of traditional family values, now draws an even larger share of voters who believe in traditional gender roles, conventional masculinity and heterosexual family norms. And the party has gotten more conservative on these issues over the past few years.

For example, the percentage of Republicans who view “gay or lesbian relations” as “morally acceptable” fell this year to 35 percent, according to Gallup, from 56 percent in 2022.

A 2024 Pew Research Center report found that 53 percent of Republican-leaning men consider themselves to be highly masculine compared with 29 percent of Democratic-leaning men. The same survey found that a plurality of Republican-leaning men (45 percent) believe that Americans in general have a mostly negative view of “manly or masculine,” while a plurality of Democratic men believe Americans generally have a positive view of masculine or manly men (46 percent).

These intragender gaps may have begun to open up before Trump took center stage, although his dominant presence has prompted an intensification of — and reverence for — hypermasculinity among Republican voters, especially men.

The gender gap is a relatively simple comparison of the differences between men and women in their votes for Democrats or Republicans, or the different levels of support for such policy issues as military and welfare spending.

In the case of women in particular, the intragender gap is more subtle. But before going there, let me register a note of caution and frustration.

In comparison with scholarship on, say, voting or polarization, a disproportionate share of academic work that might provide objective analysis of gender and politics for a lay writer like me is riddled by advocacy in place of research. Fortunately, much of the work on hypermasculinity and femininity, while sometimes jargony, does not suffer these evidentiary weaknesses, with claims often backed up by polling and other data.

In their 2021 article “Beyond the Gender Gap: The Role of Gender Identity,” Elisabeth Gidengil and Dietlind Stolle, both longtime political scientists at McGill University in Montreal, sought to capture “a person’s gendered sense of self.”

In a survey, they asked white men and women “how feminine they feel and how masculine they feel, using seven-point scales.”

Having two dimensions, they wrote, was crucial

to identifying hypermasculine men: These men do not just exhibit an exaggerated form of masculinity; they fear feminization. In order to take account of the strength of their gender identity, respondents were also asked how important it was to them to feel feminine or masculine on a scale from 1 (not at all important) to 7 (very important).

What did they find?

In comparison to the 13.6-point gender gap in support for Trump, the intragender differences between hypermasculine men (81.9 percent favored Trump) and men with a “weak” sense of their masculinity (a little less than 30 percent backed Trump) was much larger at over 50 points.

Put another way, the intragender gap for men is nearly four times as large as the gender gap between men and women.

There is evidence that the growth of gender identity among men was a key factor in Trump’s victories in 2016 and 2024.

In “Gendered Personalities and the Partisan Gender Gap,” a chapter in the book “Masculinity, Femininity, and American Political Behavior,” published three months before Trump’s 2016 presidential victory, Monika L. McDermott, a political scientist at Fordham, offered an

alternative theory for the perceived partisan “gender gap” (or sex gap) between men and women. The traditional explanation — that it is differences between men and women that drive this phenomenon — assumes that the presumed causal mechanisms, such as degree of compassion, split fairly cleanly along the lines of biological sex. Gendered personalities demonstrate, however, that this assumption is out of place in today’s world. The analyses show that levels of both masculinity and femininity influence party affiliation, vote choice and ideology, regardless of an individual’s sex. The more feminine an individual is, the more Democratic in both identification and voting, and the more liberal. The more masculine an individual is, the more Republican and conservative. These effects occur not only regardless of sex but also in place of them.

The argument receives support from a different vantage point from Melissa Deckman, the chief executive of the Public Religion Research Institute, and Erin Cassese, a political scientist at the University of Delaware.

They argue in their 2019 paper “Gendered Nationalism and the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election: How Party, Class, and Beliefs about Masculinity Shaped Voting Behavior” that the 45 percent of American voters who agreed that the United States had become “too soft and feminine” were exhibiting “gendered nationalism” and provided Trump a key bloc of votes.

“Once we controlled for gendered beliefs,” Deckman and Cassese wrote, “specifically support for the notion that America had become too soft and feminine, gender differences in vote choice were not significant. Instead, holding more nationalist views helped to shape voters’ decisions in 2016.”

These findings, Eric Knowles, a professor of psychology at New York University, wrote by email,

make a great deal of sense. One thing that “highly masculine” men and “highly feminine” women have in common is their adherence to traditional American gender norms. Since the G.O.P. has long been the party of culturally conservative values — including those around sex and gender — it makes sense that these men and women would be relatively likely to vote Republican.

Knowles argued that Republican consultants and strategists “are thinking specifically of sex and gender” as vital in fending off defeat in the midterm elections next month. “Republicans are banking on traditional gender values to snatch victory from the jaws of defeat.”

He cited Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, who has portrayed James Talarico, his Democratic opponent, as “Tofu Talarico,” “Six-Gender Jimmy,” “James Tala-freak-o” and “Low-T Talarico.”

For men, the gender identity gap is relatively straightforward. For women, it’s complex and seemingly contradictory.

The women whom the Bem Sex Role Inventory test identified as high in femininity favored Democrats over Republicans. Conversely, women who self-identified as feeling highly feminine were more likely to support Trump and identify as Republican than those who ranked themselves lower on femininity.

But it turns out there is no contradiction. In fact, the two different methodologies identify two separate groups of women with little overlap.

White women who say they feel highly feminine, according to Gidengil and Stolle, are the “most closely linked to the traditional binary gender system.” It follows they would support traditional sex roles, marriage, heterosexuality, motherhood and religious observance — all values linked to the Republican Party.

The Bem Sex Role Inventory, in contrast, uses a series of questions to determine whether the subject is affectionate, compassionate, gentle, sympathetic, sensitive to the needs of others, warm and understanding. These traits are associated with the Democratic Party, and women high on these personality characteristics are more likely to support Democratic candidates.

I asked Stolle for help explaining the antithetical outcomes for women depending on the measurement test used.

“Our measure of hyperfemininity,” she replied,

is how feminine do you feel / how masculine do you feel? (it sometimes adds a measure of salience). This is essentially a subjective gender-identity measure. A woman who places herself very high on femininity and very low on masculinity is saying something like: “I am distinctly feminine, and not masculine,” is part of how I understand myself. That can capture a more strongly differentiated or traditional gender identity, which could plausibly be associated with Trump voting. The B.S.R.I. femininity items, by contrast, select characteristics that have been traditionally associated with being female and being male. For feminine traits, these are mostly communal personality traits and include being affectionate, compassionate, gentle, sympathetic, understanding, warm, sensitive to others, tender and so on. In contemporary politics, those traits could quite plausibly correlate with Democratic voting.

The expanding role of sex, masculinity and femininity in American politics has been a long time in the making.

“During the past three decades, Americans have come to view the parties increasingly in gendered terms of masculinity and femininity,” Nicholas J.G. Winter, a political scientist at the University of Virginia, wrote in 2010.

With considerable prescience, Winter argued that there were “interrelated developments in the late 1970s and early 1980s that we might expect to have mapped masculinity and femininity — already important for politics — onto the Republican and Democratic Parties, respectively.”

These include:

- “The polarization of party elites over the Equal Rights Amendment and other issues of women’s equality in the late 1970s.”
- “Republicans are thought to handle better such issues as defense, dealing with terrorism and controlling crime and drugs; these are precisely the sorts of issues that Americans associate with men or with masculine traits.”
- “The association of women with the Democratic Party is further reinforced by the fact that substantially more women have been elected as Democrats than as Republicans over the past several decades.”
- “The concept of leadership and the political realm itself both carry symbolically male connotations. Perhaps because of this, since the early republic presidential candidates and their campaigns have often emphasized their own masculine credentials and tried to undermine those of their opponents.”

The growing differences between the parties and their voters over masculinity, femininity and sex generally are sharpening the split between Democrats and Republicans over matters of life and death.

Amid rapid advances in technology, artificial intelligence and scientific research, the use of stem cells, the advents of state laws allowing assisted suicide and the disposition of embryos have all become partisan issues, following the path of abortion.

The basic question of whether differences between men and women are rooted in genetics or provoked by social expectations has also become intensely political. Pew Research reports that “majorities of Republicans point to biology as the main driver of differences between men and women,” while, on many issues, Democrats tend to believe these differences are “mostly based on the expectations society has for the two genders.”

As I finish this essay, it occurs to me that the larger issue is that partisanship has become a metastasizing cancer with no boundaries in sight. Soon there will be nothing that partisanship doesn’t distort.

Matthew Tobin contributed research to this article.

SUMMARY

I was in Greece last week attending the Athens Democracy Forum — a gathering of democracy experts and activists from around the world — so I have been thinking a lot about the privilege and the responsibility that go with living in a democracy. ARTICLE

Two Democracy Heroes on America
Sitting on your hands is not an option when democracy is at stake.
By Thomas L. Friedman
Published 2026-10-06 20:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/opinion/middle-east-democracy-iran-us-yemen.html

I was in Greece last week attending the Athens Democracy Forum — a gathering of democracy experts and activists from around the world — so I have been thinking a lot about the privilege and the responsibility that go with living in a democracy. Every morning I ate breakfast at my hotel’s rooftop restaurant, which had a view of the Parthenon — the iconic Greek temple built in the fifth century B.C.E., at the height of Athenian democracy. And every morning the waitress would ask me: “Do you have any allergies?”

Every morning I would bite my tongue to keep from saying: “Well, since you asked, I have two allergies — but they’re political, not biological. I have an allergy to lazy, performative online activism, like ‘Hey, I tweeted about that,’ or ‘Hey, I posted my favorite pop star’s denunciation of Israel on my Facebook page, so get off my back.’ But I also have an allergy to no activism when your own democracy is on the line, like ‘Hey, my law firm does a lot of business with the federal government — we had to cut a deal with Trump.’”

What got me thinking hard about my political allergies was talking to two old friends from the Middle East. Both have taken huge personal risks to tell hard truths and fight for the right to vote in a free and fair election. So they are vexed that so many Americans would sit on their hands in the face of the greatest threat to our democracy in my lifetime — President Trump’s willingness to break rules to hold power.

One of these courageous democracy activists is Tawakkol Karman, the first Yemeni and the first Arab woman to win a Nobel Peace Prize. She won it for her nonviolent leadership of Yemen’s Arab Spring protests demanding democracy, women’s rights and freedom of speech. Karman played a leading role in the peaceful uprising in 2011 that led to the ouster of Ali Abdullah Saleh, the strongman who ruled North Yemen from 1978 and a unified Yemen from 1990 until 2012.

Karman told me over coffee at the Democracy Forum (which is held in association with The New York Times) that she was shocked to see how easily American law firms, universities and even some media companies bent to Trump’s political demands without a fight.

“For me,” Karman said, “as someone who opposed dictatorship, who knows how dictatorship works and knows what we needed to free our country from the dictatorship, it all starts when the head of state controls the media, accuses the media of lies and discredits the media — and then does not play by the rule of law, and the institutions work only for the benefit of him and his family.”

The trigger for the democratic revolution in Yemen was when President Saleh “put his son and his family in the most important institutions,” Karman added. “He attacked the judiciary and emptied it of its work. He escaped all accountability through immunity and interfered in the work of Parliament and the legitimate institutions. And now all of this I am seeing in the United States. What is that?”

The most dangerous thing in a democracy, she said, is when you start to ask yourself: “‘If I do this, what will happen to me? What will the leader do to me?’ Whether you are a journalist, a student or a teacher, you question yourself.” That is what the dictator wants — “to spread fear,” she said. “And when the lawyers don’t do their work, when the journalists don’t do their work, when the scholars don’t do their work, when they all watch themselves before doing or saying something, that is the dictator’s way to control the narrative.”

Karman hasn’t given up hope on America, though. “I gave a speech in North Dakota,” she told me. “There were a lot of conservative people there. They were so welcoming. I told them: ‘Don’t think you are divided because you have the soul of division. It is because someone wants to divide you through hate speech.’ People got very emotional.”

Karman and I first met in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital, in 2013, when I went to observe Yemen’s broad-based national dialogue. New parties, young people, women, Islamists, tribes, northerners and southerners all took part, with the aim of writing a new constitution and holding presidential elections. The process fell apart when the Houthi movement seized the city in September 2014. The Houthis, a Shiite group based in the north of Yemen, were backed by Iran and allied with forces loyal to Saleh. The Houthi takeover plunged Yemen into a catastrophic civil war from which it still has not escaped.

Karman travels the world now promoting democracy through her foundation, while working every day with followers in Yemen to try to win its democracy back from the long arm of Iran.

“What we need from the world is to stand with the Yemeni people and confront Iran’s project to control Bab al-Mandab through the Houthi militia,” she said, referring to the strait at the mouth of the Red Sea. “If Iran, through its Houthi proxy, succeeds in controlling Bab al-Mandab in addition to its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, the consequences for global security could be even more dangerous than Iran possessing a nuclear bomb. This is Yemen’s battle for freedom, democracy and sovereignty, but it is also the world’s battle for peace, security and the freedom of global trade.”

While I was in Athens, a Palestinian democracy activist from East Jerusalem, Samer Sinijlawi, reached out to me with a similar alarm bell. Sinijlawi leads Masar Jadid (New Path), one of the many new parties seeking seats in the Palestinian Legislative Council elections — the first such elections since January 2006.

Yes, folks, there are three big elections coming up that will shape the Middle East: Israel’s on Oct. 27, America’s on Nov. 3 and the Palestinian Authority’s first legislative elections in two decades, scheduled for Nov. 28. Unfortunately, there are forces around the authority’s leadership pressing to have these elections postponed again. Sinijlawi urged me to tell the world: “Do not let that happen.” (At least seven parties have submitted candidate lists for the council’s 132 seats.)

It is such a breath of fresh air to talk to someone like Sinijlawi. He understands that no matter how many European or American rallies there are to “Free Palestine,” the only thing that will do so is a freely elected, legitimate Palestinian government and legislature ready and able to be a partner for a two-state solution.

The repeated postponement of Palestinian legislative elections in the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem “reinforced Hamas’s argument that change could never be achieved through democratic or peaceful means,” Sinijlawi wrote in a Sept. 18 essay in The Jerusalem Post urging President Trump to support the Palestinian elections. “When ballot boxes are closed, extremists offer other boxes — filled with weapons, funerals and false promises. We must not repeat that mistake.”

His party, he said, is drawing the support of registered Palestinian voters — women and students, professionals, academics, entrepreneurs and people entering political life for the first time, even young Gazans living in tents.

“We support a demilitarized Palestinian state, regional economic integration and a negotiated two-state solution that provides Palestinians with freedom and dignity while ensuring security for Israelis,” Sinijlawi wrote.

An East Jerusalem Palestinian, Sinijlawi speaks both Arabic and Hebrew. He learned his Hebrew largely during five years in Israeli prison after being arrested as a teenager in the First Intifada. He told me: “I believe 70 percent to 80 percent of Israelis, if convinced they can live in security next to a Palestinian state, will prefer a smaller democratic and Jewish Israel over a greater Israel that will not be Jewish and not be democratic — and lives in permanent insecurity.”

There is no way to pressure the Israelis, Sinijlawi explained; “the only way is to persuade them.”

“We Palestinians continue denying the historical links of Jews to this land,” he continued. “Instead, we must move from a question of who belongs and who does not belong to this land to the question of how we both belong to this land.”

This is a point Sinijlawi and I have long had in common: There are seven million-plus Jews and seven million-plus Palestinians living between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea — and neither are leaving. The only solution is two states — no matter how long that takes.

And the person who understands the power of that logic best is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Why do you think he made it a top priority for most of his premiership to strengthen Hamas in Gaza? He wanted to keep it divided from moderate Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem who accepted the Oslo peace accords. Netanyahu knows what would happen if a noncorrupt, legitimate, unified Palestinian leadership came together — one that had learned from past mistakes. The whole world would insist that Israel negotiate with it on a two-state solution. It is not going to happen tomorrow, but I will continue to elevate every voice advocating it. The alternative is forever war.

What I admire about Tawakkol Karman and Samer Sinijlawi is that they know how to get off Facebook and into somebody’s face — to actually fight for democracy, not just pop off with slogans, which are a substitute for both thought and action. That used to be us in America. We used to model that for the world.

If there was ever a time to get back to that spirit, it’s now. It starts with voting on Nov. 3 in our election and getting others out to vote too — for any candidate who puts loyalty to our democratic institutions over loyalty to any single person.

ARTICLE

The Science That Has Oil Companies Running Scared
However the U.S. Supreme Court rules, the work of holding oil companies accountable for climate change has a bright future.
By Jeff Goodell
Published 2026-10-06 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/opinion/oil-companies-supreme-court.html

On Monday, the U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Suncor Energy, Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a case that could give fossil fuel companies a get-out-of-jail-free card for the harms caused by climate change.

That is not exactly how Kannon Shanmugam — who represents Suncor and Exxon Mobil, another petitioner in the case — framed the argument. He said that dozens of active lawsuits that use state tort law to sue fossil fuel companies for damages because of their role in causing climate change are superseded by federal law. “This case and others like it reflect an all-too-regrettable trend of trying to resolve political issues in court, rather than leaving them to the political branches where they belong,” Mr. Shanmugam argued.

If the justices agree, the lawsuits filed in state courts will likely be dismissed. If that were to happen, it would not be a big surprise. The court has made any kind of regulatory structure or legal action on climate very difficult. Indeed, the Roberts court is the place where climate action goes to die.

Right now, more than 20 civil lawsuits have been filed in state courts by municipalities that attempt to hold the industry responsible for climate damages. Two tribes have filed similar lawsuits. Eleven state attorneys general are pursuing consumer fraud and related claims against the industry. All in all, several cases are now in the discovery phase and moving toward trial. In addition, Vermont recently passed a climate superfund law that, if it survives court challenges, could force fossil fuel companies to pay an assessment for climate damages. In Washington State, the first wrongful death lawsuit against fossil fuel companies is moving forward. The plaintiff is asking the courts to hold the companies liable for the death of a 65-year-old woman, Juliana Leon, who died in her car during a 108-degree heat wave.

Most of these lawsuits were not filed by tattooed, vegan anticapitalists, but by sober-minded public officials desperate for money to repair sea walls, fight more intense wildfires and prepare their cities for a hotter world. Many are motivated by a lesson that many of us learned when we were children: You break it, you fix it. Why shouldn’t that apply to fossil fuel companies whose products have ruptured the climate?

The Supreme Court’s decision in Suncor v. Boulder, depending on how broadly it is written, could kill many, if not all, of these cases. If it does, it could save fossil fuel companies hundreds of billions of dollars in damages and punitive awards and help them avoid high-profile courtroom showdowns in which they are cast as greedy, deceptive planet wreckers.

If that happens, it will not signal the end of accountability. In fact, the age of accountability for the fossil fuel industry has just begun and has a bright future. The reason for that is the emergence of a powerful field of climate science known as attribution science.

Once upon a time, extreme weather events were seen as the expression of angry gods. In the mid-19th century, scientists figured out that carbon dioxide traps heat and that rising levels would warm the climate. In the 1990s, scientists detected a human “fingerprint” in the earth’s atmosphere, a distinctive pattern that differs from warming caused by changes in the earth’s orbit or the sun’s output. But whose fingerprint is it? Are all of us responsible, or are some of us more responsible than others?

The British climate scientist Myles Allen asked himself those questions as he watched the Thames River rise outside his house after an epic rainstorm in 2003. In an article he later wrote for the journal Nature, Mr. Allen asked: “Will it ever be possible to sue anyone for damaging the climate?” His answer: Given the rapid advances of science, maybe soon.

Mr. Allen’s reasoning was straightforward. Fossil fuel companies sell oil, gas and coal that, when burned, heat up the atmosphere, which increases the likelihood and severity of events like the flood that had threatened to swallow his house. Mr. Allen knew that climate scientists could do the math. Basically, they plug all the data for an extreme weather event such as a flood or a heat wave into a climate model and run it. Then they lower the carbon dioxide level in the model, creating a counterfactual world without human influence in the earth’s atmosphere and estimate the probability of the event. This allows them to calculate the role climate change likely played in amplifying or increasing the likelihood of the flood or heat wave. The art of the science is in determining exactly how much and in what ways higher carbon dioxide levels shaped the event.

In the more than two decades since Mr. Allen’s paper, scientists have made remarkable advances in these explorations of climatological cause and effect. One recent study found that heat waves between 2010 and 2019 were about 200 times as likely with global warming. And using data compiled on fossil fuel industry emissions, scientists have been able to connect climate harms to individual companies. Last year, a study by scientists at Dartmouth College found that carbon dioxide emissions from the top 111 fossil fuel companies from the burning of coal, oil and gas between 1991 and 2020 accounted for up to $28 trillion in global economic damages from heat waves alone. For comparison, $28 trillion is about equal to all goods and services produced in the United States in 2025. The same study found that Chevron, ExxonMobil and BP caused $1.98 trillion, $1.91 trillion and $1.45 trillion in losses, respectively.

In the highly politicized world of climate science, these kinds of studies attract a lot of pushback from allies of the fossil fuel industry. “Attribution science is not science,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said, arguing that you can’t link individual extreme events to long-term trends. (Attribution science comes in many forms, and much of it does not depend on connecting individual events with long-term trends.)

Critics also point to the fact that climate models are imperfect, though these imperfections are well understood by scientists. Like those of any evolving science, the methodologies are new. And how a future jury might evaluate this kind of evidence is unknown.

But attribution science is not a fringe theory. A 2021 report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the gold standard of climate science, devotes many pages to it. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine has issued two reports specifically about the attribution of extreme weather events. And as climate models improve, attribution science will only get stronger. Will it ever be able to say that a heat wave amplified by the carbon dioxide emissions of X company was responsible for Y person’s death? Maybe not. There are too many confounding local factors. But what attribution science does, writes Prof. Aisha Saad of Georgetown University’s law school, is “bring about an epistemic shift, rendering climate change not only legible but litigable.”

Exactly how that will work is still unclear. Tobacco companies fought off litigation for decades before attorneys hit upon the idea of the states suing for Medicaid costs. Lawsuits that held asbestos manufacturers responsible for causing mesothelioma in workers succeeded only after years of failed attempts.

With those precedents, it’s no wonder the fossil fuel industry appears desperate to avoid wrestling with attribution science in the courtroom. A long, well-documented history of deception about how much they knew about the harms that the burning of their products causes to people and the planet only adds to their vulnerability. Several fossil fuel-friendly states have already passed legislation to protect the industry from liability. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Representative Harriet Hageman of Wyoming — two of the best friends the industry has ever had in Congress — have introduced bills to give fossil fuel companies sweeping immunity from virtually any kind of climate accountability.

More broadly, climate accountability extends far beyond the reach of Congress or the Supreme Court. Recent opinions in Germany and the International Court of Justice have endorsed the basic legal principle that entities that contribute to climate change owe something to the people who suffer from its impacts. As attribution science becomes more sophisticated, it will articulate that debt with ever more precision.

The simple truth is, the climate accountability genie is out of the bottle, and the Supreme Court is unlikely to jam it back in. Even if the court sides with Suncor, attribution science will continue to move forward, filling in the gaps between cause and effect in our understanding of how climate works

“New science drives social and political change,” Abigail Dillen, the president of Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization, told me. Learning about the risks of the ozone hole brought a quick crackdown on ozone-destroying chemicals. The iconic 1968 photo of the earth from space helped trigger the modern environmental movement.

In the end, the promise of attribution science is that it helps us see a storm or a heat wave or a flood not as an act of a god or the whim of Mother Nature, but as a disaster that has been knowingly shaped or intensified by particular human actions. And by identifying perpetrators and victims, it transforms the question of who should pay for climate damages into a moral question as much as a legal one.

This is a science that not only articulates new ideas about accountability but practically demands that we explore them. It is only a matter of time before the courts catch up.

Jeff Goodell is the author, most recently, of “The Heat Will Kill You First: Life and Death on a Scorched Planet.” He is working on a book about climate attribution science and its impact.

ARTICLE

This L.A. Power Broker Is Suing Over His Uninhabitable $20 Million Mansion
Austin Beutner has filed a lawsuit that highlights a central dispute after the 2025 Los Angeles fires: Who pays when a house survives the flames but not the smoke?
By Rukmini Callimachi and Shawn Hubler
Published 2026-10-06 13:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/us/austin-beutner-chubb-lawsuit-palisades-fire.html

Behind a towering hedge in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Pacific Palisades sits a house that Tom Cruise bought in 1990 and Nicole Kidman sold after their divorce. A few doors down is Steven Spielberg’s estate. Across the street is Bill Cosby’s.

The property shares a fence line with that of the boxing legend Sugar Ray Leonard — “our dogs bark at each other,” said Austin Beutner, who bought the house from Ms. Kidman in 2002.

Few blocks in America hold more fame, money and access. But nearly 21 months after the house was damaged in the Palisades fire, it sits empty. Valued at around $20 million, it is uninhabitable, its walls laced with lead at levels far above what federal regulators consider hazardous, according to testing commissioned by the family.

On Monday in Los Angeles County Superior Court, Mr. Beutner and his wife, Virginia, sued their insurer, Chubb — whose subsidiary Bankers Standard Insurance Company issued their policy — and two environmental consulting firms Chubb hired. The suit accuses Chubb of breach of contract and professional negligence for refusing to pay for the full cleanup of lead and other toxins. In a letter to Chubb last month, the family’s lawyer accused the company of relying on “pay-to-play” consultants and “junk science.”

A Chubb spokesman, Michael Tomaso, declined to comment. The two consulting firms did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit joins a mounting pile of litigation filed by homeowners whose houses survived the January 2025 fires, but not the smoke. What sets it apart is who filed it.

Mr. Beutner has spent his career in rooms where decisions are made. At 29, he became the youngest partner at the Blackstone Group, and then co-founded the investment bank Evercore. He is the former deputy mayor of Los Angeles, the former publisher of The Los Angeles Times and the former superintendent of the nation’s second-largest school district. In 2022, he authored a ballot measure that now sends around $1 billion a year to arts and music programs in California’s public schools.

“I’ll be fine either way,” he said in a telephone interview before filing the suit. “But there are thousands of others who have claims like mine who may not have the agency I do. They may not be able to afford the lawyers.” Insurers are pushing families back into contaminated homes and keeping the danger quiet — a public health crisis — and litigation might be one of the few ways to sound the alarm, he said.

The Los Angeles fires killed 31 people and incinerated more than 16,000 buildings. Of the more than 40,000 insurance claims filed in the aftermath, approximately 13,000 — or nearly one out of three — were for smoke-damaged homes, according to the California Department of Insurance.

Many of those claims remain unsettled and families continue to be displaced, according to advocates for policyholders.

At a news conference in Los Angeles on Tuesday hosted by the California Community Foundation, a local nonprofit, displaced fire survivors spoke of the difficulties smoke damage had posed for them. Local officials, including Mayor Karen Bass and Kathryn Barger, a Los Angeles County supervisor, urged policyholders to file insurance claims for testing and remediation ahead of a January legal deadline.

Blanca Perez, a grandmother in Altadena, said in Spanish that she and her neighbors had been struggling for months to determine whether their 40-unit apartment building is safe for habitation, but that they lacked money for testing.

Brenda Solórzano, the president and chief executive of the California Endowment, a statewide nonprofit, said she wished her smoke-damaged house in Altadena had burned down entirely.

“It’s really frustrating,” she said. “I’m educated, I have connections, I have resources. And I, too, have been struggling with our insurance company.”

At the heart of this issue is a regulatory vacuum: With no state or national standards for when a smoke-damaged home is considered clean, insurers often test only for soot, char and ash — the visible traces of a fire — and pay for equally visible fixes: vacuuming, wiping and painting, a New York Times investigation found.

Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, signed two bills that are meant to address that issue. One directs the state to create science-based standards for measuring and cleaning heavy metals and other contaminants inside homes. The other requires insurers to pay for cleanup in line with those standards, and presumes that smoke damage in a fire zone is a result of a fire.

Those laws, the first of their kind in the nation, take effect over the next three years and are not retroactive, stranding homeowners like the Beutners and thousands of others of lesser means.

Disputes over insurance claims normally unfold out of sight, in adjusters’ letters and confidential settlements. But the scale of the Los Angeles fires has pushed them into the open. The 2025 fires were the costliest wildfire disasters on record for insurers, with estimates putting insured losses at as much as $35 billion, more than double the previous record, set by the 2018 Camp fire, according to Verisk, an insurance data firm.

Smoke has turned out to be one of the main reasons: In the first 30 days after the fires, 30 percent of homeowners’ claims were for smoke damage, compared with just 3 percent after the Camp fire, according to data collected by Verisk.

The Beutners had insured their home with Chubb for 18 years, paying millions of dollars in premiums, the lawsuit says. And while Chubb writes only around 2 percent of homeowner premiums in California, it took an outsize hit: In 2025, it recorded about $1.7 billion in California homeowner losses — roughly five times the premiums it earned on those policies, state data show.

On Jan. 7, 2025, the Palisades fire swept through the Beutners’ neighborhood but stopped short of their house, even as 100-mile-per-hour winds drove soot, char and ash inside. The family’s first Chubb adjuster called it the “worst house we have seen,” according to the suit filed on Monday.

Two weeks after the fire, Chubb sent Environmental Testing Associates, one of the two firms now being sued, to test the house. The firm’s 17 tape samples measured soot, char and ash, but not the heavy metals inside them, nor did it test in concealed spaces like wall cavities and attics. The firm recommended air filters, cleaning and vacuuming — treating the damage “as if the problem could be fixed with Lysol wipes,” the Beutners’ lawyers later wrote.

Like so many other families affected by the wildfire, the Beutners soon found themselves locked in a battle of experts. When the family hired its own industrial hygienist to test the house, he found alarming levels of toxins — including in the ceiling of the front hallway, which contained 9,575 micrograms of lead per square foot, a reading that is 239 times the federal limit for lead found indoors, according to the testing results shared with The Times.

By contrast, the consultant hired by Chubb insisted that the lead came from old paint in the home, built in the 1940s, and that lithium and arsenic came from the soil or else from the Earth’s crust, according to the reports they produced, which were shared with The Times, as well as the family’s suit.

Chubb has paid millions of dollars in claims so far for repairs and relocation assistance for the Beutner household. Mr. Beutner said that money has amounted to less than a quarter of the cost of remediating the smoke damage.

Regulators have set limits for the amount of lead found inside homes, but there are no such limits for the numerous other poisons unleashed in an urban fire — including lithium and arsenic, as well as cadmium and chromium. Several of these toxins are regulated in workplaces such as factories, but the lack of a corresponding standard for residential settings has left families in limbo.

The families who have sued are only a small share of the more than 13,000 households whose homes survived the fires but not the smoke. For many, time is running out: January marks the deadline to sue their insurer.

ARTICLE

It Can Keep Cancer in Remission. Why Is No One Talking About It?
Despite mounting evidence that exercise programs can improve cancer outcomes, access to them remains limited.
By Nina Agrawal
Published 2026-10-06 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/well/cancer-prevention-exercise-treatment.html

Lee Colker powered on an iPad in the basement of his Pittsburgh home and logged into a virtual exercise session with Olivia Masten, a trainer who specializes in working with cancer patients.

Mr. Colker, 66, had been dealing with unpredictable fatigue and brain fog since beginning a clinical trial for metastatic kidney cancer this year. When staff at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center told him an exercise program could improve his energy, he jumped at the opportunity. “That was a clincher for me,” he said.

The program is part of a growing effort around the country to help cancer patients exercise, as the benefits of doing so become increasingly clear.

Observational research has long suggested that exercise improves cancer survival, particularly for breast cancer patients. Last year, a landmark randomized controlled trial showed that colon cancer patients who participated in a structured exercise program with a trainer-coach over three years were less likely to see their cancers come back and had a better quality of life. Among those in the program, 90 percent were alive after eight years, compared with 83 percent in the control group.

A later study showed the program, which altogether cost $3,000 per person, also saved the health system money — “a home run,” said Dr. Scott Ramsey, a cancer researcher and health economist at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center in Washington State.

That combination of benefits is rare among cancer therapies: The new pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib, for example, costs $480,000 annually, has unpleasant side effects and, while it prolongs life by several months, does not increase overall long-term survival.

“If we had a drug with this magnitude of benefit, it would immediately become standard of care and funded” by insurance companies, said Dr. Christopher Booth, an oncologist and professor at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario, and the leader of the exercise trial.

While guidelines now recommend that oncologists help colon cancer patients achieve at least 150 minutes of moderate to rigorous exercise per week, many patients need support in the form of a structured program, with a trainer and supervised sessions, to get to that level and stick with it. But there’s not yet an insurance pathway to pay for such programs — a major barrier to rolling them out more widely.

“You can tell patients that if you do this, you may survive longer,” Dr. Ramsey said. But unfortunately, he added, “we just don’t have the infrastructure.”

Current programs are largely limited to major cancer centers and dependent on philanthropy or individual out-of-pocket payments to cover costs, leaving poorer patients and those who live far from these centers without access.

Dr. Jeff Meyerhardt, a gastrointestinal oncologist at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, refers his patients to the hospital’s center for alternative therapies, where they can consult with a trainer and access in-person and online exercise classes. But the trainer can’t continue supporting patients over time.

At the University of California, San Francisco, doctors refer eligible patients for physical therapy and rehabilitation, which can be reimbursed by insurance, while many Y.M.C.A. branches offer a free or low-cost 12-week program for cancer survivors.

Improving outcomes among cancer patients isn’t as simple as telling them to exercise more, said Kathryn Schmitz, an exercise oncology researcher at U.P.M.C. Hillman Cancer Center. “Exercise is not just biology,” she said. “It is also behavior.”

Dr. Schmitz is the founding director of Moving Through Cancer, the program in which Mr. Colker is participating. It is tailored to each patient: Some need more support, while others “are well enough to go out and play some pickleball,” she said.

Kimberly Barker, 68, suffered from low back and hip pain and fatigue after treatment for bladder and uterine cancer. A quilter who used to bicycle with her husband on trails near their home in Butler County, Pa., Ms. Barker lost the motivation to do the things she loved.

“I was just so tired, no energy, no stamina,” she said.

She met with Ms. Masten, the trainer, once a week for 12 weeks, and also did the suggested exercises between meetings. She continued doing them after the program ended, and now feels back to her normal self. She and her husband have resumed their bike rides.

Because of the success in people like Ms. Barker, U.P.M.C. has decided to offer the program through its employee health plan for breast cancer patients beginning next year.

The health system will be the first in the country to offer insurance coverage for exercise oncology, Dr. Schmitz said. She and her colleagues argued for it based on randomized trials that showed it saved costs by reducing hospitalizations, emergency room trips and unplanned office visits.

“This U.P.M.C. rollout is a giant experiment,” Dr. Schmitz said. If it’s successful, the hospital plans to expand it to all cancers in 2028. Dr. Schmitz also pushed to incorporate exercise into standards that cancer hospitals must follow to receive certain accreditation, which will happen later this year.

“This is no longer just something that would be nice to have,” Dr. Schmitz said. “This is a therapeutic intervention, it needs to be done — and it needs to be done for all patients.”

The counterterrorism police in Britain have now arrested seven men in connection with the puzzling incident near the base in southern England, R.A.F. Fairford, in the early hours of Sept. 27.

The police said that a London property linked to the man was also searched in connection with the events near Fairford.

“This remains a live investigation, and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near R.A.F. Fairford,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing. She added that the police were “working around the clock” to identify the motivation behind the incident.

One of the men dialed the emergency services at 12.45 a.m., prompting a major counterterrorism response. The village where the men were arrested was cordoned off, explosive experts were called in and speculation began about what exactly the men had been doing.

The five were released on bail a day later after the authorities did not discover explosives and found only a container of fuel in the vans. Another man, a British-Iranian national, was arrested on Thursday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts and has also been released on bail.

None of the men have been named, in line with British rules that grant suspects anonymity until charges are brought.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened.”

British and American security officials believe the operation was connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps or a separate military headquarters in Tehran. Iran has rejected the accusations.

Over the weekend, the United States abruptly pulled its 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from R.A.F. Fairford. American officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said the withdrawal took place after commanders received information about a potential drone attack on the base ordered by the Revolutionary Guards.

The bombers had been stationed at the base since the spring, after Britain gave permission for American aircraft to use R.A.F. Fairford for so-called defensive strikes against Iran.

There is a long history of British and American cooperation at the site, and because of the length of its runway, it is one of only a few European airfields that can be used by heavy U.S. bombers.

On Monday, some plane spotters who post regularly in online forums about the movements of the American aircraft into and out of the base were lamenting how quiet it would now be. Others were glad that the bombers would no longer be leaving from England to be used against Iran.

In July, after Britain gave the United States permission to conduct its operations from the site, Iran warned that R.A.F. Fairford was a “legitimate target.”

Trump Administration Investigates Wells Fargo for Race-Based Lending

By Rob Copeland

The Trump administration on Wednesday accused Wells Fargo, one of the nation’s largest mortgage lenders, of discriminating against home buyers by creating programs that favored minority applicants for loans.

The allegations came in a letter from the Department of Housing and Urban Development to Wells Fargo’s chief executive, Charles Scharf.

The letter, signed by Craig W. Trainor, an assistant secretary, said the San Francisco bank was being investigated for violations of the Fair Housing Act, a civil rights-era law that barred banks and other lenders from considering race, religion, sex and national origin, among other factors, in their underwriting.

In his letter Mr. Trainor cited “repeated public promotion of explicit race-based policies,” including offering Black homeowners lower-cost refinancing and the creation of a $150 million so-called credit program “to advance racial equity in homeownership.” He raised the specter of expanding the investigation to include the Department of Justice.

Black and Hispanic families are far less likely to own homes than their white and Asian counterparts, according to the Pew Research Center.

“Attempting to close statistical racial gaps in homeownership by doling out loans based on race is no way to do business,” Mr. Trainor wrote.

Jennifer Langan, a Wells Fargo spokeswoman, declined to comment. The bank’s shares ended the day 1.5 percent lower. The letter was reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal.

The behavior in question dates to when “under the Biden administration, race-conscious lending programs proliferated throughout the financial sector,” according to the HUD letter.

Wells Fargo publicly promoted its minority-focused program in news releases and on its website. It has since deleted many of those references.

The new investigation adds to the Trump administration’s efforts to punish corporate America for expanding programs aimed at Black Americans after the nationwide protests set off by George Floyd’s death in 2020.

The Trump administration has repeatedly raised instances of what it considers reverse discrimination, most recently accusing the law school at the University of California, Berkeley, of penalizing white and Asian applicants.

Under President Trump, federal agencies, including the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Department of Justice, have criticized diversity, equity and inclusion programs for favoring minority employees over white ones.

Mr. Trump said in an interview this year that he believed laws and policies dating to the 1960s, such as affirmative action, had resulted in white people being “very badly treated.”

Financial institutions, however, have until now mostly escaped the White House’s criticism of race-based programs. Mr. Trump in his second term has been more focused on whether banks have discriminated against conservatives — including him personally — by closing certain customers’ accounts, a process known as “debanking.”

Wells Fargo was among the large banks cited last year by the administration’s regulators for engaging in the practice. Industry representatives have said bank accounts are not closed for political reasons.

Mamdani Draws Anger With Oct. 7 Statement Focused on Palestinians
After calling the anniversary of the attacks on Israel “profoundly painful,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani denounced Israel’s military action in Gaza, prompting criticism from some Jewish leaders.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani ignited intense anger from Jewish groups on Wednesday when he issued a statement marking the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 attacks on Israel that focused largely on the suffering of Palestinians in Gaza.

The mayor posted a 211-word statement on social media that made reference to “the horrific war crimes” committed by Hamas and called the anniversary “profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers.”

However, the bulk of the statement provided a detailed denunciation of Israel’s military actions in Gaza since the attacks, which Mr. Mamdani described as a “devastating, ongoing genocide.” He did not provide a similarly detailed account of the killings of Israelis and abductions of hostages.

“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he said, referring to Oct. 7, adding: “That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing.”

The remarks by Mr. Mamdani, who has a fraught relationship with much of New York City’s Jewish leadership, were highly anticipated and closely scrutinized because this is the first anniversary of the attacks on Israel since he took office in January.

“You cannot proclaim empathy and care for the Jewish community and then fail to show basic humanity toward us in our grief,” he added. “Turning this anniversary into an indictment of the Jewish state is not only hurtful and deeply offensive, but it also makes Jewish New Yorkers less safe.”

The UJA-Federation of New York, a major philanthropy, took issue with Mr. Mamdani’s description of the war in Gaza, saying he had chosen “to respond to the grief of Jewish New Yorkers by advancing false and inflammatory attacks against Israel — not only inappropriately shifting the focus away from the victims of Hamas’s cruelty, but also placing Jewish New Yorkers at risk.”

But some progressive Jews defended the mayor. Sophie Ellman-Golan, a spokeswoman for Jews for Racial and Economic Justice, a group supportive of Mr. Mamdani, said his statement on Wednesday had “struck exactly the right tone.”

“I think this is a really painful day for so many reasons,” she said. “It has been three years since that day, and three years of genocide. To act like there was a horrific attack and then nothing happened afterward — we cannot fail to acknowledge that.”

The uproar was a reminder of the degree to which the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has infused the mayoralty of Mr. Mamdani. The mayor’s comments echoed a statement he made on last year’s anniversary, reflecting his consistent stance on the issue even as his platform has grown significantly.

Mr. Mamdani has clashed with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, most recently last month when Mr. Netanyahu denounced the mayor in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly, calling him an antisemite and saying that Jewish New Yorkers were less safe under his leadership. Mr. Mamdani, who has repeatedly called Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal, accused the prime minister of using the speech to spread “baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

The terrorist attack on Israel resulted in the killings of roughly 1,200 people, including civilians and military members, and the abduction of 251 hostages. Israel’s subsequent campaign in Gaza has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to a count from Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants but which includes thousands of children.

Israel’s conduct of the war has drawn broad international condemnation and caused a significant drop in public support for the country in the United States, its most important ally. That shift in public opinion has been especially pronounced among Democrats and young people, with a majority of both groups expressing a negative view of the Jewish state, according to the Pew Research Center.

On Wednesday, pro-Israel and pro-Palestinian groups held separate events to express their grief and outrage over the Oct. 7 attacks and the ensuing war, which has devastated Gaza and spread to Lebanon, Iran and elsewhere in the Middle East.

Many Jewish groups organized ceremonies to remember those who died in the attacks, including an event at the Museum of Jewish Heritage and a candlelit vigil in Union Square organized by Israelis for Peace New York, where organizers said they would also mourn those killed in Gaza.

For their part, pro-Palestinian groups protested Israel’s military action in Gaza — which a U.N. commission and some international and Israeli human rights groups have described as a genocide, a claim the Israeli government has denied — as well as the wars in Lebanon and Iran.

The mayor’s outreach to pro-Israel Jewish groups has outraged some pro-Palestinian activists who accuse Mr. Mamdani of betraying their movement. To underline that point, some attendees at a pro-Palestinian rally outside City Hall on Wednesday expressed opposition to Mr. Mamdani.

“He is just as complicit,” Jon Brule, one protester at the rally, said as he held a sign that referred to Mr. Mamdani as “on the side of genocide.” “He’s betrayed the interest of the Palestinians.”

Tamar Glezerman, an organizer of the Israelis for Peace vigil in Union Square, said it was important to treat Wednesday as a day of mourning “while also not ignoring the aftermath of this massacre,” which she described as a genocide in Gaza.

“There is this fallacy out there that if you mourn or feel the pain of one side, that somehow cancels the other side or legitimizes violence against the other side,” added Ms. Glezerman, whose aunt was killed in the Oct. 7 attacks.

Wesley Parnell contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

The Woman Whose Software Guided the Apollo Missions Has Died
Margaret Hamilton, the first female programmer hired to work on the space project at M.I.T., was 90.
By Trip Gabriel
Published 2026-10-07 23:05 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/obituaries/margaret-hamilton-dead.html

Margaret Hamilton, who led the 100-person team that wrote the onboard software for the Apollo missions, guiding Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to a safe landing on the moon, died Sept. 30 in Cambridge, Mass. She was 90.

Her death, in a hospital, was confirmed by her daughter, Lauren.

Ms. Hamilton was a young mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the early 1960s, putting her husband through law school by working in a computer lab. When she learned that M.I.T. was designing in-flight computers for the moon mission, she eagerly joined the team.

She was the first female programmer hired to work on the Apollo project, housed at M.I.T.’s Instrumentation Laboratory, in 1965. Her skills led to her promotion to director of software engineering on the project, which developed the two 70-pound onboard computers for the Apollo flights: one in the command module, which carried the astronauts from Earth, and the second in the lunar module, which set down on the moon’s surface.

Ms. Hamilton, who would bring her young daughter to work on weekends and evenings, is credited with popularizing the term “software engineering” to describe the complexity of the work her team did, thus elevating software coding to a status equal to hardware design.

A 1969 photograph of the 5-foot-4 Ms. Hamilton standing beside a head-high stack of printed code developed for the moon landing has been widely shared on social media in recent years.

Primary navigation for the Apollo flights was guided from Houston on mainframe IBM computers. But the onboard Apollo Guidance Computer that the M.I.T. lab created was a crucial cog.

Developing its software was a major lift in an era when computers had limited memory. The onboard computers contained only 72 kilobytes of storage memory (an iPhone 16, by comparison, can have more than seven million times as much storage).

As Apollo 11’s lunar module, Eagle, touched down on the moon on July 20, 1969, Ms. Hamilton, then 32, was patched into Mission Control in Houston from M.I.T.

“I was not concentrating on the mission per se, I was concentrating on the software,” she recalled in a 2017 interview for the Computer History Museum. She compared the moment before touchdown to the instant before death when a person’s life is said to flash before them. “I could see the Apollo life, just: ‘Look what happened. We did it. It worked,’” she recalled. “It was exciting.”

But it almost didn’t happen. As Eagle neared the moon, its onboard computer famously flashed alarms, and Mission Control was faced with a decision about whether to abort the landing.

One of the astronauts, according to some historians, flipped a switch that overloaded the computer’s processing unit, which set off the alarms. Ms. Hamilton had foreseen just such an event. Her software told the onboard computer to prioritize essential tasks and cancel less important ones. The alarm was the signal that the procedure had occurred. Houston chose to continue the mission, and Eagle’s computer guided it to a safe landing on the Sea of Tranquillity.

“If the computer hadn’t recognized this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the successful moon landing it was,” Ms. Hamilton wrote in a 1971 letter to a computer magazine, Datamation.

Ms. Hamilton worked on the six lunar landing missions from 1969 to 1972. Her programming also contributed to Skylab, America’s first space station, launched in 1973, and to the early design of the space shuttle. She left M.I.T. to found a company, Higher Order Software, in 1976, as well as a second firm a decade later, Hamilton Technologies.

In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded Ms. Hamilton the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Its citation reads that her work for NASA “set the foundation for modern, ultrareliable software design and engineering.”

In 2019, on the 50th anniversary of the moon landing, Google trained more than 100,000 mirrors at its Ivanpah solar power farm in the Mojave Desert to create a nighttime portrait in reflected moonlight of Ms. Hamilton, bigger than Central Park.

Margaret Elaine Heafield was born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Paoli, Ind., the oldest of four children of Kenneth and Esther (Partington) Heafield. The family moved to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. Her mother was a high school teacher, and her father was a poet and a college professor of English and philosophy.

Margaret enrolled in the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College in Richmond, Ind., where she received a bachelor’s degree in mathematics in 1958.

The same year, she married James Hamilton, also an Earlham student. The couple moved to Cambridge, Mass., where their plan was for Ms. Hamilton to support her husband in law school and then to have him pay the bills while she earned a doctorate in math and became a professor.

Instead, her computer work led her in a starkly different direction.

Her first job at M.I.T., in 1959, was in the meteorology department for Edward Norton Lorenz, the founder of modern chaos theory, for whom she helped develop software to predict weather.

In 1961 she moved to an M.I.T. team working for the Air Force on a system known as SAGE to track enemy aircraft. She was assigned a puzzle given to all new programmers: to decipher a program no one could get to work, whose author had left notes in Latin and Greek. Ms. Hamilton was the first person to get the program to run.

Based on her work on SAGE, she was hired for the M.I.T. Apollo computer project, led by a professor of aeronautical engineering, Charles Stark Draper, who had won the NASA contract for the navigation and guidance system for the moon flight, announced by President John F. Kennedy in 1961.

Ms. Hamilton was initially the only woman on the programming team, she recalled at a 2021 conference about the history of the Apollo computers.

She became known as the “rope mother,” because of the unusual way code was stored on the in-flight computers, in an era before the wide use of silicon chips.

Programs were written in binary arithmetic, a series of 1s and 0s. The digits were stored using copper wires woven around tiny doughnut-shaped material called cores. A wire passing through a core was read as a 1 and a wire that bypassed a core was a 0. The long assemblages of cores and threaded wire were called ropes.

The ropes were woven by women capable of fine hand work, many of whom had worked in New England textile mills. Ms. Hamilton, who was responsible for getting everything right, was the “rope mother.” (A 1965 film shows how the M.I.T.-designed computers were built at Raytheon’s space division plant in Waltham, Mass.).

Her first marriage ended in divorce in 1967. Two years later, she married Daniel Lickly (pronounced “likely”), a supervisor on the M.I.T. Apollo project, who was responsible for hiring her. They divorced in the early 1970s.

From the late ’70s, Ms. Hamilton was the partner of Ron Hackler, a musician she met when he helped move her office and then trained in systems engineering and was employed at her company Hamilton Technologies, which developed software. He died in 2025.

Besides her daughter, Lauren, Ms. Hamilton is survived by two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn Heafield (pronounced “hayfield”).

Like most of the legions of engineers, mathematicians and scientists who worked behind the scenes to make the moon landings happen, Ms. Hamilton is little known to the public.

But in 2017, she achieved a kind of pop culture eminence with the introduction of Lego Margaret Hamilton, a play figure that was part of a Women of NASA set. She is represented as longhaired and bespectacled, standing beside a teetering stack of computer code.
