ARTICLE

Billionaires Love This School Policy. Many Regular Parents Hate It.
In Texas and Iowa, Democrats are successfully tying universal school vouchers to corruption.
By Jessica Grose
Published 2026-10-07 09:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/school-vouchers-midterms.html

“I’ve been voting Republican my whole life. I’m super conservative,” Pine Tree superintendent Steve Clugston tells the camera in an Instagram reel. “I’m gonna tell you what, when Greg Abbott sold us out to the billionaires and sold out our schools, I’m done with his leadership.” In the Texas governor’s race, Clugston is voting for Abbott’s Democratic opponent, State Representative Gina Hinojosa.

The Pine Tree public school district is in the bright red, small city of Longview in East Texas, between the big cities of Dallas and Shreveport, La. The majority of its 4,400 students are economically disadvantaged. When I caught up with Clugston on Friday, hours before the Pine Tree football team trounced its opponents under the lights, he was at his farm. “My wife’s a teacher, my daughter’s a teacher, my son-in-law’s a teacher, both my sisters are teachers, my brother-in law’s a retired superintendent. So I’d say education’s kind of in our blood,” he told me over the phone.

Clugston told me he’s sick of his fellow Texas conservatives straying from their principles of fiscal common sense and straight talk; he even attempted a run for the Texas State Senate as an independent conservative. He is particularly appalled by Texas’ voucher program, known as Texas Education Freedom Accounts, which went into effect earlier this year. This program puts state money in accounts for Texas families to use outside the public school system: up to nearly $10,500 for children enrolling in private school, up to $30,000 for children with disabilities and up to $2,000 for those who are home-schooled.

The State of Texas has no say over the curriculum taught at the institutions that accept vouchers, and participating schools can discriminate against applicants for any number of reasons, including religion and disability status. Texas’ vouchers are universal, which means anyone can apply for them, regardless of financial means, though poorer students have been prioritized.

Around 70 percent of this year’s voucher recipients were already enrolled in private or home- school. Vouchers are costing the state about a billion dollars this year alone, and could ultimately end up costing $4.4 billion annually. While funding for vouchers comes from a budget that is separate from the public school pot, the state’s funding for public schools has not kept up with inflation.

Texas public schools will lose a projected $227 million just this year, as they shed head count, according to The Houston Chronicle. More public schools may close as a result of vouchers siphoning that money away from them. In Clugston’s opinion, vouchers are “a billion-dollar giveaway program for the rich and we’re gonna have no accountability in it. Zero.”

Hinojosa has made saving public education central to her campaign for governor, and it is what got her started in politics. Her child’s school was on the brink of closure, and she describes her political trajectory as concerned parent, to local school board member, to Texas House member. If elected, Hinojosa has vowed to “end the voucher scam.”

I have long been frustrated at the way both parties barely talk about K-12 public education, despite plunging test scores and post-Covid woes. But the reason politicians don’t talk more about education is because voters don’t care about it. What makes Hinojosa’s message on schools effective beyond irate public school parents and educators is that she ties the passage of vouchers to larger themes plaguing Republicans in the age of Trump: corruption and the outsize power of billionaires.

Vouchers failed in the Texas Legislature multiple times, with rural Republicans tending to side with Democrats to block the measures. In rural areas, “school choice,” even with vouchers, tends to be a mirage. There are few private schools, and public schools are often the biggest local employers and the heart of small-town life; nearly every Texan I spoke to for this newsletter said the reverence for “Friday Night Lights” is real.

When Gov. Greg Abbott couldn’t get vouchers passed the honorable way, he decided to primary Republican state legislators who opposed the policy. Abbott took $12 million from Jeff Yass, a pro-voucher Pennsylvania billionaire, got most of his preferred candidates into office, and got vouchers passed in 2025, as The Washington Post noted.

The outcomes for students participating in voucher programs in other states have been decidedly mixed, but Yass doesn’t give a rip. “If the mother or the parent wants the kid to go from one school to another, who the hell is anyone to tell them not to?” Yass told The Post. “I don’t care what the studies say.”

Yass isn’t the only billionaire who meddled in vouchers in the Lone Star State. The religious Texas billionaires Tim Dunn and Farris and Dan Wilks, have also poured money into pro-voucher candidates over the years. As The Texas Tribune explains, “Dunn is also the founder of Midland Classical Academy, a private school that offers its approximately 600 K-12 students a ‘Classical Education from a Biblical Worldview,’ according to its website.” (It’s worth noting that many of the elite, popular and highly ranked private schools in Texas refused to accept vouchers this year.)

Some voucher proponents claim that Texas offers more choice to underprivileged children in underperforming schools. But the data we have on other states with universal voucher programs, like Arizona’s, suggest that they are redistributing money to the highest income and most educated ZIP codes in cities and suburbs. An Arizona ABC station found that parents were spending their voucher money on everything from trampoline parks to ski tickets.

In Iowa, which has a universal voucher program for private schools that’s similar to Texas’, the Democratic candidate for governor and the current auditor, Rob Sand, has made a similar connection between vouchers, special interests and corruption. “The current school voucher program is an open invitation to waste, fraud and abuse of taxpayer dollars,” Sand explains on his campaign website.

Sand lists his voucher stance under the headline Accountability for All, where he also talks about protections for whistle-blowers and banning stock trading. By doing so, Sand is saying that you don’t have to care about what’s going on in the classroom to be outraged that a New York-based company called Odyssey, which manages his state’s voucher program, allegedly got a “sweetheart” deal for the work. As auditor, Sand found that the company “more than doubled its rate less than a month after signing their no-bid contract, costing taxpayers an additional $2.7 million.” (Odyssey, which has ties to Yass, also administers the voucher system in Texas.)

Whatever you think about public schools, it is difficult not to seethe at the fundamental unfairness of voucher programs that give money to schools that don’t have to educate all students. The Texas Observer found that of 291 private schools approved for voucher funds from the state, over 90 percent were religious or faith-based schools, “more than 100 of those schools require or prioritize for admission students of the same faith, and more than 60 have a written policy that discriminates against L.G.B.T.Q.+ students, the schools’ own data shows.”

Though the Texas vouchers prioritize students with disabilities, The Observer also noted that most of the private Texas schools they analyzed lack special education services. A Dallas Morning News analysis found that thousands of students with disabilities returned state money, in part because private schools either rejected them or didn’t even respond to their applications.

Some educators I spoke to in both Texas and Iowa told me that they’d already seen students ricocheting back to public schools because their private or home-school experience wasn’t all it was chalked up to be. Another outrageous part of this legislation is that Texas public schools are still required to do the disability testing for families that choose vouchers, and it’s straining their limited resources.

When put to a public vote, school vouchers have been unpopular; they’re perennial losers on the ballot. It’s maddening that ideologically motivated billionaires, who likely never sent their own children to public schools, have been able to push this policy through.

According to the latest New York Times/Siena University polling, Hinojosa is up by four points, and Sand is up by 11. Texas is obviously the tougher battle, but after spending the week talking to parents there, I’m cautiously optimistic. Rebekah Baus, who described herself as a conservative Christian and lives in the Dallas-Fort Worth area with her husband and two kids, told me she is so upset about the state of public school policy that she doesn’t know which way she is voting.

The State of Texas, Baus said, is trying to pretend “our public school system is failing, but in the reality, we’re failing our public school system by not funding them properly.”

End Notes

- Rural schools tend to be particularly ill served by vouchers. If your rural school is closing, or at risk of closure for any reason (including a declining population of children), I want to hear from you: drop me a line.
- ProPublica has been doing excellent work on vouchers and the lack of oversight into vouchers and private schools. They tried to start a fake private school as an experiment and found that the requirements were so scant, “we could enroll students in two states right now, if we wanted to. Arkansas even suggested ways our school could accept public money through the state’s voucher-style program.” They even created a quiz to show how “many states invite anyone with a dream and a heartbeat to start a school.” Take it here, you’ll be shocked.
- Given that I adored the Sharon Horgan show “Catastrophe,” I was not surprised to find that I also love her new HBO show “Youth.” Horgan plays Alex, a divorced literary agent who is struggling with sandwich generation headaches while she tries to get back into dating. Her 18-year-old won’t launch, her ex-husband pretty much stopped parenting and her parents are in poor health. Horgan always manages to make the mess of life into something funny and real, and I want half her outfits. (If someone can source her booties or the perfect cropped sweatshirt she wears in Episode 1, please tell me.)

trump-los-angeles-ethics.html

SUMMARY

President Trump’s choices violate — not alter — them.

ARTICLE

The Trump Outrages Keep Piling Up
Readers react to President Trump’s “take out Los Angeles” remarks and his ethics flaws. Also: Climate risk; colleges and A.I.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-07 17:29 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/trump-los-angeles-ethics.html

To the Editor:

Re “‘Take Out Los Angeles’: What Trump Said, Exactly” (news article, Oct. 7):

The latest outrage from our norm-busting so-called leader of the free world? President Trump’s comments to his supporters suggesting that Iran “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, which were understandably met with anger by California officials.

Whether he is threatening the military destruction of another nation’s civilization or suggesting the obliteration of American cities, the level of depravity in this man’s soul appears unmatched by any of his predecessors.

Regardless of his intentions, words from a president matter, and those who wish us harm are listening. Mr. Trump is utterly unfit to be commander in chief or a leader of any kind.

Anthony Arnaud Laguna Niguel, Calif.

To the Editor:

President Trump’s latest stream-of-consciousness abomination was bad enough, but what sickened me even more were the cheering and smiles on the faces of his adoring fans in response.

Many of these same people often demand that voters like me, on the left side of the political spectrum, make a good-faith effort to respect them and sympathize with their grievances.

Despite the convoluted efforts of spinmeisters such as the White House communications director, Steven Cheung, to have us believe otherwise, Mr. Trump’s casual remarks remain repugnant in the extreme. Anyone who laughs at them deserves no respect.

Bryan L. Tucker Boston

To the Editor:

Re “Trump Has Moved the Boundaries of What Is Ethical,” by Peter Baker (White House Memo, Oct. 5):

The online summary of this article says, “The president’s decision to hold an international summit at his own private golf club, an idea rejected in his first term, illustrates how much he has shattered norms.”

Even more striking is how much it illustrates how willing we have all been to go along with him.

Jonathan P. Levin Northampton, Mass.

To the Editor:

No! Ethical boundaries are still the same. President Trump’s choices violate — not alter — them. We will all do well not to confuse the two.

M.B. Barlow Eugene, Ore.

Remember Climate Risk

To the Editor:

Re “A.I. Threat Grabs Attention From Climate Risks” (front page, Sept. 23):

This synopsis of twin crises matches my thinking, and my fears. But the A.I. crisis could be shut down more efficiently than the climate crisis.

Even if we curtailed fossil fuel use tomorrow, our planet would continue to warm, and the symptoms of this catastrophe — deadly heat waves, sudden floods and insidious wildfires — would continue to plague us for some time.

If only we had taken robust action to eliminate climate pollution decades ago, we would be in a much better place today. Eight million to nine million people would not die prematurely from fossil fuel pollution every year.

Oceans would be closer to their ideal temperature, allowing coral reefs to thrive. Thousands of acres of forests would be healthier. Heat waves would be far tamer. Droughts would have less of an impact.

In 1987, a group of world leaders met in Montreal to tackle the destruction of the ozone layer. At that meeting they chose to ban ozone-damaging chemicals, and the ozone layer has been recovering ever since. Let’s find our collective sanity!

Sally Courtright Albany, N.Y.

Colleges and A.I.

To the Editor:

Re “Universities in U.S. Sound the Alarm on A.I., Even as They Embrace It” (news article, Sept. 17):

Educational institutions need to double down on what it means for students to be in community with one another and what it means to be human. Instead, higher education is mired and entangled in a never-ending struggle over A.I. use.

Institutions need to take a step back, refocus on their missions and remind educators that nurturing the core values of collaboration, creativity, purpose and ethics will stand the test of time and technology. It’s not the technology. It’s us.

A recent M.I.T. report warning that A.I. is causing “cognitive surrender” has come the closest to getting this.

Matt Levinson Los Angeles The writer is the head of school at the Wildwood School and the author of “From Fear to Facebook: One School’s Journey.”

SUMMARY

Before he created “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling was stuck. Serling didn’t want to make that kind of show. With “The Twilight Zone,” Serling realized he could use allegory to make his political points.

ARTICLE

America Feels Trapped in the Twilight Zone. This Man Can Help.
With “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling created a durable blueprint for understanding our surreal reality.
By Alan Sepinwall
Published 2026-10-07 19:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/twilight-zone-tv-america.html

Before he created “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling was stuck. He’d established a reputation in the TV industry as, basically, Aaron Sorkin before Aaron Sorkin: a celebrated writer of weighty adult dramas that grappled with big contemporary issues like political corruption or the dehumanizing nature of corporate life.

He also frequently battled sponsors over what he was allowed to write and how far his scripts could go. When he worked to create a fictionalized version of the 1955 lynching of the Black teenager Emmett Till, for example, the final product was so watered down by sponsor and network pressure that it resulted in what he’d later describe in an interview with Mike Wallace as “a lukewarm, vitiated, emasculated kind of show.”

Serling didn’t want to make that kind of show. So after he was instructed to remove virtually all references to contemporary politics from a teleplay about a United States senator titled “The Arena,” he had a realization: “I probably would have had a much more adult play had I made it science fiction, put it in the year 2057, and peopled the Senate with robots,” he wrote of that experience.

Serling apparently applied the lesson of “The Arena” to a broader canvas, as he started writing speculative stories that were at sharp right angles to our own reality, in an anthology series that premiered in 1959 with the title “The Twilight Zone.” Because the series, which often featured fantastical scenarios, always with a surprising final twist, was so stylized, Serling found he could finally tell the unvarnished truth.

Almost 70 years later, at a moment when our own situation can seem increasingly ominous and surreal — when it’s hard to look anywhere, from political corruption to corporate malfeasance to the barrage of everyday headlines, without feeling as if you’ve traveled into a fifth dimension, beyond that which is known to man — Serling’s shrewd tactic for addressing political subjects offers an instructive response.

Contemporary television has often struggled to respond to the current political darkness; while shows like “The Good Fight” directly confronted the first Trump administration, few shows have done that during the second term. Some satires like “South Park” have taken direct aim, while others like “Saturday Night Live” have often seemed at sea when it comes to dealing with political turmoil.

With “The Twilight Zone,” Serling realized he could use allegory to make his political points. After all, how could a network censor or a viewer angrily insist that a story was saying something controversial about the world when it centered on a three-armed Martian?

This might help explain why “The Twilight Zone” still seems so incredibly — and at times, depressingly — relevant. Serling and his collaborators repeatedly and stealthily tackled such subjects as prejudice, creeping authoritarianism, the dangers of humans being replaced by technology and the peril of conformity as a societal ideal in ways that still resonate. Many episodes, when rewatched now, feel like they could have been written five minutes ago.

The show hit on social questions we have yet to adequately answer. Serling, a Jewish American who enlisted in the Army to fight Nazis during World War II, wrote often with his collaborators about the dangers of fascism and how easily people can succumb to its allure, including in such episodes as “The Obsolete Man” (a librarian is sentenced to death in a dystopia where books are outlawed) and “He’s Alive” (a hatemonger rises to power through coaching from Hitler’s ghost). In “The Brain Center at Whipple’s,” an aloof owner of a manufacturing plant gleefully replaces his flesh-and-blood workers with machines, unmoved by pleas from his former factory manager about the value of human thought and emotion; eventually, he himself is replaced by a robot.

“Number 12 Looks Just Like You” is set in a future where everyone upon turning 19 is forcibly transplanted into one of a handful of conventionally attractive bodies. It’s like today scrolling an Instagram feed where everyone is using the same filters or going down a rabbit hole about looksmaxxing. And the impulsive, destructive behavior of President Trump has often been likened to aspects of the plot of “It’s a Good Life,” an episode about an omnipotent child named Anthony Fremont who holds an entire town under his thumb.

Serling’s influence is evident all over modern culture. A legion of current storytellers, in television, film and literature, owe him a debt, from Steven Spielberg to Guillermo del Toro, from Curry Barker (as seen in his 2026 horror hit “Obsession”) to Ryan Coogler (“Sinners”). Charlie Brooker, creator of the anthology series “Black Mirror,” has talked about what he learned from Serling’s use of genre devices and the freedom they gave Serling to say what he wanted to say. “If he hadn’t had that rock for the river to flow around,” Mr. Brooker told me, “would the stories feel so resonant now? Or would we only read about them in academic books about the history of television?” Mr. Brooker went on to note: “Because he was forced to enter the world of metaphor, it’s the thing that gives him a superpower.”

Serling’s storytelling superpower grew from a desire to regain a lost affection for humanity — another effort that might prove instructive to us today. During his service as a paratrooper in the Pacific theater of World War II, a teenage Serling witnessed people dying under gruesome, often pointless circumstances. At 20, he watched as a close friend was decapitated in front of him by, of all things, a supply crate dropped from an airplane, and soon came perilously close to death himself.

These experiences left him traumatized and despairing about the depths to which his fellow man was capable of sinking. They also forced Serling to examine why people so often make terrible choices and whether there’s hope for them to do better in the future, a theme that would animate his TV writing. In “The Twilight Zone,” characters are often offered a magical second chance — and the ones who can’t change frequently earn karmic justice of a supernatural variety.

Despite his celebrity and acclaim — and his unnerving prescience — Serling struggled with self-doubt for much of his career. In the years leading up to his 1975 death of a heart attack at the age of 50, he gave an interview suggesting his accomplishments would soon be forgotten.

“I’ve written articulate stuff, reasonably bright stuff over the years, but nothing that will stand the test of time,” he said in 1972. “The good writing, really good writing — like wine — has to age well with the years, and my stuff is momentarily adequate.”

Not only did Serling underestimate his influence, but he also failed to see how the tactic he adapted would prove to be the most successful way to process perilous times. If the Serling who gave that interview could, like some of his characters, travel forward through time, he might be dismayed that so many of the problems he wrote about still aren’t resolved decades later. But he would also see that the best way to describe the legacy of his work isn’t “momentarily adequate,” but a different phrase he repeatedly recited as the host of “The Twilight Zone”: “as timeless as infinity.”

Alan Sepinwall is a TV critic, most recently for Rolling Stone, and the author of the forthcoming “Serling: A Journey Into the Twilight Zone With TV’s First Visionary.”

SUMMARY

At about 194 years old, Jonathan is the world’s oldest known land animal. Jonathan gave scientists the rare opportunity to study what happens to an animal’s genome over the course of nearly 200 years. “If we had 1,000 animals like Jonathan, it would be easier to understand his longevity,” said Dr. Stephen Clark, lead author of the study and the founder of Kallel, a nonprofit dedicated to studying the genetics of aging.

ARTICLE

At 194, Jonathan the Giant Tortoise Knows About Aging
Scientists have sequenced his genome for the first time, hoping the world’s oldest land animal can offer clues into the genetics of longevity.
By Monique Brouillette
Published 2026-10-07 18:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/science/jonathan-giant-tortoise-genome-aging.html

Dr. Joe Hollins slides a thick welding glove onto his left hand and grips a cotton swab tightly in his right. He squats down to eye level with a 400-pound giant tortoise, cradles its head with his gloved hand and carefully wedges a finger into its mouth to prop open its razor-sharp beak. With his other hand, he tries to swab its cheek.

Dr. Hollins, a veterinarian, has only about five seconds to get the DNA he’s after before he risks getting punched with a thick, scaly leg.

The first swab comes back covered in half-chewed carrot — a favorite snack. He tosses it aside and tries again. The tortoise, named Jonathan, looks mildly annoyed.

At about 194 years old, Jonathan is the world’s oldest known land animal. He’s an Aldabra giant tortoise living 1,200 miles off Africa’s west coast on the remote island of St. Helena, spending his days on the sun-dappled grounds of the official home of the governor. (At the time of his arrival on St. Helena, he was at least 50 years old, a determination his keepers made based on size.)

Although he shows some signs of aging, like cataracts that have left him mostly blind, he still has excellent hearing and a strong libido. He enjoys greeting visitors, having his neck petted and delivering loud belches for the crowd that gathers around his paddock during mealtimes.

In June, after Jonathan was erroneously declared dead by some media organizations, the Guinness World Records added him to its list of global icons, honoring his superlative status. And on Wednesday, he reached another milestone when a study announced that his genome had been sequenced for the first time.

“We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive,” said Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies aging at the University of California, Los Angeles, and an author of the study, which was published in the journal Science Advances.

Jonathan gave scientists the rare opportunity to study what happens to an animal’s genome over the course of nearly 200 years. But obtaining the DNA wasn’t easy: The researchers were not permitted to take a blood sample, the gold standard in DNA sequencing, because of the risk of infection. And because the island is served by only one often delayed commercial flight per week, the swabbed saliva had to travel by boat.

The researchers were committed to the idea, though, because they were curious if Jonathan’s DNA held secrets about aging or longevity. Just think: When this tortoise was presumably born in 1832, Charles Darwin was only 22 years old and hadn’t yet visited the Galápagos Islands, where he would dream up his theory of natural selection.

After sequencing the sample, the scientists compared Jonathan’s genome with those of tortoises 100 years his junior and found some molecular differences, especially in genes involved with DNA repair and the maintenance of the protective caps on chromosomes, called telomeres. As organisms age, DNA accumulates damage and the telomeres shorten, a process thought to drive aging. The results hint that this species may have evolved to be more resilient to age-related decline, but further testing is needed.

The team also discovered that Jonathan shared some genes with other long-living species like naked mole rats, which can live to 40 and rarely get cancer.

Perhaps most interesting is what they found when they looked at the tortoise’s epigenome, which is a map of the chemical tags that regulate the genome. These tags change with age and can lead to erratic gene activity. As expected, Jonathan had age-related changes in his epigenome similar to older humans, but there was an exception. Notably, the control switches linked to mitochondria were well preserved, similar to those of a young tortoise. Mitochondria, the molecular power plants inside cells, have long been linked to healthy aging.

The potential for learning from the biology of animals that live extraordinarily long lives is exciting for scientists who study aging. “Each of these long-lived species has some kind of special trick,” said Steve Austad, a biologist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. “And some of those may turn out to be relevant to human aging.”

“The results integrate very well in the wider puzzle of what longevity is,” said Björn Schumacher, who studies aging at the University of Cologne in Germany. He urged caution, though, in concluding that Jonathan would help us understand why humans age and what we can do about it.

Jeanne Calment, for example, was the world’s oldest person at the age of 122. She attributed her long life to a diet rich in olive oil and port wine. She also smoked cigarettes. Does that mean we should all smoke and drink red wine? Probably not, Dr. Schumacher said, and we should use similar caution when drawing conclusions from Jonathan.

Jonathan’s advanced age could be an outlier because of his round-the-clock veterinary care, diet of fresh vegetables and protected lawn at the governor’s house.

The molecular results offer tantalizing clues, however — ones that scientists are keen to explore further. “If we had 1,000 animals like Jonathan, it would be easier to understand his longevity,” said Dr. Stephen Clark, lead author of the study and the founder of Kallel, a nonprofit dedicated to studying the genetics of aging. In the future, Dr. Clark hopes to analyze more Aldabra tortoises and other long-lived species by gathering data that offers some hints for us spry chickens, too.

august-lamm-influencer-smartphone-book.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 42  Words: 2219/2223

SUMMARY

One hot summer day, August Lamm stood cheerily behind a booth in Tompkins Square Park, offering a stack of pamphlets titled “You Don’t Need a Smartphone.” Lamm, who is 31, was like them once. “Have you heard of August Lamm?” she asked.

ARTICLE

The Luddite Influencer
August Lamm wants you to put down your smartphone and reclaim your life.
By Amanda Hess
Published 2026-10-07 13:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/style/august-lamm-influencer-smartphone-book.html

One hot summer day, August Lamm stood cheerily behind a booth in Tompkins Square Park, offering a stack of pamphlets titled “You Don’t Need a Smartphone.” The cover featured a retro photograph of a woman lying on the floor and talking on a landline. She looked ecstatic.

Lamm had come to the park, in part, to invite participants to a “downgrading” event that evening, in which she would lead phone addicts toward less-connected devices. The crowd floated silently past. Their ears were stuffed with AirPods. Their eyes were watching their phones. The people who most need Lamm’s help, she has found, are the least likely to look up and notice her.

Lamm, who is 31, was like them once. Four years ago, she was an art influencer with 200,000 social media followers. Then she traded in her smartphone for a 2002-era Nokia cellphone. Later, she pawned her laptop. Now she’s working to divest herself from email. And she’s become an advocate for disengaging from technology and, as she puts it, “reclaiming your life.”

At the park, Lamm wore a thrifted black top with a paper clip in place of a missing button. She appears somewhat out of time, her face cleansed of TikTok makeup trends and her silhouette freed from the long jorts that have seemingly drop-shipped onto everyone in her age bracket. Unled by Google, unfed by DoorDash, unmatched on Hinge, she navigates a version of New York where seemingly everyone else is locked in a tragic embrace with a personal device. When she walks outside, she is now the rare human who is alert and open for engagement.

Soon Louis Toledo, 73, sidled up to the booth, the white cords of his headphones swinging from his chest pocket. “Phones, huh?” he said. “No one calls me.”

He told Lamm about his divorce, his relationship with his siblings, his difficulty in grade school, his service in the Air Force and his condominium in Puerto Rico, before returning finally to the topic of the smartphone, and his suspicion that “the G5, G4, 5G, whatever” can “kill your sperms.”

“Well,” Lamm said, empathizing: “At least you don’t need them now.”

He saw things differently. “Listen, I got more to offer you today than you could imagine,” he said. “We can have two kids and live beautifully in Puerto Rico.”

She asked if he would be willing to get rid of his smartphone, and when he said no, she smiled sadly. “That’s a dealbreaker for me,” she said.

A young couple approached, brandishing a flip phone. They had been experimenting, they said, with leaving the house with one smartphone between them.

Passerby asked if Lamm was affiliated with dumbphone companies, or the Luddites, or the Summer of Ludd. Over the past few years, the smartphone resistance has grown: there is the phoneless weekly Brooklyn gathering Phone Free Adelphi; the 30-day group challenge Month Offline; the biweekly techno-critical event bulletin NYC Off Tech; and the Luddite Club, with chapters from Santa Monica High School to Stockholm, Sweden.

Lamm has emerged as a kind of bard of this scene, writing about her own experience divesting from technology and encouraging her peers to replace mindless scrolling with actual books. Now she’s selling one: After moving 20,000 copies of her self-published $10 zine “You Don’t Need a Smartphone,” Vintage published an updated and expanded paperback under the same title this week.

It’s a practical guide to a post-smartphone life: Lamm draws her own maps and checks her email once a week at the public library. She advises carrying a compact mirror and deck of cards, as if passing down the ancient texts. The book is also a deeply observed account of what everyone else is missing. “Ironically, looking at screens is how we tune out the sad state of our public spaces,” she writes. “We can’t bear to face a crowd of indifferent souls. It’s mass rejection.”

After an hour and a half at the booth, Lamm packed up her materials and dragged them under the sidewalk umbrella of a nearby poke spot. She was underslept. The previous evening, she had attended a birthday party for the publisher of an offline low-tech zine, and “as happens when you don’t have a smartphone, I did not take the optimal train trip back home,” she said.

Downgrading is the inverse of optimizing. It’s a wandered path, logistically and socially. “I feel very out of touch,” Lamm said without concern. “People don’t feel the need to communicate any cultural trends in real life anymore, because they’re assuming that you’re getting it online,” she said. “I didn’t know who Chappell Roan was for like a year.”

As we finished our rice bowls, it began to rain, which caught Lamm by surprise. Soon it was pummeling the Lower East Side. A stream formed down Avenue A, rushing toward her “downgrading” event. She worried the storm would suppress turnout.

“I really need to start looking at the weather,” she said. “I need to get a newspaper delivered to my house.”

Life at 200,000 Followers

Lamm got her first iPhone shortly after she got her first period. It was, she writes in the book, “a treasure chest,” a “dozen gifts in one.” Later it would bring a bigger prize — she would leverage it to become a working artist, one who made a living not through connections in the art world but through followers on social media.

After college, where Lamm studied South Asian art history, she took up crosshatching, a drawing style forged in the Middle Ages that she savvily repositioned for the Instagram age. As she worked by day in a Berlin ice cream shop, she gained an online following for drawings of tiny ink animals that she photographed posed with a pen in a kind of digital illusion — a koala seems to hug the barrel; a pigeon perches on the uncapped tip. Lamm posed herself for Instagram too, where she had morphed into a recognizable type — an indie artist of the 2010s, with bangs and slim high-waisted jeans. She sold drawings and consultation sessions to her followers, as well as an online guide to how they, too, could make a living as an artist on social media.

Art Instagram is assumed to be one of the cozier parts of the internet, but for Lamm it was high-stress. When the fire alarm went off in her apartment building one morning, and she missed posting her daily drawing at the optimal time, she had a panic attack on the lawn.“I was going to lose my credibility, my algorithmic rank, my income if I took that day off,” she said.

But she also found that the more emotional she got on the app, the more attention she got for her work. “When I posted about being anxious, having a breakdown, going through a breakup, I would sell more,” she said.

She took a break from Instagram in 2022, but not on purpose. After entering the wrong password too many times, she was locked out of her account for three months. The timing felt catastrophic: She had a book on crosshatching coming out that she hoped would be a bridge to a writing career. She had been diagnosed with a degenerative spinal disorder, and when it flared, she said it was difficult to draw, and to use her phone. “I couldn’t tap with my thumb,” she said. Now, on the eve of her book’s publication, her platform collapsed.

When Lamm’s account was finally restored, she felt as if she had returned to a different Instagram, one ruled not by static photographs but by looping short-form videos. Meta paid her a few hundred dollars to make her first reel, and she was overwhelmed by how much time it required — time she could be drawing or writing. Her monthslong banishment had shown her just how reliant she was on tech companies.

This knowledge was at first horrifying, and then liberating. By the end of the year, she had traded in her smartphone for a less advanced model and deactivated her social media accounts.

With the phone gone, “my thoughts grew back,” she writes. Her memory was so sharp that she wondered fleetingly if she could be a “late-blooming genius,” she jokes. She read “Anna Karenina” and “Moby Dick,” recorded diaristic folk songs in her bedroom, and wrote a novel, “Lambing Season,” based on her experience moving into a ramshackle home with a student pilot she met on the internet. She supported herself by busking, freelance writing and selling that pamphlet, which answered all the questions she kept fielding about surviving without a smartphone.

Sometimes strangers examine Lamm’s life (she is from Connecticut) and assume she must be secretly rich. Her real secret is living “very cheaply,” she said. “It’s not a comfortable existence.”

Lamm said she left home when she was 16, shortly before her stepmother was incarcerated for running a pyramid scheme out of the living room. When her father died in 2024, Lamm was left to pay the funeral costs. The privilege of the low-tech lifestyle is not necessarily one enjoyed by the leisure class, which, she writes, “devotes much of its leisure time to screens.”

In 2025, Hilary Redmon, the head of nonfiction at Knopf, was working from home one day when her college-age daughter wandered into her office, looking at her phone. “Have you heard of August Lamm?” she asked. “I have to get rid of my phone.”

Redmon downloaded a PDF of Lamm’s zine, and was struck by her voice. “It made an impact on my daughter, who is pretty quick to dismiss people trying to influence her to do anything,” Redmon said. Soon Lamm had been offered a two-book deal, for the anti-smartphone book, and her novel.

Fans and Their Phones

Lamm arrived for her downgrading event at Nightclub 101 looking as if she had run through a sprinkler, which did not trouble her. Without the practice of constant self-surveillance, she had lost “the reflex of self-consciousness,” she said.

She dried off as she zipped around the moody basement space, preparing her various offerings. She set out a group of bound short stories published by Loose Tooth Press, which she co-founded with her friend Magdalene Kennedy.

Kennedy is one of the people Lamm calls on her flip-phone when she needs a human being to access the internet on her behalf. “She was at the bookstore and she was like, ‘I’m looking for a book on how to make decisions, can you look it up for me?’” Kennedy said. “And I tried, but there were so many books on how to make decisions.”

Next to the Loose Tooth stories were copies of Lamm’s new zine, “Archaic,” which you can’t read or buy online. The first issue includes a letter from Dave Eggers and poems by Tao Lin.

It’s an outgrowth of Lamm’s Center for Archaic Networks, a group she founded that’s “dedicated to the study and revival of human networks pre-dating social media.” She recently spent $100,000 of her book advance to put a down payment on a $320,000 house in upstate New York, where she will live and host a residency where applicants can stay for a week or two and lock their devices in a safe for the duration.

“I’m so excited to have this privilege that everybody else in human history had,” she said, “which is just to live in a house where everyone is present.”

In the end, the rain did not deter dozens of young New Yorkers from Lamm’s event. Gabriel Hurlbert, 26, met Lamm at a downtown literary reading in 2024, and started exchanging letters with her. He arrived at Nightclub 101 that evening with two smartphones, one provided by his employer, Deloitte.

“My relationship to my phone, for long stretches of time, has been like that between a heroin addict and heroin,” he said, though he believes the phone itself is symptomatic of a deeper problem. “I haven’t really located the source of the malaise,” he said.

On a bench, Lamm handled a small collection of minimalist phones that she had been gifted by Keyphone, which sponsored the event; by night’s end, she’d have given them all away. She has become a kind of Luddite influencer. Dumbphone companies have offered to pay for a mention in her book, and her publisher’s marketing team has floated the idea of a brand partnership. (She’s not interested).

I asked Lamm if she’d considered reactivating her dormant 180,000-follower Instagram account for the book launch. She had never fully deleted it, in case of emergency. “This does not qualify as an emergency to me,” she said.

When Lamm stepped onstage, the stakes of her project became clear. In battling the smartphone, she was fighting for her time, and for her mind, but also for some company. She could not bear to do this alone.

Lamm read an excerpt from the book, in which she lamented that her fans often told her that her zine changed their lives. But they still have smartphones. “They were theoretically in favor of the movement, and yet personally unable to partake,” she said. “They wished me the best with my activism. They had no doubt it would make a difference.”

As she spoke, a woman in the audience lifted her phone and zoomed in.

Chris Gallant dressed for an afternoon of shooting at a Long Island gun range in a tight Adidas T-shirt and purplish jeans. It was a Tuesday a little more than a month from Election Day, when Gallant, a 37-year-old Black Hawk helicopter pilot, will face Nick LaLota, the Republican incumbent who is vying for a third term representing New York’s First Congressional District, which stretches from Huntington past the Hamptons to the tip of Long Island. Gallant denies any such thing happened.

ARTICLE

Bondage Photos Weren’t Part of the Campaign Plan
But Chris Gallant, a Black Hawk pilot and Democrat who is running to represent Long Island in Congress, is making the most of life post-tabloid reveal.
By Jacob Bernstein
Published 2026-10-07 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/style/chris-gallant-campaign-photos.html

Chris Gallant dressed for an afternoon of shooting at a Long Island gun range in a tight Adidas T-shirt and purplish jeans.

In his right hand, he held a Sig Sauer case containing two of his own handguns. A third was tucked into his jeans.

It was a Tuesday a little more than a month from Election Day, when Gallant, a 37-year-old Black Hawk helicopter pilot, will face Nick LaLota, the Republican incumbent who is vying for a third term representing New York’s First Congressional District, which stretches from Huntington past the Hamptons to the tip of Long Island.

Gallant, who was taking a break from canvassing and phone banking, headed down a flight of stairs, handed the attendant his firearm license and ordered up his rounds.

“It’s just practice,” he said, with the rehearsed modesty of a fledgling politician. “Trying to get good at something.”

Gallant then proceeded to fire dozens of shots at or close to the bull’s-eye at the end of his lane.

“Pretty good, right?” he said.

Beyond practice, of course, Gallant allowed that shooting is also a way to relieve stress, which has been in ample supply recently.

Last month, The New York Post revealed that Gallant had appeared in varying degrees of undress in promotional photos for Mr. S Leather, a San Francisco fetish brand.

The images were taken for the company’s website in early 2010 when Gallant wasn’t yet 21. One shows him in a cage, wearing a harness and a muzzle, with another man behind him performing a sex act on him.

A second image had him above the same man, again in leather, this time receiving oral sex.

At Gallant’s request, the people at Mr. S deleted the shots sometime before he announced his candidacy for Congress in August 2025. But thanks to publicly available web archives, finding them was perhaps inevitable. (Despite calling it part of a political hit job, he said he has “no idea” who was responsible for alerting The Post.)

The Post presented the story with typical tabloid panache, with a headline that read, “NY Dem House candidate modeled for XXX-rated BDSM ads while serving in National Guard.”

A photo of a much younger Gallant in a harness at the Folsom Street Fair in San Francisco also became the subject of a Suffolk County Conservative Committee Facebook post that said “Is this who you want to represent us in Washington D.C.?”

The LaLota campaign did not directly address the images. And Gallant seemed to decide that the photos were a chance to show that a person in public life can contain multitudes.

Specifically, Chris Gallant can be a Long Island-raised Black Hawk pilot in the Army National Guard who flew choppers during one of his two tours in Kuwait, worked for five years as an air traffic controller at John F. Kennedy International Airport, serves as a volunteer firefighter and is an unabashed gun owner as well as a union man who posed for those photos almost 17 years ago, not because he was manipulated but because he was into it.

“I mean, all my friends know I’m kinky” as hell, he said, using a saltier word. “I make Christian Grey look like amateur hour.”

It was his first in-depth interview since the images were widely shared. He wanted to make clear that he — like his outfits in those pics — had little to hide.

We were seated on a red leather sofa in the living room of his cozy clapboard house in Amity Harbor, which happens to be just outside the limits of the district he hopes to represent. (LaLota lives in Amityville, also outside the district, he pointed out.) Recent issues of The Advocate and Army Aviation Magazine were stacked on the coffee table.

In front of the house was a small yard and a white picket fence.

“I just thought, ‘If my family can accept me, the world can,’ and that’s how I lived my entire life,” said Gallant, who was wearing jeans and a fitted gray Rag & Bone sweater.

His mother, Barbara Solony-Cohen, was in the kitchen, having driven up from her home in North Carolina, along with his friend Jason Hewitt, a TD Bank branch manager, whom he met at a gay ski week in 2014. They were scheduled to go canvassing later that evening. Absent was his fiancé, Mike Ingram, a National Guard infantryman who Gallant said is stationed in the Middle East.

Gallant said he hadn’t anticipated that this long-ago campaign for a fetish-wear brand would become public as it did. “I mean, you had to go hunt for this,” he said.

After The Post published its article, his team had conversations about the viability of his candidacy. But there are limited options available seven weeks out from an election.

So Gallant, who has the air of many a good-looking guy who has seldom if ever been told there’s anything he can’t do, started to see about working the situation to his advantage.

Maybe it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” he said, only half jokingly.

Less than 48 hours after the Post story, he uploaded a video of himself to Facebook, speaking into the camera and calling the photo release a “coordinated political hit meant to drive me out of this race.”

Then, his social media team posted a new ad of him in a tight black T-shirt that showed off his Marvel-worthy biceps. The slogan running across it read, “Make Politics Sexy Again.”

Sexiness, the ad went on to say, includes his plans for improving the lives of the voters in his district, including support for veterans and lowering the cost of living on Long Island.

If Gallant somehow prevails, several Democratic consultants said, it will most likely be in a squeaker.

Jon Reinish, a Democratic strategist and former aide to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, said New York’s First Congressional District had not been won by a Democrat since 2012. “But in a wave election, it’s definitely in play.”

One option for Gallant? Lean further into his image as a fit guy enjoying his sexuality, Reinish argued. “The Democrats have been librarians for too long.”

In the interview at his home, Gallant seemed to be contemplating just that kind of playbook. At least, he was not wringing his hands over photos from 2010.

“My most difficult thing was always getting my name out there or trying to improve that,” he said. “And there’s definitely been a name-recognition increase on the world stage.” He noted that “The Daily Show” had covered his modeling: The first joke told was that Gallant was getting his butt beaten, “but not in the polls.”

Gallant knows that the punchline is a little generous; it is an uphill climb in a district that has been represented by a Republican since 2015. His newfound attention might not help him “in the district” with the voters who matter.

And there remains the question of whether the photographs for Mr. S will be the biggest bomb to drop.

Messenger Papers, a conservative news site, published a piece about Gallant that insinuated that he had worked as an escort as recently as 2024 under the name Joe Flint, and that Flint was discussed on a site where patrons of escorts go to compare notes.

Gallant denies any such thing happened. He said that there may have been stolen pictures floating around online, and that perhaps, they could have wound up on escort sites.

Emails to the men who had discussed hiring Flint on the site went unanswered.

But at a recent town hall, held at a sports bar in Middle Island, more than a hundred people showed up, and no one seemed interested in his sex life.

“Whatever, everyone has a social media history,” said Renee McKeon, 50, an independent voter who works as an administrator at the Suffolk County Sheriff’s Office and who said she planned on voting for Gallant, despite having cast a ballot for President Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. “During Trump’s first presidency, there were guardrails,” she said. “The corruption is much more rampant now.”

For more than an hour, Gallant was hazy about policy, but he was perfectly capable of running through his opposition to everything he believes President Trump has helped bring about, from the war in Iran to the fast-tracking of ICE agents.

During a question-and-answer session, one person asked Gallant about a recent comment made by LaLota, in which his opponent called him “weak and woke.”

“I’ve carried people out of burning buildings; I’ve flown helicopters in the Middle East,” Gallant said. “If that’s weak and woke — well, I just think that’s inaccurate.”

Another asked him what should be done regarding misinformation online.

As a supporter of free speech, Gallant said he wasn’t sure exactly.

Still, he had some advice. “Don’t get your news from social media. Unless you’re going to look at mine.”

ARTICLE

How an Influencer Has to Say ‘I’m Sorry’
A dispute over online misinformation about the F-Factor diet led to an unusual agreement: an apology video that must be pinned to the top of social feeds for three and a half years.
By Katherine Rosman
Published 2026-10-07 16:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/style/f-factor-diet-influencer-apology-zuckerbrot-gellis.html

When an Instagram influencer named Emily Gellis shared a new video late Friday night, many followers noticed the contrast to her usual fare of shopping, family and sponsored posts.

“I am here today to take full responsibility for the harm I caused to Tanya Zuckerbrot, her company F-Factor and her family,” Gellis began. In a shot that captured her from the shoulders up in a black turtleneck in front of a white wall, she seemed to read a prepared statement about her conduct toward Zuckerbrot, a registered dietitian, entrepreneur and — like Gellis — a prolific sharer on Instagram.

“I am deeply sorry,” she said in the six-minute mea culpa, her usually animated affect flat. “Yes, I want to say that again. I am deeply sorry.”

Her followers flooded her comments. “This is like a hostage video,” one said.

Gellis’s video is the centerpiece of a settlement of a lawsuit that Zuckerbrot filed in October 2020, which claimed Gellis defamed and harassed her.

The video apology must remain “pinned” to the top of Gellis’s Instagram and Facebook accounts for three and a half years, according to a transcript of court proceedings filed last month.

The Puritans had scarlet letters, and now the content creators have scarlet posts: video apologies usually negotiated by lawyers for brands and public figures that have come under criticism from influencers pushing commentary not always rooted in facts.

For the women who whittle their free time on New York lifestyle Instagram accounts, Gellis’s austere video was startling as it appeared amid a scroll of the standard imagery that generates likes, comments and commerce. “I found it very unusual,” said Molly McPherson, a crisis communications consultant. “It seemed like less of a heartfelt apology than a negotiated correction.”

Chatter about the video spread across Instagram and around New York last weekend, revisiting F-Factor, a pre-Ozempic-era high fiber diet, as well as Gellis’s relentless campaign, which created a pandemic-days internet spectacle-cum-unscripted reality show.

Apologies and retractions are longstanding remedies sought by lawyers when a client’s reputation has been tarnished by misleading advertising and by misinformed commentary presented as fact, said Daniel Watkins, a defamation lawyer whose clients have included the Rev. Al Sharpton and Robert Sarver, the former owner of the Phoenix Suns.

“What’s changed is that more are now posted online,” Watkins said. “Less common is a public apology where the plaintiff’s fingerprints and the legal pressure behind it are this visible.”

And to people viewing the spectacle of the Gellis apology, those fingerprints seemed very visible: Plenty of comments took note of the pressure she must have faced.

Indeed, defamation lawyers caution that apologies like Gellis’s don’t come cheap. This one was a result of six years of litigation, an involved discovery process and most likely hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees.

Gellis declined to comment.

In an email, Zuckerbrot said, “After six years, having the truth publicly acknowledged brings relief, but an apology cannot rebuild the company I spent 25 years creating, restore my employees’ jobs or give my family back the years and sense of safety we lost.”

Gellis’s public criticism of Zuckerbrot and her diet company, F-Factor, began in the summer of 2020, at a specific moment in internet culture when most Americans were isolated and easily fixated on drama spilling out on the internet.

Gellis has admitted that she never followed Zuckerbrot’s F-Factor weight-loss program, which is based on a high-fiber diet that she laid out in books and Instagram videos. The program also included packets of F-Factor fiber powder, fiber bars or personal consultation with Zuckerbrot or her employees. (Some clients paid as much as $25,000 to consult with Zuckerbrot directly.)

Relying on anonymous tips that Gellis said she received on social media, she began telling her followers — often posting on her Instagram story dozens of times a day, or more — that the F-Factor diet, especially the fiber packets, were making some people sick. Zuckerbrot denied any widespread problem and questioned Gellis’s research and authority.

In a New York Times article about the public clash, reporters spoke to some F-Factor clients whom Gellis said had complained to her about health problems. They confirmed that Gellis had correctly represented their experiences.

But the reporters also found that one of the most serious allegations Gellis publicized — that the diet caused a miscarriage — was untrue, and was the result of a setup by a woman who purposely lied to Gellis to see if she would propagate this claim without evidence.

In the article, Zuckerbrot defended her products.

In October 2020, Zuckerbrot, who is married to a real estate investor and who has been active in sharing images on social media of her luxury lifestyle, filed her lawsuit against Gellis, claiming that Gellis’s posts resulted in the loss of about 90 percent of F-Factor’s monthly revenue.

In 2023, after the negative publicity and as GLP-1s surged in popularity and caused the entire diet economy to reconfigure, Zuckerbrot shuttered her business. She turned her online attention to speaking out against antisemitism and in support of Israel.

But her legal battle with Gellis continued. This summer, according to a court filing, the two women agreed on a settlement.

The agreement demands that Gellis pay Zuckerbrot $500 a month for 40 years, totaling $240,000. (Zuckerbrot’s spokeswoman said the amount is equal to medical and therapy costs Zuckerbrot incurred as a result of Gellis’s actions.)

More than the video, lawyers said, this financial arrangement is novel and was probably structured to force Gellis to be reminded every month of her transgressions. “It shows someone who wants this woman to pay for the rest of her life,” said Aaron Minc, a First Amendment lawyer.

When it came to the video, Zuckerbrot imposed what is essentially a no eye-rolling rule. “In reading the apology for the purposes of video recording, Gellis shall read it taking effort to look at the device recording as much as practicable,” according to the court filing of the settlement agreement, which continues “so as to limit the appearance and/or number of times she’s looking away from the recording device when reading the apology.”

And the settlement decrees that the video apology will be the first thing scrollers see when they visit Gellis’s page. “The video and written apology will be pinned to the top of all of Ms. Gellis’s social media accounts including but not limited to Instagram and Facebook for three and a half years, and will remain in her social media feeds for an additional one and a half years after,” according to the settlement, which also forbids Gellis from setting her feed to “private” or disabling public comments.

Looking directly at the camera, Gellis admits being responsible for “a sustained and harmful campaign that was not grounded in verified facts,” and said that she was wrong to compare Zuckerbrot to Harvey Weinstein, Jeffrey Epstein and the Sackler family, members of which helped market OxyContin as a minimally addictive painkiller. “I now understand that this behavior was excessive, invasive and harmful,” she said in the video.

Last week, before Gellis had posted the video herself, Zuckerbrot did so on her own accounts, first reaching out to friends to ask that they too share it. “I want it to go viral and for the truth to get out,” she wrote in a text message reviewed by The Times.

But what she posted was not Gellis’s six-minute apology. It was a 13-minute edit of the video that Zuckerbrot had spliced with highlight clips of Gellis’s years-old posts, mocking Zuckerbrot’s manner of talking and making health claims that she lacked evidence to support, including that the diet caused someone to suffer a heart attack.

Zuckerbrot’s post was widely shared and received thousands of comments of support like, “It’s about time!!” and “Justice is finally served.”

Hours later, Gellis shared the six-minute Emily’s version on Friday evening. Her supporters, some of them critics of the diet, offered her comfort. “Everyone knows exactly what this is. You did what you needed to do,” one person wrote. “Emily blink twice if you’re OK,” another said.

Zuckerbrot succeeded in the legal battle, noted McPherson, the crisis P.R. consultant. But public opinion can be a different matter. “It’s clear from the sheer volume of her negative posts that Gellis veered from being an online critic to being a hater,” she said. “But the video apology is a hard watch and to some it can appear a hollow victory.”

To Zuckerbrot, it feels like a fresh start and she plans to focus on her business. “I am looking forward to relaunching F-Factor and returning to the work I love,” she said in an email.

Arizona Congressional Candidate Says She Was Raped While Fixing Sign
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, said the attack in August occurred while she was repairing a damaged campaign sign.
By Reis Thebault
Published 2026-10-08 03:41 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/us/bernadetta-green-placentia-campaign-sign-rape.html

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democratic candidate for Congress, said on Wednesday that she was repairing a damaged campaign sign in her district northwest of Phoenix this summer when two men attacked her.

The assailants sneaked up behind her in a parking lot, struck her on the head and raped her, according to a police report she filed with the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office. She lost consciousness, she said, and woke up with one of the men on top of her.

Ms. Greene-Placentia said her memory of the episode was spotty, but she recalled kicking her attackers until they fled.

She said the assault took place in the pre-dawn hours of Aug. 14 in Sun City, Ariz., a suburb of Phoenix.

After the attack, she said, she withdrew from her staff and family. For about two days, she did not respond to messages or phone calls, and she missed a campaign event.

“When it first happened, I didn’t want to tell anybody,” she said in an interview on Wednesday. She initially resolved to not report the rape to the police or to discuss it publicly. “I was embarrassed that I couldn’t defend myself,” she said.

But back on the campaign trail, she said, her promises to fight for Arizonans if elected to Congress began to feel hollow. How could she make that pledge, she reasoned, if she was avoiding an opportunity to speak out on behalf of other survivors of sexual assault?

“It just flashed in my head, like, ‘Well, you’re not standing up for everyone, are you?’” Ms. Greene-Placentia said. “I cannot be a hypocrite.”

On Aug. 31, about two weeks after the assault, she reported it to the police.

She then shared her account with the Phoenix New Times, the city’s alternative newspaper, which published it on Wednesday.

She said she was braced for the backlash that has become an unavoidable feature of modern politics. Ms. Greene-Placentia, a former long-haul trucker, feared that her campaign’s messaging around affordability and health care would be overshadowed. And she worried that voters would think her disclosure was a political gambit in her long-shot bid to flip a district that the incumbent, Representative Abraham Hamadeh, a Republican, won by 13 percentage points in 2024.

“I don’t want my campaign to be about this,” she said. “But women need to know it’s OK to come forward.”

In a statement, Mr. Hamadeh said he had read Ms. Greene-Placentia’s account, and he urged the authorities to “investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place, in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law.”

“No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community,” Mr. Hamadeh said.

The Maricopa County sheriff’s detectives are still working to gather evidence, including possible video footage, in the case. A department spokesman, Dave Moyer, said the investigation was ongoing and declined to comment further.

It’s unclear what physical evidence might exist to support Ms. Greene-Placentia’s account or whether detectives have identified any suspects.

Ms. Greene-Placentia said she did not seek medical care following the attack and did not undergo a sexual assault exam. She told the police she went home and took three showers and a bath. As she rinsed off, she noticed gravel from the parking lot in the base of the tub.

When officers asked if any of the perpetrators’ DNA might be found on the jeans or campaign shirt she wore that morning, Ms. Greene-Placentia told them that she had already washed the clothes. She did not get a good look at either attacker, she said, but described them as white men. One of them had small feet and was wearing black boots, she said.

Ms. Greene-Placentia at first told investigators that one of her attackers used a profanity that made her believe the assault was politically motivated, but she said on Wednesday that she could not be sure what she had heard.

Craig Beckman, Ms. Greene-Placentia’s director of communications, was one of the first people she confided in, outside a campaign event a little over 48 hours after the incident.

Mr. Beckman said he immediately knew something was wrong. “It was a shock to see her in this vulnerable state, to see her cry,” Mr. Beckman said.

Ms. Greene-Placentia’s staff members told her she could suspend her campaign, or even drop out of the race, if she felt that would be best for her health. But she was emphatic.

“It never occurred to me to quit,” said Ms. Greene-Placentia, who resumed a jam-packed campaign schedule over the following weeks. “I was just like, ‘This happened, it sucks, let’s move on.’”

But the campaign, which operates on a shoestring budget, has made some security adjustments. For one, Ms. Greene-Placentia no longer installs or repairs campaign signs alone after dark, a habit she had adopted to avoid the punishing Arizona summer heat.

Now, whenever she does go out, she is accompanied by a member of her staff and brings with her one of her many firearms, which she said she is “very good” at using.

Nearly two months after the assault, she said her resolve to speak out has strengthened. She said she had at times been skeptical of the #MeToo movement and had occasionally doubted the accusers of powerful men. Now, she said, she understands.

“I apologize to every woman that I doubted, and thank every woman for coming forward,” she said. “I’ll do anything I can to help more women come forward and recognize that there are people who will stand up for you.”

Fatal Stabbing of a 7-Year-Old Girl Rattles Chicago: ‘That Was a Baby’
The attack has raised questions about whether the suspect was overlooked by authorities despite a history of mental health problems and violent offenses.
By Bill Ruthhart and Robert Chiarito
Published 2026-10-07 20:27 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/us/chicago-stabbing-girl.html

Tiera Whalum sat in her parked car in Chicago on Saturday morning, waiting for a hair appointment. Outside her window, she saw a woman waving her arm while approaching a pair of young sisters who were holding hands while walking down the sidewalk. Then one girl screamed.

“I thought she was swatting away a bee or a bug from the girl,” Ms. Whalum, 30, said of the woman. “But she was actually stabbing her, and she walked away like nothing happened.”

Eddimar Hernandez Chacon, 7, lay on the ground with multiple wounds to her back. As the girl’s 17-year-old sister sobbed and bystanders subdued the attacker, Ms. Whalum and a police officer took turns administering CPR to the girl. But they couldn’t save her.

Days later, the brazen and unprovoked killing of a child in broad daylight continues to rattle Chatham, a neighborhood on Chicago’s South Side. The authorities have said there is no evidence that the girl was targeted. But the attack has raised questions about whether the woman charged with her murder — Shavon Gayden, 48 — had been overlooked by the criminal justice and health care systems despite a history of violent offenses and mental health problems.

“Obviously, this woman had mental health issues to do something so heinous to a child just walking down the street with her sister,” said Roderick Sawyer, a longtime Chatham resident who represented the area in the City Council for 12 years. “I’ve not seen this kind of random violence in Chatham, and I’ve been here all my life.”

The stabbing has also renewed attention to violent crime in Chicago, at a time when Mayor Brandon Johnson, a Democrat, is proclaiming amid his re-election campaigning that the streets are getting safer.

Chicago is on pace this year to record fewer homicides than last year’s 60-year low. Even so, President Trump, who for years has cast the city as a den of violence, on Tuesday again raised the idea of federal intervention, citing “a particularly violent crime wave that is getting worse by the day.” He did not mention the girl’s death.

Mayor Johnson told reporters on Sunday that while the city was working to eliminate all violence, “anytime a tragedy happens to a young person, it’s that much more egregious.”

Ms. Gayden, who has been charged with first-degree murder, remained hospitalized on Wednesday with a head injury she sustained when bystanders chased her down. She has not yet appeared in court.

Prosecutors said at a court hearing on Monday that Ms. Gayden first threatened a store clerk on Cottage Grove Avenue, a busy commercial thoroughfare. Soon after exiting the shop, she approached the girls and pulled a knife out of a pumpkin-themed bag, they said. The older sister ducked, and Ms. Gayden pulled Eddimar to the ground and stabbed her multiple times in the back, the police and prosecutors said.

Over the past decade, Ms. Gayden has twice faced charges of domestic violence, but the cases were dropped, court records show. In 2024, she pleaded guilty to felony aggravated battery for threatening to stab a bus driver and was sentenced to two years’ probation, according to prosecutors and court records.

In 2025, she pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery for striking a police officer and an employee of a homeless shelter where she was staying, prosecutors and court records say.

A warrant was issued for Ms. Gayden’s arrest in February 2025 after she violated the terms of her probation in the case involving the bus driver. She went on to appear in court four times for the 2024 homeless shelter case but was never arrested under the warrant, court records show.

It is unclear whether Ms. Gayden would have been held in jail if she had been arrested — and if so, for how long. A judge ordered her release less than two months after her arrest at the homeless shelter, according to the Cook County Sheriff’s office.

“She had a lot of mental health challenges over the years,” Ms. Gayden’s mother, Christine Gayden, said in a brief phone interview on Tuesday. “I went through hot water trying to get her help.”

After the stabbing on Saturday, bystanders knocked Ms. Gayden unconscious, the police said.

Ms. Whalum, who is a nursing student, said she jumped out of her car and applied pressure to Eddimar’s wounds with a jacket and a blanket before assisting with CPR.

“It’s really, really heartbreaking,” Ms. Whalum said, adding: “That was a baby. She didn’t even get to live her life.”

“I said, ‘Oh man, I didn’t know she was on probation,’” Mr. King said. “If I would have said something, maybe they would have locked her up and this wouldn’t have happened.”

Most of the focus at the memorial, however, was on Eddimar. Tiger Thompson said he had visited the site two or three times a day since her death. The girl’s mother works for him as a construction laborer on drywall and painting projects, he said.

“She’s an excellent mom. She works and takes care of her kids, and that’s why I keep coming here and crying,” said Mr. Thompson, 55, who lives in suburban Dolton, Ill. Mr. Thompson said he had recently driven Eddimar and her siblings to school.

“They left a bunch of candy under my seat, and I was fussing at them about it. She said, ‘I’ll get it, I’ll get it,’” Mr. Thompson recalled.

He said he believed that Eddimar’s tragic death showed the need for more mental health resources.

“If they give people the mental health they need,” he said, “a lot of this can be prevented.”

Christa Pike, Awake and Confused, Is at the Center of a Legal Storm

Six days after being shot full of a drug meant to kill her, Christa Pike awoke in a Nashville hospital, shackled to a bed and in a room where she knew no one.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers had been told to expect life support to end because her brain was not functioning after the attempt on Sept. 30 to execute her for killing a classmate decades before. But now, she was awake and in a swirl of what one lawyer called a mix of anger and confusion.

Her condition, disclosed on Wednesday after a court hearing, remains severe. She has a blood clot in one arm and pneumonia, and had not eaten — she was unable to swallow when her lawyers saw her. She could not move her arms, and her hands had swollen to resemble inflated surgical gloves, said the lawyer, Randy Spivey.

“She woke up in a hospital surrounded by people she didn’t know with a tube down her throat,” Mr. Spivey said during a news conference. “We don’t know the toll all of this will take, but Christa is a survivor.”

Ms. Pike’s awareness and evolving condition heightened the stakes of a procedural hearing in Nashville on Wednesday. A judge said she would order Tennessee to preserve records and evidence tied to the execution attempt and to ensure Ms. Pike could communicate easily with her lawyers.

The hearing came as Tennessee grapples with the ethical and legal questions surrounding the case of Ms. Pike, 50, the first person to survive injection drugs that were supposed to be lethal. A lawyer with the office of the state’s attorney general told a judge on Wednesday that he could not say whether Tennessee would try again to end her life.

A spokeswoman for Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, who paused executions while an independent investigation is underway, has not responded to questions about whether he would grant Ms. Pike clemency. Her lawyers have pleaded for him to allow her to spend the rest of her life in prison, arguing that she has suffered enough at the hands of the state.

“The dynamic is different because she’s now awake,” said David Raybin, a Nashville lawyer who helped write the state’s death penalty statute. The avenues for litigation, including for violations of her civil rights and constitutional protections against cruel punishment, have suddenly expanded, he said.

Ms. Pike has been on death row since she was a teenager, after she was found guilty in 1996 for her role in the torture and murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, 19. Ms. Pike, along with two other people, lured Ms. Slemmer into the woods, where they slashed at her with a box cutter and smashed her head with pieces of asphalt.

Ms. Slemmer’s family, who raised money to drive to Nashville from Florida for the execution, had supported capital punishment for Ms. Pike. Ms. Pike was 18 at the time of the murder and the only one of the three students to receive the death penalty.

Ms. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has since expressed frustration that the justice promised to her family has been denied.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers had repeatedly warned that Ms. Pike’s medical conditions, including her small veins, could lead to a complicated and unnecessarily painful execution. But on Sept. 30, they said, she was “at peace” after repeatedly expressing remorse for her crime.

The execution was first delayed by a flurry of last-minute legal maneuvering. It resumed after about nine hours, when word came just after 5:45 p.m. that the conservative majority on the Supreme Court said it could proceed.

But over the next two hours, witnesses described Ms. Pike as alert and lucid for stretches of time. Behind curtains, for nearly an hour, they could hear her breathing.

“She helped the execution team find what they thought was venous access,” Mr. Spivey said. “She was kind and polite as they worked for an hour, stabbing her arm with needle after needle.”

Just before 9 p.m., witnesses were told to leave. An ambulance arrived, and Ms. Pike was taken to a private Nashville hospital. Through the weekend, she had been unconscious, on a ventilator and intubated, as medical staff members worked to remove the drug, pentobarbital, from her veins. The drug shuts down electrical activity in the brain and could have caused long-term complications by lowering her oxygen levels or weakening circulation.

The details of the current lethal injection protocol in Tennessee, implemented in 2025, has been largely concealed. That was among the factors that prompted Ms. Pike’s lawyers on Wednesday to ask a judge to order the state to preserve all records and evidence related to the botched attempt.

“Today’s hearing was about transparency,” Luke Ihnen, one of Ms. Pike’s lawyers, said after the hearing. The state’s word, he added, “is shrouded in secrecy and legal jargon in attempts to obfuscate and obscure what really happened.”

John W. Ayers, an assistant attorney general, argued that the request was unnecessary, given that the agency was already required to preserve evidence. He said observation logs, medical waste and products were among the records already collected by the Department of Correction, in addition to pictures taken the night of Sept. 30.

But the judge, I’Ashea Myles of Davidson County Chancery Court, sided with Ms. Pike’s lawyers and outlined the contours of an order that she said she would sign. Among the records she listed were waste, needles, catheters, medical supplies, restraints, gurneys, syringes, drugs and IV lines, as well as communications that night.

“You will take special care not to lose, misplace, accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent,” she told Mr. Ayers.

The judge also instructed the state to allow easy communication between Ms. Pike and her lawyers, ensuring they have the same access as when she was held in prison.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers also raised concerns that one hand, as well as her feet, remained shackled to her hospital bed, despite requests from medical staff that they be removed. Chancellor Myles said that she was likely to consider the request if it directly came from the medical staff. That is expected to be kept private in order to shield the privacy of both Ms. Pike and the staff members tasked with her medical care.

Mr. Spivey said that Ms. Pike still had “a lot of cognitive confusion.”

But, he said, “she is very aware that the state tried to execute her.”
