SUMMARY

Emily Bazelon: Hi David, it’s great to be back here with you for the beginning of the Supreme Court’s new term. But there has been so much action from the court over the last few months on the emergency docket that I don’t feel like we had a break. Many district court judges feel like the Supreme Court does not have their backs when they rule against the Trump administration.

ARTICLE

Third-Country Deportations Are Only the Half of It
The real-world consequences of the Roberts court are coming into view.
By Emily Bazelon and David French
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/alito-supreme-court-deportation-colorado.html

Emily Bazelon: Hi David, it’s great to be back here with you for the beginning of the Supreme Court’s new term. Usually, this is like the first day of school for me — a fresh start. But there has been so much action from the court over the last few months on the emergency docket that I don’t feel like we had a break. I hope this is a fleeting feature of Trump’s second term rather than the new normal.

David French: It’s the new normal, I’m afraid. At least for the foreseeable future — for as long as presidents try to rule through executive actions rather than actually govern by executing laws passed by Congress.

Emily: I think it’s bad for two reasons: I am not a fan of the emergency docket except in actual emergencies and I liked having a break to think about other things. (I bet the justices did, too — remember the teaching gigs in Italy and Austria?) Oh well. Let’s pretend it’s time to get all dressed up and start with the first big case of the term. On Monday, the justices heard arguments in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. Boulder, Colo., wants Exxon Mobil, the biggest energy company in the country, and Suncor, a company based in Canada that operates two oil refineries in the state, to pay the state back for some of the costs of dealing with climate change.

Boulder says this is like the public health damage unleashed by tobacco or opioids, which states have sued companies for causing in the past, settling for large sums. A lawyer for Exxon and Suncor says this is an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” clearly pre-empted by federal law. Their best argument, I think, is that federal laws have historically governed interstate pollution. The open question, however, is whether that rule applies to carbon-dioxide emissions.

A few weeks ago, I thought that this pro-corporate court, as I see it, would be a sure bet for ruling in favor of big oil. But last week Justice Samuel Alito recused himself (he did not say why), taking out one likely vote for the companies and creating the possibility of a 4-4 split. Then at oral argument, Chief Justice John Roberts asked some intriguing questions suggesting that he has doubts about whether Boulder’s suit is in fact pre-empted by broad principles of law. Justice Elena Kagan did a good job of pressing the point by asking for the source of this pre-emption — “Where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that?” Seems like the answer was weak.

What do you think about where the justices will land and also the underlying question — should a state or county or city be able to sue a company for this kind of harm, or is it a problem Congress is supposed to pass laws to address?

David: This is one of the rare cases where I must confess that I’m a bit stumped, even after reading the oral argument more than once. I don’t know how it will turn out and — quite frankly — I’m a little bit stumped on how it should turn out.

I’m clear on what I think the ideal legal regime should look like, and that’s a comprehensive, sensible federal system that provides rational legal uniformity across the country. After all, as Kannon Shanmugam, who argued the case for Exxon and Suncor, pointed out (and here I should note that Kannon is a friend of mine), a patchwork of state and local cases would almost certainly create a chaotic legal environment. Shouldn’t industries that create interstate effects be subject to interstate regulations? And that can only really come from the federal government.

But we don’t decide cases on the basis of what the law should be, but on the basis of what the law is. And it’s far from clear that the Constitution or any currently enacted federal statutes mean that state law can’t be used to impose liability on energy producers.

Chief Justice Roberts came out swinging, confronting Kannon with a number of scenarios in which states can impose liability for harms that occur inside a state, even if the initial action occurs outside the state. (He used the simple example of someone throwing a rock from State B and hitting someone inside State A).

Justice Kavanaugh argued that the court’s precedents “make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law.” But after reading the argument, I’m not sure that a majority of the justices see the same clarity.

Add Chief Justice Roberts’s aggressive questioning to Justice Alito’s recusal, and you’ve got the possibility of a very unsatisfying 4-4 decision that would leave in place the Colorado decision allowing the lawsuit against Suncor and Exxon to go forward without really resolving the underlying issue.

Also, we should mention that there’s at least some chance that this case might also get tossed out of SCOTUS on jurisdictional grounds. So there is a good possibility that arguably the most important case of the term could go out with a fizzle and not a bang. I honestly don’t know how it’s going to go.

Emily: Last week, the court put two huge cases about deportation on the upcoming docket. One of them, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., is a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting people to “third countries,” meaning countries with which they have no ties (often when their countries of origin refuse to take them back). This case is a big deal for several reasons. The administration has deported at least 25,000 people through this avenue, according to human rights groups. The evidence suggests that the government is in fact doing this with little or no regard for human rights. Some people wind up indefinitely detained or in awful and dangerous conditions. Trump officials appear to view this as a feature, to deter immigration, not a bug. They’ve spent or pledged more than $400 million to persuade 31 countries to take people.

David: This is yet another example of how the Trump administration sometimes treats undocumented immigrants worse than we treat many of the most hardened criminals in the United States. Under the relevant federal statute, third-country removals are to take place when conventional deportation is “impracticable, inadvisable or impossible.”

That’s a last-resort provision, not a loophole. It’s not a catchall provision that gives the Trump administration carte blanche to punish immigrants by sending them to nations where neither human rights nor the rule of law are paramount. American deportees should not be imprisoned in conditions that would violate both the United States Constitution and international treaties prohibiting torture.

Emily: Another big issue in D.V.D.: The Trump administration violated Judge Brian Murphy’s order in April 2025 to halt third-country deportations to places like Libya and South Sudan — not safe — if the deportees had no meaningful chance to object. Yet in an emergency docket ruling last week, a majority of the justices gave the Trump administration a pass for now, saying that the third-country deportations can continue until the court issues a permanent ruling. The case is fast-tracked for arguments in December. But it’s remarkable and dismaying that in the meantime and maybe forever, a majority of justices is willing to look the other way on disobeying a court order. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote a powerful dissent to an earlier stay, but only her two fellow liberal colleagues joined it. She describes people narrowly escaping arrivals amid violence in Libya and writes, “Only the District Court’s careful attention to this case prevented worse outcomes. Yet today the Court obstructs those proceedings, exposing thousands to the risk of torture or death.”

Many district court judges feel like the Supreme Court does not have their backs when they rule against the Trump administration. This case illustrates why and the attending harms.

David: You raise an important point — litigants are required to follow court orders until those orders are reversed. In my law practice, for example, I didn’t ever tell my clients, “Sure, the judge ruled against us, but keep doing what you’re doing; I’m confident we’ll win on appeal.” Nope, that would be a great way to be hit with a contempt order.

Even if the Supreme Court ultimately reverses the lower courts, I do think it needs to make it very clear that defying orders on the expectation of reversal is completely unacceptable and that contempt orders are an appropriate response.

Emily: One more note about these third-country deportations: Many of these people are deportable because they committed crimes, often serious ones. The question of where they should live after they complete their prison sentences is also serious. But effectively disappearing people to places where they are mistreated and have no recourse is the equivalent of the United States abusing them.

David: You raise an important point — many, but certainly not all, of the people who’ve faced third-country deportation are violent criminals. There are no easy solutions in those cases where they’re deportable and their home countries don’t want them back. But one thing I do know is that deportation to countries that impose indefinite detention and engage in systematic human rights violations is morally grotesque.

To actually celebrate Trump’s policy is more grotesque still. At a minimum, there should be no deportation to countries that violate the Convention Against Torture, an international treaty that President Ronald Reagan signed and the Senate ratified.

When President Reagan transmitted the treaty to the Senate, he sent a message to the Senate declaring that ratification “will demonstrate unequivocally our desire to bring an end to the abhorrent practice of torture.” The Trump administration has no such desire.

Emily: The second big immigration case, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, is perhaps even more chilling.

David: I feel the same way.

Emily: It’s about whether ICE can detain anyone who crossed the border illegally, no matter how long ago and how law-abiding they have been since then, without a bond hearing before an immigration judge — in other words, no court review unless and until you can bring a habeas petition. When ICE adopted this position in July 2025, some government lawyers said they couldn’t believe it. “Mandatory detention is the dream of every hard-line anti-immigration activist,” one ICE lawyer told me. “This is as big a deal as ending birthright citizenship. If the Trump administration does that, then they have changed immigration law forever. If the Supreme Court signs off on this, it’s effectively saying we don’t do asylum here anymore.”

The appeals courts have split on whether the Trump administration’s expansion of mandatory detention is allowed by the 1996 immigration law that it is relying on. This statute is a notorious mess, but still, I think the answer is no. When this litigation started, I thought this was pretty much a slam-dunk. District Court judges largely rejected the Trumpian interpretation. But now I see two appellate courts twisting the text in the government’s anti-immigrant favor and while nine have ruled the other way, I’m not at all sure what the Supreme Court will do.

I have to point out that Congress could fix this problem. It’s supposed to write laws, not cede its power to the president and the justices. But I realize that is a futile point to make at the moment, though I keep trying.

David, do you think this case is chilling because mandatory detention with no bond hearing is bad, because it locks up so many people, including those with deep roots in our country, or bad and also illegal?

David: I think it’s terrible and illegal, but I’m not completely confident the court will agree, in large part because, as you say, the statutes are an absolute mess.

Emily: Is this 1996 law — an update of the Immigration and Nationality Act — one of the worst-written statutes ever? It’s a product of Newt Gingrich’s House leadership, but passed with Democratic support. (It was part of the budget bill that year, so voting no meant risking a shutdown.) The thing about this law is that it had draconian provisions that were not enforced because Congress did not authorize the spending for huge numbers of detention beds. Until, that is, last year, when Congress sharply increased the budget for ICE. We don’t have a new immigration law. We have new immigration policy because we made ICE the law enforcement agency with the highest funding in the country.

David: There’s serious competition for the title of worst-written statute, but it’s definitely a contender. I wrote about this issue at length in February, but here’s the short version. One statute, 8 U.S.C. Section 1225, says that “an alien who is an applicant for admission” shall be detained unless he or she is “clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted.”

Another statute, 8 U.S.C. Section 1226, says that an alien may be “arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States,” but in that circumstance they may be released on bond.

For roughly 30 years, presidents of both parties harmonized those statutes by applying the detention requirement to people stopped at the border and applying the bond provision to people arrested in the interior of the country (often after they’ve been living in the United States productively for years). No president read those statutes as requiring mandatory detention, much less permitting indefinite detention.

And there’s a good statutory reason presidents from both parties adopted the same reading. As Judge Dale Ho, a federal judge in the Southern District of New York, put it in a 2025 ruling, “Someone who enters a movie theater without purchasing a ticket and then proceeds to sit through the first few minutes of a film would not ordinarily then be described as ‘seeking admission’ to the theater.”

I believe the Supreme Court will agree with Judge Ho, but I’m far from certain. Let’s check in again after oral argument.

Emily: Gulp, yes, let’s.

Speaking of close textual readings, which you are carefully doing, what do you think of Justice Alito’s recent op-ed in The Wall Street Journal laying out his “Text? What text?” theory of originalism?

Here is the part that made me grind my teeth the morning I read it (not a metaphor). Alito goes after what he calls “insecure originalism” (subtext: any analysis he doesn’t like by a colleague, especially if her name is Amy Coney Barrett). Alito writes: “Insecure originalists remain in what Prof. Adrian Vermeule has called a ‘defensive crouch.’ Wary of being charged with ‘results-oriented’ decision-making, they are allergic to any evaluation of results. That is a mistake.”

Alito continues, “Insecure originalists may worry that they are subconsciously engaging in ‘judicial activism’ in the service of their own policy preferences. As a result, they may welcome occasions when their originalist analysis leads to results they dislike.”

Well, yes. Isn’t this the whole justification for originalism? The method’s claim to superiority is that it binds judges to the text of the Constitution as it was understood in 1788. They can’t take into account results because that would mean making a judgment call based on the outcome they would prefer, which could reflect their values. They are proud of reaching decisions they don’t personally like because this proves they are dutifully following the instructions of the framers.

Justice Antonin Scalia, originalism’s most brilliant salesman, often cited his vote in favor of ruling that the First Amendment protects flag burning. In 1989, Scalia published an essay in which he admitted to a bit of Alito-like wobble: “I hasten to confess that in a crunch I may prove a fainthearted originalist,” he said. “I cannot imagine myself, any more than any other federal judge, upholding a statute that imposes the punishment of flogging.”

But many years later, Scalia said, “I repudiate that,” in an interview in New York Magazine with the journalist Jennifer Senior. I think Scalia had no choice. If you can make an exception to the rule whenever you feel like it, then it’s not a rule. “I will take the bitter with the sweet!” Scalia said. “What I would say now is, yes, if a state enacted a law permitting flogging, it is immensely stupid, but it is not unconstitutional.”

I don’t think the court has ever consistently applied originalism (or the conservative justices’ latest expandable “history and tradition” test). Of course judges take into account real-life consequences and reach different results in difficult cases informed by who they are. But isn’t Alito giving away the game here? David, you are a committed originalist. If Alito gets to have no bitter with the sweet, can I have a world in which the Constitution reflects today’s reality? I look forward, for example, to the Supreme Court upholding the ban in Cook County, Ill., on many semiautomatic rifles, the big Second Amendment case on the docket this term. Now originalism will not bar the justices from letting the people of Chicago do their best to address the modern — that is to say, decidedly not pre-1800 — crisis of gun violence, right?

David: I had three thoughts about Justice Alito’s op-ed, two positive, one negative. First, I’m glad he wrote it. I want justices to be more transparent about their legal philosophies. I think he did a great public service in explaining how he approaches cases and explaining his own ideas about originalism.

Second, it’s important that people understand that originalists can and do disagree all the time. Originalism isn’t a plug-and-play form of legal philosophy that creates precisely predictable results in every context. It’s a way of thinking about the law. It’s not an outcome-generation machine. That’s why the conservative majority isn’t a monolith. They disagree all the time.

But on to my beef. I strongly disagree with his framing of “insecure originalism,” beginning with the word “insecure.” It echoes a particular New Right style of argument that claims that conservatives failed in the past because they lacked courage or craved the affirmation of elites. Think of it as the “if only Mike Pence had the courage” argument.

I don’t think Alito is going as far as all that, but I wasn’t the only person to read Alito’s piece and see echoes of the New Right.

As Jack Goldsmith, a Harvard Law School professor who served as assistant attorney general for the Office of Legal Counsel under President George W. Bush, wrote in The Atlantic on Tuesday: “In their attacks on the Court and its moderate conservatives, the Trump administration and its allies are articulating a New Right idea of conservative judging. That view despises originalism’s value-neutrality, prizes conservative results, admires judges with the ‘courage’ and ‘loyalty’ to uphold Trump’s program, and views adverse decisions as evidence of timidity, establishment capture, or betrayal.

“Alito claims no association with the New Right, but his essays and work on the Court make plain why its legal camp venerates him.”

I’m very worried about the future of originalism. One of originalism’s appeals is that it was supposed to diminish judicial discretion (by privileging the text above all else) and make legal outcomes more predictable and durable.

For example, to come full circle: My originalist approach to the Suncor case isn’t to ask which outcome I’d prefer (federal regulation), but rather which outcome the text of the Constitution and the relevant statutes requires, and that may well mean that Boulder, Colo., wins, at least until Congress says otherwise.

But in the wrong hands, originalism can become exactly what it was supposed to combat — a malleable doctrine that answers the “living constitutionalism” of some more left-wing judicial philosophies with what Sherif Girgis, a conservative professor at Notre Dame Law School, calls “living traditionalism” that can rest too much on the accidents of history, much less the judge’s own interpretations of that history, or personal preferences.

Emily: Indeed. At some point, let’s talk about Dobbs, Exhibit A of Alito opinions and Supreme Court jurisprudence based on misleading, cherry-picked history. I think you strongly disagree. But that’s for another day and the draft of the book I’m working on (more on that at some point, too. I hope).

For now, I will note that three red states (Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana) are suing three blue states (California, Massachusetts and New York) over the blue states’ telemedicine shield laws, which protect abortion providers in their states who prescribe abortion pills to women in states with abortion bans. This one is worth the whole conversation next time! But let’s see whether the Supreme Court accepts the invitation to exercise original jurisdiction, meaning it acts as the trial court, an option that exists when states sue each other. I doubt it. (During this administration, I keep having to pretend I remember bits of the Constitution I’ve forgotten from law school or maybe never learned. Thank you, President Trump, for your attention to this matter.)

What movies or TV shows do you have for me? I offer you “Colin From Accounts,” a light but sometimes deep Australian comedy that features a dog on wheels. My dog likes it. I bet you will, too.

David: As you suspected, Emily, we’ll have to agree to disagree on Dobbs for now, though I’d love to have a real discussion with you about that case. I thought it was one of Alito’s best opinions (though I have small quibbles at the edges).

But let’s end with a point of agreement. I loved “Colin From Accounts.” My wife and I watched that some time ago, and if you like that show, I’ve got one I recommended on The Opinions last week. The Apple TV show “Last Seen” stars Patrick Brammall (the same actor who starred in “Colin”), and it’s about a missing child who … might have been found.

I won’t say more, except that Episodes 4 and 6 are among the most gripping episodes of television I’ve ever seen. Enjoy!

Nonconsensual sex is always wrong, but that doesn’t mean consensual sex is always right. Whether or not the student who would come to be known as Jane Doe — at the time under the influence of alcohol and ketamine, in an upstairs room full of fraternity brothers — had agreed at some point to sex has become a flashpoint in the discourse around Cornell University’s rape investigation. ARTICLE

The Cornell Case Exposes What We Can’t Say
We are unable to recognize and critique bad behavior outside of a narrow definition of criminal sex.
By Christine Emba
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/cornell-sex-consent-rape-criminal.html

Nonconsensual sex is always wrong, but that doesn’t mean consensual sex is always right.

Whether or not the student who would come to be known as Jane Doe — at the time under the influence of alcohol and ketamine, in an upstairs room full of fraternity brothers — had agreed at some point to sex has become a flashpoint in the discourse around Cornell University’s rape investigation. But regardless of where one falls on that debate, we should all be able to name the way a 20-year-old sophomore was treated by her peers as degrading and perverse, deserving of sanction regardless of the legal outcome of the case. And while the dozens of frat brothers who were sent a Snapchat message advertising an intoxicated woman as “free pussy” were not under legal obligation to intervene, their broad refusal to do so should also be regarded as a moral failure.

The lurid account has haunted the public imagination since The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper, published the details in mid-September. While the alleged assault happened in 2024, its re-emergence this year has resulted in a steady drip of shocking and at times conflicting evidence into the public conversation.

Campus sexual assault isn’t new. Something about this case — the coarseness, the extremity, the failure of trusted institutions to forcefully respond — has triggered widespread revulsion, a sickening shared sense that a boundary no one thought to name has been broken. It has attracted a different kind of attention, as well — with some observers defending the perpetrators, some interrogating the rush to judge them.

There are discussions to be had about agency, responsibility and justice. But we don’t have the shared language to talk about what, exactly, went wrong.

Not that we aren’t trying to talk about it. It’s just that our public conversation feels quibbling, inadequate to the outrage at hand and insensitive to the victim’s humanity. Where does this fall under New York State’s laws? Don’t some women like rough sex? Was it a rape, or was it just a bad experience regretted after the fact?

The last question is at the heart of our shrunken moral vocabulary. “Consent” has become the consensus standard of our time, a compromise between “her body, her choice” sex positivity and a societally necessary condemnation of sexual violence. The consent standard is meant to remove ambiguity without prescribing a larger framework: Sex without consent is rape, and rape is a crime. The certainty of those categories fits neatly into our existing accountability mechanisms as defined by the legal system. Anything outside of rape is a personal affair.

In a society that treats judging others as inappropriate — or at least unfashionable — consent has the appeal of being values-neutral: It defines harm without requiring anyone to make the case for a certain idea of the good. Our reliance on consent as the ultimate arbiter of acceptability has left us unable to recognize and critique bad behavior outside of its narrow definition of criminal sex.

After all, consent here is a legal criterion, not an ethical one — a floor, not a ceiling. It defines the bare minimum, but it doesn’t define the good. That gap between “legal” and “decent” is where moral criticism does its work, but a lack of a moral language strips us of the nuance needed to empathize with victims and to come up with a social, not just a juridical, response. Without that vocabulary, it’s difficult to express what we want our shared sexual culture to look like.

Consent doesn’t help us account for the power differentials of age, gender, experience or intoxication. It doesn’t ask whether the alleged victim entered into the encounter out of genuine desire or because of social pressure, or where one stops and the other begins. It doesn’t leave room to acknowledge that even “just” a regrettable experience can cause lasting harm and that the woman involved is deserving of compassion. What do we owe to each other? Is there no higher standard to which we can hold ourselves?

Any eventual court verdict won’t cure a culture in which misogyny is gaining traction at the highest levels of government and society, embodied by a president who has sheltered virulent misogynists and has himself been found liable for sexual abuse. It won’t reassure skeptical young women that they should trust their male peers. But restoring a moral framework from which to explain why certain beliefs and behaviors are either good or bad would make us better at holding our institutions — and one another — accountable.

“I was a sex doll for all intents and purposes, which is sad,” Jane Doe told a police interviewer in the weeks after her assault. It would be tragic to have the conversation end there.

Christine Emba is a board member of the American Institute for Boys and Men and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

SUMMARY

And does the city believe in its mayor? If you’re going to advance anything big as a mayor, you have to have a coalition on the City Council. Look, we know this: There are three major areas that a city, a mayor have to deal with.

ARTICLE

Opinion | Who Should Be Los Angeles’s Next Mayor?
Times Opinion convened a panel of experts to help voters make sense of the race.
By New York Times Opinion
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/08/opinion/los-angeles-mayor-election.html

Karen Bass

Nithya Raman

Our Panel’s Ratings

We asked panelists to rate the leading candidates on how they would approach governing. Each chart reflects an average of their individual ratings.

This is the most frustrated L.A. residents and L.A. voters have been in the 40 years that I have been observing and studying Los Angeles. At Loyola Marymount, we conduct one of the largest annual surveys in urban America on Los Angeles, more than 2,000 residents every single year. When we ask about trust in government, efficiency in government, does government care about you, can government solve problems — all have declined dramatically. Voters have no belief in the ability of local government to improve their lives.

In any mayor’s race, we ask the question: Is the city working for us? Are residents able to get basic services? And does the city believe in its mayor? And I think all of those questions are up for debate right now because a lot of community members, people that we talk to every day, are feeling that services are not being delivered.

Everybody is either frustrated, unhappy or angry. And as a consequence of that, they’re uninspired by leadership. A mayor’s race often can be a moment of civic inspiration and of civic imagination, right? In 2013, Eric Garcetti had a vision for Los Angeles that he was selling to voters: a forward-leaning city. In 2005, Antonio Villaraigosa had a very clear vision of Los Angeles. “Come dream with me” was sort of the slogan of his inauguration speech. And in this campaign, I’m not seeing anybody articulating a vision for Los Angeles and trying to sort of lead people to a common civic mission.

Los Angeles has undergone two major catastrophes in the last two years — first, the ones with the Palisades and the Eaton fires. And even though the Eaton fire was in Pasadena, it’s still part of our larger community. The second major crisis we’ve had most recently is the Lineage fire in Boyle Heights, where a cold storage warehouse burned and the decomposing food took a long time to clean up. That’s of great concern to the community right now because it kind of traffics a longstanding history of people being promised so much by these candidates.

Right now, if she were to get elected today, her mandate is she’s not Bass. But that’s not the same thing as an agenda, and that’s something she should focus on building in the final weeks of the campaign. She can be very, very good at articulating a vision for Los Angeles when she wants to; she has a sense of the future, of what a multiethnic, complex city is supposed to be. And if she can articulate that, that will be a real strength. She is also very good at identifying and fixing the things that prevent government from working right.

I think if Raman wins, it’s notable that she’s not endorsed by her colleagues on the City Council. If you’re going to advance anything big as a mayor, you have to have a coalition on the City Council. And if you’re a council member that wants to advance anything big, you have to work with the mayor. So how does she reset relationships should she win, not just with the council, but also with labor and with the business community, in order to make some big moves and shift this mood?

I feel like she’s still learning how to be a politician. She has learned how to deliver her message better. I definitely do think that she will bring an outsider’s perspective. We haven’t really seen that in the city leadership. Most of the mayors that we’ve had have all had those traditional coalitions and things behind them, though she has very interesting people that are behind her, including the pro-transit community and environmentalists. We’re watching, I think, the plane being built in real time.

She understands policy and systems at a very minute level. And I think that was the strength of hers going into this race. I would say the biggest question, I think, from my perspective as a civil-rights leader in South L.A., is: Can we trust you on issues around race and equity in our community? I’ve seen her doing more work with the immigrant and primarily Latino community. But what about the other, more solidly Black communities that have been a part of this coalition bloc?

Bass has a truly cross-sector coalition. She has the business community behind her. She has older white liberals behind her. She has sizable support from the Latino community. So what is she going to do with that cross-sector coalition should she win? Every re-elected mayor has about a year, year and a half to do something really interesting and sort of ride that wave of optimism that may come from a victory. What will she do with that?

Mayor Bass spent a lot of time in Washington as a legislator. It’s like if you were used to driving a gas-powered car, and you came back to L.A. and the whole city is an electric vehicle. You have to learn how to work the machinery. Over the last couple of years, she’s been trying to figure out how the machinery actually works. If there is a second term, it’s got to be about implementation. We know what did not work around homelessness. What big tweaks are you making to actually move that forward? We know you did the executive directives around land use. But improving permitting is not the same as completing units. So if she wins a second term, the challenge would be how to get more completed units online. The strength is she knows the machinery better. The question I think most people are asking is: If we give you a second term, can you actually effectively drive this car, which is L.A. city? Can you actually effectively manage the department managers to get what we need?

Bass has tremendous relationships at all levels of government. She has been effective at leveraging that for support from Sacramento and Washington. That is a huge asset, and if Democrats retake the House and Senate, it be very helpful. The mayor’s biggest weakness is that she acts more like the legislative leader she was for two decades than as the executive and a manager a big city mayor is supposed to be.

One of the things that’s really disappointing about this race is that I had thought that with two smart, policy-savvy, progressive candidates, we would have some thoughtful conversations about housing policy, and we’re not. And to the extent that we have, it’s basically been: Should we build any apartments in what are exclusively single-family neighborhoods now? That’s a question, but there’s so many others that aren’t being asked.

Look, we know this: There are three major areas that a city, a mayor have to deal with. First and foremost is public safety. Second is land use. And then the third area is city services. Public safety, I think, is going OK for Bass. It’s that land use, the inability to build housing and affordable housing. One of the root causes with homelessness is the rent. That’s going to be Bass’s legacy if she gets re-elected, whether she wants it or not. She cannot give up on that issue of homelessness and housing.

The basics around housing are the three P’s, right? How are you doing protection, preservation and production? And what I’m hearing with Raman, it’s a lot about production. Her biggest challenge would be convincing these neighborhood associations that you could actually build density in your area and not disrupt the historical fabric of your neighborhood.

So I’m going to come at it a little bit differently, as someone who does work with the developer community quite a bit. I’ve worked for affordable housing developers and regular market-rate developers. And I will tell you that people aren’t interested in building in Los Angeles. A lot of times, the people who are opposed to a project, they are very savvy, with requirements and conditions on these projects, knowing that they won’t get built. We need a real sherpa in city hall to get us over the hump, to rebuild the trust of people who want to invest in our city at all levels of housing and bring all parties to the table, especially developers. And I think we have to figure out that we can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

The other big question is: What generation do we have at the front of our minds when we’re talking about housing policy? Are our decisions on housing policy being dictated by the needs of people my age, who are homeowners? Or are they being dictated by thinking about kids who are in kindergarten and high school now, and what Los Angeles they get to live in or not?

The median age right now to buy a home in Los Angeles is much higher than in most of the country. I have two daughters in their 20s. To know that they would not be able to buy a home — a single-family dwelling or even a condo — for a long time is concerning. When younger voters are looking at this race, I think they’re thinking about that.

It is a generational issue. Most of the people in Los Angeles rent. But we’re kind of still beholden to the homeowners. It has huge implications: There is a concentration of intergenerational wealth into the hands of a minority of the city, which was on display with the first debate these candidates had, which was hosted by a homeowners’ association.

The most important thing the mayor needs to do — and it isn’t easy, cheap or fast — is to create enough long-term housing for people who are currently unhoused. Inside Safe isn’t housing. It is temporary shelter, in a motel or hotel room, to get people safely off the streets. The city should focus more on leasing apartment units, for a likely cheaper cost, and it is actually long-term housing.

While L.A. overall needs a much greater supply of housing, preventing homelessness could best be achieved by specifically constructing units that offer below-market rent.

The next mayor needs to focus on a sustained cost-of-living reform program that decreases the cost for all renters in L.A. Too many families find themselves in precarious housing situations where they need reliable, clean and affordable pathways to long-term housing, including public housing, new development and land trust options.

The next mayor needs to build a robust coalition of serious public and private leaders to streamline the intake pathway, and deploy prevention dollars — like basic income, or utility rates cuts and freezes to stabilize affordability — alongside coordinated services.

It’s the major event in Los Angeles since Covid. And it has structured the narrative about how a city can respond, how a city can prepare. And then the mayor being out of the country when the fires broke out symbolized the city being out of touch and not engaged. And so all of that, I think, is where we are right now for the mayor’s race, but also the way people view the city. Some of this is unfair when you look at the overall pace of response compared to other places. But the fires just showed the inability of communications with the fire department, how they deployed, all of that. It’s just a reflection of the inability of the city to respond and communicate.

We’re now at a point where we know we are going to have crises that we have not experienced before. We’re going to have coastal crises. We’re going to have more environmental crises. I don’t think we think enough about the potential for cyberattacks that could shut the city down or screw up the entire water system.

To go back to our discussion about coalitions, it doesn’t matter if you have a coalition if you don’t do anything with it. Then it’s just optics and representation. The city needs more than that. It needs action. We need strong leadership to solve some of the biggest crises we’re going to face. We’re about to face a big El Niño. Are we really prepared to take that on? Are we in communication in pushing the federal government to provide us greater resources so we can tackle some of these needs?

I think first and foremost, being the mayor of the second-largest city in the United States is a sort of right and responsibility all in itself. You absolutely have the bully pulpit. You absolutely have the ability to share your opinions. You can call upon the council to do all sorts of things. You hire general managers. You establish budgets. You appoint some seats to the Metro board, to the air quality management districts. It’s a myth that we don’t have the power. It’s just a matter of learning how to use it and being willing to use it.

The bully pulpit point is so important — we’ve seen Mayor Bass do that on a couple of occasions. With ICE, she was very strong. People heard it. They saw it. But I’m not sure in other areas we’ve seen it in the same way. Many of us are looking right now at New York City, and people are seeing what appears, at least, to be bold leadership and use of a bully pulpit in multiple ways. There is a little bit of envy and a desire to have that in our city.

There’s also an element to the job that involves diplomacy skills and a lot of soft skills to build a coalition on the City Council, to be able to build a coalition on the board of supervisors, to mobilize other mayors, to mobilize legislators so you could advance a policy at the state level. A mayor has a tremendous amount of power through appointment of general managers and commissioners, though, as well as being the most recognizable public figure in Southern California. It gives them the ability, if they are able to use it effectively, to make bold and ambitious moves.

The mayor has a lot of power on paper and controls some major entities, like power or the port. But in total, the mayor of New York has more power specifically for a few issues that cities are dealing with right now. The mayor of New York controls health, education and social welfare. The mayor of L.A. doesn’t. Those are three very important policy areas that many Angelenos believe that the mayor controls. And when you’re trying to deal with homelessness, let me tell you, it’s really tough when you don’t have health and welfare under your control.

I remain optimistic that it is possible. A lot of people believe that L.A. is ungovernable. It’s very difficult to achieve your goals when you’re not exerting that level of focus and discipline, and there’s not the engagement, there’s not the communication. I think there are ways to identify some simple, quick wins that, if I were advising her, I would sit down and say, three to five things, what can we do infrastructure-wise? It’s not sexy, but Zohran Mamdani is doing it. He’s fixing the play equipment in New York City. He’s getting after Amazon for their unpaid parking tickets.

I just want to say that as a person who is a millennial in this city and a renter, the biggest frustration is that the city does not work, meaning that there’s potholes, the sidewalks don’t work, that El Niño’s going to come, it’s going to be flooded. And the question is: Why are you paying so much money?

What I’ll add, as someone who had to vote on budgets and try to get services done, is I do not envy whoever is in office next year in trying to dramatically improve the quality of city services because it’s going to be very, very difficult. We still haven’t recovered, in terms of city services, from the Great Recession era. And the funding situation is not good.

Bass did a great job in terms of ICE. But part of it is because she hardly had to spend any money. It wasn’t budget constraints. She didn’t have to deal with the City Council on that. This was on her own, her instincts of having been a coalition builder and knowing to respond. She did a great job.

We know that undocumented immigrants generate tremendous income in our city — around $250 billion, I believe, every year. That’s 17 percent of the county’s G.D.P. The L.A. Economic Development Corporation in their survey found that 82 percent of businesses reported negative impacts. And of those experiencing declines in revenue, nearly half said that those declines were over 50 percent. So I think when we’re thinking especially about Latino communities, A.A.P.I. communities impacted by ICE, we get back to the question of: How is this city delivering services for them that enable them to thrive? That’s where the rubber meets the road on this, is that it can’t just be about symbolism. It’s got to be about the delivery of services by the city as well.

The mayor does have to thread a needle when it comes to the president of the United States, whoever that is. I think the mayor has a duty to stand up for their citizens and to speak out against what’s morally wrong. But at the same time, they can’t afford to be an ideologue all the time. The job requires that the mayor solve problems and deliver city services. So that might take a different approach, a different strategy, depending on what the need is, whether it’s working behind the scenes, in front of the scenes to get to solutions with the federal administration. Sometimes that’s being inspirational and taking a moral stand. And sometimes it’s being a pragmatist.

Just don’t poke the bear. Basically, ignore Trump unless it’s about ICE, unless it’s about the Olympics. Don’t give in to Trump just because of the Olympics. He’s going to want to make it a showcase for himself anyway; he will be investing money in that. And if not, that’s the risk we’re going to have to take. I wouldn’t give up the soul or the identity of L.A. just because the Olympics might have a cost overrun.

L.A. is a city that you have to find. There are hidden pockets of nature; there’s urban grit; there’s every ethnicity and all the food and all the things. But you have to go find it. It operates very much like a small town in a lot of ways. The politics are very hyperlocal.

L.A. is the epitome of everything that the Trump administration is against. Cultural diversity — we have a large population of foreign-born people. We have creative capital that’s not seen anywhere else in the world. And we have a vibrant democracy where, on a cultural level, on a citywide level, people come together all the time, every single day.

L.A. is one of the most diverse and segregated cities in America. But the beauty of Los Angeles is that it is filled with people who believe that the possible is possible. We show up because we believe the possible is possible for everyone, even though we are very diverse and segregated.

L.A. remakes itself constantly, and we are a city of entrepreneurs. And I don’t mean that just economically, but also socially, culturally, in every single way except for city government. And that’s the disconnect. We are a bunch of cultural, social, economic entrepreneurs, and city government is not.

Whoever takes office needs to have a tremendous amount of courage. I know we gave a lot of credit to Mayor Bass, but the real people that stood up to ICE were your everyday citizens. It was people getting arrested, getting deported in some cases. There’s so much a mayor can do. But how does a mayor take the cues from their citizens? It’s this big city that’s very diverse and very complex. We disagree on a lot. But there are certain things that we will all stand by. We’re an immigrant city. And we’re going to stand by our people.

SUMMARY

Surveillance technology has spread quickly through Uganda since 2019, when the government installed a $126 million closed-circuit television network from the Chinese telecommunications conglomerate Huawei to monitor public spaces. That’s not to say it was free: Uganda now owes China about $2.6 billion. Speaking to his Chinese counterparts “with an air of enthusiasm and shared objectives,” according to a party write-up, Mr. Todwong secured a funding pledge from China that would “apply these transformative lessons within Uganda.”

ARTICLE

The Authoritarian Future Is Already Here
A crackdown in Uganda shows how new technologies, Chinese influence and America’s moral retreat are making the world safer for autocrats.
By Megan K. Stack
Published 2026-10-08 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/surveillance-autocrats-uganda.html

This essay is part of “The New World Disorder,” a series exploring the disintegration of the postwar international system and how countries are adjusting as America steps aside.

Plainclothes thugs frog-marching a radio commentator from the microphone midbroadcast. An opposition activist dying after reportedly being barricaded in his house, which was then set on fire. Security forces raiding a powerful independent media company, cutting electricity and imposing a monthlong closure.

A reign of terror grips Uganda. Specifically, the reign of Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the country’s belligerent and erratic military chief, who also happens to be the only son of Yoweri Museveni, the octogenarian autocrat who’s ruled Uganda for four decades. Critics of General Kainerugaba, who recently announced his intention to become Uganda’s next president, risk finding themselves in the “basement,” his nickname for the torture chambers he brags about on social media.

Ugandans have discovered that, increasingly, there is nowhere to hide. Civic life here is defined by thickening webs of state surveillance built with foreign help. Chinese cameras and facial-recognition software monitor the streets; Russian radio frequency chips implanted in license plates have been tracking cars in real time; Israeli software plunders the private contents of phones. Technology has created an intrusive eye that never blinks — a stealthy weapon for dictators keen to stifle speech and thought.

Welcome to our menacing new world, a place where authoritarians — established and aspiring alike — enjoy tolerance from the international community; wield cheaper, quieter and far more powerful surveillance tools at home; and reach across borders to help one another hang on to power.

Africa has become a testing ground for all of this. Authoritarianism is spreading on the continent, where Freedom House’s 2026 report found that only 10 percent of people now live in countries classified as “free,” a dismal statistic outdone only by the Middle East.

China has quietly fueled this political hardening. With unparalleled trade reach, a voracious appetite for natural resources and a compelling authoritarian model, Beijing has deepened its economic and political presence across Africa. Along the way, it has exported many of the technologies that the Communist Party uses for political and social control at home. African governments have spent at least $2 billion on the Chinese artificial-intelligence-powered surveillance systems that hound dissidents from Mozambique to Zimbabwe to the Republic of Congo.

China is not the only one. Israeli spyware such as the notorious Pegasus piracy software, which can use a phone to spy on its owner, has been snapped up by rulers around the world. And companies from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Germany and other European states have exported surveillance technologies to Africa and other regions. Such tools have sometimes been used to target opposition figures, journalists and activists.

I visited Uganda recently to explore the aftermath of President Trump’s abrupt retreat from human rights, clean government and public diplomacy. I was told, over and over, that American silence during this clampdown has made it easier for other Western countries to remain similarly quiet and has radically emboldened an increasingly ruthless Ugandan regime.

This is not to overstate past U.S. altruism. America has always chased its interests overseas — sometimes violently, often cynically, selectively calling out the abuses of disfavored regimes while ignoring repression carried out by strategic allies. But it’s also true that America stood up for dissidents and human rights defenders when it was not inconvenient and sometimes when it was. It pressured despotic governments, criticized rigged elections and imposed sanctions on officials.

Now, suddenly, Beijing’s rules prevail: Make money, extract resources, turn economic ties into leverage. Whatever you do, respect local power; don’t criticize other governments for tyranny or abuse. Mr. Trump plays by those rules, too — “trade, not aid,” his administration pithily calls it.

“I really believe, if we look at the next 20 years, our politics will be influenced by the Chinese very, very much,” said Job Kiija.

I met Mr. Kiija in Kampala, the Ugandan capital, at a coffee shop wedged over a gas station on a ramshackle street fringed with palms and groaning with traffic. He runs Innovations for Democratic Engagement and Action, a civil society group that now works in the legal shadows since it was shuttered and defunded by government crackdowns.

He showed me threatening texts he’d been receiving on his phone (“U said some not nice things … U mayb in trouble soon”). He fretted about whether his group should publicly release an extensive report about the much-criticized elections this year that — yet again — kept Mr. Museveni in power.

To depend upon international law or support from friendly Western diplomats, Mr. Kiija said, is “no longer sustainable.”

“You live knowing you’re in danger,” he said. “But if you don’t do something about it, nobody will.”

It’s a mask-off moment in Uganda. For people caught in the cross hairs, these are days of dread.

Kakwenza Rukirabashaija has read the classified documents that list, in black and white, the arms of state power and surveillance tech that attacked him.

Mr. Rukirabashaija is a Ugandan lawyer and novelist. His first book, “The Greedy Barbarian,” is the sprawling, satirical story of a president who becomes a dictator, spiraling deep into greed and corruption until he is finally ousted by popular revolt.

The regime was not amused.

Over the next two years, Mr. Rukirabashaija was repeatedly detained and tortured. He was viciously flogged and beaten so badly that his ankle bones were fractured, his kidneys damaged and his back laced with scars. He said that General Kainerugaba, the president’s son, twice visited him in detention.

During the first visit, he said, the general ordered the author — the taller of the two men — to bend over to make himself shorter and to remove his pants to reveal the size of his penis. Then, as the general recorded the exchange on his phone, he told Mr. Rukirabashaija to kneel on the floor and apologize, the author said.

On the second visit, he said, General Kainerugaba offered him a bribe to keep quiet about the abuse he had suffered. Mr. Rukirabashaija was stunned.

“I just looked at the floor. I couldn’t believe what he was telling me,” Mr. Rukirabashaija said. “He could see that I could not even stand.”

Even upon release, awaiting what he considered to be a show trial, Mr. Rukirabashaija remained in the virtual prison of constant surveillance. Soldiers surrounded his house. He was certain his phone was compromised. In 2022 he managed to smuggle himself out of his house and sneak to the border, leaving his phone at home to mislead the authorities tracking its location. He now lives in Germany.

It wasn’t until Mr. Rukirabashaija read his classified police file — sent to him in Germany by his lawyer — that he was confronted with the full machinery of his suffering. The secret court order authorizing the search of his phone. The tables laying out how a person identified only as Investigator No. 9 began to extract data from his phone at 3:44 p.m. The software tools the government had bought from the Israeli company Cellebrite to analyze his social media posts and the Canadian company Magnet Forensics to pull his data from the cloud.

Mr. Rukirabashaija knew Uganda’s government was brutal, and he said he didn’t expect much from an Israeli company, either. But the cameo appearance of a Canadian company rankled him — the cold, corporate touch of a Western democracy. He wondered whether the people involved in these deals ever questioned their moral responsibility for the products they sold.

“When they see what happened to me, when they see my pictures — all the mutilations, all that software extraction, all that information,” Mr. Rukirabashaija said, “what do they think about?”

A Cellebrite spokeswoman told me the company has stopped selling technology in Uganda, “based on our ethics and integrity standards and risk assessment framework.” Magnet Forensics did not reply to a request for comment.

Surveillance technology has spread quickly through Uganda since 2019, when the government installed a $126 million closed-circuit television network from the Chinese telecommunications conglomerate Huawei to monitor public spaces. Uganda is among dozens of countries worldwide to buy such security packages, which are typically marketed as smart city systems — cutting-edge weapons against crime.

Huawei engineers were embedded in the offices of Uganda’s security forces, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal. At the same time, Uganda made a deal with a shadowy Russian company called Joint Stock Company Global Security to buy a license plate monitoring system, which Human Rights Watch has called a threat to privacy. The Russian company was to help operate the system for the first 10 years.

Huawei declined to speak on the record, but it previously denied that it or its staff helped Uganda’s government spy on political opponents. My efforts to speak to the Ugandan government resulted — after many unanswered calls and ignored messages — in nothing. As for the Russian company hired to install trackers on cars, the Ugandan attorney general this week declared the contract null and void. The future of the license plate monitoring project is unclear.

Ugandan dissidents have rarely been so vulnerable. State security apparatchiks who once relied on radio transmitters and word-of-mouth informants now wield technological superpowers, vastly expanding their ability to keep tabs on even ordinary citizens in far-flung corners of the country who criticize the regime online.

It is perhaps no accident that Uganda’s surveillance buildup came just as a credible, popular opposition was gaining ground against the 82-year-old Mr. Museveni. That challenge arrived, somewhat improbably, in the figure of Bobi Wine, a reggae and Afropop singer affectionately nicknamed the Ghetto President.

Mr. Wine, who grew up in the Kampala slums, gained fame churning out dance hits and songs that addressed social problems like corruption, poverty and police violence. In 2017 he pivoted to electoral politics, galvanized young Ugandans with his charisma and talk of clean, democratic government and easily won a seat in Parliament. The crowds thronging his campaign rallies suggested that Mr. Wine, whose real name is Robert Kyagulanyi, had awakened a dormant political energy.

Mr. Wine became a prime target for a paranoid and ossifying regime, which used Huawei technology to penetrate his encrypted messages, according to The Wall Street Journal. (Huawei and the government have denied that allegation.) In 2018, Mr. Wine was arrested, tortured and charged with treason. His outraged supporters filled the streets, where they clashed violently with security forces.

Undeterred, Mr. Wine went on to run for president twice against Mr. Museveni, first in 2021 and again in January of this year. Both times, Mr. Wine lost in elections that were marred by violence and allegations of vote-rigging and intimidation. At least 16 people were “likely killed” by security forces during and shortly after this year’s election, according to Amnesty International, including a woman who was shot in the back of the head while walking home after casting her ballot. People were detained (or abducted, in at least one case) and interrogated about their support for Mr. Wine.

While campaigning, Mr. Wine and his supporters said, they were placed under tight surveillance and often arrived at events and rallies to find security forces waiting. The police have acknowledged using facial recognition and license plate readers to track Mr. Wine’s supporters.

In Kampala, I visited the headquarters of Mr. Wine’s party, National Unity Platform, to meet its secretary general, David Lewis Rubongoya. Inside the sprawling compound, we crossed a courtyard ringed with murals commemorating slain party activists interspersed with ones featuring Nelson Mandela, Malcolm X and Bob Marley. No matter where we stood, we couldn’t seem to escape the view of cameras mounted on a tall mast just outside the walls, angled to peer down.

“They’re aware that you’re here right now,” Mr. Rubongoya told me cheerfully. “They monitor everything that happens.”

After the 2026 election, when the president’s son took to social media to say he was praying for Mr. Wine’s death and threatened to “handle him accordingly,” Mr. Wine went into hiding and eventually fled Uganda to live — temporarily, he insists — in the United States. I asked several people close to him how he managed to evade security and leave the country. Mr. Wine, I was told, was helped by supporters inside the security forces.

“Not everyone in the security establishment is pro-government,” Mr. Rubongoya said. “The country is silent, but there is a lot of anger.”

Uganda’s other major opposition figure, Kizza Besigye, hasn’t fared any better. He was Mr. Museveni’s comrade and personal doctor back when they were rebels fighting their way into power from the bush in the 1980s. Mr. Besigye eventually turned on his old friend, accusing the president of selling out their shared principles, and challenged him in elections starting in 2001.

In recent years, Mr. Besigye drew closer to Mr. Wine and formally endorsed his candidacy in the 2026 election. The regime appeared to be rattled by a growing political alliance between the young, trendy singer from the slums and the 70-year-old, establishment-connected physician: Mr. Besigye, like Mr. Wine, was hunted down.

Mr. Besigye was abducted while visiting Kenya in 2024 for a book release and was transferred illegally back to Uganda, where he was charged with treason and illegal gun possession. The Kenyan government at first denied any involvement, but its foreign minister eventually admitted to cooperating with the Ugandan regime in an extrajudicial operation that bypassed Kenya’s Extradition Act.

Like-minded regimes, many of them in Africa, have increasingly colluded in this manner to silence or seize critics, according to the U.S.-based Action for Democracy, which has built a searchable online index tracking global collaboration among authoritarian governments. The group says, “Autocrats are treating repressive techniques as portable assets that can transcend borders.”

Mr. Besigye’s ongoing trial is, to put it mildly, flawed. A former mayor of Kampala signed on as the lead defense lawyer, but he was grabbed from his home and forced into General Kainerugaba’s torture chamber for two days before being charged with failing to report a treasonous plot. Other lawyers for Mr. Besigye have been arrested, jailed or barred from entering the country. Last month a key prosecution witness shocked the courtroom by testifying that the guns that Mr. Besigye was accused of having when he was arrested in 2024 were planted by the police. The case is continuing regardless.

General Kainerugaba has repeatedly vowed to hang his father’s old friend, calling Mr. Besigye “a dead man walking.”

Abuse and repression are not exactly new phenomena in this young, volatile country, which has never experienced a peaceful transition of power since gaining independence from Britain in 1962. But the current crackdown is moving so fast, so publicly and with such impunity that several Ugandans I met likened it to the violent excesses of the infamous dictator Idi Amin, who oversaw the killing of untold thousands of Ugandans in the 1970s.

Some in Uganda see it as a project by General Kainerugaba to terrify critics into silence and weed out any officials perceived as insufficiently loyal to a man who would soon, if he has his way, be president. The general banters on his X account about kidnapping and torturing people, posting pictures of battered captives, taunting enemies and threatening his next prey. Over the years, Ugandans have grown accustomed to disappearances and street clashes surging as elections approach, then receding once the results are announced. But this year, after the January election, the crackdown persisted.

Perhaps there is a method to the madness of the president’s son, who trained at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in England and the U.S. Army college at Fort Leavenworth, Kan. Maybe he, or the people around him, has cannily read the moment and wagered that the United States and other governments in a newly indifferent West will not complain over Uganda’s sharply repressive turn.

The United States used to push back. The Biden administration called Uganda’s 2021 election “neither free nor fair,” restricted the visas of Ugandans blamed for “undermining the democratic process” and, as political repression continued, kicked Uganda out of a program offering crucial tax and customs waivers to African countries.

Then Mr. Trump returned, and America stopped complaining. In July 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio effectively forbade his staff to utter so much as a euphemism that might hint at criticism of undemocratic values or flawed elections in other countries.

In describing their government’s relationship to the United States, almost every Ugandan I met pointed to Mr. Trump’s abduction of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela and the U.S. seizure of that country’s oil. They saw Ugandan officials as anxious to do whatever the impetuous Mr. Trump asks because, if he gets angry, who knows what he may do?

That may explain why Uganda accepted some of Mr. Trump’s third-country deportees and offered to send troops to Gaza. The government has uncomplainingly moved ahead with a health funding deal allowing the United States to have access to Ugandans’ private health data, ostensibly to monitor disease outbreaks. The political opposition is concerned that the United States may use the agreement to press for preferential rights to minerals or oil. Similar deals have been frozen or rejected in Zambia and Zimbabwe.

A Ugandan human rights lawyer, Agather Atuhaire, who said she was abducted in 2025 by security forces in Tanzania during a trip to the country and that she was tortured and dumped near the Ugandan border, can pinpoint when the change in the U.S. government’s attitude became clear. After security forces mercilessly beat voters and journalists during a 2025 by-election, Ms. Atuhaire, who now lives in Kenya, called a friend at the United States Embassy in Uganda to describe the violence she had documented. Just the previous year, she was flown to Washington and feted by Jill Biden and Antony Blinken as one of the State Department’s “international women of courage.”

This time, Ms. Atuhaire recalled, the message was different. Washington had told the embassy it didn’t give a damn, her friend said, using a harsher expletive.

The Trump administration’s moral retreat has effectively opened the field for China.

Beijing has cultivated political ties across Africa since the Cold War, when it backed anticolonial liberation movements with arms, money and training, and courted newly independent governments with aid. As China’s economy boomed and its global influence grew, it expanded its presence on the continent with loans, investment, infrastructure projects and resource deals. Unlike the aid doled out by Western governments, Chinese cash generally came without any fretting over human rights or the environment. That’s not to say it was free: Uganda now owes China about $2.6 billion.

“It’s like we’ve mortgaged our country,” said Joel Ssenyonyi, the leader of the opposition in Parliament. Speaking of China, he added, “The time will come when they will have all these countries on a very short leash.”

China played a major part in building and financing projects, including two of Uganda’s major hydroelectric power plants; oil fields to extract recently discovered crude oil that Mr. Museveni has proudly branded Pearl Sweet; a huge pipeline that will move the oil to port in Tanzania; and an expressway from the capital to the Entebbe airport. The terms often favor China: A $200 million loan from the Export-Import Bank of China to upgrade the airport, for example, requires the Ugandan government to fork over airport revenues for 20 years to ensure the debt. Arrangements like this already have caused debt distress in some countries and a backlash against doing business with China.

Chinese construction sites, factories and industrial parks are scattered in and around Kampala. Thousands of teenagers are learning Chinese through the government curriculum, imports from Chinese factories dominate shops and markets, and Chinese investors have been buying up and leasing land. China is also deeply enmeshed with the Ugandan military, inviting officers to train in China, equipping soldiers with armored vehicles and air defense systems and teaming up with Uganda to manufacture explosives and drones.

Perhaps it was only a matter of time before China began exporting not just consumer goods and surveillance systems but its political and governance ideas as well. Autocracies, after all, make for stable trading partners. They don’t badger Beijing about human rights and can push deals through without messy debate. Fostering such systems is good business for China.

That may explain why Chinese officials are working with local ruling parties to create leadership training schools that blend local nationalist and Pan-African traditions with Chinese Communist Party approaches to party discipline, political organization and governance. This suggests China is quietly working to undermine weak multiparty systems by nudging ruling parties in the direction of perpetual domination.

China has an undeniably enticing model: a durable ruling party with a rigid grip on power, decades of extraordinary economic growth and clean, safe streets with low crime. Foreign dignitaries, including officials from Uganda and other states that buy Chinese surveillance systems, get whisked off on junkets to the northwestern Chinese region of Xinjiang, where Beijing is accused of crimes against humanity over its mass detention and severe repression of ethnic Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities. Visitors tour the sites and marvel at the harmonious streets gripped by an extraordinarily intrusive high-tech mass surveillance apparatus. Chinese officials deny committing crimes against humanity, saying the security crackdown combats Islamic extremism and terrorism.

When Richard Todwong, the secretary general of Uganda’s ruling party, visited China in 2023, he announced plans to open an ideological orientation school in his country. Speaking to his Chinese counterparts “with an air of enthusiasm and shared objectives,” according to a party write-up, Mr. Todwong secured a funding pledge from China that would “apply these transformative lessons within Uganda.” The school is yet to open. Similar schools already exist in Tanzania and Zimbabwe, with another planned for Kenya.

Still, I detected strains of buyers’ (or borrowers’) remorse.

At Kampala’s Makerere University, I met Nansozi Muwanga, one of Uganda’s leading political scientists. She was born into the churn of Ugandan politics. Her father, Paulo Muwanga, was vice president, prime minister (briefly) and de facto president (even more briefly) in the tumult of the 1980s. Her office is set in a cottage on the edge of a rolling, sun-dappled lawn where clusters of students picnicked under the trees.

When China began to take a keener interest in Uganda, Ms. Muwanga said, it was regarded as a useful counterweight to the “sense of being constantly threatened” by the United States and Europe. “If you don’t have multiparty democracy, we’re going to take the money away,” she intoned. “Accept L.G.B.T.Q. rights, or we’ll take it away.”

Lately, though, “the honeymoon is over,” Ms. Muwanga said, referring to China.

Unlike some Ugandans I met who are convinced their rulers would have found novel ways to spy on them with or without Beijing’s help, Ms. Muwanga believes China influenced the government to build up its surveillance state. When I asked her what Beijing’s motivation might be, she responded, to my surprise, by talking about land. China has a huge population, she pointed out, and Uganda has plenty of empty space.

“The Chinese have proved they don’t have to bend to your rules or way of life,” she said. “They can come and create a little China in Uganda without being disrupted.”

I was struck by this leap from explaining the tools used to control people to anticipating another round of colonization — the idea that the unspoken final prize was not the resources contained in the land but the land itself.

People feel keenly the retreat of the Americans, Ms. Muwanga said. She feels it herself, and not just because she had a U.S.A.I.D. grant for a research center she runs yanked back when Mr. Trump abruptly slashed its funding.

As it turns out, you sometimes end up missing the very same meddling you once chafed against.

“The knowledge that there was a gatekeeper somewhere and someone who’d slap your wrist if you really went rogue,” she mused. “It had a certain power.”

The increase in his use of profanity is what you would expect, given how language works. We often think of slurs as distinct from swear words, but it’s an indication that they are, in fact, today’s profanity that even someone as heedless of etiquette, decorum, restraint and reflection as Trump has tended to avoid them.

ARTICLE

What to Make of Trump’s Uptick in Profanity
The president’s speech is getting filthier.
By John McWhorter
Published 2026-10-08 19:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/trump-profanity.html

President Trump has been especially potty-mouthed lately. In his second term, he has used significantly more profanity in public than in his first, according to an analysis by The Washington Post in May. Just last week we were treated to him telling interviewers from Time, “You haven’t asked me one positive question” — but dropping an F-bomb to modify “positive” — and at a rally in Ohio calling Democrats “dumb son of a bitches” and saying he was “working my ass off.”

At that same rally he made another gluteal reference of a more pugnacious nature when he said that a Republican victory would “shove it up” Democrats’ something or other.

Some have argued that the uptick in Trump’s lexical filth is a symptom of cognitive decline, a disinhibition suggestive of dementia. I doubt it. The increase in his use of profanity is what you would expect, given how language works.

When we use language, we often want to get and keep people’s attention. But the words and expressions we use to do that can lose their force over time. They require freshening up. This is how you get nonsensical words like “irregardless,” where “regardless” alone should do the trick but the “ir-” gets tacked on for added punch — the extra rhythmic oomph of “irrespective.” “Advance warning,” “close proximity” and “final outcome” are similar cases: redundancies from a logical point of view, but useful for vividness.

Trump has always been fond of “damn” and “hell,” which were part of his populist shtick from the outset. So we would have predicted that he would progress to more piquant profanity.

In this way, Trump’s public speech retraces the evolution of popular profanity over the past hundred years. In the early 20th century, religion-related terms like “hell” were people’s “hit your thumb with a hammer” words. A woman having repeated trouble with her glasses in the 1929 film musical “Glorifying the American Girl” keeps saying “damn it!” — as did film stars in blooper reels from that era. But by the 1960s, things had changed. My parents’ “hit your thumb” profanity of choice began with an “s.” To me (born 1965), that is a tad tame, and I go for the F-bomb, which is common among people my age and younger.

Profanity is all about escalation. “Damn” is reinforced as “goddamn,” with “bull” modifying the S-word and “mother” serving an analogous purpose for the F-bomb.

That said, it’s highly unlikely that Trump will turn up the volume much more when it comes to bad words. In English, profanity comes in three stages of shock value. Stage 1 is blasphemous words. “Damn” and “hell” were once considered such strong drink that in the 19th-century opera “H.M.S. Pinafore,” the captain prides himself on never saying “damn” (or hardly ever, he admits). Today, in our less pious age, those are mild expletives at best.

Stage 2 is sexual or graphic words about the body, and Trump revels in those. We will recall a notorious comment of his about grabbing women by a certain body part and his scatological characterization of countries such as Haiti and El Salvador. But these sorts of words, which are used publicly today much more than in the past, now qualify more as salty or tasteless than genuinely taboo.

Stage 3 is racial and other slurs against groups. Though Trump has been accused of using the N-word, he has long avoided using slurs in public. We can, of course, expect him to push the envelope. Indeed, just this week he used an anti-transgender slur when referring to Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina. But it’s notable that Andrews, who has expressed support for transgender youth, is not transgender herself. I’m willing to bet that Trump wouldn’t use that slur in public to refer to a transgender person like Sarah McBride, the congresswoman from Delaware, just as I wouldn’t expect him to use a homophobic slur to publicly attack a gay opponent.

Today, it is such words that qualify as truly profane. We often think of slurs as distinct from swear words, but it’s an indication that they are, in fact, today’s profanity that even someone as heedless of etiquette, decorum, restraint and reflection as Trump has tended to avoid them.

Because the Stage 1 and Stage 2 words are now more naughty than profane, Trump uses them to thumb his nose at propriety. In this, he is like an 11-year-old, snapping towels at people in the locker room — and snapping them ever more to get a rise out of the people looking on.

Yet he does not typically risk Stage 3 profanity. Amid his staggering megalomania and chronic logorrhea, Trump, if only for pragmatic purposes, maintains a twinkle of — of all things — decorum.
