ARTICLE

How Much Space Does $400,000 Get You?
The median national home price gets you a vastly different spread, depending where you are.
By Arnesa A. Howell
Published 2026-10-08 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/realestate/how-much-space-does-400000-get-you.html

Over the past six years, the national median home sales price has jumped over 20 percent to $400,000, according to a PropertyShark market study. Just how much space the median price gets you largely depends on — you guessed it — location.

PropertyShark analyzed the 100 largest U.S. cities to find that those in the Northeast and West offered the least space for the national median sale price. In Manhattan (New York City’s boroughs were considered individually in the report), a $400,000 budget would nab only 267 square feet, the least among all places studied. In Brooklyn one could expect 476 square feet. Of the 10 most expensive places, six were in California.

The study culled data from the U.S. census, PropertyShark sales data and other sources for its analysis, factoring in a mix of single-family homes, townhouses and condos.

“What these cities typically have in common are thriving economies, the major employment opportunities,” Laura Pop-Badiu, the author of the PropertyShark study, explained. Despite that $400,000 purchased only 393 square feet in San Francisco, Ms. Pop-Badiu said the city’s proximity to Silicon Valley attracted many professionals. Most downsize, the study found.

Comparatively, houses in the Midwest had the most floor space at the national median home price. The roomiest homes were in Detroit, where $400,000 could buy you a spacious, nearly 5,000-square-foot home. The cost: $81 a square foot.

While the national median sale price of $400,000 was the study’s point of comparison, in expensive markets, finding any home at that price is unlikely. In Manhattan, last year’s median sale price was far greater, $1.65 million, and the median home size, 1,100 square feet.

ARTICLE

Man vs. ‘Terminator’-Like Robot in a Cage. California Called It Illegal.
A tech start-up’s stunt in San Francisco tested the boundaries of combat sport safety and regulations.
By Adeel Hassan
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/technology/human-robot-cage-fights-california-rek.html

The 6-foot-tall, steel-framed humanoid robot, which looked like James Cameron’s original “Terminator,” entered the cage, followed by a 5-foot-5 male human in a helmet and other protective gear.

You can probably guess what happened next.

The robot, which was operated by a human pilot using a remote virtual-reality system, pummeled its fleshy opponent, Frankie LaPenna, repeatedly knocking him to the canvas and driving him into the walls of the octagonal enclosure.

Mr. LaPenna, a social media influencer, injured his hand while punching one of the metal robot frames during one of the three bouts he had with different robots. He landed a few punches, but each time he knocked a robot down, it bounced back almost instantly. The crowd of about 100 (humans, not humanoids) was thrilled.

The fight, promoted as “Human vs. Robot,” was staged on Sept. 18 in San Francisco by a tech start-up called REK, which stands for Robot Entertainment Kombat.

It caught the attention of the California State Athletic Commission, which sent the company a cease-and-desist letter. The commission, which regulates professional and amateur boxing, kickboxing and mixed martial arts, had not sanctioned the event.

REK, which bills itself as “the humanoid robot fighting league” (“Real robots, real combat”) — celebrated the letter.

“We made it boys,” its chief executive, Cix Liv, said in an online post.

The letter said that the commission must grant approval to any boxing or mixed martial arts contest, match or exhibition that involves any human in the state of California.

It is a misdemeanor, it added, to promote or participate in an unlicensed boxing or martial arts contest, match or exhibition involving any human.

Mr. Liv dismissed the regulator’s claims.

“The law clearly states that a ‘match’ is between two persons,” he said in an interview, adding that state regulators were welcome to try to argue in court that a humanoid is somehow human.

He said that his company, whose goal is to create a sport in which humanoids engage in MMA-style fighting, did not need permission from the authorities.

However, Mr. LaPenna repeatedly sought permission from REK to fight its robots, which a human operator controls similarly to how one operates a drone. Mr. LaPenna, who did not respond to a request for comment, is known for posting videos of himself getting hurt.

The event produced the most-viewed content that REK has so far shared online, but Mr. Liv said there wasn’t a plan to repeat it. Instead, the company plans to host the first fight between humanoids armed with blades on Friday night in San Francisco.

“We’re going to democratize MMA so we can essentially experience the blood sport without anyone getting hurt,” he said.

Mr. LaPenna had to sign a legal waiver that said if were killed during the fight, it would not be REK’s fault.

“Our hope was to basically get some good shots without actually hurting Frankie,” Mr. Liv said.

The athletic commission said in a statement that it was “committed to protecting the safety of the public and integrity of combat sports.”

“Unsanctioned activity puts the physical and financial well-being of all those involved at risk and such activity will not be tolerated,” it said, adding that it would consider new guidance as robot technology evolves.

Combat sports are regulated by states and tribal commissions in the United States, said Erik Magraken, the managing partner of MacIsaac & Company, a law firm specializing in combat sports regulatory issues and the publisher of the blog Combat Sports Law.

“These laws were written with no contemplation of people fighting machines, so many commissions will be ill equipped to address this novel form of fighting,” he said.

“Many athletic commissions will simply have no ability to shut down such events without amendment of their legislation or regulations,” he added.

Humanoids have been developing faster than lawmakers can keep up. In April, a humanoid robot named Lightning ran a half-marathon in Beijing in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the human world record of 56:51, which Yomif Kejelcha of Ethiopia set in August.

The Humanoid Robot Games, first held in Beijing last year, and again this summer, featured running, kickboxing and soccer. While there was plenty of running, kicking and punching, the robots also flailed around, crashed and fell over many times.

Those who know humanoid robots best highly recommend against fighting them.

“It’s very unfair to put a human in with a heavily motorized system that’s only going to dominate,” said Ken Goldberg, a professor who oversees the automation lab at the University of California, Berkeley. “There’s not nothing surprising about that.”

Dr. Goldberg boxed a smaller robot last year, for educational purposes and not in a cage. “I gave it one of my old kung fu side kicks from high school and it stumbled back and it tripped and fell,” he said. But they bounce back quickly, he added.

He said he understood the appeal of the fights that REK was staging, noting that it tapped “into some of the fear and frustration with robots that people feel.”

“I mean, they love to see the human kick the robot’s gearbox,” he said.

But the odds of that human fighter getting his gearbox kicked are much greater, Dr. Goldberg said, given that REK’s humanoid robots can weigh several hundred pounds and are made of steel.

“If you program that thing to just come swinging and punching at you, I don’t think you’ll get away from it,” he said. “It’s pretty scary.”

ARTICLE

Amex Supersizes Newark Airport Lounge Before It Even Opens
To meet skyrocketing demand, lounge operators like American Express are racing to build bigger, and the Centurion in Newark’s Terminal A will be a giant.
By Christine Chung
Published 2026-10-08 12:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/travel/amex-centurion-lounge-newark.html

American Express is going big at Newark Liberty International Airport.

The credit card issuer announced on Thursday that its Centurion Lounge at Newark — the only major New York metro airport without one of the premium Amex retreats — would occupy a 30,000-square-foot, two-floor space instead of the 18,000 square feet that Amex had originally planned.

That lounge, scheduled to open next year in Terminal A, will leapfrog Amex’s current largest offering, the 26,000-square-foot Centurion at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

Audrey Hendley, the president of American Express Travel, said that Newark’s opening would solidify its presence in the New York metro area’s airports.

“New York is unique because travelers move among three major airports, and Newark is an important addition to our network,” Ms. Hendley said in a statement.

The Centurion Lounge will be Newark’s first lounge operated by a credit card issuer, beating out both J.P. Morgan Chase, which operates Chase Sapphire Reserve lounges, and Capital One, which runs lounges and lounge-restaurant hybrids it calls Landings.

Newark’s Centurion Lounge will have three bars, including one that celebrates New Jersey’s Italian heritage, in addition to a coffee bar. Like other Centurions, it will also feature dishes created by notable chefs such as Kwame Onwuachi and Sarah Grueneberg.

Amex also announced a series of other expansions: a second lounge at Heathrow Airport in London, as well as renovations to existing lounges at Philadelphia International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston.

In Philadelphia, the lounge will double in size to 12,000 square feet over two stories by late next year. In Houston, the overhaul will be even more substantial: Amex plans to triple the lounge space to more than 23,000 square feet by 2028.

Amex opened its first Centurion lounge in 2013 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. It now has 33 Centurion locations globally, making it the credit card issuer with the most airport lounges. Chase offers Sapphire Reserve lounges at nine airports. Capital One has five lounges and two Landings locations.

In April, Amex also teased a new Centurion lounge at Boston Logan International Airport, expected to open in Terminal C in 2029, and updates at the Centurion location at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

Access to lounges is increasingly influencing the way that customers fly. In a survey of more than 1,400 travelers conducted last fall by J.D. Power, the analytics firm, nearly half of lounge customers said they planned their flights based on preferred lounge access.

To cater to this growing market, lounge operators appear to be in a race to build bigger. This week, American Airlines announced it would open its largest Admirals Club lounge, a 40,000-square-foot space at Charlotte Douglas International Airport, in North Carolina, most likely by early 2028, a spokeswoman said. Later this month, United is expected to open a 54,000-square-foot lounge at George Bush Intercontinental Airport. This will be its most spacious United Club and also the largest airline-owned lounge in North America, a United spokeswoman said.

Lounges are also expanding in response to increasing grumbling about overcrowding.

“To protect that value proposition and keep cardholders paying those annual fees,” said Sally French, a travel expert at the personal finance website NerdWallet, “lounge operators have no choice but to build bigger and bigger lounges.”

ARTICLE

21 Birds Are Found at Miami Airport Stuffed in Underwear and Hidden in a Belt
Two men, who arrived separately from Cuba days apart, each carried clutches of live birds concealed in their clothes, the authorities said.
By Rebecca Chao
Published 2026-10-08 21:20 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/us/birds-smuggled-cuba-miami.html

Twice this week, men arrived at Miami International Airport from Havana and aroused the suspicions of customs officers for the same reason.

Something seemed to be concealed beneath their clothing.

The something, they found, turned out to be clutches of live birds hidden on their persons. In one of the arrests, 10 birds were stuffed in the man’s underpants, according to charging documents. The other man was smuggling 11 birds.

That man, Alberto Hernandez Castillo, disembarked from his flight on Sunday in a pair of gold-sheened sneakers, according to a criminal complaint. He appeared nervous and authorities observed an “unexplained bulge” around his pelvis.

The second man, Roberto Perez Quincosa, 41, who arrived on Tuesday, was also arrested after officials made similar observations about him.

Each man was charged with smuggling.

Authorities have not said if the cases were related. A lawyer for Mr. Hernandez Castillo did not respond to a request for comment. It was unknown if Mr. Perez Quincosa had a lawyer.

A pat-down found that Mr. Hernandez Castillo had black pouches sewn into his underpants, according to an account in the complaint from a special agent with Homeland Security Investigations. Nestled inside were six slim tubes, bound in beige tape and affixed with black mesh at the opening. Each contained one or two breathing birds, the complaint said.

Mr. Perez Quincosa had devised a belt-like garment to hold the 11 birds he carried, according to an account from a special agent with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that was included in a criminal complaint. He had used hair roller tubes “with holes along their length and capped with netting material,” wrapped in electrical tape, the complaint said.

Some of the birds that were recovered, such as the two blue grosbeaks that the authorities said Mr. Castillo had on him, are protected species. Eight yellow-faced grassquits were also found on him. Mr. Perez Quincosa had transported six Cuban melodious finches and five Cuban bullfinches, according to the complaint.

Yellow-faced grassquits are native to South and Central America and are named for the bands of yellow above the eyes and across the throats of males. Blue grosbeaks are North American songbirds.

Mr. Hernandez Castillo and Mr. Perez Quincosa were both born in Cuba and are now permanent U.S. residents, according to the complaints. Neither had filed the appropriate paperwork to legally import wildlife into the United States, and they had also checked “no” on customs declarations forms when asked if they were bringing animals or wildlife into the country.

Mr. Hernandez Castillo was released on Monday after posting a $25,000 bond, according to court records. The authorities did not say on Thursday if Mr. Perez Quincosa was still in custody.

Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Customs and Border Protection referred inquiries to the Fish and Wildlife Service, which said in an email that it could not comment because it was still investigating.

The authorities did not say what happened to the birds, although trafficked animals sometimes are handed over to a zoo or shelter.

Miami is a gateway for smugglers seeking to bring wildlife into the United States from Latin America and the Caribbean, many of them to be offered for sale. The World Wildlife Fund estimates that, globally, as many as 1.5 million birds have been trafficked in a single year. Exotic birds with colorful plumage can sell for a thousand dollars or more. Global profits can reach the tens of billions of dollars, according to Bird Life International, a conservation group.

Last year, a man crossed from Mexico into California with two sedated parrots hidden in his trousers. In 2018, at least 200 finches made their way from South to North America stuffed in plastic hair rollers or in luggage. And six years before that, Interpol raids on airports, post offices, pet stores and other settings in 32 countries uncovered more than 8,000 wild animals, most of them birds.

According to the complaints, Mr. Perez Quincosa told law enforcement that he knew bringing in the birds was unlawful and that he intended to breed and sell them for $100 to $120 each. Mr. Hernandez Castillo said that the birds he was carrying were intended for his “personal use,” according to the complaint. He then invoked his right to remain silent.

ARTICLE

‘He’s Not Making Sense’: How Trump Has Alienated Voters for the G.O.P.
Signs are emerging that dispirited Republican voters may stay home in November, bringing a Democratic surge without many conversions.
By Sabrina Tavernise and Jamie Kelter Davis
Published 2026-10-08 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/us/elections/trump-voter-enthusiasm-midterms.html

If Democrats make big gains in the midterm elections in four weeks, it may not only be because their most loyal voters come out in force, or because their candidates have converted Republican voters to their cause.

Instead, the Democrats’ dream blue wave could come from Republicans who sour on President Trump and stay home. It already has a name: the red undertow.

Across the country, signs are emerging of an enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans, even among those who consider themselves likely to vote. A stretch of rural southwest Michigan — long a Republican stronghold — illustrates the point, with more signs for blueberries and eggs than for political candidates. Volunteers are not showing up to door-knock. And many voters say they are tuning this election out.

“People are just more focused on everyday life,” said Lindsay Kronemeyer, 35, a conservative Christian mother of two who works in the construction industry. “I don’t hear the chatter on the Republican side of ‘Trump this, Trump that.’ He’s just not there in my head anymore.”

Jim Pasek, a retired pharmaceutical plant maintenance worker who lives in the tiny town of Gobles, Mich., was baffled by a president he has voted for twice.

“He’s not making sense,” Mr. Pasek, 80, said. “It confuses me, and then I just get disgusted and tune out.”

The idea of the red undertow was introduced last month by the political analyst Charlie Cook, who argued that the Democratic brand was still underwater, but that this election was not about a rising Democratic tide. It was about a drowning Trump brand.

In its wake, Mr. Cook wrote, an undertow will “pull many Republicans under.”

In nearly three dozen interviews in Western Michigan, a sense of fatigue was constant, and that feeling goes beyond that region.

“President Trump has been saying, ‘Vote as if I was on the ballot,’ and that’s exactly what I’m going to do — not vote,” said Brandon Tremaine, 24, a graduate student in Texas who voted for Mr. Trump in 2020. “You do not campaign on being the ticket of peace and start a war of choice that is directly hurting Americans here at home and gotten Americans killed overseas.”

Polls can be unreliable, and moods may be fleeting. Trump loyalists are also known for not taking the calls of polling outfits, and that may be overstating Democratic strengths. Disaffected Trump voters may yet rally to vote as the possibility of a Democratic victory nears, and many Americans still love Mr. Trump.

“I’ll go the length with Trump,” said Jeff Gilbert, 67, a friend of Mr. Pasek in Gobles.

The numbers aren’t drastically far apart. A New York Times/Siena University national poll from last month found that Democrats were more likely to say they were absolutely certain to vote than Republicans, 61 percent to 56 percent. While Democrats led Republicans nationally by seven percentage points among registered voters, that advantage rose to nine points among likely voters.

But in close races, a small gap could prove meaningful.

“People are tired,” Al Pscholka, a Republican and a former member of the Michigan House of Representatives, said of Mr. Trump. “The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.”

The concern is showing in unlikely places. Representative Bill Huizenga, a Western Michigan Republican whose four House victories were all by comfortable margins, is in “the fight of his life” against a well-funded centrist Democrat from Kalamazoo named Sean McCann, said Rob Pocock, a retired Republican political consultant who has worked on campaigns in the region.

Nancy DeBoer, the local Republican state representative, also faces a serious fight against Joseph McClusky, a graduate of Hope College, a conservative Christian liberal arts college in Holland, Mich., who is openly gay.

“I would be shocked if Joseph wins, but I can’t believe he’s done as well as he has,” said Mr. Pocock, who teaches at Hope and had Mr. McClusky as a student. He said in Ottawa County, he was seeing Democratic yard signs in numbers he’d never seen before.

Western Michigan — home of Gerald Ford — may be seeing the ebb tide of the president’s MAGA movement, which had surged in this region, once known for a sober, Christian-inflected conservatism. In Ottawa County, ardent Trump supporters secured 8 of the 11 seats on the county commission after Covid. Pro-Trump forces won control of the state party, too.

Today, the MAGA wing is down to three seats in Ottawa County. They have also lost posts in Berrien and Kent counties.

“I think there’s a shift in the party back toward, we need a little bit of the establishment folks,” Ms. Kronemeyer said. “They exist for a reason.”

If anybody should be enthusiastic about the election, it is Ms. Kronemeyer. She ran for a statehouse seat in 2022. She door-knocked for Mr. Trump in 2016 and 2020. But she said that when a friend asked her recently about the races in her area, she had to admit she hadn’t been following them closely. She lives in deep-red Allegan County, where “traditionally in election years, yard signs would be peppered everywhere,” she said.

But the only signs she’d seen this year were for a judge, she said.

Ten years have passed since Mr. Trump took the country by storm, bringing a message of economic populism that appealed to millions of working-class Americans.

“He was a ball of energy,” Mr. Pasek said, sitting at breakfast in Gobles last week with his friend, Mr. Gilbert. “You could feel it. You could see it.”

Now, Mr. Pasek said, Mr. Trump seems to have lost his way. He started a war when he said he wouldn’t, sending the price of gas through the roof. And he seems to talk more about ballrooms and arches than he does about how he will bring prices back down.

“He’s losing touch with the American people,” Mr. Pasek said.

Mr. Gilbert said that he had stopped following the news closely, choosing to spend more time outside with his dog, Mabel. But he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, and he said he stands by that choice. He said he believed Mr. Trump had a plan for Iran.

Mr. Pasek countered, “He says he has a plan, but then he doesn’t tell us what it is.”

Mr. Pasek cited gas prices: “He says it’s chump change. No, it’s not! It’s killing the people.”

He has noticed someone living in a car in a parking lot when he drives into town, he said. He worried about his granddaughter, 28, a college graduate from Michigan State University, who is working three jobs — one full-time and two part-time — but can’t find a house she can afford.

Those misgivings are being felt at the local party level. Doug Koopman, a member of the Kent County Republican Party’s executive committee, said that it had been a struggle to get the foot soldiers of the midterm elections — volunteer door-knockers and canvassers — to pick up brochures to distribute door to door, leaving bags of them sitting around the party headquarters.

“There’s very low energy on the Republican side,” he said.

In 2024, people lined up for nearly a mile in the rain in Grand Rapids to see Mr. Trump speak the night before the election. His campaign was dominant on social media, reaching younger people who’d never voted before, such as Sebastian Covey, who remembered Mr. Trump “popping” on his feeds. Mr. Covey had not voted before 2024; he did that year, for the president.

Now 24, he said his focus was elsewhere. He lives more than an hour away from his landscaping job in Hudsonville, a bustling suburb just west of Grand Rapids, because rents are cheaper, but the rising gas price has made his commute painful. He swapped his truck for a car, but a colleague he had been car-pooling with just found another job. He and his girlfriend have been looking for a rental closer to work, but so far they have not found anything they can afford.

He said he hadn’t thought about whether he would vote.

“I should care more, but it’s hard to keep up,” he said during a lunch break in a Wendy’s restaurant.

Even Republicans who are in politics say they are tired — worn out by the battles between pro-MAGA politicians and traditional Republicans. Bob Harrison, 76, a Republican county commissioner in Berrien County, where MAGA forces won control of the county G.O.P., said those forces took away the right to vote on party decisions from local elected officials like him.

Those officials “pretty much all walked away from the Berrien County Republican Party” to raise funds for their own political candidates, said Dr. Harrison, a retired community college president.

Dr. Harrison, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said the hard-core Trump supporters remained unchanged, but “they’ve lost the support of the moderates like myself, people who think and choose and maybe split their votes.”

Warren Stewart, 69, who lives in Stevensville, Mich., and works restoring old homes, said he liked to think that Mr. Trump was working to restore the country, but he is starting to have doubts.

Clients often get nervous when the project is only halfway through, he said, but he assures them that he always has a plan for bringing the home back to its original beauty. He wonders if Mr. Trump does, too.

“Does he really know what he’s doing?” Mr. Stewart said.

He would never vote for a Democrat; he feels bludgeoned by liberals online, he said. But he’s not sure he’ll vote for Republicans, either.

“I just spent $60 on $30 worth of groceries and am about to go fill up for $5 a gallon,” he said, carrying two bags of groceries to his car. “It feels like they’re stress-testing us.”

Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting and research.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

India’s Cockroach Party Leader Carries Gen Z’s Demands. They Are Many.
Abhijeet Dipke started the movement as a joke. But after ousting a minister over a dysfunctional college entrance exam system, India’s youth say they now want to save democracy.
By Somini Sengupta and Pragati K.B.
Published 2026-10-08 07:10 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/asia/india-cockroach-janta-party.html

He uncorked a generation’s anger at a broken college entrance exam system.

Now, the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government.

The cockroaches’ latest aim is the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, over what they say is a politically motivated purge of 130 million voters from the election rolls.

This Saturday, in perhaps their biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration, they are calling on supporters to defy a police ban and stage a mass protest in New Delhi.

“For the nation, its democracy and our future, let’s all come together,” Mr. Dipke, 31, said on social media Thursday, appealing to Indians of all generations and ideologies. “Irrespective of your political inclinations, march with the youth.”

In fact, India’s youth have many more grievances: failing schools, insufficient jobs, violence against women, a lack of government accountability. Their frustrations have been boiling for years. There are so many of them — 367 million people between ages 15 and 29, the world’s largest Gen Z cohort.

Mr. Dipke says he feels intense pressure.

“It’s like someone has dropped a baby at my doorstep,” Mr. Dipke said on a recent road trip to highlight the problem with public schools in the countryside. “It actually scares me, to be very honest.”

“People have too many expectations, too many hopes,” he went on. “It’s like people are expecting me to resolve everything at once.”

Mr. Modi has not commented on the cockroach protests, though criticism has come from senior politicians of his Bharatiya Janata Party, including the chief minister of Maharashtra state, Devendra Fadnavis, who said their “fake narrative” over the voter roll revision would not succeed.

For Mr. Dipke — and the cockroaches — the risks are enormously high.

In a country where space for dissent has shrunk, they could be crushed as quickly as they appeared. The Delhi police have detained hundreds of people who defied the ban and protested in Delhi this week.

The cockroaches’ four leaders are all under the age of 32, with no political experience. Signs of friction have appeared with the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress. Its leader, Rahul Gandhi, is holding another rally across the country, in Chennai, on Saturday.

The cockroaches already have one win under their belt: the rare ouster of a government minister in connection to the entrance exams. They seem to have emboldened many more Indians to speak out against the government. Over the last week, a range of groups, from left-wing student activists to conservative regional politicians, have rallied in several cities.

“We are just frustrated by everything. Everything” said Aayushi Gaikwad, 18, who traveled three hours by train to attend a cockroach protest in Mumbai last Friday.

It was her first time at a protest. Around her, thousands of people waved Indian flags. As evening fell, Mr. Dipke led the crowd in singing the national anthem.

Ram Guha, a historian and an outspoken critic of Mr. Modi, credited the cockroach leaders for puncturing the “invincibility of the Modi government.”

“They clearly have a raw courage,” he said.

A Campaign to Fix Schools

Not long after they forced the resignation of the education minister in July, the cockroaches turned to India’s rural schools. A range of Instagram-worthy horrors awaited them at government schools. Clogged toilets. Broken water taps. Overheated tin sheds for classrooms. Rotten onions in a school kitchen. Children wading through floodwaters to reach school.

We joined Mr. Dipke as he visited a remote district in western Maharashtra state, called Nandurbar, where he had spent the first five years of his childhood before his family moved to a city.

For Mr. Dipke, fixing schools is personal.

He was born to a Dalit family, seen as low on the Hindu caste ladder. He attended private schools. But his cousins, whose parents were not as educated as his, attended rural government schools, and the contrast was obvious to him, even as a child. He sat at a desk; they sat on the floor. He drank filtered water; they sometimes had no water. He went on to Boston University for a master’s degree; they repaired cars or worked construction.

“That has been one of the most neglected things since independence. Government schools have never been given the attention they need,” he said.

At a residential girls’ school in a village called Sari, he learned there was no running water in the fourth-floor bathrooms. The girls hauled buckets of water up four flights of stairs.

At a primary school, he met the one teacher who taught a class of first through fourth graders. There was no electricity, and the girls had to fetch water for their bathroom from across a field. The boys had no toilet at all.

Vishwas Thakarey, the teacher, said he, like many teachers, had been diverted from the classroom because he had been told to work on the voter roll revision. (Teachers are often pulled away on other government duties.)

At another residential school an hour’s drive away, Mr. Dipke found a dormitory for girls made of tin walls and a tin roof. There were no beds, only thin cotton mattresses to lay out every night. Mr. Dipke compared it to “an animal shed.” “If there are no basic facilities, how can we expect a quality education?” Mr. Dipke said.

The schools in the area serve mostly Indigenous children, among India’s most neglected.

Some education advocates say that the cockroaches’ focus on school infrastructure is neither new nor especially useful to improving educational outcomes. The latest Annual Survey of Education Results, an independent assessment, found roughly 30 percent of eighth graders in rural schools struggle with second grade-level texts, and around half with basic arithmetic.

In a measure of his naïveté, and also his awareness of it, Mr. Dipke said he had not yet read the ASER reports. He said he would.

Nor was he schooled in the realities of Nandurbar. The district’s top administrator, Mittali Sethi, is. She is trying to fix the electricity system in Sari village, address its groundwater shortage, and train teachers in schools that have fallen behind.

She said she welcomed the attention on school conditions, whether it came from the cockroaches or not. “If someone has raised a problem and it’s a problem, I will fix them,” she said.

(Since Mr. Dipke’s visit, a district water engineer and a health official had visited the village, a local activist said.)

Education experts said they hoped the cockroaches would continue their schools campaign to shine a light on an issue politicians had long ignored.

“The kind of attention they’ve been able to bring to schools, no one I can think of has been able to do that for 20 years,” said Reetika Khera, an economist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi who has researched rural schools for decades.

‘Not Scared’

Last May, Mr. Dipke saw that India’s top judge had referred to young Indians as “cockroaches.” On a lark, he came up with the idea of the Cockroach Janta Party. Its website welcomed the “lazy” and the “unemployed.”

The idea caught fire, thrusting him into the public eye after anger boiled over at the leaked exams. “We didn’t plan or strategize this movement at all,” he said.

He admits to being no expert, on education or anything else. He says he is not a veteran activist nor a skilled orator. His sister reminds him that he was so camera-shy that he refused to take selfies with her. Now everyone wants a selfie with him.

In Mumbai last week, he went, as hundreds of fans do daily, to gawk at the home of Shah Rukh Khan, a Bollywood actor who played a character Mr. Dipke has long admired — only to be stopped for a selfie by one of his own fans. More people were looking at Mr. Dipke today, the fan said, than at the actor’s house.

Mr. Dipke smiled sheepishly, looked at the house, and said, “Oh ho. I’m still a big fan of yours.” He promptly shared the video with his 5.9 million followers on Instagram.

The next day, he stood on a makeshift stage with his fellow cockroach leaders, speaking to a crowd of thousands with a copy of the Indian constitution in his hand.

“Finally someone’s asking for accountability. Finally not being scared,” said Madhur Manohar, 26, who joined the protest.

“For the longest, everybody’s had frustrations,” her friend, Surabhi Apte, 30, said. “They didn’t know how to channel it. It was only dinner conversations, where your parents were like, ‘Ignore it.’”

“This is finally us doing something,” Ms. Manohar added.

Indian Opposition Leaders Detained as Protests Over Voter Rolls Intensify

Protests by Indian opposition leaders were broken up by police in New Delhi for a second day on Wednesday, with many lawmakers dragged off the streets, as anger over a revision of voter rolls that dropped more than 130 million names continued to intensify across the country.

Videos show Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, being lifted by police and shoved into a bus as he struggled to fight them off. Earlier in the week, student protesters who were also trying to reach Jantar Mantar were met by a similar show of force, with many of them rounded up by police and herded into buses. Security around Mr. Kumar’s residence has been tightened, Indian media reported.

The issue is boiling toward a possible showdown this weekend. The Cockroach Janta Party, the Gen-Z backed movement that organized mass protests over an exam leak scandal over the summer, and other youth groups are calling for demonstrations in the capital on Saturday to demand the resignation of Mr. Kumar.

ARTICLE

U.K. and Israel Agree to a Scaled-Back British Mission in East Jerusalem
Israel had threatened to close the British Consulate in East Jerusalem, a center of outreach to Palestinians for decades. A last-minute agreement means a smaller diplomatic service will remain.
By Michael D. Shear and Adam Rasgon
Published 2026-10-08 07:53 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/europe/uk-israel-consulate-east-jerusalem-palestinians.html

British and Israeli diplomats reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure of the British Consulate building in East Jerusalem, Britain’s foreign secretary announced on Thursday, leaving behind a scaled-back diplomatic mission to Palestinians.

Israel threatened last month to shut the consulate, which has served as the center of British outreach to Palestinians for decades, in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have been expanding rapidly.

Until Thursday, both countries appeared to be locked in a series of escalating retaliations. British officials had privately warned that the closure of the consulate would be met with retaliation that might include expelling a number of Israeli diplomats from London.

Instead, the two countries issued statements early Thursday morning that each declared the issue resolved but described the compromise they had reached in significantly different ways.

In his statement, the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that the consulate building would not close but would be renamed.

“Our Consulate General building will not be closing, and will be known as the U.K. Mission, Jerusalem, from today,” Mr. Miliband said. He noted that the new facility “is independent, operational, and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people.”

Mr. Miliband said that Britain stood by the sanctions imposed on the settlements in the West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law.

“We do not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years,” he added, pointing to Britain’s “longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”

He also suggested that the reduction in staffing at the building would be temporary.

“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence,” he wrote.

Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister, issued a very different statement, asserting that Israel had followed through on its threat.

“The British Consulate in Jerusalem is ending its operations today,” he wrote on social media. “Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed.”

In Mr. Saar’s telling, what remains at the building will be “a task force of only seven diplomats,” and “their scope of activity will be very limited.”

Mr. Saar added that the British consul general and 19 other diplomats would be ending their assignments. Mr. Miliband said only that a number of British officials who had been stationed at the consulate had been “temporarily withdrawn” to ensure their safety.

Mr. Saar also said that British officials had been removed from an international support center in Gaza and that British officials would no longer be able to train Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank.

Ahmad Majdalani, a member of the Palestine Liberation Organization’s executive committee, said Palestinian leaders in the West Bank were relieved that Britain would be maintaining a diplomatic mission in East Jerusalem.

“What is important for us is that there’s diplomatic presence and that it is able to maintain relations with the Palestinian leadership and provide consular services to Palestinian citizens,” he said.

The agreement came after Jonathan Powell, Britain’s national security adviser, traveled to Israel last week for meetings aimed at reaching a compromise that could avoid a more serious breakdown between the longstanding allies.

By the time Mr. Powell left Israel last week, it appeared that the Israelis had rejected his suggestions, according to three people familiar with the private discussions who talked about them on condition of anonymity. But negotiations between Israeli and British officials continued until late Wednesday night, according to one Israeli official who was briefed on the ongoing discussions.

Despite the differences in their statements, Britain and Israel agreed to coordinate their publication at 7 a.m. British time, the Israeli official said.

Within minutes of the announcement of the change, the Israeli Foreign Ministry distributed before and after pictures showing the consulate entrance with signs and then without signs by the door.

ARTICLE

How a U.S. Diplomat Suppressed and Altered Reports Critical of Israel
A top aide to Ambassador Mike Huckabee skewed information to portray the Netanyahu government in a favorable light, according to multiple officials and documents obtained by The Times.
By Natan Odenheimer and Adam Rasgon
Published 2026-10-08 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/middleeast/israel-embassy-milstein-huckabee.html

In late March, at the height of the Iran war, Israel quietly approved more settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank than it ever had at one time.

Staff members at the United States Embassy in Jerusalem saw the move as potentially flouting one of President Trump’s explicit red lines for Israel — no annexation of the West Bank — and drafted an urgent report intended for policy makers in Washington.

That memo never reached Washington. It was quashed by David Milstein, a top aide to Ambassador Mike Huckabee, according to three U.S. officials briefed on the process.

This was no isolated incident.

Since taking up his post in April 2025, Mr. Milstein, 36, has repeatedly suppressed or significantly revised embassy reporting on Israeli activities to present the Netanyahu government in a favorable light, according to a dozen people who work with or interact with Mr. Milstein in both Jerusalem and Washington:

- As settler violence in the West Bank surged in the spring, for instance, he stymied embassy reporting suggesting that the Israeli government was failing to take action, according to the three officials. Instead the embassy sent a cable to Washington, viewed by The New York Times, praising Israel for “cracking down” on the attacks.
- When members of Congress pushed for accountability over the killings of nine Palestinian Americans by Israeli settlers and security forces, he suppressed a detailed report that the embassy staff had written, effectively stonewalling lawmakers’ efforts to gain information, according to multiple officials briefed on the matter.
- Soon after arriving in Jerusalem, Mr. Milstein began insisting on approving communications from the embassy section that handles Palestinian affairs, multiple officials with direct knowledge of the process said. The flow of cables plummeted from several a week to a few a month, as some staffers refrained from writing reports for fear that Mr. Milstein would block or rewrite them, these officials said.

Mr. Milstein’s interventions go far beyond those of any recent predecessor, several officials said. They and others said they were speaking out of concern that officials in Washington were getting a distorted view of Israeli actions through core diplomatic channels.

Mr. Milstein’s efforts have helped insulate Israel’s right-wing government against potential blowback from a Trump Administration that has been its closest ally.

Among the most contentious issues on which Mr. Milstein has intervened is the accelerating expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

It’s an inflammatory subject that has soured Israel’s relationship with some of its longtime allies. Last month, Britain, Canada and France announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in response to the Israeli policy on settlement expansion. Britain accused some settlers of “ethnic cleansing.”

It is unclear to what extent Mr. Huckabee is aware of his adviser’s actions. Both he and Mr. Milstein declined requests for an interview.

The ambassador, a longtime advocate for the Israeli settlement movement, has denounced specific attacks by settlers, calling them “Israeli terrorists,” but he has played down settler violence more broadly, saying it is being carried out by a small group.

Mr. Huckabee is required to sign off on most cables and significant decisions, but officials said Mr. Milstein sometimes acts on his own. The ambassador has also sometimes worked in concert with Mr. Milstein to suppress or recast information, these officials said. But in several cases when he believed Mr. Milstein had gone too far, they said, Mr. Huckabee has reined him in.

Earlier this month, after an article critical of Mr. Milstein for inviting wedding guests to give him money appeared in Politico, Mr. Huckabee posted on social media that he had “absolute confidence” in his aide, whom he said possesses “impeccable integrity.”

Mr. Milstein is a familiar figure in right-wing circles in the United States and Israel, and has organized meetings between Mr. Huckabee and some top Israeli officials. But he is not well known in either country, and his role as a gatekeeper of information sent to Washington has drawn little attention.

His effort to shape embassy reporting was first reported a year ago by the online magazine of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a Washington think tank that advocates de-escalation and U.S. military restraint.

But fresh reporting by The New York Times unearthed documentary evidence and previously unreported instances of Mr. Milstein’s effort to skew information to the benefit of the Netanyahu government, which has continued throughout this year.

The Times interviewed 15 U.S. officials for this article, including many in Washington, all of whom worked with Mr. Milstein in some manner. The Times also talked to nine former diplomats who provided context on the role and responsibilities of senior embassy officials. All spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. The Times also obtained or reviewed dozens of documents, cables, memos and other internal communications.

The people who spoke to The Times were career government officials and political appointees, including strong supporters of the United States-Israel relationship. Most said they were speaking out of concern that Mr. Milstein’s actions are undermining standard diplomatic work, expressing worry that, in some cases, they contradict the president’s stated policies.

The concern extended to senior administration officials in Washington, including in the White House, who have expressed frustration to colleagues over some of Mr. Milstein’s actions, according to four officials, who have either witnessed or been briefed on the dissatisfaction.

It is not clear whether Mr. Milstein’s interventions have affected White House policy. But since Mr. Trump declared a year ago that he would not allow Israel to annex the West Bank, he has said little about the issue beyond briefly reaffirming in February that he opposed annexation, even as Israel was extending more control over the territory.

In response to questions sent to the embassy about Mr. Milstein’s actions, Mr. Huckabee did not address specific instances cited by The Times. He wrote in a statement: “The elements of the story The New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors.” He added: “I personally and categorically refute the elements of your proposed ‘story.’ ”

Asked about The Times’s reporting on Mr. Milstein, the State Department provided the following statement: “The entire team at State remains focused on advancing President Trump’s America First agenda.”

The White House referred The Times to the State Department.

A Chilling Effect

Mr. Milstein is the stepson of the right-wing radio host Mark Levin — a close ally of both Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu. That relationship is well known in Washington and the embassy, and has been a factor in how he is treated, officials in both Jerusalem and Washington said.

As an adviser to Mr. Huckabee, Mr. Milstein is one of the most senior officials in the embassy, acting as a chief of staff of sorts to Mr. Huckabee. The ambassador has empowered him to oversee much of the mission’s portfolio, particularly the West Bank and Gaza.

Previous ambassadors to Israel have had political appointees as senior advisers who, like Mr. Milstein, tried to influence the reporting back to Washington. And Mr. Milstein’s responsibilities include reviewing and amending information sent to Washington.

People who interact with Mr. Milstein professionally, however, say he goes to unusual lengths to frame Israel in a positive light. He has blocked reporting from being sent, rewritten cables to deliver a different — sometimes opposite — message from the original, and delayed approving drafts until the topic was no longer relevant, these officials said.

In the summer of 2025, for instance, dozens of Palestinians seeking food were killed near the distribution sites run by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, backed by Israel and the United States. American diplomats in Israel drafted a cable, viewed by The Times, warning that the foundation’s distribution process was chaotic and deadly and risked more “mass casualty events.”

Mr. Milstein rewrote the cable to declare GHF’s operation a success while overlooking the mass casualties, according to people who saw the cable and were briefed on the editing process.

Troubled by glaring discrepancies between news coverage and the embassy’s official reports, White House and State Department officials seeking a clearer picture of events bypassed standard channels at least twice to communicate directly with embassy staff, according to two officials briefed on the outreach and an internal communication from late this summer seen by The Times.

Veteran American diplomats said that withholding or twisting the information sent to Washington should raise serious concerns.

“The embassy ought to tell Washington everything — the good, the bad and the ugly,” said Dan Kurtzer, who was the U.S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush. “If they’re not doing so, they are damaging the policy-making process and possibly undermining the president’s policies.”

Mr. Milstein also questioned several colleagues on whether they were “pro-Israel” or “pro-Hamas,” according to four officials, who found the question inappropriate and said it made some people fearful of speaking freely.

A conservative and longtime Republican, Mr. Milstein served as an aide to Senator Ted Cruz of Texas from 2013 to 2018 before relocating to Israel to study at a Jerusalem yeshiva, a school for Jewish religious studies. In 2020, he landed a job as an assistant to David M. Friedman, Mr. Trump’s ambassador to Israel between 2017 to 2021.

During the Biden Administration, Mr. Milstein worked for Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, handling outreach to pro-Israel voters.

In April 2025, Mr. Milstein was back at the embassy in Jerusalem after Mr. Trump was elected to a second term.

Questions About American Deaths

In February, Nasrallah Abu Siyam, 19, was trying to stop settlers from stealing livestock when one of them shot him dead in his West Bank village.

He was the ninth American citizen of Palestinian heritage killed in the West Bank by Israeli settlers or soldiers in four years. Weeks later, seeking an update on the investigations into the killings, 30 members of Congress led by Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanding answers from Israel.

In response, officers in the embassy compiled a report that was completed in March detailing the status of each investigation, according to multiple officials briefed on the process.

Its central findings suggested that, in most cases, investigations had made little progress, that some cases had been closed, and that no one had been charged in any of the killings, these officials said. Instead of forwarding the report, Mr. Milstein argued that the embassy should send a letter saying that Israel was properly handling the investigations, two officials briefed on the discussions said.

On May 4, Paul D. Guaglianone, a State Department official, sent a letter responding to Mr. Van Hollen, saying that the embassy, which had reduced staff because of the Iran war, was focused on security cooperation with Israel and protecting Americans against Iranian attacks. (The intense fighting had wound down nearly a month earlier, after a cease-fire was struck on April 8.)

The letter, provided to The Times by Mr. Van Hollen’s office, said the embassy was working with Israel to “ensure accountability for these deaths.”

The response did not reassure Mr. Van Hollen.

“If you don’t get accountability, you endanger more American citizens,” he said in a phone interview.

Downplaying West Bank Expansion

In February, the Netanyahu government passed a measure that made it easier for Israelis to buy land in the West Bank, a move widely condemned internationally as speeding the way to annexation.

Any formal Israeli annexation of the West Bank, which Israel captured in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war, would carry immense consequences. But in embassy discussions, Mr. Milstein portrayed the government’s announcement on land purchases as a domestic matter with little significance to the outside world, according to two officials.

An embassy report sent to Washington, reviewed by The Times, said the Israeli policy was meant “to address humanitarian needs” of Israeli settlers, without detailing those needs.

A similar intervention occurred in April, when top Israeli military commanders publicly warned that West Bank settler violence could set off a new Palestinian uprising. Embassy staffers tried to alert Washington to those warnings, but Mr. Milstein prevented the reports from being sent as drafted, according to three officials.

In a cable viewed by The Times on which he is listed as the first author, Mr. Milstein praised Mr. Netanyahu’s “unprecedented new initiatives to combat” rising violence in the West Bank. The report’s title read, “Government Cracks Down on Escalating West Bank Violence.”

David M. Halbfinger and Isabel Kershner contributed reporting from Jerusalem.

ARTICLE

Millions Lose Private Medicare Plans and Face Rising Costs
As enrollment for Medicare Advantage begins this month, older Americans are confronting fewer options because insurers are discontinuing coverage in many areas.
By Christopher Rowland and Reed Abelson
Published 2026-10-09 14:52 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/medicare-private-health-care-costs.html

Millions of people with private Medicare coverage are being forced to change their insurance for 2027 and will pay higher prices for prescriptions and medical care, prompting some experts to warn that more older Americans will face greater financial hardship.

Major insurers, like UnitedHealth, Centene and state Blue Cross plans, have shuttered plans that they viewed as unprofitable in certain markets, leaving some people with fewer choices of policies, and even more limited choices of doctors in 2027. In some rural counties from Oregon to New Hampshire, older Americans shopping for private Medicare Advantage plans will find that options have vanished completely or are dwindling to just a few plans.

Overall, as open enrollment begins this month, roughly five million people will be forced to switch plans because their current policy has been canceled or is no longer offered in the county where they live, according to an estimate from Duos, a health technology firm. Other estimates are lower, but analysts who have been studying the issue said cancellations would probably surpass the number this year, which was the highest on record.

Dependent on Social Security and other fixed incomes, recipients also will be paying substantially more in out-of-pocket costs next year when they need a prescription drug or go to a doctor or hospital.

The upheaval and confusion in some areas of the country are in sharp contrast to the Trump administration’s claims that the Medicare Advantage program is “stable” and that average premiums will be lower next year. Now that about 35 million older Americans are covered by Medicare’s private plans, many will face an enrollment period that is likely to be volatile, according to insurance brokers, industry analysts and experts.

The disruptions risk angering older voters before the midterm elections. Many voters say they are unable to afford increases in health care, groceries and gas. A KFF poll released this week found that nearly twice as many likely voters trust Democrats more than Republicans to handle health care costs.

President Trump has announced that the administration was sending out pre-election payments of at least $90 to 20 million traditional Medicare beneficiaries — but not those covered by private plans. Democrats called it a “desperate” move in the face of voter disapproval.

The changes to Medicare Advantage will require members to carefully scrutinize the fine print of plan options, because costs are rising in multiple ways — from co-payments for doctors and prescriptions to deductibles, health analysts said.

In Pahoa, on the Big Island of Hawaii, Ann and Mick Kalber received a registered letter last week advising them their plan was being discontinued.

Mr. Kalber, 78, has a history of throat cancer and jaw surgeries, and he is now on a feeding tube. This year he was hospitalized twice in nearby Hilo. Together the couple are paying less than $300 in monthly premiums. Now they are bracing to pay hundreds more. A high priority for the couple is maintaining access to a Mayo Clinic surgeon in Florida who has operated on Mr. Kalber’s jaw.

Asked if they could afford any increase while living on a combination of Social Security income, an inheritance and savings from careers making videos of volcanic eruptions, Ms. Kalber said, “No — but we can’t afford not to.”

Republicans and many Democrats have long championed privatization of Medicare, but some supporters are concerned that Medicare Advantage is losing its luster. For years, the private market for Medicare plans seemed like a gold rush for insurers, which offered low-cost plans and policies that offered benefits like vision and dental care that were not available in the traditional program. By 2023, more than half of the people eligible to enroll had signed up for a private plan.

But the insurance companies soon came under sharp criticism for overbilling the program, prompting government officials to reduce reimbursements. Health care costs also began to climb more sharply, and some insurers say they struggled to make money.

Health Care Service Corporation, which operates nonprofit Blue Cross plans in several states, is sharply reducing the number of places where it offers plans and exiting some half-dozen states.

Like other insurers, the company points to numerous reasons for dropping out of various regions of the country, including changing government policies, medical costs in certain communities and the number of people enrolled in its plans.

The company said it remained committed to the market. “Medicare Advantage is very important to us,” said Stephen Harris, who oversees government programs for the insurer.

Cutbacks by UnitedHealth, the nation’s largest insurer, are causing some 390,000 people to switch policies.

The company emphasized that 94 percent of individuals eligible for the program would still have access to one of their plans. “The program is delivering real value today,” said Bobby Hunter, the president of UnitedHealthcare.

Some of the extra benefits, like dental care, that have made Medicare Advantage especially popular and have been used by insurers for years to woo new customers and build market share are being pared back.

In announcing what plans would be available for 2027, the Trump administration emphasized the program’s stability. It said people would pay lower premiums overall and pointed out that most parts of the country would have a robust number of plans competing for business.

Medicare “is fighting to keep high-quality care options affordable and accessible for the millions of beneficiaries who rely on Medicare Advantage and Part D prescription drug plans,” said Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. “By slashing handouts to big insurance companies,” he said, the government “is keeping premiums stable.”

“Individual plans make business decisions every year about where and how they participate, but those decisions should not be confused with M.A. instability,” Dr. Oz said in a statement, referring to Medicare Advantage.

But industry experts estimate that millions of people will no longer have access to the plans they had chosen, particularly those plans that did not charge a premium.

“In my decade of working in the industry, I have never seen the announcement so disconnected with what the market is experiencing as a whole,” said Jenn Kerfoot, the president of Duos, which helps people navigate Medicare. “We’re seeing the compounding forces of changes in this program.”

Many older Americans on fixed budgets will see monthly premiums rise — and what they must pay toward their medical and drug expenses will also go up. By one estimate, the average out-of-pocket limit on a typical plan will rise to $6,600, from about $5,000 in 2024.

Michele Harris-Padron, 74, who lives in Santa Barbara, Calif., can keep her plan but will have to pay $30 more a month in premiums next year. Her out-of-pocket costs could also go up. The amount she pays to see a specialist will go up from $45 to $60 a visit.

She and her husband switched plans two years ago from Blue Shield of California to UnitedHealthcare when her Blue Shield plan no longer covered her doctors.

“I’m really struggling to see if there are any other options for us, but I don’t really believe that there are,” Ms. Harris-Padron said.

Some states are getting hit harder than others. Insurers in Minnesota cut plans in 2026 and plan to again for 2027, with another 387,000 people caught in plans that are ending coverage either because companies closed the plan or left a county, according to Duos.

The number of counties with no plans available at all in 2027 rose to 187, from 118 this year, out of the nation’s 3,069 counties, according KFF, a nonprofit health policy organization. States with counties that have no plans in 2027 for the first time are New Hampshire, North Dakota and Oklahoma. Alaska’s vast rural area and tiny population have made it prohibitive for Medicare Advantage insurers for years.

One of those places where all plans have dried up is Minnesota’s Crow Wing County, a two-hour drive from Minneapolis in the center of the state. Nicole Converse, a broker at RG Insurance, said she was advising Medicare Advantage beneficiaries there that they would have to switch to traditional Medicare and purchase a supplemental Medigap plan, which she said would cost $330 a month in premiums. They also will have to purchase a separate Medicare Part D drug plan. She said the firm had about 1,000 Medicare Advantage clients in the county who would be affected.

“It’s been pretty rough so far having to explain that to people,” Ms. Converse said. “The biggest concern is they are going to have a hard time affording this.”

Rural states are experiencing more turmoil because paying for care in those places can be more expensive for insurers. The limited number of hospitals and doctors outside urban areas makes it difficult for insurers to negotiate favorable contracts, said Roshan Desai, vice president for product and strategy at Rebellis Group, which advises health plans.

“There’s a lot of volatility,” he said. “Before, plans would never reduce a service area. Now it’s common.”

For many people in traditional Medicare, their stand-alone prescription benefit insurance, called Part D, also will be changing. About four million people who received this drug insurance with no monthly premium will now be required to pay, because the Trump administration is ending temporary subsidies.

The number of stand-alone Part D plans has declined by two-thirds, to 316 from nearly 1,000 in 2021, according to Duos.

Whether erosion and higher costs in Medicare Advantage will continue after next year depends on a number of factors, including any government response.

“This doesn’t have to be the new normal, and it shouldn’t be,” said Rebecca Buck, senior vice president for public affairs for the Better Medicare Alliance, which represents the private insurers. “It all starts by fully funding Medicare Advantage and good stable policymaking.”

She Was Offered $40 Million for Silence on Elon Musk. She Spoke Out Instead.

Ashley St. Clair is sick of people asking her the same questions about Elon Musk. “People treat me like I’m some Elon psychoanalyst,” she said during a visit to The New York Times in September. “They want to know, ‘What’s it like to hang out with him?’ or they say, ‘Not many people have spent time with him one-on-one.’” She sighed. “It’s annoying and laborious.”

This fall, she’s a significant figure in “Musk,” Alex Gibney’s nearly four-hour-long documentary about the world’s first trillionaire, and she has more pressing points. “This is about a deeper rot in our society, where we’ve equated capital with morality,” she said. “There’s a level of societal and individual trust that we give to people if they have money.”

Musk did not respond to requests for comment. After TMZ reported that Ashley St. Clair rejected a $40 million N.D.A., Musk responded via X, stating, “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims.” He also condemned Gibney’s documentary with another post on X reading, “Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me.”

Below, St. Clair shares her side of the story.

These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

Were you at all nervous about participating in the film?

No. I was familiar with some of Alex’s documentary work, like “Going Clear.” I liked that he didn’t have any fear. He has a history of treating facts and narratives with respect.

You’ve seen the film. How did you feel watching it?

What was both validating and terrifying was the way the narratives harmonized. Me, Justine [Wilson, Musk’s first wife], Sam Harris [the New Atheist philosopher] and Geoffrey Hinton [the so-called Godfather of A.I.] — there are so many similarities in our experiences with Elon. SUMMARY

Parents, politicians and best-selling psychologists are increasingly anxious about how much time children and teenagers spend on screens and how it may affect their mental health. It’s not how much time children spend on screens that raises their risk of the most severe mental health outcomes, including suicide, but whether their use becomes addictive. But the amount of time children spend on screens has only a small effect on their mental health.

ARTICLE

I’m a Child Psychiatrist. Screens Are Not the Problem.
If we make screens the villain, then we let the people who control children’s health care — Congress, insurers and health systems — off the hook for their failures.
By Jonathan Slater
Published 2026-10-09 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/opinion/children-screens-parents-health.html

Parents, politicians and best-selling psychologists are increasingly anxious about how much time children and teenagers spend on screens and how it may affect their mental health. In May, the Office of the Surgeon General warned about the harms of screen use and called for a limit of two hours a day of screen time at home for children ages 6 to 18. Last month, the Department of Health and Human Services released a digital book called “The Magic Tablet” that encourages “children and adolescents to get off screens and live real life.”

It’s easy to see why alarm bells have gone off. Children and teenagers today spend far more time in front of screens at home and at school than previous generations did. Rates of youth anxiety and depression have been climbing for years.

But as a doctor who treats children with mental health problems, I see screen time as a tantalizing distraction from bigger problems: America doesn’t offer enough mental health care for children or sufficient health insurance to pay for it. If we make screens the villain, then we let the people who control children’s health care — Congress, insurers and health systems — off the hook for the fact that half of American children with a treatable mental illness get no treatment at all.

In my office, I see children who use phones, iPads and other devices compulsively, but the compulsive use is usually a sign of something deeper — depression, anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism or family history of addiction — which can both feed the screen use and, in turn, be fed by it. These are teenagers who game so compulsively that they fail out of high school or college. They are children whose moods collapse or turn violent when an adult takes the device away.

It’s not how much time children spend on screens that raises their risk of the most severe mental health outcomes, including suicide, but whether their use becomes addictive. It’s specific activities, such as using social media in a compulsive way, that harm mental health. The harm from social media in particular appears to hit girls hardest.

The case for screen time limits rests in part on an unproven assumption that fewer hours will mean fewer anxious and depressed kids. The best evidence doesn’t support it. Limiting screen time can promote children’s overall health. But the amount of time children spend on screens has only a small effect on their mental health. Genetics and certain experiences in childhood, as well as the lack of proper diagnosis and treatment, appear to be far more influential. Limiting screen time is not the first line of treatment for children with anxiety or depression.

In 2025, JAMA published a study examining data on the screen use of more than 4,000 9- and 10-year-olds over the course of four years. Among other things, it measured how many hours children spent on screens and the degree to which their screen use had become addictive.

Self-reported screen time that was measured at ages 9 and 10 — before most children had substantial social media exposure — showed no association with depression, suicidal ideation or suicidal behaviors four years later. But addictive use of those same screens was associated with all three. Adolescents who used their phones compulsively — who felt anxious when separated from them, who kept scrolling despite knowing the cost — had more than twice the risk of suicidal behavior. Nearly one in three children showed a rising pattern of addictive social media use beginning at age 11.

The JAMA study did not account for A.D.H.D. or children who had adverse childhood experiences such as neglect, abuse, poverty, homelessness, parental violence or substance abuse. This matters because children exposed to four or more of these experiences had three times the odds of problematic video game use. Kids with attention issues are also more prone to addictive screen use, as are children who come from families with addictive behavior.

If we truly wanted to see improvements in the rates of mental health issues among kids and teenagers, then we would focus on expanding access to the interventions that work — finding the children who need treatment and getting them the treatment — and the insurance reimbursement to pay for them.

Right now, schools, which are the country’s largest mental health provider for kids, don’t have the funding to screen for underlying mental health issues. Student-to-counselor ratios run at 376 to 1, while the recommended ratio is 250 to 1. Regardless of the setting, in counties with mental health professional shortages, youth suicide rates are higher.

We know that cognitive behavioral therapy reduces problematic screen use in adolescents. And treating the mental health disorders that drive these often compulsive behaviors is the heart of the work. Every major clinical guideline says the same thing: For kids with anxiety, depression or A.D.H.D., we have proven treatments that work.

To its credit, the acting surgeon general’s advisory notes the warning signs of compulsive screen use: trying and failing to cut back, withdrawal when screens are unavailable, continued use despite consequences. The advisory acknowledges the limitations of the available research, and notes that “developmental effects depend on multiple factors.” Yet the advisory proceeds to recommend specific time limits. This stands in contrast to the recommendations of global researchers, who recently cautioned that screen duration “is not the main factor influencing mental health outcomes.”

Instead of screen limits, the government should prioritize tracking and funding youth mental health. Lately, it’s gotten harder to know what’s happening with youth anxiety and depression because the federal surveys built to track the well-being of the country’s youth are losing the staff and funding they need to function.

In 2022, Congress established a $1 billion bipartisan federal program to train and place mental health professionals in schools. Those school-based mental health programs both help kids and are cost-effective. Nevertheless, this administration has terminated the grant, despite a judge’s order, and 15 states are back in court to save it.

Even when a child with a mental health problem is identified, insurance doesn’t always adequately pay for it. The fix isn’t mysterious: Make insurers cover mental health care the same way they cover everything else and raise Medicaid’s low payment rates.

Blaming screens is a convenient way to avoid harder, deeper issues: inadequate mental health care and a system that chronically underfunds treatment. Policymakers and health system leaders instead must focus on providing the therapy, medication and support that troubled kids and families need.

Jonathan Slater is a clinical professor of psychiatry at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.
