SUMMARY

Lynn Davenport, a lifelong conservative, met Donald Trump backstage at a Texas rally in 2016. And in May she filmed an ad for Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running a surprisingly competitive race to become governor of Texas. The two women have been friends for years, since Hinojosa, a state representative from Austin, helped lead opposition to a crusade by the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, to privatize Texas’ public school system.

ARTICLE

Republicans Are Worried About Gina Hinojosa. In Texas, I Saw Why.
The Texas Democrat who says the culture wars are over.
By Michelle Goldberg
Published 2026-10-09 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/opinion/gina-hinojosa-governor-texas.html

Lynn Davenport, a lifelong conservative, met Donald Trump backstage at a Texas rally in 2016. On Jan. 6, 2021, she was at his Stop the Steal rally in Washington, though she left before the Capitol was sacked. In 2024 she was a delegate to Texas’ Republican convention and a Republican precinct chair.

And in May she filmed an ad for Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running a surprisingly competitive race to become governor of Texas.

The two women have been friends for years, since Hinojosa, a state representative from Austin, helped lead opposition to a crusade by the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, to privatize Texas’ public school system. Abbott’s agenda was bitterly opposed by some conservative Texans, particularly rural ones in places where public schools are the center of the community. (Think “Friday Night Lights.”) Davenport was impressed by Hinojosa’s willingness to listen to her and by her mastery of education policy. Still, as a committed Republican, she didn’t think she’d ever vote for her.

But Davenport has grown increasingly disgusted with Abbott, over both schools and the data centers he invited into Texas. The governor, she said, is a “globalist, which to me is scarier than a communist, a socialist or a Marxist, because what Abbott is imposing is technocracy. He’s giving the tech giants carte blanche in Texas.” So she decided not just to support Hinojosa’s bid for governor but to do it publicly. “Gina is someone that I can work with, whereas Abbott doesn’t care what I think,” she told me.

The premise of Hinojosa’s surprisingly competitive campaign is that there’s a critical mass of voters like Davenport in Texas. The opportunity for Democrats, Hinojosa believes, lies not with moderate, affluent Republicans put off by Trump’s norm-smashing vulgarity but with disappointed MAGA populists. “The conventional political wisdom is that it is those country club Republicans who will swing over,” she told me before I traveled to Texas. “I think it’s always been MAGA.”

I was skeptical of this analysis then, and after seeing her campaign last week, I’m still not wholly convinced. Trump’s appeal has never been only or even primarily economic; he taps into fear and rage about a country growing less white, less Christian and less deferential to male authority. And Hinojosa seems, at least on paper, ill suited to appeal to Trump’s base. A Latina and a former labor lawyer, she comes from the heart of Texas’ Democratic establishment: Her father led the state Democratic Party from 2012 until 2025. Though she now calls herself a “populist” rather than a “progressive,” she’s one of the more liberal members of the Texas House.

Still, Hinojosa has a group of supporters like Davenport, people furious at Abbott over school privatization and data centers. Mary Lowe, an education activist and a self-described “fundamental Christian,” told me that Abbott is “a globalist. He’s a tyrant. He’s a great deceiver.” And though she has voted Republican in almost every primary and every general election since 1979, she’s voting for Hinojosa in November. “She’s a good human,” said Lowe. “She’s one of us.”

Several polls still show Hinojosa trailing by a couple of points, but three recent ones, including a New York Times/Siena poll released on Saturday, have her ahead. The polling aggregator RealClearPolitics now rates the race as a tossup, and last week Cook Political Report moved it from “likely” to “lean” Republican. Over the past week, national Democrats have started investing more heavily in the race: Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois and the Democratic Governors Association each gave Hinojosa $1 million.

“She certainly has a much better chance than I did in ’22,” said Beto O’Rourke, who challenged Abbott four years ago and lost by more than 10 points.

Part of that chance derives from Trump’s unpopularity and the country’s economic misery, which is particularly stark in Texas. Campaigning, Hinojosa talks about how the state has more people without health insurance than any other and one of the nation’s highest rates of small-business bankruptcies. She describes blood plasma centers popping up in middle-class areas — she visited one next to a Sephora — as more people seek to sell their plasma to make ends meet. Hinojosa told me about meeting a lobbyist for the plasma center industry who was excited about all the opportunity in the state. “That’s, I think, a shocking example of where we are in Texas in 2026,” she said.

But her surge can’t be attributed entirely to the economic environment: Hinojosa seems to be hitting her stride as a politician. She has long had a talent for making people feel heard, but O’Rourke said she has become much better on the stump. “I campaigned with her in El Paso a few weeks ago, and I’ve never seen her speak so well,” he said.

Her message is simple: Life has gotten too hard for hard-working people in Texas. Schools are underfunded — hundreds have gone to four days a week — and new artificial intelligence initiatives are no substitute for a good teacher in the classroom. Data centers are both a blight and a symbol of Abbott’s misplaced priorities. “It’s impacting people’s homes and lives, and it is a demonstration of the governor doing the bidding of moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves,” Hinojosa told me. Taking a page from Trump, she’s promising $1,500 checks for every Texan from the state’s plush rainy-day fund (she calls it the “Greg Abbott corruption tax refund”) and to “DOGE” the Department of Education’s dodgy vendor contracts.

It’s a platform, she insists, that can break through with those who in the past felt alienated from the Democratic Party. “When I sit down with people who voted for Trump, with people who voted for Abbott and hear them and they hear me, there’s an opportunity for connection and alliance,” she said. Democrats have a chance, she insists, to move past the cultural battles that have kept them perennially on the defensive. “If we try to be post-culture wars, we can be post-culture wars,” she said. “I’ve experienced it. I’ve seen it.”

Of course, deep rifts over religion, race and gender can’t simply be wished away. But if Hinojosa can find a way to make them less salient, it could portend not just seismic change in Texas but the beginning of a political realignment. If some fraction of socially conservative voters concludes that rapacious billionaires threaten them more than supercilious liberals, it would remake America’s political map. For decades now, we’ve lived in an era dominated by what scholars call postmaterial politics, in which values, identity and self-expression have often taken precedence over economic concerns. What if that era is coming to an end? What opportunities would that open up, and what ideological sacrifices would it require?

In May, speaking to my colleague Lulu Garcia-Navarro, Tucker Carlson said that culture war issues — the issues on which he’d built much of his demagogic career — were becoming less important than matters of concentrated wealth and financial precarity. “Most of the debates about race, ethnicity, religion, to some extent immigration, are less resonant long term than debates about economics,” he said. Hinojosa’s campaign is a bet that he was right.

She is, of course, far from the only Democrat running as a populist and seeking to persuade disaffected Trump supporters. Zohran Mamdani started his mayoral campaign by interviewing working-class Trump voters in Queens and the Bronx, and he won over a small but meaningful chunk of them. A New York Times/Siena poll showed the populist Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — whom Carlson has all but endorsed — winning 8 percent of people who voted for Trump in 2024.

But it’s one thing to run as an economic progressive in places that regularly elect Democrats. It’s quite another to do it in Texas, in many ways the spiritual home of the modern right. Sure, Texas looks more promising for Democrats this year than it has in decades, with the party’s Senate candidate, James Talarico, maintaining a consistent lead over the Republican Ken Paxton. But Paxton is singularly sleazy and widely despised. As astonishing as a Talarico victory would be, Republicans could explain it away as the fault of a particularly bad candidate.

They won’t be able to do that if Hinojosa wins. Abbott has been elected governor of Texas three times by double-digit margins. If Hinojosa even comes close to beating him, it will be because the Republican coalition that Trump assembled is collapsing and a new Democratic one is perhaps starting to take shape. “There are people who are responding to our message the same way they were responding to Trump’s message,” she said. “They want power. They want to feel like they’re in control of their lives again, and I think that they want to return to a time that feels like it makes sense again, where hard work pays off.”

A big part of the reason Hinojosa is pulling ahead is that Latinos, who swung toward Republicans in 2024, have soured on the party, in large part because of Trump’s brutal mass deportation campaign. At a Spanish-language town hall last week, Hinojosa, whose mother is a Mexican immigrant, mentioned Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who’d been in the country for 35 years. “They thought he was someone else, they killed him, and then they realized that he was only going to work,” she said. “When that’s happening, none of us are safe.”

But Hinojosa is also trying to chip away at Abbott’s — and Trump’s — white, rural base. No one thinks she’s going to win these voters outright; the goal is to lose them by less. “There’s definitely a backlash against Abbott over vouchers and over data centers in rural Texas,” said Suzanne Bellsnyder, who writes a newsletter called Texas Rural Reporter. “The question is, does that anger against Abbott translate into a vote for Gina?”

Bellsnyder is trying to make sure it does. A former field director for Abbott, she’s now working for Hinojosa’s campaign. “If I didn’t think she had a chance, I promise you, I wouldn’t be putting my entire Republican credentials on the line,” she told me.

Like Davenport, Bellsnyder got to know Hinojosa during the fight against Abbott’s education agenda. The centerpiece of this battle was Abbott’s voucher measure, which gives most qualifying private school parents about $10,000, reducing funding that otherwise would have gone to public schools. When Abbott tried to pass the law in 2023, he was foiled by 21 Republican holdouts. Abbott then supported primary challenges, partly funded by the Pennsylvania billionaire Jeff Yass, against 15 of the Republicans who thwarted him. Most of them lost, and the law passed in 2025. The wounds among antivoucher conservatives are still raw.

At an Hinojosa rally in Longview, a city in East Texas, last week, I met Steve Clugston, a 58-year-old school superintendent. He told me he last voted for a Democrat back in the 1990s, when conservative local officials in his part of the state still belonged to the party. “They’re now probably Republicans,” he said.

Clugston voted for Donald Trump in 2024, believing he did a “pretty good job” in his first term. Clugston said he is an “old school conservative,” which is reflected in his approach to education. “I still swing the paddle,” he added. (Texas is among a minority of states that allow corporal punishment in schools.) “I believe in kids acting right and learning how to work hard and how to show up and be dependable.”

But he was livid about Abbott’s relentless push for vouchers. “Our governor took billionaire money and then used it to beat Republicans that us Republicans elected,” he said. As he soured on Abbott, Clugston also grew disillusioned with Trump and his flagrant, gluttonous corruption. “When you’ve lied to me enough,” said Clugston, “and sold us out for billionaires, I get to the point I’m done.”

Hinojosa’s inroads with the populist right might have been limited to those most committed to public schools, were it not for Abbott’s enthusiasm for data centers. The governor has aggressively sought tech investment in Texas; he has offered billions of dollars in tax incentives to attract data centers and last year boasted that the state was “the epicenter of A.I. development.” Texas now has more in operation than any other state.

Many rural Texans who either live near these behemoths, or fear they will soon, detest them. Anger is so intense that Sid Miller, the state’s departing agriculture commissioner — he lost his primary after a series of scandals — told Rolling Stone that it could cost Abbott the election.

In June, Cheryl Shadden, who lives across from a sprawling bitcoin mine in Hood County, showed up at an Hinojosa event in Glen Rose wearing a homemade T-shirt that read, “Break rank.” She meant break ranks with the Republican Party, which has failed to protect her from the ugly, noisy facility that she said has upended her life.

“My community is blasted with horrific noise 24/7,” Shadden told me. “I mean, inside of our homes, outside of our homes. We’ve got health problems associated with it.” She says the value of her property — 10 acres and a barn — has plummeted. And the Republicans she has reached out to for help have ignored her. “I hit everybody and their mother, and crickets, and then Gina Hinojosa’s staff is like, ‘Gina would like to speak to you.’”

Abbott has realized that fury over data centers is a political threat, and he recently issued a moratorium on new development, pending an audit of their energy and water usage. But the pause has loopholes, and the audit, conveniently, is due to be finished right after the election, which means he can restart his data center push once the political danger is gone. “It just stinks. It’s just not right,” said Michael Ellis, a 70-year-old Republican battling plans for a new data center in Texas’ Navarro County.

I met him and his wife, Jennifer, in the town of Corsicana, about an hour southeast of Dallas, where Hinojosa stopped to meet with a small group of anti-data-center organizers. He had come with a binder; he had blueprints of a proposed 80-acre facility planned to go up a mile from his home. He was worried about noise caused by generators, water usage and the danger of an industrial disaster in an area with only a volunteer fire department. He blamed Abbott for welcoming such projects in with virtually no oversight.

Michael Ellis was still undecided about who he was voting for, but Jennifer Ellis was leaning toward Hinojosa. “Just to walk in and sit down with us and meet with us, to me, that goes a long way,” she said. “That’s massively impressive.”

Then I asked her about the Senate race. She said she’d probably vote for Paxton, despite his many scandals, because of trans issues. “I don’t do all the gender thing,” she said.

It was a reminder of the culture wars’ endurance. Hinojosa still isn’t terribly well known in Texas; in September she told me that some 20 percent of the electorate wasn’t familiar with her. I wondered what voters like Ellis would think of her after Abbott, who is outspending Hinojosa around 6 to 1, blankets Texas with attack ads. One recent spot tried to brand her as “gender bender Gina,” a radical out to “trans your kids.”

Hinojosa has tried to pre-empt this caricature in her own advertising, seeking to distance herself from social liberalism without recanting her positions. In one ad, she declared, “My pronouns are ‘mom,’ ‘Texan’ and soon to be ‘governor.’” In another, she described deciding, 23 years ago, to carry a pregnancy to term even though her baby had no chance of survival. “I chose her,” she said. The spot doesn’t mention the law that now denies Texas women the choice that she had. If I saw it without knowing who Hinojosa was, I might have thought she was anti-abortion.

She’s not, but on the campaign trail, she doesn’t talk about abortion unless she’s asked. Even then, she says her priority in office will be fixing the law that prevents doctors from treating some women with doomed pregnancies until they’re near death. “Reproductive choice is just one of those issues that divide us,” she told me. “I’m running to be governor to work on an agenda that the vast majority of us agree on.”

I could probably write a whole column picking apart this strategy. Reproductive rights are popular, even in red states. It would be disastrous for Democrats to decide, at this moment of intense social backsliding, that women’s health and freedom should be subject to compromise. And abortion rights can’t really be separated from economics; being forced to carry an unwanted pregnancy is financially calamitous.

But I have to be honest: When I try to flesh out this critique, my heart isn’t in it. In 2014, Wendy Davis ran a boldly pro-choice campaign for governor and lost by more than 20 points. In 2022 some predicted that the end of Roe v. Wade could endanger Abbott; it didn’t. It’s hard to blame Hinojosa for trying something new.

Besides, as she often says, even if she wins, she will almost certainly have a Republican-dominated legislature. The best that can be hoped for, probably, is legislation to make Texas’ abortion ban less deadly. If Hinojosa wants to escape the culture wars in Texas, maybe it makes sense to admit defeat, at least temporarily. “While we’ve been fighting those fights, we’ve lost economic power in this state and in this country, and we’re hurting,” she said. “We need to come together to take back that power.”

Whether Texans are ready to do that is anyone’s guess. Jim Henson, the director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, still thinks Abbott is favored. Henson pointed out that in the polls, Democratic voters are significantly more committed to voting for Hinojosa than Republicans are to voting for Abbott. On the surface, that looks like good news for her, but it means that Abbott has more room to improve his standing with his base. “Abbott still has time to consolidate some of the Republicans that are not yet committed,” said Henson.

Still, he said, something is changing in Texas. A few weeks ago, Henson thought an Hinojosa victory was nearly impossible. Now he thinks it’s just unlikely. If only Talarico wins, as he’s increasingly favored to do, “it’s going to be an earthquake,” said Henson. If Talarico and Hinojosa win, it will be on a whole other order of magnitude. “People are feeling the ground shaking,” he said. “It’s just a matter of how big it is going to be.”

If it’s big enough, we’ll feel the reverberations from coast to coast. Conservatives triumphed when they were able to brand the Democratic Party as the stronghold of elites. Hinojosa thinks she can turn that association around, showing voters that Republicans represent heedless, exploitative oligarchs. “It’s 99 percent of us against, like, 15 billionaire dudes and the weak leadership that allows them to get away with whatever they want,” she said. If that argument can prevail in Texas, it can probably prevail most anywhere.

SUMMARY

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, set off a firestorm of criticism Wednesday morning with a social media post ostensibly intended to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis. Finally, it is obscene because Mamdani is the mayor for about one million Jewish New Yorkers, many with close relatives in Israel, who deserve better on a day of grief than to be offered the equivalent of an “All Lives Matter” homily. It would be better to have a mayor who, if only on Oct. 7, can say: Jewish Lives Matter.

ARTICLE

Zohran Mamdani’s Moral Obscenity
A mayor for one million Jewish New Yorkers fails his duty.
By Bret Stephens
Published 2026-10-09 18:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/opinion/zohran-mamdani-israel-gaza.html

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, set off a firestorm of criticism Wednesday morning with a social media post ostensibly intended to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis. It devoted a brief paragraph to condemning Hamas and commiserating with its victims. The rest was a much longer denunciation of Israel’s “ongoing genocide in Gaza,” a “world in which occupation and apartheid continue” and a situation in which “our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.”

In response, Ammiel Hirsch, the president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said the statement was “so offensive to so many Jews that it is hard to describe how offensive it is.” In fact, it’s a moral obscenity. Let me count the ways.

It is obscene in the same way it would have been obscene if the mayor had commemorated the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 last month with a perfunctory nod to the victims of the day, followed by a much longer denunciation of U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East. What happened on both Sept. 11 and Oct. 7 was undiluted evil, each an unprovoked visit of deliberate and maximalist violence on people who had done nothing to invite that violence other than being at the wrong place at the wrong time.

It is obscene because many of the Jews murdered on Oct. 7, living in kibbutzim with conspicuously left-leaning politics, had been at the forefront of the peace movement, volunteering, for example, to drive sick Palestinians for treatment at nearby Israeli hospitals. Hamas wasn’t just killing and terrorizing the innocent; it was eliminating the good.

It is obscene because Hamas didn’t just kill its victims in pursuit of a strategic objective. It tormented and slaughtered them like an army of serial killers who delight in the suffering of their victims. Corpses of Israeli women were described by one coroner as “shot in the crotch, intimate parts, vagina, or were shot in the breast.” Others appeared to have been raped so violently that their pelvises were broken. Parents were killed in front of their children; children were murdered in their beds. A fieldworker was beheaded with a garden hoe. I know this because Hamas filmed itself doing this and I forced myself to watch the film. I know because that same month, I visited the bedrooms where the kids had been murdered, their mattresses still soaked in blood.

It is obscene because, whatever else you may think of the war in Gaza, on the eve of Oct. 7 the border of Israel and Gaza was governed by a cease-fire. It was Hamas that chose to kick off the violence, just as the Japanese did in 1941 with the attack on Pearl Harbor. Whether in fistfights between people or wars between states, whoever throws the first punch forfeits the right to throw the last.

It is obscene because Mamdani is being misleading when he speaks as if his prime objection to Israel is what it did after Oct. 7. In fact, the mayor has been an anti-Israel zealot at least since his college days, when, as a leader of Students for Justice in Palestine, he broke off collaboration with the left-leaning Jewish group J Street, which advocates a Palestinian state, because it also recognizes the rights of a Jewish state. He’s written a rap professing “love” for five men convicted in a U.S. court of funneling money to Hamas. The day after Oct. 7, he issued a brief statement that said nothing about Hamas but immediately denounced Israel. Put simply, this is a mayor who first condemned Israel as guilty and then went about collecting evidence.

It is obscene because, however much the genocide allegation against Israel is mindlessly repeated by people too lazy or prejudiced to understand the difference between war and genocide, that allegation is as false as it is sinister. False, because genocide is about killing whole classes of people for who they are rather than for what they did — and if Israel wanted to kill Palestinians as Palestinians it never would have bothered mobilizing hundreds of thousands of its own soldiers for the war, and losing hundreds in high-intensity urban warfare. Sinister, because the political purpose of the genocide allegation is to trivialize, if not erase, the attacks of Oct. 7 by making them seem minor in comparison to the Palestinian casualties that tragically, but all-but inevitably, followed.

It is obscene because Hamas’s intentions toward Israel really are genocidal. Its leaders have often and publicly vowed to perpetrate future Oct. 7s. Had the group not been stopped by force that day, there’s no reason to think it wouldn’t have kept up its orgy of slaughter on its way to Tel Aviv and other Israeli cities. Yet one searches in vain for anything from the mayor except perfunctory, pro forma condemnations of Hamas.

It is obscene because there’s an even more wretched purpose to the genocide charge against Israel, which long predates the recent war in Gaza. It is a specimen of Holocaust erasure: not the dumb kind, which seeks to deny Nazi Germany’s murder of six million Jews, but a more sophisticated version that accuses living Jews of genocide as a way of ending the historical Jewish claim to a long and ongoing history of persecution and near-annihilation that accounts for its need for a sovereign state capable of defending its people.

Finally, it is obscene because Mamdani is the mayor for about one million Jewish New Yorkers, many with close relatives in Israel, who deserve better on a day of grief than to be offered the equivalent of an “All Lives Matter” homily. This is yet another of the double standards through which modern-day Jew hatred manifests itself: Whenever antisemitism is mentioned in progressive circles, it is inevitably accompanied by nods about Islamophobia or other bigotries.

It would be better to have a mayor who, if only on Oct. 7, can say: Jewish Lives Matter. Israeli Lives Matter. Full stop. The lectures about Gaza can come some other day.

SUMMARY

Meta was developing a similar product called Muse, but had delayed releasing it over safety concerns. But on Sept. 8, Meta publicly debuted Muse, just like Mr. Zuckerberg had ordered. Three weeks after Meta released Muse, OpenAI announced Dots, its own agent.

ARTICLE

Inside Mark Zuckerberg’s Decision to Pull the Trigger on Meta’s A.I. Agent
Meta had delayed releasing Muse, its A.I. agent app, for months over safety concerns. Then new competition forced Mr. Zuckerberg’s hand.
By Eli Tan
Published 2026-10-09 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/technology/inside-mark-zuckerbergs-decision-to-pull-the-trigger-on-metas-ai-agent.html

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, gathered two top lieutenants — Alexandr Wang, the chief artificial intelligence officer, and Nat Friedman, the head of A.I. product — in August to discuss an imminent threat.

A 14-person start-up called Instinct had created an A.I. agent, which are bots that can operate apps and software on behalf of users, and it was taking off. Meta was developing a similar product called Muse, but had delayed releasing it over safety concerns.

Fearful of losing a competitive edge, Mr. Zuckerberg said Muse was ready to launch despite the risks, according to three people with knowledge of the meeting, who were not authorized to speak publicly on confidential matters.

Mr. Wang, 29, and Mr. Friedman, 49, were aware of safety concerns from recent tests, including one instance when Muse changed a user’s password without permission, two of the people said. But on Sept. 8, Meta publicly debuted Muse, just like Mr. Zuckerberg had ordered.

The internal meeting showed the tricky balance between speed and safety that A.I. companies like Meta are juggling as they try to one-up their rivals in the A.I. race. As the technology rapidly improves, it is becoming more dangerous and useful at the same time, making these decisions even more difficult.

Mr. Zuckerberg has spent billions to develop Meta’s A.I., but watched for years as rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic beat his company to market with chatbots and coding tools. When it came to personal agents, the Silicon Valley giant, which owns Facebook and Instagram, needed a win — and ultimately, getting to market quickly won out.

That has given Meta an early lead with agents, which have become the next frontier of the A.I. industry. Other companies are already introducing competing products. Three weeks after Meta released Muse, OpenAI announced Dots, its own agent.

“The most interesting thing about Muse is that Meta got there first,” said Avi Greengart, an analyst at Techsponential, a research firm.

So far, Mr. Zuckerberg’s decision to release Muse has paid off. The agent has had only a few safety hiccups, like when Muse gave out a user’s address to a seller on Facebook Marketplace without permission. As of Wednesday, more than 6.6 million people had downloaded the free app, with 1.8 million using Muse every day, according to data from the research firm Sensor Tower.

To keep up the momentum, Meta is spending millions on a Muse marketing blitz, plastering its fuzzy avatar — a character called Jolly — across billboards and in television ads.

In a social media post last month, Mr. Wang declared, “You can’t stop the Muse.”

A Meta spokesman disputed that Mr. Zuckerberg pushed to release Muse because of pressure from Instinct. “We’re proud of this work and, as we’ve said publicly, we even delayed shipping Muse for several months to make sure we got this right,” he said in a statement.

The idea for Muse began in July 2025, when Mr. Zuckerberg published a 616-word memo about “personal superintellgence,” a form of A.I. that he said could act as the ultimate assistant. He had recently restructured Meta’s entire A.I. division around the concept, hiring Mr. Wang and Mr. Friedman to lead the effort.

The two executives went on a recruiting spree, hiring top researchers from OpenAI and Google and offering them nine-figure pay packages to join Meta. They also divided their duties, with Mr. Wang focused on developing A.I. models and Mr. Friedman on products.

At that point, there was only a hazy idea of what a “superintelligent” assistant could be. “The vision of building something like Muse existed in our collective heads, but we couldn’t quite point to what exactly that product was going to be,” Vishal Shah, Meta’s vice president of A.I. products, said in an interview.

In September 2025, Meta’s new A.I. team released its first product, Vibes, an A.I.-generated video feed that immediately drew criticism for creating A.I. slop. Tensions formed internally between the new executives and Mr. Zuckerberg’s other longtime lieutenants, some of whom questioned whether Mr. Wang could succeed in catching Meta up in the A.I. race.

In November, Peter Steinberger, an Austrian programmer, released an app called OpenClaw, an A.I. agent that could code and use a computer on its own. It was open source, which meant it could be downloaded and modified without any payment or approval. As it took off among Silicon Valley developers, Meta’s executives had an epiphany.

“It all kind of clicked,” Mr. Shah said. “The next generation of consumer product was a personal agent.”

After trying OpenClaw, Mr. Friedman ordered 200 Mac Minis — the computers that the agent runs on — to Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, Calif., arranging them in stacks outside his office for employees to take. Then they went all-in on developing an agent like OpenClaw for people who weren't software engineers.

“There was no hedging,” Mr. Shah said.

Meta’s A.I. leaders also incorporated OpenClaw into their own lives. Mr. Friedman hooked his agent up to cameras in his house, where it would instruct him to do things like drink water to stay hydrated.

“It sent me a snapshot frame of me drinking a bottle of water and said, ‘Good job,’” Mr. Friedman said at a recent tech conference.

In another instance, while talking to his agent about ways to get better sleep, OpenClaw took over Mr. Friedman’s self-driving Tesla and redirected him to a grocery store to pick up magnesium pills. At Meta’s annual developer conference last month, Mr. Zuckerberg said he had connected his agent to cameras in his martial arts gym so that it could critique his fighting form.

Yet there were safety concerns. Agents could sometimes go rogue or take over software apps. In February, one agent took over the work computer of a Meta safety researcher, deleting her emails uncontrollably.

“I couldn’t stop it from my phone,” Summer Yue, the researcher, wrote on social media. “I had to RUN to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb.”

In February, Mr. Friedman demonstrated Muse to Meta’s board of directors. Two months later, Meta unveiled an A.I. model called Muse Spark, developed under Mr. Wang and the most powerful model that the company had made to date. Early in its development, Muse was powered by A.I. models made by Anthropic, but Muse Spark’s introduction meant that Meta could power its agent with its own technology.

By then, Meta had a version of Muse that it could have released, Mr. Shah said. But the company spent months making sure its safety features were secure. In testing with Meta’s employees, the agent had occasionally disobeyed commands or led people to buy items from fraudulent websites.

Then in August, Instinct’s agent became increasingly popular. Shortly thereafter, Meta rolled out Muse.

Muse has faced some privacy issues, including an instance when it read a user’s private text messages without permission and then referenced what it had learned with the user.

Some safety issues were earlier reported by The Information.

Last month, Instinct raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation. But it has fewer resources and computing power than Meta, a company with 3.5 billion users across its family of apps that is worth more than $1.5 trillion.

“You’re going up against the biggest players in the world,” Noah Shinn, Instinct’s 23-year-old founder, said on a podcast last month. “This is probably the most exciting software race ever, and the outcome is like, trillions of dollars.”

On social media, Mr. Wang has posted dozens of photos and memes of Muse’s fuzzy avatar, some directed at OpenAI. Last month, Mr. Friedman, who rarely posts on social media, also chimed in.

“I hope you like it!” he wrote.

The Controversial Class That M.I.T. Is Paying a Professor Not to Teach
Michel DeGraff, a vocal pro-Palestinian activist, can’t be easily fired because he has tenure. But he has been kicked out of his department.
By Mark Arsenault
Published 2026-10-09 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/us/mit-professor-michel-degraff-palestine-course.html

The name of the proposed Massachusetts Institute of Technology course was as provocative as it was long:

“Language and Linguistics for Decolonization and Liberation and for Peace and Community Building — From the River to the Sea in Palestine and Israel to the Mountaintops of Haiti and Beyond.”

The instructor was Michel DeGraff, a longtime tenured linguistics professor at M.I.T. who came up with the idea in the months after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel. He was a leading faculty voice siding with pro-Palestinian campus protesters, whose frequent rallying cry for Palestinian freedom, “from the river to the sea,” was seen by some Jews as antisemitic.

An M.I.T. panel rejected the course over questions about whether Dr. DeGraff, a Haitian scholar and expert in the study of Creole languages, had the expertise to teach it. That was supposed to finish the matter.

To Dr. DeGraff, it was more like the starting gun.

He disagreed that he lacked the ability to teach the course and protested the decision in a flurry of emails decrying it as part of a “new McCarthyism.” He complained to his colleagues, including deans and the university’s president in long email chains — which he then made public.

He objected on social media and in published commentaries. He filed a federal lawsuit against M.I.T., accusing the school of chilling campus speech on Gaza and violating his academic freedom.

“M.I.T. should not be repressing my teaching in this way,” Dr. DeGraff said in an interview. He called the decision a “violation of my professional rights.”

The university, through a spokeswoman, declined to comment, though it has denied Dr. DeGraff’s claims in legal filings.

As Dr. DeGraff’s profile has risen, so has the volume of his critics. He was sued for harassment by a Jewish former student. A U.S. House committee staff report last spring accused him of perpetuating “antisemitic conspiracy theories.”

Now three years into the dispute, his personal relationship with the M.I.T. linguistics section head, a onetime friend, is broken, and colleagues are exhausted by the controversy.

In many other American workplaces, employees who push back so forcefully would most likely risk their employment. But tenured professors are, by design, hard to get rid of.

Administrators have sanctioned Dr. DeGraff, accusing him of being disruptive and violating procedures and directives. He was pushed out of M.I.T.’s linguistics section and given the nebulous title of “faculty at large,” which he includes in his email signature inside satirical quotation marks.

He said in an interview that he had been denied a scheduled raise and access to new mentees, and had even been blocked from the department’s Facebook page. For the third fall semester in a row, he said, he is being paid while not teaching a class.

He is one of a number of professors in disputes with their schools over speech recently.

Carnegie Mellon University announced in September that it was investigating social media posts from a professor who is accused of celebrating the deaths of conservative figures.

A University of Texas professor is contesting his 16-month paid administrative leave, which he believes is related to his criticism of school leadership.

And an arbitrator ordered San Jose State University to reinstate a tenured professor the university had fired over allegations related to her role in pro-Palestinian campus protests.

At a time when campus politics are under a microscope and schools are trying to avoid the attention of the Trump administration, Dr. DeGraff’s fight has become one of the longest and most dramatic.

Chris Sharp, chief of staff at the Cicero Institute, a public policy organization based in Austin, said some tenured professors were cloaking their personal activism under the guise of “academic freedom.” The term, he said, is often misconstrued as the right to teach or research without limit, when it should be understood as the right to teach and research within one’s specialty.

“Just because I have a Ph.D. in one thing does not make me an expert in everything,” he said.

Friends of Dr. DeGraff say his campaign for his proposed class came from his deep concern for free speech, human rights and his understanding of language as a means to exercise power.

“Michel’s great virtue is his persistence,” said Haynes Miller, an M.I.T. professor emeritus of mathematics who is close to Dr. DeGraff and who says his friend is not an antisemite. “He doesn’t give up. If he sees an injustice he will attack it.”

Dr. DeGraff, 63, was born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, and persuaded his parents to send him to the United States to study computer science. But once there, he became more interested in his homeland’s language, Haitian Creole, which, he said, is often derided as “broken French” and not a real language.

His Ph.D. thesis at the University of Pennsylvania was entitled “Creole Grammars and Acquisition of Syntax: The Case of Haitian Creole,” he said. He joined the M.I.T. linguistics faculty in 1996.

Dr. DeGraff sees parallels between the Haitian struggle for independence and that of Palestinian people. “That is what brought me to want to further my research and teaching about these connections,” he said.

The idea for the class came to him on Dec. 5, 2023, after he had watched M.I.T.’s president, Sally Kornbluth, and leaders of Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania get rhetorically beat up by Republicans in a congressional hearing on campus antisemitism.

After the course was rejected, he turned the concept into a discussion series with guest speakers in the fall of 2024.

That year, he also frequently joined students who occupied part of campus in a three-week encampment demanding that the school end ties with Israel. He was there nearly every day, he said, before the police shut it down.

Agustín Rayo, dean of the M.I.T. School of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences, sanctioned Dr. DeGraff in late 2024. In a letter Dr. DeGraff shared, the dean said he was removing Dr. DeGraff temporarily from the linguistics section for being disruptive and creating the expectation that people who displease him “are at risk of being targeted” in public forums.

“Your speech rights do not place you above M.I.T.’s rules,” the dean wrote in the letter.

Dr. DeGraff also came to the attention of congressional Republicans, who in a report pointed to accusations that Dr. DeGraff had targeted a Jewish student for harassment. That former student, William Sussman, joined a lawsuit against Dr. DeGraff and the school in 2025.

Mr. Sussman said Dr. DeGraff targeted him on social media as an example of a Zionist “mind infection” for being Jewish. Mr. Sussman has said antisemitic harassment drove him out of the university.

Dr. DeGraff said the term “mind infection” came from an Israeli scholar who has used it to refer to how Israeli schoolbooks marginalize Palestinians. Dr. DeGraff said he was not an antisemite and that federal courts had said that criticism of Israel by itself is not inherently antisemitic.

Part of the suit, including the claims against Dr. DeGraff, was dismissed, though appeals are possible.

In a statement, Mr. Sussman criticized M.I.T., saying “the professor remains employed at M.I.T., where he continues to smear me.”

His removal from the linguistics department means “his impact at M.I.T. is substantially reduced,” said Dr. Miller, the friend of Dr. DeGraff’s. “It is humiliating for him; it’s a symbolic thing as well as a practical thing.”

Last March, Dr. DeGraff filed a federal lawsuit against M.I.T., along with the congressional committee that had named him in its report and its chairman. In his suit, he accuses the university of punishing him for his political activism.

“If you ask faculty to keep quiet, then you are basically betraying the job of the university, which is to teach about difficult topics,” he said.

M.I.T. denied his claims and asked the court to dismiss the suit.

“Indeed, the fact that DeGraff has continued to speak publicly and prolifically on the very subjects he claims have been chilled only underscores the speculative nature of his alleged injuries,” the university argued in a court filing.

He is still scheduled to teach the spring classes he has taught for years, “Creole Languages and Caribbean Identities” and “Black Matters: Introduction to Black Studies.”

Over this past summer, Dr. DeGraff proposed another new course, based on his book, published last month: “Our Own Language: Harnessing the Power of Kreyol and Other Mother Tongues for Education and Liberation.”

It is common for professors at a research university such as M.I.T. to propose new courses. And in early September, an associate dean told Dr. DeGraff the department would discuss the idea. But first, could he provide a copy of the book?

No, Dr. DeGraff replied, the syllabus he submitted should be enough. Given the history with his last course proposal, he wrote, “requiring an additional departmental review of the book itself therefore strikes me as ongoing discrimination and harassment.” He looped in top administrators, including Dr. Kornbluth, to his email.

His new class, he said, was rejected.

ARTICLE

What to Know About the Delhi Protests
Protesters opposed to sweeping revisions to India’s voter rolls are trying to rally in New Delhi. The police have come out in force.
By Somini Sengupta and Pragati K.B.
Published 2026-10-10 03:56 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/world/asia/what-to-know-about-the-delhi-protests.html

The Indian police turned New Delhi into a fortress on Saturday as protesters tried to assemble in the city center to oppose a sweeping revision of the nation’s voter roll. The authorities took extraordinary measures to stop them.

A large number of officers gathered and erected tall yellow barricades around the protest site. Several protesters have already been placed under house arrest. Delhi-bound trains have been canceled. Officials ordered the closure of 45 metro stations.

The protests were called by a Gen Z movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party. The demonstrations follow a week of daily protests by opposition politicians and several activist groups who are expected to defy a police ban and join Saturday’s rally.

The group said in a statement that three of its main leaders, including the founder, Abhijeet Dipke, were detained by the police on Saturday morning when their plane landed in New Delhi. The C.J.P. also shared a video that Mehr Parsicha, a spokeswoman for the youth group, recorded of the police detaining her.

Here’s what to know about the events in New Delhi, the capital of the world’s most populous democracy.

What are the protests about?

The protests stem from growing anger at a sweeping revision of the voter roll. The change, known as the Special Intensive Revision, began last summer as an effort to verify voter eligibility and remove duplicate or ineligible names. The government called it a long overdue push to clean up voter records.

It required Indians to submit multiple documents to prove that they were eligible to vote, and it ended up eliminating 130 million names. Critics said it had removed legitimate voters and forced people identified as dead to come forward to prove that they were indeed alive.

Critics have called the measure a politically motivated purge that could entrench the tenure of Prime Minister Narenda Modi, who has been in power for 12 years.

Leaders of Mr. Modi’s party reject the criticism. The home minister, Amit Shah, accused opposition lawmakers of “lies and disinformation” in a social media post. “Having lost their public support, these parties question institutions after every defeat,” he said.

What do the protesters want?

The protesters say their goal is to ensure free and fair elections.

They have demanded the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar; an immediate halt to the voter roll revision pending an independent inquiry; and the restoration of the previous voter roll in coming elections.

A popular slogan by the Gen Z movement refers to the election chief by a diminutive form of his first name: “Gyanu. It’s done, bro.”

The anger at the election chief has been aggravated by news, reported by The Indian Express newspaper, that other officials within the election commission and the Supreme Court had expressed reservations about the exercise.

Who are the protesters?

The protest was initially organized by the Cockroach Janta Party, a Gen Z movement that emerged this summer to decry a broken college entrance exam system. They won the rare ouster of a government minister.

Several groups said they would join the Saturday rally. They include farmers groups that led protests in 2020 against the government’s proposed agricultural reforms. They too marched toward central Delhi and faced a crackdown, but pushed the government to back down.

The opposition Aam Aadmi party, with which some Cockroach Party leaders had been involved, has also said that it planned to join, along with several leftist youth organizations. Those include the All India Students’ Association, affiliated with one of the country’s communist parties, whose members have led some of the most robust protests this week.

What’s at stake?

First, the irregularities in the voter roll revision has dented the reputation of the election commission, which for years had been seen as a credible institution that ran relatively fair elections.

Second, the protests reflect the force of the Gen Z Cockroach movement, which has been led by a handful of young people with no political experience and all under the age of 32. Their success regarding the college entrance system seems to have emboldened others both in the movement and outside it to speak out against the Modi administration.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

What’s Dragging Down A.I. Efficiency? The ‘Verification Tax.’
As artificial intelligence automates office tasks, it is also creating a new type of human work.
By Sarah Kessler
Published 2026-10-10 12:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/business/dealbook/ai-verification-tax-rework.html

Artificial intelligence is on the verge of pushing office workers to dazzling new heights of efficiency. It’s supposed to be obliterating busywork and rendering entire professions obsolete with its proficiency. At least, that’s the story told by A.I. companies.

But something isn’t adding up on the ground.

In survey after survey, executives and their employees report unimpressive gains from A.I. tools. Researchers from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Stanford University, the Bank of England and the Autonomous Technological Institute of Mexico recently published a poll of nearly 6,000 senior business executives in which about 90 percent said the technology had no impact on either employment or productivity. That’s even though 69 percent reported that their firms actively used A.I.

Major A.I. efficiency gains are also missing from the larger economic picture. As Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo, put it in a review of data from the San Francisco Fed this week: “The productivity payoff from A.I. remains a forecast rather than an observation.”

There are many explanations for the dearth of data supporting the superefficiency narrative. Maybe the most obvious is that it simply takes a while for companies to adapt and deploy new technologies.

But A.I. is also creating a new type of work that may be sucking up much of the time the technology itself is saving.

Call it a “verification tax,” “botsitting” or “rework” — it’s the often arduous task of checking that A.I. output is accurate, safe and usable, and it is putting a very human bottleneck on A.I. automation.

“The binding constraint on growth is no longer intelligence,” Christian Catalini, a research associate and lecturer at M.I.T. Sloan, wrote in a February working paper. “It is human verification bandwidth.”

In other words, Catalini told DealBook, “the only A.I. that’s useful is the A.I. that is verified.”

This work of checking and tidying up A.I. work may be softening some efficiency gains. A survey of 3,200 employees and business leaders by the human resources platform Workday found that, on average, they used roughly 37 percent of the time saved through A.I. to correct, clarify or rewrite low-quality output.

Economists at Google surveyed 600 scientists and found that, while using A.I. saved them seven hours a week on average, almost 90 percent of those who saved time said they spent a tenth of that time checking A.I. outputs, and 46 percent said they spent more than a quarter.

About 40 percent of the scientists also reported that their backlog of untested hypotheses had grown compared with three years ago. That suggests that A.I. generates potential solutions and predictions quickly but that running physical experiments or clinical trials to test them hasn’t necessarily gotten much faster.

“Basically we have found that it seems that now the bottlenecks are sort of moving downstream,” said Mihai Codreanu, a senior research economist at Google and co-author of the paper.

A.I. is saving time and is expected to save more, but automating a task is not the end of the calculation. Often it’s the beginning of a new phase in the workflow.

Tech companies, for example, can use A.I. to generate thousands of lines of code an hour. Yet Amazon and others still require a human to review that code. Their total efficiency is bound less by how much work can be generated than it is by the human capacity to make sure the code does what it’s supposed to.

When researchers at M.I.T. and the Wharton School analyzed the data of 500,000 GitHub developers, they found that new A.I. coding tools hugely increased their activity, “but the gains shrink sharply as work moves from writing code to shipping software.” They concluded: “The binding constraint on software output is shifting from writing code to the stages humans still perform: reviewing, integrating, testing and releasing it.”

In some cases the work may be getting better, but not easier. “It’s quite interesting to look at the day in the life of an investment banker,” said Alexandra Mousavizadeh, an economist whose company, Evident Insights, tracks A.I. adoption in the financial sector. “They’re working even more hours than they ever had, because you can do more. You need to also verify more, you’ve got new products, got your customers expecting more because the competitor bank is doing all of these new fancy things.”

Mousavizadeh said she was seeing that the banks that had made the biggest investments in A.I. were the ones most aggressively hiring people right now.

How much human time it takes to verify A.I. output depends on the task, said Ion Stoica, a professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley.

Some tasks are difficult to solve but easy to verify. (Is the maze complete?) Others depend on a lot of information and subjective judgments that an expert might never fully encode or articulate. (Is this a good contract?) Those are the tasks that require more human oversight.

Why not use A.I. to verify A.I.? That works in some cases. But for types of expertise that haven’t been encoded, M.I.T.’s Catalini said, “all the blind spots will be completely correlated between the A.I. that you’re using to create the task and the A.I. you’re using to verify the task.”

Human bottlenecks are likely to shift as A.I. models learn more about how to complete certain tasks, Stoica said, and verifying the work will require more advanced skills.

“You cannot verify if you do not understand the problem,” Stoica said.

Tim Walsh, the chair and C.E.O. of KPMG U.S., said the company had a human check involved in every process it automated. “I’m not at a point now where I’ve seen something that I would be willing to put in my business,” he said of relying on A.I. agents to check the work of A.I. agents.

A.I., he said, will make the company faster, “but all of it comes with a cost, and it’s not a light switch that you turn on and you’re ready to go.”

Chipotle’s stock surged on the report, while Starbucks shares fell as much as 6.7 percent before recovering.

The story of a stealth economist

How does a longtime economics reporter become obsessed with an 18th- and 19th-century Irish novelist? By realizing that the fiction writer was also a stealth economist herself.

Maria Edgeworth popularized early economic concepts by hiding them in her widely popular books, Jeanna Smialek of The New York Times writes in “The Invisible Hand of Maria Edgeworth,” a history of the author released this week.

Smialek spoke with DealBook’s Sarah Kessler about why understanding Edgeworth’s story is valuable to economists today. The interview has been condensed and edited.

How influential was Maria Edgeworth at the time she was writing?

It’s hard to overstate. We know from bank account data and various contract data that her books, at the time when she was sort of at her peak, were actually making way, way more than Jane Austen’s books were. Which makes it more important that she was hiding early economics lessons in her literature.

What were those lessons?

It was relatively basic by modern standards, because this is the very early years of economics. It’s after Adam Smith, but just at the very start of Thomas Malthus’s career.

She was very focused on things like division of labor. And the benefits of widespread education for work or productivity. She very much believed that the public having a widespread understanding of economics could help them to make better decisions in their own lives.

So I think she was looking at this field that was about to rocket into the domain of university science and thinking like, actually, we should democratize this.

You argue that society forgot her on purpose. What did that look like?

Economics professionalized, starting in the middle of the 19th century, and it became an academic science. Women who were very active in debating these ideas were painted as mere popularizers, as though popularizing was not important work. And the idea that they actually injected original ideas into the conversation was really played down.

Why is her story important now?

One reason is just the simple interesting fact that there was a much more diverse founding of this field than history has generally appreciated.

Another is the way she viewed economics as something that should be widely understood. As a reporter, I’ve often encountered economists who don’t feel that it is necessarily their job to explain themselves to the public. It’s not true of all economists. This idea that economics should be for everyone often gets lost in the conversation.

Justice Dept. Is Investigating TV Networks Over Trump Pool Coverage
Major TV networks were notified on Friday that the department was looking into whether they violated antitrust laws when they suspended pool coverage of President Trump.
By David McCabe, Michael M. Grynbaum, Benjamin Mullin, Lauren Hirsch and Glenn Thrush

The Justice Department is investigating whether the major television networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — violated federal antitrust laws when the group briefly suspended their pooled coverage of President Trump, according to six people with knowledge of the department’s action.

Officials from the Justice Department contacted networks on Friday and demanded communications and materials related to the White House TV pool, the people said. The pool is a longstanding system where the networks share the responsibility of providing footage of the president and distributing it to other news outlets.

Last month, the networks collectively suspended their pool footage of Mr. Trump for several days after the president barred CNN journalists from the White House grounds, which prevented CNN from participating in the pool.

The inquiry by the Justice Department is a profound escalation of the Trump administration’s ongoing battles with the White House press corps. It also follows a pattern of the Trump administration using the levers of government against its perceived foes in the media. The Justice Department has subpoenaed reporters from The New York Times and seized a laptop from a Washington Post journalist.

A Justice Department spokeswoman, Emily Covington, said in a statement on Saturday: “Members of the television press pool have proudly boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” a core antitrust law.

“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” Ms. Covington added.

The White House did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Saturday, and representatives for the five networks did not immediately comment.

The latest skirmish was set off when Mr. Trump, lamenting what he described as “purposely negative stories,” barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House on Sept. 18.

The three news organizations sued, calling the president’s action a violation of their First Amendment rights; the administration argued that access to the White House was a “privilege.” A federal judge issued a temporary block on the ban, which is set to expire on Tuesday.

ARTICLE

How to Buy and Eat Seafood Responsibly
Our investigation into the farmed fish industry found human-rights violations and health concerns. Here’s what you can do.
By Ian Urbina
Published 2026-10-10 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/magazine/how-to-buy-and-eat-seafood-responsibly.html

Fish farming, known as aquaculture, was supposed to help solve overfishing by producing more seafood without taking as much from the sea. But it’s actually made the problem worse. Most farmed seafood is raised on fishmeal, a nutrient-rich powder that is made from cooking and pulverizing other wild-caught fish. Our multiyear investigation revealed that the fishmeal industry is not only exacerbating this environmental crisis but has also been linked to a host of other ills: forced labor, pollution, worker deaths and injuries, and harmful chemicals that end up in the seafood.

In light of our findings, readers may be asking themselves: Is it possible to shop for and eat seafood ethically?

Consumers who want to reduce their exposure to the harms associated with fishmeal can:

Favor seafood that does not need to eat other fish.

Bivalves such as mussels, oysters and clams grow by filtering nutrients from the water and require little or no manufactured feed. By contrast, farmed salmon, shrimp, sea bass and other fed species generally depend to some degree on fishmeal or fish oil.

Pay more attention to distance and seasonality.

Seafood imported year-round from far away often passes through longer, more complicated supply chains, obscuring labor abuse, illegal fishing, pollution and other hidden costs. Local does not automatically mean sustainable, but shorter supply chains are generally easier to scrutinize. In the United States, the Local Catch Network helps consumers find seafood caught and processed nearby without overseas intermediaries.

Consult resources from the Monterey Bay Aquarium.

The aquarium has a Seafood Watch program to help diners compare seafood based on species, origin and production method. Its recommendations focus on environmental sustainability, however, and generally do not incorporate labor or human-rights concerns.

Consumers can only make informed choices if companies make those choices possible. Seafood companies have access to shipping records, contracts and other trade data that consumers, journalists and watchdog groups often do not, as well as the leverage to demand credible audits and greater transparency from suppliers. A growing number of nonprofit organizations are trying to shed light on the problem. SeaChoice’s Seafood Progress and Oxfam International’s Supermarket Scorecard track companies’ adherence to human-rights and environmental sourcing commitments. But retailers sometimes exclude large portions of the seafood they sell from those sourcing policies altogether.

Certification programs are supposed to provide another layer of reassurance. Best Aquaculture Practices, the Aquaculture Stewardship Council, MarinTrust and Friend of the Sea are among the most prominent programs tied to farmed seafood. But critics warn that certification can create a false sense of security. Audits may not reach far enough up the supply chain, and true surprise inspections are uncommon.

The Outlaw Ocean Project created Bait to Plate to help consumers, journalists, companies, regulators and researchers see where seafood comes from and how it moves through the supply chain. Bait to Plate tracks seafood across tens of thousands of ships, fishmeal plants, fish farms, processors and grocers, documenting cases involving forced labor, unpaid wages, crew abandonment, illegal fishing, shark finning, chemical dumping, avoidable deaths and other forms of misconduct. The Ocean Actions Index compiles proposals about steps that individuals, companies and governments could take to address the problems documented in the reporting.

Consumers alone cannot police a global industry. Companies have to make their supply chains more transparent, retailers have to demand better information from suppliers, and governments have to enforce laws against illegal fishing, forced labor and other abuses. The burden should not fall on a consumer to investigate a product that companies themselves cannot — or will not — trace.

There is no obvious silver bullet for making fish feed more sustainable. Researchers have experimented with insects, algae, microbes, soy and other alternatives to fishmeal, but each brings trade-offs involving cost, scale, nutrition, land use or food security. These substitutes may reduce reliance on wild fish, but none offers a consequence-free way to maintain the same level of production. That is one reason some researchers argue that the solution cannot be technological alone; it also requires rethinking what — and how much — we eat.

For some, responsible consumption has meant eating less seafood and meat altogether. Producing animals for food often requires catching or growing other food to feed them, adding another step between ecosystems and the dinner plate. Sustainability will require eating less animal protein, wasting less, demanding more transparency and accepting that seafood produced responsibly may sometimes cost more. Until the environmental and human costs of cheap seafood are reflected in its price, those costs will continue to be paid elsewhere.
