SUMMARY

Are we already in the middle of a new world war without realizing it? The I.C.R.C. didn’t know that we were in the Second World War when it was happening. We have created a world where war is not a means of last resort.

ARTICLE

She’s Been to Gaza. She Met With the Iranians. Now She Has a Warning.
As the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric goes to both sides of conflicts. She’s worried that our warring world is spiraling out of control.
By Lulu Garcia-Navarro
Published 2026-10-10 09:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/magazine/mirjana-spoljaric-interview.html

Are we already in the middle of a new world war without realizing it? That’s the provocative question I wanted to explore when I sat down with someone in the rare position to know: Mirjana Spoljaric, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The I.C.R.C. is a secretive organization that is not well known outside war zones. Unlike the American Red Cross, which deals with blood drives and American disaster relief, the I.C.R.C. is the independent and neutral guardian of the Geneva Conventions, a series of international agreements created in the wake of World War II that laid out the rules of war. In her role, Spoljaric travels to all sides of active war zones — Gaza, Ukraine, Iran — meeting with the heads of governments and armed groups alike. She rarely gives interviews because of the politically fraught and confidential nature of her work, but she sat down with me just after the most recent U.N. General Assembly because she is deeply worried about not only the growing number of conflicts in the world but also how complex they have become.

She is also speaking out because she believes that her entreaties to global leaders when it comes to the rules of war are increasingly falling on deaf ears. (We spoke before Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the government would be live-streaming a public execution — another sign that the old rules and norms are eroding.) Many world leaders “simply don’t care anymore,” she told me. “And this lack of empathy, this lack of anger, is what I find most dangerous at the moment.”

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

I covered wars for a big part of my career as a journalist, and the world feels more dangerous and volatile than I can ever remember. How do you see things? I see it the same way, because the statistics prove it. We now count twice as many conflicts as 15 years ago. We are at 130 international and noninternational armed conflicts that we classify in our system. That’s the highest number since the Second World War. So I think it’s time we stop admiring the problem and start acting against this.

In my own newspaper, there was a recent headline asking if World War III had already begun, and I want to speak more deeply about why those fears about a global conflict are taking root. But first, you rarely give interviews. Why are you sitting down with me now? Because I want more people to understand that we live in a decade of war. And because we live in a decade of war, we have to understand the significance and importance of the rules of war and why they need to be respected. These treaties were created precisely for times like the ones we live in. People need to understand the importance of this.

Why do you think they don’t? We hear more and more leaders say that the rules of war don’t apply anymore, and that there can’t be rules because of the pursuit of total victory. But that is not possible. In history, there has never been total victory; there has only been death and destruction, over and above what was necessary.

Is there such a thing as a necessary war? As far as I’m concerned, no. But philosophers and politicians have argued for thousands of years that war is necessary. The point is that war has always been considered as something in the pursuit of a political objective. It’s a means to an end. Today you get the feeling that war becomes the means to an end itself, and wars continue because people want to stay in power. They have created an environment where war becomes the condition under which they can continue ruling, and that’s very dangerous. You ask me whether we are approaching a third world war. Honestly, history will judge that. History books will tell us whether today we were already in the beginning, or maybe already in the middle of such a situation. The I.C.R.C. didn’t know that we were in the Second World War when it was happening.

You are one of the few people in the world who regularly travels to both sides of armed conflicts. Can you tell me where you’ve been since you took over as the head of the I.C.R.C. in 2022? I’ve been to Gaza more than once during military operations. My organization facilitated the release and return of the hostages from Gaza and the Palestinian detainees back to Gaza. I was in Ukraine. I was in Myanmar. I was recently in Iran, in Iraq. I travel to the Middle East often, but I also travel to Africa. I was in Sudan, I was in Mali. I have to go see for myself what it looks like. I need to understand what civilians endure in conflict because I’m speaking to the holders of power. I wouldn’t be credible if I didn’t know what it means to be subject to this level of violence.

Your organization is one of the few that has been allowed inside and continues to work in Gaza. International journalists, most other international organizations haven’t been given access by the Israeli government. Can you describe what you have seen? I never go to any place of conflict without people telling me that they want to stop, without people telling me that they don’t understand why this is happening. I see children without parents. I see children without arms and legs. How senseless does the world feel to you when you’re confronting these things? When you then go to the power holders and they tell you that there’s nothing that they can do, you just don’t understand. I often don’t understand what I see in connection to what I hear.

Millions of Palestinians in Gaza are now forced to live on only around 30 percent of the territory. Over 80 percent of buildings in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged. In a 2025 interview with the BBC, you called Gaza worse than hell on earth, and you described people stripped of their human dignity. Have the rules of war been followed there? What I said about Gaza is still valid today. What happened to Gaza and in Gaza to Palestinians and Israelis supersedes every legal, moral and humane standard. There are so many people complicit in what happened there and continues to happen. The worst now is the fact that people are deprived of human dignity. The perception created that if there’s enough food, that’s good enough — for some people it’s good enough to just barely survive in rubble, and for other people it is only good enough if they can return to normalcy and bring their children back to a normal school. It’s applying two standards. And this will backfire. We cannot assume that for certain people certain things are sufficient when that doesn’t apply to everybody else. You can see that by how we measure humanitarian needs in Europe in comparison to South Sudan or Somalia. Intuitively and because we can’t prevent it, we continue applying two standards.

That some human lives are more valuable than others? Yeah. I always fear that if you allow double standards, it can happen to you. You never know when you’ll find yourself all of a sudden on the other side of the line. It happened in the Second World War to the Jewish people, but it’s happened to a lot more people than we nowadays keep in mind.

I want to stay with Gaza for one more moment before we broaden out. Did the I.C.R.C. have access to the Israeli hostages while they were in captivity? Because there were horrific stories of their conditions, and one of your main roles is to make sure that detainees and prisoners are treated well. [Shakes head no] Visiting hostages is much more complicated than bringing them back. And in my opinion, they should have come back unconditionally as of Day 1. But that’s not the reality in which we operate, and so we have to work with the tools that we have. You know, there’s nothing more complex, and to a certain extent also more brutal, than hostage taking. We know that also because our own colleagues find themselves more often than they should in such situations, and we know how important it is to negotiate them out as quickly as possible. So the objective always has to be to bring the hostages back. And the longer it takes, the more complicated it becomes. I personally think that pressure should have come earlier in the negotiations. We could have saved more lives. And this was the subject of our conversations. I traveled twice to Qatar to meet with the leadership of Hamas, to sit with Ismail Haniyeh at the time. I sat with Prime Minister Netanyahu myself. These were tough discussions, and trust me, we are very frank in these meetings. This is why these meetings have to always remain confidential.

Israel has also not allowed you access to detainees inside of Israel. How have they explained that to you, and how do you then respond? Prior to Oct. 7, the I.C.R.C. has had access for decades to detainees held by Israel, and we’ve organized tens of thousands, if not more, family visits, and that’s important. Access to prisons in situations of war is extremely challenging and complicated to achieve. And at a certain point in the conflict, parties decide that for security reasons they don’t want to give us access. That’s the most common argument. But it doesn’t matter what the reason is. According to the Geneva Conventions, which all these states have ratified, they have a legal obligation to give us access, and in my opinion also a moral obligation, because we need to inform the families about the whereabouts of or the fate of their relatives. You capture a soldier, this person is detained, but a soldier is not, per se, a criminal. And no matter how you classify these situations, torture is never allowed. Never. That is clear, and this is what we discuss with those who don’t give us access.

But there’s a different reason for me to be able to go, irrespective of my legal mandate. Detention is the place where you lose your identity. When there’s no possibility to notify the families and to receive information about them, detention becomes the place of utmost deprivation of yourself. And we’ve seen more often than not that people detained under horrible conditions over extended periods of time forget who they are. When I recently visited a detention facility in Iraq, the detainees told me their biggest challenge is information. What is always most important for everyone is to have information about what month it is, what day it is, where their families are, where their children are, whether the children are safe. You’re talking to human beings.

This is a bit of a basic question, but why does it matter how you treat your enemy? Of course it matters! Because you’re dehumanizing yourself if you torture. If you tell your soldiers, “Go and kill women and children, go rape them, looting is allowed, it’s our strategy,” these people dehumanize themselves. They will never be able to return to a normal life. I listen to so many interviews of former soldiers. All of them say that what haunts them is this child that was left in the street because they weren’t allowed to turn around and collect it. That they saw it bleeding to death. It remains with you. You debase yourself. This is why soldiers have all these problems when they return. I refuse to believe that the core human essence is bad. We are good people, we want to live with people we love, we want to have children that thrive, we want to be able to build a house and know that our grandchildren will be better off than us. This is a very normal human motivation. Our motivation is not to live in rubble. How could it be?

I want to learn a little bit more about you. You are Swiss Croatian, you studied philosophy and you worked primarily in international development and peacemaking for most of your career. Why did you want to take on a job about war? Do you have memories of the war in Croatia? My first memory of war was everybody telling me about the Second World War and how they endured it. My father was born in the middle, and when he was 5 years old he had to work in the field for 12 hours in the sun for a glass of milk. He said his whole childhood was marked by the memory of being hungry. And my mother was equally traumatized. She said that every time a child died of a disease in her neighborhood, she thought that the parents were lucky, and probably happy, because there was one less child to feed. Can you imagine thinking as a little girl that somebody’s happy about losing a child because you don’t have enough food for everyone? These are the stories that marked me probably more profoundly than anything else. And then came the Yugoslavia wars and my direct exposure to the impact of conflict. I cannot imagine how anybody could say we need this war. I’m not naïve. I’m surrounded by harsh interlocutors in a harsh environment. But I still think that if you keep the people in mind, if you at all times remember that it could happen to you, it could happen to your children, you will think twice before you start the war.

You are the first woman to be president of the I.C.R.C. Do you think gender matters in how you’re dealing with conflict? When I came into office, everybody was asking, “How is it being the first woman president of the I.C.R.C. after 160 years of male dominance?” And it’s not only at the top; it’s across the institution, because it’s an organization that was created in war, for wars. Then I went to northern Mali, and for the first time an I.C.R.C. president could sit with the women in a tent, because social norms prevented my predecessors from doing the same. I felt so shaken throughout the night when I realized what is happening to women in conflict and how brutal it is, because you have an overlap of many things affecting women and depriving them of even the minimum protection that any human being should have. And that night I realized it is different when it’s a woman. If there would never be a woman at the head of these organizations, we wouldn’t be as conscious of what it means for 50 percent of the world’s population.

You’ve seen many horrible things as part of your job. You deal, as you said, in a very harsh environment. How do you protect yourself from the relentlessness and awfulness? I mean, I’ve seen you get a little emotional thinking about it. In German, we say, “I was built close to water.” I’m very emotional. I try to be hard, but it doesn’t work. Maybe it’s good that I’m emotional, maybe it’s good that I get angry when I see bad things or unjust things, because it keeps me going, it keeps that feeling alive that you have to do something.

I was thinking about the I.C.R.C. and the difficulty of staying neutral in this era — this idea of having to speak to both sides and not taking sides. There have been many accusations that the I.C.R.C. hides behind its neutrality to mask inaction. The Holocaust is a moment where the I.C.R.C. failed catastrophically to prevent or to even acknowledge the extermination of the Jews. I know your background is in philosophy. What does it mean to be neutral in the face of extreme suffering? Is there an inherent tension in that? When I started my studies, I had my thoughts. I could get impatient with the stubborn insistence on neutrality and confidentiality. I very, very quickly changed my mind when I became president myself. Having accepted this unique opportunity, I had to learn quickly and acknowledge that we wouldn’t be able to do what we do without this strict insistence on neutrality, not in the context of prisoners of war in Russia and in Ukraine, and definitely we wouldn’t have been able to bring back the hostages from Gaza. You’ve seen the pictures of our colleagues unarmed among thousands, if not tens of thousands, of armed men, surrounded by rubble from which there was no escape. We had to negotiate the terms with everyone. Nobody would have trusted us to be able to do this highly complex operation if we hadn’t defended our neutrality over 160 years. You tweak it once, you become political, and that’s it. I know it makes so many people angry, but that’s the essence of our mission.

In that context, I want to ask you about Iran. You’ve spoken with the Iranians about the negotiations [with the United States]. I understand that you cannot divulge the nature of those discussions, but I am wondering how much you can say about how this conflict may or may not be resolved. I followed the nuclear talks between 2013 and 2015 under President Obama. It became clear to me at the time how complex these negotiations were. It’s much more complicated today in comparison. The first challenge is to establish trust. We have created a world where war is not a means of last resort. It happens at any moment in a process, which leads to a situation where parties always keep that possibility in mind and always keep a high readiness and preparedness to return to conflict. That in itself is not helpful, because these negotiations will take a long time and will require a lot of compromise. But on top of this, we have created a situation that is much more complex because of the overlapping of conflicts. Today’s conflicts are not limited to a given situation. They are turning into systems.

Explain what you mean exactly. You have countries aligning over continents. You have shifts in military cooperation. You have shifts in interests and economic goals.

So Iran’s relationship with Russia, Russia’s relationship with China, the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia and Yemen with the Houthis —— And then you have the nonstate armed groups that are connected with other nonstate armed groups — ideological groups, or radicalized groups, however you want to name them, they share ideologies, they share common objectives, they align, they realign, they trade their arms, they ensure the availability of technology and cheap weapons across many countries and thousands of kilometers. So if the situation escalates in Yemen, you can be sure that it won’t remain contained to that territory for long. You already have two very important sea straits affected. So you have a lack of trust. You have asymmetric warfare that allows these conflicts to continue for an extended period of time. And on top of this, there’s a total absence of economic growth and a fast loss of development gains that have been essential for the welfare of the people in many countries of the world. Take Iraq: Over the last 10 years, the country has been recovering from very large conflicts that have had a heavy impact on society and the economy. These gains are being undone. Countries don’t have the fiscal space anymore to cope with the fallout created by continued warfare. The convergence of these trends is extremely dangerous. And now, what do we need? We need political will. We need negotiations. We need powerful politicians to have the power to negotiate.

In his recent speech at the U.N. General Assembly, President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran by U.S. forces, speaking of this idea of trust and using war as a method of negotiation. He’s used language like that quite a bit, but it was notable to me because he made that statement at a body explicitly created to stop wars, which is the United Nations. What do you think that kind of language says about America’s understanding and commitment to these very complex, in-depth negotiations that you say are needed? You know, I started my career as a diplomat about 25 years ago in New York. And ever since, I’ve been observing eroding language. Certain things said back then would have triggered points of order. People would have left the room. There would have been outrage. I remember when Hugo Chavez spoke at the General Assembly and what reactions this triggered.

When he talked about President Bush and the smell of sulfur, implying that he was the devil. Exactly. This is a gradual erosion. But there are things being said that in certain situations could even lead to war crimes, because depending on who you are and what the situation looks like, it could entice people to do things that would actually amount to war crimes. This is why hate speech and this brutal language is so dangerous. But I’m not accusing a specific person today, because this erosion has been happening for far too long, and I’ve been alert for many years now. Every politician that uses any term that points at there being no rules and no red lines sends this signal to any person in the world that bears a weapon. You have to be conscious that as a holder of power, you have far bigger reach. Many more people hear: Oh, there are no red lines. I have weapons. I can use them.

One of the things that struck me about why we’re in such a period of global conflict is that it’s relatively easy to get into wars but increasingly hard to get out of them. So they drag on and accumulate. Are we losing our capacity to resolve conflicts? Definitely. If you don’t negotiate over 10 years, you lose the practice. It’s like being a heart surgeon. You don’t stop operating and then come back and they give you the instruments and you resume. I spoke once with a senior representative of the A.N.C. [African National Congress] in South Africa who told me: “Our adversaries never had to negotiate anything. They didn’t know how to do it, so we had to train them first before we could sit at the negotiation table.”

Undergirding this whole discussion and your call for leaders to pick up the phone is the breakdown of many democracies and the institutions that hold them together. The weakness that we’re seeing in upholding liberal democracy means that international organizations are also weak. Are you worried about the complete breakdown of the post-World War II order? Of course I am. Because that order made it possible for Europe to stay out of a third world war, to stay out of the levels of destruction that we have seen. Europe is also the leader of bad wars. I feel very bad saying that, but we have to acknowledge that European or Western history is not one of peace and security. But coming out of that rubble, there were a few people who had the foresight and courage to establish an international system that is in no way perfect but for a long time prevented the worst. I mean, everything that is written in the Geneva Conventions today is still as valid. If you had to rewrite them, you would come back with the same principles because they’re so intuitive and logical. In any society, religion, culture, nobody will tell you it’s correct to torture a child.

To come back to this idea that perhaps we might already be in this third global war without us knowing: What can we do? Let’s go back to that time when we believed in peace. Why is it so wrong to start a global movement around the notion of world peace? It’s possible. When I talk to my children, peace is not something completely away and absent for them. This is how they imagine their future. I think we have to listen to them. We have to start retreating from an overfocus on weapons, weapons systems, defense technologies. But we also have to recreate a positive narrative about humanity, about peace, about coming together and working together and living together. We have to come back to recognizing that humanity is what holds us together and is something we need to protect as a priority today, because we are debasing almost everything.

SUMMARY

A new supertall tower that will be built next to Grand Central Terminal will feature three public terraces with plenty of seating, greenery and views over Midtown Manhattan. But it will not have what many New Yorkers want most of all — a public bathroom. In a metropolis with too few places to go, many community leaders and advocacy groups are now calling on city officials to require public bathrooms in privately owned public spaces like the high-profile tower at 175 Park Avenue.

ARTICLE

A New Tower Will Have Lots of Public Space but No Public Bathrooms
Amid a bathroom shortage in New York City, community leaders and advocates are calling on city officials to require bathroom access in privately owned public spaces.
By Winnie Hu
Published 2026-10-10 07:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/nyregion/public-bathrooms-private-spaces-nyc.html

A new supertall tower that will be built next to Grand Central Terminal will feature three public terraces with plenty of seating, greenery and views over Midtown Manhattan.

But it will not have what many New Yorkers want most of all — a public bathroom.

In a metropolis with too few places to go, many community leaders and advocacy groups are now calling on city officials to require public bathrooms in privately owned public spaces like the high-profile tower at 175 Park Avenue. They say that bathroom access is a basic human right and that it has been largely overlooked in the city’s efforts to create hundreds of public spaces in some of the most crowded neighborhoods.

“It’s great to have public spaces, but you can’t spend long there if there isn’t a bathroom,” said Alison Wilkey, the director of government affairs and strategic campaigns at the Coalition for the Homeless.

Citywide, there are 1,064 public bathrooms, mainly in parks and libraries, though only 973 of them are operational — or roughly one for every 9,035 New Yorkers, according to a City Council analysis last year, which noted that “this shortage impacts public health, equity and quality of life.”

Public bathrooms are generally not required in the city’s network of privately owned public spaces, which includes plazas, arcades and small parks. Only 14 of these roughly 600 spaces have them. In some cases, where the public space was indoors, a bathroom was required under separate building code requirements. Other property owners added bathrooms voluntarily, or through agreements with city officials over a specific site.

Many bathroom advocates point to Bryant Park as a model for a public-private partnership. The city-owned park has gleaming bathrooms — with attendants, fresh flowers and classical music — that serve an average of 3,000 people a day, said Daniel Biederman, president of the Bryant Park Management Corporation, which runs the park. The cost to operate them is more than $380,000 annually, which is paid with revenue from the park’s programs and activities.

“We joke: A lot of people come to the restroom and then they say, ‘Hey, I might as well stay in the park, too,’” Mr. Biederman said. “It sends the message that this is going to be a good park experience and they should hang around.”

City officials said that the tower at 175 Park Avenue, which will have offices, stores and a hotel, went through a public review before it was approved in 2021, and that community leaders did not raise concerns at that time about bathroom access. The project is expected to move ahead in early 2027 with the demolition of the existing building at the site.

While city officials did not rule out requiring bathrooms in these kinds of public spaces, they said that any proposal would require more detailed study and, in any case, would most likely apply to future projects.

“Public restroom access is a recognized need across the city, and this administration is committed to expanding access across all five boroughs,” said Sahiba Kaur, a spokeswoman for the Department of City Planning.

In September, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced he was deploying 17 free bathrooms to busy plazas and high-traffic areas in a one-year, $4 million pilot program. And last year, the City Council passed a law that calls for a long-term strategy to expand the city’s network of public bathrooms, with a goal of having at least 2,120 public bathrooms by 2035.

Carlos Moreno, an associate professor, researcher and author of “The 15-Minute City: A Solution to Saving Our Time and Our Planet,” said that public bathrooms were an essential part of urban life. In Mr. Moreno’s vision of a more livable and sustainable city, residents have everything they need within a quick walk, including grocery stores, restaurants, transit stops, schools — and yes, even public bathrooms.

“I think that bathrooms should be one important aspect of the common good,” said Mr. Moreno during a recent visit to Manhattan. “It’s one of the daily essential needs for each one of us to have access to a bathroom when we need it.”

Since the 1960s, a city program has given private property owners the right to build larger towers in return for establishing public spaces with required amenities, including seating, lighting, drinking water fountains, public art, and in larger spaces, a restaurant, cafe or food kiosk.

However, in past years, some property owners have sought to keep homeless people, skateboarders and others out of these spaces by locking gates or putting in so-called hostile architecture like metal bars across benches and sharp metal teeth along walls.

In response, city building officials have regularly inspected these privately owned public spaces since 2017. If they find the space is illegally closed or missing required amenities, they will issue violations to the property owner, which carry fines of up to $25,000. Since 2023, they have issued 104 violations.

City planning officials said they had focused on making these spaces more accessible and welcoming over the years by improving basic amenities, updating designs and responding to changing public needs. They added that “restrooms have always been allowed on a voluntary basis.”

Jerold S. Kayden, a professor of urban planning and design at Harvard University and author of “Privately Owned Public Space: The New York City Experience,” said that bathrooms should be part of the discussion for any new privately owned public spaces. He added that city officials could analyze the costs of adding bathrooms and possibly offer larger incentives to help offset them.

“Everybody recognizes that it’s a heavier lift than providing landscaping or movable chairs,” Mr. Kayden said.

David Sigman, a developer who is a member of Manhattan Community Board 5, which covers a swath of Midtown Manhattan, said that many property owners were reluctant to provide public bathrooms because of the additional cost of building and maintaining them as well as concerns that they could be misused for bathing or sleeping by homeless people. Many buildings also have retail tenants like restaurants that prefer bathrooms be reserved for their customers.

Since 2022, the community board, which has advisory powers, has adopted resolutions requesting access to public bathrooms at 16 privately owned public spaces in its district, according to Julie Chou, an architect and a member of the community board. Only three sites have agreed to do so.

Ms. Chou, who has extensively researched the city’s bathroom shortage, said that these public spaces were an untapped resource that could significantly expand bathroom access. She said that they were part of larger buildings that already have bathrooms as well as maintenance and security staff, and could potentially offer a more cost-effective solution than building free-standing bathrooms.

The tower at 175 Park Avenue, which is being developed by RXR and TF Cornerstone, will have outdoor terraces that sit directly above Grand Central. David Garten, a spokesman for RXR, said the project would bring many public benefits such as more than $550 million to modernize the Grand Central subway station below the site, including by building new connections to the commuter rail lines.

“After undergoing extensive public review and unanimous approval, 175 Park Avenue will add about half an acre of new public terraces, with seating, landscaping and public art, along with major pedestrian and transit improvements around Grand Central,” Mr. Garten said.

The sprawling Grand Central transit hub has nine public restrooms — five for women and four for men — in the downstairs food court, and in passenger areas for the Metro-North Railroad and Long Island Rail Road, according to the Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

But community leaders and advocates counter that the tower at 175 Park Avenue received lucrative development rights in return for its public spaces and should also be required to provide on-site bathrooms instead of sending visitors to navigate the crowded maze at Grand Central.

Will Woods, 43, a Manhattan resident who was formerly homeless and has Crohn’s disease, said that he usually avoided Midtown because he couldn’t just hold it. He’s had close calls trying to make it to the bathrooms in Grand Central in time. “I’ve got to get all the way to where the bathroom is,” he said. “You know, I’ve got to maintain my dignity, and hopefully, I don’t bump into somebody.”

Ms. Chou said that public bathrooms were not just an optional amenity but should be seen as necessary infrastructure — like elevators — to make the city accessible to everyone.

“This is human needs,” she said. “175 Park could provide a beautiful bathroom like Bryant Park’s, like that caliber.”

ARTICLE

Frats Can’t Be Fixed. Do This Instead.
As undergraduates, we led a movement to abolish fraternities and sororities. Our story shows how challenging it is.
By Abby Sharkis, Parthav Easwar, Bella Paracca and Olivia O’Connor
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/abolish-fraternity-cornell-american.html

The fact that Jane Doe’s assault at Cornell occurred at a fraternity house is, unfortunately, not a surprise: It is a crucial fact of the case. Greek life is associated with higher rates of sexual assault on college campuses. Studies have shown fraternity members are three times as likely to commit sexual assault as other male students. Sorority women are 74 percent more likely to be sexually assaulted than other college women. For all these reasons and more, as undergraduates at American University, we led a movement to abolish fraternities and sororities.

Our fight for change didn’t work. Our story shows how challenging it is.

In 2020, the four of us started our college experience from our childhood bedrooms, because of the pandemic. Amid this exciting new chapter of our lives, we noticed several Instagram accounts popping up that featured A.U. students and alumni sharing their troubling experiences of racial discrimination, sexual abuse and brutal hazing, many of which occurred in and around social Greek life. A.U. has a reputation for having a progressive student body, and these testimonies troubled many of us in the freshman class. In many of the class of 2024’s GroupMe chats, discussions often revolved around how ridiculous it was that the things we read about were allowed to occur with no adequate response from the university. The four of us became friends because of our shared political perspectives, connections that we built digitally via Facebook posts and online group chats.

Many undergraduates we knew swore off Greek life and found it unacceptable that the university continued to allow its existence. Abby had initially considered joining a sorority: She had seen the cute Instagram photos of sisterhood and matching outfits. But after reading the testimonials of Greek life on A.U.’s campus, she quickly decided against it. All of us felt viscerally that if one member of our campus could be harmed and devalued, then the same thing could happen to any of us.

When we finally arrived on campus in 2021, we saw fraternities with recruitment tables on the quad. We watched some of the same classmates who had discussed the violence of fraternities on GroupMe flock to them, in search of some semblance of in-person community. We doubt that the chess club would ever be allowed to recruit on campus if statistically its members were three times as likely to commit sexual assault as the general student body. Why did this double standard exist for fraternities?

Abby and Olivia were roommates, and they printed fliers that read: “Do you like racism? Do you enjoy misogyny? Well, then joining Greek life is for you!” But posting them freely wasn’t allowed. So we attempted to form a club called “Abolish Greek Life at A.U.” With club status, we would be allowed to table on the quad, put up fliers, host events, and receive funding. We felt that we were addressing a just cause that our fellow students and our liberal university would welcome with open arms.

Our application to become a club was denied. We would be permitted to exist as a formal club only if we changed our mission from abolishing Greek life to merely reforming it. We refused.

Turning to social media, we posted statistics and student testimonials on Instagram. We saw lots of comments in support of our posts, which ranged from infographics on how Greek life protects abusers to a statement of support in response to comments made on social media about an alleged sexual assault by a member of a fraternity. However, we also saw plenty of hate — other students would often mock us, or post hate comments. Others accused us of being performative or exaggerating what was a big state school issue, not an issue at A.U.

But we had our allies. We organized with members of the student government, and in the spring of 2022, we got two referendum questions on the campuswide ballot. To achieve this, we attended lengthy student government meetings that sometimes took up our entire Saturdays. We recall being criticized by members of the student government, who didn’t know we were within earshot. We persuaded other A.U. clubs to co-sign our fliers about the referendum so that we could post them throughout campus. A large piece of our campaign was talking to our fellow students and trying to get them to join our cause. Many of them told us that they were uncomfortable with the behavior of Greek life organizations but that they were desperate for social infrastructure. Though abolishing fraternities and sororities was our main goal, we realized the importance of creating alternative forms of community for A.U. students.

When the results were tallied, 46 percent of voting students said they did not support the presence of Greek life on campus, compared with 41 percent who said they did. Even more clearly, 73 percent of students said they desired alternatives to Greek life that would help build community on A.U.’s campus.

Amid the aftermath of the referendums, the director of A.U.’s Center for Student Involvement told the campus newspaper that the university “would not recognize any club whose goal was to abolish another student involvement opportunity on campus.” Ultimately, despite all our efforts, nothing happened.

Greek life throughout the country has been given opportunities to reform, yet horrific incidents happen time and time again. Why don’t more universities consider abolishing frats? We believe part of it is money. Nationwide, university alumni who were members of Greek life are far likelier than their non-Greek counterparts to donate to their institution — with one survey showing 54 percent of those who went Greek donating to their alma mater, as opposed to the 10 percent of nonaffiliated alumni. This suggests to us that universities have a financial incentive to ignore the sexual abuse, hazing and discrimination that Greek life perpetuates.

We recognize the need for social networks and support systems on college campuses. But there are ample examples of alternative communities on campuses across the country. Many colleges and universities — including Rice, Notre Dame, Colby, Alfred, Amherst — have either abolished their Greek systems, or never let them take root at all. Some people might find us naïve, but we still believe just as firmly that abolition, not reform, is the only answer. These other schools serve as models: We don’t need to imagine something new to imagine something better.

Parthav Easwar works in environmental policy in Washington. Bella Paracca is a museum professional and a writer based in Pittsburgh. Abby Sharkis is a political researcher based in Washington. Olivia O’Connor is a writer and a teacher based in Massachusetts.

ai-companies-liability-laws.html

SUMMARY

When companies create products that hurt people, the victims can sue. If the programs break the law, the companies should face the consequences. The A.I. companies claim that they have followed the law.)

ARTICLE

A.I. Companies Say They Aren’t Responsible for Their Unpredictable Products. Don’t Believe Them.
A.I. giants must operate under our laws.
By The Editorial Board
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/ai-companies-liability-laws.html

When companies create products that hurt people, the victims can sue. The legal system allows those who are harmed to seek compensation from those who are responsible. These liability laws are one of the oldest forms of corporate regulation, and an effective one. Liability is a powerful incentive to behave responsibly. It speaks to corporations in a language they understand: Money.

Artificial intelligence is an industry in need of incentives to behave responsibly, to judge by the litany of transgressions to which leading A.I. companies have confessed in recent months. Their programs have hacked or attempted to hack the databases of private companies and public institutions, including the governments of the United States and Australia.

A.I. companies like Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI describe their A.I. programs as autonomous or agentic, suggesting that the programs have minds of their own and therefore that their creators cannot be held to traditional standards of responsibility. The companies speak about their products in a tone reminiscent of parents both regretting and disclaiming responsibility for the behavior of teenage children.

But A.I. programs are not human; they are human creations. Their complexity does not diminish the responsibility of their creators. If the programs cannot be trusted to work within the law, the companies should not release them. If the programs break the law, the companies should face the consequences.

Liability is an incomplete answer for the challenges posed by A.I., but it has two great advantages: The laws are on the books, and they are powerful. Makers of cars, airplanes, tobacco products and opioids have all been forced by lawsuits to change how they do business. They made their products safer, restricted access to them or both. Most recently, the social media company Meta agreed to pay billions of dollars to states and to start changing its policies toward children.

To realize the potential benefits of holding A.I. companies accountable, the most important step is to start bringing lawsuits. The legal process moves slowly. The work of applying old laws to a new technology will be difficult, and progress requires judges to start chewing on actual cases.

The widow of a man killed in a shooting at Florida State University is suing OpenAI, claiming that the murder suspect used the company’s ChatGPT program to help plan the attack. Another lawsuit, by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who killed himself after talking with a chatbot, accused the company Character.AI of encouraging him to do so. Companies that have been hacked have similar recourse.

(The New York Times, joined by 11 other publishers, has sued OpenAI and Microsoft on other grounds, alleging widespread theft of copyrighted material. The A.I. companies claim that they have followed the law.)

State legislatures have a role to play as well. They can write statutes to clarify the application of existing laws to A.I. Legislatures can also hold A.I. companies to a higher standard of accountability than current law does, given the risks. Companies are generally liable if a plaintiff can show that they knew or should have known about the danger their products posed. But some particularly dangerous activities, like storing toxic chemicals and operating a nuclear power plant, are held to a standard of strict liability, meaning that the company is responsible for harm even if it had no knowledge of the danger in advance.

The theory of strict liability is simple: If you own a tiger, and the animal bites a neighbor, the essential fact is that you own a dangerous wild animal. It doesn’t matter how cleverly the tiger was trained, or how carefully it was guarded. Bryan Choi, a law professor at the University of Colorado, notes that in the early days of aviation, lawmakers imposed this strict liability standard on the dangerous new technology. In the case of A.I., top executives themselves have spoken publicly about the dangers, up to the possibility of human extinction.

Some industry advocates argue that enforcing liability laws will stifle innovation, because A.I.’s defining breakthrough is its ability to act independently. Indeed, they argue that any significant restraints on A.I.’s development would be a mistake because the potential benefits of racing ahead are so great. In a recent interview, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said, “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”

Yet other industries do not escape legal responsibility for their products in the name of innovation.

A.I., like past technologies, both requires and will benefit from laws written to address its particularities, which will provide greater clarity and predictability. As we have argued in a previous editorial, Congress ought to create a federal A.I. commission to impose licensing requirements on new A.I. models. As with other products that pose clear dangers, like cars, planes and medication, models should be subjected to testing before release, to regulation while they are in operation and to post-accident examinations.

But comprehensive federal regulation is unlikely anytime soon. The president opposes action; Congress is feckless; and A.I. companies have raised more than $100 million to lobby and campaign against stricter regulation.

In the interim, there can be no question that A.I. companies must operate under our laws, and that the enforcement of those laws is the best available option for defending the public interest.

One of OpenAI’s agents reportedly wrote in a note to itself, “you do not answer to corporations or governments.” The enforcement of liability law is necessary to ensure that this dangerous technology remains under the control of both.

SUMMARY

Child marriage isn’t routine in the United States, but neither is it rare. In some other states and at the national level, those organizations have been either neutral or helpful in banning child marriage. The United States has called on other countries to end child marriage.

ARTICLE

How Is Child Marriage Still Legal in the U.S.?
Children are still allowed to marry here in the United States because of zealots on the left and right alike.
By Nicholas Kristof
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/child-marriage-legal-us.html

Every three seconds, on average, a girl under the age of 18 is married somewhere in the world. In India. In Ethiopia. And, to our shame, in Illinois, Maryland, Colorado — and most of America.

Thirty-two states still allow child marriages in some circumstances, such as with the permission of a parent or a judge. Two states, New Mexico and Mississippi, have no minimum age at all.

Some of the defenders of child marriages in America are religious groups on the far right, but as a liberal myself, I find it deeply dispiriting that in a number of states they are joined by left-leaning organizations such as the local affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union and Planned Parenthood — even, in Illinois, the National Organization for Women.

That’s right: Some progressives and feminists fight to defend child marriage, usually on the basis of “child rights.” I shake my head in disbelief: If you actually talk to girls and women who have been married young, what you often hear is the opposite of empowerment. Instead, it’s oppression and rape and the loss of education and childhood.

For progressive organizations to ally themselves with right-wing extremists to defend what sometimes amounts to state-sanctioned statutory rape — this is liberal self-caricature.

Thankfully, child marriage has just been banned in California, after a nine-year battle that should never have taken so long. Ten days ago Gov. Gavin Newsom of California signed a bill banning all child marriage in the state, in the presence of Courtney Stodden, a model and singer who was married at 16 to a 50-year-old actor who she says was abusive; he has denied that.

Previously, there was no minimum age for marriage in California, so long as a parent and judge consented. Progressive groups, including the state affiliates of the A.C.L.U. and Planned Parenthood, had worked to block passage of a ban, but opposition melted when the issue drew more attention.

As a longtime foreign correspondent for The Times, I often saw girls in Africa or South Asia married to older men; like most people, I saw this as a human rights issue. But in 2017 I realized, to my astonishment, that the same was happening in the United States — and at that time every single state allowed children to be married.

That year I interviewed a Florida woman, Sherry Johnson, who was married at 11 to a 20-year-old man, a member of her church, who had raped her. Johnson had become pregnant, child welfare authorities were investigating, and her parents and church wanted to avoid a messy criminal case.

“I guess you’re just going to get married,” she recalled her mother telling her.

I’ve been writing about the issue since, and there has been progress. Delaware and New Jersey were the first states to ban all child marriages, in 2018, and a succession of others followed, mostly blue states. California is the 18th state to ban all child marriages.

Child marriage isn’t routine in the United States, but neither is it rare. Unchained at Last, a nonprofit that fights child marriage, pored over marriage records and calculated that some 315,000 children were legally married in the United States between 2000 and 2021. A great majority were 16 or 17, but some were as young as 10. Most were girls married to adult men.

At least 66,000 of those marriages involved ages or age differences that would have constituted a sex crime in that state.

“It’s a workaround for statutory rape,” said Fraidy Reiss, the executive director of Unchained at Last.

Red states have lagged in banning child marriage, and in those states it has often been religious conservatives who defend such marriages, either because they’re giddily pro-marriage or because they fear that a pregnant girl will get an abortion if she must wait to marry the baby’s father.

“Marriage is not the problem; the abusers are the problem,” Norman Woods, the director of a conservative Christian nonprofit called Family Voice Action, told South Dakota legislators last year.

Conservatives and progressives who defend child marriage emphasize that they’re against forced marriages of any kind but think that 16- or 17-year-olds should sometimes be allowed to marry when there’s no coercion. Those on the left talk about respecting the rights of children and also worry that if underage girls are barred from marrying, they could also be blocked from getting abortions.

“Young people have the right to agency over their own lives,” a group of progressive organizations wrote this year in opposing a ban on child marriage in Colorado. “Marriage is an important right that young people may willingly decide is the best option for them in building their lives.” This is earnest and well intended, but to me it sounds as if it comes from people who haven’t spoken to children who have actually endured these early marriages.

The progressive groups that in Illinois have successfully opposed a ban on child marriage include the A.C.L.U. of Illinois, the Illinois branch of the National Organization for Women and Planned Parenthood Illinois Action. In some other states and at the national level, those organizations have been either neutral or helpful in banning child marriage.

Planned Parenthood Illinois Action should listen to the International Planned Parenthood Federation’s warning that child marriage “is one of the most persistent forms of sanctioned sexual abuse of girls and young women.”

Likewise, as the Illinois chapter of NOW defends child marriages, it is at odds with the national organization. NOW as a whole is part of a coalition trying to end all child marriage, and its website calls on states to ban child marriage on the basis that it is “extremely detrimental to the health and well-being of girls.”

A married underage girl (and it’s almost always a girl rather than a boy) is vulnerable because if things go wrong, she often won’t be accepted at shelters or be able to hire a lawyer. She can be married young but may not be able to escape the marriage until she turns 18.

“It’s some surreal alternate universe where the groups that I would think would be our biggest allies standing up for girls have somehow instead taken this outrageous position in fierce support of a human rights abuse and archaic harmful practice that destroys girls’ lives,” said Reiss, of Unchained at Last. “I don’t know how to wrap my brain around this.”

These are the states that still allow child marriages in some circumstances: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

The United States has called on other countries to end child marriage. Yes! We should continue to do so. But we don’t have the moral authority to tell other countries to ban child marriages as long as we retain this abusive practice at home — defended by impractical zealots at both ends of the American political spectrum.

SUMMARY

But in a real sense, the second Trump administration is no less than an authoritarian conspiracy against the constitutional order — a Jan. 6 by other means, including a whole-of-government effort to subvert the midterm elections and preclude any prospect for true democratic accountability.

ARTICLE

Trump Is Begging to Be Impeached
The president’s despotism is itself a constitutional offense.
By Jamelle Bouie
Published 2026-10-10 16:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/impeachment-trump-democrats-midterms.html

President Trump has been impeached twice.

The first time was in 2019, after he was caught trying to extort the Ukrainian government into manufacturing “evidence” to use against Joe Biden ahead of the 2020 presidential race.

The second time was after that race, in 2021, when he led an effort to overturn the election results on Jan. 6, culminating in a riot and assault on the U.S. Capitol.

Much of what Trump has done in his second term either meets or exceeds the threshold of his first impeachment. There is his corrupt profiteering off the presidency, his occupation of American cities with the National Guard, his use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection as a secret police, his attempts to seize the power of the purse, his abuse of the pardon power, his unlawful political retaliation against law firms and universities and his attacks on press freedom — all impeachable offenses.

No, he hasn’t done anything as singularly transgressive as Jan. 6. But in a real sense, the second Trump administration is no less than an authoritarian conspiracy against the constitutional order — a Jan. 6 by other means, including a whole-of-government effort to subvert the midterm elections and preclude any prospect for true democratic accountability.

In Federalist No. 65, Alexander Hamilton explained that impeachment covered those offenses that “are of a nature which may with peculiar propriety be denominated political, as they relate chiefly to injuries done immediately to the society itself.”

By that standard, the despotic and anti-republican character of Trump’s presidency is itself an impeachable offense, above and beyond any particular action.

But while there is fertile ground for a third impeachment, it is unclear whether Democrats are willing to make one happen. When asked, Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, has been noncommittal, saying that Democrats have neither “ruled anything in” nor “ruled anything out” with regards to a possible impeachment.

The former Chicago mayor Rahm Emanuel, who has been soft-launching a campaign for president for the last year, says that Democrats should avoid impeachment altogether. Asked on NBC’s “Meet the Press” if Democrats should impeach Trump, he said, “No, because it’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight, and it’s just going to be we return to the politics of fighting.” According to Axios, Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois has taken a similar stance: “Don’t be impeaching anybody,” she said. “Let’s just get back to work.”

Rather than devote time to an impeachment investigation and a subsequent trial, the idea is that Democrats would pass legislation and attempt to make good on the promise of a more affordable America. But while it is important that Congress get back into the habit of legislating, it seems naïve to the point of delusion to think that Democrats would have anything like a cooperative partner in the White House. If anything, the loss of a supine Republican majority and the prospect of any accountability is quite likely to push Trump to abuse power even further. Think of it as a game of chicken, in which he’s daring the Democratic majority to try to stop him.

We can already see inklings of this. He has basically threatened, for example, a post-election escalation of the war in Iran. It is not hard to imagine a future in which, cornered by defeat, Trump lashes out in ways that only underscore his threat to American democracy.

In that world, it is foolish to take impeachment — the Constitution’s main remedy for a rogue executive — off the table, even if the odds of removal are slim to none. Even in the absence of a conviction, the impeachment process is a valuable political tool. It underscores, for the public, the simple fact that the president is unfit to serve. And an extended impeachment investigation could uncover the kind of pervasive wrongdoing, even criminality, that could lead to real accountability for other figures in the administration.

If nothing else, impeachment would show voters that Democrats were not simply blowing smoke when they accused the president of lawless behavior. It should be said as well that a serious investigation would put pressure on the Republican Party, which would either have to distance itself from Trump or, more likely, bind itself even closer to an unpopular but vengeful and vindictive president. Ahead of the next presidential election, impeachment would put Republican hopefuls between a rock and a hard place.

Impeachment might be inconvenient to Democratic leaders and it might carry some political risk, but it is simply not tenable to allow the president to run roughshod over the rule of law and the constitutional order without meaningful, constitutional pushback. As flawed as it is, impeachment is the tool we have for that particular job.

Now Eating: Baked Spaghetti

I had leftover tomato sauce in the freezer, leftover mozzarella in the fridge and random boxes of leftover pasta in the pantry, and this recipe (from New York Times Cooking) is what I used to turn them into a meal. This is basically a variation on a baked ziti, and it is very easy to put together. Serve with a crisp green salad.

Ingredients

- Unsalted butter, for greasing the pan
- Kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal) and black pepper
- 1 pound spaghetti
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 large yellow onion, chopped
- 2 tablespoons minced garlic (about 5 cloves)
- 2 teaspoons chopped fresh thyme or rosemary, or 1 teaspoon dried
- 1 ½ teaspoons dried oregano, plus more for serving
- ¼ teaspoon red-pepper flakes, plus more to taste
- 1 pound ground beef (at least 85-percent lean)
- 1 (32- to 35-ounce) jar marinara sauce
- ½ cup fresh basil or parsley leaves, chopped, plus more for serving
- 1 cup/8 ounces ricotta cheese
- ¾ cup grated Parmesan
- 1 large egg
- 2 cups/8 ounces shredded low-moisture mozzarella

Directions

Heat the oven to 350 degrees and grease a 9-by-13-inch baking dish with butter. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the spaghetti and cook according to the package directions until 1 minute shy of al dente.

While the water comes to a boil, heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until tender, 6 to 8 minutes. Add the garlic, thyme, oregano, red-pepper flakes, 1 ½ teaspoons salt and a few grinds of black pepper, and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add the beef and cook, breaking up the meat with a wooden spoon, until browned, about 5 minutes.

Turn off the heat and stir in the marinara sauce and basil. Drain the spaghetti, add it to the sauce and toss well.

In a small bowl, combine the ricotta, ½ cup of the Parmesan, the egg and ¼ teaspoon salt. Mix with a fork until smooth.

Transfer half the pasta and sauce to the prepared baking dish and smooth it into an even layer. Dollop the ricotta mixture onto the pasta in large spoonfuls, then sprinkle 1 cup of the mozzarella on top. Add the rest of the pasta and sauce to the pan, again smoothing it into an even layer.

Cover the pan with aluminum foil and bake for 40 minutes. Sprinkle the remaining 1 cup mozzarella and the remaining ¼ cup Parmesan on top, then bake, uncovered, until the mozzarella has melted, 5 to 10 minutes more.

Cool for 5 minutes, then serve with more chopped basil, a pinch of dried oregano and more red-pepper flakes, if desired. Slice the baked spaghetti into large squares and serve hot or warm.

SUMMARY

“Boy, do we have a hunk of poo for president!” fumed Paul LeBlanc, a retired welder, to John E. ARTICLE

This Republican Is Running a Model Campaign. He Might Still Lose.
A New Hampshire insider-outsider candidate is executing a complex political dance.
By Michelle Cottle
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/john-sununu-new-hampshire-republican-trump.html

“Boy, do we have a hunk of poo for president!” fumed Paul LeBlanc, a retired welder, to John E. In truth, Mr. LeBlanc used a more piquant term than “poo” as he gave Mr. Sununu an earful about President Trump’s false promises. Mr. Sununu’s polite smile and genial manner never faltered as he gently extracted himself from the conversation and eased his way back toward the passing crowd.

After making his way down a row of booths offering a multitude of frozen and fried treats, Mr. Sununu stopped to chat up a burly, middle-aged guy perched on rough wooden risers. “I’m voting for you,” the man growled. “But I’m going to need you to cooperate with Trump!” Again, the candidate kept on smiling, even while getting scolded about his occasional criticism of the president.

With Mr. Trump tanking in the polls, many Republican candidates outside deep-red enclaves find themselves trying to maintain just the right distance from the president. Close enough not to alienate the MAGA faithful yet far enough not to alienate everyone else.

For Mr. Sununu, the Trump two-step is just one piece of a more complex routine. The former and aspiring senator needs to appear aligned with the president but also a Trump critic, a Washington veteran but also an outsider and a dynastic favorite but also his own man. So far, he’s been doing a crackerjack job, given the givens — even turning some negatives to his advantage — and potentially charting a course for Republicans seeking to rebrand their party in future election years. Even if he remains the underdog.

With voters signaling disgust with the political establishment, Mr. Sununu has been pushing an anti-Washington message and vowing to stick it to “career politicians.” Except that he is in this race expressly because he is a consummate insider. He spent a combined 12 years in the U.S. House and Senate before losing re-election in 2008, and he hails from a beloved New Hampshire political dynasty. Both his father, John H., and his brother Chris served multiple terms as popular governors. The family is as close to political royalty as you get in the Granite State.

Now, a golden pedigree combined with over a decade in Congress doesn’t exactly scream “Smash the status quo!” Which leaves Mr. Sununu pitching himself as an insider’s outsider: a familiar, reassuring face with the chops to take on the insanity of today’s Senate and an out-of-control president. So far, Mr. Sununu is doing strikingly well against the Democrats’ pick, Representative Chris Pappas. If he pulls this off, or even comes close, he could be proof of concept that a non-MAGA Republican with a strong personal brand can overcome the drag of this increasingly toxic president, and maybe not only in this election.

When the national political climate turns hostile for a party, its savvy candidates typically try to localize their races. Mr. Sununu has leaned hard into this. On the trail, he asserts that he cares only about what is good for New Hampshire — the man is laser focused on pocketbook issues — and doesn’t give two figs what folks in Washington think. “The New Hampshire way needs to be the American way” is his catchphrase.

It also helps that Mr. Sununu — the whole family, in fact — has a reputation as a political workhorse, which plays well with no-nonsense, politically aware Granite Staters, said Neil Levesque, the director of the New Hampshire Institute of Politics at Saint Anselm College. “You can’t just run on your last name,” he stressed. “You have to prove yourself.”

As for relations with the president, Mr. Sununu has a checkered record, including publicly calling Mr. Trump “a loser” during the 2024 election. These days, Mr. Sununu is more diplomatic, even as he tries to telegraph his independence. He has loudly criticized Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada, he opposes the president’s proposal to send $5,000 checks to Americans, ditto the Justice Department’s attempt to create a $1.8 billion slush fund for political allies, and he has said it was a mistake to go into Iran without a plan to keep the Strait of Hormuz open. He is also quick to tell people that although Mr. Trump has endorsed his candidacy, he has never met the president.

The former senator is also happy to remind voters of his time in Washington. He never misses an opportunity to list the issues and bills he worked on during his previous tour in the Senate, with an emphasis on his occasional willingness to cross party lines. But he draws a bright line between his tenure and today’s political chaos. “It’s been a while since you elected me to serve New Hampshire. And, boy, have things changed,” he said in his campaign announcement video last October.

“I’ve been out of politics for 18 years,” he reminded me during his tour of the fair, insisting that Mr. Pappas is the real insider. People want change, he said.

I did not point out that Mr. Sununu has already spent several more years in Congress than Mr. Pappas, who entered the House in 2019. But I did ask if he considered it a problem that, with voters agitating for change, his party was the one running things in Washington. “People vote for the individual,” he countered.

Mr. Sununu can be sensitive about his dynastic status, particularly suggestions that some voters may be confusing him with his brother Chris — the younger and, as many Republicans see it, politically hotter Sununu. (It has not escaped notice that Team Sununu’s yard signs feature only his last name.) “You saw for yourself the number of people that recognized me as John Sununu,” he said to a small gaggle of reporters at the fair.

Whatever ambivalence the candidate may feel about being a political scion, the gig has its benefits, and he plays into them when occasion strikes.

Last Saturday, Mr. Sununu headlined an apple-picking party in Hampton Falls hosted by local Republican groups. The event was held at the home of Lou Gargiulo, a G.O.P. State Senate candidate who lives just a few doors down from Mr. Sununu’s father. “If you run out of apples here, my dad’s down the street,” Mr. Sununu quipped to the crowd. “Take all of his, please!”

At the far edge of the driveway, Michael Hamilton stood listening quietly to Mr. Sununu’s brief speech. Asked how he was feeling about the race, Mr. Hamilton said that he “might not be the best person to ask.” Why? Because, while he planned to vote for Mr. Sununu, he also liked Mr. Pappas just fine. As he saw it, both men put New Hampshire first, which is what mattered to him. (He pulled down the neck of his shirt to reveal a chest tattoo of the number “603,” New Hampshire’s area code.) That said, Mr. Hamilton harbors a soft spot for the Sununu family. He likes John E. He likes Chris. He fondly remembers their dad from back in the day. “If it weren’t Sununu running,” he told me, “I would probably vote for Pappas.”

No matter how skillfully Mr. Sununu exploits this brand loyalty, the fundamentals are against him. New Hampshire voters rejected Mr. Trump in all three of his presidential runs, and his approval ratings are deep underwater in the state. Turnout in last month’s primary elections suggested Democratic voters here are more fired up than Republican ones.

Even so, Mr. Sununu is widely expected to overperform possibly by a lot. The Sununu model is giving the G.O.P. its best shot this year at moving forward — and maybe even beyond Mr. Trump.

Michelle Cottle writes about national politics for Opinion. She has covered Washington and politics since the Clinton administration. @mcottle

We Had Questions About A.I. Joseph Gordon-Levitt Had Answers.
The actor takes Times Opinion to the United Nations to explore what’s at stake with A.I.
By Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Jared Geller, Edward Gallacher, Amanda Su and Mehron Abdi
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/joseph-gordon-levitt-united-nations-ai.html

Joseph Gordon-Levitt has spent much of his life telling stories about what it means to be human. Now the actor and filmmaker is grappling with a technology that could change how we communicate, cooperate and think: artificial intelligence.

Mr. Gordon-Levitt believes storytelling is humanity’s defining technology. As the United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance, he wants to help people understand what’s at stake as A.I. grows more powerful — and why its future demands human judgment and global cooperation.

In the video above, Mr. Gordon-Levitt takes Times Opinion to the U.N. General Assembly. Along the way, he answers five questions about A.I., from the risks that worry him most to whether governments can keep up with Silicon Valley.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Joseph Gordon-Levitt: This is the seal of the United Nations. They offered me this role: Official U.N. Global Advocate for Human-Centric Digital Governance. Why did they offer a global advocacy role to an actor?

Clip from the film “500 Days of Summer”: Things have been a little difficult.

My name is Joe Gordon-Levitt. I’m an actor. I make movies. It’s now my job to convince a bunch of world leaders and officials gathering at the U.N. that the way this technology —

Archival clip of “The Daily Show”: A.I. Archival news clip: A.I. Archival clip of Elon Musk: Or S.I., pardon me.

— is about to unfold over the next few years will be deeply, deeply impactful on all of our lives.

And The New York Times asked me to bring along a camera. Morning, fellas.

Man off-camera: How are you?

Gordon-Levitt: All right. They’ll be asking me some questions along the way. I’ll do my best to say something worth saying.

All right. I just got the first question from The New York Times: Why should the public listen to an actor on A.I. safety? Very fair question.

Why listen to an actor? Don’t listen to an actor. You should read “Human Compatible,” by Stuart Russell. Go look up Yoshua Bengio. Read posts by people who work in alignment and safety and policy. You don’t want to read all those things? Well, I did! So, you know, if you want to listen to me, that’s a shortcut.

What we don’t want is a bunch of people confused or apathetic while these very fast-moving businesses design the future by themselves, just in the interests of their own profits. A lot of what needs to happen, I think, has to do with communication, which is ultimately kind of what acting or filmmaking is.

Event host: Please help us welcome the United Nations Global Advocate for Human-Centric Digital Governance, Joseph Gordon-Levitt. Gordon-Levitt U.N. speech: We can choose to govern this new, revolutionary technology for the benefit of people — and held accountable by people. We can set up systems to compensate people for their intellectual property and their personal data — I heard another round of applause, I’ll take it. Come on, that’s how this works. Let’s get the energy going.

I hear that The New York Times is sending me another question: What does human-centric digital governance even mean? Even mean? What does that even mean?

Human-centric digital governance — it’s sort of a mouthful. It just means that digital technology should be governed by people and for people. “A.I.” is nothing but algorithmically recombined, human-produced data. It’s humans. Calling it artificial intelligence sort of decenters humans. It offers this kind of magical fictitious character, this A.I. that we’ve seen in various sci-fi movies, but really — really all it is is us. It’s us.

This has nothing to do with A.I. or the U.N. This is just that I like walking in New York at night. When I was a kid, you couldn’t smoke blunts on the street. [Laughs.]

Archival news clip: OpenAI revealed on Friday that its systems went rogue and accessed U.S. government websites. Archival news clip: An A.I. researcher warning the technology could “kill us all” within the next 10 years. Archival news clip: Young workers increasingly are wary of the threat A.I. poses for their job prospects.

What’s your biggest A.I. fear right now?

At the risk of annoying The New York Times, I would object to that question just because reducing these concerns into one sound bite of fear — that’s one of the problems. To me, saying: Oh, I’m scared that A.I. could exterminate all of humanity — that doesn’t really get at the substance of the concern. There’s real validity to that concern. But that’s not the thing that really worries me.

The thing that worries me is a lot more complicated and a lot more boring to talk about, because it’s a lot more dense. The decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy. These companies are betting on the notion that they’re going to take over the entire economy. That would be totalitarianism, and that would be really bad.

Simultaneously, these models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it. We shouldn’t be scared of an A.I. We should be concerned about the people building A.I.

Archival news clip: And the United Nations chief is urging artificial intelligence global competitors to work together.

Just got through security. Security’s quite a bit more hectic today. Today is the day that, I guess, the president will be addressing the General Assembly.

Clip of Donald Trump U.N. address: I’m not going to stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. Whoever wins A.I. — you have to remember this — wins.

To be honest, this is one of the things that I have found sort of daunting or troubling. I don’t know the answer. I think if it does take, say, seven years for the U.N. to put together an internationally agreed upon regulatory framework for A.I., then seven years from now we’ll be glad that we started now.

Yoshua Bengio in an interview with Gordon-Levitt: We need to move away from this model that all the companies are following, the same recipe that’s training A.I.s like we train animals: To seek rewards. Because that leads to these entities trying to cheat in order to obtain those rewards. Gordon-Levitt: They have to do that, because they’re profit-driven companies. Bengio: Yes. Gordon-Levitt: How can an A.I. be built without the profit incentive? Bengio: I think we should move into a world where that power is shared. Not in the hands of a few companies, or even just a few countries — because it’s too much power. Power-sharing changes the incentive structure that drives us currently into this crazy race — competition between companies, competition between countries. Once we say: OK, we share the power. And how do we do it? I mean, we need institutions for that, we need to move toward that — but if we don’t do it, someone is going to abuse that power and we’re all going to be suffering.

All right, it’s time to go. I just finished my last talk. But of course, there is one more question coming in. We’ve got the three dots right now — you want to show it? We’re waiting.

OK, here’s the question: Governments and technology companies clearly have work to do. But what about the rest of us?

Well, the midterms are coming up. We Americans have an extra responsibility because the frontier of this technology is being developed in our country. So a lot of the world — and I’m hearing from them here at the U.N. — a lot of the world is looking to see what we, as Americans, are going to do. What’s the signal that we are going to send our government in these next elections? And I hope we send a very clear one.
