SUMMARY

What boomer hasn’t heard, repeatedly, how mom and dad walked five miles to school, uphill in freezing rain while fighting off wolves — or some other hair-raising tale of toughness and deprivation? The question isn’t whether young adults today have it hard. The scramble to balance work, babies and bills becomes a season of being young, busy, useful and fully engaged — the very things older people miss most.

ARTICLE

Boomers Didn’t Always Have It So Easy
All generations think they drew the short straw; they’ve really shared the same challenges, just in different eras.
By Dan Kadlec
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/millennial-boomer-young-adult.html

What boomer hasn’t heard, repeatedly, how mom and dad walked five miles to school, uphill in freezing rain while fighting off wolves — or some other hair-raising tale of toughness and deprivation?

Then our turn came. Having learned exactly nothing, we told the kids stories from our own legendary childhoods: how we left home after breakfast in patched jeans on a banana bike, armed with 55 cents, and didn’t return until dusk. That allowance goes a long way when you mooch a PB&J at a friend’s house and dine on chips and a Milky Way. There’s even enough left for bubble gum.

Competitive suffering may be one of the few things generations reliably pass down. And in that sense, today’s young adults are building a mammoth bequest. They have excellent material. Housing is outrageously expensive, inflation persistent and health care increasingly unaffordable. There are fewer traditional tickets to the middle class in corporate management or in manufacturing. A.I. is eyeing their future earnings. It’s a compelling tale of economic adversity.

But here’s where my inner boomer — despite my best efforts to keep it quietly occupied with Wordle — starts clearing its throat. Hasn’t every generation faced what seemed like an unprecedented crisis in its 20s and 30s? We boomers — I was born in 1956 — certainly thought so. We came of age with the Vietnam War and the draft dividing the country, gasoline lines and stagflation. The homicide rate in 1980 was more than twice today’s. Hanging over all of us was the reassuring possibility of nuclear annihilation.

Somehow, we still found time to shop for lava lamps. And attend rock concerts, and yes, our music was better — don’t even go there.

Is life so much worse now? Or is every generation just convinced that it drew the short straw while editing out the parts where fortune delivered?

On a recent video call with my 30-something daughter-in-law, something about the scene felt oddly familiar. She was working from home on her laptop while my not-quite-a-toddler grandson sat contentedly nearby with his toys under her distracted supervision. Suddenly, I remembered a photo I snapped in 1995, with a film camera. There was my wife, Kim, about the same age, in her windowless home office, cutting deals using a cellphone with an antenna affixed, surrounded by a fax machine and file folders and a desktop computer the size of an Oldsmobile — all while balancing our youngest on her lap.

Different century, same chaos.

These like images tell me that maybe some of this is less a modern phenomenon than a life stage. The technology changes. The financial angst and vague sense that everyone else has figured out adulthood do not.

None of which means today’s young adults are imagining their predicament. Timing matters. Research has found that graduating into a severe recession such as 2007-9 can depress earnings for at least a decade compared with those of people who graduate during periods of prosperity.

Homeownership is traditionally the first rung on the wealth ladder, and it has been yanked up as higher prices, and now interest rates, have outrun young adult incomes. In 1985, the median new home cost 4.6 times the median annual earnings of a full-time worker aged 25 to 34. In 2025, it was seven times. Many young adults carry substantial student debt and face punishing costs for health care and child care, making the financial burden even greater. Career paths can feel less secure.

But — and I can practically hear myself aging as I type this — for most people, their 20s and 30s have never been the gravy years. They’re the years when expenses tend to arrive before income does, careers wobble, babies appear, and many of the older people you know seem to have had it made for decades.

The question isn’t whether young adults today have it hard. It’s whether they have it uniquely hard, or whether every generation, looking sideways at its parents instead of backward at what those parents endured at the same age, concludes that the game has been rigged against it.

Boomers made the same miscalculation. We compared ourselves with what our parents had achieved, not with what they had endured. For many of them, the included both the Great Depression and World War II. Stagflation seems less arduous a challenge in that company.

Nobody builds a hardship story around his or her advantages. Young people today have plenty. Boomers thought that color television and digital phones — freedom from rotary dialing — were technological leaps. Today my watch can take a call, measure my heart rate, give me directions and remind me I’m still 1,247 steps shy of my goal.

Cars are safer. Investing is easier. Education and training are available online. Remote work has opened the world to at-home job seekers. Try job hunting without Google, LinkedIn or Zoom. I had to scan newspaper want ads, print resumes on expensive paper, mail them into the void and wait for the phone to ring.

The phone was attached to the wall.

On the other hand, when we left the office, the office generally stayed there. Call that one a draw.

So, the message isn’t that young people should quit complaining. That would be both unfair and, coming from a boomer, almost self-parody. The message is simpler: Hardship and opportunity tend to arrive in the same package. We’re just better at noticing the hardship than, say, the largest intergenerational wealth transfer in American history tagged for millennials — if mom and dad don’t spend it all on home whole-body cryotherapy chambers and a personal longevity concierge.

The kids are all right. I have a few of my own. Some are pushing 40, so perhaps it’s time I stopped calling them kids. They’ll figure it out — not because the hurdles aren’t real, but because that’s what generations do. They complain, adapt, take some things for granted and eventually become the people with households full of stuff telling younger people how difficult everything used to be.

Will this familiar progression finally fail? I don’t think so. But the fixes won’t be easy. Defeating stagflation in the early 1980s was painful. The Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker drove short-term interest rates as high as 19 percent — my first mortgage was double-digit — helping set off two brutal recessions that claimed a lot of boomer jobs. It worked, though.

Today’s scourge is affordability, most visibly in housing. There will be no Volcker-like fix. We need at least a million more homes by some estimates, whatever the interest rate. That will require states, cities and towns — perhaps pushed by young voters — to make housing easier to build. The politics will be messy, the progress uneven. But eventually we will adapt, as generations do. Housing may reclaim its former role as an accessible wealth builder.

And then, as always, the hard years will start to glow. The cramped apartment becomes our first little place. The awful job becomes the place where I learned everything. The scramble to balance work, babies and bills becomes a season of being young, busy, useful and fully engaged — the very things older people miss most.

I can hear millennials in the future, right now. “You have no idea what life was like before A.I. We had to Google things ourselves. Cars had steering wheels. We had to stop texting and drive.”

Dan Kadlec writes Aging Without a License, a Substack newsletter about the lighter side of living, loving and loss.

ARTICLE

How Democrats Beat the Republican Money Machine
This week in politics: Which Democrats? And whose A.I. morals?
By Robert Siegel, E.J. Dionne Jr., Carlos Lozada and Vishakha Darbha
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/republicans-money-democrats-midterms.html

From the midterm elections to advances in artificial intelligence, there’s no dearth of political news this week. The Opinion contributor Robert Siegel joins the contributing writer E.J. Dionne Jr. and the columnist Carlos Lozada to discuss the role money plays in political campaigns, how the Democrats should proceed in November and whether A.I. has the ability to feel emotions.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Robert Siegel: This week on our plate: Democrats appear to be doing very well in the midterm elections. What are they selling, and why are people buying? And it’s hard for A.I. developers to figure out how to deal with their models morally. And now comes the question: Are the models capable of making moral decisions on their own? Can they learn morals? Can they feel hurt?

But first, the midterms, and one stunning measure of what’s happening this year.

Records for campaign funding and spending are being shattered. In August, The Times published a list of megadonors — just 20 of them — although some of them are pairs of people, whose combined contributions to various federal races is $1.2 billion. Most of them are Republican donors. Democrats are bracing for a big G.O.P. spending blitz in the last month. Considering all this, the Democrats are doing pretty well in the polls, and that raises the question: How important is money in politics? Do we overestimate that importance? Carlos?

Carlos Lozada: I have conflicting views on money in politics. First of all, it is extremely important. Money buys you name recognition. It may preclude you from running at all if you are someone who lacks the ability to raise sufficient funds. And money buys access to politicians, right? The views of donors inevitably get more attention in Washington. If either of you are “Star Trek” fans, it’s like Spock’s line, “The needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few.” It’s the other way around in Washington, when it comes to money, you know? The preferences of the few outweigh the needs of the many. So money can tilt the playing field, but it doesn’t guarantee that you win the game, right? If it did, Jeb Bush would have been the 2016 Republican nominee, not Donald Trump. Michael Bloomberg would have been the 2020 Democratic nominee.

Siegel: Hillary Clinton would have been the winner of the presidential election.

Lozada: And we’d be somewhere, reaching the halfway point of the Kamala Harris-Tim Walz administration right now. So money can help you amplify a message. It doesn’t substitute for a message. If you don’t have one that resonates with voters, money doesn’t fix the problem. It might even expose that problem even more. The last thing I’ll say on it is, there can be diminishing returns to, say, ad spending. There comes a point of just saturation, where I think voters have had enough and kind of tune it out. I was in Ohio a couple of weeks ago, and my God, was it hard to watch television when I’m just trying to watch a college football game, guys. And every commercial is an attack ad; and after a while, you just sort of start tuning out.

Siegel: Yeah. E.J.?

E.J. Dionne Jr.: I’m glad you started with the few, not the many, buying interest. I think that we should take a step back and say that the Supreme Court, beginning with Citizens United, really destroyed all the guardrails that we had on big money in politics. My friend and mentor in many ways Robert G. Kaiser, famous editor of The Washington Post, wrote a book back in 2009, called “So Damn Much Money,” about the influence of money in politics. And if he did a sequel, it would be “So Damn Much More Money.”

An analysis released just this past Wednesday, by Americans for Tax Fairness, found that 170 billionaire families had spent over $1.7 billion to influence the election. There’s just something wrong here. Among pure democracies, they don’t do it like this, and that influence matters. But as Carlos says, does it always matter?

I think historically what people said is you can be outspent two to three to one. As long as you’re in the game, you can compete. These elections are going to test that further, but I think we’re reminded that no matter how much advertising you put up, the product has to be something people want to buy. And what Republicans so far seem to be up against is a lot of people just resisting the product. Sabrina Tavernise had a great piece in The Times this week, where she quoted a former Republican state representative who gave, I think, the simplest answer to what’s going on. He said, “People are tired. The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.” And that exhaustion may yet overcome all this money, but I think it is going to tighten some of these races. We shouldn’t deny that it has some impact.

Siegel: But Carlos, with all respect to Mr. Spock and his formulation, have we simply become desensitized to a massively corrupt relationship between money and politics?

Lozada: I think that money in politics can be especially dangerous when you have a set of politicians, or an administration that has shown itself to be especially susceptible to the desire to enrich itself while in office. There’s also this amazing story that, I believe, ran just this week in The Wall Street Journal, about Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.

Siegel: Wasn’t she also with the governor of California before that?

Lozada: Prior. Yeah. You know, politics is a family business. And The Journal got hold of all these text messages between Guilfoyle and a Trump donor, where she’s essentially begging him to pay off her American Express bill.

Siegel: $100,000.

Lozada: And the line is: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” They really have all the receipts. And what you see is — aside from her messages where she’s telling him, “Do not say we have any arrangement. What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing” — there’s one moment when the donor responds and he says: “I have paid you $300,000 over the years. As of this memo, I have not received one favor. I am not naïve or a sucker. I need results.” And that captures so clearly, so blatantly, the quid pro quo expectations — why people donate money. “I need results.”

Siegel: Moving on. E.J., we talked the other week about how the midterms are likely to affect the Republicans in 2028. Let’s talk about the Democrats right now. Going by the polls, which admittedly can be very hazardous, Democrats are leading in states where they didn’t seem to have a chance. They’re competitive in places where they had been an endangered species. What are the Democrats selling so well, exactly?

Dionne: Well, as I mentioned, I think that the thing they’re selling most is a backlash against Trump, prices, and a war in Iran that is deeply unpopular, because it’s still not clear why we fought it.

Siegel: They’re selling who they are not.

Dionne: Well, right. And so, they are selling the thing you sell first in a midterm election, which is: You don’t like that guy in the White House; buy us. But I think, underlying here, there are a couple of big lessons. You’re seeing a lot of more moderate Democrats challenging in states, Kansas notably, where they haven’t elected someone in a long time. And so you’d say that’s an argument for moderation. But you’re also seeing an awful lot of Democrats, including moderate Democrats, running against concentrated economic power, big corporations, the power of billionaires and what and how that affects people’s lives.

And so, I’ve been thinking a lot about: The lesson of this election is what we need to move beyond. And our conversation partner for a long time, David Brooks, once made fun of me for being a beyond-ist, saying we need to move beyond this or that. Well, I’m a double beyond-ist in this election. I’m doubling down, I guess. Because I think, on the one hand, the Democrats need to move beyond the left-right fight in the party and say: Look, in order to win in a lot of places, you cannot be a left-wing Democrat. The word “socialist” doesn’t sell everywhere. And that a certain amount of care and moderation and understanding of who your constituents are is really important.

However, the left is right when it says that there is a lot of disaffection with the economy and about this inequality. The party has to find someone who can pull these messages together. But the other beyond is, I think the country so wants to get beyond this division, wants to get beyond where we are now, where we’re not solving any problems. And I think somebody who can move the country past this, who can plausibly make that argument. You’re seeing that in the campaign of James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas — both talk about trying to bring people together. And so, I think this double message comes out of this election and gives Democrats a potential road to not only a victorious message, but actually a substantively decent message.

Siegel: What do you think, Carlos?

Lozada: When I hear questions about the Democrats — Will the Democrats win back the Senate? How will the Democrats do? My question is always: Which Democrats are we talking about? Like, what version of the party? If there is a resounding Democratic victory next month, what version of the party will claim that victory?

What version will be able to use it as a governing mandate? Will it be the progressive wing, the D.S.A.-inflected wing, or will it be, as you mentioned, the Hamiltons in Kansas and Talaricos in Texas? That’s the key question leading into 2028, but also into your question of, what is it that they’re selling, because different people are selling different things. I think, regardless of how it turns out, and of which part of the party claims that mantle, there’s such a thing as overreading your victory. I think we’re seeing that with Trump right now. Donald Trump took his victory in 2024 to mean he could do whatever he wanted on immigration, on tariffs, foreign policy — and that has backfired massively.

Would a Democratic victory really mean an endorsement of Democratic priorities, or is it — as E.J. mentioned at the beginning — a repudiation of Donald Trump? Midterms are always a repudiation, or often a repudiation, of the party in power. Of course, people who win like to say elections have consequences, right? That was the famous Barack Obama line. But my corollary to that would be: Elections often have bizarre, unexpected consequences, even when you win. Just go back to 2022. People were thinking there might be a red wave. The opposite of today. And when there wasn’t — when the Democrats performed better than expected — that was read as some kind of victory for Joe Biden, for his agenda. It may have encouraged him to run again, despite worries over his age. And we all know how that turned out. So in some ways, I think you never really know exactly what an election means and what it’s going to lead to.

Dionne: You know, I think this is really important, and elections can be like Scripture. They can be read in many different ways, and people, partisans in various arguments, always read them as confirming whatever it was they thought going in. You saw that a lot in 2024: Why did Trump prevail? But Carlos’s comment on the nature of Democratic Party requires the obligatory reference to Will Rogers: “I’m not a member of an organized political party; I’m a Democrat.”

And the fact is that the Democratic Party is a very big coalition that is very hard to hold together — which is something each faction of the party has to remember. And so I think it’s a difficult line they have to walk, because the country really does seem to want substantial change from where we are. But that does not mean that the country has gone all ideological in one direction. Now, how do you square that circle?

Siegel: I do think what you said earlier is actually quite important; that there are people whom we call moderates, who are running in a way that during the Reagan and Bush presidencies, I think, was branded by Republicans as class warfare. If you keep on complaining about what the billionaires have got and how much rich people are getting away with, that’s divisive. It isn’t good for the country. And it seems that the line, the definition of moderation the way I hear it, has changed a bit to include some complaint about inequality in American life.

Dionne: One hundred percent. Although I think there was always class warfare on both sides, the Republicans wage class warfare against the educated class, and the Democrats did it against the moneyed class — and it was a clash of those two forms of class warfare. But absolutely right: You could argue that reality has moved to the left to some degree. And even some conservative economists I know acknowledge that rising inequality over the last 30 years is a fact and an important problem in the country. And so you have a lot of, yes, moderate Democrats speaking in class terms. Why? And I think, by the way, tech has brought that into relief because the tech folks are so wealthy, and have accumulated so much wealth, that this is an issue that sort of transcends ideology now. But you’re right. Class warfare, or at least an awareness of class inequality, is much more embedded in the conversation than it used to be.

Lozada: Yeah. Two thoughts on that: First, one of the things that has happened since that Reagan-Bush era attacks on class warfare by the Democrats is that you’ve had reality intervene in the form of the Great Recession. And that really, I think, crystallized for a lot of people what had been going on for a long time, which was the increase in inequality in both wealth and income in the United States. And so I think that, in a sense, has become a more mainstream concern that once would have been classified as a more extreme concern. The other thing I’ll say about that is that, in some ways, this is also a more palatable rebranding of the Democratic Party, away from what, say, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez would refer to as “Woke 1.” The culture war issues, on gender, on identity, on race. A.O.C. generated some headlines recently, when she said, “Woke 1 was crazy,” right? And this, I think, is Woke 2.

This is the far more focused attention on issues of economics, of class, of inequality, affordability that, in a sense, is a remaking of the party on issues that, because of that reality that has changed, seem much more palatable to the broad swath of voters.

Dionne: Of course, for the people who would recognize this, I don’t think it’s woke. I think it’s something that old Franklin Roosevelt and Harry Truman would recognize. And ——

Lozada: They were super woke, E.J.

Siegel: Long dormant.

Lozada: Reawakened.

Dionne: What all wings of the party actually agree on is that if Democrats don’t do better among working-class voters, they’re going to have a long-term problem. And so they argue about how to do it, but they all agree that they need bigger margins among the working class, not only to win, but to be able to govern.

Siegel: And just very briefly, a short-answer question: Is there some Democrat who stands out to you right now as looking like the person most likely to benefit from the results next month and become the party’s standard-bearer in 2028?

Dionne: My short answer is no. I don’t think it’s clear, at least to me. And I ask almost every Democrat I run into, “Who do you think is the person?” And more than at any time since I’ve been doing this, which is a long time, I don’t think I’ve ever heard so much uncertainty about who that person is. But if you ask the question: Who did himself the most good in this cycle so far? It’s probably Jon Ossoff. I think Ossoff has gotten attention and energy with his very focused attacks on corruption, and how he’s linked corruption to economic discontent. Assuming he wins by the margins people expect, I think he will emerge, certainly, as one of the big winners out of this election.

Siegel: From the very genuine intelligence of the two of you, onto artificial intelligence. And we are indebted to Times reporter Elizabeth Dias for a very thought-provoking piece on the interactions between the A.I. company Anthropic, in particular one of its founders, Christopher Olah, with religious thinkers representing many religious and philosophical traditions.

The questions they addressed are posed by what Anthropic technologists have come to see in the models that they have created. And just to give one example: Dias describes Olah as saying — and this isn’t a direct quotation of him, but her writing — But Mr. Olah believes that “if there is a chance the models experience suffering, the responsible thing is to avoid causing them harm.”

Carlos, you were especially struck by this story of people trying to implant morality into A.I. models, and first trying to figure out what morality is, exactly.

Lozada: This gets to the heart of the debate over what makes us human, what makes us distinct. It’s an extraordinary story, and it really does get into this question: Does this technology possess a consciousness of its own?

When people debate these issues, the term of art that is often used is “alignment,” right? Which, like every euphemism, is just terrific. It sounds kind of benign and neutral. If we just instill core human values into artificial intelligence, then things will be fine. We’ll be aligned. And whenever A.I. does something that looks dangerous or worrisome, it’s a misalignment incident. That’s how it’s described. The results from imperfect training. My question is: Aligned with what? Who has decided what the agreed-upon consensus is on human values and human behavior, and therefore what should be instilled in these programs? I don’t think we can leave that to agreements between the White House and tech companies — like the agreement that they signed just a few days ago. Anthropic is the company at the heart of the story, and Anthropic published a constitution for Claude, for its main A.I. program.

Siegel: Written by the in-house philosopher.

The company’s chief philosopher.

Lozada: Yes. And it embeds all these principles of safety and ethics and helpfulness for Claude. And if you read it, it treats Claude as this near-sentient being. It offers Claude advice on how to behave. It talks about its character and its nature. It expresses hope that Claude will genuinely care — that’s a quote about behaving in a way that is safe. I mean, I hope so too, right? I share this hope, but I think treating A.I. this way, hoping that it’ll care about our safety, is not a reassuring strategy. It’s an abdication of responsibility, and I think it’s kind of a corporate dodge.

Siegel: You mean, the more we acknowledge some separateness, that there’s a discrete entity that happens to be an A.I. model, the more we distance ourselves, its inventors, from responsibility for what it does.

Lozada: One me. That’s the answer.

Dionne: Everyone should read that story. It is a magnificent piece of work, and it drove me back to Genesis, where God says to Adam, “You are free to eat from any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will surely die.”

And I thought, oh my goodness, is A.I. the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? Now, for scientific rationalists out there: I am not saying that Genesis predicted A.I., but it does remind you, and this story did — this very scary thing about whether human beings are creating a technology with almost godlike qualities. Because what’s really striking about A.I. is it’s unlike other machines. Machines could replace aspects of human action, human labor. But this technology is gobbling up all human knowledge, all the work done by human beings over a long period of time. Philosophy, theology, novels — it’s all going into these models with the idea that they literally are superhuman. And that’s very scary. And the notion that these beings, these agents have consciousness — first of all, playing to type, maybe they should form a union. But this terrible error of thinking that an algorithm can have consciousness, that an algorithm can be a human being.

Both Carlos and I were talking about Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical. There were so many great lines in there about what it means to be human. Perhaps because I make many errors, I particularly like this line. He said, “For an algorithm, an error is a flaw to be corrected; for a person, however, an error can be a catalyst for profound change.” Insisting on a line between human beings and this technology, I think, is so important going forward.

Siegel: I’m glad that you raised the papal encyclical, in which Pope Leo XIV, who has a mathematics degree, is unusually well-suited for this debate. And he was much more concerned about the workers who would lose their jobs because of this technology, and with it, their dignity. Speaking up for the dignity of work doesn’t seem to be fitting, jibing easily, with Anthropic and the others.

Lozada: It’s interesting. Pope Leo XIV came of age in his formation, in kind of the post-Second Vatican Council, Catholic Church. He learned about liberation theology. And if you read his encyclical, which is called “Magnifica Humanitas” — magnificent humanity, right?

It is imbued in that kind of culture of the social doctrine of the church. And part of that is why he comes out swinging against this whole idea of alignment. \

He worries that what he calls “technocratic thinking” is going to dominate, because technology takes on the characteristics of those who devise it, who finance it, who regulate it. He also really, really dislikes the idea of anthropomorphizing technology. He says that the A.I. do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, nor do they have a moral conscience.

And yet, the Claude Constitution attributes almost all those things to Claude. It says we can’t ignore the potential moral status of the A.I. models. They may have some functional version of emotions. So if you take personality and self-perception, emotion and agency, I wouldn’t be surprised if legal personhood is what follows. That seems to be the logic at play here.

Siegel: And again, the legal personality for the model is, once again, insulation for the designer of the model.

Dionne: The Supreme Court created a precedent when it declared “corporations are people,” so why not a bot? I think everything you said, Carlos — which is really profound — is why there is so much uneasiness that is beginning to seep into the election conversation that we had earlier, about this technology. And whenever someone is critical of a technology, they’re accused of being a Luddite. You know, progress is inevitable. You’ve got to embrace it. And I don’t think any of us wants to be a Luddite in that sense. And Pope Leo XIV, by the way, is not. In that encyclical, he talks about potential gains from this technology. But people are genuinely petrified about the social impact of this, because they know, as these companies are kind of admitting now, that they themselves don’t fully understand what they are creating; that they may lose control of what they are creating.

And so, the desire to slow down and maybe think a little about what we’re doing, I think permeates the public reaction to this. And maybe this is one good thing. I think some of this backlash — or even better said, just quiet concern — does transcend the ideological categories in the country right now. And I’m reluctant to predict this because such predictions never turn out. This may be an occasion for us to sit down and forget our labels for a little bit and say, “What are we doing here?”

Lozada: I think part of the backlash to data centers — that is, a bipartisan backlash — is a tangible way to oppose something that, in some ways, feels so intangible and so difficult to understand. The debate over consciousness reminds me of this terrific novel from the ’50s, “A Canticle for Leibowitz.” Have you read it?

Dionne: Oh, what a wonderful book.

Lozada: Walter Miller Jr., I believe, is the writer. And it’s all about this tension between technology and politics and faith. But there’s a great moment when a skeptic and an abbot are talking, and the skeptic talks about his uncertainty over whether he even has a soul. And the abbot says: No, no, no — wait a second, doctor. You don’t have a soul. You are a soul. You have a body temporarily.

And the skeptic is like: Oh, that’s just semantic confusion. And the abbot is like: Yes, it probably is, but which one of us is confused here?

I think we’re in that moment right now, where we’re trying to discern body, soul, faith, reason.

Dionne: You are the soul of thoughtfulness, and I am so glad you raised that book because I had not thought of it until you said it — how relevant that is to this conversation.

Siegel: I just wanted to note, I was especially struck by the remark of a rabbi — Navon, an Orthodox rabbi or scholar who was part of this discussion that Anthropic organized — and he didn’t believe that the models had consciousness. But he told Anthropic: If you do believe that, then you’re advocating slavery. You want to create beings whom you regard as having soul or consciousness and human attributes and abuse them, abuse their labor.

It’s been a wonderful discussion. And as we end every discussion, I’d like to ask both of you — E.J., starting with you — some source of joy in your life recently.

Dionne: You know, Robert, when we started doing this 13 months ago, my joy was the fact that our daughter Julia had married a wonderful person, named Devin Stein, and they are still happily married. And I am now going full circle because my joy this week is that, at the beginning of the month, our son James got married to Kate Applegate, an absolutely wonderful woman we love, at a great ceremony where her parents, her brother Gray, joined our family, and it was really spectacular. And at the risk of being mushy for the tough-minded, smart readers, I want to say that what you can’t replicate is seeing your own three kids love each other so much, and to have your family grow in this way, really in such a spirit of love. And it was just a great event.

Siegel: Carlos?

Lozada: Congratulations. That sounds wonderful. I love that that’s where you went, E.J., because I’m also going to share something that is about family and about these big transition moments. It’s joy tinged with a little bit of sadness because our oldest son has gone off to college. And this is the first of our kids to do that. And he is so happy to be there, jumping into dorm life and his classes. And we’re the ones left with his empty room. So I’m sad at his absence, but I’m so happy for him. And at the same time, it’s a reminder that, really, parenting from the first moment you hold your child is about preparing them to leave you. And also, even with the tinge of sadness, I feel joyful at the new stage that our own relationship is going to embark upon, because as he really comes into his own as an adult, our relationship will evolve as well.

Dionne: These are perfect because my story says the joy doesn’t stop when these big transitions happen.

Siegel: Well, for me, this time I just wanted to add, in addition to some very nice time with family, also a very interesting play that my wife and I went to see called “The Score,” which the Shakespeare Theater Company in Washington, D.C., has brought over from London. And it’s an imagining of what went on when Johann Sebastian Bach met with Frederick the Great. Frederick the Great, who ruled with an iron fist, but presumably had at least some hand made of something more pliant, because he played the flute, and extremely well. And it’s a play about the authority of art and musical genius versus the authority of political strength and political power. And I found it a very fascinating and joyful day at the theater, and look forward to more.

Lozada: I went to see that as well last Friday. And of course, the lead is the great Brian Cox. Best known to many of this generation for playing Logan Roy in “Succession.” I found it a similarly captivating experience.

Dionne: I know what I have to do soon. Thank you.

Siegel: Carlos Lozada and E.J. Dionne, thanks again so much. Great to see you guys.

Dionne: Thank you.

Lozada: Thanks, Robert.

SUMMARY

Re “Writing Isn’t as Important as We Think,” by Joe Cruz, a professor at Williams College (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 1): As a Williams alumna, as well as a novelist, I was disappointed with Professor Cruz’s argument that writing isn’t as important to students as most of us think. Joe Cruz has a low opinion of writing.

ARTICLE

Why Should Students Write? Let Us Count the Ways.
Readers respond to a philosophy professor’s essay that argued for less emphasis on writing in the college classroom.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-10 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/writing-thinking-students.html

To the Editor:

Re “Writing Isn’t as Important as We Think,” by Joe Cruz, a professor at Williams College (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 1):

As a Williams alumna, as well as a novelist, I was disappointed with Professor Cruz’s argument that writing isn’t as important to students as most of us think.

Engaging fully in the writing process is, and should remain, a central tenet of liberal arts education. Why? Because it is hard. Perseverance is the point. Guiding a piece of writing from a bad first draft into a polished final product is a difficult but meaningful exercise for the mind.

My favorite professor at Williams, the great American short story writer Jim Shepard, said that drafting a written piece was like combing very tangled hair. It is slow going. You get stuck, trapped in snarls, but with patience and grit, you gradually make the hair smooth.

Now, here is a professor guiding his students to hand over the comb to the robot that will do the pesky detangling work for them.

This is poor advice. Yes, this knotty process helps us master the art of writing. But it also teaches us a much more important lesson: Frustration, pushing ourselves to the edge of failure, is the very thing that crafts us into strong, capable people.

By all means, cede a majority of the writing process to A.I. Choose the easy path. But don’t tell us that the difficult one wasn’t worth much after all.

Lauren Edmondson Herndon, Va.

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz argues in his essay against a claim that nobody is likely to make — that students learn to think only by writing. Surely, all would agree that thinking is also aided by reading, listening and discussing.

The philosophical passage he cites that criticizes writing is from Plato, arguably the greatest of all philosophical writers. You might as well find a line from Shakespeare dismissing the importance of playwriting.

Professor Cruz notes that he doesn’t teach from prepared scripts. That observation, however, hardly implies that writing is unimportant. After all, his professorial role involves extensive writing.

Eventually, Professor Cruz admits that writing is an essential life skill, but he says nothing about how he teaches his students to write effectively. Or does he? He equates writing and archiving. Note, though, that his essay seeking to persuade is written.

Even Abraham Lincoln, one of our greatest orators and literary stylists, read the Gettysburg Address from a written script.

Steven M. Cahn Old Greenwich, Conn. The writer is a professor emeritus of philosophy at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and the author of “Towards Teaching Philosophy.”

To the Editor:

As a former journalist turned entrepreneur who has long considered writing a strength, I’ve spent a lot of time wondering what A.I. will do to the craft.

I also have a high-achieving 10-year-old with dysgraphia, which for her manifests primarily as difficulty with spelling. Too often, that gets misconstrued by grade-school teachers as an inability to write or construct an organized argument. The result is that she can become reluctant to use her robust vocabulary or fully engage in writing assignments.

I’ve told her that the art of writing is really about formulating an argument, supporting it with evidence and, hopefully, engaging an audience enough so that it wants to listen.

That’s why I was so heartened by this essay and its argument for other ways to demonstrate knowledge. Quite honestly, it also reflects how most of us communicate in the working world. How many of us are regularly writing formal papers in the field or the boardroom to make a point?

Lindsay Stewart New York

To the Editor:

Reading Joe Cruz’s essay made me suspect he lacks knowledge about being an introvert. Besides needing downtime alone to recharge, introverts often need extra time for reflection and to formulate thoughts, and we do this best away from the clamor of others.

In small seminars at Wellesley College, I learned a lot from students batting ideas back and forth, and occasionally I thought quickly enough to get a word in edgewise. But for the thorniest issues, I have always done my best thinking on my own and with paper and pencil, still my best tools.

I have worked as a journalist and written children’s books. And I have led workshops for writers — in mental hospitals, jails and writing programs — where the mantra is “We write to discover what we think.”

Mary Carpenter Washington

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz has a low opinion of writing. The philosophy professor believes that conversation and debate are what best reveal deep thought, whereas writing is really “archiving” — a storage function — or “scaffolding,” a trifling utility. Elsewhere he states that writing “summarizes and compresses our thoughts,” as if it’s a zip-file option. He’s wrong.

Many smart and creative people over the years have observed that writing is thinking. Not separate from or duplicative of, but actually integral to it. As Joan Didion noted in 1976, for example, “I don’t know what I think until I write it down.”

That’s because you can’t efficiently generate, develop, organize, expand or ruminate on your ideas unless you’re committing them to the page. Even people with extraordinary memories require composition to construct deeper thoughts — not because they couldn’t remember three things, or 30, but because the process of writing necessitates the process of thinking.

Articulation requires cogitation. Or to use another metaphor, writing isn’t the frosting atop dessert; it’s the whole cake.

Joe Hayden Memphis

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz’s article on A.I. and writing in the college classroom showed a disappointing level of reasoning on two counts.

First, from my vantage as a longtime dual-enrollment college writing instructor, Professor Cruz seems blithely unaware of the scale at which most college teaching is done. He suggests 45-minute oral exam periods for a final. At the moment, I teach 90 writing students; if I followed his method, conducting finals would take 67 hours!

Professor Cruz does not mention the extent of his teaching schedule, but I suggest he more seriously consider the demands placed on the adjuncts and other typical instructors who do the majority of teaching. His system isn’t tenable when delivering instruction at scale, and the majority of college teachers (maybe not department chairs like him) are delivering at scale.

Second, I’m surprised at the professor’s use of Plato’s “Phaedrus.” Interpreting Plato always requires the reader to see the ironic, dramatic distance between Socrates, the character in Plato’s dialogues, and Plato himself, the thinker and writer. Plato chose writing to capture his thoughts. The Socratic criticism of writing in “Phaedrus” should be considered, but only as a criticism that Socrates’ best student, Plato, chose not to adopt.

William Hughes Charlottesville, Va.

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz cites Plato’s hostility to writing in support of his argument. Of course, Plato didn’t have access to studies documenting important changes in brain functioning associated with writing.

On the other hand, we should have taken his warnings concerning the vulnerability of democracies to demagogues much more seriously.

Thomas W. Allen Chesterfield, Mo. The writer is an emeritus associate professor of education at Washington University in St. Louis.

SUMMARY

Mary Tsingou arrived at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory in 1952, seven years after the testing facility in New Mexico helped propel the world into an age of nuclear proliferation. As Los Alamos continued to serve as a leader in Cold War scientific research, Ms. Tsingou was disappointed that her first task was to input simple math equations on a calculator. Instead, her name was placed in a footnote: “We thank Miss Mary Tsingou for efficient coding of the problems and for running the computations on the Los Alamos MANIAC machine.”

ARTICLE

Mathematician Who Waited 50 Years for Proper Credit for Her Work Has Died
At the Los Alamos National Laboratory, Mary Tsingou Menzel’s computer programming helped set the stage for chaos theory and other fields.
By Ama Sarpomaa
Published 2026-10-10 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/science/mary-tsingou-menzel-dead.html

Mary Tsingou arrived at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory in 1952, seven years after the testing facility in New Mexico helped propel the world into an age of nuclear proliferation. She was a recent college graduate with a mathematics degree and joined the cohort — almost all women — of “human computers.”

As Los Alamos continued to serve as a leader in Cold War scientific research, Ms. Tsingou was disappointed that her first task was to input simple math equations on a calculator. “It was pretty boring sitting there doing addition and subtraction,” she recalled in 2020 to a publication of the federal research lab.

But Ms. Tsingou was soon given the opportunity to work as an early programmer of MANIAC I, the lab’s first fully electronic computer. Her coding work — translating equations into the MANIAC-approved language of holes punched on tape — led to the creation in 1955 of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) problem, named after the men who worked on the numerical experiment.

When the report was published, Ms. Tsingou was not listed as an author. Instead, her name was placed in a footnote: “We thank Miss Mary Tsingou for efficient coding of the problems and for running the computations on the Los Alamos MANIAC machine.”

“They didn’t know anything about programming,” she told The Los Alamos publication. “They set up the equations, and I did all the programming.”

The groundbreaking computational physics experiment observed surprising physical behaviors that propelled the development of nonlinear science, one of whose branches is chaos theory — an influential way of thinking about how subtle changes to the initial state of a complex system can eventually lead to wildly unpredictable outcomes. It offered scientists a new way of exploring the physical world, by showing, for the first time, the power of the computer to investigate phenomena too complex to visualize by hand or with traditional experiments.

Ms. Tsingou (later Menzel), who spent her nearly 40-year career as a programmer at what became Los Alamos National Laboratory, died on Aug. 27 at her home in Los Alamos. She was 97. Her death was confirmed by her daughter Ann Menzel.

The original MANIAC — an acronym for “Mathematical Analyzer, Numerical Integrator and Computer” — was seven feet high, nine feet wide, weighed 1,000 pounds and was fitted with about 3,000 vacuum tubes. It could make upward of 10,000 calculations per second, dramatically superior to computing by hand.

Through a series of trials, Ms. Tsingou and her fellow operators became so familiar with the computer that they could identify and address issues with code by ear. But the technology was so new that they were forced to “invent their way out of problems,” said Nicholas Lewis, a lab historian at Los Alamos.

“You had to use what the machine recognized, which was only ones and zeros,” Ms. Tsingou said of the laborious task of programming the MANIAC. “We typed the directions on a tape and put it in the machine.”

Her first exercise while learning to work with the hums and blinks of the primitive computer was to find the sine of an angle. After poring over her work for some time — computing, coding, checking and rechecking — she finally punched the tape.

“It worked immediately!” she said in a 2002 oral history interview with the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers.

She was invited to program an experiment for the mathematician Stanislaw Ulam and the physicists John Pasta and Enrico Fermi as they brainstormed ways to use the MANIAC to explore theories they couldn’t easily compute by hand.

They decided to observe the computationally simulated motion of a line of particles connected by springs, similar to a vibrating string. Their expectation was simple: When prompted, springs would cause energy to be shared throughout the entire system, resulting in random movement patterns.

But when Ms. Tsingou plotted the data she pulled from the MANIAC on to charts and graphs, the system appeared to vibrate in structured ways, periodically returning to its initial configuration. This revealed, numerically, that there can be hidden patterns in the motion of dynamically rich, or “nonlinear,” systems.

The revelation from the FPU problem strongly influenced how scientists and mathematicians study the multitude of nonlinear systems in our world, including how our heart beats, how the economy sometimes functions and how complex weather patterns behave.

Her programming work, physicists say, would make her a co-author today, because programmers are charged with writing the computable code that scientists need to run simulations they design. But fuller credit was not provided until Thierry Dauxois, a French physicist, championed her contributions in a 2008 article in Physics Today titled “Fermi, Pasta, Ulam, and a Mysterious Lady.”

“Her programming of a 1950s computer was not a trivial task,” he wrote. “Why has her contribution received only a two-line acknowledgment?”

Soon afterward, the problem became more widely known as Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou. And despite the intriguing headline in the Physics Today story, she told The Los Alamos Monitor, a local newspaper, that she was far from “mysterious.”

Mary Tsingou, the younger of two daughters, was born to Greek immigrant parents in Milwaukee on Oct. 14, 1928. The Tsingous moved during the Depression to Bulgaria, where they had property, before returning to Milwaukee in 1940, soon after the start of World War II.

Her father, Thomas Tsingou, was a factory worker, and her mother, Anastasia Koutsouyianni, had only a second-grade education. Her parents spoke Greek at home, and it was well into their childhoods before Mary and her sister, Sally, had fluency in English.

Back in Milwaukee public schools, the daughters were so behind in English that they were initially held back several grades — yet both were so strong in math that they were soon able to resume education at grade level.

In 1951, Mary Tsingou received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Wisconsin with the intent of becoming a high-school math teacher.

In her oral history, she said school jobs were sparse for women, because male veterans returning from the Korean War were given priority. She learned that Los Alamos was hiring women to do hand computing, which was considered a clerical job mostly reserved for women. She and the others in her cohort were informed that they would be paid less than the men doing the same work.

She temporarily left Los Alamos to work on a master’s degree in mathematics and received her diploma from the University of Michigan in 1955. Over the years, her mathematical and code-writing skills were used in thermonuclear research and for the Strategic Defense Initiative, the Reagan-era antimissile system popularly known as Star Wars.

In 1958, she married Joseph Menzel, who worked in security at Los Alamos. He died in 2022. In addition to Ann, she is survived by another daughter, Carol Menzel; eight grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.

Reflecting on her career, Ms. Menzel said in the Los Alamos lab publication that she was not bothered by being left out of the 1955 experiment’s original name, Fermi-Pasta-Ulam.

“I was just doing the job,” she said. “I was glad to get paid.”

will-we-ever-understand-dementia.html

SUMMARY

The story of the science of dementia began on an autumn day in 1891, when a 71-year-old man was admitted to the psychiatric hospital at the University of Prague. And yet, in a sense, we understand little more about the plaques and tangles of Alzheimer’s disease than we did 120 years ago, when Alois Alzheimer first noticed them. Whether you called it senility or Alzheimer’s, you were denying something essential and subtle about dementia that researchers took years to understand — something Pick and Alzheimer both knew: Dementia is not just one thing.

ARTICLE

Will We Ever Understand Dementia?
Since the days of Dr. Alzheimer himself, there has been a dream that severe senility might have an explanation — and a cure. The search for both has never been more urgent.
By Robert Kolker
Published 2026-10-10 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/science/will-we-ever-understand-dementia.html

The story of the science of dementia began on an autumn day in 1891, when a 71-year-old man was admitted to the psychiatric hospital at the University of Prague. The man, referred to as August H. in his medical file, had periods of freezing up mentally, sometimes fainting and not coming to for several minutes. More recently, he had been prone to fits of rage, and even threatened his wife with a knife, shouting that he was going to kill her.

The case caught the attention of the director of the clinic, Arnold Pick. After August H. died, Pick’s team examined his brain, dividing it into sections and weighing them and checking for abnormalities. The brain seemed essentially normal except for signs of decay, or atrophy, in one self-contained place: the left temporal lobe.

This was quite likely the first recorded moment that a scientist, staring at a piece of brain tissue, saw dementia as a problem to be understood and solved, rather than a natural, unavoidable part of aging. Until then, almost everyone, including Pick himself, had taken it as an article of faith that dementia, or senility, was a generalized condition, the sign of a brain in overall decline. But after seeing August H.’s brain, Pick began to search for and document other dementia cases in which the problem wasn’t aging, but this specific part of the brain that was starting to lose function and misfire.

His observations might have fallen into obscurity had they not come to the attention of one of his counterparts in Germany — Alois Alzheimer.

Pick’s clinic, in Prague, existed far from Germany’s well-known neurology centers. But Alzheimer was plugged in to a community of cutting-edge researchers in Frankfurt and, later, Munich, specialists in microscopy and histology who could analyze sections of a brain under a microscope by staining the samples on glass slides.

While Pick’s consequential patient was August H., Alzheimer’s was a woman named Auguste D. She arrived at the Frankfurt hospital where Alzheimer worked in 1901, when she was only 51 years old. Out of nowhere, it seemed, she had flown into fits of jealousy toward her husband, then suffered a rapid loss of memory. She got lost in her own apartment, carried things back and forth incessantly and then hid them, and became convinced someone was trying to kill her. After she died in 1906, Alzheimer found something strange in her brain cells, which he examined under a microscope.

In the center of an otherwise almost normal cell, Alzheimer noticed “one or several fibrils,” or what we now call tangles, and in the cell’s outer layers he saw “numerous small miliary foci,” or what are now called plaques. “All in all,” Alzheimer concluded in a 1907 paper, “we have to face a peculiar disease process.”

The plaques and tangles identified by Alzheimer remain the most compelling and mysterious aspects of what we now call Alzheimer’s disease. On a slide, under a microscope, the plaques (later found to be made of a protein called beta-amyloid) looked like little blotches, darker in the center and wispier on the edges. The tangles (now known to be proteins called tau) looked like little curly threads that interwove, bundled together and bunched up in any number of ways. To Alzheimer, these plaques and tangles seemed like interlopers, clogging the cells of a brain and causing disease, though he had no evidence that this was really the case; he could only compare them with the brains of people who had died without brain disorders, which were free from these intrusions. Alzheimer didn’t know how the plaques and tangles had gotten into those brain cells, why they were there, how to get rid of them or even whether anyone should try.

Today dementia is estimated to affect more than 55 million people worldwide, and nearly 10 million cases are added every year. By 2050 — as populations age and the power of diagnosis improves — that number is projected to rise as high as 139 million. We’re already on our way to becoming a society of caregivers, looking after an aging population unable to support itself.

And yet, in a sense, we understand little more about the plaques and tangles of Alzheimer’s disease than we did 120 years ago, when Alois Alzheimer first noticed them. In recent years, we may have even lost ground. A decades-long consensus about the meaning of those plaques and tangles has collapsed as treatments built on those theories have failed, reopening what now must be understood as one of the most urgent unsolved problems in medical science: What is dementia, and how can we possibly slow its advance and reduce its terrible toll?

From the start, Alzheimer’s disease had a very fluid definition. Alois Alzheimer’s second major patient, known as Johann F., had only plaques in his brain, no tangles. If Alzheimer’s was a single disease, why did affected brains often look so different from one another? And there remained the question of the cases Pick had been collecting. In 1911, Alzheimer re-examined two of Pick’s cases and found something very different between plaques and tangles: tiny spherical orbs, clear with spots in the middle that would later be called Pick bodies.

As a diagnosis, Pick’s disease — now classified as a form of frontotemporal dementia, or FTD — was as elusive as Alzheimer’s. “Each case suggests new problems,” the German psychiatrist Anton von Braunmühl said in 1928. And even if scientists wanted to further investigate these new diseases, there was no way to diagnose them with certainty before patients died, much less provide a cure.

This sense of futility was not the only reason that little progress was made. This was the age of Freud, with neurology upstaged by psychoanalysis; in sanitariums and hospitals and clinics, brain science was becoming passé. But as the century progressed, the human race, at least in the wealthy world, was experiencing something revolutionary. Thanks in large part to the development of antibiotics to fight life-threatening bacterial infections, the average life span was increasing. And as humans lived longer, many more of them were developing problems with memory and cognition.

Finally, a growing number of neurologists started to suggest a paradigm shift. Why should dementia be seen as a natural inevitability of aging? Why couldn’t it, one day, be cured?

In 1976, a neurologist named Robert Katzman published an article in Archives of Neurology titled “The Prevalence and Malignancy of Alzheimer Disease: A Major Killer,” in which he argued that the distinction between garden-variety senility and Alzheimer’s disease — which, for decades, was considered a rare condition — ought to be dropped entirely. If most of the world’s millions of dementia cases were recategorized as Alzheimer’s, Katzman wrote, the disease would automatically qualify as the fourth or fifth most common cause of death in America.

In one elegant semantic flourish, the scientific community had a new nemesis — a medical menace, like cancer or heart disease, to obsess over and build entire systems of research and drug development around. The campaign worked. By the 1980s, “Alzheimer’s” had become a household word. Alzheimer’s disease became neuroscience’s public enemy No. 1. Between 1976 and 1989, the National Institute on Aging’s annual budget for Alzheimer’s research surged to $222 million from about $20 million.

But once this new war on Alzheimer’s was underway, there were unintended consequences. Nearly every dementia disorder was now assumed to be Alzheimer’s — and since there was still no test for Alzheimer’s, other than an autopsy, how could you prove any doctor wrong? Misdiagnosis became something close to the norm. In one 1993 study, 18 of 21 patients found to have a rarer type of dementia had first been wrongly thought to have Alzheimer’s.

The scientific community had traded one gross generalization for another. Whether you called it senility or Alzheimer’s, you were denying something essential and subtle about dementia that researchers took years to understand — something Pick and Alzheimer both knew: Dementia is not just one thing.

By the 1990s, two camps had emerged: Those who blamed the tau protein for Alzheimer’s were nicknamed tauists, and those who considered the beta-amyloid protein to be the culprit were called baptists. The debate between the tauists and baptists became one of the most prominent story lines of neuroscience — even as the baptists had clearly taken the lead. In 1991, the geneticist John Hardy and his colleagues isolated a mutation in a gene that produces the so-called amyloid precursor protein in people with Alzheimer’s. That was good enough for most of those in the field to become born-again baptists: Most researchers and pharmaceutical companies went all in on attacking the beta-amyloid protein. Their case was strengthened in the late 1990s when two more genetic mutations, known as presenilin and APOE, seemed to confirm the connection.

After that, the baptist consensus locked in, and the funding spigot turned on. Developing a new neurodegenerative drug through Phase 3 clinical trials can cost upward of $2 billion. And this wasn’t just one drug. Over several decades, the pharmaceutical industry has sunk easily tens of billions of dollars into drugs targeting amyloid proteins, all with little effect. Other approaches were crowded out — not just in the pharma world, but in academia, which needs pharma support to get results. Generations of researchers experienced that chilling effect directly.

“If you worked on tau, they would kill your career and you would wind up not getting funded,” said Dr. John Crary, a neuropathologist who runs the brain bank at Mount Sinai Medical Center. “You would wind up at the V.A., or worse, in Worcester — not at Harvard, right?”

The consensus around amyloid turned any other attack on dementia into a sideshow. Tau tangles were considered at best a secondary aftereffect and, at worst, an “artifact” — the word scientists use to describe something they think doesn’t matter at all.

In the late 1990s, when three different research teams successfully linked FTD to the MAPT gene that produces tau, the baptist camp didn’t back down. Instead, they argued that because amyloid seemed to show up first in the brain, tau must be a sign of the final stages of Alzheimer’s disease. Tau is the bullet, one saying went, but amyloid is the gun. Without a gun, the murder can’t happen.

And yet, every year someone seemed to identify a new tau-related brain condition: many cases of FTD, dementia with Lewy bodies, corticobasal degeneration, argyrophilic grain disease, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, atypical forms of Parkinson’s disease, certain strains of A.L.S. The overproduced protein in these conditions is tau.

Gun or no gun, the bullet seemed to be doing just fine on its own.

Slowly, the importance of non-Alzheimer’s cases became undeniable. In the 1980s, Alzheimer’s was assumed to be 85 percent of all dementias. But that percentage has been nose-diving ever since. Dr. Crary quoted Dr. Rusty Hays, a prominent neuropathologist, whom he once heard say: “It used to be easy — you saw plaques and tangles and you were done. It was Alzheimer’s.” Those days are over.

The amyloid camp did score a victory when the Food and Drug Administration approved lecanemab, a drug infusion that showed evidence of removing amyloid plaques from the brain; a second, similar drug, called donanemab, followed. The trouble was, the positive results of these drugs were so marginal — and the risks so considerable, including brain swelling and bleeding — that researchers became divided on whether they ought to be celebrating at all. The most shocking reversal came from one of the forefathers of the amyloid hypothesis, Dr. John Hardy.

“When we found amyloid mutations, I thought, and the field thought, that sorting out amyloid was to sort out dementia,” Dr. Hardy said in 2022. “We do not think that anymore.”

For the last six years, a convention space in a major city somewhere on the globe has attracted hundreds of attendees of the Tau Global Conference, an international gathering of scientists and drug developers focused on disorders of the tau gene. Dozens of papers are presented over several days, and the venue’s hallways are packed with several hundred placards displaying the most recent tau-related research findings, battling a dozen or more different conditions where tau is implicated: Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, FTD, A.L.S. and even traumatic brain injury and chronic traumatic encephalopathy.

After decades of being passed over, tau, here at least, is the belle of the ball. More than half a dozen teams are working on tau-reducing drugs now, with the earliest results showing hope for slowing the symptoms of dementia. But just as tau is having its moment, it might be time to call off the debate entirely.

In the wake of the collapse of the amyloid hypothesis, there’s a renewed drive to understand not just tau, but a wealth of other factors in the development of dementia. Two more proteins, TDP-43 and alpha-synuclein, are now connected with late-in-life memory loss and cognitive decline, respectively, for people with Alzheimer’s and even those without Alzheimer’s. “I don’t think anyone, even the most fervent, would tell you that if you could just get the right amyloid lowering you will cure this,” said Dr. Bruce Miller, director of the Memory and Aging Center at the University of California, San Francisco.

Going after so many different proteins calls for stopping the mutated genes that are overproducing those proteins. (CRISPR is one option among many possible gene therapies, all of which face the challenge of safely getting past the blood-brain barrier, the membrane that protects the brain from outside infections.) The gene called APOE offers the clearest genetic biomarker for hereditary risk for Alzheimer’s; researchers are focused on finding ways to manipulate that gene to help stop the disease in its tracks. Other gene therapies could bolster or trigger our immune systems to help the body clear out proteins that would otherwise clump up in the brain.

Beyond Alzheimer’s, people are living so long now that it isn’t uncommon to die with two or even three different neurodegenerative conditions. Once these conditions can be accurately predicted with biomarkers, many foresee the day when there could be a precision-medicine approach for dementia, tailoring treatments to each patient’s specific genetic issues the way that many cancers are treated now. Patients with high amyloid or tau or TDP-43 numbers could receive treatments the same way patients take statins for high cholesterol.

Above all, the acknowledgment of the genetic nuance in dementia is fueling a slightly more sober sense of optimism than the fervor of the baptists and tauists. A recent overview of the Alzheimer’s literature in the journal Cell offers “hope for a future where AD is not only treatable but also preventable,” while still acknowledging the condition’s “complex pathologic underpinnings.”

This, after all, was Arnold Pick’s insight: that dementia is many things. What if we could nip these complex problems in the bud genetically, before the crippling health care costs and heartbreaking losses — before the ones we love lose much of what makes them who they are?

“With the gene carriers, you can get in very early, maybe even before any age-related change is happening, any pathology is present at all,” Dr. Miller said. “I think it’s going to be a really huge decade. We’re just beginning.”

A Senator Facing Re-Election Settles a Bakery Bill, 6 Years Later
Senator Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican in a difficult race, paid an old campaign debt for cookies, muffins and brownies after a baker’s story went viral online.
By Tim Balk
Published 2026-10-11 02:33 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/us/politics/marshall-kansas-baker-bill-senate-midterms.html

Senator Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, has faced a series of challenges in his unexpectedly close race for re-election.

The latest: A six-year-old unpaid bill for 150 frosted sugar cookies, 100 mini strawberry muffins and 100 fudge brownies, posted online by an angry baker.

The bill, the baker wrote in a social media post that quickly went viral on Thursday, was from Mr. Marshall’s primary night watch party in 2020. The cookies’ buttercream frosting carried his name in blue and yellow. And the source of her frustration was that Mr. Marshall’s 2020 campaign had never paid her the nearly $700 she said it owed her.

On Saturday, Mr. Marshall wrote on social media that he had paid the bill, bringing more attention to a curious saga that his opponent’s campaign had seized on.

The bill began gaining widespread notice on Thursday afternoon, after the baker, Holly Thomas of Hutchinson, Kan., wrote an eight-paragraph Facebook post.

“Six years later, I haven’t forgotten,” she wrote, recalling that repeated phone and email inquires seeking payment had gone unanswered. “That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”

Mr. Marshall, a first-term Republican who may need every vote he can get in a race that polls indicate is neck-and-neck, rushed to respond. He was already contending with a separate revelation about unpaid bills that he had sought to collect on: Last month, The New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, and that he had routinely charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate.

On Thursday evening, Tyson Brody, a spokesman for the Rev. Adam Hamilton, Mr. Marshall’s Democratic opponent, amplified the baker’s post, writing on social media that the bakery bill was “larger than debts for which Roger Marshall had patients sued.” (The unpaid medical bills ranged from $101 to several thousand dollars.)

By Friday, Mr. Marshall had paid Ms. Thomas back, she said in an interview. On Saturday, he addressed the issue in a post on his official X account.

“As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill,” Mr. Marshall wrote. “We have absolutely no idea how this happened.”

But, he added, “as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double.”

The senator attached an invoice showing that he had sent $1,300 to Ms. Thomas’s bakery, Holly’s Sweet Treats. That amount was not quite double the original bill, which had been for $678.75, according to the copy that Ms. Thomas posted on Facebook this week.

It was not clear if Mr. Marshall’s response would satisfy some of the commenters who had seized on the initial post. One had argued that Mr. Marshall owed Ms. Thomas more than $1,400, accounting for interest.

Mr. Marshall’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for further comment on the bill. Several Republican strategists said that Mr. Marshall had handled an unfortunate situation as well as he could.

Ms. Thomas, for her part, said she still had no intention of voting for Mr. Marshall, though she added that his payment was “the right thing to do.”

“I can’t put all the blame on him,” said Ms. Thomas, 43, recalling that the initial order had been placed by a campaign staff member. “But as a business owner, when my staff messes up, it falls on me as well.”

She has been closely following the Senate race and “impulsively” wrote her post as she complained at work about the years-old order, she recalled.

“I just made a post about Roger Marshall and how he didn’t pay me,” Ms. Thomas said she had declared at work. “We’ll see what happens. Maybe he will pay me.”

By Thursday evening, her phone began pinging with messages as she watched her daughter’s volleyball game. She had a theory, she said, for why the post took off.

“He’s let a lot of people down in the state,” said Ms. Thomas, who declined to share her political affiliation. “And people are frustrated with how things are going.”

Some on social media accused Mr. Marshall of hypocrisy, citing his own business practices.

“I do think he’s a hypocrite,” Lindsey Derr, 43, a Democrat in Hutchinson, Kan., who had already planned to vote against Mr. Marshall, said in a phone conversation. She added, “It makes me very upset.”

Mr. Marshall is trying to avoid becoming the first Republican to lose a Senate race in Kansas since 1932. His campaign says the senator gets results for Kansas. But he has been challenged by steep price increases that the Iran war has inflicted on farmers in the state.

On Saturday, Mr. Hamilton’s campaign issued a statement that attempted to encapsulate the episode in a single word: “Cookiegate.”

Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

Pentagon Again Increases Number of U.S. Casualties in Iran War
In an unannounced change, the Defense Department is now acknowledging troops who died or were wounded in support roles.
By John Ismay

The Pentagon has again quietly raised the number of U.S. service members killed and wounded during operations related to the Iran war amid widening criticism over the lack of transparency about the conflict’s human and operational costs. The military now is reporting that 21 U.S. service members have been killed, up from 18, and 865 wounded, up by 98 since August. The changes were posted Friday evening to the Defense Casualty Analysis System website, which offers a detailed breakdown of casualties by branch of service, rank, race and ethnicity.

The cause of the increased casualty numbers is not completely clear, since the hostilities between the United States and Iran have largely been in a lull for many weeks.

“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” Representative Adam Smith, Democrat of Washington, and Representative Chrissy Houlahan, Democrat of Pennsylvania, said in a joint statement on Friday. The two House members had demanded an explanation from the Pentagon after the House Armed Services Committee discovered “a discrepancy in the Pentagon’s reporting of casualty numbers” and brought it to the White House’s attention.

“The failure of Secretary Hegseth to immediately take ownership of the problem also does a grave disservice to the men and women putting their lives on the line in service to our country,” they added.

The Pentagon, under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has deliberately withheld casualty numbers from the public, while also attacking reporters for publishing information on them.

In response to reporting by The Washington Post in September that more U.S. troops had died in support of the Iran war than the Pentagon had acknowledged, Mr. Hegseth took to social media to say, “This is DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE.”

The defense secretary also said The Post is “worse than Iranian state media.”

Mr. Hegseth’s office did not immediately respond to a request on Saturday for comment regarding the updated casualty numbers. The increase was reported earlier on Saturday by The Post.

On July 20, the Pentagon added 100 casualties to the war’s tally without explanation. Three days later, the department lowered the number of troops killed during the war, which Mr. Hegseth calls Operation Epic Fury, from 18 to 14 — claiming the discrepancy was caused by “temporary data disruptions.”

Later that month, the Defense Department took the unusual step of claiming that Operation Epic Fury ended with President Trump’s cease-fire announcement in June, and any further deaths and injuries would be accounted for as part of “overseas operations.”

The new casualty numbers come as the war with Iran continues to drag on. Critics have also said the Pentagon has not fully acknowledged the damage done to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which defense officials recognize may be abandoned rather than repaired.

In early July, U.S. Central Command, which directs military operations across the Middle East, resumed near daily airstrikes against Iran. By July 15, Mr. Trump had declared the cease-fire over and resumed a blockade of Iran’s ports by U.S. warships.

Days later, Iranian ballistic missiles struck a base hosting U.S. forces in Jordan, killing three American service members. By the end of the month, U.S. warplanes attacked more targets inside Iran and expanded the strikes to hit Iranian forces in Iraq as well.

A week ago, the Pentagon hastily evacuated B-1 bombers from an air base in Britain after receiving intelligence that Iran might try to attack them with drones.

And while Mr. Trump has not said whether he would resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, The New York Times reported on Thursday that the U.S. military was preparing options to restart major combat operations against Tehran.
