And other Republicans running in competitive Senate and House races had little to say about the agreement, which Mr. Trump trumpeted Friday on social media as a “very big and important” deal, claiming it would swiftly bring down energy costs.

“It’s a grave error by the president,” said Representative Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican from a battleground district who is not running for re-election. “People realize that the sanctions on Russia are appropriate when Russia’s invading a country and bombing cities at night.”

Mr. Bacon predicted the deal would have little effect on soaring diesel prices but would offer a victory for one of America’s adversaries. And the congressman said that the agreement would not help Republican candidates. “It looks desperate,” he said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The deal received some Republican praise. Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Florida Republican running in a competitive race, wrote on social media that it would “massively benefit the American people.”

The United States introduced sanctions on energy exports from Russia after the country started its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Mr. Trump’s deal, and his declaration Saturday that Ukraine should “get a new president,” escalated U.S. tensions with Kyiv. The issue of U.S. support for the country has for years divided Republicans; the two Republican Senate candidates who questioned the deal have long been supporters of Ukraine.

Some Midwestern Republicans have called for a pause on diesel exports to try to lower costs for American consumers, a notion that Mr. Trump has ruled out.

Energy experts say the deal is not likely to have a major impact on the cost of diesel, which has spiked to around $6.28 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club, up from $3.67 a year ago. Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, an energy consulting firm in Houston, said the deal would introduce a “very small” amount of diesel into the market “compared to U.S. demand.”

In Michigan, Mr. Rogers, who has recently sought distance from Mr. Trump by calling for the president to end both the Iran war and his tariff fight with Canada, told reporters on Friday that he supported an agricultural rebate for diesel, but not the president’s approach.

Mr. Rogers, long a foreign policy hawk, cited concern about offering Mr. Putin a victory. “You just don’t want to give that guy an inch,” he said.

In Alaska, a spokesman for Mr. Sullivan, Nate Adams, said in a statement that the senator “believes American energy dominance is the answer to high prices, and that means producing more of it in Alaska, for Alaskans, by Alaskans, not importing it from Russia.”

Democrats pounced on the deal. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader, wrote on social media that the president had made a “deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes.”

Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee in the competitive Senate race in New Hampshire, said in a statement that the agreement was a “slap in the face to Ukraine and our allies overseas.” The campaign of his Republican opponent, former Senator John E. Sununu, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The high cost of diesel poses a particular risk for Republicans running in states whose farming-heavy economies are powered by diesel, such as Nebraska, Iowa and Kansas.

The campaigns of the Republican Senate candidates in two of those states, Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the president’s deal with Russia. Their hotly contested races, staged in conservative states, could help decide control of the Senate.

Mr. Rogers, Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Hinson have all called for the United States to pause diesel exports. Last month, Mr. Trump proposed banning or limiting U.S. diesel exports, worrying European countries. But last week, he said, “We are not going to be doing the export ban.”

In Wisconsin, another heavily agricultural state, Representative Derrick Van Orden, a hawkish Republican in a battleground district who has been a forceful supporter of the Iran war, said Saturday that he had no comment on the president’s deal with Mr. Putin.

SUMMARY

When you sit for hours, your entire body takes a hit — from your neck to your glutes. Keep your hips on the floor and avoid arching excessively through your lower back. Keeping your back flat, hinge forward from your hips and lower as far as you comfortably can, until you feel a stretch through your glutes and hamstrings.

ARTICLE

Sitting All Day? This Mobility Routine Can Help You Loosen Up.
Try these simple moves to avoid aches and pains.
By Hannah Singleton and Theodore Tae
Published 2026-10-10 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/well/move/mobility-routine-sitting.html

When you sit for hours, your entire body takes a hit — from your neck to your glutes.

Our bodies crave movement variety, said David Jou, a physical therapist in New York City. But when you spend all day at a desk, your body starts to conform to the position it knows best, a process he calls “creep.”

“Once your tissues start to assume a shape, it becomes really hard to get out of,” he said. Eventually, an overly sedentary lifestyle can lead to muscle imbalances, joint issues and chronic pain.

It’s important to counteract long periods of sitting with exercises that take your body out of that hunched position, said Katie Hillery, a physical therapist and strength and conditioning coach in Chappaqua, N.Y. That means opening up areas along the front of your body, including your chest and hip flexors, while engaging and strengthening muscles along the back of your body — called the posterior chain — including your upper back and glutes.

This 20-minute routine, designed with Mr. Jou and Ms. Hillery, combines mobility and strengthening exercises to move your neck, back and hips through ranges of motion you don’t experience at a desk. Work through the entire routine during a break or in the evening, or pick a few movements to sprinkle throughout your workday.

Overview

Time: 20 to 25 minutes

Intensity: Light

What You’ll Need

- Chair or bench
- A mat
- A long resistance band and a short resistance band
- Light to moderate dumbbell (optional)
- Foam roller (optional)

Chin Tucks

Repetitions: Two sets of 10 reps

Targets: Activates the deep neck muscles

Start seated with your shoulders relaxed and spine upright. Look straight ahead and gently draw your head straight back, as if you were trying to make a double chin. Keep your gaze level rather than dropping your chin toward your chest. Hold for three seconds, then relax.

Neck Rolls

Repetitions: One minute, each direction

Targets: Stretches the muscles along the front, side and back of the neck

Start sitting or standing with your spine straight and shoulders relaxed. Slowly lower your chin toward your chest. Roll one ear toward your shoulder, and continue in a circle, tilting your head back before bringing your other ear toward your shoulder and returning your chin toward your chest. You should feel a stretch but no pain — only go as far as feels comfortable. If any spots feel particularly tight, hold the stretch and take a deep breath. Repeat in the opposite direction.

Seated Thoracic Windmills

Repetitions: Two sets of eight repetitions per side

Targets: Stretches the chest and mobilizes the mid-back

Sit on a chair or a bench. Reach down with your left arm and grab your right leg as far down as is comfortable. Rotate your torso to the right as you reach your right hand toward the ceiling, opening your chest. Aim to stack your shoulders, but go only as far as your mobility allows. Return to the starting position and repeat. Switch sides.

Thoracic Extension on Foam Roller

Repetitions: Three sets of eight repetitions

Targets: Stretches the chest and mobilizes the mid-back

Lie on your mat and position the foam roller horizontally beneath your shoulder blades. Place your hands behind your head, keeping your elbows wide. Slowly extend your upper back over the foam roller, allowing your chest to open. Keep your hips on the floor and avoid arching excessively through your lower back. If you need to release pressure, keep more weight on your feet. Hold for five seconds, and then return to the starting position.

Seated Row

Repetitions: Three sets of 15 repetitions

Targets: Strengthens the upper back muscles

Sit on the mat with your legs extended in front of you, keeping a slight bend in your knees. Loop a light to medium resistance band around the soles of your feet and hold one end in each hand. Engage your core and sit tall. Pull the ends of the band toward your hip bones, drawing your shoulder blades back and together. Avoid shrugging your shoulders to your ears. Slowly extend your arms and control the movement back to the starting position.

Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch

Repetitions: Two sets of 30 seconds per side

Targets: Stretches the hip flexors

Kneel on the mat with one knee on the ground and the opposite foot planted in front of you. (Place a pillow or cushion beneath your knee if needed.) Put your hands on your hips or on top of your knee, tuck your pelvis and tighten the glute on your kneeling side. Keeping that position, shift your hips forward until you feel a stretch in the front of the hip on the kneeling side. Rock in and out of the stretch for the allotted time. Switch sides.

Banded Hip Flexor March

Repetitions: Two sets of 20 repetitions (10 per side)

Targets: Strengthens the hip flexors and engages the core

Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and loop a short resistance band around both feet. Keeping your torso upright, raise one knee until your thigh is parallel to the floor. Keep your foot flexed and avoid leaning back. Lower your foot with control and repeat on the other side. You can keep your hands on your hips or swing the opposite arm as you march.

Seated Good Mornings

Repetitions: Three sets of eight repetitions

Targets: Strengthens and stretches the hips

Sit on a bench or chair with your feet wider than your hips and your toes out in front of your knees. Slightly angle your feet outward. Hold a light to medium dumbbell in both hands between your legs. Keeping your back flat, hinge forward from your hips and lower as far as you comfortably can, until you feel a stretch through your glutes and hamstrings. Press through your feet and squeeze your glutes to return to sitting.

Sit-to-Stand Squat

Repetitions: Three sets of eight repetitions

Targets: Strengthens the glutes and thighs

Stand in front of a bench or sturdy chair with your feet hips-width apart. Bend your knees and lower into a squat until you tap the chair. Press into your feet to stand back up and squeeze your glutes at the top, being mindful not to arch through your lower back. To make this movement more challenging, you can hold a dumbbell at your chest.

On-set trainer: Cadence Dubus

Exasperation and Resignation in Greece Over Allegations Against Kimberly Guilfoyle
The U.S. ambassador to Greece is facing accusations that she asked a donor to pay off her credit card bill before she took up her post in Athens.
By Niki Kitsantonis, Lara Jakes and Lynsey Chutel
Published 2026-10-10 17:48 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/world/europe/kimberly-guilfoyle-greece.html

As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle has cultivated a highly visible profile, attending late-night parties and appearing on the cover of Vogue Greece. Lately, however, she has drawn a different kind of attention from Greeks.

Revelations this week that a Republican donor said Ms. Guilfoyle asked him to pay her American Express bill in exchange for access to senior Trump administration officials were the latest allegations of hardball tactics or outright misconduct to emerge against her.

Greeks interviewed in Athens in recent days expressed exasperation and cynicism about the steady drip of reports about Ms. Guilfoyle’s dealings, and some said they saw them as signs of what smaller countries are forced to endure from larger, wealthier nations.

“Greece is not a major power,” Petros Malliaros, 35, a freelance lighting technician, said. “We have to get along with the U.S. and whatever representatives it chooses to send us.”

The accusations against Ms. Guilfoyle are “hardly a shock,” said Anna Markaki, a 38-year-old school teacher. Of President Trump, she added, “He probably thinks she’s done a good job.”

Pavlos Iliopoulos, a 47-year-old pizza store owner, shrugged it off. “Greece is a small country and pretty much has to play along with the U.S.,” he said. “One corrupt diplomat staying or going isn’t going to make much of a difference.”

Anta Rapaki, 52, a former health care worker, criticized the administration’s decision to send Ms. Guilfoyle to Greece in the first place. “They’re underestimating my country as a faithful ally — instead of honoring that friendship, they sent her here as a favor,” she said.

She added, “Because we’re a small country, we have to have friends, and we need the U.S. But we’ll dance the dance up to the point that serves us; we won’t knuckle under.”

Ms. Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Mr. Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., was one of the first ambassadors to be nominated in the president’s second term. She has said that her experience with Greece before being nominated as Mr. Trump’s envoy last November came from college history classes and a honeymoon trip. She has served in Athens with a mixture of MAGA glitz and what her supporters have described as relentlessness in securing business deals involving American interests.

She has come under fire in recent weeks in reports in The Wall Street Journal, which reported last month on potential conflicts of interest in Ms. Guilfoyle’s involvement in energy deals in Greece.

This week, the Journal revealed her communications with a Republican donor, Eric Deters, who said that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her credit card just before her confirmation hearing, which he did not pay. The New York Times confirmed their discussions.

A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle declined to comment. The U.S. Embassy in Athens directed requests for comment to the State Department in Washington, which did not respond.

In a visit to Athens, Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to answer questions on Thursday about the ambassador’s conduct. Ahead of his trip, he had described her as “an incredibly effective advocate for the President’s agenda in Greece,” adding that she had “successfully advanced U.S. energy interests in Greece and across southeastern Europe.”

Mr. Trump said he knew little about the allegations against Ms. Guilfoyle. “I don’t know too much,” he told journalists on Friday. “But she was always very nice.”

For some Greeks, more troubling was a comment she was reported to have made at a dinner in Athens in March insinuating that the United States could replace the Greek government. “The fact that they would send someone like that here, with no tact or diplomacy skills, shows how low we rank in Trump’s priorities, how insignificant Greece is for them,” Maria Stefanou, a 68-year-old retiree, said.

Ms. Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed the characterization of the dinner, and the foreign minister, George Gerapetritis, said on Friday that the Greek energy minister who was there denied it as well.

Asked about Ms. Guilfoyle’s purported comment, Pavlos Marinakis, a government spokesman, said, “There was never any question of the Greek government being threatened, nor would anything of the sort ever be tolerated.” He added that the Greece-U.S. partnership was founded on “mutual respect.”

In Parliament on Friday, Mr. Gerapetritis said it was not necessary to summon Ms. Guilfoyle to explain herself. “Summoning an ambassador and potentially creating a diplomatic incident would serve no purpose,” he said.

Their responses were part of a Greek government effort seeking to tamp down a national debate over Ms. Guilfoyle. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has aligned himself with the Trump administration, seeking cooperation on security and other issues.

“As long as Ms. Guilfoyle enjoys the support of the U.S. president and secretary of state, the Greek government has to respect the position of the U.S. government,” said Constantinos Filis, a prominent analyst and director of the Institute of Global Affairs at the American College of Greece, said. “It’s as simple as that.”

Leftist parties have called on the government to demand clarifications from Ms. Guilfoyle.

“Favors from Trump’s America come with a price tag,” Rena Dourou, a prominent lawmaker of the leftist Syriza party, said Friday. “The question is: How much will the Greek people ultimately have to pay?”

Ms. Guilfoyle is the latest of Trump administration ambassadors accused of engaging in decidedly undiplomatic behavior. Many serve in Europe, which long has been a destination for American political appointees of both parties who have little to no experience in official diplomacy.

Bill White, the U.S. ambassador to Belgium, was asked by that country’s foreign minister to stop making derogatory statements about government officials. Charles Kushner, the chief envoy to France (and father of Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law), ignored summonses by the French Foreign Ministry after criticizing Paris for doing too little to combat antisemitism.

Sharon LaFraniere contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Rebuking Ukraine Over Oil Strikes, Trump Says It Should ‘Get a New President’
Hours after President Trump said the United States would buy Russian diesel, the Kremlin said there would be no immediate resumption of discussions to end the war.
By Marc Santora and Andrew E. Kramer
Published 2026-10-10 12:13 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/world/europe/ukraine-russia-trump-diesel-talks.html

President Trump on Saturday accused Ukraine of causing a “world problem” with Russian refinery attacks and said it should “get a new president,” further undermining Kyiv a day after saying he would open U.S. markets to Russian diesel.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Saturday, he said the United States had told Ukraine, “you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, he said, “wants to make problems for the world.” He added, “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Over four years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Ukraine has pursued a strategy of mid- and long-range strikes that have battered Russian supply lines and oil infrastructure. The attacks have helped Ukraine stall Russian advances and even claw back some territory, but Mr. Trump on Saturday linked them to high fuel prices, which spiked this year after the United States and Israel attacked Iran.

“He wants to make problems for the world,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Zelensky. “He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”

Later on Saturday, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said that Mr. Zelensky “has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide.” He added, “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well.”

Mr. Trump’s announcement on Friday came despite a Russian ban on exporting fuel and was followed by the lifting of U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April. The Kremlin apparently offered no concessions in return.

Hours later, Russian officials said peace talks would not resume immediately.

“We will think about when these negotiations might be resumed,” Yuri Ushakov, President Vladimir V. Putin’s foreign policy adviser, said in a statement Friday night.

The diplomatic efforts fizzled shortly after Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami to meet with Mr. Trump’s top envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. As those talks were about to begin, Mr. Trump spoke at length with Mr. Putin over the phone.

While Mr. Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal made no mention of Ukraine, it was poised to hurt Ukrainian efforts to defend itself, as any major purchase of Russian fuel would help fund Moscow’s war machine.

Ukrainian officials said on Saturday that the talks in Miami had ended without a breakthrough.

In an online chat with reporters on Friday evening, Mr. Zelensky did not hide his sense of betrayal.

“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen, and that is certainly not fair,” Mr. Zelensky said. He has worked hard to maintain a stable relationship with the White House as Mr. Trump has steered America closer to Russia and away from traditional democratic allies.

“It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Mr. Zelensky added, calling Mr. Trump’s diesel announcement a “weak decision.”

For Kyiv and its European allies, the short-lived talks in Miami laid bare how U.S. diplomacy has drifted from pursuing a durable peace settlement to hunting for business deals with Russia. The Trump administration has placed the burden of compromise almost entirely on Ukraine and put little pressure on Moscow to stop its campaign to destroy the Ukrainian state.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump similarly did not suggest that Mr. Putin should make compromises. The U.S. president said that Mr. Zelensky, though, “could have settled this war many times, many many times, and he chooses not to.”

On Saturday, Mr. Zelensky said Russia had directed five guided bombs at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, killing at least 20 people, including three children. “In Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities,” he said.

Daniel Fried, a longtime senior U.S. diplomat and former ambassador to Poland, said it was “very clear that the Russians are completely uninterested in any diplomatic approach and are simply standing back waiting for the West, the U.S., the Ukrainians to come to them with some bigger and better offer.”

“When you start chasing after them, they simply smirk and wait for you to purchase bigger and better bouquets to throw at their feet,” Mr. Fried said.

He said Mr. Trump was undermining not only Ukraine’s security but also Europe’s.

“All of this is taking place at a time when Russia is escalating its shadow warfare against Europe, and we are acting as if that is not occurring,” he said.

It is unclear whether Mr. Trump’s move to import Russian diesel will have much immediate impact on prices before the U.S. midterm elections.

In a statement after his call with Mr. Trump on Friday evening, Mr. Putin said that Russia had “confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. market and global markets at large,” but he did not specify any amounts.

Mr. Trump’s end run around Ukraine continued a pattern that had been playing out since he started his second term claiming he could end the war in 24 hours.

Last year, Kyiv agreed to Mr. Trump’s call for an immediate, unconditional cease-fire, but Moscow flatly rejected it. That first round of diplomacy established a dynamic that still defines negotiations: Ukraine received no reward for saying yes, and the Kremlin paid no price for saying no.

Since then, ambitions of forging a lasting peace have largely evaporated. Instead, only a handful of hastily announced tactical pauses and holiday truces have emerged.

Still, when the Trump administration opened the latest diplomatic track on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in late September, Ukrainian officials were startled by how far Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff went in their offerings to Russia.

According to officials familiar with the discussions, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential diplomatic talks, the Americans put three lucrative economic incentives on the table to coax Moscow into a limited cease-fire, either on energy infrastructure or at sea.

Washington floated releasing billions of Russian sovereign assets immobilized in the West. The money, the officials said, was viewed as an upfront incentive for partial truces, not a reward for their enactment. This revived a proposal from last year to release funds to Russia. Then, the suggestion was to release up to $100 billion.

The Americans also revisited a plan to sell off parts of the Russian oil giant Lukoil in a multibillion-dollar deal that would go to a group of Middle Eastern investors, including some with business ties to U.S. negotiators.

And Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner revived a U.S. proposal that would allow Belarus, the Kremlin’s ally and neighbor, to export potash, according to officials familiar with the talks.

Kyiv has avoided rejecting any proposal outright but has demanded guardrails. For instance, it has suggested dollar-for-dollar mirror payments of frozen assets to Ukraine or guarantees of additional military aid upon any truce breach.

But Mr. Zelensky’s frustration with Washington was clear earlier this week when he visited the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in northern Ukraine, hundreds of miles from the front lines. The strike killed 22 people, including five children — among more than 100 civilians killed in Russian strikes last week alone.

Asked about Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s comments that talks to end the fighting were “proving elusive” because the war had reached a “strategic stalemate,” Mr. Zelensky bristled.

“We are not at a diplomatic dead end,” he said. The problem, he added, was that there was not enough pressure on Moscow.

“Shut down their entire economy,” he said. “Sew Russia’s mouth shut. Don’t feed them with your own sales.”

Valerie Hopkins and Ivan Nechepurenko contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

At Least 12 Killed and 300 Injured in Houthi Attack on Saudi Airport
The strike on Saturday was the deadliest attack in a Gulf Arab country since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February, and forced the airport to temporarily suspend operations.
By Vivian Nereim and Euan Ward
Published 2026-10-10 16:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/world/middleeast/riyadh-airport-attack-energy-congress.html

The Iran-backed Houthi militia launched a deadly attack on an international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital on Saturday that Saudi officials said killed at least 12 people and injured over 300 more, in a dramatic escalation of the war between the kingdom and the Houthis.

The strike, which a senior Houthi official said the militia was responsible for, was the deadliest attack in a Gulf Arab country since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February.

The latest toll was announced early Sunday morning by the Saudi civil aviation authority, which said four Saudi nationals and one U.S. citizen were among the 12 dead. It added that of the 309 people injured, some were in critical condition.

Earlier, the Saudi aviation agency announced the temporary suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh. Repeated, deadly Houthi attacks on the airport this week have struck at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions to turn the city into a global travel and business hub, threatening to disrupt major international events planned for the coming weeks.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen said in a statement on Sunday that the Houthi attack had targeted a passenger terminal at the airport, and vowed a decisive response.

Across the border in Yemen, Saudi warplanes have been waging a deadly bombing campaign against the Houthis, who say that the country has been subjected to hundreds of airstrikes in recent weeks. Since Sept. 3, airstrikes have killed 91 people in Yemen, mostly women and children, according to Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi government-affiliated health ministry.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Houthi official, said the militia was responsible for the attack in Riyadh on Saturday, which he said was in retaliation for Saudi strikes, including on civilian infrastructure in Yemen.

The Houthis carried out the attack “so that the world understands that airports, seaports, wedding and mourning halls, hospitals, and markets in Yemen are civilian facilities that must not be targeted or harmed — and that the same rules that apply to these facilities in Yemen must also apply to their counterparts everywhere else,” he said.

Saudi officials did not immediately respond to questions about details of the attack. A reporter for The New York Times, however, saw at least six ambulances heading toward the airport, where the police had blocked entry.

The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, along with other Western embassies, urged its citizens to avoid the area and warned of travel disruptions.

Speaking at the White House, President Trump told reporters, “we just found out about the recent attack.” He said the United States would “make a decision” about possibly intervening in the conflict, without offering further detail. Mr. Trump carried out a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, declaring a swift victory after the United States burned through weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone.

The Houthis also carried out attacks earlier this week on airports in Riyadh and Abha, in the south of the kingdom, killing and injuring several people, according to the Saudi authorities.

Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, said early Sunday that “a projectile fell” in the area of King Fahd International Airport, in eastern Saudi Arabia, without elaborating.

Saudi Arabia previously led a disastrous bombing campaign against the Houthis in 2015, after the militia took over Yemen’s capital of Sanaa, routing the Yemeni government. During the brutal war that ensued, hundreds of thousands of people died from violence, hunger and disease, but the Houthis survived, cementing their rule over northern Yemen.

A truce in 2022 brought a fragile peace to the country, until the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, igniting a regional war.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis re-emerged in July, after the Houthis accused the kingdom of bombing the airport in Sanaa. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed responsibility for that bombing, saying it was acting to prevent an unauthorized Iranian plane from landing.

The Houthis have long bristled at restrictions on their airspace that are enforced by Saudi Arabia, calling them a blockade. They soon announced that they intended to enforce a “blockade for blockade” policy and declared an embargo on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea — which has become an important alternative route for Saudi oil exports after the Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway near Iran.

Yemen’s internal war soon reignited, with fierce clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces allied with the Yemeni government.

The Houthis seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline last month in a lightning offensive that gave the group greater control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, an important choke point for global trade.

Finally, a full-blown war broke out last weekend. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government announced a new military campaign against the Houthis, pledging to oust them from all of the territory they had seized over the past 12 years, and Saudi Arabia began a new bombing campaign against the militia.

That decision has plunged the kingdom deeper into the regional fallout of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Houthis’ main backer. Prince Mohammed now faces the difficult task of stopping the Houthi attacks while avoiding another prolonged war that could derail his economic plans.

Analysts say that a political solution to the conflict has become increasingly challenging to work out as the Houthis’ demands continue to grow. Houthi officials, battle-hardened by a decade of warfare and ruling a countryside with much of its infrastructure already destroyed by the fighting, appear to be calculating that they can inflict greater pain on Saudi Arabia than the kingdom can inflict on them.

Over the coming weeks, Riyadh was expected to host visitors from around the world for major global events, beginning on Sunday with the W.P.C. Energy Congress, an international gathering of energy officials and executives.

In an email to participants late on Friday, organizers of the event said it would proceed as planned and offered alternative travel options, including coordinated flights with Saudia, the national carrier. The airline’s flights were among those diverted on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data.

Later this month, Riyadh is also expected to host the Future Investment Initiative, Prince Mohammed’s annual investment summit, which typically draws world leaders, billionaires and top global executives. Organizers have yet to announce any changes to that event’s schedule.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

SUMMARY

Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. This is an interesting letter, because I’m not sure the advice you need is the advice you’re looking for. What advice would you give to someone returning to the office from self-employment?

ARTICLE

A Contagious Aversion to Overhead Lights
Plus: How far to go for a colleague, and now your chance to give someone advice.
By Max Read
Published 2026-10-11 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/business/office-lighting-work-advice.html

Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend, I manage a team of about 20 people in an open-plan office suite. A few months ago, one of my staff members asked that we disconnect the overhead lighting above his pod because he is prone to migraines. His co-workers didn’t object, so I complied. That corner of the office is now permanently dark, which isn’t ideal, but I’ve been willing to tolerate it. Last week, a worker in another corner of the office asked to work from home in the morning because her husband’s schedule had changed and she needed to be home to care for her two preschoolers. I said she could change her schedule if necessary, but not work from home while also caring for a 2- and 4-year-old. She escalated to the union, but the union supported my decision. Yesterday, she came back with a request to have the lights above her desk disconnected as well, saying she also suffers from migraines. Today, a third employee, a close friend of the second, said that she, too, suffers migraines and needs the lights disabled. This feels like a retaliatory protest, and obviously, I cannot agree to the entire office being plunged into a perpetual state of gloom with no overhead lights. My question is, in declining the two new requests, should I then also revert to full lighting for the whole office? That feels like penalizing a person with a legitimate health need for two disgruntled staffers. — Anonymous

This is an interesting letter, because I’m not sure the advice you need is the advice you’re looking for.

The answer to your specific question is pretty obvious: No, you should not revert to full lighting for the whole office. Your migraine-suffering employee’s accommodation was made separately from these two later (and, to your mind, suspicious) requests. Right now you have two apparently disgruntled employees; why would you add a third?

I understand why you’re looking to assert some authority here. You’re afraid of being undermined by employee rebellion. (And afraid of a darkened office.) But being a manager isn’t solely about maintaining dispensatory power, and flexibility and creativity can often defuse tension more effectively than a rigid commitment to particular rules — or, for that matter, to particular office lighting schemes.

Rather than roll back accommodations for the sake of fairness (or to make a point), I would at least consider trying to meet your other employees halfway. For all you know, their requests are legitimate and the connection to the contentious schedule change is coincidental. (“Bad migraines” doesn’t seem like a far-fetched condition for a woman with two young kids and a stressful schedule.) Could you, for example, move the two newly incapacitated employees to the same darker section of the office as the original migraine sufferer? This might blunt their frustration, and even earn some good will, without darkening the entire office.

Or you might go in one day this week and try to look at the office lighting as lighting rather than as leverage. Is a less brightly lit office really “gloomy”? Is that one corner “permanently dark,” or naturally — even soothingly — lit? Would individual desk lamps be better for everyone? Is it possible that the migraine sufferers have a point? You could even consult some of the other employees to see how they feel. Some of them may hate the darkness as much as you do, which would at least give you more ground to stand on in rejecting the newer requests.

These exercises may amount to nothing; creativity is not a panacea. And it’s true, you’re backed into a (particularly ill-lit) corner right now because you made the original accommodation informally. But the best alternative to casual flexibility is a formal, neutral and transparent process, not arbitrary rollbacks. In other words, if you can’t absorb tension through creative management, absorb it into bureaucracy.

Your team is big enough and organized enough to run management decisions through the union; why aren’t you also running their accommodation requests through your own process? Ask for medical documentation and discuss alternatives, both for the two new requests and, retroactively, for the original one. If the new requests are bad-faith, you can defensibly shoot them down. And if those two employees can demonstrate need, you’re empowered to help them without feeling undermined.

How to Stand Up for a Colleague

Dear Work Friend, A technologist at the laboratory where I work was scheduled to come in at 2 a.m. to relieve the holdover from the second shift. He collided with a deer on his way to work, and his car sustained severe damage. He notified the technologist covering the lab that he’d be returning home rather than risk driving the damaged vehicle any farther. Because this employee had a history of arriving late to work, the laboratory manager filed an incident report. The technologist went to human resources to plead his case. He was told that in a year’s time the incident would be expunged from his personnel file, but that he needed to address the matter with his manager. When he went to the manager’s office, he found the manager focused on his computer screen. He tried to hand him the garage’s detailed bill as proof of what had happened, but the manager continued looking at his computer and simply said, “I wouldn’t worry about it.” This man is well liked around the office, and a group of us wrote a letter on his behalf with the intention of giving it to the C.E.O. He was grateful for what we’d done but, in keeping with his nonconfrontational nature, refused to sign the letter. Was the laboratory manager justified in maintaining his incident report? Should H.R. have followed up on this matter? And what responsibility, if any, did the manager or H.R. have for what happened to the incident report? — Anonymous

I agree with your sense that the manager was being unfair in filing the report and that H.R. perhaps should have intervened or declined to escalate the report. I also appreciate the methodical detail with which you recount this story, which probably speaks highly of your skill as a laboratory worker.

But I think the surplus of incidental facts, and your overall sense of frustration with the injustice and unfairness, may be distracting from the practical takeaway of these interactions, which is that most of the people involved seem to want to let the mess die down.

H.R. has said the report will be expunged from his personnel file in a year. The manager has explicitly said not to worry about it. Even the employee in question has declined to join you and your colleagues in your attempt to get the report overturned.

Obviously this doesn’t mean your co-worker is safe from escalation as far as possible escalation goes. And given the manager’s fussy report filing, I understand why you feel concerned.

But your colleague (and you) should be cheered that he has such supportive and well-organized colleagues willing to stand up for him. If the situation develops further — if you get better evidence that the manager or H.R. is truly looking to escalate or retaliate — you already have a protest letter in place. But for now I would listen to H.R., the manager and the technologist themselves and keep it in the drawer.

Asking for a Friend

Dear Work Friend, I have worked for myself for over 20 years, but the kids are gone, the house is being sold, and I’m contemplating going back to work for someone else. I have some dated experience about what corporate, government and nonprofit workplaces are like. My question is: What has changed in the past 10 to 20 years that I should take into account as I prepare to do this? As a woman, I expect there to be additional challenges — by most statistics, women over 50 who have not recently been in the work force are not at the top of the hiring list. There’s lots out there on how to make yourself relevant, how to fill in the gaps in résumés; how #MeToo has had an effect, and a backlash; even how to address ageism. But I don’t get a sense of how the culture itself has changed. What would you qualify as the biggest workplace cultural changes in the past decade or so? What are things to absolutely avoid, but that might have been acceptable in the past? Your thoughts are welcome! — Anonymous

The Lord (and my editors) know that I’m usually all too happy to weigh in on circumstances with which I don’t have a huge amount of personal familiarity. (What kind of advice columnist would I be if I didn’t?)

But given my own demographic categories (a man in his 40s) and work history (checkered), I think any attempt I could make at answering this letter would fall badly flat. Plus, I recently re-entered office work myself, and could use the advice. So it seems like a good opportunity to turn this question over to readers.

What has changed in the workplace? What advice would you give to someone returning to the office from self-employment? What have you had to learn, and what do you wish you’d known?

Send your advice for Anonymous to workfriend@nytimes.com or fill out the form below, and we’ll publish a selection of the letters in a future column.

san-francisco-housing-conversions.html

SUMMARY

In the years after the pandemic, many city officials and developers saw an opportunity to turn unused offices into apartments. San Francisco, with roughly a third of its 100 million square feet of office space vacant, had the potential to be a nucleus for office-to-residential activity. And since then, San Francisco has yet to see a single office conversion even as thousands of projects are underway and being completed in other cities.

ARTICLE

San Francisco Isn’t Giving Up on Turning More of Its Offices Into Homes
The city has not completed a single office-to-housing conversion, despite hopes to meet housing demand and inject life into empty downtowns.
By Joe Gose
Published 2026-10-11 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/business/san-francisco-housing-conversions.html

In the years after the pandemic, many city officials and developers saw an opportunity to turn unused offices into apartments. San Francisco, with roughly a third of its 100 million square feet of office space vacant, had the potential to be a nucleus for office-to-residential activity.

But as cities like New York, Washington and Chicago began offering tax incentives for conversions, San Francisco did not offer similar programs for builders. And since then, San Francisco has yet to see a single office conversion even as thousands of projects are underway and being completed in other cities.

The city is now is trying to change that. This year, officials adopted a law that allows developers to get back a portion of their future property taxes, over 30 years, on commercial buildings converted to new housing.

The financial reimbursement is available for projects downtown, which includes the Financial District, South of Market area and Civic Center neighborhood, and is meant to help alleviate the financial risk of conversions.

So far, three developers have submitted projects for the program.

“We’ve got about 30 million square feet of vacant space, so we knew we had a significant problem to tackle,” said Anne Taupier, executive director of the city’s Office of Economic and Workforce Development.

City officials are hoping the new tax incentive will fuel conversions the way tax abatement programs have in New York and Washington. Those are the top two markets for office conversions, with nearly 25,000 units in development combined as of the start of this year, according to RentCafe, an apartment search platform and research firm.

In 2023, a study by a group of public policy, planning and architecture firms determined that many office buildings in San Francisco were suitable for conversion because of factors like shape, size and layout. The city then relaxed several building codes, requirements and fees. Measures waived included mandates for bike parking and open space. And in March 2024, San Francisco voters eliminated a property transfer tax on buildings that were turned into housing, helping to ease some financial burden.

Despite those initiatives, developers remained reluctant to convert properties. Meanwhile, the housing crisis in San Francisco worsened as the expansion of artificial intelligence companies pushed up rents in an already pricey market. In September, the median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the city was over 25 percent more than it was the prior year and at an all-time high, according to Zumper, a rental platform.

In all, San Francisco’s efforts to make it easier and more financially feasible to convert offices to housing are expected to cut 25 percent off total costs in projects, said Marc Babsin, president of Emerald Fund, a residential development firm in San Francisco. That is a sizable amount even if those reductions, he noted, would be realized only after developers increase property values that go on to generate higher property taxes.

One of the developers trying to take advantage of the tax incentive is Mr. Babsin’s firm, which submitted an application and teamed up with another local developer to buy a midcentury office building. They plan to convert it into 106 apartments. Another developer, Hudson Pacific Properties, a real estate investment trust that owns some 12.5 million square feet of offices and production studios on the West Coast, wants to turn the upper floors of a landmark, 114-year-old building it owns into 136 apartments.

The new tax break “gives developers a way to put together a financing package that can make conversions work,” said Chris Pearson, senior vice president of Hudson Pacific.

The incentives are also playing an important role in the city’s Future of Downtown initiative, a rebuilding program the city’s planning department introduced in 2023.

San Francisco’s office vacancy rate, though improved recently, is among the highest in the country at 30.1 percent, according to Cushman & Wakefield, a commercial real estate brokerage. City officials see more people living downtown as a way to keep the area lively well past 5 p.m. and on weekends. That requires a mix of housing, shops, restaurants and entertainment, said Jacob Bintliff, manager of economic recovery initiatives for the Office of Economic and Workforce Development.

“Everybody feels the pain of where downtown has been since Covid, and there has been a lot of political will to go further with incentives for this category of projects,” he said. “If we were proposing them for some other type of development, maybe we wouldn’t have the same political coalition.”

More of that type of development is needed to give developers confidence to build even bigger, said Steve Luthman, global head of real estate at Hines, a global real estate investor.

The company wants to redevelop a block in the Financial District that could include converting a late-1940s-era office building into housing along with constructing the tallest office skyscraper in the city containing a mix of offices, housing and retail.

But without a broad office conversion effort, the Hines project will remain an island in a district of underused office buildings, Mr. Luthman said.

“The Financial District has always been a single-use district, and every one of our cities in America has one like it,” he said. “So we believe that creating more experiential urban districts is a winning formula, and the leadership shown by a historically anti-development city like San Francisco is giving developers a palate for those projects.”

Even with the new incentives, the advent of A.I. is an unknown in the future of office conversions in San Francisco. Lately, leasing activity and office building values are rising, partly because of the increasing number of A.I. firms looking for space.

More office leasing activity could slow momentum for conversions, as building owners and lenders have become reluctant to part with buildings at a price at which a conversion works financially, Mr. Babsin said. But he is confident that more conversion opportunities will become available.

“There are a lot of A.I. start-ups generating a lot of headlines and a lot of buzz,” Mr. Babsin said. “Nonetheless, dozens of Class B and C office buildings continue to struggle, so we’re bullish on office-to-residential conversions and see an opportunity to bring new energy into downtown.”

mark-zuckerberg-social-network-reckoning.html

SUMMARY

By 2010, the year Jesse Eisenberg played the Facebook chief executive Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” the real Zuckerberg had made only a modest number of public appearances. But that was not yet the Zuckerberg we saw in “The Social Network.” Who is the real Mark Zuckerberg?

ARTICLE

Three Mark Zuckerbergs, Three Surprisingly Different Men
Jeremy Strong in “The Social Reckoning,” Jesse Eisenberg in “The Social Network” and the real Meta executive are all playing parts. But only one has changed his approach.
By Alissa Wilkinson
Published 2026-10-11 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/movies/mark-zuckerberg-social-network-reckoning.html

By 2010, the year Jesse Eisenberg played the Facebook chief executive Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” the real Zuckerberg had made only a modest number of public appearances. The first was in 2004, when the 19-year-old executive talked to CNBC about what was then called TheFacebook. In the video he’s composed and articulate, explaining his site’s purpose to an audience that largely wouldn’t have used it, since at the time it was open only to students at select colleges. He maintains direct eye contact. His head moves slightly; his body not at all. His lines sound rehearsed, as if he had practiced a script before this big opening performance.

His body language had barely changed by the time the movie was released six years later. In an interview with Diane Sawyer, his eyes have the same fixed quality. Seated onstage at an advertising conference, his body remains still while he gesticulates with his arms.

The real Zuckerberg’s appearance is a performance from a not particularly gifted actor, though nobody expects a coding genius to be an entertainer. His mannerisms barely shifted as he became more famous. That blankness made it easy for actors to project onto him — Eisenberg, but also Jeremy Strong, who plays him as a seething, embattled middle-aged executive in the new follow-up, “The Social Reckoning.” By now it has become clear just how much of Zuckerberg’s real persona has been an act.

But that was not yet the Zuckerberg we saw in “The Social Network.” As portrayed by Eisenberg, he was a different kind of guy. The general public wasn’t all that familiar with him yet, so Eisenberg didn’t need to do an impression. He had free rein to play the executive as an idea: a smug, insolent teenager secretly desperate for connection.

Thus the Zuckerberg of “The Social Network” is a motormouth, twitchy, brilliant, a brat. He’s a force in perpetual motion, tossing staccato zingers at his opponents and skirting the rules and hierarchies that govern stodgy Harvard. When he comes to rest, it’s to gather energy to strike again. In a scene in which he’s called before a Harvard disciplinary board, his foot taps rapidly, not with nerves so much as pent-up energy, and his eyes dart around the room.

The performance was mesmerizing and netted Eisenberg an Oscar nomination, but it wasn’t much like the real Zuckerberg, who was showing up more and more on TV, still sitting stiffly and only intermittently emoting. After “The Social Network” was released, he told “60 Minutes” that he had liked the movie, but that they had gotten him all wrong.

A month later, Eisenberg hosted “Saturday Night Live” and explained to Andy Samberg — a cast member who’d been impersonating Zuckerberg as a doofy bro — that to play the role, “I speak in short, clipped sentences and I keep my head very still.” (The latter part is debatable.)

In a backstage shot, the real Zuckerberg joked with Lorne Michaels about wanting to join the stars onstage. As he talked, he gestured with his arms in the same way he did in media appearances: bent at a right angle, forearms parallel, cantilevering up and down. Back onstage, Eisenberg continued: “I wasn’t really doing Mark Zuckerberg; I was interpreting a fictional character in a movie script.”

Then the real Zuckerberg walks onstage, ready to play himself. “Jesse, I don’t know if it came off that way,” he says with a practiced smile.

OVER THE YEARS, the possibility of a “Social Network” sequel was floated repeatedly in interviews, and Eisenberg eventually declined to take part in “The Social Reckoning,” the new follow-up. “I don’t want to be associated with that character” anymore, he told Variety.

Instead, Jeremy Strong stepped in. His section of “The Social Reckoning” is set in 2021, just before the release of The Wall Street Journal’s “Facebook Files” investigation. In the conceit of the film, Zuckerberg is preparing, with the aid of lawyers, to testify before Congress. His team is coaching him on the body language required to, as he puts it, appear likable. Nod your head to signal you’re listening. Be nice.

Strong’s Zuckerberg is not Eisenberg’s, and no wonder. We’ve had 16 years of watching Zuckerberg as he grew from wunderkind to chief executive of one of the most powerful, consequential and mistrusted companies in Silicon Valley. We know who this guy is, sort of. He does jiu-jitsu and goes to White House state dinners and makes decisions that affect billions of lives.

Strong’s performance has elements of impersonation. His hair is cropped short and colored a reddish brown. His demeanor is formal and stiff, unlike Eisenberg’s vibrating ball of nerves. He’s sitting at a desk on a stage, with harsh lighting and lines to learn. Strong is a great actor playing a lousy actor who’s preparing for the performance of his life.

But what Strong really nails is Zuckerberg’s eyes. They are unblinking. If Zuckerberg’s expression is generally blank on TV, Strong plays him as though there’s fuming impatience and rage just beneath. Eisenberg’s version was angry, too, but he was jumpy, antsy, annoyed with the sluggishness of the world around him. Strong’s version seems to be filled with molten lava ready to boil over. Even when he’s talking to his employees, he’s frustrated that they’re around at all.

If we were to trace a Zuckerberg arc from Eisenberg to Strong, we’d imagine that the cocky teenager who built a website discovered that when your user base outnumbers the population of whole countries, running a company becomes very difficult. The kid who just wanted to connect became a man who wished everyone would leave him alone. He was never prepared for the consequences of his actions.

But of course, these are fictional versions of Zuckerberg. They’re portrayals of a public figure who dodges efforts to know him.

And that is what’s most interesting about anyone playing the role of Mark Zuckerberg. Unlike some of his colleagues in Silicon Valley, those who ooze charisma and those who seem simply unhinged, Zuckerberg has stage-managed his persona: First he was an awkward genius, then a cool and competent business guy. Lately, he’s played a man’s man, telling the podcaster Joe Rogan that “the corporate world is pretty culturally neutered” and calling for “masculine energy” and “a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more.” It comes off as a line reading, an echo of something somebody said on the internet.

Who is the real Mark Zuckerberg? It’s hard to say. Eisenberg played him as a type; Strong plays him as the dark side of a guy we know from TV. Zuckerberg himself seems malleable, depending on what’s expedient. Maybe it makes sense that someone who thought we could connect with one another through data-driven profiles and glowing flat screens turns out to be fundamentally unknowable.

ARTICLE

‘He Went Inside, and We Waited as People Started to Stream Out’
Losing a precious item on a night out, recalling a big Knicks spring and more reader tales of New York City in this week’s Metropolitan Diary.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-11 07:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/nyregion/metropolitan-diary.html

Hidden Gem

Dear Diary:

We went to see Jerry Seinfeld at the Beacon Theater, the early show.

Upon getting home across town, my wife noticed that the stone in her sapphire engagement ring was missing. We looked at a picture we had taken in front of the marquee before the show and saw that the stone had been there then.

We called the theater, but all we got was voice mail. So we took an Uber back to the West Side. We retraced the steps we had taken when we left to no avail.

We found a sympathetic security guard and asked whether we could look for the stone near our seats when the late show was over.

He looked at a picture we had of the stone that showed its shape and color and took a look at our digital tickets that showed where our seats were. He said we could not go in until everyone had left but that he could go and begin to look before that.

When the show ended, he went inside and we waited as people started to stream out.

Finally he returned and opened the door slightly.

“I’m sorry,” he said, “but I can’t let you in.”

Before we could respond, he added: “Because I found it! It looked like a piece of candy and was exactly under the seat you had been in.”

— Steven Goldstein

Knicks Spring

Dear Diary:

The sun had finally come out on the last afternoon of the Memorial Day weekend.

We took advantage, setting up our volleyball net in a dry spot between puddles at McCarren Park.

After one particularly hard spike, the ball rolled in front of four men decked out in Knicks gear, presumably on their way to watch the game.

One picked up the ball and threw it back.

“Go Knicks!” he yelled.

“Knicks in four!” I yelled back.

And just like that, everyone around us in the park began to chant: “Knicks in four! Knicks in four!”

— Elliot Warner

Mr. Zhang

Dear Diary:

The owner of my neighborhood Chinese restaurant in Harlem lit up excitedly once when I came in.

He came out from behind the counter, waving his checkbook and a piece of mail. His young children scampered past him into the kitchen.

We took a seat, and he showed me a credit card statement. His name was Mr. Zhang.

He had no English and I had no Chinese. I pointed to the amount due, and he nodded. I filled out a check, including his account number on the memo line, then the payment coupon and his return address on the envelope.

He seemed especially pleased when I reviewed it with him. I offered to help again any time, gave him my phone number and headed home across the street.

When I got out of the elevator on the sixth floor, a new voice mail was waiting. There was no message — just the sound of voices chattering in the background, and the clattering of pots and pans in a noisy kitchen.

— Paul Klenk

Double Take

Dear Diary:

It was winter 2018, and I was rushing across Washington Square Park to meet a friend for drinks.

Cutting through the center of the park, I made eye contact with a man walking toward me. As we passed each other, we both did a double take.

“Julia?” he asked.

I turned around and walked back to meet him there in the center of the park. We were both bundled up: hats, scarves, gloves, big jackets.

I couldn’t quite place him, but he obviously knew who I was — he had called out my name.

We chatted for a few minutes. He said he was so happy to run into me, asked when I had moved back to the city and where was I living and what I was up to that very moment.

Surprised by his level of interest, I scanned his face, trying desperately to figure out who he was. Maybe an acquaintance from high school?

I had just moved back to the East Coast from California, so his questions all made sense, and I answered them readily.

“Wait a second,” he asked after a few minutes of back and forth. “Is your last name …?”

“No,” I said.

“But your name is Julia?”

“Yes.”

“Who did you think I was?”

“I’m not totally sure,” I said sheepishly.

“I don’t think we know each other,” he said.

We parted ways and dove back into the cold, dark, winter night.

— Julia McCarthy

Not So Uniform

Dear Diary:

A nun stood outside our high school, St. Vincent Ferrer on the Upper East Side, every morning to check our uniforms: skirts past the knees, tie in place, beret on head.

She had come to New York from Indiana and found the city to be a strange place.

One morning, just as the bell rang, one of the girls from Queens walked up the street wearing a single loafer.

“Where’s your other shoe?” the sister asked.

“Someone stole it at 59th Street,” the girl replied.

— Monica Coffey

SUMMARY

When he was 20, Mr. Gallant modeled for promotional photos for Mr. S Leather, a San Francisco fetish brand; many of the photos, which capture Mr. Gallant engaged in sex acts with other men, were too explicit for even a tabloid to publish. Every time I posted a celebrity’s leaked photo on Gawker’s sex blog, Fleshbot, I told myself that I was helping to destigmatize taking sexy selfies with an X-rated take on “Stars — They’re Just Like Us!” Being tagged in embarrassing photos has become a rite of passage; it’s hard to work up outrage when someone else’s erotic exploits wind up in the tabloids.

ARTICLE

The Sex Scandal That Wasn’t
It’s hard to work up outrage when someone else’s adult exploits wind up in the tabloids.
By Lux Alptraum
Published 2026-10-11 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/opinion/chris-gallant-campaign-photos.html

It wasn’t all that long ago that if The New York Post published photographs of an aspiring congressman wearing a leather collar and a chain-link leash, his campaign would have immediately been over. Yet that doesn’t seem to be the case for Chris Gallant, the gay, gun-toting former Black Hawk pilot who’s running for Congress on eastern Long Island. He still may not win, but these photos alone haven’t sunk his chances.

When he was 20, Mr. Gallant modeled for promotional photos for Mr. S Leather, a San Francisco fetish brand; many of the photos, which capture Mr. Gallant engaged in sex acts with other men, were too explicit for even a tabloid to publish. Instead of apologizing or withdrawing his candidacy in disgrace, Mr. Gallant has embraced his naughty brand, running ads that urge voters to “Make Politics Sexy Again.” “I mean, all my friends know I’m kinky,” he said in an interview with The Times. “I make Christian Grey look like amateur hour.”

His approach raises a question: Has our historically prurient politics finally gone post-shame?

In 2007, I started my first media job at Gawker Media, where there was no hot gossip or leaked photo of a public figure that was considered too salacious to publish. Sometimes our muckraking turned seemingly promising political candidates — like the Democratic congressional candidate Krystal Ball, who made headlines after bloggers leaked a photo of her as a sexy Santa with a dildo-nosed Rudolph at her side — into sideshows; in other cases, like the anonymous confession of a one-night stand with the Delaware Republican Senate candidate Christine O’Donnell, it further weakened an already rickety campaign.

But it always felt as if we were publishing on borrowed time. Our Gen X founder, Nick Denton, would often muse that millennials like me who’d come of age on Facebook would reshape notions of what was newsworthy. How could a saucy photo be seen as shocking when sexting, online porn and the anything-goes era of the internet and early social media had inoculated an entire generation to much worse? Then, I firmly believed that this post-shame era was just around the corner. Every time I posted a celebrity’s leaked photo on Gawker’s sex blog, Fleshbot, I told myself that I was helping to destigmatize taking sexy selfies with an X-rated take on “Stars — They’re Just Like Us!”

My cohort grew up, and that stigma didn’t subside. In 2019, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez had been in Congress for less than a week when she became the subject of a nude photo scandal. Though the photo supposedly of Ms. Ocasio-Cortez turned out to be fake, the implication that such a photo would be shameful was real. Later that year, Katie Hill resigned from the House of Representatives after her real nude photos were leaked to the press. She might not have been ashamed of the adventurous sex life those photos depicted, but that hardly mattered when it came to holding on to her political career.

So what, exactly, has changed?

Millennials and Gen Z now make up nearly half of the electorate. These generations have grown up online, documenting a wide range of formerly private moments in public. Being tagged in embarrassing photos has become a rite of passage; it’s hard to work up outrage when someone else’s erotic exploits wind up in the tabloids.

These generations have also been exposed to significantly more ideas about once-taboo topics like sexuality and drugs, turning moments that might once have ended careers into total shrugs. Attitudes toward sexuality, in particular, have become increasingly laissez-faire, thanks in part to the L.G.B.T.Q. people, kink and fetish aficionados, and sex workers who’ve found community and cultivated online fans. Catchphrases like “sex work is work” and “don’t kink shame” may, at times, be nothing more than empty posturing, but they also illustrate a growing values shift. In a world where OnlyFans is increasingly seen — among young people, at least — as a wholly legitimate occupation, it’s hard to get worked up over someone else’s nudes. So what if a politician once modeled for a saucy advertisement?

In an earlier era, there was a plausible argument that a member of Congress who was engaging in so-called sexual deviance could pose a national security risk. What better way for foreign forces to blackmail a government official than by threatening to reveal sexual secrets? But as people have lived more openly, social mores have become more accepting. What better defense against having your secrets exploited than refusing to have any secrets at all?

In Mr. Gallant’s case, it’s refreshing to see a gay politician openly embrace the more outré (but relatively common) aspects of queer culture, particularly after stories like Pete Buttigieg’s allegedly refusing to campaign in a gay bar with a dancer pole on the premises. At a time when “authenticity” is a buzzword in political circles, being willing to admit that queer life isn’t always a monogamous suburban lifestyle, perfectly calibrated to offend the fewest people, feels genuine.

However, I’m hesitant to take Mr. Gallant’s example as a sure sign that our society has changed for good. Handsome white men are often more indulged, whatever their proclivities. His masculine profile and military bona fides make it easy to imagine him fitting comfortably in the halls of power. It’s notable that Mr. Gallant referred to Christian Grey — a fictional character mainstream enough to be idolized by millions of women across America — rather than a gay subcultural figure like Robert Mapplethorpe. Female voters, in particular, might be less shocked than titillated by it all.

It is harder to imagine a relatively unknown woman of color being able to bounce back from bondage photos leaked to the press. Being seen as a sexual being is still treated as a black mark on a woman’s record. Not because it makes her more susceptible to blackmail but because, unlike a BDSM dominant like Christian Grey, sexual women still are seen not as powerful, capable leaders but rather as submissive objects who can’t be taken seriously.

Hopefully, we can one day achieve a world where all of us are post-shame. But in order to arrive there, we’ll need to fully grasp that there’s nothing demeaning about consensually enjoying sex, leashed or not.

Lux Alptraum was an editor in chief of Fleshbot, a blog about sex and adult entertainment, and is the author of “Faking It: The Lies Women Tell About Sex — and the Truths They Reveal.”

ARTICLE

The Neuroscience of Decluttering
Decluttering is a challenge for many Americans, but neuroscience indicates we can make the process easier on ourselves and our loved ones.
By Emily Falk
Published 2026-10-11 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/opinion/clutter-spring-cleaning-psychology.html

When I came across old high school notebooks of mine while helping my mom declutter my childhood home, I knew I should throw them away. Even if I’d wanted to brush up on Latin American history, they would be a poor resource. And yet I didn’t want to let go.

Many of us face clutter when we do our spring cleaning or, far harder, when we deal with a deceased loved one’s things. Americans spend billions of dollars each year on storage, and many live with jam-packed basements and attics. As a neuroscientist studying how people make decisions, I have also seen that when given the tools, people can choose to work with, rather than against, the brain systems that regulate decision making to help themselves let go of old ideas and behaviors. Knowing how our minds work is the first step to aligning our decision making with our goals and values.

It isn’t irrational to have trouble letting objects go. The parts of our brain that help us decide what is valuable overlap with the parts that keep track of what feels like us. As a result, we feel that what is ours is good, and we increase the value we attach to objects, ideas and behaviors from our past.

People given an object typically place more value on it than they assign to a similar object they don’t own. In one study, participants were asked to sort objects into a basket that would be theirs and one that would be someone else’s. Placing objects in their own basket immediately produced more brain activity in the self-relevance system, and those objects were later remembered and preferred over other objects. Such research helps make sense of why when I held my old notebooks, they felt like pieces of me — objects of real value that I didn’t want to throw away.

In these moments, loss aversion is powerful. In studies in which people made choices about what to buy and sell, the sellers who had the most difficulty parting with items showed the most brain activity in regions that process pain, risk and attention. So we hold on to family heirlooms — as well as pants that no longer fit and piles of travel mugs cluttering the pantry.

Objects can also become cues that activate memories, momentarily bringing them back into focus. One brain-imaging study indicated that past versions of ourselves compress in our minds, similarly to how faraway objects blur in the distance. Holding a hat you used to love activates memories from that past self, creating a portal between who you are now and the person you once were. For me, it’s hard to let go of things that offer that sense of connection, however tenuous.

Still, my research told me that holding on to objects like my old notebooks was the wrong approach. My lab studies what happens in people’s brains when they are making choices and how we can use that understanding to make change easier. One way to make change easier is to switch from the standpoint of possessor to buyer. Instead of asking, “Do I want to keep this?” ask, “Would I buy this today?” Modifying the decision-making framework allows a neural calculation in reward and self-relevance systems to shift, too. A teakettle becomes something you can choose — or not — rather than something you stand to lose.

Another way to think about things from a different perspective is to borrow someone else’s eyes. In my team’s research, when we asked people to imagine another person’s perspective, it altered their behavior to be more similar to that imagined person’s. Brain scans show that taking another person’s perspective also changes our brains’ reactions to unpleasant situations and can even affect how we think of ourselves. When I showed my partner my old notebooks, he reminded me that he isn’t enthusiastic about storing musty old papers in our basement. He’s less sentimental because his brain doesn’t treat the old notebooks as part of me, as mine does.

Researchers have found that people going through old things feel more willing to part with an item if they are coached to take a photograph to remember it by. In one study, two sets of dorm rooms were equipped with posters encouraging students to donate unwanted items. One set of posters also encouraged the students to take a picture of the items before donating them. The dorms with posters suggesting a photo had 15 percent more donations.

For me, the goal isn’t to get rid of every single thing, but to see clearly why I choose to keep things and become more purposeful in those choices. Research documents the brain’s tendency to prioritize immediate rewards, so figuring out how to make the process of change feel better is crucial.

Taking a moment to connect with others is one way to activate the brain’s reward systems. I make sure to respond enthusiastically to a photo of nine boxes ready for donation on a friend’s porch, knowing that positive social responses can be fuel to keep her going. Connecting with others also helps manage stress. When I found an old doll from a friend’s mother who collected dolls when she was alive, I texted him. “She loved you so much, and dolls meant the world to her,” he told me, adding, “I have a creepy doll in my house, too.” Giving advice to someone in the same situation can also help us do the right thing ourselves. When I hold up objects for my mom to photograph and ask whether she’d buy the items today or how a neutral observer might react to them, the questions remind me of the tools I need, too.

We must also recognize how the environment we’re in got us here. Ubiquitous targeted advertising, frictionless buying and cheaper manufacturing have tricked us into accumulating so much more than we need. If we want to avoid the pain of decluttering later, we can also actively remove the technologies that push us to accumulate in the first place.

Letting go isn’t hard because the objects themselves are objectively so precious. It’s hard because the brain sees it as changing who we are — and resists that. The same is true for our old ideas and behaviors. But if we take a step back and use our imagination and connection to others to see the problem in a new way, we can more purposefully let go of the things that aren’t serving us without losing the core of who we are.

Emily Falk is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and the author of “What We Value: The Neuroscience of Choice and Change.”
