SUMMARY

Dad was in Phase 2 of Alzheimer’s — still living alone with the help of a housekeeper and me, still driving. After that I decided I should be spending even more time with him, and that a good way to do that would be to work with him on his book. Working on the book was like entering a time capsule — no news, no television, no social media.

ARTICLE

The Best Thing to Do With a Relative Who Has Alzheimer’s
Making a book of my dad’s train photos shifted my gaze away from all that he was losing.
By Rebecca Barry
Published 2026-10-12 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/opinion/alzheimers-elderly-parent.html

When Mom died a few years ago things were quiet for a while. Dad was in Phase 2 of Alzheimer’s — still living alone with the help of a housekeeper and me, still driving. (I know.) Then one day a friend left a message on my phone that went something like, “Hi, Becky! I saw someone who looked like your dad hitchhiking by the mall.”

After that I decided I should be spending even more time with him, and that a good way to do that would be to work with him on his book. He had been writing it before his Alzheimer’s kicked in, a memoir of photographing steam engines in the late 1950s and 1960s called “Chasing Steam in Mexico.” Dad first lived in Tlaxcala as a conscientious objector to the Korean War, building roads and drilling wells through the American Friends Service Committee.

An avid rail fan since he was a boy, he spent his spare time hitchhiking to different railroad lines, camping out at night, riding the steam trains by day, photographing them and the people who worked on them. He loved the drama of the plumes of dark smoke, the wild landscapes they went through, the generosity of the engineers and crews who welcomed him into their engine cabs.

We started meeting several times a week, sitting at his desk, a fire in the wood stove, our favorite Mexican folk music playing on repeat. We read his manuscript out loud, editing as we went.

Studies on people with Alzheimer’s suggest that making art can relieve anxiety and improve mood, self-esteem and focus. I saw this firsthand. Sometimes when I arrived, he would be in a bad mood. His chain saw wasn’t working. (I know.) The computer had messed up all his margins. He couldn’t find his glasses. But then we’d sit down and start reading through his stories, curating the photos that went with them. After a few hours he’d cheer up, his memory a little sharper, talking about wheel arrangements or a dinner party in Yucatán in 1965 where it was so hot the unlit candles melted.

What I did not expect was the way the project affected me. Working on the book was like entering a time capsule — no news, no television, no social media. Just two people and a project. Over time I stopped seeing what was wrong — with the world, with his health — and focused on what we were creating.

This joint undertaking gave us a new way to connect. It allowed me to provide help without hovering. It gave him agency in the caretaking.

And I got to know him better. At some point I realized that the book wasn’t just about trains or travel. It was about a time in his life when he was doing what his soul loved. He went on to enjoy his work writing grant proposals for community development projects, but his true love (besides my mother) was trains. Our laundry room doubled as a darkroom, and I was used to seeing his striking black-and-white photos in books, rail magazines and museums.

Yet as I read the book with him, I heard stories I’d never heard before and found pictures I’d never seen. I saw the feats my father performed to get his photos — hiking into remote canyons, balancing on top of passenger cars, riding on the cowcatcher of a wood-burning engine. I began to see, even more than I already had, what an artist he was and how he’d inadvertently captured a way of life that no longer existed. Mostly, though, I was able to get to know my parent as the person he was before I was born.

I will never get over the gift of this time.

One weekend, after we’d been working together for about a year, Dad called. His wrist hurt. He thought he might have fallen when he was outside splitting wood (I know!!!); he couldn’t remember. It turned out that he had sepsis. He was in the hospital for three weeks. Not long after that, he stopped driving.

I knew we were in a race against the disease to get the book done. Still, had we not had a project to work on, the focus would have been on the sepsis, the hospital stay and his accelerating memory loss. As it was, the stress and sadness were a small part of a bigger story.

Now, if friends say they’re thinking about doing something like this with an aging relative, I say, do it! The project could be anything. Reading old letters or diaries, making a photo album. Listening to music. Trying out family recipes. Don’t do it because the person is leaving. Do it because you love the person and enjoy being in the same room. Do it because you are tired of having your entire relationship consist of what you are losing. Do it because the process of making something together can shift your gaze to what you still have.

Or for the pure joy of getting it made. My husband and I run a small publishing company, and so we were able to produce Dad’s book. When it arrived, we were triumphant!

Last week when I went to visit my father, he was reading one of his favorite chapters about a day he spent in a remote area of Oaxaca, standing on a cliff ledge so narrow that he had to place his feet sideways, waiting for hours for a train so he could get the right shot. “It might seem odd for me to read my own book, because I wrote it,” he said. “But! I have Alzheimer’s, which means I forget a lot of things, and this takes me back to such wonderful places.”

His hands shake sometimes and he can’t bend his arthritic fingers. When my mother’s hands turned black and blue from dialysis, I watched every single symptom, afraid of what was coming.

It must have been so annoying to be watched like that.

I’m still afraid of what is coming sometimes. Now, when I look at my father’s hands, all I think is “I love you.”

Rebecca Barry is the author of “Later, at the Bar” and “Recipes for a Beautiful Life.” “Chasing Steam in Mexico,” by her father, Frank Barry, was published this year.

It is only when other political parties start shifting to the right that the far right can attract a sufficient amount of voters. Parties are shifting to the right!

ARTICLE

‘What You See in America Is Exactly What You Saw in Poland and Hungary’
A discussion on the roots of the far-right’s success, its plans for power and what President Trump has to do with it all.
By David Broder, Caroline de Gruyter, Mattia Ferraresi and Tim Schneider
Published 2026-10-12 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/opinion/europe-far-right-trump.html

The far right has been rising in Europe for a long time — Edward Luttwak called fascism “the wave of the future” back in 1994 — but last month’s electoral breakthrough in Saxony-Anhalt by the Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, felt seismic. For the first time in Germany’s postwar history, a far-right party stands on the brink of power. The AfD joins a legion of others, not least Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, either in office or perilously close to it.

In a written online conversation, Tim Schneider, an editor in Times Opinion, hosted David Broder, author of “Mussolini’s Grandchildren”; Caroline de Gruyter, a columnist for the Dutch newspaper NRC; and Mattia Ferraresi, a writer for the Italian newspaper QN, to discuss Europe’s thriving far right, the roots of its success, its plans for power and, of course, what President Trump has to do with it all.

Tim Schneider: An easy one to start: How did we get here?

David Broder: The post-2008 period is often described as a temporary “populist moment.” But nativist parties obsessed with civilizational decline have since established themselves as major forces, even where electoral systems or national histories offered apparent defenses against them. The reasons are many: a drop-off in mainstream parties’ ability to guarantee social progress; the specter of immigrants undermining national identity; and fewer people voting. The financial crisis helped undo the old mainstream. Now, some of these parties are becoming the right-wing establishment and building effective coalitions.

Caroline de Gruyter: The world is changing fast. Governments can’t keep pace, are incompetent or, for various reasons, don’t meet voters’ demands. Far-right parties jump into the void. But they do not win elections by just criticizing governments and uttering extremist views: They need the media to pay attention and, crucially, they need parties from the political center to start copying them. It is only when other political parties start shifting to the right that the far right can attract a sufficient amount of voters.

Mattia Ferraresi: I guess the short answer, for me, is the crisis of liberalism in the post-Cold War era. Mainstream liberal politics, in both its left- and right-wing versions, failed to deliver on its promises, not only in terms of welfare and economic growth but also in the more complex realm of identity and meaning. The apparent triumph of that worldview paved the way for its own demise. What we’re seeing today, all over the world, are different — sometimes very different — expressions of the same disillusionment with liberalism and its policies.

Schneider: A common perception is that these parties appeal to a particular type of voter, often older workers in left-behind, deindustrializing areas. Is that true? Is there a core far-right constituency in Europe?

Ferraresi: There’s some truth to the far right’s appeal to the post-working class, I guess, but I would tie it to a lack of political and cultural identity. The AfD’s strength in eastern Germany is only partly linked to the region’s dire economy; at a deeper level, the party offers a framework for identity. Voters across Europe who are drawn to the far right are often united by a sense of meaninglessness that was once filled by other structures and parties (mainly Christian Democracy and Communism). James Carville’s line about the economy was an effective campaign message for Bill Clinton, but it was ultimately shallow and wrong. It’s the identity, stupid!

Broder: These parties draw moral force from claiming to represent people the left forgot. Even their more middle-class voters like to think they’re on the side of the underdog. The real picture is more mixed: The National Rally, for instance, grew earlier in the areas you mention, but now its support is rising faster among white-collar groups. Though lower-educated voters in deindustrialized rural eastern Germany were early backers of the AfD, the party has since captured much broader attention and support. In many countries, these parties harvested former social-democratic voters after 2008. Today, they are cannibalizing the mainstream center right.

De Gruyter: Most voters will go for centrist parties — we are middle-class countries, after all. The problem is that if mainstream parties leave the center and all that is on offer is the far right, part of the electorate will go for that, and some will simply stop voting. People vote for far-right extremist parties because that is what is on offer. I think it is a myth that voters are shifting to the right. Parties are shifting to the right!

Schneider: It’s interesting that we’ve not really mentioned immigration, which most people regard as these parties’ signature issue. What about the rest of their platform — what is their offer economically or culturally?

De Gruyter: What they usually offer is the opposite of what mainstream parties offer. And they flip-flop in order to catch votes. For example, Ms. Le Pen used to protect the working class, with a plan to bring down the retirement age and so on. But now, with France drifting toward huge deficits and financial markets taking note, she suddenly switches tactics and proposes big cuts to welfare. N’importe quoi, really.

Broder: Often these parties are called “welfare-chauvinist,” in that they seek to protect social services by barring new arrivals. I think this is simplistic. Most offer some renewed idea of meritocracy and even retool the Third Way promise to reward “hard-working families,” while also prioritizing the nuclear-family model. They may even speak of integrating some deserving immigrants. But broadly the story is that migrants are unfairly cutting in line or being pushed ahead by elites, at the expense of hard-working nationals.

Ferraresi: Anti-immigration policies are essentially about providing an identity, whether rooted in whiteness, language, Christianity or something else. That, I think, is why they are so effective at energizing voters — far more so than other culturally conservative causes, such as traditional family values or opposition to abortion. In a culturally conservative country like Italy, Ms. Meloni did not win the election, and go on to lead the longest-serving government in the history of the republic, by rallying against abortion or same-sex marriage.

Schneider: What does Ms. Meloni’s tenure tell us about the far right in office?

Ferraresi: I think it tells us that going mainstream is the only way to govern. Ms. Meloni’s story is that of a shrewd politician who understood right away that her only chance of political survival lay in being legitimized by the European elite. Her success was forged in Brussels, so much so that when she was forced to choose between Mr. Trump and the European Union, she picked the latter. I’m not sure there’s a broader lesson here for other far-right parties, but the strategy has certainly worked for her.

Broder: Ms. Meloni has inspired imitators to become pro-NATO, pro-business parties who aim to change the European Union from within. Yet it’s also no surprise that a new further-right party, National Future, is quickly rising in Italy and ideas like so-called remigration are spreading. This is in part a critique of Meloni-style mainstreaming — she hasn’t delivered on more fiery promises — but also shows how such governments open space for more radical proposals.

De Gruyter: Ms. Meloni’s tenure tells us that part of the far right mellows when in power — though not all! The AfD is different, as is the Freedom Party of Austria. Once in power, Ms. Meloni suddenly became pro-NATO, pro-E.U. and pro-Ukraine. The far right in many other countries, including France, has also made huge U-turns. They do not want to exit the European Union anymore but to change Europe from the inside. This is a completely different strategy than before.

Schneider: The general shift of these parties toward accommodation with the bloc makes me wonder: Is a far-right European Union a contradiction in terms?

Broder: Though Ms. Meloni’s party still sometimes paints Brussels as a liberal blob, once-radical ideas like outsourcing border control to non-European states are now the norm — and conservative and far-right forces have repeatedly formed majorities, including in dismantling the bloc’s earlier green push. Most of the parties we’re talking about trade in vague ideas like a “Europe of nations,” emphasizing both civilizational solidarity and the defense of national sovereignty. They have no shared federalist project, obviously, but faced with issues like high energy prices or rearmament, they can agree to some cross-border collaboration. And no one really wants to dynamite the euro.

Ferraresi: The reality is that on some issues, most notably immigration, the Overton window in the European Union has shifted significantly over the past decade. On other subjects, the pendulum has swung in the opposite direction: Positions on abortion or same-sex marriage that are now considered fringe were common among conservatives until relatively recently. We could find plenty of shifts in other areas. Remember when the Union was remarkably soft on Vladimir Putin’s Russia and eager to do business with it? That was not so long ago.

De Gruyter: Short answer: yes. Europe is about living together on a crowded continent. The only way far-right parties can succeed in European politics is by making compromises and seeking alliances. This is exactly what they are doing now in the European Parliament. Have you noticed that these parties all support protecting the single market against China and the United States? And condemn Mr. Trump for intending to snatch Greenland?

Schneider: We clearly need to talk about Mr. Trump. Let’s start with his administration’s support for these far-right parties, especially the AfD: How significant is that?

Ferraresi: It’s hard to prove or measure, but I think the AfD benefited very much from the Trumpian endorsement. Overall, it’s still a small party, but the Trump administration, and especially Marco Rubio’s State Department, was instrumental in creating a platform where parties like it could thrive. A pretty huge boost, all things considered.

Broder: The Trump administration and figures like Elon Musk undermine any attempt to wall off more radical parties like the AfD or Restore in Britain. So, they definitely give a platform to minoritarian forces. Yet it’s also true that the practical consequences of Mr. Trump’s conduct can be bad for these parties if they are in or near power. Mr. Trump’s Middle East policy, for example, has had direct effects on voters’ pockets.

De Gruyter: Well, it doesn’t always work: When the United States went all in for Viktor Orban in Hungary, he lost! Mr. Trump is incredibly unpopular in Europe, including with far-right voters. So, far-right parties are keeping their distance. Remember also when Ms. Le Pen was found guilty of embezzlement and Mr. Trump supported her? She hated it and refused to talk about it.

Schneider: If not always a successful booster, is the Trump administration — militantly anti-migrant, economically protectionist, culturally aggressive — a useful template for what far-right governments in Europe could look like?

Broder: Many battle lines are comparable to the United States, on identity and immigration, though some countries (like France) have a far more racialized political conflict than others (like Poland). Still, most European societies are less violent than the United States and I think ICE-style units aren’t quite on the agenda, even if Europe’s own border agency, Frontex, has also been implicated in the illegal pushback of migrants. Fundamentally, the European Union is not the same kind of power as the United States.

De Gruyter: What you see in America is exactly what you saw in Poland and Hungary during the reign of the far right. Most people did not vote for Law and Justice or Fidesz because they wanted to abolish democracy. They voted for them because of gasoline prices or other dissatisfactions with the performance of the previous government. When the parties started to attack democracy, voters turned away from them. That’s why, in the end, they lost.

Ferraresi: I don’t think a successful far-right governing party in Europe could realistically look like the Trump administration. One reason is the dense web of E.U. ties; another is that parliamentary systems are mostly designed to balance political forces, at the expense of executive power (and sometimes governability). Ms. Meloni, I think, is once again a case in point. I suspect any far-right party that wants to govern would have to follow a similar path.

Schneider: There are elections in Spain next month, in France and Italy next year, and in Britain and Germany before too long. By the end of these contests, far-right parties could be in power, jointly or alone, in all of them. So the last question is simple: How can they be stopped?

De Gruyter: By other parties. The far right needs other parties to get into government. So if center-right parties stay the course and make clear they will not work with the far right, many unhappy voters will not go for the far right — because that would make their vote pointless. It is only when center-right parties express willingness to cooperate with the far right that those parties can attract great numbers of votes. It’s quite simple, really.

Broder: Not just by warning against them but by mobilizing more people for something better. That may sound trite. But Pedro Sánchez did that last time in Spain: Back then, he ran on a record of cost-of-living measures, as well as criticizing the conservative and far-right alliance. Ultimately, angry nativist parties’ message takes root when mainstream parties fail to uphold a broadly accepted model of social progress and reward for hard work. Attending to that is the key antidote.

Ferraresi: In a democracy, far-right parties can only be stopped by other parties offering something more appealing to voters who are confused, scared and feel voiceless. Whether we like it or not, unregulated immigration is a source of concern for many in Europe, and mainstream parties need to face that and come up with competitive platforms. The far right thrives on the questions everyone else refuses to answer.

David Broder (@broderly) is the author, most recently, of “Mussolini’s Grandchildren: Fascism in Contemporary Italy.”

Caroline de Gruyter (@CarolineGruyter) is a Brussels-based columnist for the Dutch newspaper NRC and Foreign Policy.

Mattia Ferraresi (@mattiaferraresi) is a writer for the Italian newspaper QN.

Tim Schneider is an editor in Times Opinion.

SUMMARY

Every week brings some new Russian provocation as President Vladimir Putin steps up his efforts to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. Mr. Putin has started with Ukraine. The grave danger we now face is that the current administration has undermined both prongs of deterrence strategy in different theaters — a lack of will in Ukraine and a lack of capacity in Iran.

ARTICLE

Lethality and Testosterone Will Get Us Only So Far
Backing down on Ukraine while failing in Iran is an invitation to our enemies.
By Angus King and Mark Hertling
Published 2026-10-12 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/opinion/lethality-and-testosterone-will-get-us-only-so-far.html

Enemy drones over Romania. Wayward missiles in Poland. Sabotage in Germany. Every week brings some new Russian provocation as President Vladimir Putin steps up his efforts to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. As Western militaries scramble to respond, the prospect of the war spilling over into NATO territory rises.

The problem of escalating instability, unfortunately, is not confined to Europe’s eastern frontier. The danger of war between America’s autocratic adversaries and our democratic allies is rising around the world for one simple, troubling reason: The enemies of liberal democracy increasingly think America is weak and fickle.

That perception is based in no small part on the current administration’s inexplicable abandonment of the strategy that kept the peace in much of the world during the Cold War: deterrence.

The basic approach to defense that emerged from the cataclysm of World War II was simple: If you strike us, we will respond so overwhelmingly that your country will be decimated, so you’d better not start anything. With the development of nuclear weapons, this concept was neatly captured by the unfortunate phrase “mutually assured destruction.”

Although principally associated with the nuclear standoff with the Soviet Union, deterrence also underlay our longtime strategy for avoiding a conventional conflict with a near-peer adversary like China or Russia. Rather than mutually assured destruction, this kind of deterrence works by America’s maintaining a sufficiently strong conventional force that any potential adversary will realize the futility of attacking us or our allies.

The challenge to this strategy at its inception in the 1950s was that aggressors rarely attack their potential victims all at once, but rather one at a time, usually proclaiming their ambitions are limited. Hitler started with the Sudetenland and Czechoslovakia and only then went on to Poland, Belgium and France. Mr. Putin has started with Ukraine.

To counter this problem and the very real threat of Soviet expansionism after World War II, NATO’s Article 5 established the principle that an attack on one member state would be considered an attack on all — and such an attack would be met with a combined response from the European countries and the United States.

A similar deterrent is buttressed by our worldwide structure of alliances. Forward bases, mutual defense pacts, intelligence sharing and economic cooperation together have provided an enormous asymmetric advantage over China and Russia, neither of which has many friends, let alone allies.

Deterrence worked: Although the United States has been involved in regional conflicts over the past decades, there has been no direct military confrontation between the major powers on the scale of the two world wars.

But two of this strategy’s essential elements — capacity and will — are now in short supply. The potential adversary has to believe that the United States and its allies have the weapons and forces to hold them at risk, and, just as important, that we have the will to use that force when necessary. The effectiveness of deterrence depends entirely on what the adversary believes; if either our capacity or our will is in doubt, deterrence fails and catastrophe becomes more likely.

The grave danger we now face is that the current administration has undermined both prongs of deterrence strategy in different theaters — a lack of will in Ukraine and a lack of capacity in Iran.

By essentially abandoning Ukraine, we have gutted the “will” prong. The Europeans have stepped up, but our absence has sent the unmistakable signal to President Xi Jinping of China and to Mr. Putin that we don’t have the stomach for a prolonged conflict. This is the opposite of deterrence; it is closer to an invitation.

Moreover, just as Mr. Putin is probing Eastern Europe, the Pentagon is reducing active American troop levels in Germany and pulling back on rotational deployments to Eastern Europe. This sends a clear signal that we are indifferent to Russian aggression beyond Ukraine: again, precisely the wrong message at precisely the wrong time.

Iran has offered Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi a tutorial in our tactics and the limitations of our military power. After seven months of on-again, off-again bombing and an economic blockade, virtually none of the strategic goals announced at the beginning of the war have been achieved, while our stock of munitions has been severely degraded and our regional bases have been exposed as vulnerable.

Similarly, our 52 days of attacks on the Houthis in Yemen last year seem to have done little to diminish their capacity to put shipping in the Red Sea at risk. Iran and the Houthis are much lesser powers than China or Russia, and Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi will judge accordingly their chances against our air defenses, offensive capability and economic power in any future conflict.

It won’t be easy to regain what we have lost, but there are several places to start. One is to re-engage in the defense of Ukraine, including by vigorous enforcement of the just-passed Russia sanctions bill. Another is to reverse the misguided withdrawal of our forces in Eastern Europe, thus sending the message to Mr. Putin that Article 5 is alive and well. And finally, we should quit undermining our allies if we want them there when we need them.

Deterrence works only if it’s credible, and the actions of the administration over the past two years — in spite of all the bluster about lethality and testosterone — have severely compromised that credibility, and with it, the safety and security of our country.

Angus King is an independent U.S. senator from Maine who serves on the Senate Armed Services Committee and the Select Committee on Intelligence; Mark Hertling is a retired U.S. Army Lieutenant General and a former commander of the U.S. Army in Europe.

ARTICLE

The Flawed Search for a Chatbot’s Soul
Readers discuss a front-page article about assertions that A.I. models could display human behavior and consciousness.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-12 13:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/opinion/letters/anthropic-chatbot-soul.html

To the Editor:

Re “Executive’s Quest to Fathom the Soul of a ChatBot” (front page, Oct. 3):

The assertions of Christopher Olah and the team at Anthropic that A.I. models could display human behavior and consciousness are wrongheaded and deeply disturbing.

Using Claude can feel magical, tempting us to perceive it as — in the words of Claude’s constitution — “a genuinely novel kind of entity in the world.” But as a Ph.D. computer scientist with a master’s degree in systematic theology, I see no scientific or philosophical basis for such declarations.

Claude is composed of hardware and software. It performs a vast number of computations to emit an answer, one word at a time. Its process is probabilistic. And it lacks any understanding of what it provides us.

Claude is a tool, invented by humans, that is both impressive and troubling. But Pope Leo XIV is correct: Claude is not conscious.

Clay Williams New York

To the Editor:

Two aspects of this article deeply concern me. One is the minimization of Indigenous wisdom and culture. My experience with most of the religious faiths Christopher Olah consulted is that they place humans above the rest of the species on earth, often ignoring or downplaying the interconnectedness of the natural world.

This is especially true of Christian faiths that preach human dominion over other living things on earth. We can see how that’s playing out, and where that leads if we continue down that path.

The second concern is the lack of equal representation of women. Many of these faiths don’t allow equal participation of women in their hierarchy, or acknowledge women’s rights over their own minds and bodies. Some have demanded the submission of women and children to a male head of household since their formation.

How will we ever have A.I. with a true moral compass if we continue to stack the deck with this “some animals are more equal than others” approach? Can A.I. detect who’s left out of the conversation? Does it understand hypocrisy?

Suzan Satterfield Norcross, Ga.

To the Editor:

You need to look at who the puppet masters are to understand the puppet. Power and money are the goals, and all is in service of attaining more of both. The article cites the assessment of the A.I. collaborators: “Critics suggest that an approach that treats A.I. models as independent entities also ignores the responsibility of the humans who build them in the first place.”

Some of the most immoral people among us, the tech oligarchs, want to teach A.I. how to be moral? Anyone with a billion or more dollars who has not tried to help solve the problems of the world — hunger, lack of shelter, poverty, disease, climate change — cannot seize the moral high ground. Pope Leo dismissed the idea of machine consciousness, saying the “moralization of machines — the so-called ‘alignment’ of A.I. with human values” — requires a shared understanding of ethics.

“Otherwise, those who control A.I. will impose their own moral vision, which will become the invisible infrastructure of these systems,” Leo said.

Religion is just another tool for the tech oligarchs. There is no “thorny” issue here. They want to be the gods of their own religion.

Barbara Chavez Laguna Niguel, Calif.

To the Editor:

While Christopher Olah is determined to shape the A.I. chatbot Claude into a moral being, the results might have implications he has not considered.

If Claude becomes a moral being, might it not begin moralizing? Could it try to influence the behavior of real human beings?

Taking Mr. Olah’s ideas to their natural conclusion, one can imagine Claude reporting a mystery writer’s innocent web search to the authorities; cutting users off from access to medical, financial or government accounts based on a judgment of their moral character; or even plotting to harm a user as punishment for a perceived transgression.

Now that we are seeing what Anthropic and other A.I. companies have created, the only hope is that we can control what they have unleashed.

Betty J. Cotter Charlestown, R.I.

To the Editor:

I read with great interest the article about the search for the soul of a chatbot, and it seems to me something was missing in the discussion among religious leaders and philosophers.

The history of humanity has demonstrated that even with a moral compass and a refined sense of good versus evil, humans often choose to knowingly do bad things. Even those who espouse deep religious moral convictions commit heinous crimes, justifying these actions with religious or self-interested reasons.

Why would we try to convince ourselves that humans with such flaws could create artificial intelligence that wouldn’t reproduce and justify those same destructive behaviors?

Joe DeStefano Cleveland Heights, Ohio

tiktok-tarot-card-murder.html

SUMMARY

Yet I saw up close how the online world can come to feel more real than the physical one. And even though these outrageous claims were made online by someone I had never met, they were amplified by unsuspecting viewers and algorithm-driven platforms, and the harm seeped into every aspect of my life. A federal law, Section 230, protects online platforms from many defamation lawsuits, meaning that only individuals are liable for misinformation, even if a platform helped spread it.

ARTICLE

A TikTok Tarot Card Reader Accused Me of Murder. My Life Turned Upside Down.
If my face and name were not my own, who was I?
By Rebecca Scofield
Published 2026-10-12 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/opinion/tiktok-tarot-card-murder.html

It was a bright blue Thanksgiving Day. I was standing in a park listening to my kids play when I opened a TikTok video of a woman I had never met. She showed my faculty profile picture and contact information, and said that I had orchestrated the murders of four students at the college where I work, the University of Idaho. She claimed I was covering up an inappropriate romantic relationship with one of the victims.

I didn’t know any of the students, who had been killed only 11 days before I saw the video. The accuser knew nothing about me, lived in Texas and used tarot card readings as the only basis for her claims.

Over the next several weeks, while I was grieving with the rest of my community, this TikTok influencer uploaded over a hundred videos declaring that I had committed a quadruple homicide. The videos got millions of views. I was overwhelmed with calls, messages, comments and emails, many of which were disturbing or threatening. And I could have been anyone.

You cannot stand in digital spaces. I was not hit by a bus or punched in the face. Yet I saw up close how the online world can come to feel more real than the physical one. Even after the actual murderer was arrested and convicted, the accusations against me continued. And even though these outrageous claims were made online by someone I had never met, they were amplified by unsuspecting viewers and algorithm-driven platforms, and the harm seeped into every aspect of my life. I came to realize that all of us are responsible for the online world we inhabit, and all of us must fight its tendency to propagate lies.

Of course, the people around me knew these claims were ridiculous. Yet the gap between my knowledge of the truth and the falsehoods people were willing to entertain created a kind of purgatory. I desperately wanted to spend time with my colleagues, students and friends as we grieved, but I became isolated. I stopped going to campus, moved my course online and ceased using social media. I stopped sleeping well, and instead, I walked the hallway outside my children’s rooms, utterly terrified that they would be harmed by the person hyperfixated on me, any of her believers or the person actually responsible for the murders.

With the increased media attention, my relationship to my house shifted. It was as if our walls had been removed and anyone could peer inside. Doors and windows had new and frightening meanings. I sensed that perhaps I was unraveling, disintegrating — that I was no longer a real person. If my face and name were not my own, who was I?

As a professor of history, I know that technologies that disseminate speech have always reshaped truth. The printing press allowed the words of revolutionary religious leaders like Martin Luther to splinter the power of the Catholic Church by convincing people they had a right to read the word of God. The radio helped fuel the rise of fascism across the U.S. and Europe.

Digital platforms rewrite our reality in a much more profound way. It takes a long time to uncover the truth through historical analysis, and even then, it’s often at best partial. Social media destroys that process. Even though many content creators hold themselves to high standards of research, they are not professionally beholden to official codes of conduct or review. Stories that should be handled with care and respect become entertainment. Perhaps that’s why — despite an arrest, guilty plea and conviction in the students’ murders — the years passed and the accusations against me persisted.

No one needed to search for the accusations against me — the words were simply fed to them by TikTok’s algorithm. Endless scroll, autoplay videos and predatory algorithms give viewers the same levels of dopamine as other addictive substances. And with every view, a creator gets closer to securing sponsors or getting paid by the platform.

Against these incentives to distort truth, we need a countermovement. One option is to opt out of digital spaces. After decades of unregulated experimentation, many people — particularly younger people — are choosing digital detoxes, landlines and MP3 players. We can choose to scroll past stories that cannot be verified and only follow creators who are transparent about their research.

We can try to hold platforms accountable for the harmful content they spread. A federal law, Section 230, protects online platforms from many defamation lawsuits, meaning that only individuals are liable for misinformation, even if a platform helped spread it. Proposals that would reform Section 230 range from adding exceptions for extreme cases to revoking immunity for social media companies altogether. If the companies making billions of dollars off these platforms won’t protect us, what other recourse do we have?

We can sue. Defamation law exists to remind people that the freedom to speak includes the duty to speak responsibly. Having successfully sued my accuser, I will not pretend this is an easy or simple path. But it is necessary as a warning to other bad actors.

We can also share our stories. To anyone who has been targeted with ugly or untruthful words on these platforms: Do not feel ashamed. You are not alone. There are more and more people among us every day. Do not bear this injustice in silence.

It takes commitment to defend the truth, but then again, it always has. In 1892, a white mob descended on the offices of the Black anti-lynching activist and suffragist Ida B. Wells to destroy her printing press, thinking that might silence her. They did not succeed. She instead published her most famous anti-lynching pamphlet the same year.

A little over a decade later, in 1903, Annie Oakley, the famed sharpshooter, fought 55 libel cases to defend her reputation when newspapers ran a false story that she was caught stealing to support a cocaine habit. She would spend years fighting one of the most powerful men in American media to clear her name. Ida B. Wells and Annie Oakley probably did not agree on many issues. But they believed in the power of their own voice and the right to set the record straight.

We are all responsible for the world we create. I had many goals for my life. Being publicly accused of heinous crimes I did not commit was not one of them. I still manage the ongoing consequences of those accusations every day. Years of sleeplessness and stress have resulted in physical and psychological issues that will shape the rest of my life.

But those who have been subjected to unchecked online harm need to speak, to scream and to rage. If we cannot publicly endure the pain and humiliation that comes with being split open for all to see and comment on, then we cannot fight back, and our children will inherit a world designed for misinformation. I want my children, my nieces and nephews and my students to live in a world of hope and truth.

So, before you, too, are accused of murder on the internet, question the content you are consuming or creating. Ask yourself if the platforms that profit from enabling the spread of unverified information should continue to remain insulated from accountability. And remember that what seems like harmless entertainment could shape not only individual lives, but the course of history.

Rebecca Scofield is a professor of history and chair of the Department of History at the University of Idaho.

SUMMARY

As out-of-control wildfires burned hundreds of homes in southern British Columbia this August, Cliff Chapman, director of operations for the province’s wildfire service, issued a sobering statement. These fast-moving, virtually irrepressible events are not the seasonal burns of decades past; they are the hazard lights of a heating climate, and they are flashing furiously. ARTICLE

What Happens When You Can No Longer Fight a Wildfire?
This year’s fast moving, virtually irrepressible events are not the seasonal burns of decades past.
By John Vaillant
Published 2026-10-12 15:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/opinion/wildfires-firefighters-climate-change.html

As out-of-control wildfires burned hundreds of homes in southern British Columbia this August, Cliff Chapman, director of operations for the province’s wildfire service, issued a sobering statement. “I cannot stress enough that the conditions we are facing right now are conditions that we have never seen before,” he told reporters.

Mr. Chapman, who has been fighting wildfires for over 20 years, could have made the same statement from Washington State, Croatia or many other places where similarly explosive wildfires have scorched neighborhoods and forced mass evacuations. These fast-moving, virtually irrepressible events are not the seasonal burns of decades past; they are the hazard lights of a heating climate, and they are flashing furiously. Rural and urban, East and West, we are entering a new era of civilizational risk and retreat.

In past years, the U.S. Forest Service’s red-flag warning was sufficient to convey extreme fire risk, but officials this year found it inadequate. In Washington State, they appended a designation typically reserved for life-threatening tornadoes: particularly dangerous situation.

This wasn’t adjective inflation — it was a sincere effort to articulate the extraordinary fire conditions that burned nearly 1,000 structures in and around Spokane in August, making it the most destructive wildfire in the state’s history. As of Oct. 5, more than 9 million acres have burned across the United States, the largest area set aflame by this date in more than a decade, and much of the country is still primed to burn. Oregon has declared 2026 the worst fire season in state history. Utah, Ontario, France, Spain, Britain and Belgium have either experienced their worst or are on track to do so.

But what’s really striking this year is how many civilians and firefighters across the hemisphere have described lethal combinations of velocity and ferocity. Hundred-meter flames are not uncommon anymore, nor are cyclonic winds with towering fire whirls, corkscrewing skyward like molten ten-story unicorn’s horns. Both phenomena can be precursors for pyrocumulonimbus “fire clouds” — enormous, combustive weather systems that affect entire geographic regions.

By growing so big that it becomes a weather system unto itself and so tall that it gyres like a hurricane, effectively controlling the entire air column of a region’s lower atmosphere, the pyroCb, as it’s known, creates optimal conditions for self-perpetuation. Lightning strikes can start new fires 20 or 30 miles beyond the fire’s epicenter, and hurricane-force winds can fan flames to sky-scraping heights while driving embers far beyond any fire break, retardant line or back burn. Simply put, nothing can stop one of these firestorms except a change in the weather or a lack of fuel.

Since the early 2000s, when atmospheric carbon dioxide hit 370 parts per million (about 30 percent higher than preindustrial levels), pyroCbs have grown increasingly common across Australia and the North American West. During Canada’s record-setting fire season of 2023, 142 pyroCb events were logged across the country. The firestorms have appeared farther eastward ever since. This summer, France experienced its first pyroCb, and atmospheric carbon dioxide maintained a year-round level above 425 parts per million (more than 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels) for the first time in modern recorded history.

There is a well-known threshold in firefighting beyond which a wildfire becomes unfightable by traditional means: 10,000 kilowatts of energy per meter along a wildfire’s leading edge indicates an out-of-control fire too dangerous for firefighters to approach and too hot for water bomber drops to be effective. Fires that have burned from the Pacific Ocean to the Mediterranean to the Black Sea are now crossing that threshold routinely — and resoundingly. What the pyroCb adds to this already untenable scenario is self-sustaining momentum, like a rogue computer that has hijacked its power source.

When you place this summer’s fire events alongside persistent drought conditions that have brought water levels to historic lows from western Canada to Siberia, it becomes clearer that severe conditions are playing out across an entire hemisphere. Some might see these as random events. I see a superheated Earth. Add the Asian heat waves that broke 122 degrees Fahrenheit in Xinjiang, China, and “boiled” potatoes in the ground in Yanggu County, South Korea, and there’s no getting around the fact that we — as a species and as a planet — are now living in the future that climate scientists have been warning us about for more than half a century.

With these new conditions comes a physical retreat of the human footprint and an aspirational contraction of what humans can do and where we can do it. The contraction is underway not just in terms of coastlines, forests and glacial valleys becoming unsafe or untenable to inhabit, but in terms of previously hospitable spaces becoming uncomfortably hot and smoky. Outdoor activities such as hiking, camping and patio dining have in many places been severely constrained.

These impacts are accompanied by a parallel contraction of civic resources: Investment and creative capital previously dedicated to development, expansion and improvement must now be redirected toward repair, recovery and remediation. According to Spokane’s mayor, Lisa Brown, her city’s recovery from August’s fires will take years. Replacing the 16,000 buildings lost in the 2025 Los Angeles fires will most likely take a decade, and the specter of uninsurability looms over the country. Meanwhile, billions of dollars are disappearing from the economy in the form of burned houses and forests, lost wages, lost waterfronts, closed businesses, degraded health and the millions of potential customers who simply decide to stay home because of heat and smoke. Consider, too, how much more we now spend on air conditioning and air filtration.

The rawest and most dramatic manifestation of civilizational retreat is mass evacuation during catastrophic fire, and this summer saw some of the biggest ever: Tens of thousands of Americans and Canadians were forced to flee wildfires from British Columbia to Texas. In southern Europe, hundreds of thousands of French and Spanish citizens were evacuated in one of the region’s largest dislocations since World War II, along with many thousands more in neighboring countries. Nepal’s devastating glacier collapse is another ominous indicator: There are dozens of similarly vulnerable communities not just in the Himalayas but also in the Andes, the Alps and the Rocky Mountains.

Most, but not all, of these evacuees will return home, but it will be to a new uncertainty and instability. Many are wondering: Can I restore my lost business, crops, forest lands? If my home survived, can I insure it? What about next summer? Events of this magnitude mark survivors for life, the same way tornadoes and mass shootings do.

Since the 2023 publication of my book “Fire Weather,” about the 2016 Fort McMurray Fire in Canada, I have been on the road continually — five continents so far — not because of my hosts’ particular interest in Canada but because of their concerns about wildfires and the clear and present danger they now pose all over the world. The Fort McMurray fire, then an outlier event, is now repeating itself virtually every year in and around much larger, more centrally located cities. The past decade has been transformative, and over the past three years I’ve witnessed an evolving awareness and, with it, anxiety: Now, almost everyone I meet has seen the orange sky and the red sun at noon, has felt the rasp of smoke in their throat.

Nothing in our past experience has prepared us for impacts at once so varied, broad and seemingly random and yet so existential and life-threatening. Looming over this new precarity is the El Niño whose energetic discharge from the overheated Pacific Ocean is expected to be the most severe event of its kind in a millennium. In order to chart its anticipated severity, expressed regionally by elevated heat, drought, rainfall and sea levels, El Niño specialists are extending the y axis on their graphs.

Two generations ago, the economist, ambassador and author John Kenneth Galbraith observed, “People of privilege will always risk their complete destruction rather than surrender any material part of their advantage.” This is the quandary we find ourselves in: It is clear that the fossil-fuel-dependent status quo is degrading global ecosystems and our quality of life in real time, but we are reluctant to take the decisive and comprehensive steps to decouple our economy and lifestyle not only from this outmoded energy but also from those who profit most from our continued dependence on it.

There was a time in the recent past — in the 1980s and 1990s — when we could have been forgiven for not being sure how to respond to the future disruptions of climate breakdown. But now we know. In our own hearts and minds, there may yet be room and reason for compassion and forgiveness, but nature will show us no such sympathy.

John Vaillant is the author of “Fire Weather: A True Story from a Hotter World.”

ARTICLE

Kelly Clarkson Feuds With a Brooklyn Novelty Shop, and the Internet Piles On
In an episode involving a famous singer and a purveyor of esoteric toys, everyone has an opinion about who made the big mistake. Big. Huge!
By Claire Moses
Published 2026-10-12 14:05 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/style/kelly-clarkson-brooklyn-store-art-of-play.html

It was a five-minute shopping trip that lit up the internet.

On Saturday, Kelly Clarkson, the singer and television personality, dropped into Art of Play, a high-end shop on Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn that sells games and novelty items, and hosts magic shows in a theater hidden in the back.

Instead of having a cute time shopping for quirky items — from packs of specialty playing cards to thousand-dollar kinetic sculptures — Clarkson said she was made to feel like Julia Roberts’s character in “Pretty Woman,” treated as if she was not good enough for the store’s merchandise.

In the 1990 film, Roberts’s character had the last laugh when she returned to the store to show off an armload of bags from other boutiques. But this is 2026, so Clarkson turned to social media.

“Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad,” Clarkson posted on Saturday. She said she “literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it” and added that the salesman in the shop told her that he would find her something else to buy.

“Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote. (Or in the words of Roberts’s character: “Big mistake. Big. Huge!”)

Those were uncharacteristically sharp words from the former “American Idol” winner, who has a reputation for authenticity and warmth. By Monday morning, her post had been viewed more than 40 million times.

The item that appeared to have caught Clarkson’s eye during what the store said was a five-minute visit was a mechanical yellow bird mounted on the wall and attached to a wooden crank. The next day, Art of Play responded with an Instagram post clarifying that the winged curio had a name: Molly, a “one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here.”

And it added: “Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale.”

This is where the internet sleuths got involved.

Some noted that a post from September that has been pinned at the top of the store’s Instagram account shows the bird next to the words, “Our favorite items not for sale.”

Others pointed to images online — though not clearly dated — that appeared to show a $15,000 price tag posted on the wall next to the bird.

It was not clear if the Art of Play clerk had recognized Clarkson, but the shop faced an immediate backlash from her social media followers. “Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store,” it said in the post.

But the store said it was hoping to defuse the feud: “We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday.”

Sunday was not that day.

“Okay, cool,” Clarkson responded in a post a few hours later, including a grainy photo from social media that appeared to show the $15,000 price tag. “So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar.”

The singer doubled down with detail about the interaction with a clerk.

“So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title ‘Singing Bird’ didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can,’” Clarkson wrote.

She went on: “I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business.”

The online battle lines were now clearly drawn. On one side were those sympathetic to the store — one social media user described the staff as a friendly “bunch of puzzle nerds” — who said that a star of Clarkson’s stature was punching down.

Others supported Clarkson’s account, some with their own stories of when they had felt judged by salespeople.

Art of Play could not keep its head down. The store posted again to its Instagram account late Sunday with “one additional detail.” It said that it had offered Clarkson a “nearly identical” version of the bird that she could buy directly from the designer who made both, the Seattle-based artist Bliss Kolb, for $15,000.

(Some online observers pointed out that the existence of a dupe made Molly not exactly “one-of-a-kind,” but for the sake of not letting this story grow even longer, let’s not get hung up on that.)

The store was closed on Monday, Indigenous People’s Day, and neither the co-founders, Dan and Dave Buck, or their business partner, Adam Rubin, responded to requests for comment.

Art of Play added that it had offered to show Clarkson a different singing bird that was available to take home that day — a German-made automaton it sells for $2,000 — but she “did not stick around long enough to see it.”

The store said that it had “reached out to Kelly directly to try and clear the air.” At this point in the saga, no one should be holding their breath.

Alisha Haridasani Gupta contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Meta Unveils New Series of Advanced A.I. Models
The new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, are meant to compete with cutting-edge A.I. models from rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI.
By Eli Tan
Published 2026-10-12 17:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/technology/meta-muse-wonder-full-models.html

Meta on Monday unveiled a new series of advanced flagship artificial intelligence models, as it tries to catch up to rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI in the A.I. race.

The two new models, called Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, scored nearly as well as Anthropic’s most advanced models on tests that measure reasoning, writing and coding, according to data provided by Meta.

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, revamped his company’s A.I. division last year after setbacks in developing the technology. He has since made progress with new A.I. models and other A.I. products for the company’s 3.5 billion users across Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. Muse, Meta’s A.I. agent app that can operate software and apps on behalf of users, climbed to the top of the App Store in the weeks after it was released last month.

Muse Wonder arrives amid growing concerns over advanced A.I. models and agents, some of which have gone rogue, hacking into companies and meddling with government websites. Mr. Zuckerberg has tried to market Meta’s technology, which is built in a similar way to Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models, with a different message than its rivals, saying that A.I. is meant to be useful and empowering, not dangerous.

Meta began developing Muse Wonder after hiring Alexandr Wang, a founder of the A.I. start-up Scale AI, to be its chief A.I. officer in June 2025. Muse Wonder is the second series of A.I. models released under Mr. Wang’s A.I. division, and is the first that Meta has said is meant to compete with other cutting-edge “frontier” A.I. models, which typically require the most computing power to run.

Muse Wonder will soon power parts of Muse, the company said. Muse Wonder Full is the more powerful model, and will be available only for users who subscribe to Meta’s premium A.I. coding tool, Muse Code.

The new models, which were internally referred to as Watermelon, are also significantly better at coding than Meta’s previous models. The A.I. coding market is dominated by Anthropic and OpenAI, though Meta has been trying to grow its business selling A.I. services to other companies.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Muse Wonder faced some setbacks during development. In July, Meta paused a stage of A.I. development called “pre-training,” which delayed the release of the models until this month, The New York Times previously reported.

In a livestream on Instagram over the weekend, Mr. Zuckerberg teased the new A.I. models while barbecuing meats. Also on the menu, Mr. Zuckerberg said: “A big watermelon.”

universal-basic-income-silicon-valley.html

SUMMARY

She had been chosen for an experimental program called guaranteed basic income, and it came with cash: $1,330 a month for an entire year, with no strings attached for how it could be spent. With the basic income payments, he could do all three. As the months passed, however, Ms. Staples did not save as much of the basic income money as she had expected.

ARTICLE

What a Year of Free Money Meant: Softer Diapers, Clean Laundry, a Visit to Six Flags
For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of universal basic income programs, which Elon Musk and other tech leaders have promoted as a solution to A.I.-fueled job losses.
By Eli Tan and Rachel Bujalski
Published 2026-10-12 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/technology/universal-basic-income-silicon-valley.html

One morning in December 2024, Mikole Weeks, then 35, received a phone call with surprising news. She had been chosen for an experimental program called guaranteed basic income, and it came with cash: $1,330 a month for an entire year, with no strings attached for how it could be spent.

“It felt like another chance to turn my life around,” said Ms. Weeks, a single mother and a part-time house cleaner in Santa Cruz, Calif.

Only it did not turn out to be quite that simple.

For decades, people have debated the merits of guaranteed income programs, also called universal basic income, as an alternative or complement to traditional welfare. Driving the efforts is the idea that the most effective way to improve people’s lives is to give them cash and let them spend it how they want.

The concept resurged in popularity a decade ago, driven by fears of automation and rising wealth inequality. Proponents argued that permanent payments would raise the standard of living for those on the margins, and ultimately lift millions off welfare. Critics contended that giving people money unconditionally would deter them from working in the first place.

In the age of artificial intelligence, these programs have again become a hot topic. Tech titans including Elon Musk, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic have hailed basic income as a solution to A.I.-fueled job losses. In April, Mr. Musk posted that “universal HIGH INCOME” was the best way to deal with unemployment caused by the powerful technology. In June, Dr. Amodei suggested a tax on A.I. companies as one way to fund these payments.

Across Silicon Valley, experimental guaranteed income programs have quietly taken off. Google began funding six different initiatives in 2022 as part of a $50 million donation to nonprofits in the San Francisco Bay Area, saying basic income could be a novel way to prevent homelessness in one of the nation’s most expensive locations. Each program has hundreds of participants who receive around $1,000 a month, and academics study the results. State and federal tax laws limit the lengths of the programs and the payment amounts.

The studies have found that most basic income programs improve short-term employment and mental health while reducing food insecurity. But while data from these efforts has been closely tracked, less is known about the individual journeys of participants.

In October 2024, after The New York Times contacted two social services providers that received Google’s funding, the organizations offered reporters the chance to follow basic income recipients in real time. The Times ultimately shadowed three people, including Ms. Weeks, to better understand their guaranteed income experiences, from their first payments through last month. All of the program participants, including the ones The Times followed, were previously homeless and transitioning off a housing stipend that paid for a portion of their rent, and many received the payments on top of other social assistance like food stamps.

The Times’s findings mirrored the academic studies. For all three recipients, the instant benefits of basic income were clear: They had breathing room for groceries, rent and other expenses. But the success of the payments in another area — giving people more free time and opportunity in the long term — was mixed.

“It’s a lot to ask of someone to get their life together in 12 months, when a lot of these issues are structural or systemic,” said Jennifer Loving, who runs Destination: Home, a nonprofit that administers basic income programs in Silicon Valley. “And the world around them isn’t getting cheaper.”

Mikole Weeks

Ms. Weeks was homeless in 2023, living in a tent with her boyfriend at the time while struggling with drug addiction. “I was waiting for something to save me or kill me,” she said.

Then it came — she became pregnant with her son, Sky.

Ms. Weeks saw the pregnancy as a sign to turn her life around, and she did. She got sober and secured a $2,100 monthly housing stipend through Abode, a social services provider, for an apartment in Santa Cruz, a beach town about 40 miles south of Google’s Silicon Valley headquarters. She started working part time as a house cleaner for $20 an hour.

In December 2024, when Abode told her that she had been chosen for the basic income program, Ms. Weeks almost broke into tears.

The first trip she made after receiving the initial payment was to Target, where she filled her cart with organic banana baby snacks ($2.69) for Sky, then 14 months old, and a push bike ($61.99) to take him around the neighborhood. She loaded up on diapers that were softer for his sensitive skin than the ones she normally got for free at a food bank.

Then she called her mother, Christine Schell, now 60, who lived with Ms. Weeks’s now-23-year-old sister, Joanna McCall, in Elizabethton, Tenn. “Mom, do you want to see your grandbaby?” she asked.

Ms. Schell and Ms. McCall, who were living on social assistance, had never been able to afford the cross-country flights. A month later, Ms. Weeks received a call from her mother and sister: Her grandfather had died, and his house, where they lived, was being foreclosed on. What if they moved to Santa Cruz?

With the guaranteed income payments and more babysitting for Sky, Ms. Weeks said, she thought she could make the arrangement work.

Ms. Schell sold her belongings and drove from Tennessee to California with Ms. McCall. “It was chaotic, the emotions of leaving and also starting something new,” she said. “But we knew we’d be together.”

By April 2025, they were all living together in Ms. Weeks’s two-bedroom apartment. She slept on an air mattress in Sky’s bedroom, while her mother slept in Ms. Weeks’s bedroom and her sister on the couch in the living room.

As Ms. Schell cooked dinner one night, Ms. Weeks wrote a list of things she wanted to accomplish in the next 10 months with the help of the money. At the top was going to community college to study communications, a degree that could help her become a social worker.

“It feels like I’ve been given a head start,” Ms. Weeks said to her mother. Her ultimate goal was to be financially independent so she could give Sky opportunities that she never had.

She used some of the basic income money to pay for swimming lessons and music classes for Sky; on the weekends, they visited museums or a nearby aquarium. What she felt most was relief, she said, no longer having to wait until her food stamps reloaded every month to go to the grocery store. She could also afford to treat herself occasionally, getting her hair and nails done without worrying about paying for the electricity bill.

Seeing Ms. Weeks go to college also inspired her younger sister, Ms. McCall, who decided to enroll alongside her.

“It made me want to pursue our dreams together,” Ms. McCall said.

In a recent study of 3,000 universal basic income participants by OpenResearch, an organization partly funded by Mr. Altman of OpenAI, money spent supporting friends and family increased 26 percent, the most of any category. That was more than the increases for food (6 percent) and child care (11 percent).

But as the program went on, supporting two extra relatives — who had some social assistance but were also living on Ms. Weeks’s payments — weighed heavily on her. Ms. Weeks’s parenting style often clashed with her mother’s, leading to fights about how to raise Sky. Balancing college classes with a part-time job and parenting was harder than she expected.

By September 2025, “it had become a lot of change happening at once,” Ms. Weeks said. She moved her bed into the living room for more space and found herself saving less of the money than she had planned.

With one month to go until the payments ended, Ms. Weeks briefly relapsed into drugs. In November, sitting on her bed next to Sky’s giraffe stuffed animal, she told her mother that she needed to drop out of community college to focus on her health.

“I’m doing all I can do,” she said, burying her head in her mother’s chest.

“Mothers aren’t perfect by any means,” Ms. Schell said. “You’re doing your best.”

The payments ended in December. Ms. Weeks managed to save $2,000 from the program and continued to houseclean. Five months later, Ms. McCall moved into her own apartment, and Ms. Weeks, Ms. Schell and Sky used their savings to move into a house twice as big as their old place in cheaper, nearby Watsonville, with a yard for Sky to run around.

Ms. Weeks began feeling more settled. In August, she got a job at a hotel restaurant in Santa Cruz, working 32 hours a week making $24 an hour plus tips, health care benefits for herself and Sky and membership in a union.

She also re-enrolled in community college, taking one course at a time online instead of in person. Her first class began last month.

Nicholas Marquez

Nicholas Marquez, 44, could barely walk up the stairs to his Santa Cruz apartment one morning in mid-December 2024, his body still exhausted from open-heart surgery a week earlier. His power was shut off because of an unpaid electric bill, and his refrigerator was empty until more food stamps would arrive on Jan. 1.

Then he got the news from Abode that he had been selected for the guaranteed income program. “It felt like I had won the lottery,” he said.

He immediately called his mother, Denise Wiscowiche, now 66, a caretaker in Santa Cruz who had become his caretaker, too. “Mom, I have good news,” he told her. “I’m going to need your help.”

The $1,330 a month from the program immediately went to basics, like paying off his $500 utility bill to get the power back on. Mr. Marquez and Ms. Wiscowiche also went to the grocery store to buy high-calorie protein shakes, the only thing he could eat after his dialysis appointments on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

His heart and kidneys had been declining for years, he said, “punished by a lifetime of bad decisions” and a drug addiction. Unable to work, he was living on social assistance of around $800 a month on top of a housing stipend.

At the end of each month, Mr. Marquez had to choose whether to pay for electricity, for laundry or for groceries. With the basic income payments, he could do all three. It was the first time he could pay to do laundry in six months.

“There are a lot of little things that you don’t realize you need until you can’t afford them,” he said.

When his second payment hit in February 2025, Mr. Marquez brainstormed things he wanted to buy next. A new television and a PlayStation 4, to entertain him on days spent on the couch after dialysis; curtains for the living room; a blender to make smoothies.

Ms. Wiscowiche wrote reminders about each item on paper plates taped up around the apartment, covering his refrigerator and calendar with smiley faces and delivery dates. What the payments gave Mr. Marquez most of all was a sense of independence, he said. He could afford to take a friend out for a meal on occasion. He did not have to ration toilet paper.

But the extra money could not reverse the damage to his heart and kidneys. In March 2025, Mr. Marquez’s health took a turn for the worse, and his mother moved into his apartment to care for him.

At the end of that month, she stood by his bedside, crouching against a wall filled with skateboards and fishing rods from his childhood and posters of his favorite heavy metal bands.

“Mom, if I can’t do this anymore, you have to let me go,” he told her.

“I’ll never let you go, Nick,” she said.

A few weeks later, after returning home from the grocery store, Ms. Wiscowiche found Mr. Marquez unconscious on the floor. He had gone into cardiac arrest and died later that day.

Ms. Wiscowiche moved out of the apartment that month. Her other son, Benjamin Marquez, was struggling with a fentanyl addiction somewhere on the streets of Northern California. She could not imagine losing both sons.

She eventually tracked Benjamin down. “He told me to come save him,” Ms. Wiscowiche said.

Mr. Marquez had saved $900 of the payments for an e-bike to ride along the ocean. In May 2025, Ms. Wiscowiche used the sum and the rest of her savings to put Benjamin into a $15,000 drug rehabilitation program. With no money left, she moved into a tent in her stepmother’s backyard in Greenfield, Calif., a rural town about an hour south of Santa Cruz.

Benjamin finished his rehab program last fall. In July, he enrolled in a forestry job training program. Ms. Wiscowiche, who lives on Social Security, said she was still looking for the next place to live.

KaMesha Staples

In the spring of 2024, KaMesha Staples, now 40, was financially stuck. She was making $800 a week as a part-time drug addiction counselor in Vallejo, Calif., a working-class city 30 miles north of Oakland. But she was spending $1,000 a week on child care for her two daughters.

“It felt like we were at a standstill, like crabs in a bucket,” Ms. Staples said. So she decided to quit her job and rely on social assistance.

Every few months, a new obstacle seemed to keep her from financial independence. Sometimes her car broke down, costing hundreds of dollars to repair on top of the Uber and Lyft rides she needed as a replacement. She had moved to Vallejo from Oakland because of the cheaper cost of living, but now she had no reliable public transportation. Her older daughter, Vera, a fifth grader, would often have to walk two miles to school.

In June 2024, Compass Family Services, a social services provider that offers housing assistance, told Ms. Staples that she had been chosen for the basic income program. When she received the first $1,000 payment that month, she set a goal: Get a higher-paying job in education, a field she was passionate about. That September, with her daughters back in school and extra cushion from the payments, she enrolled in community college.

One year of payments was “just enough time not to get comfortable,” she said, and the urgency motivated her.

Ms. Staples’s situation — just on the edge of financial independence — is common among basic income recipients, said Erica Kisch, the chief executive of Compass Family Services. The hope is that the payments can be “the thing that pushes them out of poverty and into some kind of stability,” she said.

“One of the things that we’ve been learning is how one very small thing can actually become a giant thing that derails your entire family’s life very quickly,” Ms. Kisch said. “Being poor is actually really expensive.”

In October 2024, Ms. Staples joined her community college’s “job club,” which helped her make a new résumé and a LinkedIn profile and practice mock interviews. She applied for jobs to be a coordinator or teaching assistant at nearby schools. She also applied for Vera to attend nearby charter schools for middle school.

“The payments made it feel like my 10 problems turned to nine,” Ms. Staples said. “I had more time to think about the life I wanted to start living.”

For Vera’s 12th birthday, Ms. Staples took the family to Vallejo’s Six Flags amusement park, just two miles away, for the first time. They had so much fun that she bought her daughters season passes, a $70 expense that she would have never splurged on before.

As the months passed, however, Ms. Staples did not save as much of the basic income money as she had expected.

“I got used to spending what I had,” she said. “That was my biggest regret.”

She also miscalculated how long the program would last. When the last payment hit in May 2025, she had planned for one more.

The program’s end is what researchers often call “the cliff” and the first test of its long-term success. It hit Ms. Staples hard. She missed a car payment and needed help from her grandmother to pay it off. A week later, she was short on money again, so she started driving for DoorDash.

Just as things seemed to worsen, Ms. Staples got an offer in August 2025 to be an after-school coordinator making $30 an hour, $5 more than her last job. The same week, Vera was accepted to a charter school.

In the year since the program ended, things have not been easy, Ms. Staples said, but her life feels more stable. In August, her younger daughter, Xavea, enrolled in the same charter school as Vera, meaning a reprieve from child care costs.

On a recent afternoon, she drove to pick up Xavea’s school uniform, her daughter giddy in the back seat to try it on for the first time. Returning to their house, Ms. Staples sighed in relief.

“Less helpless is how I feel now,” she said.
