SUMMARY

Democrats who have spent months emphasizing the high cost of living in their fight to win control of Congress are increasingly invoking corruption in Washington to sharpen that message in the closing weeks of the campaign, blaming self-dealing by politicians for driving up prices. “There is a cost to corruption.” But Republicans, in control and responsible for the government, have less freedom to link corruption to high costs, giving Democrats an opening.

ARTICLE

Democrats Tie Corruption to High Costs in Final Midterms Push
Party leaders are working to connect Washington profiteering and the influence of billionaires and corporate America to affordability, in what they hope will be a potent closing message.
By Carl Hulse
Published 2026-10-12 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/democrats-midterms-corruption-affordability.html

Democrats who have spent months emphasizing the high cost of living in their fight to win control of Congress are increasingly invoking corruption in Washington to sharpen that message in the closing weeks of the campaign, blaming self-dealing by politicians for driving up prices.

Armed with research showing that voters have grown numb to the idea that politicians cannot be trusted, Democrats are using the message to stoke anti-incumbent sentiment as Republicans attempt to defend their slim House and Senate majorities. Their claim is that rampant corruption in Congress and the administration is directly costing average citizens who are paying more for necessities like groceries, gas and medicine while those in power get rich through insider knowledge, pay-to-play schemes and the backing of billionaires and powerful corporations.

That message is taking center stage in political ads, speeches and debates in some of the most competitive races in the country.

“You aren’t the problem and neither are your fellow Americans,” Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for re-election in Georgia, says in a campaign video. “Corruption is why things don’t work for the American people.”

Democrats are using the message in multiple competitive House and Senate contests, with candidates pointing to increases in the net worth of lawmakers and administration officials and vowing to embrace an anti-corruption agenda, including banning congressional stock trading and ending the revolving door between lawmakers on Capitol Hill and lobbyists on K Street.

Democratic candidates also are hitting Republican members of Congress with accusations of protecting enablers of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, after the G.O.P. had to be forced into taking up and passing legislation directing the Justice Department to release files in his case.

It is yet another way that Democratic leaders are trying to yoke Republican candidates to President Trump. Multiple accounts have shown his family and others connected to the government enriching themselves during his presidency through cryptocurrency trading, peddling influence, securing lucrative real estate deals with foreign entities and negotiating pardons.

The Democratic candidate in Pennsylvania’s Seventh Congressional District, a firefighter named Bob Brooks, has an ad declaring that he has “never seen a dumpster fire” like Washington, where “corporate PACs and Big Tech” back lawmakers, “and your paycheck goes up in smoke.”

In Virginia’s First District, the Democratic county prosecutor Shannon Taylor released an “accountability agenda” that she said was aimed at pursuing “elected officials who are looking out for themselves while raising our costs and hurting our community.”

And in Kentucky’s Sixth District, where the two parties are vying for an open seat, a recent ad for the Democratic Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor Zach Dembo promises that he will take on health insurance companies denying care “and go after corruption in both parties.”

Democratic leaders, increasingly confident of their chances of grabbing the House majority, see the anti-corruption theme as a significant element of their platform, one they say they intend to deliver on if they take control of the House, Senate or both.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to be speaker should his party win the House, has repeatedly said Democrats intend to “hold the crooks accountable” if their candidates prevail. In a meeting with reporters this week, he called corruption “an incredibly important theme” for Democratic House candidates.

“The reality facing the American people is that the cost of living is way too high, and Donald Trump, along with his Republican sycophantic members of Congress, have actually decided not to do anything about it because so many of them are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends and their donors,” Mr. Jeffries said. “There is a cost to corruption.”

Accusations of corruption and political misconduct have been a staple of congressional campaigns for decades, though the emphasis has shifted from election to election. In the 1990s, Republicans recaptured the House after 40 years by successfully branding the entrenched Democratic majority as corrupt, citing multiple scandals such as rampant abuse of overdrafts at the House bank. In 2006, Democrats regained power by accusing the Republican majority of fostering a “culture of corruption” with various scandals, including one involving a lawmaker who sent sexual messages to teenage House pages.

But Democrats say their research, including in focus groups, uncovered a unique aspect to the corruption issue in recent months. In those discussions, voters blamed a “rigged system” for the high costs they were facing. Internal surveys revealed that voters favored taking on the corrupt system even more than other Democratic priorities, such as bringing down health care costs.

Public polling showed similar results. A mid-August Reuters/Ipsos survey found that more than 60 percent of Americans believe that corruption influences the decisions made by the federal government and that the president and his family had inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency. A narrow majority said that corruption was worse under the Trump administration than under other recent presidencies. The poll found that the view that corruption plays an undue role in the government spanned all ideologies.

In making the link between corruption and affordability, Democratic strategists said they had found a sweet spot that gives the issues more heft together.

“When you tie the corruption issue to the cost of living, that resonates more than the corruption issue itself,” said Brian Fallon, a Democratic strategist providing advice to groups and candidates on the subject.

Republicans, too, are trying to leverage the issue. They are also raising it on the campaign trail, with new ads going up in recent days in Florida hitting incumbent Democrats on the stock trading issue. Party officials note that it was Senate Democrats who blocked a recent attempt to limit stock trading by members of Congress. (Democrats called the bill watered down since it would not bar such trading outright and would not apply to the president.)

Republicans say that voters will reject Democrats’ focus on corruption as a politically motivated artifice.

“Voters see through the facade, and they know Republicans are cleaning up the rot left behind by Democrat leaders,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But Republicans, in control and responsible for the government, have less freedom to link corruption to high costs, giving Democrats an opening.

Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and minority leader deeply involved in Senate campaign strategy, credited Mr. Ossoff for the way he has distilled the issue. He said Democratic strategists have been circulating Mr. Ossoff’s message on how corrupt practices contribute to high costs.

“When you tie the two together,” Mr. Schumer said of corruption and high costs, “the sum becomes greater than the parts.”

Democrats also like the message because it unites their party all along the ideological spectrum, steering clear of the divisions between more progressive and moderate candidates that have complicated races this year.

Still, the focus raises a potential challenge for Democrats if they succeed in their push to take over Congress. Under any scenario, they would still have to work with the Trump administration on legislation to reduce costs, while simultaneously conducting inquiries into the corruption allegations that are fueling their campaigns.

Mr. Jeffries said Democrats could do both.

“We certainly have a steadfast commitment to continuing to make significant and decisive progress on addressing the affordability crisis,” he said. “But at the same time, recognize that we have to visit accountability upon those individuals who’ve been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people or screwing over the American people.”

SUMMARY

Elon Musk has quietly funneled more than $276 million into Republican groups and his super PAC since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections. And Mr. Musk’s $158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Mr. Paxton after months of reluctance.

ARTICLE

Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans
The world’s richest person has quietly become by far the biggest known midterm donor, trying to save Republicans’ Senate majority with some of the largest donations in American political history.
By Theodore Schleifer
Published 2026-10-12 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/elon-musk-midterms.html

Elon Musk has quietly funneled more than $276 million into Republican groups and his super PAC since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.

The staggering amount of money makes Mr. Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Mr. Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Thursday.

In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, he gave a total of $158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team. In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.

Mr. Musk has also built a major Republican turnout operation through a super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. He donated over $76 million this summer to the group, which in turn spent that much on building a sprawling canvassing program to try to turn out hard-to-reach Republican voters. The group is active in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races.

Mr. Musk has already given far more money, about $366 million, to federal committees during the 2025-26 election cycle than he did during the 2024 election, when he laid out roughly $290 million to help return President Trump and Republicans to power. He has given even more in undisclosed donations during both elections, according to people briefed on the giving.

The latest torrent of spending has helped give the Republican Party a financial advantage in the midterms, as well-funded outside groups like Mr. Trump’s powerful super PAC flood the airwaves with advertising in the final weeks. No Democratic billionaire is spending nearly as much as Mr. Musk, and money remains a central worry for the party in an otherwise favorable political environment.

The donations also clear up the mystery of how much staying power Mr. Musk wants to have in American politics.

“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.

Mr. Musk, who oversees a vast business empire that has benefited from enormous federal contracts, is famously unpredictable and often jumps from one project to another. He has been far quieter about his political work since his dramatic blowup with Mr. Trump last year. After months of wielding vast influence inside the White House and overseeing Mr. Trump’s government cost-cutting project, he raged against the president’s major domestic policy bill and floated threats to start a third party.

But the two men have warmed back up, appearing together at three events in the last two weeks and praising each other.

Now Mr. Musk has donated more than a quarter-billion dollars to help Mr. Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The money signals his commitment to the right and sets him up as a potential player in the 2028 presidential election, when his super PAC says it intends to remain active — the first time it has confirmed such plans.

Beyond Mr. Musk’s donations to his super PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund, his representatives said that from July through September, he had given smaller but still substantial amounts to other conservative groups:

- $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans
- $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas
- $10 million to the Republican Governors Association
- $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” said Andrew Romeo, a spokesman for America PAC. “These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”

Pushing for Paxton

On voters’ doors across Texas, the campaign literature carries a stark warning: “Radical Democrat socialists are winning elections all across America. Could Texas be next?”

The hanging door cards are the work of Mr. Musk’s voter-turnout operation, which deployed nearly 3,000 paid canvassers last week around the country, according to America PAC officials.

The group has devoted most of its more than $76 million in midterm spending so far to this canvassing program, shelling out smaller amounts on advertising, mail, phone calls and text messages. Much of the messaging targets Democrats, sometimes in misleading or overheated ways.

This spring, Mr. Trump’s political advisers asked Mr. Musk to reprise America PAC’s 2024 field program, a person familiar with the conversation said. Despite the challenging environment for Republicans, some party strategists believe that a field program can make the difference in particularly tight races.

America PAC relies on a few voter-canvassing firms that compete aggressively with one another for work and for staffing, according to people briefed on the operation.

Turnover in the canvassing industry is high. One canvasser who worked for America PAC told The Times that he was paid between $1.50 and $3.00 for each door he knocked on across Texas in the heat. America PAC says it has knocked on about 6.5 million doors across the country so far.

Mr. Musk and his operation, people close to them say, have been particularly focused on the Texas Senate race. The group has unloaded over a third of its disclosed spending in that expensive race, more than in any other. It is uncommon to run an extensive field campaign in large states like Texas, where television ads are more often used to reach voters.

Mr. Musk, a resident of Austin, has extensive business interests and property holdings in Texas. Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, has investigated Mr. Musk’s opponents, like Media Matters, a liberal group.

Mr. Musk’s $10 million donation to Mr. Paxton’s super PAC came at a critical time, when the Republican candidate was being badly outspent.

And Mr. Musk’s $158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Mr. Paxton after months of reluctance.

That is because Mr. Musk’s donations preceded the decision in late August by the super PAC, led by allies of Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, to start what has become a $149 million pro-Paxton ad campaign.

A Focus on Transgender Issues

As it did in 2024, Mr. Musk’s operation is focused not on persuading swing voters, but on registering and turning out voters with conservative beliefs — especially “low-propensity” ones who are less likely to cast a ballot.

This is a lot harder for Republicans in a midterm election, without Mr. Trump at the top of the ballot.

To do it, Mr. Musk’s super PAC is leaning hard into the culture wars, especially transgender issues. (Mr. Musk’s daughter, who is transgender, has spoken about their clashes over her identity, and he has suggested that this led to his increased political engagement.)

At voters’ doors in Texas, canvassers are told to target Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, over her record on transgender issues, according to parts of a script reviewed by The Times.

Similarly, the Musk operation is leaving literature on doors that claims that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, has a “radical trans agenda.” And America PAC’s top ad in the state, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, denounces Mr. Talarico over his past comments suggesting that “God is nonbinary.”

The Musk group is also targeting other Democratic Senate candidates over transgender issues, including Josh Turek, the party’s nominee in Iowa. Nationally, one of the super PAC’s most visible ads on Facebook features a man in makeup and reads: “He made his plan to vote. Did you? Don’t stay home while crazies elect radicals.” The group is running ads and sending mail on a broad range of topics, but socialism is a core theme. The Musk super PAC regularly attacks Democrats as socialist and ties them to figures like Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, according to 48 pieces of direct mail shared by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm.

Online, it is even running personalized messaging that invokes a voter’s first name. For example, in a video showing smiling Democrats: “Why are they smiling? Because Christopher hasn’t made a plan to vote yet.”

Much of this outreach points voters to an America PAC website where conservatives can learn about how to register to vote. The super PAC is pushing what it calls an “America Pass,” a digital card on Apple or Google wallets on voters’ phones that lists their registration information, along with election dates and deadlines in their home state.

A Big Spender With a Back-Seat Role

While Mr. Musk is spending big again and using some tactics that are similar to those he deployed two years ago, this is not 2024 anymore.

He is in a different place politically. While he and Mr. Trump appear to be on good terms again — “our modern-day Thomas Edison,” the president called him on Thursday — Mr. Musk is taking a hands-off approach this election and does not appear as personally passionate.

He has not brought up the midterm elections or the Trump presidency much in private conversations with friends, according to people who have spoken to him in recent months. He is focused on his businesses, these people say, and he and his business lieutenants have taken a less active role in America PAC’s operations, entrusting major decisions to Chris Young, his top adviser.

And on X, a semi-reliable indicator of where the billionaire’s mind is, Mr. Musk has written just seven direct posts this year about candidates in competitive midterm races, according to a Times review, a far cry from his relentless calls throughout 2024 to elect Mr. Trump. Five of those posts focused on Mr. Talarico — and one appeared critical of Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican in Maine.

Gone, too, are Mr. Musk’s barnstorming campaign stops, like the ones he did in Pennsylvania in October 2024 or a Wisconsin judicial election in the spring of 2025. There are no more sweepstakes where he personally hands an oversize check of $1 million to some registered voters who sign a petition, a gambit that drew legal challenges.

Mr. Musk has not evidently grown infatuated with candidates this time around, as he did with Mr. Trump. The closest he came was a $10 million donation for a long-shot Republican running for the U.S. Senate in Kentucky — an investment that went poorly.

The $276 million figure is, of course, just what is publicly known. Mr. Musk has also made some seven-figure donations to support midterm candidates through groups that are not required to disclose their donors, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

Juliana Castro Varón contributed analysis.

SUMMARY

Federal agents executed a search warrant at the home of Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Monday, according to three people briefed on the matter, the kind of investigative step the Justice Department has long shied away from so close to an election. The court-approved search of her Washington-area home comes after Department of Homeland Security officials said in recent months that they were investigating Ms. Omar, a Democrat, over her family’s immigration paperwork. A Justice Department spokeswoman said that Homeland Security Investigations agents — a part of ICE — executed a judicially authorized search of a home in the Washington area, as part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

ARTICLE

Homeland Security Agents Search Home of Rep. Ilhan Omar
The search takes place within the 60-day window of the midterm elections, when the Justice Department has historically avoided such investigative steps related to political candidates.
By Devlin Barrett, Hamed Aleaziz, Ernesto Londoño and Alan Feuer
Published 2026-10-12 14:14 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/ilhan-omar-home-searched.html

Federal agents executed a search warrant at the home of Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Monday, according to three people briefed on the matter, the kind of investigative step the Justice Department has long shied away from so close to an election.

The court-approved search of her Washington-area home comes after Department of Homeland Security officials said in recent months that they were investigating Ms. Omar, a Democrat, over her family’s immigration paperwork. More recently, some federal investigators have also sought to investigate other issues, such as Ms. Omar’s finances, campaign funds and interactions with a foreign citizen, as The New York Times previously reported.

The three people who described the execution of the search warrant spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss it.

The search warrant, executed 22 days before Election Day, lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge, according to a person familiar with the document.

The search warrant was the subject of significant back and forth between prosecutors and the federal judge who eventually approved it, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity. The first application for the search was submitted by prosecutors more than a week ago, and was only approved after a discussion of the possible constitutional issues, like the speech or debate clause, surrounding her status as a member of Congress, the people said.

In a statement posted on social media on Monday, Ms. Omar called the raid “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she wrote, adding: “I will not be silenced.”

President Trump has frequently attacked Ms. Omar, focusing on her Somali heritage.

“I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” Mr. Trump told reporters on Monday ahead of a campaign rally in Ohio, adding: “She comes from a country that is a non-country. And then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution. I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the D.O.J.”

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that Homeland Security Investigations agents — a part of ICE — executed a judicially authorized search of a home in the Washington area, as part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The spokeswoman declined to comment further.

In September, Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, said his department was investigating issues surrounding Ms. Omar and her family’s immigration to the United States, and suggested the end result could be deportation.

Ms. Omar was born in Mogadishu in the early 1980s. Her family fled their hometown when she was around 8, as a civil war engulfed Somalia, according to a memoir she wrote. In the mid-1990s, after spending time at a refugee camp in Kenya, Ms. Omar and her relatives were admitted as refugees in the United States. They started a new life in Minnesota, which is home to the largest Somali diaspora in the United States.

Ms. Omar has long said that suggestions that she and her family committed immigration fraud were false and politically motivated.

“I will say it again so it’s as clear as possible: I’m not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams,” she wrote in a fund-raising email in September.

Monday’s search of her home, which was reported earlier by Fox News, takes place within the 60-day window before an election. Justice Department policy has long urged prosecutors not to take any overt, unnecessary investigative steps that could affect an election during that period — especially if such actions could be taken after the election without causing any harm to the investigation. The guiding principle of the 60-day rule is that prosecutors should exercise caution in regard to politically sensitive cases.

The rule is not absolute, and there are exceptions, such as instances where prosecutors believe evidence could be destroyed, ongoing crimes are being committed, or people are in danger. The rule is also largely an interpretation of Justice Department regulations, and as such has been the subject of significant debate about its exact parameters. For many years, however, Justice Department officials have concluded that a publicly observable search — such as of a politician’s home or business — is the kind of overt activity that should be avoided during the 60-day period.

In the last federal election, Mr. Trump cited the 60-day rule in his own criminal cases to accuse the department of acting improperly in 2024 as he campaigned for election. He and his lawyers, some of whom now run the Justice Department, argued that the special counsel, Jack Smith, broke the 60-day rule when he filed court papers in September 2024 describing the evidence supporting charges that Mr. Trump had conspired to obstruct the results of the 2020 election. In that instance, however, the key filing was made in response to a court order, which is not subject to the department policy.

In a statement on Monday, the House Democratic leadership — Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Pete Aguilar of California — condemned the search of Ms. Omar’s house as a “rogue abuse of power.”

“The Trump administration’s raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries,” they said.

Ms. Omar has represented a solidly blue district that includes Minneapolis since 2019, and she faced no serious competitors during the primary this year.

Scores of Omar supporters gathered Monday afternoon at a park in Minneapolis for a rally, many holding signs that said “Stand with Ilhan” and “Hands off the Somali community.”

Jason Chavez, a member of the Minneapolis City Council, predicted that the search of the congresswoman’s home would galvanize her constituents and perhaps boost her victory margin in November.

“Folks are riled up,” he said. “What is happening is just wrong.”

Ms. Omar’s immigration history has been scrutinized since she first ran for a seat in the State Legislature in 2016 and made history as the state’s first Somali American lawmaker, according to people familiar with the inquiries.

The Justice Department under the Biden administration also opened an investigation into Ms. Omar in 2024 that examined her finances, campaign spending and interactions with a foreign citizen, as The Times previously reported.

Previous federal inquiries — including one seeking to establish whether Ms. Omar married a sibling to get him a green card — ended without any charges. Ms. Omar has called such claims “absurd and offensive.”

Late last year, Tom Homan, the White House border czar told Newsmax that earlier efforts to investigate Ms. Omar’s immigration matters were stymied by statute of limitations.

Investigators were reviewing her immigration files again, Mr. Homan said, adding that he had no doubt Ms. Omar had committed fraud.

In March, Vice President JD Vance reiterated that claim, which he said he had discussed with the White House senior aide Stephen Miller.

“We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud,” Mr. Vance told a conservative podcaster. The next step, he said, was to figure out how to “build a case necessary to get some justice for the American people.”

In recent months, federal investigators opened an investigation into Ms. Omar’s immigration history, focusing in part on whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied or omitted information as he sought legal status in the United States before becoming a U.S. citizen.

Among the questions investigators have looked at is whether Ms. Omar derived citizenship from a father who may have been ineligible to obtain naturalized status, according to a person familiar with the case.

If there is conclusive evidence that Ms. Omar derived citizenship improperly, the Justice Department could pursue a criminal or civil denaturalization case against her. In cases in which prosecutors prevail and persuade a federal judge to order someone denaturalized, the immigrant may be placed in deportation proceedings.

Annie Karni contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?
It’s Oct. 12 — 22 days away from the midterms. Here’s the state of play.
By Reid J. Epstein
Published 2026-10-12 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/whos-winning-the-race-for-congress.html

The Republican Party’s hopes of saving its majorities in Congress increasingly appear to depend on a few possible outcomes: G.O.P. advantages in money and on the map pay off, the polls are wrong, or a major news development suddenly brightens the party’s prospects.

In the meantime, Republicans in competitive races are doing whatever they can to try to loosen their ties to President Trump’s agenda, which is dragging their party down with just over three weeks to go before the midterm elections.

There have been new ads stating opposition to Trump’s tariffs from candidates who supported them, calls to end the war in Iran from candidates who backed it and efforts to look bipartisan from candidates who pledged to be Trump’s top allies.

The debates last week made clear that Republicans are on the back foot. Questions about high prices, tariffs and the war dominated the sessions in battleground states. While G.O.P. advertising often aims to link Democrats to their party’s left-wing figures and stoke disputes about transgender athletes, cost-of-living issues are paramount to voters this year.

Trump’s rhetoric is not helping his party. Even as his own approval ratings have plummeted, he urges voters to pretend that he is on the ballot. He touts data centers that are even less popular than he is. And he has shown no inclination to back off from his positions on the war in Iran or tariffs.

But then there is the money.

Thanks to Trump’s super PACs and well-heeled political allies, Republicans still hold a commanding financial advantage. The billionaire Elon Musk has directed more than $276 million to Republicans since the start of July.

Republicans hope that will help them pull through on a House map they sought to redraw in their favor and Senate map that features plenty of races in red states. But the time to change minds and move votes is shrinking by the day.

The Battle for the Senate

Republicans have all but conceded the race in North Carolina to Democrat Roy Cooper, a popular former governor. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff has a commanding lead over Representative Mike Collins. And now Democrats are on offense in deep-red Kansas, with Senate Majority PAC, the party’s main super PAC, beginning $5 million worth of ads in the state.

Democratic candidates are leading or running neck-and-neck in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — all places Trump won three times by substantial margins. He and Vice President JD Vance have aimed to energize the base with appearances in those states, but the polls suggest the Democrats are holding their own.

In the eyes of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, Democrats even have a chance to take back the majority because of his recruiting efforts. In an interview Friday, he claimed credit for getting Cooper, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio and former Representative Mary Peltola of Alaska into their races and helping Josh Turek win his primary in Iowa.

“I couldn’t accept the map as is because the map as is consigns us to a minority, all things being equal, just because of the way the states are structured,” Schumer said. “So we had to expand the map. I didn’t accept the original map. I worked to build a better one.”

Still, some Democrats worry about Senate races that ought to be easier for them. Contests remain tight in Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire.

The Race for the House

Things do not look promising for House Republican hopes of retaining their majority.

The Cook Political Report on Friday shifted 18 districts toward Democrats. Two Iowa seats, held by Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, are now considered “lean Democratic.”

That is in addition to Republicans already punting on the Omaha-based district held by the retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska.

Representative Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the House majority whip, said the issue is that Republican voters may be too “satisfied” with Trump to vote in November.

“The midterms, you typically have the party that wins the White House is satisfied,” Emmer said Sunday on ABC’s “This Week.” “If our people will turn out — you may be satisfied, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t vote. You show up and vote, we’re going to be fine.”

Democrats need to flip just three seats to take a House majority. Many election forecasters now suggest they will do much better than that. During a discussion last week, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, repeatedly declined to predict how many seats his party would win.

He did, however, suggest that Democrats would be able to repeat their successes from 2018, the last midterm with Trump in the White House.

“Past performance is not evidence of future results,” he said. “But it provides at least a path for us to ascertain what is possible.”

The Money

Even for Musk, a quarter-billion dollars is a lot to spend on politics in just three months.

The billionaire has once again become the largest single donor to Republican causes. The roughly $276 million he directed to groups during July, August and September means his tab for the 2026 elections is now about $366 million.

Musk’s funds are split between $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Senate G.O.P. super PAC; over $76 million to America PAC, his own outlet that focuses on voter turnout; $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which supports House Republicans; and other donations. One of them reflects Musk’s interest in the Texas Senate race: He gave $10 million to a super PAC backing Ken Paxton, who polls show trails James Talarico, the Democratic candidate trying to become the first in his party to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988.

The Early Vote

In five states with competitive Senate races, 615,100 ballots have already been cast.

Top Talker

After vanishing from the campaign trail for nine days, James Talarico, the Texas Democrat running for Senate, emerged at the Austin City Limits music festival Friday. He said he’d been home sick with the flu.

Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, had been making hay out of Talarico’s whereabouts. What is next in the Texas campaign is unclear: Talarico on Saturday challenged Paxton to debate, and Trump has suggested Paxton should debate, but Paxton has yet to agree to a debate.

One Poll Number

76 percent.

That’s the percentage of Ohio voters who said Trump’s policies have increased cost of living in the state in a CNN/SSRS poll. The poll found Brown, the Democrat, up by 6 percentage points over Senator Jon Husted, the Republican. Trump and Vance have both visited the state recently in an attempt to boost support for Husted.

On the Issues

Trump’s latest idea to bring down gas prices — importing diesel fuel from Russia — got a chilly reception from some of his fellow Republicans, including a few in battleground races. Former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan and Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are both locked in tight Senate races, panned the idea. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said on Saturday that he would force a vote to block Russian oil purchases. The U.S. has forbidden importing Russian fuel since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine.

On the Ground

In Maine, the cost of home heating oil is surging along with prices of seemingly everything else, forcing voters to pay more to stay warm just as fall temperatures drop.

Republicans concede the costs — up 80 percent over a year ago to fill a standard heating oil tank — are a problem for Senator Susan Collins, who backed the Iran war that drove up oil prices before she called for it to end.

Quote of the Week

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.” — Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia

Ossoff pulled no punches in his debate attacks on Representative Mike Collins, his Republican opponent in Georgia’s Senate race. He said Collins had “hired half the Third Reich,” a reference to Collins hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views.

Collins responded that he had “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.”

ARTICLE

NATO Details Plan to Shield Ukraine’s European Allies From Russia
With the Russians intensifying sabotage, arson and cyberattacks against European nations supporting Ukraine, NATO divulged a blueprint, in case of war, to deter the Kremlin.
By Marc Santora and Steven Erlanger
Published 2026-10-12 17:06 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/nato-strategy-russia-europe.html

With Russia intensifying efforts to destabilize European nations that support Ukraine, NATO’s top military commander on Monday detailed a blueprint to deter Moscow in the event of outright war, a concept he summarized as “block, blunt and break.”

The commander, Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich of the U.S. Air Force, said the alliance does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable,” despite Russian sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and disinformation aimed at rattling European resolve and severing weapons supply lines to Ukraine.

But in that environment, the general said he had made a deliberate decision to publicly disclose the core of NATO’s classified war plan — known as its “theory of victory” — to bolster confidence across 32 allied countries.

“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this,” General Grynkewich said on Monday at the Warsaw Security Forum. “We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”

Yet even as the American four-star commander stressed that NATO’s ultimate defense rests on unity, stark geopolitical contradictions echoed through the conference hall. President Trump’s decision to unilaterally ease sanctions on the Kremlin in order to purchase Russian diesel fuel highlighted a jarring disconnect between NATO’s military planning and European support for Ukraine, and the White House’s transactional diplomacy and hostility toward Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump appeared to blame Ukraine — not for the first time — for the war, and said it should “get a new president.”

By injecting hard cash directly into the Kremlin’s coffers, the administration risked undercutting years of allied economic pressure, muddying the Western coalition’s deterrence messaging and testing the very solidarity General Grynkewich was in Warsaw to project.

Even if the amounts of diesel purchases are small, the symbolism of division is large. Ukraine and Europe argue that only economic and military pressure will persuade President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to end the war he started. Mr. Trump and his envoys apparently favor enticing Mr. Putin with “deals,” instead.

The tension was evident earlier in the day when Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland warned that the defense of Ukraine and the security of NATO are inextricably tied.

“Anyone who, for any reason — treason, stupidity, or money — wants to weaken Ukraine in its defense against Russian aggression is clearly acting against their own nation, the security of their own state, and its sovereignty,” Mr. Tusk said.

Pressed afterward on whether European allies could count on Washington to defend them, General Grynkewich dismissed suggestions that the United States would waver, citing the thousands of American forces along NATO’s eastern flank, including in Poland. He also pointed to recent summit communiqués that reaffirmed the bedrock collective-defense guarantee of Article 5.

European fears of an emboldened Russia have been increasing. Michal Koudelka, the director of the Czech Security Information Service, the country’s domestic spy service, warned his Parliament on Monday that Russia could escalate “in a matter of months rather than years to a significantly riskier and more serious operation,” which could include, down the road, limited military action against a NATO state.

General Grynkewich said the new NATO doctrine draws directly on modern battlefield lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East.

Specifically, he said, the blueprint pairs precision weapons with what he described as “affordable mass” — large numbers of autonomous systems, drones, and electronic warfare assets designed to sustain a protracted war of attrition.

The “block, blunt, and break” strategy he outlined is designed to stop an invasion in its tracks without trying to conquer the enemy’s homeland.

First, he said, allied forces immediately “block” an attack at the border to prevent the enemy from seizing territory, a change in strategy since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Next, they “blunt” the offensive by hitting advancing troops from the air, sea and land to strip their momentum. Finally, if the attack continues, they “break” the enemy by targeting the supplies, communication links and command networks that keep their frontline forces fighting, weakening the aggressor to the point of collapse.

General Grynkewich stressed that NATO is not interested in taking an adversary’s land. By limiting the objective strictly to the tactical and operational neutralization of the adversary, NATO intends to deny the enemy any pretext for escalation, he said, placing the moral and strategic burden of expanding the war squarely on the aggressor.

“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt, should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”

Kremlin officials have routinely dismissed the alarms being raised across Europe.

“We have no intention to fight Europe, to engage in warfare with Europe; that is utter nonsense,” Sergey V. Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, said during a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly in September. “But Europe is preparing for war with us,” he said. “This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy.”

Adam Goldman contributed reporting from London.

ARTICLE

Trump Gives Putin a Hand in Russia’s Economic War With Ukraine
President Trump is moving to buy Russian diesel while also pressuring Ukraine to halt attacks on refineries, a lifeblood of Moscow’s war machine.
By Constant Méheut
Published 2026-10-12 16:17 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/russia-diesel-trump.html

With the front lines largely frozen, Russia and Ukraine have turned the war into a contest of economic endurance. Kyiv has gone after Russia’s oil refineries. Moscow has hit Ukraine’s ports and heavy industries.

On Friday, President Trump sided with Russia in this all-important battle.

The American leader announced a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel and stepped up pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries. The diesel agreement, if it goes ahead, could send some $4 billion of American money into the Russian economy, energy experts said. A halt to refinery strikes, if Ukraine accedes to one, could be much more valuable to the Kremlin.

Mr. Trump is enlisting Russian help in his effort to bring down sky-high diesel prices, caused mostly by the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, before the midterm election early next month. Ukraine is expected to get nothing in exchange, even as the American president demands an end to Kyiv’s refinery attacks, its most potent tool for depriving the Russian war machine of income.

Moscow remains free to continue hitting Ukrainian ports, steel factories, warehouses, power plants and data centers, a campaign that is gradually pushing Ukraine’s economy toward a breaking point. Such attacks destroy nearly $10 billion in business assets each year, Ukraine’s economy minister has said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine has condemned Mr. Trump’s decision to buy Russian diesel, saying in a social media post on Friday that “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”

Mr. Trump, who lifted sanctions to allow Russia to sell the fuel to the United States, struck an economic deal with Mr. Putin even as Russian attacks have driven civilian casualties in Ukraine to what the United Nations called a “new horrifying level.”

More than 100 Ukrainian civilians were killed in the past week alone. Moscow is striking Ukraine with an ever growing arsenal of increasingly powerful and precise weapons, taking advantage of gaps in Ukrainian air defenses.

Mr. Zelensky said on Monday that Ukraine had refrained from attacks on Russian oil refineries overnight. But he has said that Ukraine will agree to an extended cease-fire only if Moscow stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. There are fears of a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine this winter if Russia succeeds in its goal of taking down the Ukrainian power and water systems.

The diesel deal is another sign of Mr. Trump’s willingness to tip the scales toward Russia, the aggressor in the conflict. This time, he is offering the Kremlin assistance in an economic battle that could help decide the fate of the war, with both armies largely bogged down at the front.

Ukraine’s campaign against Russian oil infrastructure began in 2024, with strikes on oil depots and refineries. The effort at first had little effect. But as Ukraine expanded its fleet of attack drones and learned how to target critical components that are hard to repair, the effects increased.

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, combined with those on other businesses, have cost Russia about 1 percent of its gross domestic product, President Vladimir V. Putin acknowledged this month.

Reported gasoline output is down by 20 percent compared with 2025 levels, and diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30 percent, the International Energy Agency said in a report last month. The Ukrainian attacks prompted Russia to impose restrictions on diesel exports that Moscow now says it will lift to sell fuel to the United States.

The energy agency added that Russia’s oil tax revenue from January to August was nearly 17 percent below the level of the same period in 2025.

Should Kyiv be forced to halt its refinery strikes, Russia’s advantage in the two countries’ contest to starve the other of money will only grow.

Nowhere is that imbalance clearer than in the near closure of Ukraine’s ports.

For months, Russia has attacked commercial ships sailing in and out of the ports in the southern region of Odesa, aiming to discourage them from calling there. The ports are a lifeline for Ukraine’s economy, accounting for 60 percent of the country’s total export volume. They are used to export grain from the country’s fertile farmland, a key source of revenue.

Because of the Russian attacks, traffic through the three Odesa ports was down nearly 95 percent in August and September, compared with the same period last year, according to port data obtained by The New York Times. In September, only 12 ships made it out of the ports, compared to 266 in the same month last year.

Ukraine has tried to redirect some of the traffic to its ports on the Danube River, which connects the country to Romania. Ships can travel down the river through Romania and back into the Black Sea, sailing off the coast of NATO countries toward Turkey. But the Danube ports can handle only about half of the cargo that normally moves through the Odesa ports.

And the Danube route is now under threat, too. Last week, drones struck three ships off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, sinking two and killing several crew members. All three vessels had carried Ukrainian grain in the past, according to Romanian authorities and port data.

Ukraine has accused Russia of carrying out the attacks, though Romania and Bulgaria have steered clear of assigning blame. Russia did not comment on the attacks.

The halt to Ukraine’s seaborne exports could have catastrophic consequences for the country’s economy, with effects across many sectors. Ukraine’s agriculture minister said this month that farmers were unable to export about 30 million tons of agricultural products, worth about $30 billion.

Russia has also suffered from Ukrainian strikes on its Black Sea ports, which have constrained its agricultural exports. But economists say the impact is not comparable because Russia has more export routes than Ukraine, including through the Baltic and Caspian Seas, which Ukrainian weapons cannot reach as easily.

In a sign of that imbalance, Russia became the world’s largest exporter of sunflower oil in the 2025-26 marketing year, overtaking Ukraine for the first time in two decades, according to estimates from the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Russia appears to be following a methodical approach to dismantling Ukraine’s economic base, striking all kinds of assets that an economy needs to function, including export routes, factories and energy facilities.

The fate of Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel manufacturer, is a case in point.

Its factories, including two large steel plants in southeastern Ukraine, were already suffering from power outages caused by Russian strikes on the grid. Then came attacks on the ports, which blocked a key export route, and on the railways, which left its products stranded inside the country. Finally, strikes on the plants themselves forced them to shut down last month.

The collapse of Ukraine’s steel industry, which contributed more than 7 percent of Ukraine’s economic output last year, will have severe economic consequences, said Oleksandr Myronenko, Metinvest’s chief operating officer. The company is planning layoffs for administrative personnel, and towns that depend on steel plants will see their budgets shrink.

In September, for the first time in a century, not a single metric ton of steel was produced in Ukraine for one week.

After Russian Diesel Deal, Trump Faces New Crisis Over Ukraine
President Trump’s surprise decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel fuel stunned Ukrainian and European officials, who were meeting with U.S. envoys at an exclusive golf club near Miami.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/russia-ukraine-war-us-diesel-deal-negotiations.html

President Trump’s new diplomatic crisis over Ukraine first erupted at Steve Witkoff’s exclusive golf club outside Miami on Friday.

Senior Ukrainian and European officials had traveled to the club, Shell Bay, for talks with Mr. Trump’s peace envoys, Mr. Witkoff and Jared Kushner. They had planned to discuss updated proposals to end the war in Ukraine ahead of another trip to Russia by Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner.

But Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner soon made an announcement that stunned the visitors and much of the world when the news became public shortly thereafter. The United States, the Americans said, would suspend sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. The Americans added a firm request from Mr. Trump: that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries.

One of the Ukrainians asked what they would get in return.

The Americans responded that the United States was doing a lot for Ukraine already, according to three people familiar with the meeting, and should not have to make a trade for Ukraine to stop its refinery attacks. The Americans then mentioned U.S. intelligence assistance, considered vital to the Ukrainian war effort.

Some in the room heard that as a veiled threat, according to two of the people. A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy, denied any suggestion of a threat to withhold such support. But the official also said that Mr. Trump had grown so angry with Ukraine that it was hard to say what he might do.

Now, the dispute has ballooned into the biggest crisis between Washington and Kyiv since the Oval Office blowup with Ukraine’s president last year. The future of U.S. support for Ukraine again appears to be hanging in the balance. The escalating back-and-forth showed how Mr. Trump’s efforts to bring down energy prices before next month’s midterm elections have threatened to destabilize the fragile Ukraine talks.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are now indicating that they have put their expected trip to Russia on hold until President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine mends fences with Mr. Trump, two people familiar with the talks said.

To the Ukrainians and their European supporters, the attacks on Russia’s fuel refineries are Kyiv’s most effective way to respond to Russia’s bombardment of Ukraine’s energy grid. Ukraine is prepared to stop attacking energy infrastructure, Mr. Zelensky has said, if Russia does the same.

Russia has refused such a deal. Nevertheless, to Mr. Trump, Ukraine’s attacks are an affront to a U.S. administration that has continued to provide intelligence and some military support to Ukraine despite the American president’s harsh words about Mr. Zelensky. “We are ready for an energy cease-fire: We are ready for any mutual format, anything that is not one-sided,” Mr. Sybiha told reporters while entering a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Luxembourg.

The meeting on Friday at Mr. Witkoff’s golf club lasted about six hours, two people familiar with it said. Much of the meeting involved brainstorming about what the future peace talks might require to work, and the focus was on the standard issues, according to several people. The issues included accession to the European Union for Ukraine, for instance, and the question of territorial control.

Mr. Witkoff stepped out at one point to join a call between Russia’s president, Vladimir V. Putin, and Mr. Trump, according to one of the people, who was in the room for the meeting. In addition to Ukraine’s three-person negotiating team, the national security advisers to the leaders of Britain, Germany and France, as well as top officials from the European Union and NATO, joined the meeting.

But Mr. Trump’s diesel deal with Mr. Putin quickly overshadowed the rest of the talks. Mr. Zelensky on Friday called Mr. Trump’s deal with Mr. Putin to allow imports of Russian diesel fuel in order to lower prices a “weak decision.” As the dispute intensified, Mr. Trump on Saturday said Ukraine needed “a new president.”

European leaders, including France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the head of the E.U.’s executive arm, Ursula von der Leyen, issued statements of support for Mr. Zelensky. Members of Congress criticized the diesel deal as helping fund Russia’s war machine.

“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” a bipartisan group of six senators, including the Republicans Susan Collins of Maine and John Curtis of Utah, said in a statement on Sunday. “The administration must immediately reverse course.”

Björn Seibert, a senior E.U. official who attended Friday’s meeting in Florida, gave ambassadors from across the European Union’s 27 nations a briefing on the meeting on Sunday, according to one European official who was there and three diplomats briefed on the matter.

Both the official and two of the diplomats said that the Europeans in Florida were taken by surprise by the Trump administration’s diesel announcement. The official said the ambassadors were stunned by the announcement.

One major takeaway from Florida, Mr. Seibert told ambassadors, was that the Americans were engaging more with the Russians than they publicly acknowledge, the official and one of the diplomats said. No further details on those engagements were given during Mr. Seibert’s briefing, which lasted about 20 minutes, according to the official.

The Trump administration has argued that energy deals with Mr. Putin, in addition to lowering energy prices, could help pave the way for a settlement in Ukraine by showing the Kremlin that reintegration into the world economy was possible for Russia if it compromised in the war.

We Know How to Fix Homelessness. Look at Denver.

They have surrendered public spaces to the homeless and their encampments to the point that it’s difficult to describe these spaces as truly for the public anymore.

Denver shows what happens when a city puts into place proven policies with determination and focus. Not only has it significantly reduced homelessness; it embarrasses every other urban jurisdiction that has failed to deal with its Covid-era surge of homeless encampments. Other cities no longer have an excuse.

Denver has recorded the biggest recent drop in street homelessness among the largest U.S. cities, according to my analysis of local data. The city’s drop was roughly 13 times the national rate in 2025, the most recent year for federal statistics. Since 2023, Denver’s unsheltered population is down 64 percent. “What they’re doing is working,” said Samantha Batko, a senior fellow at the left-leaning Urban Institute, which is independently evaluating the city’s progress.

Since Mayor Mike Johnston of Denver took office in 2023, he has focused on getting unsheltered homelessness to zero. He has done so by using some fairly standard ideas. Police officers break up homeless encampments, warning that repeated violations could lead to arrest. With the help of social workers, the city connects those people to services and shelters. Crucially, it has expanded those services to ensure that officers and social workers have something to connect people to.

By successfully combining enforcement and social services, Denver demonstrates that cities don’t need to choose between those binaries. They should do both.

Politically, none of this is easy. On the policing side, progressives remain skeptical of using law enforcement to deal with what they see as largely an economic issue. On the housing side, the constraint is money. Building housing and shelters requires public and private funds that cities often don’t have and aren’t willing to prioritize over other spending and tax cuts.

Speaking from an office stuffed with Colorado memorabilia, Mr. Johnston said he wanted to go further. He laid out a vision to ensure that all people are housed and that public spaces are actually available to the public. “Our fundamental mantra when we started was our belief that all of our problems are solvable and we’re the ones to solve them,” he told me.

On a Monday afternoon, Mr. Johnston played tour guide. He wanted to show me the city’s new homeless shelters and how they differed from traditional facilities. We walked 10 minutes from City Hall — the mayor stopped to congratulate a wedding party on the way out — to a block of tiny houses known as Elati Village.

Each resident there gets a small house that offers a level of privacy not typical for homeless shelters. Valentino Ortiz, a former Elati Village resident and a transgender man, said privacy was important for his safety. He recalled a previous stay at a more traditional shelter. “The third day, I was already getting sexually assaulted,” he said. At Elati, “you have a beautiful tiny home to call your own. You have hot showers. You can cook your own meals and do laundry.”

Next, Mr. Johnston took me to the Aspen, a city-owned hotel. For residents, it is like an apartment complex. The rooms weren’t too different from places I lived in before. Mr. Johnston said he wanted the city’s shelters to feel like real homes — “a room of one’s own.”

As we walked through the building, residents told the mayor they finally had been able to get their lives in order. Staff members at the Aspen and other shelters spend much of their time preparing people to leave. They help residents get the documents they need to find a job and permanent housing. They connect them to training, education programs and additional government aid, including housing vouchers and rent subsidies. Residents don’t face hard limits on how long they can stay, but providers are, under their contracts, evaluated on how many people they help get on the right path.

The goal is to keep people off the streets for good. To that end, the city still has to address the high cost of housing. Denver has enacted some reforms, but buying and renting a home remain too expensive for much of the poor and middle class.

Ana Miller, an organizer for the homeless rights group Housekeys Action Network Denver, criticized the Aspen for some of its rules and their enforcement, particularly the staff’s room inspections. She also panned the shelter’s provider, Urban Alchemy, which has faced criticism in other cities for its unorthodox tactics, including its hiring of ex-convicts as staff members. Ms. Miller said Elati Village offers a better model than typical shelters, but she worried about resistance from neighborhoods to building more such communities. The neighbors living in apartments near Elati “literally point cameras at the community and watch them,” she said.

Still, the numbers speak for themselves. Mr. Johnston said that no one has declined an offer to move into one of the new facilities and that they are consistently at or near capacity. The city’s biggest problem is how it can buy or build more places like Elati Village and the Aspen to meet demand.

Much of the tens of millions of dollars the city has spent on shelters came from temporary federal funds that have expired. The Trump administration has also moved to cut housing subsidies across the country. The financial constraints have led some local officials to question whether the cost of the city’s efforts is worth the benefit. If that sentiment spreads, it could doom progress.

At 6:30 a.m. on Tuesday, I met with a Denver police squad to see the enforcement side of the city’s strategy. Officer Michael Nierenberg, who led the group, told me his goal was not to arrest people. Tall and imposing, he said the threat he presented was only an incentive to push people to get help. Social workers rode along.

Early in the patrol, we came across a tent. Inside, a couple slept with all their belongings scattered across the floor. Officer Nierenberg waited patiently as they woke up, and then he explained the consequences of breaking laws against camping outside: a verbal warning, then a written warning, then a ticket or arrest. He started asking about the couple’s situation. They were from Texas, they said, and still had family there. They would like to go back, but they didn’t have the means to do so, they added.

Officer Nierenberg told them to pack up their tent and said he would see what he could do. He sat in his car, making calls and looking through his computer. After about 15 minutes, he came back with a bus ticket. The man, who identified himself as Chance, cried tears of joy.

We continued like this for the rest of the morning. Sometimes the encounters were less pleasant. One man told the officers, in colorful language, to go away. Other times, people were cordial. “It has been a typical morning,” the officer told me as we headed back to the police station.

Progressives tend to view the enforcement side of anti-homelessness strategies with disdain because it can involve criminalizing an economic or a mental health issue. At the same time, other residents don’t want encampments clogging up parks and sidewalks. Progressive cities have tried to get around the dilemma by flooding the streets with social services, hoping that offers of help would get people on the streets to pack up. The reality, as cities have painfully learned, is that people often need a stronger push to abandon their tents.

The balanced approach has shrunk the number of encampments across Denver, the Urban Institute’s evaluation found. From 2023 to 2025, the number of active encampments fell by nearly half. The number of large encampments, with 10 or more tents or structures, dropped by 91 percent. “It’s pretty much night and day,” said Anthony Mantelli, whose family runs the West Saloon and Kitchen in the city’s 16th Street Mall. “I close the restaurant four or five nights a week. I don’t deal with many issues at all.”

Mr. Johnston described his strategy through his perspective as a former school principal. “Your job is to keep everyone safe,” he said. “That means I love every single kid in the building. And if there’s one kid who’s making other kids in the building feel unsafe, my job is to either help him change his behavior or hold him accountable for it.”

I asked Mr. Johnston if it’s realistic to think a city as large as Denver can eliminate street homelessness. “I genuinely believe we can do it,” he said.

The next phase will be more difficult. Those who continue to live on the streets are much more likely to suffer from mental illness and addiction. They need more than a roof over their heads.

For this step, Mr. Johnston has begun an initiative that focuses on connecting people to mental health and addiction treatment. That will be hard to execute. Many of the sick and addicted are resistant to treatment, and getting them to accept help can require a kind of coercion and policing of low-level crimes that many progressives are uncomfortable with.

I came away from Denver convinced that the mayor’s focus and determination are the most crucial factors. I’ve seen this happen nationwide: Policies that work in one place fail in another because officials can replicate the law or the money but not the leadership — the force of will — behind the original success.

But Democrats around the country should figure out how to copy Denver’s program. The party’s failure to tackle homelessness and public disorder more broadly has haunted it nationwide. It’s one reason the party is unpopular, even as President Trump has approval ratings in the 30s, leaving many voters with two options on the ballot they don’t particularly like.

“When you see a problem in front of you every day and nothing happens, your only option is either to blame your neighbor or to blame democracy,” Mr. Johnston said. Mr. Trump “has proved that if things are bad enough, Americans are open to both of those arguments.”

He added: “I think the opposite’s also true. If you can prove that there’s something hard to do and we work it out together and it gets better, you train people’s muscle memory to turn to each other — not to turn on each other.”

SUMMARY

The Supreme Court justices took the bench last week to hear oral arguments, but the start of this term feels different from previous ones. That’s one of the reasons fixing the Supreme Court must be a top priority — and why Democrats, if they take control of one or both houses of Congress in November, must place Supreme Court reform at or near the top of their list. But if you’re a fan of the Supreme Court, you should also support Supreme Court reform.

ARTICLE

The Supreme Court Has Grown Too Powerful. This Is How to Rein It In.
Why Democrats must prioritize court reform.
By Kate Shaw
Published 2026-10-13 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/opinion/supreme-court-reform-democrats.html

The Supreme Court justices took the bench last week to hear oral arguments, but the start of this term feels different from previous ones. For one thing, with the sharp increase in activity on the shadow docket, the justices don’t really take the summers off the way they used to.

It also feels different because this is a precarious moment for American democracy and for the mechanisms of democratic participation — and because it’s impossible to ignore the Supreme Court’s role in creating this instability. In this election cycle, state legislatures have aggressively redrawn congressional districts to maximize their partisan advantage and, in Southern states, to extinguish Black political power; the ultrarich are spending tens of millions of dollars helping to elect their preferred candidates; and the president has sought to radically change the rules for voting by mail, while openly promising voters payouts for helping his party retain control of Congress.

True, the court has rebuffed some of the most egregious efforts at election subversion this year. But it has laid the foundation for the electoral upheaval we are experiencing.

That’s one of the reasons fixing the Supreme Court must be a top priority — and why Democrats, if they take control of one or both houses of Congress in November, must place Supreme Court reform at or near the top of their list.

Beginning with John Marshall’s 1803 pronouncement in Marbury v. Madison that “it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is,” we have gradually come to view the Supreme Court as the final arbiter of the meaning of laws and the Constitution. When the court is functioning properly — when it plays a meaningful but limited role in our system — that’s a reasonable state of affairs, whatever the merits of any particular Supreme Court decision.

But when the court develops an outsize sense of its own authority and when it uses that authority to impose its policy preferences and, increasingly, its partisan preferences on the rest of us, the arrangement becomes untenable. That has happened before, and it is manifestly the case now.

This court has asserted extraordinary power and has, again and again, used that power to undermine democratic participation and thwart meaningful self-governance. It substituted its judgment for the judgment of Congress about how to make real the Constitution’s promises of equality and voting rights. It insulated the president from various criminal laws. It hobbled the ability of administrative agencies to respond to pressing problems like climate change. Many of these decisions conspicuously depart from the court’s professed commitments about how legal interpretation should be done, leaving the distinct impression that the court is simply announcing its policy preferences as binding law.

The consequences of these decisions are everywhere. Take presidential lawlessness. Since it declared presidents all but above the law in Trump v. United States two years ago, the court has created a permission structure for much of President Trump’s second-term lawlessness. In the June decision Trump v. Slaughter, it handed Mr. Trump complete control over most of the last remaining pockets of independence — and checks on the president — inside the executive branch.

When the lower courts have challenged his lawlessness, the Supreme Court has regularly interceded to greenlight the president’s actions — allowing the unilateral canceling of billions in funding, granting the so-called Department of Government Efficiency access to sensitive Social Security information, permitting the rendition of individuals to third countries without complying with the Convention Against Torture, letting ICE agents stop citizens and noncitizens alike simply because of their appearance. Both the court’s rulings in these cases and its approach to them — rushed dispositions, failure to provide full reasoning and disregard for the careful rulings of lower courts — are impossible to square with the rule of law.

Then there are the court’s decisions overriding congressional efforts to protect the democratic process. The ones invalidating key provisions of the Voting Rights Act have undermined both electoral stability and an inclusive and representative democracy. The most recent case, last term’s Louisiana v. Callais, functionally rendered the Voting Rights Act a dead letter while declaring partisan gerrymandering a god-given right. After that decision, orders from the shadow docket — also now referred to as the emergency or interim docket, the practice of issuing orders and summary decisions typically without full briefing or oral arguments — allowed states to put the decision into effect immediately. That rushed effort resulted in the elimination of majority Black districts throughout the South and ever more extreme partisan gerrymanders. The court has also, through Citizens United and its progeny, paved the way for wild distortions of our electoral process by ultrawealthy individuals and corporations.

When the delegates to the Constitutional Convention gathered in Philadelphia in 1787, they considered a number of approaches to designing the process of lawmaking. One proposal, part of the Virginia Plan, would have included judges in a “council of revision” that, together with the executive, would review proposed legislation and either approve or reject it. The convention actively debated this proposal, and in the end decided against including judges in a council of revision; instead, the delegates gave the president alone the power to sign or veto legislation.

The current court has fashioned itself into a council of revision, with the power to decide whether it approves of laws passed by Congress and thus whether those laws will have force at all.

Facing the reality of what the Supreme Court has become is critically important — especially for people, and I count myself among them, who think of themselves as institutionalists. If you detest the Supreme Court, I probably don’t need to convince you that the court needs fixing. But if you’re a fan of the Supreme Court, you should also support Supreme Court reform.

As a new book by the law professors Nikolas Bowie and Daphna Renan argues, there is a rich American tradition of pursuing court reform. At critical moments in our history — before and after the Civil War; leading up to and during the New Deal era — the Supreme Court acted to undermine democratic participation and to routinely substitute its judgment for the will of the people as expressed by their elected representatives. In response, political actors and the people pushed back, including legislatively. The current moment calls for nothing less.

A legislative package should include term limits, for which there is now bipartisan support. According to a recent Brennan Center analysis of polls, 73 percent of the public supports such limits, including 61 percent of Republicans. With a law that sets terms at 18 years, justices could transition to senior justice status and would no longer be able to spend decades wielding enormous public power without any meaningful accountability.

Any law imposing term limits should contain binding ethics rules that would prohibit justices from receiving large gifts and luxury travel from wealthy benefactors. The rules should also mandate detailed financial disclosures and include a meaningful enforcement mechanism — either an inspector general for the judiciary or a committee of current or former federal judges.

Congress could also rein in the court from issuing too many rulings on the shadow docket by codifying which cases deserve emergency consideration and requiring the justices to provide reasons for any shadow-docket ruling. It could require the agreement of a supermajority of justices to disturb a lower court ruling on the shadow docket. It could also impose such a voting rule more generally, requiring a supermajority to invalidate any act of Congress.

Finally, the law should include a mechanism for regularizing appointments across presidential terms while also increasing the size of the court. Each president might get two or even four Supreme Court nominations at designated points during a presidential term.

This list is just a start. If Democrats win the upcoming midterm elections handily, there will be much debate about the specific shape a reform package should take. But for the future of the court and the country, it’s critical that the discussions begin now.

Kate Shaw is a contributing Opinion writer, a professor of law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School and a host of the Supreme Court podcast “Strict Scrutiny.” She served as a law clerk to Justice John Paul Stevens and Judge Richard Posner.
