SUMMARY

People have long searched for a way to extend life, but the obsession has reached a new height in recent years. Here are six myths longevity researchers would like people to stop repeating. A 2021 meta-analysis of 30 studies also found that weight loss among people aged 65 and older is associated with a 59 percent higher risk of death.

ARTICLE

6 Things Longevity Experts Wish People Would Stop Saying
Living longer and healthier is important. But don’t believe everything you hear.
By Melinda Wenner Moyer
Published 2026-10-13 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/well/longevity-experts-advice.html

This article is part of our Longevity special section on living longer and healthier.

People have long searched for a way to extend life, but the obsession has reached a new height in recent years. According to a 2026 report by XRC Brand Capital Fund, longevity-inspired web searches were four times as high in late 2025 as they were a year earlier. YouTube and TikTok teem with anti-aging hacks, from supplements to peptide injections.

Yet many popular anti-aging claims are inaccurate, if not downright dangerous. “A lot is circulating in this space that is not science-based, and it’s really important to dispel some of that,” said Dr. Sofiya Milman, a professor of human longevity studies at the Institute for Aging Research at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

Here are six myths longevity researchers would like people to stop repeating.

The goal of longevity research is to make people live longer.

Most aging researchers don’t want to extend the life span. They want to extend the length of time people remain healthy, or what is known as “health span,” said Steven Austad, a professor of biology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

“If extra years turn out to be a side effect of keeping people healthy longer, well, that’s great,” he said. “But that’s not the goal.”

People are getting healthier and living longer.

A 2025 study reported that the average life expectancy in the United States rose by only about six months from 2009 to 2019, while healthy life expectancy actually declined. In fact, from 2010 to 2019, the United States was the only high-income country in which healthy life expectancy decreased. Put another way, we’ve gotten slightly better at keeping people alive, Dr. Austad said, but we’ve also been “increasing the period of ill health at the end of life.”

Dr. Austad compared this trend to a game of Whac-a-Mole: As researchers have found effective treatments for diseases like cancer and heart disease, other serious conditions, like dementia, have become more prevalent. Studies even suggest that young adults today are more likely to have chronic health conditions than they were a decade ago. Some experts have argued that the American medical system’s emphasis on treating disease, rather than preventing it, is part of the problem.

Drugs and supplements can extend life span.

Peptides, resveratrol, NAD+, growth hormone — influencers claim that products like these can extend the human life span, but no drug or supplement has been shown to do that, said Aladdin Shadyab, an associate professor of public health, human longevity science and medicine at the University of California, San Diego.

Some substances have been shown to increase life span in worms and mice, but human bodies are very different, he said.

One common claim says that low levels of the coenzyme NAD+ are a marker of aging and that older people can benefit from taking supplements that boost it. But a 2026 study found that NAD+ levels in the blood remain stable in old age, suggesting that replenishment may not be necessary and is unlikely to offer any benefit.

Some of these hacks may actually do harm: A review of clinical trials found that human growth hormone (H.G.H.), which is popular in some longevity circles, can actually increase the risk of health issues like joint pain, swelling and carpal tunnel syndrome in healthy older adults.

Women stay healthy longer than men do.

On average, women live about five years longer than men. But they often spend a greater proportion of their late life suffering from illness and disability, said Pankaj Kapahi, a professor who studies aging at the Buck Institute, in Novato, Calif.

“Especially after menopause, there is a significant decline in multiple facets of their health,” Dr. Kapahi said.

The discrepancy may be a byproduct of the fact that aging research has traditionally focused more on men than on women and, according to recent research, still does.

Among other things, older women are at a higher risk for autoimmune diseases, arthritis and Alzheimer’s disease, and on average, conditions that are more prevalent among women have been studied less than those that are more prevalent among men.

In addition, most compounds that have been shown to increase life span in animal studies seem to work better in males than females, said Viviana Perez Montes, director of the aging biology division at the National Institute on Aging. No one knows exactly why.

Weight loss is always good for you if you’re overweight.

Some studies have linked weight loss with a lower risk of death, but others have not, especially among adults over 65. In a 2023 study, Dr. Shadyab and his colleagues found that both intentional and unintentional weight loss among women 61 to 81 were linked with lower odds of surviving to 90, regardless of their starting weight or B.M.I.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 30 studies also found that weight loss among people aged 65 and older is associated with a 59 percent higher risk of death. The literature is “pretty mixed,” Dr. Shadyab said, adding that weight loss may not always be protective.

Why is this? Some studies suggest that when older people shed pounds, they disproportionately lose beneficial muscle and bone mass rather than fat. The findings illustrate a broader point in longevity research: What benefits younger adults does not always benefit older adults.

If you take good care of yourself, you can live to 100.

Recent data suggest that genetics shape half of a person’s life span, on average, while lifestyle and environmental factors account for the other half. But among people who live to 95 or older, genetics seem to play an even larger role in their exceptional longevity, Dr. Milman said. Studies have shown that people who live to at least 95 do not lead healthier lives — as measured by their weight, diet, physical activity, alcohol use or smoking habits — than people who don’t live that long.

“There’s really nothing different about their lifestyle,” Dr. Milman said.

SUMMARY

For one day last week, much of Israel united to commemorate the anniversary of the deadliest attack in the country’s history. Many in this liberal bastion are likely to vote against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his hawkish policies, holding him responsible for failures leading to Oct. 7, said Daniel Rahamim, 72, a spokesman for the community, who survived the assault along with his family. Some attitudes have hardened here, too, since the Oct. 7 attack.

ARTICLE

The Oct. 7 Attack Changed Israel, but Not Its Politics
As Israelis prepare to vote for the first time since the Hamas-led assault, they remain divided over whether to hold Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responsible for negligence or fault the “treason” of his generals.
By Isabel Kershner
Published 2026-10-13 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/middleeast/israel-october-7-attacks-elections.html

For one day last week, much of Israel united to commemorate the anniversary of the deadliest attack in the country’s history.

But when Israelis head to the ballot box this month, they will be carrying sharply disparate versions of who is to blame for failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led assault. Though the attack traumatized Israel, it did not produce the kind of rage that would create a political transformation, leaving the country more polarized than ever.

The political divide is nowhere clearer than among the Israelis living closest to the Gaza border, where thousands of gunmen overran communities, army bases and a music festival.

In Nahal Oz, a pastoral kibbutz half a mile from the border, the gardens are blooming again with the return of residents evacuated during the war. Many in this liberal bastion are likely to vote against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his hawkish policies, holding him responsible for failures leading to Oct. 7, said Daniel Rahamim, 72, a spokesman for the community, who survived the assault along with his family.

“We don’t have the privilege of giving up on peace,” he said.

Barely eight miles away in the working-class town of Sderot, the scene of a fierce firefight during the Hamas-led attack, Mr. Netanyahu remains a hero. In the view of many residents, he was let down — or even betrayed — by his security chiefs in the run-up to Oct. 7 and on the day of the assault.

“If the left wins, we’re done for, it will be the end of Israel,” said Shlomi Aragon, 55, referring to anybody critical of Mr. Netanyahu.

The election, set for Oct. 27, will be the first since Hamas militants and their allies surged across the border from Gaza, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, according to the Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages.

Israel’s devastating war in response reduced much of the Palestinian enclave to rubble and left more than 74,000 people dead, including thousands of children, according to Gaza health officials, who do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Many Israelis view this month’s vote as the most momentous since their country’s establishment nearly eight decades ago, and for reasons that are not limited to Oct. 7. Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, Israel’s most hard-line and religiously conservative, has undermined the country’s democratic foundations, critics say, and left it diplomatically isolated.

Hanging over the election most intensely are questions about the missteps in the prelude to Oct. 7 — for the policies aimed at fostering quiet in Hamas-run Gaza in the years before the attack and for military and intelligence lapses that left Israel vulnerable. These failures have profoundly shaken people’s confidence in the state’s ability to protect them.

The wars that spread from Gaza to Lebanon and Iran in the aftermath of the Oct. 7 attack remain unfinished. Three years on, Israel’s enemies are battered but not out, defying Mr. Netanyahu’s promises of total victory.

Yet all this upheaval has not produced the radical shift that would upend Israel’s politics.

“Like everyone, after Oct. 7, I thought there would be an earthquake,” said Tamar Hermann, a professor of political science and expert in public opinion at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group in Jerusalem.

Instead, she said, it has reinforced people’s previously held positions as they retreated to their political “comfort zones.”

Like past elections, this one, too, revolves largely around the question of “Yes Bibi or no Bibi,” Ms. Hermann said, using Mr. Netanyahu’s nickname, and the choice between a “more Jewish or more democratic” Israel.

The Netanyahu camp, for its part, says Israel’s security services failed to respond to the grave threat posed by Hamas, not the prime minister or the policies of his ruling Likud party.

There is little argument among most Israelis over the government’s new willingness to carry out sustained attacks beyond the country’s borders and occupy territory in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon. A majority of Israelis fear a repeat of Oct. 7, according to a recent survey by the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

But that view does not extend to confidence in Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership. Surveys indicate a split electorate and a typically tight race with a high likelihood that neither Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, nor his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist and former military chief, will secure an easy path toward forming the next government.

A Tale of Two Communities

On the Israeli side of the Gaza border, the air of renewal masks sharp disagreements over the lessons of Oct. 7.

During the attack, 15 people in Nahal Oz were killed, and eight residents were kidnapped, including one who died in captivity. Most of the residents have since returned to the kibbutz. At night, the lights of Israeli army positions visible along a ridge inside the Gaza Strip provide some sense of security.

Mr. Rahamim, the Nahal Oz spokesman, has a fresh tattoo on his arm bearing the date of the attack and the words, “On the path of hope.” The image of a sunflower climbing his forearm symbolizes a local crop — and hope, Mr. Rahamim said, “because it always faces the sun.”

In the last national election, held in 2022, 83 percent of the voters in Nahal Oz supported centrist and left-leaning parties. In the upcoming election, Mr. Rahamim said he and many neighbors will likely vote against Mr. Netanyahu again.

Mr. Netanyahu’s handling of Gaza is not the only reason. Mr. Rahamim also pointed to the government’s efforts at curbing the powers of the judiciary and at the influence Mr. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies have over him, leading Mr. Rahamim to ask, “Will Israel be a liberal democratic state or gradually turn into a religious or fascist state?”

Some attitudes have hardened here, too, since the Oct. 7 attack. “If there is a consensus here in community, it is that Hamas has to be destroyed,” Mr. Rahamim said.

Unlike many in Mr. Netanyahu’s camp, Mr. Rahamim also said he believes that Israel must eventually negotiate an accommodation with moderate Palestinian leaders. “We have an obligation to our grandchildren,” he said.

In Sderot, forests of construction cranes rise from new neighborhoods. A serene memorial park has replaced the police station where a deadly battle raged. More than 50 people were killed in the city, including civilians, police officers, firefighters and soldiers.

Sderot has historically been a stronghold of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, and in the last election, 79 percent voted for the right-wing and strictly Orthodox parties that made up his governing coalition.

Here, residents espouse conspiracy theories spread by Mr. Netanyahu’s camp that treasonous generals and security chiefs kept the prime minister in the dark about the start of the Hamas attack.

Mr. Netanyahu has asserted that Israeli security officials had chosen not to awaken him in the early hours of Oct. 7, despite worrying signs from Gaza.. He has blocked the establishment of an independent inquiry into what went wrong, despite a strong public demand for one.

Mr. Aragon, who owns a shawarma restaurant, said he narrowly escaped death on Oct. 7 when gunmen drove behind him and started shooting. About 20 years ago, he said, his house was hit by a rocket from Gaza that severely injured his wife.

He described Mr. Netanyahu as “the war leader of a generation” and suggested that the Israeli air force, if activated, could have halted the Hamas invasion within an hour. “There was a betrayal. It’ll come out,” he said.

Living opposite the site of the destroyed police station, Evelyn Sayada, 60, whose son-in-law survived the assault on the music festival, said she felt constant anxiety because Hamas had not been disarmed. But she said she would almost certainly vote for Mr. Netanyahu, as her family has always done.

“I don’t think he failed,” she said. “There was treason.”

‘Afraid of change’

One of the worst-hit Israeli border villages was Kfar Aza, home to Yonatan Shamriz, 36. His brother, Alon, was taken hostage and later killed accidentally by Israeli soldiers in Gaza who had mistaken him and two other captives for militants.

Mr. Shamriz emerged from a life of relative obscurity and founded a grass-roots movement to cultivate new leadership and change called “Kumu!” — Hebrew for “awaken!” or “rise up!”

Faced with what they call government efforts to blur and forget, he and Kumu organized Israel’s main Oct. 7 memorial ceremony for the last three years, embracing families of victims from across Israeli society — left and right-wingers, religious and secular, Jews and Arabs. Tens of thousands attended this year’s memorial, and Israel’s leading television channels aired it live.

Mr. Shamriz now lives far from the Gaza border, in a trailer with his wife and three young children in a kibbutz on the coast north of Tel Aviv. He said he believes another attack like the one on Oct. 7 is a matter of time. “If not next year, then in 10 years,” he said.

Last year, Mr. Shamriz announced that he was entering politics, aiming to create a new, unifying force with a vision based on the lessons of Oct. 7. “Something young and fresh,” he said.

In September, he quit, concluding that Israelis weren’t ready to leave their old politics behind.

“For now, people are afraid of change,” he said. “Everyone wants to vote for an experienced politician or general — someone they know.”

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Tim Janus, One of the World’s Greatest Competitive Eaters, Has Died
He brought rigor and strategy to the sport, rising to No. 2 in the world and eating 141 pieces of nigiri in six minutes in the process.
By Clay Risen
Published 2026-10-14 20:13 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/obituaries/tim-janus-eater-x-dead.html

Tim Janus, one of the world’s highest-ranked competitive eaters who, at various competitions, consumed four pounds of tiramisu in six minutes, 10.5 pounds of ramen in eight minutes, 71 tamales in eight minutes, 7.7 pounds of boneless Buffalo wings in 12 minutes and 141 pieces of nigiri in six minutes, died in Boston on Sept. 16. He was 49.

He was diagnosed with an aggressive form of lung cancer in 2022, said his sister, Tess McNair.

For more than a decade, Mr. Janus reigned at the top of his sport, peaking at No. 2 and racking up records that remain standing two decades after he set them.

Some eaters specialize; Mr. Janus ate it all. Cannoli. Marshmallow Peeps. Shoofly pie. And, of course, hot dogs — he frequently placed in the top three at the Nathan’s Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest, where contestants eat frankfurters by the score every July 4.

His career, beginning in 2004 and ending, with his retirement, in 2016, tracked the evolution of competitive eating from a state-fair novelty to a serious undertaking, with televised events, sponsorships and a governing body, the International Federation of Competitive Eating.

The early days were often more spectacle than sport, with outsize characters with outsize names — among them Crazy Legs Conti, Badlands Booker and a 100-pound woman known as the Black Widow. Mr. Janus, who went by the nom-d’estomac Eater X and painted his face with a luchador-style mask, fit right in.

“He wanted to win these contests, and he practiced and positioned himself to win,” said George Shea, who with his brother, Richard, operate the governing federation. “But he also understood throughout that process that there was an absurdity to all of it, and he could hold those two things in his mind.”

Mr. Janus stood out because he actually looked like an athlete: lean and muscular, he was 5 foot 10 and just 170 pounds — ten pounds less than when he started to compete.

He was also more intellectual and analytical in how he approached competitions. Like any serious athlete, he trained constantly, developing a unique regimen of cottage cheese and water to expand and maintain his stomach capacity, not to mention his ability to force feed himself long past the point of satiety (he also ran four days a week).

He watched tapes of his competitors. He filled notebooks with data. And he developed eating strategies: Tiramisu, he decided, should be eaten cream first, since it is denser than the ladyfinger portion, and competitors are judged based on the weight remaining on their plate.

“He had a real science-meets-tomfoolery approach to competitive eating,” Mr. Conti, who lived with Mr. Janus for over a decade, said in an interview.

After leaving the world of competitive eating, Mr. Janus began a new career as a Foreign Service officer. In 2023 he had to cut short a deployment to Mexico City when he was diagnosed with cancer.

Like many of the earliest competitive eaters, Mr. Janus stumbled into the sport. He was working as a day trader in Manhattan, hating the stress of his job. One day he went looking for a way to relieve the pressure and found it in a St. Patrick’s Day eating contest — corned beef and cabbage.

He didn’t win, but he was hooked. He started going to more events on the East Coast, and within months was named rookie of the year by the International Federation of Competitive Eating.

“He brought this unique level of thoughtfulness and earnestness to competitive eating,” Jason Fagone, the author of “Horsemen of the Esophagus: Competitive Eating and the Big Fat American Dream” (2006), said in an interview. “He took this thing that a lot of people just throw off as a joke, and he took it seriously.”

As he evolved as a competitor, so did the sport. Safety standards were imposed. Vomiting — euphemistically called “the Roman method” — was deemed a disqualifying misfortune. A circuit emerged, based around state fairs and regional foods and anchored at the Nathan’s contest, which draws tens of thousands of spectators to Coney Island every summer.

With his good looks and everyman demeanor, Mr. Janus became a poster boy for the sport’s aspirations to seriousness. He appeared on MTV and “Good Morning, America.” In a video interview with The Wall Street Journal, he gamely squared off against two journalists in a hot dog eating race.

Before they started, he offered some tips.

“The first thing is, you have to open your mind to the possibility of eating more hot dogs than you think you can,” he said.

Timothy Peter Janus was born on Dec. 31, 1976, in Farmington, Conn., and raised in nearby Simsbury. His mother, Lucinda Hannon, was a licensed social worker and his father, Peter Janus, was a labor attorney.

Along with his sister, he is survived by his parents and his stepmother, Nancy Janus, a licensed clinical social worker.

He studied political science at Southern Methodist University. Following graduation in 1999, he moved back to Connecticut for two years, where he tended bar, before moving to New York to work in finance.

After he took up competitive eating, he began working nights at a pizza parlor, and eventually quit day trading to make pies full time. He never earned enough money in the sport to live off it exclusively — at the time, no one did — but he also insisted that money didn’t interest him.

“It’s never been about the cash; it’s always about the adventure,” he told The New Era, a newspaper in Lancaster, Penn., in 2006. “One of these contests recharges me more than a week at the beach ever would.”

SUMMARY

I didn’t want to see “Digger.” As a result, “Digger” may be the best climate crisis movie ever made, cleverly disguised as the worst. Yet beneath the shouting, the ungodly animatronic cat and Mr. Cruise’s layers of prosthetics, “Digger” is a surprisingly empathetic, nuanced film about the difficulty of confronting, let alone averting, climate change.

ARTICLE

Tom Cruise’s Big Flop Is a Secret Masterpiece
The film has been panned by critics and shunned by audiences, but its message about the climate crisis is one we need to hear.
By Jayson Greene
Published 2026-10-14 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/opinion/digger-tom-cruise-movie-climate-flop.html

I didn’t want to see “Digger.” The trailers, in which Tom Cruise, in heavy old-man makeup, plays a cartoonish oil baron named Digger Rockwell, looked empty, grating, unfunny. What’s more, I already knew the film’s big twist, which has been widely spoiled, and which I will also spoil below.

My premonition turned out to be well founded. The film has been roundly savaged as a critical and financial catastrophe, a soon-to-be legendary flop that will go down alongside Mr. Cruise’s biggest public missteps, like the couch jumping, the Matt Lauer interview and “Knight and Day.”

Perversely, I decided to see “Digger” anyway, hoping to rubberneck, and the first 30 minutes played out just as I suspected. The film begins as a rickety “Dr. Strangelove”-esque satire, coated in flop sweat and whiffing on all the jokes. Sandra Hüller, playing Digger’s little sister, screeches her lines and dresses like a Spirit-of-Halloween Annie Hall, while John Goodman, as President Compson, roars like a community-theater George C. Scott. Everything is unendurably loud; nothing is funny.

Yet, by the time the credits rolled two hours later, I was moved and engaged, and no longer hiding my face in my hands. The director, Alejandro G. Iñárritu, has hidden a quiet, thoughtful movie about our collective failure to act on climate change inside the husk of an earsplitting, empty one. As a result, “Digger” may be the best climate crisis movie ever made, cleverly disguised as the worst.

Climate crisis movies have always been notoriously hard to make, for the same reason the climate crisis is hard to combat: It’s too big. Everyone’s affected, but not in the same ways, on the same timelines or at the same scale. We can see and comprehend elements of the problem, but no one sees the whole picture or how its disparate causes and effects connect.

Paul Schrader’s 2017 film “First Reformed” tackled climate change by focusing on one tortured man’s psyche, following a priest, played by Ethan Hawke, who crosses paths with the radical environmentalist husband of a parishioner and descends into spiritual despair. Adam McKay’s “Don’t Look Up” in 2021 parodied our societal indifference through a parable about alarmed scientists warning everyone about a meteor coming to destroy Earth. Climate change has been exploited for apocalyptic action-movie spectacle, as in “The Day After Tomorrow” and “Snowpiercer,” and fashioned into allegory, as in Bong Joon Ho’s “Parasite” and Valentyn Vasyanovych’s war-fallout film “Atlantis.” But it’s always the backdrop.

“Digger” succeeds where previous climate-warning films have fallen short because it truly captures what the cultural critic Amitav Ghosh called “the great derangement,” our total imaginative failure in the face of the scale of what is happening to the planet. To do so, the film takes a different and unusual tack — and here’s where we get to that oft-spoiled twist.

Around the half-hour mark, having endured that outlandish opening, we learn that what we’re watching is actually a dress rehearsal for a play called “Fossil Fools,” and Mr. Cruise’s real character is a disgruntled actor named Curtis Markson who’s playing the role of Digger. The climate apocalypse being depicted in the play has already happened, and the world survived it, sort of — and this play has become an unlikely hit, offering its audience a sense of catharsis and a chance to boo its cartoonish villains.

Watching Markson wander backstage, muttering about his ridiculous role, I slowly started to grasp that none of the actors involved in the play seem to think it’s particularly funny or, really, any good at all. The actors are mostly the opposite of their onstage personas: They’re subdued, respectful, kind to one another and maybe a little sad. This dynamic cleverly flips the usual play-within-a-play structure in which the hysteria tends to occur backstage while the show goes on.

It also neatly mimics the sensation of climate despair: Mostly, you just go about your life. But every once in a while, you need to freak out — and when you do, you too might resemble one of the two-dimensional characters depicted in “Fossil Fools.”

In one of the many memorable pans of the film, New York magazine’s Bilge Ebiri wrote that watching the film felt like “being trapped inside a tuba for two hours.” He’s not wrong — the movie is loud and overwhelming and in many ways repellent. But for me, that’s how “Digger” succeeds. It acknowledges the ways in which art about the climate crisis almost always resembles being stuck inside a tuba: The pitch of our indignation and our terror and panic at what is being lost reliably render us overwhelmed and incoherent.

By daring to make the movie this way, Mr. Iñárritu not only courts audience rage (at this writing, the film sits with a deadly C+ on CinemaScore, which measures viewer reaction), but also risks making himself, having twice won an Oscar for best director, look incompetent. For a movie about Method acting, role-playing and artistic failure, it’s an apt gesture, if a slightly insane one.

In the film’s final moments, Mr. Cruise’s Markson character derails the play’s dress rehearsal. How do you play someone like Digger Rockwell, he demands — someone who knowingly ushered the planet past the point of collapse? The play offers us a cartoon, he argues, but this was a real man.

Jesse Plemons, playing a mysterious producer, reveals that he is the nephew of the real-life Digger Rockwell, and he reminds everyone: Yes, his uncle was real, as were all the other ghoulish characters on the stage. The planetary devastation is also real, as is the communal need for catharsis. During productions of the play, we learn, audiences cheer and weep, indulging their atavistic urge for punishment and retribution. They hoot at the death of Digger Rockwell — and then they line up to see it again and again. The play might not be perfect, or even good. But as the credits roll, and as we follow its audience out the doors into the surrounding devastation, Mr. Iñárritu asks us to consider what a better version of that story might look like. How might we tell future generations of our failure?

“Digger” is such an accurate portrayal of the necessity of bad art that it’s very easy to mistake it for bad art. It’s certainly provoked that response from many viewers: During its second weekend in theaters, its audience plummeted even further, fueled in part by toxic word of mouth.

Yet beneath the shouting, the ungodly animatronic cat and Mr. Cruise’s layers of prosthetics, “Digger” is a surprisingly empathetic, nuanced film about the difficulty of confronting, let alone averting, climate change. It strives to understand what has happened already, what will happen to us next and even why. We know all of this is too big, the film says, and it’s going to make shrieking cartoons of us all.

Jayson Greene is the author of the novel “UnWorld.”

ARTICLE

Five Who Lived Along Walking Trail Are Dead and the Police Hunt a Killer
Lansing’s police chief says the string of attacks along a greenway raises the possibility that a serial killer has been at work. A man is under arrest in one of the deaths.
By Bill Ruthhart and Ryan Patrick Hooper
Published 2026-10-14 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/us/lansing-michigan-serial-killer.html

The Lansing River Trail, a greenway that winds through Michigan’s capital, has long drawn walkers and cyclists to the Grand River. But lately, the trail has become known for something else: suspicious deaths.

In less than a year, five homeless men died from injuries suffered in the middle of the night on a one-mile stretch near downtown Lansing, Mich. Each was lying down, possibly sleeping, the police said. Four suffered head injuries. A fifth was stabbed.

A suspect has been charged with murder in that attack, but the others remain under investigation.

Public awareness of the deaths among the homeless spread only recently. In September, The Lansing State Journal noted similarities among four of the killings. Soon after, investigators confirmed the details of a fifth. Then Robert Backus, the police chief, raised the question that has the city on edge.

“Do we have a serial killer in Lansing?” Chief Backus said during a news conference, adding: “We are looking at the idea — or the possibility — that these may be related cases.”

The prospect of a killing spree in a public park has frightened residents and prompted nighttime patrols by community groups and the police. The deaths have also renewed questions about how Lansing handles homeless encampments, park safety and public communication about crimes. The Police Department has faced sharp criticism from local leaders, homeless residents and a victim’s father for failing to warn the community.

“It’s scary knowing that even if you’re homeless, you can’t even lay out here and go to sleep without somebody beating you,” said Derick Byrd, 56, who has stayed along the river and knew three of the men who were killed.

Chief Backus said that temporary cameras were now along the trail, and that the city was considering better lighting and permanent surveillance. The chief said he considered the trail safe — except overnight.

Along the trail downtown, public squares, playgrounds, art installations and apartment buildings sit near woods with homeless encampments. The path winds under bridges that are dark and isolated at night, serving as popular sleeping spots. On Friday evening, homeless people on the trail far outnumbered others.

At Lansing Shuffle, a bar steps from the greenway, bartenders discussed the deaths, and Austin Smith, 28, a patron, said talk of a serial killer had kept friends off the trail. They “just pass it by, find a different route,” he said, “because why even take the chance?”

Lansing’s homeless population has grown in recent years, officials said, with clusters of tents scattered in the same downtown where Michigan lawmakers and lobbyists gather in marbled hallways and high-dollar restaurants. A 2023 study estimated the city of more than 113,000 had a homeless population of 2,371.

Along the river, the string of deaths among the homeless began on Oct. 14, 2025, when Gino Chouinard, 54, was found unconscious with injuries to his face. He died 13 days later. The medical examiner listed his cause of death as undetermined, but Chief Backus said it was now under review.

Then, over the summer, four more men died within two months of one another.

Denis Dunnebacke, 70, was found unconscious on July 9 with facial injuries under a bridge. Four days later, Robert Smith, 57, was found unresponsive and bleeding from his head. Both men died within days. Mr. Dunnebacke’s cause of death remains under investigation, while Mr. Smith’s has been ruled a homicide, the police said.

A little more than a month later, on Aug. 20, Daniel Lusk, 22, was found stabbed to death under a bridge. Ten days later, Louis Woodruff, 57, was found with facial injuries under another bridge. Mr. Woodruff’s death is being investigated as a homicide, the police said. He died on Sept. 1.

The next day, the police arrested Edward Joseph Smith, 23, and charged him with murder in Mr. Lusk’s death.

Surveillance footage from nearby buildings captured a man leaving the scene and walking across downtown, including a stop at a drinking fountain to wash his arm, court records show. Police found blood on the fountain, recognized Mr. Smith from the video and found a sweatshirt in his tent that matched the one worn by the suspect on the surveillance footage, the records show.

At his news conference, Chief Backus noted that while all five deaths had similar circumstances, Mr. Lusk’s was the only one that involved a known weapon — a knife. The stabbing involved a victim and a suspect in their 20s, the police said, while the other victims were over 50.

“We are looking at every case with the idea of, is this a similar suspect or the same suspect?” Chief Backus said. “But we cannot move forward in an investigation thinking that these are all the same person. We have to look at these on a case-by-case scenario.”

He said the investigations had been hindered by limited surveillance cameras, few witnesses and, in some cases, inconclusive or unfinished findings from the medical examiner.

Dean Lusk said the death of his son, Daniel, was too fresh for him to watch the chief’s news conference. Mr. Lusk, 67, said his son had battled drug addiction and had been in and out of rehab and jail. He visited him regularly by the river, bringing food and clean laundry.

Mr. Lusk said his son’s death might have been prevented had the police said more publicly and increased patrols.

“There were incidents that happened down there before my son got murdered,” Mr. Lusk said. “The cops were well aware of it, and they refused to do anything about it.”

Sarah Anthony, a state senator whose district includes the trail, called the deaths “terrifying,” and said that had the victims not been homeless, the police would have acted more urgently.

“It’s really infuriating, the lack of information and clarity we’ve received,” Ms. Anthony said. “There’s no perfect time to tell the public news that could scare them, but bringing the community along is something leaders do.”

Mayor Andy Schor, a Democrat, declined an interview, but said in a statement that the attacks did not target “the general public,” a line echoed by Peter Spadafore, the City Council president. Mr. Spadafore said that “the Police Department is treating these deaths as serious as any other suspicious deaths,” but added that officials would look to improve communication. A police spokesman, Eric Pratl, declined to comment.

In his news conference, Chief Backus apologized for not issuing a news release about one of the deaths. He said that in other cases, medical information about victims and their causes of death arrived slowly, and he didn’t want to alarm the public unnecessarily.

Ryan Kost, a council member whose ward includes the trail, said the city’s homeless population had “exploded” over the past eight months and previous city sweeps of homeless encampments had pushed more people toward the river. He said the police should have done more to warn and protect them.

“You’re talking about a population that has no defense mechanism — they’re sleeping on the damn ground,” Mr. Kost said. “That’s the frustrating part: They had no way to fight back.”

Walking the trail Friday evening, Mr. Byrd, the homeless resident, said he had known Daniel Lusk and grown up with Mr. Chouinard, calling him “my best friend.” He referred to Mr. Woodruff as “Uncle Louis” and said he “didn’t bother nobody” and “would give you the shirt off his back.”

Mr. Byrd said he suspected the person or people behind the attacks were not part of Lansing’s established homeless community. Many people along the river have long known one another, he said

“Everybody here, we’re normal — this is us,” Mr. Byrd said. “But when the sun goes down, some people come up in here who don’t live here, don’t know us and we don’t see them.”

ARTICLE

Democratic Donor Emerges to Blitz Red-State Senate Races With Late Ads
Steve Pajcic, a lawyer and philanthropist in Florida, started a group that is airing ads in Kansas and South Carolina. Florida and Mississippi are next.
By Shane Goldmacher and Theodore Schleifer
Published 2026-10-14 22:56 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/us/politics/democratic-donor-senate-red-state-ads.html

A surprise Democratic donor has emerged as a financier of a late effort to help the party deliver upsets in four red-state Senate seats.

Steve Pajcic, a lawyer and philanthropist in Florida, and his children are spending at least $7 million for a blitz of ads in Florida, Kansas, Mississippi and South Carolina, a quartet of Senate seats in traditionally Republican territory. Mr. Pajcic, a co-founder of the personal-injury law firm Pajcic & Pajcic, is behind a new group called New Deal for All that was formed in the beginning of October and started to air ads Tuesday in Kansas and South Carolina.

The group will soon expand to Florida, where it plans to spend most of its money, and Mississippi. The injection of even a modest amount of cash shows the optimism among Democrats about winning Senate seats that were thought beyond their reach as recently as last year.

“Democrats have been way too timid and modest in their expectations in the past,” Mr. Pajcic, 80, told The New York Times. “There’s a real chance for something big happening with this election, and I’m kind of old. So why not see if you can if there’s anything you can do to help?”

Mr. Pajcic has never donated at this scale before. He contributed $147,000 to a Democratic Senate super PAC in 2024, but he said he did not want to simply hand over $7 million — the most he has ever donated, he said — to outside groups.

“If I’m going to put this much into it, I want to make sure it’s effective and doing what I want it to do,” he said.

He said that he named his super PAC New Deal for All because he wanted to see Democrats win as many as 56 Senate seats and usher in a historic movement “comparable to the changes we had with the New Deal.”

National Democrats in recent weeks have begun shifting more of their resources to these red states, particularly Kansas. But they are still spending relatively little in Florida — one of the country’s most expensive states to campaign in — as well as South Carolina and Mississippi.

They Voted for Trump.

How are they feeling about high grocery prices?

Donald J. Trump rode to the White House in 2024 on a pledge to make America more affordable and bring down the cost of everyday essentials.

“I won on groceries,” he told NBC News in 2024, referring to his electoral victory.

But as the midterm elections draw near, grocery prices have been climbing, driven upward by the Iran war, which has caused a surge in diesel and gasoline costs and made shipping goods more expensive.

Consumer prices overall are up 3.7 percent from a year ago, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Wednesday, well above the government’s target. Food costs have risen 2.5 percent over the past 12 months. Among the goods whose prices are rising: fruits and vegetables (up 3.7 percent since last year), nonalcoholic beverages and materials (up 3.8 percent), and cereals and bakery products (up 2.1 percent).

The cost increases pose an intensifying problem for Republican candidates, and a growing number of them are distancing themselves from Mr. Trump and his policies. Sexual Assault Report at Chicago Frat Upends Another Elite Campus
The University of Chicago said the suspect and victim were not students at the school. But the accusation drew scrutiny after revelations of a reported gang rape at Cornell University in New York.

A 21-year-old woman reported that she was sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago, the city police said, putting another campus on edge over accusations of misconduct tied to Greek life organizations.

The woman said the assault occurred in the early hours of Sunday during a party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity, the police said, though neither the victim nor the suspect were students at the school. One witness said in an interview that she had interrupted an attack. That prompted the suspect to flee the house, according to the university, which called the episode “deeply concerning.”

The Chicago city police are investigating and did not provide further details, nor say whether there had been an arrest. On Tuesday, the school said it had identified a “person of interest” in the assault, adding that the person has been barred from campus.

Accusations of sexual misconduct are grimly plentiful on American campuses, and the report at the University of Chicago, a campus of Gothic architecture and intellectual rigor, came after a reported gang rape at Cornell University in New York propelled the issue back into the national debate.

The Chicago episode took place at a Saturday night fraternity party boisterous enough to be heard blocks away. Klara Grant, an 18-year-old chemistry student, said there was a D.J., dance floors on two levels of the house and a bar.

Mia Lara, a 21-year-old student at a nearby university, said she had seen the event advertised on the fraternity’s Instagram account. She and the woman who reported the attack, along with a third friend, decided to go.

It was the first time any of them had been to a fraternity party, Ms. Lara said. At the door, they were asked for identification, but not whether they attended the University of Chicago.

The trio danced in the basement. Ms. Lara’s friend and a man began kissing and Ms. Lara lost track of them. She searched the house, eventually finding a small group of men cheering outside a locked bathroom door in the basement, she said.

“They were saying things like, ‘When’s it my turn?’ and, ‘I want to go in there,’” Ms. Lara said.

Ms. Lara jimmied the lock and forced her way inside. She found her friend sitting on the floor, slumped against the wall with her clothes and undergarments pulled down. The man whom her friend had been kissing had his hands on her wrists, Ms. Lara said.

Her friend began saying, “Make it stop” and “Get me out of here,” Ms. Lara said. Ms. Lara began screaming and the man left. She and her friend carried the woman out of the bathroom.

Outside the fraternity house, Ms. Lara chased the man, a scene captured in a social media video. In the clip, Ms. Lara yells at the man, accusing him of assaulting her friend.

“She wanted to,” the man replies. Ms. Lara swats the man with her hands, and he runs.

Ms. Lara said the man got away and she was intercepted by a campus police officer. The officer drove the three friends to the University of Chicago hospital, she said, where the police took a report and her friend underwent a rape exam.

In a statement posted on Instagram, the University of Chicago’s chapter of Alpha Epsilon Pi condemned what it called a sexual assault, asking for respect and privacy for the victim.

The fraternity’s national organization decried the episode in a separate statement, saying, “No one should attend an event on any campus — fraternity-based or otherwise — and have to fear for their safety and well-being.”

Jonathan Pierce, a spokesman for the fraternity’s national organization, said the suspect was not a member of the Alpha Epsilon Pi chapter at the university.

“We do not believe that any AEPi members were involved in this horrible act, nor were they complicit with it,” Mr. Pierce said in an email.

Fraternities at the University of Chicago are not formally affiliated with the institution, the school said, but are still “subject to university policies and disciplinary procedures.” Alpha Epsilon Pi has been told not hold events or programs during the investigation, according to Mr. Pierce.

Gerald McSwiggan, a spokesman for the university, declined to be interviewed.

Fraternities and Greek life overall have been under scrutiny after allegations of a gang rape at Cornell in 2024 recently came to light when a woman sued over the episode. On Tuesday, Cornell announced that it would ban fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year.

Around the country, the necessity of Greek life has been called into question, as some reflect on the history of hazing, violence and even death that has long marred institutions promising friendship and professional networks.

Ms. Grant, the chemistry student in Chicago, left the party with her friends before the incident, she said. They were stunned when they learned about it the next day, she said.

“There’s definitely going to be a different sense in the air for the next little while,” she said.

ARTICLE

Sally Rooney Says Her Novels Will No Longer Be Sold in U.K.
Ms. Rooney and her publisher said that she could no longer receive royalties from British sales because she pledged to donate book revenues to Palestine Action, which is banned in Britain.
By Stephen Castle
Published 2026-10-14 19:44 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/world/europe/rooney-britain-palestine-book-sales.html

Sally Rooney and her publisher said Wednesday that her novels will no longer be sold in the United Kingdom because of her support for a pro-Palestinian protest group that the British government banned last year as a terrorist organization.

The publisher, Faber, said in a statement that “current legislation” meant it could no longer pay royalties from the United Kingdom to Ms. Rooney. It has therefore decided, the statement said, not to supply her work “in the U.K. in any format.”

Payment of royalties to Ms. Rooney could violate the law because she has promised to donate funds from her book sales to the banned group, Palestine Action.

Ms. Rooney said, in a statement released by her agent, that the publisher’s decision to halt U.K. sales had come “after a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement.”

The decision to withdraw her books means that Britons will no longer be able to buy best-selling novels including “Normal People” and “Conversations with Friends,” which have both been adapted for TV and proved highly popular.

The development will likely intensify the debate over the Labour government’s contentious decision in 2025 to use terrorism legislation to ban Palestine Action, which has claimed credit for several acts of vandalism but does not promote violence against individuals. The group’s members repeatedly damaged facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and in June 2025 broke into R.A.F. Brize Norton, Britain’s largest air force base, spray-painting two aircraft.

The ban of Palestine Action was the first time the British government had used terrorism powers against a group for “serious damage to property,” rather than because of the use or threat of violence against people, prompting criticism from a broad range of human rights groups and international bodies.

As a result of the ban, more than 3,000 people have been arrested for expressing support for the group at demonstrations, including by holding signs or wearing T-shirts saying “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” The arrest of peaceful protesters has prompted a fierce debate over free speech and the right to protest.

It is has also put Ms. Rooney and her publisher at risk of breaking British law because, after Palestine Action was banned last year, Ms. Rooney said she would use money raised from her book sales to support the group. In an article in the Irish Times last year she wrote: “I want to be clear that I intend to use these proceeds of my work, as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action.”

Giving any kind of support to organizations designated under the Terrorism Act is a criminal offense in Britain, and paying royalties to the author, given her open intentions, could therefore expose her publisher to prosecution.

In a statement released by her agent, Ms. Rooney reiterated her intention to support Palestine Action, “which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland,” even though publishing her work in the United Kingdom “could now constitute a serious criminal offense.”

Ms. Rooney said she had “made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions,” and was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

In its statement, her publisher said that “to sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.”

It added: “We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”

Britain’s home office, which introduced the ban on Palestine Action, said that the ban “followed a rigorous and evidence-based decision-making process, endorsed by Parliament.”

In a statement it added: “The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right.”

Palestine Action’s co-founder, Huda Ammori, described the forced halt of sales of Ms. Rooney’s books in the U.K. as “a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action.”

In a statement, she added: “A world-renowned author fearing arrest and being forced to remove her books from our bookstores, exposes the chilling consequences of this authoritarian law, which has been used to make over 3,700 arrests for simply holding seven word signs.”

The ban on Palestine Action as a terrorist group has been challenged in a succession of legal hearings. Britain’s High Court initially found that the ban was unlawful, saying it was disproportionate and breached free speech rights. But judges in the Court of Appeal overruled that in June. Ms. Ammori appealed that ruling, and the ultimate decision now falls to the country’s Supreme Court, which is expected to hear the case next month.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

As a Child Evangelist, He Roused the Faithful. Later He Exposed the Con.
An ordained minister at 4, Marjoe Gortner went on to star in a documentary that revealed the flimflammery of his former profession: “You go into it like a business.”
By Penelope Green
Published 2026-10-15 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/movies/marjoe-gortner-dead.html

By the time he was 4, Marjoe Gortner was an ordained minister, coached by his parents into a tiny simulacrum of a Pentecostal preacher, belting out hellfire and brimstone.

He was born into the business, the fourth generation of a family of ministering men. But it was his mother, Margaret, known as Sister Marge, who taught him the trade, writing the scripts for his sermons and drilling him in daylong sessions.

He rarely stumbled. When he did, Marge’s teaching method involved pressing a pillow over his face or holding his head under a running faucet. These tactics were successful not only because they were terrifying, but also because they didn’t leave any telltale marks.

He was a hit on the evangelical circuit. Clad in a little white suit and cowboy boots, his hair a nimbus of blond curls that his mother had bleached and permed, he gestured and lunged, delivering his lines in a piping voice from a pint-size pulpit and rolling his R’s as his mother had taught him:

“Hell is a place of extrrreme suffering.” “I’m herrre to give the devil two black eyes.” “I thank God for my good Chrrristian mother.”

Marge sewed special pockets into his suits so that when he went through the congregation collecting offerings — $20 would get you a kiss from “Little Marjoe” — there was ample room for the money. Not long before he turned 5, he officiated at the wedding of a young couple, earning copious press coverage and a spot in “Ripley’s Believe It or Not!,” as well as opprobrium from religious leaders who found the publicity stunt unseemly.

He was good at his job, and he enjoyed being onstage, but he never believed in God. And he certainly didn’t believe in hell.

By the time he was 14, the novelty of preaching had worn off, for him and his congregants. His voice was changing, and his father had abandoned the family and absconded with Marjoe’s earnings — some $3 million, he later estimated.

Marjoe decided to leave, too.

He drifted a bit through his native California, living first with an older woman and then, at 16, marrying a girlfriend. He worked as a shoe salesman, as a barker on the Santa Cruz Wharf and as a doorman at a dance club in Los Angeles before starting a rock band and melting into the nascent hippie scene there.

Yet by his 20s, he had returned to preaching. He needed the money, and missed the limelight. At first, he thought he might introduce his pacifist beliefs into his sermons, skipping the sin-and-hell part. That didn’t go over so well — he was not invited back to the churches where he tried it. So he returned to his revivalist techniques, adding some vocal moves he borrowed from Black preachers and some physical ones from Mick Jagger.

Once again, Marjoe was a hit and his collection buckets overflowed. He stayed in the game for another few years, though by then he was thoroughly sick of the con and longed to perform legitimately: He wanted to be an actor. With the help of two documentary filmmakers, he succeeded at that.

Mr. Gortner, who exposed the flimflammery of his former profession in the 1972 Oscar-winning documentary “Marjoe” and went on to become a hard-working mid-list actor, died on Oct. 2 in Santa Fe, N.M. He was 82.

His wife, Susan Magestro Gortner, said the cause was congestive heart failure.

In the spring of 1971, Mr. Gortner was between preaching gigs when he visited New York City, where he hoped to study at the Actors Studio, he told The New York Times. Instead, he ended up pitching his story to Howard Smith, a columnist at The Village Voice, who teamed up with a co-worker, the writer Sarah Kernochan, to make a documentary.

Neither had filmmaking experience, but many of the crew members they hired had worked on an award-winning 1970 documentary about Woodstock, and they all set off with Mr. Gortner that summer as he barnstormed through the country on what would be his final tour.

What they captured was mesmerizing, a lens turned on the evangelical world. Mr. Gortner, handsome and charismatic, roused the faithful in tents and auditoriums across California, Texas and Michigan. He sweated and pranced and sang and prayed, delivering ecstasies to his congregants by pressing a “healing” hand to their foreheads. Many fell to the ground, writhing and speaking in tongues, the inscrutable “language” that signaled communion with the Holy Spirit.

The filmmakers also captured how well those performances made bank, with scenes of Mr. Gortner and another minister counting out the take from the collection buckets. In between performances, Mr. Gortner, often clad in a tie-dyed tank top, hung out with the film crew in motels, smoking pot and explaining the mechanics of his trade. He was a hustler, he admitted, but so were his peers.

“You go into it like a business, and you work it like a business,” he said. “I enjoy getting it off onstage, but I wish I was getting it off as a rock star. I like to think that I’m bad, but not evil. I’m a hype, but I don’t feel I’m a bad hype.”

The film was mostly a critical hit — Judith Crist, writing in New York Magazine, called it “a striking example of intelligent cinéma vérité” — although Vincent Canby of The Times was unmoved by Mr. Gortner’s charms, describing the documentary as a “feature-length screen test for Marjoe.” In that regard, Mr. Canby would be proved correct.

The film won best documentary at the Academy Awards in 1973, the same year that “The Godfather” won best picture and “The Poseidon Adventure” best song (for “The Morning After”).

By then, Mr. Gortner was a star on both coasts, having traded the tent-revival circuit for that of the talk shows. He hung out at Max’s Kansas City in Manhattan, dated beautiful women like the actress Berry Berenson, partied with the Rolling Stones, attended fashion shows with the model China Machado and was featured in Rolling Stone, the magazine, as well as Life. Judith Jamison, the Alvin Ailey dancer, named her marmalade cat after him. He made a rock album, “Bad but Not Evil,” which The Times, while noting that he was a promising pop singer, described as “bad but not hopeless.”

As Ms. Kernochan said in an interview, “He was slurped right up. He had the best agent; he was everybody’s favorite dinner guest.”

“It’s a turn-on for people to have me at their parties,” Mr. Gortner told The Times, which described him as “the celebrity-seeking crowd’s latest bauble.” “But I get so tired of telling the same stories. That’s why I’d like to do something completely opposite as an actor, to show I can make the change.”

He did that with gusto. During the 1970s and ’80s, he was a ubiquitous television presence, landing middling roles on series like “Kojak,” “Barnaby Jones,” “Police Story” and “Falcon Crest.”

He played the outlaw in “Bobbie Jo and the Outlaw” (1976) — a kind of poor man’s “Bonnie and Clyde” — with Lynda Carter, who had recently begun starring in the TV series “Wonder Woman,” playing Bobbie Jo.

In the disaster film “Earthquake” (1974), he played a grocery store manager turned unhinged National Guardsman. The screenwriters had a bit of fun with Mr. Gortner’s past: When his character summons a beat cop to get rid of the Hare Krishna followers outside his store, the policeman, a sour George Kennedy, snaps, “You got something against religion?”

Hugh Marjoe Ross Gortner was born on Jan. 14, 1944, in Long Beach, Calif. His parents, Margaret Ellen (McMillan) Gortner and Vernon Gortner, were ordained ministers, which explains their choice of the name Marjoe, a portmanteau of Mary and Joseph.

The family traveled constantly, preaching in churches and tents throughout the country. Marjoe and his younger siblings, Vernoe and Starloe, were home-schooled by Marge while they were on the road.

Once Vernon left and Marjoe stopped preaching, money was tight. Marge tried unsuccessfully to mold Starloe — now Starr Padilla — to follow in her brother’s footsteps. Recalling her debut at 7, terrified and trying to choke out a sermon on juvenile delinquency in front of an enormous audience, Ms. Padilla said in an interview, “Mom realized I wasn’t Marjoe, by any means.”

“She was a ‘Mommie Dearest,’” Ms. Padilla added, referring to Christina Crawford’s 1978 memoir about her abusive upbringing at the hands of the actress Joan Crawford. Like her brother, she married young, at 17, mostly to get away from Marge.

Mr. Gortner’s marriages to Carol Raney, Virginia Humphreys, Agnes Benjamin and the actress Candy Clark ended in divorce.

He met Ms. Clark when he produced and starred in “When You Comin’ Back, Red Ryder?,” a 1979 film adaptation of a Broadway play by Mark Medoff about a disturbed Vietnam vet who imprisons and terrorizes the patrons of a New Mexico diner. Mr. Gortner played the menacing vet, and Ms. Clark his flower-child girlfriend. (The movie was not a success: “Punishment passed off as entertainment” is how The Los Angeles Times described it. Neither was the marriage, which lasted about a year.)

Mr. Gortner married Susan Magestro in 2019. In addition to her and Ms. Padilla, he is survived by a daughter, Gigi Gortner, from his first marriage; a son, Dylan Becker, from another relationship; two stepdaughters, Marie Ciattini and Stella Magestro; and a step-grandaughter.

Starting in the 1980s, Mr. Gortner produced charitable sporting events for various philanthropies, including Dream Foundation. He retired in 2012, and lived in Sun Valley and Santa Fe, N.M.

For much of his life, Mr. Gortner was estranged from his family, Ms. Padilla said, although they both always reached out on their birthdays. He eventually made amends with his father, she said, but after the documentary was released, he and his mother never spoke again.

“I loved him, and I thought he was a remarkable man,” Ms. Padilla said. “He was flamboyant and outgoing, but also extremely private. All of his life he was made to be a performer, and people always wanted something from him, so he was very guarded with allowing anyone in.”

As Ms. Kernochan put it, “He had been in costume his whole life, and in a way he found he couldn’t take it off.”

She added: “We lost touch after the movie came out. Things were already thorny between us; he was a very paranoid and calculating fellow. The reason the movie begins with him as a child was that you’d forgive him anything if you saw what he went through.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

It’s instructive that Holmes isn’t the first person you see in the movie given how she appears in the movie. Again and again, Fielder presses Holmes about her past and her present.

ARTICLE

‘You Can See Everything’ Review: The Slippery Mind of Elizabeth Holmes
The disgraced tech entrepreneur and the comic Nathan Fielder chat and joust in a dizzying movie about truth, reality and the contours of knowledge.
By Manohla Dargis
Published 2026-10-15 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/movies/you-can-see-everything-review-elizabeth-holmes.html

The nominal subject of the trippy “You Can See Everything” is Elizabeth Holmes, the celebrated entrepreneur turned celebrity jailbird. As a portrait, the movie is intimate and analytic, informative and incomplete. It’s also off-the-charts bonkers, which isn’t surprising given the participants. Directed by the comic Nathan Fielder and the filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, the movie is, among other things, a wily, disturbing, self-aware exploration of the relationship between documentarians and their subjects. It’s often funny, even if the questions that it raises about truth, reality and knowledge can make it feel like a tragedy — few movies speak as uncannily to the pathos and destabilizing confusions of the present moment.

At this point, it’s a tossup whether Holmes is better known for her pop-cultural profile or her real-world exploits or if Fielder, the creator of absurdist comedy TV shows like “Nathan for You,” is now the bigger draw. Her fame was relatively brief but sensational. In 2014, Forbes deemed Holmes, the founder of a blood-testing start-up named Theranos, the youngest self-made female billionaire. She claimed, among other things, that her technology would revolutionize health care, which proved untrue. By 2022, Holmes had been found guilty of four charges of fraud for deceiving investors, a turn of events that seemed to baffle even the presiding judge. “What was it that caused Ms. Holmes, regrettably, to make those decisions that she did,” Judge Edward J. Davila asked, before sentencing her to 11 years in prison.

That question hovers over the movie, and is as much a head-scratcher as how Fielder and Oppenheim came to make it. At one point there’s an approving reference to Fielder being someone who looks “at things differently.” It’s a rich line for those familiar with his work; it’s obvious that Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, were not. It’s also obvious that they were out to shift public perceptions about her or, at least, the ostensible narrative, and that the filmmakers were aware of the role they were being solicited to play. It’s not for nothing that the documentary opens on a tight shot of Evans’s face. “Nobody knows who she is,” Evans says to someone on the phone, shortly before dropping the words “radical transparency.”

It’s instructive that Holmes isn’t the first person you see in the movie given how she appears in the movie. She was the most famous woman tech entrepreneur to emerge from Silicon Valley, which helped elevate her profile and added frisson of her fall. Her signature look was striking, including long hair that always seemed a smidge messy, as if she were just too busy innovating to comb it. She didn’t seem to blink, which emphasized the whites of her eyes and presumably held others rapt. It’s a neat movie actor trick for creating dominance, which might have been useful in tech-bro land. She blinks in “You Can See Everything” and her distinctive low-pitched voice also seems more natural; it’s about the only thing that does.

Shot over several years, the documentary opens in 2023, 34 days before Holmes entered prison. Throughout it, the filmmakers mix original and extant material, and embrace different documentary approaches (participatory, ethnographic and so on). For the most part, though, “You Can See Everything” — the title refers to a text Holmes sent Fielder — unfolds as a series of intense conversations with Fielder serving as the on-camera interlocutor. Many of these take place in Holmes and Evans’s beachfront place in Del Mar, Calif., where Fielder prods and pushes them in the dining room, on the sofa, wherever, sometimes with the couple’s two young children and her parents in attendance. A number of encounters are shot in such extreme, dermatologic close-up that you become intimately familiar with Fielder’s zits.

Every so often, other members of the small film crew show up on camera, too. These onscreen appearances are reminders of the inherently constructed aspect of the movie and, by extension, the documentary genre, and they dovetail with a movie’s preoccupation with questions of authenticity and artificiality. All the conversations in the movie take place, after all, in front of a small audience that is, in turn, recording these interactions for the far larger movie audience. Whether Holmes’s occasional blinks and tears in these chats are performative is open to question as are her grasp on language, truth, science and reality itself, all of which Fielder seizes on in a series of interactions that grow progressively weirder.

One of Fielder’s superpowers as a performer is his deadpan, which he generally manages to maintain no matter how outlandish the conceit. He’s put it to recurrently unsettling effect on shows in which he — or a version of himself — aggressively toys with the genre of reality television through his interactions with real people. In “Nathan for You,” he offers absurd advice to small-business owners, successfully persuading a frozen-yogurt store manager, for instance, to sell a lab-created fecal-flavored offering, a.k.a. “poo.” The more conceptually ambitious show, “The Rehearsal,” involves him helping people work through assorted personal issues with the use of hired actors and elaborate re-creations of real life.

Both shows are finally less interesting for what they say about their putative subjects than what they say about those of us who watch them and keep on watching in stitches, shock or horror. Fielder likes to test the limits of propriety and (canned) reality, and he’s having some laughs in the process. He’s also creating social psychological experiments that, in their effect, bring to mind Orson Welles’s 1938 broadcast of the H.G. Wells novel “The War of the Worlds,” about an alien invasion. Welles presented part of the drama as breaking news, which panicked listeners, made headlines and irked the Federal Communications Commission. Welles later said that he had underestimated “the extent of our American lunatic fringe.”

That fringe no longer seems marginal, if it ever was. That the world in “You Can See Everything” appears sane is partly because of the legitimacy conferred on Holmes by her fame and the hundreds of millions of dollars that went into Theranos. Serious people took her seriously, which can seem hard to believe given how slippery Holmes and Evans seem here. Indeed, the first image of Fielder in the movie suggests that he and Oppenheim have come to this project with a degree of incredulity. It’s a murky shot of Fielder peering through a window with what looks like comic skepticism. If it’s uncertain what Fielder is thinking at that moment, it is certain that he and Oppenheim have already begun to test your preconceptions.

One of the most gob-smackingly wild things about Holmes is how she was able to scam so many. That’s part of the story here, though the more interesting one concerns what we mean by truth in a world of profound epistemological uncertainty. Again and again, Fielder presses Holmes about her past and her present. He stares into her eyes, and she stares right back, as he interrogates her linguistic elisions and wonders about her grasp on a famous old comedy routine. He also watches her as she watches the 2022 TV drama series “The Dropout,” in which Amanda Seyfried plays Holmes. It’s a dizzying moment, all the more so given that we’re watching, too, swept up in a ricochet of gazes in the mirrored fun house we now live in.

You Can See Everything Rated R for language and male nudity. Running time: 2 hours 54 minutes. In theaters.

SUMMARY

The French have a phrase for it: “un engrenage,” a vicious spiral. France, truly, is on the brink. But France is no longer in control of its destiny.

ARTICLE

France Has a Phrase for What’s Happening, and It’s Not Good
A fiscal crisis threatens to bring the country to ruin.
By Mujtaba Rahman
Published 2026-10-15 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/opinion/france-protests-debt-budget.html

The French have a phrase for it: “un engrenage,” a vicious spiral. That’s what France is in. Several crises have been long in the making; each now threatens to accelerate the others.

The first is a crisis of liberal democracy. Polls suggest that the far right may take power in the presidential election next spring. The second is a crisis of fiscal mismanagement. France’s public debt has reached a record $4 trillion, with the cost of new government borrowing surging above that of Italy and Greece. The third is a crisis of youth disaffection. French students, protesting against dilapidated schools and diminished life chances, have blocked nearly half of the country’s high schools in the past few weeks.

Clashing with police and bearing inspiring banners, the students have riveted the world’s attention. The protests are certainly dramatic and significant. So too is the rise of the far right. But the fiscal crisis is the most dangerous, underlying many of the country’s woes and threatening to bring it to ruin. France, truly, is on the brink.

The high school protests began in the poor suburbs of Paris in mid-September. They have spread to state-run schools in every region of the country, from big cities to provincial towns. The 15- to 18-year-olds are rebelling against long hours, large class sizes, frequent teacher absences and crumbling school buildings. They also worry about global warming, the rise of the far right and the A.I. threat to jobs for the young. At the center of their complaints is chronic underinvestment.

This is something of a conundrum. After all, the French state spends a great deal on education: around $100 billion a year, or 5.1 percent of gross domestic product, above the European Union average. So what’s going on? Crucially, more than a quarter of that money goes not to the young but to the old, paying the pensions of retired teachers. That points to one of the root causes of the country’s problems. About one-quarter of all state spending goes to pensions; another quarter goes to social services, from health care to unemployment benefits.

No French government has balanced its books for 52 years. Even so, the French debt pile, at 119 percent of G.D.P., is lower than that of some other countries, including the United States. As recently as 2019, President Emmanuel Macron managed to bring the annual deficit within the E.U. target of 3 percent of G.D.P.

Then came the pandemic. Mr. Macron’s pledge to spend “whatever it takes” to keep the French economy alive during lockdown sent the deficit rocketing to 9.2 percent of G.D.P. in 2020. Accumulated debt rose by $335 billion in one year. France was then slower than other E.U. countries to ease its pandemic subsidies. The government spent another $95 billion to shelter France from rising energy prices after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

After that, Mr. Macron lost control. He was re-elected in 2022 but failed to win a majority in the National Assembly. He imposed a modest pension reform in 2023, increasing the official retirement age gradually from 62 to 64. He argued, rightly, that France needed to work longer to afford its generous pensions and welfare system. Yet over 70 percent of French people disagreed, some violently.

In response, Mr. Macron called an ill-advised snap election in 2024, which further reduced the size of his centrist coalition. Since then, two prime ministers have proposed solutions to French overspending. Both were booted out by a majority of left-wing and far-right lawmakers in the National Assembly. The result has been a curious blend of stalemate and chaos.

Mr. Macron deserves some of the blame for the mess. So does the opposition, from the far-left France Unbowed to Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally. They have preferred to play political games rather than address the gathering fiscal disaster — especially the stifling weight of pensions and other social payments. In February, the center-left Socialists allowed a budget to pass for this year but only at the price of suspending Mr. Macron’s pension reform.

The current prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has proposed painful but scarcely punishing changes in the 2027 budget, which would bring the deficit down to 5 percent of G.D.P. He faces a first critical vote in the Assembly on Oct. 20. If his government fails to pass the budget, the cost of servicing French debt may explode. France could be forced to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund and to pray for it from the European Central Bank — a humiliation for the world’s seventh-biggest economy.

France remains in many ways a robust and wealthy country. Yet market distrust of France is not so much economic as political. The markets doubt whether a poisonously splintered political system, increasingly dominated by extremes of right and left, will ever agree to the painful changes that are needed to get the public finances back on track. The country, they fear, is becoming socially volatile and institutionally paralyzed. That explains the withdrawal of confidence that has pushed France’s borrowing costs sky-high.

There is no easy way out. Whoever wins the presidential election in May will struggle to win a parliamentary majority in the legislative election that follows in June, setting up further political turmoil. What’s more, many doubt the willingness of Ms. Le Pen, the current front-runner, to confront the crisis honestly. She presented a five-year budget plan last week that was stuffed with ideological obsessions and creative accounting.

On the other hand, Ms. Le Pen knows that the markets could make or break her presidency. She wants to prove that she is a stateswoman, not a wrecker. With that in mind, she will probably order her bloc of 139 deputies in the Assembly to abstain to allow the budget to pass. That may avert, for now, the kind of meltdown suffered by Greece after the financial crash. But France is no longer in control of its destiny.

“L’engrenage” — the vicious spiral — is here to stay.

Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group and a senior visiting fellow at the London School of Economics.
