ARTICLE

Trump’s Deal With Russia Inflames War He Vowed to Swiftly End
The Ukrainian president’s defiant decision to continue attacking Russian refineries underscores President Trump’s inability to end a war he had promised to resolve.
By Anton Troianovski and Luke Broadwater
Published 2026-10-15 23:26 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/politics/trump-russia-ukraine.html

On the campaign trail in 2024, President Trump promised lower prices and a swift end to the war in Ukraine.

Two years on, neither has been accomplished. And in his scramble to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has wreaked further havoc in his efforts to make peace in Ukraine.

Mr. Trump’s relationship with President Volodymyr Zelensky, already strained after last week’s U.S. decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, hit new headwinds on Thursday when the Ukrainian leader declared he would not abide by the U.S. plea not to attack Russian refineries. And with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia refusing Mr. Trump’s demand for a cease-fire, an end to the war appeared to recede even further.

The spat with Mr. Zelensky and the escalating conflict have combined to create a new liability for the White House, highlighting Mr. Trump’s remarkable friendliness toward Russia and his inability to end Europe’s biggest war in generations.

Russia is not known to have made any concession in exchange for Mr. Trump’s decision to lift diesel sanctions, and the move has not yet eased the pain at the pump. The average U.S. diesel price was around $6.32 a gallon on Thursday, compared to $6.29 a week earlier, according to the AAA.

But the White House appears to be hoping that voters care more about Mr. Trump’s push to lower prices than about the fate of Ukraine, and that they are no longer surprised by Mr. Trump’s forgiving attitude toward Mr. Putin. The diesel deal has already become a talking point for Mr. Trump as he tries to help Republicans avoid losing control of Congress in the Nov. 3 elections.

At a recent rally in Syracuse, N.Y., Mr. Trump cited the deal as proof that he was working to bring down gas prices.

“Russia agreed to send us millions and millions of barrels of oil and its diesel,” he said. “That’s what we really need.”

Administration officials have argued that doing deals with Russia could pave the way for peace in Ukraine by showing Mr. Putin and the hard-liners around him that a strong, postwar relationship with the United States was possible.

But Democrats and even some Republicans reacted to Mr. Trump’s diesel deal with Mr. Putin with outrage. Many saw it as the starkest Russia-friendly move yet by an administration that, for all of Mr. Trump’s kind words toward Mr. Putin, kept in place many Biden-era policies in support of Ukraine.

“We need to lower diesel prices,” the Iowa G.O.P. Senate candidate Ashley Hinson said in a debate Tuesday, “but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.”

This week, a bipartisan group of senators called on Mr. Trump to reverse his decision to ease the diesel sanctions, describing the deal as a “gift to our adversary.”

Mr. Trump “has been embarrassed by Putin,” Ms. Mobbs said in a phone interview from Ukraine, referring to Russia’s almost immediate violation of the cease-fire on energy targets that Mr. Trump declared last weekend. “I don’t know of a bigger middle finger than that.”

Still, Mr. Trump’s friendly attitude toward Mr. Putin puts him on the fringe of American public opinion, even among Republicans, polls show. The Pew Research Center found in March that 83 percent of Americans had an unfavorable view of Russia, as did 83 percent of Republicans.

In recent months, Mr. Trump’s main envoys for the Ukraine war, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as Mr. Vance, have all asked Mr. Zelensky not to strike Russian oil refineries, according to a person familiar with those conversations. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy.

Mr. Trump declared on Sept. 13 that “Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.”

Export statistics showed that most of the diesel supply crunch came as a result of the war on Iran, though the attacks on Russian oil refineries also played a role. Ukraine said it was willing to halt its refinery strikes if Russia halted its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Mr. Putin refused.

Mr. Trump suspended sanctions on Russian diesel anyway on Friday. Mr. Zelensky’s anger built this week amid suggestions by Ukrainian officials that the United States was stopping intelligence support and Starlink satellite internet service for the Ukrainian military.

U.S. officials have said intelligence sharing has not been cut back. On Thursday, a bipartisan group of senators demanded a Pentagon investigation into the disruptions.

Mr. Zelensky told The Financial Times in an interview published Thursday that Ukraine had paused refinery strikes for three days to comply with Mr. Trump’s request, but was now resuming them. He criticized Mr. Trump for making deals with Mr. Putin and for openly admiring authoritarian leaders who have clung to power.

How can Mr. Trump “be friends with him?” Mr. Zelensky added. “I think that it’s a mistake.”

Republican supporters of Ukraine now fear that Mr. Zelensky’s attacks could make matters worse. As the U.S. president stewed over Mr. Zelensky over the weekend, some of the Ukrainian president’s critics in Mr. Trump’s orbit called Mr. Trump to air those grievances, the person familiar with the matter said.

bonds-investors-interest-rates.html

SUMMARY

The bad news for bonds isn’t over. The intuitive explanation is straightforward: When rates rise, a bond you bought yesterday isn’t worth as much today because new, otherwise identical bonds are now available, and they pay more in interest. Should rates rise further, price declines would be less painful for shorter-duration bonds and bond funds.

ARTICLE

Why Bad News in the Bond Market May Be Good News for Investors
In the contrarian logic of investing, rising interest rates have made bonds much more attractive, our columnist says.
By Jeff Sommer
Published 2026-10-16 05:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/business/bonds-investors-interest-rates.html

The bad news for bonds isn’t over. Far from it.

Yet I’ll stick my neck out and say that for careful people with long horizons, this is a fine time to make selective purchases of high-quality bonds. That includes Treasuries, inflation-protected, corporate and municipal bonds, and bond funds.

Today’s high interest rates are painful for borrowers. But at their current levels, they have begun to provide a comfortable buffer against further losses for investors and promise richer income streams for the future.

“With interest rates where they are now, it’s a good moment for long-term investors and for people in retirement to lock in some high yields,” Kathy Jones, a bond maven who was formerly a chief strategist at Schwab, told me.

Even so, jumping into bonds now requires fortitude because trouble is likely to continue. Interest rates, which soared in September, could easily rise from here, and their pernicious economic toll is still spreading. Nor is this just a U.S. problem. In France, a debt crisis is underway, raising concerns that it could worsen financial problems elsewhere in Europe and around the world.

A hot inflation report in the United States on Wednesday heightened expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise short-term rates again this year. It’s possible that longer-term rates set by thousands of traders in the bond market will rise, too. That means that bond buyers who sell before their bonds mature could face short-term losses.

Still, months of rising rates have already led to a major and positive change for investors. The 10-year Treasury yield, which serves as a benchmark for all others in the bond world, surpassed 5.3 percent last month, up from 4.2 percent at the beginning of this year.

It is hovering above 5 percent. While that may seem shocking after rates were so low for so long, current yields are only approaching the average of 5.4 percent since the 1950s, based on my own computation of data compiled by Robert J. Shiller, the Yale economist. Investors are being compensated at rates that haven’t been available for years. These higher interest rates imply better returns for bondholders in the years ahead.

Yes, It’s Been Rough

Still, if you’re leery of buying bonds, I don’t blame you. They have performed dismally. There’s no sugarcoating it.

Why did this happen? Recall some basics. Rising interest rates mean falling bond prices, as a matter of fundamental bond math.

The intuitive explanation is straightforward: When rates rise, a bond you bought yesterday isn’t worth as much today because new, otherwise identical bonds are now available, and they pay more in interest. Yields have soared since the start of the war with Iran at the end of February. Oil prices rose, the pace of inflation increased, and traders in the bond market demanded better yields — and lower prices — for the risks they were taking.

Perhaps more important, this year’s rate increases are built on a deeper shift in the market.

Bond rates have been trending upward since the Covid-19 pandemic, when the 10-year Treasury yield fell as low as 0.6 percent. That benchmark yield had begun dropping much earlier. It approached 2 percent during a steep recession in 2008 and fell below 2 percent in September 2011. In those years, deflation was a far bigger concern than inflation.

Interest rates have taken a long road upward. Seen in this light, their increase may be viewed as a return to normal — to the interest rates that prevailed before the great financial crisis that started late in 2007.

A variety of factors help to explain the decades-long increases in interest rates. They include: widening government deficits in the United States and other countries; a downturn in bond purchases by central banks; repeated inflationary shocks from disease, wars, tariffs and other disrupters; and, lately, increased global demand for capital to finance development of artificial intelligence. There’s been a sea change in interest rates.

Watch Out for Duration

Ordinary investors who held bonds and bond funds through these shifts have endured losses. If yields are approaching a peak, those losses could be coming to an end.

Consider the returns for two funds this year and over the five years through Thursday.

- iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond E.T.F. (short for exchange-traded fund). It contains Treasuries with a maturity of at least 20 years. Shareholders lost 6.3 percent this year and 8.2 percent, annualized, over five years.
- Vanguard Total Bond Market Index fund. It tracks a benchmark for the entire U.S. investment-grade bond market and the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond index, and it contains shorter- and longer-term Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and corporate bonds. The bond fund declined 2 percent this year and 0.5 percent, annualized, over five years.

The numbers are much worse for the iShares fund because it includes only long-term bonds, with an average “duration” of 14.5 years, according to FactSet. Duration measures a bond’s price sensitivity to interest rates. The Vanguard fund has a much shorter duration — less than six years. Duration is the main reason for the return differences.

That’s important if you’re contemplating purchases of investment-grade bonds or bond funds now. Should rates rise further, price declines would be less painful for shorter-duration bonds and bond funds. (The contrary would also be true: Should rates decline sharply, which often happens in economic downturns, longer-duration bonds could have spectacular returns.)

Note that I’m talking only about investment-grade bonds. High-yield bonds, known as junk bonds, are more hazardous. Hold junk bonds only if you have examined the specific risks, and have chosen to embrace them, in exchange for the somewhat higher yields they offer.

Personally, I take on all the investing risk I can handle through stock index funds. For bonds, I want greater safety. That means short- to moderate-duration funds — with a rough maturity of up to five or six years — containing only investment-grade bonds.

The Silver Lining

This backward look at the bond market is gloomy. But in the contrarian world of investing, it’s why the future looks better.

“The higher yields in the market now are a silver lining for investors,” Gina Martin Adams, chief market strategist at HB Wealth, an independent investment management firm, said in a phone conversation. Yields are in a historically reasonable range now, she said. “It would be worth nibbling at some bonds now, if you have been staying away from them.”

Ms. Jones has a similar perspective. “I’ve been looking at high-quality bonds for myself,” she said.

How should people think about the risk that rates would rise further? To produce losses over the next 12 months, yields would need to jump appreciably from current levels, with the 10-year Treasury yield approaching roughly 6 percent. That could happen. Even so, the income stream generated by bonds at current 5 percent-plus yields “should hold up well” over the next decade, Ms. Jones said, assuming the Fed tames inflation.

The Fed raised the short-term rates it controls by one quarter point at its last meeting. While the market deems it unlikely that the central bank will raise rates again when policymakers meet this month, further increases are expected later this year and next. Longer-term rates set in the bond market are likely to moderate if inflation is perceived as being under control.

That’s a benign outcome, of course. There are other possibilities.

A nastier one, modeled on history, would be something like this: Inflation remains hot, forcing interest rates high enough to slow the economy. That would set off more bond losses and, ultimately, could start a recession.

A recession would end the interest rate increase cycle emphatically. Interest rates typically plummet when the economy is weak, and bonds, especially Treasuries, tend to rise in value. That happened in the 2007-9 recession. While the U.S. government no longer has a pristine, AAA bond rating, I believe that Treasuries would probably serve as a haven again.

Bonds are where investors have traditionally gone for stability. They haven’t done a great job lately, but they can still play that role. And if solid income is what you’re looking for, high-quality bonds can do the job.

But don’t expect too much from them. Over the long haul, even when bonds have performed reasonably well, returns in the U.S. stock market have been much better. For very short periods, too, money market funds and Treasury bills have been more reliable than bonds because they don’t lose value when rates rise. (That’s because money market funds and Treasury bills have very short durations.) Government-insured certificates of deposit and high-yield savings accounts are also good places to park money.

The turmoil in the bond market is opening opportunities. The negative bond headlines are disconcerting, but they signal better buys for prudent investors.

SUMMARY

In Thailand’s carmaking hub of Rayong, China’s largest electric vehicle maker, BYD, built its first factory outside China, a complex the size of 180 football fields. Tossophol Kunsri, president of the Automobile Labor Congress of Thailand, one of the country’s biggest autoworkers’ union, said Chinese electric vehicle makers often hired Thai workers for short-term contracts in brief production runs, then laid them off without severance pay.

ARTICLE

After Welcoming China’s Electric Vehicles, This Country Is Paying the Price
Thailand introduced subsidies and tax cuts to encourage electric vehicle adoption. Now it is trying to recalibrate, alarmed by the threat to its industrial landscape.
By Sui-Lee Wee, Kittiphum Sringammuang and Nicola Longobardi for The New York Times
Published 2026-10-16 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/business/china-ev-thailand-cars.html

In Thailand’s carmaking hub of Rayong, China’s largest electric vehicle maker, BYD, built its first factory outside China, a complex the size of 180 football fields. Twenty miles south, a plant once run by General Motors is now owned by China’s Great Wall Motor. A 10-minute drive away, Ford took over a vehicle assembly plant from the Japanese automaker Suzuki.

All of this happened in the past five years — evidence of an industry in upheaval.

For decades, Japanese automakers dominated Thailand. They arrived in the 1960s, built supply chains and transformed the country into the “Detroit of the East.”

Then the Chinese automakers arrived.

Today, they control about 85 percent of Thailand’s electric vehicle market, up from almost zero four years ago. Japanese automakers, slow to embrace the technology, have struggled. In 2024 and 2025, Subaru and Suzuki shut down their Thai plants, while Nissan and Honda have scaled back production.

Several Thai auto-parts suppliers that depended on Japanese manufacturers went bankrupt, threatening a supply chain that employs about 700,000 workers.

“It was much faster than anything we had expected,” said Supavud Saicheua, chairman of the National Economic and Social Development Council, the central economic planning agency in Thailand.

“We didn’t think of the full picture,” he added. “The impact on Thailand has been much more adverse than we had thought.”

To some, Thailand is a cautionary tale about the unintended consequences of opening the door to China’s electric vehicle manufacturers. The lesson could resonate elsewhere. President Trump has seemed open to welcoming China’s E.V. brands to manufacture in the United States despite tariffs that effectively block their entry into the market. The European Union is struggling to rein in Chinese vehicles, despite imposing tariffs.

Thailand is trying to contain the damage. Last month, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul traveled to Tokyo to reassure Japanese automakers. A month earlier, he had ordered a review of policies that Japanese firms say put them at a disadvantage.

Few in Thailand think gas-guzzling cars are the future. Electric vehicles made up a third of new car sales in the first seven months of 2026. It is easy to see the consumer appeal of the Chinese cars. Many offer technology like large display screens and autonomous driving at low prices. (Mr. Anutin owns BYD’s electric S.U.V., the Sealion 7.)

But policymakers are concerned about the influx. In the first seven months of this year, about two-thirds of electric vehicles sold in Thailand were imported, primarily from China.

The government is trying to curb the flood. Last month, it unveiled a three-tier tax system that imposes the highest rates on automakers importing vehicles with no plans for local production and the lowest on those that source a large share of their parts locally.

But Ruth Banomyong, a professor of supply chain management at Thammasat University in Thailand, said there was little evidence that Thailand was benefiting. Chinese automakers, he said, operate within a “closed ecosystem” that makes it difficult for Thai companies to enter their supply chains because the core technology remains in China.

He and his colleagues have estimated that 300,000 jobs could disappear within five years if electric vehicles dominate Thailand’s auto market.

“The trickle-down effect is very minimal,” said Mr. Ruth, a former adviser to Thailand’s previous commerce minister.

Tossophol Kunsri, president of the Automobile Labor Congress of Thailand, one of the country’s biggest autoworkers’ union, said Chinese electric vehicle makers often hired Thai workers for short-term contracts in brief production runs, then laid them off without severance pay.

He said the Chinese companies rejected unions. By contrast, he said, he maintained respectful relationships with Japanese automakers, which were willing to negotiate annual salary increases and bonuses.

Mr. Tossophol said that he had complained to the government about the Chinese companies’ labor practices and that the labor minister had agreed to investigate.

“We’re standing at a crossroads,” he said. “Are we still going to be an actual automotive manufacturing base, or are we just going to be a market for cheap Chinese E.V.s?”

‘We Thought It Was Still Far Off’

In 2011, Netsana Sakulpolpanya started working at a car parts factory in Thailand’s Samut Prakan Province, making exhaust systems and mufflers for Toyota, its biggest customer.

Her company embodied the homegrown industry that supplied Japan’s automakers. Ms. Netsana earned $440 a month operating molds and pressing machinery.

Her first years were a boom. In 2012, she received an extra five months of salary and a $740 bonus. The money helped her care for her disabled sister and pay for her niece’s education at a university.

In 2022, Thailand’s prime minister at the time, Prayuth Chan-ocha, declared electric vehicles crucial to the country’s economic future and its fight against pollution. He set a target for zero-emission vehicles to account for 30 percent of the country’s vehicle production by 2030.

Ms. Netsana said union leaders had warned workers about the changes that electric vehicles could bring.

“We honestly thought it was still far off,” she said.

Then the government rolled out tax cuts and subsidies and allowed electric vehicles to be imported for two years before automakers had to meet local manufacturing requirements. A free-trade agreement between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meant the vehicles faced no customs duty.

Within months, Chinese brands like Changan, GAC Aion, Neta and Chery were driving on Thai roads.

Ms. Netsana watched orders fall. Overtime disappeared. Her company began telling workers to stay home some days and cut wages to 75 percent of normal pay.

In September 2023, Srettha Thavisin, a billionaire real estate developer, became prime minister with a mission to court foreign investment. His first stop was China. Chinese carmakers were looking abroad to escape a domestic market saddled with overcapacity and brutal price wars.

Mr. Srettha said he felt he had little choice but to court them. Otherwise, they were likely to have gone to Vietnam or Malaysia. In hindsight, he said, his government should have tracked more closely how many Thai workers the Chinese companies employed and how much they sourced from Thai suppliers.

Ms. Netsana’s company declared bankruptcy and shut down in 2024. Nearly 900 Thai workers lost their jobs without severance pay.

Ms. Netsana, 49, now earns $11 a day working at a supermarket. She said she did not apply to the Chinese factories because a friend told her that they hire only young workers.

“I blame the government for failing to manage the transition fairly,” Ms. Netsana said.

A Factory Under Scrutiny

At BYD’s factory in Rayong, workers intertwined multicolored wires into wiring harnesses, the nervous systems of electric vehicles. A sign warned: “No playing with mobile phones or loafing on duty.”

Elsewhere, robotic arms welded together the frame of the BYD Atto 3, an electric sport utility vehicle. When it launched in Thailand, customers lined up overnight to buy it. This section operated around the clock.

An overhead monitor displayed the day’s production target of 4,000 cars. By 3.52 p.m., 3,409 were complete.

Opened in 2024, the BYD factory exports cars to across Southeast Asia, Australia and Europe. But American and European trade regulators have scrutinized it, questioning whether it functions as a final assembly plant to circumvent tariffs.

Asked what percentage of car parts came from China, Benson Ke, BYD’s general manager in Thailand, said there were so many components that “it’s difficult to go into great detail.”

He said BYD bought steel sheets locally and assembled batteries in Thailand with local partners. The factory employs 5,600 workers, 94 percent of them Thai, he said, and has received “high ratings for genuine localized manufacturing” during inspections.

When we first met Mr. Ke, he was at a Bangkok motor show unveiling new models. Several attendees said they were considering buying their second BYD.

Mr. Ke welcomed the government’s policy to raise excise taxes on imported vehicles, saying it would help control supply and price competition.

It is easy to see why. BYD has invested more than $1 billion in its Rayong factory.

Yet on a recent visit, signs of BYD’s connections to its Chinese supply chain were plentiful. BYD used Kuka robots, once German-owned, now controlled by China’s Midea. Boxes carrying wiring components bore Chinese addresses. Battery cells were imported from China.

To Thai consumers, it might not matter.

Nithi Thuamprathom, a Bangkok-based automotive reviewer with 1.2 million YouTube subscribers, said his Thai viewers asked him to review Chinese electric vehicles that offered features like adaptive cruise control and 360-degree cameras at prices that often undercut Japanese competitors.

“The era of Japanese carmakers’ enjoying 60 years of easy profits in Thailand is over,” Mr. Nithi said. “Now they have to adapt to real competition.”

ARTICLE

Warsh Vows to Tame Inflation as A.I. Delivers ‘Shock’ to Economy
The Federal Reserve chairman stuck to his pledge to avoid providing guidance about the path forward for interest rates, but did nothing to convey an urgency to raise them later this month.
By Patricia Cohen and Colby Smith
Published 2026-10-16 05:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/business/warsh-fed-imf-bangkok.html

Kevin M. Warsh, chairman of the Federal Reserve, reiterated his commitment to “deliver price stability,” amid rising energy prices and soaring investments in artificial intelligence, which he called a “shock” to the economy. But he did not convey an urgency for the central bank to raise interest rates at its meeting at the end of the month.

Mr. Warsh spoke Friday in Bangkok before a standing-room-only crowd at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. He stuck to his approach to avoid giving specific guidance about what the Fed might do next in terms of policy adjustments.

“I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have in the balance of this year,” Mr. Warsh said. “It’s a new chapter at the Fed, and we’re not in that business anymore.”

The chairman conceded he would only “make some judgments at the October meeting and the December meeting,” the final two gatherings of the year.

His comments, made in conversation with the I.M.F.’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, came right after she had warned of inflation pressures and the need for central banks to keep a tight rein on monetary policy in an earlier session.

“Central banks should be laser-focused on price stability,” she said, adding that she welcomed the “firm language” coming from the Federal Reserve and other central banks.

“Rate hikes today are better than falling behind the curve” and having to impose bigger rate increases later, she said.

Mr. Warsh also noted most central bankers around the world were tightening monetary policy in sync in response to rising global inflation.

Mr. Warsh’s comments were the last scheduled remarks before the Fed enters its communications blackout on Saturday, ahead of its policy meeting on Oct. 27-28. That meeting comes just days before the U.S. midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress.

New inflation data this week that showed price pressures accelerating in September has complicated to some degree the Fed’s deliberations in October.

Overall consumer prices rose 0.6 percent, the largest monthly increase in five months. Compared with the same time last year, prices were 3.7 percent higher. Wholesale prices also rose, while retail sales figures showed consumers continued to spend.

Mr. Warsh on Friday expressed optimism about the overall state of the economy, highlighting specifically the enormous impact that A.I. is having.

A.I. promises huge economic benefits in the long run, he said, but warned the path there “is likely to be a very bumpy one.”

“The advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change in the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime,” said Mr. Warsh.

Booming A.I. spending is one of many factors that have pushed up inflation this year. Another driver is the war with Iran, which has led to soaring energy prices.

According to the I.M.F.’s projections, inflation in the United States is not expected to return to its 2 percent target until the middle of 2028.

Still, several top policymakers made the case in recent weeks that the Fed could raise rates gradually after voting unanimously in September to lift them by a quarter of a percentage point to a new range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent.

According to rate projections released alongside that rate decision, most Fed officials expected one more quarter-point increase this year after September’s move.

If the Fed stands pat in October, as is widely expected, Mr. Warsh will be under pressure to explain why the central bank is not moving more aggressively in the face of broadening price pressures.

Raising rates will keep the central bank in the cross hairs of President Trump, who has repeatedly attacked it for failing to acquiesce to his demands for substantially lower borrowing costs.

Mr. Trump has spared Mr. Warsh, whom he handpicked for the job, from the bulk of the criticism. Instead, he has directed his ire at the chairman’s colleagues on the Board of Governors.

Mr. Trump is engaged in a protracted legal fight with one of those seven members, Lisa D. Cook, whom the president has tried to fire for over a year over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud. The White House last week announced an investigation into Ms. Cook, culminating in a hearing that she was directed to attend.

Mr. Warsh made a point on Friday of defending the Fed, its previous leaders and its staff. “Power comes from our institutional credibility, bestowed on me by the great chairmen that came before me,” he said.

Since taking over as Fed chairman, Mr. Warsh has sought to recast how the central bank operates in a range of dimensions. In addition to jettisoning the provision of guidance over the future path of rates, he has also downplayed the importance of specific data releases and instead described data-point dependence as “a dangerous preoccupation.”

As part of Mr. Warsh’s goal of enacting “regime change” at the central bank, he has announced five task forces to examine issues ranging from how the Fed communicates to how it measures inflation. One of those task forces is focused on productivity gains tied to A.I. and the broader impact on the labor market. Mr. Warsh said on Friday that there would be a “hearing” on the subject on Nov. 16 in San Francisco.

Mr. Warsh noted that A.I. could transform how the Fed did its work because of its enormous analytical potential. This is “a big deal for central banks,” he said, adding that it will “fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy.”

ken-russell-the-devils-re-release.html

SUMMARY

Perhaps the most in-demand screening at the Cannes Film Festival in May had no red carpet and required no formal wear. The occasion was the unveiling of a new restoration of Ken Russell’s “The Devils,” or “Ken Russell’s The Devils,” as the distributor Warner Bros. Kermode added that it was important to Russell that “The Devils” look contemporary.

ARTICLE

In 1971, This Film Was a Scandal. In 2026, It’s a Respected Period Piece.
“Ken Russell’s The Devils” was deemed shocking for scenes with orgiastic nuns and a debauched priest. But its serious aims are clear in a new restoration.
By Ben Kenigsberg
Published 2026-10-16 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/movies/ken-russell-the-devils-re-release.html

Perhaps the most in-demand screening at the Cannes Film Festival in May had no red carpet and required no formal wear. The movie, showing just once in a packed 300-seat theater, also had no chance of winning an award.

The occasion was the unveiling of a new restoration of Ken Russell’s “The Devils,” or “Ken Russell’s The Devils,” as the distributor Warner Bros. Clockwork is calling it for its release on Oct. 16. This period piece, about the targeting of a debauched 17th-century priest (Oliver Reed) for supposedly instigating a case of demonic possession among nuns, was greeted in some quarters as a scandal in 1971. But it has long been a cause for cinephiles, who have been intrigued by its modernist aesthetic, its bouts with censorship and its extended stretches of unavailability.

By a certain light, this is the first time that the British director’s vision will be seen properly. The restoration contains censored moments once thought lost, like frenzied, naked nuns writhing sexually on a giant crucifix or a Mother Superior (Vanessa Redgrave) making love to a phallic bone fragment. Those additions were first shown in 2004. But even that material hasn’t been seen in top visual quality until now.

In 1971, “The Devils” faced fury and dismissals. Reviewing the film in The New York Times, Vincent Canby wrote that the picture was “of so little substance, obscene or otherwise, that I can only believe that the men and women of the Motion Picture Association, who rated the film ‘X,’ must be in league with Beelzebub, or with Warner Brothers.” Russell tangled on television with the London Evening Standard critic Alexander Walker, who had excoriated the movie, and hit him on the head with a newspaper.

The uproar makes sense in context. “When people saw the film, because Ken’s imagery is so visceral, they were shocked by it,” said the critic Mark Kermode, who befriended Russell in the 1990s and was instrumental in finding the lost footage and reintegrating it into the director’s cut, which he provided to Clockwork. “This produced a kind of scandalous air. The censors had problems with it, the studio had problems with it, and the story became, ‘This shocking film.’”

Yet Russell, who died in 2011 at 84, was adapting a respected 1952 nonfiction book, “The Devils of Loudun” by Aldous Huxley, and a stage version by John Whiting that followed in 1961.

The plot centers on a Roman Catholic priest, Urbain Grandier (Reed), who unabashedly pursues sexual relationships with women, but also presides over the walled city of Loudun as a sort of secular stronghold where Catholics and Protestants live together peaceably. The community’s self-governance poses a threat to Cardinal Richelieu’s authoritarian aspirations for a unified France. And when Redgrave’s Sister Jeanne, repressing lust for Grandier, insinuates that the priest has engaged in demonic activity, the authorities sense an opportunity.

In short, this may be a movie famous for being filled with sexualized nuns, but their performance of ecstasy is coerced. Father Barré (Michael Gothard) tortures Sister Jeanne and goads the other nuns, who are under threat of their lives, into a state of orgiastic delirium.

“It is really a brilliantly serious, heartfelt story about brainwashing, about the politicization of religion, about the use of hysteria,” Kermode said on a video call. He noted that this is a through line in the work of Russell, a Catholic convert who had a complicated relationship with his faith.

“Ken was very interested in religion, but also in false religion, in false messiahs,” Kermode said. “If you look, for example, at something like ‘Tommy’” — Russell’s 1975 screen adaptation of The Who’s rock opera — “‘Tommy’ is absolutely a story about false messiahs.”

The use of religion, or at least the perception of how it was being used, surely factored into the reception. “The Devils” opened five years after the incalculably more conservative, best picture-winning “A Man for All Seasons,” about the 16th-century martyr Sir Thomas More. Each film ends with a man on trial forced to choose between his beliefs and his life in a dispute that has fused church and state. But More, unlike the sweaty, flesh-and-blood Grandier, is never shown to be a hypocrite, and Russell treats Grandier’s hypocrisy as deeply human, worthy of sympathy.

In an interview, Richard Crouse, author of “Raising Hell: Ken Russell and the Unmaking of ‘The Devils,’” pointed to another 1966 event: Time magazine’s publication of a cover emblazoned with the words “Is God Dead?” Crouse said that satanic themes were also working their way into movies like “Rosemary’s Baby” (1968) and “The Exorcist” (1973).

But in his book, Crouse points out that “The Devils” never achieved the popular success of those films. The difference, he said in an interview, was the Russell film’s sheer bleakness. “It was widely condemned as sacrilegious when it first came out,” Crouse said, noting objections at the Vatican and from the British conservative activist Mary Whitehouse.

And, he added, the film “fought and lost more battles with censor boards than almost any other film that I could think of that was made by a major studio, that starred big international stars, that was directed by a director like Ken Russell, who had big hits before this.”

Russell moved on quickly. Incredibly, “The Devils” was the second of three features he put out in 1971, along with “The Music Lovers” and “The Boy Friend.” And for a long time, the only home-movie version was an R-rated cut available on a miserable VHS tape. In recent years, “The Devils” has appeared on disc in certain territories, and it has intermittently turned up on streaming services like the Criterion Channel, but never in a complete or visually uncompromised form.

Russell’s boundary-pushing pictorial sensibility may be the biggest revelation of this restoration. Two years off the critical acclaim for his polished D.H. Lawrence adaptation “Women in Love” (1969), which had a comparatively easy ride past the censors, Russell used “The Devils” to begin advancing the more hallucinatory style that would define later films like “Lisztomania” (1975) and “Altered States” (1980).

His production designer was Derek Jarman, who went on to become an important experimental filmmaker, and who created a convent interior that looks like nothing so much as a white-tiled bathhouse, an image that Kermode said was derived from Huxley.

Kermode added that it was important to Russell that “The Devils” look contemporary. “If you were in Loudun at that point, it didn’t look like an old, mossy city,” he said. “It looked like a modern city. He wanted viewers of the film to see the film as modern.”

That also accounts for the deliberate anachronisms. Some viewers find it jarring that Father Barré, in tinted sunglasses, resembles John Lennon. “He wanted to show that it was always happening, this kind of thing,” Lisi Tribble Russell, who met Russell in the 1970s and was married to him for the last decade of his life, said on the video call with Kermode. “And so he intentionally cast someone that was extremely out of the front row of the Beatles.”

While Tribble Russell cited other hallmarks of the era that may have been on Russell’s mind — the Vietnam War, the mind-control experiments of MKUltra — she emphasized that classical music was his first love.

At Cannes, she told the audience that when Russell had the lost footage returned to the film, he responded, “Now I have my rhythm back.”

SUMMARY

A decade or more into an era of populist upheaval in American politics, voters are angrier than ever at a system they rightly believe is ignoring their priorities. Yet somehow, after years of voters saying as loudly and clearly as possible that they want decisive government action on the cost of living, nobody is actually doing much about it. But voters really care a lot about the cost of living.

ARTICLE

Voters Say It Is Their Top Concern. Why Aren’t Politicians Acting on It?
Can 1990s-style politics make a comeback?
By Matthew Yglesias
Published 2026-10-16 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/opinion/affordability-republicans-democrats.html

A decade or more into an era of populist upheaval in American politics, voters are angrier than ever at a system they rightly believe is ignoring their priorities.

Affordability is dominating the midterms, just as inflation dominated the 2024 presidential campaign. Yet somehow, after years of voters saying as loudly and clearly as possible that they want decisive government action on the cost of living, nobody is actually doing much about it.

President Trump is even making the cost of living higher through an agenda of tariffs, regressive tax cuts and war with Iran. And while Democratic candidates are benefiting politically from voter fury over high prices for beef, gas and diesel and mortgages, the party has not rolled out a credible national agenda to tackle the issues underlying the lack of affordability. When given the chance in the Biden administration, Democrats instead gave us an Inflation Reduction Act, which did little to reduce inflation but authorized lots of spending to combat climate change and inject money into the economy.

It is the biggest mystery in politics: How come neither party will actually address the thing voters say is their top concern?

Government policies influence consumer prices in direct and indirect ways, but one big macroeconomic reality is key: The federal government is running a budget deficit that is the equivalent of close to 6 percent of the American economy.

If we were in a recession, a deficit that large could help kick-start the economy. But with unemployment low, deficit spending fuels inflation — which the Federal Reserve in turn tries to control with higher interest rates. Those higher rates then push up the cost of mortgages, auto loans and other forms of consumer credit. With deficits this large, there is no good solution to the high cost of living.

Pulling out of this spiral is going to require tough choices, but it is achievable if politicians prioritize costs rather than ideological activist goals. In other words, it’s also going to take some technocrats.

On one level, it’s easy to understand why both parties are not more responsive to voters’ top concern. Both parties are organized around the ideological goals of their key stakeholders. Republicans push regressive tax cuts; Democrats push funding for health care, environmental, welfare state and other programs.

The solution is simple: good old-fashioned deficit reduction. According to Washington conventional wisdom, politicians don’t embrace this because it’s unpopular. But that’s not entirely true. Raising taxes on the rich, for example, polls extremely well.

In recent years, Democrats have preferred to pair that idea with spending the money on new programs rather than on addressing inflation and curbing spending in an effort to lower interest rates. Fiscal responsibility annoys political elites because it constrains their ambitions and makes it harder to pursue their pet projects. Bill Clinton’s decision to prioritize macroeconomic prudence irritated many people in his coalition, but it helped produce a very strong economy. Voters don’t care all that much about fussy budget details, but they do care a lot about good economic outcomes.

For Democrats and technocrats, there are plenty of opportunities to go after wasteful spending. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that preventing traditional Medicare beneficiaries from using private supplemental insurance (like Medigap coverage) to help defray out-of-pocket costs like deductibles and co-payments could save more than $250 billion over the next decade; at the moment, nearly 90 percent of them do have such coverage, which encourages them to use more medical services, driving up Medicare’s costs. The Medicare Advantage program has even bigger problems, featuring major overpayments to private providers that will cost the government an estimated $1 trillion over 10 years.

This kind of relatively low-hanging fruit is not enough to balance the budget, but paired with taxing the rich, it would make a big dent in the deficit and reduce the upward pressure on inflation and interest rates created by stimulating an economy that doesn’t need stimulus.

From there, a technocratic, affordability-focused administration would work line by line through the array of federal laws and regulations and try to strip away everything that raises the cost of living.

The Jones Act, for example, forbids the use of foreign-made or foreign-owned ships to transport goods between American ports. But it not only raises the price of everything shipped by water, it also helps pad margins for overland freight (rail and road) by ensuring there is no seaborne competition.

New American commercial jet pilots generally must have 1,500 hours of training flight time before they can qualify to co-pilot a plane — over five times as much time as required by perfectly safe European airlines. These are not rules with bona fide safety or environmental benefits. They exist primarily as job-creation or (in the case of the pilot-training requirements) job-protection measures, which contribute to higher fares.

Similarly, a 2024 study concluded that federal “Buy American” procurement rules to increase manufacturing employment cost $111,500 to $137,700 per job created (future tightening of the criteria will push those costs higher). Congress recently explored ways of bringing down regulatory barriers to home building with its ROAD to Housing Act. But a bolder federal government should go further in punishing jurisdictions that refuse to allow new homes while easing up on rules adopted in the wake of the Great Recession that have made it much harder to get a starter home mortgage.

Policy wonks across administrations have long deplored these kind of rules but have struggled to persuade presidents (and Congress) that curtailing them is worth the effort. But if affordability is truly Job 1, technocrats and politicians should spend political capital on reducing it.

It seems likely that the next administration, particularly a Democratic one, will shift from Mr. Trump’s approach on immigration. But few Democratic politicians are framing immigration reform as a way to bring economic benefits: using work visas in sectors like construction or hospitality, for instance, to improve affordability.

Neither party seems interested in new free trade deals. There are certainly national security reasons to worry about reliance on certain kinds of imports from China, but most of America’s pre-Trump trade barriers have no such rationale and often increase costs for American consumers. Whether it’s Canadian lumber, Japanese pickup trucks or Central American sugar cane, there are lots of goods from friendly countries that we could welcome in to bring down costs.

Are these the kind of solutions the voters are demanding? Probably not. But voters really care a lot about the cost of living. And that’s worth taking seriously not just as guidance for what politicians should talk about, but also for what they, and associated technocrats, should do in office.

Voters know what they want — a government that focuses on tangible progress on the cost of living — but are not technical experts in macroeconomics or regulatory cost-benefit analysis. The whole point of representative government is to elect politicians who are willing and able to empower the people who are experts to solve the problems voters want solved.

This kind of 1990s-style politics — progressive taxation, fiscal discipline, deregulation, free trade and modesty about policy — has been unfashionable for so long that it scarcely seems imaginable. But when we had it, people loved the results.

Matthew Yglesias (@mattyglesias), a contributing Opinion writer, is the author of “One Billion Americans: The Case for Thinking Bigger” and the newsletter Slow Boring.

ARTICLE

What if the A.I. Economy Crashes?
Azeem Azhar and Paul Kedrosky debate the case for and against an A.I. bubble.
By Ezra Klein and Rollin Hu
Published 2026-10-16 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-azeem-azhar-paul-kedrosky.html

This is an edited transcript of “The Ezra Klein Show.” You can listen to the episode wherever you get your podcasts.

Right now, A.I. is the driving force behind the gains in the U.S. stock market and U.S. economic growth.

It is sucking up so many construction resources, it now appears to be crowding out housing, manufacturing facilities and basically everything else you might need to build.

And the question, if only from a financial perspective, is: Is this all worth it?

Is all of this investment going to pay off? Or is A.I. a bubble, and one of these companies is going to miss an earnings target or get downgraded, and the whole thing is going to pop — taking all of our retirement portfolios with it?

So I wanted to have two different perspectives on this.

Paul Kedrosky is a partner at the venture capital firm SK Ventures. He’s a fellow at M.I.T.’s Initiative on the Digital Economy and has a popular newsletter at paulkedrosky.com. He thinks we are in an A.I. bubble and has been very vocal about it.

Azeem Azhar is a British technology entrepreneur, an author and an analyst. He is a creator of the Exponential View, which is both a great Substack I read often and a research platform where, among other things, they have been creating dashboards tracking whether there’s financial stress in the A.I. industry.

I think it’s fair to say that Azhar’s view is somewhat more optimistic than Kedrosky’s. So I wanted to put the two of them into conversation together to try to see why you might or might not think we are in an A.I. bubble.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft claiming copyright infringement. The companies have denied those claims.)

Ezra Klein: Paul Kedrosky, Azeem Azhar — welcome to the show.

Paul Kedrosky: Hey, Ezra. Good to be here.

Azeem Azhar: It’s great to be here. Thanks.

So Paul, make the case to me that this is a bubble.

I mean, it’s a big claim. You’re saying that all these investors, all this money pouring in, all these sophisticated analysts at BlackRock and Goldman and wherever — along with the hyperscalers like Google and Meta — are all getting this wrong on some level, and you’re not.

So why do you think it’s a bubble, and they’re all idiots?

Kedrosky: Well, I wouldn’t go quite so far as they’re all idiots. [Chuckles.] That may be true, though I’ll step back on that one.

So what’s unusual about this — let’s just talk about, really quickly, what a bubble is. A bubble occurs whenever asset prices detach from any semblance of economic reality.

We have one of the largest competitive capital expenditure spending waves in history. So in Western economic history, there have been eight or nine of these moments when we build out some giant general-purpose technology — a G.P.T. Not the ChatGPT kind — but a general-purpose technology.

And we’re building it out like we were the railroads, like we were electrification, like we were the canals, like we were the interstate highways. And every one of those moments has led to overbuild.

There isn’t a major economic capex episode in Western economic history that didn’t end in a rolling series of crises, vastly inflated asset prices and a vast oversupply of capacity of whatever the thing was — railroads, fiber-optic cable, take your pick.

And so that’s the bubble. The bubble is — once again, we’re vastly oversupplying something because of the availability of capital and the eagerness of the suppliers of the capital to continue building out in anticipation of future demand.

Now, none of this is to say that A.I. is frivolous or it doesn’t work, or that there aren’t incredibly useful cases for it. That’s not the point any more than that was the point for railroads. Railroads were incredibly useful, and it still ended up where something like 50 percent of the track miles ever laid in the U.S. turned out to be useless.

So the bubble is this vast oversupply of something, largely fueled now by credit, which in turn will lead to massive business failures and write-downs of assets. And all of that credit has spread through the economy. It’s inside of insurers, inside of private credit, it’s inside of sovereign wealth funds.

We’re on the order of trillions of dollars now. And it’s probably going to hit $10 trillion before it’s done.

So all of this investment is at risk, and it’s across the entire economy and sitting inside of all kinds of — I mean, it’s even sitting inside of your individual 401(k)s. We’ve all seen the data that something like the Top 10 stocks in the S&P 500 are now 40 percent of the market capitalization of the index. So if you’re holding an S&P 500 index — my friend, you are very, very long on A.I.

Get out of my portfolio, Paul.

Kedrosky: In fact — yeah, get that [expletive] out of my portfolio.

So you’re very, very long on A.I., and this is the problem. The expression you hear all the time: It’s a one-factor world. Everything is leveraged to A.I. across every asset class, across all of retail investing.

And then the last stat I’ll give you, and the reason that matters, is we’re at record percentages in terms of the percentage of people’s net worth that is tied to equity. Half of people’s net worth is now in equity.

So follow that math through. If half of net worth is in equities, and that’s driven by the A.I. trade, people are even more overleveraged to this single trade than they ever were to dot-coms, and that creates this incredible fragility.

So all of this — this nexus of factors — is what creates this bubblish moment, which has nothing to do with whether A.I. is useful but has everything to do with why the other side of this will see a rolling series of crises that could potentially become really catastrophic.

I want to focus for a minute on the rationality of the core players — your Metas, your Alphabets, your OpenAIs and Anthropics, all of which believe that there’s only going to be a couple of A.I. winners.

Kedrosky: Right.

I mean, Mark Zuckerberg made this amazing statement where he said: “If we end up misspending a couple hundred billion dollars, that would be unfortunate. But the risk of not acting aggressively enough is considerably higher.”

And so there is this dynamic where I think they believe this is going to be a highly concentrated or oligopolistic market, where maybe it’s one model that rules them all or three models that rule them all. And so there is this race to be one of the three.

But that creates a pressure to invest way beyond what the market can collectively sustain.

Kedrosky: Right. That’s the classic competitive dynamic that has existed in every one of these capex build-outs.

It existed with the railroads. You could not afford to be left behind. You had to invest in it. And that’s why we ended up with duplicate routes between cities.

I mean, that’s the essence of the competitive dynamic crossed with a prisoner’s dilemma: I would like to slow down, but I can’t because no one else will.

And so we all continue on with this frantic competitive dynamic. And so that’s what you’re seeing incarnate there. And we saw that even a couple of weeks ago: Dario Amodei at Anthropic was suggesting that we need to — and this is a ridiculous expression — “pace the frontier.” Which sounds vaguely like we’re training for the Boston Marathon. But it’s this idea that we need to slow down.

Well, of course, everyone, in a classic prisoner’s dilemma, said: Go for it. You slow down. I’m not slowing down. And even worse, they said: Even if we all agree here, in the U.S., for frontier companies to slow down, China won’t. And then you get into this terrible discussion — the what-aboutery with respect to what China will do.

So this is the problem: There’s a race dynamic that has been created, that if you stop, there’s a fear that either my competitors will gain an advantage or my shareholders will punish me. And so as a result, the race dynamic continues, and that’s what guarantees the overbuild.

As long as you have a supply of capital and a race dynamic, you’re guaranteed overcapacity, much like whether it’s canals, railroads, electrification — take your pick.

Azeem, you and your team, over the past year to year-and-a-half, have been building out this dashboard, trying to track how much stress there is in the A.I. industry financially — trying to think through what it looks like for this to be on a healthy financial path and what it looks like for this to be a bubble.

So why don’t you walk me through your perspective — the indicators you watch most closely — and why you’re a little bit more optimistic right now than Paul is?

Azhar: Well, Ezra, when we’re looking at a technology boom — a technology cycle — we’ve got to keep two different things under consideration.

The first is: Are customers finding it useful? Are they paying for it? Are they increasingly paying for it? In other words: Is demand real? And is demand there?

And when you look back at bubbles that burst, it is almost always connected to a problem in the financing mechanism: the refinancing of shorter-term debt. It runs into a problem, and capital goes away, and you see all of the things that we associate with bubbles.

The question is: Where are we today? And where we are today is that demand is very strong from American and global enterprises.

There is not an overbuild yet. There is vast, vast undersupply of the compute needed for A.I. And the race seems to be: Can we get enough chips and power enough chips over the next two to three years to keep up with the demand?

On the financing side, we are certainly moving off the cash the hyperscalers have earned over the last 20 years or so. And we’re bringing debt on board.

But it’s not yet at the levels at which you would say: This is a historically high and complex position. So for me, today, it’s in that productive boom with the hints of maybe getting — forgive my French — a little bit stinky.

So I want to focus on the supply versus demand at this very simple level. What Paul is basically saying is that there is a strong incentive to build too much supply, and what you are saying is that there’s actually plenty of demand. So I want to decompose what we mean when we talk about “demand.”

So this is demand for A.I. usage, which is tokens — which, again, for people who are not as used to this, are: When you ask a question, the A.I. model is consuming tokens to answer it. When you ask the A.I. coder to code you a program, it is consuming tokens to code the program.

And so, functionally, what is happening with a company like OpenAI or Anthropic is people are buying token use from them. They don’t sell you Claude, they sell you tokens at the high levels. So that’s the reason tokens are an important concept here.

And so there’s first these questions of: How many tokens are people going to want, and how strong is the demand for tokens going to be? And then there is a secondary question of: How much will they pay for them?

Because the price per token is plummeting. So there’s this question of: Even if there is a lot of demand, is it going to be demand for the kinds of very expensive models that the American companies are investing in, or not?

So I’d like you to walk me through how that demand picture looks to you.

Azhar: Well, we have to start at a layer below the tokens. The asset we’re investing in is data centers, about 65 percent of the cost of which is the chip — the graphics processing unit or the A.I. accelerator.

So what I think is important to look at is: What is the demand for those chips to do the computing that, in some cases — most cases — produces tokens? And who are the customers of those GPUs?

And when we look at this, we see these hyperscalers — Amazon, Microsoft and Google — and then new labs called neoclouds. These people buy millions of these GPUs. They put them together in data centers that will now start to cost billions of dollars, and they rent those GPUs out.

And the thing that I spend a lot of time thinking about is: Is that capital expenditure on the actual productive asset turning into revenue with just enough return on investment to pay itself?

And right now, the reason we know we’re in a compute-constrained environment is that people are making extremely good returns in 18 to 24 months on an asset because they’re able to charge essentially Uber surge pricing for their GPUs. And about 50 percent of their revenues go to the two big A.I. companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, for their spending.

The other 50 percent is a mix of other A.I. companies and firms — companies directly running those open-source models that you alluded to or open-weight models on the hyperscalers’ infrastructure.

And then I think we get to your other question, which is: Well, if 50 percent of this is coming from Anthropic and OpenAI, what percentage of that is actually real customer spending?

And what I’d say is, if those ratios stayed the same for the next three or four years, we’d very much be in a world where this is someone effectively paying themselves around the back door.

But what has been happening is that ratio has been declining. Essentially, the hyperscalers are getting more and more business from real customers. And all of that, for me, is a sign of a market that is maturing week after week, quarter after quarter.

Paul, how do you see that differently?

Kedrosky: I hardly know where to start. So let me just start.

A lot of the “discussion” — and I use that word advisedly — with respect to how people talk about this stuff reminds me of that old joke: Mother comes downstairs in the morning, finds her daughter under the Christmas tree, and there’s a giant pile of horse manure. An awful lot of what’s happened with frontier models is people confusing the early customers of frontier models for what you and I want.

So who were the early customers of A.I. models? Who really drove this? Coders. Something like 80 percent of the token usage and the revenues from the largest A.I. frontier model companies are coders or developers. And developers are really idiosyncratic for at least two reasons.

That’s not anything like what you and I do, for the most part. A lot of what normal people and normal businesses do is closer to a 1:1 relationship.

Or even compressive. Like I’ll say: I got 25 emails from Goldman Sachs babbling about something or another. Are any of those things worth reading?

And that’s compressive, right? Because I’m taking a whole lot of stuff and turning it into something small, and that feels efficient to me — or, similarly, some other email or a calendar, whatever. So the point being that normals — the people who these frontier models want to sell to now — are not really well represented by what people in the early days of the market were doing. Because coders are really unusual.

And you’re already seeing some of that: Meta’s cutting in half the number of developers in-house who are allowed to use external frontier tools. Microsoft, the same thing.

The days of token-maxxing — where you had charts internally that said who’s winning at using the most tokens — those are long over. Normal companies can’t tolerate that. People are blowing their entire budgets in months.

So my point is, we’re already moving away from the early days of profligate token use and everybody looking for ponies inside of giant piles of manure.

I want to ask you both this question: What, for you, counts as the bubble popping?

Azhar: Well, historically, when bubbles have popped they have resulted in two things. One is a huge decline in the level of investment in that particular asset. And they have been accompanied by a significant crash in a relevant asset market — whether it’s the stock market or something else. And that is the test that I would use.

I think we may end up in a world where there are grindingly low and embarrassing returns for credit funds and for hyperscalers because of the investments they’ve made. But that degree of pain is not a bubble bursting. That is just: Somebody made some bad investments, and they bought high when they should have bought at a lower price.

I mean, I think I would use a very, very classic historical definition, which is that we need to see the level of investment drop by 50 percent, and we need to see a really, really substantial — and typically it’s been 50 percent or more — correction in whatever the relevant market is.
