What Wall Street is very, very good at is making it less pristine because they’ll continue to raise money for you, and raise and raise and raise for you. Because the fees are tremendous. And as they do so, your credit rating declines.

And we’re seeing that with Oracle. We’re seeing that we’re on the cusp of that with Microsoft. We’re on the cusp of that with some of the other hyperscalers, because that’s what Wall Street does.

They see a pristine balance sheet, an “unlevered company” in the term of art in the industry. And they’ll continue to burden it with credit.

And so the way that these companies try to get around it — Meta is probably the best example — is they use somewhat more exotic structures so the debt doesn’t actually sit on their balance sheet. They use things called special-purpose vehicles. They use things that are off-balance-sheet financing.

They’ll say: Hey, hey, hey, that’s not my debt. I know I control it, but it’s over there with that funnily named thing that sounds like a New Orleans bagel. That’s somebody else’s debt.

And so this is all just a shell game. And the reality is that rolled up, we’re now at a point where tech, whose main advantage historically was fast growth, no debt — tech is now the largest issuer of investment grade bonds in the United States.

This is an industry whose main claim to fame, other than growth, was that they were relatively clean. They’re now the exact opposite.

These are hugely debt-encumbered companies, increasingly, that are dominating the issuance marketplace to the point that it’s even having an impact on sovereigns. So one of the reasons we had the bond market freakout over the last two or three weeks was because of the role of hyperscalers in issuing credit at the same duration as the tenure in the United States. Which, at the margin, was actually outcompeting the U.S., which caused yields to have to go up on the tenure.

So that’s how crazy things have become. So yeah, no, it has completely transitioned. Which is going to have huge consequences down the road in terms of this debt overhang that starts to look increasingly like Japan circa 1990 — all these corporations with giant balance sheets loaded with debt that are trying to work it off.

Well, the other side of that, Azeem, is that it’s not just debt that is being crowded out where these hyperscaler companies are competing with everybody else for money. It’s also construction, it’s also real materials.

I’m sure you’ve seen these charts going around that imply there’s real crowdout happening. That yes, we are building, we are pumping money into A.I. capex, but home building, in a country that does not have enough homes, is going down. Spending on manufacturing plants and factories is going down, or at least the share.

And so there does appear to be a movement from investing in other parts of the economy, at a construction and capex level, into investing in A.I.

I guess if A.I. works out — great, that’s fine. But if it doesn’t, or even if you just think these other things are underrated, as say, maybe, for homes — homes are a more stable investment. They don’t give you returns like investing in Nvidia does, but they’re pretty important, and I have a cleaner way of explaining why more homes would make more people’s lives better.

How do you think about the crowdout question here?

Azhar: A year ago, back in the summer of 2025, I wrote about how I assessed whether we’re in a boom or a bubble. And one of my observations was that at the moment, the hyperscalers are spending out of their own cash flows and their own balance sheets.

As soon as that starts to change, and they go to external finance, you introduce lots more risk. And my threshold for more risk was about 30 percent, which is about the level that we are approaching now at the end of 2026. These things are not set in stone.

The crowding-out problem is a real problem, and it’s really a complicated and thorny issue. I think one place to think about is what happened in the Netherlands in the 1970s, when they discovered a lot of offshore natural gas in the North Sea, and the entire economy oriented around gas extraction. And you got this thing called Dutch disease, where effectively that part of the economy was sucking up all of the activities.

And there could be a risk that will happen in the U.S., if it isn’t already happening right now. And I think then the question is: What do you do about it? And how do you actually adapt to that?

And I’m afraid my only answer is that it requires something of a policy stimulus to make sure that those sectors get the activity that they need. Because I’m not persuaded that market forces on their own would do that.

That seems like a tough prescription at a time when, I’d say, we have both very erratic leadership, but also our borrowing costs are going pretty high amid incredible levels of debt.

Azhar: Well, look, your politics are your politics, and you get to vote every four years and make the choices that you make.

[Laughs.] And then live with them.

Azhar: Right, and then live with them. [Chuckles.] But it doesn’t have to involve subsidies. It can involve other types of policy interventions.

It’s a really difficult problem. And it will continue to happen as long as the returns on the other investments are higher and as long as that is creating a supply shock for electricians and construction workers and HVAC technicians and all the other things that are needed in data centers.

There is a “but” to all of this, which is that, of course, there’s a lot of upskilling going on. There are many, many electricians being trained. There are many HVAC engineers being trained. There are many construction workers being trained. There are construction firms that are growing and that will start to have spare capacity.

And I don’t know how that ends up. But in a year or two or three, that capacity and those skills will be in the economy and able to be used.

So I want to ask this not in terms of stock markets and financial flows: What does this economy look like in which companies and people — and governments, for that matter — are using enough A.I. to make these investments, writ large, pay off? Even if some companies may not end up being in the winner’s circle here and may fail?

So Azeem, you spend a lot of time thinking about this. If you were to try to paint a picture of what things look like at normal companies — your GEs, your Coca-Colas — in this world where the A.I. bet pays off, what does it look like?

What is different? What is not being spent on if so much money is being spent on A.I. tokens? Like, what is happening here?

Azhar: When I talk to bosses, and I talk to them across Europe and the U.S. — dozens every year — I hear this same sort of thing, which is: We’re making progress with A.I. It’s harder than we thought. We’re going to keep doing it, and we’re starting to get results.

And the more confident ones say: We’re getting more and more results.

But a large part of it is coming now — I think will come, unless businesses grow very, very quickly — from just a slow reduction in the replacement of workers. Companies that are getting more productive with A.I. will be delivering more dollars per employee. And if they’re not growing faster than that productivity growth, then their headcounts will start to fall.

But we should just add that there are very few A.I. native companies. When we think about electricity, the electricity-native companies were companies like the Ford Motor Company, with its end-to-end production line. But most of America didn’t get fully electrified for another 15 or 20 years after that.

And I don’t think I can really point to a Main Street firm that is outside of Silicon Valley that you could say: This company has become A.I. native. What you can see are bits of the business that look like they’re using a lot of A.I. ——

OK, but if the A.I. native company that you’re talking about is a company where you’ve managed to replace people with A.I.s — now you seem to be really quickly tipping into the much-worried-about world in which A.I. is net negative for jobs across the economy.

Unless you believe there are all these new companies starting that are somehow very human-labor intensive, even though, in theory, the new companies starting are going to be more A.I. native, so less human-labor intensive — so is that actually a good world?

And then if that’s the world, who’s spending more money in this world where people are losing jobs?

Azhar: Well, I think there are a number of different things going on. One is that there are still things that the A.I.s won’t be able to do. And those will be the layers of humans doing verification, doing the last sign-off, doing the things that the models cannot do well. What would typically happen is that those people will end up being paid more and more, and better and better, as a consequence of sitting at that choke point.

I think that the second thing that you will start to see is a whole class of roles that we can’t imagine within companies — whether it’s things like the webmaster, which didn’t exist in 1993.

And then I think the third thing is really the cultural dimension of a general-purpose technology. This is where Paul was describing the G.P.T., is that they tend to construct entire new classes of work and behavior that we hadn’t been able to put our fingers on.

And if you just think about Henry Ford — well, because of Henry Ford, we ended up with motorcars. Because we have motorcars, we ended up with people having suburbs and suburbs to vacations and vacations to all the services that sit around them.

Now, I’m not blasé about that. I think the challenge we may find is that it takes longer to create those new roles than anything else that happens.

But the other observation I would make is that my time horizon for this runs in five, seven, 10 years — not one or two, not two or three. Because I do think it just takes time for management teams to absorb what it is they have to do with this technology.

And it’s just not the case that you get the best model from OpenAI and say: Fix my company — and it fixes it. These things take time. And that’s what I hear when I talk to bosses. However fast they want to move, it just takes time.

Paul, how do you see this?

Kedrosky: We’re basically repricing labor, right? I mean, this is the fastest adopting technology in history, and its fundamental function is to reprice cognitive labor.

And I mean, this is the deep struggle. Because the article of faith — the West Coast ideology on this stuff — is technology always creates more jobs than it destroys. And so it becomes just a thing that people repeat — like a mantra that they hope will become true.

And the reality is we’ve never seen a general-purpose technology that had such broad applicability, was adopted so quickly and was repricing labor at the same time. And when I say repricing labor, I mean it’s making it vastly cheaper to run things like call centers, for example.

And as a result, this change is going to be destabilizing long before we figure out how to turn them all into — I don’t know what the equivalent of webmasters is.

And so this is the problem: It’s happening so much faster than any prior G.P.T. This arm-waving about creating more jobs than it destroys belies the lived experiences of people who are affected by this stuff.

And so it can quickly become just some strange mantra like: Don’t worry your pretty little head — everything will be fine.

So no, I think the disruption will vastly outpace our ability to create new positions.

This has also struck me as another form of economic risk for not just workers but actually A.I. and for some form of this bubble popping or deflating, if it is a bubble.

Because you can imagine a world where the problem is not whether companies are willing to adopt A.I. That actually — particularly under more economic strain — interest rates keep going higher, maybe there’s a recession of some sort, and companies begin moving very aggressively to replace human labor — which needs health care and unionizes and has opinions — with A.I.

And then there’s a huge backlash. There’s already a huge A.I. backlash. People are organizing against building data centers. They don’t want them where they live.

But if you know anything about the history of occupational licensing or building homes or anything else, it’s actually not that difficult for, say, teachers to organize and say: No A.I. in the classroom. Actually, education is off-limits for A.I.

Doctors all of a sudden start to organize. Maybe there are a couple of bad events where people are getting bad diagnoses off A.I., and so it’s locked out of hospitals.

Anthropic, in its risks to their I.P.O., says existential risk to humanity is possibly one of the risks of this I.P.O.

If there’s some major control incident where, instead of hacking Hugging Face or OpenAI, it hacks Wells Fargo, it hacks something in China, and all of a sudden regulation comes in not a little bit but all at once.

All of those things seem like real risks. The possibility of discontinuous regulation seems higher to me than elsewhere. It also seems — I don’t want to say inevitable, to me — but quite likely, to me.

So what do you think about that?

Kedrosky: This has been my complaint from the very beginning of the process by which these companies have launched models.

They’ve essentially been conducting unlicensed drug trials on the public. In the sense that these are hugely consequential technologies that are launched in a way that, were they a drug company, you would immediately have the F.D.A. on your back.

And yet, because of their technology, companies can do these mass trials: Oh, by the way, we’re going to transform all of education. We’re going to launch these things that can penetrate government websites and other things.

So this idea that you can do this with impunity in technology, because we live in the timeline where, so far, these things haven’t killed us, is just ridiculous and indefensible.

And I think we’re inevitably headed toward a world where there’s going to be — after some kind of terrible event — some kind of post-hoc regulation imposed. But it will only be after consequential damage.

And I’ll give you a specific example. This is the way I often try to characterize it for people. Because they’ll say: Well, what’s going to cause that? As if you can just come up with this stuff.

If you think about it, there are probably five, 10, 15 different sorts of scenarios we can come up with that might lead to regulation, none of them probably having a probability of, let’s say, maybe more than 5 percent.

So let’s say I have six events, each of which has a 5 percent chance of happening. What’s the likelihood that any one of them happens? It’s about 20 percent.

If I have a dozen events or possible scenarios that are all bad, but each of which has no more than a 5 percent chance of happening, what’s the likelihood that one of those happens? It’s more than 50 percent.

We have way more than a dozen ways that these things could cause trouble and end up requiring regulation. So looking at it that way, it’s almost inevitable. It’s like a 50 or 60 percent chance that something happens that drives regulation. And yet people continue to sit around and say: Well, you know, this isn’t that likely. Or: That isn’t that likely.

So no — regulation here is inevitable. It will take the form of something like the F.D.A. Maybe like some kind of Atomic Energy Commission — because it’s just as consequential and because there are so many different ways for them to have broader consequences in society.

And it’s amazing to me that people sort of glibly pass that off.

Azeem, how do you see this political risk dimension?

Azhar: Well, I think, when you look at industries — industries grow quite well when there’s a little bit of regulation. The pharmaceutical industry is a great example.

And when we think about who’s going to pay for this, the A.I. companies — from the model labs through to the hyperscalers — are going to be making a lot of money. So it’s fairly clear that there is money in the system, and there are firms that can cover some part of the bill.

And I think one of the things that’s really exciting about the data center protests that you’re seeing, particularly in the U.S., is that actually it is people expressing their sense of unease about this technology, the way it’s manifesting itself.

And the way to look at that is that is a democratic expression. That is an expression of will. That is an expression of uncertainty. And what you would hope to come out of something like that would be a better social license that people are more and more comfortable with.

Now, I suspect that within the U.S., because you have state-level governance power, that some of this may be done on a statewide basis. What’s happening in the U.K. is that there is an attempt to get people developing data centers to reinvest annuities into the local community.

Because one of the things that we don’t really talk about much is that a huge data center might employ very, very few people, indeed. I mean, it may be billions of dollars, but it’s a handful of jobs, and that’s not really ——

Which is crazy — two to six people for a multibillion-dollar facility.

Kedrosky: Well, and if you do the math in terms of the cost per jobs created, it’s often — I was looking at one in New Mexico recently. It’s $4 million in terms of subsidies per job created, leaving aside the cost of the center. If you look at the tax abatements and the required improvements to local utilities, the numbers are insane.

Azhar: So none of that works long term. But the useful thing is that there’s money in the system. Because there are profits being made up and down the stack. And one would feel that because of that, there’s an obvious place for that bill to land.

And that bill can land through — I don’t think self-regulation works. And I would agree that we will need to find — whether it’s local, national or international — real rules about how these systems work and the harms and the damages that they might cause.

But the thing to me that’s interesting in that — of course, there’s going to be regulation. That’s clear to me.

The range of how that could fall — all the way from pharmaceutical regulation, where what we want is for pharmaceutical companies to produce safe drugs, although people may argue we’ve made that too slow, also. All the way to, say, nuclear power regulation, where, fundamentally, what we’ve ended up wanting is no new nuclear power plants.

And depending on what happens with A.I. and given how negative people are on it already, one of the possibilities here is that it could swing such that the answer on a bunch of things is simply: No, we don’t want to be replaced by robots. Which, actually, when you say it aloud like that seems like a fairly straightforward thing and probably the kind of thing that people are going to express in a democracy.

Or: No, we don’t want robot agents crawling all over the economy. No, we don’t want to be called endlessly, as a restaurant, by your Muse agent trying to get reservations everywhere. Because now you’ve just made it functionally impossible for a restaurant to ever answer the phone again with a human being.

And that the collective expansion of all this — I mean, I know people who are managers at different firms, and they’re just saying: I’m just drowning in A.I.-produced reports all of a sudden. My email is just full of obviously A.I.-written inquiries, which is making my responsiveness all across the board go down.

I’m not just saying: Will there or won’t there be regulation? But I think one risk is if people decide they don’t want this in fairly large swaths of the economy or used in some of the ways people are expecting.

There’s a very good piece by John Herman in New York magazine about the beginning agony of companies that all of a sudden are absorbing tremendous amounts of Muse agent inquiry.

And we’re not prepared for everybody to have an agent calling you as a robot, trying to negotiate down the price or get a reservation or sell a concert ticket or just whatever it might be. And people may actually not like it.

Kedrosky: Yeah.

Azhar: They might not like it. And the trouble is there appears to be some revealed preference here, and that picture is not even.

So only about 2.5 percent of Americans pay for an A.I. subscription, which — considering they’ve been available for three years — is a very slow takeoff.

I love this stat in one of your newsletters recently, that a larger number of Americans pay for a G.L.P.-1 than for A.I.

Azhar: Well, yeah, because one is really quite useful, and you feel the impact within a matter of a few weeks.

But hundreds of millions of people in America and around the world do use A.I. through the free version, and when companies like Meta start to put these tools in front of you, I’m sure people will end up using them.

Even if they vote with their complaints and with their social media posts saying they don’t want any A.I., either it will become inescapable or they will still have it on their phone, and they’ll be using it. And I think we have to just contend with that possibility.

I think we also have to realize — and this is where we think about technology as being this gigantic, unpermissioned experiment —which it has been for 40 or 50 years. That what you’re describing about robocalls from A.I. agents into hotels and restaurants — or as my orthopedic surgeon was telling me, he just gets long, 10,000-word emails from patients who have clearly given ChatGPT their medical notes.

This is unfortunately going to happen, and that cost has now been pushed into the system, and we’re going to have to figure out how to deal with it. I now pay — it’s not a lot — about a buck a month to my phone operator to screen out spoof phone calls that are essentially robocalls.

That’s what’s going to happen. And we’re going to call that gross domestic product, those additional costs.

Kedrosky: I think, though — your comment, Ezra, really reminded me of this: We have this idea in Western capitalism that it’s always about efficiency.

In a weird way, societies require friction. And when you take away frictions, even frictions that you didn’t realize existed, all of a sudden, it has consequences. There have been examples of people using large language models to launch claims in small claims court, for example.

Do we want that to have less friction? Do we want more of that? Do we want your example of the restaurants?

And we have all of these frictions that exist in society, and blithely removing all of them is creating, in tech parlance, almost a denial-of-service attack on modernity, where all of a sudden, we’re having stuff launching at us from every angle, almost like Russian bots attacking a website. Except it’s coming from all angles because of the increasing number of bots and other things.

And I think that’s what people are responding to. It’s this out-of-control feeling as all of the frictions drop away. And suddenly, I can’t get access to things, or nothing works the way I’d expect.

So simply dealing with the reduction in frictions has huge consequences across society, and I think people are reacting to that.

And what’s going to happen is it’s going to be these two A.I.s bouncing things back and forth. And it’s just going to be a more and more and more unpleasant economy.

Which is why I do think there are going to be large areas where people just say: Maybe not.

Let me end on this question, which is first, for you, Azeem. What would you need to see to start thinking: Oh no, this is getting pretty bubbly?

And then to you, Paul, the reverse. What would you need to see to think: Oh, maybe I do have this wrong, and these investors have it right, and there’s a lot of money to be made here?

Azhar: Well, there are so many risks that we have talked about, and there’s all the complexity and fragility in the financing. The thing that keeps this on the other side of healthy is whether real customers are spending real money and getting real results.

So the thing that would make me uneasy would be if I saw a couple of quarters where the amount that American enterprises were spending on A.I., that the growth rate was halving, say, two quarters in a row. That would suggest that they’ve filled their appetite, and there’s not going to be the revenue to keep this on the right side of healthy.

Paul?

Kedrosky: There are so many. I mean, I’m convinced I’m wrong about most things, so I’m always happy to find more things I’m wrong about.

So I just look at economic data. If we began to see, I don’t know, productivity growth go well beyond trend, that would be striking.

I mean, so far we’re sitting at around trend data with respect to U.S. productivity growth. There’s no sign of A.I. improving productivity. If we saw participation rates sharply increasing, that would be something that would help to tell me: OK, A.I. is an inclusive technology in bringing people back into the economy. That would really help.

If we saw G.D.P. growth going back above trend — we’re still sitting around the levels of the post-World War II trend, at the low end of it — any of those things would tell me that something big was going on, like a true productivity shock in the economy that warranted the kind of expenditures.

So if any of those, and probably, the three of them at once happened, that would tell me I was wrong. If those productivity numbers come through, then fine, everything changes. But if it doesn’t, you’re looking at something that looks more like the 1930s than it does like the 2000s.

All right. I think that’s a good place to end.

So always our final question: What are three books you’d recommend to the audience? Paul, why don’t we begin with you?

Kedrosky: Sure. “Middlemarch” by George Eliot is my go-to on thinking about normal people being swept along by the winds of change as a major technology revolution is taking place. It’s set at a time when the Industrial Revolution was taking hold, and I think it’s a tremendous book about that.

So the other one that I like to recommend is “Liberty’s Dawn” by Emma Griffin, which is a collection of the average workers’ biographies and notes from during the Industrial Revolution. It’s just a wonderful, wonderful look at what it was like in the middle of that wrenching transition. And as people would talk about economic data and everything else, what it was like to live through it.

What did it feel like? What was the pain I felt? And what are my hopes for the future? It’s just a wonderful book about that.

And the last one that I always point to is about Samuel Insull, a largely forgotten figure. He was probably one of the most important entrepreneurs of the 1920s. His empire in electricity shows what happens — building an empire on top of a G.P.T. and even doing that successfully can still end up in collapse and calamity. But it’s a wonderful story. So “Insull: The Rise and Fall of a Billionaire Utility Tycoon,” by Forrest McDonald.

Azeem?

Azhar: So my three books — the first is “The Day the Universe Changed.” It was written by BBC science journalist James Burke back in the 1980s. I read it as a teenager, and I’ve just reread it, and it is all about how, as we develop new types of knowledge, we start to rethink our role in the world, what matters to us and how unsettling that is. And he walks us through 1,000 years-plus of that through Western and Asian history.

The second book is “Fathers and Sons” by Ivan Turgenev, which is a book written in the 19th century. It’s at that moment where the ideas of science and modernity are making their way into Russia, and you have the generational conflict between the more traditional generation and the younger generation, and what stays as a bond between them — what even the most recent breakthroughs in science can’t tell you about what it is to be human. I think it’s very relevant.

And then the final one, which I’m just rereading again, is “Candide” by Voltaire.

Azeem Azhar, Paul Kedrosky, thank you very much.

Kedrosky: Thanks, Ezra.

Azhar: Thank you.

SUMMARY

Overall, members of Wesleyan’s all-male fraternities were twice as likely as nonmembers to be found in violation of nonacademic regulations. The hypermasculine culture in all-male fraternities often feeds on denigrating women, and people feel pressure not to intervene. Fraternities would have to admit women or become off-limits to Wesleyan students.

ARTICLE

Fraternities Can Change. This Is How.
A fellow college president warned that the blowback from my decision would end my presidency. Instead, it produced some extraordinary conversations.
By Michael S. Roth
Published 2026-10-16 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/opinion/fraternities-cornell-men-women.html

Like most everyone else, I read about the accusation of gang rape at a Cornell fraternity with anguish. As a former leader of a fraternity and the current president of a university, I felt a connection that was much more personal. My Greek organization, Alpha Delta Phi, was already coed when I was a student at Wesleyan in the 1970s, and it was the source of friendships I still treasure. About a dozen years ago, however, our campus went through a period of heated debate about Greek life. The significant changes that resulted made life here better — and have important lessons to offer other colleges and universities.

A few years after I was appointed to my current role, it became clear that a disproportionate share of Wesleyan’s disciplinary infractions were tied to parties at the large houses of three all-male fraternities. Numerous people who attended those parties left in ambulances because of excessive alcohol consumption, and students reported harrowing cases of sexual assault on the premises. Overall, members of Wesleyan’s all-male fraternities were twice as likely as nonmembers to be found in violation of nonacademic regulations.

The problem of sexual assault was not confined to fraternities alone, but reasonable people — and insurance companies! — saw a high degree of risk in these institutions. After a survey found that almost half of Wesleyan undergraduates reported feeling “less safe” in fraternities than in other social spaces, in the spring of 2014 the student government passed a resolution demanding that residential Greek societies become coed or disband. (The university has at times had a sorority, but it has been nonresidential.)

Faculty members and students signed petitions along these same lines, arguing that fraternities as they existed discriminated against women in ways that made them fundamentally inequitable and unsafe. At the same time, other students, along with alumni, rallied to fraternities’ defense, making the case that they were being unfairly singled out for punishment while their community-building activities were being overlooked.

I did my best to listen to all these positions. I also considered evidence from social psychology that in spaces controlled by a tightly knit group, people are less likely to speak out when bad things happen. The hypermasculine culture in all-male fraternities often feeds on denigrating women, and people feel pressure not to intervene.

I explored a range of options, from banning all Greek societies to incentivizing them to better police themselves to changing the terms of their official relationship with the university. At the end of summer of 2014, I came to a decision. Recognizing that our residential Greek organizations do inspire loyalty, community and independence, but that they undermined the ability of women to have full access to the benefits of a Wesleyan education, I concluded that they should be permitted to remain open but not to remain single-sex. Fraternities would have to admit women or become off-limits to Wesleyan students.

We also implemented a strong bystander-intervention program to train all the members of our community to take action when they see someone in harm’s way. At Cornell, no one intervened; one young man’s Snapchat invitation to a chain of buddies to have sex with an intoxicated woman was like-minded bro culture at its worst. Bystander intervention breaks this kind of chain apart. Opening up previously all-male societies makes it less likely in the first place.

My decision, to put it mildly, was controversial. A fellow college president warned that the blowback would end my presidency. Instead, it produced some extraordinary conversations. I spent time with young women who recounted horror stories of being sexually assaulted at large frat parties. I also spent time with fraternity members who felt I’d made the wrong choice. In many cases, these young men were proud of their progressive credentials, yet here they were defending male privilege. I reminded them that their organization used to exclude Catholics, Jews and Black people but eventually changed course; admitting women was the next step in that process. But no, some of these students told me, women are different.

In addition to requiring coeducation, I decided to close one fraternity — Beta Theta Pi — altogether, after a wild party it sponsored resulted in serious injuries. A second fraternity, Delta Kappa Epsilon, whose home sits across the street from mine, sued the university and its leadership. After much discussion, Psi Upsilon, the third all-male fraternity, agreed to admit women as full members.

The campus today is safer and it is more equitable. Its largest social spaces are no longer controlled by all-male organizations, and the incidence of reported sexual violence is way down. Violence against women and trans people is still far too prevalent nationwide, and many incidents go unreported. Our campus continues to be plagued by these factors, but people who see someone in a vulnerable position here are more likely to speak up than they were in the past. I can’t be certain how much of our progress can be attributed to the fact that we no longer had all-male fraternities, and how much is a result of greater mainstream awareness of sexual consent and a generational shift away from alcohol. The strong indications, however, are that it helped.

As for the Greek organizations, the outcomes are striking. My old organization, ADP, remains a vibrant, creative, coed community. After years of litigation, the lawsuit from DKE was settled in 2022. The fraternity’s house sits empty; the undergraduate organization now exists only as a nonresidential club.

Psi Upsilon, on the other hand, is thriving. Not long after ceasing to be exclusively male, the fraternity had a female president. It recruits an impressively diverse, talented group of students each year, and they make every effort to be a resource for the campus and for the city of Middletown, Conn. They still have parties and concerts (I can hear them from my window). Last homecoming, my wife and I danced with students there as an alumni band rocked out.

I am not suggesting for a moment that all Wesleyan’s efforts in this regard have been successful, or that ending all-male Greek life will end sexual assault on any campus. Sexual violence has many causes, and every campus has its own cultural dynamics. In places where all-male fraternities play an important role in social life, however, there are just too many horror stories waiting to happen. Forcing these organizations to admit women, as well as trans and nonbinary students, can be an important step in making campuses safer for all who inhabit them, whatever their gender.

Michael S. Roth, the president of Wesleyan University, is the author of “The Student: A Short History” and “Safe Enough Spaces: A Pragmatist’s Approach to Inclusion, Free Speech, and Political Correctness on College Campuses.”

But it’s worth pausing to recognize that, with Trump’s attempt to banish Omar, we’ve crossed yet another once-unthinkable line.

ARTICLE

Trump’s Attempt to Deport Ilhan Omar Is Another Leap Toward the Abyss
This is more than just another persecution of one of the president’s political enemies.
By Michelle Goldberg
Published 2026-10-16 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/opinion/ilhan-omar-deportation-trump.html

In his final speech as president, Ronald Reagan emphasized the essential role of immigration in American greatness. “We lead the world because, unique among nations, we draw our people — our strength — from every country and every corner of the world,” he said. Reagan cited a letter he’d received about how one can’t simply move to France and become a Frenchman or move to Japan and become Japanese. “But anyone, from any corner of the Earth, can come to live in America and become an American,” he said.

Donald Trump, who launched his political career with lies about Barack Obama’s birthplace, is devoted to destroying this ideal. For Trump and his movement, real Americans are defined by race and ancestry. The administration’s war on birthright citizenship stems from that belief. It’s the reason Trump, who accused immigrants of “poisoning the blood” of our country, has limited refugee resettlement almost exclusively to white South Africans. JD Vance channeled the same idea last year when, attacking the Jewish Anti-Defamation League, he said, “I think the people whose ancestors fought in the Civil War have a hell of a lot more claim over America than the people who say they don’t belong.”

And now the Trump administration is attempting to strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, who was born in Somalia, of her citizenship so as to deport her. This is more than just another persecution of one of Trump’s political enemies. Rather, his government is tacitly declaring the citizenship of all foreign-born people provisional, their Americanness something that can be revoked. It’s a frontal attack on the idea of constitutional equality. As Hannah Arendt wrote — a quote that the writer John Ganz reminded me of — “One is almost tempted to measure the degree of totalitarian infection by the extent to which the concerned governments use their sovereign right of denationalization.”

This week, as you might have read by now, around 20 Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s home in Washington, seizing her phone and computers, among other things. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that the investigation is aimed at denaturalizing her, a prelude to deporting her. In its attempt to cast out Omar, the administration is looking not just at her own actions, but also at those of her father, who applied for citizenship when she was a teenager. Apparently, the case hinges on whether she was 18 rather than 17 at the time.

I have no idea whether Omar or her father (who died in 2020) did anything wrong, but the details of her immigration paperwork are somewhat beside the point. What matters is that Trump targeted Omar for her politics and, even more, her ethnicity. Just months into her first term, he was calling for her expulsion from America, his rally crowds lustily chanting, “Send her back!” In a cabinet meeting last year, he called Omar “garbage” and attacked Somalis more broadly, saying, “I don’t want them in our country.” As his political fortunes have waned, his rhetoric about Somalis has grown increasingly fascistic. On Truth Social last week, he wrote that the “once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants.” As if trying to incite a pogrom, he urged: “Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

Under these circumstances, it would be willfully credulous to assume the administration’s good faith in the Omar investigation. Even if the government ultimately fails to take away her citizenship, as it’s failed in most of its other attempts at political vengeance, it’s sending a message to every foreign-born American. Oppose Trump too loudly, and the government will comb through your paperwork — including paperwork filled out by your parents — for errors that could upend your life.

There is an obvious progression here. This regime has already tried to deport green card holders like Mahmoud Khalil for their political speech. It’s turned hundreds of thousands of Haitians — the group Trump demonized as pet-eating savages — into illegal immigrants overnight by ending their temporary protected status. Now it’s escalated to naturalized citizens. Omar probably won’t be the last. Though Trump has been charmed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, other Republicans have called for his deportation. Representative Andy Ogles, a Tennessee Republican, has asked the Justice Department to review Mamdani’s naturalization documents. In the Trumpian schema, some Americans are here by right, and some only on sufferance.

It’s chastening to think back to 2019, when Trump first tweeted that a group of progressive Democratic congresswomen, presumably including Omar, should go back to the “totally broken and crime infested places from which they came.” At the time, his bigotry was considered shocking. Four Republicans, as well as the Republican-turned-independent Justin Amash, joined Democrats in passing a House resolution condemning his words. Even Representative Elise Stefanik, who’d go on to become one of Trump’s most slavish lackeys, felt the need to denounce him. “While I strongly disagree with the tactics, policies and rhetoric of the far-left socialist ‘Squad,’ the president’s tweets were inappropriate, denigrating and wrong,” she said.

Now that Trump is acting on his gross rhetoric, the response has been more muted; by mass-producing outrages, the administration has numbed America’s ability to recognize their individual gravity. But it’s worth pausing to recognize that, with Trump’s attempt to banish Omar, we’ve crossed yet another once-unthinkable line.

For now, Trump’s power may be waning as his popularity collapses, but if the Republican Party continues on its current course, the next Republican president is likely to begin where he left off. The logic of this brand of politics moves inexorably toward atrocity.

Here’s Arendt again: “Mass cancellation of naturalizations, such as the one introduced by Nazi Germany in 1933 against all naturalized Germans of Jewish origin, usually preceded denationalization of citizens by birth in similar categories.” If there’s one lesson of the last decade, it’s never believe it can’t happen here.

Things Are Bad’: How Texas Border Voters Feel Ahead of the Midterms
With control of the Senate at stake, Mara Gay traveled to this Texas border region to hear from voters.
By Mara Gay and Emily Holzknecht

The Rio Grande Valley, along the U.S.-Mexico border in South Texas, has long been a Democratic stronghold. But in 2024, the region swung to Donald Trump. How do voters there feel now? To find out, the Opinion writer Mara Gay traveled to the region, where voters described fears about immigration enforcement, frustration with the economy and a desire for stability.

With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, their votes could help determine whether Texas sends a Democrat to the U.S. Senate. What would it take to win their support?

ARTICLE

Avalanche of G.O.P. Cash Keeps the Party Competitive Despite Its Problems
Republican Senate and House candidates are being out-raised by their Democratic rivals, but the party has received a huge boost from groups tied to Elon Musk and President Trump.
By Theodore Schleifer and Matt Zdun
Published 2026-10-16 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/avalanche-of-gop-cash-keeps-the-party-competitive-despite-its-problems.html

The political fund-raising picture in the final month of the midterm elections is something of a Rorschach test.

If you’re a Democrat, new election filings show many of the party’s Senate and House nominees raising more than their Republican rivals. This campaign cash is the most important money in politics, because candidates can control it directly and buy ads at cheaper rates.

If you’re a Republican, the same filings show that the G.O.P. has a significant advantage in money from super PACs and other outside groups tied to Elon Musk, President Trump and the party’s big donors. In many races, this edge has allowed the party to club Democrats with advertising even though Republican groups have to pay more for ads.

In fact, both of these perceptions are true. And for Republicans, the ability to hold their own — at least — in the midterm money fight is a rare bright spot as the party faces a gloomy political environment. This financial resilience has allowed Republicans to put up a robust defense of the Senate, in particular, as they try to keep control of Congress.

A bonanza of Federal Election Commission filings on Thursday offers a view of how much every federal candidate in the country raised and spent from July through September, as well as the finances of many of the outside groups supporting them. Even more filings for those groups will land next week.

Here are seven takeaways from the filings:

Democratic Senate contenders have raked in cash.

In eight of the Senate races expected to be most competitive in November, Democrats have raised more money this year through their main campaign committees than their Republican challengers, the filings show.

No Democrat raised money like James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas. His campaign hauled in a staggering $114 million from January through September, about $100 million more than his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, raised.

The Democratic edge was also striking in Kansas, a surprising Senate battleground. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, raised $13.4 million in the first nine months of the year, roughly six times as much as his Republican opponent, Senator Roger Marshall. (In just the third quarter, Mr. Hamilton brought in nearly $10 million, compared with Mr. Marshall’s roughly $800,000.)

The money will help Democrats’ effort to take back the chamber, but many of the seats the party needs to flip are in solidly red states — and Republicans have more money from outside groups.

Democratic House candidates also have an edge.

A similar story played out in the House, with Democrats out-raising Republicans in 38 of the 42 races currently considered competitive.

One of Democrats’ largest fund-raising advantages was in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, a tossup race that was thrown into turmoil when the incumbent Republican, Representative Chuck Edwards, dropped his re-election bid amid sexual harassment allegations. The Democratic nominee, Jamie Ager, raised about $4.6 million in the first nine months of the year, versus about $350,000 for the Republican nominee, Jennifer Balkcom.

But Republicans are winning with outside money.

Despite Democratic candidates’ fund-raising strength, party leaders have expressed profound concerns that Republicans hold a financial advantage.

Why? Because Republican super PACs and other outside groups have raised and spent far more than their Democratic counterparts.

That helps explain why Republicans are currently slated to have an advantage of about $650 million in general-election advertising, according to a review of past and future ad reservations across federal and state races by AdImpact, a media-tracking firm. (Ad reservations are fluid and are likely to change before Nov. 3.)

The main super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, the Senate Leadership Fund, out-raised its Democratic rival by about $122 million this quarter. The Republican group also revealed on Thursday that it had been the sole funder of super PACs backing several of the party’s battleground candidates: Mr. Paxton in Texas and Senators Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, Susan Collins of Maine and Dan Sullivan of Alaska.

The parties’ main House super PACs appear to be in a more competitive financial fight, according to advertising data. The main House Republican group raised $94 million in the last quarter, but its Democratic counterpart will not disclose its finances until Tuesday.

Nationally, some of the gap between Republicans and Democrats can be traced to three Trump-affiliated super PACs, which have combined to spend over $210 million on advertising, according to AdImpact. These groups’ finances will not be revealed until Tuesday, either.

If Paxton wins in Texas, he owes Elon Musk big time.

For weeks, it wasn’t quite clear how national Republicans were able to spend close to $160 million to help Mr. Paxton, who has long struggled to raise money and faces the single strongest Democratic midterm fund-raiser, Mr. Talarico.

The answer was Elon Musk.

The filings on Thursday suggested that the world’s richest person indirectly funded Texas PAC, the biggest-spending super PAC backing Mr. Paxton. He did it by sending enormous sums to the main Republican Senate super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, which had long resisted spending on behalf of Mr. Paxton. The group feared that doing so in a pricey state like Texas would divert resources from other competitive Senate races.

But Mr. Musk, the new filings show, made two huge donations to the Senate Leadership Fund: $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23. After each one, the Senate Leadership Fund sent an identical amount the next day to Texas PAC — which had no other donors through Sept. 30.

So even as Republicans worry that Mr. Paxton could do the unthinkable and lose to a Democrat in Texas, Mr. Musk appears to have given him a better chance of hanging on.

Republican megadonors are still giving generously.

Democrats have their own big donors. Two super PACs funded by the Soros family entered October with about $174 million on hand. And two of the party’s biggest donors, the Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, put $16 million into the midterms fight, the new filings show.

But most of the biggest midterm donors are supporting Republicans.

Dick Uihlein, a Midwest-based billionaire industrialist, put a staggering $67 million more into his super PAC last quarter, which in turn gave $15 million to the anti-tax Club for Growth.

Jeff Yass, a hedge fund investor, gave $10 million more to a super PAC backing Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio. Mr. Yass has now spent $30 million backing Mr. Ramaswamy.

Mr. Yass and Mr. Uihlein have each now donated well over $100 million this cycle to federal political committees.

And then there’s Mr. Musk, who backed a few Republican groups beyond S.L.F., including about $89 million he gave to his own super PAC. In sum, Mr. Musk disclosed on Thursday a total of about $289 million in third-quarter contributions to federal committees, making him the biggest known midterm donor.

Mysterious dark-money groups are everywhere.

Several political groups made disclosures on Thursday that did not actually disclose much of anything about the true origins of their cash.

That is a reflection of the rise of dark money, with both parties relying more heavily on nonprofit groups that are not legally required to report the identities of their donors.

A lot of Democratic money traces its way back to super PACs with names like Government That Works PAC, Your Community PAC, and United Futures. Those groups, in turn, got their cash from a battery of liberal dark-money nonprofit groups.

The main Democratic Senate super PAC raised a majority of its money in the third quarter from dark-money groups, according to an analysis of its donors.

On the Republican side, a super PAC called Defend Us PAC, which is spending against Mr. Talarico in Texas, said it raised $8.3 million last quarter. Of that, $6 million came from a group called the American Prosperity Caucus Inc., which does not appear in state records in Georgia, where it says it is based.

And most of the money raised by a super PAC backing Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, $5 million, came from a dark-money nonprofit in Delaware nonprofit that was created in May.

There are plenty of other examples. Confused? In modern campaigns, that’s the point.

There were other revelations, too.

Here are a few other things that caught our attention in the third quarter:

- Democrats are getting $38 million worth of digital help at the last minute from a new super PAC. That group, Lower Costs Now, received that much in late September.
- Trump administration officials continue to be major donors to political causes even while serving in government. The ambassador to Britain, Warren Stephens, and the White House chief design officer, Joe Gebbia — both of whom are billionaires — each donated over $1 million to Republican efforts.
- The Republican Governors Association seems particularly invested in electing Zach Lahn to lead Iowa. The group’s super PAC sent $12.5 million to his campaign, an investment it did not make for any other candidate.
- A super PAC for the sports-betting industry, Win for America, has now raised $82 million this cycle, making it one of the wealthiest industry interest groups in the midterms. About half of that sum has come from the company DraftKings.

About the data

Fund-raising figures in the graphics include total contributions to each candidate’s main campaign committee, not including refunded contributions and contributions that candidates made to themselves. The totals also include transfers to the main campaign committee from other committees.

One summer around 14 years ago, a young elk ditched the American mainland, swam alone to a misty island and never left. “Everyone has a Bruiser story,” said Margaret Nichols, 71, who lived on Whidbey Island for years and returns monthly. Whidbey Island was enough for Bruiser.

ARTICLE

Bruiser the Elk Left His Herd for an Island and Made It Home
After swimming across chilly waters to Whidbey Island in Washington State, the solitary elk charmed residents for more than a decade with his antics. He died at 15 to 18 years old.
By Ishani Desai
Published 2026-10-16 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/elk-whidbey-island-bruiser-dead.html

One summer around 14 years ago, a young elk ditched the American mainland, swam alone to a misty island and never left.

The animal chose Whidbey Island, a stretch of rolling hills and steep bluffs north of Seattle. Known as Bruiser, he was the only one of his kind on that strip of land. And now, the elk — who enchanted locals with his ironclad loyalty and wily antics — has died, leaving residents heartbroken.

“Everyone has a Bruiser story,” said Margaret Nichols, 71, who lived on Whidbey Island for years and returns monthly.

To a degree, she said, Bruiser was the island’s mascot, his likeness immortalized on keychains, earrings, T-shirts and stickers. “We were practically hyperventilating,” Ms. Nichols said of the first time her family saw him.

But why did a nearly 1,000-pound, 6-foot-tall wild beast inspire such devotion?

The elk was to some a unifying animal, which was welcome for an island divided along political lines like many other communities. He had come to symbolize conservation and independence and his presence reassured some residents that they chose correctly when trading the bustling city life for a quiet island.

Whidbey Island was enough for Bruiser. So he was right for the people, too.

And Bruiser, who had a penchant for snacking on apples he found on trees in people’s yards, was entertaining in his own way.

His antlers somehow became hopelessly entangled in all sorts of things: a bicycle, yard art, clotheslines. He often butted against fences and tarps, residents said.

“He was always up to something,” said Cynthia Mason, 64, a resident on Whidbey Island. “There was a little mischievous side to him.”

The island, about 169 square miles covered in lush forests, beaches and stunning cliffs, is a study in contrasts. The U.S. Navy erected an air base on it in the 1940s, at one point housing more than 11,000 people. There’s agriculture: farmers growing tomatoes, peppers and berries. Some of the island’s 71,000 residents commute by boat 75 minutes or longer each way to Seattle for office jobs, locals said.

Bruiser once was a member of the North Cascades elk herd managed by the state and the Point Elliott Treaty Tribes in Skagit Valley, Wash., about 60 miles north of Seattle. The herd is the northernmost pack in the state. At about 1,600 animals, it is the smallest of the 10 herds recognized by the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife.

For motives unknown, Bruiser braved chilly waters and dangerous currents in Skagit Bay, leaving the U.S. mainland and arriving on the island’s shore around 2012, said Kurt Licence, a wildlife biologist with the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. The route is about two to four miles, though it is not exactly known what course Bruiser took, Mr. Licence said.

The morning of Sept. 13, 2012, Fred Goodman was walking on his property near Strawberry Point, by the eastern shore of Whidbey Island. There, he spotted a tawny coat and antlers, much to his astonishment.

Mr. Goodman, who spent a career in wildlife management, knew.

It was an elk.

An elk had not been spotted on Whidbey Island for more than 100 years after the island’s elk population was hunted to zero around the early 1900s, officials and residents said.

At the time, Mr. Goodman called an officer with the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Ralph Downes, who confirmed that an elk was roaming Whidbey.

The local newspaper, The Whidbey News-Times, published a story recounting how the elk had graced its shores, Mr. Downes said, and word spread. The newspaper documented a relationship between Mr. Downes and Bruiser, with the officer receiving about a half-dozen calls about the elk’s exploits in a single year.

A well-known Bruiser tale involved him playing with a rope swing attached to a buoy in February 2017. The rope was wound around the antlers, and the bull couldn’t get it off.

Bruiser bucked and thrashed when Mr. Downes and others tried to free him. He ran, but the buoy kept hitting his face, and Bruiser became more angry, Mr. Downes recalled.

He crashed in the woods, went over a bluff and fell on a beach, still furious and wearing the unwanted crown, he said.

Mr. Downes was part of a group that tranquilized Bruiser. “He woke up just as pissed off as when he fell asleep,” he said. “He wasn’t very thankful.”

Perhaps Bruiser longed for a way back to his herd. During the rut, or the mating season when an elk becomes more aggressive, he would be spotted bugling — making a mating call — toward the Washington State mainland.

Despite his frustrations, Bruiser stayed.

Ansel Santosa, 35, and co-owner of the Ballydídean Farm Sanctuary, said Whidbey Island’s politics are narrowly split. Only 33 votes separated the Republican from the winning Democratic candidate for governor in 2024 in a district that includes the island. But Bruiser was a topic everyone could rally behind. He never saw the animal, and yet felt a special connection from the pictures posted on social media.

“He gave me hope that we could become part of the community in that way,” Mr. Santosa said.

After Bruiser’s death, The News-Times published a 1,602-word tribute to “the neighbor who never paid rent.”

As he grew in years, the residents’ love for Bruiser grew. But the beast — who was anywhere from 15 to 18 years old — grew haggard. Bulls rarely live more than 12 years, according to the state’s Fish and Wildlife Department.

Detective Sergeant Ed Wallace, a spokesman for the Island County Sheriff’s Office, recalled a video posted about a week before Bruiser’s death, which showed the elk had damaged antlers and was moving with a limp.

On Oct. 6, the sheriff’s office was called at about 1 p.m. to a private property for a report of a dead elk. A couple came across the carcass while walking on the beach, the detective sergeant said.

It was Bruiser. He wasn’t shot. He was at the base of a cliff with his antlers broken.

Perhaps, Mr. Downes said, Bruiser wanted one last glimpse across the bay from the top of the cliff. He had left behind his herd, but had found a new place to belong, Mr. Goodman said.

“Maybe we were his herd,” he said.

SUMMARY

Terence Tao is typically described as one of the world’s greatest living mathematicians, but right now he is doing very little math. Theoretical, or “pure” math — the math of Dr. Tao — is loved as much for its art as its science. To Dr. Tao, the next few years will require the reinvention of math, or at least of math education.

ARTICLE

Why One of the World’s Greatest Mathematicians Is on a ‘War Footing’
The Fields Medalist Terence Tao is on the front lines of a debate about artificial intelligence and the future of his field.
By Elisabeth Bumiller
Published 2026-10-16 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/math-ai-terence-tao.html

Terence Tao is typically described as one of the world’s greatest living mathematicians, but right now he is doing very little math.

“I’m on a war footing,” he said while grabbing coffee during a two-day math workshop at the University of California, Los Angeles, that was rife with talk about the existential crisis that artificial intelligence has created in his field.

Days earlier OpenAI had announced that it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven “Millennium Prize problems” that had stymied the greatest minds in math for nearly a century.

“There are no rules any more,” Dr. Tao, 51, said in an interview before the workshop in his modest office on the U.C.L.A. campus, his home since 1996, when he arrived after completing his doctorate at Princeton at the age of 20. “I’m just numb to what would have been jaw-dropping events for me a year ago. At some point, maybe I’ll get hit by a whole wave of PTSD.”

Instead he was hit by a bigger bomb on Oct. 6, when OpenAI released more than 350 findings in nearly every subfield of the profession, including algebra, number theory, theoretical computer science, mathematical logic and topology. Stunned mathematicians, some who were close to solving problems they had worked on for years, found themselves beaten in an instant by A.I.

Dr. Tao, who has been a tenured professor since the age of 24, said senior academics like himself are not as threatened by A.I. as those starting out. But the math world is looking to him for answers. He has accepted that his celebrated status has made him an unofficial spokesman for the field, a job that for now is consuming most of his time.

Until recently his job was as a bridge between the slow-moving world of higher math and the scorching speed of A.I. Dr. Tao, who uses A.I. as an assistant to run calculations, write code, search vast troves of literature and brainstorm ideas, has been experimenting with OpenAI’s models since 2023. He was an enthusiast for a “best of both worlds” future.

OpenAI’s releases have now left him feeling used. “As recently as a year ago, I had a pretty good relationship with many employees at OpenAI,” he said in a recent phone conversation.

“A lot of people I interacted with shared a very common vision of how A.I. should be used — you know, to empower scientists.” But the rush to publish new findings, he said, shows their true purpose. They “used math for what they needed, which was to evaluate their models,” he said. “At this point, I don’t see a way to constructively engage.”

His anger was clear in a post on the widely read math blog Proofs and Prompts after OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release. “I am horrified by the many person-years” of research, particularly by young mathematicians, “being casually disrupted or destroyed,” he wrote.

“Much as one cannot unhear a movie spoiler or a crossword clue, one cannot explore a problem as profitably and richly once one is aware of an existing solution.” He mourned, he added, “the path not taken, and the opportunities lost in the frantic race to develop this technology.”

As Much Art as Science

At the heart of the crisis in the profession is a menacing question. If solving hard problems is a mission of math, what happens when machines can do it faster? So much of higher math — hiring, promotions, graduate training and acclaim — is based on the difficulty, quality and the impact of papers (the written documents explaining proofs) that a mathematician produces.

The consensus is that A.I.-assisted problem solving is the inevitable future, but no one knows exactly what that new world will look like. “Deep uncertainty will persist in these next years,” a draft report by a group of mathematicians meeting at Harvard on Ph.D. education concluded last month.

A.I. does offer “exciting new possibilities” the report reassured. But implicit in its pages was the sense of loss among humans drawn to math for the intellectual adventure of problem solving — often deeply frustrating, sometimes thrilling and euphoric if a personal breakthrough leads to an advance in the field.

“You’ve had epiphanies, right?” Ravi Vakil, a prominent Stanford mathematician and the president of the American Mathematical Society, asked in an interview. “Suddenly everything in the room becomes clear.”

Theoretical, or “pure” math — the math of Dr. Tao — is loved as much for its art as its science. Its primary goal is to add to the understanding of the vastness of math itself. Unlike applied mathematicians, who have generally embraced the power of A.I. to help them solve practical problems in engineering, finance, weather forecasting and other sciences, pure mathematicians study shapes, structures, numbers and abstract concepts.

Still, pure math ultimately has led to, among many other advances, the creation of the internet, microchips, GPS, cybersecurity, encryption, CT scans and other medical procedures. In 2006 Dr. Tao and three partners created the mathematical theory of compressed sensing, which sped up the scan times of MRIs. Today MRIs can produce real-time images of the beating heart, and many children can be scanned without sedation.

‘Screaming for Help’

He may say he is battle ready, but Dr. Tao hardly projects as a warrior. In his office, he spoke softly in a lilting Australian accent, was self-deprecating, occasionally funny, upset about the relationship he once had with OpenAI and far from the stereotype of a tortured, brooding math genius. He is known for his sunniness in the rarefied realm of pure math, and students remark on his modesty.

He was dressed in faded blue jeans and a loose polo shirt that seemed to hang absent-mindedly from his slight frame. A blackboard that ran nearly the length of the room was covered with computations by one of his three current Ph.D. students, Ben Goldman. Nearby was the bike Dr. Tao had ridden to work, with his lunch from home in a plastic bag strapped onto the rack over the back wheel.

“It’s leftovers from three days ago,” he said.

He spends much of his time in what he calls “community organizing” — pulling together groups of mathematicians, strategizing, responding to the media, delivering lectures on A.I., counseling. “It’s someone screaming for help,” he said. “I can’t help them because I have no bandwidth, but I can identify somebody else they can talk to.”

His own 20-year-old blog has become math’s front page, filled increasingly with guest posts from others but also notes from the graduate class he is teaching and breaking math news. The day he posted a statement he signed along with 24 other winners of the Fields Medal, math’s version of the Nobel Prize, that called OpenAI’s math “detrimental” to the field, his blog shot to 100,000 views.

“My wife says I’m The Huffington Post,” he said.

His lightheartedness faded as he talked about appearing in a promotional video for OpenAI earlier this year. Its roots were in the Trump administration’s suspension last year of $600 million in research grants to U.C.L.A. that threatened the existence of the university’s Institute of Pure and Applied Mathematics, where Dr. Tao is director of special projects.

Dr. Tao reached out to OpenAI as part of an emergency fund-raising drive, and the lab agreed to sponsor a workshop at the institute for what Dr. Tao said was $60,000 to $70,000. It was held in March, when OpenAI conducted an hourlong video interview with him in which he talked about the benefits and risks of A.I.

He expected the entire video to be posted. OpenAI instead cut it to one minute: “I think it’s ready for prime time,” Dr. Tao says of A.I. as he writes rapidly on a blackboard and a soundtrack of joyful music seems to urge him on.

He gave OpenAI permission to use the ad, he acknowledged in his blog. But in retrospect, he wrote, he should have “pushed back harder.”

An OpenAI spokesman, Laurance Fauconnet, said in a statement that “we value our engagement with Terence and the wider mathematics community.” The lab, he said, is “working with the community to turn progress in A.I. into deeper human understanding and new discoveries, and we will continue to act on its feedback.”

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Dr. Tao was not impressed with the writing in OpenAI’s proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. “It is technically readable,” he said. “But no expert I’ve talked to has actually understood the whole argument.” He said the writing is better in the latest release, though he called it a “mixed bag.” Some papers appropriately cited his work, he said, and seemed to have advanced it in a way he thought was plausible. Still, “there is no author that I can have a real conversation with about the results.”

Dr. Tao was aware last month that OpenAI was working on the Oct. 6 release and at the time called the coming results “toxic waste.” Now he calls them “maybe treated waste.”

A 760 on the Math SAT at Age 8

The first day of the math workshop — the topic was the field of partial differential equations “in the age of A.I.” — got underway in a small auditorium at 9 a.m. The institute’s director, Dimitri Shlyakhtenko, welcomed several dozen academics, including a batch from Harvard, Princeton, the University of Tokyo and Sandia National Laboratories, the home of the nation’s nuclear stockpile testing. The room was expectant, waiting to hear from Dr. Tao on what he thought A.I. might have in store for them.

“Our first speaker does not require introduction,” Dr. Shlyakhtenko said.

Indeed he did not. As Dr. Tao popped up from his seat to take his place at the lectern, it is safe to say that most in the room already knew him as a legend. Born to Chinese immigrant parents in Australia, he taught himself to read at the age of 2, scored 760 on the math portion of the SAT at 8 and won his Fields Medal at 31.

The medal was for his advances in harmonic analysis — the study of breaking down complex waves into simpler ones — but also for work in partial differential equations and the fields of additive number theory and combinatorics. The Fields Medal Committee cited Dr. Tao for his most famous work, with the mathematician Ben Green, on what is known as the Green-Tao theorem, which proved that there are arbitrarily long, evenly spaced sequences of prime numbers — a monumental achievement in the field.

Up at the lectern at U.C.L.A., Dr. Tao began with an apology. His plan, he said, had been to spend the summer developing a “living spreadsheet,” or network, built and maintained by A.I., of academic results about explicit analytic number theory, an unforgiving subfield of math. “But I’ve been a bit distracted in the last few weeks, and I have not actually devoted as much time to this project as I wanted to,” he said.

He finished with another apology. The network was not complete. He had budgeted all of September to get it done, but “some things happened in the meantime.” The crowd chuckled knowingly.

The most intense discussion on A.I. came after lunch. Sometimes it seemed like a group-therapy session.

“As we soul-search about what the role of the human mathematician is, shouldn’t we go back to where mathematics came from?” said Tatiana Toro, the director of the Simons Laufer Mathematical Sciences Institute at the University of California, Berkeley.

Andrea Bertozzi, a U.C.L.A. professor of math and mechanical and aerospace engineering, said that one thing she liked about college math was that “you sat down with your pencil” and coffee and paper, “and you could prove things.” She brought up the cost of solving Navier-Stokes, which OpenAI said took a swarm of 10,000 agents 88 hours to produce a 165-page proof. Was it “something like $6 million?” she asked.

“More like 22,” someone in the audience said.

This led to a round of comments that the cost of A.I. is undemocratic, particularly to mathematicians in developing nations. “Half the world is going to fall behind,” Dr. Toro said.

Dr. Tao, who had the last word, agreed that the field needed to do some soul-searching. But, he mused, given how fast things were moving, maybe he was doing “soul-searching at gunpoint.” At that point, the room laughed.

‘The Elephant in the Room’

Mr. Goldman, like Dr. Tao’s two other Ph.D. students, is facing an ambiguous future. He is 25, a graduate of the University of Chicago and now in his fourth year of a five-year program. He doesn’t know what he wants to do after he gets his doctorate, but he said he has long been drawn to the creativity of math research.

“I’m not saying I was necessarily trying to prove the thing that’s going to be in every textbook 30 years from now,” he said. But he would be happy with a proof “that feels like the argument is me somehow, that has my DNA in it and that people will at least for that one result want to know the way I thought about something.”

After the latest OpenAI release, Mr. Goldman said he was plowing ahead with the research for his dissertation, “even if it can be made obsolete by some messy manuscript released by these companies in the next coming months.” He was upset, he said, “to see a field that I love being sort of strip mined.”

Siddharth Mulherkar, a fifth-year Ph.D. student of Dr. Tao, is applying for postdoctoral research jobs for next fall, the next step on the long pursuit of a tenured professorship. Dr. Tao has given him, like the others, the OK to use A.I. in his work. And yet when he discloses on a job application that A.I. helped with the proof he submitted, how will he himself be evaluated?

“Obviously I don’t want to just be pushing buttons and getting answers to problems,” said Mr. Mulherkar, 27, who was born in California but moved to India with his parents and lived there until he arrived at U.C.L.A.

OpenAI’s latest release, he said, has made him even more uncertain. “I’ve spent quite some time training to become a research mathematician in the traditional sense,” he said. He knows he’ll need new skills, but what they are and “what this career is going to look like and what it will value is completely unclear to me.”

Arian Nadjimzadah, 26, another fifth year Ph.D. student of Dr. Tao, said he was shocked by OpenAI’s latest release claiming to have solved the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and other problems related to his own work. “I had to take a couple days from working on math,” he said.

He was particularly frustrated, he said, with the writing in OpenAI’s proof explaining the conjecture. “The result is extremely difficult to read and uses very unfamiliar jargon to us in the field,” he said. “That’s the nice thing when a person posts a result. They’re accountable. They give talks about it, and they help people understand.”

Mr. Nadjimzadah is studying this academic quarter at the Institut Mittag-Leffler outside of Stockholm and is looking for a postdoctoral job. At the advice of Dr. Tao, he is including in his job applications how OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release connects to his current work and future plans.

“He just said it’s important to address the elephant in the room,” Mr. Nadjimzadah said.

Therapy Sessions

To Dr. Tao, the next few years will require the reinvention of math, or at least of math education. The Harvard report recommended, essentially, that math become more human-centric: Doctorate degrees should not be rewarded primarily on the text of a dissertation, as they are now, but more on a rigorous in-person defense. Students should regularly show professors they can speak fluently about their work.

Dr. Tao went further last week when he presented what he sees as the future of math in a lecture at the California Institute of Technology. Despite OpenAI’s releases, he said, most problems at the frontiers of math are unsolved, math remains infinite and the difficulty of problems is therefore boundless. Since A.I. has given mathematicians the ability to collect data on such a vast scale, they will increasingly work in large groups collaborating on once-unimagined projects.

Dr. Tao, who sees each of his three students once a week, said every meeting is “increasingly a therapy session more than technical guidance.” His answer to them is that “if you focus on only the things you could do before, it looks bleak.”

So he has offered hope with advice that amounts to acceptance born of necessity rather than fighting a war. Problem solving is not a destination but a journey, and lessons learned along the way are often more important than the answer itself. Rather than solving a single problem on their own, they can use A.I. to solve 10 problems and find new patterns and more questions to ask.

“They will have to use their imagination,” he said. “This is a time for creativity, and I do hope students rise to the challenge. They didn’t ask for it. But I think many of them will surprise us.”
