ARTICLE

M.I.T. Scientist Wins $6 Million in Sexual Harassment Defamation Suit
David Sabatini, once a prominent scientist at M.I.T., sued a former colleague who accused him of inappropriate behavior. A jury found in his favor.
By Mark Arsenault
Published 2026-10-17 01:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/mit-scientist-sexual-harassment-defamation-lawsuit-david-sabatini.html

A prominent Massachusetts Institute of Technology biology professor forced out of his job over sexual harassment allegations won a defamation case against his accuser on Friday, along with a $6 million award.

The biologist, David Sabatini, was among the most prominent scientists in his field, and ran a research lab at the Whitehead Institute, in Cambridge, for 24 years. His lab studied cellular biology to better understand neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, diabetes, and aging.

He was forced out of his lab in 2021 after an internal Whitehead investigation concluded he had a past sexual relationship with a younger and less experienced colleague, Kristin Knouse, over whom he had a career-influencing role. The investigation also found that his lab had maintained a sexualized atmosphere. Dr. Knouse said that the relationship was coerced.

But Dr. Sabatini denied his lab had an improper atmosphere. He maintained that his relationship with Dr. Knouse had been consensual and that Dr. Knouse had schemed to get him fired and disgraced after he became interested in another woman.

“It’s surreal,” Dr. Sabatini, 58, said in a phone interview after the verdict. “I’ve been dreaming about this moment for all this time, but often thinking I might not make it, financially, emotionally or physically.”

Nearly five years to the day after he filed his defamation lawsuit, a Suffolk County jury agreed with him, finding that Dr. Sabatini had proved in court that Dr. Knouse had defamed him and interfered with his ability to work.

The jury rejected Dr. Knouse’s counterclaims that Dr. Sabatini had harassed and retaliated against her.

Dr. Knouse’s lawyer, Ellen Zucker, said in an interview Friday evening that Dr. Knouse would appeal the decision.

“The sad reality of our time is that society still has a difficult time believing women and appreciating the difficulty they encounter with men who too often control their fate,” Ms. Zucker said. She said Dr. Knouse “came into court and told the truth.”

Dr. Knouse is an assistant professor of biology at M.I.T. and on the faculty of the Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research, which is affiliated with M.I.T.

Dr. Sabatini’s career was derailed by the allegations. After he was pushed out of M.I.T. and the Whitehead, he had talks with New York University about a job. But N.Y.U. staff members and students protested in the streets against his hiring in 2022, and the university did not hire him.

In 2023, he was hired by the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry, in Prague, and later opened a Boston-area branch of that institute. He has been splitting time between Massachusetts and the Czech Republic.

Dr. Sabatini said he hopes the verdict is a step toward regaining his reputation. “Before, I was judged as having a great lab and for providing great mentoring,” he said. “For the most part my trainees have been there for me through this.”

“I hope that I can get back to being judged by my science and my training,” he said.

The Whitehead Institute, in a statement after the verdict, said that earlier legal claims against the institution had already been dismissed, adding, “Therefore, Whitehead was not a party to this case, and the decision and judgment only apply to Drs. Sabatini and Knouse, the parties in the case.”

A spokeswoman for M.I.T. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Most of Ken Paxton’s Money Can Be Traced to One Man: Elon Musk
The world’s richest person, who has become the biggest known midterm donor, gave $158 million to a group that quickly spent that much to help Mr. Paxton’s Senate bid in Texas.
By Theodore Schleifer
Published 2026-10-16 04:51 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/politics/elon-musk-ken-paxton-texas-senate-race.html

If Ken Paxton wins in Texas, he may have Elon Musk to thank.

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest person and a Texas resident who has major business interests in the state, sent $158 million in September to a super PAC that immediately flipped that much money to a group backing Mr. Paxton’s Senate bid, according to campaign-finance filings released Thursday.

The donations from Mr. Musk, collectively some of the biggest ever recorded in American politics, have allowed Mr. Paxton to remain financially competitive even as he is vastly outraised by his Democratic opponent, James Talarico. Republicans in Texas have grown increasingly worried about the race, one of this year’s most expensive and high-profile contests, fearful of losing a statewide election in Texas for the first time in more than three decades.

Mr. Musk sent the money to Senate Republicans’ top super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, in donations of $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23. Each time, the very next day, the super PAC cut a check of the same amount to Texas PAC, a group that the Senate Leadership Fund had set up to support Mr. Paxton.

The money sent to the Texas group was not necessarily Mr. Musk’s, and super PAC officials have said publicly that they were seeking new donations to finance a pro-Paxton operation. But without Mr. Musk’s historic donations, it’s unlikely that such a large amount would have flowed Mr. Paxton’s way.

Rarely has an individual donor been effectively tied to such a large commitment for a single candidate.

The New York Times reported on Monday about Mr. Musk’s contributions to the Senate Leadership Fund and how they could end up helping Mr. Paxton, but the campaign filings offered more detail on the choreography of Mr. Musk’s donations.

Mr. Musk also donated $10 million to a separate pro-Paxton super PAC, money that allowed the group to start running television ads in late August. Mr. Musk, who lives in Austin, and Mr. Paxton, who as the state attorney general regulates Mr. Musk’s businesses in Texas, have been allies in state politics.

Mr. Musk has not shown much enthusiasm in public or private about any midterm candidates, rarely posting on X, his social media site, about Republican nominees. But in recent days, he has posted negatively multiple times about Mr. Talarico.

On the campaign trail, Mr. Talarico has criticized the political influence of billionaires like Mr. Musk.

ARTICLE

Katie Zacharia Is Ousted After 5 Days as White House Press Secretary
Her abrupt departure came after she was shadowed by questions about how she had presented her legal career and handled her first press briefing.
By Shawn McCreesh, Tyler Pager and Hamed Aleaziz
Published 2026-10-16 17:33 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/politics/katie-zacharia-fired-press-secretary.html

President Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was forced out of her role Friday after five days on the job, a rare reversal by the White House that capped a week of upheaval.

Ms. Zacharia, who had gained Mr. Trump’s attention as a conservative commentator, had gotten off to a shaky start with her first and only press briefing on Tuesday. She largely read off a script and ended questioning after just five and a half minutes. That was followed by an onslaught of headlines about whether she had misrepresented herself as a lawyer — the president called her “an attorney” — despite failing her bar exam.

Subsequent interviews she gave in the media, in which she tried to defend herself by pointing out how unprepared she had been to go before the Washington press corps, also went poorly.

Finally, after days of unrelenting press coverage, the Trump administration decided on Friday afternoon to do something it almost never does: It folded.

Mr. Trump was walking across the South Lawn to depart for a midterm rally in Georgia when he stopped to talk to reporters, telling them how he’d just encouraged his press secretary to “reconsider” her new job.

“Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” he told the reporters, recounting his conversation with her. “Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this.”

Three people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions, said Ms. Zacharia was ousted from her role as press secretary.

The president told reporters that Ms. Zacharia might continue to work for him “in some form, but maybe a more pleasant form.”

Later Friday, Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, said that Ms. Zacharia would be “transitioning into a new role that will be announced at a later date.”

Ms. Zacharia, in her own social media post late on Friday, wrote that it “was an honor to work for” Mr. Trump.

The president, she added, “is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to.”

Ms. Zacharia had just started on Monday, and hadn’t even moved to Washington yet.

It was last Friday that the president offered her the job. A little-known, unpaid Fox News commentator with whom many in the White House were unfamiliar, she was a surprise pick. While Ms. Zacharia did have the support of Natalie Harp, the powerful West Wing aide who rarely leaves the president’s side, others in the building believed her debut had been a disaster.

She was not a deft communicator.

She had represented herself as a lawyer in the news media, but when asked repeatedly by a New York Times reporter on the South Lawn of the White House to say in which state she had passed a bar exam, she twice replied, “When I moved to China.” She later told The Times that she had simply misheard the question — even though the president had repeated the reporter’s question to her while standing feet away.

The end was nigh after she appeared on Fox News on Thursday night to be interviewed by the president’s friend Sean Hannity, who asked her a few tough questions and treated her with rare skepticism.

The reception she got on Friday morning on “Fox and Friends” wasn’t exactly friendly, either.

“Do you wish you would have disclosed to the president about the bar and not passing the bar?” one of the hosts, Lawrence Jones, asked her.

“Well, Lawrence,” Ms. Zacharia responded, “those questions weren’t asked.” On Wednesday, Mr. Cheung had posted that “up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job.”

“At the end of this second term, she’ll be remembered as one of the all-time greats,” he wrote.

She may be remembered as having had what seems to be the shortest tenure in the history of the White House press secretary job: five days and one briefing.

In Mr. Trump’s first term, Anthony Scaramucci was fired as the White House communications director (a different role from press secretary) just 10 days after he was hired.

After news of Ms. Zacharia’s ouster broke, Mr. Scaramucci posted on X: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

The ousting of the administration’s top spokeswoman was the culmination of a week of remarkable turmoil inside Trumpworld.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece, was fired on television on Tuesday (during Ms. Zacharia’s only briefing). The president spent time in the Oval Office trying to get to the bottom of a vicious fight between two of his loyalists, Richard Grenell and Alina Habba Mildon.

Paolo Zampolli, a longtime Trump confidant who claimed to have introduced the president to his wife, was pushed out at the State Department after one of his internecine feuds spilled into the press. And the daughter of Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, and others in her circle, came under scrutiny for their moneymaking overseas.

ARTICLE

Is Retirement Unhealthy? It Depends.
As more Americans live longer and as the population ages, measuring the effect of retirement on physical, cognitive and mental abilities is a complex undertaking.
By Alina Tugend
Published 2026-10-16 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/well/longevity-retirement-health.html

This article is part of our Longevity special section on living longer and healthier.

Joe Casciani, a 77-year-old psychologist, always dreamed of playing the drums. But with his busy work schedule, he never had the time to pursue this passion.

In 2019, he stepped back from clinical work and during the pandemic bought some electronic drums, playing them with a headset so his wife couldn’t hear. Now he has a soundproofed studio behind his house in San Diego and plays with a band once a week at a local senior center.

“My whole life has been so cerebral and I just love the physicality of drumming,” he said.

Mr. Casciani could be considered a retirement success story. He is hitting all the important marks experts say are key to fulfilling retirement: a sense of purpose, socialization and stimulating mental and physical activity.

That’s no accident. Mr. Casciani, whose website, the Living to 100 Club, focuses on aging well, was very aware of the common belief around getting older: It’s a steady decline both physically and mentally.

While he knows that is often a part of later years, he pushes back against a retirement where “we talk a lot about what we lose.”

“I like to put the spotlight on what we gain,” he said.

As more Americans live longer and as the population ages — the percentage of people 65 and older in the United States has nearly doubled over the past 50 years — retirement is now measured for many in decades, rather than years. Understanding what that means and how much control we have over the later stages of life has taken on a new urgency.

Not surprisingly, measuring the effect of retirement on physical, cognitive and mental abilities is a complex undertaking. It involves disentangling factors like career status and satisfaction, voluntary or involuntary retirement, socioeconomic class and financial stability, and overall health and health choices — such as smoking.

There is also the difficulty of separating the effects of aging versus those of leaving the workplace.

With all those caveats, however, a 2025 analysis of 22 studies between 2013 and 2023 on the impact of retirement on cognitive functioning — drawn from a variety of countries — suggests “that retirement tends to decrease cognitive functioning and increase the rate of decline.” The international study, led by Chilean researchers, however, noted that “to fully establish a link between retirement and cognitive decline,” there must be more and better studies to reach a definitive conclusion.

Findings are also mixed in the area of physical health. So much in this area depends on the type of job and occupation one is leaving and why; retirement shows more benefits for those leaving physically demanding, low-quality jobs or poor working conditions.

Research does consistently show it matters significantly whether someone chooses to leave a job or is pushed out. Those who are forced to retire from highly satisfying careers that are a major source of their identity are more likely to experience depression after they leave the workplace than those who dislike their jobs or leave voluntarily.

Although the actual impact of retiring may be hard to tease out, there is more solid evidence about how to make the last stages of life as healthy and rewarding as possible.

But those are general guidelines, not prescriptions. For example, research shows that meaningful social connections are very important for both good physical and mental health, but it’s the quality not the quantity. Some need a wide group of friends they see frequently; for others, it can be a few close relationships.

Some studies have shown that in addition to friendships, joining or maintaining a membership in a group — something that meets regularly and is formed around a common interest — correlates with better physical and mental well-being in retirement.

Having a sense of purpose, while harder to define and establish than, say, an exercise routine or a book group, is increasingly seen as an important aspect of a satisfying retirement. It has been found in some studies to predict better physical health, and in others to protect against self-reported cognitive decline.

But purpose does generally decline over time, said Elliot M. Friedman, a professor of gerontology at Purdue University. During research for a paper that found sustained purpose in life is associated with slower cognitive decline, Professor Friedman and his colleagues looked at a decade of data from 9,800 Americans included in the Health and Retirement Study. Conducted by the University of Michigan, it used data from the Social Security Administration and the National Institute on Aging.

As part of that survey, participants were asked seven questions from what is known as the Ryff Scales of Psychological Well-Being to measure purpose, such as “I sometimes feel as I’ve done all there is to do in life,” or “I enjoy making plans for the future and working to make them a reality.”

There may be a number of reasons for reported decline in purpose as people age, Professor Friedman said. But he added that “opportunities for purpose and meaning in later life are just fewer and farther between as older people are expected to slowly detach themselves from society.”

There are even debates about how to define purpose. Is it doing something that benefits others? A legacy that lives on after death?

“Purpose manifests in different ways, so there’s not a one-size-fits-all,” said Patricia A. Thomas, an associate professor of sociology at Purdue and a co-author of the paper on sustained purpose in life. “Focusing on the small things that make you feel like you want to get up in the morning might be a simpler way to look at it than this giant, ambitious type of goal. It’s the small acts that can still be very meaningful and that can contribute to better cognitive function, better health and longevity in general.”

For example, Professor Thomas’s grandmother, Eileen Veselka Thomas, 95, retired from her job as a full-time nurse at 70 after her husband died. She continued to work part time until she was 88 as a registered nurse, but also joined a writing group led by professional authors and traveled widely.

She has finished a work of historical fiction around the conquest of Mexico, which has been accepted by a publisher.

“I had been wanting to write the book for years before I actually began, but I was too busy with my job and family,” she said in an email interview.

Ms. Thomas said she does not feel she has experienced cognitive decline as she has aged, so she doesn’t think writing the book has helped keep her mentally sharper, “but other people think it has.”

Ms. Thomas’s retirement crystallizes many of the trends experts see these days that can be connected with slowing down physical and mental health deterioration — including her decision to keep working part time after retiring and joining a writing group. Or in the parlance of academia, engaging in bridge employment and lifelong learning.

In Sweden, for example, the proportion of individuals who continue to work after starting to withdraw their pension has doubled, said Isabelle Hansson, a co-author of the study “Retirement as Risk or Relief?”

“On average, one-third of retirees continue to work in some way or another after retirement,” she said. “That shows that retirement is no longer like a permanent exit from the labor market.”

Whether later employment has a positive effect on health and well-being depends on why someone is looking to work; having to because retirement income and savings fall short can cause more stress versus wanting to work for enjoyment or a sense of purpose.

But even as people can try to fashion their lives to be as meaningful and healthy as possible in the latter years, much is out of their control. These include socioeconomic class, and the lack of affordable programs that serve the aging and support caregiving.

The Stanford Center on Longevity, with its New Map of Life, lays out a world where schooling, work and time-off are far more integrated and overlapping throughout a lifetime than they are currently.

“In the United States and beyond, 100-year lives will be common for those born today,” the introduction to the map states. “Yet, the social institutions, norms and policies that await these future centenarians evolved when lives were only half as long and need updating.”

Perhaps most important, people need to realize that the type of retirement they experience grows out of the type of life they have lived. Learning to be curious about the world, volunteering to help others and developing friendships has to start much earlier than 65.

As Baowen Xue, an associate professor at University College London and a co-author of a paper on the effect of retirement on cognitive functioning, said in an interview: “Your life after retirement already started when you were a baby.”

ARTICLE

Japan’s Leader Says She Loses Hours to Makeup and Chores. Opinions Abound.
Sanae Takaichi said she has a busier schedule than her male predecessors, a nod to the disproportionate share of household tasks in Japan that fall to women.
By Javier C. Hernández and Kiuko Notoya
Published 2026-10-16 09:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/world/asia/japan-women-makeup-chores.html

Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, stood at a lectern in Parliament this week fielding questions about the budget, Russia, an emerging political scandal and nuclear de-escalation.

Then came an inquiry about her schedule. Ms. Takaichi, the first woman in Japan’s history to serve as prime minister, seized the moment to make a point. She said her daily agenda was far busier than her male predecessors because she spends at least three hours on makeup, bathing, cooking and other chores.

“Finding the time to sit down and focus with a truly clear head is a challenge,” she told the room of lawmakers, a vast majority of them men. “I feel that, compared to a male prime minister, I might be spending an extra three or four hours on these tasks.”

Ms. Takaichi’s remarks have prompted debate in Japan, where women still shoulder a disproportionate share of household chores and face pressure to conform to rigid expectations known as midashinami, or looking presentable in public. These guidelines include wearing makeup (but not too much) and high heels while avoiding short skirts and low-cut tops.

Some of Ms. Takaichi’s supporters praised her remarks, saying she had helped bring attention to the extra effort women invest to succeed at work and the role they play in running households.

“Are they saying she should show up to the Diet barefaced?” Kotoe Hashimoto, a conservative writer, said on X, using the name for Japan’s Parliament.

But some lawmakers and commentators criticized Ms. Takaichi, a staunch conservative, saying she was promoting stereotypes about women.

Yoshiko Kira, an opposition lawmaker in Japan’s Senate, said in an interview that Ms. Takaichi was reinforcing gender norms and undermining efforts to improve women’s rights in Japan.

“I find it deeply unsettling that the prime minister would speak as if these specific expectations regarding appearance and demeanor are simply ‘the natural order of things’ — as if they were immutable, foundational premises that cannot be challenged,” she said.

Ms. Takaichi’s remarks came during a routine budget hearing on Wednesday in response to a question about a recent report that argued Japan’s prime ministers spend too much time dealing with legislative procedures.

The report, by NXJI Research, found that Japanese leaders can spend up to seven hours a day answering questions from lawmakers. The prime minister, the report found, is expected to attend Parliament sessions on average about 72 days each year, compared with 50 days in Britain and 13 days in Germany.

Ms. Takaichi, a self-described workaholic who gets “zero to three hours” of sleep a night, responded by describing the demands of her schedule. She said she “found it quite difficult to carve out time to sit down and think strategically about the direction our country should take or the kind of nation we aim to be.” She said she takes home a “mountain of paperwork” each day.

She went on to describe how her all-male team of aides has had trouble adapting to her schedule, not even setting aside time in her diary for makeup before television appearances.

“They haven’t quite gotten used to the fact that I am a female prime minister rather than a male one,” she said, eliciting laughter from lawmakers.

Ms. Takaichi has made a point of modeling traditional values while in office. She has spoken about caring for her ailing husband, cooking meals and cleaning her residence.

By some estimates, Japanese women take on more than three-quarters of household chores. That burden is exacerbated by the fact that many Japanese workers are expected to routinely work overtime — as much as 22 hours per month — according to recent surveys.

While Ms. Takaichi receives support in her official duties, she is not given a staff of butlers, chefs and gardeners, as in the White House.

According to an interview this year with Ms. Takaichi’s husband and former lawmaker, Taku Yamamoto, the official residence has limited domestic help. In the interview, published by the monthly magazine Bungeishunju, Mr. Yamamoto said that a cleaner comes to the residence once a week, but there is no cook. He sometimes orders pizza, he said, making sure to get the delivery person’s name so the order can get through security.

“Access to the building is so strictly controlled, it’s like being in a prison!” he told the magazine.

In Japan, it is relatively uncommon for families to hire domestic help; only about 2 percent of households employ housekeepers, according to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.

Ms. Takaichi, who vowed to “work, work, work, work and work” upon her election last year, has frequently highlighted her grueling schedule to reinforce an image of a down-to-earth leader. Her comments in July about her sleep schedule prompted debate in the country over work-life balance. At the time, she recounted that she spent a holiday weekend ironing undergarments, sewing fraying skirts and reinforcing loose jacket buttons.

Ms. Takaichi rose to power in Japan’s male-dominated political system and has embraced some policies that critics say erode women’s rights. As prime minister, she supported legislation aimed at preserving the male-only lineage of Japan’s imperial family. She also opposes changing a longstanding law that requires married couples to share a surname.

She has sometimes been subject to sexism, including commentary on her wardrobe, hair and makeup.

Midashinami is such a large part of the culture in Japan that schools do routine checks on hair, nail and skirt length, and workplaces enforce strict rules. While there are expectations about grooming for both women and men, in practice women often face more scrutiny.

Tokyo’s governor, Yuriko Koike, has apologized several times over the past few years for forgetting to wear lipstick at news conferences. Japan was abuzz earlier this year when a television anchor for NHK, the public broadcaster, rushed to the studio after an earthquake and appeared on the air wearing glasses and seemingly no makeup.

Some companies have worked in recent years to ease the burden on women. Japan Airlines last year relaxed its dress code, allowing flight attendants and ground staff to wear sneakers instead of high heels.

Outside a subway station in Tokyo this week, women expressed mixed views about Ms. Takaichi’s comments. Some said they were baffled how she could spend so much time on makeup and bathing.

Rina Sumi, 22, who works part time at a cafe, said that Ms. Takaichi’s remarks “weren't appropriate in this day and age.”

“Why bring up her gender like that — as if it were an excuse?” she said.

Mika Okado, 27, a nurse, said she spends an hour each day getting ready, including preparing a bento box for herself. She said she was surprised by Ms. Takaichi’s ability to devote so much time to her routine, adding that she admired her frankness.

“In a way, it’s actually quite refreshing — she’s speaking without overthinking it,” she said. “There’s a certain human quality to the fact that she isn’t calculating every move or anticipating how it might be perceived.”

ARTICLE

What Life Is Like in Kyiv as Russia Tries to Make It Unlivable
A day in the Ukrainian capital, a new kind of battlefield far from the front, where daily life means assessing — and accepting — deadly risks.
By Kim Barker, Maria Varenikova, Oleksandra Mykolyshyn and Jędrzej Nowicki
Published 2026-10-16 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/world/europe/ukraine-war-life-in-kyiv.html

The air-raid alarm went off at 3:11 a.m. but offered little warning. Within three minutes, the missiles started to hit, almost 10 teeth-rattling booms that jolted Nikita Horskyi and Alona Horska awake.

The couple launched into what has become a familiar ritual in recent weeks. Mr. Horskyi scooped up their two children. Ms. Horska assembled makeshift beds in the hallway. Their 16-story apartment building has no shelter, and they knew that two walls offered more protection than the exterior wall alone.

Mark, their 10-year-old, thought, “God, help us,” as he said he does after every explosion. He hugged his stuffed goose and curled up in the hallway on a thin mat and a pillow resembling a smiling green monster. Arina, 5, lay down on a blowup bed with sheets of pastel bunnies and hedgehogs.

The family fell back asleep, accustomed to this particular nightmare, until the next missiles hit, two of them nearby, including one that killed a pair of security guards. Mark woke to the sound of glass shattering outside. He fell asleep for a bit longer, then he and his sister got up for school. Soon the jet-powered drones would arrive.

“Of course, it affects my mental state and my nerves,” Mark said. “I have to come up with things to calm myself down.”

This is the story of the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on a recent Wednesday, and how life here has deteriorated. The Russian missiles come more often now, not just at night but all day.

In August, new Russian drones, powered by jet engines and capable of going up to 375 miles an hour, began streaking into cities in exponentially larger numbers. They hit almost without warning. Ukraine has not figured out how to consistently intercept them.

President Trump has recently lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales, pressured Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and suggested that Ukraine get a new president. He has said nothing about what Russia is doing to Kyiv. Moscow is killing more civilians in Ukraine than at any time since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

This Wednesday would be an average day. Not too quiet, not too loud. The air-raid alarm would go on and off seven times, keeping Kyiv under alert a total of about 10½ hours. Parts of the city would lose power and running water. Six people would die.

In the fifth year of war, Russia is trying to make the capital unlivable, drive people away and force Ukraine to capitulate. Kyiv, a city shaped like a heart, has become a new kind of battlefield far from the front in eastern Ukraine, where Russian forces have been unable to win the war.

Kyiv has given no indication that it will give up. But it will suffer.

People here once coped with major missile attacks every seven to 10 days and the occasional drone that made it past Kyiv’s defenses. Life was sometimes miserable, like during power cuts last winter. But it was often joyful, with “Blade Runner”-themed raves and pouty influencers parading down hipster streets with camera crews. That Kyiv has been muted. Life has become grayer.

Russia has threatened to knock out power, heat and water in Kyiv this winter. This month Moscow started trying to cut the city in two by hitting bridges over the Dnipro River, which divides the east, where rents are lower, from the west, where most people work.

Every decision, small or big, feels fraught with what-ifs that could be life-changing. People in Kyiv first decide where to sleep. A tent in a subway station. A car in an underground parking garage. A mattress in the hallway. A gamble in bed.

Shopping has turned into a Sisyphean task, because many larger stores make people leave when the sirens start. School is constantly interrupted, because children must go to the schools’ shelters for every alert.

Mark often finds himself in his school’s basement, which is rented out to a gym called the Shogun Fight Club.

There are punching bags, wrestling mats and concrete walls, but no desks or chairs. The children cannot study there. Some follow the paths of drones on apps.

Others play games, like one where a few boys pretend to be Ukrainian recruitment officers and then tackle other boys on the wrestling mats to send them to imaginary front lines. Or the one where the boys throw paper airplanes and paper drones at a burning building drawn on the gym wall in pencil, complete with people waving their hands for help.

The Decision

Anatoliy Kavunenko, 66, woke before dawn on Wednesday for his early shift. Despite the ongoing alert, he decided to go to his nearby job as a security guard. His wife, Antonina, packed him lunch: eggplant with garlic and buns stuffed with mushrooms. Mr. Kavunenko walked out the door.

About 5:12 a.m., the second round of ballistic missiles hit. Mrs. Kavunenko heard a thundering explosion and tried to call her husband. His phone rang and rang.

Every missile, every drone, changes a neighborhood’s life, a Russian roulette that has damaged thousands of buildings in Kyiv. When the alert ended at 7:05 a.m., people emerged into the acrid, smoky air that has blanketed Kyiv almost every morning for the past two months.

On the east side of the river, a missile set fire to garages over an area the size of a tennis court.

Mrs. Kavunenko, 64, ran there, still wearing her dark-green velvet pajama pants and a light black coat. Firefighters told her that one of the two burned corpses on the ground in front of her was the body of Anatoliy, her husband.

“My brain can’t accept that this black piece of coal is my Tolik,” she said, using his nickname. She held her hand over her heart and took a deep breath.

“Please help me. How can I find out if this is him?”

The Alarm

The Shogun Fight Club shelter doesn’t have room for all students during air-raid alerts, so they attend school in morning and afternoon shifts. Mark’s classes last from 8:30 a.m. until noon. Some days, he never leaves the basement.

Things were better on Wednesday. His fifth-grade class made it through math. In English, the children learned how to pronounce different rooms in a house. At 9:48 a.m., as students practiced the word “bedroom,” an alert went off. Some students cheered. Everyone packed their bags.

The rest of the morning was quiet. Mr. Horskyi, 36, risked driving his motorcycle over the bridge to his office in the frequently battered neighborhood of Lukianivka on the west side.

Mr. Horskyi’s office looks out at two buildings hit by jet-powered drones the week before. Moving trucks had shown up at one building. Mr. Horskyi, who has a business designing motorcycle clothing, had thought about moving, too.

“Sometimes I think that Kyiv is suffering even more than the cities located closer to Russia,” he said. “Right now, it’s like a tricky, tricky question, a tricky choice to leave or to stay. Because actually I love Kyiv.”

About 1 p.m., the air had cleared of smoke, and Oksana Stelmashchuk, 40, who lives a few blocks away, decided to go for a walk with her baby, Sophia. She looked up at an apartment building where pieces of window frames hung from blown-out windows, and stepped back.

Sophia was born into this reality, on Aug. 26, as drones hit a building next to the maternity hospital. Now, her baby was crying, so Ms. Stemaschchuk sat down on a bench in a nearby playground to feed her.

“All the playgrounds in our area are empty now,” she said. At 1:24 p.m., the air-raid alert sounded again. Ms. Stelmashchuk grabbed her phone to check what was flying: only one drone on the outskirts of Kyiv.

“It is still far away, my girl,” she told her baby.

The Jet Drones

At a nearby McDonald’s, which has been hit at least nine times, the menu was a shadow of its former self. All the attacks in recent months meant it had been stripped to the essentials — burgers and fries. There was no Coca-Cola.

At 3:29 p.m., the air-raid alert went off. Everyone inside the restaurant left for the nearby subway station, the customers hurriedly eating fries. Seventeen minutes later, the alarm ended. The workers filed back up the stairs.

Nearby, people waited for a tram. The air-raid alarm sounded again.

“We’re just so tired of it all,” said Heorhii Vasyliev, 52, who travels all over Kyiv for his construction job.

A drone hit in the distance, a low boom. “Oh,” he said, exhaling. “What can you call normal about any of this? Is this normal? Is war normal?”

On and off, off and on, the alerts continued. A drone on the west side of the river set fire to a Soviet-era, five-story apartment building, where mostly retired people lived. A charred piece of a balcony hung from a nearby tree. Firefighters rushed to put out the flames.

Inna Sadova, 68, who lives next door, was in her kitchen when the explosion shook her home. Her building has no shelter.

“The neighboring building has a basement, but a basement like that is more of a mass grave than a shelter,” she said.

The jet-powered drones kept coming, and the list of minor atrocities unknown almost anywhere else in the world continued. Two people died on the west side of the river when debris from a drone interception hit a parked car. Two more people would die on the east side after a drone hit a 12-floor apartment building about nine miles north of the Horskyi apartment.

The power went out in much of the city. The water, too, stopped working in parts of Kyiv. So did trams, trolley buses and parts of the subway on the west side. On the east, an entire district of high-rise apartment blocks blinked out, one after the other.

The Horskyi family made the best of it. They lost electricity for three hours, the first time in months, but it came back on, and they had water. In the early evening, they took their French bulldog, Marcy, for a walk, near a building that had been hit 10 days earlier by a drone, where Mark’s history teacher lives. Mark was fascinated that people still lived on the floor above the strike.

The children ate burgers for dinner. They brushed their teeth, put on their pajamas and climbed into their twin beds in their bedroom.

“I didn’t sleep very well last night,” Mark said. “I’ll probably fall asleep really quickly. I’ll just pass out.”

Still, it was a good day, all in all, the children said. Soon they turned off the lights.

Published 2026-10-17 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/arts/television/east-of-eden-florence-pugh-cathy.html

Zoe Kazan’s “East of Eden” makes her intentions for Cathy Ames, deftly personified by Florence Pugh, clearer in one scene than John Steinbeck does over the course of almost 600 pages.

Based on Steinbeck’s 1952 novel, the Netflix limited series devotes its second episode, “Cathy,” to the backstory of the book’s notorious femme fatale and possible Devil incarnate. In a flashback, we see her as cherubic child reading “Alice in Wonderland” in a field. A faceless older boy offers her candy and disappears into the nearby woods; Cathy, intrigued, toddles after him. Though the director Garth Davis doesn’t follow her down the rabbit hole, the sight of a tiny girl disappearing into the brush is unmistakably sinister.

The incident scars Cathy and trails her throughout the series, which traces the entirety of her extraordinary, damned life. Whenever she remembers it, Pugh’s face clouds over with resigned revulsion before re-calcifying into Cathy’s default expression of grim self-possession. The bruise of this childhood memory becomes darker, uglier and angrier every time a man — whether he’s her father, pimp or husband — tries to have his way with her. Her pain embarrasses and enrages her.

Unlike her grandfather Elia Kazan, who directed the film adaptation of “East of Eden” (1955), Zoe Kazan is too fascinated by Cathy’s motivations to let her be two-dimensional. Instead, she digs into Steinbeck’s subtext to excavate an astonishingly human portrait of a traumatized woman committed to self-preservation above all else.

Pugh, also an executive producer, does her part to flesh Cathy out with a performance that is sensational in dramatic moments and heartbreakingly precise in quieter ones. The choice to root Cathy’s ruthlessness in something so human as trauma is a risk, but one both the writer and actress take on with care.

Where Steinbeck’s Cathy Ames is larger than life, Kazan and Pugh’s is familiar and depressingly relevant. You can draw a straight line from their interpretation of Cathy to a modern-day character like Catherine, the sex trafficking victim turned serial killer of “Furious,” the hit Hulu crime drama. Their anger is palpable, their coping mechanisms warped, their sense of self inextricably tied to the damage wreaked by selfish men.

But Cathy and Catherine (played by a riveting Lola Petticrew) split in their reactions to the destruction they keep causing. Catherine’s lust for revenge weakens with every kill; Cathy, who began her journey to hell by setting fire to her parents’ house with them still in it, only feels more empowered.

For as much empathy as Kazan has for Cathy, she doesn’t shy away from the awful impact of her decisions. Cathy is not the only character in “East of Eden” who had a terrible childhood, but she is the only one who murders her parents, shoots her husband, leaves her children for dead and takes over a brothel by slowly poisoning its motherly madam (a terrific Martha Plimpton). Confronting Cathy only seems to make her more vicious. If anything, contextualizing her malice as a response to sexual trauma — one of the world’s oldest and most common evils — only makes her more terrifying.

Kazan’s take on Steinbeck’s villain has proved contentious. The book is thick with biblical allusions — it is based roughly on the story of Cain and Abel — and Cathy is more traditionally understood as an unholy version of Eve, the original temptress, or even Lilith, Adam’s treacherous first wife in Jewish folklore. For those who read “East of Eden” as strictly allegorical, turning Cathy into a flesh-and-blood person — especially since the novel suggests she was born a “monster” — is practically sacrilegious.

From the start, Steinbeck’s Cathy is more slippery and shocking than Kazan’s. While the series hinges on that eerie sight of the woods swallowing her up, the book’s introduction of Cathy describes a different, more visceral scene: Cathy’s mother finds her daughter in a barn, half-naked and bound, with two older boys. Cathy, seemingly in shock, offers no explanation, but the boys insist she lured them and tied herself up.

Many don’t believe them — but others, including Cathy’s own father, are more skeptical of her than of the boys. Without solid evidence to convict her, the novel’s narrator — not some omniscient authority but a tertiary grandson who frequently second-guesses himself — can only point to the vague queasiness she seems to inspire in people.

Whenever a boy found her alone, he says, he was magnetically attracted to “a force he could neither understand nor overcome.” When a teacher’s fixation on Cathy ends with him dying by suicide, the insinuation is that she pushed him to the brink. When she finally snaps, to devastating ends, the narrator takes it as proof that she was always irredeemable.

What Kazan’s adaptation proposes is that the simpler explanation is the true one: Cathy is the victim of a crime that scars her for life.

Decades later, Cathy’s long-abandoned husband, Adam (Christopher Abbott), finds her at the brothel she now owns. He is floored to realize the woman he once mistook for an angel is actually deeply bitter and won’t — or can’t — see the good in anyone. Caught out, Cathy brags about making men like her schoolteacher do whatever she wants, then notes that “all he wanted was to go to bed with me, a little girl.”

Adam’s response in the novel is that “he must have been very sorry about something” to die by suicide. But in the series, he doesn’t rush to defend the teacher’s honor; instead, he lets the implications of the revelation sink in. After years of confusion about her wretched actions, he can finally see their rotting foundations.

Kazan didn’t invent Cathy’s inability to shake off the pain of her past when taking such scenes from the page to the screen. She just moved it from the margins to the center, where it is impossible to ignore.

The viewer, like Adam, can then decide if Cathy deserves any sympathy — but it doesn’t particularly matter. The greatest achievement of Kazan’s “East of Eden” is that its audience doesn’t have to sympathize with Cathy Ames to understand her.

Ms. Branswell “saw the pandemic coming well before anyone was paying attention,” Dr. Ashish K. Jha, the White House Covid-19 response coordinator in 2022 and 2023, posted on social media after her death. By the end of March, Ms. Branswell had written about 50 articles about the pandemic.

ARTICLE

A Reporter Who Saw Covid Coming Has Died
Helen Branswell recognized the threat of the pandemic ahead of the vast majority of journalists and even medical experts. She was 69.
By Jeré Longman
Published 2026-10-17 14:49 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/health/helen-branswell-dead.html

Helen Branswell, a leading reporter on infectious diseases who wrote with foresight, urgency and clarity about the emerging danger of the Covid-19 pandemic, ahead of the vast majority of journalists and even many medical experts, died on Tuesday in Ottawa. She was 69.

Her death, in a hospital, was from complications of a recurrence of breast cancer, her sister, Brenda Branswell, said.

Ms. Branswell “saw the pandemic coming well before anyone was paying attention,” Dr. Ashish K. Jha, the White House Covid-19 response coordinator in 2022 and 2023, posted on social media after her death.

Reporting at the time for STAT, the medical and science news site, she posted on Twitter on New Year’s Eve 2019 about a report of “unexplained pneumonia” in China, saying, “Hopefully this is nothing out of the ordinary.” Two days later, she posted a South China Morning Post article about the outbreak and wrote, with more concern, “Not liking the looks of this.”

On Jan. 4, STAT published her first article on the “growing cluster” of unexplained pneumonia cases, in which she noted the possibility of “a new virus and perhaps even a new coronavirus.” By the end of March, Ms. Branswell had written about 50 articles about the pandemic.

That February, Ms. Branswell moderated a panel in Washington that included Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, the longtime director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. At that point, there had only been 13 confirmed cases of Covid in the United States, and Dr. Fauci said that the risk of the coronavirus spreading seemed “relatively low.”

Ms. Branswell, clearly skeptical, replied: “Explain to me why the risk is low, somebody. Because to me, when I look at this virus spreading, it’s spreading very efficiently.”

She continued: “Like, there’s no force field around China. It’s not going to stop there.”

This drew a blunter response from Dr. Fauci: “Is there a risk that this is going to turn into a global pandemic? Absolutely, yes.”

That was not the only time Ms. Branswell challenged the response of public health officials to the outbreak.

In an interview two months later with Dr. Robert R. Redfield, then the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, she asked why the agency had not held a public briefing in a month.

“You’re invisible now, sir,” she told Dr. Redfield. “Your agency is invisible.”

Rick Berke, the executive editor of STAT and a former reporter and editor at The New York Times, said in an interview that Ms. Branswell’s coverage “was the definition of authoritative and meticulous.”

She won a 2020 George Polk Award, the prestigious journalism prize, and was cited by the judges for her “relentless coverage of all aspects of the pandemic that became must reading for the medical community and the general public.”

She and two colleagues at STAT were named finalists for the 2021 Pulitzer Prize in breaking news reporting for their “prescient, expert and accessible” work.

“She was the best in the business of covering public health and communicable and infectious diseases,” Dr. Lawrence K. Altman, a physician and former medical reporter for The Times who befriended Ms. Branswell when both were covering the SARS epidemic of 2002 and 2003, said in an interview.

“I was always struck by how penetrating her questions were,” Dr. Altman added. “She had the ability to cut through the fog and B.S. to get to the heart of whatever was being discussed. She asked questions that often surprised scientists, questions about issues that the scientists hadn’t thought about.”

Mary Helen Branswell was born on May 19, 1957, in Sherbrooke, Quebec, roughly 100 miles east of Montreal. Her father, John Branswell, taught high school English and history. Her mother, Margaret (Steele) Branswell, ran a household of six children and later did clerical work.

Helen received a bachelor’s degree in English literature in 1978 from St. Thomas University in Fredericton, New Brunswick. Wanting to be a writer, she fell into journalism as a freelance reporter and then as a staff writer at The Daily Gleaner, a newspaper in Fredericton.

In 1986, Ms. Branswell joined The Canadian Press, serving in the news agency’s bureaus in several Canadian cities, and in London as its European correspondent. She covered politics, foreign affairs, health and sports. She was hired by STAT at its start in 2015.

Her interest in covering infectious diseases was spurred by the SARS epidemic, which began when she was reporting in Toronto.

At first, she found it stressful to wade through the dense jargon of scientific studies, but “she quickly got up to speed,” her sister said, adding that a three-month fellowship at the C.D.C. in 2004 was “career-altering” for Ms. Branswell.

She went on to cover Ebola, Zika and other outbreaks, as well as polio and influenza, and became known for her nuanced, evidence-based writing.

Ms. Branswell’s reporting was so vital during the coronavirus pandemic that William Hanage, a professor of epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, called her a “godlike figure to people who are infectious-disease epidemiologists” in a March 2020 interview with The Times.

Her understanding of the science, history and politics of the outbreaks she covered made her “a journalist who knew more than most of the experts she interviewed,” Dr. Jha, the former Covid response coordinator, wrote.

In addition to her sister, Ms. Branswell is survived by four brothers, Kevin, Larry, Rick and Jack Branswell.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the World Health Organization, wrote in a tribute that Ms. Branswell demonstrated “an unwavering commitment to evidence, science and truth.”

At a time “when misinformation competes with facts,” he added, “her reporting was a trusted source of clarity, honesty and insight.”
