SUMMARY

Advertisers are projected to spend more money on political ads in the 2026 midterms than in any previous election cycle. What are campaigns selling — and what do they think voters want? But I think that ad probably has stuck with me as one of the classic ads of just optimism.

ARTICLE

The Cringiest and Craftiest 2026 Midterm Ads
Sex, video games and grandparents on the campaign trail.
By Stephen Stromberg, Emily Keegin, Carlos Lozada and Jillian Weinberger
Published 2026-10-17 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/opinion/midterms-election-politcal-ads-voters.html

Advertisers are projected to spend more money on political ads in the 2026 midterms than in any previous election cycle. What are campaigns selling — and what do they think voters want? The Opinion editor Steve Stromberg examines the ads shaping these elections with the Opinion columnist Carlos Lozada and Emily Keegin, a photo editor and creative consultant.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Steve Stromberg: Just to get us started: I’m wondering, is there a political ad or a slogan that has really stuck with you? Maybe it’s the first one you remember or one that stood out, something that can really show how powerful these images, these words, these slogans can be when they really work. Carlos, why don’t you start?

Carlos Lozada: I think the one that I remember, from a young age, probably has to be Ronald Reagan’s “Morning in America” ad from 1984, from his re-election campaign.

Archival clip of “Morning in America”: It’s morning again in America. Today, more men and women will go to work …

And I think I remember it, in part, because my father just loved Reagan and I wasn’t so crazy about him. Not that I had strong, strong views at the time, but the ad was so optimistic. It kind of captures that very sunny Reagan vibe. The ad says, “It’s morning again in America,” and people are getting married and buying homes and raising the flag, and it’s like: Why would you want to go back to how things were four years ago? And, like, poor Jimmy Carter.

But I think that ad probably has stuck with me as one of the classic ads of just optimism. And that’s where the whole “Are you better off than you were four years ago” comes into it as well. The case was: Things are better. Stick with me.

Emily Keegin: The ad I go back to, over and over again, is the “Daisy” ad by Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964.

Archival clip of “Daisy” plays.

And the idea here is to play on fear and to say: Don’t you want someone you know will protect you and your family? And what’s interesting to me about this ad is that not only is it a horrifying ad to watch — it is incredibly effective — but that it’s then used over and over again in the ’70s. And then again during the 1984 re-election campaign, Walter Mondale used a very similar ad structure. And it’s the same concept. You use a child, and you place that child against the biggest fear that we have. This cycle, I think what’s interesting is how little fear we’re seeing in the advertisements that are becoming viral or that we see on the national stage.

Stromberg: In a headline, what’s the mood of this midterm election?

Lozada: I’m not one for vibe checks and mood checks and the like. But if we had to pick one, the mood of the midterms right now, to me, feels best captured by House Speaker Mike Johnson wondering aloud recently if maybe after the election he might have to move back to Louisiana and start a lawn care business. Those are not the musings of a confident man.

And meanwhile, on the Democratic side, you hear a lot about expanding the map, which is the term you always hear in elections when one side is just daring to dream and is so confident that it imagines blue spreading all over the place. So the expectations seem pretty cemented at this point for a big night for Democrats, so much so that I instinctively, in a contrarian way, I’m not trusting it. So we’ll have to wait for the vote.

Stromberg: With that, let’s start with our first ad. The Washington Post did an analysis of 8,000 midterm ads. The majority focused on the economy — affordability, housing, the cost of living. But the first ad we’re going to watch went in a different direction. It’s for Steve Hilton. He’s a Republican running for governor of California. Let’s watch.

Archival clip of “Just Try It, California,” plays.

What we just saw was a video of two young ladies on a bed, seemingly talking about one thing but then filling in an absentee ballot for Steve Hilton, the Republican running for governor. And then the ad ends by saying, “Steve Hilton for governor. Just try it.” Emily, you’re our California resident. What do you think?

Keegin: I think the reaction is just ick. It’s very, very icky. This one, because of its ick factor, I think, went viral. So at least we’re talking about it, I suppose. The question is: Does that make you want to vote for the man who created it? I’m not sure that you want to be sexualizing young women in 2026. I’m not sure that that’s going to inspire a lot of voters. Ugh, it’s just ick.

Stromberg: Carlos, what do you see here?

Lozada: Well, let’s just stipulate the creepiness and tackiness of the ad. I was just wondering, is this sort of like some older guy’s fantasy of what young lesbians are like? The Pride flag and the nose rings and the tattoos and the hair dye. Like, it was all a bit much. But that aside, two things really jumped out at me: One was the moment when the reluctant voter, who’s almost being coerced into voting for Hilton here, says, “What if my dad finds out?”

It reminded me immediately of the ads in 2024 when you have these progressive suburban women, married to Trumpy guys, who are secretly voting for Kamala Harris and they don’t want their husbands to know. Now, instead of keeping your vote secret from your conservative husband, it’s keeping it secret from your progressive parents. But it kind of paints voting, for one side, as this thing that you’re kind of forced to do, whereas voting for the other side is this thing that you’re free to do. It’s like this kind of liberation.

The only other thing I’ll say is that I don’t necessarily have a problem with ads that feature sex or imply sex. Sex has, for better or for worse, always been a political issue in the United States. This ad — the Hilton ad — it just uses sex to try to get us interested in the candidate without any substance to it. To me, that’s why it’s a fail. Not because it’s salacious but because it’s salacious with no other purpose except for being salacious.

Stromberg: Let’s stay on the West Coast and head far to the north, to Alaska, where I recently spent some time reporting on Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign. She is a Democrat, but you might not necessarily know that from this ad.

Archival clip of Mary Peltola ad plays.

Emily, what do you make of this? Peltola isn’t the most polished candidate, but she has a lot of “Alaska first” authenticity. Does that come through convincingly? Can you unpack some of the images that she uses?

Keegin: I don’t think this is a hugely successful ad, insofar as it’s pretty standard. I think we’ve seen this type of political ad a lot. And I, to be perfectly candid, don’t think that advertisements alone get a candidate elected, in the same way that I don’t think you bought the shoes on your feet because of an advertisement.

There’s a lot that goes into what we choose to buy or who we choose to vote for. Most often it’s about our relationship to the brand or our relationship to the party long term or who our friends and family members are supporting or what they’re buying on the shelves. I guess if you do look at all presidential campaign ads — say, starting in 1952 — you do notice that the winners tend to do a handful of things over and over again. And you do notice that the losers have a tendency to make certain choices over and over again.

To talk about good ads: Whether you’re a shoe brand or you’re a politician, you want to see the same principles that you use in classic propaganda, really, which is that you want a simple image and a simple slogan that, when seen together, inspire in the viewer a big and kind of complicated feeling. And that feeling can be hope. It can be optimism. It could be fear.

But look at classic 20th-century propaganda. Look at Rosie the Riveter. Simple image: arm up, eyes facing forward. Simple slogan: “We can do it!” And that together inspires in you some hope, some optimism. Or my personal favorite, Smokey Bear. Simple image: bear in a hat, pointing at you. And the text, “Only you” — so romantic, so powerful. “Only you can prevent wildfires.” And we want the same principles in advertising. You see it all the time. “Think different” is a classic example. If you’re speeding down the highway, you want to be able to engage with it and understand it easily and quickly.

If you’re scrolling, same. What Peltola’s doing here is something that doomed candidates have a tendency to do, which is that they center themselves in the ad, they focus on their biography and their accomplishments, and they show themselves politicking. And one of the biggest things that I think politicians do — a mistake that politicians make — is that they think they are more charismatic than they are and so they put themselves in their ads and clip pieces of speeches. And it’s just not as compelling as they think they are. You really want to create an advertisement that is Smokey Bear: Bear in hat says great slogan. And the best ads, the most popular ads, and the ones that stick have that.

And frankly, Hilton’s ad is terrible in comparison. We’ve just spoken about that. But it is something that sticks because it’s a simple image with a simple piece of text attached to it.

Stromberg: Carlos, what did you make of Peltola’s pitch here?

Lozada: You joked at the beginning that it might be hard to remember that she’s a Democrat from this ad. And to be honest, when I was going through these ads and I was watching them with my wife, I had to turn to her and be like, “Wait, she’s the Democrat in the race, right?” And she’s like, “Oh, of course she is. Right, right.” I just had a brain freeze for a second because of the ad. And I think that’s very deliberate. She literally says at the beginning, “Forget party, forget politics.” It’s trying to help voters forget that she’s the Democrat and all the baggage that label has.

What she doesn’t want you to forget is her N.R.A. rating, the fact that she stuck it to Joe Biden on the border, the fact that she’s pro-oil projects development. When she says something that seems vaguely critical of President Trump, she doesn’t even name him. She says, “I‘ve got no tolerance for any politician who uses their office to get rich.”

Stromberg: It could be even just a generalized attack on D.C.

Lozada: Yeah, exactly. It’s very anti-conventional politician. Like, “they’re all corrupt,” “pox on both your houses” kind of thing. It’s a smart move when you’re running in a state that Donald Trump won by 13 percentage points last time around. You recently wrote about Peltola, so I’d be interested in your thoughts on this.

There’s a moment in your piece, I believe — and correct me if I’m getting it wrong — where you’re talking to her and trying to get her to engage on, like, what a broader centrist or center-left vision would be like for the party on a national level. And she just doesn’t engage.

Stromberg: Totally.

She’s either not willing or not able to. And that comes across in this ad. It doesn’t feel like a pose. It feels like this is who she is. Alaska first, Alaska always, completely parochial, in kind of the smartest way.

Stromberg: That’s exactly right. It does come off as authentic. And as you point out, there are just a ton of Republican-coded issues highlighted in this ad. But one thing that did strike me is that, even though she emphasizes how Alaska-focused she is, she highlights a national issue, and that national issue is securing the border. And she’s a candidate, remember, in Alaska, which is as far north of the southern border as you can get and doesn’t have a huge undocumented population. It sort of shows the extent to which immigration has become a cultural issue that defines people’s political identity.

Lozada: And it’s not just saying that she favors securing the border: She says that she opposed Biden’s border policies. It’s also a sign of how she realizes that the Biden brand is not a strong one for the Democrats, and so she’s creating distance there.

Stromberg: Right. And she was in Congress during the Biden administration, and so she has to come back and say: Well, I wasn’t for all that. And this is one way that she does that. I mean, one way to look at the ad is that Alaska Democrats don’t need to worry too much about keeping the left on side and can go really hard for disgruntled Trump voters. And there are a lot of those in Alaska. And some of these other red to purple states.

Let’s move on to our next ad. This one is from Sarah Huckabee Sanders. She is running for re-election as governor of Arkansas. Unlike Peltola, her party affiliation is pretty clear in this spot. Let’s take a look.

Archival clip of “Work” plays.

What we just saw, for the listeners out there, is a young white man, in a dark room, playing video games and munching on chips and various other bad-for-you things. At the end, though, he puts on a tie and is presumably employed. So, Carlos, Huckabee Sanders is basically a shoo-in to get re-elected, but this spot drew a lot of backlash, with some MAGA guys calling it anti-white and anti-men. What do you see here?

Lozada: It’s an aggressive ad, to be sure. I mean, most welfare recipients in Arkansas are white, so I don’t quite grasp the racial complaint here. The gender one, I think, is more interesting. There’s a long history of personalizing political rhetoric around specific kinds of welfare recipients, casting them as lazy or as fraudsters. Reagan in the ’70s was quite good at this.

Sarah Huckabee Sanders, I think, is trying to have it both ways. First, she does blame Brad, when she introduces him: “Meet Brad. Brad has turned relaxing into a full-time profession.” And she stresses the word “choose,” that Brad has chosen to behave this way, to do this — that he’s choosing not to work. But then she also suggests that it’s really a matter of incentives. It’s not just that Brad has terrible character. It’s that the system is set up in such a way that if you tweak it, you create this requirement: Brad will clean up, put on a tie and get to work. It’s both kind of blaming Brad and blaming the system writ large.

I think it’s also easier to criticize her because this ad could’ve been done with a kind of generic voice-over, kind of a faceless narrator. But instead, she puts herself forward. You see Sarah Huckabee ——

Stromberg: She’s on the TV screen.

Lozada: —— on the screen, right at the beginning, and she says, “That’s why I launched a welfare-to-work requirement.” She’s very much taking full ownership of it in a way that these ads sometimes don’t do. One little detail that I find interesting in this ad is that there’s a sense in which she’s telling it with a bit of a wink. If you hear her voice at the very beginning, she’s not just saying, “Meet Brad”; she’s kind of laughing. There’s this little undercurrent of laughter as she’s saying it, and she’s like, “Brad has turned relaxing into a full-time profession.” There’s, like, a little smirk there.

What is that? Is that her mocking Brad a little bit, or is that her acknowledging that, look, this is a caricature? This is a little bit of a joke. It’s a little bit funny, because Brad does look funny. He’s throwing the cheese puffs in the air. They’re falling on his face. He’s way too into the video game. I mean, clearly that was a choice. I’m sure they shot this many times, and choosing to have her laugh a little bit when she’s saying those things is something very deliberate. When people inject that undercurrent of laughter into something they’re saying, they’re creating some distance from the point they’re making. They’re trying to say: Look, this is not exactly an attack. I don’t fully stand by this, but I’m just going to put it out there anyway.

The last thing I thought of is that, when I think of Brad as a character, I immediately thought of other fictional characters that are created in political ads, and I thought of Pajama Boy. If you remember Pajama Boy ——

Stromberg: Obama’s Pajama Boy.

Lozada: It’s this guy in this holiday onesie, drinking hot chocolate, talking about how you’ve got to sign up for Obamacare. And it also made me think of Julia. I don’t know if you remember “The Life of Julia.” It was this slide show that the Obama administration put out, showing all the ways that women are cared for by the state throughout their lives, from Head Start to health care. And that got some criticism because it had a nanny-state vibe. But I just imagined — I wonder what Brad and Pajama Boy and Julia would say to each other if they could sit down and talk about the role of government in their lives.

Stromberg: Emily, I would love to hear from you. What did you make of the laugh, if anything? What did you make of the imagery?

Keegin: Well I think the strangest part, for me, is that she put herself on the TV, and I understand this in the narrative of the story on it, but that’s not something that most candidates do. They usually put their opponent on the TV, and there are a lot of those ads. That’s a trope that’s been going on since the ’60s, really.

You put your opponent on the TV, and you talk, and you show the opponent flip-flopping or saying something that you think you disagree with. And the reason you put the opponent on the TV is that the TV kind of acts as a barrier and a remove from everyday life — from the concerns of the Everyman, and it isolates the candidate. So when I see her on the TV, there’s this Big Brother vibe, a little bit. It’s an interesting choice. I think it’s probably fine. It works fine for the ad, but it’s something most candidates don’t do — put themselves on the TV like that.

Stromberg: And it also does sort of feel like: Well, this is the state government that’s going to drop in and make you shape up and put on that tie.

It feels a little bit like an attempt to play into the alpha male/beta male thinking on the right. She’s making alpha males out of beta males like Brad, and maybe that chuckle is that we all kind of know a Brad in our lives. In the process, she gets to make the old “welfare queen” attack lines seem new and sort of less race-oriented. But to me, this all still feels a little bit like a throwback. Like an old, different era of Republican politics. Even the lazy-kid-living-in-the-basement thing feels pretty last decade. Does this work?

Lozada: Well, it’s also, weirdly, one of the more substantive ads I’ve seen in this campaign. It’s not just biographical. It’s not just shock value, like the Hilton ad. It’s engaging on a policy issue, and that feels like a throwback to me. Like maybe being substantive is a luxury you have when you are very likely to win re-election.

Stromberg: Or you have a record that has substance behind it, which not everyone, not every politician, can claim. OK. Let’s get to our next ad, our final ad. We’re looking at an ad out of Michigan from the Democratic Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed.

Archival clip of “Jan & Judy” plays.

For the listeners out there, we saw an elderly couple on a sofa discussing their grandson, Abdul El-Sayed. There are some images of El-Sayed campaigning with Bernie Sanders. At the very end, he emerges, gives the grandparents a hug. Carlos, this ad reminds me of when President Barack Obama referred to himself as a “skinny kid with a funny name” when he came to national attention in 2004. And Obama followed that up by talking about how his family’s from Kansas, his grandfather fought in Patton’s army. Is that what El-Sayed is channeling here?

Lozada: This ad, and in some ways this campaign, has given me a lot of Obama flashbacks to that period. There’s been efforts to paint Abdul El-Sayed as something of an outsider — just the way that the grandmother says it, like, “Where did Abdul El-Sayed come from?” She’s channeling that feeling. People have often used his full name, in a very unsubtle way, to depict him as sort of distant and foreign and untrustworthy — Abdulrahman Mohammed El-Sayed. And that’s just like Barack Hussein Obama, right? It’s a very similar kind of approach.

The opening of the ad, where you have the grandmother seemingly playing into that ominous, suspicious tone, before pivoting to the lovely “Here! We’re his grandparents!” It reminded me — it’s another Obama moment, but it’s actually about Obama’s opponent in 2008, John McCain. And there was that famous instance where it’s a McCain rally and an elderly white woman has the mic and she’s asking McCain a question.

Archival clip of John McCain rally, October 2008, plays.

And when I saw this ad, I felt like that face that the grandmother is making — where she’s pretending to be suspicious of him — that could have been the face of that woman that you never see at the McCain rally.

And finally, like Obama also, El-Sayed is relying on these lovely, white grandparents to vouch for him: Look, if you worry about me — worry about my name or something — look at Judy. Look at Jan. They’re harmless, they’re sweet, and they love me.

And that was not just the way that, I think, Obama felt compelled to use that part of his biography, but it’s also, in a weird way, how he picked Biden — this avuncular guy who you all know, who’s been there forever, who will be with me when I’m in the White House if you don’t quite know me or don’t quite trust me.

Stromberg: Emily, what do you see in this ad?

Keegin: Can I be a photo nerd for a minute? Can I talk about aesthetics just for a minute? Because I find there’s this really kind of beautiful overlap between how politicians want to present themselves either as the adult in the room — part of the establishment, having a long history of success — versus being an outsider, being of the people, being just like you and me. These two directions.

And if we look at photography, photography really could be split into two: One is photography that’s made by professionals. This is the kind of photography that traditionally you see in magazines, television. And by photography, I mean photography and film. And this kind of photography is made by professionals with high-quality cameras, and the results are kind of a clean lighting and flat, even horizon lines and bold colors, and there’s never grain, and there’s never fingerprints, and there’s never dust — and this is establishment photography.

And then there’s the kind of photography that’s made by amateurs. This is the kind of photography that you and I know really well, because this is what we make, and it’s made with disposable cameras and your iPhone, and it’s made with cheap, consumer-grade equipment. And so it looks like a mess. It often is not slick. In video think of, like, a camcorder or Super 8. You see dust flying across the screen.

And the other important part of amateur photography is that because we have used cheaper equipment, we often see grain or digital noise in that imagery. Those are the hallmarks of these two types of photography, and people in advertising pick different pieces of those two types to communicate with us silently. They don’t have to say anything. We know immediately how we should be interacting with the content because of the quality of the film and the choices that are made by that photographer or by that advertiser.

The same is happening in this advertisement. He’s using the aesthetics of amateur photography — the photography that we understand — and it comes from our own background and our own homes. The imagery that he’s showing is full of grain. We have sprockets on some of them. It’s full of mistakes. There’s some light leaks. It looks like there’s some Super 8 kind of vibes happening. It looks like things that we understand to be of the home, of ourselves and of the popular. It’s a populist look at this point.

If the sound was off, if you never heard anything that was said in this ad, you would know where he stands. You would know what he comes from and what he believes in, because he’s not using establishment photography. He’s using the photography of the Everyman, of the citizen. And his opponent’s doing the same thing, as it turns out.

Stromberg: And this is something that you might think would die out with generational change and technological change. But do you find that it’s not, because people use Instagram filters and they manipulate their digital images to convey precisely those sorts of messages?

Keegin: Right. It just compounds. The more we use photography, the more we understand all of those small details. And we are photographers, too, and advertisers will use the language — the vernacular that we are the most familiar with — which is your iPhone, to connect with you.

Stromberg: You mentioned an ad from El-Sayed’s opponent, Mike Rogers. We do have that, so why don’t we quickly watch that, and then we can compare and contrast?

Archival clip of “Where I Came From” plays.

The ad is titled “Where I Came From.” There are a lot of politics of identity in this ad also. The ad shows Mike Rogers in a button-up shirt but with no tie, and he’s talking about his neighborhood, which you see, and you see “Michigan values” sort of stamped. Emily, can you do a compare and contrast for us?

Keegin: Right. I think one of the things that’s also interesting about both of these campaigns is that they’re using a lot of collage animation and typography that has a sense of texture to it, which we’re seeing across the culture outside politics. But part of the reason that we’re seeing this is this backlash to A.I. and backlash to technology. And using both those kinds of amateur photography aesthetic, plus this kind of cut-and-paste feel to the text and the type, is to show an interest in the human hand and an interest in something that’s authentic and tactile. Which is, if we think about what that means politically, it means that the politician is anti-establishment, anti-tech and trying to feel grass roots, trying to feel human.

Stromberg: I think the big, if not the dominant, theme this year is that candidates recognize that this is an anti-establishment environment. They’re trying various strategies to deal with it. People hate the parties. Hilton runs away from his party label and mentions almost nothing of substance. Peltola goes hard on local issues. Huckabee Sanders reverts to this sort of old-school Republican message. El-Sayed associates himself with this sort of insurgent anti-establishment left. He’s hugging Bernie Sanders in his ad. Mike Rogers claims he has always been a working-class populist.

They’re appealing to different constituencies, many of these candidates, but you can see they’re all trying to do the same thing. What’s your read on what’s working the best here? Emily, why don’t you start?

Keegin: Well, I think the best advertisements, now and forever, are advertisements that have a strong, simple visual and strong, simple language that together inspire something powerful in the viewer. I think what we’re seeing right now are candidates that want to seem human and real and warm, and that’s actually happening across all branding. I think we’re having a Captcha moment — you know: Prove you’re not a robot. And I think both parties are taking some aesthetic risks to communicate this. They’re using different types of film stock, and they’re using different types of typography just to get the point across that they are authentic and they believe in the human spirit.

And I think it’s interesting, in the time of Trump, that Democrats themselves — I would expect them to portray themselves as the serious, competent alternative, right? We look at what’s happening in Washington, and maybe we want an adult in the room. But instead, I think we’re seeing a lot of Democrats specifically go for something that’s warmer and kinder and human and humorous. There’s lots of humor happening in these ads. And I wasn’t expecting to see that this time around.

Stromberg: Carlos, what do you make of the populist moment and the political advertising we’re seeing?

Lozada: It’s hard to distill the essence of the parties out of a handful of ads, but let me give it a shot. If you look at the two Democratic ads, they’re both efforts at reassurance. Peltola is saying: Look, I’m not that loony left you might be worried about. Like: I’m N.R.A., and the border and oil, and I’m Alaska above all, you know?

And Abdul El-Sayed — that ad is explicitly acknowledging the criticisms and concerns that he has raised through his campaign at the very beginning. And then he says: But look, I’m Michigan. I’ve got these people vouching for me. If you’re a little concerned about me, look at my adorable grandparents. They both seem to be saying: I’m safe. I’m normal. I’m of this place. I’m just like you. And therefore you can vote for me. I’m not Woke 1. I’m something else.

On the Republican side, I feel they’re a little bit more scattered. The Hilton ad just feels like the desperation shot at the buzzer, when you’re down by way more than three points, actually. What’s interesting to me about Sarah Huckabee Sanders and that ad is not just that it’s far more substantive than any of the ones that we’ve talked about, as I mentioned earlier, but that she’s someone who’s so associated with the Trump administration, certainly the first term.

And yet she seems to be creating distance from that. Both these ads are disregarding Trump’s request that you should vote like “I’m on the ballot.” There’s nothing about Trump being on the ballot in these ads that we’ve discussed. If I squint really hard, I see Sarah Huckabee Sanders kind of distancing herself from the tough-guy, masculinity, Hegseth vibe of the second Trump term, by kind of poking fun at someone like Brad.

And I don’t have to squint at all to see the Hilton ad leaning into the sexualized language of the Trump era in general. This ad seems very risqué and controversial, but when you have a president who campaigned talking about the size of Arnold Palmer’s anatomy — and recently talked about Jon Husted’s body and having a great butt or something like that — then the Hilton ad seems like less of a big deal to me or certainly in keeping with that kind of discourse.

ARTICLE

Trump’s Bubble Is About to Burst
The president’s crazy actions have Democrats on the cusp of victory — and they’ll be coming for him.
By Maureen Dowd
Published 2026-10-17 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/opinion/trump-photo-zacharia-harp-doug-mills.html

Sometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era.

It happened when L.B.J. yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style.

It happened when a photographer captured W. being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle.

It happened in 2009 when every living president gathered in the Oval Office and Jimmy Carter so obviously kept his distance from Presidents Obama, Clinton and both Bushes that his sense of superiority was made clear.

It happened when Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a Black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.

It happened again when Doug Mills, The Times’s dazzling White House photographer, took a picture on Tuesday of President Trump on Marine One with his blond aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his wobbly new press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing.

Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy.

The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knockoffs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss.

It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in America.

He desperately craves being the center of attention, and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.

Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetizing slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base.

In Mills’s photo, Marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble — at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview.

Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called Human Printer, who trails — and sometimes sprints — behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies.

Zacharia reposted Mills’s photo with the caption, “Best President in U.S. History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”

Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia.

But actually, the two women — scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash talk them — were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet who told them to hang in there.

But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot.

They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story on Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only.

“Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several longtime advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’s daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.

The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared, “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’”

Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’s picture, but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap.

We can’t see the expression on Wiles’s face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture.

Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president, and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted — in vain — to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder and likely end up in an “S.N.L.” cold open blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.

Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when The Times’s Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar.

“When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump — who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment — snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere.

But by the time they got to Alaska eight hours later, she was beaming at her boss and doing damage control.

(She told a far-right Pizzagate conspiracist in an interview that she wanted to be played on “S.N.L.” by “a Scarlett Johansson-type character.”)

Zacharia tried to fight back on “Hannity,” no doubt assuming she would be in friendly territory.

But she wasn’t. Sean Hannity asked her why she had put up 15 media posts identifying herself as an attorney. She lamely protested that they were “retweets of a title that had been given.” (Mistakes were made.)

Hannity pressed on: “Why didn’t you just say ‘I never practiced law’?” and asked about her first news conference, “Why only three questions in 14 minutes?”

Zacharia looked unnerved, as though she had been sandbagged by her foes in the White House.

As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard.

Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fueled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.

This week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; the Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Center, accused by the Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the center; and our ally Volodymyr Zelensky saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution.

Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent — and dangerous — court.

Doug Mills has proved once again that a picture is worth 1,000 words, or in my case, 1,283.

SUMMARY

Scott Kirby wants to be known as someone who moves on quickly after a disappointment. But after telling his wife, his next call was to a board member of United Airlines. I am a better C.E.O. of United Airlines because of what happened than I would have been a C.E.O. of American.

ARTICLE

United’s C.E.O. Says It Should Cost More Not to Sit in the Middle Seat
Scott Kirby of United Airlines said that “it’s expensive to fly airplanes” and that airfares may have further to rise.
By Jordyn Holman
Published 2026-10-18 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/business/scott-kirby-united-airlines.html

Scott Kirby wants to be known as someone who moves on quickly after a disappointment.

Ten years ago, he was let go from American Airlines after being passed over for the top job. He was furious. But after telling his wife, his next call was to a board member of United Airlines. He was hired at United in 2016 and named chief executive in 2020.

His goal was to best his former employer.

“For a long time, I said our goal is to be the best airline in the history of aviation,” Mr. Kirby, 59, said. “I think we’ve become the best, not at everything, but in totality, I think we’re the best.”

Mr. Kirby took over at United during the Covid-19 pandemic, the worst crisis the airline industry had faced since 9/11. Things have largely turned around for the industry since then, and United’s stock has risen more than 300 percent during Mr. Kirby’s tenure.

While things may be looking up for United, for many travelers, flying is miserable: delays, lost luggage, chaotic boarding processes and cramped seats.

It’s United’s job — and his — to take stress away, Mr. Kirby said. As a father of seven children, Mr. Kirby often looks at air travel through a parent’s eyes. Investing in better Wi-Fi, having more movies and TV shows available and developing a user-friendly app, he said, all help reduce the stress of traveling, especially with children.

But Mr. Kirby pushed back on one common customer gripe: rising airfares, which nationwide were up more than 22 percent in September from a year earlier. He said that fares are still lower in inflation-adjusted terms than they were in 2019.

Unlike many chief executives of large public companies, Mr. Kirby seems to relish expressing contrarian opinions. He defends fees for aisle and window seats. He dismisses most of the ways that people use artificial intelligence as “ridiculous.” And he endorses the idea of a national wealth tax — not your usual C.E.O. stance.

This interview was edited and condensed.

Air travel can be arduous and frustrating. If you’re not a frequent flier with United, you have to pay $70 to not be in a middle seat. How do customers without frequent-flier status fit into your strategy?

We made a lot of investments in premium, but most of investments we’ve made apply to every single person on the airplane. We’re going to have fast, free Starlink. Seat-back entertainment for every customer.

Some people just want to get from A to B at the cheapest price possible. There are some customers who want to sit in a window seat or a better seat, and that costs money to deliver. The way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want.

Then do you disagree with the premise that the frequent fliers are the haves and other travelers the have-nots?

I would never describe it that way. There are customers that pay more that get more.

With the war in Iran, fuel prices have risen and airlines, including United, have raised prices. Where will we be on prices long term?

Prices have gone up this year, but the truth is they’re really bouncing off an artificial low from Covid. This year, Spirit Airlines shut down. Four out of the eight publicly traded U.S. airlines are going to lose money this year. We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes.

What’s your management style? It’s been described as brusque.

People confuse management and leadership. Management is about compliance.

Leadership is about inspiration and vision. I’m more focused on leadership today than I was in the past. As C.E.O., if you are making too many decisions, you have to make all decisions. Everything gets punted to you. My job is really to make five decisions a year — the big decisions with no clear right or wrong answer that only the C.E.O. can make.

Was that hard to learn?

That was hard. But once I started doing it, you realize how much better the team around you gets.

What was the inflection point?

One was going through the experience of being told you’re going to be the C.E.O. and then, “Oh, I changed my mind and now you’re fired.”

At American Airlines?

At American.

The biggest thing I’ve changed is realizing that even when I know the right answer, taking the time to make sure everyone else feels good about the answer is 100 times more effective.

You’ve been at United for 10 years. Does how it ended at American still sting?

Stinging isn’t the right word. It felt more like a betrayal. I wanted to go somewhere else and prove something.

So what’s your advice on moving past a bad work experience like that?

I am a better C.E.O. of United Airlines because of what happened than I would have been a C.E.O. of American. It did force introspection.

I firmly believe in no excuses, and when bad stuff happens to you, it doesn’t matter if it’s fair, it doesn’t matter if somebody treated you wrong, it doesn’t matter why. The only person that can make it better is you.

Do you have any concern that the general public seems to have less trust in C.E.O.s, and do you have any responsibility for dispelling that?

Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that.

We should have a national wealth tax — it won’t work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100 percent at some level. I would pay them.

How are you personally using A.I.?

The way that most people use A.I. is ridiculous.

Say more.

Using A.I. to summarize is like reading a summary of the CliffsNotes. I want to read a book because the interesting stuff is in the spaces in between. I want to find the things that nobody else has figured out.

I think A.I. is incredibly powerful for a certain class of problems. I actually hired an A.I. tutor to learn to program.

Like a human tutor? We have to clarify these days.

Yes. I took three one-hour lessons. It was eye-opening. That made me an evangelist for using A.I. for programming in particular.

Let’s rewind. You grew up outside of Dallas. Tell me about your upbringing.

I have five brothers and sisters. I hit the jackpot on parents. My mom was the most involved mother you could be. She raised six kids, and, when she was in her 40s, she went back to law school, graduated summa cum laude and became a lawyer.

My dad was an accountant. What he gave me, which I now really appreciate, was time. His mother lived in a place called Goldsboro, Texas, and had cattle. We would go at least every other weekend, help with the cows, hunt. In fourth grade, I got my first shotgun.

You have seven children yourself. You live in Dallas, but United’s headquarters are in Chicago. What does work-life balance look like for you?

I am really efficient with time. My normal schedule, I sleep eight and a half hours a night. I work out every day for about an hour. I read three hours a day. I limit myself to no more than four hours of meetings on average a day, usually a lot less. I spend a lot of time calling people and talking to them.

My job is not to work hard. My job is to think hard.

I also spend lots of time with my kids when I’m at home. We have a routine at night: I start the putting-to-bed process — it’s about an hour — and we play hide-and-seek and chase and we read books. We tell spooky stories.

What is it like to travel with your family?

It’s not easy, but I get a lot of help.

Let’s go to the lightning round. What’s the first thing you look for when boarding a plane?

Smiling, positive flight attendants.

When interviewing someone for a job, what’s the most revealing question you ask?

The only question I ask every single person is: What advice do you have for me? Are they willing to tell me things that they think we can do better?

What’s the last question you asked A.I.?

My son started buying baseball cards, and he wants to try to sell them. I asked about the best place to buy and sell cards.

It gave bad advice.

What’s your most contrarian take?

I don’t know if this is contrarian or not: I think A.I. is going to be really powerful, but we are in an investment bubble. There’s just no way it’s going to generate that amount of revenue.

Give me one more.

I think the future of the United States is incredibly bright. I am not down in the dumps like a lot of people. I think, by the way, people on both sides of the aisle want to do the right thing for the country.

What’s your biggest pet peeve as C.E.O.?

I cannot stand anything that wastes time.

Do you always fly commercial?

Almost exclusively. I occasionally fly private. It’s rare, but if I do, it has a P.R. risk.

It’s important to fly commercial: I’m seeing our product. I fly other airlines, too. I see competitors’ products, and I learn a lot.

SUMMARY

I recently met a friend and his daughter for a drink on the Upper West Side. As my friend was walking me home, we came upon a group of young people — two men and three women — under some building scaffolding. Once I started to hang, my friend pulled out his phone to get a picture.

ARTICLE

‘My Friend Pulled Out His Phone to Get a Picture.’
Getting the hang of things uptown, pausing for a praying mantis and more reader tales of New York City in this week’s Metropolitan Diary.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-18 07:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/nyregion/metropolitan-diary.html

Getting a Lift

Dear Diary:

I recently met a friend and his daughter for a drink on the Upper West Side. As my friend was walking me home, we came upon a group of young people — two men and three women — under some building scaffolding. The men were doing pull-ups almost effortlessly.

I rushed forward.

“Hey, I read that if you’re a certain age and weight you should be able to hang for a certain amount of time,” I said. I had just turned 80. “Can you lift me up?”

The men obliged. Once I started to hang, my friend pulled out his phone to get a picture.

The young women began to chant: “One 1,000, Two 1,000 …”

After about 20 seconds, I asked the guys to let me down. Once I was on the ground, I asked them how they had done it so easily.

“We are Alvin Ailey dancers,” they said.

— Meredith Bernstein

Praying Mantis

Dear Diary:

It was one of those humid July days that take everything out of you. I was walking along East 57th Street when I noticed a praying mantis on a dusty tree with battered bark.

I had only seen perhaps two or three mantises in my life, and I couldn’t fathom how this one had wound up on a tree on a busy Upper East Side street.

I saw an older woman walking down the block. She noticed me staring at the tree.

Was I OK? she asked.

“I am now,” I said.

— Paul Aaronson

A Brooklyn Ocean

Dear Diary:

I was forced out of my Carroll Gardens home so a developer could tear it down. As a divorced mother, where would I find a three-bedroom for my two teens and me at an affordable rent?

I searched high and low and ended up moving south to Sunset Park. I found a raw loft space, which I fixed up. (Yes, I invested my own money in a rental.)

The apartment was directly above a 24-hour sex shop and it had a view of the Brooklyn Queens Expressway. I refused to open the windows and bought air purifiers.

Our first night there, I cried. What have I done? The noise from the B.Q.E., the constant shaking of the apartment — it all felt unbearable.

I was so depressed I wanted to leave the city altogether, but my kids were still in high school. I had no choice. I was trapped.

The next morning, I went for a long, anxious walk. I bumped into a barber who had been born and raised in the neighborhood, on Third Avenue.

I asked how he dealt with the noise and traffic.

He laughed.

“Are you kidding me?” he said. “It’s my ocean.”

The big trucks, he explained, were crashing waves; small cars, ripples; and the whirring engines, the steady flow of water. He told me he missed these sounds whenever he went to the country.

His perspective changed everything. The second night, I slept like a baby, with a sound machine accompanying the “waves” of nighttime traffic.

Two years later, my home is a haven for my kids and me, and I fall asleep each night to the soothing rhythm of a Brooklyn “ocean.”

— Mara Stephens

Gershwin Plays

Dear Diary:

I was an art history graduate student in the mid-1980s with an internship at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s medieval department.

At some point, I was assigned to accompany a staff member to an apartment in an old walk-up building that I think may have been in Greenwich Village. We were there to collect a painting or drawing that would be part of an exhibition unrelated to the medieval department.

A lovely older man welcomed us into a cozy apartment that was brimming with books, art, and personal treasures.

The talk turned to the man’s player piano, and he kindly pulled out original piano rolls of George Gershwin performing.

I was absolutely entranced as we listened to what was essentially Gershwin giving a performance in a warm, intimate setting.

I have completely forgotten what we were there to pick up but I have never forgotten the charming musical interlude.

— Leslie DiNella

Pork Chop Scar

Dear Diary:

I was standing on a packed subway train on my way into Manhattan when I overheard two women having a lively conversation.

“I just don’t eat pork anymore” the louder of the two said. “See here? Pork chop scar!”

“What do you mean?” the other woman asked, turning to get a look at her friend’s face.

“Right here,” the first woman said. “My right brow bone. See? Look closely!”

I couldn’t resist trying to get a peek myself as her friend leaned in for a closer inspection.

“Like how?” the second woman said in amazement.

“One day, when I was a teenager, I came home from school absolutely starving,” the first woman said, “and I peered over my mother’s shoulder as she was in the midst of seasoning some T-bone chops for the grill.”

She then recounted the exchange that followed:

“‘What’s for dinner tonight, Mom?’”

“‘Pork chops,’” she replied.”

“‘Oh no, not pork chops again!’”

“Thwack! Pork chop scar!”

— Jacqueline Rush Lee

SUMMARY

China becomes so technologically advanced, and its human and robotic work force so huge, that Americans are left with only the dimmest comprehension of what is playing out on the economic, scientific and perhaps even geopolitical frontier. But I find it easy to imagine how human control and comprehension of much of society could be handed over to machines. Isn’t the story of modern society human beings trading comprehension and control of their world for technological and economic advancement?

ARTICLE

This Is the Good Scenario?
We may not want it to, but A.I. is asking us how to live.
By Ezra Klein
Published 2026-10-18 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/opinion/ai-bubble-catastrophe-investors-control.html

Imagine Americans were offered this deal: Hit a big red button and China becomes the world’s first hyperpower. It rockets past the United States in technical sophistication, manufacturing capacity and wealth generation. China becomes so technologically advanced, and its human and robotic work force so huge, that Americans are left with only the dimmest comprehension of what is playing out on the economic, scientific and perhaps even geopolitical frontier.

But the rewards for disempowering ourselves are magnificent. The global economy booms, and Americans grow richer than ever before. We are given new cures and cheap energy and wondrous entertainments. Machines perform our labor and mood-enhancing drugs protect our psyches. We need not struggle — perhaps we need not even work — to live lives, long lives, of luxury and ease.

There, then, is the trade: Cede control and much that we have struggled for can be ours. But control, once gone, is gone.

Would you press the button?

The A.I. conversation centers questions of catastrophe. I want to center the question of success: What if A.I. works not as its architects fear, but as its inventors and investors hope? Wander outside of Silicon Valley’s p(doom) — their shorthand for the probability that A.I. extinguishes the human race — and you might notice that their p(utopia) has problems, too. They imagine something like the world I sketched above, but more extreme, with A.I. playing the role assigned to China.

An amusing collision of these visions came when Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old OpenAI and Anthropic whistle-blower, sat down with Jon Stewart on “The Daily Show.” Coxon was there to warn that A.I. might kill us all, but when Stewart offhandedly mocked the “future utopia” of the A.I. architects, Coxon stopped him. “Well, I am a believer in the future utopia,” Coxon said. But what he said next sounded grimmer: “So I heard you talking about jobs. I think there will be no jobs.”

Coxon went on to describe “the world that is being envisioned by the people building this technology” as “no jobs. Universal high income. The dividends from entirely automated economic production can be distributed among real humans.”

This vision, or some variant of it, is common enough at A.I. companies. I have heard it often. But most people, face to face with this idea, are incredulous at hearing this world — in which virtually all advanced cognitive work is done by A.I. — described as utopian. Stewart certainly was. “So we’ll all just be performing in a play?” he asked.

I tend toward skepticism of the jobless future. Human beings are good at nothing if not finding something to do. (Who would have imagined, in our grueling agrarian past, that podcasting could be a full-time job?) But I find it easy to imagine how human control and comprehension of much of society could be handed over to machines. A few recent developments — some reflecting the outer boundary of what advanced A.I. can do and the other reflecting its advancing utility in daily life — reveal the ways it is already happening.

A few weeks ago, OpenAI dumped more than 700 manuscripts proposing solutions to nearly 400 advanced mathematical problems all at once. If you’re not a mathematician, and you are not close to any mathematicians, this may have passed by unnoticed. Within mathematics, it was an earthquake.

I am not a mathematician, but my father is. The area of math he worked in had to do with the way electrons move through disordered crystals. Sitting at the center of his field were two problems that were more than just unsolved; they were, my father says, “totally out of reach — nobody had any idea how to solve them.” OpenAI’s systems solved them in an afternoon. “It is the end of mathematics as we know it,” he texted me. “It is the first time I am glad I have retired.”

The newly formed Association for Human Mathematics, which has about 1,000 members, quickly released a statement: “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done.” It’s an interesting sentence. Should mathematicians be able to decide which math problems do and do not get solved? How do we weigh the benefits and costs of a world where the frontier of mathematics is advancing rapidly, but human beings no longer understand it?

Imagine the OpenAI process running repeatedly, over a period of years: A.I. swarms solving problems no human being has solved, then using those solutions to pose new problems, which are solved by other A.I. swarms that have absorbed the work done by their predecessors, which allows for the formulation of yet more problems, and on and on. It is too much new math for humans to comprehend, but A.I.s can absorb it easily, and they do, driving forward advances in material sciences and energy production. Human beings do not understand all this new science, but they do benefit from it.

Is that world so different from the one we now inhabit? Few of us understand much about the borderlands of human knowledge. I cannot remotely comprehend the math my father did. How different is it if none of us can understand the math the A.I. does? And yet, a world where the farthest edge of knowledge and progress rests in algorithmic systems, rather than human minds, does seem different to me. Human control — which is, in my view, inseparable from human comprehension — is worth something, is it not?

As I was writing this, I read about a study in which theoretical physicists posed 50 complex, unpublished problems to advanced A.I. systems. These problems were difficult but solvable, taking a physicist who was expert in the particular area of the problem about a day to solve. The best A.I. solved 98 percent of them, at a cost of less than $3 per problem.

The physicists initially thought the A.I. had performed worse than it had, but the model insisted that it was the humans, not the A.I., that had erred, and it was right. “Frankly, I wasn’t expecting this day to come as soon as it has,” Suvrat Raju, one of the physicists behind the study, wrote. “After we found these results, I couldn’t sleep properly for a couple of nights.”

The grimmest A.I. stories often center on a single moment when superintelligence slips out of our control and begins plotting our demise. But the scenario I find more likely and more irresistible is called “gradual disempowerment.”

In this telling, there is no one moment when humanity loses control; there is instead a progression of small moments when we willingly give control away because it is the rational thing to do. Firms turn first more of their work and then more of their decision making over to advanced A.I.s because it gives them a competitive edge. Governments turn more battlefield decisions over to A.I. because it makes their forces swifter and more lethal. A.I. companies turn to recursive self-improvement — where the A.I. autonomously creates the next A.I. model — because it vaults them ahead of their competitors.

The key to this process is competitive pressure. Companies and governments and A.I. labs that resist are outcompeted by peers that give A.I.s more control and autonomy. Advances in A.I. systems — and, eventually, in A.I.-controlled drones and robotics — keep expanding the amount of work A.I.s can do better than human beings. Even assuming the A.I.s remain helpful and pliant, more and more of society’s basic functioning slips beyond the grasp of human beings.

Which brings me to a second, more mundane, story in A.I. Meta’s Muse assistant has topped the Apple app charts for weeks now. At its core, Muse is a fairly simple A.I. model. What makes it useful is that it is designed to operate with access to much more of your digital life — your email, your calendar, your social media, your bank accounts, your cloud storage — and then automatically take actions on your behalf.

I feel queasy about offering an A.I. so much access to my life, but my friends who use it tell me it has made them feel superhuman: They are more responsive and more responsible than they have ever been, because there is an always-on A.I. agent monitoring their digital life and catching problems and following up on emails and making reservations and reminding them of their priorities. The catch, of course, is that there is someone on the other side of all these A.I. actions.

Already, we’re hearing of businesses getting swamped by automated calls and emails. As Muse-like agents spread, those businesses will employ their own A.I.s to answer the influx. As A.I. agent use like this becomes more widespread, anyone who doesn’t use an agent may begin to fall behind. We will be less responsive than those who do use agents, or simply overwhelmed responding to other people’s agents.

Eventually it will be our A.I.s bargaining with other A.I.s, our A.I.s calling the restaurant’s A.I. for reservations, our A.I.s emailing our colleague’s A.I.s. The edge will go to those who grant them more intimate access or autonomous control. And the logic of competition will roll forward. What would seem bizarre one year will become commonplace the next. Much of our world will be turned over to A.I.s.

We have seen this before. There was a time when we could resist using email or smartphones, but for most of us, that time has past. It is too much of a disadvantage in modern society for most of us to forgo these technologies, even if we lament their consequences in our lives. The same will likely prove true with A.I.

Perhaps this is just how it has always been. Isn’t the story of modern society human beings trading comprehension and control of their world for technological and economic advancement? I would not trade places with my ancestors, even though society is less legible to me than it was to them. That air-conditioning or M.R.I. machines work is enough; I do not need to know, at a fundamental level, how they work. But that story has, until now, remained a fundamentally human story. That day may be ending.

It’s easy enough to answer the question of whether we want A.I. that kills us all. We don’t. But do we want A.I. that enriches us all, if the cost is our control and comprehension over the world in which we live? What is the value to human beings maintaining primacy over our own struggle, and how do we weigh it against the easing of that struggle? I want the cures and the theorems and even, on some level, the capable digital assistants. And I also believe the struggle for human progress is essential to the human story, and even the human soul.

I don’t find these questions easy to answer. I don’t even find them easy to clearly pose. But right now, we are on a path to letting them be answered for us, in countless small and mostly unnoticed moments when it will make competitive or personal or political sense for the humans to step back and let the machines step forward.

In his much-misunderstood book “The End of History and the Last Man,” Francis Fukuyama posed a similar question. It seemed unlikely, Fukuyama thought, that any political or economic system would surpass capitalism and liberal democracy at driving forward material prosperity. The question was whether there were human drives that liberal democracy would not only fail to meet, but fundamentally betray.

Fukuyama thought there was: Man did not just want a paycheck and an apartment; he wanted recognition and struggle. He wanted to be seen as not just equal to other men in some spiritual or political sense, but as better than other men. The fight for recognition is a fundamental human drive. And the inability of technocratic, liberal societies to even comprehend that urge might destabilize them.

“We inhabitants of liberal democratic countries are by now so used to accounts of current events that reduce motivation to economic causes, so thoroughly bourgeois in our own perceptions, that we are frequently surprised to discover how totally noneconomic most political life is,” Fukuyama wrote. “Indeed, we do not even have a common vocabulary for talking about the prideful and assertive side of human nature that is responsible for driving most wars and political conflicts.”

A.I. seems, to me, to pose Fukuyama’s question in an even sharper form. If it plays out as its proponents hope, it promises levels of prosperity and possibility conventional political systems never imagined. But it does so at the cost of betraying the human drive for recognition and struggle. Fukuyama worried about liberal democracy because its promise of equality, even when equality could be achieved, would not be enough. He saw liberal democracy as built on an incomplete conception of what human beings actually want. But A.I. goes further: It promises inferiority as a condition of prosperity.

Stewart saw this problem immediately. “If I may poke a hole in that utopia,” he said to Coxon, “I think, for the most part, even when we’re doing jobs we don’t particularly like, that humans like to feel relevant …. When people my age retire, they often die, because they’re no longer connected to purpose.”

Coxon, to his credit, didn’t dodge the question. Many people hate their jobs, he said. And I’d add: Many people love retirement, though they loathe unemployment. But I don’t think the problem here is best understood as jobs, or at least not solely as jobs. There is much human beings will prefer to do for and with each other even if A.I.s can do it better. That a machine can beat a chess grandmaster has not meant the end of human beings playing chess. But humanity’s sense of purpose and control and primacy is a harder and more ineffable thing to replace.

“Once you began admitting explanations in terms of purpose — well, you didn’t know what the result might be,” Aldous Huxley writes in “Brave New World.” The book imagines a world in which all desires are fulfilled but struggle is absent. In the society Huxley imagined, debates over purpose were considered subversive. They could leave people believing “that the purpose of life was not the maintenance of well-being, but some intensification and refining of consciousness, some enlargement of knowledge. Which was, the Controller reflected, quite possibly true. But not, in the present circumstance, admissible.”

Liberal democracies are threatened today not because they failed to deliver prosperity that was unimaginable to our predecessors, but because they allowed so much inequality and alienation and powerlessness to fester amid that prosperity. We want wealth, but we want wealth in part because it promises to grant us dignity. You can see, in the fury of the politically radicalized rich, how insufficient wealth is when severed from the recognition they believed it would accord them.

I am not saying that A.I. will, or even can, create this world. But it is the world many of its architects envision. Their vision for A.I. is not merely that it replaces white-collar work but that it races ahead of our most brilliant minds, and with each day that passes, with each new model that is released, with each new piece of evidence that A.I. can solve problems we cannot, this becomes a little more plausible.

The people building A.I., Stewart said, “don’t particularly seem like they have an understanding of the human condition.” If given the chance, almost all of them would push the button. Would you?
