SUMMARY

This essay concludes The New World Disorder, a series exploring the disintegration of the postwar international system and how countries are adjusting as America steps aside. By now it is clear to most of America and much of the world that America and what it stands for have changed. Is that the future of America in the world?

ARTICLE

The Old World Order Is Over. This Is What Could Come Next.
Here are three scenarios for what the new global order might look like.
By Serge Schmemann
Published 2026-10-18 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/opinion/america-world-order-democracy-trump.html

This essay concludes The New World Disorder, a series exploring the disintegration of the postwar international system and how countries are adjusting as America steps aside. Read more in the series below.

By now it is clear to most of America and much of the world that America and what it stands for have changed. The dominant face of that change is President Trump and his determined and deliberate efforts to accumulate greater powers than the Constitution apportioned to the president, to create a cult of personality based on grievance and vengeance and to challenge every aspect of the postwar global order, demeaning allies and courting autocrats.

Is that the future of America in the world? An increasingly autocratic, rude and unpredictable superpower guided by populism, rancor and whim? Or will Americans, once Mr. Trump is gone, try to restore the United States as the world’s repository of democratic values and human rights?

It is hard to imagine that even a MAGA-minded successor to Mr. Trump (say, Marco Rubio or JD Vance) would be as petulant, inconsistent and vindictive as this president has been. Yet too much has already shifted in the world — beyond anything Mr. Trump has done — to believe that the liberal, rules-based and values-driven order shaped by America and its allies after World War II can ever fully return to what it was.

New realities have come to the fore since the Berlin Wall came down almost four decades ago: the emergence of China as a greater economic and military rival to the United States than the Soviet Union ever was; the re-emergence of Russia as a menacing police state and its starting of a European war; the global retreat of liberal democracy, led by the premier democracy, the United States; fast-evolving technology undertaking tasks once reserved for the human brain. Globalization, once promising a borderless world and worldwide prosperity, has revealed its dark side: mass migration, inequality, cybercrime, polarization.

There is no reboot mechanism in history; there is no way back to the conveniently binary world of the last century any more than Mr. Trump can realize the illusions of Make America Great Again. The world is moving on.

What lies ahead? There is no way to know. But we must consider possible scenarios, if only to prepare as best we can. The exercise is especially critical for Americans, because any coherent action against global disarray will have to begin with the return of American democracy, as Charles A. Kupchan argues in his book “Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.” Though Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, might have articulated a widespread longing at Davos in January when he urged middle powers to join forces and “create a third path,” the power, wealth and traditions of a renewed United States would be critical for any meaningful reversal of illiberal and autocratic trends.

The scenarios below, looking a dozen years or so into the future, are drawn from conversations with and the writings of people who professionally gaze into the crystal balls of politics and world affairs, as well as with people who are concerned with what we leave behind. They are meant not to be scientific or comprehensive but to reflect on this critical moment, because, as the great American sage Yogi Berra once said, “If you don’t know where you are going, you might wind up someplace else.”

America Makes a Comeback

This is our most hopeful scenario. A leader committed to the primacy of law, honest governance and liberal democracy across the globe is back in the White House, and the United States has begun to clamber back to its place as the “shining city on a hill.”

Europeans have taken on greater responsibility for their defense and are warily coming to accept the United States as a friend and ally again. Vladimir Putin has been ousted and the conflict with Ukraine frozen, allowing Ukraine to make a rapid economic recovery and eventually have its territory returned. China has surpassed the United States economically but not militarily, and the two superpowers work to avoid conflict and find a modus vivendi.

A reinvigorated and re-empowered United Nations, no longer undermined by Washington, is mobilizing once again to combat climate change and public health challenges and find ways to regulate artificial intelligence. The consensus formed among rich nations after World War II — that aid to poor countries builds stability, fosters growth and reduces suffering — is restored as America retreats from Mr. Trump’s “America first” use of foreign aid purely as a transactional lever.

Before exiting, Mr. Trump called off the war in Iran, declaring victory even though Tehran retains its mullahs and its nuclear fuel. But at least the Middle East is calm, and with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel voted out of power, the new administration in Washington gets to work on beginning another peace process between Israelis and Palestinians.

Its own house in order and its democratic allies behind it, the United States is able to begin guiding the world to a new order. The verities long taken for granted about the benefits of globalization, free trade, automation, digital technology and liberal democracy have given way to a far more fragmented world, with multiple centers of power competing over influence and status, but at the same time, as Mr. Kupchan writes, “more tethered together and interdependent than it was during the 20th century.” A new system of global governance begins to take shape, perhaps along the lines of what Mr. Kupchan envisions: a global concert of major nations to preserve peace and cooperation while acknowledging the ideological and cultural diversity of a complex world.

The recovery of America is central to this future. However great the degradation of American ideals in the MAGA era, the United States remains unique in its power, resources and embedded values and in its ability to overcome serious failings. It took fourscore and seven years and a cruel civil war before the proposition that all men are created equal was expanded to include Black people and an additional century to translate that into law. Women have had the vote for only a bit more than 100 years, and the struggle for equality is far from finished. Yet to borrow further from Abraham Lincoln, America has succeeded in “a new birth of freedom” again and again, and it can do it once more.

We Muddle Along

In this version of our collective future, the world carries on much as it is. A new U.S. administration ends Mr. Trump’s tariffs and tries to restore relations with allies and avoid conflicts, but a deep polarization continues to grip American politics, feeding constant tensions among the branches of government and destabilizing the executive.

America’s wealth and military power command fear and respect, but after all the back and forth of the Trump and Biden administrations, most of the world — including Europe and Canada — can no longer view the United States as either the democratic standard or a moral leader. American-led alliances and economic institutions weaken. Governments around the globe form shifting economic groupings and increasingly turn to China for trade and security.

As China surpasses the United States economically and draws closer militarily, Beijing forges ever closer economic ties to Europe and emerging economies and escalates pressure on Taiwan, though it avoids confrontations that could provoke American action. Several of the countries once relegated to the developing world — like India, Mexico, Brazil and Indonesia — approach first rank but without a shared vision for how the world should work together.

In the Middle East, Mr. Trump finally found an exit ramp in Iran before leaving office, restoring passage through the Strait of Hormuz, but the mullahs, with much of their enriched uranium, remain in power in Iran. Mr. Netanyahu is gone, but Gaza remains devastated, and new Israeli settlements in the West Bank continue to fan Palestinian resentment. Mr. Putin has been overthrown by a junta of siloviki — the military and security barons through whom he ruled — but the war with Ukraine remains a smoldering stalemate. Europe accepts greater responsibility for its own defense but struggles to find a unified approach to China, Russia or the problems of the world.

Global tasks like battling climate change continue in fits and starts, without major commitments or progress. The United Nations and its major agencies, like the World Health Organization and UNICEF, remain suspect to much of America and thereby limited in reach and financing. The world is largely at peace, but this can change at any moment as China rapidly gathers force.

Unchecked Decline

Here, polarization and recriminations paralyze the United States. NATO and other American-led alliances lose meaning in a maelstrom of tariff wars and mutual rancor. Major international organizations — the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund — founder as countries north and south seek security and trade in shifting alliances and trading blocs. Beijing succeeds in annexing Taiwan without international military resistance, but China’s growth stalls, leaving the world without a dominant center. Unregulated A.I. leads to a host of new crises — rogue incursions and raids, proliferation of misinformation, loss of countless jobs, dangerous advances in cyberwarfare.

An America distrusted by other nations and trapped in debilitating internal struggles leads to a deeply fragmented and unstable world, increasingly vulnerable to Chinese demands. Xenophobia and ancient grievances become the stuff of local politics and international relations, leading to flare-ups in the Caucasus, the Balkans, the Horn of Africa and other places where demagogues fan animosities.

Unchecked global warming creates chaos the world over, from seawater sloshing through the Bowery to flooding and drought in Africa and Asia, setting off vast new migrations and conflicts. A total breakdown of alliances and international organizations leaves the world vulnerable to the full range of historical scourges, from famine to war.

Russia, its oil and gas fields battered by Ukrainian drones, threatens a tactical nuclear strike against Ukraine. The United States and Iran remain at a yearslong stalemate, rendering passage through the Strait of Hormuz sporadic and dangerous, pushing the price of oil ever higher and adding, most grievously, to the woes of developing countries and the poor with rising energy, transportation and food costs. Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern powers lose faith in America. Terrorist attacks multiply in Israel and the occupied territories, the threat of war hanging over the region.

Even in this scenario, a major clash of great powers — the United States, China, Russia or even Europe — remains unlikely, given that such conflicts tend to be over historical wrongs, artificial crises or regional borders, but the threat of regional conflicts going out of control is ever present. The strongmen in power are not above using conflict to extend control over their subjects.

The world is a dark place, and America is no longer there to offer light.

There are, of course, innumerable other ways things could play out in coming years and decades. As our great American sage, again, reputedly said, “It’s tough to make predictions, especially about the future.”

The dangers are huge, but the future need not be dystopian. However the old liberal order is viewed, its achievements cannot be denied — or quickly undone. Even as autocracies spread, the yearning for freedom remains strong. Ukrainians have demonstrated an extraordinary determination to stay free; American judges still often stand up to Mr. Trump’s efforts to subvert the law; journalists the world over risk freedom and even death to report the truth; countries still rush to help others when catastrophe strikes, as they did when floods ravaged Nepal and Tibet in August.

Elections can reverse an extremist drift, as they did in Poland and Hungary, but they can also raise warning signals, as with the gains of the Alternative for Germany in Germany’s recent regional elections. The midterm contests in the United States next month will be scrutinized the world over, the presidential race in 2028 even more.

In the words of the hymn, the fate of humanity still turns on the decisions that people and nations take “in the strife of truth with falsehood.” They do not always make the wrong choice. The key is not to wait too long.

business-school-mba-harvard-cornell-cambridge.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 39  Words: 2580/2656

SUMMARY

This fall, another cohort of ambitious young professionals has arrived at business schools around the world for two-year programs with price tags in the six figures. I have taught in business schools for over 20 years, at Harvard, Cornell and Cambridge. We don’t need to “fix” business schools.

ARTICLE

I Teach at a Business School. It’s Time to Shut Them Down.
Students come in with noble intentions and leave with flawed expertise.
By Chris Marquis
Published 2026-10-18 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/opinion/business-school-mba-harvard-cornell-cambridge.html

This fall, another cohort of ambitious young professionals has arrived at business schools around the world for two-year programs with price tags in the six figures. Their presence at some of the nicest and shiniest buildings on campus renews a familiar question: What exactly is an M.B.A. for?

This question has become more urgent as business education has expanded dramatically in the past decades. Today, nearly one in five American undergraduates majors in business, and the M.B.A. is the most popular graduate degree in the United States.

I have taught in business schools for over 20 years, at Harvard, Cornell and Cambridge. While some students appear to care only about their future compensation, I have met many with nobler goals: engineers who want to commercialize clean energy, physicians determined to fix the health care system, nonprofit leaders who have watched good missions fail for want of good management.

These students enroll hoping to learn what business schools say they teach: how to manage people, how to allocate capital and resources and how to make the world a better place through leadership. But I’ve come to see how the institution can reshape the worldviews of those who enter it, often undermining the very ambitions that brought them there.

This change can take place in a single semester. Again and again, I have watched students abandon their altruistic intentions, instead becoming consumed by whether to choose careers in consulting or finance and who will land a summer internship at McKinsey or Goldman Sachs.

The modern business school is designed to promote dealmaking, simplification and optimization. This mind-set has escaped containment and has spread to the wider world. Business-educated elites increasingly populate political leadership, bringing with them a transactional view of public life. One investigation found that out of 45 current heads of state who had studied in the United States, 10 were business majors, and six of those also earned M.B.A.s. President Trump, a Wharton graduate, has treated foreign policy and government itself as extensions of dealmaking and personal gain.

Surely, not every business graduate governs this way. But recent research by the Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu and colleagues shows what tends to happen when you put an M.B.A. in charge. In both the United States and Denmark, firms that appointed managers with business degrees cut wages and reduced labor’s share of income. Yet these companies didn’t become more productive, nor did they grow sales, investment or employment any faster. What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer — value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.

I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system — they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to “fix” business schools. We need to abolish them.

Business schools have always struggled to justify their place in the university. A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice — undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they “need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.”

When schools like Wharton and Harvard Business School were established, they were seen as overly vocational, and to build legitimacy their founders framed management as a profession, on par with law and medicine. But education in those fields rested on established bodies of knowledge — centuries of case law, natural sciences like biology — that management lacked.

The solution, devised in the 1920s by the Harvard dean Wallace Donham, was to borrow the teaching style used in law and medicine: the case study. It became the signature method of business education. To this day, professors assign 10- to 20-page descriptions of business challenges culminating in a decision point that students then debate in class. The method is pervasive: In 2024, Harvard Business School sold nearly 17 million case studies to various business programs around the world.

One well-known case study that I have taught many times is “Rob Parson at Morgan Stanley.” The facts are simple enough to produce a lively classroom debate. Mr. Parson has delivered impressive results and is viewed as a star performer, but his abrasive and go-it-alone style has alienated people across the firm. In the classroom, students take the position of his manager, Paul Nasr, and decide whether to promote him, delay the promotion or push him out.

Nearly three decades after publication, it remains among H.B.S.’s most widely used cases, and the dilemma is enduring: Should results be rewarded even when the person producing them damages the culture around him? In class, students vote on Mr. Nasr’s options and often role-play the difficult conversation between him and Mr. Parson. The discussion can be dramatic, engaging and effective.

But my experience has shown that by asking students to inhabit Mr. Nasr’s role, the case study narrows their imaginations to the decision facing one senior manager. Deeper questions — like whether Mr. Parson is himself a product of investment-banking culture — are rarely raised. Mr. Parson becomes an individual problem, when the larger issue may be an industry that rewards rainmaking, hierarchy and masculine performance norms, then acts surprised when they cause conflict.

When the case method is used in medicine and law, it serves a different set of goals. Medical students work through detailed patient scenarios — symptoms, test results, histories and social and economic context. Law students read real court opinions, dissecting facts, arguments and judgments. In both fields, students are confronted by the messiness of reality, and the goal is to foster disciplined skepticism: ask what’s missing, challenge assumptions and test how an analysis could be wrong.

Business school cases operate on another logic, focused not on inquiry but on decision making. H.B.S.’s own overview of the method describes students imagining “themselves in the decision-maker’s role” and “taking decisive action.” The point is to practice acting like the person in charge — or, as George W. Bush, a graduate of Harvard Business School, put it, “the decider.”

By overestimating the importance of individual decision makers, the business school classroom avoids harder questions: Who made this person the legitimate protagonist? Whose knowledge is absent? Why are workers, regulators, communities, ecosystems or citizens rarely given equal standing?

I wrote dozens of case studies during my decade at H.B.S., some of which are described as classics and best sellers. These are not products of independent research, but carefully packaged corporate narratives. The disclaimer printed in tiny type on every H.B.S. case concedes this point: Cases “are not intended to serve … as sources of primary data.” The data they include can be selective, biased or even fabricated.

For the many cases I wrote under the guidance of senior faculty members, events that reflected poorly on the company were softened or omitted and the roles of certain executives were burnished. The companies held final approval, with drafts reviewed by their lawyers and P.R. staff. Rather than being vehicles for disinterested learning, as one might expect at a university, the case studies end up as instruments of reputation management.

Corporate influence feeds a larger problem: The cases almost always feature winners, making it easy to mistake luck or timing for a proven strategy. Failures, dead ends and nonmarket solutions are rarely considered. Before Enron’s fraud was exposed, its business model was presented in admiring terms by at least five H.B.S. case studies. More damning still, the strategies that later led to its collapse — its asset-light model, its trading platform — were portrayed as innovations. Questions about deregulated energy markets, revolving-door oversight and opaque accounting went unasked.

Furthermore, edits that push the case narratives away from reality are often meant to make it “work” in a classroom. Complexity is systematically shaved away, and dissenting voices often go unheard. Real organizations don’t move in clearly delineated phases toward a decision point, but business school teaching materials often do — compressing timelines, dropping messy subplots and smoothing over contradictions to produce clean narrative arcs and satisfying problems to debate.

The result is a curriculum built around false narratives. Some of the most celebrated ideas in management have not been the ones that survived peer review or replication, but the ones that could be turned into TED Talks, consulting frameworks or airport best sellers. Faculty members are rewarded not for knowledge but for performance — selling a big idea with a memorable label that promises “success” or “disruption.”

Business schools have a divided mission: They seek to legitimize an economic system focused on private gain while also developing guardrails to tame it. They found a remarkable way to manage this tension: the “win-win” story in which the conflict between private gain and public good simply evaporates.

A classic win-win is the contention that environmental programs like reducing waste or using LED lights can save money or that decent pay and benefits lower costs by reducing employee turnover. Business schools now claim to educate “leaders who make a difference in the world,” as H.B.S. proclaims in its mission, while Wharton pursues a “quest for positive global impact.”

These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of “stakeholder capitalism”: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.

During the 2010s, stakeholder capitalism was quickly woven into M.B.A. syllabuses. But when researchers examined whether the corporations that signed on to a statement pledging commitment to this ethos actually changed their behavior on wages, investment, governance or climate, they found little evidence of a shift. The statement was less a new doctrine than an effort at reputation management — and a ploy to avoid oversight.

Recent evidence shows that many foundational studies supporting the win-win idea were based on flawed data or couldn’t be replicated. Yet faculty members keep researching, writing about and teaching the topic — suggesting an ideological project more than an academic exercise.

Much of what has happened in business schools turned out to be the leading edge of a broader transformation: the corporatization of the university itself. Institutions now chase rankings, donors and corporate partnerships, tout their contributions to innovation and growth and treat everything else as overhead. Students are “customers,” and the degrees are “products” with greater and lesser “market shares.” University strategic documents talk about “brand positioning” for departments and “R.O.I.s” on tenure lines.

Once you accept this frame, it becomes hard to defend the existence of a philosophy seminar or a history department for any reason other than the revenue it generates. The hiring of non-tenure-track adjunct professors follows: If education is “content” delivered to fee-paying “customers,” why keep full-time scholars on the payroll when you can hire contingent, low-wage instructors?

Business schools’ success in placing their graduates in high-paying jobs boosts their rankings; high rankings attract more applicants and allow higher tuitions; and wealthy alumni fund new programs and buildings that elevate the school’s status. It is a self-reinforcing cycle — a flywheel, in M.B.A. parlance — that pulls money, attention and legitimacy away from the disciplines best equipped to question this logic: history, philosophy, sociology, political theory.

The university’s capacity to cultivate historical memory, moral judgment and democratic imagination is weakened, even as its capacity to churn out data analysts, financial engineers and “innovation” managers grows. The irony — and danger — is that in the age of A.I., the thinking fostered in the arts and humanities is increasingly urgent. The domination of business schools is not only physical and financial; it is intellectual, and it is crowding out liberal education.

I’ve come to a grim conclusion: The problem with business schools is not repairable misalignment but the design itself. Business schools are not malfunctioning institutions; they are highly efficient machines doing exactly what they were designed to do. An ethics elective here, a sustainability center there, a “responsible leadership” badge — they all serve to legitimize the machine, not change its output.

The most honest solution I’ve come across is to replace the category entirely. Stuart Hart, an emeritus professor at Cornell and an early sustainability champion, told me he reached that conclusion after trying every internal route to make M.B.A. curriculums more responsible. The institution itself was the problem. At the University of Vermont, Dr. Hart has since developed a new form of business degree focused on societal impact — a small but concrete test of the case for starting over. In this program, sustainability is not a lone elective but run through the whole curriculum, and students spend the summer embedded in a mission-driven company.

What would that clean-sheet logic mean across an entire university? One starting point is the organization theorist Martin Parker’s call to create “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business, centered on how humans coordinate for shared ends. Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from “How do we maximize shareholder value?” to “How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward — and which should we strengthen?”

Dismantling the business school as a single high-status silo that professionalizes private gain may seem a heavy lift. But universities can create cross-disciplinary pathways for students who want to work in business without submitting them to the business school worldview. Some already offer “business and society” majors or master’s programs in organizations and public purpose, drawing on sociology, law and public policy. The point would not be to abolish the study of markets, but to return it to settings where questions of power, history, democracy and ecological limits cannot be so easily avoided.

For most of my career, I’ve taught electives focused on responsible business and sustainability — gratifying work, but largely preaching to the converted. Recently, at Cambridge, I introduced a required sustainability course filled with future bankers, consultants and tech executives who once would have steered clear.

Many arrive deeply skeptical, convinced that any time a corporation acts in a responsible way it must be a marketing ploy; some push back hard on ideas they see as threats to growth. But forcing them out of their bubbles into a shared conversation about the natural environment, inequality and discrimination has produced the kind of debate that is so often missing in education today.

This is not enough. One required course cannot redeem the business school model. If anything, teaching it has intensified my disappointment. The course is relegated to the very end of the program — a telling signal of its importance — and amid a growing backlash against sustainability, there is some pressure to reduce or eliminate the class, to appease the customers who now drive decisions in higher education.

Still, the experience has reminded me why abolishing business schools cannot mean abandoning the people in them. The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.

Christopher Marquis is a professor at the University of Cambridge Judge Business School and the author of “The Profiteers.”

ARTICLE

Defending the Right to Choose Death
Readers respond to an Opinion guest essay about medical assistance in dying. Also: An assault on federal science.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-18 13:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/opinion/medical-assistance-in-dying.html

To the Editor:

Re “We Implemented Canada’s Assisted Dying Law. We’re Concerned,” by Gary Rodin and Madeline Li (Opinion guest essay, nytimes.com, Oct. 5):

As a physician who has assessed and provided medical assistance in dying (MAID) in Manitoba for nearly a decade, I read this essay with concern. I agree that patients considering MAID deserve careful exploration of their suffering and access to counseling, palliative care and social supports. But counseling should support patients’ decisions, not be another test they must pass before their choice is respected.

The authors say clinicians focus on whether patients can receive MAID rather than whether they should. There is an important distinction between understanding why people want MAID and deciding whether they should want it. Medicine often follows the golden rule, treating patients as we would want to be treated. When a patient’s experience differs profoundly from our own, the platinum rule serves better: treating patients as they would want to be treated.

I have asked patients requesting MAID what they would need to no longer want it. Overwhelmingly, the answer is not counseling, housing or companionship. It is a cure, or a reversal of irreversible decline, something that medicine cannot offer.

Shared decision making means listening, exploring alternatives and identifying vulnerability. But in the end, intolerable suffering belongs to the person living it.

Kristen Creek Winnipeg, Manitoba

To the Editor:

As a retired cardiologist and an advocate of increasing access to medical aid in dying in the United States, I appreciated the concerns raised by Drs. Gary Rodin and Madeline Li. However, it’s important to highlight the differences between Canada’s MAID process and America’s.

Thirteen states and Washington, D.C., have legalized MAID, with legislation pending in at least 16 other states. Opponents of MAID are quick to refer to Canada and suggest that America is on the “slippery slope” that these authors describe.

Here, access to MAID is state-based, while Canada has established a federal right to it. In the United States, the patient must be terminally ill with less than six months to live, which is not the case in Canada. Finally, American patients must be able to self-administer the medication; in Canada, the physician can participate in the administration, often by IV.

Opponents of this choice for Americans raise fears that we will “become like Canada.” However, this hasn’t happened in almost 30 years of experience, starting with Oregon’s passage of MAID legislation in 1997.

Shannon J. Winakur Baltimore

To the Editor:

There is no reason to involve medical or legal professionals in one’s end-of-life decision. No one else needs to be deciding as if we were children. Whether pain or sadness or poverty leads one to choose death, all that matters is the decision.

All the hand-wringers who complicate the issue would do a greater service by providing access to therapies without forcing these on people who know they are ready to die.

I should be able to purchase from a pharmacy the necessary means to a serene death at the time of my choosing. Period.

Beatrice Shushan Carlsbad, Calif.

If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for a list of additional resources.

An Assault on Federal Science

To the Editor:

Re “Science Agency Diverts Money Meant to Fund Basic Research” (news article, Oct. 4):

Your report that the National Science Foundation withheld $1.4 billion — 19 percent of its primary research budget — describes one part of a much larger assault on federal science.

In the first 18 months of President Trump’s second term, more than 10,000 scientists and health professionals with doctorates left federal service. Thousands of research grants that had survived peer review were terminated, suspended or delayed.

Scientific advisory committees were abolished or reconstituted; databases and observing programs were disrupted; foreign students and scholars faced new restrictions; and the United States withdrew from international scientific and public health efforts.

Some measures have been blocked by Congress or the courts. But the cumulative effect reaches far beyond any single budget.

American scientific leadership was built over decades on stable institutions, peer review, continuity and international cooperation. Once those foundations are weakened or dismantled, they cannot simply be restored by reversing a policy or replenishing a budget.

James Lawrence Powell Buellton, Calif. The writer is the author of “The Rise and Fall of Federal Science: From Jefferson’s Republic of Knowledge to Trump’s War on Science.”

ARTICLE

Even a Blue Wave Can’t Stop Trump
Congressional powers may be less than they appear to be, especially lately.
By Jeffrey Toobin
Published 2026-10-18 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/opinion/midterms-congress-trump-democrats.html

Think potential Democratic majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate will prove to be formidable adversaries for President Trump? Think again.

The problem isn’t the fecklessness of whoever leads both chambers. It’s the structure of our constitutional system, which is more tilted than ever in favor of the executive branch.

True, under the Constitution, the government can spend only money that Congress appropriates (in a bill that is subject to the president’s veto). Likewise, congressional committees, which are led by the majority party in each house, have long enjoyed wide latitude to conduct investigations, including by issuing subpoenas for testimony and documents.

But those congressional powers may be less than they appear to be, especially lately. Democrats controlled the House in the last two years of Mr. Trump’s first term, and he was able to stonewall most attempts at meaningful oversight. He refused to comply with subpoenas and fought enforcement in the courts, where he exploited the inevitable delays that come with appeals to run out the clock on his term.

To cite just two examples, the House Oversight Committee sued over access to information about the census, and the case ended with President Joe Biden providing the information over two years later. The Ways and Means Committee sued to obtain Mr. Trump’s tax returns, and the Biden administration settled that case, too — nearly four years after it began.

That kind of resistance from the White House will be a certainty once again if the Democrats take control. And if a new majority in one or both houses targets private parties with ties to the Trump administration, like the Trump family’s partners in grift in crypto and other businesses, those companies and individuals will still have recourse to use the courts to delay, or to prevent, compliance.

Even better for President Trump, the law is now more skewed toward the executive branch, thanks to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States. Its main holding was that former presidents, including Mr. Trump, enjoy absolute criminal immunity for actions in connection with their core constitutional powers and presumptive immunity for other official acts. In short, the president could not be criminally prosecuted for any “official” actions he undertook while in office.

There is also language in Chief Justice John Roberts’s opinion that suggests the president cannot even be investigated for his official actions.

The president, the chief justice wrote, has “‘exclusive authority and absolute discretion’ to decide which crimes to investigate and prosecute.” In a future fight with Congress, President Trump’s lawyers could cite that language to argue that the lawmakers have no right to examine any of his most controversial actions — like the Justice Department’s sham prosecutions of the former F.B.I. director James Comey and New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, and the Department of Homeland Security’s search of the home of Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

That same principle — that the executive has absolute discretion when it comes to investigations and prosecutions — will also limit the ability of Congress to use its power of the purse to control the president. The lawmakers can use their budgetary authority to cut back on prosecutions of certain crimes; a lower court, for example, ruled that Congress could bar the Justice Department from using government funds to bring cases against medical marijuana providers. But the president, as Chief Justice Roberts made clear, retains the power to decide which individuals to prosecute.

The congressional budget rules allow lawmakers to impose some prohibitions on how money is spent, but they can’t use spending to usurp authority that belongs to the president, like the power to issue regulations. For this reason, Congress can change the budget for the Environmental Protection Agency, but it can’t use its power of the purse to force the leaders there to repeal its recent regulations that reward polluters.

On the even more consequential question of whether Congress could bar continued funding for the war in Iran, the answer is yes — sort of. Toward the end of the Vietnam War, Congress did use the budget to stop the bombing of Cambodia. During the Reagan administration, the Boland Amendment barred military aid to the contras in Nicaragua.

But even that power has important limitations. Congress cannot usually block the use of previously appropriated dollars, and given the vast size of the Pentagon budget, the administration can surely use existing funds to keep paying for that war. Even more to the point, the federal budget — with any restrictions that Democrats might seek to attach — is subject to a presidential veto. Following any plausible outcome of the midterms, the chances are remote that two-thirds of the lawmakers in each house will vote to override any of President Trump’s vetoes.

Indeed, funding battles are likely to be the chief preoccupation of Congress in the next two years even if only the House (and not the Senate) goes Democratic. Standoffs over the budget have made government shutdowns almost routine in recent years, and that pattern is likely to recur, and could accelerate, after the midterms. As in previous years, confrontations over the budget will probably end in grudging compromises, not a soaring rejection of President Trump’s policies.

If Democrats take control of the Senate, they will have the chance to vote on the president’s nominees. That power will probably not matter a great deal when it comes to votes on the president’s choices to lead cabinet departments. Whoever winds up in those positions, even if they are only in “acting” capacities, will certainly be doing Mr. Trump’s bidding.

The judiciary is another story. In a Senate controlled by Democrats, they will have the absolute right to reject any Trump nominees to lifetime appointments to the federal courts. The new majority will be, and should be, under enormous pressure from supporters to exercise that power with a heavy hand.

This is especially true if there is a vacancy on the Supreme Court. When Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016 with nearly a year left in President Barack Obama’s term, Senator Mitch McConnell, then the leader of the Republican majority, refused to hold hearings or a vote on Mr. Obama’s nomination of Merrick Garland to the Supreme Court. Democrats can — and must — return the favor if Mr. Trump tries to fill a seat on the court in his final two years in office.

Democrats should exercise that power because it’s the right thing to do, but also because they are going to have little power to do much else.

ARTICLE

Some MAHA Voters in Arizona Question Their G.O.P. Ties
MAHA’s alliance with MAGA had energized voters to support President Trump’s 2024 campaign. Now, some aren’t so sure.
By Sejal Govindarao
Published 2026-10-18 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/maha-voters-republican-split.html

When Winston Ledger stops by Firefly Coffee in Scottsdale, Ariz., he opts for an off-the-menu drink: a “naked” iced vanilla latte.

It’s a standard iced latte by most measures — except for the fact that it’s milkless. Mr. Ledger instead purchases raw milk from Firefly’s refrigerator and mixes it into the organic espresso and syrup in his cup. Local health inspectors said the shop cannot use raw milk in its drinks, according to one of the shop’s founders, but can sell it.

“That’s my go-to,” Mr. Ledger said, sitting beside his raw milk latte and a Bible he was studying.

Firefly is somewhat of a hub for Make America Healthy Again-minded patrons in the affluent, right-leaning and health-conscious city of Scottsdale, attracting athleisure-wearing young people, stroller moms, entrepreneurs and Bible study groups.

For co-founders Patrick Sullivan Jr. and Ashley Leroux Sullivan, both Republicans who embraced the marriage of MAHA and MAGA, Mr. Ledger is the exact type of wellness-minded regular they had in mind once they opened in 2025. Now, however, the couple finds themselves part of a contingent of MAHA voters who are slipping from the Republican Party and searching for candidates who prioritize the movement.

While it’s difficult to pinpoint the number of MAHA supporters who are pulling their support from the Republican Party, nearly 70 percent of rural supporters of the movement said the Trump administration’s policies have had an adverse effect or no impact on the health of people where they live, according to a KFF and A.P. poll earlier this year focused on the midterms.

The driving forces behind the MAHA movement are people seeking to be healthier and looking to remove harmful substances in food, the poll found. Few MAHA supporters specifically expressed support for President Trump or Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who runs the Health and Human Services Department.

Still, a majority of MAHA supporters are Republicans, with about half identifying as MAGA, the poll found. The two coalitions were bound for friction as the alliance marries a traditionally pro-business Republican Party with skeptics of industry who have rallied against chemical exposure.

Rifts formed last fall after Mr. Kennedy released a draft report on childhood health that activists criticized for not doing enough on pesticides.

Then in December, Lee Zeldin, the administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, loosened restrictions on harmful chemicals, prompting MAHA activists to call for his resignation.

And earlier this year, Mr. Trump signed an executive order intended to increase the production of glyphosate, a widely used weedkiller and possible carcinogen that has been the target of thousands of lawsuits, including one brought by Mr. Kennedy. Activists rebuked the move and railed against the administration after it backed the manufacturer of the weedkiller.

The moves, particularly on glyphosate, have caused Mr. Sullivan to feel “a little allergic” to the Republican Party, he said.

“My team did that?” said Mr. Sullivan.

“It makes you feel like you want to be an independent,” Ms. Leroux Sullivan chimed in.

Some conservatives, like Alex Clark, a health and wellness podcaster for the conservative group Turning Point U.S.A., are fretting that the MAHA coalition is “up for grabs.”

“I believe that vibes have been off for awhile, started with the Epstein debacle, continued with the Iran war, and then if we completely fumble the bag on MAHA, you can kiss 2028 goodbye,” Ms. Clark said.

Ms. Clark said it was likely too late for the Republicans to earn back the trust of MAHA voters with just weeks before the midterm elections.

Eden Marie James, co-founder of the MAHA Mom Coalition, said the 2028 presidential election could determine whether MAHA is a durable Republican constituency or a voting bloc that is willing to move. Ms. James has cast her ballot for both Republican and Democrat presidential nominees, like others in her coalition, she said.

“I don’t think that MAHA’s future is guaranteed to belong to either party,” she said.

That doesn’t stop politicians from trying to tap the coalition.

Representative Andy Biggs, the Republican nominee for Arizona governor, has a MAHA platform. Among its priorities: allowing restaurants and coffee shops to sell and serve raw milk; limiting the purchases of soda and junk food with SNAP benefits; making ivermectin, an anti-parasitic drug, available over the counter; and requiring schools to educate parents on vaccine exemptions for their children.

“I hope it brings people back” to the G.O.P., Mr. Biggs said in an interview. Mr. Biggs is hoping to unseat Katie Hobbs, the Democratic incumbent who recently tapped a former Republican as her running mate. If successful, Mr. Biggs would be the first Republican elected to Arizona’s top office since 2018.

“Ivermectin, raw milk, I mean we’re going deep here,” Ms. Clark said. “This isn’t just, you know, fluff stuff.”

The move on raw milk would allow Firefly to make and serve raw milk lattes, moving Mr. Ledger’s makeshift drink to the actual menu.

When the coffee shop founders learned of Mr. Biggs’s MAHA platform, they were optimistic, but wary.

“I don’t know if that’s pandering,” Mr. Sullivan said of Mr. Biggs’s platform. “I hope it's not.”
