ARTICLE

O.J. Simpson, a Secret Informant and a Decades-Old Mystery
An “extremely reliable” informant told authorities about the missing murder weapon, according to newly unsealed records. The informant’s brother told The Times his sibling was at the crime scene.
By Mike Baker and Tim Arango
Published 2026-10-18 09:45 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/oj-simpson-ippolito-informant-accomplice.html

O.J. Simpson entered a Miami hotel suite in June 2006 and sank into a chair. His eyes scanned the room, as if looking for a way out. His fingers rapped on the armrest.

The former N.F.L. superstar, television pitchman, movie star and onetime murder suspect had agreed to this meeting with his ghostwriter. Mr. Simpson planned to publish a confession — or at least a “hypothetical” confession — to the murder of his ex-wife and her friend. But he seemed to be having second thoughts.

He leaned in and scooped up a handful of nuts. He reached for a water bottle. The ghostwriter turned on his audio recorder, signaling the start of a conversation.

Mr. Simpson paused for a moment, the room draped in silence.

“You know I couldn’t have done this alone,” he began.

In the story Mr. Simpson told that day, later published in the book “If I Did It,” he described a version of the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman in which Mr. Simpson had help from a friend who got rid of the murder weapon and Mr. Simpson’s bloody clothes.

Prosecutors who had failed to convict Mr. Simpson of murder have given little credence to the notion of an accomplice. The police, too. Many people considered the details of Mr. Simpson’s hypothetical confession a fantasy, part of a desperate effort to cash in on his waning fame and notoriety amid growing money struggles and scrapes with the law.

But today, more than 30 years after the “trial of the century,” newly uncovered evidence suggests that Mr. Simpson’s account should not have been so readily dismissed.

A New York Times examination, based on recently unsealed court files, interviews and other evidence, details long-hidden information about the missing murder weapon, Mr. Simpson’s supposed efforts to cover up the crime, as well as the possibility of an accomplice. Together, the findings challenge the popular narrative around a case that has been dissected in countless books, podcasts and documentaries, and they stir doubts about law enforcement’s decision not to do more to pursue a promising lead.

A decades-old document filed in an unrelated, obscure criminal case in New York — recently unsealed at the request of The Times — outlines the account of a prized informant who came forward with tantalizing information while Mr. Simpson’s 1995 murder trial was proceeding.

The informant — a man considered “extremely reliable” by a veteran federal prosecutor and praised heartily by a longtime federal judge — was an associate of Mr. Simpson and a close friend of Mr. Simpson’s confidant, Al Cowlings. As part of his sweeping cooperation deal with law enforcement, the informant shared information about the supposed location of the murder weapon and the efforts to dispose of it. The document outlines the broad nature of what the informant offered prosecutors, but does not specify what he said, or to what degree he implicated himself or others.

His account was forwarded to Los Angeles prosecutors late in Mr. Simpson’s murder trial — so late that prosecutors had already presented their version of events to the jury and rested their case, but had yet to offer closing arguments. The documents in the New York case were ordered 30 years ago to be kept secret. They have remained so, until now.

The informant’s role in the case may go even deeper. Earlier this year, the informant’s brother told The Times that the siblings were in Los Angeles on the night of the murders. And he saw the informant with his hands apparently covered in blood after going out to help Mr. Simpson.

None of the new evidence uncovered by The Times definitively untangles the mystery. No one has come forward with new forensic evidence. Even the informant’s brother has since sought to disavow the explosive statements he made to The Times. Taken together, the material points in different directions but veers significantly from the official account that has been proffered by the police and prosecutors.

The double murder prosecution of Mr. Simpson, who was acquitted by a jury, remains one of the most scrutinized cases in popular culture, spawning endless theories. With many of the key players now dead, it’s possible the full truth will never be known.

Still, the notion that an accomplice participated in the murders has drawn the notice of Los Angeles Police cold case investigators, who as recently as last winter were quietly making calls about potential leads.

“The O.J. Simpson case remains an open and ongoing investigation,” a spokesman for the L.A.P.D. said. Because there was no conviction in the murders, “the department has an obligation to continue to pursue justice in this matter.” The spokesman added, “at a point that new evidence is found, detectives will follow those investigatory leads.”

As part of a re-examination of the Simpson case, The Times has unearthed tales of secret audiotapes, mafia links, a prison escape, and backchannel communications between state and federal prosecutors. The reporting also came across a dramatic account from the rapper Fat Joe that bolsters the informant’s supposed role in the case.

Much of the new information centers on the informant, a dead drug runner named Joseph Ippolito, known as Joey. He was a mafia associate, a serial felon, a prison escapee — and a friend of Mr. Simpson. The story of the New Jersey native’s high-flying life and his link to the Simpson case, were they not buttressed by police reports, court files and interviews, might seem too fantastical to be true.

A mobster escapes prison

Mr. Ippolito was raised in the mob underworld of New Jersey, where his father was part of the DeCavalcante crime family. As a young man, he went on to receive acclaim in Florida as a professional cigarette boat racer. He built a network of high-profile and well-heeled friends, such as the actor James Caan, and he built a reputation as a guy who embraced danger and took risks. Those risks included running drugs up the East Coast.

He was eventually caught in 1981, in a drug bust so large that it appeared on the front page of The Times. He served three years in prison for helping traffic 20 tons of marijuana from Colombia to Long Island.

In the late 1980s, fresh from prison, Mr. Ippolito moved to Los Angeles to start a new life.

He began managing an Italian restaurant, PCH Bar & Grill, which occupied a prime location near the Santa Monica beachfront. It offered sunset views across the Pacific Coast Highway, luring some of the city’s rich and famous. Among the people he hung out with: Al Cowlings, a former football star turned fledgling Hollywood actor.

Mr. Cowlings was also best friends with Mr. Simpson — they had been teammates in high school, college and the N.F.L.

Mr. Cowlings and Mr. Ippolito became fast friends. They went on hikes and took walks along the beach. They were so close, Mr. Cowlings later credited Mr. Ippolito for helping him kick his cocaine habit.

“My situation was getting so dismal that I know that if it were not for Joe, I probably would have died,” Mr. Cowlings wrote in a letter to a judge, while requesting leniency for Mr. Ippolito.

But while he helped Mr. Cowlings avoid cocaine, Mr. Ippolito was funneling it to others. Authorities found that Mr. Ippolito was trading on his proximity to Hollywood’s power brokers to move drugs. A major federal sting, involving secret recordings and an undercover mob informant, led to his arrest in Los Angeles in 1992. A jury found him guilty the following year.

Family and friends rushed to support Mr. Ippolito, lobbying the judge and attesting to his character. One friend, Julie Mijares, offered to house Mr. Ippolito in Los Angeles if he were released on bail. “I love Joe like a brother,” wrote Ms. Mijares, who met him more than a decade earlier in Florida.

A stylist to stars such as the pop group TLC, Ms. Mijares managed two retail shops of the Hollywood boutique Fred Segal in the 1990s. She was a regular at Mr. Ippolito’s restaurant.

Mr. Ippolito’s brother Sam, one of nine siblings in the Ippolito family, told the court that his brother had kept the family together after their father died, and served as the family’s figurehead.

“Joseph has worked hard his whole life, not for himself but for his family, and would not do anything to hurt them,” Sam wrote.

Mr. Ippolito was sentenced to 10 years in prison and sent to a minimum-security facility in Florida.

But prison couldn’t slow him.

In May 1994, eight months after his sentencing, he escaped by leaving a work duty before the 4 p.m. count. He stepped into a car he had called and got a ride to Panama City, Fla. His lawyer would later say in court it was the only known prison escape by way of private limousine.

His brother Sam said in an interview this year that he picked up Mr. Ippolito in Florida, began driving westward and eventually reached Los Angeles. He said they stayed at an apartment that belonged to Ms. Mijares, the stylist friend who had previously offered Joey refuge amid his legal troubles.

Records show that she once had an address in West Hollywood, in a four-story complex on Doheny Drive just off Sunset Boulevard.

Then one night — June 12, 1994 — Sam Ippolito recalled that his brother left the apartment. He said he needed to help a friend.

A double murder in Los Angeles

The authorities contended that, on that night, Mr. Simpson drove to his ex-wife’s condo. The former couple, who shared two children, had a volatile relationship, and he had a history of domestic violence.

Prosecutors said he stabbed her to death outside the home, and fatally slashed Mr. Goldman nearby.

At the crime scene, investigators found Mr. Simpson’s blood, along with footprints that matched both the style and size of his rare Bruno Magli shoes. They also found a single leather glove that matched the type Ms. Brown Simpson had once purchased for Mr. Simpson. Investigators also recovered a cap that contained hair consistent with Mr. Simpson’s hairs, and another hair on Mr. Goldman’s shirt, also consistent with Mr. Simpson. Another glove was found at Mr. Simpson’s home, with blood from both victims. Mr. Simpson had a cut on his hand.

The mountain of evidence against Mr. Simpson appeared clear-cut. The trial would be anything but.

When the authorities issued an arrest warrant for him five days after the killings, Mr. Simpson fled. The nation was transfixed as a white Ford Bronco, driven by Mr. Cowlings, with Mr. Simpson in the back seat, led the police on a slow-speed chase through the Los Angeles metro area.

Mr. Simpson eventually surrendered after returning to his home.

The chase not only captivated the country, it also drew the attention of authorities who were trying to track down Mr. Ippolito.

U.S. marshals knew Mr. Ippolito and Mr. Cowlings were friends. And the authorities knew the men were in close contact.

When Mr. Cowlings was briefly detained after the Bronco chase, the police found in his wallet the phone number to a mess hall where Mr. Ippolito worked while he was incarcerated, said John Cuff, one of the marshals tasked with finding Mr. Ippolito. In the Bronco, detectives also found photos of one of Mr. Ippolito’s girlfriends, along with her phone number.

The hunt for Mr. Ippolito grew more urgent, and the authorities began looking coast to coast. Their pursuit persisted for months. They conducted stakeouts and developed sources, at times believing they were on his tracks, only for Mr. Ippolito to slip through their fingers.

Then, as Mr. Cuff assessed a network of pager activity, he identified one likely belonging to Mr. Ippolito. Marshals made plans to apprehend him when he went to get the pager serviced at a store in New York’s Little Italy. They staked out the store for days until they saw a man who looked like Joey. Instead of a balding head, however, the man had flowing hair.

Still, they closed in.

“Joe,” Mr. Cuff said to the man.

“What do you mean? Who?” the man replied.

“What’s with this?” Mr. Cuff said, snatching at the man’s hair and pulling off Mr. Ippolito’s toupee. The escapee simply smiled, Mr. Cuff recalled, as he was brought back into custody.

The ‘snitch of the century’

Mr. Ippolito knew trouble and how to get out of it.

But options were limited for the repeat felon and recent prison escapee.

While Mr. Ippolito settled back behind bars in custody in New York, Mr. Simpson was on trial for murder, the proceedings playing out on television before a global audience.

Each man was fighting for his freedom. But Mr. Ippolito didn’t want to go to trial, or back to prison. So he turned snitch.

Drawing on his connections as a coast-to-coast drug trafficker, he quickly worked from behind bars to help undercover agents buy narcotics from high-priority targets. Records show he began to provide key information that helped federal agents piece together the racketeering activities of major mafia figures. Law enforcement officials said that Mr. Ippolito put himself “at great risk” to help them.

His extraordinary assistance was later outlined in a sealed 5K letter, a legal document filed by federal prosecutors to reward a defendant’s service. The letter, filed in court in December 1996, detailed Mr. Ippolito’s cooperation “almost immediately” after his arrest in August 1995.

“From the outset, Ippolito was completely forthright in our debriefings, during which we found Ippolito to be a remarkable source of information,” the letter reads. “This information has proven valuable as both investigative leads and to buttress several cases under indictment, and is likely to result in significant prosecutions at which Ippolito, if called, should prove to be a valuable witness.”

The first example cited? The O.J. Simpson case.

While trafficking drugs in California, the letter stated, “Ippolito became close to several individuals at the center of the Simpson/Goldman murder case. Through his close personal relationships with Al Cowlings, Simpson’s confidant, and others involved in the cases, including O.J. and Nicole Simpson, Ippolito had become privy to many facts relevant to the case, including Simpson’s alleged domestic violence, the Simpsons’ narcotics usage, Simpson’s attempted flight from justice, and his disposal of the murder weapon.”

Mr. Ippolito’s claims may have seemed outlandish, the type of storytelling that spouts from inmates desperate for leniency. Except Mr. Ippolito had been a “tremendous resource” to authorities while the Simpson case was playing out in California.

Federal prosecutors in New York began quietly sharing information to local prosecutors in Los Angeles. Mr. Ippolito made himself available to the authorities, and his information was provided to prosecutors “during the murder trial,” which was “at that time important to their case, particularly Simpson’s flight and his remarks to Cowlings concerning a murder weapon,” the cooperation letter stated.

“While Ippolito ultimately was not called as a witness — he was arrested and began to cooperate as that trial drew to a close — my conversations with the Los Angeles authorities indicate that Ippolito’s information was, at the very least, very helpful to their case,” the letter, written by then-federal prosecutor David Kelley, said.

Reached recently, Mr. Kelley said that he remembered Mr. Ippolito speaking about a knife concealed around Mr. Simpson’s property and that Mr. Ippolito had learned of the information from a close associate of Mr. Simpson. He declined to name the person, though the cooperation letter he wrote years earlier suggested Mr. Cowlings was the conduit. Mr. Kelley added that he did not believe Mr. Ippolito was involved in the killings.

Mr. Cowlings did not respond to text messages, phone calls or a letter sent to his home.

Mr. Kelley said in an interview that he recalled having a series of conversations with the prosecution team in Los Angeles, including the lead prosecutors Marcia Clark and Christopher Darden.

Mr. Darden declined to comment.

Ms. Clark, in a recent message, said she had no knowledge of Mr. Ippolito. “If anyone had spoken to him and found him to have relevant and credible information, I surely would have been informed,” she said. “The fact that I was never so informed establishes he had no credible or relevant evidence to provide.”

But others said there was significant back-and-forth between the agencies. One Los Angeles law enforcement official who was involved in the prosecution recalled receiving a call in the summer of 1995 — in the middle of the murder trial — from a federal official in New York who said that Mr. Ippolito had information about the case and was willing to talk. The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity around the case, recalled that Mr. Ippolito was later reluctant about “being the snitch of the century in the trial of the century.” With the prosecution of Mr. Simpson underway, and the L.A.P.D. and the district attorney’s office being inundated with tips, the official in Los Angeles said they didn’t press the matter.

Mr. Kelley, the former federal prosecutor, said he did not recall Mr. Ippolito being unwilling to help local authorities and that any such reluctance would have violated his cooperation agreement.

Mr. Ippolito was on the radar of L.A.P.D. investigators and prosecutors well before the murder trial, according to the case files reviewed by The Times.

Police detectives — with Mr. Darden, the prosecutor, present — interviewed Marcus Allen, an N.F.L. star and friend of Mr. Simpson, on Sept. 22, 1994, in Kansas City, according to investigative files. The interview took place months after the killings and while Mr. Ippolito was on the lam.

In the interview, investigators asked Mr. Allen whether he knew about Mr. Simpson’s friends and associates, including Joey. The report noted that Mr. Allen said he “did not know a Mr. Joey Ebalito” — an apparent misspelling of Mr. Ippolito’s name.

Around this time, Mr. Simpson’s defense lawyers also took interest in the drug runner with mafia ties. The group investigated whether Mr. Ippolito was linked to the murders, and at one point mulled whether he could be considered a suspect, according to Patrick J. McKenna, a private investigator from Florida who worked for the defense team.

Mr. McKenna said the team had another investigator, Jack McNally, a former New York Police Department detective with contacts in the city’s underworld, pursue this angle. Mr. McKenna recalled that Mr. McNally spoke to contacts in “the highest of the five families” in New York and reported back to the defense team, saying, “I don’t think he’s got any involvement.” (Mr. McNally died in 2023.)

Mr. Ippolito was never called — by the defense or the prosecution — to testify as a witness in the murder case. One of the complicating factors, as suggested in his cooperation letter, centered on timing.

At the time of Mr. Ippolito’s arrest in August 1995, the trial against Mr. Simpson had been underway for eight months. The prosecution had already rested its case. Closing arguments were approaching.

A jury acquitted Mr. Simpson in October 1995. The prosecution was marred by the police department’s history of racism and questions about the handling of key evidence. (A jury in a civil case later held Mr. Simpson liable for the deaths.)

At the time of Mr. Ippolito’s own sentencing in late 1996, federal prosecutors and a district judge heaped praise on him for his cooperation.

In addition to having him inform on mob associates, federal law enforcement placed him in a federal detention center in Brooklyn to spy on high-profile inmates, most notably suspects detained for their alleged roles in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, according to two people who were close to Mr. Ippolito.

In a 1996 hearing closed to the public, Judge Kimba M. Wood said the government wrote on Mr. Ippolito’s behalf “one of the strongest letters I have ever received, possibly the strongest.”

Judge Wood said she was “inclined” to do whatever she could to “make sure” he received “the credit he deserves for this cooperation,” according to a transcript of the hearing.

She issued the most lenient sentence she could, under law.

For his prison escape, Mr. Ippolito was sentenced to time served. The government also agreed not to prosecute him for distributing drugs in California for the five years up until his arrest.

Records indicate that Mr. Ippolito was released from custody in 1998. He died in 2006. His obituary vastly understated his colorful life, describing him as “a self-employed restaurateur in the Florida area.”

Bloody hands and a mysterious bag

The new information collected by The Times suggests that Mr. Ippolito’s role may have extended beyond what he told authorities.

Mr. Ippolito’s brother Sam said Joey was at the scene of the killings.

Sam Ippolito said that on the evening of the murders, Joey left the apartment around 6 p.m. Hours later, around midnight, his brother returned to their apartment carrying a bag with a heavy object inside and he appeared to have blood on his hands, Sam Ippolito said. Next, Joey undressed and stuffed his own clothes in the bag. He then asked Sam to get rid of it while he showered.

Sam also said he saw Joey call Mr. Cowlings from the apartment, and heard his brother say that he had just been “helping” Mr. Simpson.

Sam Ippolito told The Times he didn’t ask questions. He went outside and found a dumpster along Doheny Drive, near a construction site. He tossed the bag in.

Soon after, Sam said, he and his brother left Los Angeles and headed back to the East Coast. Sam brought up Mr. Simpson during the brothers’ trip. Sam said Joey refused to answer specific questions about what had transpired except to say that he “went to go help O.J.” that night.

An attorney for Ms. Mijares released a statement denying Sam Ippolito’s claim about Joey’s bloody appearance at her apartment, calling it absurd. “She has known Joey since she was a teenager,” the statement read. “She cannot be expected to remember every time they were together, especially events from 30 years ago.”

Ms. Mijares did not address questions about whether the Ippolitos stayed at her home in June 1994.

Sam Ippolito said in an interview that he was “100 percent” sure that Joey was with Mr. Simpson at the scene of the murders. He said he should have disclosed this information long ago.

But revealing secrets can have consequences. In 1997, two years after Joey became a federal informant, a mafia gunman shot Sam repeatedly and ran him over with a vehicle — authorities called it retaliation for Joey’s cooperation with the government. The gunman was later convicted of attempted murder and witness tampering.

In his conversations with a reporter earlier this year, Sam Ippolito maintained for months the story about his brother’s involvement.

Then, in a follow-up exchange this past summer, Sam Ippolito asked for compensation. He said he had been “offered a ton of money” and was under contract to tell his story elsewhere. And now, he wanted to recant what he previously told The Times, saying he previously could not differentiate what was real and what was not.

Peacock has announced that it is airing a documentary, “OJ’s Accomplice,” later this year about theories in the Simpson case.

Friends and some family members of Joey Ippolito have rejected any suggestion that he was involved on the night of the murders. They said that Sam Ippolito could not be trusted and might be trying to win attention and compensation.

Over the years, many have wondered about the case’s unexplained mysteries, such as where the murder weapon might have gone. Some have posited the brutal, efficient nature of the killings meant it likely that more than one person was involved.

Under the timeline presented by prosecutors, Mr. Simpson was in a hurry on the night of the murders, rushing home to catch a limousine that would take him to a previously scheduled flight.

Detectives hunted the route for the knife — in the woods, dumpsters and even the bowels of an airport waste tank that could have held the discharge from the airplane. None was ever found.

Tom Lange, who was the lead detective in the Simpson case and is now retired from the L.A.P.D., said he has never believed Mr. Simpson had help, and said if there was any evidence to support that theory it would have been disclosed by now.

Mr. Lange recalled Mr. Ippolito’s name coming up during the investigation of the murders, but that he “never really became an issue” for investigators. He said they received hundreds of tips during his time on the case and that only a handful were related to Mr. Ippolito.

During the criminal trial, Mr. Simpson’s defense team suggested there was evidence two people had been at the crime scene — an idea that prosecutors rejected. Robert Blasier, a lawyer who was part of Mr. Simpson’s defense team for both the criminal and civil trials and lived with him at his Brentwood home during the civil case, said Mr. Simpson had also maintained his innocence in private conversations. Still, Mr. Blasier believes the theories about having an accomplice could be true.

“My take is that these other theories are certainly possible,” he said. “But none of them amount to proof beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Over the years, Mr. Ippolito told people varying stories about his role in the case.

Eddie Trotta, a longtime friend of Joey, said Mr. Ippolito phoned him, talking about how he was telling law enforcement that Mr. Cowlings was the one who hid the knife, and that Mr. Cowlings ultimately discarded the weapon. Mr. Trotta said it seemed to him Mr. Ippolito was inventing tales.

Rob Brisolari, a former Drug Enforcement Administration agent who regularly spoke with Joey Ippolito, was skeptical that Mr. Ippolito was involved in the murders. He believed Mr. Ippolito had no motive to do so. Still, Mr. Brisolari did not rule out the possibility.

“It seems a little far-fetched to me, but that doesn’t mean it didn’t happen,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Brisolari remembered that Mr. Ippolito did disclose to him that he had received a call from Mr. Cowlings after the murders, seeking help to get Mr. Simpson out of the area. Mr. Ippolito reported to Mr. Brisolari that he told Mr. Cowlings that it would be difficult to do so — Mr. Ippolito himself was on the run from the authorities.

That request for assistance was in line with yet another tale that has emerged about Mr. Ippolito. The rapper Fat Joe, the man behind the hit song “What’s Luv?”, told a seemingly random story on his podcast about a friend named “Joe” and O.J. Simpson.

He said this deceased friend in Miami went by the name Joe Bentley, a name used by Mr. Ippolito because of the many Bentleys he owned.

On the podcast, Fat Joe said that Joey, who was released from federal custody in 1998, confided to him that when Mr. Cowlings and Mr. Simpson were in the Bronco chase, Joey had been at an airport, waiting with a private jet to help them escape. (Investigators did find in the infamous white Bronco a travel bag with a passport and a disguise kit.)

Fat Joe said he once went to Joey’s home for the birthday of Joey’s wife. Mr. Simpson was there. When it came time to cut the cake, Joey handed a “machete” to Mr. Simpson and declared: “You did it!” Mr. Simpson then chased Joey around with the weapon, apparently all in jest.

Reached recently, a spokesperson for Fat Joe said the rapper declined to comment. Mr. Ippolito’s widow declined to comment.

The tale meant that there were at least three versions of Mr. Ippolito’s link to the murders. In one told to federal prosecutors, he shared information from Mr. Cowlings, including about the supposed location of the murder weapon. In another version, as told by his brother, Mr. Ippolito was at the scene of the killings and had apparent blood on his hands. In another version, as told to Fat Joe, Mr. Ippolito was ready to help Mr. Simpson escape.

An accomplice named ‘Charlie’

Mr. Simpson, who died in 2024, was coy about the truth through the years. He vacillated between professing innocence and admitting guilt in a “hypothetical” confession.

In his hypothetical account of the night of June 12, 1994, Mr. Simpson told a ghostwriter that a friend of his, identified by the name “Charlie,” had come to his home that night, and their conversation triggered Mr. Simpson’s anger. The two hopped into Mr. Simpson’s white Ford Bronco and drove to Ms. Brown Simpson’s home to “scare” her. He described Charlie as a horrified observer to the bloodshed that ensued.

“Jesus Christ, O.J. — what have you done?” he quoted Charlie as saying as they looked over the scene of the two bodies crumpled on the ground. But after they arrived back in Mr. Simpson’s neighborhood, Mr. Simpson said he had handed Charlie a bundle of bloody clothes and the murder weapon. Charlie warily agreed to get rid of it.

But there’s yet another wrinkle to the “Charlie” story. A man whose real name is Charlie once suggested that he was the hypothetical accomplice.

Charlie Ehrlich was charged alongside Mr. Simpson during a robbery case in Las Vegas in 2007.

Mr. Ehrlich said in an interview that before the “If I Did It” book was published, Mr. Simpson told him over dinner that he had used his name as part of his hypothetical account.

Several years ago, Mr. Ehrlich went on to work with a producer, Erik Laibe, to tell his life story. The pair envisioned a film.

In hours of audiotapes never made public but reviewed by The Times, Mr. Laibe and Mr. Ehrlich do not directly confront the question of whether the “Charlie” in Mr. Simpson’s book was a reflection of Mr. Ehrlich. Mr. Ehrlich said on the tapes that he had met Mr. Simpson before the murders. Mr. Laibe at one point brings up that Mr. Simpson’s hypothetical account had used the name. “Regarding that: Use your imagination,” Mr. Ehrlich said. “I’ll leave it at that.”

Mr. Ehrlich suggested at another point that he had insights into Mr. Simpson’s mind-set on the night of the murders.

Those tapes fueled the theory that Mr. Ehrlich was the accomplice.

In a recent interview, Mr. Ehrlich said it was all a lie. He said he had played along with the idea that he was the hypothetical accomplice as part of an effort to cash in on the infamy.

Mr. Simpson’s ghostwriter, Pablo Fenjves, said he recalled being the one to propose Charlie as the pseudonym of Mr. Simpson’s supposed accomplice.

Mr. Ehrlich said he didn’t meet Mr. Simpson until Mr. Simpson moved to Florida in the years after his trial — well after the killings.

Mr. Ehrlich recalled that Mr. Simpson was impressed he had done seven years in prison, “kept his mouth shut” and “never ratted nobody out.”

“O.J. loved that about me,” Mr. Ehrlich said.

Unspoken was that the man who introduced them was himself a superstar snitch. His name? Joey Ippolito.

Kirsten Noyes, Alain Delaquérière, Kitty Bennett, Sheelagh McNeill and Susan C. Beachycontributed research.

SUMMARY

The last time Larry David waded into politics with a satirical essay, it was to take aim at a very safe target in his liberal circles — President Trump. Mr. David, who is known for his brand of anxious, observational comedy, mocked Bill Maher for dining with Mr. Trump at the White House in a guest essay published in The New York Times Opinion section last year headlined “My Dinner With Adolf,” in which he imagined dining with Hitler in 1939. Another post described the essay as “Larry David has a boomer crashout over Israel.”

ARTICLE

Larry David Mocks the D.S.A. Some Are Not Amused.
The comedian satirized the Democratic Socialists of America, its platform and its opposition to Israel in an essay that some did not LOL at.
By Lisa Lerer and Evan Gorelick
Published 2026-10-19 03:09 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/politics/larry-david-dsa-satire.html

The last time Larry David waded into politics with a satirical essay, it was to take aim at a very safe target in his liberal circles — President Trump.

Mr. David, who is known for his brand of anxious, observational comedy, mocked Bill Maher for dining with Mr. Trump at the White House in a guest essay published in The New York Times Opinion section last year headlined “My Dinner With Adolf,” in which he imagined dining with Hitler in 1939.

But Mr. David’s latest satire took aim at topics that are likely to be far more controversial within the coastal enclaves where his work is popular: the ascendant Democratic Socialists of America and its hostility toward Israel.

In a new essay published by Air Mail, the 79-year old comic channels the satirist Jonathan Swift and offers a dozen “modest proposals” for the manifesto of the socialist organization, whose actual proposals and guiding principles have been widely debated this year as several candidates aligned with the organization won primaries.

Mr. David’s suggestions start with ideas rooted in core planks of the movement, as he parodies proposals to abolish prisons and restrictions on immigration.

“In our Socialist America,” Mr. David writes, “everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes.”

“Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner,” he writes.

He rapidly progresses to more outlandish ideas, including national paid leave for the death of pets, mandating that employers provide cots for two siestas a day, allowing humans who identify as animals to “relieve themselves” wherever they wish and reparations that would enlist white people to serve as slaves for Black families.

Mr. David then aims his pen at one of the biggest fault lines dividing the Democratic Party, wading into the fraught debate over the line between opposition to Israel and antisemitism. Jews, he writes, will no longer be allowed to call themselves “the Chosen people” — a part of Jewish identity dating back millenniums — and will be known instead as “the Bagel People.”

“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” the proposal says. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty. We think the Bagel People will be very happy there.”

Best known for the hit TV shows “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Mr. David has long been a prominent Democratic donor in Hollywood with an interest in political satire.

A national spokesperson for the D.S.A. declined to comment on Mr. David’s article. But online, some took umbrage at Mr. David’s satire of the democratic socialists. Matthew Gauna, a 29-year-old student in San Antonio who agrees with D.S.A. ideas but said he is not a member of the organization, replied online to a post comparing Mr. David to Mr. Maher by calling Mr. David “my problematic king,” with a wilted flower emoji.

“I don’t know if Larry is on top of his comedic game right now,” Mr. Gauna said in a phone interview.

Another post described the essay as “Larry David has a boomer crashout over Israel.”

Zack Wall, 35, of Columbus, Ohio, replied online to that post, writing, “Someone take the phone from gramps,” along with three crying-face emojis.

Mr. Wall said in a phone interview that Mr. David’s piece was an “utter disappointment.”

“Not so much that he was ragging on D.S.A. I don’t care about that part,” said Mr. Wall, who added that he identifies as a democratic socialist but is not a member of the D.S.A., with which he has some disagreements. “It was just so low-brow and unfunny. It can’t be the same person who wrote ‘Curb.’”

Many posts focused on Mr. David’s age while criticizing his views, and others described him as unfunny and racist.

“Maybe I’m just too young, but who is Larry David and why would any person alive care what he has to say?” said a user who identified themselves as DSA_Girly.

The Times sought to confirm the identities of the users who wrote these posts, but some declined to be interviewed or did not immediately respond to interview requests.

Mr. David, whose comedy has made him a millionaire many times over, did not mock the D.S.A.’s economic proposals, which include universal health care, raising the minimum wage and expanding public housing and child care. The movement’s focus on economic inequality is central to its appeal for many voters, who are struggling with higher costs and a dismal view of their financial future.

Mr. David seemed to anticipate the backlash his piece would provoke, daring his socialist targets to take the joke.

His last proposal mandates that any comedian who causes “emotional discomfort” be sent to be “re-programmed” to emerge with greater sensitivity.

And if that effort fails, Mr. David offers one final “modest” suggestion: “The repeat offender will be sent to Pitcairn Island to live with the Bagel People.”

SUMMARY

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California spent his Saturday weaving through New Hampshire, campaigning with midterm candidates as he faced questions about his presidential ambitions. Next weekend, former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is weighing another White House bid, plans to be in the state with the Democratic Senate nominee. The Democratic schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race.

ARTICLE

The 2028 Presidential ‘Shadow Primary’ Descends on the Midterms
The schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race Democrats are flocking to this month.
By Evan Gorelick
Published 2026-10-18 19:47 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/politics/midterms-2028-presidential-race-democrats-republicans.html

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California spent his Saturday weaving through New Hampshire, campaigning with midterm candidates as he faced questions about his presidential ambitions. Next weekend, former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is weighing another White House bid, plans to be in the state with the Democratic Senate nominee. And days after that, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, who is also considering a run, will appear there, too.

In the final stage of this year’s midterms, prospective presidential candidates are parachuting into battleground states to rally support for candidates on the ballot this fall, road-test their stump speeches, and introduce themselves to voters and activists. The Democratic schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race. While New Hampshire has lost its long vaunted first-in-the-nation Democratic primary status to South Carolina, it will go third in 2028.

“Got here last night from the most un-Trump state in the United States of America, California,” Mr. Newsom told the crowd in Exeter, N.H., at a rally on Saturday with Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate nominee, as well as other Democratic candidates. His 10-minute speech focused primarily on President Trump.

Ambitious Republicans, too, are trying to leave lasting marks across the country in this year’s high-stakes elections. Vice President JD Vance and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas are hitting the road for midterm candidates, including in states expected to figure prominently in the next G.O.P. presidential race.

In both parties, the possible presidential candidates’ itineraries reflect their standings, showing where they are in demand and where they are not. At times, midterm candidates have subtly or loudly distanced themselves from some of them.

In other cases, midterm contenders have welcomed the extra attention and support. Mr. Newsom’s trip to New Hampshire follows recent visits by Senator Raphael Warnock, Democrat of Georgia, and Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, among others. Mr. Pappas, whose roster of surrogates from outside New Hampshire has grown, is facing former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican.

“I think of political campaigns like building a house. You have to build the foundation first before building the walls. That’s what these visits are,” said Jim Demers, a veteran New Hampshire Democratic strategist, who like other operatives refers to the current phase as the “shadow primary.”

At the town hall event in Exeter, Mr. Newsom popped out from behind a curtain, beaming as Macklemore and Ryan Lewis’s “Can’t Hold Us” played in the background. Asked about his political future, he waved his hand and said, “It’s all about 2026.”

While others similarly say they are solely focused on this year’s elections, Democratic and Republican strategists see multiple purposes in these visits.

“A campaign for president is like having an endoscopy and a colonoscopy at the same time,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “A lot of candidates are truly deciding whether they want to do this.”

Midterm travel may be especially attractive to lesser-known politicians looking to raise their national profiles, and to those who don’t hold public office.

Mr. Buttigieg, who left his post in the Biden administration in early 2025, has endorsed more than 100 candidates this cycle and campaigned for them in more than 30 states. Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky has headlined Democratic Party dinners or conventions in nine states, including several that will hold early presidential primaries. Representative Ro Khanna of California has campaigned for more than 70 candidates.

Others have been more selective with their travels. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, recently campaigned in Michigan, another early-nominating state, with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate. She plans to appear in Maine this week with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee there.

The country faces a “pivotal and consequential moment,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said in Michigan on Friday. She brushed aside speculation about her 2028 plans, saying, “What matters right now is the next 19 days.”

Ms. Harris also recently appeared with Dr. El-Sayed. She plans to visit Nevada, an early-nominating state, as well as Mississippi, Georgia and Wisconsin.

But Senate candidates in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas have publicly and pre-emptively uninvited Ms. Harris, whose ties to the Biden administration have made her unwelcome in some conservative-leaning states.

Tensions have flared in other ways. In recent weeks, Latino leaders became angry that the Democratic Governors Association, chaired by Mr. Beshear, was not investing more money into Gina Hinojosa’s race for Texas governor against Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent. They made veiled threats to withhold their support from Mr. Beshear should he run for president in 2028.

Within a week, the D.G.A. made a seven-figure donation to help elect Ms. Hinojosa.

Some potential presidential candidates have sought to balance their own re-elections: Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania are on the ballot in November. Mr. Shapiro recently started a federal political-action committee that enables him to give money to congressional candidates.

On the Republican side, Mr. Vance has campaigned in Kansas, Michigan and other battlegrounds. In Michigan on Thursday, he called the Senate contest “the most important race in the United States of America,” as he stumped for Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee.

Mr. Trump’s sinking approval ratings have made the president and, by extension, Mr. Vance a liability for some battleground candidates, as they seek to energize the party’s base voters. When Mr. Vance held a rally in Iowa last month, Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, didn’t attend, citing scheduling conflicts.

Republican “candidates in swing seats want his voters, not necessarily his baggage,” said Matt Klink, a Republican strategist in California, speaking of Mr. Trump.

Mr. Cruz, who has clashed publicly with Mr. Vance, has raised money and campaigned in his home state of Texas for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in a tight contest, and visited Iowa, which has been an early Republican nominating state, among other places.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a frequent target in Democrats’ campaign attacks, has also campaigned for Republicans this cycle in Iowa and Kentucky, a departure from past Pentagon officials who have stayed out of politics.

In New Hampshire, Derek Thibeault, 55, the chair of the Nashua Democratic City Committee, said he approached Mr. Newsom at an event on Saturday and asked the governor to let him know when he’d be back to campaign for the White House.

“He gave me a big laugh, but he didn’t say no,” Mr. Thibeault said.

Andrew Sylvia contributed reporting from New Hampshire.

ARTICLE

Trump Outlines Rapid Plan to Close and Overhaul D.C. Golf Course
The plan to begin work transforming the course in four weeks injected fresh urgency into a federal lawsuit opposing changes to East Potomac Golf Links.
By Zach Montague
Published 2026-10-18 18:06 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/politics/trump-golf-course-east-potomac-washington.html

President Trump said on Sunday that his administration had finalized plans to transform East Potomac Golf Links in Washington into a “World Class Championship Golf Course,” saying the municipal course would close within four weeks and that its replacement would be playable in about 15 months.

The announcement set up another frantic legal clash over the site. A federal judge ordered the administration in July to present her with any long-term plans for the course and not to carry out a surprise overhaul as the president had with the East Wing of the White House and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The Interior Department appeared to have done just that earlier this month, taking down hundreds of trees over a holiday weekend and giving the court and a group suing to stop any changes to the course less than a day to react.

In a post on social media on Sunday morning, Mr. Trump appeared to affirm what a historical-preservation group and two Washington residents had warned of in a federal lawsuit: that the administration might move to seize the existing course before they had a real chance to oppose the plan.

Mr. Trump wrote that he had already notified professional golf organizations that “they will soon have one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World to put on their list of great places to play, and hold Major Events.” He added that he had secured a design by Tom Fazio, a well-known designer who has planned other courses owned by the Trump Organization.

The president shared a rendering of the planned course that resembled a blurred-out image sitting on his desk in a photo shared on Friday by Katie Zacharia, his press secretary who was ousted from the role after less than a week.

In response to the post, Judge Ana C. Reyes, who has presided over the case, ordered the Justice Department to reconcile the announcement with what had been said in court by Sunday at 8 p.m.

She noted that the government had consistently denied that any decisions on the future of the course had been made along the lines of the vision Mr. Trump has shared publicly. She quoted a Justice Department lawyer who, as recently as Friday, said that Mr. Trump “at most” had given only “preliminary thought to” the future of the course.

The group opposing the plan has argued that the existing course provided an affordable and accessible option to players in the Washington area who would be harmed by its conversion into a more exclusive, professional-level destination. Critics and local golfers have also expressed doubt that the isolated Hains Point peninsula, where the course is situated, could handle the traffic that professional tournaments would demand.

The map Mr. Trump shared on Sunday showed the new course covering the bulk of East Potomac Park, with the proposed 12th hole situated over what is now a public picnic area and playground at Hains Point. In addition to the current municipal course, the perimeter of the island is also a popular cycling circuit.

“East Potomac Park is a national park, golf course and recreational facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy,” said Skye Perryman, the president of Democracy Forward, which is representing the group challenging the plan. “Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves.”

Mr. Trump has signaled for months that he intended to realize the plan, and he was photographed touring the site and studying blueprints with Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Mr. Fazio in June.

But because there had not previously been imminent plans to move forward with the redevelopment, Judge Reyes was hesitant for months to preemptively block the Trump administration from making any changes to the existing course. Instead, she had prevailed upon the Justice Department to notify her before making any major changes.

During a hearing in July, a Justice Department lawyer said that no decision had been reached on the fate of the course.

After it was revealed that the Interior Department cleared hundreds of trees last weekend, Judge Reyes excoriated the Justice Department for failing to keep her apprised during a fiery hearing on Monday. She accused the government of “double speak” for representing in court that the work was planned maintenance, despite Mr. Trump’s public vision to transform the course.

Seething at a government lawyer, Judge Reyes turned an extended portion of the four-hour hearing into an effort to identify who had given the go-ahead to begin the work. She ordered the government to track down several senior officials in the Interior Department to testify on the spot but was able to reach only one.

Judge Reyes lamented that she had tried to avoid “playing parks and rec” or policing landscaping decisions at the course. But confronted with signs that the administration was rushing forward, she ordered the government not to remove any more trees until Oct. 26 to give the group opposing the plan time to respond.

The question of who authorized the work is expected to be the focus of a hearing on Monday, at which Judge Reyes had ordered Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee at the Interior Department, and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify.

But the Justice Department escalated the standoff on Friday and filed a motion to disqualify Judge Reyes, citing her frustration at the hearing in order to question her impartiality and ask that she recuse herself from the case. She ordered both sides to file a response to the request by Sunday afternoon.

On Sunday, Judge Reyes also ordered Stanley Woodward Jr., the associate attorney general who filed the motion to disqualify her, to attend the hearing on Monday in which more senior Interior Department officials are scheduled to testify.

In the post on Sunday, Mr. Trump repeated an argument the government had made in court that clearing trees from the course was meant to return it to its original 1920s design, which featured open sight lines. But while the government indicated last week that the tree removal was proposed in a seven-year-old historic-restoration concept, Mr. Trump appeared to suggest that it was linked to the “Fazio Design” that he said would be built starting on Nov. 15.

ARTICLE

Some MAHA Voters in Arizona Question Their G.O.P. Ties
MAHA’s alliance with MAGA had energized voters to support President Trump’s 2024 campaign. Now, some aren’t so sure.
By Sejal Govindarao
Published 2026-10-18 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/maha-voters-republican-split.html

When Winston Ledger stops by Firefly Coffee in Scottsdale, Ariz., he opts for an off-the-menu drink: a “naked” iced vanilla latte.

It’s a standard iced latte by most measures — except for the fact that it’s milkless. Mr. Ledger instead purchases raw milk from Firefly’s refrigerator and mixes it into the organic espresso and syrup in his cup. Local health inspectors said the shop cannot use raw milk in its drinks, according to one of the shop’s founders, but can sell it.

“That’s my go-to,” Mr. Ledger said, sitting beside his raw milk latte and a Bible he was studying.

Firefly is somewhat of a hub for Make America Healthy Again-minded patrons in the affluent, right-leaning and health-conscious city of Scottsdale, attracting athleisure-wearing young people, stroller moms, entrepreneurs and Bible study groups.

For co-founders Patrick Sullivan Jr. and Ashley Leroux Sullivan, both Republicans who embraced the marriage of MAHA and MAGA, Mr. Ledger is the exact type of wellness-minded regular they had in mind once they opened in 2025. Now, however, the couple finds themselves part of a contingent of MAHA voters who are slipping from the Republican Party and searching for candidates who prioritize the movement.

While it’s difficult to pinpoint the number of MAHA supporters who are pulling their support from the Republican Party, nearly 70 percent of rural supporters of the movement said the Trump administration’s policies have had an adverse effect or no impact on the health of people where they live, according to a KFF and A.P. poll earlier this year focused on the midterms.

The driving forces behind the MAHA movement are people seeking to be healthier and looking to remove harmful substances in food, the poll found. Few MAHA supporters specifically expressed support for President Trump or Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who runs the Health and Human Services Department.

Still, a majority of MAHA supporters are Republicans, with about half identifying as MAGA, the poll found. The two coalitions were bound for friction as the alliance marries a traditionally pro-business Republican Party with skeptics of industry who have rallied against chemical exposure.

Rifts formed last fall after Mr. Kennedy released a draft report on childhood health that activists criticized for not doing enough on pesticides.

Then in December, Lee Zeldin, the administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, loosened restrictions on harmful chemicals, prompting MAHA activists to call for his resignation.

And earlier this year, Mr. Trump signed an executive order intended to increase the production of glyphosate, a widely used weedkiller and possible carcinogen that has been the target of thousands of lawsuits, including one brought by Mr. Kennedy. Activists rebuked the move and railed against the administration after it backed the manufacturer of the weedkiller.

The moves, particularly on glyphosate, have caused Mr. Sullivan to feel “a little allergic” to the Republican Party, he said.

“My team did that?” said Mr. Sullivan.

“It makes you feel like you want to be an independent,” Ms. Leroux Sullivan chimed in.

Some conservatives, like Alex Clark, a health and wellness podcaster for the conservative group Turning Point U.S.A., are fretting that the MAHA coalition is “up for grabs.”

“I believe that vibes have been off for awhile, started with the Epstein debacle, continued with the Iran war, and then if we completely fumble the bag on MAHA, you can kiss 2028 goodbye,” Ms. Clark said.

Ms. Clark said it was likely too late for the Republicans to earn back the trust of MAHA voters with just weeks before the midterm elections.

Eden Marie James, co-founder of the MAHA Mom Coalition, said the 2028 presidential election could determine whether MAHA is a durable Republican constituency or a voting bloc that is willing to move. Ms. James has cast her ballot for both Republican and Democrat presidential nominees, like others in her coalition, she said.

“I don’t think that MAHA’s future is guaranteed to belong to either party,” she said.

That doesn’t stop politicians from trying to tap the coalition.

Representative Andy Biggs, the Republican nominee for Arizona governor, has a MAHA platform. Among its priorities: allowing restaurants and coffee shops to sell and serve raw milk; limiting the purchases of soda and junk food with SNAP benefits; making ivermectin, an anti-parasitic drug, available over the counter; and requiring schools to educate parents on vaccine exemptions for their children.

“I hope it brings people back” to the G.O.P., Mr. Biggs said in an interview. Mr. Biggs is hoping to unseat Katie Hobbs, the Democratic incumbent who recently tapped a former Republican as her running mate. If successful, Mr. Biggs would be the first Republican elected to Arizona’s top office since 2018.

“Ivermectin, raw milk, I mean we’re going deep here,” Ms. Clark said. “This isn’t just, you know, fluff stuff.”

The move on raw milk would allow Firefly to make and serve raw milk lattes, moving Mr. Ledger’s makeshift drink to the actual menu.

When the coffee shop founders learned of Mr. Biggs’s MAHA platform, they were optimistic, but wary.

“I don’t know if that’s pandering,” Mr. Sullivan said of Mr. Biggs’s platform. “I hope it's not.”

ARTICLE

On the Campaign Trail, Trump Tries to Outrun a Bad Week in Washington
As Trump held rallies around the nation, his White House was consumed by dramas that reinforce how his presidency has become a drag on his party’s prospects in the midterms.
By Tyler Pager
Published 2026-10-18 19:20 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/trump-midterm-elections-republicans-approval-ratings.html

President Trump continued to sell himself as the Republican Party’s savior as he crisscrossed the country in recent days, making it clear in words and sheer presence that this midterm election is about him.

But back in the nation’s capital, Mr. Trump’s White House was consumed by dramas that reinforced why polls show that his presidency itself has become a drag on Republican tickets.

On Monday, Mr. Trump asked for the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, his ambassador to Greece, after a string of embarrassing reports, including that she urged a donor to pay for her $100,000 credit card debt. The president on Thursday canceled the Pentagon’s planned livestream of an execution of the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting after bipartisan outrage. And on Friday, he ousted his press secretary of five days after her bumpy debut.

Meantime, the White House Counsel’s Office was investigating a dispute between two prominent Trump allies and former administration officials over claims one of them misallocated funds for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a heated conflict stemming from a transaction from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company. And the administration deepened its standoff with the federal judge presiding over a lawsuit challenging the president’s plan for a golf course, pushing to disqualify her after she excoriated federal officials for ripping up hundreds of mature trees with little notice.

Together, the string of controversies invoked the chaos of Mr. Trump’s first term, when infighting among his aides regularly burst into public view. The week also encapsulated how Mr. Trump’s approval ratings have been dragged down by his administration’s policies and allegations of self-dealing that have shadowed much of his inner circle.

“It feels like late 2020,” said Alyssa Farah Griffin, who served in Mr. Trump’s White House during his first term. “There’s almost too much chaos. It's drinking from the fire hose, and you can’t anticipate the next plot twist from this administration.”

She added: “You couldn’t dream up a worse week for the White House heading into the midterms.”

Mr. Trump's approval rating sits around 37 percent, the lowest of his presidency, according to The New York Times average of polls. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll conducted Oct. 9-13 and released on Sunday shows his approval among Republicans dropped from 88 percent near the start of his term to 79 percent. The survey also found, for the first time in a decade, that voters trust Democrats more on the economy, and 66 percent of voters said Mr. Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself.

A Fox News poll from this month found that government corruption ranked first among voters’ concerns, followed by inflation, gas prices, government leadership and health care. Democrats are making the case that corruption is in fact a cause of higher prices.

“To the extent that Republicans are successful in keeping the Senate, it will be because of their success in distancing themselves from some of the president’s policies,” former Senator Jeff Flake, Republican of Arizona and longtime Trump critic who served as ambassador to Turkey in the Biden administration, said in an interview. “And that’s not a position you want to be in. And it’s not just the policies. It’s the weirdness of it. The crass and crude and vulgar language. It’s awful. It doesn’t help Republicans.”

On the road, Mr. Trump made no mention of the latest controversies. He held rallies in six different states, stretching from Alaska to Georgia, serving up a familiar message: His presidency has been an unbridled success, and Democratic victories next month threaten America’s future.

Inside the cosseted bubble of a Trump rally, composed largely of MAGA superfans, that message was met with hearty concurrence from the president’s adoring fans.

Tara Green, a front desk office administrator who attended the rally in Wasilla, Alaska, said seeing Mr. Trump was “an opportunity of a lifetime.”

“Trump has a vision, and it might take time, but it is fixing things,” she said. “I have every belief and trust in him.”

Still, there were signs of Mr. Trump’s eroding support, even inside his bubble. The president was interrupted by protesters at each of his rallies, once a rare occurrence. And swaths of the arenas, which Mr. Trump used to pack with ease, remained empty.

At a check-in desk for special guests on Saturday outside Truist Arena in Highland Heights, Ky., one volunteer asked a staffer for Mr. Trump how many people they were expecting at the rally. The staffer, outfitted in a “Team Trump” jacket, said they had expected a larger audience than was on hand. (The entire upper level of the arena remained empty during the rally.) The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Trump’s closing message also was notably meandering, even for a man who boasts about “the weave,” his description of how he bounces from one topic to another without any discernible connection.

The president kicked off most rallies this week by praising the appearance of Republican male candidates. (He seemed particularly enthralled by the backside of Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, bringing it up at two different rallies this week.)

He recounted his own political successes and margins of victory in the states he was visiting, most of which are historically Republican strongholds and a sign of how much ground his party is defending this year.

And he reminded voters of the basket of incentives he’s offering if they elect Republicans, expanding it from cash bonuses to pardons and investments from the Pentagon.

But even the president downplayed the impact of his signature midterm giveaway: a controversial promise to give $5,000 for every American adult — which he calls the “Trump dividend” — if Republicans retain control of Congress.

Describing a hypothetical conversation about a couple looking to spend the money, “Let’s go to Palm Beach and join the president for lunch. Let’s have lunch at Mar-a-Lago, where for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert,” he said, with a laugh. “I shouldn’t say that.”

That line in particular underscored how Mr. Trump has repeatedly seemed to minimize voter anxieties about rising costs, one reason Republicans have tried distancing themselves from the president.

Even among rally-goers, there seemed more wariness than in earlier elections, and loyalty to Mr. Trump seemed more important than concerns about policy or the turbulence in his administration.

Ustun Yuksel, a Trump supporter who has a Ph.D in political science and lives in Dawsonville, Ga., acknowledged that he needs to work on addressing cost of living issues.

“They can definitely do better,” he said, while waiting for Mr. Trump in Dalton, Ga.

But he said he likes Mr. Trump’s foreign policy. And he had no interest in discussing the latest headlines out of the White House.

“I don’t want to talk about it,” Mr. Yuksel said just after the news broke that Katie Zacharia, the White House press secretary, was ousted. “I don’t want to say anything.”

A few hours later, as Amy Thomas, a bail bonds agent from Cleveland, Tenn., waited in traffic to exit the rally, she jumped out of her car to capture Mr. Trump depart on Marine One. She said Mr. Trump was “getting the job done” and demurred when asked about the turmoil in the administration.

“My friend follows it more than I do,” she said of the firings and latest drama.

France Reels After Largest Riots in Years
Centrist and leftist leaders blamed each other after anti-government protests devolved into chaos.
By Catherine Porter and Ségolène Le Stradic
Published 2026-10-18 08:44 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/world/europe/france-protests-shock-arson.html

France was in a state of shock on Sunday, as citizens woke to streets littered with shattered glass and images of burned-out government buildings after the country’s largest demonstrations in years devolved into riots and looting.

The unrest on Saturday — which led to some 1,200 arrests — caused widespread damage to several symbols of the state, including a 19th-century city hall in Limoges, a town in central France renowned for its porcelain, that was largely destroyed in a nighttime arson attack.

Rioters attacked city halls from Lille in northern France to Marseille in the south, where masked infiltrators broke into the local government headquarters and tipped over a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic. Fires also destroyed a tourist office in Lyon.

On Sunday, that violence had given way to a political blame game. Government officials accused the far left of stirring up the unrest, and a left-wing leader blamed the government.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu placed the blame for the chaos squarely on a far-left party, France Unbowed. The leader of that party, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, stands a chance of making the runoff in next year’s presidential election to succeed President Emmanuel Macron.

Mr. Lecornu accused the leaders of France Unbowed of sowing distrust in the police among student protesters all week. He also said that intelligence suggested that the earliest rioters — who started attacking riot police and government buildings before official protests were set to begin — were members of the “ultra-left.”

“Behind all this, there is obviously a political battle to wage,” Mr. Lecornu said, adding that the country was at “the point of no return.”

“It’s also time to choose sides,” he said. “Either you are in the camp of the Republic, and therefore of law enforcement — and of those who protect people and property and enforce the laws — or you are on the side of the rioters.”

In response, Mr. Mélenchon blamed the government. He said on social media that Mr. Lecornu was “responsible for the chaos” — due to “incompetence or a worst-case strategy to create a party of order that would make people forget his failure in public finances.”

Mr. Lecornu did not respond to that allegation, but had earlier urged Mr. Mélenchon to call out the perpetrators of looting and violence.

Mr. Mélenchon had offered a qualified condemnation of the violence, stating that “those who share our fight have no place in looting, in pillaging.

“Regardless of the “responsibilities of those in power,” he said on Saturday night, the left “must refuse to take part in actions without political meaning and contrary to our methods.”

Protest organizers had hoped that the demonstrations on Saturday would lead to a convergence between the student demonstrations that have roiled France since September demanding better school conditions, and a broader social movement that addressed a wider array of concerns, including the rising cost of living.

What emerged on Saturday seemed like a split-screen event, with marches occurring peacefully in one part of a city and groups of black-clad agitators sparring with police and causing damage in other areas.

Then, as things unraveled, opportunist rioters joined in, exploiting the chaos, government officials said.

In Paris, the police said they were confronted first by “wildcat marches” and violent groups of 500 to 1,000 people. The situation changed in the late afternoon, the Paris police prefecture said in a statement on Sunday morning, with “the massive arrival of individuals whose sole objective was to commit theft and looting, taking advantage of the disorder to act.”

“If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand,” Mr. Zelensky told NBC’s “Meet the Press,” in an interview conducted in English. “If United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable. It’s a tragedy. It’s a historic mistake and a big tragedy.”

Mr. Zelensky’s comments capped a week of rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington that began with President Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement that he had brokered a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel, in a bid to lower gas prices before the U.S. midterm elections. To let Russian oil flow back into the market, Mr. Trump demanded that Ukraine halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, which it begrudgingly did for a few days.

But Kyiv said it got nothing in return, while Russia continued its devastating bombardments of Ukrainian cities. Then on Friday, Mr. Trump announced a rollback of new U.S. sanctions on Russia.

Mr. Zelensky has denounced the moves as benefiting Russia, the aggressor in the war, and complained about a string of developments that he said hampered Ukraine’s ability to fight and that he strongly suggested were orchestrated by Washington — deepening the rift between the two countries.

The Ukrainian leader has taken particular issue with what he has described as “a planned operation” to cap the speed at which Ukrainian forces can use the satellite internet service, Starshield.

The service, the military-grade version of Starlink, is provided under a Pentagon contract through the company SpaceX. Kyiv uses Starshield to provide connections for its drones in both offensive and defensive military operations.

Kyiv has said that drones relying on the service stopped working at speeds above 100 miles per hour, and also experienced disruptions when flying at lower speeds.

Mr. Zelensky has not explicitly said who he believed was behind that “operation.” But in his NBC interview on Sunday, he said “the message came from government,” in a reference to the Trump administration. “I don’t know from whom, what cabinet, and et cetera,” he added.

Mr. Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Starshield and said he did not think the SpaceX founder, Elon Musk, had done so either.

Mr. Musk has suggested that any restrictions on the service came from the Trump administration, saying that Starshield systems are “owned and controlled by the U.S. government.” A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has demanded an investigation into the disruptions.

The Ukrainian military first reported the restrictions on Wednesday morning, saying they had disrupted operations at the front and endangered the country’s air defense capabilities. Kyiv has since contacted the Pentagon and SpaceX for answers, but said neither had responded. Some disruptions to the service persisted as of Saturday evening, according to Ukrainian officials and commanders.

“Based on the information currently available to us, we cannot confirm that Starshield’s full capabilities have been restored,” Denys Sienik, a senior Ukrainian diplomat in the United States, said on Saturday.

“Four (4!) days after we submitted our inquiries, we have yet to receive a response from the Pentagon or SpaceX,” Mr. Sienik added in a social media post. “We hope to receive confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously, providing reliable communications essential to protecting our people amid intensified Russian aerial attacks.”

Ukrainian commanders offered mixed accounts of the situation on Saturday evening, with some saying disruptions continued while others said the service had returned to normal.

Separately, arson attacks on Starlink ground stations have been reported in Poland and Bulgaria. The Polish authorities have accused Russian intelligence services of carrying out the attack on the station in Poland, and the Bulgarian authorities have said that an investigation is ongoing. It was not clear whether the stations relay internet traffic to the Ukrainian military. Russia’s embassy in Poland did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Ukrainian military uses Starshield for a wide range of operations, including on attack drones that strike Russian command posts and on ground drones that deliver supplies to frontline troops. Mr. Zelensky has said interceptor drones also rely on the service to shoot down Russian long-range drones, although use in those cases appears to be limited.

Ukrainian forces use Starshield only for operations inside their country. The service does not work over Russian territory, meaning that Ukraine cannot use it to strike the Russian oil facilities that Mr. Trump wants spared.

Frustrated by Mr. Trump’s preference for putting pressure on Ukraine instead of on Russia, Mr. Zelensky said on Wednesday that he had ordered Ukrainian forces to resume strikes on Russian oil facilities, defying the American leader.

A first attack on an oil refinery southeast of Moscow took place Thursday. It was followed on Sunday by a drone assault on St. Petersburg which set ablaze a large oil terminal, according to St. Petersburg’s governor and a Ukrainian drone company that said its weapons were used in the strike.

Ukraine has long argued that the strikes on Russian oil refineries have little impact on gas prices, which have been largely driven by the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and the resulting drop in oil product exports. The strikes, however, have strained Russia’s oil industry, helping erode revenues that Moscow uses to finance its war effort.

“Our deep strikes, our attempts to target Russian oil refineries — it’s not damaging the United States, it’s not damaging the world,” Oleksandr Merezhko, the chairman of the Ukrainian Parliament’s foreign affairs committee, said in a phone interview. “It’s damaging only Russia and gives us a chance to bring Putin to the table of negotiation.”
