SUMMARY

The online right has that old spring to its step. The accusations brought by Jane Doe against seven men at Cornell have given the online right what it’s been missing most: a woman to hate on. It’s clear the right has abandoned any effort at drawing more women, particularly young women Doe’s age, into its fold.

ARTICLE

I Have Never Seen the Online Right So Happy
Online right-wingers are doxxing and smearing the accuser in the Cornell rape case, in tactics that reek of desperation.
By Nathan Taylor Pemberton
Published 2026-10-19 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/opinion/cornell-rape-political-right-smear.html

The online right has that old spring to its step. The infighting brought on by Donald Trump’s chaotic second-term agenda has settled down and the anonymous accounts have been posting at a furious clip. What is the source of this newfound unity? The accusations brought by Jane Doe against seven men at Cornell have given the online right what it’s been missing most: a woman to hate on.

The social-media celebrities and talking heads of the right have jumped at the chance to pick apart Doe’s allegations of a gang rape — labeling it a “hoax” and a “witch hunt.” Unable to dispute the basic narrative of the assault, including a lurid fraternity group chat, they’ve elected to argue that Doe is the actual aggressor, a once-willing participant in sexual debauchery now seeking vengeance against her hapless partners.

Her most hostile critics on the right have sought to portray Doe as a kind of out-of -control sexual fiend or “super slut,” as the conspiracist Alex Jones has labeled her. Not content to simply degrade her, Nick Fuentes, the white-nationalist streamer and self-proclaimed virgin, has used the Cornell case as an opportunity to espouse his vision of male dominance by suggesting that Doe should not only be “put in jail” but that he would “absolutely beat” a woman who behaved like her.

Elsewhere, far-right online communities of young groypers, anonymous MAGA chuds and Christian nationalists have been relentlessly harassing Doe. Tactics have included doxxing her by posting her legal name and her address, as well as attempting to flood social media with intrusive images and videos supposedly ripped from her social media accounts. As a result of these obsessive efforts, Doe was subjected to a “swatting” incident that resulted in the police descending on her family’s house with their weapons drawn.

The message embedded in the right’s freakout is that feminism’s moral permissiveness is corrupting women, our institutions, traditional values and even the left as a whole. The conservative influencer Michael Knowles suggested that Doe is not a victim of violent masculinity, but rather of “hookup culture” run amok. Another conservative, Matt Walsh, declared that “feminists fundamentally reject the idea that women can ever be truly responsible for any wrongdoing of any kind.”

This hangdog argument, that women can get away with things and men can’t, is a staple of the manosphere. It’s here where men’s rights advocates like the podcaster known as Myron Gaines, one of the more prominent and vociferous voices in this sinister space, have declared that the Cornell case reflects a culture that demands “zero accountability” for women. And now, Mr. Gaines believes, it’s time to give the #MeToo moment a “real re-evaluation.”

The onslaught against Doe and her supporters is taken directly from the playbook that established them: Gamergate. In 2014, a mostly anonymous digital horde waged a full-scale assault on women working in the gaming industry in an effort to damage their reputations and drive them from their professions. They harassed and doxxed their victims and fabricated and disseminated conspiratorial rumors about them, all at a critical moment when the online world was first starting to function like the social media-dominated internet we know today.

Gamergate is a formative origin point for the alt-right, whose members and ideas have been absorbed into what is now called the new right. Once a subset of the broader conservative movement, the intellectuals and policy wonks of the new right, who almost all share atavistic visions of a masculine-obsessed politics, helped pave the way for Mr. Trump’s rise to power.

Today, their ideas are shaping both the G.O.P. and the actions of the federal government. What was once a style practiced by the fringes, out on the hard edge of the American masculine psyche, has now become an everyday tactic among the MAGA mainstream and the heart of government.

As a political tactic, resorting to a decade-old strategy of harassment should be evidence that the right’s bag of tricks is painfully meager. It’s also a bit baffling. In the face of a midterm election that could knock Mr. Trump’s presidency down into a posture of feeble lameness, the right’s online surrogates are instead burning crucial bandwidth on a grotesque persecution of a sympathetic woman — all while pushing a scolding grievance message about sexual values that is more likely to scare away new voters than bring them into the tent.

So who is this for? It’s clear the right has abandoned any effort at drawing more women, particularly young women Doe’s age, into its fold. It might be reasonable to conclude, then, that the right-wing response to the Cornell case is some end-run play for the votes of young men, the angry disaffected kind. But this noncommittal voting bloc appears to have reconsidered its support for the president. A mid-September survey of 800 young men, aged 18-30, revealed a mass retreat from Mr. Trump and his agenda, with a double-digit preference for a generic Democratic ticket among young men who are likely to vote in the midterms.

Even for those young men who still lean toward Mr. Trump, a misogynistic digital blitz that blames women and feminism for male woes isn’t likely to inspire them to go to the polls. Which isn’t to say young men don’t feel aggrieved. It’s just that they’re more aggrieved about more material issues, like rising living costs. Affordability and inflation are issues that polling has consistently revealed to be the top anxieties weighing down young men. It just so happens that, for the party of Donald Trump, it’s the single issue it cannot address with a shred of credibility.

But to suggest that this reactionary effort to smear women stems from a lack of political imagination or tactical savvy misses another important point. The new right’s obsessions with masculine dominance, policing gender norms and traditional values are some of the rudimentary urges shaping its worldview. And of the vast discontents that seem to energize the right — nationalism, racial animus, antisemitism, contempt for elites, Islamophobia — few have the ability to bring together the right’s various factions like misogyny.

The writer Helen Lewis recently put a label on this political dynamic, calling it “masculinism.” More than attitude or a style or a culture war tactic, Ms. Lewis argues, it’s an energy far more intrinsic to the conservative worldview; she describes it as one of the “single most important forces uniting the American right.” Seen through this lens, the right’s campaign against Doe is something more rewarding and essential to how it does politics. It’s an opportunity to convey the purpose of the movement in the clearest possible terms.

It’s why one can sense a whiff of nostalgic euphoria in the right’s recent vulgarities against Jane Doe. Could it be that these reactionaries, in the face of an overwhelmingly complex and challenging political moment, are pining for the pleasant simplicities of the not-so-distant past? A nostalgia for their own reactionary uprising — back when a hysterical outcry against the so-called woke scolds or the liberal managerial state or the demonic left was a winning pitch to American voters?

Having won the presidency twice in less than a decade with its masculinist grievance politics, the right is now functioning much like an addict, flailing about for a quick fix and a familiar high, even if a brutal comedown is all but certain.

Nathan Pemberton writes about influence and the new right.

SUMMARY

This weekend, hundreds of thousands of French men and women joined the students on the streets in an expression of mass frustration over the cost of living, extreme wealth disparity, government paralysis and a faltering social welfare system.

ARTICLE

The French Fantasy Is Coming to an End
With Saturday’s enormous, and enormously destructive, protests, the dream of Paris as a place of escape may be nearing an end.
By Glynnis MacNicol
Published 2026-10-19 15:57 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/opinion/france-protests-paris.html

On Saturday, protests shut down large swaths of Paris. In parts of the city and around the country, pockets of these demonstrations turned violent. Looting and arson marked streets near the Place de la République and in the First Arrondissement, where shop windows were broken and electric bikes were set on fire. In the city of Limoges, the 19th-century Hôtel de Ville went up in flames; in Lyon, a tourist office blazed.

Protests here began in late September with students in the suburbs exhausted by the conditions of their schools, including their inability to cool or heat classrooms, keep out rats or simply keep teachers. This weekend, hundreds of thousands of French men and women joined the students on the streets in an expression of mass frustration over the cost of living, extreme wealth disparity, government paralysis and a faltering social welfare system.

For the past decade, I have spent part of every year in Paris. Protests are a fact of life here, but Saturday’s were different, larger, more intense. Many groups, including the Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vests) — a protest movement that seized the country in 2018 and 2019 over the falling quality of life — joined the students, along with labor unions.

I left the Left Bank and set out on foot for the Bastille, 30 minutes away across the Seine, on Saturday around noon. The Bastille column was covered in graffiti from a demonstration the previous week. There I caught the tail end of a procession of people making their way toward Place de la République. It was a largely peaceful group of mostly young people, some holding signs mocking President Emmanuel Macron, some waving French flags. Intermittently, marchers would break out in chanting and clapping.

At République, police officers ringed the square, dressed in riot gear as though preparing to go to war. It was crowded but civil. Some people wore surgical masks, others gas masks, ready for tear gas, the faint smell of which was already in the air. Television crews interviewed protesters. A few climbed the statue of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, and waved French flags. Shortly after I arrived, flash bangs began going off on one of the side streets toward Canal St. Martin, and canisters of tear gas could be seen sailing through the air. Crowds began running back into the square. As the tear gas grew thicker, I sought a quick exit down the narrow path the police had provided for people to leave.

It was only on Sunday that I saw the shattered windows, looted stores and charred remains of electric bikes.

The violence of the protests, which was amplified on social media and apparently the result of rioters exploiting the moment, threatens to undermine the message of the students and risks resulting in the exact opposite of their goals, which is to petition for more government resources devoted to education and, by extension, a more sustainable future.

These days of protest and rage have struck me as more than just a rebuff to the French government. The students’ fury is giving voice to some larger social failures many of us, in France and elsewhere, often fail to face directly: the climate catastrophe, the terror of artificial intelligence, the faltering economic picture. The students’ determination to voice their anger and frustration over the future is a necessary and courageous reminder that we all need to be facing facts and acting on them.

On my bike ride home from République on Saturday, I encountered an impromptu gathering of students singing “La Marseillaise,” the French national anthem. As they passed the intersection, some set down bikes and other objects to block cars and make the trip more difficult for everyone. That’s as it should be, I thought, as I navigated past the makeshift barricades. Against the backdrop of so many destructive forces, none of us, anywhere, should be allowed to proceed easily.

Since late spring, a series of calamities, in quick succession, have taken a battering ram to the fantasy that Paris is some sort of respite from the problems plaguing the world. A number of punishing, record-breaking heat waves roiled the country, beginning in May. Temperatures in Paris soared above 100 degrees Fahrenheit again and again this summer. Joyful images of young Parisians leaping into the Canal St. Martin and the Seine were sobered by a national death toll of nearly 8,000 and fires that burned tens of thousands of acres. The spectacle of haute couture shows held in the extreme heat felt especially grotesque. Walking through the city this fall, I still see the tattered remains of silver foil hacked together to keep out the heat fluttering from windows. Every piece of store-bought chocolate I’ve purchased since summer is white from having melted and resolidified. As October began, I wandered into the Pride parade rescheduled after the extreme heat made it untenable.

And then the streets were aflame.

All this is happening against the impending presidential election next spring, which currently favors the far-right candidate Marine Le Pen. To paraphrase F. Scott Fitzgerald, chronicler of the interwar period (another era known for its wild abandon), a restlessness approaches hysteria, with menacing undertones that have finally burst to the fore with the protests. Mr. Macron, the target of much of the students’ anger and derision, didn’t help matters much by spending his Friday night with Celine Dion, dancing at the city’s most coveted concert just before parts of Paris burned.

In a speech broadcast live Sunday night, Mr. Macron made a point to differentiate between the protesters’ “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed and looted.” He said, “We all feel anger and shame.”

Americans, in particular, have always been susceptible to the country’s siren call. Last year, France had a 14 percent increase in first-time residency permits issued to Americans. As life and politics in the United States have grown ever harsher and more punishing, Americans have craved France’s monthlong vacations and universal health care (if not the tax burden that supports them).

But now, with Saturday’s enormous — and enormously destructive — protests, the dream that there is a place of escape may be nearing an end. With their anger and determination to tap into France’s long history of revolution, students are showing the rest of the world that the only way to march into the dark future is together.

Loudly. And with cleareyed resolve. Their challenge now is to keep the violence at bay. If there is a French fantasy to pursue in these tumultuous times, this must be the one.

Glynnis MacNicol is a contributing Opinion writer. She is the author of “I’m Mostly Here to Enjoy Myself.”

SUMMARY

Which raises the second Zionism, the easiest one for American liberals to disdain. The first two, political and religious Zionism, while dicey for American liberals, are easier for them to understand. In contrast, few Americans — or American Jews, for that matter — can perceive, let alone appreciate, Israeliness, or the cultural Zionism as it exists in the Jewish state.

ARTICLE

There Is a Zionism That Needs the Support of Progressives
American liberals should not abandon Israel’s cultural Zionists.
By Bernard Avishai
Published 2026-10-19 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/opinion/international-world/israel-us-liberals-zionism.html

For nearly 60 years, I have split my time between Israel and North America. After a string of Benjamin Netanyahu’s governments, the Gaza war, the Iran attacks, plus more than a half-century of occupation and at least $300 billion in American aid, I cannot recall a time when being identified as a Zionist seemed so awkward among American liberals, whom I count as kindred spirits.

In 2024, Pew reported that among Democratic and Democratic-leaning respondents under 30, 47 percent said their sympathies lay more with Palestinians, and just 7 percent with Israelis. Democratic candidates who decline to use the terms apartheid or genocide when talking about Israel flunk the progressive wing’s entrance exam. Last year, a flier reportedly distributed by a local activist group blamed “Zionist white supremacists” for rent increases in Crown Heights.

Ordinarily, I would not be inclined to defend Zionism as a movement. It’s not because I reject its history and achievements. It’s because as a movement, it has long been anachronistic. Fifty years ago, I was already arguing that we were in a “post-Zionist” era — that Israel had graduated into a diverse, established country, with culture wars of its own, and did not need to present a united front as if it were still soliciting, say, recognition from the Truman White House. If what one means by Zionism is being pro-Israel, well, I’m pro some Israelis, anti others.

And yet, the debate over Zionism now seems inescapable in America, especially since some Israeli leaders seem unable to retire the term. Zionism, as my late friend, the writer A.B. Yehoshua, put it, is “the ketchup poured onto every plate.” In the current Israeli election campaign, even centrist leaders opposing Mr. Netanyahu are promising a Zionist government, their proxy term for a coalition not reliant on Arab Israeli parties to make a majority — not in wartime, anyway. More generally, they say, they want a Jewish and democratic state, yet feel the need to signal that they will not sacrifice the former to the latter. Just what they mean by democratic, if cooperation with Arab parties is precluded, they leave to our imaginations.

Which brings us to the real issue at hand. The most fair-minded critics of Zionism pose a question, which is not a bad one. Can any Jewish state, any product of Zionism, possibly be a country worthy of the democratic liberalism that progressives in America are fighting for? Is a Jewish and democratic state a contradiction in terms? Prominent critics of Zionism — Jewish ones included — insist that Americans ought to advocate equality of citizenship in any state, irrespective of ethnicity, religion and race, while Zionism seems to presuppose some sort of Jewish supremacy. Haven’t Mr. Netanyahu’s grotesque governments been, in this context, more the effect of Zionist ideology than the cause of its debasement?

In some ways, yes, and in another, no, actually. There were three distinct Zionist ideologies in Israel’s prehistory — political, religious and cultural — which have left marks on the country’s current political leaders. These ideologies can coexist in our imaginations, but each defines a distinct historical crisis, each presents a distinct solution, and each has implications for the kind of state Israel can be.

The first Zionism, political, is arguably inconsistent with democratic life; the second, religious Zionism, inarguably so. Yet the third, the cultural kind, is consistent with democracy. Its acolytes — secular Israeli liberals who are the most affluent, educated and internationally minded third of the country — are in a multigenerational struggle and fighting for the future of their country. They could use the support of American progressives, not some sweeping dismissal of Israel’s very existence, which, ironically, only plays into the hands of Israel’s right-wing populists and theocrats.

The first Zionism is the most familiar. The problem it purported to solve was unyielding persecution of Jews and the psychic wound of powerlessness. Good luck trying to assimilate into Western countries; the Holocaust is the ultimate proof that this hope is forlorn, political Zionists would say. Israel’s rejection by the Arab world fell in the same category. Defiance, in this rubric, is also a mass therapy. Citizenship in the Jewish state is embodied in the Law of Return: Jews were hunted on racial grounds, and so their state includes, and privileges, anyone with a single Jewish grandparent. So long as Israel sustains a Jewish majority, and accords civil rights to minorities, it is democratic enough for the Middle East. Though political Zionists are often secular, they may also bow to Orthodox piety to engender national solidarity.

Which raises the second Zionism, the easiest one for American liberals to disdain. Call it cultic Zionism, so as not to degrade the word religious. Cultic Zionists want a Jewish — or more precisely, a “Jewist” — state, quite like Islamist theocracies: promised land, a holy city, holy law, perfect (or at least superior) commandments underlying ethics, a metahistory of kingdoms and messianic projections, a skewed archaeology turning Judean artifacts into irredentist claims. Rabbinic courts and Halakhic law would supersede civil courts. About the role of women, or the rights of homosexuals, the less said the better.

But a third Zionism, the one that built the country, saw things quite differently: cultural Zionism, which morphed into the Labor Zionist settlement project from 1905 on. This focused on the adoption and development of modern Hebrew, along with the socialist political economy that enabled Hebrew to proliferate as a language of work and self-reflection in pioneering internal colonies.

Cultural Zionism’s cadres are products of the 18th- and 19th-century Jewish Enlightenment, or Haskalah, in Europe, who saw secular modern culture to be inevitable and attractive. Rabbinic authority, they thought, would justifiably be superseded by liberal norms and evolutionary science. Yet they also saw themselves as custodians of liturgical Hebrew, fabulous texts, legal precepts and prophetic ideals not bound by Talmudic constraints, of musical forms and poetic grandeur — all of these — which might be transformed into material for individual artistic innovations.

The problem cultural Zionism sought to allay was not the impossibility of assimilation but the certainty of it — that is, in Western liberal countries such as the United States and Western European nations, where granular Jewish life would be dissolved by the languages and cultures of host nations and so would be reduced to synagogues and kitsch. The goal of cultural Zionists was a secular and distinctly Jewish national home as un-self-consciously and inclusively liberal as France is, well, French.

By 1925, Labor Zionist culturalists, settling in collectives on land purchased from absentee landlords, had begun dispossessing thousands of Palestinian tenant farmers, helping to provoke the bitter conflict that we know. But these settlers considered that their lands would amount to a small sliver of Arabia and that a modernizing Hebrew-speaking civil society could, with statehood, assimilate Arabs and Druze as full citizens.

How do these various Zionisms fare in America? The first two, political and religious Zionism, while dicey for American liberals, are easier for them to understand. That’s because they refract Israel through the prism of American Jewish experience: a dream palace of religious longing and ethnic solidarity in the face of bigotry — a big synagogue with an air force.

In contrast, few Americans — or American Jews, for that matter — can perceive, let alone appreciate, Israeliness, or the cultural Zionism as it exists in the Jewish state. They don’t typically sit in cafes on Tel Aviv’s Rothschild Boulevard, go to a Shalom Hanoch concert or read a Lea Goldberg poem. They don’t go to Hadassah hospitals, where, entirely in Hebrew, they are treated by an integrated team of Jewish and Arab Israelis — physicians, nurses and pharmacists. They don’t see, in short, that a democratic Hebrew Republic, while not yet fully realized, is plausible, or that Israelis advancing the political and religious Zionist ideas that Americans default to continue to obstruct it.

The tragedy of this lack of understanding of cultural Zionism is that instead of American progressives expressing fellow feeling for Israeli progressives, they assume that the latter, owing to their Zionism, cannot exist. So, they engage in boycotts of Israeli technology start-ups, news organizations, film institutes, scientific labs and universities — the very institutions that incubate Israeli liberalism, and which Mr. Netanyahu is already only too happy to starve. Indeed, their boycotts seem to justify Israeli rightist tropes that Jews are condemned to be hated.

Since American sympathies are on the line here, I hasten to add that sympathy for Palestinians is possible in Israel, too, and especially for Palestinian leaders who are reciprocal enough to choose a common future over a fight to the finish. Palestinians need Israeli liberals as much as they need American ones, after all. Israelis, Palestinians and Americans can safely consider the moral prestige of historical Zionism as beside the point. But in no country does liberty defend itself. Americans should realize that Israeli liberals, too, need them for that fight.

Bernard Avishai, a visiting professor of government at Dartmouth College, is the author of “The Tragedy of Zionism,” “A New Israel,” and “The Hebrew Republic.”

SUMMARY

But above all, Guilfoyle must be baffled. Guilfoyle, 57, and Donald Trump Jr., 48, broke up in 2024. Guilfoyle was an Einstein of avarice and an avatar of Trump.

ARTICLE

Kimberly Guilfoyle, Sacrificial Ham
The exiled ambassador didn’t defy the president. She mimicked him.
By Frank Bruni
Published 2026-10-19 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/opinion/kimberly-guilfoyle-fired.html

Kimberly Guilfoyle must be frenzied. She was abruptly ousted from her role as the U.S. ambassador to Greece and needs to scram, but I doubt she’s capable of packing in a jiff. She probably fills a half dozen steamer trunks with the wardrobe needed to maintain her busy social calendar.

Guilfoyle must be panicked. Normally, a disgraced or displaced Trump-administration showboat can hope for lucrative harbor at Fox News, but she already worked for the network years ago, and that arrangement also had a tawdry finale. According to an article by Jane Mayer in The New Yorker, she was forced out after a female assistant accused her of such inappropriate behavior as sharing photographs of the phalluses in her life.

But above all, Guilfoyle must be baffled. What exactly did she do to warrant President Trump’s contempt?

The rap against her is that she crassly exploited her ambassadorship for pleasure and profit, as a recent series of reports in The Wall Street Journal detailed.

But with her fame-hungry dreams and money-ravenous schemes, she didn’t violate the Trump ethos. She paid tribute to it. She didn’t contradict the Trump brand. She was its gaudy, greedy hood ornament.

In conventional political circles in ordinary times, an aide gets the ax because he or she has fallen out of step with the other members of the team and misunderstood the operation’s ideals. Guilfoyle understood and embodied them perfectly.

That’s what makes her banishment so interesting. It speaks to one of Trump’s favorite parlor tricks: pretending to be the opposite of who he is by feigning offense at behavior that’s a mirror of his own. He accuses Democrats of the very political thievery that he has attempted. He calls his predecessors economic ignoramuses as he redefines incompetence in that arena. And he signals disapproval of how Guilfoyle took advantage of her station as if such unscrupulous opportunism isn’t the very essence of him, his family and his friends.

The way I figure it, Trump made an example of Guilfoyle so that he doesn’t have to crack down on others in his rancidly corrupt administration. She’s the sacrificial ham. And he allowed himself an extra measure of cruel fun by acting as if he barely knew her.

“She wasn’t a member of my family,” he told reporters who asked about her resignation when it was announced last week. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”

A long time ago? Guilfoyle, 57, and Donald Trump Jr., 48, broke up in 2024. The president guesses? She and Junior were engaged and owned a house together in Florida. And she shrieked her allegiance to his wretched clan in speeches at both the 2020 and the 2024 Republican conventions. People in the front rows still haven’t gotten their hearing back.

Then Junior pivoted to Bettina Anderson, a sometime model 18 years younger than Guilfoyle, and married her. Greece was Guilfoyle’s runner-up prize. And from the moment she arrived there, touching down in the private jet of a rich Greek American businessman, she began clubbing and hobnobbing and styling her ambassadorship as an ego odyssey of ever-changing outfits.

Those articles in The Journal — whose claims she has disputed — recount how she cozied up to Greek business leaders in inappropriate ways, accepted lavish gifts and played financial footsie with a Trump donor who promised to pay her as much as $1 million if she helped him win access to and the favor of key administration officials. That donor gave The Journal what appeared to be text messages in which Guilfoyle pleaded with him to take care of a $100,000 American Express bill of hers in advance of her Senate confirmation hearing. Instead, he exposed her, and the nakedness of their transactions apparently rankled the president to a degree that the sprees and spending of other Trump aides — Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, and Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, come instantly to mind — haven’t.

Trump is quicker with pink slips for the women in his employ than for the men, as Erica L. Green recently recognized in The Times and as Katie Zacharia discovered last week, when she was terminated as White House press secretary just five days after assuming the post. That surely isn’t lost on Guilfoyle, and I’m betting she also noticed that Junior let a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a post-nuptials bacchanal in the Bahamas for him and the lovely Bettina. Guilfoyle’s platinum panhandling was no more shameless than his.

And he’s the one who’s really getting richer — he and his brother Eric, his stepmother Melania, his brother-in-law Jared Kushner and a grifter’s gallery of money-mad, morally bereft hangers-on. In Trump’s second stint in the presidency even more than in his first, he leverages misbegotten policy and misguided diplomacy for personal profit — for his kin, his associates, his donors and most of all himself. He eschews do-gooders restrained by ethics; go-getters don’t encumber themselves with such self-effacing silliness. And smart people maximize perks that dullards and weaklings don’t even spot.

Guilfoyle was an Einstein of avarice and an avatar of Trump. In thrall to the television camera, she long ago traded real lawyering for on-air legal analysis for CNN and ABC and then Fox News, where she ascended to the role of co-host of “The Five.” She was inconstant in her ideology but consistent in her attraction to celebrity, segueing from a brief marriage to Gavin Newsom to her aborted engagement to Junior. And she was — and is — unabashed in her self-adoration. She decorated Jefferson House, the Athens residence of the American ambassador, with enormous portraits of herself.

From her vanity-driven messes to her cartoonishly voluminous tresses, she’s MAGA incarnate, and if imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, then she flattered Trump as sincerely as anyone ever did. For that, she’s exiled? I’m not sure if that’s irony, tragedy or comedy. In Trump’s world, the three have a habit of blurring.

For the Love of Sentences

As is often the case after the newsletter has gone dark for a few weeks, I’m allotting this section extra space, so I can fit in a few more of the accumulated nominations.

In his newsletter, Ron Charles recognized the impossibly high bar that an author’s previous novel set for her follow-up: “To say it’s no ‘Demon Copperhead’ hardly seems fair. But that’s the unenviable starting point for Barbara Kingsolver’s new novel, ‘Partita.’ One squints to read it in the glaring light of its predecessor.” (Thanks to David P. Barash of Goleta, Calif., for nominating this.)

In The Times, Jeff Giles described what he saw when he read the book: “Kingsolver is interested in what we accrue over our lifetimes, like iron filings to a magnet. Or shrapnel.” (Donna Stephens, Cape Cod, Mass.)

Also in The Times, Rukmini Callimachi explained why many of the omelet-mad Americans who joined the craze for miniature coops in their backyards got a loud and eggless surprise: “A chick is a fluffy question mark, and even the professionals tasked with determining the sex of chicks sometimes get it wrong. As a result, a meaningful share of ‘hens’ carried home during the great chick rush grew up, found their voice and started using it at 4:30 in the morning.” (Julie Jennrich, New Glarus, Wis.)

In The Wall Street Journal, Dan Neil reported that while nobody in Monterey, Calif., batted an eye at the Ferrari Amalfi that he was driving, it drew a different reaction in Raleigh, N.C.: “The rakish Amalfi would have high schoolers jumping around like the early hominids in ‘2001: A Space Odyssey.’” (Andy Laster, Charlotte, N.C.)

In The London Review of Books, Adam Mars-Jones contemplated the limits of the “absolute outrage” that “The Disappearers,” a celebrated new novel by Marlon James, asks readers to feel: “Outrage is no more than anger in the key of helplessness.” (Val Traversy, Clam Bay, Nova Scotia)

In The Washington Post, David Von Drehle rued the tawdry and transactional religion of the televangelist Jim Bakker, who died this month, and his spiritual kin. “God is a celestial A.T.M., coughing up the cash we’ve banked through our displays of virtue plus the interest earned by his grace, provided we enter the right scriptural PIN,” he wrote, then asked: “How all-knowing is a deity that needs constant reminders in the form of tithes and offerings? That needs TV preachers to manage his miracles? The God of the prosperity gospel was really no greater than the squabbling mercenary gods of the Greeks and Romans, jealous clerks in the great department store of nature, this one dispensing rain, that one arranging harvests.” (Matt Bai, Bethesda, Md. and Stan Martin, Andover, Mass., among others)

Also in The Post, Megan McArdle deconstructed many Americans’ shock at the botched attempt to execute Christa Pike. “As long as we do not confront certain brutal realities, we can keep imagining that death looks like the peaceful portrayals in television and movies, where patients apparently suffering from Extreme Paleness murmur loving final words and quietly close their eyes.” (Carey Winfrey, Amenia, N.Y.)

In Slate, Chason Gordon mulled melons: ”There’s always been a cutthroat rivalry between honeydew and cantaloupe. Honeydew’s a little sweeter and firmer, and cantaloupe — with its bright orange flesh and netted rind — looks like a sofa from the 1970s, and when bad, can kind of smell like one, too.” (Harold Gotthelf, Fords, N.J.)

In The Atlantic, Rogé Karma asserted that there are problems well shy of humanity’s erasure — bank heists, disinformation campaigns, attacks on power grids — that argue for firm guardrails for A.I.: “If those have the side benefit of averting the apocalypse, it wouldn’t be the end of the world.” (Mike Shelton, Sand Springs, Okla.)

Also in The Atlantic, Alexandra Petri ventriloquized Katie Zacharia, then the new White House press secretary, giving her a script truer than the one she used for her dubious debut: “You may know me from my appearances on Fox News; I am pretty sure that is how the president knows me. That is how he identifies all possible candidates for jobs: turning on the TV and pointing. My successor will be a Kalshi commercial.” There was more. “I’m bringing a kind of ‘unlicensed bus driver’ energy to this speech: unsteady at best, with many seemingly random stops in unexpected places. Just call me Vote by Mail, because my delivery is raising a lot of questions in the White House.” (Stan Shatenstein, Montreal)

In The Dispatch, Jonah Goldberg responded to Trump’s apparent belief that Republicans can triumph in the midterms by insisting that the economy is great and pretending that he’s on the ballot: “Also, the best way to repel grizzly bears is to slather yourself in a thick paste of salmon, honey and vanilla ice cream and then grab a bear cub for a selfie.” (Dan Markovitz, Corte Madera, Calif.)

And in her newsletter, Joanne Carducci, a.k.a. JoJoFromJerz, saw pure shtick in the performance of Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, during that tragicomical Senate hearing into the former special counsel Jack Smith’s investigations of Trump: “Kennedy has a law degree from the University of Virginia and studied at Oxford, but point a television camera at him and suddenly he’s three syllables away from telling us his meemaw always said you can’t prosecute a possum during crawfish season. It’s not folksiness. It’s intellectual drag.” (Julie Lalo, Glenshaw, Pa.)

What I’m Reading, Watching, Writing and Doing

- Not everyone has the emotional honesty and intellectual nimbleness to love a country madly while seeing its faults clearly, but that’s what my Times colleague Jason Horowitz brought to his coverage of Italy during the years — 2017 to 2025 — when he served as our Rome bureau chief. He reflects on that experience in a memoir, “The Italian Job,” that was published early this month.
- The new HBO Max series “War” imagines “the biggest divorce trial in British legal history,” as one of the many shady lawyers involved in it says. And so far (just three of eight episodes have been released), it delivers the snippy, snappy pleasures you’d expect.
- My Duke colleague Phil Napoli, working with a team of students at the school, confirmed and quantified an impression that I — and, I bet, many of you — have had: Fox News lavishes an inordinate amount of airtime on trashing journalists and journalism. Read more in their article in Nieman Lab.
- In our most recent exchange, Bret Stephens and I debated the meaning of the midterms. We previously examined the resistance to artificial intelligence. Before that we parsed the president’s attempts to quash journalism he doesn’t like.
- I have long enjoyed and admired the perspectives of Katherine Mangu-Ward, the editor in chief of Reason magazine, including recent essays in The Times about the wisdom of libertarians and the loneliness of the Republican congressman Thomas Massie. She’s an unconventional thinker and a spirited communicator, and that combination should make for a great evening at Duke University on Monday, Oct. 26, when I’ll chat with her onstage about American politics, the midterms and the country’s uncertain future. On a Personal (and Partly Regan) Note

The newsletter went dark for the last two weeks because I was dealing with a serious medical issue, and both the time consumed by daily treatments and their painful side effects slowed me down significantly.

I’ll perhaps at some point say more about that; I just haven’t figured out what or if there’s any purpose. For one thing, those treatments, which lasted six weeks, are over; the side effects shall slowly fade; and my long-term prognosis is excellent, probably allowing me to put this challenging chapter firmly in the past. For another, I reflected on illness, vulnerability and aging in my 2022 book “The Beauty of Dusk,” which recounted a rare stroke that compromised my vision, and in several essays in The Times related to that. (Here’s the first of those articles; here’s another.) I’m not sure I have additional insights.

Except about my beloved Regan. I went through that medical odyssey before she shared my home with me. I went through this one in her furry company.

My friends, who know how strong the bond between Regan and me is, kept asking: Did she sense that I was hurting? Did she hover, cling, console? At first I said no, not really. She seemed to me no more or less affectionate than usual, which was plenty affectionate.

Then, well, she did start to cling. Maybe. I couldn’t definitively tell, and I couldn’t be trusted to decide: I was too primed to detect some extrasensory perception in her, too eager for a storybook uptick in doggy empathy. Isn’t that the great flaw in all our observations? They’re tainted by what we want — and have been coached — to see.

Here’s what I indisputably noticed: As I struggled, she adapted. As I focused more and more on my needs, she relaxed hers. She made no visible protest over fewer walks, earlier bedtimes, long spells in the middle of each day when I was away at the medical center. I teetered; she didn’t.

Dogs have a way of surrendering to changes beyond their control. It’s a part of their wisdom, an aspect of their grace. I can’t say that Regan doted on me, nor am I sure what, exactly, that would look like. But she did something simpler and better: She stood steadily by me. Slept snugly beside me. As if nothing were wrong. Which made everything a crucial bit more right.

republican-party-trump-future.html

SUMMARY

“Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” President Trump has been pleading with Republicans in midterm campaign stops. That cacophony of voices representing itself as Republican would have been unthinkable before Mr. Trump. The state party accepted him even though he refused an explicit demand from Mr. Trump.

ARTICLE

The Midterms Look Dark for Republicans. Their Future Looks Brighter.
The G.O.P. will not always be focused around the strong personality and charisma of Trump.
By Michael Brendan Dougherty
Published 2026-10-19 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/opinion/republican-party-trump-future.html

“Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” President Trump has been pleading with Republicans in midterm campaign stops. He has a point. With him on the ballot, in 2016 and 2024, Republicans fared much better than they expected. In 2018 and 2022, without him, they stumbled.

But two things can be true at once. Mr. Trump is the party’s great unifier, and going into 2026, he’s the party’s biggest drag.

G.O.P. candidates can read polls as well as anyone, and those in the toughest races are reacting almost in real time. Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa, Mike Rogers in Michigan and Senator Jon Husted in Ohio have broken with the president on some issues, and all three have called for an end to the fighting in Iran.

The midterm outlook for Republicans may be poor, and Mr. Trump’s unpopularity may be dragging the party down. But by smashing the former consensus in the party, he has allowed new elected figures and influencers to start building a different G.O.P.

The Dallas midterm G.O.P. convention may have looked like yet another event to focus attention on Mr. Trump as the main attraction and the biggest draw. But we actually got a glimpse of the post-Trump road ahead. We saw figures who disagree with Mr. Trump, and with one another, to one degree or another.

That cacophony of voices representing itself as Republican would have been unthinkable before Mr. Trump. And it is this collection of voices — the mismatched set of impulses and ambitions on display — that may very well represent the future of the Republican Party.

It will be a big tent, and bring in people who didn’t feel welcomed in the G.O.P. before and who may even disagree on some issues — and yet a party with the real potential to grow into a majority. Yes, it will have to transition from one focused around the strong personality and charisma of Mr. Trump to a coalition. It doesn’t lack for potential leaders who could fit that model.

So 2026 may be rough. But in the years ahead, that party may be electorally stronger than what preceded it, even if it is far more diverse and fractious than the old one.

There is a model for what this kind of Republican Party can become. The New Deal Democrats were the most dominant political coalition of the 20th century. That party joined urban Catholics with Southern segregationists, farmers with union workers and, increasingly, Black Americans as well.

A restive coalition, it was held together by patronage and shared enemies. Southern committee chairmen in the House and Senate with seniority shaped the New Deal to fit their region and constituents. Political machines in Chicago, Kansas City and New York turned relief jobs and money into votes from Catholic and Jewish immigrants. Unions organized workers as a matter of loyalty to one another, not to New Deal intellectuals. Farmers got price supports and rural electricity.

The New Deal coalition was undone by historical upheavals like the civil rights era, the Vietnam War and the social revolutions of the 1960s that would split the party. But the long, multifarious life of New Deal Democrats shows that a looser coalitional arrangement can dominate electorally, and even manage enormous internal cultural differences and contrasting priorities for decades.

Before Mr. Trump, the Republican creed was easy to state: smaller government, lower taxes, free trade and global leadership. The party isn’t going back to it whole. Nor does what’s coming look like a contest between two ideologically grouped sides, the Tea Party-style libertarian populists and the conservative nationalists.

That’s too simple and neat. Many nationalists are against wars. Take Vice President JD Vance and Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri. Though he supports the president publicly, Mr. Vance is widely reported to have advised against the Iran war. Both suspect NATO can be a debit on American sovereignty, not just a force multiplier. Mr. Hawley voted against Swedish and Finnish membership in NATO. Libertarian types believe the government is too intrusive in Americans’ lives, and the MAHA movement says regulators are captured by corporations. They are united by suspicion of the state. At the Dallas midterm convention, programming moved through the party constituencies hour by hour: “America First” trade police, school choice and opposition to gender ideology in youth sports, chronic disease and “corporate influence in public health agencies.” Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. drew cheers for praising his uncle Ted Kennedy’s authorship of Title IX. John Fetterman, a Democratic senator, sent a video introducing and praising a Republican Senate colleague, Dave McCormick, vowing to “defend the steel way of life” in western Pennsylvania.

Or take the example of glyphosate, a controversial pesticide used on millions of acres of farmland. For years, Mr. Kennedy has railed against its overuse. When the Trump administration declared glyphosate production a matter of national security, Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida was behind an amendment to strip a liability shield for pesticide makers from the farm bill. She was joined by Chip Roy from the Freedom Caucus. It is another glimpse of party members not walking in lock step but clashing over ideas and positions.

Almost every Republican wants to restrain the reach and ambitions of government, but they no longer agree on where. Just look at how the September outcry about Flock cameras scrambled Republicans. Some Republicans defended them as a tool for law and order, others an unholy alliance between Big Tech and big government against our rights and privacy. Senator Hawley, who heads the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, opened an investigation into the company in August, and ripped it in a televised hearing.

Take data centers. A Fox News poll in July found that 70 percent of voters opposed building data centers in their area. Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance defend them, but Mr. Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, backed a moratorium on new ones. Senator Husted supported them in his state but also introduced a bill to shield residents from higher electricity costs.

Debate and negotiation give even the losers a stake in the party. They may not win this time, but there will be other opportunities to fight for their cause. And the contestation over ideas makes a party seem to voters like it is more engaged with the vital questions about the future of the country.

Over a decade ago, Peter Harris, a political science professor at the Colorado State University, said that the problem with the G.O.P. was that it was “not diverse enough.” He meant ideologically, but he also believed that a little less party discipline and more internal debate would change the demographics of the party. He noted that figures like the stalwart libertarian Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky or the evangelical culture warrior Senator Ted Cruz of Texas serve an important function as “outriders.” These figures, he said, would flummox the party establishment but “excite and engage large numbers of young Americans, racial minorities and others not usually tempted by the G.O.P. brand.”

Mr. Harris was right: The outriders — none more so than Mr. Trump — dragged in exactly those voters. In a New York Times/L2 analysis, between 2020 and 2024, Republicans gained 2.4 million registered voters, while Democrats lost 2.1 million. Democrats lost ground in voter registration in 30 states in that time period. Similarly, Gallup’s three-year trend showed Republican identification broadening among groups that don’t fit into the traditional business wing or the evangelical wing: Hispanics, voters under 30, lower-income Americans. Republicans gained among Catholics and African Americans, too.

This G.O.P. coalition is under strain in 2026. The most notable break is among Hispanic voters. In a New York Times report on polls, Democrats lead among Hispanic likely voters on the generic congressional ballot by 35 points. The same pollsters found Kamala Harris, then the vice president, ahead by only seven points in their final 2024 surveys. Republican gains among young voters are also in jeopardy. Polling by Echelon Insights found Mr. Trump’s net approval among 18- to 34-year-olds at minus-44 in August.

Voters soured on Mr. Trump for familiar reasons: the deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Renee Good, among others, in ICE encounters, an Iran war that drags on and pushes up energy prices and inflation. What ties these complaints together is that Mr. Trump has governed less like the outsider who ran in 2016 and more like the party he had come to change. He signed tax cuts with a Republican Congress and made the market a measure of his success. Instead of draining the swamp, he has presided over a Washington where graft now looks rampant.

But this isn’t a simple reversion to the old status quo either. It looks more as if younger voters and Hispanics are at the volatile edge of longer-term trends. Hispanic voters may swing toward Democrats this year, but as a TelevisaUnivision executive said recently, Latino voters “aren’t locked into one party.” Gallup, meanwhile, found that a record 45 percent of adults called themselves independents in 2025.

These trends are the environment the party sits in now — and they suggest the party has room to grow.

The potential leaders of a future Republican Party seem to be pulling in different directions. This just so happens to be the physics of building a big tent.

Mr. Vance is the likeliest nominee for the 2028 presidential election. His recent book about his conversion to Catholicism puts economic concern for families at the center of his conservatism. Traditional conservatives regularly denounce him for his views on “America first” foreign policy and trade restrictions. Mr. Trump himself noted that Mr. Vance had a “philosophically” different view on Iran, code for advising against it. His more populist views probably work to his advantage in a general election.

Still, even if a Fox News Poll shows that 70 percent of voters are at odds with Mr. Trump on data centers, Mr. Vance has defended the building projects as essential for our competition with China. In Dallas, Mr. Vance acknowledged the discontent and heterogeneity in the Republican coalition, telling voters he wouldn’t ask for agreement on every issue.

Although some cast them as antagonists, and they may have some disagreements on foreign policy, Secretary of State Marco Rubio is quite similar to Mr. Vance. Both were initially hostile to Mr. Trump and eventually became loyal to him and began to echo him on trade and reindustrialization.

Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, who has generally been seen as more acceptable to the traditional business-friendly wing, is taking a stance on artificial intelligence that is more populist than Mr. Vance’s. He pushed hard for A.I. regulation in Florida, barring data centers from passing infrastructure and electricity costs on to residential ratepayers. Mr. Hawley is also fighting Mr. Cruz in the Senate over a federal A.I. moratorium.

The older Reagan-Bush Republican Party may get the closest thing to its own champion in Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia, who not only hews to the conservative movement’s orthodoxy on taxes and small government but whose political persona has been shaped by his clashes with Mr. Trump over the 2020 election. A Kemp nomination would represent the return of the repressed.

Still, Mr. Kemp’s own survival in the Trump era is instructive. The state party accepted him even though he refused an explicit demand from Mr. Trump. In Mr. Kemp there is a lesson: There is a way for competent politicians to survive big internal battles, manage a fractious coalition and still win.

There are also the many well-known figures and influencers who have become influential in various parts of the G.O.P. coalition and the wider new media world that now surrounds it.

Tucker Carlson is a wild card. He has all but sworn a vendetta against President Trump over the war in Iran. Mr. Carlson’s current passion over issues of foreign policy regularly drives him to describe America, or its politicians, as being enslaved to the ambitions of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel or his government.

Mr. Carlson also shows that the party’s coalitional openness is a two-way street. It’s one thing to cheer when Senator Fetterman crosses over to cheer a Republican senator. It’s another to watch the party’s most influential podcaster praise a Democrat — something Mr. Carlson did when he said he wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers in Michigan at gunpoint and lauded the agenda of the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, as “literally Trumpian.” A coalition loose enough to let Mr. Fetterman in the front door is also loose enough to let Mr. Carlson escape.

The MAHA moms and the wellness right look to figures like Jillian Michaels, a fitness trainer and a TV personality. There’s the manosphere in its varieties, from extreme misogyny to more mainstream “save our boys” concerns among parents who see their sons failing to thrive in school. There are the national populists who tune in to Steve Bannon’s “War Room.” And there are people Mr. Bannon denounces, like the tech bros and A.I. optimists on the “All-In Podcast.”

There are the foreign-policy restrainers who think the liberal world order is a threat to America’s independence and solvency, and there are the hawkish diaspora groups from Iran, Venezuela, Ukraine and Cuba who want the G.O.P. to press harder on foreign policy. And there are still the stalwarts: gun owners and pro-lifers.

Yes, Mr. Trump’s personal charisma and the way he could turn any controversy into one about himself rather than the substance have papered over these differences for a decade.

When the midterms end, the party will go through a rambunctious primary in 2028 — and eventually it will rally behind a nominee. Throughout, the G.O.P. will disagree about tariffs, A.I. and foreign policy.

What will unify this fractious coalition after Mr. Trump is a common enemy in the liberals of the credentialed class. That class staffs the very institutions — such as universities — that Americans have come to broadly distrust. The G.O.P. will continue to cast its antagonist as a national H.R. department: intrusive, entitled and not really more qualified than you, just empowered.

Republicans must beware of a big vulnerability of coalitional politics: factional capture. In the past, the G.O.P. has suffered when it could be caricatured as a party beholden to the country club or as the political wing of an evangelical tent revival.

Democrats are now suffering from this very problem with the dominance of their college-educated faction and their values. Their influence on the party is disproportionate to their numbers.

The most important battle line between the parties in the years ahead might come down to a simple question: who can appeal to normal people? Winning that competition requires, at the very least, demonstrating that your party isn’t hostage to one faction and threatening to rule everyone by its norms.

But it bears noting that normal people can seem politically weird. The same person can be paranoid about Flock cameras and enthusiastic about A.I., antiracist but gender-critical, distrust the Food and Drug Administration but want food additives to be better regulated.

A coalitional party doesn’t exhaustively try to resolve those contradictions; it just tries to contain them and draw what is useful from them without letting one faction or figure try to speak for 330 million citizens.

Mr. Trump shattered the image of the G.O.P. as a vehicle dominated by the conservative ideological movement. Now the post-Trump Republican Party is freer to rebuild itself again as a more fractious coalition.

The traditional stalwarts for small government are still in there, and still have influence. But the party is no longer in their grip. They may find that the party lasts longer and goes a little harder under conditions of anarchy.

Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review.

SUMMARY

Covid has been around long enough that the once wildly unpredictable virus has finally settled into a few recognizable patterns. But repeated Covid infections can take a toll, he and other researchers said. Covid infections have generally become milder as the virus has mutated and new variants have circulated.

ARTICLE

How Bad Is Another Case of Covid?
Repeated infections are “a fact of life” at this point, experts say. But they warn there is no such thing as a risk-free case.
By Dani Blum
Published 2026-10-19 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/well/covid-reinfection-risks.html

Covid has been around long enough that the once wildly unpredictable virus has finally settled into a few recognizable patterns.

Cases normally rise in the late fall and winter, so repeated infections seem inevitable in the coming months. “Reinfection is more or less a fact of life, with an asterisk,” said Dr. Ziyad Al-Aly, a senior clinical epidemiologist at Washington University in St. Louis who studies Covid. “The asterisk here is that we tend to trivialize this.”

And people who have already been sick with the virus three, or five or seven times may think they know what’s in store should they test positive again: a cough, an aching throat, full-body fatigue or other common symptoms.

But repeated Covid infections can take a toll, he and other researchers said.

Milder Infections, Continued Risk

Covid infections have generally become milder as the virus has mutated and new variants have circulated. Additionally, scientists suspect that the more times you’ve been exposed to Covid — whether through infections or vaccination — the better your immune system becomes at recognizing and responding to the virus.

On average, the risk of getting seriously sick from an infection — whether it’s your first or your fifth — has significantly declined, Dr. Al-Aly said.

But, he added, that does not mean an infection is inconsequential. There’s no such thing as a risk-free case, experts said.

“It doesn’t really mean it’s a nothing burger,” he said. “It doesn’t really mean that people should forgo vaccination or not really care about it. It doesn’t really mean they shouldn’t stay at home when they are sick.”

The virus remains especially dangerous for people with compromised immune systems, those with underlying conditions like diabetes or heart disease, pregnant women and people over 65.

With repeated infections, the virus can set off symptoms before enough viral load builds up to turn a rapid test positive. As a result, people who test for Covid too early may have a false negative result. Doctors recommend taking a second test 48 hours later.

Scientists are split on whether your first bout with Covid predicts how you’ll fare the next time. A pivotal study, published in 2024 in the journal Communications Medicine, examined electronic health records from more than 200,000 people who were first infected between 2020 and 2022, and then infected again before the spring of 2023. The paper found that people who were hospitalized during their first infection were likely to have a bad case of Covid the next time. People with mild first infections tended to have another mild bout, the study found.

But it’s been challenging to find more recent health record data that examines cases of reinfection with the latest variants of the virus, said Richard Moffitt, a researcher at Emory University, who was an author on the 2024 report.

“How many times have you gotten Covid, and then how many times, of those, does your doctor know about?” he said. “The surveillance as far as how many people getting Covid end up in the medical system has really plummeted.”

Researchers do know that the severity of a case, as well as the symptoms, can vary from one infection to the next. A person who was asymptomatic during one Covid infection could develop a sore throat and cough the next. Someone who had cold symptoms during a first infection could have an upset stomach as part of another bout.

“Every infection is a chance at something going wrong,” Dr. Moffitt said.

Long Covid as Russian Roulette

Doctors tend to be more concerned about the chance that someone will develop long Covid from repeated infections than they are that a person will get very sick in the acute phase of the illness. Covid can cause long-term damage to nearly every part of the body and repeated cases can compound those harms.

A number of studies have shown that each time someone contracts Covid introduces an opportunity to develop long-term symptoms. Researchers often compare it to Russian roulette: Any infection could be the one that leads to long Covid.

“Every time there’s a wave, there’s another wave that’s going to follow with patients developing new onset long Covid,” said Akiko Iwasaki, an immunologist at Yale University.

Some researchers think that reinfections are part of why the number of people with long Covid has plateaued. Even though some people have recovered from their long-term symptoms, there’s continually a new influx of patients developing the condition, said Dr. Danny Altmann, a professor of immunology at Imperial College London. And if someone already has long Covid and then contracts the virus again, that patient risks experiencing more severe symptoms.

Doctors said that the possible harms of repeated infections are significant enough that people should take precautions, like getting vaccinated and masking when traveling or in crowded areas.

At this stage of dealing with the virus, we’re not “helpless,” Dr. Iwasaki said. “There are things that we can do.”

ARTICLE

Priest Dies After Crucifix Falls on Him During Livestreamed Mass
The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari was addressing his congregation in Guayaquil, Ecuador, when a wooden cross detached from a wall and struck him.
By Karla Adam
Published 2026-10-19 14:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/world/americas/ecuador-priest-dies-crucifix.html

A priest in Ecuador died on Saturday after a large wooden crucifix fell from a wall and fatally struck him during a livestreamed Mass.

The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, the pastor of Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church in the city of Guayaquil, was speaking to his congregation on Saturday when the accident occurred.

A video streamed live to the priest’s Facebook page, and verified by The New York Times, shows Father Sánchez Molinari standing in a flower-filled sanctuary framed by a sweeping wall mural, at the center of which is a large crucifix. He put on his reading glasses and began speaking — “Let us pray to the Lord” — moments before the crucifix detached from the wall.

The priest, facing his congregation, did not see the cross falling behind him, and he collapsed when it struck him.

Minutes before the accident, he had reflected on mortality, saying during his sermon that people lose hours to scrolling on their phones or watching television but give too little time to God or to the people closest to them.

“All of us are going to die,” he said. “Sometimes the time we have spent on things has far less meaning than the time we spend with God, the quality time we give to God, to our brothers and sisters, to our husbands, wives, children and families. That is the time best spent.”

After the crucifix fell, parishioners in the nave could be heard shouting in shock. Several rushed to the altar to help before the video cut out. It was unclear what had caused the accident. Local authorities did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed the priest’s death in a statement on social media on Sunday, writing that he had “departed for the Father’s House to rejoice in His presence and glory.”

Mourners gathered at the church on Sunday evening for a service in the priest’s honor.

ARTICLE

What Makes Men in Groups Behave So Badly?
Why do men in groups behave this way?
By Kate Manne
Published 2026-10-20 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/opinion/cornell-chi-phi-group-chat-bro-code.html

I keep thinking about an emoji posted in a group chat of more than 50 young men: a devil’s face (😈). And a text: “This is crazy work” — which I take to mean wild, out of bounds, outrageous. These and other Snapchat messages written by members of Cornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity have provoked intense outrage on behalf of Jane Doe, who says she was sexually assaulted by seven men that night, because the misogyny on display is so transparent. “Free pussy”; “Like you can walk in and whip it out”; “Shop still open?” This, almost everyone agrees, is abhorrent behavior. It is the language of rape culture.

Why the devil emoji? I think the forbidden nature of sex with Jane Doe was part of the chat’s collective excitement. I see a tacit awareness that a severely intoxicated woman can’t consent to sex — and an insistence on going ahead anyway. Then: a shared delight that the group of brothers is getting away with it, together. The men cheered: “I fucking love chi phi”; “CHI PHIII.” Masculinity is performed, proved and reveled in: You show yourself to be big men on campus by collectively preying on a vulnerable woman.

Why do men in groups behave this way? What makes a man in front of an audience of other men offer up a woman like a piece of meat for consumption? Two of the men whom Jane Doe describes assaulting her that night were something like friends to her. In the days after, they sent messages that appeared sympathetic and caring. “I’m so so sorry,” one texted. Another wrote, “How’ve you been coping with the stress? You need anything?” These same men were the ones who advertised her body for the taking to their fraternity brothers. (All the men accused by Jane Doe have denied wrongdoing.)

I am a professor at Cornell, and a few days ago I spoke to Diego Estrada, a former student of mine who served as the president of a fraternity on campus, graduated and was working as a live-in adviser at a different fraternity in fall 2024, when news broke of Jane Doe’s allegations. I wanted to understand what the conversation was like within fraternities at the time.

Mr. Estrada described to me the mood he observed at one of the frats he thought of as socially comparable to Chi Phi. The members there overall seemed sympathetic to the Chi Phi men; they felt bad that these men were being “ruined” by what Jane Doe was saying. Their response, Mr. Estrada said, was identical to the victim-blaming comments we now see spreading online: that Jane Doe brought what happened on herself by drinking and going to the fraternity house.

He told me he was appalled by what he heard, but said nothing. He didn’t want to be seen as a scold. Nor did he want to lose his job at the time, and consequently his meal plan and housing.

My term for the sympathy shown to male perpetrators over female victims is “himpathy.” I see this insidious sentiment at work in the Chi Phi chat in the loyalty that bonds frat brother to brother, which would make any attempt to hold each other accountable feel like a betrayal. It appears that nobody who saw the group chat that night openly objected to the behavior; on the contrary, many of the men egged one another on and seemed to escalate it. At least two men entered the room where Jane Doe was after seeing the chat, and one reported back to it that she was still in there. (To be fair, one member of Chi Phi did share the Snapchat conversation, perhaps feeling enough moral compunction to document what was happening.)

The Chi Phi group chat fits into a clear pattern of men subjugating women as a way of bonding with other men. According to the norms within many all-male groups, when one man proposes doing something immoral or illegal, the bro code dictates that other men go along with it. Sociological research has shown that one of the ways men demonstrate their masculinity to one another is through misogynistic sexual violence, as well as aggression and coercive control of women.

It’s easy to see, then, how male group dynamics can turn toxic all too quickly: One particularly entitled or cruel man decides to prey on a vulnerable woman, and invites other men to participate. They feel not only excited but even honor bound to take up that invitation. A 2007 study found that men who join fraternities are three times as likely to commit sexual violence during their freshman year, even though they were no more likely to have committed assault beforehand. That data has since been further supported. Frats appear to have the power to take men and turn them into rapists.

A secondary rule of the bro code is that you don’t call out another man’s bad behavior or intervene to protect the victim. A fraternity brother has a strong sense of duty to protect and uplift his own. And he in turn feels entitled to loyalty from his brethren. After Jane Doe’s allegations came out on campus, one of the accused men complained to another that he felt abandoned by Chi Phi. “Talking about ‘brotherhood’ and then no one except a couple real ones check in, much less acknowledge our existence,” he wrote. “Dead ass bro,” was the response. These men felt sorry for themselves. They even felt like victims.

I recently read a report titled “Campus Gang Rape: Party Games?” that analyzed more than 50 cases of gang rape on university campuses of all kinds: Ivys, small liberal-arts colleges, state schools. It identified a pattern:

A fraternity holds a party. In many cases … a young woman often has had too much to drink and/or too many drugs. Therefore she may be unaware that the “friendly” persuasion of the brothers is actually a planned pursuit of easy prey. By the time she recognizes her predicament, her confusion has changed to fear and panic, and escape seems impossible. She is unable to protest or her protests are ignored. Anywhere from two to eleven or more men rape her.

The report was published over 40 years ago, in 1985. What is new in the case of Jane Doe is that old patterns of sexual predation are being enabled and facilitated in terrifying ways by modern technology. Groups of men can now form and coordinate with far greater ease than they could in any previous era. They can invite one another to commit rape from behind the anonymizing shield of their screens. Online, the misogyny and rape culture that can foment within all-male spaces operates on a grand scale, at the speed of light.

The effects of this are evident far beyond the university. In France, Dominique Pelicot recruited upward of 50 men from a website to rape his drugged wife. An Italian Facebook group devoted to trading nonconsensual photos of wives and girlfriends numbered in the tens of thousands. This year a CNN investigation reported on a chat room in which men from around the world shared strategies for, and videos of, drugging and assaulting their partners; one French lawmaker referred to such groups as online rape academies.

Even in the more mundane corners of the internet — gaming, YouTube, social media — we find groups of men congregating to air their resentments toward women and plan sexual exploitation. In September, Wired wrote about Maddie Kowalski, a university student who was recorded during sex acts without her consent. The videos were circulated on Snapchat, where they were picked up by an online doxxing community and further disseminated on X. The videos, with Ms. Kowalski’s name attached, were ultimately viewed millions of times. The devastating impact on her and other women who have been similarly victimized can hardly be overstated.

The internet is where young people come of age, and it is soaked through with such misogyny. Perhaps this is why sexual violence has not diminished in the post-#MeToo era. Indeed, at Cornell sexual violence appears to be increasing. The university’s 2025 survey data showed that 35 percent of female undergraduates had experienced some form of sexual assault during their time at Cornell, compared with 23 percent in 2023.

Last week, Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, suspended fraternity parties until the end of the school year. But ultimately this policy is likely to be as successful as Prohibition was in ending alcohol consumption: Parties will be driven underground while Greek life remains in operation.

Ban the frats, I say, and Mr. Estrada, the former frat president, almost agrees with me. But he is struck by how he feels when he says it: guilty, ashamed, as if he is betraying his brethren in even contemplating their dissolution.

He told me that his girlfriend asked him recently what he would have done if he’d been part of the Chi Phi group chat that night. He was characteristically honest and insightful in his reply. “I was thrown off by my internal response because immediately what I thought of was, well, am I still fraternity president?” he said. “It’s kind of terrifying. That’s how much it’s been drilled into me, as president, that my job is to protect my brothers and defuse the threat, versus the need to be a good person.”

Kate Manne, a moral, social and feminist philosopher at Cornell University, is the author of “Entitled,” “Down Girl” and “Unshrinking” and writes the newsletter More to Hate.

No country right now better reveals the transformation in the way the world sees America — the way we’ve turned from ally and partner to bully and predator — than Canada.

In late August, Prime Minister Mark Carney, of Canada, walked away from trade talks with the Trump administration. He did so knowing that the retaliation could be ruinous for the Canadian economy.

But it’s also ruinous and revealing about the shambles of Donald Trump’s foreign policy — how what Trump is doing is not getting America what Trump wanted. I mean, Trump wanted Canada to be the 51st state. Instead, it might become an associate member of the European Union.

Trump wanted to weaken China in the global sphere. Now Carney and Canada are negotiating deals and agreements with all manner of other countries, including China, in an effort to diversify away from America.

America and Canada are hurtling toward a January deadline when massive new tariffs will go into effect. So who is this helping?

And what does it mean, not just for Canada but for America, for our relationship with our neighbors and for our relationship with the rest of the world?

From 2013 until earlier this year, Chrystia Freeland was a member of the Canadian Parliament. She served in a number of senior roles in the Canadian government, including deputy prime minister, minister of finance and minister of foreign affairs, where she was a lead negotiator for Canada in trade talks with the first Trump administration.
