But I think that if they see that President Trump and MAGA no longer deliver at the ballot box, you may start seeing some very different behavior.

I think that might be right. So there’s this idea of preference cascades, which are situations where a lot of people hold a preference that they don’t yet feel comfortable voicing, and so something changes, and then everything spills out because there’s been pressure building up behind a wall.

So many people will make the argument that there was a preference cascade toward Trump in 2024, that many in the American business community and in the American cultural elite, and so on, had actually become, at the very least, against the Democrats, right? They hated wokeness. They hated Joe Biden. They hated Lina Khan. They hated the whole kind of situation.

But supporting Trump had been culturally looked down upon. Maybe you wouldn’t get invited back to your galas.

Well, you might get invited, but people would think, like ——

They’d think you’re a jerk. So people were sort of holding back, and it was once Musk did his endorsement, and Andreessen, and then things began. All these people who had actually been quietly pro-Trump, at least somewhat, there was this rush toward it.

Then in the Trump era, because there is a real punishment for getting on Trump’s bad side, lots of people at different levels of society — but particularly in the business community here, who actually can’t stand this — they have the opinions they had in the first term. They think this is grotesque, but they’re mostly quiet because it’s a risk.

Even something like the Jamie Dimon Op-Ed you’re describing. Yes, if you know how to read trade debates, Dimon is disagreeing with Donald Trump, but as you say, it doesn’t come out with a critique of Donald Trump.

But it’s a disagreement at a profound level, right?

Sure. But the thing that will tell me the dam has burst is when people say the thing that is true: This guy is insanely corrupt, and he is harming America’s interests. And this is a grotesque way of using the Oval Office, and it is against what we stand for, both as a country and as citizens.

Right? I agree, I’m glad Jamie Dimon is standing up for decent trade policy, but I see that as a fairly low bar to clear.

Agreed. And I would also, just going back to these preference cascades, I think part of what was kind of pent up was very well expressed in a great piece that the Financial Times ran right after Trump’s re-election, where they quoted an anonymous top banker saying: “We can say ‘retard’ and ‘[expletive]’ without the fear of getting cancelled. It’s a new dawn.”

Yeah. Congratulations, guy. Also that they quoted him anonymously is so — some of these people ——

It’s so revealing that like: Wow, we were so oppressed. We weren’t allowed to call people “[expletive]” or “retards.” Terrible, the oppression that we suffered under Democrats.

But I think there clearly was that, and I guess I do think that there is now pent up, among very privileged people, appreciation that the policies of this administration are bad for America. They are bad for the country as a whole. They are bad for the country economically. They are bad for the country in terms of security.

And business leaders are starting to see that. Even people who describe themselves as very conservative — who are quite sympathetic with some of the stated objectives — I don’t think they ever were supportive of America turning into a kleptocracy that was Putin’s best friend, that was seeking for Ukraine to lose the war and that was breaking up the NATO alliance. And that’s what’s happening.

So I want to bring this back to the U.S. and Canada. If before Jan. 1 there is a deal, what do you think that deal will look like?

What do you think are the core issues that actually could be resolved, such that both sides would say: That’s good enough. Can we step back from this?

So the first thing I would say is that there doesn’t have to be a deal before Jan. 1. There just has to be getting into a negotiation and sort of saying: We’re going to have a cease-fire on further tariffs while the negotiation happens.

I think that would be a good place to begin.

In terms of where negotiation goes, what I think would definitely be the outlines of a plausible deal — and this is not just a deal with Canada, actually, I think this could be a deal with the allies writ large, so including the E.U. and the U.K. — is for America to say: Actually, we want to be your friends. We want to be your trading partners. We actually recognize that trade between us is mutually beneficial. It makes us richer, it makes us safer. But we’re concerned about China. And so, what we would like to do is to have a common policy on China.

And by “common,” I don’t mean exactly matched tariff policy but a common approach that has real teeth.

Look, I think it’s important not to frame it as anything punitive toward China, but to create a space where our economies can flourish, as well, and where we do not have a dangerous dependence on China. That, to me, would be the basic logic of the kind of deal that you could have.

I’d love to see two things happen: The first is that the rest of the democratic world should join Canada in retaliating against U.S. tariffs.

It’s great to have declarations of solidarity and say we’re all friends, but what should really happen right now is a more in-sorrow-than-in anger-united response from the allies who say: This is not acceptable to us, and we’re happy to have negotiations. If there are elements of the trade relationship that you want us to work on, we’re happy to do it, but we are not going to accept unilateral tariffs. And actually, we’re going to match them dollar for dollar.

And if you had Canada, Mexico, the E.U. — I’ll throw in Japan, South Korea, Australia, just for fun — basically, America’s democratic partners all respond together, I think you would see real, meaningful pressure on the United States in the right direction. So I would love to see Canada not standing alone.

The second thing I would love, and this did happen in the first Trump administration, is for Americans to say to the White House: This is nuts. You have to stop doing this.

You need to see American business speaking up a lot more, I would say, starting with the auto industry. That’s where we build things together.

I think the midterm results will be really, really important. I would say Senator Grassley was someone who really had guts last time around, and said to the president: You have to stop this — this is not a good idea.

There needs to be more Republicans who say that. And that poll that you cited — showing that Americans support Canada’s counter-tariffs but don’t support American tariffs against Canada — what that says to me is that this would be a popular position.

I think that is a good place to end. Always a final question: What are three books you’d recommend to the audience?

OK. So my books are two golden oldies, which I reread often, but they’re almost like characters in my life.

One is “The Dispossessed: An Ambiguous Utopia” by Ursula K. Le Guin. Do you know it? So I love this book, and it speaks so much to our time, actually, when you think about both the dystopian universe that it describes — but also the hope for a small, hardy band of people standing for their values. So I love that book.

The second one is “The Player of Games” by Iain M. Banks.

You’re a sci-fi head.

Oh, I totally am. I always have been. I’ve read sci-fi, like, since I started to read. And I think that is darker but also has light and hope.

I recommend both of those books because I do think — we haven’t talked that much about A.I., but the combination of A.I. and a geopolitical order, which is all smashed up, and people having questions, partly because of the economy, partly because the geopolitical order, partly because of A.I. — it’s about what it means to be human. I think that reading sci-fi is a really good way to explore those issues. So anyway, those are two great books I highly recommend.

Then my third pick is “Book of Lives: A Memoir of Sorts” by Margaret Atwood, and it’s really wonderful. She’s obviously a brilliant writer. The book kind of reveals her to be just an amazing person, who doesn’t take herself too seriously, who is able to laugh at her own weaknesses and failings, who is not self-indulgent.

And since, Ezra, we’ve been talking about how suddenly people are kind of interested in Canada, her life is a really Canadian story, and reading her account of parts of her life tells you a lot about Canada.

Chrystia Freeland, thank you very much.

It has been wonderful.

ARTICLE

France Comes Unglued, Again
A model for progressive policies has become a model for their flaws.
By Bret Stephens
Published 2026-10-20 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/opinion/france-american-liberals-riots.html

American liberals have often looked to France for a model of what they would like to see in the United States: universal health care; low-cost day care; affordable universities; strong worker protections; sacrosanct social benefits; high taxes; large investments in green energy; a secular republic in a multicultural society; constrained defense budgets, modest economic growth but lots of joie de vivre.

For a long time that model seemed almost plausible. Not anymore.

What has unfolded in France in recent weeks — student protests against deteriorating schools turning into mass demonstrations against deteriorating economic conditions turning into violence and rioting against the state itself on a level not seen in years, and all this ahead of presidential elections that could wind up pitting the extreme left of Jean-Luc Mélenchon against the extreme right of Marine Le Pen — are scenes from a country coming unglued.

That’s not because its finances or politics are broken, although both are. More deeply broken are the promises that were supposed to hold the country together: that the young would find opportunity and the old would have support; that the country could carry on as a vast entitlement state without having to compete as a nimble and enterprising one; that France would maintain its identity and its security within a peaceable Europe open to itself and to the rest of the world.

Those promises were never really tenable, though it’s remarkable how tenaciously the French have held on to them.

A succession of French prime ministers have struggled to enact a reform raising the retirement age to 64 from 62, which would bring it more in line with the European Union average and help address the crushing fiscal burden of paying generous pensions in an aging society. Yet the measure is a political nonstarter, which has now been kicked past the next election so the current prime minister can hold on to his job.

France’s youth unemployment stands around 20 percent, nearly three times the rate in Germany. Yet statutory social costs for employers are higher in France — about 45 percent of gross salary — than anywhere else in Europe, discouraging hiring.

A whopping 57 percent of the country’s gross domestic product is spent by the state. Yet the quality of France’s public schools, hospitals, policing and other social services is in manifest decline, not because the government spends too little but because it tries to do too much.

France is hardly the only country in which people are unwilling to let go of government benefits for the common good. But its problems are compounded by its elite traditions of étatisme, even under Emmanuel Macron’s supposedly reformist presidency, and deep-seated hostility to free markets and enterprise. One recent survey of 34 countries put French attitudes toward economic freedom in the bottom quarter of the table.

Of course the French are fully within their rights to distrust or repudiate what they call, usually as a slur, “neoliberalism.” But they should accept the consequences that come with that distrust.

Average annual wages in France, measured in U.S. dollar purchasing power, are over 30 percent less than they are in the United States. The last time the World Bank published its “ease of doing business” rankings, in 2020, France came in 32, in league with Turkey. That may explain why France gets relatively little foreign direct investment — only 15 percent of what tiny Singapore takes in.

In a list of the world’s 100 largest companies as measured by market capitalization, 62 are from the United States, 11 are from China and Hong Kong, and just four are from France. Last year, Le Figaro reported that “nearly 15,000 recent graduates from French engineering and management schools choose to begin their careers abroad each year,” the primary reasons for wanting to go being France’s low salaries.

Policies of national self-impoverishment have broader effects on social cohesion and national security. Resentments against migrants inevitably fester when people feel they are sharing dwindling national resources with newcomers. So do most other resentments — of class and age and religion and race — when people are fighting over how to divide those resources rather than thinking about how to grow them.

Demographic forecasts expect net immigration to jump an additional 50 percent in the coming decades compared with the net increase over the past 30 years. Barring draconian immigration restrictions or a miracle of economic growth, this is a recipe for civil strife, if not outright war.

It’s also a formula for a different kind of danger. Though they are ostensible opposites, both Le Pen and Mélenchon oppose military aid to Ukraine and want a partial or full withdrawal by France from NATO. To the extent that the protests and riots have boosted their presidential chances, they’ve also made it likelier that Vladimir Putin will eventually win his war, especially as the Trump administration turns, shamefully, on Ukraine.

It’s always possible that the weekend’s spasms of violence will remind the French, some of whom are now under curfew, that their politics tend to end badly when taken to the streets. There’s a warning there for all the naifs who used to extol the virtues of a country that thought it really knew how to live.

SUMMARY

What the chatbot probably didn’t know was that this customer is in a position to fight back. “Companies are increasingly deploying A.I. chatbots as the mandatory gateway between consumers and the help they need,” states a new report on the ubiquity of A.I. customer service intermediaries. Companies whose chatbots and automated voice systems mislead people, leave them stuck without help or only pretend to offer support would face significant penalties, with fines per violation (per customer) ranging from $525 for a first-time offender up to $3,500.

ARTICLE

Help! A Chatbot Hijacked My Customer Service Call.
An effort to fix a hotel bill illustrates why New York City is now trying to crack down on A.I. chatbot-powered customer service.
By Samuel A.A. Levine
Published 2026-10-20 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/opinion/mamdani-ai-rule-customer-service-doom-loop.html

Press 1 if you’ve heard this story before. Press 2 if it has happened to you.

After a recent trip, I noticed several mysterious charges on my hotel bill. Certain I hadn’t raided the minibar, I went hunting for a customer service number to get an explanation. I searched and I searched. Nothing. Instead, all I could find was an offer for a “live chat” blinking in the bottom-right corner of my phone screen. I gave it a try.

Three dots danced. A friendly name appeared. Cheerful pleasantries were exchanged. I began explaining my problem until an F.A.Q. menu suddenly interrupted me. That’s when I realized I had been communicating with a chatbot all along.

I had stumbled into the digital labyrinth — a veritable Hotel California, and I was just a prisoner of my own device. I explained my predicament. I re-explained it, supplying information it already seemed to have, answering prompts that had little to do with the the question I was asking, and rebuffing discount codes and propositions to book another stay. At one point, I pleadingly typed a single word in all caps: HUMAN. The machine whirred, ignoring me.

As I floundered, I found myself reflecting on the future of customer service. Based on my 25-minute ordeal, I began to suspect that the chatbot was not designed to solve my problem. It seemed to be designed to test how much friction customers would tolerate — how much information we would provide to train future models — before giving up. What the chatbot probably didn’t know was that this customer is in a position to fight back.

In my job as commissioner of the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, I hear similar complaints from New Yorkers of every stripe. Automated customer service systems tasked with handling our data and money are driving us crazy. Whether you’re trying to return a purchase, cancel a subscription or recover a hacked account, getting actual help requires a Homeric quest past a morass of junk.

It’s easy to dismiss these exhausting mazes of chatbots, robocalls, irrelevant pop-ups and consent forms as the routine irritations of life lived on tiny screens. But taken together, these episodes can amount to something much larger — delayed medical care, denied insurance coverage, predatory subscription practices and scams that cost Americans an estimated $119 billion a year.

Now, artificial intelligence is starting to make a bad situation worse. “Companies are increasingly deploying A.I. chatbots as the mandatory gateway between consumers and the help they need,” states a new report on the ubiquity of A.I. customer service intermediaries. “That includes tenants, borrowers, insurance policyholders and fraud victims seeking assistance with services that can be enormously consequential in their lives.”

While the technology is still evolving, a common trend is emerging. In a recent global study, nearly one in five consumers reported that A.I. customer support failed to provide any benefit at all. Just artificiality, no intelligence. Little wonder then that states such as California, Maine, New Jersey and Utah are moving to require companies to disclose chatbot use.

Today, New York City is going a step further, proposing some of the most rigorous rules in the nation to protect customers against automated doom loops, including automated voice systems and chatbots. Our proposal is simple: Companies can still use A.I. and other automated tools, but they need to tell consumers when they are communicating with a chatbot — and make it much easier to reach a human being.

Companies whose chatbots and automated voice systems mislead people, leave them stuck without help or only pretend to offer support would face significant penalties, with fines per violation (per customer) ranging from $525 for a first-time offender up to $3,500. Reminder: There are roughly 8.6 million people living in New York City, according to the latest census.

We’ve faced these dilemmas before. At the dawn of the modern internet era — the last great technological inflection point — government leaders took the view that markets could self-correct and that technology companies could police themselves. Individuals, rather than companies, were expected to shoulder the burden of protecting their own privacy, a burden we still bear every time we helplessly click “I agree” just to use a website or an online service.

The confidence with which companies subject customers to onerous hoops to process returns and get their money back, which I saw firsthand at the Federal Trade Commission with online retailers, is no accident. It reflects decades of policy choices that allowed corporate America to unilaterally control the direction of new, powerful technologies: a philosophy born of the Reagan era that held government could create problems but not solve them.

In the month ahead, my department will solicit written testimony from the public, review comments, consider feedback and issue a final rule, in the hopes of establishing guidelines ahead of this year’s holiday season, when we expect retailers to roll out new chatbot “assistants” along with their Black Friday sales.

For the moment, Washington politicians have taken little action on this issue. Many of the industry insiders who hold sway on Capitol Hill have proposed fighting A.I. with more A.I.: developing personal digital assistants that can negotiate with corporate chatbots, spawning algorithms to go toe to toe with algorithms while consumers stand on the sidelines.

Our hope is that New York’s rule will offer a template for other municipalities and for states to follow. The more cities and states that follow suit, the more financial pressure on companies to comply — regardless of the gridlock in D.C.

When I finally resolved my mysterious hotel bill, it wasn’t because the chatbot had a breakthrough. It was because, eventually, I reached a person. As it turned out, that was the solution all along.

Samuel A.A. Levine is the commissioner of the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and a former director of the Federal Trade Commission.

ARTICLE

Could Mississippi Elect Its First Black Senator Since Reconstruction?
A once-in-a-generation shot to turn a solidly Republican state blue.
By E.J. Dionne Jr.
Published 2026-10-20 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/opinion/trump-mississippi-scott-colom-democrat.html

On a recent Sunday morning at the Pilgrim Missionary Baptist Church in Natchez, Miss., a large sign facing the worshipers described the congregation’s goal for 2026: “The Year of Re-Alignment.”

The banner proclaimed a spiritual aspiration, not a political objective. But the warm shouts that greeted Scott Colom, the Democrat seeking one of Mississippi's U.S. Senate seats, suggested hope for political change in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in 44 years.

“Y’all,” Mr. Colom declared, “we need a realignment on so many fronts.”

President Trump’s unpopularity is opening vistas for Democrats in places they never expected to contest, and the party must decide how far it wants to extend its reach, even as it lags Republicans in fund-raising. Mr. Colom, a district attorney for four eastern counties, makes a persuasive case that his campaign against Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith deserves national attention and support. This really could be the year for a Mississippi miracle. He’s right: Democrats can make inroads in the Deep South and upend national politics. But the national party needs to show up.

Mr. Colom, a religious man who typically concludes conversations with “bless you,” insists that you don’t have to believe in miracles to think he can win a state Mr. Trump carried by nearly 23 points in the last election. The problem, as he sees it, is that Democrats have fallen into a vicious cycle by assuming that Mississippi is irretrievably Republican. They starve the state of resources, so potential supporters decide that Democrats have given up on them. The effect, Mr. Colom said in an interview at Johnny T.’s Bistro and Blues in Jackson, is that a party claiming to champion the working class is casting aside what he calls the country’s “most working-class state.”

“They want to be Democratic,” Mr. Colom said. “They want to believe that we’ll make their life better. They want to believe we care about working people. But they just have been frustrated that we haven’t competed in Mississippi.”

There is hard math behind Mr. Colom’s thinking. Mississippi Democrats start with a strong base in the Black community, which represents 37 percent of the population, the largest share of any state. The longstanding rule of thumb, as Mr. Colom’s pollster Margie Omero told me, is that a Democrat can win by securing high turnout among Black voters and roughly a quarter of the white vote.

In several recent elections, Democrats have come close to hitting the magic numbers. In 2023, Brandon Presley, a longtime member of the Mississippi Public Service Commission (and, yes, Elvis’s second cousin) came within roughly three points of defeating the Republican governor, Tate Reeves. In 2018, former Representative Mike Espy lost to Ms. Hyde-Smith by just over seven points. Like Mr. Colom, Mr. Espy ran in a year of revolt against Mr. Trump — and the anti-Trump backlash is even stronger now than it was then.

Mr. Colom has begun to turn skeptics into believers — or, at the least, into hope-mongers. One sign of his success: Sabato’s Crystal Ball, one of the leading adjudicators of what’s happening across the political map, recently shifted the Mississippi race Mr. Colom’s way. Sabato still judges the seat to be “likely Republican,” but the move away from “safe Republican” was an indication that even hard-nosed election analysts sense that something is happening.

Part of it is Mr. Colom’s relentless campaigning, including some 60 town halls. His energy was on display on a recent weekend when he worked a crowd at a Black rodeo in Greenwood, spoke about raising the minimum wage and protecting voting rights at Pilgrim Baptist, then did a Q. and A. at a community center. He closed there by leading his audience in a chant of his pithy campaign mantra: “Higher wages! Lower costs! Save health care! Save hospitals!”

Like many Democrats this year, Mr. Colom links his Christian faith to his politics. “When we talk about policy issues,” he told me, “we need to talk about it through a faith and values lens. Sometimes we talk about numbers, like we talk raising the minimum wage. We just need to raise the minimum wage because this is the proper thing to avoid inflation. No, people deserve the dignity of work. If somebody works, they deserve dignity, and that’s a values proposition to me.”

But there is a sharp, practical focus to his appeal: He knows the voters he needs to get and has a strategy for how to win them over. He believes that widespread economic anxiety and Mr. Trump’s broken promises create an opening for Democrats to begin winning back working-class voters, including whites. “There’s a lot of working-class people that we can get in Mississippi if we just talk to them about the issues we agree on,” Mr. Colom told me. “We haven’t made clear to them that we have their back.”

Former President Barack Obama encapsulated the campaign in a recently released ad. His imprimatur, along with campaigning in the state by Senators Cory Booker and Raphael Warnock and promised stops by former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, bolsters Mr. Colom’s case for making his race a priority.

“Scott is a devoted husband and dad, a seventh-generation Mississippian,” Mr. Obama declared. “Guided by his Christian faith, Scott made his community safer prosecuting violent crimes as district attorney and fighting corruption in Columbus. Now he’s running for Senate to raise wages, lower costs, and save your health care and hospitals.” The first half casts Mr. Colom as a safe pair of hands who shares voters’ values. The second places economic issues front and center.

They form the core of his critique of Ms. Hyde-Smith, whom he sometimes refers to as “Cindy High Prices.” With inflation a central issue everywhere, she gave him an unexpected opening when a local television interviewer asked her about the rising price of beef. She replied, “You know you have so many proteins to choose from.”

In a digital ad that went viral, voters mocked her answer. “Pick another protein?” one asks incredulously. “I’d rather pick another senator myself.” One of Mr. Colom’s innovations has been a food truck run by his wife and their 8- and 9-year-old daughters, who give away tacos at events on college campuses and at housing projects and community gatherings. Lately, they have taken to referring to the truck’s chicken or beef taco offering as a “pick your protein taco.”

Senator Warnock, first elected in a dramatic December runoff after President Joe Biden’s 2020 victory, alluded to the not-so-behind-the-scenes battle over whether national Democrats should add Mississippi to the growing list of states in which they’re investing. “Believe me when I say Mississippi has the ingredients of our win in Georgia, and then some,” he said. “I’m also pushing the Democratic Party to invest more in the South. I think the Democratic Party fails to invest in the South at its own peril.”

Although he would make history if he wins, Mr. Colom plays down the prospect of being the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. “That’s not a motivating factor for me,” he said, and argued that it’s far less meaningful to voters than health care cuts, high prices and Mr. Trump’s “betrayal” of his 2024 campaign promises. Voters, he insists, are not interested in who is “first.”

At the same time, he identifies with the anger of Black voters over the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, which this year further eviscerated the Voting Rights Act and allowed states to eliminate districts likely to elect Black members of Congress. In response, Black turnout has been up across the South, and in Mississippi’s primary, nearly as many Democrats voted as Republicans.

The Republican-controlled Mississippi Legislature is threatening to redistrict away the seat of Bennie Thompson, the state’s sole Democrat and African-American House member, and Mr. Colom typically ends his stump speeches by denouncing racial gerrymandering, offering a homage to Mississippi’s central role in the civil rights movement, and pleading with his audiences to exercise the rights won through an earlier generation’s sacrifices.

“They want to carve you up in a way your where your vote is really not going to matter,” he told his Pilgrim Church audience. “They want to decide what votes matter in Mississippi.” But thanks to civil rights heroes, the right to vote itself was still alive. “They sacrificed, they died, they went to prison, the lost their jobs,” he thundered. “They did that so we could have the one power they knew we needed at this moment, the power to vote.”

Mississippi may be the prime example of a maddening problem for Democrats in the closing weeks of this campaign: They have more opportunities than resources. But the chance to revolutionize the country’s political map doesn’t come along very often. Mr. Colom’s campaign slogan is “Mississippi Matters.” In this election, it surely does.

E.J. Dionne Jr., a Times contributing Opinion writer, is the author of “Why Americans Hate Politics,” “Our Divided Political Heart,” “Why the Right Went Wrong” and, most recently, “100% Democracy,” with Miles Rapoport.

ARTICLE

The Overseas X Factor That Could Swing Israel’s Election
Thousands of Israelis living in the United States are expected to fly to Israel to vote in the country’s national election this month.
By Yair Rosenberg, Debra Kamin and Gabby Sobelman
Published 2026-10-20 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/israel-election-netanyahu-voters.html

Bar Luzon, an Israeli citizen living in Cambridge, Mass., never considered herself “a political person.” An assistant professor of linguistics and philosophy at M.I.T., she had not voted in an Israeli election since she came to the United States for graduate school eight years ago. But after the events of Oct. 7, 2023, she said, she could no longer sit on the sidelines.

“It feels like the country is not functioning, in a scary way,” Ms. Luzon, 32, said. She cited Israel’s failure to quickly stop the Hamas-led attack, a lack of vision beyond “war until the end of times” and recent efforts to ban Arab parties from the upcoming elections. “I’m very afraid of how racist my government is, how much it hates its own citizens,” she said.

She now plans to vote against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies when Israelis go to the polls on Oct. 27. But there’s a catch. Unlike many democracies, Israel does not allow most citizens to vote absentee from abroad. So Ms. Luzon will be canceling classes and crossing an ocean to try to make her voice heard.

She is far from alone in making the trip.

Uriel Guy, a software engineer in New York, recalled that at a Rosh Hashana dinner he attended last month, “out of the seven Israelis there, all of them were going to vote.” It will be Mr. Guy’s first time voting in Israel since moving to New York in 2013. He has asked his siblings there to pick for him among the different opposition parties, because they are the ones “who will have to actually live with the consequences.”

According to the London-based Institute for Jewish Policy Research, some 630,000 Israeli citizens live abroad, the equivalent of about 6 percent of the country’s population. The American-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group helping Israeli voters living elsewhere with logistical support and chartered flights, announced last week that it expected more than 50,000 to return and cast ballots.

In such a tight contest — polls show a dead heat between the governing coalition and its opposition — those voters could prove pivotal.

In 1996, Mr. Netanyahu, who is often referred to by the nickname Bibi, won his first term as prime minister by a single percentage point. One political consultant later chalked up the victory in part to conservative voters who flew in at the time to support him. This past June, Peru’s presidential election was decided by votes from abroad.

What’s more, in a chaotic parliamentary system like Israel’s, small swings can have outsized impacts. In 2022, the parties that made up Mr. Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition won 48.4 percent of the vote but obtained 64 of the parliament’s 120 seats because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just shy of the electoral threshold for making the Knesset. The government that was in place on Oct. 7 and oversaw Israel’s response to the attack had come to power by the thinnest of margins.

For many who did not vote in Israel’s last election, the events of that day and its aftermath have served as a wake-up call. “Israelis abroad typically lived in their own bubble,” said Jonathan Barsade, president of the AID Coalition, which is nonpartisan in its current messaging but has supported protests against the Netanyahu government in the past. “Since Oct. 7, all of a sudden, they came out of that bubble.”

In theory, far-flung Israelis of any political persuasion could attempt to tilt the electoral outcome by returning to vote. But secular and more educated Israelis, who tend to lean left, are more likely to have moved abroad for work opportunities — or as an act of political protest — and are more likely to be able to afford the trip back. Many of those outside the country are also more aware of and alarmed by its deteriorating international standing.

Yael Shomer, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University, said that Israelis who departed the country in recent years — well over 100,000, according to official data — tended to have advanced degrees and hail from liberal areas, like Tel Aviv.

“The Israeli Central Bureau of Statistics actually analyzes the characteristics of those Israelis who left,” she said, “and we know from other research that those characteristics are correlated quite strongly with center-left leaning voters who support the current opposition parties.” In other words, the composition of the Israeli community abroad has changed, and so has who it benefits when they vote.

In recent interviews with The New York Times and other outlets, many Israelis living elsewhere said they intended to vote against Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.

Among them was Amit Stern, a 51-year-old dual American-Israeli citizen who moved to the United States when he was six and has gone back and forth since. After watching the Hamas attack unfold from his New York living room, he returned to Israel in 2023 to assist his former army unit, patrolling the Gaza border for several weeks. Three years later, Mr. Stern will be returning to cast a ballot against the country’s leadership.

“There is huge dissonance between the Israelis as a population and the government that is managing them,” he said. He hopes that the election will empower a new government composed of “people with more integrity,” he said, not divisive leaders who “scare people, as Bibi often likes to do.”

Some Israelis abroad feel compelled to vote out of civic duty. Others express a deep sense of foreboding about Israel’s future if the country does not change course.

“I have five grandchildren and there won’t be an Israel for them,” said Susan Lax, a co-owner of the Israeli footwear brand Na’ot, who grew up on a kibbutz and lost a friend on Oct. 7. She and her partner split their time between New York and Tel Aviv, and will be returning to Israel to vote against the current coalition.

Guy Ben-Aharon, an Israeli in Boston, is currently deciding between the two main Arab parties, in part because he does not feel that the Jewish opposition parties “speak openly enough against the occupation and the apartheid reality and the war in Gaza,” in which tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed. “Do I think that a change of regime in Israel is going to change everything I care about?” he said. “Not at all. Do I think it’s important to vote Bibi out? Very much so.”

If the current leadership manages to stay in power, “I’m afraid that thousands of Israelis will leave,” said Danny Peleg, a former Israeli special forces captain living in Boulder, Colo. “Israel will no longer be a democratic state, and I’m afraid that the decisions will be led by a person who has the fear of going to jail” — a reference to Mr. Netanyahu’s ongoing corruption trial — “and wars will continue forever.”

Mr. Peleg and his wife have two children living in Israel, and another who works at an Israeli embassy in Europe. He bought plane tickets as soon as the election was called.

Israelis abroad are not a political monolith.

Ricki Alon, an entrepreneur from Los Altos Hills, Calif., who arrived this week to vote in Israel, said she will vote for Mr. Netanyahu despite significant misgivings. She said she considers him the most qualified to run the country out of the available options, adding that he has “the most experience, ability, and skills to manage this crisis.”

Last month, one former Israeli chief rabbi ruled that religious expats — who tend toward the right — could use certain charity funds to fly to Israel to vote for one party in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition. But in practice, both the Israeli government and opposition understand that voters abroad these days are most likely to support the challengers.

“When we look at the profile of those coming this time, the profile is liberal Israelis living abroad,” Yaron Deckel, a former regional director of the Jewish Agency, an Israeli nonprofit that operates in 65 countries, said at an Israeli political conference last week.

“That’s why it worries Likud so much,” Mr. Deckel said, referring to Mr. Netanyahu’s party, as opposed to “in the past when ultra-Orthodox Jews from New York came to vote, because they were more identified with parties that support the right.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have criticized efforts to increase international turnout. “The left is now trying to bring in masses of people from abroad,” Shlomo Karhi, Israel’s communications minister, told a radio program in August. “Anyone who doesn’t live here in the country shouldn’t come.”

In May, Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud Party threatened legal action against the AID Coalition, and later filed a petition against it, alleging that the group’s neutral veneer concealed a partisan purpose. Likud withdrew the suit this month after the AID Coalition agreed to several restrictions on its work.

None of these machinations have deterred Ms. Luzon, the M.I.T. professor. “I have to do the only thing I can do, even though its effect is minuscule,” she said. “I want to be there to celebrate if we manage to replace this horrible government.”

And if that fails? “I spent a lot of time crying in the last three years. I’d rather do it with my friends in Israel than do it here alone.”

ARTICLE

The Mayor Who Chose ‘to Stay and Fight’ as Gangs Laid Siege to His Town
The mayor of Kenscoff, a town near Haiti’s capital, wrote government officials hundreds of letters to warn of gang threats. Then dozens of people died, and he did, too.
By Frances Robles
Published 2026-10-20 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/world/americas/mayor-kenscoff-haiti-gangs-massacre.html

The mayor had a 9-millimeter handgun tucked in his waistband under his suit jacket. Police officers and civilians wearing balaclavas over their faces gathered outside the police station, gearing for battle.

Gangs seeking to control Kenscoff, his picturesque town in the hills above Haiti’s capital, had already attacked twice this summer, burning houses and killing people, he explained.

“The gangs want to kill me, too,” the mayor, Jean Massillon, told a team of visiting New York Times journalists in late September. “I have chosen to stay and fight.”

Police and government officials hadn’t listened when Mr. Massillon repeatedly told them that the gangs would attack, making him something of a Cassandra whose warnings went unheeded until many people were dead.

But Mr. Massillon, a longtime city administrator, refused to leave, even after other residents fled in August. He became the public face of the resistance against illegal armed groups wreaking havoc in his homeland.

He was also a symbol of how the Haitian state has effectively collapsed.

He suddenly fell ill on Oct. 9, while walking up a mountain on foot to reach an area the police had recently cleared of gangs. But the ambulance service had abandoned his city a year ago because of gang violence.

After six years serving as the appointed interim mayor of this town of about 50,000 people, Mr. Massillon died — another victim of Haiti’s yearslong decline and inability to protect its most vulnerable citizens. He was 53.

“There is a total decline of health care and security in Haiti; it’s like the country is dying,” Mr. Massillon’s brother, Christophe, said. “The whole of Haiti will remember that Jean stood up to defend the commune of Kenscoff and never gave up on this, even if he had to pay for it with his life.”

We met Mr. Massillon on the last Saturday in September, when we visited Kenscoff to report on a new United Nations-backed gang suppression force in Haiti.

Kenscoff had long been known as a peaceful mountainous farming village where Haiti’s elite went for weekend respites from the traffic-clogged capital, Port-au-Prince, a dozen miles away. But in recent years, Kenscoff had become a strategic point in Haiti’s battle against gangs that were increasingly making incursions into new territory.

It’s tactical because it borders Petion-Ville, a suburb where most diplomats and wealthy people live.

More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang violence in Haiti since 2021, and hundreds of them have died in Kenscoff.

“Twenty-one months we’ve been resisting and fighting,” the mayor said when we visited.

He showed us the bullet holes in the walls of City Hall.

The first attack, in January 2025, killed 139 people, according to the National Network for the Defense of Human Rights, a leading Haitian human rights organization.

Since then, Mr. Massillon sent at least 200 letters to police and government officials begging for help, the city manager, Emmanuel Pierre, said. He compiled them in a binder, which he was quick to show us.

Gang surveillance drones flew over his house. He fired off more letters.

“I can show you the papers that I wrote to the chief of the police to tell him that something has to be done, because we heard about something that is going to happen in the city,” Mr. Massillon told us.

His letter to the national police chief, Vladimir Paraison, was dated June 30. Between July 4 and 9, gangs arrived, killing 61 people, according to a United Nations panel of experts. The mayor put the body count at 105.

Despite the threats, the Haitian National Police withdrew key personnel and armored personnel carriers from the community, according to Kenscoff’s former police inspector and a report from a leading human rights group.

“We didn’t have any help,” Mr. Massillon said.

On Aug. 23 and 24, gangs conducted coordinated attacks on the city, killing 47 people, according to the mayor and the United Nations.

Yvener Metellus, a member of a local self-defense brigade, found his 79-year-old father burned alive in his home.

“I think the state is responsible,” he said, standing beside the home’s charred ruins.

The head of the National Police, Mr. Paraison, did not respond to repeated requests over several weeks for an interview. The police’s director of communications said he would refer a detailed list of questions to the agency’s high command.

The mayor also wrote Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé and the justice ministry. The prime minister’s office referred questions to the justice ministry, which did not respond to requests for comment.

Government officials in the capital had reached out to the local police inspector in charge of Kenscoff before the August massacre, and the commander claimed to have the situation under control, according to a senior Haitian official. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

The police response may have been complicated, the official said, by the fact that there were tensions between the mayor and the local police inspector, Nikenson Cadet.

Mr. Cadet has been removed from his post and is facing disciplinary hearings.

Mr. Cadet, in an interview, acknowledged that the police had withdrawn equipment and personnel before the latest massacre. But he said that, in his view, this indicated his superiors must have believed he was doing a good job and did not need additional resources.

He, too, had written to his superiors about the threats, but instead he became a scapegoat, he said.

“The problem is that we have a lack of human resources at the police department,” Mr. Cadet said. “We don’t have enough fire power to meet what the other guys have. We are overwhelmed by this situation.”

He said gangs had more machine guns than his officers did and that they had burned an armored personnel carrier.

In the hourslong telephone interview, which was conducted before Mr. Massilon died, Mr. Cadet also accused the mayor of complicity in the attacks. Mr. Massillon, he said, had suspiciously disarmed members of civilian self-defense groups just before the August killing spree.

Mr. Massillon’s brother called the accusation “absurd” and stressed that it was the job of the police, not the volunteer self-defense brigades, to protect the city.

A report by the National Network for the Defense of Human Rights said two members of the self-defense brigade had been disarmed after they committed an unlawful killing. The mayor “strongly denied” disarming them and stressed that he held no authority over them, the report said.

Marie Rosy Auguste Ducéna, who helped prepare the human rights group’s investigation, said the Haitian government was to blame for what happened in Kenscoff. Though the police inspector was the only person removed from his post, she confirmed that he had written at least two letters asking for ammunition, guns and armored vehicles.

“The first thing is the absence, not even the lack, but the absence, of will to protect the population,” she said. “They are never held accountable, really, in Haiti — never.”

Mr. Massillon died before The Times had the chance to ask about the police inspector’s accusations. His family and colleagues said the allegations had upset him, particularly after a political enemy denounced him on local radio.

Dr. Jean William Pape, a Weill Cornell Medical College professor who runs a clinic in Port-au-Prince and has a home in Kenscoff, spoke to the mayor the day before he died.

He said he had sounded tired and had not been taking medication for his high blood pressure.

“When politicians were lying about him on the radio station, he was profoundly hurt,” Dr. Pape said.

Dr. Pape’s home, just steps from the police station, was set ablaze during the August massacre. A security guard, a dozen horses and several dogs were killed.

Dr. Pape said he believes he was targeted because of his support for the mayor, who had spent the past year moving every few weeks to dodge gangs.

Mr. Massillon most likely died of heart failure or a stroke, Dr. Pape said. With the closest ambulance about 40 minutes away, his family drove him from one clinic to another, only to be told he had already died, Mr. Pierre, the city manager, said.

A month after the massacre, the Haitian National Police posted videos of the police and private military contractors taking back gang-occupied territory in Kenscoff. The U.N.’s gang suppression force never responded to Kenscoff, but took over positions in the capital previously manned by the Haitian National Police, enabling the police to deploy.

Townspeople in reclaimed areas are slowly returning, though people from other communities are still too afraid to go back. Several we spoke to had moved four times in two years, each time fleeing a massacre with just the clothes they had on.

Lerionne Louis, 63, is not even sure how many of her relatives died that August weekend. She saw about 23 cadavers.

Bodies are still missing.

“If there’s no security and no police presence,” Ms. Louis said, “that will take place again.”

Michael Anthony Adams and André Paultre contributed reporting.

alzheimers-disease-brain-head-shape.html

SUMMARY

The illnesses that rob people of the ability to think, remember and create identity often begin, with pinpoint precision, in specific parts of the brain. Take Alzheimer’s, a disease that typically takes root years before memory unravels, when tangles of a protein called tau begin to accumulate and cells die off in a structure near the base of the brain called the entorhinal cortex. And the architecture of the brain did not by itself predict who would develop Alzheimer’s.

ARTICLE

Alzheimer’s Researchers Look at an Unusual Data Point: Head Shape
Could the geometry of our brains increase the risk of Alzheimer’s disease? It’s a provocative question, but one that some scientists are beginning to explore.
By Carolyn Y. Johnson
Published 2026-10-22 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/22/science/alzheimers-disease-brain-head-shape.html

The illnesses that rob people of the ability to think, remember and create identity often begin, with pinpoint precision, in specific parts of the brain. It’s one of the biggest mysteries about brain diseases: Why do they start where they do?

Neuroscientists call this phenomenon, in which specific areas and cells in the brain are damaged by a disease while others are unaffected, “selective vulnerability.” Figuring out why it happens — and how to prevent or stop it — is a holy grail of the field.

Take Alzheimer’s, a disease that typically takes root years before memory unravels, when tangles of a protein called tau begin to accumulate and cells die off in a structure near the base of the brain called the entorhinal cortex.

In a preliminary study, scientists found that tau buildup in that origin area was linked to the progression of Alzheimer’s disease only when the region also lay close to the edge of the tentorial incisura, a notch in the brain’s outer lining.

This correlation prompts a series of unorthodox questions: Could the repeated mechanical stresses of everyday life, paired with the sag of gravity over a lifetime, create pressure points in the brain? And could that biomechanical wear and tear influence people’s risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease? And, as a result, could differences in the anatomy of a person’s head help explain why some people develop dementia and others do not?

“It really started in hushed tones in neuropathology circles,” said Dr. John Crary, a neuropathologist at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York, who partnered with Frank Provenzano, a neural imaging bioengineer at Columbia University, to test the idea in a small sample of 47 patients with mild cognitive impairment. Their paper was published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia this month.

The idea is provocative — not least in how it carries a whiff of some long-discredited ideas from the 19th century, when head shape was used to predict personality and justify racism. But outside scientists said the approach is intriguing, though the evidence is preliminary and suggestive and would need to be rigorously tested. They applauded the study for injecting a new idea into the scientific discussion.

“It’s really outside the box, which I love,” said Dr. Gil Rabinovici, a neurologist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the study and cautioned that the idea needs more evidence to build a convincing case. “I think we should be thinking more outside the box, in terms of understanding risks for neurodegeneration.”

Pressure points in the brain?

Much of what we know about the human brain comes from autopsies, after the organ has been removed from the skull. In other words, it has often been mapped entirely out of context. The relationship between the skull and the soft, fragile brain are studied in head traumas, but largely untested in many neurodegenerative diseases. But it was precisely this relationship that Dr. Crary, who runs a brain bank, became interested in.

Dr. Crary had studied a form of neurodegeneration caused by repeated head trauma, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or C.T.E. C.T.E. has shown scientists that mechanical forces can indeed trigger the accumulation of toxic tangles of the protein tau.

Dr. Crary had also read a 1958 scientific paper that reported an unconventional set of autopsy data, in which a portion of the skull was removed. It sparked his curiosity because it showed wide variation in the size of an opening in the middle of the brain called the tentorial notch, the lip of a pass-through area between two compartments.

After an acute injury or a stroke, brain tissue can swell and press against the edge of the rigid tentorial notch. Would smaller, cumulative effects of a lifetime of movement have a similar effect?, Dr. Crary wondered.

“Some people have big ones, some have small ones, some have long ones, some have short ones,” Dr. Crary said of tentorial notches. “And as I was looking at this, I was thinking this could be a risk factor.”

Dr. Crary, a self-proclaimed contrarian who has an “X-Files” poster in his office with the slogan, “I want to believe” inscribed on it, readily admits that it was hard to get other scientists interested in an idea so far outside the mainstream. But he needed a partner, one with both open-mindedness and the requisite technical chops, to tackle the project.

That partner appeared on a trans-Atlantic flight back from a conference in Lisbon. Dr. Provenzano, who had been up until 4 a.m. working on grant reviews, was feeling crummy and sat down next to Dr. Crary.

As they started chatting, Dr. Crary pulled out his laptop and began explaining his theory that a lifetime of jostling, at a spot in the brain uniquely situated at the junction of soft tissue and stiff structures, could explain why the entorhinal cortex is where Alzheimer’s takes root. Dr. Provenzano, who has a 3-D printed model on his desk of the brain region, perked up.

“As a biomedical engineer, I’m kind of like a rhinoceros to a fire. I have to put it out,” Dr. Provenzano said. “I was like, ‘John, this is outstanding — we can address this.’”

Measuring the distance

To take a first swing at the question of whether brain anatomy could help explain Alzheimer’s risk, the researchers analyzed medical scans from 47 people with mild cognitive impairment, with tangles of tau in the vulnerable area. They measured the distance between the hard edge of the tentorial notch and the entorhinal cortex.

This distance did not predict the amount of tau tangles in the brain. And the architecture of the brain did not by itself predict who would develop Alzheimer’s. The researchers did find, though, that tau in the risky region was linked to developing dementia over the next three years only among people with a tight gap between the notch and the entorhinal cortex.

Both scientists acknowledge that their small study is only a starting point, not a proven case. They hope, though, that their work will encourage follow-ups. The Alzheimer’s field has long been focused on toxic clumps of a protein called amyloid-beta, and more recently on tangles of tau. Multiple drugs that remove amyloid have been approved, but they have produced limited benefits for patients.

David Attwell, a neuroscientist at University College London, wrote in an email that Dr. Crary and Dr. Provenzano’s paper showed an “intriguing correlation” and raised many other questions that could be studied.

He said it was easy to speculate as to the possible ways that everyday mechanical stresses could contribute to Alzheimer’s risk. For example, brain cells called microglia that clear amyloid-beta protein from the brain are sensitive to being stretched. But he, like others, said there were other factors that might correlate with the distance between the two brain regions that could also play a role.

The ideas proposed by Dr. Crary and Dr. Provenzano still need to be tested to see if they bear out. Even if they do not, though, they may still generate other ideas or observations that spark new research directions.

Michael Yassa, a neurobiologist at the University of California, Irvine, said he was cautiously excited about the paper. His own lab published a paper last year in Nature Communications that examined the changing shape of the brain over the course of a lifetime. Dr. Yassa’s team chronicled the effects of the “slouch of gravity,” which compresses the brain in some directions and stretches it in others. Certain aspects of this resculpting, they found, tended to be pronounced in older adults experiencing impairments in memory and cognitive functioning.

Dr. Yassa said that, from his perspective, the Alzheimer’s field had long failed to embrace new ideas, and he hoped that keeping an open mind could lead to benefits for patients and families.

“It’s so dominated by the classic ideas — classic, as in, from 1909,” Dr. Yassa said. “Pushing the envelope on these ideas, and breaking through some of these silos, and banging down doors is what we should be doing.”

ARTICLE

Ahead of Tight Race, Trump Swaps Tariffs on Some Canadian Goods
The move was announced by Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican who faces a tough re-election fight amid rising prices.
By Alan Rappeport and Ana Swanson
Published 2026-10-23 19:28 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/business/trump-susan-collins-canada-tariffs.html

The Trump administration announced on Friday that it will shuffle its tariffs on Canadian products, exempting some items and applying new tariffs to others, in what appeared to be a last-minute bid to provide relief to American farmers ahead of the midterm elections.

The move follows lobbying by Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican who is facing a close re-election bid in her state. The tariffs that are being lifted apply to Canadian products such as corrugated paper, refrigeration equipment, plywood and packing machinery, items that are widely used by farmers and growers in Maine. They currently face 50 percent tariffs, which Mr. Trump slapped on a variety of Canadian goods in July.

Instead, new tariffs will be applied to Canadian exports of cocoa powder, vinyl flooring, shampoo, canoes and other products.

“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Ms. Collins said in a post on social media. “I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”

Ms. Collins said the exemptions would help her state’s blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.

In a proclamation on Friday, Mr. Trump said that he had agreed to modify his tariffs, and that the changes would “offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce” in a way that was consistent with “the interests of the United States.” The new tariffs will also apply to Canadian products like wooden coffins, parts for yachts, carpets and archery equipment, and will be effective as of 12:01 a.m. Oct. 30, the White House said.

The White House said that it was responding to Canada’s “continued discrimination” against American farmers, manufacturers and workers.

“This administration will continue to use every available tool to restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships and safeguard the economic prosperity and national security of the American people,” said Matthew Middleton, a White House spokesman.

The president’s trade spat with Canada began shortly after he returned to office, when Mr. Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian exports in return for what he claimed was the country’s role in channeling fentanyl to the United States. Mr. Trump has also angered Canadians by repeatedly referring to their country as the 51st state, and threatening to withdraw defensive provisions for Canada.

The tension has devolved into tit-for-tat trade actions that have proved unpopular with many Americans, particularly in states that rely on Canada as their biggest export market.

After Canada refused to fold to some of Mr. Trump’s trade demands, the Trump administration imposed tariffs in August on more than $20 billion of Canadian exports. Canada retaliated with tariffs on hundreds of U.S. products. Then in September, Mr. Trump banned some Canadian products outright, including alcoholic beverages, dairy byproducts and molasses.

Earlier this week, a food importer filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration for those tariffs, saying they could increase its tax burden by $40 million annually. Courts have struck down other tariffs issued by Mr. Trump, but it remains to be seen how they rule in this case.

Ms. Collins and her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, have been deadlocked in recent polls. The loss of Ms. Collins’s seat could tip the Senate in favor of Democrats, upending Mr. Trump’s legislative agenda for the rest of his term. Voters in the state have been frustrated by Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs, immigration and the war in Iran.

During a debate against Mr. Jackson this month, Ms. Collins defended her record and described herself as the “most outspoken opponent of the tariffs with Canada.” She highlighted her success exempting road salt and cement from the duties.

Mr. Jackson suggested that those efforts were too little and too late.

“Mainers can’t afford to pay their bills with a press release or a strongly worded letter,” he said. “What about everything else? We can’t eat road salt.”

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Paul Stankard Has Died. Behold What He Did With Paperweights.
Yes, paperweights. Working over a nearly 5,000-degree gas flame, he created glass marvels that sold for tens of thousands of dollars. He was 83.
By Josephine de La Bruyère
Published 2026-10-23 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/obituaries/paul-stankard-dead.html

Paul Stankard, whose decades-long obsession with replicating the natural world in glass transformed the American paperweight from tchotchke to fine art, died on Oct. 6. He was 83.

The cause of death was cancer, said his daughter, Christine Kressley.

In 1972, with three young children and a newborn at home, Mr. Stankard skipped out on a steady job blowing glass for chemical laboratories. He was in love — with paperweights. The form’s pioneers had filled their weights with stylized glass garlands, pansies and primroses. Not Mr. Stankard, a sprightly, self-taught naturalist. He set out, he told a film crew in 2024, “to invent a new language to interpret native flowers in glass.”

For the next 54 years, over a nearly 5,000-degree gas flame, he melted and joined canes of colored glass into hyper-realistic buttercups and spiderwort. Within three-inch hemispheres, he created spectacular, increasingly intricate natural worlds from glass: root systems, worms, moths and honeybees in flight; kaleidoscopically colored bouquets crammed with foxglove, moss, blueberries and sprites.

Mr. Stankard meant his pieces, which commanded prices in the high five figures and landed in the permanent collections of the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, to astound and delight. Could those stamens, lilacs or veined and dappled leaves really be made of glass? The technical precision his illusions demanded in turn drove and delighted Mr. Stankard, who was fanatically serious about his craft.

“Paul just loved glass,” David Graeber, his longtime studio assistant, said in an interview. “He lived it, breathed it, ate it.”

Paul Joseph Stankard was born in North Attleboro, Mass., on April 7, 1943, to Martin Stankard, a chemist, and Mary Florence Stankard.

School was torture. As an adult, Mr. Stankard discovered that he was dyslexic. But his childhood home opened onto woods where the swamps, ponds and hills teemed with mountain laurel and touch-me-nots. Roaming free there, Mr. Stankard remembered in 2024, “you felt like a pioneer.”

Impressed by a trade school brochure his son brought home, Martin Stankard coaxed Paul into a program for scientific glassblowing. Afterward, Mr. Stankard spent his workdays blowing apparatuses for chemists. On weekends, he took his torch and tool kit home.

‘Paul just loved glass. He lived it, breathed it, ate it.’

He blew glasses in his utility room and sold glass animals at craft fairs for a quarter. But nothing enchanted him like paperweights. Magnified by a clear crystal dome, imperfections were impossible to hide — a challenge to which Mr. Stankard thrilled. Paperweights, he told The Palm Beach Post in 1996, “embody my attitudes about Mother Earth and nature. The spherical shape gives me a parameter, and within that, I’m able to create.”

For $10, he sold his first paperweight to an antiques dealer at an Atlantic City craft fair in 1971. By 1975, his weights fetched between $250 and $400, said Alan Kaplan, an antiques dealer who began working with Mr. Stankard that year. In 1989, Mr. Stankard had begun stretching his orbs into prisms that sold for nearly $10,000. That year, he hired David Graeber. The men met through Mr. Graeber’s uncle, the owner of a Mobil station where Mr. Stankard settled his account in paperweights.

“Paul was the almighty barterer,” Mr. Graeber said. “Paperweights for service — with the butcher, with the dentist, with the lawyer.” The weights could buy a lot of steak.

As he aged, Mr. Stankard pushed himself toward increasingly ambitious designs. In his Mantua, N.J., studio, experiments with roots turned into knobby spirits that danced at the bottom of his weights. He played with reflection, refraction, plants’ life cycles and microscopic words. He made glass resemble sand. Within poured orbs and blocks of optical glass, he squeezed whole bouquets. Could he fit three? Five? He could.

Mind-bogglingly, taxonomically true to nature, his pieces turned the paperweight world on its head. “A paperweight had been an attractive object,” Douglas Heller, a glass dealer who sold Mr. Stankard’s work in his New York City gallery from 1980 onward, said in an interview. “But looking at Paul’s was like looking through a window to another world. He took it to unprecedented heights.”

Mr. Stankard showed his work in New York at the Museum of Modern Art in 1998 and the Museum of Arts and Design in 2004.

As his star rose, so did the paperweight’s. “There’s a Before Stankard and After Stankard,” Mr. Heller said. Mr. Stankard’s creations convinced a generation of American craftsmen of the object’s creative potential. In 1994, The Chicago Tribune named the paperweight the year’s hottest collectible.

Which is not to say that Mr. Stankard’s work conquered all. A critic in The New York Times wondered aloud in 1989 whether Mr. Stankard packed his paperweights with such imagination out of fear “that he might be viewed merely as a craftsman rather than a true artist.” In a 1993 cover story — “Revenge of the Philistines” was the headline — Forbes lumped a Stankard piece in with “junk collectibles.”

If he heard the sneering, Mr. Stankard did not seem to care. A devout Catholic, he saw melting his woodland worlds into miniature as a higher calling. Wearing purple didymium lenses to protect his eyes from the sodium flare heated glass emits, Mr. Stankard worked beneath a Benedictine motto: Laborare est orare, Latin for “to work is to pray.” He strove for excellence. It was “to respect God’s beautiful creations,” he said in a documentary.

“When I look at a flower, I don’t think that God, after creating man, took a rest and then went around creating the plants,” he said. “I think that he worked just as hard on the flower.”

Mr. Stankard is survived by his wife, Patricia Stankard; five children; six siblings; and six grandchildren.

ARTICLE

The Meaning of the Republican War Over Ramaswamy’s Vile Ad
The G.O.P. nominee in Ohio has given conservatives space to reckon with the ethical degradation of Trumpism.
By Michelle Goldberg
Published 2026-10-23 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/opinion/acton-ramaswamy-ad-trump-ohio.html

It’s quite a feat, in this numb and debased era, to create a political advertisement so shocking and indecent that people from across the political spectrum feel the need to denounce it. The Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has long fashioned himself as a kind of Donald Trump 2.0 — younger and brainier but just as brash — has managed it.

By releasing what may be the most disgusting ad in American political history, he’s done more than just reveal his own low character. He’s opened a kind of proxy debate on the right about whether a post-Trump conservatism should try to reclaim some base-line morality or continue along its current smash-mouth course.

As you might know by now, the story behind Ramaswamy’s ad involves child sexual abuse. His Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, was 12 when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, known as Bud, was arrested and indicted on charges of raping her, though he skipped town before he could be tried. Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, stood by him and lost custody of her children; she never saw her daughter again. (Bud Arthur died in 2004.)

In 2020, when Acton was serving as Ohio’s health director, Donna Arthur, fashioning herself as a concerned Christian, gave an interview to the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue attacking her estranged daughter. It was deeply if unintentionally self-incriminating. Arthur speculated that Acton got the idea to say Bud Arthur raped her from his daughter from a previous marriage, who’d made a similar claim. By Donna Arthur’s own account, then, she brought a man accused of sexually abusing his child into her children’s home.

Now Ramaswamy’s campaign has dug up this elderly woman to make a video calling her daughter a liar who can’t be trusted to lead the state. At first, the ad featuring Arthur circulated online, without attribution. As outrage about it grew, Ramaswamy’s campaign admitted that it created the spot, and then, in Trumpian style, doubled down, saying it would spend millions to air it on television and promote it online.

By tacitly siding with a man indicted on charges of child rape, Ramaswamy has shown us all who he is. But he’s also given conservatives space to reckon with the ethical degradation of Trumpism, though without quite admitting that that’s what they’re doing.

Take, for example, the conservative magazine National Review. Early in 2016, it put out an issue with the words “Against Trump” emblazoned in gold on its cover. “Donald Trump is a menace to American conservatism who would take the work of generations and trample it underfoot on behalf of a populism as heedless and crude as the Donald himself,” said the lead editorial.

Over the following decade, some of the issue’s contributors remained anti-Trump stalwarts, but several — along with the magazine as a whole — turned into apologists and bootlickers for the president. As long as Trump offered the right new peaks of political power, many of his onetime conservative critics were happy to swallow their qualms. Now, as the whole gaudy edifice of MAGA crumbles — with Trump so unpopular that Republicans risk losing states like Texas and Kansas — at least some of his enablers may be feeling ashamed.

Denouncing the Ramaswamy ad gives conservatives a chance to try to drag their movement out of the Trumpist gutter. National Review, tellingly, has helped lead the charge. It ran a sober article backing up Acton’s story, and then several columns lambasting Ramaswamy, including one titled “When Character Was Obliterated.”

The conservative broadcaster Erick Erickson has taken a similar line. He was one of the contributors to “Against Trump” who then turned around and endorsed Trump for re-election. “I still struggle on the character issue,” he wrote in 2019, but argued, “We cannot have the Trump administration policies without President Trump, and there is much to like.” Now Erickson is back to believing that character is crucial. “We keep being told we must surrender our decency to win and then we lament how indecent the country is becoming,” he wrote about Ramaswamy, as if he had not been one of the ones counseling such surrender.

If conservatives were to suddenly decide that moral depravity is disqualifying, it would be bad news for Trump and those closest to him. It’s not surprising, then, that on Wednesday, JD Vance praised Ramaswamy’s “audacity” in running the spot, declaring himself “disgusted” by Republicans who are “whining” about it. Trump, on Thursday, celebrated the ad on Truth Social, writing, “I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse.” Both men seem to understand that Republicans who criticize Ramaswamy are also implicitly criticizing them.

That’s particularly true of Vance, because he and Ramaswamy are such similar figures. The two men were friends at Yale Law School. Both worked in venture capital and developed ties to the tech right before positioning themselves as inheritors of the MAGA movement. Both have to contend with anti-Indian bigotry — Vance’s wife is Indian American — which has cost Ramaswamy some far-right support. And both are charmless, awkwardly imitating the president’s cruel provocations without his dark charisma or comic timing. If Ramaswamy loses a state as red as Ohio despite Trump’s imprimatur, Vance might start to look like a bad bet in 2028.

Seventy-two years ago, Joseph Welch, the attorney representing the U.S. Army, rebuked Joseph McCarthy with the immortal line, “Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last?” Despairing observers have been asking the same thing of the Republican Party for the last 10 years. Both Ramaswamy and Vance had better hope that the answer is still no.
