ARTICLE

What Hundreds of Focus Groups With Trump Voters Revealed
Sarah Longwell has conducted hundreds of focus groups with Trump voters, and many of them are feeling betrayed.
By Ezra Klein, Annie Galvin and Jack McCordick
Published 2026-10-23 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-sarah-longwell.html

This is an edited transcript of “The Ezra Klein Show.” You can listen to the episode wherever you get your podcasts.

Since he took office in 2025, Donald Trump’s net approval rating has collapsed, falling by more than 30 points. As we head into the midterms, Democrats now have the opportunity to do something that seemed unthinkable just a year ago: to take back not just the House but the Senate, possibly even winning in places like Texas and Kansas.

So how did Donald Trump go from winning his first popular vote victory ever to, in less than two years, what now looks like it could be an electoral wipeout for Republicans?

Sarah Longwell is a political consultant and the founder and publisher of The Bulwark. Since the 2016 election, she has conducted hundreds of focus groups with thousands of voters across the political spectrum that have become this really extraordinary source of qualitative evidence of how voters have evolved in the Trump era — particularly voters who had leaned toward Trump but maybe now don’t.

Longwell is also the host of “The Focus Group Podcast” — you can hear some of these groups there — and author of the recent book “How to Eat an Elephant.” She joins me now.

Ezra Klein: Sarah Longwell, welcome to the show.

Sarah Longwell: Thanks for having me. I’m superexcited to be here.

Donald Trump takes office again in January 2025. His approval rating is above 50 percent. He has his biggest electoral victory ever.

He’s now at 36 percent.

I think you’ve probably personally done more focus groups with Trump voters of different flavors and variants than anybody else in America.

So what happened?

It’s easy, actually. This is the easiest question in politics right now. Donald Trump made some very specific choices, and they were his choices, and everyone knows they were his choices.

The first one was when he did all of the unilateral tariffs, didn’t consult Congress and just got into trade wars with a whole bunch of people. And the second was starting the war with Iran.

Voters completely identify those two things with Trump. You can’t say Joe Biden did that. You can’t say it was someone else or Congress. There was nothing else.

The deep state went to war on Iran.

Donald Trump made these choices, and voters know it.

The consequences of both have been to raise prices for the American people at a time when they elected Donald Trump to do one thing: lower prices.

And as a secondary matter, they said: No more stupid wars.

So the voters right now recognize that their life is not getting better and that Donald Trump has broken his promises. That is the easiest way to explain what’s happening right now.

Tariffs were a promise from Donald Trump. He ran for office saying again and again and again: Tariffs on everyone, tariffs in all directions.

I can imagine, if you’re him, you look at your tariff policy as promises kept. So when his supporters tell you what they don’t like about them, what do they say?

Well, the thing about voters is that they are often not interested in the policy minutiae of how one gets to a place. They’re just saying: What are we going to do to lower prices?

The thing that has shocked me the most listening to voters — not even shocked, it’s more the thing that I find has changed my relationship with voters — is that the first thing we do is ask people: How do you think things are going in the country?

And every focus group, every single time, doesn’t matter — whether left, right or center — right now, people say: bad. And then they immediately start talking about the prices of something.

They talk about the prices of gas. They talk about the prices of beef. But they talk about something they did: I walked into the store today, and the beef cost X dollars, and that’s $2 more than it did, and it wasn’t even the good stuff.”

Americans don’t necessarily connect policy rhetoric to the outcome. They live through something, see the outcome, and then they decide how they feel about it.

On that point, about the ground beef, I want to play a clip that your team shared with me from one of the focus groups. This is someone who voted for Trump in 2024.

Archival clip: I grocery shop every week, so I know when prices are going down and up, and I’m like: He’s lying. Nothing has changed — OK, maybe the eggs have gone down, but that’s it. I’ve never paid $9 for ground beef before — ever — even the good kind. So that is really, really crazy and getting very scary. I really thought that it was going to be about us here at home.

When that woman says to you: “I really thought it was going to be about us here at home” — what did she think?

What did the people who had swung toward Trump in 2024 see in him that they maybe hadn’t seen in 2020?

Well, this is the promise of “America first.”

“America first” has a lot of racist origins. But for the voters, “America first” is an idea that the president is going to prioritize them — Mr. and Mrs. American — and they like that promise. They like the idea of not sending all this money to other places.

I hear versions of this in basically every group that I do, which is: We want to be taken care of. We want money spent on our schools.

It’s interesting watching Abdul El-Sayed, because he’s doing a version of this right now, his own version of “America first.”

Often when he gets asked the question about Israel, he says: I don’t want our money going overseas. I want it spent here in Michigan. I want it spent on our schools, on taking care of our people.

Archival clip of Abdul El-Sayed: I’m opposed to unconditional military aid for any country. That is Israel, yes, but that’s also Egypt, where my family immigrated from. That’s Pakistan, that’s Saudi Arabia, that’s U.A.E. And that’s not because of a focus on what’s happening anywhere except for a focus on what’s happening here. We’ve got communities in my state where the median income is $14,000. And I believe they have a right to their tax dollars.

And that is something that appeals to Americans deeply. They say: Yes, we want to be taken care of.

They feel like, in the big maelstrom of conversations — whether it’s sort of the weird social issues that people get wrapped around the axle about or whether it’s the big geopolitical questions that politicians are always talking about — what they really want to know is: What are you going to do for me?

That disconnect between people whom we talk about as elites — but let’s just say you and I — we should admit this. We do not walk into the grocery store and say: I can’t buy this now because it’s $2 more expensive.

Nobody in Congress has that experience. Nobody who is in a lot of decision-making authority has that experience. And so it is so easy to forget that is the thing everybody wants.

I think this is a problem that ends up afflicting both sides. It happened to the Biden administration during their term, and now it’s happening to Trump, which is: You get elected, and the voters who crucially put you over the top — not your big base of voters who are always going to vote for you but the people who made the difference in the election — they hire you to do often a job that is maybe not the job that you’re most excited about doing.

Voters want lower prices. They’re maybe not as bought-in on climate change questions as Democrats are.

And there are all these people around you who have your ear — who, in fact, do not have problems buying groceries in the grocery store. They have things they are much more excited about doing. So you have this constant pressure to get off the course of what the swing voters wanted from you.

That seems, to me, to be a lot of the Trump story here. He won because inflation was high, but he didn’t really care about inflation. That’s not what gets him out of bed in the morning.

No, what gets Donald Trump out of bed in the morning is Donald Trump’s interests in enriching himself. This goes back to the earlier question: Why do Americans think that Donald Trump is in it for them?

The way that I heard so many voters characterize it is that the process was so slow and sclerotic, and they felt like nothing was changing, and the way that politicians talked all sounded the same.

But mostly, they thought: This guy is a businessman — and that means that he is going to figure it out. Because this is what Donald Trump pitched all the time: I’m going to cut deals for you. I know how this system works. It’s rigged against you. I’m going to unrig it.

And voters really did think, whether it was because of “The Apprentice” — and I cannot tell you how important “The Apprentice” is and was to the lore that sits inside voters ——

Still, by 2024, it was so important?

He lived, in their living rooms, at the top of a boardroom where he made decisions about business, and that is what voters really internalized about Donald Trump.

So when inflation was high, they thought he was going to come in, and in some way that is magic from him — sort of like the Kool-Aid Man busting through the window — and say: Here, I’m going to lower grocery prices on Day 1.

They think he has some secret sauce that allows him to do that. When, of course, it is just a lie. He couldn’t do it.

There are a lot of ways that the people who interpret politics publicly — my job, for instance — end up having a lot of trouble understanding voters.

One of the ways is that we think of the primary divide in the electorate as left or right. But the primary divide in politics, I always think, is between interested and uninterested. The hard-core left and the hard-core right, MAGA, the liberals, resistance, whatever it is, they’re all interested. They’re all following some media source constantly.

But a lot of voters don’t like politics. And they’re not that interested.

So I’d like to hear you talk about the different ways that people who decide elections but do not follow politics that closely in between elections — that difference in the electorate and how they then understand what is happening.

We talk in political science terms. We’re always slicing and dicing the electorate, and we often talk about “low-information voters.” I always think that is an unfair term to people who are just not sick in the head like us, who are not following everything, who don’t let their nervous systems be hijacked on a daily basis by the vicissitudes of political wrangling.

Low neuroticism voters. [Laughs.]

Yeah, that’s right. I think it’s a perfectly acceptable thing to be like: Actually, I’m going to focus on my family and getting my kids out the door, and then I’ve got to go to a job that’s quite demanding. And both parents in the household are working.

One of the things we ask about in the focus groups all the time is: Where do people get their information?

And it is unsatisfying now, because it used to be that people would be pretty clear. They’d be like: I watch Fox News. Or: I watch CNN. I read this newspaper. I read The New York Times. Or: I read my local newspaper.

The majority of people would often say that they watch their local news. But now what people mostly say is: I don’t know where I saw that.

They’re scrolling. They’ve got their favorite cooking influencer, or they’re scrolling on Instagram or TikTok — an algorithm-driven information environment where they mostly want basketball or sports. But then there’s Stephen A. Smith talking about politics.

So this is why, when people said: The left needs its own Joe Rogan — and they tend to reach for people who are actually political pundits. But that’s not what Joe Rogan is.

Joe Rogan is a comedian. I mean, I don’t watch a ton of his content, but I do think there’s a fair amount of getting stoned and figuring out who would win between a shark or a gorilla if they fought each other. And then they have a guest, and the guest says whatever, and Joe Rogan really doesn’t challenge him because he’s not a subject matter expert in much.

That’s about culture. There are cultural people all over the place where politics is injected.

There used to be this phrase: Politics is downstream from culture. I think, increasingly, the overlap between politics and culture combines into something that is a deeply nonpolitical-science term, which we would call a vibe.

And that vibe is what a lot of the low-information voters are getting. Something that washes over them, that is algorithmically injected into the cultural things that they imbibe.

Say more about that. What changes in politics — or what have you watched change in politics — as it has become more, in your language here, vibe oriented?

I think it’s the big difference between news seekers and news receivers.

We used to live in a world where you spent time with the news, and it was a specific time. You sat down at the breakfast table, and you read a newspaper. You watched the evening news. You made time for the news.

I just think that the news receiver means: I didn’t sit down to find something out. Information just washed over me, and there was no mechanism to verify it. I didn’t really sit and spend time with it and ask: Is this true? Does it even matter to me? It just hit me for a second.

It just flashes over them. So they wake up with an opinion without any idea of how it was formed.

I want to talk about something that seems to have begun breaking through. And I don’t really know why it’s finally breaking through now, but it is: corruption.

I want to play a clip from a Trump voter talking about corruption and how it has changed in his view.

Archival clip: I’m a Republican. I’m just saying he’s front and center now. And he’s just blatant with corruption. But we tolerated corruption in a way, or looked the other way. Corruption has just been constant in the Trump administration. I was watching corruption in polls through the whole administration, waiting for it to attain salience.

It was just like nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing — and then suddenly, it’s the top issue.

What broke through?

It’s prices again. Everything comes back to people’s relationship to the economy. And this is a bummer, actually, of an observation, but the American people — especially Trump voters and more low-information voters — would probably let Trump get away with corruption. In fact, we know they would — he was doing a lot of corrupt things in his first term.

People didn’t really care. You couldn’t get them to care about how much he was spending on golf or having big meetings at all of his hotels with the rich.

All the insane crypto stuff during the 2024 election, that was the one I always thought was crazy — the Trump family getting involved in crypto scams and meme coins during the election and the post-electoral period.

They don’t care. But again, it comes down to people’s relationship with their own money. If they thought Trump could do something for them — and you can see this especially with people who are superengaged on the crypto stuff — if they think they can make some money off Trump, they don’t care about his corruption.

There are two reasons that corruption is breaking through right now. The first is, people are suffering economically.

And so all of Trump’s focus on his ballroom and the Reflecting Pool frustrates voters that he is not focused on them — he’s focused on himself.

But also, the enriching himself is becoming difficult to ignore because it’s so out in the open. And when people are not doing well, they’re angrier about it.

The second reason, though, that corruption is now a very high-salience issue, is the same reason that democracy became a high-salience issue.

To some of your work on polarization, there’s a backlash effect that happens when Democrats start accusing Republicans of being corrupt because Donald Trump is doing this brazen corruption.

The thing that happens for Republicans is that they do the “What about…?”

So they say: No, Democrats are corrupt. Or: They’re all corrupt.

Part of what happens is this national conversation where one side is accusing the other of something, and so the other side does: What about…? — and then quickly it becomes a dominant issue.

Democrats were also accusing Republicans of being a threat to democracy after Jan. 6. But Republicans were accusing Democrats of having stolen the election. And pretty soon, democracy is the No. 1 issue.

And Democrats think: Oh, look, everyone cares about democracy. And I’m going: No, no, no, no, no — they don’t care about it the way you want them to care about it.

The Democrat who seemed to really figure out how to make the corruption case against Trump and get people to pay attention to it this cycle is Jon Ossoff.

There’s more interest in whether or not he’s going to run for president than in whether he’s going to win in Georgia.

Jon Ossoff is taking it slow. He’s taking it one bite at a time, and he is writing to say: Hey, you’ve heard about this.

Are they just grabbing people and putting them in camps? Voter 3: I do agree that we should stay on top of actual illegal immigration and criminals, but there’s plenty of criminals already here that we could do a better job with instead of focusing on people that are — even if illegal — working and kind of minding their own business.

What I hear when I hear that — and I’ve heard a lot of this also on podcasts like Rogan’s and from some of the people who swung toward Trump on this issue in 2024 — is that Democrats always have this problem where they don’t like to deal with the fact that the public has ideas of the deserving and the undeserving poor.

Democrats want to say: There’s no distinction, and everybody deserves help. But that’s not where the public usually is. They want people to work and to show up, and that often gets Democrats in trouble.

Republicans on immigration, the MAGA right at this point, don’t have “good immigrants” and “bad immigrants.” It definitely doesn’t have “good illegal immigrants” and “bad illegal immigrants.” It just really has an antipathy toward immigrants.

And now you see this spilling out into crazy things, like saying there are too many Indian American students at a college-football game. It’s going into crazier and crazier places, more and more racist places, to be blunt about it.

But Trump always sort of merged these ideas. He would sometimes talk as if he were just talking about the bad illegal immigrants and was going to be discerning — and then sometimes just promise mass deportation. He’s been much more on the mass deportation side, and people don’t seem to like it.

No, and I actually really try to speak up for the American people on the issue of immigration sometimes. Because I do think that people think everyone who is a Trump voter is just profoundly racist, and that’s where their desire to see immigration curbed is coming from.

There is a spectrum of Trump voters on this. There are racist people, and there are people who are just like: Deport harder — get every single person out of here. That is not the majority of Trump voters.

The majority of Trump voters make a couple of distinctions. One is the one we’ve talked about, where they say dangerous criminals should go. But the person who’s paying taxes and has been here for 25 years, who lives down the street — leave that guy alone. That’s part of it.

The other distinction they make, though — and I hear this all the time from voters — is a sense of fairness. They say: I want immigrants to come here, but I want them to come — and this is the key phrase you hear — “the right way.”

And what they mean, and this is very important for people to understand, is that Americans have no idea what it is to go through the immigration system.

So when they say: Come the right way — they assume that there is some easy process by which one can become a naturalized citizen. They just have no idea what it looks like, though.

When they see people coming across the border illegally, they say: Hey, somebody is standing in line over here, trying to come the right way, and this person is breaking the law coming in.

They do not want a country in which immigrants don’t come. Americans actually are quite good about talking about this. As soon as you start talking about immigration, one of the first things they will tell you is their own immigrant story: when their grandparents came here or the immigrant who they know or the person they’re married to who is an immigrant or their family.

Americans are not that hostile to the idea of immigration, they are hostile to the idea of coming here illegally across the border.

Is this another example of where people perceive Trump’s priorities diverging from their own? Because there were two instrumental arguments I would hear Republicans, including Trump, make. One was the dangerous criminal illegal immigrants. The other was that immigrants were taking your jobs, buying your homes and pushing up prices in different places.

Both of those things fit into a sense of disorder under Joe Biden. New York City was a place where there was a big swing toward Trump in the election, and something I heard from a lot of people in New York City was that they just didn’t like seeing the disorder around them.

They don’t like the sense that their government is not holding order. People prize order very highly. That is a job they entrust government with.

Trump comes in with “law and order” Republicanism. There’s a reason “order” is in that phrase.

But he, Stephen Miller and Greg Bovino created disorder. When people looked at what was happening in Minnesota and Americans getting shot by government agents, when they looked at these deployments — the Trump administration seemed to be creating disorder.

They were creating violence. They were creating frightening visuals. What instead seemed to be happening was things were getting all the more out of control, just in the other direction. Is that ——

No, I think that’s completely right. This is happening where they live. This is not abstract to them. When you talk to voters in the focus groups, they’re the people living in the places that we’re talking about on the news.

So they will say: I took my kid to school, and there were ICE agents who showed up at the school, and they had masks on, and there are kids there. What are we doing here?

And yet they’re seeing images on their TV of masked agents shooting an I.C.U. nurse in the back.

I can’t tell you how much the agents covering their faces is a problem for voters. They don’t understand why their faces are covered. That’s not something they’re used to seeing from law enforcement.

I don’t agree. I think people understand exactly why their faces are covered.

Well, I think that’s true. I think what I mean is they don’t like it. They don’t like their faces being covered. That’s not something they normally see from law enforcement.

When people say: Well, they’re worried about being targeted — people are like: That’s not a thing. We have accountability in this country.

The police go without face covers. I’ve heard this, too, and it drives me insane. Everybody knows what it means when the government begins sending people in masks after you.

It means two things. It means the thing they are doing is bad enough that maybe they are worried about being targeted. It also means the government knows the thing they are doing is bad enough that it is a problem if their faces can be seen.

When the government starts doing that, they are creating a zone of action that is wider because they are creating anonymity. They are shifting the relationship between the agents and the public because there is no face-to-face relationship between them.

Everybody knew what it meant. And God bless the people of Minnesota who stood up to push back on this. And Alex Pretti and Renee Good lost their life doing it.

But I recognize, I’ve talked to many political consultants — and you’ll probably tell me the same thing — that this was not the most salient issue to most of the American people. As you say, Trump is still doing better on immigration as an issue than he is doing on trade or prices or a million other things.

But as a signal that the country was falling into a different regime, like an equilibrium that is more like fascist takeover, that was a profound signal.

A midterm is not just where people are in the polls. There are the polls, and then there’s who’s actually going to come out to vote. And the people who had reactions to the masked men in the streets, they’re going to come out to vote.

When I listen to Trump voters in focus groups, they’re sad. They’re bummed out. They don’t like their candidates. They think they’re lame. Often in a bunch of these places — Georgia, for example — hard-core Trump voters aren’t voting for Jon Ossoff, but they understand that everyone else seems to be voting for Jon Ossoff, and that makes them annoyed.

It’s one of the reasons I like qualitative work more than I like polling. Because you can gauge an energy and the absence of enthusiasm among Republicans right now for Trump. Some of them will still defend him because it’s deep in their bones to do that. But they know things aren’t going well and that he’s not doing a particularly good job. So they stay home.

Then what animates people to come out to vote? Are they animated to come out to vote because they want to lower prices? I’m not sure people actually think a Democratic Congress is going to do something about prices.

But the things that animate them are things like America betraying its relationship to the world. Donald Trump is cozying up to all of these dictators. They’re shooting Americans in the streets.

I think that the anti-ICE sentiment is a motivating factor for people that gets them to turn out in a way that immigration has been a turnout mechanism for Republicans in the past but will not be now.

We’ve been mostly talking here about things where Trump is the central driver. He drives the war in Iran. He has a lot of space for action on prices, tariffs and immigration.

We’ve been talking about corruption, but the other thing that seems to be driving races all across the country, though doesn’t seem to be directly emanating from Trump, is data centers.

When I look at a bunch of the key Senate races — Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Josh Turek in Iowa — you see a lot happening around data centers.

I’m curious how those have begun playing into what you’re hearing in your focus groups.

The data center issue started to come up in 2025 in the off-season races, where you had Mikie Sherrill and Abigail Spanberger. This is again why I love focus groups. It caught me off guard.

It was the dominant thing that voters in those races were talking about. In their minds — and again, like immigration, A.I. is one of these issues that activates people across multiple vectors — their energy prices are going up. They think that the data centers themselves are a blight or disruptive in their communities in some way. And the third thing they say is: Are we building these things in our communities that are ultimately setting up to take our jobs from us?

And the companies are like: Maybe. Maybe.

Maybe — that’s right.

So in 2025, it was coming up entirely organically as a dominant issue, mainly around energy prices then. But then I have watched it just go up and up and up in salience in terms of what voters are talking about.

And it is dominant in 2026. In fact, in Ohio, Jon Husted, who is running against Sherrod Brown ——

Oh, yeah. That’s another race where it’s been central.

It has been really central. And as much as Donald Trump can talk about his rear end ——

Husted’s rear end.

Husted’s rear end. He likes talking about Husted’s [expletive]. He’s on a weird bender about men’s bodies right now.

He has been for a long time.

Yeah, I know. I think people say we’re not ready for a gay president, but I disagree. I think we’ve already kind of got one.

A bisexual president?

[Laughs.] So Husted’s big liability is that he had helped secure funding for a bunch of new data centers, and so that is how Sherrod Brown is defining him.

Archival clip of Sherrod Brown: He was the guy who was the point man for the 200-plus data centers in Ohio, $2.5 billion in tax breaks, higher electric rates. We have some of the highest electricity rates in the country now, and did this without anybody locally having any input. It really is part of the rigged system that Jon Husted has been part of and tried to increase, frankly, and make even more rigged through his whole political career.

When I go home to central Pennsylvania, in the more rural areas, that’s where you see the “No Data Center” signs. It’s another thing that is taking the rural voters, who usually show up in enormous numbers for Republicans, and diminishing their enthusiasm for Republicans. Because they don’t want the data centers. It’s in the rural communities where there’s lots of land that these are actually happening.

The other reason I think data centers are frustrating people is that they’re turning out in their local communities to vote against them. But then they’re often happening anyway, which is creating a real sense of frustration among voters that this is a thing being done to them.

I want to hold on that. We were looking at some clips of voters talking in your groups about this, and you really get at this sense of powerlessness, so I want to play them.

Voter 1: People are voting here in Pittsburgh, in these old mill sites, and they’re putting these data centers. People are saying: We don’t want them. We don’t want them. We don’t want the pollution. We don’t want this anymore. But yet they just keep coming, and there’s no stopping. It doesn’t matter who the governor is or who the mayor is. They’re all on board because it’s job creation. And it’s just not job creation. It’s short-term gain for long-term pain. Voter 2: We’re actually having one right now in our town. Everybody voted no on it, and then it came out that it was already in the process and a done deal. The farmers had already sold their property and everything for this to start being built. So basically, everybody that showed up to city hall was for nothing. Our word doesn’t matter.

One of the things I’ve always thought Trump really understood is how powerless people felt in politics, and he sort of presented himself as an answer to that. Like: You might be powerless, but I am powerful. I know how the system works. I have worked it. I have bribed these politicians before.

Totally.

And then this happens, and where’s Trump? Trump is completely pro-data center. He calls Jensen Huang during the All-In Summit, and they’re all just talking about how Trump isn’t going to fall for this anti-data center hoax.

Archival clip of Donald Trump: Google wants to build a big one in Finland — which I’m not happy about because they were unable to get permitting. And I’m telling you, it’s all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy. And it’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years. It’s bigger than the internet and the A.I., you know, much more so.

Look, Trump is not an ideological person, and he certainly doesn’t care about regular Americans. He does care what the All-In podcast guys say about him. He cares what the donor class that he is talking to says and how they talk to him. Those are the people who stand to benefit the most from the data centers, and he is on their side.

I’m sure a lot of those people are coming in and explaining to Trump all of the long-term benefits and how we have to compete with China. That competitive instinct is something that I do think Trump gets into.

But what’s interesting about Trump is that for all the credit he gets for being a good communicator, he’s not trying to have a conversation about this with the public at all. He’s not trying to explain what the benefits might be. I mean, he throws a couple of things out there, but mostly he just tells voters: Stop caring about this. Affordability is a hoax. We’re going to do data centers. They’re great.

Archival clip of Trump: The data centers, you want to put them in the right location, but if you want to get rich as a state or as a town, and if you want to pay lower taxes, if you want to create tremendous wealth, if you want your house to be more valuable and everything else, you’re going to want a data center. If you want to go through poverty, crime and squalor, I would say don’t approve data centers. You know, you have your choice.

People give him credit for his instinct for understanding Americans. But people are extraordinarily anxious about what’s coming because of A.I.

Is this technology going to replace me? It’s something that I hear now all across these focus groups.

If Democrats come in and just say: We’re anti-data centers — but take the exact opposite role of Republicans, I think they will miss an opportunity to demonstrate that they can talk to the American people about a complicated thing that is changing in real time.

What voters really want is someone to take them through it: How should we feel about this?

The problem is — I will say this, having talked to many Democrats and Republicans in office about this — none of them actually know how they feel about it. That is the hard thing about A.I. — and the interesting thing about it as a political issue.

It is unsettled and nonpolarizing. If you look at the polling on data centers, it’s not like Democrats oppose data centers and Republicans don’t, or vice versa. Both sides poll in very, very similar numbers.

With A.I. itself, I don’t think you yet see politicians who really know what to say on this and know how to take people through it. I don’t think they know what to say, and I don’t think they know what “through it” even means — we’re so early in the first innings of it.

This is why I’m so obsessed with finding a Democratic candidate in 2028 who is a good communicator. By that, I don’t mean somebody who knows all the answers or has a firmly held opinion on this.

Americans will let you say: I don’t know, but I’m working to figure it out, and I’m going to figure it out in a way that doesn’t leave you behind. I’m not going to side against the American people on this. I’m going to figure out what is in their best interest.

I am convinced that we are in a new moment of communication, which isn’t just: Go on more podcasts, be like Joe Rogan. It is that the American people are hungry to trust someone who is going to walk them through an incredibly complicated world now with a lot of things changing and an economy that they haven’t seen before.

It’s one of the reasons that I think people want younger candidates, too. They feel like there’s a new generation of problems coming fast that older politicians don’t understand, and they want people who live in that world, too.

One of the things that voters, especially people under 40, say about the economy all the time in focus groups is: I would like a politician who understands that I’m not going to go get a job and then be at that job for the next 35 years. That’s not the economy we’re living in anymore. Will somebody talk to me about the world that we actually live in as it is?

That is why it’s not that I think Dems need better messaging around their issues. It’s that I think people desperately want somebody who’s going to level with them about the problems America is facing and be open-minded about the solutions.

Who are the Democrats that the more Trump-leaning voters in your focus groups actually like?

Right now, Jon Ossoff couldn’t have more juice with voters. In fact, when I do focus groups in Georgia, even if people aren’t voting for him, they want to talk about how he’s clearly winning people over.

A lot of that, too, is constituent services. Constituent services are his bread and butter. All these Trump voters say: I call his office, and they talk to me, and somebody helps me out.

Josh Shapiro, when I was doing focus groups in Pennsylvania the first time he ran for governor, they all had stories about dealing with him and his office, personally, where he helped them. Josh Shapiro is about to win by real margins in the largest swing state in the country, and I think people should take a serious look at him.

I think Pete Buttigieg is doing something very interesting. He’s walking into red states, holding these big town halls and refusing to say that there’s such a thing as a permanent red state.

One of the things I like about Ossoff, obviously, is that Georgia is a redder state.

This is why I’m so suspicious of California politicians who run for national office — I think you have to be surrounded by the people who live in the swing states to have an instinct for what matters to a median voter. If you’ve cultivated your political career in California, you simply don’t have the gut-level instinct to be around a Georgia, Pennsylvania or Michigan swing voter.

So I am looking at politicians who both have that gut instinct — because they come from these places and their political careers were forged there — and who are good at talking to people and have a record of good governance.

People want a candidate who feels like they care about them. And Donald Trump conned people into believing that he cared about them when he didn’t, but people were so desperate for it that they were willing to be conned.

We’ve talked a lot here about people who voted for Trump and are maybe souring on him. But obviously, he maintains support from a huge number of his voters and a lot of Republicans.

So when you hear from the people who are still very pro-Trump — they voted for him in 2024, think he’s doing a great job and don’t regret that vote at all — how do they understand him? What is different in the picture they’re seeing from what we’ve been talking about?

The number one thing that people say to indicate that they’re still appreciative of what Donald Trump is doing is that he has made it clear that there are two genders, and that he is keeping biological men out of women’s sports.

They are still deeply into a lot of the cultural fights — the places where they think that Democrats are weird or overly woke. They tend to be people who are so polarized and so deeply anti-Democrat that, out of tribal allegiance, they continue to support Trump and will brook no dissent on that because they’re very dug in.

It is part of their personality and identity. The Trump thing is who they are. Which is again why I’m a bit skeptical about the future of the Republican Party without Trump.

It is mostly on the cultural things. Which leads me to the thing I am most curious about coming up in this election — something that I’ve been pretty obsessed with: Is it vibes or turnout then?

If it’s enthusiasm, vibes or turnout, Donald Trump turns out rural voters at Assad-like margins. So what happens when he’s no longer there to turn out these voters who were never part of the political process before but are Trump-only voters?

For Democrats, who have college-educated voters, those people are much more in tune. They read everything, they closely follow the election, and they show up to vote.

Whereas a lot of these low-information voters who turn out just for Donald Trump might not turn out in the midterms. But even more, when you add on top of that people who are depressed about what Trump is doing and don’t like their Republican candidates, I think that is why you end up in wave territory.

I think that is a good place to end. Always our final question: What are three books you’d recommend to the audience?

OK, so I just read “Intermezzo” by Sally Rooney, which I really loved.

My favorite book that I have read recently is a reissue. I don’t know if it had gone out of print, but it is by John Williams, and it’s called “Stoner.”

It’s so funny, that book has just been coming up in my field a lot. I haven’t read it.

My understanding is that it had sort of been out of print, and a new publisher picked it up and reissued it. It is the best piece of fiction that I have read in a long time. It’s what I think fiction should be. It’s a wonderful book.

And then the third book — you know, I wrote a book of nonfiction, so that meant that I wanted to just surround myself with fiction — is “The Poisonwood Bible” by Barbara Kingsolver, which I had not read. I don’t know if I read it in high school or something, but I didn’t remember it at all. I just reread it — or read it for the first time, unclear to me. It is so incredibly good.

Those are my three.

Sarah Longwell, thank you very much.

Thanks.

Last week, federal agents searched the Washington home of Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat and a Somali immigrant, apparently as part of a federal investigation of her citizenship.

ARTICLE

Trump Is Turning to an Old Tool of Authoritarian Repression
It evokes dark periods in American history.
By The Editorial Board
Published 2026-10-23 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/opinion/ilhan-omar-trump-citizenship.html

The revocation of a political opponent’s citizenship has long been a tool of authoritarian repression.

The Soviet Union stripped Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, the dissident author, of his citizenship in 1974 and deported him to West Germany. Czechoslovakia revoked the citizenship of Milan Kundera, another celebrated author, in 1979. East Germany and Romania, under Communist rule, took similar steps against critics, as did Chile under Augusto Pinochet, Greece under its military dictatorship, Germany under Hitler and Italy under Mussolini. More recently, Nicaragua stripped more than 300 government critics of their citizenship.

Now comes a new effort to do so from President Trump’s administration. Last week, federal agents searched the Washington home of Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat and a Somali immigrant, apparently as part of a federal investigation of her citizenship. The search should disturb all Americans, regardless of whether they agree with Ms. Omar’s political views.

The investigation of her is a chilling example of the federal government using its immense power to silence a critic. It is an affront to free speech, the rule of law and American ideals. It continues the Trump administration’s use of denaturalization as a weapon. In May and early June alone, the government began proceedings to take citizenship from 33 people, more than in any other entire year since at least 2008.

Ms. Omar is by any definition a political opponent of Mr. Trump’s. She is among the most progressive representatives in Congress, an original member of the so-called Squad, along with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and a frequent critic of the president. Mr. Trump, for his part, has repeatedly vilified her in public over the past seven years, often in ugly, racist ways that play into his broader fearmongering and lies about immigrants and Muslims. He has called her “garbage,” “scum,” “a disaster,” “a troublemaker” and “a terrible person.” He has mocked the head scarf she wears. He has said she should return to Somalia, which he has derided as having “nothing but crime, bedlam, filth.”

In an interview with The New York Times in January, he called for her deportation. “Ilhan Omar is a woman that should be immediately thrown out of Congress and sent back to her, her country, from where she’s always complaining about,” he said. When Tyler Pager, a Times reporter, followed up to ask if she should lose her citizenship, Mr. Trump replied, “Oh, absolutely.” Nine months later, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security entered her home and seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport. They did so in the final weeks of Ms. Omar’s re-election campaign, violating a Justice Department standard against taking public action in an investigation of a candidate within 60 days of an election.

Mr. Trump’s allies have claimed, among other things, that Ms. Omar’s father misrepresented her age during her naturalization process 26 years ago by saying that she was 17 — and thus still a child — rather than 18. We do not pretend to know whether the allegations have merit. Yet as tempting as it may be to focus on them, they are not the main issue.

Sometimes, Mr. Trump makes claims about his perceived enemies that are simply false. Other times, his claims have some connection to reality. Repeatedly, though, he and his appointees use their law enforcement powers selectively and thus unjustly.

The list of critics whom they have targeted for investigation and prosecution includes John Bolton, E. Jean Carroll, James Comey, Lisa Cook, Cassidy Hutchinson, Gen. Mark Milley and Miles Taylor. At the same time, the Trump administration has failed to enforce the law against or has pardoned flagrant and violent criminals, so long as they are friendly to the president.

In the case of Ms. Omar, the administration has gone back more than a quarter-century to investigate a prominent critic. If her naturalization can be revisited, it suggests that no naturalized citizen is safe. It also indicates that the federal government can go searching for any decades-old problem to hound somebody who has criticized the White House. Those are the tactics of authoritarian societies.

They also evoke dark periods in American history. During the Red Scares of the early and mid-20th century, the federal government attempted to strip citizenship from labor leaders and others it accused of being radicals, often focusing on immigrants. At the time, officials like A. Mitchell Palmer, J. Edgar Hoover and Joseph McCarthy used the cases to whip up anti-Communist fervor and justify their efforts to undermine American democracy.

Mr. Trump is following a similar playbook with Ms. Omar. The investigation of her should end immediately.

ARTICLE

She Won His Family Over Years Before Their First Date
Kibriyaá Morgan and Caleb Freundlich had been in each other’s orbit since early childhood. It took a mutual friend and glowing reviews from his mother, the actress Julianne Moore, to bring them together in college.
By Sadiba Hasan
Published 2026-10-23 04:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/style/kibriyaa-morgan-caleb-freundlich-wedding.html

Kibriyaá Sahara Morgan won over Caleb Moore Freundlich’s family before the two ever even met.

They were both New York City kids who had been in the same prep school orbit since they were 5. Freundlich, who grew up in the West Village of Manhattan, attended Friends Seminary in the Gramercy neighborhood, and Morgan, who grew up primarily in the Prospect Heights section of Brooklyn, attended the Chapin School on the Upper East Side.

In 2013, Freundlich’s younger sister, Liv, was considering transferring to Chapin and visited the school with her parents. Morgan, then a sophomore at Chapin, was part of a panel tasked with persuading parents of prospective students to enroll their children in the school. “I was a heavy hitter,” Morgan said, recalling her impressive recruiting record.

Among the parents she won over was the actress Julianne Moore, Freundlich’s mother, who was so impressed by her charisma and sense of humor that Freundlich recalled his mother coming home that day and telling him, “I chatted to this girl Ki, she was so great. She was so cool.” (Liv graduated from Chapin in 2020.)

Morgan’s name came up again after she and Freundlich — who go by Ki and Cal — graduated from high school in 2016. While in Montauk that summer, Moore ran into Veronika Kailich, Morgan’s best friend at Chapin, who mentioned that Morgan would be attending Davidson College in North Carolina that fall. As it happened, Freundlich was headed there, too. Moore returned and gave Freundlich the update about the hilarious, cool girl she had met at Chapin years ago.

Freundlich, intrigued, looked Morgan up on Facebook. “I saw that she was a baddie and played basketball” at Chapin, he said. “Captain of basketball,” Morgan clarified.

Kailich tried to get the two to hang out that summer, but it wasn’t until an honor code signing at Davidson, just before the fall semester began, that the two finally met. They were seated close to each other, and Freundlich recognized her. He nervously deliberated what his opening line should be before tapping her on the shoulder and saying, “You know Veronika, right?”

“Cal?” Morgan said.

“Ki?” Freundlich responded.

When they saw each other again a few days later in French 102, they found out they lived in the same dormitory, one floor apart. They started doing homework together and watching the U.S. Open from student lounges. She brought him to parties thrown by the Black Student Coalition, where they danced to Fetty Wap and Drake.

Morgan and Freundlich, now both 28, became best friends. Both were in relationships, so there was no romantic intention, but they said they had an undeniable chemistry.

Over winter break that freshman year, Freundlich invited Morgan to his family’s West Village home. “We were having a great time and clearly really flirting,” said Freundlich, who, by this point, was single. Morgan’s relationship was approaching its end. “But she still kind of has this boyfriend, and my mom is saying to her, ‘What’s up with this boyfriend?’” Freundlich said, adding that his family picked up on their chemistry.

When their food arrived, Freundlich experienced his first anxiety attack. As a member of Davidson’s basketball team, Freundlich felt pressure to gain weight, and the stress surrounding food and eating had begun to take a toll on him. Morgan was able to console him and uplift him through the episode.

“This was something that really plagued me in college,” Freundlich said about the anxiety attacks. “And she was the only true person that I felt like I could be comfortable with this part of me that I was trying to figure out over the years.”

ARTICLE

‘I Have to Go In’: Dad Describes Killing Gunman in Oregon School Shooting
Kaylub Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting that he happened to be driving by the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend when he saw a gunman preparing to enter the school.
By Michael Levenson
Published 2026-10-23 21:33 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/oregon-shooting-gunman-kaylub-giamanco.html

The father who has been credited with helping to stop a gunman at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., last week described in his first public interview how he pursued the assailant and fatally shot him.

The father, Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter from Bend, said in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting published on Friday that the day of the attack, Oct. 15, started like any other. Mr. Giamanco, who did not respond to messages from The New York Times on Friday, said he woke up, helped his two daughters get ready for picture day, dropped them at Silver Rail Elementary School then drove to a job site.

Mr. Giamanco had packed lunch that day, but had to run into town to buy supplies for the job he was working on, so he called his wife and said he would come home for lunch instead. He asked her to reheat some leftover tacos.

Those choices led him to a fateful moment. As he drove onto Brentwood Avenue, which runs right by Silver Rail, Mr. Giamanco said, he saw a figure in black with a long gun fire twice at a red pickup truck and once into a field. Then he saw the gunman throw his weapon over a fence by the school.

“And that’s when panic flooded into my brain,” he told Oregon Public Broadcasting. Mr. Giamanco opened the center console of his truck, “and just said ‘No, no, no, no, no,’ and I grabbed my gun, and I put the magazine in it, and I racked the action.”

Mr. Giamanco, who the police said had a .40 caliber handgun legally stashed in his truck, drove into the school parking lot. He watched as the gunman, armed with a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, walked along the school’s exterior.

“I was just in full panic, like, ‘No, there’s children, there’s babies in there,’” he said. “I told my Siri to call 911,” he said, and apologized to the dispatcher as she continued to ask him questions.

“I said, ‘I’m sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,’” Mr. Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting. Mr. Giamanco hopped over a fence, and crept behind the attacker around a wall-ball court. He heard the assailant fire into the side doors of the school as he blasted his way inside.

“And that’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives, and then I started hearing gunfire, and I just started army-crawling faster and faster,” he said. “And I told myself, ‘This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do.’”

Mr. Giamanco crawled into the school through a window that had been shot out, and peered into a special education classroom, where he saw the attacker — later identified as Griffin J. John II, 16, a former special education student at Silver Rail — wrestling with a teacher.

Mr. John had already killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, in the classroom, the police said. He had also wounded a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher. But another teacher — the one Mr. Giamanco saw — had thrown her cellphone at Mr. John and had started wrestling with him in what the police called a heroic confrontation that prevented more bloodshed.

Mr. Giamanco, who grew up hunting birds with his grandfather, prepared his gun.

“At that point, I swung the door out and open, and I stepped in, and I fired,” he said. The teacher and the gunman dropped to the floor, he said. The teacher then ran out of the room, fearing Mr. Giamanco was another attacker, he said.

Mr. Giamanco said he saw Mr. John scrambling for his shotgun and shot him two more times, killing him. A heavily armed police officer arrived moments later.

Mr. Giamanco said he put his gun on the floor, put his hands up and told the officer, “‘We need your help over here right now — please, please, please.’”

Then Mr. Giamanco went back to his truck, unloaded his gun and picked up his phone.

“I call my wife to tell her that I’m not coming home for tacos,” he told Oregon Public Broadcasting. He said he also told her: “I just had to shoot and kill somebody, and that I had to watch him take the lives of children and teachers.”

The police have not identified a motive for the attack. They have said the gunman still had 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. In the days since the rampage, Mr. Giamanco said he had been reflecting on the shooting with a heavy mix of emotions.

He said he wanted to meet the families of the victims and “just cry with them and hold them.”

“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Mr. Giamanco said, adding that the “gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome. But there’s ones that I didn’t save, and that’s probably the hardest thing for me right now.”

President Trump, Gov. Tina Kotek of Oregon and the Bend police have all praised Mr. Giamanco, saying he helped prevent even more deaths at Silver Rail.

Mr. Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting: “I want to be a hero in this world. It feels like I was meant to be here and do this.” He added: “I’ve always wanted to change the world, but I’ve felt small. You know, I’m just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon.”

ARTICLE

What to Know About Alaska’s Senate Race
President Trump told the Justice Department to intervene in the race, where polling shows Republicans at risk of losing a seat.
By Jess Bidgood
Published 2026-10-23 23:16 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/alaska-senate-race-explainer.html

The tale of Alaska’s two Dan Sullivans has been an uncanny subplot of the midterms, involving the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S. Sullivan, and a constituent turned long-shot challenger with an almost identical name.

That story is now a really big deal.

In a highly unusual move, President Trump directed the Justice Department to ask a federal court to block the certification of that race if Sullivan, the senator, loses narrowly. His primary rival for the seat is Mary Peltola, a Democrat and a former congresswoman who has led him in several polls.

But Alaska has a complicated ballot, and the Trump administration is arguing that the inclusion of another Republican, Daniel J. Sullivan, merits this unprecedented federal intervention.

Who are the Senate candidates in Alaska? And why are there so many of them?

The best-known candidates in the race are Sullivan, a first-term senator seeking re-election, and Peltola. But they’re not the only candidates.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which asks voters to list the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate secures a majority of the vote in one round, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their supporters’ ballots are transferred to the next-ranked choice.

This year, the Senate ballot (see it here!) includes a Republican named Gerald L. Heikes, as well as the other Dan Sullivan.

Who is the other Dan Sullivan?

Daniel J. Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher, and Republicans have accused him of entering the race at the behest of Democrats as a spoiler who could siphon votes from the incumbent.

He told my colleague Kellen Browning that he was running of his own volition, figuring his name would give him an “instant megaphone.”

Alaska is a red state. Could the incumbent really lose?

In 2024, Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points, so the state was hardly anyone’s idea of a major battleground heading into 2026.

But the incumbent Senator Sullivan has found himself in a tough re-election fight — and it’s not because of the guy who shares his name. It’s because Peltola, the Democrat in the race, is an imposing rival.

Who is Mary Peltola?

She is a former member of Congress who won that seat twice in 2022 — first in a special election to fill the vacancy left by the death of Don Young, a Republican, and then again in a regular election that November. Alaska’s small population means it has only one U.S. representative, who has to run statewide.

Peltola lost re-election in 2024 and then jumped into the Senate race early this year. An Alaska Native, she’s a conservative Democrat who supports gun rights and drilling for oil. She’s been accused of being an unforgiving and chaotic boss.

But she has shown strength on the ballot already. In the primary this summer, in which a slew of candidates from different parties competed for the four slots on the general election ballot, she led the incumbent Sullivan by eight percentage points. (In that race, the other Dan Sullivan won 2.5 percent of the vote.)

Has anyone tried to kick the other Dan Sullivan off the ballot?

They have. As soon as Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race, Republicans swiftly filed complaints with the state’s Division of Elections, arguing that he had not filed to run in “good faith” and that he should be removed from the ballot.

Their evidence? Sullivan had only recently registered as a Republican. He seemed to have ties to a Democratic strategist. And it appeared he had donated to Democrats — including Peltola — in the past.

The election agency agreed and kicked Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot. But a judge reversed that decision, and the state’s highest court upheld that reversal.

Trey Grayson, a Republican and former Kentucky secretary of state, said that whether the second Dan Sullivan could appear on the ballot was a question for the state of Alaska — and that it had already weighed in.

“The states run the elections,” Grayson said. “There are federal laws. They have to be followed. But there doesn’t seem to be anything under federal law that would allow this kind of litigation to succeed.”

How unusual is the Justice Department’s lawsuit?

Highly. The move, my colleague Devlin Barrett wrote, signals an effort to intervene in the outcome of the election.

David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, said he could not recall a similar instance in which the federal government had sought to block certification of an election, “and certainly not 11 days before an election.”

“D.O.J. making this claim this late smells of political interference and is against D.O.J. policy,” Becker said.

SUMMARY

The Pentagon had set up review boards at bases around the globe, manned by everyday uniformed service members with narrow orders that all but ensured that the trans troops appearing before them would be voted out. Navy and Marine Corps boards have voted to retain trans members in nine of 12 cases. Navy and Marine Corps hearings have followed the same pattern.

ARTICLE

Hegseth Barred Trans Troops. Military Boards Are Rejecting Those Orders.
The service members at Navy and Marine Corps hearings are finding ways to keep trans troops in uniform.
By Dave Philipps
Published 2026-10-23 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/trans-troops-military-boards-retain.html

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a slur to proudly announce to an auditorium of Marines in September that he was ridding the military of all transgender troops.

The Pentagon had set up review boards at bases around the globe, manned by everyday uniformed service members with narrow orders that all but ensured that the trans troops appearing before them would be voted out.

But just steps from the auditorium where Mr. Hegseth spoke, at Marine Corps Base Quantico, boards assigned to carry out those orders were doing the opposite. Instead of firing trans Marines, the boards were voting to keep them.

The same was happening in the Navy: Boards given strict rules instructing them to force out sailors were rebelling and voting to let them stay.

It is not just a few outlying individuals. Navy and Marine Corps boards have voted to retain trans members in nine of 12 cases.

The Pentagon keeps the proceedings secret. Outsiders — even spouses — are not allowed to attend. Officials won’t release numbers. Leaders won’t discuss the outcomes. The New York Times compiled the figures through interviews with service members and lawyers involved in the hearings.

The number of Navy and Marine cases is small and could easily change as more hearings are conducted. The same pattern has not been seen so far in the Army or Air Force, which have overwhelmingly voted to discharge trans service members.

Still, the votes are a stunning rebuke from the armed forces, where following orders is bedrock. And they suggest the military’s transgender ban is being rejected by the very troops the administration says the ban is meant to serve.

“These boards are being told to do something that they know is wrong — to rubber-stamp a non-choice given to them by the administration,” said Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer and a professor at Southwestern Law School who has been tracking the cases. “We are seeing them say they’re not going to play that game. We are seeing them nullify a process they see as unjust.”

The board decisions are only recommendations, and could be reversed by the politically appointed secretaries overseeing each service branch. There are also pending legal challenges that could pause the ban or rescind it entirely.

The Trump administration claims that trans troops, who account for about 4,250 people or about 0.1 percent of the military, are a costly burden on military effectiveness — a position that military findings contradict. President Trump signed an executive order barring trans troops during his first week in office, saying the action was needed to weed out dishonorable radicals who poison morale and waste resources.

“For the sake of our Nation and the patriotic Americans who volunteer to serve it, military service must be reserved for those mentally and physically fit for duty,” the order read.

The Pentagon designed a policy that paid transgender troops to leave voluntarily. Hundreds of highly qualified people left, including doctors, lawyers, pilots and nuclear technicians. The troops who stayed to challenge their dismissal waited in limbo, sometimes for more than a year.

While they waited, the administration set up a system of three-member separation boards to process the remaining cases using a narrow set of instructions. Under the rules, any evidence of transgender feelings or tendencies — even if there is no formal transition — requires dismissal.

The three-person boards are made up of everyday officers and enlisted personnel plucked temporarily from their normal jobs to hear one case, like civilian jurors. They are not allowed to consider whether a person is a top performer, a specialist in a critical career field or a decorated combat veteran.

The members are given a one-page findings sheet and instructed to circle a few words to find that a service member exhibits evidence of being transgender and therefore is not qualified to serve and should be discharged.

At least, that was the plan.

Trans Marines and sailors who went before boards said in interviews that after months of being vilified by top government officials, they expected a quick dismissal, but instead encountered thoughtful respect from fellow service members who voted to keep them.

Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras was one of them. The Marine Corps pulled him from his job and put him on paid leave in April to await his discharge. In late August the Marine Corps flew him from Hawaii to Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia to face a board.

He walked in with his head down, sure that his career was over.

The government’s lawyer presented documents from 2017 showing that he had changed genders.

The three members then reviewed his decade of flawless service as a supply and logistics specialist, his three overseas deployments, and his good performance reviews.

They then crossed out instructions on their findings sheet regarding “a history of cross sex hormone therapy” and circled “remains qualified,” and voted to retain him.

“I was shocked at first, but when you come down to it, it makes sense,” Sergeant Contreras said in an interview from Hawaii, where he is stationed. “You have war fighters looking at war fighters,” he said. “They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules. They say, ‘Hey, this is a good Marine, why wouldn’t we retain him?’”

Sergeant Contreras’s lawyer, Priya Rashid, has represented dozens of trans service members and has a broader understanding of the boards than anyone else. After losing nearly all of her initial cases, she saw a stark shift this summer. She has no idea why.

The Army was the first to hold hearings, beginning in February. It has held about 50, according to Ms. Rashid, and voted to discharge soldiers in all but about five cases.

The Air Force started this summer. It has reviewed about six cases and voted to discharge in every known case.

But the Navy and Marine Corps, which began holding hearings in July, have voted to retain in the majority of cases.

“I don’t understand why this pattern is occurring,” Ms. Rashid said in an interview. “And I’m worried that if the pattern becomes too apparent, the government will just change the processes and procedures again so that the pattern can be extinguished.”

Last week Ms. Rashid won another — this time in the Army.

Across the military, the hearings follow a pattern. A lawyer for the government briefly presents medical records and other documents showing evidence that a service member is transgender. The defense then often spends hours presenting a portrait of a service member’s years of service and accomplishments, submitting binders of awards and evaluations, and calling witnesses to vouch for character.

“It all made no difference,” said Maj. Kara Corcoran, an infantry officer who has served for 18 years and deployed to Afghanistan twice. An Army board voted in May to dismiss her in what she called a “kangaroo court.”

“They cut off my character witnesses halfway through and said, ‘We get it, your service is commendable, that’s not what we’re here to decide,’” said Major Corcoran, who now heads the trans advocacy group SPARTA Pride. “The government lawyer, the board, they thought it was ridiculous, but I think they felt they had no choice.”

Navy and Marine Corps hearings have followed the same pattern. But their decisions have been an about-face.

In the Navy, which began hearings in July, nine boards have led to seven votes to retain sailors, according to lawyers involved in the cases.

In the Marine Corps, which began hearings in August, three boards have led to two votes to retain. In the third, the board voted to dismiss a Marine, but wrote on the findings sheet that its members unanimously believed that the Marine should “be retained based on his commendable service record and unique skills.”

What’s driving the shift is far from clear. The military branches, citing ongoing litigation, declined to discuss the outcomes or make board members available for interviews. The Defense Department also declined to comment.

Ms. VanLandingham, the former military lawyer, said the votes might be influenced by growing concern in the ranks that the current Pentagon is preoccupied with wedge issues and gives little thought to the welfare of the force.

Mr. Hegseth in his speech to the Marines, she noted, said the force should have “No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals,” but did not mention those killed or wounded in the war with Iran.

“There’s been a chipping away at any kind of confidence that Hegseth actually cares about service members,” she said. “I think that’s given the boards license.”

There may be cultural factors, too, she said. The board instructions in all the branches are nearly identical. But each branch has different values. The Army is often seen as the most bureaucratic and least likely to buck orders. The Navy is the most diverse. The Marine Corps prides itself on a culture of loyalty.

The Navy has nearly twice as many people who identify as gay, bisexual or transgender — 9 percent — compared to other branches, according to a 2015 report by the RAND Corporation.

That was clear to a Navy paramedic who was retained by a board in July. The paramedic, who asked to not be named because he feared retribution, said he was stunned when his lawyer asked a chief, a lieutenant commander and a commander sitting on his board if they knew any trans sailors.

“They all said yes,” the paramedic recalled in an interview. “The chief said his liberty buddy in Thailand was transgender and was a phenomenal sailor. The lieutenant commander said her first work center supervisor was transgender, and she learned a lot from her. The commander said he’d worked with several transgender sailors, and he barbecues with his next-door neighbor, who’s trans.”

There were other factors working in his favor. He had been meritoriously promoted twice for superior performance; remained able to deploy his entire five years in the Navy; and had saved several lives working in emergency rooms.

For his last assignment he was attached to Marines deployed to the southern border. “I never ran into people who cared if I was trans,” he said. “They just cared that I did my job well.”

His lawyer, Steph Kral, a former Air Force officer, represented a second sailor a short time later in front of a different board that she said had no relationships with trans sailors. That board also voted to retain.

“I don’t think they are trying to make any grand policy statement,” Ms. Kral said. “I think they’re just trying to do what’s best for the Navy.”

The Marine Corps has the lowest reported percentage of women, gay and transgender personnel. It also has a tradition-bound culture based on masculine toughness. But Marines have an almost cultlike loyalty to fellow Marines, expressed in their motto, Semper Fidelis — Always Faithful.

“The questions from the Marine boards have focused in on how the policies of higher-ups may have changed, but the Marines in question never did anything wrong,” Ms. Rashid said. “I think they are looking for a way to give a fellow Marine the benefit of the doubt.”

When Sergeant Contreras went before a board, he produced years of performance evaluations and letters from superiors — some who never knew he was trans — that vouched for his good work.

After deliberating for about three hours, the board scratched out language on the instructions sheet about evidence of being transgender and voted to let him stay.

“It was very humbling to see the things that they had to say about me,” the sergeant said. “It had nothing to do with being transgender. I honestly don’t think they care about that. It was about how I was a great Marine.”

ARTICLE

Your Sleep Habits May Point to a Specific Type of Depression, a New Study Finds
Researchers say people with ‘circadian depression’ might benefit from therapies that help adjust the body’s clock.
By Christina Caron
Published 2026-10-23 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/well/mind/circadian-depression-subtype.html

It is well known that clinical depression is linked to disruptions in circadian rhythm, the body’s internal 24-hour clock that controls the sleep-wake cycle. Reduced daylight in autumn and winter, for example, can set off a type of depression known as seasonal affective disorder, or SAD.

But, according to Dr. Ian B. Hickie, a professor of psychiatry at the Brain and Mind Centre at the University of Sydney, in Australia, SAD is “just the tip of the iceberg.”

In a study published this week in the British Journal of Psychiatry, Dr. Hickie and his collaborators have proposed a new subtype of clinical depression called “circadian depression,” that is estimated to affect about a quarter of the people who have major depressive disorders. And it is not dependent on seasonal changes.

The researchers assessed more than 11,000 Australians who had been diagnosed with depression and found that over 2,600 of them, or about one in four, met the criteria for circadian depression.

It is not a formal diagnosis but rather a suggested subtype, defined as meeting three or more of the following criteria:

- Waking up “very tired”
- Waking up late
- Identifying as a night owl
- Sleeping much later on “free days” than on “working days”
- Seasonal changes in sleep duration, social activity, mood, weight, appetite or energy level
- Sleeping more when feelings of depression are at their worst

Dr. Hickie and his colleagues found that people who met those criteria reported that their depression started at an earlier age than those who did not. In addition, they were more likely to have gained weight during depressive episodes, and exhibit more severe symptoms like brief hallucinations and suicidal thinking.

Identifying this subtype is important, Dr. Hickie added, because people who have it may derive greater benefit from treatment that helps adjust the body clock than from conventional therapies.

Those who showed symptoms of circadian depression reported having a worse response to the antidepressants selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or S.S.R.I.s, and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, or S.N.R.I.s. They also reported more side effects from those drugs.

Some of the symptoms associated with circadian depression are similar to depression with atypical features, which is already considered a subtype of depression. With atypical depression, patients often report feeling sleepy during the day and hungry even after they have eaten. And they do not usually respond well to modern antidepressants.

In the study, there was some overlap among the participants who had atypical depression and those who were found to have circadian depression. But about 1,400 patients with atypical depression did not meet the criteria for circadian depression, the researchers said.

Circadian depression, according to the study, was also associated with genetic signals that suggested a higher risk of developing attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or A.D.H.D.; major depression; anxiety; bipolar disorder; inflammation; and insulin resistance.

Dr. Hickie hypothesized that the people in the study who were labeled with circadian depression might benefit from treatments including melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate the body’s internal clock, and light therapy.

People who don’t respond to antidepressants “very quickly get labeled treatment-resistant,” Dr. Hickie said. “We would argue they’ve probably been on the wrong track since the start.”

More research is needed to know whether those with circadian depression would benefit from such treatments, but earlier studies have shown the mental benefits of resetting the body clock and staying consistent.

“Circadian features, such as difficulty becoming alert in the morning or oversleeping, point to treatments that target sleep and circadian timing,” said Michael Terman, who was among the first researchers to show that bright artificial light early in the morning has an antidepressant effect.

“Bright light therapy is an established treatment for seasonal affective disorder, and research has also shown benefits in nonseasonal depression and bipolar disorder,” said Dr. Terman, who currently serves as president of the Center for Environmental Therapeutics and was not involved in the new study.

Circadian depression is “a plausible” medical condition, he added. But, he said, the study’s findings don’t establish a new diagnosis or show that circadian depression will respond to specific types of treatments.

A significant limitation of the study was that the participants, who were predominantly of European ancestry, self-reported their sleep-wake cycles, and it was unclear whether they did so accurately. It was also unclear whether the patients were in the midst of a depressive episode during the study — depressive episodes are known to cause sleep disruptions.

“If it’s a circadian type of depression, that should mean that the circadian problems should go away when the depression goes away, and that, they have not shown,” said Dr. Nina Kraguljac, a psychiatrist at the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center and chair of the American Psychiatric Association’s Council on Research, who was not involved in the study.

Even so, she said, it’s worthwhile trying to better understand to what extent the clock in the brain contributes to depression.

“Almost every patient who is depressed either sleeps too much or doesn’t sleep enough,” she added. “So it is important to think about circadian rhythms as a potential way to personalize treatments in depression.”
