SUMMARY

The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen is not only firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, but also waging a propaganda war against the kingdom on social media. Saudi officials have not responded to the Houthi accusations about Mr. Epstein or the reports about the tapestries after new Justice Department files were released this year. Since July, as fighting with Saudi Arabia has reignited, the group has turned back to their own conflict and shifted their messaging accordingly.

ARTICLE

The Epstein Files Produce an Unlikely Weapon for the Houthi Messaging Wars
The Yemeni militia is using the culture of its sworn enemies in the renewed fighting with Saudi Arabia.
By Ephrat Livni
Published 2026-10-23 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/world/middleeast/houthis-saudi-arabia-propaganda-epstein.html

The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen is not only firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, but also waging a propaganda war against the kingdom on social media.

A key character in the group’s communications campaign is, oddly, Jeffrey Epstein, the deceased American sex offender, some of whose files the U.S. Department of Justice has released.

The Houthis have recently homed in on a particular set of revelations to try to undermine Saudi Arabia’s leaders — namely, reports showing that associates of the Saudi royal court sent tapestries that had draped the holiest site in Islam to Mr. Epstein’s private island.

The Houthis control much of Yemen. Their communications show a profound awareness of news that their sworn enemies generate. They are willing to deploy the information in many forms — songs, videos, speeches, statements, influencer posts and more — to build support and target foes, including Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognized Yemeni government they are fighting. They portray themselves as defenders of Islam against corrupt foreign influences.

Now, the group has stepped up its messaging efforts, after Yemen’s civil war reignited this summer amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Plugged In

The Saudis last month accused the Houthis of firing a drone at the Muslim holy city of Mecca, saying the attack was a “disgraceful” act that intended to provoke Muslims. The Houthis denied the accusation.

Rallying their expansive network to try to turn the accusation of religious betrayal against the kingdom, the Houthis pointed to the reports that Mr. Epstein had received tapestries that had draped the Kaba, the cubed building in Mecca that is the spiritual center of Islam.

“Those who gave Epstein the Kaba’s cover are the ones targeting Mecca,” Mahdi al-Mashat, the Houthi president, said in a statement to the group’s official news media.

Saudi officials have not responded to the Houthi accusations about Mr. Epstein or the reports about the tapestries after new Justice Department files were released this year.

Variations on Mr. al-Mashat’s message were echoed across the Houthi network, including video commentary from a Yemeni comedian with more than 270,000 followers on X and a song by a traditional musician in Yemen.

“They are very plugged in,” said Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the risk advisory firm Basha Report and a Yemen analyst in Washington who has tracked the evolution of Houthi communications over more than 20 years.

The group’s messaging operations have morphed from essentially “a two-man crew,” Mr. al-Basha said, to an organized media system. It spans television channels, websites, radio, newspapers, email campaigns and official and unofficial social media accounts. There is also a brigade of cultural influencers — a support network involving people who are ideologically aligned with the group and other Iranian proxies but not necessarily paid — who amplify a range of content in line with their ideology.

Like other groups in Iran’s “axis of resistance,” the Houthis are “obsessed” with Mr. Epstein, said Mr. al-Basha. The disgraced financier, he added, serves as shorthand for the corruption of the United States and Israel and is invoked to bolster antisemitic conspiracy theories that Jews and Zionists run the world.

A secular American Jew who officials said killed himself in a New York jail in 2019 while facing criminal charges on the trafficking of underage girls, Mr. Epstein frequently features in speeches by the Houthis’ leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi. He mentioned Mr. Epstein in a speech this month celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war and in another in September about the Houthis’ 2014 takeover of the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.

“Epstein’s files demand serious attention,” Mr. al-Houthi said in a February address. “They unveil a Zionist incubator that trains leaders and elites.”

The Houthis have positioned their fight with Saudi Arabia as part of the broader war the Iranian axis says it is waging against the United States and the “Epstein class,” including Saudi leaders, said Moustafa Ayad, who leads research at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue in London on Islamist movements’ online ecosystems.

The Houthi motto calls for death to America and Israel. Connecting the rulers of Saudi Arabia — the birthplace of Islam — to these core enemies reinforce’s the group’s stance that, although the Saudis have no diplomatic relations with Israel, they are “one block” with the United States, Mr. Ayad said. U.S. weapons and military support were essential to the yearslong bloody bombing campaign that Saudi Arabia waged against the Houthis.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government has its own approach to propaganda, though it does not have the same unity of messaging, Mr. al-Basha said, because its Presidential Leadership Council is made up of leaders with various ideologies and affiliations to different military groups. They are unified in their opposition to the Houthis, but “there is no one voice for these groups,” he added.

Laser-Focused

The Houthis’ messaging to the Arab world has been prolific, and their content went truly global after they targeted commercial ships in the Red Sea in 2023 in alliance with Hamas during the Gaza war. Since July, as fighting with Saudi Arabia has reignited, the group has turned back to their own conflict and shifted their messaging accordingly.

“Now, they are very specifically singling out Saudi Arabia” and “almost laser-focused on decimating” the standing of the kingdom’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said Mr. Ayad.

The Yemeni comedian Mustafa Al-Moumr was previously critical of and jailed by the Houthis, but since his release in 2023 he has aligned his content with the group’s talking points. It is not clear what is behind his new work, or whether he is operating under duress.

In the current conflict, he has produced a stream of content critical of the kingdom and Prince Mohammed, including music videos, commentary and short dramas. One music video posted in July shows him as the Saudi crown prince singing about his fear of the Houthis while aides report militia attacks, and ends with the royal captured in his palace at gunpoint. The post has had more than 300,000 views.

Another major theme in Houthi content is the toll of Saudi Arabia’s intervention in Yemen. A Saudi-led bombing campaign in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which began in 2015, precipitated one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen from violence, hunger and disease.

When Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, was filmed last month in New York being berated by an activist in Arabic, a Houthi spokesman, Ameel Hayyan, posted the clip on social media, writing that Saudi Arabia is loathed globally “due to its crimes against Muslims and especially the savage massacres it committed in Yemen.”

Since the civil war in Yemen reignited in August, some 260,000 people have been displaced, according to the United Nations. Nearly 1,600 people have been killed, the World Health Organization said this week. And the Houthis have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians.

Some of the content has emerged in the recent conflict is “essentially a mimicking of the Iranian approach” to propaganda, Mr. Ayad said.

Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, Iran has been adept at reaching an international audience on the messaging front.

Explosive Media, an Iranian group that has produced viral Lego videos, last month created “a Lego retelling of Yemen’s battles and victories,” a fantastical take on Houthi fighting with Saudi Arabia that shows the militia storming a Saudi military base with a golden statue of Mr. Trump and ends with a Houthi commander sipping from a mug marked “mocha,” alluding to their capture of the Red Sea port of Mokha, a gateways of early coffee trade.

The narratives are traveling far and wide, reaching seemingly unlikely sympathizers, at least some of whom share an obsession with conspiracy theories and Mr. Epstein.

Jake Shields, a retired mixed martial arts champion and popular right-wing podcaster and influencer, whom the Southern Poverty Law Center has accused of promoting “antisemitism, racism and bigotry,” posts about the Epstein files regularly. On a recent episode of his show, he spoke about the fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, expressing admiration for the militia’s resilience.

“I’m a big fan,” he said of the Houthis. “I think they’re kind of badass.”

It was precisely the kind of reputation and response that experts say the Houthis have sought to cultivate with their military and messaging campaigns.

James McManagan contributed reporting.

trump-epa-chemical-air-pollution.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 117  Words: 3858/3861

SUMMARY

Within sight of a southeast Texas middle school stands a chemical plant that President Trump excused from new federal rules intended to curb its cancer-causing pollution. Mr. Trump gave it a similar waiver from recent clean-air rules. Many of the details of how the Trump administration aided the chemical industry are being reported here for the first time.

ARTICLE

How Trump Gave the Worst Polluters a Free Pass
The president temporarily waived clean-air rules for industrial facilities that spew cancer-causing gases. Then his appointees worked to gut the regulations altogether.
By Eric Lipton, Maxine Joselow and Mira Rojanasakul
Published 2026-10-24 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/climate/trump-epa-chemical-air-pollution.html

Within sight of a southeast Texas middle school stands a chemical plant that President Trump excused from new federal rules intended to curb its cancer-causing pollution.

About a 30-minute drive from Pittsburgh, a steel-making facility has spewed carcinogenic chemicals near homes for years. Mr. Trump gave it a similar waiver from recent clean-air rules.

And on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., the owners of an industrial warehouse emailed the Trump administration asking for their own waiver. Their wish was granted. Nine months later, the facility accidentally released a large plume of carcinogenic gas into the community.

In total, since taking office again, Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from clean-air regulations that were going into effect. Some were among the country’s worst industrial polluters, including chemical manufacturers, copper smelters and coal-burning power plants. About 3.3 million people live within three miles of at least one affected facility.

The exemptions represent the biggest presidential intervention in enforcement of the Clean Air Act in the half-century since President Richard M. Nixon signed the bedrock environmental law. And that is only one of the ways the Trump administration is dismantling a variety of federal environmental protections.

Before Mr. Trump’s return, the chemical industry was losing its fight to block or at least delay tougher E.P.A. requirements to reduce toxic emissions. It had pleaded with agency officials, filed lawsuits and appealed to Congress. But officials and the courts had largely rejected the industry’s claims of undue expense and regulatory overreach.

Now, Mr. Trump is prioritizing the economic interests of corporations and easing costs for polluting industries, and their immense clout is striking.

The president’s exemptions were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the Environmental Protection Agency with appointees who had lobbied for the industries they now regulate. Those officials then quickly went to work from the inside to gut the rules altogether.

Mr. Trump has taken an expansive view of executive power in his second term. On the environmental front, he has unilaterally shredded regulations, withheld science funding appropriated by Congress and ordered coal plants that planned to shutter to continue running.

Even so, his evisceration of the new Clean Air Act rules stands out.

Many of the details of how the Trump administration aided the chemical industry are being reported here for the first time. In one upside-down moment, industry executives provided the agenda for a meeting with E.P.A. staff and then effectively presided over it.

Mr. Trump also nominated Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade group, to lead the E.P.A.’s air regulation office. Once there, Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement, documents show.

To understand how Mr. Trump gave a free pass to some of the worst polluters, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and spoke to more than 70 people familiar with the efforts, including former E.P.A. officials and industry executives.

“These companies, with their campaign contributions and the revolving door of former lobbyists and executives that now work in the regulatory agencies — that is where the petrochemical industry gets its power,” said Brent Coon, a Beaumont, Texas, lawyer who has spent decades squaring off in court against petrochemical firms over environmental and health risks.

The Clean Air Act requires the E.P.A. — created in 1970 to protect public health and the environment — to periodically review the latest pollution controls and impose them broadly if they are affordable and effective. The most recent review began under the Biden administration, which in 2024 finalized new, tougher requirements.

In granting the waivers to those rules, Mr. Trump cited an obscure clause in the act that allows exemptions if complying with new rules would threaten national security and if the necessary technology is not widely available.

Yet the president approved the waivers even though the equipment was readily accessible and the industry’s national security claims had little detail to substantiate them, documents show.

The Biden administration pushed through the new pollution requirements after evidence emerged about the health threats posed by ethylene oxide, a colorless gas used to make products like plastic soda bottles and to sterilize medical devices like pacemakers.

E.P.A. researchers had concluded that ethylene oxide was 30 to 60 times as carcinogenic as previously thought, particularly for people who live near plants where the gas is made or used. The agency held meetings to warn community members about the elevated risks.

Outside Richmond, home to one of the country’s largest commercial sterilizers of medical devices, some residents left one of these briefings wondering whether recent cancer diagnoses among neighbors were tied to the plant, though it is virtually impossible to prove pollution caused a specific cancer case.

“You see these pretty buildings, and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from the plant, which resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

As recently as April, the plant, owned by Sterilization Services of Virginia, had a mishap. A faulty valve caused 580 pounds of ethylene oxide to leak from large drums and waft in a toxic plume over nearby homes, state records show. The plant’s state permit allows it to discharge no more than 400 pounds of ethylene oxide in an entire year.

Representatives for Sterilization Services of Virginia did not respond to calls seeking comment.

The new rules required not only sterilizers but also chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If certain amounts of the gases got out, the operators had to fix the leaks. Some facilities also had to build special containment systems — akin to giant breadboxes — to reduce gas releases.

Though the facilities would still have to follow pollution limits already in place, the industries fought the E.P.A.’s new mandates, calling them expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. They also challenged the Biden administration’s scientific findings.

“It is critical that regulation of our industry is based on sound science and that those regulations reflect a reasonable assessment of the risks and benefits involved,” Brendan Bradley, a spokesman for the American Chemistry Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.

The Trump administration did not ask companies to present an exhaustive case for why they deserved a waiver from these new requirements. It was as easy as sending an email to the E.P.A. and invoking the obscure exemption language in the act, a provision that no president had ever used.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement the waivers were necessary to protect American manufacturing.

“Exemptions were issued due to crushing Biden-era regulations that required large swaths of our industrial base to adopt technologies that don’t exist outside the imagination of Biden’s E.P.A. bureaucrats,” she said.

Mr. Trump’s decisions rewarded industries that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he won.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off, saving the industry millions of dollars in upgrades.

“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.

‘A Sense of Urgency’

The chemical plant in Port Neches, Texas, just south of the meandering Neches River, is a vital cog in American manufacturing. It is among the country’s biggest producers of ethylene oxide.

The plant’s owner, Indorama Ventures, is a major employer in the region and supports local schools, including Groves Middle School. It provides a football training complex through which its chemical pipelines run. It also sponsors the annual Fish-O-Rama Fishing Tournament to raise money for local science and math programs.

The plant also has a long history of releasing toxic pollutants into the community, state records show.

On more than 500 occasions since 2003, it has experienced malfunctions or other failures that resulted in releases of air pollution or toxic chemicals, frequently in violation of its permit, Texas records show.

From his front yard, dotted with baseballs and children's bikes, Cody Coburn can see the flares that burn off excess toxic gases from the plant across the street. Some nights they rattle his windows, suggesting a possible malfunction at the plant.

The incidents leave Mr. Coburn and his wife wondering if they are taking a risk living there with their young sons. “We’ve talked about moving away,” he said.

The violations continued after Indorama, based in Bangkok, purchased the facility from the Texas-based Huntsman Corporation in 2020.

A particularly alarming incident occurred in early 2022. A control valve failed, sending 57,000 pounds of pollutants into the air, including ethylene oxide, records show. The discharges continued for nearly a week.

That 2022 incident, and others like it, put Indorama on the radar of E.P.A. officials who were rewriting the rules for chemical plants.

These kinds of facilities had long used models to estimate their emissions. The problem was, no one could say if the estimates were accurate.

The E.P.A. decided to find out. The agency emailed the managers of the Indorama plant and 10 other facilities, ordering them to install temporary devices at the edges of their properties to measure toxins in the air.

Career E.P.A. employees were stunned by the results, said Brenda Shine, then the agency engineer who supervised the data collection.

Based on data provided by the plant, agency staff had estimated the tests for benzene, a gas linked to cancer, would find about 0.02 micrograms per cubic meter of air — a relatively small amount. But the actual air sampling revealed benzene levels nearly 50 times as high. It also found three times as much ethylene oxide in the air as estimated.

Similar conditions were found at other plants, but Indorama’s tests showed the worst results.

The public health implications were enormous.

An additional one in every 500 people who lived near the plant for most of their lives was likely to develop cancer from exposure to ethylene oxide, a March 2024 EPA report concluded. That risk is 20 times the 1-in-10,000 level that the E.P.A. typically considers to be the highest acceptable cancer risk when it evaluates carcinogens.

That cancer threat from the Indorama plant could be cut by 95 percent, the E.P.A. found, if better pollution controls were installed.

“There was a sense of urgency,” said Joseph Goffman, who supervised Ms. Shine’s work as the head of the agency’s air office during the Biden administration. “It really alarmed local communities.”

Indorama executives argued that the E.P.A. had gathered samples while the plant was undergoing maintenance, so the results did not reflect normal operations, records show. But when agency inspectors returned in 2024, they still found ethylene oxide leaking in multiple locations and drifting across the facility’s fence line.

A spokeswoman for Indorama declined to address detailed questions from The Times about the plant and cancer risks because they involve continuing regulatory discussions.

“Indorama Ventures recognizes the importance of protecting the health and well-being of our employees, neighbors and surrounding communities,” Patricia Sakamiti, a company spokeswoman, said in a statement.

The test results were a critical factor in the E.P.A.’s approving the new air toxics rules.

Those rules required Indorama and other facilities to limit leaks from valves and upgrade flares so that they could burn off more toxic gases before they were released. The companies also had to install monitors around a plant’s fence line. The results would be publicly posted, letting neighbors see what they were breathing.

The E.P.A. estimated that similar improvements would cost about $440 million to install and $163 million a year to maintain for all affected facilities. That would constitute less than 1 percent of the industry’s national sales.

For that price, millions of people who live near these plants would be at a lower cancer risk, the agency concluded.

Indorama said the E.P.A. had acted “beyond its statutory authority” when it required the fence line tests and that the demands were based on a “flawed risk assessment.” Executives from plants that use ethylene oxide to sterilize medical devices, including the one outside Richmond, joined the protests.

So did companies like U.S. Steel, which operates a facility in Clairton, Pa., near Pittsburgh. The plant bakes coal at up to 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, turning it into coke, an ingredient in steel making.

U.S. Steel, in a statement at the time, said it was committed to working with the E.P.A. in supporting regulations that were “well grounded in law” and science. “Unfortunately, the 2024 coke rules do not meet these criteria,” it said.

Lobbyists Turned Regulators

Eleven days into the second Trump administration, Lee Zeldin, the newly sworn-in E.P.A. administrator, received a request from the American Chemistry Council and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, the two biggest trade groups for the chemical industry.

They wanted Mr. Zeldin, a former Republican lawmaker, to push the president to give them relief from the Biden-era rules.

The trade associations, in their petition, laid the groundwork for the Trump administration to intervene for national security reasons, arguing that the new requirements could cause them to curb or cease production. “National security includes economic security and protection of domestic production of chemicals vital to public health,” the petition said.

The chemical and medical device industries were also busy writing a flurry of checks to Mr. Trump’s causes.

AdvaMed sent $125,000 to his inauguration fund and $1 million to MAGA Inc., one of Mr. Trump’s campaign affiliates. The latter donation was made on the same day in April 2025 that AdvaMed’s chief executive, Scott Whitaker, attended a candlelight dinner with Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort.

“Yes, I met with President Trump and was grateful for the opportunity to introduce our lifesaving industry to him,” Mr. Whitaker said in a statement, adding that ethylene oxide did not come up.

One of the E.P.A. officials who was copied on the request for regulatory relief was Mr. Szabo, a senior adviser who was awaiting confirmation to lead the agency’s powerful Office of Air and Radiation, which oversees regulations intended to curb toxic pollution.

In Mr. Trump’s first administration, Mr. Szabo had served as a White House lawyer, helping review new regulations. But before that term ended, he moved to the lobbying world, representing oil and gas companies, chemical manufacturers and coal-burning electric utilities.

His clients included AdvaMed, and Mr. Szabo secured private meetings with the E.P.A. and the White House through 2024 to help the medical device industry fight the Biden-era changes, records show. Before Mr. Trump’s re-election, Mr. Szabo also helped draft the E.P.A. chapter in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint for a second Trump term.

From his new perch within the E.P.A., Mr. Szabo began participating in gatherings at the agency’s headquarters with former clients and working on the industry’s wish list, according to emails reviewed by The Times.

Brigit Hirsch, an E.P.A. spokeswoman, said in a statement that an ethics agreement Mr. Szabo signed last year permitted him to work on “general” matters that affected various industry players but not “particular” matters that narrowly affected his former clients until one year passed.

E.P.A. officials held at least 40 meetings with chemical industry executives in 2025, agency entrance logs show.

Mr. Szabo coordinated these efforts with two deputies who had joined the E.P.A. after stints in industry: Abigale Tardif, a former lobbyist for the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, and Alexander Dominguez, a former American Petroleum Institute lobbyist.

Mr. Szabo also reached out to Emily Underwood, a senior White House lawyer, suggesting that the president could invoke the Clean Air Act exemptions, documents show.

“Thanks Aaron! Can we just see the copy for POTUS’ proposed mention of/remarks on this?” Ms. Underwood responded.

Ms. Underwood, when reached by phone, told The Times that the agency took the lead on these efforts: “The best person to talk to on that would be Aaron Szabo at the E.P.A.”

Mr. Szabo declined to comment. Ms. Tardif did not respond to requests for comment.

The same day that he corresponded with Ms. Underwood, Mr. Szabo appeared before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for his confirmation hearing. It was Ash Wednesday, and Mr. Szabo, a Catholic, bore a cross of ashes on his forehead.

Mr. Szabo told senators that he had a personal stake in clean-air rules because he had cystic fibrosis, a lung disease exacerbated by air pollution.

“Growing up, I could feel the impact of poor air quality in my lungs,” he said.

A week later, the E.P.A. created a special inbox to receive requests for waivers from the rules. Companies soon flooded the agency with submissions.

Presidential Exemptions

To understand the newfound power of the chemical industry inside the E.P.A., consider a meeting in May 2025 at the agency’s satellite offices in North Carolina.

Nearly a dozen senior chemical industry executives flew in and gathered in a large conference room. Another 30 industry members joined on a video call. The participants represented some of the industry’s biggest players, including Dow, BASF and Huntsman.

The agenda was set by the chemical industry rather than its regulators.

“To provide some structure to our discussions, we prepared the attached agenda,” Leslie Bellas, a vice president for regulatory affairs at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, wrote to the E.P.A. team.

The de facto moderator was Brendan Mascarenhas, a lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council, according to meeting minutes and participants.

Industry officials were not shy about their demands then and at follow-up gatherings with E.P.A. officials, the minutes show.

First, they wanted the E.P.A. to rescind its scientific finding that ethylene oxide was much more likely to cause cancer than previously thought. The determination had formed a legal basis for many regulations, and with it gone, the rules would fall like dominoes.

Companies also wanted to roll back requirements for fence line monitors. And in the event of a leak, they wanted to keep plants running longer before shutting down for repairs.

That same month, the chief executives of Dow, Chemours, OxyChem and the American Chemistry Council gathered with Mr. Zeldin at his office in Washington.

Chris Jahn, the head of the chemistry council, wrote on social media afterward that they discussed transforming the E.P.A. so that it focused on “pro-growth policies,” while also “protecting human health and the environment.”

By July 2025, when Mr. Trump had still not granted the waivers, executives grew anxious.

The deadline for the first of the new pollution controls was only a year away, and it would take nearly that long to install the necessary equipment. So the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman wrote a letter directly to Mr. Trump and shared it with the E.P.A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for Presidential Exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E.P.A.,” they wrote.

Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

He issued his first exemptions for 50 chemical plants and 40 sterilizers. His order said that “the current compliance timeline would undermine our national security,” and that the sterilizer rule relied on “technologies that do not exist in a commercially viable form,” even though the breadbox-like enclosures were already in use in some states.

The E.P.A. pointed to Mr. Trump when asked about the exemptions. “This decision was made by the White House, as it is a presidential authority,” Mr. Szabo wrote to one Texas Republican lawmaker.

Then, two of the former lobbyists within the E.P.A. turned to weakening the underlying rules.

One was Ms. Tardif, who had represented the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum in meetings at the E.P.A. as recently as December 2024. In a June 2025 email, an official at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers thanked her for “productive discussions” about “reconsideration” of the chemical plant rules and copied an official at Marathon.

The other was Mr. Szabo, who asked his staff this spring to strike the same provisions from the sterilizer rule that he had once represented AdvaMed in opposing, including the requirement to install the enclosures.

He delivered an even bigger victory to his former clients by summer.

In a memo dated Aug. 13, E.P.A. staff members warned Mr. Szabo that removing the fence line monitoring requirement for all affected chemical plants would be “difficult to justify” in court. They also noted that the Clean Air Act required the E.P.A. to address “air toxics that pose the greatest potential health threat,” including those tied to cancer.

Despite those warnings, Mr. Szabo issued the order to kill the mandate that same day.

It would be one of Mr. Szabo’s final acts at the agency. This month he resigned and took another job at a law firm that has represented industry groups in their challenges to some of the same Clean Air Act rules.

Weighing Risks

In Clairton, smokestacks at U.S. Steel’s facility release clouds of steam and chemicals. Thanks to the Trump administration, the plant no longer has to curb some of its toxic emissions, at least for now.

Melanie Meade’s house, in her family for generations, sits on a ridge overlooking the plant. In her backyard, it often smells like rotten eggs or burning rubber, and time outdoors makes her feel lightheaded.

Ms. Meade said she knew she faced an elevated risk of cancer, which killed her older sister and several of her neighbors. But she cannot afford to buy a comparable house elsewhere. So she stays.

A spokesman for U.S. Steel, Andrew Fulton, said in an email that Clairton Coke Works had never been fined for exceeding benzene emissions standards. The company plans to invest up to $2.5 billion in its plants in southwestern Pennsylvania, but none of it will be spent on new pollution controls in Clairton, Mr. Fulton said.

“It would be premature for U.S. Steel or any other regulated company to invest in controls while the rule is under reconsideration,” he said.

In Groves, Texas, which sits adjacent to the Indorama plant, some residents were surprised to learn that Mr. Trump had waived requirements designed to protect their health. Their reactions were mixed.

Chris Borne, the mayor of Groves, appreciates Indorama.

“I have full faith in our facilities where I live,” said Mr. Borne, an electrician who has handled jobs in many of the area’s chemical plants. “Sometimes the rule makers, they go too far.”

Others were angry about the administration’s moves.

“Making things great again — I thought that meant making all things great, including our health,” said Lance Bridges, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2016.

As Mr. Bridges spoke, his 22-year-old daughter pushed a toy scooter carrying his granddaughter in front of their house.

A few weeks later, the Indorama plant had another accidental discharge. Gases started seeping into the community at 6 a.m. on Sept. 11, shortly before students began streaming into school.

State records show that the leak continued for eight hours.

Andrew Chavez and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

ARTICLE

The Eyes of Elizabeth Holmes
Look into that unblinking gaze and see the abyss.
By Maureen Dowd
Published 2026-10-24 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/elizabeth-holmes-you-can-see-everything.html

You’d think we’d be weary of flimflam artists, tech vampires and alternative realities by now. But no.

It’s like Gertrude’s lust in “Hamlet”: “As if increase of appetite had grown / By what it fed on.”

In a time of deceit — political, algorithmic and every other way — a meditation on deceit has taken the culture by storm.

Meditation is not the right word, actually. It’s more like a film noir thriller, with a manipulative femme fatale, a destructive romance, a man who’s meant to play the fall guy, and an atmospheric cottage by the sea.

The three-hour documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything,” is paradoxically titled, because you can’t see much of anything. (Except her naked narcissistic fiancé preening in the shower.) Holmes is busy obscuring the truth and building an illusory world where her dangerous fraud about comprehensive medical testing with a pinprick of blood was just an innocent hiccup.

“I know I didn’t commit any crime,” she assures the filmmaker Nathan Fielder, training her big, blue Furby eyes on him. She doesn’t think she has ever lied in her life, she says. It was all just a misunderstanding. Never mind the threatening lawyers like David Boies she sicced on anyone who questioned her phantom technology.

Holmes abandoned her Steve Jobs black turtleneck in favor of J. Crew-looking soccer mom sweaters. But she remains the perfect avatar for our age: She promised tech that would help humanity and then unleashed a deception that could have hurt humanity.

Holmes and her partner, who had two children before her 11-year sentence for fraud began in Texas in 2023, wanted a sympathetic documentary charting her last weeks with her family before she got locked up. They stumbled upon Fielder, who directed the movie along with Lance Oppenheim, and ended up starring in it.

Fielder originally did not intend to appear onscreen, but Holmes irresistibly drew him into her web, and the resulting game of cat-and-mouse between the two magicians is astonishing.

The deadpan Fielder is a Canadian-born satirist who worked with Sacha Baron Cohen on the 2018 mockumentary “Who Is America?” and on his own shows, “Nathan for You” on Comedy Central and “The Rehearsal” on HBO, where he has built elaborate ruses. He is a master at spinning his own absurd reality, and so is Holmes.

The sparring of these two raises the question: ls there any point searching for the truth or is it better to settle into our own fractured, subjective realities?

At 30, Holmes became the first self-made female billionaire, after she dropped out of Stanford at 20 and started Theranos. But she’s no role model for women. When she got in trouble she embraced victimhood, turning from a confident Silicon Valley founder who dominated every room into a damsel in distress. In court, she blamed her lover/partner, Sunny Balwani, who got an almost 13-year sentence for helping Holmes defraud investors of more than $700 million. She said he abused her psychologically and sexually and controlled everything, from her clothes to her diet. The jury was unconvinced.

Holmes tries to turn Fielder into a film noir sap, someone who will believe her lies about her lies, be drawn to her emotionally and come to her rescue. And the documentary projects, then calls into question, a scenario where her current lover/partner, Billy Evans, is manipulating her, asking for a cut of the documentary’s profits supposedly behind her back, taking over her X account and putting up foul-mouthed posts pretending to be her, releasing a hologram of Holmes that he nonchalantly acknowledges might be used by some men online for porn.

The woman famous for her guile — suckering George Shultz, Jim Mattis, Henry Kissinger, Sam Nunn, Larry Ellison, Rupert Murdoch and other brainy older men — plays guileless, acting as if she can’t even scramble eggs without her controlling fiancé’s help, or understand the simplistic joke in the classic Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” comedy routine. Fielder jokes that if Holmes had “just said that Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free.” The couple talk about building “monuments of love” to each other, but it’s more like monuments of manipulation.

Tyler Shultz, George Shultz’s grandson, who was an intern and researcher at Theranos and then left and blew the whistle on Holmes, said on “CBS Mornings” that Holmes took in Fielder enough to allow doubt to creep in about Holmes’s guilt.

“She knows that she was lying,” Shultz said, “because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies.”

Shultz said the harm to real patients was horrible and Fielder never laid out the dimensions of her crimes.

“We told people that they had H.I.V. when they did not,” he said. “We told people that they had cancer when they did not. We told expecting mothers that they had lost their unborn child when they had not.”

Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy for playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” also wonders if Fielder is too “protective of her.” The actress reprises her role in some scenes in the documentary and visits Holmes’s family after she goes to prison, getting chided by Evans for her Hulu portrayal.

Evans is a handsome, buff man, the scion of a wealthy hotel family who is now determined to work with Liz, as she is known now, to straighten out the problems with her blood-testing method. But as the film goes on, there’s a Dorian Gray effect, where his face grows scarier, twisted into a mask of rage and subterfuge. Is Evans, not Fielder, the sap? As in film noir, the boyfriend carries a rod and is vowing vengeance.

Whether or not you think Fielder isn’t tough enough on Holmes, it is impossible to look away from her. Her unblinking gaze is like the disembodied blue eyes in the haunting billboard in “The Great Gatsby,” and both represent the same thing: moral decay.

ARTICLE

Lena Dunham: The Day I Met My Parents
It was a busy Tuesday with news of acid rain, insider trading, nuclear radiation and (at least) two new babies.
By Lena Dunham
Published 2026-10-24 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/lena-dunham-nyt-175.html

To mark The Times’s 175th birthday, Times editors asked writers to reflect on — and imagine a little bit about — the newspaper’s front page on the day they were born. This is the first in a series. Look up your own birthday page here.

It was a mild Tuesday in Manhattan. On May 13, 1986, the trains spit out throngs onto Wall Street, and while their suits were gray and rumpled, the men had a spring in their step: that fresh itch that accompanies skirts getting shorter, women revealing the dimpled flesh of their thighs as they arrange themselves on the subway seats. Many of the gentlemen, stopping for their daily newspapers, smiled and said, “Keep the change” — pennies, really, but it felt like largess to them. A spirit of generosity had overtaken essentially ungenerous people.

Somewhere in Barnes, England, that day, Robert Pattinson had been born. His mother gazed at him misty-eyed, full of hope for what he would be: a scientist who finds the cure for a rare (or even common) cancer? A professor of classics? A traveling instructor of water sports, spending winters in Fiji and summers in Aspen? She went over so many options it made her laugh, but never considered that he might become an actor and play an alluring and pure-hearted vampire, inciting lust in tweens, then switching to more independent fare and doing gangbusters there, too.

But on Wall Street, nobody yet knew about Robert Pattinson — and some of them never would, either dying before his reign or missing it altogether, since they were the types who skipped right to the finance section. Had they bothered to take a moment to extend their interests, they might have learned from the front page of The New York Times that France had reported “a captive Arab” admitting to attacks, while at Yeshiva University the refuseniks Anatoly Shcharansky and Yelena Bonner reunited after Mr. Shcharansky’s release from a Soviet labor camp, greeting each other with such joy, you’d have thought they were lovers. The General Accounting Office’s investigation of Michael Deaver, a member of President Ronald Reagan’s staff, found several potential violations in his handling of efforts to move the United States toward an agreement with Canada on acid rain. (What exactly acid rain is, and what it could do, were questions few people bothered to ask in either country.) NASA had been warned of cold weather risks to the Challenger space shuttle, but sent it up anyway. The death toll from Chernobyl radiation and burns had reached six (according to Moscow). The only headline that piqued the men’s interest was about the Wall Street “merger specialist” charged with insider trading, a reminder to stay on the up and up, or at least appear to.

In the stairwell, a secretary from the float pool — a recent Smith College graduate — smoked a cigarette, ate a bagel and read every word of the front page, promising herself after each article that she would go back to her temporary desk very soon. As happened with the drinks she’d had last night, she was breaking her own rules. The world has never been bleaker, she thought, although maybe that was the hangover talking, and she tried to remember her history professor — the squarely handsome one with the sandy hair — reminding his students that “the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.”

Uptown at Roosevelt Hospital, two 36-year-olds, who had arrived dressed like teens on summer break, were in an icy operating room. She was awake on the table, though numb from the waist down, and he wore blue scrubs over his ripped, paint-stained khakis and tennis shoes with the backs crunched down. He was trying his hardest not to avert his eyes as a doctor cut his wife’s lower abdomen horizontally. If she has to go through it, he thought, then I should have to watch it.

He’d slept horribly the night before. All the joy and fizz of the past nine months had given way to a sense of profound dread, as if he had agreed to turn himself in at the police station come morning on a federal charge. He was considering this — Why now? What did he think he was losing? — when all at once the doctor pulled an infant, slack and blue but eyes wide, from his wife’s stomach and slapped its back with dramatic flair. The baby sputtered, then let out a cry so ferocious and oddly pitched that one of the nurses began to back out of the room.

Another nurse rubbed the screaming infant with a towel and wrapped her expertly, and one of them grinned at the man: “You want to hold her, Daddy?” Daddy — he knew instantly he would not like this to be his new name.

He looked at his wife, but she was staring up, at the light or seemingly something beyond it. And as they handed him the baby, his body was flooded with a sense of purpose that had previously eluded him. Like an EpiPen chased with a shot of Jack. Like your high school crush saying, “I don’t just like you; I need you.” Like knowing what you’d be doing every day for the next 40 years.

“Hello, Lena,” he said. He was staring into her eyes, trying to understand if she looked like his father or if he just felt like his father.

The doctor began to stitch up the incision. “Wait a second — I can feel that,” the new mother said. “Please, stop — I feel it.”

But everyone had moved on, and no one was really listening.

Lena Dunham is the creator of the TV series “Girls” and the author, most recently, of “Famesick.”

ARTICLE

Republicans Are Crude, Craven, Cruel. It’s Not Working Anymore.
Republican candidates are in a sorry state.
By Jamelle Bouie
Published 2026-10-24 15:35 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/midterm-elections-republicans.html

In my column last week, I wrote about the Democratic Party’s dramatic change of fortune in the race to control the Senate. The expectation at the start of this election cycle was that Republicans would hold the chamber easily and, depending on the course of events, even expand their majority.

After all, just to maintain the status quo, Democrats had to defend incumbents in states that President Trump won handily. And to have any chance at a majority, they would need to defeat at least one incumbent — Susan Collins of Maine, for example — and overcome the Republican Party’s home-field advantage in at least two states.

A tall order if there ever was one.

But thanks to a set of Trump’s bad decisions — from his authoritarian occupations of American cities that enraged liberal voters to a war in Iran that has angered swing voters and independents with inflation and high prices — Democrats have turned what was supposed to be a bad Senate map into one where they stand a real chance of winning a decently sized majority in the chamber.

But while the fundamentals determine the overall shape of the electoral landscape, candidates and campaigns play a meaningful part in the final outcome. And it is in the realm of candidates and campaigns that I want to remark on two particular aspects of this campaign season.

The first is the wide gap in candidate quality between the Republicans and Democrats. In race after race, Democrats have managed to recruit and advance candidates who are well positioned to capitalize on changing political circumstances. Even if he were not facing off against Ken Paxton, an experienced but still strikingly weak candidate, James Talarico would still be an impressive recruit. He is a natural communicator — whose seminarian background and personal faith have been a great asset in winning over Texas voters — and he has proved to be both nimble and aggressive, able to hold Paxton’s feet to the fire despite facing an onslaught of cash from outside groups and actors, like Elon Musk.

You could say similar things of Adam Hamilton in Kansas, perhaps the surprise candidate of this cycle, who is running a competitive race against the Republican incumbent, Roger Marshall. Hamilton is a religious leader — the founder and senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the United States — with broad appeal in a state that is, like Texas, known for its deep religious feeling. With his moderate politics, Hamilton has successfully presented himself as a bipartisan figure, with support from prominent Republicans in Kansas. It also helps that Marshall, a doctor, has struggled in the face of revelations that he took harsh and punitive action against his patients, dragging them to court for trivial amounts of money.

Other Democratic candidates, such as Josh Turek in Iowa, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Troy Jackson in Maine, have also successfully capitalized on the Republican Party’s worsening electoral position. And even those Democrats who might be a little more progressive than their electorates — Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — show a great deal of political talent and are well-positioned to win.

As for the Republicans, the opposite appears to be true. There are a few candidates in the field who may well outperform the fundamentals, like the Iowa Senate nominee Ashley Hinson. Michele Tafoya in Minnesota also seems to be keeping up with her opponent. But beyond them, Republicans are working with candidates who are just not up to snuff. In Georgia, Mike Collins has been marred by his associations with white nationalists and other extremists, and is headed for a crushing defeat in his race against the incumbent, Senator Jon Ossoff. Darline Graham in South Carolina is barely ahead of her Democratic opponent, and again, this is South Carolina. The aforementioned Ken Paxton is such a lackluster candidate that he may well deliver the Texas Republican Party its first statewide defeat for federal office since 1988.

Perhaps the most striking example of a candidate ill-equipped for a competitive race is Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio. Ramaswamy ran unsuccessfully for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, then returned home to Ohio to try to lead the party there. Perhaps the fact that Republicans were not anticipating a competitive year is how Ramaswamy managed to win the nomination. Either way, he is currently poised to lose to the Democratic nominee, Amy Acton.

In apparent desperation, the Ramaswamy campaign commissioned an advertisement featuring Amy Acton’s mother. The two have not seen or spoken to each other since 1978. As a child, Acton testified against her stepfather, who was charged with sexually abusing her. Acton’s mother took her husband’s side, and the two fled the state. In the advertisement, Acton’s mother calls her daughter a liar, someone who “lies about her past.” The evidence says otherwise. To give one example, documents released by Mahoning County officials in Ohio corroborate Acton’s claim that she lived in a tent as a child.

The Ramaswamy camp, which includes fellow Ohioan JD Vance, thinks the ad is effective. But it’s been condemned by people on both sides, including the state’s Republican governor, as crude, craven and cruel. There is a chance, as well, that it blows back on Ramaswamy, undermining his campaign in the critical final stretch of the election. It is the kind of move that a more seasoned and competent candidate might have avoided. As it is, Ramaswamy’s gambit may well drag down the entire statewide ticket.

We’re still 10 days away from Election Day, so I’m not going to make any grand pronouncements about the outcome. But I will say that if Republicans do lose the Senate, and if they lose it badly, it will be a testament to one of the most striking political dynamics of the Trump era.

It is very possible that Trump was the only Republican who could have stitched together his particular electoral coalition. It is undoubtedly the case that Trump has some special sauce that makes him a formidable general election candidate. But this has not extended to the rest of the Republican Party. No other Republican is able to mimic Trump’s particular style of politics. And while Trump’s endorsement is a powerful force in Republican primaries, the president does not actually have a great track record of picking candidates who go on to win general elections.

Trump is in absolute command of the Republican Party, but outside of his own victories, he has steered it, more often than not, into troubled electoral waters.

It should be said that the drive to denaturalize Omar is, by itself, a startling attack on the liberty of all Americans. It’s a move that harks back to the worst of the nation’s past — those moments when the government sought to shape, define and ultimately choose who would be “the people” of the United States.

Now Eating: Baked Spanakopita Pasta with Greens and Feta

A delicious way to use up the odds and ends of herbs, greens and cheeses you might have in your fridge. Also very kid-friendly if, like me, you have to think about those things. Recipe comes from NYT Cooking.

Ingredients

- Salt and black pepper
- 4 cups chopped spinach, Swiss chard or other mild greens (tough stems removed)
- 4 cups chopped arugula, watercress or other peppery greens
- 1 cup chopped fresh dill or parsley leaves and tender stems, or a combination
- 6 scallions, trimmed and thinly sliced, whites and dark green parts separated
- 1 pound tubular or curvy pasta, like rigatoni or fusilli
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 4 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced
- 8 ounces cream cheese (1 cup), cut into ½-inch cubes
- 4 ounces mozzarella, grated (1 cup)
- 4 ounces crumbled feta (1 cup)

Directions

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Heat the oven to 450 degrees.

In a 3-quart/9-by-13-inch baking dish, toss the chopped spinach, arugula, herbs and scallion greens with 2 teaspoons salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Squeeze the mixture with your hands to wilt, then set aside.

Cook the pasta in the boiling water until 2 minutes shy of al dente; reserve 1 cup pasta water, then drain pasta and set aside. Return the pot to the stove.

Melt the butter in the pot over medium heat. Add the scallion whites, garlic and a pinch of salt, and cook until softened, 4 to 5 minutes. Add the cream cheese and pasta water and stir until smooth. Stir in the wilted greens, half the mozzarella and half the feta until combined. Stir in the pasta until combined. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed.

Transfer the pasta to the baking dish, then top with remaining mozzarella and feta. Bake until the sauce has thickened and turned bubbly, and the top has browned in spots, 10 to 15 minutes. If you like a crisper top, broil for a few minutes.

SUMMARY

The principles and strategies that over multiple generations have made the United States the world’s leading nation in effect are on the ballot, and these midterms mark a potential turning point. Yet President Trump, with the acquiescence of congressional Republicans, is vandalizing education, from Head Start for 4-year-olds living in poverty to elite universities researching new treatments for cancer. ARTICLE

None of This Is Normal
The fundamental issue is Trump’s shredding of the model that made America the world’s leading country.
By Nicholas Kristof
Published 2026-10-24 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/midterms-trump-america.html

America’s midterm elections will probably be determined primarily by issues like affordability. But what is at stake goes far beyond the quotidian concerns that many voters are focused on.

The principles and strategies that over multiple generations have made the United States the world’s leading nation in effect are on the ballot, and these midterms mark a potential turning point.

Let’s focus on three pillars that explain the rise, strength and resilience of our nation.

First is education: The United States pioneered mass education in the 19th century and today operates great universities and research institutions that are among the nation’s crown jewels. These have given us an edge in the global economic competition. Yet President Trump, with the acquiescence of congressional Republicans, is vandalizing education, from Head Start for 4-year-olds living in poverty to elite universities researching new treatments for cancer.

Trump is trying to dismantle the Department of Education, cut student aid and slash support for the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health. His war on America’s leading universities is particularly alarming, for he has variously attempted to defund them, cancel their tax-exempt status and make it harder for foreign students to enroll.

“The U.S. is committing suicide,” Yasheng Huang, a professor at M.I.T., told me, referring to the Trumpian campaign to demonize higher education and hobble cutting-edge research.

Another source of American greatness that Trump is throttling is immigration. The United States gained immensely from successive waves of newcomers from around the world, often arriving destitute and without English (like my father in 1952) but lifting their families up over a generation or two. One reason we’re a global leader in science and technology is that we’ve been able to recruit the brightest minds and hardest workers from across the globe.

When I lived in China decades ago, I was an interviewer of applicants to Harvard, and one of the students I told the university it would be lucky to have was a brilliant young woman named Sofie Qiao. She was admitted and went on to earn a Ph.D. and become an American. Today she is a serial biotechnology entrepreneur in Silicon Valley, helping develop treatments for breast and prostate cancers and for mesothelioma. She is now helping save the lives of other Americans.

Under Trump, fewer of today’s Sofies are coming to America. The number of international students arriving in August 2025 for the fall semester dropped by almost one-fifth, and the number in August 2026 fell by another 12 percent.

A third pillar that has made America the world’s leading country is the bundle of norms that govern our politics, economics and society.

Until Trump came along, I believed it was laws and the Constitution that were the country’s primary guardrails, but as I’ve seen how Trump has bullied his way past Congress and the courts, I’ve come to think that norms are just as important in underpinning democracy and economic strength. I’m thinking of simple traditions — such as that presidents will honor election results, won’t persecute rivals and will refrain from starting reckless trade wars with, well, everyone.

Norms of self-restraint historically made the system work. Presidents did not try to crush law firms or universities, nor did their administrations mislead federal courts or send armed officers into cities, where they shot people. Presidents quarreled with allies but didn’t threaten to invade Greenland.

Trump has tried to pulverize those norms by vilifying immigrants, denigrating women and threatening to “annihilate” Iran. Just this month, he called a female federal judge a “crazed lunatic.”

“The vitriol is toxic,” says David Beasley, the former Republican governor of South Carolina, “and it is undeniably feeding into the hearts, minds and souls of Americans.”

Trump is attempting to establish what feels to me like a personality cult, putting his name on the Kennedy Center and his photo on national park passes and some passports; I’m reminded of Bangladesh under its last dictator, who had herself named “mother of humanity” and put her picture and her father’s everywhere. Other presidents redecorated; Trump tore down the East Wing of the White House, is building a ballroom and aims to construct a so-called Arc de Trump.

Then there’s the greed, on a new level altogether. Trump reaped at least $2.2 billion last year, in his first year back in the White House, much of it from his family’s cryptocurrency businesses, a Times analysis found. That’s more than $6 million per day. When Amazon reportedly paid $40 million to acquire the Melania Trump documentary, I recalled covering corruption in Indonesia in the 1990s, when the wife of the president, Madame Tien, was nicknamed Madame Tien Percent.

The mix of grandiosity, authoritarianism and sleaze dribbling out of the White House is polluting government, civil society and the economy. Having spent much of my journalistic career reporting in two-bit dictatorships, I see so much that is familiar; it’s heartbreaking to see this unfold in my own country.

Trump has worked to undermine the entire international system the United States created after World War II — for our benefit and the world’s — to promote peace, trade, prosperity and health. Ebola, poverty and Vladimir Putin are beneficiaries. Imagine if in 1943 President Franklin Roosevelt had abandoned Britain and switched to back the Third Reich; that is a bit like Trump’s seeming pivot from Ukraine to Russia.

We may not have reached bottom. A particularly dangerous step would be for Trump to invoke the Insurrection Act and dispatch troops to crush protests or seize ballot boxes. Asked about the Insurrection Act, Trump told Time magazine: “I could use it. A lot of people think I should use it sometimes.”

None of this is normal. We are betraying other countries but also our own history and culture. I always wondered what citizens of ancient Rome, a proud and sophisticated empire, thought when one of their crazy emperors came to power; now I have a glimmer of understanding.

“This is the greatest heist in the history of the world: stealing America,” the singer Bono said of what has unfolded. “Everything we love is on the line,” he told me.

So those are the stakes in this election: Will we accept the loss? Or will we try to get our nation back?
