ARTICLE

What Happens if Trump Doesn’t Like the Midterm Results?
Hope, dread and the final stretch to Election Day.
By Michelle Cottle, Jamelle Bouie, David French and Derek Arthur
Published 2026-10-24 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/trump-midterm-elections-results-predictions.html

We’re less than two weeks out from Election Day. In their last conversation before Americans head to the midterm polls, the national politics writer Michelle Cottle joins the columnists Jamelle Bouie and David French to take stock. While Jamelle makes the case for cautious optimism about a possible blue wave, David worries about what could happen if Trump doesn’t like the results.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Michelle Cottle: I’m Michelle Cottle. I cover national politics for New York Times Opinion, and I am here this week with my brilliant colleagues, columnists Jamelle Bouie and David French. Gentlemen, how goes it?

Jamelle Bouie: It goes well.

David French: Doing well, Michelle.

Cottle: All right. We are less than two weeks out from Election Day. This is our last episode before the will of the voters becomes clear, and I have so many pressing questions for you, most of which fall into the category of: What in God’s green earth is going to happen?

So I know, I know, we can’t really know, but from everything we’re seeing and hearing, how do we think this is going to play out? And maybe this is just my PTSD from 2020 talking, but how might a certain president try to undermine the results if things don’t go his way? So let’s dive in.

There has been a lot of optimism in the air for the Democrats in recent weeks. Our latest newsroom poll has Democrats leading nationally by 11 percentage points. Are we expecting a blue puddle, a blue wave or, maybe more accurately, what has been termed a “red undertow”? David, you go first.

French: You know, it’s really interesting, Michelle. Everything empirical is saying that this could be a blue wave, this could be a blue tsunami. You’re starting to see things, like polling in South Carolina, in Mississippi, within the margin of error, and it’s becoming so blue-ish in all of the data ——

Cottle: Blue-ish.

French: That a lot of smart people I know are like: Wait a minute, can we trust this data? Because it feels like people have been through this before. They have been through optimistic polling waves. We’ve also been through years and years and years of very closely divided politics, where it doesn’t feel like something like Democrats +11 in a popular vote, if you’re going to like ——

Cottle: That’s not a real thing.

French: Take the whole House and put it at, would it actually end up Democrats +11? Highly doubt that. Highly doubt it. But at the same time, there’s nothing really empirical to point at to diminish the optimism.

I keep going back, though, to the sense I felt when I was in Texas recently. When I was talking to Democrats, I would call it “cautious, guarded, daring to dream, but not really dreaming,” if that makes sense. Which I think is actually a pretty healthy attitude to take.

Cottle: Jamelle?

Bouie: Yeah, I would advise people, if they’re thinking about this, to just stress-test it against previous elections, when you’re thinking about, OK, how, how might this be off? And I think that’s useful, because it forces you not just to look at the polls, but at the larger national conditions. And that’s where I think it’s worth just taking seriously what the polls are saying.

So if you look back at 2018, Donald Trump was not this unpopular. He just wasn’t. He was in, I believe, the low 40s, right? So at the moment, he is about 10 points on average less popular than he was in 2018. And I really think it’s important to stress that he’s never been this unpopular before. Economic conditions under Trump have actually never been this bad before, other than, again, the early days of the pandemic.

And so in a lot of ways, we’re in a situation that is actually quite distinct from previous situations when Trump has been on the ballot — and the results we’re getting in terms of polling are consistent with that. It doesn’t mean that things might be better for Republicans than the polling suggests, but I do think that it’s a good reason to think this is capturing something. The exact contours of what that something is, we won’t know until all the ballots are counted. But as far as where the national mood is and what appears to be competitive, that all seems quite right to me.

Cottle: OK. Well, this makes me feel a little better, because I tend to be a pessimist with a lot of these things, and I tend to look at, say, Maine, where I’m not so sure Susan Collins isn’t on track to pull this out. So if I look at Texas, where, yep, the polling looks good for James Talarico, and I don’t think Beto was ever ahead in the polls.

French: No.

Bouie: No.

French: Never like that.

Cottle: People always compare it to that. At the same time, I’ve been reporting and waiting for Texas to turn blue. I remember doing a story about how the Black and brown coalition was going to turn it blue, I think, like a quarter century ago.

I tend to pick the states and areas that make me the most nervous and obsess a lot about those. In part because one of the just broader things that I’m worried about is that Democrats — not even the electeds, but like a lot of the voters or the activists or the kind of watchers — I worry are playing the expectations game badly, that they’re so excited, that they want to win in Texas.

They want to win in some of these red states — in Alaska, that sort of thing; Iowa — that they’ve got expectations so high that, unless they just completely wipe out the Republicans in the House and claim the Senate, I still worry that they’re going to just be declared underperformers, which is going to give Trump an opportunity to stand up and say, “See? We’re fine, and I can just continue running amok,” and all of that. So aside from the people that you talked to in Texas, David — just like broadly — is anybody else worried about the expectation game being played wrong?

French: Absolutely, Michelle. Let’s put this in perspective for a second. We’ve long been thinking that the Democrats could hold in Georgia. We’ve thought that Ohio could possibly be in play. Ohio is a swing-ish state. Even Iowa, swing-ish somewhat recently. Maine, a relatively blue state. So these are states that nobody would just fall out of their chair in shock about. But now we’re talking about Kansas. We’re talking about Nebraska. We’re talking about South Carolina, Mississippi, Texas. And so I do think, if the Republicans hold those states — sort of ending up by going, “Ha, ha, we narrowly held Kansas” — it’s not the flex that you think that it is. But I do think that expectations are building to such a point that there would be at least some degree of disappointment and upset if Democrats don’t win Kansas. I think there might be some real disappointment, again, if Democrats don’t win in Texas.

To Jamelle’s point — I think Jamelle makes a ton of valid points — about the fundamentals of this race, they are enough to make anyone who’s wanting to see the MAGA era end feel more optimistic. I think those fundamentals are there. It’s just, for me, it’s becoming sort of so overwhelming as state after state and race after race goes from likely R to lean R to tossup, that you start to wonder, could this be something realigning? Could this be something truly resounding that we haven’t seen for some time in American politics? And that’s when all of the skepticism lights start to come on. And we’re just going to have to wait and see.

Cottle: Jamelle?

Bouie: I will be surprised if Adam Hamilton wins in Kansas. That’s kind of a crazy outcome. If Darline Graham only wins by one point, that’s a crazy outcome. But having said that, I guess I’m not as shocked by this development as David might be, in part because of the point I made earlier: The actual fundamentals, the national conditions right now, are different. The closely divided elections of the past since 2016 have all operated under a kind of similar set of circumstances: a relatively strong economy; relatively evenly matched, in terms of popular sentiment, political parties; coalitions that aren’t that fluid because there aren’t any new issues changing the nature of the political debates. And all that stuff has changed, right?

Again, the president’s very unpopular, the economy is sluggish, inflation is still relatively high, still with us. Fuel prices are high. There are these new issues on the table — A.I., data centers — that are scrambling partisan coalitions somewhat. There is the fact that Trump simply isn’t on the ballot. And if you think of Trump as an issue and not just a person — the dividing issue of the past 10 years or so of American politics — him not being on the ballot, and thus voters aren’t being forced to choose about their view of Trump’s role in American politics, that itself maybe opens things up a bit. “Oh, now I’m not voting about Trump; I’m voting about diesel prices. Now I’m voting about the fact that I don’t like data centers.”

So there are all these things happening below the surface of American politics that the divided nature of American politics over the last 10 years may have somewhat obscured, and now, as Trump is leaving the scene, they’re kind of bubbling up again. Again, that’s not to say that I think it’s going to be a big Democratic sweep, but that when you look at a place like Mississippi, which apparently is competitive, the high levels of racial polarization in that state actually mean that Democrats have a pretty high floor, right?

Cottle: Sure.

Bouie: They’re usually winning 45, 46 percent. Is it really that crazy to think that, in an unusually bad time for the incumbent party, some percentage of white Mississippians may decide either to sit it out or switch votes? And in that environment, is it really that crazy that the state becomes competitive? I don’t think so. For so much stuff, it’s like tiny changes on the margins can produce these big effects, and I kind of think that’s what we’re seeing.

Cottle: Well, I do think you touched on something interesting there, which is that it’s not that Republicans need to vote for Democrats; they just need to stay home. You hear these discussions about, “Oh, well, there’s no way with the Democratic brand that somebody who’s been voting Republican forever is going to come out and pull that lever.” But this is a midterm election. Midterm elections are always about who you can get to show up at the polls. I do think that from what we saw, certainly, during the primaries, the enthusiasm gap in Democrats’ favor is enormous, which could always make the difference in these sorts of places.

French: And this is a point in Jamelle’s favor on why you should be looking at some of these polls and saying, “OK, they’re measuring something real.” I can’t remember the last time in an election where you could trace voter anger at specific issues to very specific actions by the administration. Normally, when you’re talking about things like inflation rates or job creation, it’s kind of debatable what’s causing all of the inflation or how are these jobs being created, how much is the government versus the private sector, etc. But here you’ve got: Why are gas prices high? The Iran war. Why is background inflation creeping up again? Why are wages falling behind? Tariffs.

You can look at very specific things that this administration has done, which is one of the reasons I think that that term you used — the red undertow — is very appropriate. You can go issue by issue by issue and say, “On what planet does a smart political party do this? On what planet do you do this if you’re actually trying to win elections?” And rarely have I seen a party squander a victory more thoroughly and more efficiently — and more comprehensively — than what the Republican Party has done to the 2024 victory. It is astounding what the Republican Party and what Trump has done after this vibe shift in 2024. And so that’s to Jamelle’s point: Voters can look at very specific things that Trump and the Trump administration have done that have made their lives worse, and I think it makes it easier to vote against them.

Cottle: Yeah, I think you make an important point there, when you’re like, what party would do this if they want to be successful? It’s not a party. It is one man who has never cared about his political party. Donald Trump has no interest in the success of the broader Republican Party. He is only interested in how people talk about him or what he wants to do. And so there has been, obviously, plenty of frustration among Republican lawmakers about some of these issues. Now, if they were really frustrated about it, they should have stood up and done something before now. But, here we are.

So we’ve laid out basic expectations. Let’s turn now to the kind of dark, weird possibility of what happens if all of this comes to pass — blue tsunami, blue wave, blue whatever — and a certain president doesn’t like the outcome. Does he try to meddle with it, to overturn it? I mean, it wouldn’t be the first time. Earlier this week, the Department of Justice charged 28 people with violating federal voting laws. And after claiming that there are likely 20,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, I mean, are you guys worried about any of this, and the efforts that seem to be kind of percolating along?

Bouie: So I’m of two minds: The first is that all of this is obviously very bad, right? It seems to be the administration doing what it typically does: abusing its power, harassing innocent people, that sort of thing. The claim that there have been 20,000 noncitizens registered — you know, California disputes that, and every time D.H.S. or the administration has made this kind of assertion, it’s promptly fallen apart, so there’s no reason to believe that it’s true. So all of that is very worrisome, right? I think one should have every expectation that the administration is going to say that the elections were tainted by fraud, etc., etc., etc.

My question always is: OK, so what, practically speaking, does that matter? Because practically speaking, it’s not like the White House can’t overturn the election. When I say that, people are going to hear something like, “Well, that’s illegal. He can’t do it.” No, I mean that in the very literal sense. What specific person talks to what specific person to invalidate 435 congressional elections, to invalidate 30 Senate elections, right? That’s not a thing.

Cottle: It’s just not a thing.

Bouie: It’s just not a thing! And in the event that there is a big Democratic win, that disincentivizes regular Republicans from going along with this stuff, because at a certain point, it’s like, well, what’s the point? What’s the point in causing all this grief if we know we’ve just got our butts handed to us? So I see this stuff very much as a desperate administration lashing out in whatever way it can to try to intimidate people, right? To try to convince people not to turn up, not to vote, to create enough fear and uncertainty to make people think that something truly catastrophic might happen.

But when you think about it rationally, they don’t have much they can do in terms of subverting the outcome. And what they can do is not something they can do without opposition, right? Localities will, states will, the Democratic Party will, in terms of being able to file litigation. There’s all this room for pushback and relatively little room for action from the administration. So for me, it’s these two things at once. It’s a problem and it’s bad, but it’s also not, like, apocalyptic.

Cottle: David?

French: I’m a little darker than Jamelle, not on the front end. I draw a distinction between the voting and counting and certifying. I think it’s just so hard. It is really, truly so hard to mess with the actual voting.

Now, where I’m more concerned is that some of these states, if you win — if the Democrats win Ohio by seven or eight, or Jon Ossoff wins Georgia by eight or nine — I’m not worried about that. But what about Talarico up 0.6 percent on Ken Paxton in Texas? That’s when I’m saying all bets are off at that point. Or you have Hamilton 1 percent or less up in Kansas. And in those circumstances, you’ve got the very red-state election officials. And if there is a contest — the contest in the House, for example — as to who sits in the House is settled by the House. And this is something under procedures that are really pretty cursory and not really fully defined very well.

And then at that point, yeah, Jamelle’s right: There’s lots of opportunities to contest this and to fight this. But as we learned with Jan. 6, and Trump in 2020 and 2021, they don’t even need a credible legal argument. They can get people storming the Capitol over stupidity, like, just lunacy. That’s the thing: The 2020 election conspiracy theories weren’t just wrong; they were stupid and wrong. They were incandescently stupid and wrong, and he got people storming the Capitol in that circumstance. And so that’s where I’m a little bit more worried — the back-end certification challenge in maybe some of these very red states that are suddenly competitive.

Cottle: Yeah, I tend to be more nervous about the structure, and I tend to be specifically nervous about the very low-down officials, like precinct-level type stuff. I just remember, after the Jan. 6 hoo-ha, there was this shift in the Trump world where they were basically readying the playing field to take over. Steve Bannon did this call-out, the precinct strategy, where he called for MAGA people to go in and get elected, or get appointed or volunteer, to take over all these low-level offices, so if there was a question next time, it would be Trump loyalists who would be making the calls about: Did this look like fraud? Should we have this recount? Should we do this, that, or the other?

And then on top of that, of course, you have Trump doing what he always does, which is just to sow distrust and undermine the public’s confidence that any of this works. So that if something gets thrown to this board or that recount, people are kind of primed to think, “Oh, well, there must be something wrong.”

So I have to say, that does make me nervous. On the other hand, I do think that the difference is Trump’s not on the ballot. And on some level, if things don’t go his way, maybe he just wants to throw up his hands and say, “See, you guys are total losers when I’m not there. This just proves that I am the only thing that matters, and I’m just going to go forward for the next two years and fight it out with Democrats, and enjoy my status as the undisputed only Republican that matters.” So his lack of give-a-crap-ness, on some level, makes me feel a little better, I guess.

Bouie: I would say as well that I think it’s just important to think of all this stuff as part of a larger dynamic system, right? So Trump claiming fraud is significant, certainly, but it also has to be weighed against the fact that Trump is very unpopular. So he’ll claim fraud, and what percentage of people will hear that and be like, “Yeah, well, of course he’s going to say that,” and they just move on, right?

The extent to which public sentiment is just not on his side — the extent to which, if it’s a big election victory for Democrats, there’ll be tangible evidence of that — really does, I think, diminish the actual capacity of Trump and his allies to do shenanigans. They may still have the mechanical ability to do it, but you also need some sense that this sentiment is going to be on your side. And an election where, let’s say, Republican turnout collapses — which is very possible — would suggest that it isn’t. So they can do stuff, but I think the response is going to be “OK, whatever,” and you move on.

French: Fox has about 787 million reasons to not go along with stolen election theories this time around. And we’ve actually seen this since 2020. You’ve actually seen, in certain circumstances, when someone goes on Fox and spouts some crazy election conspiracy now, you will have a host come on and say, “There was no evidence. All courts ruled —” etc., etc. And so you are seeing some, for lack of a better term, quality control, editorial standards locking in here a bit. So I do think that’s an absolutely better environment than in 2020 and 2021, and that does give me some optimism. But mark my words ——

Cottle: Mark your words.

French: If it’s Talarico by 0.5 percent, watch what’ll happen in Texas, in conspiracy land.

Cottle: Are you worried about the certification process, Jamelle? I mean, not the voting, but the after — the process.

Bouie: Not particularly. In part because Republicans will be on these ballots, too, right? They’re going to want their offices, too, and the secretary of state, state boards of election, which are responsible for certification, are going to want to certify those people as well. If it were the case that these were the only elections where the competitive Democratic Senate wins, then maybe. But the fact that — in terms of do you get your office, do you get your staff, do you get your salary — everyone’s kind of bound up together. I think that leads me not to worry, not to worry as much.

Cottle: What you’re telling me is that you’re feeling good.

Bouie: What I’m saying is that I think that there is a tendency to treat the desire and will of the president as equivalent to ability and capacity. And so they say, “We want to do these things,” and they make these threats, and I think that there’s a tendency — because of all the crazy stuff we’ve experienced over the last 10 years — to say, “Well, if they say they really want to do it, then it must be a thing that they can do.” And my view has always been: Is it, though? They can both practically — and thinking politically — thinking about the interplay of forces and institutions and people — they may try, but that doesn’t mean they’re going to succeed.

It doesn’t mean people should be complacent, but I do think it means that one should try to, um … I’m going to, I’m going to do a me thing. So in his memoirs, Ulysses S. Grant tells this really interesting story that during the Mexican War, he is out with a riding partner and they hear wolves. And Grant’s like: We’re surrounded by wolves, what are we going to do about this? And his riding partner’s like: Let’s just go check out and see what this is. And they go find the wolves, and there’s only two wolves. And Grant says: There’s always more of them before you count them.

That’s where we are.

Cottle: Nice. OK.

Bouie: There’s always more of them before you count them. Being able to have a clear view of what the landscape looks like I don’t think should, again, make you complacent, but should give you a better sense of what the actual possibilities are here, and how we can deal with those.

French: I hate to contradict one of my childhood heroes, Yoda, who famously said, “Do or do not. There is no try.” There is a try, and the try can be really dangerous and destructive, even when the try fails. Like Jan. 6, for example. That was a very damaging thing to Americans, the American body politic, even though it failed. And I’m with Jamelle. Can they do it? I’m skeptical. Will they try it? If the conditions are at all where there’s any shouting distance, any kind of possibility at all, I think they would try it. And then you’re in the realm of how destructive does the effort get? And that’s what I get worried about.

Cottle: We have been talking about polls and the radioactivity of Trump rubbing off on the Republican Party. It’s not like Americans are really happy with either party. There’s a lot of just general disgust and frustration. That said, as we wrap up this very weird midterm conversation, I want to go positive. Tell me something that you think each team has done well. I mean, obviously, operating within the circumstances that they’ve been given. So give me some high points for each team.

Bouie: I mean, I think Democrats have done an actually exceptional job at candidate recruitment this cycle. Talarico; Hamilton in Kansas; getting Sherrod Brown to jump back into it in Ohio. I mean, when you start looking at the people who are running in these races, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, you’re looking at a set of just strong candidates that match the states, match the circumstances and aren’t really making major mistakes, right? There aren’t a ton of missteps. And it’s a real contrast with, I think, how Republican candidate recruitment has gone, especially in the Senate races.

In fairness to Republicans, when the cycle began, there was no expectation that these races would be all that competitive. So sure, you can let a below-replacement-value person get the nomination because you’re like, “Yeah, well, we’re going to win anyway.” So there’s a certain sense of Republicans not quite understandably realizing where the puck was going. But I think Democrats basically recruited the strongest possible candidates they could, and that, as much as anything, is contributing to their good fortune here.

Cottle: And do you have anything from the red team that you want to say something positively?

Bouie: I mean, no. I can’t ——

Cottle: Fair. Fair.

Bouie: But seriously, seriously, seriously — just in terms of how the Republicans have been trying to, or have been approaching this election cycle, it is genuinely difficult for me to think about or think of a good choice. I mean, they have one very strong candidate on the table: That’s Ashley Hinson in Iowa. Great recruit. But beyond that, the big, strategic mistake Republicans made was to just completely defer to Trump for 18 months, and now they can’t separate themselves from him.

Cottle: They’ve made their bed.

Bouie: Yeah, they’ve made their bed, so.

Cottle: David?

French: So I would say, if you’re going to look at a red bright spot, it would be Michele Tafoya in Minnesota. That is much more competitive. That race is a lot more competitive than Democrats expected it would be. I think that the Democrats will still pull it out, but if you’re going to look across the country and see where a Republican did overperform expectations, I’m betting Minnesota is going to be at the top of that list. Again, I think the odds are against her. Minnesota’s a blue state. It’s been closer and closer blue, but it’s still a blue state. All the fundamentals are with the Democrats, but I think that this is one race to keep an eye on from the Republican perspective.

On the Democratic side, I think watching the Democrats more intentionally compete for the faith-based vote is one of their better decisions, quite frankly. And this is something I wrote about at some length, about the “God gap,” where in 2024 it wasn’t just white evangelicals who came out in large numbers for Trump; 18 of 22 Protestant denominations moved more red, including some of the more liberal and most liberal denominations in America.

So you had a faith-based problem. The Democratic Party had a real problem with faith-based voters. Now, Black Protestants still went overwhelmingly, obviously, for Kamala Harris, but you saw even movement in those numbers in a more red direction.

And so I think by getting candidates out there like Hamilton, like Talarico and others — and Raphael Warnock, in many ways, showed that way and blazed that trail in Georgia — to have very faith-forward candidates, no, you’re not going to peel off too many of the conservative white evangelicals. They’re too closely wedded to the Republican Party, but those are not all the people of faith in this country. And so diving in and fighting over that turf and over that ground, I think, has been very, very smart by Democrats. Necessary.

Cottle: Yeah, and I think, beyond the specifics of the individual candidates, what the Democrats are trying to do is shuck some of their aura of being extremist and anti-traditional and anti-everything along those lines. So I think that this helps. I do think that this helps with that on a bigger picture.

I take the point that Republicans have done some truly wretched things in the recruiting department, most of which can be tied to the MAGA brands like Paxton or the situation in Georgia, where Ossoff is up against a very weak Mike Collins. But I also think that where they’ve got their swing state moderates like Susan Collins in Maine, the party — and by that you have to say Trump in particular, has let them separate themselves. I mean, I guess that’s damning with faint praise, but, you know, it is what it is.

And as far as the Democrats, this time they seemed to have gotten serious about trying all kinds of different things to appeal to the particular electorates. So in addition to the great candidates within the party that they have put forward, they’ve also — say, in Nebraska, you guys know I went out there to talk to Dan Osborn, who’s an independent running against Pete Ricketts — the Democrats have fully thrown in behind him because the Democratic brand in Nebraska is a disaster, and they are looking at this as: It’s better to have a like-minded independent in the race than to just throw in behind somebody with a D just for the sake of it.

So that’s it. But before we go to recommendations, I’ve got to take a minute, and I want to let folks in the New York City area know that on Nov. 5, just two days after the midterms, the three of us will be together live and in person, taping “The Opinions” at the Central branch of the Brooklyn Public Library. We really would love to see our fellow political sickos come out while we chat with one another altogether for the rare, rare face-to-face confab. So see our show notes or check out the Brooklyn Library’s events pages for more info. You know you want to come out and see these guys in their hats live and in person. So I look forward to seeing everybody there.

And with that, it’s everybody’s favorite moment. It’s time for recommendations. David?

French: So I’m going with a little bit of lighter fare this time, Michelle. And this is not a new show. It’s been around for a few years, but my wife and I just discovered “The Gilded Age” on HBO, and it’s a historical period drama. And I say lighter because the stakes in any given episode are not necessarily huge, because it’s a story about social life in Gilded Age-era Manhattan. And so sometimes the stakes are things like, is one of the main characters going to get invited to a box at the opera house, signifying ——

Cottle: Very important.

French: Like, increasing social status. And you’re thinking: Why would anybody watch that? Well, it’s incredibly well acted. I’m a sucker for history, for anything that is set in real-world history and modeled, at least to some degree, on real-world history. And it’s just really well done. It’s not as dark and murdery as my typical fare that I’m watching. So every now and then you need a break from it, Michelle. Just every now and then.

Cottle: Are the costumes pretty? Because this is important to me.

French: Oh, everybody is dressed, like, this is the kind of thing ——

Cottle: That’s what I need to know. That’s what I’m here for.

French: Where people are going to dinner with their family in tuxedos. That’s the kind of thing.

Cottle: There you go. I’m sold. Jamelle?

Bouie: I have a recommendation that involves the same time period. I recently watched the 1975 Peter Weir film “Picnic at Hanging Rock,” which is this very important film in Australian cinema. It’s the film that made Peter Weir a big-name director, and it is about the mysterious disappearance of a group of girls at a picnic in 1900, at a place called Hanging Rock. The best way I can describe this movie is that it feels like you’re watching someone’s memory of a dream. It’s a very enigmatic film. With the mystery that doesn’t really resolve itself, but you’re there as much for the vibe as you are anything else. And I was really taken with it.

Cottle: Where can I watch this?

Bouie: I believe it’s on the Criterion Channel. Or you can just rent it from Apple TV or whatnot. It’s like an hour and 40 minutes. It’s not particularly long. But I found it kind of enchanting, and very strange, but enchanting.

French: Jamelle, one day you will recommend a movie that I have seen. And it is not this day.

Cottle: Hope springs eternal. All right, well, it’s October. We’re coming up close on Halloween, and as pod fans may know, I’m a fool for Halloween. My house turns into — it’s like Spirit Halloween threw up in my front yard. The neighbors wait on it. We have a party. That sort of thing. So I watch horror movies or horror series during the month, because that’s just how I roll, and I want to recommend something that I thought was going to be absolutely horrible but turned out to be wildly entertaining, and that is the Mike Flanagan mini-series just remaking “Carrie,” the original Stephen — I think that was Stephen King’s first novel.

Bouie: Stephen King, yeah.

Cottle: But it’s actually kind of fantastic. They play around a little bit with the supernatural element of it. I won’t get into details; I don’t want to spoil anything. It’s not a big commitment. It’s streaming. Mike Flanagan, for those who follow this sort of thing, he’s the guy who did “The Haunting of Hill House,” “The Fall of the House of Usher.” He does horror movies as well, but they tend to be smart, and they’re not slasher movies. So anyway, that’s my recommendation for the Halloween spooky season people out there. Check it out. And with that, we’re going to land this plane. Guys, it has been delightful, as always. I will see you on the other side of Election Day.

Bouie: Yeah. See you, and we’ll find out what happened to our country.

Cottle: Speaking of spooky. So spooky.

French: Looking forward to it.

ARTICLE

In Alaska, Some Early Voting Sites in Rural Villages Have Not Yet Opened
“There is no legal excuse” for the failure of 18 polling sites to open for early voting, a state lawmaker said.
By Anna Griffin and Emily Schwing
Published 2026-10-24 22:06 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/alaska-early-voting-sites.html

As the Trump administration launched a pre-emptive attack on election results in Alaska’s critical U.S. Senate race, some polling places in rural villages key to Democratic hopes have been slow to open, tribal leaders and voting-rights activists say.

What they don’t know is if the closed polling places are a result of a purposeful attempt to block thousands from voting or because voting has always been tricky to manage in the far-flung, rural villages of Alaska’s wilderness.

On Thursday, the U.S. Department of Justice sued the state of Alaska at the president’s request seeking to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses.

Their argument, which many legal observers have dismissed as unlikely to succeed, was that voters intending to cast ballots for the incumbent, Dan Sullivan, could mistakenly choose another candidate with the same name. They asked the federal court to preemptively agree to intervene should that happen. National Democrats and the League of Women Voters, among others, have asked to join the defense.

Now Democrats and people who organize rural Alaskans to vote are sounding a warning about polling places.

In a letter sent Friday to the state elections division and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, a Republican who oversees the office, a state lawmaker warned that at least 18 voting locations in rural Alaska listed on the election division’s website have not actually opened.

“There is no legal excuse for the failure to open these sites,” wrote Senator Bill Wielechowski, a Democrat who represents east Anchorage, adding: “To say the Division’s failures are shocking would be a profound understatement.”

Alaskans vote in person, though anyone in the state can vote early at a polling place or request an in-person absentee ballot. That’s how most rural villages vote.

This is far from the first time Alaska has struggled to get ballots to voters in its remote villages, many accessible only by plane or boat.

In 2024, mail delays prevented some rural polling places from opening for early voting on schedule. And in 2022, ballots from several villages arrived too late to be fully counted.

In his letter, Mr. Wielechowski also highlighted problems with Alaska’s primary election in August, citing “dozens of rural Alaska voters whose votes were not counted because it took too long for their ballots to reach election counting sites by mail.”

He said that for the November election, in at least 18 places, “local partners who were supposed to operate voting sites reported that they did not receive the necessary materials or even know the were expected to operate a voting site.”

“I think some of these systems that we’re being told are broken systems are actually working the way that these people have designed them to work,” said Mike Jones, tribal president for the Haida Organized Village of Kasaan. “They’re designed to be confusing and hold people up and frustrate people to the point where they don’t want to bother with it.”

Michelle Sparck, director of Get Out the Native Vote, didn’t spot any menace. “This is just the usual logistical failure.” she said.

Ms. Sparck said missing polling places represented “a systemic issue that we have every single election cycle” and blamed a gap in understanding — and interest — among state leaders about just how hard it can be to reach a more established polling location.

This year, voting access in Alaska is a national issue, because the state is a surprising battleground in two important races.

Former Democratic state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has led polls since the August primary in the four-person race for governor, and is seeking to become the first Democrat to lead the state since 1998.

The U.S. Senate race looms even larger in national conversations.

Senator Dan Sullivan finished second in the primary to Representative Mary Peltola and has trailed her in polls since then. The Alaska Senate race is considered critical to Democratic hopes of taking back the chamber. Republicans worry the presence of another Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, will confuse voters enough to hurt the incumbent under Alaska’s ranked-choice system.

Republicans outnumber Democrats in Alaska, 23 percent to 11 percent, though independents make up the bulk of the state electorate, and they’re largely clustered in the more urbanized Railbelt region around Anchorage.

Thus, Ms. Peltola and Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins have focused much of their campaign efforts on reaching the small but important pockets of potential Democratic voters in rural, usually Native-dominated villages.

The state elections division could not be reached for comment Saturday.

Ms. Sparck said she did not see a way for state leaders to solve the missing polling place problem in time for people in the affected areas to vote.

ARTICLE

A New 2028 Poll Finds Vance, Rubio and a Mishmash of Democrats in the Mix
The Democratic presidential primary race appears to be wide open, while JD Vance and Marco Rubio led among Republican voters, a New York Times/Siena survey found.
By Reid J. Epstein and Ruth Igielnik
Published 2026-10-24 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/democrats-republicans-presidential-primary-poll.html

Democrats still have significant disagreements about their party’s future direction, even as more of them want the party to move to the center than the left, according to a poll from The New York Times and Siena University. The party’s voters also had no consensus on who their 2028 presidential nominee should be.

Republicans, on the other, hand, want their party to follow President Trump’s lead in 2028 and say they prefer Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio to be their next presidential nominee.

The poll shows that while a meaningful slice of Republicans would like to change direction from Mr. Trump, the party remains much more united than Democrats. Still, Republicans face a generational divide, with far more older voters wanting to stick with the Trump path than their younger compatriots.

Both parties are days away from a midterm election that is likely to serve as an inflection point.

Democrats hope that a backlash to Mr. Trump’s policies will power them to victories deep in parts of the country where Republicans have long prevailed. Republicans, for whom Mr. Trump has been the dominant figure for a decade, are betting on his ability to turn out the party’s base. The president himself has urged Republican voters to pretend he is on the ballot.

Mr. Trump’s lasting grip on his party is clear in the poll: When asked an open-ended question about whom they wanted to be the next G.O.P. presidential nominee, 8 percent of Republicans named him, even though he is constitutionally ineligible.

Harris, Newsom or … no clue.

Democrats had no consensus in the poll about whom they would be most likely to vote for in a presidential primary race.

Those surveyed named more than 20 Democrats — including former President Barack Obama and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, who are both ineligible — as their top choice.

Nearly half of potential Democratic primary voters said they did not know whom they wanted to support for president.

The question asked respondents to volunteer their choice of candidate, rather than providing a list of names. With more than two years until the 2028 election, it can be difficult for people to come up with the names of potential contenders.

Still, the party faces a broader fight over its direction as the midterms conclude and the 2028 presidential race takes shape. About 48 percent of Democrats wanted to see the party move toward the political center, compared with 27 percent who thought it should go to the left. About 21 percent of Democrats said the party should stay where it is.

The chasm is wider among independent voters, whom both parties need to win national elections. Of those, 72 percent thought the Democratic Party should move to the center, compared with just 11 percent who wanted it to shift left.

Younger Democrats are more inclined to want the party to move left, while their elders want to see it move to the middle.

When Democrats were asked in the poll whom they would be most likely to vote for in the 2028 primary race, no candidate received more than 12 percent support.

Two of the best-known potential candidates, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, topped the list with 12 percent and 9 percent, respectively. They were followed by some of the party’s other prominent figures: former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (7 percent), Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York (6 percent) and Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia (4 percent).

No major Democratic candidate has announced a presidential campaign yet, though several potential contenders, including Mr. Newsom, Ms. Harris and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, have publicly deliberated about the possibility. Mr. Buttigieg has traveled the country stumping for Democratic candidates in the midterms. Mr. Ossoff, who is running for re-election, said during a debate last week that he would serve his full six-year Senate term if re-elected and declared that he had “zero interest in running for president.” (Mr. Obama said similar in 2006.)

Fifteen other Democrats were named by at least two poll respondents as preferred 2028 options. Some of these figures are highly unlikely or ineligible to run, including Mr. Obama; Michelle Obama; Mr. Mamdani (he is ineligible to be president because he was born overseas); Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is 85 and has said he does not expect to run again; and Hillary Clinton, the party’s presidential nominee in 2016.

Vance, Rubio or … Trump again.

Mr. Vance has widely been seen as the most likely heir to Mr. Trump’s political movement since they won the 2024 election together.

The Times/Siena poll indicates that potential Republican primary voters tend to feel that way, too: Thirty-three percent said they would most likely vote for Mr. Vance in a Republican primary, compared with 23 percent for Mr. Rubio, who has said he will defer to Mr. Vance.

A large majority of Republicans in the poll, 63 percent, said they wanted a continuation of Mr. Trump’s policies. Eight percent went so far as to say that he was their first choice for 2028, even though he cannot run because of term limits.

Eleven other Republicans were named by at least two poll respondents. They included Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida (3 percent), Donald Trump Jr. (1 percent) and Mitt Romney, the party’s 2012 nominee, who broke with Mr. Trump long ago.

The poll suggested that it would be challenging for a Romney-like figure who represents the pre-Trump Republican leadership to win the 2028 primary. Just 34 percent of Republicans said they wanted the party to move in a new direction, away from Mr. Trump.

Independent voters have a different view. More than 80 percent of them want Republicans to move away from Mr. Trump, an indication that the president has lost ground with the voters who often decide battleground elections.

SUMMARY

The Justice Department is sharply intensifying efforts to intervene in the midterm elections, goaded by a president unfettered by even the limited restraints of his first term. ARTICLE

In Second Term, Trump’s Justice Dept. Submits to His Election Demands
With moves in Alaska and California, the department has stepped up interventions in the midterm elections as the president’s instrument of unmediated executive power.
By Glenn Thrush, Katie Rogers and Zolan Kanno-Youngs
Published 2026-10-24 18:11 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/alaska-senate-election-trump-justice-department.html

The Justice Department is sharply intensifying efforts to intervene in the midterm elections, goaded by a president unfettered by even the limited restraints of his first term.

The next several weeks represent a critical moment for federal law enforcement, a test of whether a department repurposed by President Trump as an instrument of unmediated executive power will be effectively mobilized as a guarantor of his political power.

In recent weeks, the department has taken several new steps, including an extraordinary effort to invalidate any potential Democratic victory in the Alaska Senate race, that reflect Mr. Trump’s growing agitation as his party faces the possibility of losing control of Congress precipitated by his sagging popularity.

On Thursday, the department asked a federal court to block certification of the election if the incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, were to lose narrowly, claiming that the presence of another candidate with a nearly identical full name tainted the election. The move, the first of its kind in generations, came in response to the president’s rants about the issue, officials said.

Hours after the papers were filed, Mr. Trump abandoned any pretext that department officials had acted without his say-so, telling reporters, “I’m the one that said do it.”

Mr. Trump has grown increasingly agitated about the dueling Sullivans, among other election-related grievances. He has demanded the department take legal action, even as some department officials raised concerns about the merits and constitutionality of the case, according to two people with knowledge of the situation, speaking on the condition of anonymity to avoid retribution.

The episode comes amid the department’s widening push to exclude large batches of mail-in votes on suspicion that some had been cast by noncitizens, despite evidence that such voting is exceedingly rare. At the same time, Attorney General Todd Blanche has abandoned departmental norms by promoting prosecutions and investigations of politicians, within 60 days of the election.

Late Friday, the department escalated the fight, sending letters to local election officials across California demanding that they help identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls and set aside their ballots. The letters came with a threat. Those who failed to comply would “risk significant federal scrutiny.”

All of this has administration critics, and even some in the department, asking: Just how far are Justice Department leaders willing to go?

“The department is taking commands from the president and throwing spaghetti at the wall to file meritless lawsuits,” said Vanita Gupta, the No. 3 official at the department under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. “The ultimate goal is undermining faith in the election, intimidating voters and discrediting results the administration doesn’t like.”

It is by no means certain that any of these legal actions will ultimately succeed. But election officials from both parties have expressed concerns that it represents a dangerous effort to discredit functional election systems administered by the states.

Democrats on the Senate Intelligence Committee have grown increasingly worried that Mr. Trump may claim foreign interference in the election as a reason to seize voting machines, citing Mr. Trump’s dubious claims in a speech over the summer.

Over the past year, the department’s civil rights division, under an outspoken Trump ally, Harmeet Dhillon, has undertaken a series of actions intended to demonstrate they would aggressively pursue his agenda. This included an unsuccessful legal effort to obtain sensitive state voter data and dispatching 1,000 federal monitors to oversee elections, all the while sowing broader doubts about election integrity.

This has apparently not been enough for Mr. Trump, who has become increasingly impatient. He was especially fired up after a meeting in the Oval Office this month with election deniers, including Tina Peters, a former Colorado election official who was imprisoned for her role in a security breach of election systems before obtaining a pardon, two people with knowledge of the meeting said.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that Mr. Trump “has done more than any other president to ensure our country has free and fair elections” and that “the Trump administration has been clear that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable.”

Responsibility for executing this agenda has fallen to Mr. Blanche, who espoused a maximalist vision of executive power as Mr. Trump’s lead defense lawyer. He has charted a course of calibrated ambiguity when asked about the election, issuing words of reassurance even while plowing ahead with the new lawsuits.

Mr. Blanche has maintained that he will be guided by evidence, citing federal statutes that prohibit illegal voting by immigrants and others that require retention of records by state and local election officials.

He defended the department’s actions in a statement to The New York Times, saying the suit relied “solely on federal law” and was not intended to benefit any candidate or party.

“The Department of Justice does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election,” he wrote. “This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or misled.”

Shortly before one of his deputies filed the Alaska suit, Mr. Blanche cast the department’s recent lawsuits as a good-government effort and dismissed the likelihood of a department effort to block certification of the results in any given state as a “doomsday scenario.”

Yet Mr. Blanche’s presence atop the department is itself significant. While he has pushed back on some White House directives, he is operating at the pleasure of a president who will not tolerate the institutional guardrails that existed in his first term, and personally steered the department’s legal campaign to punish his perceived enemies.

And he has made it clear that he believes Mr. Trump has the right to dictate department actions against the advice of officials, including himself, provided the president is not violating laws or the Constitution. In a recent interview, he claimed there was a “misperception that there’s this separation and independence between the Department of Justice and the White House,” and said he worked for Mr. Trump.

Many of Mr. Blanche’s predecessors pushed back harder. An antagonist of the first term, in Mr. Trump’s view, was former Attorney General William P. Barr, who refused to deploy the vast powers of federal law enforcement to pursue fabricated claims about a rigged election after the 2020 race.

Mr. Barr quit in December 2020 after publicly dismissing the baseless claims of election fraud that have animated the department in Mr. Trump’s second term.

“There’s a growing tendency to use the criminal justice system as sort of a default fix-all, and people don’t like something they want the Department of Justice to come in and investigate,” he said at the time, referring to the president and his allies.

The president has never forgiven him. At an event at the White House in late 2025, he stunned a gathering of federal prosecutors in a vulgarity-laced tirade against Mr. Barr, according to two attendees, speaking on the condition of anonymity to disclose details of a meeting intended to remain private.

Mr. Trump’s cardinal rule in staffing up his second-term Justice Department, according to current and former officials: no more Bill Barrs.

The White House has found two particularly cooperative partners in Mr. Blanche’s top two deputies, Trent McCotter and Stanley Woodward Jr. Mr. McCotter who has worked in the past with Stephen Miller, the president’s top domestic policy aide, the official pushing the department to crack down on alleged voting by unauthorized immigrants, those people said.

Both are in frequent contact with top West Wing officials, as many of their predecessors have been, often through the White House Counsel’s Office.

Mr. Woodward’s name was affixed to the lawsuit in Alaska federal court seeking to block certification of the coming Senate election in the state. At times, Mr. Woodward’s name on a legal filing indicates that subordinates were unwilling to do so themselves, former officials said.

Legal experts are dubious about the prospects of the Alaska suit succeeding. One described it as “one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen.”

The only known effort by the Justice Department to preemptively block certification came nearly six decades ago, in a very different time and place. In 1968, the department sought to block an election by the Barbour County Democratic Executive Committee in Alabama because white members changed the rules to exclude Black candidates who had been denied their voting rights in the Jim Crow South.

Earlier this month, Mr. McCotter — who helped draft the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund proposal so toxic it imperiled Mr. Blanche’s nomination as attorney general — was the signatory on a suit seeking to block the counting of 20,000 mail-in ballots in California. It claimed, without providing detailed evidence, that many were not U.S. citizens.

One name conspicuously absent from both suits: Ms. Dhillon, whose staff would typically be responsible for overseeing election integrity cases. It was not clear why Ms. Dhillon was not listed on the lawsuit.

Ms. Dhillon, appearing in an interview on “60 Minutes” in the past week, downplayed the possibility that the department would interfere with the election.

“I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states,” she said.

She went on to dismiss the proposal of deploying agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement at polling places, even though Mr. Trump told a reporter this month that he had not yet made up his mind.

“Is the administration planning to send ICE agents out to the polling places?” asked the correspondent Lesley Stahl.

“There is no plan to do that,” Ms. Dhillon replied.

Her response was noted in the White House, which had enlisted Ms. Dhillon to appear on the show in the first place.

Mr. Trump watched the interview and was upset that Ms. Dhillon underplayed the threat posed by illegal voting and let other administration officials know about it, according to two people with knowledge of the situation.

SUMMARY

Democrats have a hefty advantage in national polls. Control of the Senate hinges on victories in red states that favored Mr. Trump by significant margins in 2024, including some that Democrats have not won in decades. Then, Republicans — and some Democrats — scoffed when Mr. Schumer publicly discussed recruiting a Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi.

ARTICLE

Why Democrats Could Find It Hard to Win the Senate Despite Their Strong Polls
Democrats are increasingly optimistic about the midterms. But they are being outspent by Republicans. And they are trying to compete in states that favored President Trump by large margins.
By Lisa Lerer
Published 2026-10-24 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/democrats-expectations-blue-wave.html

Democrats have a hefty advantage in national polls. President Trump is playing defense, campaigning through deep-red corners of the country that he won by overwhelming margins just two years ago. And assumptions that Democrats will win control of Congress have become conventional wisdom in many quarters, from longtime political observers to social media to the oddsmakers in prediction markets.

But as Democratic dreams of midterm victories grow bigger, some strategists quietly worry that expanding expectations are crowding out signs of a more challenging political reality.

Control of the Senate hinges on victories in red states that favored Mr. Trump by significant margins in 2024, including some that Democrats have not won in decades. Republicans are outspending them by eye-popping amounts in key races. And after its performance in 2024, the Democratic Party as a brand still remains unpopular among voters.

All of that has left some in both parties wondering: Could the much-discussed blue wave end up looking more like a splash?

“The election can be summed up in the following sentence: Can huge amounts of Republican money defeat huge Democratic advantages in issues, candidates and political climate,” said Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader from New York.

Strategists in both parties believe it is increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold on to their House majority. But among Democratic donors, activists and voters, hopes of winning control of both chambers have grown so high that some fear any other result could feel like falling short.

“I am concerned that we have an overheating of expectations,” said Molly Murphy, a pollster who worked on the 2024 campaigns of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and former Vice President Kamala Harris. “People often assume in a wave you win everything, and what happens in a modern wave is you win far more than normal.”

The kind of broad wins that once defined wave elections are largely a thing of the past, Ms. Murphy said, destroyed by gerrymandering that has left relatively few House seats truly competitive.

In 2018, the most recent midterm election considered a landslide election, Democrats won 41 House seats and control of the chamber. But Republicans gained two Senate seats and expanded their majority.

This year, there’s near-universal agreement among politicians, strategists and activists that Republicans face steeper political headwinds than Democrats. Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit a new low this week, views of the economy are dismal and Democrats lead by 11 points on the generic ballot — a measure often used to gauge a party’s strength.

The sharp deterioration of the national political environment for Republicans has transformed the electoral map, forcing their candidates on the defensive in surprising places. This week, Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, began airing $1.2 million in television ads in Mississippi — a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1982.

That’s a striking reversal of expectations from two years ago, when Democrats began plotting a midterm strategy and winning control of the Senate seemed nearly impossible. Then, Republicans — and some Democrats — scoffed when Mr. Schumer publicly discussed recruiting a Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi.

The question is whether the Democrats’ momentum is strong enough to lift their candidates in deep red states to victory. To win control of the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats, and keep all of their own.

Of the 10 Senate battleground contests, four feature Republican incumbents: Senators Dan Sullivan of Alaska, Jon Husted of Ohio, Susan Collins of Maine and Roger Marshall of Kansas. And five are happening in states that Mr. Trump won by 11 points or more in 2024.

“Structurally, the Senate is built to be Republican, and the question is whether this wave can breach that levee,” said Liam Donovan, a Republican strategist. “It is incredibly hard.”

Polling, early-voting turnout and the results of recent special elections suggest that Democrats are far more enthusiastic than Republicans this election cycle.

But those measures, particularly early-vote returns, can be misleading. Turnout can flip on Election Day, particularly if Republicans successfully leverage their campaign war chest and Mr. Trump’s tour through Republican strongholds to drive their supporters to the polls.

“Trump is probably going to do some good in these red-leaning states when he comes in,” said David Kochel, a veteran Republican political strategist from Iowa, where Mr. Trump held a campaign rally on Thursday. “There’s still a lot more Republicans in Iowa and Kansas than there are Democrats.”

In Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday night, Mr. Trump offered plenty of MAGA red meat, attacking Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, and urging Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, not to take down an ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent that has drawn bipartisan backlash. And, Mr. Trump told the crowd, he had the “right” to run for a third term.

“I’m asking you to pretend I’m running,” he said, repeating a frequent refrain. “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Can the polls be trusted?

This year, as in several recent election cycles, Democrats harbor considerable anxiety about the accuracy of polling. Some strategists worry that pollsters are oversampling Democrats, particularly in red states, who may be more likely to respond to questions about the election.

A historical assessment of congressional polls conducted by The Economist this week found that the more partisan a state, the more the polls have underestimated the strength of the dominant party.

If that trend held true this year, it would temper Democratic expectations in states like Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

And even if the polls favoring Democrats turn out to be accurate, many individual Senate races are quite close, in some cases within the margin of error.

“There will be two explanations if the wave is just a ripple,” said Howard Wolfson, a veteran Democratic strategist. “One is there is a massive polling error. The second is that the Democrats didn’t have enough money to put enough races into play and make the races that were in play sufficiently competitive.”

G.O.P. financial advantage

Republicans currently have an advantage of about $650 million in general-election advertising, according to a review of past and future ad reservations across federal and state races by AdImpact, a media-tracking firm.

Their edge is most pronounced in the Senate: In the seven races that the Cook Political Report rated as tossups, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by more than $320 million, according to a separate tally by AdImpact.

The lack of Democratic funds limits the party’s ability to mount aggressive campaigns in the kind of districts that would fuel a wave, said Mr. Wolfson, a political adviser for Michael R. Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York City, who spent about $80 million bolstering Democrats this fall.

So far, the polls haven’t shown significant shifts since more money started pumping into races.

But the spending is being felt not only in the barrage of campaign ads, said Jason Roe, a Republican strategist based in Michigan, but also in efforts to push Republican voters to the polls. Republicans have embraced a version of the strategy that helped them capture the White House in 2024, focusing on driving loyal Republican voters who typically skip midterm elections to the polls.

And just as in 2024, they have gotten plenty of outside help, including from Elon Musk, who has quietly funneled more than $276 million into building a huge turnout operation to help Republicans.

The impact of that work might not be clear until Election Day.

“I have never seen more money spent on the ground in my life — it is obscene,” Mr. Roe said. “If you are a Republican voter, you are going to get harassed to no end to turn out.”

He added: “The question is: How many of those people are so unhappy with Trump or Republicans that they don’t vote for us when they get there?”

Unpopular with voters

Some Democrats also worry that their party’s still-battered brand could hurt their support in November. Even as Democratic candidates gain support, polling shows lingering disapproval of their party overall.

Just 28 percent of voters said they are satisfied with the Democratic Party, in the recent New York Times/Siena poll, eight points lower than satisfaction with the Republican Party and the share of voters who approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance.

Republicans have tried to capitalize on that skepticism by casting Democratic candidates as far-left radicals who want to turn the country into “a socialist hellscape.”

Matt Bennett, a vice president at Third Way, a centrist think tank that presses for a more moderate Democratic approach, worries that some of the party’s more progressive candidates, including Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, are underperforming Democrats competing in traditional red states.

Is there a scenario in which Democrats win in red states but squeak by in blue ones? Mr. Bennett doesn’t rule it out. Midterms, he said, can produce strange results.

“Every single one of the Senate races is on a knife’s edge,” Mr. Bennett said. “The results could be super weird.”

ARTICLE

A New Level of Threat and Fear Risks Pushing the U.S. and Iran Back to Full War
With new intelligence and the possibility of all sides seeking pretexts for action, the war in Iran is entering a dangerous phase ahead of elections in the United States and Israel.
By David E. Sanger, Julian E. Barnes, Jonathan Swan, Maggie Haberman, Farnaz Fassihi and Eric Schmitt
Published 2026-10-25 00:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/trump-netanyahu-iran-new-phase-of-war.html

Inside the Trump administration, officials are expressing fears that Iran is in the “advanced stages” of planning attacks against U.S. officials.

More than 6,000 miles away, the Iranians appear convinced that Israel and the United States are preparing to unleash their third major attack in 16 months, a final push to force Iran to surrender to U.S. demands.

The conflict in the Middle East has entered a new phase in which a maelstrom of factors, from the political calendars in the United States and Israel to the potential for all sides to be seeking pretexts for action, are creating heightened levels of tension and risk.

This is how countries can escalate into full-scale war, several diplomats and outside experts noted. If the U.S. intelligence disclosed this week is right that Iran has credible plans to attack Americans at home and abroad, one senior European official said — “and it probably is,” the official added — one gunshot that appears aimed at a U.S. official could touch off a conflagration. So could a stray explosion near a bunker sheltering Iranian leaders, who already survived their predecessors’ deaths in a decapitation strike in the opening hours of the war on Feb. 28. The fact that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and President Trump are facing critical elections that could dramatically affect the balance of power in their countries feeds into the complex set of calculations that all sides are making. Even if he is defeated on Tuesday, Mr. Netanyahu could decide to launch one last strike that he may believe his successor would hesitate to execute. Similarly, Mr. Trump, who knows how unpopular the war is even among his strongest supporters, may want to show that at least when it comes to his powers as commander in chief, his authority is undiminished.

And, as in other moments of global peril — the Cuban Missile Crisis and the decision to invade in Iraq, as examples — partial or faulty intelligence, or just a failure to understand the adversary’s true motives, can carry deadly consequences. Iraq poses another cautionary tale, when selective intelligence can be used as an actual pretext for military action.

U.S. officials say they are focused on elements of the most recent intelligence suggesting that the Iranians may seek to kill U.S. ambassadors in the Middle East and American officials on U.S. soil — a longtime ambition of Iran’s elite Unit 840, which has carried out kidnappings and assassinations around the globe. But history suggests Iran’s desires often outstrip its capabilities. It has at times hired hapless hit men who have been arrested before they could do harm.

Still, those incidents are a reminder that U.S. and Iranian fears are rooted in bitter experience. And while Mr. Trump has said he would not attack before the midterm elections in 10 days, he has also hinted that all bets are off after that. Senior U.S. officials say that in private, Mr. Trump appears to be leaning toward another round of major strikes inside Iran. Plans developed by Central Command detail an expanded list of bombing targets, including energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy, according to an official with direct knowledge of the planning.

Echoing Mr. Trump’s bombast, a senior official in Iran took to social media in recent days to say the country was preparing to take on its adversaries with surprise attacks, with “zero red lines.”

A Rising Threat

U.S. officials and European allies said the intelligence about potential attacks had been rising in recent weeks, since a suspected Iranian plot against a military base in Britain used by the U.S. military.

The intelligence reviewed by senior officials included Iranian plotting of how to respond to an attack by either the United States or Israel with an assassination campaign, as well as other attacks Iran could carry out in retaliation for earlier U.S. attacks, officials said.

The intelligence about the plots remains highly classified, so it is hard to judge. Only the most senior U.S. lawmakers — members of the so-called Gang of 8 — had been briefed before the warning in a memo from Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, became public on Friday. Some officials have been puzzled by why Trump administration officials released the memo, given that they knew they could not back it up by discussing evidence of specific plots.

The gap between what Mr. Trump and most of his advisers say about the war publicly and the intelligence they are receiving is wide, and neither the White House team nor Pentagon leadership has given a briefing on the conflict in months. The president prefers to keep information closely held, but that has merely heightened the risks.

But the essence of the intelligence findings is that several Iranian plots have moved from the aspiration stage toward execution. And a Western official compared the U.S. reaction with the response to the warnings of the Iranian threats to attack American personnel and bombers at R.A.F. Fairford, a base in southern England, earlier this month. A dozen B-1 Air Force bombers were withdrawn, and Iranian officials said that if they returned, it would be taken as a sign of imminent attack.

Mr. Trump said nothing to reporters on Saturday about the intelligence, but did say he would decide soon whether to take renewed military action. He has been briefed regularly on the new intelligence, which some officials say is being taken more seriously than any warnings since the war began.

There is some evidence the Iranians have operatives inside the United States who are “not just simply Iranian nationals,” one official said. But even if Iranians are plotting attacks from the United States, it is not clear they can.

They note that Iranian officials, in their communications with colleagues, often exaggerate their ability to carry out covert overseas attacks.

Still, Iran almost always finds criminals and hit men to hire for assassination plots, particularly in Europe and the United States. The danger of any specific attack plan, U.S. officials cautioned, depends on the competence of the criminal hired to carry out an assassination, U.S. and Western officials said.

Haunting Memories From 2024

This is not the first time Washington has gone through this exercise.

The mix of real threats from Iran against Mr. Trump and some of his top advisers, along with other potential assassination attempt scenarios, created a climate of fear and paranoia for the president’s team throughout the 2024 campaign. Those threats had grown in intensity throughout Mr. Trump’s four years out of office, and were animated in part by Mr. Trump’s decision in January 2020 to order a strike on the head of Iran’s elite Quds force, Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani.

The Biden administration tracked an increase in threats, and the F.B.I. arrested a Pakistani nationalist on July 12, 2024, charging him with a murder-for-hire plot directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps against Mr. Trump.

Separately, President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s senior advisers had tracked what was described as a credible threat against Mr. Trump from Iran, and sent countersnipers to his outdoor rally in Butler, Pa., on July 13 that year. One of those snipers shot an attempted assassin, Thomas Matthew Crooks, who officials said was acting on his own and had no connection to a foreign plot.

But the back-to-back incidents — along with a hacking of campaign officials’ emails that was said to have been led by Iran — generated constant fear inside the Trump campaign.

Other perceived threats and anxieties were comical. A small item was discovered in the campaign headquarters in South Florida, prompting a 9-1-1 call and fears it was a listening device. It turned out to be a device that could be purchased online, a prank carried out by someone on the campaign.

The Trump team has continued to sift through threats, including against senior White House officials. They pay close attention to the names of officials mentioned by Iranians in intercepted chatter.

In Iran, Telegraphing the Reaction

Iranian officials believe their most inspired moves after the Feb. 28 attack included striking U.S. bases across the Middle East and closing the Strait of Hormuz, which caught U.S. officials off guard. They have made no secret about their intentions to expand the scope of the war if a third round of fighting breaks out. In public remarks, senior officials have threatened to target civilian infrastructure, energy sites and underwater fiber optic cables that carry internet and other communications traffic.

Two Iranian officials, one of them a member of the Revolutionary Guards, said in interviews on Saturday that the expansion of targets also included U.S. diplomats and personnel. The officials, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly, confirmed State Department reports about Iran’s plot to target Americans.

The officials defended the plan and noted that Israel and the United States had killed dozens of Iranian officials and some family members. In their view, they said, that made targeting Americans “fair game.” It is not clear whether they have the reach, however.

Iran’s success rate has measurably deteriorated compared with the 1980s, in the earlier years of the revolution, when it carried out a string of assassinations of Iranian political dissidents.

Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the lead negotiator and speaker of parliament, said on social media that Iran views the coming part of the war as existential.

“We are in a surprise phase of the war, and we will not fight a classic war,” Mr. Mohammadi said. “It will be an asymmetrical, fierce and conclusive war that will target the enemy’s strong points and weak spots.”
