ARTICLE

How the Most Ruthless Ad of the Midterms Divided Republicans
The fallout from Vivek Ramaswamy’s brutal spot targeting his Democratic rival in the Ohio governor’s race showed that even in the Trump era, a political attack can be seen as going too far.
By Reid J. Epstein and Campbell Robertson
Published 2026-10-24 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/vivek-ramaswamy-ad-ohio-amy-acton.html

The most explosive advertisement of the midterm elections has split Republicans and again posed the question of what is fair game for campaign attacks in American politics.

In the days since the leak of the ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, many fellow G.O.P. politicians have denounced, disavowed or distanced themselves from the spot. Yet President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, a remarkably ruthless one even by the standards of modern political campaigns.

The ad features the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Ms. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, when she was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her.

The outrage over the ad’s dark backstory has left Mr. Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur who exemplifies the anything-goes, attack-at-all-costs ethos of Trump-era politics, at the center of a self-created political firestorm.

The Republican disagreements over the ad show that major figures in the party can still become divided over the rules and red lines of political warfare in the Trump era. And they set the stage for high drama on Election Day in Ohio, a state that has trended solidly Republican in recent years but now has outsize importance in the midterms. The overarching political question is: Will a potential backlash to Mr. Ramaswamy hurt other Ohio Republicans in competitive races, especially Senator Jon Husted, who is trying to fend off a well-known Democratic rival in a vital race for Senate control?

There is now a degree of unpredictability in the state. Campaigns in both parties do not know how voters will react.

Mr. Ramaswamy, who along with his aides declined to be interviewed for this article, said at a campaign stop on Friday that he had no regrets. The ad, he suggested, was his attempt to change the rules of engagement for Republicans in Ohio — just as Mr. Trump has done in Washington.

“What we need is a governor at the top just like President Trump is for our country — a governor for this state who stands strong, who says we will not play on your terms,” he told a crowd in Strongsville, a Cleveland suburb. “We will stand for what we know is right and true, and we will not apologize for it.”

A Shocking Ad Emerges Online

There had been rumblings for weeks in Ohio political circles that Mr. Ramaswamy’s top aides were in touch with Dr. Acton’s estranged mother.

Dr. Acton’s troubled childhood was no secret, and had been the subject of reporting during her high-profile stretch as the pandemic-era health director for Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican.

Mr. Ramaswamy had been trailing Dr. Acton in many public and private polls. Like other Republicans, he was confronting voter frustration with high gas prices, tariffs and Mr. Trump’s leadership.

Producing the ad was a politically hazardous move for Mr. Ramaswamy, a 41-year-old start-up founder who has shown a high tolerance for risk since he emerged on the scene during his 2024 campaign for president. During that race, he presented himself as a full Trump acolyte and made plenty of enemies with his brash style before placing fourth in the Iowa caucuses, dropping out and endorsing Mr. Trump.

The Ramaswamy campaign was still testing the ad to gauge its effectiveness when the spot burst into public view late Monday.

D.J. Byrnes, a left-leaning local journalist known as the Rooster, published the ad online, calling it “loathsome.”

The spot, which took little time to spread widely online, showed Dr. Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, using harsh language to denounce her estranged daughter.

“Don’t let her become your governor,” Ms. Arthur said.

‘Just Plain Wrong’

The backlash was immediate and intense.

As the controversy swirled, Mr. Ramaswamy reached out privately to other Ohio Republicans to gauge their reaction, according to three people briefed on the exchanges. He felt the coverage by the news media was unfair and wanted a chance to explain his thinking, even if it did not lead to public support for running the ad.

Governor DeWine called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong,” and he urged Mr. Ramaswamy — whom he has endorsed — to take it down. Mr. Husted, who faces his own tight election against former Senator Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3, said he would not have run the ad. Republicans in close races in other states, like Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, who is running for Senate, said it should come off the air.

Not only has Mr. Ramaswamy so far declined to back away from the ad, but his campaign also bought more than $4 million in Ohio airtime to show it to viewers.

Supporters of Mr. Ramaswamy echoed his contention that he has been treated unfairly by the news media and argued that there had been no public anger when Dr. Acton’s campaign had attacked him.

“Democrats and the media are trying to change the subject from ‘she’s a liar’ to ‘she was abused as a child,’” Beth Lear, an Ohio state representative from just north of Columbus, wrote in an opinion essay published Friday in The Columbus Dispatch. “It’s a masterful attempt to manipulate voters’ emotions by making Amy a victim.”

The ad served as an attempt to shift the focus of the campaign in its final days from frustrations about Mr. Trump’s economy to a referendum on Dr. Acton’s honesty. But in so doing, it placed Mr. Ramaswamy’s own morals and ethics in the spotlight, and reminded voters that Dr. Acton survived a seriously troubled childhood.

Mr. Ramaswamy has, in a sense, run a political psychology experiment on his home state. Will voters in Ohio be outraged that he has tried to secure a political advantage through a woman estranged from her daughter over allegations of rape, or will they better recall the accusation that Dr. Acton is lying?

“We ran an ad about lying,” Mr. Ramaswamy told the crowd in Strongsville. “Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me.”

But at a pumpkin festival on Friday night in Circleville, Ohio, Mr. Ramaswamy’s running mate, State Senator Rob McColley, said the campaign did not believe Dr. Acton was lying about her childhood abuse.

“Oh no, that is horrible,” Mr. McColley said. “We are accusing her of lying in her adult career.”

Anger From the Acton Campaign

Dr. Acton’s campaign has almost run out of words to express its disgust over the ad. A spokeswoman, Addie Bullock, has called it “despicable,” “disturbing” and “disqualifying.”

“Ramaswamy will do anything, including embrace child sex predators, to get what he wants,” Ms. Bullock said.

Court documents from Mahoning County, Ohio, back up the descriptions by Dr. Acton and her brother of the events of her childhood. In 1978, when Dr. Acton was 12, her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with raping her.

He pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury, after which Ms. Arthur lost custody of Dr. Acton and her brother. A month later, court records show, Mr. Arthur fled the area, and a warrant was issued for his arrest. The Arthurs appear to have lived the ensuing decades in Pennsylvania, and according to Dr. Acton’s brother, they stayed together until Mr. Arthur died in 2004.

In the campaign ad, Ms. Arthur accuses her daughter of lying about her past but does not address the rape allegations.

It is not clear where Ms. Arthur lives now, and she did not respond to messages this week.

She had been living in her car with some cats in the Calvary Church parking lot, just outside Boalsburg, Pa., according to the Rev. Stacy Sublett, the church’s pastor. Mr. Sublett said that he had tried to find Ms. Arthur permanent housing in the area but that she declined the assistance.

He said he was not aware of friends or family who came to see her.

‘He’s Not the Same Baby’: Family of Child Found Alive in Morgue Recalls Ordeal
Vincent Fiordilino was 18 months old when he was found to be alive after having been declared dead at an Arizona hospital in February.
By Rebecca Chao
Published 2026-10-24 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/toddler-alive-morgue-parents-lawsuit-arizona.html

The mother of a toddler who was pronounced dead at an Arizona hospital in February, then found to be alive hours later in a morgue, is speaking out about her family’s ordeal and raising questions about the care her son received that night.

The mother, Alexus Fiordilino, said in an interview this week that she, her husband and her mother-in-law were at the hospital saying their final goodbyes to her son, Vincent, who was 18 months old at the time, when they thought that maybe “he was trying to breathe.” He had been found unresponsive in a backyard swimming pool hours earlier.

“As I was hugging him,” she said, “air came out of him.”

When they told a police officer and a member of the hospital’s medical staff that Vincent appeared to be exhaling, they were told that it was “agonal breathing,” or “the final death breath,” Ms. Fiordilino said.

“That’s what they confirmed with us over and over,” she added, referring to the medical staff at Dignity Health Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert, Ariz., a suburb southeast of Phoenix.

Eight months later, Vincent is unable to walk, talk, sit up or swallow, and is fed through a G.I. tube, Ms. Fiordilino said.

The family’s lawyer, John B. Brewer, said he planned to file a lawsuit as soon as next week. He contends that if Vincent had continued to receive care over the roughly four hours that he was in the morgue, the effects on his health could have been significantly different.

The Gilbert Police Department forwarded the case to the Arizona attorney general’s office for review. A spokesman for the attorney general’s office, Richie Taylor, said in an email that it had not yet decided whether to pursue the case.

In July, the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office announced that Ms. Fiordilino and her husband, Angelo, would not face charges. The office said the family “had multiple childproof locks and safety measures in place, and multiple adults were present in the home, all of whom believed someone was watching the child.”

Scott Holden, a lawyer for the doctor in charge of Vincent’s care, Aryan Toosi, and Abby Kay, a spokeswoman for Dignity Health, said in emails that they could not discuss patient care because of patient privacy laws — and, in Dr. Toosi’s case, because of “pending litigation,” Mr. Holden said.

“Dr. Toosi’s thoughts are with the young patient and family, and he wishes the child continued healing and recovery,” Mr. Holden said. “His commitment to delivering high-quality care has always been rooted in a desire to provide healing, safety and comfort to his community.”

In the early evening of Feb. 8, Vincent wandered out of his parents’ sight during a Super Bowl gathering at the family home in Gilbert and was found floating face down and unresponsive in the family’s backyard pool, according to police reports. It is unknown exactly how long Vincent had been in the water, but the reports note that family members said he might have been in the pool for 10 to 15 minutes before being found.

The Fiordilinos took turns performing CPR until the police and emergency medical workers arrived around 5:40 p.m., according to the police reports. After they failed to revive Vincent, he was taken to the emergency department at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where medical workers attempted lifesaving measures.

After several minutes, Dr. Toosi left the area where Vincent was being treated, according to the reports.

Around that time, a nurse said, “I have a pulse.” A police officer who was present went to inform Dr. Toosi, who was talking to Vincent’s parents. Dr. Toosi replied, “Please do your thing and let me do my thing; I went to medical school for a reason,” the reports said.

Dr. Toosi then walked to the room where members of his staff were still performing lifesaving measures and listed aloud the treatments the child had received, noting that Vincent had blood gas levels showing “a pH balance incompatible with life,” according to the reports, which paraphrased Dr. Toosi. The doctor then conducted a final pulse check.

“As long as there are no objections, I’d like to call the time of death,” Dr. Toosi said, according to the reports.

No one spoke up, the reports said, and at 6:20 p.m. Dr. Toosi called the time of death and asked for a moment of silence.

Several minutes later, an officer who was present heard what sounded like “gasping” and asked a nurse about it. The nurse said it was agonal breathing, according to the reports.

Vincent was moved to the morgue between 7:18 p.m. and 7:23 p.m., the reports said. At around 11:30 p.m., an employee of the medical examiner’s office in Maricopa County arrived to retrieve the boy’s body and observed that he was still alive. Vincent was then airlifted to Phoenix Children’s Hospital.

The family believes that the hours in the morgue in which Vincent was left without care contributed to the child’s current health outcomes, according to Mr. Brewer.

Ms. Fiordilino and her lawyer said in the interview that Vincent, now 2, would require lifelong care.

“He can understand his name, but that’s kind of it,” Ms. Fiordilino said. “He’s not the same baby.”

Before the accident, Vincent was “very rambunctious,” Ms. Fiordilino said. “He loved to climb on everything,” she added.

“He used to say ‘hi’ all over the place,” she said. “And he had actually just learned ‘bye’ right before this. So I heard him say ‘bye’ one time.”

Mark Walker contributed reporting and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

SUMMARY

People who graduated from the University of California in the 1960s didn’t pay a dime for tuition. The University of California, Berkeley, posted an all-in price — tuition, room, board, fees and other expenses that make up the full cost of attendance — of $54,674 this year for new in-state students living in a campus residence hall. Presumably students will not take umbrage with new campus housing that will come online in the next two years.

ARTICLE

Public Colleges Are Passing the $50,000-a-Year Mark. For Locals.
At the University of California campuses in Berkeley, Irvine and Santa Barbara, students get an unwitting education in navigating the housing market.
By Ron Lieber and Alex Welsh For The New York Times
Published 2026-10-25 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/business/california-colleges-costs.html

People who graduated from the University of California in the 1960s didn’t pay a dime for tuition. If they have offered to pay for their grandchildren to attend now, they may be in for a shock.

The University of California, Berkeley, posted an all-in price — tuition, room, board, fees and other expenses that make up the full cost of attendance — of $54,674 this year for new in-state students living in a campus residence hall.

The Santa Barbara campus lists a $50,946 price. The cost of attendance has crossed the $50,000 barrier in Irvine, too, where undergraduates are guaranteed only two years of on-campus housing. The all-in price for a student living off campus there is $50,130.

The $50,000-per-year figure is likely to act as a kind of psychological tripwire for families who thought that state schools were supposed to be a bargain.

It does come with asterisks. Plenty of people get financial aid and pay much less. These estimated list prices include health insurance, which many students do not need to buy.

And the price reflects the fact that California is an expensive place to do most anything. According to the College Board, the average list price for tuition and fees at an American four-year public university was $11,950 during the 2025-26 school year. At the California schools in question, that figure was many thousands higher.

Still, there is one big reason that many families there will indeed pay $200,000 over four years, while out-of-state students will shell out over $300,000.

Student housing — even in university-owned residences — can cost more than tuition and related fees.

This, like so many laments about what things cost in America, is a housing story. Public schools that provide a residential undergraduate education are also selling undergraduates an education in what it means to afford a residence.

Rents at the Break Point

How much housing should a university provide, and does a state school have a special responsibility to provide cut-rate beds to everyone who wants one?

If you’re a parent shopping for college, you might assume that the answers are “a lot” and “yes.” But if you’re considering Santa Barbara, you would also be wrong, at least some of the time.

The first thing you should know about the University of California’s campus there is that its Blum Center on Poverty, Inequality and Democracy saw fit to publish an 85-page “people’s guide” to the university’s “housing crisis” in 2024.

The second is that the university recently announced that it would guarantee the availability of on-campus housing for incoming undergraduates. But that promise lasts for just two years, up from one before, and it’s possible only because of some long-planned (and delayed) construction of new campus residences.

Plenty of schools don’t guarantee four years of housing. Decades ago, landlords and developers near the Santa Barbara campus rented out single-family homes and built apartments faster than the university could or wanted to on its own land.

But the housing supply both on campus and off did not keep up as the university grew, and the area’s geography is one big reason. The school is hemmed in by an airport and bodies of water, including the Pacific Ocean.

The only real neighborhood within walking distance is an unincorporated area called Isla Vista. When you visit the school’s admissions office, you can pick up a map that calls I.V. “U.C.S.B.’s college town.” It’s roughly 50 square blocks of often dated houses and low-slung apartment buildings, where landlords are effectively in charge.

Rents at the Breakpointe & Coronado, for example, start at a budget-breaking $1,336.65 per month price point, per person (per bed, technically), for a shared room in a small two-bedroom apartment. Interested parties can already join the fall 2027 wait list.

Over at the Penthouse, a climb up the cobwebbed exterior stairway leads to a top-floor landing overlooking electrical wires and a few palm trees. A sign out front directs people to an error-strewn website promising that the company “will begin leasing all 330 of it’s apartments, townhouses and duplex’s on a first come, first served basis in early January.”

If you’re a student, get in line. Seriously.

Isla Vista landlords know that campus housing won’t be available for everyone. By firing the starting gun on the race for off-campus housing for the 2027-28 academic year now, they can profit from the uncertainty.

“After October, you start hearing, ‘Have you found housing for next year?’” said Nicole Meng, the student team leader at the university’s Blum Center. “All of my friends were like: ‘What do we do? We’re 18. We don’t really have any resources. I’m first generation, low income — how am I going to come up with deposits? And I need to find roommates.’”

She did, and she does. Her rent is $2,988, split three ways among roommates who share a 450-square-foot one-bedroom apartment.

It isn’t shopping, either. “This is to find a spot,” said Jasmine Hsieh, external vice president for statewide affairs for the Associated Students of U.C. Santa Barbara. “You’re not selecting. You’re just hoping to be able to continue to go to school.”

Undercutting the Landlords

When universities spend decades ceding their undergraduate housing market to nearby landlords while the student population grows, they lose a certain measure of control. Eventually, it becomes a crisis, the school’s cost of attendance approaches $50,000 and they need to try to regain it.

There are several ways that University of California schools build dorms, according to Kyle Gibson, the director of strategic communications for U.C. Berkeley’s administration division.

You can hope for a big donation, seek grants from the state or borrow money and perhaps team up with a private developer. Then, you build in such a way that student rents will cover the costs.

After decades of debate, Berkeley is building a new dorm in a small park it has owned for decades. In the wake of protests over potential development there, it surrounded the site with unclimbable shipping containers, in lieu of normal fencing, and topped them with barbed wire for good measure.

In 1970, Isla Vista protesters set fire to the Bank of America branch there, in part because of high rents. Presumably students will not take umbrage with new campus housing that will come online in the next two years.

There will be deals. Willie Brown, the Santa Barbara associate vice chancellor for housing, dining and auxiliary enterprises, said rates would be far below rents in Isla Vista. “For us, this works well, because Isla Vista is so overpriced,” he said.

Meanwhile in Berkeley, off-campus rents on older properties have actually fallen in recent years. Does Mr. Gibson take pride in whatever role his new housing has played in creating competition? “I do,” he said.

Stable housing is fundamental to people feeling good and, for students, performing well, said Gaye Theresa Johnson, the Blum Center’s director and a professor of Black studies.

“When you want to propose a solution, whose feet do you hold to the fire?” she said. “The one steady to me is the university.”

Hers isn’t the only school that could use a little foot warming.

Flagship state schools in Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia have all posted prices over $40,000 for in-state students for at least some undergraduate programs.

This is where college shoppers can make schools uncomfortable. Ask questions of expensive public universities, preferably in large rooms in front of other visitors.

“I hear this is a tough real estate market. Why not build more housing and guarantee four years of availability?”

“Does the lack of a guarantee put lower-income students at a disadvantage?”

“Just how hard and expensive will it be to find housing off campus?"

“Does your on-campus housing lottery coincide with lease-signing season off campus, or will I need to go all in on one or the other?”

This is a service to other visitors listening in. Ms. Meng said she and her friends had arrived on campus in Santa Barbara unaware of the intensity of the housing derby that awaited them.

The best students in any state ought to be able to afford the best state schools without fearing insolvency or homelessness. If they decide to go elsewhere, hopefully they’ll tell the schools (and their state legislators) why.

And then, at last, just maybe, the ones that are losing good students will build more, cheaper and faster.

SUMMARY

Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Most people are obligated at some point in their careers to work directly adjacent to an unpleasant person. Two weeks ago, we published a letter from a woman seeking advice about returning to office work, in her 50s, after two decades of working for herself.

ARTICLE

My Co-Worker Is Losing It Over My Religion
Plus: Reader responses to a woman returning to the office after two decades of self-employment.
By Max Read
Published 2026-10-25 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/business/religion-harassment-work.html

Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend, I’m a practicing Buddhist working at a university, with a desk next to a difficult co-worker. One recent afternoon, while a colleague and a student were talking about a campus event, she loudly wondered whether they’d be “serving Kool-Aid.” The next morning, I found a piece of paper with “the cult” on it taped to her otherwise bare desk, hanging toward my work space. With H.R.’s blessing, I calmly asked her what the sign meant. She told me to keep her name out of my mouth, mocked my “Karen voice,” and insisted that “the cult is a band!” Since then, she has mimicked my typing, drummed on her desk whenever I stop typing, and moved the sign so it now faces only me. I reported everything in writing to H.R., which responded that because this co-worker has a pending lawsuit against the university, they can’t take action against her right now, since it could look like retaliation. Their solution was for me to move my desk, but there is no other space. I don’t want to sue my employer. I just want to come to work without being mocked for my faith. I’m exhausted from managing this on my own while the person causing it faces no consequences. What can I do when H.R.’s hands seem tied? And how do I keep working next to someone who clearly wants me to feel unwelcome? Anonymous

Most people are obligated at some point in their careers to work directly adjacent to an unpleasant person. This is frustrating, because “my neighbor sucks as a person” is generally not enough reason to change desks or offices, at least as far as management is usually concerned.

Your bad neighbor, however, has crossed the line into harassment, and done you the favor of giving you leverage. If you’ve made your employers aware that you’re subject to workplace harassment based on your religious practice — as you have — and they’ve done nothing about it — as they have not — you have grounds for a Title VII complaint.

Your H.R. representatives should know this, and if they don’t, your university probably has an equal-opportunity or equity office that can remind their colleagues of their duties. And if it comes to it, I suspect there are a lot of employment lawyers who would be eager to explain to a deep-pocketed university the nuances of Title VII and its obligations to its employees.

The point is that your H.R. reps’ hands are not tied here. The decision to move you rather than to address the harassment directly is a decision based on legal considerations only insofar as they have determined you are much less likely to sue the university than your co-worker’s lawyer is to file a new motion in her lawsuit. That they reached that decision and still didn’t move you suggests to me that they really, really don’t think you’re going to do anything about it.

I respect that you don’t want to sue your employer. But I don’t think you need to. You just need to make the administration think you might for them to start taking your concerns seriously. Start with a formal letter to your boss, with H.R. CC’ed, including your documentation of the harassment and asking how the university is going to meet its obligations to you.

It doesn’t need to be a threatening letter — but don’t be afraid of escalating to the equal-opportunity or equity office, or of consulting an employment lawyer who might help you draft the kind of letter they’d take seriously. I bet you’d find that all kinds of new office desks will open up to you, ideally with neighbors less interested in English post-punk bands of the 1980s.

Two weeks ago, we published a letter from a woman seeking advice about returning to office work, in her 50s, after two decades of working for herself. We asked Work Friend readers what they would suggest as advice. Across the hundreds of responses, a few clear themes stood out:

Learn to love, or live with, new tech …

By far the most consistent thread among all responses was that workplace tech is entirely unrecognizable, and you’ll need to get up to speed. It’s not just the software you use for your job, but the whole infrastructure of W2 work: “Expect to enroll in benefits, review policies, and sign contracts through payroll and H.R. platforms,” Polly Bangs writes from Portland, Ore. Ron Katz, who returned to office work in his early 60s, advises: “Make friends with the IT and support teams, not just your colleagues. They will save you more quickly than a co-worker who resents or is wary of the new person on the team.”

… especially Slack, Zoom, and GIFs.

New communications software comes with both a learning curve and a new set of expectations. “Don’t expect voice-mail messages to be responded to in a timely manner, if at all,” one writer cautions. Instead, get used to chaotic video conferences. “Remember that guy who went viral in 2017 because his toddler intruded on a BBC interview? That’s how we all work now,” explains another. For style points, “work on your GIF game,” C.A. writes. “People now communicate in GIFs over Slack or Teams.”

Adjust to a new, more casual and more flexible culture …

After technology shock, the second most-mentioned development in the workplace was the rise of more casual dress codes: “It is totally normal to wear tennis shoes on a client call, and I haven’t worn high heels since before Covid,” one reader wrote. The end of suits and ties is accompanied by a broader cultural shift, which one commenter summed up by saying, “Overall, the employment relationship has become less hierarchical and more collaborative.” What sometimes seems like laziness on the part of younger colleagues is often just different habits. Another person writes that his younger colleagues’ flexible hours “doesn’t mean they’re lazy or work less — in my experience, quite the opposite is often true.”

… and be thoughtful in how you communicate.

I’m wording this topline summary carefully, because the advice around this tended to fall into two broad camps: People who believe that young workers today are humorless scolds (“Never make a joke at work” was a common refrain), and people who believe that they’ve struck a blow for better workplaces. (“As a Gen Xer, I give all credit to much-maligned millennials for making the workplace significantly more respectful,” one correspondent writes. On behalf of millennials: Thank you.) Either way, our commenters agreed that caution and thoughtfulness is warranted. “Absolutely everything you say or do at, or even not at, work can be recorded and saved for posterity,” one person wrote.

Be curious and outgoing …

Many people wrote that workplaces are less social than they used to be, and older workers will have to make the first move in establishing relationships. “Moderating my expectations for work friends (haha) was necessary to mitigate my disappointment,” one of our correspondents admitted. But younger workers often appreciate your input, and your curiosity: “If you’re working with a lot of millennials, I’d say lean in. Ask questions, be curious, and share your experience too,” another writer suggests.

… but set boundaries for yourself.

All that new communications tech means it’s harder to leave the workplace. “It’s harder to justify taking a day off when you’re sick because most people can just work from home now,” one person writes. “There’s no such thing as snow days anymore.” For this reason, another commenter advises, “establish early on that you will not be answering work-related calls or emails when off duty.”

Be prepared for a long hiring process …

Many, many readers responded not so much with “workplace advice” as with “job-seeking advice.” “Ageism is very real,” one commenter writes. “Applying for an open position with no connections has very low odds of success.” One 53-year-old woman said she “stopped putting the dates for when I earned my bachelor’s and master’s degrees on my resume and got more responses.”

… and the difficult transition of having a boss again …

Others suggested that the biggest difficulty might be learning how to have a boss again after two decades of working for yourself: “Adjusting to someone else’s processes and priorities may be your biggest challenge,” Melanie Taplett writes. Though there are also some good things: “Relish in not having to do everything yourself,” Ron Katz suggests.

… in fact, maybe don’t do it at all?

A small minority of readers even advised our advice-seeker to avoid returning at all: “‘What advice would you give to someone returning to the office from self-employment?’ Don’t.”

But if you do, there are helpful supplemental materials.

A career counselor in Gainesville had a very specific piece of advice: “Your assignment for today is to rent ‘The Intern’ with Robert De Niro as a traditional worker returning to an office full of young people.”

SUMMARY

And in Brooklyn, a couple, at 32, confronted a generational conundrum: stay in their hometown as their parents age? In interviews, two people in their early 30s separately described feeling “like a teenager” compared with their parents at this stage. But her parents planted roots in New York with government assistance, bought an apartment and built a fulfilling life.

ARTICLE

Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This Is 30.
They’re trying to build middle-class lives in New York. But many 30-year-olds in the city feel worse off than their parents. Is it average adult angst? Or something more enduring?
By Troy Closson
Published 2026-10-25 07:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/nyregion/30-year-old-angst.html

A young woman in Queens celebrated her 30th birthday with cake, champagne — and an existential crisis over still living paycheck to paycheck.

A 30-year-old in Manhattan felt ready to consider marriage, but knew he couldn’t afford a wedding.

And in Brooklyn, a couple, at 32, confronted a generational conundrum: stay in their hometown as their parents age? Or move away to start a family?

Forget the kids.

The 30-somethings are not all right.

“Everyone I know around my age is feeling the weight of the burdens of this economy and what it takes to live a nice, comfortable middle-class life,” said Dan Iammatteo, 31, a marketing director in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood of Brooklyn.

And their angst is intensifying. People in their early 30s constitute the largest age cohort in the United States, and their frustrations have emerged as a potent force reshaping cities and their politics and demographics.

In New York, this age group turbocharged the ascent of the Democratic Socialists of America, propelling to office Zohran Mamdani, who turned 35 this month, and a slate of progressive allies to congressional primary wins.

With the midterm elections little more than a week away, these voters across the nation — their rage fueled by rent and gas prices that are devouring their paychecks — could prove pivotal in some major contests.

“This is a very real feeling across the U.S.,” said Jason Dorsey, a generational researcher who lives in Austin, Texas. “Thirty-somethings really feel like they have missed out and have been left behind.”

Nearly two dozen people in their early 30s said in interviews that the image of adult life that they had been promised turned out to be a sham.

Many work full time and earn enough to cover the cost of basic groceries (even if it means trips to three stores). But their salaries are losing ground to inflation, and their health care costs are skyrocketing. They’re cutting back on salon visits, social activities and fresh fruit runs — and they feel priced out of adulthood.

On Thursday, the long-running Harvard Youth Poll found for the first time in its history that more young Americans expect to fall behind, rather than surpass, their parents economically.

Adam Crittenden, 30, who lives in Chelsea and does data work, thought about a future wedding (elopement sounds cheap!), children (costlier for an L.G.B.T.Q. couple) or a two-bedroom apartment (median asking rent in Manhattan is $6,000).

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take,” Mr. Crittenden said. “But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach.”

‘A Lot of Hurt’

There was a time when the early 30s were described as a turning point.

“Never trust anybody over 30” was a rallying cry of the ’60s; the lead character of “13 Going on 30” awoke to a thriving career and posh apartment; a pop star even used “30” as a meditation on marriage and motherhood.

But so much about the lives of Americans has changed during the last three decades. In 1990, a wedding at 26, a baby shower (or two) by 28 or a first home around 30 was ordinary.

“It’s so crazy,” said Cat Van Holt, 31, a housing attorney in Manhattan who earns about $84,000 a year and lives in a rent-stabilized studio apartment. Many of her clients face eviction; she knows she isn’t poor. But compared with those mythical adults three decades ago, “our two realities are just leagues apart.”

Most Americans across all age groups agree: Financial milestones are harder to meet for today’s young adults than they were for their parents’ generation, according to a survey by the Pew Research Center this summer.

The share of Americans who say raising children is unaffordable jumped 20 percentage points during the last decade. And while people in their 30s today are more highly educated than earlier generations, they are more than twice as likely to remain saddled with steep student loan payments.

In interviews, two people in their early 30s separately described feeling “like a teenager” compared with their parents at this stage.

One woman in Manhattan struggled to fathom how her mother was married with two children by 35 and owned the New England home where she still lives. At the same age, she is single, and the rent on her 275-square-foot studio apartment doubled during the last decade while her take-home pay barely budged.

“You work hard and then you do better than your parents. And then your kids do better than you. And on and on,” said Maria Doulis, a New York State deputy comptroller who has researched this age group. At least, that’s how the story went.

“It almost feels like the slipping away of the American dream,” she said.

Many young professionals in their 30s have reached a breaking point in recent years and moved away in droves to raise families — contributing to an enrollment crisis in New York City’s school system.

Fiona Kearns, 31, who was born and raised in Queens, and her husband are public schoolteachers who consider themselves well paid. She is among the fortunate with no student debt. “Even with all that luck and privilege, I can’t get a two-bedroom apartment,” she said.

The couple planned to upgrade for more space last winter and try for a baby in the summer. But the search for an affordable place proved hopeless.

“I feel a lot of hurt about it as I feel myself aging — and a lot of resentment over being so careful to make responsible choices,” she said. “Am I entitled to have what my parents had? I’m not sure.”

She paused.

“But it’s hard to know that I can’t.”

Promises Dashed

Ali Sousa sometimes feels a gnawing guilt.

Ms. Sousa, 31, who lives in Central Brooklyn, needed to lean on her family to cover the $4,800 out-of-pocket cost of a recent chronic back pain treatment. She barely has savings and sometimes eats French fries for dinner.

“It can really feel like a personal failing,” said Ms. Sousa, who earns about $52,000 a year working in theater administration.

She regularly opens Instagram to a sea of stories from friends, desperate for any extra work to make their monthly bills. “I don’t know how we even begin to fix this,” she said.

In interviews, many people in their 30s felt that they were promised that graduating college, climbing the career ladder and forgoing DoorDash or Uber would put them on the path to whatever a “comfortable life” means these days.

In Manhattan, a 33-year-old nonprofit lawyer was somewhat embarrassed to admit that his parents are purchasing him a home. But it’s the only way that anyone he knows has managed to buy.

A college-educated couple, both 32, in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid reprisal from their employers, were among the many who acknowledged that these pressures have made them reconsider becoming parents.

The husband recently learned that, adjusted for inflation, he earns only about $5,000 more than he made in 2020. The wife’s monthly student loan payment jumped $600 overnight after Congress rewrote the rules for certain loans.

She pointed out that she was born to Soviet refugees who arrived in 1989 and had to learn English. But her parents planted roots in New York with government assistance, bought an apartment and built a fulfilling life.

She worries that starting a family now in Bay Ridge would push them into poverty — and refuses to bring a child into such a world. The two summed up their sense of dismay: We did all the things you’re supposed to do. And it’s not getting us nearly as far.

Still, some researchers saw reasons to feel bullish — or, at least, something other than abject despair over this extended timeline of adulthood.

“We sometimes forget the benefits,” said Jeffrey Jensen Arnett, a senior research scholar at Clark University who has written about emerging adulthood.

Kandice Hill, a 33-year-old working in sales operations, moved in March from North Carolina to a South Brooklyn house. She has 10 roommates.

To her family, it’s a curious arrangement. To her, it’s a relief. Back in Charlotte, she felt the pressure of societal expectations as a single woman; parishioners in her Bible study meetings sometimes prayed that they would find a partner.

In New York, her lifestyle comes with much less shame. At her employer’s Bring Your Child to Work Day, she noticed many parents of young children were in their 40s.

“No one’s like, ‘That’s nuts,’” she said. “They don’t even bat an eye.”

ai-bubble-financial-crisis-lehman.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 27  Words: 2008/2089
================================================================================

SUMMARY

As the money pours in, the companies involved are resurrecting bad old habits eerily reminiscent of the shenanigans deployed in the run-up to the financial crisis. With more U.S. funds in A.I.-heavy stocks than in homes, a crash could destroy more wealth than the 2008 financial crisis did. As bad as the financial crisis was, it began with a small slice of mortgages of a still-diversified economy.

ARTICLE

This Boom Looks a Lot Like the Housing Bubble
There are signs the A.I. boom is going bust. If it does, the consequences could rival the 2008 financial crisis.
By Jen Harris
Published 2026-10-25 13:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/opinion/ai-bubble-financial-crisis-lehman.html

Artificial intelligence is fast becoming the largest investment in U.S. history. As the money pours in, the companies involved are resurrecting bad old habits eerily reminiscent of the shenanigans deployed in the run-up to the financial crisis.

There are already signs that much of this investment may go bad. If it does, the consequences could rival what happened in 2008.

We know far too little about the financial plumbing propping up this surge. What little we do know looks remarkably like the tactics once employed by Wall Street firms like Lehman Brothers, the storied 158-year-old bank that collapsed in 2008, setting off a panic that ultimately cost taxpayers nearly $700 billion in bailouts in today’s dollars and nearly nine million Americans their jobs. Now as then, companies are hiding large amounts of debt off public balance sheets. Firms responsible for protecting our pensions and our insurance are again risking our money by snapping up complicated financial products backstopped by assets of uncertain value. A small group of companies are buying and selling large amounts of a hot product to one another, inflating demand for the product and obscuring the risks of the system in a web of complexity. The accountants and credit-rating firms that analyze the situation — and that are financially beholden to the debtors — are deploying shaky excuses to declare it all fine.

There are a few differences. With more U.S. funds in A.I.-heavy stocks than in homes, a crash could destroy more wealth than the 2008 financial crisis did. And the Trump administration, reportedly eager to prevent a bust, is making changes that inject new opacity and more risk into the situation.

There are already signs the nascent A.I. industry may not soon generate the trillions of dollars required to pay off all the huge debts it is incurring. Earlier this month, The Financial Times reported that the projected annual revenue at A.I. lab OpenAI was about $50 billion at the end of September, 28 percent lower than had previously been believed. Figures reported by The Wall Street Journal this month suggested that revenue growth at Anthropic, OpenAI’s chief rival, was softening. Markets are getting nervous, with the tech-laden Nasdaq falling over 5 percent over the last two weeks.

Anthropic and OpenAI are already so entangled in our economy (and in our national security) that if they sink, Washington will need a plan. Done right, any rescue would come with real safety guardrails, real insurance that we won’t cede control of the technology to China and real service to the public interest.

Lehman Brothers was born in 1850 as a cotton brokerage in antebellum Alabama. The A.I. chipmaker Nvidia was born in 1993 in a booth at a Denny’s in San Jose, Calif., and Meta in a Harvard dorm in 2004. And yet the financial circumstances surrounding those companies share an uncanny resemblance.

Start with hidden loans. A Wall Street Journal analysis in August concluded that the nine largest tech firms, Nvidia and Meta included, have managed to accrue $3 trillion of debt, or roughly 10 percent of the entire U.S. economy, off their balance sheets. Keeping the debt off the books (and away from the figures investors and regulators watch most closely) makes it easier for those companies to spend enormous sums constructing the data centers that drive A.I. — centers they believe will both improve the technology and satisfy an expected takeoff in demand.

Back in 2008, Lehman, too, accumulated lots of debt, primarily from buying subprime mortgages; those loans, which were targeted to home buyers with thin or imperfect credit histories, were the hot product of its day. The firm similarly avoided scrutiny by shuffling the debts off its balance sheet. When those mortgages went bad, so did Lehman, and its sudden demise nearly took much of the banking system with it.

Within days of its failure, Washington committed hundreds of billions of dollars to stabilize the financial system, and the Federal Reserve backstopped trillions more. Still, the rescue wasn’t enough to stave off the worst recession since the Great Depression. Millions of jobs and trillions in household wealth evaporated.

Now you might ask: Didn’t Congress pass legislation to prevent another crisis from occurring? Yes, but that law, known as Dodd-Frank, applied largely to lenders, which means banks and bank-holding companies. It left private creditors, back then a relatively small slice of the finance world, virtually untouched. In 2018, Congress, worried about the potential impact on small businesses, loosened rules to allow many private creditors to stretch their balance sheets. It ignored objections that money, like water, would always flow to the least regulated corners of finance.

Enter Silicon Valley. A.I.’s biggest players seized on the loosely regulated private credit industry to help finance their data center spree.

Another throwback to the bad old days of 2008: the way the A.I. firms and their main suppliers are buying and selling the technology and its infrastructure to each other, lending large sums to one another to fund the deals. Nvidia disclosed commitments and guarantees of over $530 billion to its own customers in July — more than triple the amount it was lending just three months earlier. Analysis by the asset manager Sona found at least 176 circular financing deals in the A.I. ecosystem that were worth $3.6 trillion over the past three and a half years.

Back in the housing bubble, major Wall Street firms came up with numerous complex ways to borrow from their rivals, with proceeds going to purchase even more subprime mortgages. The result made demand for those loans look greater than it actually was, and it built a financing web so tangled that it became difficult to parse any one firm’s exposure. As Lehman’s collapse later showed, such confusion meant that a problem anywhere can soon become a problem everywhere.

Then how about the fact that accounting firms, those given the job of calling out any warning signs, appear asleep at the wheel once again? Ernst & Young, which signed off on Lehman’s questionable accounting tactics before its collapse, is now being accused of offering more tautology than real comfort in its latest approval of Meta’s unusual accounting moves to fund its very expensive A.I. push. Everything is all fine, essentially, because Meta said it is.

Those are the similarities. Now for the differences.

This presidential administration, reportedly worried that any A.I. slowdown will beget a broader economic one (which, in turn, could worsen its political standing), is propping up the boom. Its measures likely goose the available money in the short term but will worsen the pain of any correction. President Trump wants to allow Americans to invest their retirement savings in private credit funds, ensuring they will lose directly if these data center deals go bad. The Securities and Exchange Commission has made it easier for data center owners and their lenders to slice and repackage this debt, which is exactly what banks did to subprime mortgage debts in the housing bubble. The S.E.C. is also proposing rules that allow newly public companies to disclose even less than they already do.

Another difference: This time, taxpayers are more clearly on the hook, because private creditors are more directly attaching A.I. debt to the financial products we need. Take annuities, which are often relied on by retirees. Because many Americans rely on such insurance products, their policies are usually guaranteed by the state should an insurer go bankrupt. Right now, private creditors like Apollo are funding the debt boom in part by tapping the money sitting in companies like Athene, the $470 billion insurer Apollo controls. Should the A.I. boom go bad and Athene go under, Apollo knows the state (i.e. taxpayers) will be on the hook for much of what it owes policyholders. (Athene’s opaque disclosures make it hard to know how much of its assets are in data centers.)

Private-capital-backed firms now own nearly 20 percent of the entire U.S. life insurance industry, with assets of nearly $1.5 trillion.

As bad as the financial crisis was, it began with a small slice of mortgages of a still-diversified economy. This time, the sector at risk is our economy’s growth engine. A.I.-related investment fueled an estimated one-third of the country’s recent economic growth, and the handful of companies most exposed to the A.I. build-out now comprise roughly one-third of the entire S&P 500.

In other words, the U.S. economy is fully hostage to an A.I. build-out laden with increasingly worrying financial engineering, all riding on a wager — that demand for A.I. will keep growing, that customers will soon be willing to pay what the technology actually costs to produce and that firms will manage to build the infrastructure required to supply it. Recent estimates indicate that A.I. would need to generate as much as $3 trillion annually in perpetuity to return the capital extended. That’s 9 percent of the U.S. gross domestic product, or twice what Americans spend on food.

Already, a closer look at the fundamentals of OpenAI and Anthropic, the most critical players in this bet, are perhaps even worse than the headlines suggest. Right now OpenAI expects to lose $280 billion by 2030 even assuming revenues grow tenfold over the same period. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have already slashed prices 40 percent to 50 percent from early summer, perhaps because China’s Deep Seek, the leading “open weight” A.I. model, reportedly nearly matches their latest models’ performances at about 1.4 percent of the cost. Far less expensive open weight models have roughly doubled their share of token volume this year, according to OpenRouter, a service that tracks A.I. usage across all major providers. Prices and market share are shrinking; costs are not.

Such worries may explain why tech stocks have been taking a beating, and bond markets — normally where investors go for shelter amid financial turbulence — are volatile. Many of those private creditors — a sector that has grown sharply amid the A.I. boom, to between $2 trillion and $3 trillion — are showing classic signs of financial distress.

A final difference from 2008: The government deficit has reached historic highs. The reality is our government has little money to rescue all the major players should this boom go bust. Yet national security demands will never allow the United States to cede the technology to China. So if the A.I. bet starts to falter, a range of voices including that of Palantir’s chief executive, Alex Karp, as well as those of privacy advocates have suggested that the government take over frontier or cutting-edge A.I. The technology would join America’s other big-ticket national security expenses, such as aircraft carriers and warheads, which for the most part, are critical to our military and security arsenal but lack commercial viability.

The government could separate the technology into its two constituent parts: Innovation would move to a national lab with safety protocols like the ones that govern nuclear weapons; a computing arm would run on a meter and operate similarly to a utility. A careful reorganization would help lessen the chaos of a crisis, thus softening any recession, and prevent our most formidable adversary from taking over the industry. Obviously, such a plan would raise plenty of hard design questions. But the basic aim is simple: Our most powerful A.I. models, which are perhaps proving too expensive for any private firm to build, could then answer to democratically elected leaders and be pointed more clearly to public good than to quarterly profits.

The necessary authorizing legislation could ensure the independence of this new national lab from undue political interference and also detail civil liberties and privacy protections fit for an A.I. era in a way we never got around to with the internet revolution a quarter-century ago. And as long as we’re at it, perhaps Congress and our regulators can reassess the choices that landed us where we are now.

There’s an old chestnut in finance circles that crises take longer, and then happen faster, than you think. With so many echoes of 2008, shame on us if this one catches anyone by surprise.

Jennifer M. Harris directs the Economy and Society Initiative at the William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. She was an economic official in the Biden White House.

Humanity is entering its most dangerous era yet.

According to the columnist Thomas L. Friedman, humanity has set off a second Big Bang — and we are not ready for it. In this video, he explains why the rise of artificial intelligence and other “godlike” powers will require us to build healthy interdependencies to survive what comes next.

Thomas L. Friedman: Any journalist who has been working for almost half a century is sure that he or she was here for the big one. World War I, World War II, Vietnam. The rise of the internet. The fall of the Berlin Wall. The opening to China.

Clip of Raj from “The Big Bang Theory”: What?

Here’s why we need to pay attention to this second Big Bang: We have made ourselves godlike as a species in seven different ways.

We’ve created an artificial brain greater than the creator endowed us with. We have disconnected intelligence from human biology — that is a godlike act. We’ve created a planetary nervous system where we’ve connected virtually everybody on the planet, and we can now hear one another whisper. We’re not quite as omniscient as the creator, but we’re getting there.

Third, we’ve changed the climate. We are the first species to actually drive itself into a basically man-made climate era.

Clip of Greta Thunberg: It’s just the beginning of a rapidly escalating existential crisis.

No species has ever done that before. That is a godlike act. Fourth, we’ve created our own new galaxy. It’s called cyberspace, where we’re all connected and no one’s in charge. Fifth, we split the atom.

Archival clip: The uranium atom was split, releasing its catastrophic force.

We can now destroy the planet just as much as God did in the age of Noah, with a flood. That is godlike.

Six: We’ve created deep learning, where we can now apprehend mysteries of the universe that previously were only the purview of the creator.

And lastly, coming to a theater near you, we don’t know exactly when — five years, 10 years, maybe 15 years. But we’ll get there: Quantum computing, fusion energy and A.I.

The conversion of those three things will allow us to create anything from the molecular level up. That will be our Genesis moment. Just one problem: We now have the power to part the Red Sea, but without the Ten Commandments. Without the rules, norms and institutions to govern our now godlike powers.

Clip of Yoshua Bengio: I have a vision of advanced A.I. in the future, governed safely.

We’re about to experience the greatest phase change in human history, and we are not ready.

Clip of Jensen Huang: And this is the part that people don’t see: A.I. is literally everywhere.

You’re going to love it. It’s going to be optimizing 24/7, adjusting all these kinds of things in your body and feeding all the data back. It’s going to be wonderful.” “But Doc, Doc, wait a minute — feeding the data back? Where does the data go?” “Oh, that will be back at shanghai.hipreplacement.china or whatever.”

Am I going to put that hip replacement in? Are you going to put that hip replacement in? What happens when A.I. is in everything? Your Chinese-made car. Your Chinese-made watch. Your Chinese-made toaster. Your Chinese-made glasses.

Clip of Donald Trump: During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning superintelligence.

Producer off-camera: Oct. 7.

Now, you could say, “Hey, Friedman, we’ve been able to get by episodically for a long time now, only collaborating part of the time — and not at the kind of depth I’m talking about.” But A.I. is different. This can — we cannot kick it down the road. So we have become fused by fate. Moses ain’t coming down with the two tablets.

Clip of Moses in “The Ten Commandments”: There is no freedom without the law.

We are going to have to develop those norms, those ethics, those standards, and globalize them. Because we now live in a world where more people can do unto you farther, faster, deeper, cheaper than ever before. And you can do unto others farther, faster, deeper, cheaper than ever before. And now add A.I. agents and robots to the mix.

We are going to rise together by building healthy interdependencies. Or we’re going to fall together. But baby, whatever we’re doing, we’re doing it together.

We can learn that early; we can learn that late. We can learn that before the massive global crisis or we can learn it after. But learn it, we will.

SUMMARY

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, posted an ad featuring a malicious attack on Amy Acton, Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent. After Mike DeWine, the Republican governor of Ohio, denounced the Ramaswamy ad (though he did not withdraw his support for Ramaswamy), President Trump took to Truth Social, condemned DeWine as a “RINO,” and said: “The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it’s so good! Trump supporters delight in Trump’s cruelty, of course, but they also engage in their own vile speech and actions as a virtual initiation rite into the MAGA movement — it’s the way that they demonstrate that they have the courage necessary to take on the left.

ARTICLE

Despicable Doesn’t Begin to Cover It
Trump’s culture of cruelty spreads.
By David French
Published 2026-10-25 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/opinion/midterm-ads-ramaswamy-acton-ohio.html

I’ve never seen a viler ad.

By now, you almost certainly know the story. Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, posted an ad featuring a malicious attack on Amy Acton, Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent. The ad starred Acton’s own mother, a woman named Donna Arthur.

The family story here is evil. Arthur married a man named Cledith Arthur, who became Acton’s stepfather. Cledith Arthur was indicted when Acton was 12 for raping her. He fled the jurisdiction rather than face charges.

Donna lost custody of her children and — as Charles Hilu at National Review reported — she has her own criminal history. She was convicted of theft by deception in the 1990s and accused of animal neglect in 2021.

It’s hard to imagine a more cruel and evil act than raping a child. There is no betrayal greater than the betrayal of a child by a parent. And then Ramaswamy compounded that betrayal by wielding that evil mother as a weapon against her own daughter.

I’m reminded of Sir Thomas More’s famous line in Robert Bolt’s play “A Man for All Seasons”: “Why, Richard, it profits a man nothing to give his soul for the whole world. But for Wales!”

But for Ohio, Vivek?

Long ago we learned that there is no bottom for MAGA, and there is still no bottom to this scandal. If Ramaswamy had a molecule of decency, he would take the ad down and apologize. Instead, he attacked Acton. “It is an ad from our campaign,” he said. “I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans. Unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues. She won’t debate me. She doesn’t allow cameras at her events.”

At a rally in Ohio, JD Vance, the former junior senator from Ohio and the vice president of the United States, weighed in, praising Ramaswamy. “Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” he said.

Vance, of course, is no stranger to malicious lies. He trafficked in the slanderous “Haitians eating pets” stories during the 2024 presidential campaign. There was never any credible evidence supporting those claims, yet he spread them anyway — even as Haitians faced death threats as the rumors metastasized across the body politic.

At the time, Vance told CNN, “If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention to the suffering of the American people, then that’s what I’m going to do.”

After Mike DeWine, the Republican governor of Ohio, denounced the Ramaswamy ad (though he did not withdraw his support for Ramaswamy), President Trump took to Truth Social, condemned DeWine as a “RINO,” and said: “The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt.’ ”

At a rally, Trump said that he told Ramaswamy to “leave it up and look upstairs and say, ‘Thank you God very much, I appreciate it.’ ”

“I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody,” he said.

If there were a column hall of fame, Adam Serwer’s 2018 essay in The Atlantic called “The Cruelty Is the Point” should hold a place of honor. Rarely has a single piece so completely captured the zeitgeist of a movement.

Trump’s “only real, authentic pleasure is in cruelty,” Serwer wrote. “It is that cruelty, and the delight it brings them, that binds his most ardent supporters to him, in shared scorn for those they hate and fear: immigrants, black voters, feminists, and treasonous white men who empathize with any of those who would steal their birthright.”

Serwer wrote those words eight years ago, when cruelty was already central to the entire MAGA enterprise. Trump supporters delight in Trump’s cruelty, of course, but they also engage in their own vile speech and actions as a virtual initiation rite into the MAGA movement — it’s the way that they demonstrate that they have the courage necessary to take on the left.

Indeed, in a Truth Social post, Trump applauded the “courage” of Acton’s mother. Vance, as I said, praised the ad’s “audacity.”

This perversion of the concept of courage is central to the MAGA ethos. In MAGA’s account of history, the Republican Party before Trump was a collection of cowards and quislings — people who knew the right thing to do but refused to do so because they were desperate for the approval of progressives.

That’s the origin of the famous (in conservative circles) “D.C. cocktail party” smear — the idea that conservative convictions crumble the instant that conservatives get access to elite institutions or the moment that they get the first taste of elite approval. I’ve faced this accusation for more than a decade, ever since I said I could never support Donald Trump as the Republican nominee.

In other words, there are no genuine arguments about policy or morality, there are only two kinds of people: the strong and the weak (Vance accused Republicans who condemned the ad as “whining”). Or as Shane Vaughn, a Trump-supporting pastor said in an online rant defending Ramaswamy: “Quit being soft. Quit being gay. Quit being spineless. Quit falling. We are in a war!” And one way to tell that you’re strong is if the left loathes you. The more the left hates you, the more righteous you are.

In fact, this is a less obvious reason for evangelicals’ continued support for Trump. From a young age, evangelicals are taught that they’ll be hated by the world. They’re taught to prepare for persecution, and when the secular left is angry at them, that’s treated as proof that they’re on the righteous path. It’s a message I heard for much of my life.

In the words of a common saying I’ve heard on the right, “If you’re taking flak, it means you’re over the target.”

As a result, there is a powerful incentive to intentionally trigger outrage. That’s how you establish your credibility. There’s nothing new about this — The Daily Wire, a right-wing media company, has long sold a tumbler that says “LEFTIST TEARS” for example — but with every passing year it gets worse.

A cohort of far-right supporters of Vance, for example, are fond of using the acronym WAGTFKY, which stands for “we are going to f**king kill you” as a kind of in-group signaling of their own hatred and aggression. They’re living examples of Vance’s own morality. During his campaign for Senate, he made his values clear — “I think our people hate the right people,” he said.

And then he put his hatred into practice, in one of the most powerful offices in the land.

That behavior should be self-defeating, and as a potential blue wave looms in November, it might be. Many Republicans are growing very weary of Trump and — crucially — of Trump’s most aggressive supporters. One thing that was very clear when I traveled to Texas to report on the U.S. Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico is that a meaningful number of Republicans were seething with anger and resentment toward MAGA. They were tired of being bullied. They were tired of MAGA’s corruption. Some were even open to voting for Democrats.

But they were also extremely reluctant to go on the record.

And that shows exactly how MAGA survives. Every act of resistance to MAGA carries a profound cost. The bullies are loud, the good people are often quiet, and when the good people do summon up the courage and decency to decry hatred on the right — as DeWine and many of my friends at National Review have done — they often face the wrath of the president of the United States. They will be the “RINO” in one of Trump’s vicious rants.

Given enough time, every institution takes on the character of its leader. Trump is a cruel man, he leads a cruel movement and only the total defeat of both can free the nation from their malign control.

SUMMARY

I know who I am: Grapes. I’ve been Grapes every year since 2009 — nearly two decades. Grapes is in the room with us now.

ARTICLE

This Year, Yet Again, I’m Dressing as Grapes
Every Halloween for nearly two decades, I’ve adorned myself with purple (or black) balloons. It’s a lifelong commitment to the bit.
By Michael Linares
Published 2026-10-25 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/opinion/this-year-yet-again-im-dressing-as-grapes.html

Unlike the rest of you, I’m not agonizing over a Halloween costume. I know what I’ll be. I know who I am: Grapes.

I’ve been Grapes every year since 2009 — nearly two decades. I don’t expect that I will stop, either. It’s a lifelong commitment to the bit. Grapes gives the feeling of Cronenbergian body horror: a freakish solid with near-liquid bounce.

The first time I dressed as a bunch of grapes, I was 21 and new to New York. I didn’t know what I was looking for, only that it had to be quick and easy, a bit of a gag, and within my Balthazar-server budget. I wanted armor — friendly up close, spooky at a distance; perceived but not seen. I was a weird queer brown kid navigating a new social world. I wanted attention, but not follow-up questions. I didn’t yet believe I had anything to say. I needed a costume that read as defiant, not sexily gay — a category I felt excluded from.

So, post-breakfast shift, I went to the Balloon Saloon in TriBeCa (an upscale emporium for, you guessed it, balloons). Out I came with the bags of sinewy latex that would become my exoskeleton.

A quick tutorial: Grapes as a costume is just green felt and 15 purple balloons safety-pinned to a long-sleeve shirt in an inverted pyramid. It is decidedly D.I.Y., impressionistic, hard to bungle. That first year, I wore an all-purple American Apparel outfit, but I learned it hardly mattered — your body underneath the balloons becomes invisible. I roll a sheet of felt into a cone and pin it to a hat; another rings my neck. The big to-do is blowing up the balloons, which was infinitely easier when I had five roommates, though I eventually got it down to 10 minutes solo. Each balloon gets a pin through the lip. (Keep your back and bum balloon-free so sitting is possible.) Start at the top and work your way down the front: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. By the second row, the operation becomes untenable: you’ll start pricking yourself and popping precious inventory. But by the third row, the magic sets in. The scaffold turns into structure, and the ghost enters the machine. Grapes is in the room with us now.

The first few years, Grapes was pure joy. Everyone was happy to see me. Children bopped me, dogs booped me. Straight men leaned out of cars to say, “YO, GRAPES!” — a welcome catcall rather than a menacing taunt. With the same costume every year, I could sit out the annual rat race to yassify a new profession (sexy data center worker?) or embody the most niche queer reference (Elizabeth Holmes, or the “dancing bird automaton”?). I refused to make it new.

Some years I told people I was Bacchus, or Sour Grapes, or the Grapes of Wrath. But I never stuck with the conceits. The worst part of any costume is having to explain it. Even at 21, I was tired of explaining myself — my race, my sexuality — of making myself neat in someone else’s mind. I wanted to overflow matter-of-factly. With Grapes, I could. I was Grapes, plain Grapes.

Grapes is great at parties. The first balloon crosses the threshold and suddenly everyone has a role to play. Fellow guests must see that this new being can get a drink, make way for its many bathroom breaks. All Grapes can do is smile and shrug and hope to be taken care of. People pause conversations; crowds part. I wave to the world from inside my balloon bumper car, buffered against social anxiety.

Grapes makes the awkwardness literal and unavoidable, and somehow lets me be more myself. I can take a night off from self-protective extroversion — from meeting everyone more than halfway. Now they have to come to me. Surviving the night as Grapes is a testament to the miracle of human cooperation, like crowd surfing or voting.

Here’s a thing I learned: Grapes is a divining rod for sadists. I’m not talking about the innocent boppers or mischievous jostlers — I honor both. I’m talking about poppers. Poppers are otherwise normal people who are overcome with the urge to maim Grapes. They are sleeper cells activated by the sight of sweet, bulbous me. They cannot be avoided, and rarely can they be reasoned with. Most are strangers. Some are not.

Poppers can be anywhere, and they might look like normal people — they shop at the Park Slope Food Co-op; they live on my block; I still run into them at Christmastime and at Shabbat. But Grapes remembers who popped them. There are things Grapes cannot unsee.

There were years when Grapes began to feel like an albatross around my neck — or 15, pinned to my body. Eating was impossible; going to the bathroom was risky. I had to ride contorted in the back seat of cabs, and forget about a seatbelt. Wind could ruin me. Sometimes the store ran out of purple balloons and I had to go as jet-black caviar (2018), or I had nowhere to go but a Zoom chat (2021), or I had somewhere to go but it was more of a grown-ups-drinking-wine vibe (2024). Some years I just was not in the mood, but I pressed onward (2016, 2023, 2025). There was no opting out.

To don the same costume every year is to defy the relentless passing of time, and to see how I’ve changed in turn. In early photos of Grapes, I can see how much I needed the armor. In later ones: I have more confidence and calm, more wrinkles. I forgive poppers now. I carry extra balloons. Today, under all that purple, I want to be seen, not just perceived. I have plenty to say, and I can take all the questions. I wonder how I’ll ripen and sour in the next 20 years of Grapes.

Like any piece of endurance art, Grapes took on different valences over time. It was funny, then less funny, then mundane, then ironic, then post-ironically sincere, then, God willing, funny again. I could tell what kind of year it was by people’s eyes. As I tumbled out of cars or jiggled upstairs, I might catch the wide-eyed excitement of a party host or the slow blink of an exasperated friend. Recently, I told my partner I’d be his plus-one to a fancy (plainclothes) soiree falling on Halloween — as Grapes. He looked at me witheringly. I am now uninvited.

The trail from “YO, GRAPES!” to “Oh, Grapes” is shorter than you’d think. Luckily, it is a loop.

Michael Linares writes about culture and technology and is the vice president of product for NYT Cooking.
