ARTICLE

Far, Far Away
Making a home on the world’s most remote inhabited island.
By Nick Schönfeld and Julia Gunther
Published 2026-10-25 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/world/africa/tristan-da-cunha-island.html

To reach Tristan, roughly halfway between Africa and South America, Kelly Green crossed 1,738 miles of the South Atlantic from Cape Town aboard the M.V. Edinburgh, a 205-foot lobster boat. She had never been to sea before, and she worried about seasickness, but it never came.

After a week at sea, the ship dropped anchor off Calshot Harbour, in front of Tristan da Cunha’s only settlement — Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. Its two small piers, jutting into the water, looked to Kelly like arms reaching out to welcome her.

Kelly could see most of the island’s residents (then 264 people) waving, including her mother and father, Marina and Sean Burns. Her father had been sent to the island, a British Overseas Territory, to serve as its administrator. He persuaded his reluctant 22-year-old daughter to visit, though Kelly, living in Britain, was more interested in clubs than remote islands. Kelly remembers him saying: “You have to come out, because you’ll never get the chance again.”

Among the men who helped carry her bags off the boat was Shane Green, 21. They met again that night at the island’s only pub. They danced.

Kelly went home after six weeks. The first night back in Cape Town, South Africa, where most ships leaving Tristan travel to, her hotel phone rang. It was Shane. They talked every night for months.

That was in 2012. Two years and several visits later, Kelly made the decision that would change her life: She moved to Tristan and became the first woman in over a century to settle there for good. The last had been three Irish sisters, in 1908.

Tristan was first sighted in 1506 by Tristão da Cunha, a Portuguese naval commander. Britain annexed the island in 1816 and set up a garrison for a year. A Scottish corporal stayed behind with his wife, their two children and two English stonemasons. That was the beginning of the community that lives there today.

Only 220 people now call it home, down from a peak of 300 in 1993. In the past three years, there have been 21 deaths and only six births. A few islanders have emigrated over the years.

Before settling on Tristan, Kelly’s life had been defined by travel. As a diplomat’s daughter, she had moved every few years — Antigua, Bangladesh, Senegal, Kenya — then became a flight attendant. Shane had never lived anywhere but Tristan. Where Kelly could describe the color of the sand on a beach in Mombasa, Shane knew every cove and gulch of his island and could explain, in great detail, the safest way from Green Hill to the beach called Down-Where-The-Minister-Landed-His-Things.

Part of what made it easier was that she and Shane, despite their very different lives, grew up watching the same British TV shows, which Kelly’s father had taped and brought to the island.

Living on an isolated island requires residents to be rather social — to pitch in for the common good, wear multiple hats, work long days and make their own fun.

Before Kelly moved in with Shane, he took her to dig potatoes, clean tripe and gut fish. He was impressed by how quickly she adapted. She said, “If I didn’t want to get my fingernails dirty, we wouldn’t have worked out.”

When Kelly steps outside to hang laundry, she can see the vast expanse of the ocean stretch out before her. To her right lie the remnants of the 1961 volcanic eruption, a vast lava wall nearly 300 feet high that hems in Edinburgh, which residents call “the Settlement,” on its eastern side. Behind her, a giant cliff face closes off the sky above.

There is little of the ambient hum that fills most inhabited places — no traffic or electrical thrum. Even the diesel generators that power much of the Settlement are only audible up close. At times it is quiet enough to hear the rush of wind under an albatross’s wings, or the echo of a tumbling rock kicked loose by grazing sheep.

When winter storms hit, the only sounds are the roar of the wind and the window-rattling boom of waves exploding against the cliffs. Salt spray fills the air and eventually streaks everything with rust.

Most mornings, Kelly bakes bread and packs lunches before leaving by half past eight for her job as the island’s Head of Tourism.

At work, she might deal with a private yacht mooring offshore, sending her on a run of chores and errands — arranging tours, ferrying grateful guests to and from showers and washing their clothes. The next day might be spent fielding media questions, writing posts for the island’s social media accounts, or, on Wednesdays, serving lunch for a small group of expatriates.

On fishing days, Shane is at his boat before dawn with Steve, tying frozen bait to traps by the light of their headlamps. They’ll stay out all day and return around six in the evening, to find their daughters waiting with a cooler of homemade mutton pies and cans of soda.

Tristanian children have unusually free rein on the island. In summer, Savanna spends a lot of time at the community pool across the road from the pub, running around with school friends, or dancing in the same hall where Kelly and Shane first danced, and their parents before them.

The farthest Kelly and Shane travel regularly is to the Patches, a cluster of small stone-walled plots two and a half miles west of the Settlement, where Tristanians have grown potatoes, pumpkins and cabbages for more than a hundred years.

The family’s 24 “patches” sit inside a mosaic of low volcanic stone walls and wire fencing, built to keep the island’s cows out. Antarctic terns nest in the cracks of the walls and divebomb anyone who strays too close.

Leaving Tristan is difficult, and getting back is even harder. The two ships that call regularly carry just twelve berths each, with priority given to government officials and islanders needing medical treatment. Only the SA Agulhas II, a South African research vessel, which calls at Tristan once a year, has more spaces, but those fill up quickly too.

A vacation abroad is nearly impossible: Kelly’s family alone would take four of those spaces. The only other chance is a passing cruise ship, and those cabins cost more than most islanders can afford.

Kelly last left the island in 2023, for her father’s funeral. Sean had suffered a series of strokes while serving an unexpected third term as administrator on the island. No ship was close enough to reach Tristan quickly, so the RV Meteor, a German research vessel working in the region, was dispatched. It took several days to arrive.

Sean was carried aboard, and the ship immediately turned for Cape Town. Although his wife, Marina, was able to accompany him, there was not enough room for Kelly.

Sean died during the crossing, somewhere in the South Atlantic. Kelly has the exact coordinates tattooed on her left arm.

“Raising a family here is amazing,” Kelly said, but she always reminds Savanna and Seren that there is also a world beyond Tristan. “There is life to experience before you decide what you want to do.”

Shane wants his children to study off the island if they choose to, but he is just as intent on teaching them to splice rope, plant potatoes, or catch fish from the beach — skills they can fall back on if they decide to stay.

ARTICLE

Israel’s Election: When Will We Know Who Will Be Prime Minister?
Most votes were expected to be counted by Wednesday, but forming a government could take weeks of negotiations — or require another election.
By Ephrat Livni
Published 2026-10-25 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/world/middleeast/israel-election-guide-netanyahu-eisenkot.html

Israelis turned out in huge numbers on Tuesday to choose their next government. But with exit polls suggesting no clear winner, it could take weeks, months or longer to determine who will be prime minister.

The exit polls showed that the right-wing alliance of the incumbent prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the opposition bloc led by a former military chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, were nearly even, with neither in a firm position to form a government. Most votes were expected to be counted by Wednesday, though it could take longer to reach a final tally.

In Israel’s parliamentary democracy, voters choose a party or alliance, and the leader of the party with the greatest number of seats in the 120-member parliament, or Knesset, does not automatically become prime minister. Forming a government could take lengthy negotiations among the various factions — and if those fail, the country could face another election.

Here’s what to know.

What happened on Election Day?

Turnout nationally was 77.7 percent when the polls closed, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, the highest since 1999.

Both Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Eisenkot struck triumphant notes in speeches to supporters. Mr. Eisenkot declared that “the public opted for change,” while Mr. Netanyahu said that his party, Likud, had emerged with the most seats and called for “a strong right-wing government.”

Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the population, voted in large numbers with the stated desire to oust the far right. Exit polls pointed to a strong showing by Arab parties, putting them in a position to play a possibly decisive role in forming a government. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, an Islamist party, told a television interviewer on Tuesday night that the turnout showed that “frustration and despair” in Israel’s Arab society had “turned to hope.”

How are votes counted?

Israel’s electoral system uses nationwide proportional representation. Each voter casts a ballot for a list of candidates affiliated with one or more parties or slates. Each list receives the number of Knesset seats proportionate to its share of the national vote, so long as it got at least 3.25 percent of valid votes. About 10 parties are expected to clear that threshold.

How is a government formed?

No single party has ever won a majority on its own in Israel. That means parties have to negotiate to forge coalitions that can reach a majority in the Knesset of at least 61 lawmakers.

Within seven days of the announcement of the official election results, Israel’s president meets with elected representatives from the parliamentary factions. He can take recommendations and is not obligated to select a potential prime minister from the party that won the most votes. He may instead determine that another leader is more likely to be able to form a coalition that can win a vote of confidence in the Knesset.

The absence of a clear winner in Tuesday’s election could leave the president, Isaac Herzog, facing a difficult choice over whom to ask to form a government.

Once the president decides, that candidate has 28 days to negotiate with other factions. A 14-day extension to the deadline can be requested.

If that effort fails, the president can select another candidate, who also has 28 days to try to form a government but has no option to extend. If the second attempt fails, a majority of Knesset members can ask the president to have a third candidate try. That person would be granted 14 days to form a government, and if that fails, new elections are announced.

Technically, the law allows for a minority government if the relative majority supporting it is larger than the minority opposing. Mr. Eisenkot has floated that possibility.

Historically, it has taken about 20 to 100 days to form a government, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank.

Who will likely lead Israel?

The initial exit polls do not always give an accurate sense of the final results, so it may be some time before the picture becomes clear. For example, exit polls do not reflect the votes of hundreds of thousands of Israelis who cast ballots at special polling stations, including on military bases and in hospitals, prisons and embassies abroad.

In the 2022 election, those votes tended to favor Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.

What the exit polls do suggest, however, is that neither of the main coalitions — the far-right bloc led by Mr. Netanyahu and the center-right alliance led by Mr. Eisenkot — is likely to reach a majority, meaning they would have to negotiate with smaller players and possibly have to make significant compromises.

Two Arab parties were projected to win as many as 18 seats in the Knesset, potentially making their support crucial to assembling a government. But Mr. Netanyahu has in effect ruled out including them in the coalition. Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have also balked at the prospect.

Some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have floated a unity government with Mr. Eisenkot and other centrists that could keep him in power. But that would carry a heavy political cost for Mr. Eisenkot, who has said Mr. Netanyahu is unfit to lead.

ARTICLE

Saudi Arabia Reopens Riyadh Airport Even as Houthis Threaten Further Strikes
The Houthis, an Iran-backed Yemeni militia, launched several deadly attacks on the airport this month.
By Vivian Nereim
Published 2026-10-25 12:14 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/world/middleeast/saudi-arabia-riyadh-airport-reopens.html

The authorities in Saudi Arabia reopened an international airport in the capital on Sunday after a spate of deadly attacks, even as the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen vowed to keep striking the facility.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital, said on Saturday night that flights would resume on Sunday. In a statement, it advised travelers to “verify the status of their bookings and flights before heading to the airport.”

The airport had been closed to the public since Oct. 10, when a cruise missile launched by the Houthis struck a passenger terminal, killing at least 13 people and injuring more than 300. The militia, based in northern Yemen, has launched at least three other deadly strikes on the airport this month — part of its near-daily attacks on Riyadh.

On Sunday morning, residents of the capital received an emergency alert warning of an incoming “aerial threat” and some reported hearing several loud booms. The Saudi authorities said soon after that they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh.

A Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, had renewed a warning to airlines and travelers after the airport issued its statement about reopening, saying to avoid using the airport “because it is a military target.” The Saudi government, he said, would “bear responsibility for the consequences” of reopening it.

The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to questions about how they had assessed it was safe to reopen the airport, or if they had put in place additional air defenses.

After four years of relative peace, the Houthis and the Saudis resumed attacking each other earlier this month amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the Houthis’ primary backer.

The Houthis describe their attacks as retaliation for deadly Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, including many that have killed and injured civilians.

On Saturday, Mr. Saree claimed in a statement that the militia had carried out an operation against the airport, among other attacks around the country, without specifying when.

The Saudi authorities have not said whether the airport was targeted this weekend. The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, which is fighting the Houthis, said it had intercepted missiles and drones heading toward Riyadh on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

It was not immediately clear how many flights were departing from or landing in Riyadh airport on Sunday, or whether airlines other than Saudi state-owned carriers would opt to resume flights.

Flightradar24, a flight tracking website, showed that a Saudi Arabian Airlines plane flying from Jeddah had landed in Riyadh on Sunday afternoon. It also showed that dozens of flights to and from Riyadh had been canceled.

In recent weeks, fighting has reignited inside Yemen between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

A Saudi-led bombing campaign launched against the Houthis a decade ago aimed to rout the militia and restore the government. It lasted for years and precipitated one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen from violence, hunger and disease.

A truce in 2022 brought a fragile peace to the country and left the Houthis in control of northern Yemen.

Tensions began to rise again after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, sparking a regional war. In July, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the international airport in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in order to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.

The militia declared a blockade on Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea, and both sides began to launch a series of escalating attacks. After a full-blown war reignited earlier this month, the militia turned its focus to Saudi airports, threatening to turn them into a “theater of military operations.”

In doing so, they have hit at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions to transform the kingdom from an insular, oil-dependent nation into a global hub for business and tourism.

The prince, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, recently launched a new international airline with its hub in Riyadh. His annual investment summit typically draws billionaires, executives and officials from around the world to Riyadh and was set to begin on Monday. However, it was postponed at the last minute until 2027.

The United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said on social media last week.

Despite the Houthi threats, Saudi officials have sought to maintain a sense of normalcy. The authorities kept Riyadh airport open after two deadly attacks, closing it only after the mass casualty event on Oct. 10.

In the face of the attacks, Saudi Arabia has been seeking support from allies. Last week, Britain said that it would send fighter jets to help defend Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from the Houthis.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

ARTICLE

In India, I Saw Things That Should Scare Trump
Young people have revived the country’s glorious tradition of nonviolent dissent.
By Lydia Polgreen and Abhishek Khedekar
Published 2026-10-26 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/26/opinion/india-modi-students-protests.html

Narendra Modi, the barrel-chested strongman leader of India for the past dozen years, has finally met his match — and it looks a lot like Mohini Majumdar. Just 20 years old, slender and voluble, Majumdar is an English student at Delhi University: an unlikely antagonist for an omnipotent autocrat.

Yet early on Oct. 10, she shared an early morning taxi to the center of Delhi with a gaggle of classmates. Dressed casually in flowing cotton and sensible shoes, Majumdar and her friends could just as easily have been on their way to a stroll in one of this city’s splendid gardens. But their plan, she told me, was to march across the street to a place called Jantar Mantar, a historic monument at the center of Delhi that has for decades served as a designated ground for protest.

They had been there before, over the summer, joining thousands of other young people in raucous, meme-driven protests after a leaked paper led to the cancellation of a college entrance exam. Eventually, under the banner of the upstart Cockroach Janata Party, they forced the resignation of India’s education minister. It was the first time Modi’s government had dismissed a top official under pressure from public protests.

Now, they were back for an even bigger fish: Modi’s handpicked chief election commissioner, who had overseen the deletion of more than 130 million people from the country’s voter rolls in a murky process that threatened to undermine faith in the voting process in the world’s largest democracy. “These kinds of protests really prove that you should be political, and everything is political in our life,” Majumdar told me as she waited for the march to begin.

She never did get to march that day. A few minutes after I spoke with her and her friends, a column of police officers decked out in camouflage descended on the students, manhandling them into a waiting bus. The officers drove them 40 minutes north of the city center and held them in a police station until after dark, eventually letting the women go; only when they refused to leave did the officers also release the men.

So great was the threat these students presented to Modi’s rule that his government reportedly deployed over 50,000 security personnel to the streets, shut down dozens of metro stations, blocked long-distance trains from arriving in Delhi and threw up yellow steel barricades across the capital, leaving its usually teeming streets eerily deserted. Majumdar was one of thousands of people detained that day by the authorities in an all-out attempt to quash the protest.

Despite these efforts, Modi appears more vulnerable than at any time since he was first elected prime minister. Young people like Majumdar, educated, middle-class and Hindu — the children of a generation that rocketed him to power — are in open revolt, incensed by the government’s derogation of education and democracy. Willing to risk detention and the baton blows of the feared lathi, they are setting out to make Modi, who has carefully managed his image as a civilizational figure who will lift India into glory, an object of fun. Majumdar, undeterred by her detention, joined another protest the very next day.

“The moment you oppressed me, the fear was gone,” she told me.

For Modi, it is a stunning turnabout. For over a decade, his rule seemed durable and unshakable. His rise to power, initially inconceivable and then inevitable, was a foretaste of the world to come. Before Brexit blew apart Britain, before Donald Trump ascended to the American presidency, before an influx of Syrian refugees turned European politics rightward, Modi led the world’s largest democracy toward a vision of nationalist, right-wing populism, promising a civilizational restoration.

Today, India is once again in the vanguard — this time leading, perhaps, in the opposite direction. As Modi has consolidated his power over this vast nation and its sprawling state apparatus, many Indians have grown weary of the bargain he has offered: growth and national prosperity in return for a hardening authoritarianism. Beset as Modi is by crises within and without, his iron grip on power is clanging against the steel of India’s messy democracy. As governments struggle and discontent flourishes worldwide, the country offers a lesson for us all.

When I moved to India as a correspondent for The New York Times in 2009, I discovered a place brimming with optimism and ripe with possibility. Fresh off an election victory, the Congress Party formed a sturdy coalition government led by Manmohan Singh, a soft-spoken, teetotal technocrat with a Ph.D. in economics. Unfettered by its most irksome left-wing coalition partners, his government would be free to make deep reforms and get India’s economy soaring.

It didn’t work out that way. Indians saw their dreams of prosperity founder in the wake of the global financial crisis, while their government was snarled in scandals of grubby self-dealing. An anti-corruption protest movement sprang up, expressive of deep discontent that Modi’s right-wing Hindu nationalist party rode to power. Modi pointed to the prosperous state he governed, Gujarat, and promised to do the same for the rest of India.

Abstemious and devout, Modi offered himself up as a servant leader with no personal interests to pursue beyond the uplift of the nation. For many Hindus, his assertion of Hindu pride and even supremacy proved enticing. That he allegedly stood by idly as hundreds of Muslims died in religious riots in the state he governed in 2002 — his role in this tragedy led the United States to deny him entry for nine years — was mostly ignored by the public.

One of the voters who rolled the dice on Modi was a man named Surender Kumar. I met him outside a popular market in Delhi, where he was waiting for passengers in his motorized rickshaw. Back in 2014, he was angry about corruption and thought it was time for a change. He cast his ballot, with some hesitation, for Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party. But a dozen years on, he is disappointed. “The government came with certain kinds of promises during the elections, and none of them we see right now,” he told me. “Just to protect kingmakers in the government, they are letting kids be beaten.”

Though Kumar’s parents had been penniless manual laborers, he managed to leave their world of physical toil behind. Driving his rickshaw could net him between $200 and $300 a month, before expenses, a decent working-class living. But his son and daughter, growing into adulthood during Modi’s tenure, haven’t been able to make a similar leap.

Kumar could not afford private school or tutoring classes for them, so neither made it to college. His daughter studied cosmetology and opened a small beauty salon, but has struggled to make a go of it. His son works at McDonald’s, earning what his father describes as pocket change. Inflation eats away at his own earnings: The price of the natural gas that fuels his rickshaw has more than doubled, he told me. “You can’t name a thing which has retained its price,” he said. “Rice, cooking oil, mustard oil, cooking cylinders.”

Further up the economic ladder, among the middle-class Hindu families that make up many of Modi’s most fervent supporters, the struggle to provide economic advancement for the next generation is both all-consuming and increasingly uncertain.

In a sprawling, tree-filled apartment complex at the northern edge of Delhi, Shivani Sharma, a teacher, described a life that revolved around a singular goal: getting her 17-year-old daughter, Sanskriti, into a good public university and launched into a well-paying career. This has involved expensive private schools and costly tutoring sessions to sharpen her math and science skills in preparation for the relentless battery of highly competitive government-administered entrance exams.

“You have to have a very good score,” Sharma said. “Only then you can get entry into the Delhi University,” the prestigious school where she had gotten her bachelor’s degree in the 1990s.

For middle-class families, admission to a good public university is akin to a lottery ticket — the tuition is low and the credential confers real prestige. If Sanskriti does not make the cut, the family may have to come up with upward of $15,000 per year to pay for a private college. As it is, they struggle to keep up with her current educational expenses. In addition to running a school with her husband, Sharma earns extra money by tutoring children in the neighborhood. Her husband has a part-time job in a clothing showroom.

“We live simply,” she told me. “We don’t take international tours. We don’t wear expensive clothes. We don’t spend money here and there. We try to save money for our daughter’s education.” Sharma grew up in a big family, with five sisters and a brother. Yet none of her siblings has more than two children, she said. “We didn’t opt for the second child because I knew it’s very expensive and it’s very difficult to raise both the children and give them a good lifestyle and good education,” she told me.

Given the stakes, the leaked exam paper — expressive of deep corruption in the education system — rattled Sharma. “Some children committed suicide,” she said. “Only insiders can leak the paper. Who else can leak the paper? It’s a lot of corruption.”

Even a bachelor’s degree from a prestigious college is no guarantee in a country where graduate unemployment is at nearly 40 percent for those ages 15 to 29 and starting salaries are abysmally low. Food delivery drivers often earn more than entry-level tech workers with engineering degrees. To improve Sanskriti’s chances in life, Sharma said they are considering sending her abroad for a master’s degree. That would probably cost $100,000, an unfathomable sum that would require them to go into debt.

Young people across the country increasingly see this as a fool’s bargain, a debt-filled dead end. And they are not afraid to say so, loudly and publicly. Aditi (she goes by one name), the 29-year-old president of the students’ union at Jawaharlal Nehru University, is emblematic. Her parents are stalwart supporters of the B.J.P. But like many members of Gen Z, she rejects the empty promises of Hindu nationalism. “People have gotten bored with Modi’s narrative,” she told me. “Young people have tasted blood.”

Modi’s government has faced down discontent before. In 2019, a new citizenship law that targeted Muslims was rightly seen as an affront to India’s foundational ideal of secularism, enshrined in its constitution. But Modi was mostly able to wave that away as minority special pleading. Protests the next year by farmers, heavily drawn from India’s Sikh minority, could be dismissed as separatist agitation, even as the government mostly ceded to the farmers’ demands.

But this time, the protests have been driven in part by the concerns of the aspirational Hindu families that are the bedrock of Modi’s coalition. For many of these Indians, it may have been possible to ignore the ugly aspects of Modi’s rule, indeed to retreat from politics altogether and focus on building futures for themselves and their children. But many are realizing that all their hard work can be scuppered by a purloined exam answer sheet; by the devaluation of college degrees, which command little premium in an oversupplied labor market; and by a compromised election commission that could silence their most fundamental individual choice in a country of over 1.4 billion people.

Modi’s centralization — the very thing that seemed destined to consolidate his power — has become a booby trap. He captured and muzzled the mainstream press, especially television news, only for an enormous ecosystem of independent and influential journalists to rise up on YouTube and Instagram. He centralized the process of college examinations, leaving him no one else to blame when evidence of systemic leaking of exam papers emerged. His control over the election commission has left him with few options when faced with difficult questions over deleted voters.

Modi has also discovered that despite his efforts to project global leadership, his power quickly fades at the water’s edge. After promising to elevate India to great-power status, he has found himself stuck, subject to the mundane gravity of global events over which he has little control. He has suffered a series of embarrassments on the world stage, especially at the hands of the Trump administration.

What’s more, the pressure valve of migration is tightening. On the upper end of society, the dream of sending a child abroad, especially to the United States, is dying. On the lower end, uncertainty in the Persian Gulf is making migrant labor there a shakier proposition too. For a country that is the world’s largest receiver of remittances, amounting to roughly 4 percent of gross domestic product, that’s a big problem. That’s before you consider rising prices for fuel and tariffs on exports.

There will be no sudden fall for Modi. Though leaders in neighboring South Asian countries like Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka have been swept aside by youth uprisings, there is little chance of that happening here. India may seem like a chaotic and cacophonous place, and in many ways it is. Yet India’s government has always changed through the orderly process of elections, and Modi will not face the national electorate again until 2029.

But something profound has shifted. Modi’s aura of omnipotence and serene competence has been shattered. The protests have transformed his main challenger, Rahul Gandhi of the Congress Party, as well. They have given him the chance to shed his image as the pampered and ineffectual scion of a storied political dynasty. The political landscape, settled for so long, is suddenly altered.

India’s democracy has always been improbable. It is a society of boggling diversity and deep divides of religion, ethnicity and caste. Inequality, always pervasive, has deepened as the country has grown richer in ragged, uneven ways. And yet its constitutional democracy has endured, with the brief exception of Indira Gandhi’s emergency rule, since its independence from Britain nearly eight decades ago.

It is telling that this unexpected challenge to Modi’s power was catalyzed by affronts to two fundamental features of Indian democracy. As the political scientist Pratap Bhanu Mehta explained to me, taking exams and voting in elections are perhaps the two most important pillars of individual agency in India. Each contains the possibility of self-actualization, something that can seem nearly impossible in a country that is simultaneously so multitudinous and so hierarchical.

Exams hold the promise that anyone from anywhere, with enough hard work, can improve his or her station in life. Even more fundamental, if diffuse, is the individual franchise, which carries the notion that each citizen has an equal role in choosing who governs India. These two pillars, Mehta told me, are “the self-conscious revolt against caste, kinship, religion.” This is perhaps why copies of the Indian Constitution have figured so prominently in the protests, along with images of its main architect, Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar.

It is easy to harbor romantic notions about Indian democracy. It is a project never before attempted in human history — for so many people with so much diversity to live together by common assent, under a written constitution that guarantees rights for all. For the past 12 years, India has engaged in a different experiment, one all too willing to brush aside the unfulfilled aspirations of the Constitution in the name of material progress and Hindu pride.

But a new generation of Indians has risen up, insisting that the price of that trade is far too high. Armed only with witty slogans and astonishing bravery, these young people have revived their country’s glorious tradition of nonviolent dissent. As peers from Paris to Tirana, Milan to Madrid, take to the streets demanding radical change, they would do well to look to Delhi as a guide.

SUMMARY

If, as expected, Democrats take control of at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, power in Washington would shift from unified Republican control to divided government. How will President Trump respond to that? What might come next for President Trump, Republicans and Democrats?

ARTICLE

Trump Is Not the Only Thing Unsettling About Our Politics
Conflict? Cooperation? On the potential of divided government.
By Frances E. Lee and John Guida
Published 2026-10-26 15:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/26/opinion/midterms-democrats-trump-power.html

If, as expected, Democrats take control of at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, power in Washington would shift from unified Republican control to divided government.

How will President Trump respond to that? What will Democrats do with institutional power? Will the open presidential primaries of 2028 for both parties have any effect on all this?

Frances Lee, a political scientist at Princeton, assessed these questions in a written conversation with John Guida, an editor in Times Opinion. It has been edited for length and clarity.

John Guida: Let’s assume, based on consensus polling, that we have divided government, with Democrats controlling at least the House for the next two years. What might come next for President Trump, Republicans and Democrats? Let’s start with Trump.

Frances Lee: Divided control of national government will make Trump less solely responsible for outcomes. He will be able to blame Democrats for not acting on his priorities in ways that were less available to him when dealing with Republicans during his first two years of office. He may be able to get some mileage out of that conflict.

Guida: How did Trump handle a newly Democratic House in the final two years of his first term?

Lee: That Congress, the 116th (2019-20), actually turned out to be a remarkably legislatively productive two years. That’s largely a story of the extraordinary response to Covid: $3 trillion in new spending in 2020 alone.

But there was more that got done than Covid, at least on second-tier issues: legislation implementing a new North American trade agreement; paid parental leave for federal workers; legislation to reduce generic drug prices; and multiple national parks enactments. So some degree of bipartisan cooperation persists, even in a Congress that also featured two presidential impeachments! It’s not the case that national government is totally gridlocked during divided government, even in today’s polarized politics.

Guida: Do you think the aggressive use of executive power in Trump’s second term makes that cooperation more difficult? I’m thinking of areas like immigration, investigations by the Justice Department of political opponents or in conflicts between the White House and Congress over spending authority.

Lee: It’s rather astonishing how aggressive Trump has been in using unilateral executive authority even under conditions where his party also controlled Congress. It’s honestly hard to see how he could do more on that than he has already done. He attempted to personally reset the United States’ trade relationship with practically every country in the world.

Obviously, with Democrats likely in control of at least one house of Congress, there will be more aggressive oversight as Trump uses these powers. They will have agenda control and will be able to highlight overreach, missteps and abuses of power. We should naturally expect very tough interbranch conflict. In Trump’s first term, the administration routinely stiff-armed congressional oversight.

Guida: How might Democrats handle that?

Lee: On issues like immigration, they will certainly hold more hearings on what the administration is doing. They will be able to shine a light on the collateral harms of the policies in ways that they are not able to do now. But Democratic leverage over ICE and C.B.P. (the U.S. Customs and Border Protection) will be less than normal, because those agencies are already funded for the balance of Trump’s term, as a consequence of the parties’ inability to reach agreement on appropriations for those agencies this spring. Republicans then went on to fund them via a party-line reconciliation.

Guida: You said above that Trump will be able to share blame in particular for things that don’t happen. In polling, voters have prioritized issues around affordability. Is there any chance of dealmaking between Trump and Republicans and Democrats in Congress?

Lee: Trump’s departures from conservative orthodoxy do open up some potential for cross-party dealmaking on issues such as capping credit card interest rates or lowering prescription drug costs.

That said, Trump is not strong as a legislative leader. He even has difficulty cooperating with his own party allies. He is constantly surprising them with new demands or withdrawing support at the last minute. Probably the most significant legislative effort this Congress on affordability issues was the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. This was a big bipartisan deal to lower some of the regulatory obstacles to building new housing and to open up some new financing alternatives to home buyers and home builders. But in the end, Trump pulled the rug from his own party leaders in Congress and refused to sign the package. It became law without his signature. If he has this much trouble working with his own party’s House speaker and Senate majority leader, how hard will it be to get anything done working with Democrats?

Trump prefers to do things on a unilateral basis. This is not likely to change in any way in his last two years as president. This approach clearly leaves his legacy more vulnerable to reversal by successors than if he could actually get legislation enacted. Indeed, much of what he did this way in his first term wound up being undone by President Biden.

Guida: A cliché in politics is that the 2028 election begins the day after the midterms. How much, if at all, do you think the incentives of 2028 might shape what happens in the next two years?

Lee: The Republican Party will be facing large questions about its basic policy commitments in both foreign and domestic policy. The factional lines are already drawn: whether there will be a return to the values of Reagan Republicanism or whether instead policy will follow more directly from Trump’s heterodoxies on trade, international alliances, entitlements and many other matters.

Democrats have clearly been facing considerable frustration and restiveness from their base voters on whether they have been standing up to Trump sufficiently. It will not be easy for them to cooperate with the administration, given these political pressures.

Both parties have an interest in credit claiming for doing something on the issues that matter most to Americans, such as affordability. But I have my doubts as to whether those interests will take precedence over the larger internal party pressures. After all, nothing that Congress can do legislatively is likely to move the needle much on affordability on any near-term basis. So my suspicion is that the next two years are unlikely to see major policy action on domestic policy issues.

Guida: You have emphasized that in American politics right now, power changes hands frequently between the parties from election to election. When Democrats or Republicans gain power, they often use it to enact items from a narrow partisan agenda.

Lee: Intense party competition for majority control of Congress limits bipartisan dealmaking. If there is reason to think that the majority party will shift or is likely to shift, then the party with less power now will prefer to hold off on cutting deals on major issues in hopes of getting something better in two years.

Beyond that, both parties will be preoccupied with driving narratives in the media aimed at winning advantage in that future electoral contest. The minority party will want to denounce the party in power for doing a bad job.

It cannot do that effectively at the same time as it is striking deals with that party and shaking hands on policy enactments that they can both support. The minority needs to withhold cooperation, propose partisan alternatives and message about how they would do a better job.

So all these dynamics will be very much in play across the next two years.

Guida: Is this arrangement, which has structured so much about politics, at the root of voter dissatisfaction that has been endemic for decades?

Lee: It undoubtedly fuels voter frustration. Every election they’re told that this is the most important election of their lifetimes. But then they discover that major breakthroughs don’t happen on the policy front after elections are over. Legislation generally requires significant bipartisan cooperation to get done, with the exception of reconciliation enactments that get around some of the normal veto players.

In an environment like this, there is a preoccupation with politics over policymaking. Nobody is able to think long term about policy, because our politics is so profoundly unsettled and there is no confidence about who is likely to have power after the next set of elections. Indeed, every election seems to yield a rough 50-50 outcome: This just doesn’t provide much clarity to elected officials about what voters actually want from national politics.

Guida: You have identified how our “unsettled politics” have shaped our system in two distinct ways. One is in how policy is made, more and more often by executive power; the other, in how parties respond to the shorter time horizons imposed by power shifting back and forth so often between them.

Lee: The parties often look to presidents to achieve policy outcomes that they cannot legislate.

This is one of the surprising features of our current politics. Even though Trump continually outrages Democrats with his actions, Democrats are not forcefully criticizing his aggressive use of presidential power. They criticize his specific policy actions, but they rarely denounce them as usurpations of legislative power. Clearly, Democrats would like to see a future Democratic president act boldly as well. So the current conditions incentivize presidents to go around Congress. And Congress tolerates, even sometimes promotes it.

The short-time horizons manifest in a “go for broke” attitude when parties have trifecta control. No one seems to expect it to last. So the idea is to do as much as you can as quickly as you can.

Guida: Your recent paper on the Trump-Republican One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 digs into the process of how big laws are typically achieved today. They require unified, one-party control of the presidency and Congress. And the bills are often done through the reconciliation process, which allows the majority party to avoid a filibuster and pass bills on a simple majority vote.

Lee: It is a way of enacting huge party wish lists. In each presidency with unified control since the Clinton years, the administration has used a reconciliation enactment to get some big policy wins on their priorities. This is how both George W. Bush and Trump got their signature tax cuts done. Obama used it to get his health care reform done after Democrats lost their 60-vote majority in the Senate. It’s how Biden did his Inflation Reduction Act.

These are tough bills to pass and it’s not unusual for parties to fail at the effort. They are swinging for the fences, and sometimes they strike out, as Republicans did when they attempted to repeal and replace Obamacare in Trump’s first term and as Biden attempted to do with the Build Back Better agenda. But this is a party’s ticket to getting some big wins. Trump utilized it with his One Big Beautiful Bill, which put through his full domestic policy agenda, including making his earlier tax cuts permanent along with an array of other priorities, in one single legislative vehicle.

Guida: What do these massive bills miss by being done on a party basis?

Lee: This kind of “go for broke” attitude winds up producing backlash. The minority party denounces them vociferously and campaigns against them. Neither party’s agenda is all that popular. And these big bills are likewise usually rather unpopular. These efforts generally get interpreted as overreach. In our polarized era, no party has been able to hold onto trifecta control for long. So this dynamic perpetuates insecure majorities.

Guida: Is insecure-majority politics sustainable?

Lee: We seem to be stuck in a recurring cycle. It has been a very long time since we’ve seen a truly decisive election in American politics. There has been no landslide since the 1980s. This fact means that elections fundamentally don’t settle much in terms of the future direction of policy. Parties try to make the most of any opportunity they get.

But the meaning of elections is contested. The two parties don’t agree on what to conclude from election outcomes. There is not so much sense that the “people have spoken.” The party out of power expects to be able to get back in — and soon. And they have generally been right about that.

Guida: We have seen potential emerging realignments come and go: the emerging Democratic majority, Trump’s multiracial working-class coalition in 2024, which polling strongly suggests has crumbled. Is it possible to see the emergence of a majority party in 2028?

Lee: This is one of the most mysterious features of our contemporary politics. We have been stuck in this trench warfare, closely competitive party politics for decades now.

But this pattern of politics is not the norm for U.S. history. It used to be conventional wisdom that American politics could be understood in terms of a “sun party” and a “moon party,” meaning that there was a dominant party and a secondary party and the major issues of the day would get fought out among factions in the dominant party. That seemed to be the pattern across the 20th century, where the New Deal coalition dominated national politics for so long. The Jacksonian Democrats were similarly formidable during the 19th century. The Republican Party predominated from 1894 through until the Great Depression, with the exception of a brief stretch of closely contested politics during the Progressive Era. Why is our own era so different?

Guida: You don’t seem very confident that the political system will change much in the next two years. What in the future might bring about change?

Lee: Top leadership of both parties will be very much up for grabs looking to 2028. Not just in terms of personnel, but also in terms of ideological commitments. Will Trump leave office regarded by his own party as an embarrassment, as has happened to a number of other recent presidents? Or will he be a kingmaker?

That outcome will have major effects on whether the G.O.P. continues following the Trump mode or whether there is some return to conservative orthodoxies. Things are also wide open in the Democratic Party. It is a fluid time in national politics.

Frances E. Lee, a professor of politics and public affairs at Princeton, is the author of “Insecure Majorities: Congress and the Perpetual Campaign” and, most recently, “A Case for Congress.” John Guida is an editor in Times Opinion.

SUMMARY

Around this time a year ago, President Trump and his MAGA acolytes saw North Carolina as a trough at which they could gluttonously feed. They envisioned oodles of money pouring into North Carolina to ensure that its 2026 Senate contest went Republicans’ way and that Democrats, who hadn’t won a Senate race in the state since 2008, continued their losing streak. Political analysts in North Carolina tell me that such an outcome is as good a bet as any.

ARTICLE

In North Carolina, Republicans Got Greedy. Now They’re Getting Schooled.
Why the Tar Heel State is giving me hope for the future
By Frank Bruni
Published 2026-10-26 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/26/opinion/north-carolina-midterms-republicans.html

Around this time a year ago, President Trump and his MAGA acolytes saw North Carolina as a trough at which they could gluttonously feed.

They decided that its U.S. House delegation of 10 Republicans and four Democrats — already a mockery of a purple state with roughly equal numbers of voters in each party — wasn’t lopsided enough, so they successfully pressured Republicans in the State Legislature to gerrymander the existing gerrymander, with the aim of an 11-3 split after the midterms.

They envisioned oodles of money pouring into North Carolina to ensure that its 2026 Senate contest went Republicans’ way and that Democrats, who hadn’t won a Senate race in the state since 2008, continued their losing streak. How confident they were. How cocky.

How premature.

Last week, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a prominent newsletter that tracks elections, changed its ratings for North Carolina’s First and 11th Congressional Districts, once thought to be Trump territory, to “leans Democratic,” reflecting a continued nationwide mood shift in favor of Democrats. That update coincided with the release of an Emerson College poll that put Jamie Ager, the Democratic nominee in the 11th, an astonishing 13 percentage points ahead of the Republican nominee, Jennifer Balkcom. If Democrats indeed prevailed in the 11th and the First, North Carolina’s U.S. House delegation after the midterms would probably be nine Republicans and five Democrats. Political analysts in North Carolina tell me that such an outcome is as good a bet as any.

The Senate contest also hasn’t gone as Republicans expected. Early this month, The Times reported that a major Republican super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, would stop spending money on television ads for Michael Whatley, the Republican nominee. In poll after poll, he has failed to close the gap between him and the Democratic nominee, Roy Cooper, who currently leads Whatley by about 10 percentage points, according to an average of recent voter surveys.

All in all, North Carolina is poised to prove that a president and a political party can’t outrun reality, not with shady scheming, not with mountains of cash, not with all the swagger and bluster in the world. It’s also demonstrating that the deep cynicism, deep fakes and deeply entrenched partisanship of our era haven’t rendered certain principles obsolete. The quality of candidates matters. So does the quality of their campaigns. North Carolina, my home for the past five and a half years, is reassuring me of that. It’s giving me hope for the future.

Of course nothing’s certain, and Republicans haven’t wholly surrendered the fight here. President Trump and Vice President JD Vance separately visited and held rallies in North Carolina last week, intent on reinvigorating their party’s most loyal voters.

But an Elon University poll that was released last week showed what a hostile environment Trump and Vance were entering. Only 34 percent of North Carolina adults approved of Trump’s job performance while 57 percent disapproved. North Carolinians’ frustrations with the economy and misgivings about the president are so palpable that Michael Bitzer, a professor of history and political science at Catawba College in Salisbury, N.C., questioned the usefulness of a Trump rally here.

“I haven’t seen the kind of energy and enthusiasm on the Republican side that you would think these high-profile visits would bring,” Bitzer told me. “I’m almost wondering if it’s having a backfire effect. It’s going to rile up Democrats even more.”

Those Democrats are already plenty riled. Representative Deborah Ross, a Democrat whose seat in North Carolina’s Second Congressional District is safe, told me that the degree of Democratic enthusiasm and the scope of efforts to turn out the Democratic vote remind her of 2008, which was the last time not only that Democrats won a Senate contest but also that a Democratic presidential candidate — Barack Obama — won North Carolina. “People are putting it all on the line,” she said.

The prospect of Democratic triumphs here is mostly about national dynamics, and it’s consistent with reappraisals of Democrats’ chances in House and Senate races across the country.

But the North Carolina story is also one of smart choices and discipline — virtues that the Democratic Party has not exhibited in abundance over recent years. It was smart of Democratic leaders to press Cooper, who was North Carolina’s governor from 2017 to 2025, to run for the Senate seat that Thom Tillis, a Republican, is vacating after two terms. Cooper’s name recognition, proven popularity among the state’s voters and moderate image made him a daunting opponent for any Republican nominee.

And he has run a disciplined campaign whose focus on affordability is almost comical in its folksiness, as I wrote in July. “Make Stuff Cost Less” is his slogan. His rallies are part of the Make Stuff Cost Less tour. The culture war? To hear him talk — about utility bills, grocery prices, health insurance — is to forget it even exists.

Representative Don Davis, the Democratic nominee in the First Congressional District, has painstakingly emphasized votes and beliefs that position him as moderate. That’s the only sane strategy in territory dominated by Republicans and independents who favored Trump in 2024. After that contest, the district was redrawn to make it even Trumpier, with the goal of replacing Davis with a Republican. But what polling there is suggests a tight, winnable race against his Republican challenger, Laurie Buckhout.

A series of developments have put the 11th Congressional District — in a largely rural patch of western North Carolina — into play. The Republican incumbent, Representative Chuck Edwards, ended his re-election campaign shortly before the House censured him in September for inappropriate conduct with young women on his staff. That left the party scrambling for a last-minute replacement — and meant that Ager, the Democratic nominee, had a huge head start.

More important than that, Ager has an ideal profile for a Democrat running on red turf. With a father and brother who have served in the North Carolina Legislature, he knows politics, but his occupation — he operates Hickory Nut Gap Farms, which has been in his family for generations — doesn’t carry even a whiff of the establishment. Good luck finding a photo of Ager in a jacket and tie. He’s more likely in flannel or outerwear, near pigs or wooden fences.

“He’s the guy who Democrats wanted Graham Platner to be,” Chris Cooper, a political science professor at Western Carolina University, told me. “He really is a farmer. He really runs Hickory Nut.” And he has a real knack for connecting with the district’s voters, said Cooper, who mentioned an annual parade in Canton, N.C., where Ager and his Republican opponent, Balkcom, both showed up. “She was riding a float,” Cooper said. “Jamie Ager was in the crowd, pressing the flesh.”

Matt Ballance, a former Democratic chairman for the 11th District, called Ager “a kind of silver bullet for this district.” “We can’t win it with the standard current Democrat,” he said. But with Ager? According to recent financial reports, Balkcom had raised less than $400,000 by the end of September; she had about $300,000 of that on hand. Ager had raised about $5.4 million, with $1.6 million on hand.

That speaks to his hustle, his shrewdness, his ardor. He’s not the only North Carolina Democrat with those gifts, which Trump’s corruption of the truth and attacks on the voting process can’t snuff out.

For the Love of Sentences

In The Times, Sarah Karnasiewicz savored the uncommonly diverse forms of a common fruit: “Snow White’s apple may have been crimson and comely, but these days some of the most exciting varieties in American orchards are old, odd and decidedly unpolished. Their names have the ring of Dickensian villains — Esopus Spitzenburg, Cornish Gilliflower, Fearns Pippin, Hubbardston Nonesuch — and their flavors vary from honeyed sweetness to dark clove spice.” (Thanks to Mary Margaret McGuire of San Simeon, Calif., for nominating this.)

Also in The Times, Amelia Nierenberg recognized that Danish diners’ current romance with sliced cheese on fresh bread is a 180-degree turn “from the best-known Danish cuisine, which has been foraged, fermented and tweezered into submission over the last two decades.” (Jennifer Rothschild, Englewood, Colo., and Jean Knorr, Charlottesville, Va.)

And Samuel A.A. Levine evoked a classic Eagles song to recount his futile interactions with a customer service chatbot: “I had stumbled into the digital labyrinth — a veritable Hotel California, and I was just a prisoner of my own device.” (Andrew R. Zinn, Dallas, and Kelly Frederick, Los Angeles, among others)

In The Ringer, Brian Phillips charted the humiliation of the American military under Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who prematurely declared victory in Iran, depleted our arsenal and emboldened our rivals: “If he were actually working for China, he would be their employee of the year.” (Chloe Wynns, Chicago)

In The Atlantic, Helen Lewis noticed President Trump’s fixation on the hotness of various men in his orbit, including a comrade up for re-election: “Step forward, Jon Husted of Ohio, with your glorious, rippling glutes and your valiant crusade against energy-efficient dishwashers. At a campaign stop for the Republican senator in Dayton, Trump discovered that Husted used to be a star football player. Naturally, the president looked for evidence of this in Husted’s buttocks — the windows to the soul.” Trump perhaps benefits from such effusions about male pulchritude. “Campiness is key to his political appeal — it’s the secret sauce that transforms nastiness into showbiz sass. Trump is politics’ answer to Joan Rivers, and his persona is influenced by all the flavors of American fakery: the carnival barker, the reality-TV host, the kayfabe world of professional wrestling. He looks like a man doing a drag performance as himself.” (Fred H. Lawson, Bodega Bay, Calif., and Howard Caro, San Francisco, among others)

Also in The Atlantic, Alexandra Petri reacted to remarks in which Steve Witkoff, a U.S. special envoy, called Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian”: “My dictionary just ran outside and threw itself off a bridge. Noah Webster arose from his grave and lurched around, howling and tearing at his hair. Samuel Johnson is bellowing something awful; I can hear it across the Atlantic Ocean. George Orwell is sighing; he has been here before.” (Helen Scott, Queens, N.Y., and Hilarie Lennan, Media, Pa.)

In The Guardian, Arwa Mahdawi treated the books mentioned in Usha Vance’s Goodreads account as rune stones: “‘Arwa,’ you might say, ‘you’re reading way too much into this!’ Of course I am. I have a degree in English literature: That’s three years of explaining how doorknobs in Jane Austen novels represent the hollowness of colonialism.” (David Clohessy, St. Louis)

And in the weekly publication Seven Days, Mary Ann Lickteig described how Neil Shah, a Vermont software engineer, developed a device that works with an app to let people know when their wood stoves need tending: “Shah has created a Jetsons solution to a Flintstones problem.” (Angela Simpson, Burlington, Vt.)

To nominate favorite bits of recent writing from The Times or other publications to be mentioned in “For the Love of Sentences,” please email me here and include your name and place of residence.

What I’m Watching

- Netflix recently released a new season of “The Diplomat,” and once again, I found myself howling at the story’s implausibility, rolling my eyes at the tape loop of the two main characters’ preposterous marriage, devouring the whole of it and having a grand time. “The Diplomat” isn’t about international intrigue and political gamesmanship, though some of its plotting, especially in the final three of the season’s eight episodes, is electric. It’s about tremendously skilled actors (Keri Russell, Rufus Sewell, Allison Janney, Nana Mensah, Ali Ahn) delivering smart, stylized and precisely cadenced dialogue in regally decorated rooms. Works for me.
- Enough praise has been heaped on “You Can See Everything,” about the fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, that I feel compelled to play the contrarian. That’s not hard. As mesmerizing as the documentary can be, its three-hour length is indefensible, the result of a preciously high-concept, tedious final hour and the moviemakers’ decision to let almost every sniffle, every sob, every staring contest play out for twice as long as need be. The movie’s melodramatic score and extreme close-ups give it a campy quality that becomes grating as the minutes tick by. And its principal characters — including the comic Nathan Fielder, who directed the movie with Lance Oppenheim and points the camera at himself as often as at his interview subjects — beseech attention so aggressively that it can feel icky to reward them with it.

Retire These Words!

Many of you write in with excellent suggestions for words and phrases that warrant exile. But in some cases, I’ve covered that terrain in editions of the newsletter that you missed. So I thought it might be worthwhile to provide a bit of a map to semantic sins already exposed. I’m not sure that what follows is complete, but if not, it’s close. Each link leads you to the newsletter in which a given lament of mine appeared, almost always at the end, after other topics.

My first target, back in August 2022, was “unpack.” I subsequently cried foul at the ubiquity of “amazing” and at the banality of “it is what it is.” I pleaded for the sunset of “at the end of the day.” I noted the false promise of “long story short.”

When everything is an “existential” crisis, nothing is; the same goes for people, events and objects idolized as “iconic.” And when someone qualifies an observation with the defensive words “in all honesty,” a discerning reader or listener braces for at least a dab of falsity.

Something that’s not machine made isn’t ipso facto “handcrafted,” a description I’ve seen applied to deli sandwiches, for salami’s sake. And you can select something without “curating” it, at least if you’re willing to part with your pretensions.

Pretentiousness is the handmaiden of many grating words and phrases whose retirement I’ve lobbied for: An experience needn’t be a “journey,” a partisan propaganda operation is not a “think tank” and most writers and scholars do not qualify as “thought leaders” and “public intellectuals,” no matter how readily they accept those labels.

Nonsensical dog metaphors are too prevalent in conversation and prose, and our political discussions are polluted by such jargon as these terms and these and these and let us not forget this. We suffer verbal ignominies brought about by, or associated with, the current tenant of the White House, and we should be spared forevermore from “Trump derangement syndrome,” from any four-word phrase that begins with “make” and ends with “again,” and from “trump” as a verb outside the realm of a card game.

We also serve too many “word salads” in which “community” is presumptuously used. We bemoan “pearl clutching” as if there’s no alternative expression for exaggerated offense. We applaud a “laser focus” in people whose concentration doesn’t seem remarkable at all.

The phrase “happy wife, happy life” is often sexist and always dopey. “Sleeping with” is needlessly coy — own and enjoy the sex you’re having. And let’s avoid so many double negatives. They’re not without merit (oops!), but they’re indirect routes — journeys, if you will! — to destinations reachable more quickly and cleanly.

“Retire These Words!” is an occasional feature about overused, oddly used, erroneously used or just plain annoying locutions.

SUMMARY

At an event in Jerusalem in July, an opposition candidate for Israel’s Parliament kicked things off by asking what voters feared most if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing, religious government won another four-year term. ARTICLE

Israeli Jews Across the Spectrum Face an Election of Fears
Supporters and opponents of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have expressed intense anxieties about isolation abroad, security at home and the future of Israel’s identity.
By David M. Halbfinger
Published 2026-10-26 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/26/world/middleeast/israel-election-stakes.html

At an event in Jerusalem in July, an opposition candidate for Israel’s Parliament kicked things off by asking what voters feared most if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing, religious government won another four-year term. The answers were startling.

Israel would become even more of an international pariah, one said. “I’m afraid my children would leave,” said another. “I’d want my children to leave,” said a third.

It got darker from there. “Tyranny of the majority.” “Civil war.” “Collapse.”

Every national election is important, and many play on voters’ fears. But none has felt so consequential and dire to so many Israeli Jews as the one on Tuesday.

And no wonder: They have the chance to render a verdict on polarizing decisions that have torn the country apart for years — and to choose between starkly different visions for Israel’s future.

Perhaps the rawest emotions among Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents surround the question of whether the long-serving prime minister, legendary for his political survival skills, will be held accountable for the worst national-security failure in Israel’s history, the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre.

As traumatic and shocking as that attack was, many other deep questions about Israel’s character hang in the balance.

Will the country weaken its judiciary and grant the government far more power? Will it rewrite the social contract to demand service and sacrifice from all sectors of society?

Will it arrest accelerating emigration before a brain drain threatens its tech-driven economy and, close behind, its vaunted military?

Will Israel defy global opprobrium and try to thwart Palestinian aspirations to statehood once and for all, potentially risking its relationship with the United States? Or will it reverse course and attempt to repair ties, at least with Washington?

Finally, will it end Mr. Netanyahu’s tenure precisely at a moment when his staunchest supporters believe that his fortitude and skills are most needed to face down Israel’s adversaries on the global stage?

These issues are so divisive, and the country so polarized, that even a clear election result may not begin healing the rifts.

“Whoever wins, the other side will feel that they’re not part of the Israeli state,” said Yuval Eylon, a retired Israeli rear admiral and researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv.

In a recent poll, the institute found that 39 percent of Israelis fear violence between different segments of society — as many as fear an Iranian nuclear weapon.

“It’s really a danger for the Israeli state as an idea,” Mr. Eylon said. “Ten years ago, people said we could deal even with a nuclear Iran, because we’re strong as a country, strong inside. But if you don’t have unity of the people, then the external threat becomes a mortal threat.”

Targeting the Ultra-Orthodox

Dan Ben-David, president of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research, has been warning for years that Israel faces a demographic point of no return.

He focused largely on the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi Jews, who tend to have many children and educate them in religious schools that don’t teach math, science, English or civics. They also receive far more subsidies than they contribute in taxes, largely thanks to Mr. Netanyahu, who has relied on their support to stay in power.

The ultra-Orthodox are doubling as a percentage of the population every 25 years, even as fewer of them are prepared for jobs in a modern economy.

That is an unsustainable trend, Mr. Ben-David warns, and a key driver of another: Already, just 20 percent of Israel’s workers supply 93 percent of all income-tax revenue, while half of all Israelis are so poor that they pay no income tax whatsoever.

Crucially, the ultra-Orthodox have also avoided military service — first under a decades-old exemption, and then, after the Supreme Court ordered in 2024 that conscription begin, by simply draft-dodging.

The Gaza war brought that issue to the fore. Roughly half of Israel’s citizens serve in the army, bearing the burden, in casualties and reserve duty, of defending the country, while many Haredim loudly declare they would rather die than be drafted and shut down highways and train lines with protests.

“We ourselves hang in the balance here,” Israel Friedman, editor-in-chief of Yated Ne’eman, a Haredi daily newspaper, said in an interview. “What is at stake is our right to be Haredi.”

Mr. Ben-David, whose recommendations have been embraced to varying degrees by most opposition leaders, says the resulting fury at the ultra-Orthodox has created a rare chance not only to make them enlist but to cut their subsidies, overhaul a failing education system and reorient Israel toward a sustainable future.

If the opposition fails to dislodge Mr. Netanyahu and the Haredi parties now, he says, Israel may never get another chance.

A brain drain is already underway: The country faces an acute shortage of doctors, more people are moving out of the country than immigrating to it, and those leaving are better educated and better earners than those staying behind.

Should enough of Israel’s roughly 300,000 physicians, tech workers, professors, engineers — the citizens who could most easily take jobs elsewhere — decide to emigrate, Mr. Ben-David said, those left behind would be too unskilled to save the economy or defend themselves.

Israel simply “won’t be,” he said. “It’ll be over.”

The Threat of International Isolation

Even erstwhile Netanyahu allies worry that Israel’s international isolation could cost it dearly.

Michael Oren, who was Mr. Netanyahu’s deputy prime minister and ambassador to the United States, said that the spread of sanctions against Israel as it backs settlers in the occupied West Bank could devastate the economy.

“We’re going to have a choice of whether we’re going to build in E1 or have an economy,” he said, referring to a vast tract outside East Jerusalem where the government is pushing for new Israeli settlement. Critics say doing so would effectively cut the West Bank in two, making a contiguous Palestinian state all but impossible.

Mr. Oren said that a new government, by contrast, could buy some global good will by ending vigilante violence and illegal settlement construction in the West Bank, stating its desire for peace with Palestinians and disavowing territorial ambitions in Gaza, Syria or Lebanon.

But he added that the damage in relations with some U.S. Democrats was done: “It’s no longer what we do but who we are, and no matter who the prime minister is, it’s not going to make much difference.”

Fears Over Security and the Courts

Many Israelis who oppose the government describe Tuesday’s vote as make-or-break.

“The building is burning,” said Paul Gross, a British-born author of a new book on Israeli democracy, “and this election is about putting the fire out.”

What worries him most, Mr. Gross said, is the prospect that the government could finish what it started in 2022: an effort to undermine the judiciary and give itself effectively unchecked power.

“The last time, we could always say, this isn’t what people voted for,” he said. “Netanyahu ran on security and Iran, not on judicial reform. This time, no one can claim they don’t know what the government’s intentions are.”

Without a strong judiciary, he could envision some demonstrations being barred, he said, noting that Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have already voted to ban some political parties only for the Supreme Court to stop those moves. Without that judicial check, “you really are in authoritarian territory,” he said. “That is very scary.”

Backers of the judicial overhaul, of course, see it positively, as a chance to bolster democracy by removing power from “deep state” judges and bureaucrats, and returning it to elected lawmakers and ministers.

But the prospect has many Israelis obtaining or renewing foreign passports and considering options elsewhere.

Alexandra Benjamin, who moved to Israel from London a quarter-century ago, said she was eyeing the exits out of despair over the country’s politics.

She mentioned the widespread denigration of the rights of Arab citizens and political leftists, and how some citizens had been willing to write off Israeli hostages held in Gaza for the sake of destroying Hamas.

“If we end up with the same government, I just can’t see how to be in Israel anymore,” Ms. Benjamin said. “Do my kids really have a future here? Do I? Is the state of Israel even sustainable?”

Ms. Benjamin, 49, has lived in Israel through difficult times, including the Second Intifada, when about 1,000 Israelis were killed in attacks, but had not considered leaving till now. “External” threats like from Iran, she said, had never made her afraid to stay.

“That didn’t challenge my sense of purpose and the sense of identity around this society and who we are, and who we want to be,” she said. “But you have to decide, has the country changed in a way that I can’t stay bought all-in?

She added, “It’s hopelessness about the country, but also, like, who are these voters who will re-elect these people?”

Fights Over Identity and Faith

Few supporters of the current government talk about emigrating.

Rather, many right-wing Israelis say that their determination to stay, no matter what, makes them the real Zionists, and grants them a moral superiority over others, said Shraga Bar-On, a settler and a professor of Jewish thought at the Shalom Hartman Institute.

But they, too, see the stakes as enormous.

For Israeli settlers led by the far-right Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister in Mr. Netanyahu’s government, re-election would be a chance to drive a stake through the heart of a two-state solution and declare Israel’s sovereignty over the West Bank — land they see as their biblical birthright, and the heart of a potential Palestinian state that they consider a fundamental threat.

Mr. Smotrich calls for Palestinians to submit to Israeli rule or leave.

“If, God forbid, a government from the left comes to power, its view of Judea and Samaria would be entirely different,” said Yair Frank, rabbi of the Amihai settlement, using the biblical names for the West Bank. “Development could come to a halt, or things could become even worse.”

For Mr. Netanyahu’s die-hard supporters, Israel’s international isolation is only an added reason to keep him in power. No one else, they often say, is capable of defending the country, prosecuting multi-front wars and standing up to President Trump, let alone to the rest of the world.

The rhetoric is even more apocalyptic among the ultra-Orthodox. Some say they feel hated or demonized, and compare their situation to how it felt to be Jewish in 1930s Germany.

Mr. Friedman, the Haredi editor, argued that yeshiva students ought to be exempt from the draft because the military threatens the Haredi way of life. “This is an army with a gender agenda, an army with an educational agenda,” he said. “This is what we oppose: the melting pot. I don’t want a melting pot. I want to be Amish.”

Deep Divisions

To some, perhaps the most frightening thing about the election is the possibility that the outcome does nothing to cool the tensions bubbling over in Israeli society.

Ehud Olmert, a former prime minister, said he feared the polarization could spark violence. “It was always underneath the issues of the day, but never did we arrive at a point of physical confrontation as it is now,” he said.

It felt, Mr. Bar-On said, as though “every segment of Israeli society is completely sure that the others want to crush it.”

Some Israelis have been reaching back to ancient times for comparisons, noting that Israel, at 78 years old, is roughly the same age as two Jewish states that didn’t survive their third generations: the biblical kingdom of Saul, David and Solomon, and the Hasmonean dynasty, which fell to Pompey the Great of Rome.

Amotz Asa-El, a veteran columnist, argues in a new book that modern Israel is failing to heed the grim lessons of ancient Jewish civil wars.

“I feel the willingness and ability to assault fellow Jews,” he said. “That’s how civil wars begin. Talk to people and you feel that they hate each other.”

He recalled a first-century historian’s observation: “Josephus at one point says the Jews were so divided, while the Romans approached, that arguments invaded families and split them down the middle,” he said. “I feel that happening here.”

Johnatan Reiss contributed reporting.
