ARTICLE

A Historic Show of Strength for Israel’s Arab Minority
Voters supporting two leading Arab parties turned out in record numbers to voice their opposition to the Netanyahu government in Tuesday’s election.
By Liam Stack
Published 2026-10-27 23:50 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/world/middleeast/israel-election-arab-parties.html

One of the most striking results from the election in Israel on Tuesday was the unusually strong showing by two leading Arab parties, whose voters turned out in record numbers to express their opposition to the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The final results have not been announced, but a range of exit polls conducted by Israeli broadcasters suggest that two of the parties — the socially conservative United Arab List, or Raam, and the left-wing Joint List — may have won a historically large number of seats in parliament and an important role in the formation of the country’s next government.

Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.”

He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal.

The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers.

Most Arab citizens are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence.

Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies.

Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box.

This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice.

“I’m very optimistic because people understand that this isn’t like ordinary elections — we want change,” said Kholoud Al-Zeinati, 39, an Arab Israeli voter who cast her ballot on Tuesday in the mixed Jewish-Arab city of Lod, where long lines formed at polling places. “Because we, as the Arab community, are the community that pays the biggest price across so many aspects of life, it’s important to come out and take part.”

“I expect our votes to be truly decisive in shaping the next government and making things better for all of us,” she added.

Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.

Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history.

That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout.

Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting from Lod, Israel.

SUMMARY

When I was Politics editor of The Times in 2018, polls indicated that Democrats were likely to ride a wave of anti-Trump energy to win big in the midterm elections. Are polls overestimating the Democrats’ chances? They work on our Times/Siena Poll, which is widely considered to be one of the most accurate polls in U.S. politics, and Nate recently explored the question of polls and Democrats’ chances in his newsletter, The Tilt.

ARTICLE

Are Polls Overstating Democrats’ Midterm Leads? Times Pollsters Weigh In.
Members of the team behind the Times/Siena Poll on what the data show, how they’ve improved their methodology and what it means to be “right.”
By Patrick Healy, Nate Cohn and William P. Davis
Published 2026-10-28 09:05 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/insider/polls-midterm-election.html

When I was Politics editor of The Times in 2018, polls indicated that Democrats were likely to ride a wave of anti-Trump energy to win big in the midterm elections. Democrats went on to capture control of the House of Representatives, but Republicans did better than expected in a couple of red states — Missouri and Indiana — and increased their Senate majority.

Now we face another midterm election with President Trump in office, and polls again favor the Democrats, including in the House. Recent New York Times/Siena polls also show the party with a slight edge to flip the Senate. But that may come down once more to Senate races in red states like Texas, Ohio and Kansas.

Are polls overestimating the Democrats’ chances? What are we doing to accurately capture support for candidates? I’ve been thinking about these questions in my current role focusing on reader trust in The Times. For instance, we published a poll in October showing a healthy lead for James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas. Many other polls also show Talarico leading. Given the base-line partisanship of Texas and voters’ track record of electing Republicans there, regardless of headwinds, I wondered whether readers would trust our polls or question their credibility.

I recently spoke about polling and the midterms with Nate Cohn, our chief political analyst, and William P. Davis, who leads our Election Analytics department. They work on our Times/Siena Poll, which is widely considered to be one of the most accurate polls in U.S. politics, and Nate recently explored the question of polls and Democrats’ chances in his newsletter, The Tilt. Our interview has been edited and condensed.

Let’s start with a point-blank question. Should people trust these polls showing Democrats running ahead or neck-and-neck in red states?

NATE COHN: You can trust them to a degree. You can trust the polls to usually be in the ballpark, but you can’t trust them to be exactly “right.” Polls are inherently imprecise and subject to many sources of error.

So if by “trust” you mean “assume that the leading candidate will win,” then the answer is “no.” The polls have been wrong by this standard before and they will be wrong again. But if trust means “rely on the polls as the best source of information on the electorate, even if an inexact one,” then the answer is yes.

WILLIAM P. DAVIS: There are a lot of indicators pointing in the same direction this year — polls of specific races, President Trump’s approval rating, the fact that Republican candidates in deep-red states are distancing themselves from the president, the expectation that Democrats have a turnout advantage in midterm elections, etc.

The question becomes: How good of a year will it be for Democrats? Polls suggest a pretty good one. But whether the national results swing eight or 10 or 12 points to the left from 2024 will make a material difference in whether or not Democrats are able to take the Senate, and polls can’t guarantee that level of precision.

But some people read a Times poll headline saying so-and-so is ahead and take that to the bank. What do you say to people who see our Senate polls and regard them as predictions for Election Day?

WILL: Polls measure public opinion at a specific point in time. If people are still making up their minds, or late-breaking information upends a race, any prior poll will miss it. Polls can help us understand which races are close, and why; we won’t know until the results are in how they will shake out.

As rigorous as our polls are, I’m a little skeptical that a Democratic Senate candidate will win in Texas, given historical candidate performance there. What’s your pushback on that?

NATE: I’d say that you shouldn’t be quite so skeptical. Over the Trump era, Texas Republicans have become dependent on elevated levels of support from Hispanic voters. Without them, Texas is highly competitive, as Republicans have lost enormous support among white voters in the state’s highly educated suburbs. Every available piece of evidence — from our polls to on-the-ground reporting — suggests that the G.O.P.’s gains among this group have evaporated.

For good measure, the G.O.P. has nominated a candidate — Ken Paxton — who has been investigated, indicted and impeached. Add in a hostile national political environment for Republicans, and I don’t think there would be anything surprising about a Democratic win in Texas. Nearly every nonpartisan poll since at least Labor Day has shown Talarico ahead.

WILL: It’s reasonable, even good, to be skeptical. But people also have a false memory of Texas polls in the past. Most polls did not show Beto O’Rourke ahead in the 2018 Senate race against Ted Cruz. Our Times/Siena poll of that race had O’Rourke down eight points, and he actually only lost by 2.5 points, so we underestimated him a bit in that race. This year’s race is still pretty close, but it’s undeniable that Talarico is doing better there in polls than any Democrat in recent history.

I raised the question earlier of reader trust in polls. Readers have asked me if we’re “sure” that our Texas polling is right and whether we would kill the poll if we weren’t sure. How do you see that? And do we ever not publish polls that we’ve conducted?

NATE: It might seem strange, but it’s pretty important that we publish every survey result. We’ve never withheld a Times/Siena poll result. Many smart election analysts would have never imagined Trump winning in 2016, would have never imagined that Democrats could have avoided a “red wave” in 2022, or would have never believed Trump could surge among young and nonwhite voters in 2024 — if it weren’t for polls raising it as a real possibility.

And if The Times had withheld positive polls for Trump in 2016, we would have been accused of bias.

NATE: Yes. We would absolutely be accused of cherry-picking polls that fit a partisan bias or, even worse, in order to fit or construct a partisan narrative.

Of course, there are sometimes good reasons to wonder whether our poll is in the ballpark. That’s especially true when there’s a lot of other polling or our reporting shows something different. When we get an outlier like that, we can be cautious about the result in our write-up.

Even when the poll does appear to be a true outlier, it doesn’t mean it’s wrong. In 2022, I downplayed the result of a poll in Kansas’s Third District, which showed the Democrat Sharice Davids ahead by 14 points. This seemed totally bonkers. The race was considered a true tossup, with both parties spending millions of dollars. One Democratic pollster called the result “cray” and sent the laughing-while-crying emoji. In a very rare move, the Democratic campaign even disputed the result: “I don’t know what model The Times is using but this is going to be a very tight race. Our polls show it’s a true tossup at this point.”

In the end, Davids won by 12 points. I still get flack for downplaying the result.

Even modest polling errors in the past have underestimated Republican strength. Why is that, and what have we done to account for it?

WILL: Poll error from years when Donald Trump has been on the ballot are top of mind for most people, and with good reason. The chief theory for why polls have missed relates to who polls have a hard time reaching: low-education voters who don’t vote as regularly. If those voters overwhelmingly favor one candidate over another, and if polls don’t reach enough of these voters, that can add up to the sorts of issues many pollsters saw in 2016.

At the Times/Siena Poll, we put a lot of effort into reaching these voters, in part by placing more calls to voters who are less likely to respond. That ends up costing us a lot more money, but it pays off: In 2024, we saw early on that Trump was building a lead with these voters.

And we are continually reviewing how our poll performs and making improvements. In 2024, we made a change to keep in our poll results respondents who hang up mid-survey. This year, we made significant changes to how we weight our polls, with the goal being to better account for the types of people we have a hard time reaching.

Do we know how to poll Democrats better than we know how to poll Republicans?

NATE: Not necessarily. When polls underestimate Republicans, it’s entirely possible that Democrats contribute to the problem. Imagine, for instance, if the “resistance” Democrats are much likelier to take a poll than a working class registered Democrat who sometimes votes for Trump.

What else have we learned from past polls, and what are we doing differently this year?

NATE: The thing that we’ve learned over the last decade — and that the industry as a whole has learned — is that even a perfectly designed survey will probably underrepresent Trump’s supporters.

As Will mentioned, we’ve adopted a new method for “weighting,” the technique pollsters use to give more weight to underrepresented groups. The new approach lets us leverage the rich data we have on our survey respondents while weighting the poll to more thoroughly represent the population. This approach improved our past polls when we took the data from our old surveys and applied the new weighting approach. It would have especially helped in the white working-class states where polls have erred in the past, but that’s no guarantee of better results in this cycle or the future.

WILL: There are serious challenges to making sure you have the right methodology, that you’re reaching a representative group, that your weighting is correcting for the things that matter most. We sweat every one of those decisions.

And there are other ways to mess up beyond the methodology of the poll. The specific wording of questions is difficult to get right. Our colleague Ruth Igielnik leads our questionnaire development process, and we often spend weeks refining the specific language we use. But we sometimes realize after scrutinizing the results, reviewing recordings of calls, calling back voters and comparing our results to other polls that we didn’t quite get it right.

One example was in 2023, when we found that more than 20 percent of voters in the presidential battlegrounds said they would support Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for president. We had a lot of reasons to believe that number was way too high: We compared our numbers to what others were finding, we looked at what respondents supporting Kennedy said in other questions, and we had a theory about what caused the issue.

We still released the results, but we worked hard to place it in the proper context when we wrote our story about the finding. It was uncomfortable for us, to somewhat disavow our own finding. But we thought it revealed something about how unpopular Trump and Biden were, and we tried to explain that. And a few months later, we conducted an experiment to try to prove out our theory of why we got such a flawed result. Our theory was proved correct, and we wrote that up, too, to try to help readers better understand how polling works.

We reported the other day that a fake polling firm had deceived The Times and other polling aggregators with several phony poll results. They said they were trying to “demonstrate the vulnerabilities” in the political polling field. Size this up — what did they prove and what did they not?

WILL: It’s worth noting that the “polls” put out by this group, which went by Wedgewood Polls, had no bearing on our own Times/Siena polls. They appeared in our poll trackers but did not receive prominence in our coverage.

Wedgewood certainly proved that we’re not perfect. But they claimed that The Times and others had included their polls without vetting them, and that’s not true. The Times vets all new pollsters, asking a series of questions designed to determine whether a group is attempting to field representative polls, learn where their funding comes from.

This process has weeded out untrustworthy pollsters. But Wedgewood deceived us — as they appear to have deceived others who asked similar questions or even gave them money. It’s not clear to me that their true goal was to demonstrate vulnerabilities. We are putting a lot of thought into how we could have found these issues out earlier.

One thing the episode highlighted is the way that newer pollsters can attract attention. The group was able to quickly gain traction, in part by claiming to be associated with another polling group and in part by polling some races that had little polling.

It’s gotten evermore expensive to field a high-quality poll and ever-cheaper to field a low-quality one. And A.I. is making it easier than ever to fake things. The Times/Siena Poll is one of a few pollsters left with the resources to both put a focus on quality and poll many of the key races each election. Increasingly, pollsters are having to choose between one or the other.

Last question. If Election Day results are materially different than our polling suggests, is the polling worth the risk to our credibility?

WILL: In the end, I will regard how well we did as journalists by how well our coverage reflected what ended up happening.

If Democrats do really poorly, we should do some soul searching about both our methods and the questions we asked, as we would for any other story we got wrong.

If Democrats do well but fail to take the Senate, I would ask myself how well our coverage prepared readers for that possibility. I hope the answer is that it prepared them well, because we’re constantly talking about how to ensure our coverage prepares people for this scenario. I would also ask how well our poll questions helped us understand and explain why these races were so close.

Similarly, if Democrats do much better than expected, I would ask myself how well we understood the circumstances that caused so many Trump voters to either stay home or switch to Democrats.

NATE: Polling isn’t like a lot of the other journalism at The Times. Most of the report is about facts. If Peter Baker says that Trump’s going to Illinois tomorrow, that’s a fact. A poll is not a fact. It’s a best measurement. There’s no guarantee that a “best” measurement is good enough — whether in terms of The Times’s credibility or whether it improves our understanding of politics. Historically, there have absolutely been elections when it didn’t feel like polling passed that test. The 2016 election is the easiest example; there will be another election like it again.

That said, readers come to The Times to understand American politics, which includes an understanding of public opinion during an election. For better or worse, polling is really the only quantitative measure of the attitudes of the electorate. There just isn’t an alternative. The polls will still drive the political conversation, even if The Times doesn’t conduct any of its own polling. Campaigns run on polls. Our coverage would inevitably be affected by the polls that others are conducting. If that’s going to be the case, it’s probably better that we’re conducting our own.

SUMMARY

I spent Monday morning at a breakfast hosted by the prediction market company Kalshi. The only time I have ever really considered prediction markets as a parenting issue is when I wrote about the rise of addictive gambling among young men since sports betting became legal in some states in 2018. At the breakfast, Lara said that prediction markets are not like sports books or casinos, citing the mechanics of how Kalshi works.

ARTICLE

Is This the Gateway Drug for Gambling?
We actually can regulate prediction markets, and we should do it now.
By Jessica Grose
Published 2026-10-28 09:06 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/opinion/kalshi-teens-wager-sports.html

I spent Monday morning at a breakfast hosted by the prediction market company Kalshi. At an event space in Manhattan with soaring ceilings and tables stacked with bagel towers, Emily Oster, a best-selling parenting writer and economist, and the Kalshi co-founder Luana Lopes Lara had a conversation billed as being about “how data, forecasting and probabilities can sharpen our choices,” which promised to “tackle parents’ questions about prediction markets.”

My first thought when I received the Paperless Post was: How is Kalshi going to help me sharpen my choices as a mom? The only time I have ever really considered prediction markets as a parenting issue is when I wrote about the rise of addictive gambling among young men since sports betting became legal in some states in 2018.

Prediction markets are regulated differently from sports betting platforms, where there is a house that collects and pays off bets. Kalshi doesn’t have to abide by state laws on gambling (though there are lawsuits pending about this loophole), and it doesn’t have to pay the same taxes.

What Kalshi does is provide a platform to match opposing traders and it earns fees when trades are executed. The bigger the pool of people making trades on its platform, the more money Kalshi makes. This summer, wagering on the World Cup exploded on Kalshi. The company recorded $27 billion in trading during tournament play, according to Reuters.

Most states require sports bettors to be 21, while most prediction markets allow users as young as 18. A CNN analysis published at the end of August found that Kalshi users between the ages of 18 and 21 traded $5 billion on the platform this year, though that’s only about 3 percent of the company’s trading volume.

At the breakfast, Lara said that prediction markets are not like sports books or casinos, citing the mechanics of how Kalshi works. The platform allows betting on all sorts of events beyond sports — like whether “The Odyssey” will win the best picture Oscar or whether it will rain tomorrow. Because prediction markets make their money off transaction fees, regardless of whether traders win or lose, Lara described the company as having more noble incentives than traditional sports books, and also ones that are more aligned with users.

It is true that the inner workings of prediction markets aren’t the same as sports betting apps. But according to every gambling addiction expert, psychologist and pediatrician I have ever spoken to, users treat sports books and prediction markets as interchangeable (The consensus seems to be: If it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck. …).

A majority of Kalshi’s trades come from sports. In fact, the company previously advertised itself as the “first app for legal sports betting in all 50 states.” Polymarket, the other leading prediction market in the United States, also has the highest volume of its trades from sports. The N.B.A. just made deals with both Kalshi and Polymarket.

According to an analysis by The Wall Street Journal in May, on both Kalshi and Polymarket, “losers vastly outnumber winners.” Though advertising by prediction markets suggests big paydays for regular Joes, professionals dominate winnings. My sense is that Gen Z is turning to prediction markets in part because the traditional ways of building wealth feel out of reach to them. The job market stinks, the potential for artificial intelligence destruction of many industries, if not humanity, looms, so why not put some of your piddling savings on whether the Timberwolves will win by over 5.5 points tonight?

Abdullah Mahmood, a licensed social worker who works with problem gamblers in Columbus, Ohio, told me that some of his younger clients — between the ages of 18 and 24, he estimates — started their betting addictions with prediction markets. Mahmood said that for many young men, their identity is rooted in sports, which can be communal. But that love of sports and sense of identity are “being wrapped in trading and gambling,” and that’s perverting what could have been very positive for them, he said.

Dr. Shawn Kelly, a pediatrician in Ottawa who specializes in adolescent addiction medicine, said, “From a youth brain perspective specifically, there is no discernible difference” between prediction markets and sports betting. From the time children become adolescents, until their brain fully matures in their early-to-mid 20s, they are particularly vulnerable to the allure of short-term rewards and the chemical rush of dopamine that goes with it.

At the breakfast, Lara addressed some of the risks Kalshi could pose for young users. She explained that her platform has a strict age-verification system that requires a Social Security number, name, date of birth and form of identification to keep minors from trading. Lara did acknowledge that there are specific risks for users ages 18 to 21, and that these young adults can elect to give a parent access to all of their transactions.

This week, Kalshi rolled out a $2,500 deposit limit for its youngest customers, “unless you have proof of funds or self-attestation that you know the risks associated with trading and the contracts.” Lara added that the company has a partnership with Birches Health, which provides treatment for compulsive behaviors, including a gambling addiction self-test.

While I appreciated this acknowledgment, it also reveals the contradiction at the heart of Kalshi’s public image: We’re not gambling, but we provide resources for gambling addiction and give millions to the National Council on Problem Gambling. We’re not gambling, but we acknowledge that there are higher risks for our younger users whose brains are still forming.

The company wants to be seen as taking these matters seriously and creating its own guardrails. Tarek Mansour, Kalshi’s other founder, told PBS last month that theirs is a pro-regulation company. In practice, that seems to mean only the regulations it picks and chooses.

At the event, Lara mentioned that the company sued regulators at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to expand its business to include predictions for elections. The commission argued that it was not in the public interest and that the regulator was not equipped to offer fraud protection in that context. Kalshi won and “the litigation actually helped with a lot of other markets.”

Attorneys general in 44 states signed onto a letter this year to try to claw back the power to regulate prediction markets from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, calling them a “new form of casino” and citing research that shows the younger someone starts gambling, the greater the likelihood of developing a problem. We do not have to accept the widespread availability of prediction markets as normal, even if this breakfast treated it as part of our inevitable financial future.

Toward the end, Lara said a market she follows closely is about artificial intelligence. Specifically, she likes one about whether the Citrini scenario, a doomsday forecast predicting that A.I. will destroy the economy, will happen. When I checked on Tuesday morning, 19 percent of Kalshi users wagering on the question put their money behind “yes.”

I hate those odds. As a parent, I’m not sure how that data is supposed to help me. I want to put my money behind “no” to all of it.

End Notes

- Yes, I read Alexandra Alter’s profile of the tech titan Marissa Mayer and her new personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle, which is pitched to busy working moms. Yes, I think it’s weird that she asked a bot to come up with three things that made her daughter special. But I was more struck by how out of touch she is with the user base of regular parents she hopes to reach.
- I have been doing this for so long, I wrote about Mayer’s maternity leave controversy for Bloomberg in 2012, when I was very pregnant with my now older daughter. I stand by that take, which is that her experience of maternity leave — she reportedly built a nursery next to her office — is so different from your average person’s as to be completely irrelevant. Our energy is better spent fighting for policy changes than worrying about whatever she’s doing. Feel free to drop me a line about anything here.

SUMMARY

A generation of baby boomers, aging into retirement, are starting to sell their machine shops, plumbing companies and dentistry practices to private equity firms. Then in 2022, Hoffmann Family of Companies, a Florida-based private equity and investment firm, purchased one of the two remaining ferry services. Situations like this are happening all over the country, and it’s only going to get worse as more baby boomers retire and sell their companies to private equity.

ARTICLE

Baby Boomers Are Retiring in Droves. Private Equity Is Waiting.
Investors in big cities are quietly consuming small businesses all over the country.
By Doug Lepisto
Published 2026-10-28 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/opinion/private-equity-baby-boomers-investors.html

A generation of baby boomers, aging into retirement, are starting to sell their machine shops, plumbing companies and dentistry practices to private equity firms.

Deal by deal, ownership is being extracted from the thousands of communities where businesses were built to the handful of cities where capital is already concentrated. For the new owners, the primary, and often exclusive, connection to the community is the profit they can derive from the acquired asset. Left unchecked, this historic migration will lead to a new geography of inequality.

The mass retirement of baby boomer business owners is helping accelerate this shift. The scale of this “silver tsunami” is difficult to fully appreciate. More than half of America’s small businesses have owners over the age of 55. These companies earn $6.5 trillion in revenue each year. And many of their owners do not have a succession plan.

Private equity firms, once primarily known for leveraged buyouts of large corporations, are seizing this opportunity. The formula is straightforward: Buy a downtown dentist practice for a relative bargain, merge it with a collection of other dental practices across the country and sell control of the agglomeration for a premium. In 2024, private equity firms had completed over 1,500 acquisitions under $25 million, an over 40 percent increase over the last decade.

Firms are now consolidating numerous niche industries. Alpine Investors, an $18.5 billion private equity firm based in San Francisco, founded Apex Service Partners in 2019 for the purpose of buying and consolidating ownership of independent HVAC, plumbing and electrical companies. Now it owns around 75 local brands in 46 states. The same is happening in garage door repair and roofing businesses.

This migration of ownership is playing out north of where I live in Michigan, on Mackinac Island, a small community known for its sweeping coastline, fudge and lack of cars.

For decades, thousands of visitors reached its shores via three commercial ferry services. In 2016, the third route was acquired by one of the two existing lines. Then in 2022, Hoffmann Family of Companies, a Florida-based private equity and investment firm, purchased one of the two remaining ferry services. It was a family business. “They’re keeping everything the same, including the name — nothing really is going to change from the guest perspective,” the ferry president, Chris Shepler, 59 at the time of the sale, told The Detroit Free Press.

Hoffmann later bought the other ferry service, as well as the private boat charter service and the private dock, giving it a near monopoly on transport to the island. By 2024, the firm also owned two area newspapers as well as more than 116 parcels of land, 51 buildings and 6,500 parking spaces, making it the largest real-estate owner in the Mackinac region.

Changes quickly ensued. Ticket prices rose. Ferry users had to start paying extra to bring on a bike; parking fees increased. The result was war, with the Mackinac Island government taking Hoffmann to court. The local tourism director reported spending $155,000 in additional advertising to counter the negative press generated by the dispute. A resort owner, Liz Ware, said groups interested in booking her place for meetings started to ask whether they would still be able to reach the island. Michigan sided with the island government, granting it authority to regulate the economics of all elements involving ferry access. As a result, Hoffmann has threatened to stop operations in 2027.

Situations like this are happening all over the country, and it’s only going to get worse as more baby boomers retire and sell their companies to private equity.

If we do nothing, the confluence of private equity and the silver tsunami will create an even wider gap between communities that own and control their services and those that do not. Some communities — New York, Miami, San Francisco — will gain more ownership, more wealth and more power. Others, like Mackinac Island, are drained of control, upside and civic influence. For Americans to have a say in their economic futures, they must make protecting local ownership a national priority.

Nonprofits can help, but they cannot, by themselves, solve a problem created by the market. We need capitalists — investors and entrepreneurs — willing to build investment models that treat place-based ownership as an advantage. I helped found an investment fund that backs aspiring business owners who want to acquire and expand West Michigan businesses. We operate with a mandate that our businesses should not only be profitable, but also benefit their communities. With $150 million in investment capital, our firm is a relatively small player, but it is a start.

Local government already helps communities attract employers, support expansions and encourage new business formation. But it can do more, by helping aging business owners find local successors and encouraging investments that keep ownership in communities. Economic development officials should know which sectors and firms are most important to the local economy and who needs to be connected before a succession crisis arrives.

Higher education can also help. Colleges have long trained students to work for companies or start them. They should also prepare students for careers in which they ultimately acquire and lead existing businesses. Ownership is not only a Silicon Valley start-up story. It can also be a path to preserving the companies that hold a local economy together.

Finally, we need a culture that lionizes the steward as much as the founder. America celebrates successful founders but forgets that many celebrated business figures were not there from the start. Ray Kroc bought McDonald’s. Howard Schultz bought Starbucks. Steve Jobs bought the outfit that became Pixar.

For a long time, America has treated local business ownership as a private matter. But when millions of owners reach the exit at the same time, private decisions become a national reckoning. The question is whether America will renew a culture of local empowerment or let economic control keep concentrating in the places that already have it.

Doug Lepisto is a professor at Western Michigan University and a founder of Sleeping Giant Capital.

trump-law-lawlessness-presidency-congress.html

SUMMARY

For all the power the president held, supporters of the Constitution in each of the 13 states argued, he was still bound by law. Donald Trump is not the first president to break the law. He is not the first president to disregard the law.

ARTICLE

Trump Cannot Be the End of the Story
Trump has no use for pretense and he’s not interested in playing along.
By Jamelle Bouie
Published 2026-10-28 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/opinion/trump-law-lawlessness-presidency-congress.html

Writing under the pseudonym Publicola in support of the new Constitution, the North Carolina attorney and legislator Archibald Maclaine rebuffed critics who charged that the president was little more than a king.

“It is a maxim in the British government that the king can do no wrong; that is, he is not amenable to the courts of justice, as the law has not provided any punishment for his misconduct.” But, Maclaine wrote, “the president of the United States will be liable to be impeached by the representatives of the people, and to be tried for his crimes.”

Even more emphatic, on this point, was the Federalist writer Americanus. Should the president “at any time be impelled by ambition, or blinded by passion, and boldly attempt to pass the bounds prescribed to his power, he is liable to be impeached and removed from office; and afterwards he is subject to indictment, trial, judgment and punishment according to the law.”

For all the power the president held, supporters of the Constitution in each of the 13 states argued, he was still bound by law. And his job, fundamentally, was to faithfully execute the laws. He was not subordinate to Congress, but he wasn’t its master, either.

When it comes to the actual operation of government, however, practice matters more than theory. It was George Washington’s service as the nation’s first president that, as much as anything else, structured the relationship between the two branches. Washington imbued the office with his stature. He commanded respect and so, too, would the presidency, even when held by men without his bearing or accomplishments. And as the United States democratized and the office became something like a vessel for the national mood, individual presidents also took on the respect accorded the popular will in a democratic society.

All the while, the office was bounded by law. When presidents exceeded their given authority, they worked to justify their actions in terms of law, whether ordinary statutes or the higher law of the Constitution. “Are all the laws, but one, to go unexecuted, and the government itself go to pieces, lest that one be violated?” Abraham Lincoln asked when confronted over his use of war powers in the opening months of the slaveholders’ rebellion. His point was that however much he exceeded his authority, he did so in defense of the Constitution, in accordance with his oath.

Donald Trump is not the first president to break the law. He is not the first president to disregard the law. He is not even the first president to insist that his actions cannot, on some deep ontological level, be illegal. But he may be the first president to abandon the pretense that the law matters at all.

The canonical example of presidential lawbreaking, Watergate, was a cover-up because Richard Nixon believed himself obligated to give lip service to the law. He hid his actions from the public out of fealty to the idea that he was bound by law, even if he didn’t agree. His hypocrisy, as the saying goes, was his tribute to virtue.

Trump has no use for pretense, and he’s not interested in playing along. He thinks he is a law unto himself; that he holds sovereign authority over the entire country; that he can rule by decree and punish those who resist. As one would expect, his administration has been an exercise in breaking the law, exceeding its bounds and violating its spirit. His lawyers may dutifully argue that their client is acting within his lawful authority, but the character of his actions betrays contempt for the law itself.

His basic approach, in fact, is to ignore or break the law and hope that the Republican-appointed majority on the Supreme Court will use his lawbreaking to advance its pet ideological projects. Chief Justice John Roberts, to use just one example, is preoccupied with the expansion of executive power at the expense of Congress. And it seems that in his view, an erratic, lawless president is a small price to pay for summoning the unitary executive into existence.

One important result of this interplay was the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in Trump v. United States, which shielded presidents from criminal prosecution as long as their actions related to core duties and official acts. As you might imagine, a clever teenager could find the many ways this might apply to virtually anything, legal or illegal, the president wants to do. Under this standard, even Watergate may well have been perfectly cromulent.

Trump has let it be known that he is considering a set of blanket pardons for subordinates in his administration. We don’t know for certain the extent of the lawbreaking in the Trump administration, but we know it’s there. If they win Congress next week, Democrats will investigate and perhaps, in the future, issue criminal referrals. Blanket pardons would preclude federal criminal accountability for anyone who broke the law at Trump’s behest. Worse, they would give subordinates an incentive to continue breaking the law — or enabling the president’s lawless behavior — secure in the knowledge that they, too, will walk away unscathed.

It has never been outside the realm of possibility that a president would order his officers to engage in illegal behavior and then issue pardons to shield them and himself. George Mason warned of it at Virginia’s ratification convention. “Now, I conceive that the president ought not to have the power of pardoning, because he may frequently pardon crimes which were advised by himself,” Mason said. “It may happen at some future day that he will establish a monarchy and destroy the Republic. If he has the power of granting pardons before indictment or conviction, may he not stop inquiry and prevent detection?”

Similar observations were made by skeptics of the Constitution at Maryland’s ratifying convention, as attested to by Luther Martin of Maryland, a leading anti-Federalist who had left the Philadelphia convention in protest. “It was said that no treason was so likely to take place as that in which the president himself might be engaged — the attempt to assume to himself powers not given by the Constitution, and establish himself in regal authority — in which attempt a provision is made for him to secure from punishment the creatures of his ambition, the associates and abettors of his treasonable practices, by granting them pardons should they be defeated in their attempts to subvert the Constitution.”

If this loaded gun hasn’t been fired, a major reason is that most presidents understood themselves to be stewards of a democratic republic. This kind of lawless pardon has never really been on the table, as egotistic and power-hungry as many of them have been.

It matters a great deal then that Trump does not see himself as a steward of a democracy. The country, to him, is little more than a large and lucrative piece of real estate. And his obligations appear to extend only as far as his pecuniary interests. His ideological obsession with whitening the United States can be seen in terms of his fundamentally aesthetic preoccupations. What else is mass deportation than the effort of a lifelong landlord to remove the people he thinks degrade the value of the property?

Which is just to say that of course Trump would be the first president to contemplate blanket pardons for his subordinates. The only real surprise is that he hasn’t done it already.

It is worth placing all of this in relation to the Supreme Court’s efforts to shield the president from the law. To grant the president criminal immunity on top of his plenary power to pardon is, in effect, to extend the zone of lawlessness to the entire executive branch. The part of government meant to execute and enforce the law is now — or is at least potentially — free from it altogether.

There is a word for a system where the chief executive is outside the law and can use the force of the state against his enemies without any real obstacle, a word that was very much on the minds of the framers of the Constitution: tyranny.

As dire as this is, the opposition is not without options. There are things Democrats can do to begin to deal with the crisis of a lawless president and administration. They can create a civil cause of action against executive branch officers, allowing victims of abuse to sue federal officials in court for damages. You may not be able to hold a Stephen Miller criminally accountable, but you could drain his bank account, knowing full well that Trump will not come to the rescue.

A more ambitious move would be to introduce a constitutional amendment limiting the scope of the pardon power. This would not work retroactively, but it would restrain future presidents.

Even in the absence of an amendment, Democrats should begin to think creatively about Trump’s pardons and potential pardons, from those issued to the Jan. 6 rioters to the corrupt pardons given to those with the president’s ear and a little cash to spend.

Here, it is useful to think about the Constitution not just as a collection of clauses, but as a holistic document written to establish republican government under the rule of law. The text of the document may state an unlimited pardon power, but to judge that text against the ethos of the document is to see a more nuanced picture. A Constitution that would allow the president to break the law and then pardon the perpetrators is one that becomes the author of its own demise. And because we know the Constitution was not written to facilitate its own destruction, we should treat that outcome as absurd.

If, having investigated the administration, Democrats find evidence of criminal behavior — and if they find that a pardon was issued to preclude criminal prosecution — Democrats should treat those pardons as null, void and illegitimate on their face in light of what the Constitution implies about the limits of the pardon power — and of president power itself.

We may well be less than a week away from a Democratic sweep of Congress. There are prominent voices within the larger Democratic coalition who think it is counterproductive, even foolish, to pivot to hearings, investigations and political accountability. In their telling, most Americans are tired of the noise. The only thing they want from Congress is good government.

I want good government, too. But good government, now or in the future, is impossible without accountability. To set that aside is to condemn the United States to another national exercise in corruption and authoritarian rule. And I would hazard that after nearly two years of abject lawlessness — including summary killings by agents of the state — there are many tens of millions of Americans who also want to hold the administration and its allies responsible for their actions.

Our nation’s experiment in executive aggrandizement has gone too far. If accountability means anything, it must mean binding both the president and the presidency with law. It is the essential task of the next Democratic majority, and the next Democratic presidency for that matter, to begin the reconstruction of American democracy with the rule of law in mind.

That Trump is something like the apotheosis of the dysfunction of the American system does not mean that he is the end of the story. He may well be the beginning of something much worse. Our job is to make him a blip in the history of American democracy and not the opening act of its demise.

SUMMARY

We spent months preparing a beautiful home wedding for our daughter — with many guests, a vibrant floral backdrop and a gifted guitarist. The groom’s brother and the bride’s sister officiated the ceremony together. After delivering thoughtful remarks and listening to the bridal couple exchange heartfelt vows, the groom’s brother dropped his trousers and bared his naked butt to the guests — with the first names of the bride and groom temporarily tattooed onto his butt cheeks.

ARTICLE

The Officiant Mooned the Guests at My Daughter’s Wedding. Help!
The mother of the bride feels that the groom’s brother tarnished a special day that she had worked hard to make beautiful. Should she confront him?
By Philip Galanes
Published 2026-10-28 13:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/style/wedding-misbehavior-confrontation.html

We spent months preparing a beautiful home wedding for our daughter — with many guests, a vibrant floral backdrop and a gifted guitarist. The groom’s brother and the bride’s sister officiated the ceremony together. After delivering thoughtful remarks and listening to the bridal couple exchange heartfelt vows, the groom’s brother dropped his trousers and bared his naked butt to the guests — with the first names of the bride and groom temporarily tattooed onto his butt cheeks. Cameras clicked, pictures were posted, and that single image branded the day. To me, the prank debased a beautiful event — like a cockroach in a bowl of perfect cherries, but no one in the wedding party sees anything wrong with the prank or is willing to confront the exhibitionist. I feel hurt by the gesture and disappointed by the apathy. Should the groom’s brother know this?

MOTHER OF THE BRIDE

I understand how you feel: as if all your tasteful planning were for naught. I’m almost inclined to give you extra leeway for your startling roach-on-the-cherries imagery. But as I understand it, you’ve already consulted members of the wedding party (presumably, your daughters), and they don’t share your opinion. That doesn’t make them apathetic: They simply disagree. Still, your feelings are valid.

It does raise a question, though: Why use members of the wedding party as your ventriloquist dummies? If you are upset about the behavior of your son-in-law’s brother, tell him. Now, you may have judged that scolding him is not a great way to begin what may be a long relationship. I tend to agree. But there’s probably a middle ground between silence and a dramatic proclamation that he ruined the day.

So keep calm, say your piece and carry on. The next time you see him, say: “I was not a fan of your mooning the guests, but I guess others found it amusing.” I see no problem with an honest statement, but if you worry that your daughter and son-in-law may object, check in with them first. I wouldn’t start a quarrel with your new in-laws over this.

Why Rain on a Baby Shower?

I have been invited to a baby shower for a distant relative. Included in the invitation was a card with the gift registry information, another card with a request to bring a favorite book for the baby and a third card requesting a package of diapers with a chance to win a prize. A raffle for bringing a gift? Ugh. This kind of commercialism disgusts me. I’m considering going away for the weekend so I can be far from this party. Thoughts?

INVITEE

It’s not exactly breaking news that some people get overexcited about the big events in their lives — including new babies. As a bystander, I try to give them grace: The number of joyful occasions in life is not infinite. So I try to be happy for them, even as I recognize that they may be going overboard. If I can’t be happy for them — or if I, like you, find myself disgusted by an invitation — I take that as a reliable sign that I should skip the party. I doubt that a distant relative will be missed. And moralizing about the exuberance of others is not necessary.

Can’t Share What You Don’t Bring!

I bring my toddler son to our neighborhood park frequently. Another family with a toddler is often there. The boy is sweet, but he asks me on arrival for toys and snacks. I bring both in abundance! I’ve come to dread seeing him: I’m annoyed that his family doesn’t bring their own toys and snacks. I refused him a toy recently that my son wanted to play with. May I say something to the parents?

PLAYGROUND MOM

Toddlers are not known for their impulse control. (In fairness, their prefrontal cortices have barely begun to develop.) That’s why most parents I know bring only toys and snacks to playgrounds that they are willing to share. Why be party to a toddler meltdown over a few Goldfish crackers that you brought to a communal space?

Now, I understand your annoyance that some parents are not as prepared as you. But since most toddlers last barely an hour on the playground, are all your abundant toys and snacks necessary? Perhaps the better workaround here is to minimize your supplies — not to ask that other adults come similarly equipped. When you enter a shared space with toddlers, be prepared for grabby little hands.

Nothing to Hide at a Nude Beach

On a weekend trip to a nude beach, my wife ruled out swimming. She said the water was too cold for her. Our friend replied that if she stayed close to him, she would be fine: He had enough body heat for them both. I interpreted his remark as flirtatious. My wife didn’t take it that way. She thought he was just joking about her inability to tolerate cold water. Am I being oversensitive?

HUSBAND

I can see both sides here. Your wife would have to be awfully close to your naked friend to absorb his body heat. (And that Kathleen Turner movie was racy.) But he made the remark out in the open, which suggests joking more than flirting. I would let this go — unless your friend has made you or your wife uncomfortable in the past.

alaska-dan-sullivan-conspiracy-peltola.html

SUMMARY

In the summer of 2025, a staffer for Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democrat who was eyeing a run for Senate, received unusual instructions from top campaign aides: Find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska as you can. And if the Peltola campaign or its allies could track down and persuade another Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, the confusion could cost the senator crucial votes on the state’s unusual, four-person ballot. Both the Peltola campaign and the D.S.C.C. denied participating in efforts to recruit spoilers to the ballot in Alaska.

ARTICLE

Inside Democrats’ Secret Effort to Stack Alaska’s Ballot
Operatives aligned with Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate, spent months recruiting candidates to peel votes from Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican.
By Kellen Browning
Published 2026-10-28 14:37 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/us/politics/alaska-dan-sullivan-conspiracy-peltola.html

In the summer of 2025, a staffer for Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democrat who was eyeing a run for Senate, received unusual instructions from top campaign aides: Find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska as you can.

The staffer complied, combing through voter records to produce a list of Dan Sullivans from across the state.

This was no random request. Dan S. Sullivan is the name of the state’s Republican senator. And if the Peltola campaign or its allies could track down and persuade another Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, the confusion could cost the senator crucial votes on the state’s unusual, four-person ballot.

The plan worked. This spring, a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle, reachable only by air and sea, announced his candidacy for Senate. His name was Dan J. Sullivan.

The Peltola campaign has repeatedly denied any involvement in his candidacy. But The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola’s team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader. The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent’s support and help catapult the Democrat to victory.

The endeavor, which was internally called the ballot composition project, involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs.

It also involved the Peltola campaign’s lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party’s campaign strategy in Senate races across the country. From Washington to Anchorage, those advisers participated in regular conversations about the effort and even considered forming a new political party to draw conservatives onto the ballot.

Ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska. But this operation, which has not been reported before, reveals the lengths to which Democrats went to seek advantage in a Senate race that could determine control of the chamber.

“Alaskan voters need to know,” said Elisa Rios, Ms. Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, who was fired amid a staff shake-up in August, and agreed to a series of interviews with The Times since then. “There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions.”

Ms. Peltola was not directly involved in the project, Ms. Rios said, but she was “definitely aware.”

The operation had impact. On Tuesday, Ms. Peltola will be the only Democrat on the ballot, facing off against the two Mr. Sullivans and a long-shot candidate named Gerald Heikes who was also recruited into the race, according to The Times’s reporting. Polls give Ms. Peltola a strong chance of winning.

The Justice Department, meanwhile, filed a lawsuit in federal court at President Trump’s behest last week seeking to block certification of the election results if votes for the other Mr. Sullivan cost Senator Sullivan the win.

Both the Peltola campaign and the D.S.C.C. denied participating in efforts to recruit spoilers to the ballot in Alaska. Neither group addressed a detailed list of questions provided by The Times.

“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” the campaign wrote in a statement.

The D.S.C.C. sent a similar response, saying it had “no involvement” in recruiting Mr. Sullivan “or any other Republican candidate.”

This article is based on interviews over the past two months with 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates that the team tried to recruit. The Times also obtained dozens of text messages that provided updates on the progress of the effort. The reporting included the extensive interviews with Ms. Rios, during which she shared details of the operation.

Last week, as The Times prepared to publish this article, Ms. Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit against the Peltola campaign, contacted The Times and said she wanted to take back her previous statements.

“As discussed on our call earlier today, I am confirming that I have retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race in connection with any article you may or may not be writing,” Ms. Rios wrote. “I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity.”

It is rare for a source to seek to retract comments made in previous interviews, and The Times’s standards do not obligate reporters to comply with such requests. The Times had never agreed that those previous interviews could not be published, and informed Ms. Rios last week that they would be a part of this story.

In addition, Ms. Rios’s interviews were consistent with The Times’s other reporting. She has not filed a lawsuit against the campaign.

“Our friend” Jerid

The operation began in the summer of 2025 to lure potential spoiler candidates onto the state’s unusual four-person ballot, Ms. Rios said. In one early meeting, she said, aides with the D.S.C.C. introduced a veteran Democratic operative named Jerid Kurtz to Ms. Rios and Anton McParland, who at the time was Ms. Peltola’s chief of staff. Mr. Kurtz, a native of Ohio, was introduced as a specialist in secret ballot maneuvers, Ms. Rios said.

Months later, in early 2026, Mr. Kurtz participated in a video call with members of the ballot composition team, Ms. Rios said. He told the group he had made contact with one of the Dan Sullivans. This Mr. Sullivan lived in the tiny village of Petersburg, and Mr. Kurtz described him as amenable to running if it would help Ms. Peltola, Ms. Rios said.

Mr. Kurtz “told us when he found him,” she said. He said Mr. Sullivan “said he hated Trump, and if it was going to help Mary, he liked Mary. He didn’t have any interest in being a politician, but if this could help.”

Mr. Sullivan, who has maintained that he entered the race of his own volition, did not respond to repeated requests for comment over the past week.

According to Federal Election Commission records, a pro-Peltola super PAC called 49th State PAC paid Wingspan Strategies, a firm co-owned by Mr. Kurtz, about $87,000 this fall. The PAC said in a statement this week it had “never hired or paid Jerid Kurtz for performing any services.”

Mr. Kurtz did not respond to repeated requests for comment. In recent days, he removed his LinkedIn profile from public view and made his X account private.

Text messages viewed by The Times show officials with the D.S.C.C. and the Peltola campaign communicating for months about the project. Mr. McParland asked for updates from “Jarid,” “Jared” or “our friend,” and D.S.C.C. officials quickly scheduled calls, the messages showed. (Mr. McParland, who was demoted to a consulting role in August, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.)

Ms. Rios regularly participated in the calls. She said the members sometimes chatted casually, and Mr. Kurtz occasionally grew animated when describing his tactics, saying he used pseudonyms and cover stories to keep his activities under wraps.

In late May, just before Mr. Sullivan filed his papers to run, Mr. Kurtz spoke by phone to a Peltola campaign aide, saying he had just gotten off a plane in Petersburg, according to Ms. Rios and another person familiar with the conversation.

The Peltola aides worried at times that Mr. Kurtz’s efforts would be discovered, such as when he posted an image of the Anchorage airport on his Instagram account.

“I am hearing that our friend in the state is being noticed,” Mr. McParland wrote in a text message in January reviewed by The Times. Andrew Piatt, the D.S.C.C.’s director of campaigns, replied: “We will check in.”

Alaska’s voting system makes it especially easy to add spoilers to the ballot. The state holds nonpartisan primaries, so candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. That allowed Mr. Sullivan of Petersburg, a longtime supporter of Ms. Peltola and other Democrats, to land a spot on next week’s ballot.

Republicans have also taken advantage of this system. When Ms. Peltola ran for re-election to the House two years ago, the state Republican Party backed an effort to help a Democrat — an inmate who ran his campaign from a New York prison — stay on the ballot.

This year, as soon as Mr. Sullivan entered the race, Republicans denounced him as a Democratic plant, but they haven’t been able to prove it. They attempted to remove him from the ballot, arguing that he was not a “good faith” candidate and citing his registration switch from unaffiliated to Republican just before the deadline to run.

In June, the Alaska Supreme Court brushed aside that argument, ruling there was no basis for removing Mr. Sullivan in either state law or the U.S. Constitution.

The lawsuit from the Justice Department, meanwhile, is still making its way through the court. Election law experts say the case is dubious, given that states control the administration of elections under the Constitution, and the suit seeks to challenge an election that hasn’t happened yet.

While the Justice Department is focused on the two Dan Sullivans, The Times found other Alaskans the team sought to recruit as spoilers. Not all of them, of course, shared a name with the Republican senator. Some would simply add more options to the ballot and potentially siphon support from the incumbent.

Matthew Salisbury of Anchorage said he got a call out of the blue last December from an unfamiliar Google Voice number with an Ohio area code.

A one-time candidate for the U.S. House, Mr. Salisbury said in an interview that the caller identified himself as Zane — no last name — and asked him if he would consider running in the upcoming Senate race. Zane also wanted to meet him in person.

Over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, and over more meetings and calls in subsequent months, Zane continued to press Mr. Salisbury to run for Senate. He said he was looking for independent-minded candidates, and that his backers would support Mr. Salisbury with outside spending. He seemed friendly and intelligent, Mr. Salisbury recalled, but never provided more details about his background or political party, and he wouldn’t say who was paying for the effort.

“I’m not naïve,” said Mr. Salisbury, who didn’t end up running for Senate. “I had to have that general idea that they’re not in it for me.”

When The Times sent Mr. Salisbury a photograph of Mr. Kurtz, Mr. Salisbury identified him as the man who called himself Zane. Efforts to reach the Google Voice number were unsuccessful, as were attempts to reach Mr. Kurtz at the email address he used with Mr. Salisbury, which includes the word “buckeye.” Public records show that Mr. Kurtz is from Ohio, known as the Buckeye State.

In late May, Mr. Kurtz, still posing as Zane, texted Mr. Salisbury that he had also tried to recruit several “upper level candidates, including a few of the folks currently in the gov race,” to no avail.

And he wanted Mr. Salisbury’s opinion on a recent news story, writing: “You see this craziness with another Dan Sullivan? What’s your read on that?”

A multipronged strategy

Throughout the spring, the campaign swapped leads with the D.S.C.C. on potential candidates and continued to participate in efforts to shape the ballot.

In one exchange of text messages obtained by The Times, Peltola advisers seemed to make fun of voters while watching a focus group, surmising the participants would be susceptible to being tricked into voting for a ballot spoiler.

“Do we have a scheme for you,” wrote a consultant for the Peltola campaign. A pollster on the chat wrote that one voter seemed like the perfect audience “for our ballot strategy plan :)”

The team’s spirits rose with the results of the Aug. 18 primary, as both Dan Sullivans advanced to the four-way general election. But there was one problem: The fourth spot on the ballot had gone to a Democrat who could siphon some votes away from Ms. Peltola that fall.

That Democrat, a progressive named David Leslie, quickly faced calls from his party to withdraw. One of those callers, Mr. Leslie said in an interview, was Jerid Kurtz. Mr. Kurtz met with Mr. Leslie in person, at a cafe in Fairbanks, according to a person familiar with the exchange.

Mr. Leslie soon agreed to drop out.

“I’m really proud of the action you took today,” Mr. Kurtz wrote to Mr. Leslie on Aug. 31, the day he dropped out, in a text message viewed by The Times.

Mr. Leslie’s exit cleared the way for another Republican to take his spot on the ballot, potentially dividing the G.O.P. vote even further: Gerald Heikes.

Mr. Heikes, a drywall contractor, said in an interview that he was recruited to run for Senate this spring “by a guy from the Midwest.” The man, whose name Mr. Heikes did not remember, first reached him on the phone, then met with him at a deli in his hometown of Palmer, Alaska. Mr. Heikes did not think he resembled the photo of Mr. Kurtz.

“He said, ‘Hey, if you go and file to run for Senate, we’ll back you — we can’t give you money or anything, but we’ll make things happen for you,’” Mr. Heikes said.

Mr. Heikes, who has said before that he believed God was telling him to run for office, decided after the meeting to run for the Senate.

Funding the new recruits

There were also efforts to support the new candidates financially. Back in March, Peltola campaign employees had dinner with a local political consultant named Jim Lottsfeldt. Mr. Lottsfeldt, who works with super PACs aligned with Ms. Peltola, agreed to lead an effort to boost the long-shot Senate candidates with outside spending, said Ms. Rios, who was among the attendees.

“We were talking about how we would balance the different distinct universes and create basically a Republican war in the primary,” Ms. Rios said.

Federal filings from Alaska Values, a new super PAC supporting Mr. Heikes, show that Mr. Lottsfeldt had requested advertising time from Alaska radio stations this month.

In an interview, Mr. Lottsfeldt denied any knowledge of or involvement in the effort, and said no such topic was discussed at the dinner. He argued that Ms. Rios was a source of “disgruntled, anti-Mary Peltola stuff that I think is often not true.”

He also denied an association with the Alaska Values PAC, but could not explain how his name ended up on the filings, suggesting it must have been an error.

“These forms have auto-whatever, it’s quite possible that my name was on it from a blank form and then it got moved over,” Mr. Lottsfeldt said. “Even if I had requested some time, OK, so what? There’s nothing illegal about that, there’s nothing suspicious about that.”

A new MAGA party

Even as the Peltola campaign and D.S.C.C. officials denied participation in the operation, the texts and documents reviewed by The Times show it involved the party’s Senate committee and its top law firm. At one point, when Peltola campaign aides toyed with an audacious idea to establish a right-wing state party that could challenge the incumbent senator, they contacted D.S.C.C. officials.

“Imagine if there was a MAGA party!” Mr. McParland, of the Peltola campaign, wrote in January.

“Smart,” replied Mr. Piatt, the D.S.C.C.’s director of campaigns. “Let’s see.”

Jacquelyn Lopez, an attorney with the Elias Law Group, the firm that represents both the committee and the Peltola campaign, was part of this effort, according to Ms. Rios. In a text message from April viewed by The Times, a campaign consultant asked Ms. Rios: “Do we need to follow up with Jackie about maga party stuff?”

In another message from that month that misspelled Mr. Kurtz’s first name, Mr. McParland wrote: “Jackie is calling Jarid.” Ms. Lopez did not respond to a request for comment.

The MAGA party plan fizzled out in May.

But in June, the D.S.C.C. celebrated alongside the campaign when an Alaska court cleared the way for the other Dan Sullivan to stay on the ballot.

“Other Dan won, will be on ballot,” Shelbi Dantic, a D.S.C.C. employee, wrote in an internal group chat.

Three people — two Peltola aides and a member of the D.S.C.C. staff — reacted with heart emojis.

Nathaniel Herz contributed reporting from Alaska, and Matt Zdun, Theodore Schleifer, Emily Davies and Beth Reinhard contributed reporting from New York and Washington. Georgia Gee and Julie Tate contributed research.

In Michigan, El-Sayed Faces Heat From Former Primary Rival as Election Nears
Representative Haley Stevens has been less than enthusiastic about Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, injecting late intraparty tensions into a race that could decide Senate control.

Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan, who lost to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in a bitter Democratic primary for Senate in August, has grown increasingly critical of him as the election draws near, injecting unusual intraparty tensions into the final days of a pivotal midterm contest.

While Ms. Stevens reiterated Wednesday night that she plans to vote for Dr. El-Sayed, she did so through seemingly gritted teeth in a televised interview just hours after her fiancé said that he would be voting for former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican rival. She also called on Dr. El-Sayed to denounce an ad from an outside group that she has argued amounts to “fear-mongering about Israel,” and to take down an ad from his campaign featuring Tucker Carlson.

“Of course, I’m voting for our Democratic nominee for Senate,” Ms. Stevens said on CNN. “I’m voting for the Democratic ticket. But I want to encourage this campaign to shut out the hate and to call it out and to make people who are in my coalition, right — make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.”

Ms. Stevens’s remarks are an unwelcome development for Dr. El-Sayed in a high-stakes race. It is rare for the loser of a primary who has endorsed the winner to be publicly critical this close to the general election.

It’s not the first time it has happened in this year’s midterms. In Texas, Senator John Cornyn has missed few opportunities to needle Ken Paxton, who beat him for the Republican nomination in May. Mr. Cornyn, however, has not made as many cable news appearances as Ms. Stevens.

Ms. Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, said on CNN that she is representing Jewish Michiganders who supported her and are angry about advertising that they view as antisemitic. The campaign of Dr. El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel, has said it was “not affiliated in any way” with the ad that has come under scrutiny. But Ms. Stevens said that does not go far enough.

“He can disavow these ads, and he can reassure these undecided voters who are still out,” she said.

A spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment on Ms. Stevens’s remarks.

Dr. El-Sayed, speaking to reporters earlier Wednesday, dismissed concerns that Ms. Stevens’s fiancé was backing Mr. Rogers over concerns about Dr. El-Sayed’s Israel policy.

“I’m building a movement to take on the challenges that Donald Trump is facing,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “If folks have issues that are more important to them than that, that’s fine — that’s their choice.”

The public criticism from Ms. Stevens made clear that there has been little private reconciliation between the primary rivals despite her vow to vote for him. While Ms. Stevens couched her public remarks as constructive criticism, she has been more critical of Dr. El-Sayed in private, according to a person who has spoken with her, leaving some allies wondering if she would in fact vote for him.

She said in a text message on Wednesday that she would not appear with Dr. El-Sayed in the campaign’s final week. “I am not campaigning with Abdul,” she wrote.

Ms. Stevens’s criticism of Dr. El-Sayed had been building.

On Sunday, in another CNN interview, she said, “I can’t say that I agree with everything that’s gone on.” She questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s efforts to appeal to Black voters and suggested that he was too focused on foreign policy.

“I watched Haley graciously concede an election, and open her arms and her heart to Abdul on Aug. 5, the day after the primary, and I prayed that he would moderate, and he hasn’t,” Mr. Turkish said in an interview.

Mr. Turkish said he was frustrated after Dr. El-Sayed declined to answer a question at an October debate about whether Iran or Israel was a greater threat to the United States. And Mr. Turkish expressed disappointment that the day after the primary, Dr. El-Sayed was joined by another Democratic primary contender, Mallory McMorrow, who finished a distant third after dropping out weeks before the primary, rather than Ms. Stevens at a celebratory news conference in Detroit.

Ms. Stevens’s tepid support — and the awkward dynamic between the two Democrats — is one of the most public points of tension among Democrats in Michigan, who remain far more divided than party leaders had hoped to be going into the election next Tuesday.

Opinion polls show that Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Rogers are running neck-and-neck in Michigan, a traditional battleground state where a Republican has not won a Senate race in more than three decades. The battle between Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Rogers could play a critical role in the national fight for Senate control.

Israel remains a dividing line for some Democrats in the state, and Jewish voters say they are torn about whether to support Dr. El-Sayed, who has called Israel’s government “evil.” Dr. El-Sayed is also trying to overcome tensions between Black and Arab American voters in the Detroit area.

Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Stevens clashed regularly over Israel during the primary race, with Dr. El-Sayed assailing Ms. Stevens over support she received from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a lobbying group. AIPAC is now backing Mr. Rogers.

“I don’t place blame on one over the other,” Mr. Scott said.

Representative Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who stayed publicly neutral in the primary, defended Ms. Stevens.

“I’m sick and tired of people blaming Haley,” Ms. Dingell said.
