SUMMARY

So — what was the Trump era and what might it tell us about what comes next? Bernie Sanders had made his mark on Democratic politics in 2016, of course, but it was in the Trump years — and particularly the first years of his second term — that the Democratic Socialists of America became a national political force. Then, the argument seemed shortsighted — how sure were any of these people that the new Trump era would actually last?

ARTICLE

The Trump Era Is Fading
It’s time to take stock. Here are 12 takeaways from the last 10 years.
By David Wallace-Wells
Published 2026-10-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/opinion/trump-midterms.html

Nobody wants to jinx it. The election is still days away. But Republicans are pulling money out of North Carolina, assuming they will lose there, and spending in Mississippi, where they hope to save a Senate seat. A Democrat could win the governorship of Texas. Polling suggests the biggest margin of victory in any congressional election in nearly two decades, and Republicans desperate to save their seats are repudiating each major item on President Trump’s second-term agenda: tariffs, war, and ICE. All the signs we have suggest that, historic or not, these midterms are likely to mark the end of a political era.

So — what was the Trump era and what might it tell us about what comes next? Some of that story is pretty familiar, 10 years on. But here are 12 perhaps more surprising, or counterintuitive, takeaways.

1. MAGA defined the epoch, but the movement — and its leader — was always weak.

It may seem ridiculous to say, given Trump’s domination of the American political landscape for the last decade and the concrete damage his movement has done to American institutions and the country’s faith in them. But over three presidential campaigns, Trump won eight million fewer votes than his Democratic opponents. Add up the days when more Americans approved of him than disapproved of him since he descended the golden escalator, and you get about two weeks.

During the 2016 primaries, Trump’s rise looked like a sign of Republican Party weakness — how had it lost so much institutional strength that this interloper could waltz in and take right over? In retrospect, the weakness looks more general and enduring. A haphazard demagogue who never managed to achieve a majority mandate nevertheless commanding power and attention for so long and to such consequential ends — this is not the sign of a healthy republic.

Perhaps nobody but Trump could’ve mobilized the mass of national discontent the way he did. Even so, he never approached the popularity of Bill Clinton or Barack Obama, let alone Franklin Roosevelt or Ronald Reagan. Which does raise the question: Is this about as good as anyone can manage, now? Are we doomed to weak leaders pretending to be strong? Or will one era of constrained possibility give way to something else?

2. MAGA doesn’t mean what it used to.

In 2016, conventional wisdom held, Trump was carried to victory by a resentful anti-elite coalition — in particular by surprising strength across the deindustrializing Rust Belt in the upper Midwest.

Out of power during the Biden years, MAGA nursed professional-class grievances against various tools of inclusive liberalism — first raging against C.R.T. and later D.E.I. and lamenting the loss of test-based standards in college admissions and the rise of what it saw as anti-white racism in corporate hiring practices.

Once it returned to power in 2025, the movement looked like it had been reshaped once again, this time in Elon Musk’s image — a mix of moralistic social Darwinism, anti-woke retribution and acquisitive tech accelerationism, pay-to-play access for billionaires and a kind of corruption free-for-all in the White House.

Ten years ago, Trump could somewhat plausibly claim to be giving voice to the American voiceless. Now, he is speaking largely for a different constituency, when he isn’t speaking for himself.

3. But the influence of Christian nationalism endured — even grew.

The class portrait for Trump’s second term is conspicuously full of performative macho libertines from the manosphere. But the strongest part of the Trump coalition has always been its committed white evangelical base.

In each of Trump’s three elections, religiosity was the single best predictor of voter preference, even more than it was in the George W. Bush years. As MAGA stares down a possible midterm endgame, it’s notable that Mike Johnson, an evangelical and a social conservative, is the speaker of the House — and that despite looking like such a strange match temperamentally, he is the longest-serving Republican leader of this era. Less than a week out from the election, Trump’s most loyal voters remain evangelical Christians.

4. The traditional Republican heartland is looking pretty purple all of a sudden.

The midterm map now looks like an entirely new political world, one in which Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia are solid blue, in Texas and South Carolina are tossups and in Florida and Mississippi are contested. Add in close governor’s races in Nevada and Arizona and you get a battleground band stretching through the Old South, Deep South and Sun Belt.

Not so long ago this was the spiritual heartland of red America. And in almost all these races Democrats appear to be either winning handily or competing seriously. (As they are in Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, and Alaska, among other places.)

All of these races are obviously shaped by disenchantment with President Trump and don’t necessarily signal lasting partisan shifts — wave elections tend to set a high-water mark for a new majority. But the reality that each of these historically red states is in play tells you something about just how much things have changed — and how much less secure the Republican Party’s legacy claim on the heartland has become. The upper Midwest looks redder than you might expect in a year like this, but head a little ways east and Gov. Josh Shapiro is very likely to win re-election in Pennsylvania by 20 points or more.

Where, then, are the true G.O.P. strongholds?

If Ohio, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska can be pulled into play, as they have been this year, the pretty empty states of the Great Plains and the Mountain West are the obvious answer. But even there it’s not at all clear whether the Republican Pete Ricketts can hold off the liberal-minded independent Dan Osborn. The race for the South Dakota Senate seat isn’t exactly up for grabs, but the Republican margin of victory could easily stay within single digits, too. As John Anzalone, a Democratic pollster, has taken to saying, all of America is a battleground state now — at least in this midterm.

A few years ago, you heard a lot about the possibility of a Democratic crisis given the population exodus from blue states and coastal capitals to red states and start-up cities (thanks not just to weather but also to more affordable housing, a friendlier business and regulatory environment and perhaps some frustration with liberal governance in places like San Francisco and New York).

A few years later, many of red places are still thriving, but they are also growing more Democratic. Whatever the legacy politics of those states, this probably shouldn’t come as such a surprise — in general, when places grow denser and richer they get bluer, too. The gains of this year will likely recede, but the stories about the rightward lurch of the country look much more questionable. We might’ve thought red states were winning a demographic tug of war, but the same forces are tugging leftward, too.

5. We have entered an era of whiplash politics.

After the 2020 election, many liberals believed that some natural-seeming order had been restored and the accident of Trump’s first election had been somewhat expunged. In 2024, it looked briefly like Trump and MAGA had engineered a new generational majority, poised to reduce the Democrats to the kind of rump party they had been through the 1980s. Two years later, it looks increasingly silly to extract lasting ideological meaning from any of these elections.

It also looks increasingly intuitive that we should conceptualize this period — perhaps beginning with Trump or the 2010 election — as being marked by the same serial anti-incumbency backlash visible in so much of the rest of the world. In any given election, one party seems up and the other down, but the consistent pattern is voters’ wanting change almost regardless of who is in power. Maybe most distressing is the self-reinforcing nature of the pattern: When parties are given only slim legislative majorities for a very brief period, it’s extremely hard to persuade voters they’re anything but ineffective embodiments of a broken status quo. Which makes it much easier to imagine a big blue wave next Tuesday than an enduring Democratic majority lasting long enough to pull the country out of political despondency.

6. MAGA is often framed as a reaction to progressive overreach. Maybe it’s the other way around.

It’s almost hard to believe, given how frequently they are characterized as a phenomenon of imperious liberal excess, but the Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 took place under Trump, as, in part, a response to his rule. The #MeToo era began, as well, in 2017 — in the aftermath of the “Access Hollywood” tape and the Women’s March. These were not the Obama years or the Biden years.

In fact, by the time Joe Biden took office in early 2021, the phenomenon had by many measures already crested and begun its decline. And it is remarkable how little oxygen liberal race politics now takes up in the national discourse.

The climate awakening and protest movement began in Trump’s first term, too, when the United States announced its intention to quit the Paris agreement at a news conference where “Summertime” played in the Rose Garden. Bernie Sanders had made his mark on Democratic politics in 2016, of course, but it was in the Trump years — and particularly the first years of his second term — that the Democratic Socialists of America became a national political force. (Its national star, Zohran Mamdani, first really introduced himself to New Yorkers as a candidate for mayor by interviewing Trump voters on the street and asking what he could do to win their votes.)

Public health grew tribal partly in response to Trump’s supervision of the pandemic. And though it looked for a time as though MAHA would be the lasting political legacy of Covid, it now seems quite possible that liberal former public health officials will be elected in Michigan to the Senate and the governorship of Ohio — and perhaps that measles-stricken South Carolina, too, will elect to the Senate a Democratic pediatrician who began her campaign running against Kennedy and MAHA.

7. Abortion has largely disappeared from the political landscape, but the gender wars remain.

As recently as the last midterms, in 2022, outrage about that year’s Supreme Court decision to end the federal right to abortion was seen as one driving force behind Democrats’ surprisingly good electoral performance. These days, you can find abortion ranking as low as 36th on surveys of national political issues.

But you can see the lasting legacy of the Trump-era gender wars in other ways. The number of Republicans saying women should return to their traditional role in the home nearly doubled in just a few years, and the number of Republicans who say gay sex is morally acceptable has fallen from 56 percent to 35 percent in just three years. The fight over trans rights has taken a more ambiguous turn — hysterical Republicans made it the centerpiece of their closing argument in the last election cycle, but just two years later Americans appear to trust Democrats more on the issue.

There’s been a lot of talk, over the last decade, about the crisis of the American male, but the Trump years just seemed to steer those in crisis toward gambling and crypto. Almost every job created anywhere in the country in Trump’s second term has gone to a woman, and employment is growing only in sectors traditionally coded as female. Which is all to say: These gender issues are probably not going away soon, however poorly Republicans may do with young men on Tuesday.

8. Trump’s two biggest political legacies are problems the country must solve.

One of these is a practical challenge for any future Democratic administration, with Trump responsible for more than a quarter of the national debt. The other is a political challenge: The country disapproves of ICE and mass deportation programs, but it’s not at all clear what immigration policy Americans actually want to see or to what degree they would protest a return to the old liberal consensus.

9. Trump turned China into America’s foil.

In 2016, Trump’s constant invocations of China became such a joke that you could watch supercuts mocking his pronunciation of the word. Obama had tried to shift the country’s foreign policy attention in that direction with his “pivot to Asia,” but the rise of a new geopolitical rival still lived primarily on the outskirts of public discourse. By the time Trump left office in 2021, it was central enough to a new bipartisan consensus that it served as the basis of Biden’s entire policy agenda and has shaped liberal conversations about A.I., abundance and industrial policy since.

10. And he torpedoed America’s reputation around the world.

As the sun sets on MAGA, the actual state of global status competition is a bit ambiguous. China is struggling with economic slowdown and demographic decline, but racing past the United States in green technology, robots and, increasingly, science — and now can claim to be a more popular diplomatic partner, too.

The U.S. economy has proved pretty resilient, though much of the country’s strength comes from financial firms and A.I. companies that increasingly seem to lie outside the realm of the state and operate instead almost as autonomous city-states. And in Iran, Trump has tried to impose his will militarily — only to be humiliated on the world stage in an episode of imperial comeuppance that has doubled as a lesson that the American way of war is now a thing of the past.

11. The Silicon Valley “vibe shift” may have been primarily about A.I.

In explaining their sudden lurch to Trump in 2024, the tech chief executives told a variety of stories, mostly about the excesses of Biden-era liberalism: that administration officials had gotten too involved in policing public health information on social media, that regulators had gone too far in trying to control and tax Big Tech, that the culture of the country had grown too feminine and we needed an injection of new masculinity, which happily coincided for the tech leaders’ with a hands-off approach to corporate oversight (as everyone knows, there’s nothing more masculine than a tech C.E.O.).

Then, the argument seemed shortsighted — how sure were any of these people that the new Trump era would actually last? In retrospect, the answer may be that they weren’t thinking as much about the next election cycle as about the high stakes for tech policy in the short term, given that the A.I. age seemed to be dawning.

12. Trump violated the politician’s code when he declared the country broken in 2016. Now, everyone seems to agree.

“America is already great,” Obama declared in 2016. “America never stopped being great,” Hillary Clinton echoed. Meanwhile, Trump declared that the country was a “dumping ground,” a “third-world country” and a “laughingstock” around the world. “We never win anymore,” he said again and again on the campaign trail.

At the time, Americans were somewhat evenly divided on the question of whether the country’s best days were ahead of it or behind it, according to polling by Pew. When the question was asked again last year, the gap had grown from -5 to -19. Among Democrats, almost two-thirds of the country now says our glory days were in the past.

Partly, this was a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy: Trump stripping the country for parts, exposing longstanding hypocrisies and dropping the pretenses that for so long sustained our sense of American exceptionalism. Partly it reflected just how heavy a blow his re-election had been to liberals, a vote that made the national character look far uglier to them than they might ever had acknowledged before.

But this shifting sentiment has also paralyzed the Democratic Party, which has retreated on many commitments from the previous cycles that it now considers controversial or alienating without offering much in the way of a successor vision. In 2020, Biden dreamed of a Franklin Roosevelt-scale presidency, and his party is heading for power again. But while Democrats are now much less likely to defend the status quo, they don’t exactly have an ambitious plan to remake it, either.

Many on the left have framed an expanded horizon of political possibility as the silver lining of Trump’s norm-breaking presidency. But at least at the national level, the ambitions of liberals seem to have narrowed, not widened. Even among those competing for office and national leadership positions, the rhetoric is more defiant than optimistic: “It’s the most corrupt administration of all time and everybody knows it,” Jon Ossoff recently declared on the campaign trail. “I refuse to leave my girls a world as dark and dangerous and cruel as this one threatens to become.”

And yet that generational note contains its own message of hope. Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Donald Trump were all born in 1946. Joe Biden was born even earlier, in 1942. Ossoff is a child of the 1980s, as are Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Abdul El-Sayed and JD Vance. Marco Rubio and Josh Shapiro were born in the 1970s. Among everything else, the last decade of American politics has often looked like a gerontocracy. The close of the MAGA era may bring an end to that, too.

The Best Cities to Retire in 2026
A study compared data across 45 metrics to find the best cities for senior living.
By Arnesa A. Howell
Published 2026-10-29 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/realestate/the-best-cities-to-retire-in-2026.html

Florida emerged as the best state for retirees last year, according to a study by the personal finance platform WalletHub, and this year a similar study drilled down to the local level, pitting the 182 largest U.S. cities against one another. Four categories of data contributed equally to the final ranking: affordability, activities, quality of life and health care. Sources included the U.S. Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics and WalletHub’s own research.

Once again, Florida was found attractive by retirees, with Orlando benefiting from the state’s favorable tax policies and handily ranking second for affordability, according to WalletHub. In fact, the three top retirement cities were all in Florida, and four made it into the top 10.

Ranked second and third, Miami and Tampa piggybacked on the state’s financial advantages for retirees, according to Chip Lupo, a WalletHub analyst. (With no state income tax, residents keep a larger chunk of their Social Security check and other retirement income. There are also no inheritance or estate taxes.) Orlando’s access to “very affordable” in-home health and adult day care services edged out the other two cities, Mr. Lupo explained. Overall, the city fared well in the health care category, offering older residents plenty of options for specialized care through gerontologists, quality geriatric hospitals and home health care facilities. A central geographic location helped, too, making it more weather-friendly than hurricane-prone Gulf Coast cities, Mr. Lupo continued.

Mild-weathered Scottsdale, Ariz., a city with the best quality of life and the second-highest share of people 65 and over, finished fourth overall — despite scoring 114th for affordability. Next was Casper, Wyo., cited as one of the cheapest cities to live in.

Among the five worst places to retire, four were in California: Stockton, Calif., came in last. New York City was least affordable.

“A lot of people do live on fixed incomes and don’t have a whole lot of flexibility,” Mr. Lupo said. “In that case, you may want to settle for maybe not one of the worst, but somewhere middle of the road, a place like Knoxville, Tenn., or Columbia, S.C.”

ARTICLE

Oberlin College Professor and His Wife Are Murdered by His Son, Police Say
Pipo Nguyen-duy, 64, was the studio art chairman at the liberal arts college in Ohio and had been honored for his photography, including being named a Guggenheim fellow.
By Neil Vigdor
Published 2026-10-29 22:09 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/us/oberlin-college-professor-murdered.html

An accomplished photography professor at Oberlin College in Ohio and his wife were found shot to death at their home on Wednesday, according to the authorities, who said that the professor’s son had been arrested and charged with murder.

The shootings jolted the Oberlin campus, which is about 35 miles southwest of Cleveland, and visual artists who had known him.

The professor, Pipo Nguyen-duy, 64, who had taught at the college since 1998 and was its studio art chairman, and his wife, Tran Thi Phong, 56, were identified by the Oberlin Police Department as the victims.

Daniel Jones, 31, of Ashland, Ore., who the police said was Mr. Nguyen-duy’s son and Ms. Phong’s stepson, was charged with six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and one count of tampering with evidence, the authorities said.

A motive was not immediately clear.

In a statement, Carmen Twillie Ambar, Oberlin’s president, described Mr. Nguyen-duy, who was known as Pipo, as a beloved member of the college community whose passion for photography touched everyone.

Mr. Nguyen-duy, who was born in Vietnam and came to the United States as a political refugee, had received numerous honors for his photography over the years, including a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2011, according to his biography.

“Our community will be hurting for a very long time, and when the shock of this news subsides, we will all need to process our grief,” Ms. Ambar said.

Around 9 a.m. on Wednesday, officers responded to a car fire in a parking lot at the college’s music conservatory, according to a police report. Investigators found a wood stove heater in the back seat of the Toyota hatchback, which had Oregon plates and was registered to Mr. Jones, with a makeshift chimney pipe protruding from the roof, the authorities said.

Officers discovered Mr. Jones’s wallet, passport and live ammunition rounds inside the car before finding him about a mile away over an hour later, the police said.

Based on the officers’ interactions with Mr. Jones, they went to his family’s home — about two blocks from where they had responded to the car fire — to conduct a wellness check, investigators said.

After forcing their way into the home, officers found Mr. Nguyen-duy’s body on the first floor and Ms. Phong’s in an upstairs bedroom, the authorities said. Both had been shot multiple times, the police said.

Jenifer Berki Merrill, a lawyer for Mr. Jones, declined to comment about the charges on Thursday. She said that Mr. Jones preferred to go by his birth name, Asia Nguyen-duy.

On Thursday, police officers carried him by his arms and legs into Oberlin Municipal Court for an initial hearing in his case, a video taken by WKYC-TV showed.

He slumped over in a chair while wearing handcuffs and beige-and-pink striped jail clothes during the proceeding.

A judge set his bond at $3 million and he remained in custody on Thursday afternoon, according to court records.

Edie Carey, 21, a senior at Oberlin, said in an interview on Thursday that she had taken four or five classes taught by Mr. Nguyen-duy, and that he had become her favorite professor.

“I feel like the college experience I was promised of becoming really close with someone who knows so much was really only fulfilled by my relationship with him,” she said.

“His teaching wasn’t like anything else I had experienced,” she added. “It was really kind of holistic. He really changed how I see the world.”

Ms. Carey, who worked as a photo lab monitor for the studio art department overseen by Mr. Nguyen-duy, said he would regale his students with fascinating stories about his life.

He told them about competing nationally in table tennis as a teenager in Vietnam and becoming a Buddhist monk in northern India, which required him to shave his head, she said. When he moved to the East Village in New York City in the 1980s, he was hired as a bouncer, she said.

Ms. Carey said that students had set up tributes to Mr. Nguyen-duy on campus, including photographs he had taken. She credited him with inspiring her to pursue a career as an artist after she graduates.

“I always thought about him being there for me,” she said.

ARTICLE

Nvidia Chief Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot
A Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing. President Trump was briefed and took no action.
By Jonathan Swan, Maggie Haberman, Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle and Julian E. Barnes
Published 2026-10-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/us/politics/nvidia-china-jensen-huang-trump.html

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence.

A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing.

But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive.

For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump’s, set off alarms at the White House.

Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.

This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts.

American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips.

But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Mr. Huang had insights into Mr. Trump’s thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge A.I. models.

Mr. Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services, people briefed on the surveillance said.

The surveillance of Ms. Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia said the company that employed Ms. Huang, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Nvidia is “confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Mr. Rizzo said. Customers like Megaspeed, he added, “receive ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

The White House, the C.I.A. and the National Security Agency all declined to comment. In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said that its “current leadership” takes the matter “extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations.” It added that “outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating.”

Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment. It is not clear how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed. A person familiar with Megaspeed’s operations said that Ms. Huang had become less active in the company in the wake of the American investigations.

Asked about the American conclusion that Ms. Huang has been collecting intelligence on behalf of Beijing, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said the United States was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.

When Mr. Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, U.S. officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Ms. Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Mr. Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intelligence-gathering role for China.

Questions about whether Megaspeed was providing A.I. chips to China became public through articles published last year by The New York Times and Bloomberg News.

Mr. Huang has successfully lobbied the administration during Mr. Trump’s second term to loosen regulations on artificial intelligence companies and roll back tighter restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China. He also negotiated a deal with Mr. Trump that allowed the U.S. government to take a 25 percent stake of certain Nvidia chips that the government allows to be sold to China.

The close relationship between the president and Mr. Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former U.S. officials said. They described some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia as having ground to a halt within the Commerce Department, the agency in charge of regulating chip exports.

Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. Mr. Rizzo said China’s government has “blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry.”

Many questions about the situation remain unanswered, at least publicly.

It is unclear whether concerns about protecting the surveillance played a role in the decision not to inform Mr. Huang. Telling him could have alerted Ms. Huang that she was being watched, which is a common reason intelligence officials hesitate to give defensive briefings.

It could not be determined which intelligence agency or agencies have been involved in monitoring Ms. Huang, or what prompted them to start. It is also not clear under what circumstances Ms. Huang began gathering information for Beijing, what information she passed along or its value to China.

The previous reporting about Ms. Huang by The Times described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businesswoman and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade U.S. prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips.

The U.S. government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there.

Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Ms. Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her.

The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department, administration officials said.

While the U.S. government has restricted companies from exporting the most advanced Nvidia chips into China since 2022, some firms have been found to illegally smuggle them over the Chinese border. Other companies have legally set up businesses that buy large numbers of chips to build data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese firms.

Some U.S. officials and lawmakers consider this to be a problematic loophole, and the Biden administration restricted this practice. Mr. Trump rolled back those rules. The administration is weighing whether to tighten them again.

Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centers and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from the American arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker. The U.S. has blacklisted Inspur’s parent company for funneling technology to the Chinese military, though the U.S. firm remains free of sanctions.

Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. U.S. officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run A.I. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

Megaspeed’s sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced A.I. equipment containing Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records obtained from ImportGenius, a trade platform. It was an exceptional amount of money for a small, obscure company.

Nvidia and Megaspeed have continued to do business this year. The limited data available for most of this year shows that Megaspeed and its affiliates kept buying Nvidia products, often through intermediaries.

To prevent chips from being smuggled to China, Nvidia evaluates buyers before approving a chip purchase and sometimes checks later whether the buyer still has the chips. The company continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as this month. In a job ad, Megaspeed’s Indonesian branch called itself “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

Megaspeed has continued serving its primary client, Alibaba, according to that person and other tech industry analysts.

In June 2024, just weeks before Megaspeed began its purchases, photos posted to LinkedIn showed Mr. Huang alongside Ms. Huang at a bar in Taipei following a local technology trade show. They drank whiskey with other A.I. executives.

One year later, in May 2025, they were seen together again, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with other A.I. suppliers. She waited behind Mr. Huang as he spoke to Taiwanese journalists outside the restaurant.

Those details were described in a Times article last October. But the deeper intelligence involving Ms. Huang remained closely held inside the administration.

People with knowledge of the matter said U.S. agencies had been conducting electronic surveillance of Ms. Huang. That surveillance showed that she was in contact with an American citizen.

U.S. intelligence agencies generally cannot legally surveil American citizens without a court order. But when communications involving Americans turn up in surveillance, citizens can be identified to government agencies who can show a need for the information through a process known as unmasking. In this case, the unmasking process identified Mr. Huang as the U.S. citizen.

Before 2025, Mr. Huang seldom visited Washington and stayed out of politics.

But as the Trump administration was considering a ban on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Mr. Huang and his wife traveled to Mar-a-Lago, the president’s private club and residence in Florida, to meet with Mr. Trump at a high-end donors’ dinner and sell him on the idea of allowing chip companies to do business with Beijing.

At the event, according to people briefed on the discussion there, the Nvidia executive appeared to wow the president with his descriptions of his own rise.

Nvidia later donated at least $20 million to Mr. Trump’s ballroom fund, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The company also pledged to invest $500 billion on manufacturing in the United States.

And when the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, visited the White House for a state dinner last month, Mr. Huang was at the head table.

Last year, Mr. Trump approved the sale of an older generation of Nvidia chips to China in return for a cut of the revenue. As the president sought warmer ties with China ahead of his meeting with Mr. Xi, he entertained a push by Mr. Huang to sell the Chinese even more powerful technology, rankling some administration officials and Republicans in Congress, before ultimately deciding against it.

People who have watched the two men interact say Mr. Trump has been won over by the lavish praise Mr. Huang has given the president in public, and his immense wealth and success.

It is not clear when Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang of Megaspeed first met. Before The Times reported last year on her role in purchasing Nvidia chips, Ms. Huang posted photos of herself with Mr. Huang on her social media feed, according to a person who viewed it.

Ms. Huang has a slim profile on the Chinese internet. She has described herself as Megaspeed’s chief executive, and the company listed her as its managing director for its first eight months before removing her from that role in its corporate paperwork. Megaspeed’s current director is from Singapore but has recently lived in Shanghai, according to business records and his social media accounts.

According to information posted online by a Chinese investment fund where Ms. Huang worked, she was formerly employed in China as a TV reporter, but The Times could not find any information to verify that. She later worked at several major Chinese banks, then joined a Shanghai-based fund, Hexi Capital, which has invested in a variety of semiconductor- and A.I.-related firms, according to WireScreen, a data platform.

According to tech investors familiar with the company, Ms. Huang and her associates bragged about her connections to Mr. Huang and used it to raise funds and promote their fast-expanding network of businesses, which has invested alongside the Chinese government in data centers around China. In Southeast Asia, Megaspeed has continued to pitch new data centers, hire employees and trumpet its close connections to Nvidia, according to industry analysts, online job posts and other records.

Megaspeed is pushing ahead with construction of a large data center in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new A.I. facilities have risen between palm oil plantations. In a stock filing last month, a Malaysian property developer said it had received the final payment for the 53-acre plot where a Megaspeed subsidiary has promised to build the data center.

When a Times journalist visited recently, rows of construction materials sat between the skeletal frames of partially built data centers. Outside the park, backhoe loaders dug into the reddish brown earth as workers installed concrete pipes.

The company had already secured the chips necessary for the build out, according to a person with knowledge of the plans.

Pei-Lin Wu and Zunaira Saieed contributed reporting.

Elon Musk’s Endgame
What does the world’s richest man believe in?
By Ezra Klein and Rollin Hu
Published 2026-10-30 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-quinn-slobodian.html

This is an edited transcript of “The Ezra Klein Show.” You can listen to the episode wherever you get your podcasts.

If Republicans keep the Senate, if they perform better in the House than people expect, a lot will come down to one man, and that man is not Donald Trump. It’s Elon Musk.

At this point, Musk has given around $450 million to the Republican campaign effort. That makes him the single largest donor in any election cycle ever.

Musk’s contributions are now one-quarter of all campaign donations Republicans have received. And yet the size of this, and what it throws into relief, is how hard it is to conceptualize how much money he really has.

Because for Musk, with a net worth of around a trillion dollars, giving $300 million, $400 million, is like the median American household giving, like, $100. It is for him nothing, and yet it is reality warping for the rest of us.

But his money is not Elon Musk’s only source of power. There’s his control of X, of Starlink, of SpaceX, of Neuralink, of Tesla. He has power over wealth, attention and critical infrastructure that no human being has ever had at this level, at least once you’re outside the range of, say, a Donald Trump or a Xi Jinping — somebody who controls a superpower as a state.

That’s not what Musk has, and yet he has this almost statelike thing that is completely pursuant to his whims.

So what does he want to do with it? What is he doing with it? What is this world he is flexing his power and taking real risk to build?

Quinn Slobodian is a professor of international history at Boston University. He’s the author of several books, including “Globalists,” “Hayek’s Bastards,” and very relevant here, “Muskism,” which he co-wrote with Ben Tarnoff.

Ezra Klein: Quinn Slobodian, welcome to the show.

What is he trying to buy?

I think he’s trying to entrench the dependency that he already enjoys. One is through his financial role in the U.S. political economy — and, by extension, the global economy.

SpaceX now is one of the world’s top tech companies. Tesla is a large part of the tech portfolio that people hold in their pension funds and in their individual investor accounts.

On the machine side, he’s trying to make the world ever more dependent on his infrastructures — the use of SpaceX as really the monopoly launch provider to put things into low Earth orbit, the rolling out of low Earth orbit satellites with Starlink as the default communications medium for battlefield operations and for rural consumers and so on.

But then there’s what I would think of as the messaging or the media piece of that. There he has much more targeted trying to produce communicative ecosystems in which his way of framing social problems and solutions to social problems is uncontested and uncontestable.

His purchase of Twitter, in October 2022, long described as one of the biggest business failures in American history, has proved to have been quite effective, I would say. So that people are caught in an echo chamber of his creation.

His targeting of the midterms and his flexing of his own power to make or break candidates, as he wishes, is a way he hopes to fine-tune that control over the media and messaging ecosystem and get out ahead of what he worries would be a regulatory wave that would accompany a Democratic majority.

What’s interesting to me about the description you give there is you could imagine someone with Musk’s portfolio of interests seeing a very different strategy as optimal.

Because the work he does is so intertwined with the government — being highly associated with one partisan side of the fight in America and in Europe with the right-wing parties he’s been boosting — it creates risk.

You talk about entrenching dependence. But he’s also creating a situation where, in 2029, if you have President Jon Ossoff or President Gavin Newsom or President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and a Democratic Congress, reliance on SpaceX, on Starlink, on Grok in the Pentagon could maybe be seen as a huge risk.

So from that side, this doesn’t all look purely rational, like a master businessman just entrenching himself. It looks like a man who believes things and is actually risking quite a lot to push those beliefs upon the world.

Yeah, it’s an unusual approach. The way that corporate leaders have usually tried to exercise their influence on the political landscape in the past has been slightly more from behind the scenes, of course. But I would say that he’s, again, working on two tracks.

One is to deepen that financial and structural dependency such that even if a President Ossoff or a President A.O.C. comes into power, they have a limited ability to rein in his central, fulcrum role in the health of the stock market and its dominance in certain key frontier sectors. Their hands would still be tied, I think.

But at the same time, he can use this tactic of hyperpolarization, which he’s obviously taken as his own kind of trademark, even among his own Silicon Valley leadership class, to potentially become the favored partner for a future ruling administration.

And that’s also the way he’s approaching the relationship to far-right parties in Europe. A rational person would try to come up with some kind of compromise with the ruling parties in Western Europe, to make peace with the E.U. in some way to gain market access.

He has taken an opposite approach. He’s gone on a full-frontal attack against Brussels and the existing legacy centrist parties, and tried to ally with what I’ve long thought of as who he sees as the Teslas of politics — the AfDs, the Restore Britains — that he hopes will come from marginality and nowhere to completely disrupt and destroy the legacy institutional parties of social democracy and Christian democracy.

Yes. The term “viruses of the mind” was coined by Richard Dawkins in the early 1990s — a well-respected, if an incendiary, conservative evolutionary biologist. And not, coincidentally, the same guy who coined the term “meme” in his book “The Selfish Gene,” from 1976.

Musk has absolutely swallowed this notion whole to the point that, I think if you want to understand how he understands politics or the problem of consent, or indeed the problem of truth, it’s inseparable from this idea of humans and machines being networked together into what he calls cybernetic collectives, within which problems of political affiliation, support, loss of support, dissent, anger are triggered always through the multiplication or the reduction of certain memes or certain mind viruses.

I think Musk would see that whole legacy as part of the contamination of Western civilization by empathy. I think it raises a number of questions here. One of the core ones to me is: How does his upbringing in apartheid South Africa influence or shape this set of concerns?

One doesn’t have a lot of documentary evidence to work with, so there’s a certain leap of interpretation that’s necessary. But it’s not a very big leap of interpretation.

One of the things we describe in the book is the way that being a minority privileged population, racially marked in South Africa, that drifted, through everyday life and one’s whole life course, in a way, past faceless colored masses of the African population helps to reinforce in very obvious ways a sense of the nonplayer characters and the playing characters.

South Africa itself is not a traditional modern nation-state in the sense that it’s built on an asymmetrical logic where the majority of the residents are actually just there insofar as they’re useful to the minority of residents.

So those old problems of: What is popular sovereignty? What is national self-determination? How can you get a group of people who live next to each other to see each other in bonds of reciprocal attention or minimal care? — these simply didn’t apply in late-apartheid South Africa.

It’s effectively one of the last decolonizing sites in the world. It lived on with that imperial two-tier logic much longer than the rest of the world did. So I think it’s easier for him to just set aside what to most political thinkers are things that need to be considered seriously.

I think it’s worth looking at how that breaks down concretely, as well. How have previous oligarchs, how have previous titans of industry, secured popular consent?

This is actually where the comparison to Fordism is helpful. Ford himself, virulent antisemite, violently anti-union, and yet Fordism is something we associate with collective bargaining agreements, upward generational mobility, the construction of the single-family breadwinner model, the welfare state, even.

How did that happen? Well, it happened because through social struggle, through enlightened legislation and through democratic pressure, a compromise or a social contract emerged in which people were minimally willing to go along with the way that this guy was going to design the factory and the way he was going to make his money.

What’s the equivalent for Musk? Where is the social contract that people like Musk are proposing? Where is the equivalent of Carnegie’s libraries in the case of Musk?

You can look concretely at the Musk Foundation, which few people have heard of but is one of the top 10 endowed private philanthropic foundations in the United States.

Why have few people heard of it? Because they routinely don’t spend the 5 percent of their assets that they’re required to do as a 501(c)(3) philanthropic foundation in the United States. And when they do, who do they give it to? As in the recent example, they gave it to a school called Ad Astra that is next to SpaceX in Texas that was designed pretty much exclusively for employees of Musk. That vision of outward-facing social purpose, his complete reneging of that, is itself quite extraordinary and sets him apart from others in his class.

Arguably, if empathy at a basic level is a woke mind virus, then the Gates Foundation is thoroughly infected with it. They have a vision of saving as many lives as possible, no matter where they are on the planet. Tons of critiques associated with that, of course, but a pretty standard way of trying to buy consent under conditions of grotesque inequality.

So it’s an extraordinarily bold affront to all of the normal ways historians have thought about how instability is stabilized in moments of extreme change. And what’s amazing for me is to see how resilient he’s been despite the depth of his provocations.

One of the reasons I wanted to have you on was because you wrote a book with Ben Tarnoff on Muskism that I think is important to understanding Musk — maybe to understanding some of the modern right.

The book is called “Hayek’s Bastards.” If you don’t mind, just tell me about the main argument of that.

The main argument of that is that there was a group of people who called themselves neoliberals — coined it in 1938. And when they called themselves neoliberals, they meant that they needed to figure out how to protect the principles of market freedom at a time when that was under challenge from, as they saw it, the left and the right.

So some of these people became quite famous: Milton Friedman, Friedrich Hayek, Gary Becker, George Stigler. And through the Cold War, of course, they exercised their political influence as well as they could and became favorites of Thatcher and Reagan. Come the end of the Cold War, one would think that they had reached their ultimate victory, right?

And yet, and this is what was so fascinating, when I went back to look at transcripts of the meetings that they were having, the papers they were publishing, as the Berlin Wall fell, as the Soviet Union fell apart, they were actually panicked about a new set of threats. The red enemy, as they often put it, had turned into a green one.

Remember, this was an early high point of activism against greenhouse gases and the dangers of what was then more often called the greenhouse effect and global warming than climate change.

They were worried about the resurgent demands for affirmative action and equality of representation in the workplace, equal pay. They were worried about minority sexual demands from the gay rights movement to the feminist movement.

So this becomes important because it creates the conditions for an alliance that would only really come to full fruition years later between people who wanted to defend free market freedoms as best they could with people who seemed to have opposition to those same progressive politics but for different reasons.

This is the moment of the paleoconservative alliance, for example, between a radical libertarian, like Murray Rothbard, with someone who is mostly interested in cultural nationalism, like Pat Buchanan.

Alternative for Germany is a perfect example of this, as well — founded by neoliberal economists who thought the euro was being mismanaged, creating alliances with ethnonationalists and opponents of Muslim immigration. How these two things ended up getting linked together seems to be an important question to figure out about our politics.

Well, one of the ways that I understand you as making the argument is that they’re linked together in the view that very fundamental categories and hierarchies that persist in society are natural. That they reflect I.Q. differentials, cultural differentials, people who are more or less fit either at the individual level, at the group level, etc.

And what I thought was interesting about this book in conversation with your Musk book is that, to me, there’s a lot of this sense, in the way Musk talks about the woke mind virus, that there are important hierarchies, categories in society, and that the danger comes from a constant progressive push or a woke push to dissolve them. That you can’t have Western civilization without the hierarchies upon which Western civilization was built.

I just interpret a lot of Musk’s political activity as not about free markets or any of these other things but about this.

Yeah. The subtitle to that book is “Race, Gold, I.Q. and the Capitalism of the Far Right.” And in all of those cases, there was an expressed belief that nature was an unequal place, and it distributed gains unequally, either through birth or territorial endowments, and that to deny that basic natural inequality was to pave the road to serfdom, as Hayek described it, in a new way.

Now it would be paved with green bricks and pink bricks instead of red bricks. And someone like Musk, I think, absolutely falls into that category.

Where I think the ’90s conversation gets updated and transformed in our present moment is especially around a category like I.Q. I.Q. is fascinating because in the 1990s, it came surging back. The arguments that put it back on the table were especially those of Charles Murray, the think tanker, and Richard Herrnstein, the Harvard psychologist, in their enormous best seller, “The Bell Curve,” from 1994.

That book said two things. It said at the one end of the bell curve, we’re going to get people whose I.Q. is going to be ever more determinative of economic success because of the knowledge economy we’re in. And at the low end of that bell curve, we’re going to have people who are going to be less and less able to perform in this knowledge economy, and they’re going to be a social problem.

And the incendiary part, of course, was that there are group differences in racial intelligence such that we can assume that there will be a disproportionately large number of Black people at that bottom end of the bell curve.

So the era of the knowledge economy is also the era of mass incarceration and the real turn toward more punitive police law-and-order policies. The way that this was mapped onto an idea of who is equipped and who isn’t for the big transition in how money will be made and jobs will look ends up being a pretty good kind of way to read that.

Why that’s different now is that, by their own statements, the tech leadership now assumes that almost all of those knowledge jobs are going to be automated away. So if I.Q. was predicting even at the far 10 percent of the curve for the people who would thrive in the coming internet world, then what happens if that has now been reduced to like 0.1 percent? Because all those other jobs — the coders, the project managers, the copywriters, the technical writers — are all going to be done by L.L.M.s and agents, which is what they are banking on.

Then you have a question where A.I. has actually eaten I.Q. And now you’ve gone from just a cognitive elite, which is what Herrnstein and Murray called it, to a hypersmall cognitive super-aristocracy.

I want to stay on this point because, to me, this coheres a lot of things in Musk that are puzzling from the outside. You’ve got this guy for whom the most important thing in the long-term vision is expanding the light cone of human consciousness through the stars.

There’s this bending of the psychic knee to the A.I. superiority. Musk is at the same time very worried about falling birthrates as he is destroying foreign aid, which can certainly help people thrive and be alive and live long lives and reproduce.

At the same time, he is virulently against the immigration policies of many of these countries. It’s like, where does this guy who, on the one hand, appears to believe in maximizing the quantity of consciousness fit with this guy who seems not to really like a lot of humanity? Where does this guy who believes in humanity fit with this guy who seems to be accelerating the A.I. turnover?

But if your sort of fundamental view of the world is about a kind of cognitive hierarchy, and you have certain views about where A.I. will sit in that, where different cultures sit in that, it’s not like one-to-one with any individual thing, not one-to-one with race, not even one-to-one with silicon versus flesh.

It’s just one-to-one with a certain vision of who or what qualifies as having the capacity to be a main character in this performance. Then a lot of it, I think, begins to fall into an unsettling, but a kind of coherent space.

I think there are a couple of ways to look at it.

One is to draw back on his grandfather’s ideology, which I hesitate to do too much because there’s no evidence that Musk himself was influenced by his maternal grandfather.

But his maternal grandfather, Joshua Haldeman, was a very active member of something called Technocracy Incorporated in Canada in the 1930s. And Technocracy Incorporated was proposing something very similar to what we’re talking about here.

It was about the dissolution of the existing price system, the dissolution of democracy altogether, the reduction of the unit of exchange and, I guess, store of value to something called an erg — which was the unit of energy that each human is able to produce in their life.

And the rational allocation of those ergs would be overseen by a very, very small but elite caste of engineers. That is an extremely far-fetched but very radical vision that actually, on the menu of existing political ideologies, probably comes the closest to what it seems Musk is describing.

But I think to get there, there are a few steps involved. To put it mildly.

[Both laugh.]

So there is the problem of the transition right now for Musk. I think it’s a central problem: How do we get from where we are now to this 10-year mile marker to the end of his life? Actually, he has no real plans for his succession.

One of the extraordinary things about SpaceX, from a corporate-law point of view, is that he has about 85 percent of the voting shares. If he dies tomorrow, you’d simply have to wait for those shares to be allotted.

I think he’s really banking on that transition having taken place in his own lifetime. How do you get there?

This is where the relationship to the “Hayek’s Bastards” discourse is actually relevant again. One of the arguments I make in that book is that under this atmosphere of uncertainty, in times of unrest, there is a tendency, as within the investor world, to do a flight to safety.

These far-right thinkers in association with neoliberal thinkers were offering different forms of refuge and safety where a certain value would be protected and more durable.

So those were things — your whiteness will save you, your access to a gold hoard will save you. Your citizenship value, which was one of Bannon’s talking points in the first Trump campaign, will save you.

The problem with Musk now is, if he’s saying that the people who will get through the filter are such a small minority, then how do you sell this vision to enough people to let you realize your goals in the medium term — except by defaulting to very shopworn scripts of ethnonationalism and social war?

So his decision to say: The way I’m going to win consent is simply to make you frightened of outsiders and make you believe you need my technology to save the lives of yourself and your family — is a way that politicians have used to justify a lack of material redistribution for over 100 years.

There’s actually nothing new about that, and it’s actually one of his, I would say, less innovative interventions, this belief that simply meming the fear of the invader will be enough to get you through that transitional moment until you get to, quite literally, liftoff or escape velocity.

I always thought the reason the Musk-Trump alliance was so potent, particularly in its early moments before Musk discredited himself as a direct actor through DOGE, was that they recognized in each other, and particularly Musk recognized in Trump — it’s why I think Musk endorsed him after the assassination attempt when Trump raised the fist — that Trump, in his third campaign for president, began to represent a return of masculine will to politics out of this era of woke, feminized, consensus-oriented politics.

For a lot of people, this was the idea of the builder, the industrialist, the Ayn Randian Superman.

The world spirit on horseback.

The world spirit on horseback. Yeah. Trump began to embody some of that. I don’t think he does now.

There’s this way in which, to Musk’s many, many, many fans — and pretty young to middle-aged male fans — that he represents this masculine conquering impulse.

It’s why some of the scary visions of the future he presents — at the level not of content but of texture — they don’t always scare people. Because to hear a person saying this is to hear a person saying: We will sally boldly forth and try to forge a glorious and unknown future for humanity. Even if it’s one that, on the face of it, barely seems like a future for humanity at all. But at least it is not afraid of the future.

Yeah, and I think it also sets up a Pascal’s wager or Roko’s Basilisk dynamic: The closer you are to him, the closer you adhere to his vision, the more likely it is that you’ll be one of the ones who gets through the filter.

So if he’s the one who is making the future, then to deny him would basically be to doom yourself to obsolescence — and that’s not an exchange that a lot of people are willing to make.

What’s amazing, really, is to see how resilient he’s been despite the depth of his provocations. But I think the important thing to see, just so as not to give him too much credit in this, is to see how he has actually managed to monopolize a lot of things that were the product of collective will, collective creation and collective intelligence.

That directs attention to the task of reform, which is: How can you dethrone Musk? Not in the sense of throwing away all of the technology that he produced by often piggybacking on other people’s innovations — but how can you create a different story whereby it’s the people, the nation, who decide this and not just one man and his posts?

Well that, I think, brings us back into the more material realm of immediate politics. Because one of the things that strikes me about what we are seeing now is that it is a fundamentally unstable equilibrium.

You have Elon Musk, whose companies, as you have described, are inextricably intertwined with politics. It would be hard to unwind the state from them.

But also by that very same token, if you’re a Democrat, the idea that you’re going to be dependent on Musk, and he can turn off Starlink if Ukraine or some other country or ally or even America is doing something he doesn’t like — that’s very, very dangerous. That intertwining with the state creates a vulnerability.

So it becomes very, very dangerous for him the more he becomes allied with a more extreme version of the right to have any left-wing or centrist candidates win really anywhere in the world in countries that are dependent on him.

At some point, either you end up in a situation where Musk needs to break the opposition to him or the state needs to contain the threat. It just seems fundamentally unstable.

It’s not like he gave $10 million. He just dropped $450 million like it’s nothing — because to him it is nothing.

The way that my co-author and I were talking about this — and we had, interestingly, more pragmatic conversations about Musk and Muskism in the book in Europe than we’ve had in the United States.

I think the proximity of Musk and the problems you’re describing to Americans makes it very hard to deal with it rationally. There’s such a desire to lash out at this level of cathexis — the suturing together of the future of the American economy with Musk and his products — that sometimes there’s a will to moralize and psychologize and just bat him away and denounce him without further reflection.

Whereas in Europe, we found that there was a three-R strategy that we were discussing. One is regulation, of course, and you could say that’s the route that the E.U. is taking.

The other model, though, is replacement. You look at what Musk has made, and you say: How much would it cost to make substitutes? And often the cost is very, very high.

But the third model is really to reimagine what the heck this tech is even for. And that’s where I think looking at the range of Musk’s history of business creation is actually helpful.

We alluded to this before, but the promise of electric autonomy, for example, that he was holding out when Tesla was mostly making E.V.s, but also when it was making solar panels and battery storage units, was actually much more socially useful and potentially inspiring than what he has done with his businesses ever since.

So I think one attitude there is to start from first principles and just say: What are we even investing in any of this for in the first place?

What do you want?

What do you want? And actually, one of the pedagogic virtues of Musk and his very monstrousness is he has made that question impossible not to ask. Because if the answer to that question is what we want is a continued level of being completely fused with this man, then I think a lot of people, on reflection, would not want that.

So he’s made us ask that question, and he knows that he’s put himself into a difficult situation with people asking that question — hence the impression of inevitability.

In The Economist interview, he said: It’s not like we can stop A.I. right now — that there’s no red button that says stop.

Actually, of course, there is.

Generative A.I., in its current model, requires an enormous amount of build-out of compute infrastructure that, right now, is being slowed down to the point of even stopping, through hundreds of moratoria across the country.

So it’s actually not true that there’s inevitability to the world that he’s imagining. It actually is true that we have options. Breaking out of that cosmic vector that he’s produced through the uses of the attention economy is the first step in that.

But it gets even more pragmatic than that. I’ll give you an example. In his newsletter this week, Paul Krugman — centrist liberal economist — has talked in two segments about nationalizing Starlink.

Paul’s only a centrist to you.

Right. Yeah. But this is actually not something that you would have expected him to talk about a few years ago. The use of the Defense Production Act, the comparisons to the nationalization of Montgomery Ward.

A pragmatic economist until recently would have said: If you nationalize a company that’s in the top 10 on the Nasdaq, you’re going to trigger a recession. There will be cascading effects of loss of confidence, repricing of risk ——

Loss of incentives for future companies to build this kind of capacity.

Absolutely. But the very fact that this controlled demolition of the very Muskist dependencies you’re describing is now being brought onto the agenda, I think, is very encouraging.

But this is what I actually mean by an unstable equilibrium. I saw those pieces from Paul. I thought they were very, very interesting. And as you say, it’s interesting that Paul — whom I call a progressive economist, but not a communist, not someone prone to nationalization — was talking about this.

I think it speaks to a world where you could really imagine a situation with a Democratic president, and Musk turns off Starlink at some critical moment, and the Defense Production Act is immediately engaged, and you do have this moment of genuine showdown.

I think from Musk’s perspective, this needs to be understood as a risk of what he’s doing and the way he’s acting. And from the other perspective, because you are getting to this position ——

And we should say, one reason I haven’t focused on the Ukraine Starlink question is, right now, the reporting is contested in a way I cannot untangle as to whether orders came from somewhere inside the Trump administration or were implied from somewhere in the Trump administration or the activity was from Musk.

I just don’t know the answer, and I can see it also being a miscommunication. These things happen, too. So I don’t want to say confidently what happened there.

But I think one can say relatively confidently that you could imagine a series of things happening where — and look, I don’t love Michael Bloomberg dropping $80 million at the end of the campaign, either — I don’t think this is the way campaigns should work — you begin having much more serious efforts at restricting the ability of megabillionaires to drop this much money.

Musk is a billionaire on a scale that somebody like Bloomberg cannot even touch. It is just rare for an individual person to have so much power that they’re not a state unto themselves, but they are some kind of state-capacity-size entity operating. It’s like the Vatican of technology that he’s got over there.

But I think it’s also important to keep in mind one of the things that I started this conversation talking about, which is the financial dependency. SpaceX is in the top 10 in the stock market indexes.

More than 50 percent of Americans hold some kind of equities or stocks. Most of those are directly or indirectly, mostly indirectly, through passive funds, connected to the health of Musk’s businesses. So let’s say 20 to 30 percent of Americans have some kind of stake there indirectly.

One of the things that Musk has proposed recently is that he give one stock in SpaceX to every American child. The proposal is that would happen through the Trump accounts, which are automatically made accessible to children in the United States.

If he goes through with his plan, then that number of American citizens goes up to about 50 percent. There you’re approaching a way of blackmailing, you could say, the American population away from following someone like Krugman’s plans by saying: Do you really want to hurt yourself? Are you going to hurt your child like that by punishing me, Musk, the person who’s keeping the stock market afloat?

And if you get into the granular questions of who owns the stock, it gets even more interesting. Who are the top 10 investors? The Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan — huge amount of SpaceX stock. The primary educational target of the Trump administration and often Musk himself, Harvard University, is a huge holder of SpaceX. University of North Carolina.

When you see that, although high-profile and superficially startling moments of turning on and off drone connectivity in the battlefield are the sharp edge of the wedge, the base of what anchors the dominance of the Silicon Valley digital sector in the United States is really in the stock market itself.

The fact that that’s how we do redistribution, that’s how we do the social contract, is saying: You pay into this market-determined pension fund, and you will be paid out of it. And whoever is keeping that thing propped up arguably has the real power of saying what the social contract looks like.

Then I think sitting in that bidirectional dependency, but that real dependency, it’s maybe worth ending in a strange place, but I actually do think it’s an important one.

You mentioned that the conversations in Europe are maybe a little less prone to psychologizing than the conversations in America. The problem, though, is that Musk’s psychology is very important.

There’s something that he says a lot. I was there in 2016 at the ReCode conference — I was, actually, I think, one of the first people to write about this — when he was talking about how he believed it was very likely we lived in a computer simulation.

This is a sort of idea that Nick Bostrom, that philosopher you mentioned, is very associated with. But he has kept saying it, actually in somewhat stronger terms. I want to play this clip. This is Elon Musk on Walter Isaacson’s show:

Archival clip of Musk: I once had a dinner at my house with a physicist and a computer scientist, and they’re both leaders in their field. I asked: What do you think the probabilities are that we’re in a simulation? The physicist said zero percent, and the computer scientist said 100 percent simultaneously. So I guess maybe I should go 50 percent. I don’t know. There are odd things that happen in this simulation, especially if you’re me. Think about it: If you’re me, should all these things really be happening? Should I really be making spaceships to go to the moon and Mars? That doesn’t seem real.

The simulation theory is that, if you just imagine an advanced society would create lots of simulations, the way we make lots of video games, you just shouldn’t assume that we are living in the base reality.

That’s sort of the argument in a nutshell. But he goes further, and I get, in a psychological way, why. I’ve heard him say this now repeatedly that what really seems unlikely is to be Elon Musk — to be building starships and influencing global politics and having 250 million X followers, or whatever it is, and being the first trillionaire.

The mixture of a life that is so unlikely and also not grounded in some other ontology — not some religion or some other way of imagining the world — plus an attraction to the simulation hypothesis and, of course, to be a lifelong gamer.

I just think that for a person with as much power as he has, to have that kind of psychology to suspect that this is a game where your role in it is making big moves — I don’t really know how to describe that situation. But it is a distinctive one that we all now have a lot of exposure to.

There are a couple of varieties of the simulation theory, too. One is we are all simply just artifacts of this future civilization’s computer video game.

But the other is that most people are shadow people and a small number of people are actually player characters. And it seems like that’s the one that orients him most.

In the libertarian community that reflected a lot on these things, one of the people is Robin Hanson, the George Mason University economist, who said: What kind of ways would we conduct ourselves if this were true?

And he says: If this were true, then it would make sense to first care nothing about other people — so things like foreign aid and the welfare state would be frivolous things to spend time on — to be as entertaining as possible, to accumulate as much wealth as possible and to try to simply organize the world around you in as successful a way as you can.

There’s this radical reneging on anything like social responsibility that is only possible if you embrace this incredibly nihilistic reaffirmation of your megalomania. And the question is how to remove the props and struts that hold him up in that delusion, because it is not true, and he needs to be somehow persuaded from the outside that it’s not true.

If he continues to be incentivized to indulge in those ways of thinking, then he will never be required to be divested of that.

I think that’s a place to end. Always our final question: What are three books you’d recommend to the audience?

Well, there’s so much amazing work happening right now in the world of tech criticism and political economy, so I wanted to draw attention to three exceptional recent books that move up the stack from under the ground to the clouds and the apps.

The first book would be Thea Riofrancos’s book “Extraction: The Frontiers of Green Capitalism,” which is about something that we’ve put out of our minds for the last 18 months or so, which is the challenges of climate combined with a world that still operates according to the price mechanism and where the state can fit in.

None of these machines, certainly none of the data centers, would work without the raw materials being extracted somewhere from the earth and put into their circuitry. Thea gives a wonderful description of the political settlements and tensions and struggles that emerge in the process of doing so.

The second book would be a book by Nick Srnicek called “Silicon Empires.” I think one of the handicaps we have right now in talking about tech ideology and tech political economy is a lot of things get jumbled together. When you talk about semiconductors, it’s somehow also a discussion of frontier labs, it’s also a discussion of neoclouds and data centers. But these individual market sectors actually operate under very different dynamics. And I haven’t read anything yet better than Nick Srnicek as a calm, guided tour up the stack of what A.I. actually is as a built entity.

The third book is one I think is really special. It’s called “Against Tech Oligarchy” by JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine, and both of them were organizers within tech companies in Silicon Valley.

Clarissa Redwine led the successful organization of Kickstarter, and both of them were at Twitter trying to organize employees at the time of the Musk takeover.

What they draw attention to is the fact that class struggle and class politics exist in Silicon Valley inside of tech companies, and they give the insider’s view of how you practice class power inside of the tech sector. It’s interestingly not always, as they see it, through the old-fashioned model of getting recognition for a union. That can sometimes slow down some of the dynamics that draw people into social activism.

So it’s a very cleareyed and wonderfully written insight into something that I think most people know very little about.

Quinn Slobodian, thank you very much.

It’s my pleasure.
