ARTICLE

I’m in ‘You Can See Everything.’ Here’s My Side of the Story.
I’m in ‘You Can See Everything.’ Here’s my side of the story.
By Amy Chozick
Published 2026-10-30 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/opinion/you-can-see-everything-elizabeth-holmes-nathan-fielder.html

Over opening weekend, someone posted on X: “Imagine how weird it would be to watch ‘You Can See Everything’ with Amy Chozick.”

Let me tell you how weird.

It was wild to watch the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, reading the lengthy profile of Ms. Holmes that I wrote for The New York Times on a laptop, seemingly just as it was published, in 2023. At one point, Mr. Evans reads a quote from Ms. Holmes about her depiction by actors in film and TV — “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” — and says it doesn’t sound like something she would say. He suggests Ms. Holmes must instead have said, “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character they created.” She agreed.

I had no idea that a central theme of the film would revolve around this disputed quote, which essentially opens and closes the movie.

“You Can See Everything,” a Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documentary, is, as one review put it, “an existential vortex, challenging the concept of truth.” It might not even be, by some overly strict definitions, a documentary.

It is quite funny. I howled laughing at the uncomfortable weirdness of the depictions of the couple that Mr. Fielder and Mr. Oppenheim constructed. Ms. Holmes and Mr. Evans appeared to have let the filmmakers see everything, even showing Mr. Evans taking a shower. But when I saw the film, I kept thinking: Where is the nanny?

She was nowhere to be seen. Without her, the couple comes off as harried multitasking parents, Ms. Holmes literally rocking the baby with one foot.

I met Vanessa, the Salvadoran woman who was sometimes on hand to help care for their toddler and newborn, because I also spent several days inside the couple’s canary-yellow rental home in Del Mar, Calif. My article was published on May 7, 2023, 23 days before Ms. Holmes went to prison after being found guilty of fraud at her once-hot blood-testing-device company.

We went to the zoo and for tacos and smoothies. They even offered to let me stay with them. I declined. And by the looks of the bed they dusted off for Mr. Fielder, I think I made the right call.

I left in March. Mr. Fielder and his crew arrived in April. I was struck by the film’s opening text that said Ms. Holmes hadn’t spoken publicly in seven years, since my profile was published shortly after Mr. Fielder and his crew arrived.

Ms. Holmes and Mr. Evans seemed convinced that the longer you spend with them, in the cozy kitchen, playing with the kids, walking the dog on the beach, the more you’d be hypnotized, too. How could you not be? For them, access was a conduit to a type of exoneration. They are salespeople. Their humanity is what they now had to sell.

It’s why the couple extended so much access for my Times profile, hoping it would help reshape Ms. Holmes’s image and garner sympathy. Then the story came out.

Half the internet and many of my former Times colleagues derided the story as a puff piece. I was relentlessly trolled online by people who thought I was too easy on her. Ms. Holmes and Mr. Evans, meanwhile, apparently thought I’d been too hard on them.

So they might as well embrace Mr. Fielder and — as is explored in the documentary — ask for a cut of the film’s profits.

My time in Mr. Fielder’s vortex began in June 2025, when he reached out saying he’d love to “pick your brain” off the record. He’d also spent time with Ms. Holmes before she went to prison — we’d just missed each other — and was working on a documentary. I promised not to tell anyone about the project.

We spoke a couple of times, comparing notes about our surreal experiences with Ms. Holmes. We’d so nearly overlapped that she’d worn the same camel sweater. It almost felt like a support group. It’s a pretty small circle of people who understand the dizzying experience of sitting in that canary-yellow house by the Pacific, watching Ms. Holmes nurse her baby days before reporting to prison. We’d both stared into those unblinking eyes. Both offered her Kleenex when she cried. Mr. Evans offered us both breakfast. We both felt ourselves getting swept up by Ms. Holmes’s quiet magnetism.

I’d left the house thinking I had better check my wallet. Mr. Fielder seemed to be similarly conflicted.

I wasn’t particularly familiar with Mr. Fielder’s work, but I wanted to be helpful. I tentatively agreed to appear on camera. Why not? He seems like a mensch! I mentioned this to a friend, a rabid Fielder fan who also happens to work in communications. His advice: “ABORT! ABORT!”

I told Mr. Fielder I actually didn’t feel comfortable being on camera. I apologized and wished him luck. He was disappointed. He laid on the guilt (fair). He’d already rented the camera package and had a crew traveling my way as we spoke. He promised he’d make it “very fun and easy.” I felt bad. I wanted to help a nice Canadian man make his documentary. I asked my friend what to do. His response: “LEAVE TOWN!”

I have to admit, I ghosted Mr. Fielder. As it turns out, ghosting Nathan Fielder is hard to do. He is unusually likable, persistent and persuasive — winningly awkward, as he seems to be on camera — and there’s something that makes you want to help him.

Then, in February 2026, Mr. Fielder contacted me again. He wanted help to “clarify a little thing.” Ah, yes, a little thing. Ms. Holmes, he explained, said I’d misquoted her.

In the film, after reading the quote, the couple call their P.R. team. And sure enough, back in 2023, I had heard from one of her publicists who explained that Ms. Holmes’s recollection of our conversation differed from what was published. Would I double-check the quote? At the time, I reviewed my notes with my editors, who stood by the reporting. Mr. Evans sent The Times an 80-second audio clip, but it didn’t contain the disputed exchange. We heard nothing further and considered the matter resolved. (I’ve explained the full backstory here.)

It surprised me, because Ms. Holmes and I had spoken so much about the persona she created at Theranos. When I showed up at the rental house, she looked and sounded like a completely different person from the girl boss people remembered. What was with the James Earl Jones inflection? The Steve Jobs turtlenecks? The red lipstick?

In my profile, Ms. Holmes explained that having founded Theranos at 19, she’d created a public persona to be taken seriously in business.

Now, three years later, Mr. Fielder was asking about that quote. I informed my old editor, who advised that I not reply. Instead, we referred Mr. Fielder’s inquiry to The Times’s public relations department, standard practice when a published article is being challenged.

When the documentary premiered at the Telluride Film Festival, I heard from friends who told me that my Times article was in the movie.

I sent several requests to A24, the film’s studio, asking to see it. It felt as if every culture writer and midlevel executive in Hollywood had seen the movie and was asking me about it. I heard about a big screening in Los Angeles. They said it was at capacity. A spokeswoman at a firm helping A24 offered “to assist with a ticket to a local theater” when it opened. (“No spoilers.”)

I texted Mr. Fielder to see if he could help. (Canadian mensch and all.) He said he’d try, and then reminded me that I never did answer his question about the disputed “character I created” quote (single-tear emoji). And somehow I felt guilty all over again. I apologized. I told him I knew it was too late, but to call me if he wanted me to explain.

I finally saw “You Can See Everything” as God and A24 intended at a 4:30 p.m. showing on opening day at the Landmark Theaters Sunset in Los Angeles.

I spit-laughed at the scene of Mr. Fielder sitting on the second floor of Beer Authority across the street from the New York Times building, eating nachos and trying to track me down. I haven’t worked on staff at the paper since 2022. I live in Los Angeles and write screenplays now. But hey, I appreciate a good establishing shot.

The documentary’s postscript says Mr. Fielder eventually got in touch with me, and that I stood by my story but didn’t provide evidence supporting the quote. That’s not exactly what happened. I never discussed the disputed quote with Mr. Fielder. I referred his inquiry to The Times, which has stood by the reporting.

I don’t know what Ms. Holmes told Mr. Fielder that didn’t make the cut, but the tone of their conversations on camera is different from my memory of how she and I interacted. With me, our talks felt very much mother-to-mother. After Theranos imploded, Ms. Holmes told me that she finally felt free: “I began my life again.” I remember thinking that she sounded a lot like someone who had finally broken out of a cult and been deprogrammed.

But then I remembered that Ms. Holmes had been running the cult. It was her vortex all along, and thanks to Mr. Fielder and Mr. Oppenheim, we all get to experience it.

Amy Chozick, a former New York Times reporter, is a screenwriter and an author based in Los Angeles. Her debut novel, “With Friends Like You,” was published in July.

ARTICLE

Minnesota Declined to Buy a Prison for $75 Million. D.H.S. Paid $495 Million.
The recent purchase of the prison to hold immigrants is among the acquisitions facing scrutiny in the Trump administration’s mass deportation push.
By Ernesto Londoño
Published 2026-10-30 22:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/us/minnesota-prison-homeland-security.html

CoreCivic, a private prison company, approached the Minnesota Department of Corrections last year offering to sell a long-shuttered detention facility. The price: $75 million.

State officials passed. They didn’t have the funds to buy the Prairie Correctional Facility in western Minnesota, nor did they need a prison of its size or have the ability to staff it.

Last summer, to their astonishment, the 1,600-bed prison sold for more than $495 million. The buyer: the Department of Homeland Security.

“The price tag is so different than the conversations we were having last year,” said Safia Khan, the deputy commissioner and chief of staff for the Minnesota Department of Corrections. “It was a shock.”

D.H.S. purchased the facility amid a multibillion-dollar spending spree to support the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. It plans to use it to expand its immigrant detention capacity, one part of a buildup whose ballooning budget was faulted last month by the Government Accountability Office, a watchdog agency, as a hastily and poorly planned “waste” of millions of taxpayer dollars.

The department is also facing scrutiny over the purchase of 10 used jets for $464 million this year in a no-bid contract. The department said it needed the planes for deportation flights, but most of them have largely sat idle.

Some officials in Minnesota, which the White House has portrayed as an avatar of poor governance and fraud, expressed outrage this week after learning about the amount taxpayers paid CoreCivic. The company donated $500,000 to President Trump’s inauguration committee, and its stock price soared after his 2024 victory.

“Trump scamming taxpayers out of almost half a billion dollars is outrageous, especially at a time when Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran are already raising prices for Minnesotans,” Attorney General Keith Ellison, a Democrat running for re-election, said in a statement.

When it opens, the Prairie Correctional Facility will be the sole dedicated immigration prison in Minnesota.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, referred questions about the price the government paid for the Prairie Correctional Facility to D.H.S., which did not respond to an emailed inquiry on Friday.

In a statement, CoreCivic said the federal government bought the facility following an appraisal that established its “fair market value.” It added, “For this specialized property, independent appraisers hired by the federal government used a cost-based methodology grounded in current replacement cost, depreciation, land value and other market-based factors.”

The Prairie Correctional Facility was built in 1992 by the city of Appleton, Minn., population 1,392. In its early years, the medium-security facility housed prisoners from the Puerto Rico Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation. In the mid-1990s, it was acquired and run by CoreCivic, which had contracts with several state corrections agencies, including Minnesota’s.

The prison closed in 2010 as demand for out-of-state detention bed space declined. Over the years, Minnesota officials periodically considered buying or using it again, Ms. Khan said, but it was never a good fit. Its remote location near the South Dakota border made it impractical from a staffing and infrastructure standpoint, she said.

Last year, as Minnesota officials were mulling closing one of the state’s largest prisons near the Twin Cities, state officials met with CoreCivic executives, who were seeking to offload the Prairie Correctional Facility.

In May 2025, Kelly Durham, the company’s director of state partnerships, offered to refurbish and sell the prison to Minnesota for $75 million, according to an email obtained by The New York Times. The news station KARE 11 reported on that offer this week.

During meetings, company officials seemed eager to get rid of the prison, at one point offering to sell it for a fraction of that price, Ms. Khan said. But talks between CoreCivic and the state agency gained little traction.

In August, CoreCivic announced the sale in a statement that said the company intended to use a portion of the proceeds to buy back company stock. Days after the deal was announced, the Department of Homeland Security gave CoreCivic an $18.6 million no-bid contract to run the prison for a year. It’s unclear why the final sale price for the prison jumped so much after last year’s offer.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who was in Minnesota on Friday to announce developments in the administration’s efforts to root out fraud in safety net programs, said he had not heard about the prison deal. He called questions about the gap between the 2025 price tag and what the government paid “a waste of our time.”

David A. Fahrenthold contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

For much of her adult life, the woman struggled with anxiety and depression, but it never affected her sleep. She found a case report of a man on an antidepressant who had the same drastic worsening of anxiety, depression and insomnia when he took rifampin. ARTICLE

She Was Racked With Anxiety and Crushed by Insomnia. Finally She Understood Why.
The woman’s symptoms were common, but the cause was not.
By Lisa Sanders, M.D.
Published 2026-10-30 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/well/rififi-anxiety-insomnia-tb-treatment-rifampin.html

The 35-year-old woman’s eyes snapped open; her heart pounded. Her chest was tight, and she gasped for air as a terrible and familiar sense of panic spread through her. She checked the clock: 3 a.m. She tried the breathing exercises that she had to practice so often lately. They never really helped, but they distracted her from her terror. It had been a few months since she was able to get a good night’s sleep. And she was so very tired.

For much of her adult life, the woman struggled with anxiety and depression, but it never affected her sleep. Between talk therapy and antidepressants, she had it mostly under control. Then it flared that spring, around the time she started a new position at her company. Change was hard, her psychiatrist reminded her as she tried a couple of new medications to help get through the transition. Nothing seemed to help. She started having panic attacks that seemed to come on randomly, without any triggering stressors. Even at night. In the predawn hours, she would wake up in a pool of sweat, heart pounding. The days were no better. In addition to the fatigue from not sleeping, she was in a constant state of dread and anxiety. She couldn’t focus. She was an engineer, and thinking clearly was essential to her job.

She asked her psychiatrist week after week where this might be coming from. Certainly, there were stressors. In her new position, she had a continuing conflict with a colleague. And she had some medical problems. Two years earlier, a case of Covid had caused a flare-up of her Behcet’s disease, a rare autoimmune condition that had been quiet for the 13 years since her diagnosis. After months of debilitating joint pain and extreme stiffness, she agreed to start an immune-suppressing medication to tamp down the antibodies causing the disease. It helped with the pain, but suppressing her immune system put her at risk for tuberculosis — and sure enough, she tested positive for it a year after starting on the medication.

A chest X-ray did not show any sign of an active TB infection, and that was a relief. But unless she was treated, there was a good chance that her latent TB would become active. Four months on a drug called rifampin would kill the TB bacterium before that could happen. So that summer, she added it to her new regimen of medications. The drug turned her urine and tears an orange color, a side effect she had been warned about.

In the Grips of Anxiety

That spring and summer, her psychiatrist suggested a slew of medications: for sleep, for anxiety, even for bipolar disorder. But panic and dread remained her constant companions.

She requested and was granted a leave of absence from work and checked herself into the closest mental-health facility she could find. It was in Arizona, nearly seven hours away from her home in Los Alamos, N.M. Doctors there changed her antidepressants and had her in daily therapy sessions to help her develop strategies to manage the anxiety. Despite all this, she started having suicidal thoughts. When her insurance ran out after 30 days, the doctors were reluctant to discharge her, but she couldn’t pay to stay and didn’t think their treatments helped.

Her aunt lived in the next town over and was an important source of support, but she too was overwhelmed by the woman’s anxious days and panicked nights. Her brother lived in Seattle and invited her to stay with him and his family, so the woman’s aunt drove her there. But the change of scenery didn’t help. She felt supported by her family, but her depression deepened. She cried every day. Her world seemed dark. Her chest felt so tight that it seemed like work just to breathe. The suicidal thoughts were overwhelming, and she started to think more about how to end her life.

When she asked her aunt to take her to Switzerland, which has permissive laws around assisted suicide, her family insisted that she go to the nearby University of Washington Harborview Medical Center to be taken care of by the psychiatric teams there. In the emergency room, she was evaluated by the medicine team. When they didn’t find a cardiac cause of her chest pain, she was seen by a psychiatry resident and his attending doctor. One of them asked her if she was considering suicide. Not at that moment, she told them, but she did admit that she didn’t want to continue to live if she had to feel this way. She told the team she suspected that this sudden worsening of her anxiety and depression was caused by some undiagnosed physical disorder. She wondered about an endocrine issue and had read that Behcet’s could cause psychiatric symptoms. Could that be what was driving these terrible feelings?

She was admitted to the psychiatric unit for further evaluation. The team considered the possibility that her depression had a medical cause, but she’d had lots of tests looking for this in New Mexico and nothing was found. Still, they asked their rheumatologist to see her and help them understand if this debilitating mood change could be a result of her Behcet’s, which can cause neuropsychiatric symptoms. After seeing the patient and reviewing her records, the rheumatologist thought it unlikely. In her experience, neuropsychiatric forms of Behcet’s were characterized by an acute onset of psychosis or confusion, not the subacute worsening of existing anxiety and depression.

The Troublemaker

On her second day in the hospital, the pharmacologist, who was part of the team caring for her, asked a question: How long had she been on the rifampin? The past three and a half months, she told him. She was due to stop after she had completed four months of treatment for her latent TB.

The doctor looked thoughtful. Then he explained that rifampin ramps up the machinery in the liver that breaks down some drugs, including antidepressants. And increasing the speed with which a drug is eliminated will reduce its effectiveness. A dose of an antidepressant that might have worked well before starting rifampin will suddenly not be sufficient. The timing of the rifampin matched up well with the onset of the woman’s worsening psychiatric symptoms.

The team seemed surprised by this. They had not seen many people on rifampin, and they certainly didn’t know this about the drug. But they were reluctant to cut short the treatment. TB was at least as great a danger as depression and anxiety. So they increased the dose of her antidepressant instead, saying they would monitor her mood until she finished her course of the anti-TB treatment.

The next 10 days were brutal. She went to talk therapy. She worked with the therapists on improving her strategies for managing her anxiety and depression. But she didn’t feel better. When she stopped the rifampin, there was no instant change. But over the next week, the grip of anxiety began to loosen. The perpetual sensation of fight or flight eased, and she was able to see the possibility of recovery. While she didn’t feel completely herself, she no longer felt that everything was impossible. She was even able to imagine once again doing the things she loved.

Once at home, the patient looked on the internet to see what she could find out about this drug that had brought her down so low. She found a case report of a man on an antidepressant who had the same drastic worsening of anxiety, depression and insomnia when he took rifampin. That gave her a little hope, but she knew it would take a while to fully recover. The type of antidepressant she was taking could take weeks to start working. But over the next month, she did start to feel better. Almost like her old self.

Rifampin is derived from a bacterium called Amycolatopsis rifamycinica, whose antibacterial properties were first identified in 1957. This bacterium was named after the lead character in a popular French gangster movie called “Rififi,” which became a slang term for “trouble.” It turned out to be a very good name indeed. There are now over 800 medications that are known to be altered when administered with rifampin.

It has been a year since the patient was hospitalized. Her depression and anxiety are well controlled by her antidepressant, now that there isn’t another drug messing with its effectiveness. She hasn’t gone back to work yet. She’s not eager to go back to a job that gave her so much agita. She is taking her time, enjoying the opportunity to look around and figure out what’s next.

The harrowing details of that night were described in a lawsuit filed on Wednesday in State Supreme Court in Manhattan, accusing Mr. Suh of assault and battery.

The trajectories of the two cadets appear to have diverged after that night. The woman, identified in the suit as Jane Doe, struggled to move on with her life after the traumatic episode, according to her suit, while Mr. Suh seemed to flourish as he pursued a career in public health at elite institutions.

But in June 2026, Mr. Suh was charged with one count of assault within a maritime and territorial jurisdiction. He pleaded guilty, and is expected to be sentenced to around two years in prison, according to the terms of his plea agreement.

While awaiting sentencing, however, Mr. Suh has been allowed to continue his education. In October, Mr. Suh asked the judge in his case, Philip M. Halpern, to push his sentencing to January, citing a desire to finish his academic term at Columbia, as well as complete a program aimed at rehabilitating felons. Federal prosecutors did not object.

Judge Halpern granted Mr. Suh’s request.

A representative for West Point did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesman for the Mailman School of Public Health at Columbia, where Mr. Suh is studying, declined to comment. Thomas Kenniff, a lawyer for Mr. Suh, said he would not comment on any ongoing ligation.

Columbia was unaware of Mr. Suh’s criminal conviction before The New York Times informed the university of it, according to a person with knowledge of Mr. Suh’s status who was granted anonymity to discuss a matter involving a current student. The university is taking “swift action,” the person noted. Applicants to the school are not required to disclose prior criminal convictions or charges, the person said.

At the time of the crime, Mr. Suh was competing to become the first captain of West Point, an honor earned by the top cadet in each graduating class, a federal prosecutor said at his plea hearing in June.

In March 2022, Mr. Suh and Jane Doe broke up. In May, she reported her experience on that night to the Army Criminal Investigation Division at West Point, according to her lawsuit. It is not clear what came of that investigation.

Mr. Suh would attend multiple Ivy League institutions, presenting himself as a champion of public health and launching an organization aimed at addressing systemic inequalities in America’s health care system.

Over the next four years, Mr. Suh graduated with a bachelor's degree from Cornell University, where he was a member of the school’s Center for Health Equity. He called himself an “educator committed to diversity, equity and inclusion,” according to his directory page. Cornell did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Suh was also a research coordinator at Cornell’s medical school. He co-founded an organization that sought to address health disparities through advocacy, according to its website.

Following his graduation from Cornell this year, Mr. Suh received a scholarship to attend Columbia for a master’s degree at the Mailman School.

Russell Kornblith, a lawyer representing Jane Doe, said that any parent would be “haunted” by the facts of his client’s case.

“Our client was committed to carrying this pregnancy to term, and it was taken from her,” Mr. Kornblith said in an interview. “And it was taken from her in a place where she should have been safe.”

Mr. Suh and Jane Doe began dating in October 2020, according to the lawsuit. And by around January 2022, she learned that she was pregnant. He repeatedly pressured her to terminate the pregnancy, but she resisted, the suit said.

Mr. Suh even told Jane Doe that he “would commit suicide if she did not get an abortion,” according to the suit.

Unable to sway her, Mr. Suh hatched a plan to deceive her, according to the lawsuit.

During his guilty plea in June, Mr. Suh outlined the details of the plan to a judge in federal court in Manhattan, according to court records.

Without Jane Doe’s knowledge, Mr. Suh created an account with an online pharmacy using her name, personal information and identification. He then used the account to purchase abortion medication and ship it to West Point. He also obtained Xanax through a friend, he said.

According to the suit, Mr. Suh impersonated Jane Doe on the pharmacy’s online forum and asked questions about taking the medication, including whether she would “feel the pills in my vagina.”

Then, he said, he put his scheme into action.

“I led her to believe that I had come to support her pregnancy when, in fact, I did not,” Mr. Suh told the judge, according to the lawsuit.

On Feb. 4, 2022, Mr. Suh visited Jane Doe in her barracks, where he encouraged her to drink what he called a “prenatal protein shake,” the suit said.

According to the lawsuit, Jane Doe became sick and fell asleep. At one point she woke up and felt “an odd sensation in her gums,” the suit said. She found two pills in her mouth and spit them out.

But Mr. Suh grabbed the pills and tried to put them back in her mouth, the lawsuit claimed, telling her “eat this, it’s good for you.” Mr. Suh then moved closer “and began touching her vagina” while she was incapacitated, the lawsuit said.

He left her at about 11 p.m. and returned to his barracks room.

At around midnight, Jane Doe woke up in pain, according to her lawsuit. She “vomited and experienced diarrhea,” and then stumbled into the bathroom, where she discovered that she was “profusely bleeding from her vagina,” the suit said.

Fearing a miscarriage, Jane Doe called Mr. Suh, according to the lawsuit. He did not respond.

Katherine Rosman and Emily Steel contributed reporting.

Jeff Lindbom flew with Ms. Bennett in the Navy while she was deployed on the U.S.S. Mr. Kean has said the disclosure shows that Ms. Bennett is incapable of working across the aisle in Washington.

ARTICLE

A Navy Pilot Tries to Flip a Key House Seat, Right by Trump’s Golf Club
Rebecca Bennett, a Democrat, is vying to unseat Representative Thomas Kean Jr. in a New Jersey district that includes President Trump’s Bedminster golf club.
By Tracey Tully
Published 2026-10-31 07:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/nyregion/rebecca-bennett-nj-house-race.html

To Rebecca Bennett, the limitations of the MH-60 Seahawk she flew as a 20-something Navy helicopter pilot were striking. Its computer processors were too slow to load a moving Google map, she said. Floppy diskettes were the norm. And female pilots had nowhere to safely urinate on long flights.

The problems, she said, seemed fixable, but not from a cockpit.

So Ms. Bennett, now 39 and running for Congress in one of the country’s most closely watched midterm races, applied in 2014 to the Navy’s elite Test Pilot School, where for a year she trained to assess and improve aircraft performance.

“To go try,” she said, “to make this stuff better.”

That same mind-set, she said, led her to launch her first campaign for office soon after President Trump was elected to a second term. “I was like, ‘I’ve got to go throw myself at this problem,’” Ms. Bennett, a Democrat, said in an interview.

To get to Washington, she will first need to unseat Representative Thomas Kean Jr., a New Jersey Republican who shares a name with his father, a former governor.

The race was upended this spring after Mr. Kean, 58, disappeared from Capitol Hill for nearly four months, an absence he later said was tied to a long-term hospital stay for depression. Waning public support for the president and alarm over the high prices of gas, diesel and groceries have only added to Mr. Kean’s challenges.

Democrats see Mr. Kean’s Seventh District seat as one of their best pickup opportunities in Tuesday’s elections, in spite of the congressman’s formidable fund-raising advantage, which has helped to fuel a barrage of negative ads against Ms. Bennett, a former health care executive.

Mr. Kean and his Republican allies have tried to depict Ms. Bennett as too left-leaning for the affluent district and its most famous, part-time resident: Mr. Trump, who often spends time at his golf club in Bedminster. “She’s a greedy, liberal millionaire who doesn’t care about you,” intones an ad paid for by the Kean campaign.

But a review of Ms. Bennett’s life and career offers a far more complex portrait, one that appears to be resonating with voters in a state that a year ago elected another Navy helicopter pilot, Gov. Mikie Sherrill, by a resounding margin. In the final weeks of the campaign, officials with two Republican super PACs withdrew about $2 million in ads booked in support of Mr. Kean after internal polling showed his odds dimming; early Democratic turnout has been roughly twice the rate of Republican turnout in the northern New Jersey district.

‘Incredibly driven’

Ms. Bennett spent 15 years in the Navy and the Air National Guard and was registered to vote as a Republican until she was nearly 30. She describes herself as a “patriot” at rallies where supporters hold signs that read “country over party,” a campaign slogan. In grad school at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, her similarly hard-charging M.B.A. classmates voted her “most likely to become president.”

It is a prediction that was tossed around in her childhood home in Granbury, Texas, too. Her sister, Sarah Matz, said it was a lighthearted nod toward Ms. Bennett’s tendency to “always go to the hardest thing.”

At 16, Ms. Bennett moved 75 miles away from home and into a dorm room at the University of North Texas to begin two years of publicly funded college-level math and science coursework. At 18, she won an R.O.T.C. scholarship and entered Cornell University, where she studied chemical engineering.

When Ms. Bennett, the maid of honor at her sister’s wedding, recited a long speech from memory, Ms. Matz recalled: “My husband’s friends were like, ‘Your sister’s really intense.’”

“She is incredibly smart. She’s incredibly driven,” Ms. Matz added.

“That’s who she is. She’s not trying to be anything else, you know?”

Jeff Lindbom flew with Ms. Bennett in the Navy while she was deployed on the U.S.S. Nimitz in the Persian Gulf, during Operation Enduring Freedom. Their first flight together was a nighttime training mission, he said, and Ms. Bennett was his instructor.

The helicopter they were flying came too close to another. “A not-good situation,” he said. “Definitely gets the hair standing on the back of your neck.”

Ms. Bennett took charge to get the pilots reoriented and in the coming days gave Mr. Lindbom, a friend, a failing grade. Her high standards helped to shape him as a pilot, he said; years later, he would follow her to Test Pilot School.

The school, founded in 1945 and based in Patuxent, Md., is known for its rigor. Twenty-two of its graduates, including a woman who graduated with Ms. Bennett in 2016, have gone on to become astronauts since 2000, according to a spokesman for NASA.

To save time commuting during the yearlong program, Ms. Bennett put a mattress on the floor of a classmate’s condo and returned home on weekends to see her husband, who at the time was also on active duty in the Navy.

“She knew what it would take to succeed in that kind of environment,” the classmate, Kristine Sweigart, said. “She literally lived on my floor for a year so that she could excel.”

That was also the year that Ms. Bennett’s politics began to shift toward the Democratic Party.

‘I cannot sit in this church’

In 2016, Mr. Trump, then a New York City businessman, was ascendant.

Ms. Bennett changed her party affiliation that summer and made what she said was her first-ever political contribution, to Mr. Trump’s Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton.

One of Ms. Bennett’s first television ads emphasized the apolitical nature of the military. “In the aircraft,” she says, “you’d never ask your crew if they’re Democrats or Republicans.”

But after leaving the Navy in 2022, Ms. Bennett did fully jump into partisan politics, participating in phone banks for Democratic candidates and traveling to Michigan with her sister to knock on doors in support of Vice President Kamala Harris’s presidential bid.

She has told supporters that her frustration with Mr. Trump’s 2016 victory briefly led her to stop attending church in Maryland, according to a recording first reported by The Washington Free Beacon.

“I was like, ‘I cannot sit in this church full of people who voted for Trump,’” said Ms. Bennett, a Presbyterian. “Then, ultimately, I decided they do not get to decide what Christianity looks like.”

Mr. Kean has said the disclosure shows that Ms. Bennett is incapable of working across the aisle in Washington. “That’s not a person who’s going to listen,” he told a debate audience.

After moving to New Jersey in 2019, Ms. Bennett became active in a Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) congregation in Princeton that is known for its inclusive services. David A. Davis, the church’s pastor, said she sought his counsel soon after Mr. Trump was elected in 2024. She was deciding, he said, whether to enter the race against Mr. Kean, aware it would “upend her life.” Some of Ms. Bennett’s earliest campaign videos, he noted, were filmed at Nassau.

It was a deliberate choice for Ms. Bennett, who said that her “sense of service” was heavily shaped by the church-led mission trips she participated in as a teenager in Texas.

“We were not wealthy,” she said. “But we had a roof over our head and we had food.

“Going to places in the country and seeing people who do not have that, it just made me very appreciative of what I was given.”

Early in the campaign, as she tried to set herself apart from Mr. Kean, Ms. Bennett frequently referred to the 2010 Honda Accord she drove. Mr. Kean comes from a wealthy New Jersey political family; his estimated $10 million in assets are linked largely to family trusts.

Yet during the debate, Ms. Bennett refused to state her own net worth, instead referring people to her financial disclosure forms, which show assets worth between $430,000 and $1.5 million, including two I.R.A.s and college savings plans.

Ms. Bennett and her husband also own a four-bedroom home in Montgomery, N.J., a suburban township that lawmakers excised from the Seventh District when redrawing congressional boundaries after the 2020 census.

House members are not required to live in the district they represent. But the new map created a public relations challenge for a candidate hoping to kick Mr. Kean — whose deep New Jersey roots extend to the state’s first governor — out of office.

During the summer of 2025, she and her husband moved into a rental home about 15 miles away in Bridgewater, which is in the Seventh District. Their 7-year-old daughter attends public school there and their 4-year-old daughter is in day care nearby.

‘The best of the best’

The race began as one of only a handful of tossup battleground contests in the 2026 midterm cycle and was regularly cited by both parties as a must win, drawing prominent surrogates to the campaign trail.

Gabby Giffords, a former congresswoman and a leading gun-control advocate, joined Ms. Bennett this month at a library in New Providence. The Democratic House leader, Hakeem Jeffries, spent a recent Friday night with Ms. Bennett at a small Baptist church in Linden. Pete Buttigieg, a former transportation secretary, spoke to a large crowd at a community college in Branchburg, hailing Ms. Bennett’s military experience as the “perfect background for going to the United States Congress in today’s Washington.”

“A test pilot — the best of the best — whose job is to figure out what’s broken before anybody gets hurt,” he said.

Before entering the race, Ms. Bennett worked for four health care companies — Johnson & Johnson, Midi Health, Noom and Oshi Health — and she has made repealing the deep cuts to Medicaid that Mr. Kean supported as part of the president’s so-called Big Beautiful Bill a central campaign platform. She has also called for modernizing the country’s air traffic control system, ending the war with Iran and freezing child care costs at 7 percent of a family’s income.

Ms. Bennett’s own child care costs have become a Republican talking point, after campaign filings showed she used roughly $20,000 in donations to pay for her daughter’s day care, a decision Mr. Kean has attacked. Ms. Bennett’s campaign has noted that the Federal Election Commission has since 2018 permitted candidates to use campaign contributions to pay for child care “to help parents who aren’t independently wealthy be able to run for Congress.”

Republicans have also homed in on Ms. Bennett’s work in health care in ads that suggest she led efforts to put profits over patients, highlighting her role at Midi in brokering a partnership with a private-equity-backed hospital chain. “She bragged about her deals with sketchy companies,” reads a mailer that includes a photograph of a bloody, disembodied eye.

Cindy Gentry, Ms. Bennett’s boss at Midi, a start-up focused on expanding telehealth for menopausal women, said the advertising “missed the point.”

“The point is women didn’t have access to care,” Ms. Gentry said. “What Rebecca was trying to do, was, ‘How do I create telehealth offerings that expands access and provides good, high-quality care to women who right now don’t have access to it?’”

In early October, Ms. Bennett and Mr. Jeffries sat side by side at Greater Mount Moriah Baptist Church, in front of pews packed with Democratic loyalists. The pastor, the Rev. Barry Wise II, used the opportunity to note his disappointment with Democrats who fail to follow through on promises after being elected, pointedly urging Ms. Bennett — and Mr. Jeffries — to do better.

Ms. Bennett, in her remarks, turned to face Pastor Wise.

“I will wake up every day,” she said, “and work harder than I’ve ever worked in my life to fight for you and your family as hard as I fight for my own kids.”

SUMMARY

One would think that in a state as deeply red as South Carolina, this would be enough. There’s every reason to think Graham will eke out a win — this is South Carolina, after all. Beyond the immediate politics, it is difficult to overstate the larger historical significance of liberal Democratic wins in Mississippi or South Carolina.

ARTICLE

Three Races I am Watching Closely
The future of American politics runs through the South.
By Jamelle Bouie
Published 2026-10-31 15:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/opinion/columnists/midterm-election-races-what-to-watch.html

I’m at the stage right before an election when I stop paying close attention to polls. People are already voting — millions, in fact, have already voted — and there isn’t much left to learn from new polls. Instead, I’ve turned my attention to a handful of races I think are interesting, both as potential bellwethers and as stories in their own right.

Virginia’s 5th Congressional District

The first of these is close to home. The 5th District includes Lynchburg, Danville and Charlottesville, where I live. It covers most of central Virginia, touching the Richmond suburbs in the east, the Shenandoah Valley in the west and the majority of rural Southside, reaching the North Carolina border.

Most years, the 5th is solidly Republican. But there is precedent for a Democratic victory. In 2008, Tom Perriello — who, I should say, I know personally — won the seat. He lost in the 2010 Republican wave on account of his votes for the Affordable Care Act and a climate change bill. Perriello is back this year, hoping to unseat the incumbent Republican, John McGuire.

I think Perriello is running a strong and vigorous race — the kind of campaign that can make the difference in an exceptionally close contest. But I still think the final result will hinge on overall national conditions. If we’re looking at a double-digit swing toward Democrats, Perriello wins. If it’s something more modest, I think he falls short.

South Carolina Senate

The next race I am watching is further South. Darline Graham is running to replace her brother, Lindsey Graham, in the Senate. She is a novice politician, relying on name recognition and the full support of President Trump. One would think that in a state as deeply red as South Carolina, this would be enough. But you would be wrong.

Graham has quite a few disadvantages beyond her lack of experience. Not only do place-holder candidates tend to suffer compared with those who have been elected to the seats they hold, but Graham had a bitter primary battle that left South Carolina Republicans divided. Rather than play for unity, her former opponent Ralph Norman has been an open critic, exacerbating the split. There are also conservative third-party candidates on the ballot who have eaten into Graham’s support.

It has been clear since the summer that this race is more competitive than it initially looked, and in the most recent New York Times survey, Graham is in a statistical dead heat with her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews.

There’s every reason to think Graham will eke out a win — this is South Carolina, after all. (And I spend enough time there every year visiting family to get a good sense of its deeply-rooted conservatism.) But thanks to a surge in Black turnout and potential crossover voting among Republican-leaning independents, there is a real chance of a Democratic upset.

As for Andrews? She has been on the ground for nearly two years, trying to build support and name recognition. She has been hustling, and in politics as in most areas of life, hustle can mean the difference between victory and defeat.

Mississippi Senate

The last race I’m paying close attention to is in another place that is far more competitive than you would think: Mississippi. According to many polls, the incumbent senator, Cindy Hyde-Smith, appears to be just ahead of her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom.

There’s a familiar dynamic here. Hyde-Smith is what you might call a replacement-level candidate — no better and no worse than a generic Republican. And why would she need to be? The stark racial polarization of Mississippi voters means that as long as Hyde-Smith can attract the vast majority of white voters, she is in good shape come Election Day.

But what happens if there is a slight decline in racially polarized voting among whites? What happens if there is an explosion of Black turnout — thanks to the Supreme Court’s unpopular decision in Louisiana v. Callais — in a state where Black Americans make up close to 40 percent of the population? And what happens if the candidate leading the charge for Democrats is smart and talented with a record of winning in a seemingly inhospitable environment?

In that case, you have another potential upset in a state that for decades has been written off by Democrats and taken for granted by Republicans.

Beyond the immediate politics, it is difficult to overstate the larger historical significance of liberal Democratic wins in Mississippi or South Carolina. Both states are virtual bywords for American reaction; South Carolina was the hotbed of nullification, secession and Redemption, as well as the staging ground for the 1948 Dixiecrat rebellion. Mississippi had the South’s first Jim Crow state constitution and produced a stream of racist demagogues from Theodore Bilbo to James Eastland.

Democratic victories would shake up the political landscapes in both states. They might also work as proof of concept for further investment below the Mason-Dixon line.

The South overall is a fast-growing and dynamic part of the country, with a rapidly diversifying population of white and Black Americans, Latinos, and Asian Americans. It is a hub for new immigrants and a destination for Americans from across the country. It has also been a laboratory for democratic backsliding — a place where reactionary lawmakers have done their best to limit the scope of democratic participation and impose their preferred social order.

But there’s a clear tension here between dynamism and tradition. And in the fastest-growing states of the South, economic and social dynamics have begun to produce renewed partisan competition, as new coalitions emerge to contest power.

A Democratic Party that can contest and win in both the Deep and the Upper South — Georgia, South Carolina, Louisiana, and Mississippi, in addition to Virginia and North Carolina — is a Democratic Party with far more paths to national victory than it has had over the last decade.

Which is all to say that I’m not just paying attention to Virginia, South Carolina and Mississippi because I am a Southerner with roots in and connections to those states, but because I’m convinced that the future of both parties, to say nothing of the future of the nation, goes through the South.

What I Wrote

My column this week was on President Trump’s corrupt use of the pardon power, the rule of law and the future of American democracy.

Donald Trump is not the first president to break the law. He is not the first president to disregard the law. He is not even the first president to insist that his actions cannot, on some deep ontological level, be illegal. But he may be the first president to abandon the pretense that the law matters at all.

In the latest episode of my movie podcast with John Ganz, we covered John Frankenheimer’s 1998 film “Ronin.” And if you are reading this in New York City, I’ll be speaking on citizenship and the Constitution at N.Y.U. on Nov. 11. Now Eating: Carrot-Orange Olive Oil Cake

I made this cake last weekend for a get-together, and it was a big hit. It is extremely easy to put together, and you might already have all the ingredients you need. A few recommendations. If you can, grind whole cardamom for a stronger flavor and aroma. The recipe doesn’t call for it, but you should steam the carrots before blending them; that way you won’t need a high-powered blender to get a smooth mixture. And as always for a cake like this, you’ll want to use the best olive oil you can get your hands on. Recipe from NYT Cooking.

Ingredients

- Nonstick cooking spray or butter, for greasing
- 1 ⅓ cups/175 grams all-purpose flour
- 1 tablespoon baking powder
- 1 teaspoon ground cardamom
- 1 teaspoon kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal)
- ¼ teaspoon baking soda
- 5 medium carrots (about 10 ounces/300 grams), peeled and roughly chopped (about 2 cups)
- 1 cup/210 grams extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 cup/200 grams granulated sugar
- 2 large eggs, at room temperature
- 1 orange, zested and juiced (¼ cup juice)
- Powdered sugar, to serve

Directions

Arrange a rack in the center of the oven. Heat the oven to 375 degrees. Grease a 9-inch springform pan, cake pan or cast-iron skillet with nonstick spray or butter, and line the bottom and sides with parchment paper.

In a large bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder, cardamom, salt and baking soda together. Make a well in the middle and set aside.

In a blender, combine the carrots, olive oil, granulated sugar, eggs, orange zest and orange juice; blend until smooth. Pour into the middle of the well of the dry ingredients. Starting in the center, use a whisk to slowly incorporate the flour mixture until there is no visible flour.

Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Lower the oven temperature to 350 degrees and immediately place the cake onto the middle rack. Bake for 35 to 45 minutes, until the center comes out clean when tested with a toothpick.

Let the cake cool on a wire rack for about 1 hour, then remove from the pan. Before serving, dust with powdered sugar.

SUMMARY

In the waning days of the midterm election campaign, Republicans have finally stumbled on a closing message: defending the honor of the Cheesecake Factory. Trump ran against Big Tech in 2020, when he saw it as an ally of Democrats, but he was less interested in curbing the industry’s power than co-opting it. Democrats should remember his words when they retake power.

ARTICLE

Republicans Tried to Turn the Cheesecake Factory Against Democrats. It Flopped.
It’s become screamingly obvious who represents billionaires and unchecked plutocratic power.
By Michelle Goldberg
Published 2026-10-31 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/opinion/democrats-populist-working-class.html

In the waning days of the midterm election campaign, Republicans have finally stumbled on a closing message: defending the honor of the Cheesecake Factory.

Last week, Barack Obama made a viral crack about Donald Trump’s renovations: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Conservatives feigned outrage on behalf of the humble American volk for whom the Cheesecake Factory is the height of sophistication. Fox Business interviewed the centimillionaire Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, after lunch at the restaurant; he sniffed, “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try.” (His Massachusetts beach house, which he sold for a couple of million dollars in 2012, was in Provincetown.) The Wall Street Journal suggested that Democrats had shot themselves in the foot in their quest to win back “the working man in Middle America.” The White House posted a list of Trump’s “accomplishments” in the style of a Cheesecake Factory menu.

Republicans have been trying to brand Democrats as the party of out-of-touch elitists since at least the 1960s, but this time, it felt particularly forced and desperate. After all, it’s become screamingly obvious which party represents billionaires and unchecked plutocratic power.

On the stump this week, an increasingly disinhibited Trump scoffed at the idea of “suffering at the pump” while boasting that high oil prices have been a windfall for the energy industry. Elon Musk, the richest person on earth, is almost single-handedly funding the Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s campaign. Susan Collins ran a closing ad in which a retired broadcaster seemed to mock her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, for being a logger, saying, “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here; we’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate.”

Meanwhile, Democrats all over the country are running against the ultrarich. “The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right,” the Texas Senate candidate James Talarico says on the campaign trail. “It’s top versus bottom.” In the Michigan Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed is a political protégé of Bernie Sanders who accuses his opponent, Mike Rogers, of being bought by corporations. Former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, defeated with the help of crypto dollars two years ago, may regain his seat thanks in part to widespread fury at data centers and the tech billionaires behind them.

If Democrats win big on Tuesday after running such populist campaigns, it will be more than a victory over Trump. It will be an opportunity for them to once again develop an image as the champion of working people against predatory elites. That, in turn, could realign American politics. But it will happen only if Democrats can resist the entreaties of the tech donors and lobbyists who, having realized that going all in on MAGA was a bad bet, will now spend big to rebuild bridges to the center left.

For decades now, American politics has been shaped by two very different conceptions of class. Liberals tend to view class as a primarily economic distinction: a millionaire car dealer in the Midwest has a class advantage over a Brooklyn adjunct professor on food stamps. Conservatives, by contrast, are more likely to understand class as a matter of taste, culture and education. They’ve long seen America as riven between what some called a “new class” of intellectuals, professionals and bureaucrats and an alliance of capitalists and traditionalist blue-collar workers. “The simple truth is that the professional classes of our modern bureaucratized societies are engaged in a class struggle with the business community for status and power,” wrote Irving Kristol, godfather of neoconservatism, in 1972. (He very much sided with the beleaguered businessmen.)

Neoconservatism fell out of fashion, but Kristol’s ideas about class didn’t. If anything, as the two parties sorted by education, they became a kind of cultural common sense. Obama, who was still paying off student debt in his 40s, was tagged as an elitist, while Trump, who loves to brag about his wealth, was not.

The 2024 election was a triumph for the right’s conception of class politics, with Trump making gains with low-income voters while Kamala Harris won those earning over $200,000 a year. In surveys and focus groups, voters described Democrats as elitist and condescending. When the Democratic firm Navigator Research polled swing districts after the last election, 56 percent of respondents said the party didn’t look out for working people, and a majority said Democrats didn’t share their values. The road to winning back working-class voters looked difficult and uncertain.

Trump, by abandoning all restraint in his kleptocratic smash-and-grab, has made it easier. In a September poll from The New York Times and Siena University, voters identified Republicans as the “elitist” party by 10 points. The Times quoted a 40-year-old who’d voted for Trump two years earlier: “The people that are ‘in with him,’ who look or act a certain way, are the ones that are going to be given an opportunity.”

Few things have laid bare the president’s essential elitism like his alliance with America’s tech oligarchs. Trump ran against Big Tech in 2020, when he saw it as an ally of Democrats, but he was less interested in curbing the industry’s power than co-opting it. Now that he’s done that, tying Silicon Valley’s fortunes to his own, he can’t countenance criticism of it. He’s attempted, absurdly, to rebrand A.I. as “super intelligence,” and said that communities that reject data centers risk becoming “backwards and poor.”

Silicon Valley was once seen as a bastion of liberalism, but a recent Politico poll found that voters across the political spectrum now associate it with the Republican Party. At the same time, Big Tech — and particularly A.I. and data centers — has rarely been more reviled. This summer, a leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee called data centers “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle” and warned that public fury about them could cost the Republican Jon Husted his Senate seat in Ohio.

Rob Flaherty, former head of digital strategy for Joe Biden, is a founder of Tomorrow Together, a new super PAC that goes after Republicans for their ties to the A.I. industry. He shared polling his group commissioned about A.I. and data centers in several swing districts. In Pennsylvania’s Eighth District, held by a Republican, Rob Bresnahan, 51 percent of respondents feel strongly unfavorably toward data centers. Only 5 percent feel strongly favorably. Voters see A.I., Flaherty told me, as “these guys sitting in a room somewhere cooking up technology that’s going to make your life worse, making you pay for it, and buying off the government to do it.”

Now that Democrats seem likely to retake at least one house of Congress, tech companies are rushing to hire Democratic lobbyists. Given the enormous resources Silicon Valley kingpins wield, some Democrats might be tempted to seek a rapprochement with the industry. “I worry that Democrats are going to say, ‘We need to rebuild our alliances with tech,’ and miss the opportunity that’s in front of their face here,” said Flaherty. That would be a terrible mistake. The opportunity before Democrats is about more than being on the right side of a winning issue. Democrats have a unique chance, after decades of culture wars, to wrest the mantle of populism from Republicans and thus change the terrain on which American elections are fought.

“They are unanimous in their hate for me — and I welcome their hatred,” Franklin Delano Roosevelt said in 1936 about monopolists, speculators and war profiteers. Democrats should remember his words when they retake power. A good enemy is a terrible thing to waste.

ARTICLE

This Is How MAHA Ends
Doctors like Annie Andrews, Amy Acton and Abdul El-Sayed remind us that Americans don’t trust Republicans with their nation’s health.
By Jessica Grose
Published 2026-10-31 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/opinion/doctor-democrats-midterms.html

“My name is Dr. Annie Andrews, and for almost two decades, I’ve been a pediatrician in South Carolina. Parents trust me to treat their kids for just about everything you can imagine.” That’s how Andrews, who is the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina, launched herself into the race.

In a lab coat, with a stethoscope slung around her neck, she goes on in the campaign video to talk about the damage that the Trump administration has wrought on Americans’ physical well-being. She describes Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the head of Health and Human Services, as “the vaccine-denying brain worm guy” who “is gutting our nation’s health care system.”

Andrews is not the only prominent medical professional running as a Democrat in Tuesday’s election. Amy Acton, who is running for governor in Ohio, is a physician and a former director of the Ohio Department of Health. Though the vile attack ad run by her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy put Acton in the national spotlight, this ad distracts from her public health expertise and her commitment to health care affordability, which have been pillars of her campaign.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Michigan who is an epidemiologist, has crowds chanting about Medicare for All, which he literally co-wrote the book about even as he has to defend himself against bigoted smears about Arab scientists from Kennedy.

According to The Hill, seven doctors who are not incumbents are running for Congress as Democrats, along with 14 nurses. If all the doctors running as Democrats win office, they will meaningfully shift the balance of physicians in both the Senate and the House away from Republicans. That means Democrats with medical expertise will have more of a say in confirming health-related officials, will vote for more progressive health care policies and will create viral moments arguing with ignorant Trump administration officials during hearings on medical issues.

But I think these doctors, if they can eke out victories in tight races, are poised to do something bigger: They can reclaim the mantle of health and wellness as a winning issue for Democrats.

Though Kennedy pulled off a feat of great marketing with his Make America Healthy Again movement, MAHA never represented a majority of Americans who care about health. While trust in public health, and in President Joe Biden and the Democrats especially, took a drubbing in the aftermath of the pandemic, it simply isn’t true that Americans ever trusted Republicans to have the answers for what ails us.

MAHA’s canny marketing — a symbiotic relationship with grass-roots “crunchy mama” influencers who spent years spreading bad information — was a shiny object that distracted from the truth that Democrats have been the more trusted party on this topic in the recent past. Ahead of the 2022 midterms, when the Covid mitigation backlash was arguably at its peak, a Reuters/Ipsos survey found that “more Americans believe Democrats are stronger on Covid-19.” Two years later, KFF, a nonprofit health policy research organization, did polling during the run-up to the 2024 presidential election. On every health care policy measure, it found that Americans trusted Biden more than they trusted Donald Trump.

The only health care issue on which Trump polled close to Biden in 2024 had to do with the expense of care: 38 percent of Americans trusted Biden to “address high health care costs” versus 36 percent who trusted Trump and 27 percent who trusted neither.

Trump embraced Kennedy and MAHA because it was politically convenient, and the president does seem to have some bizarre and deeply held beliefs about vaccines and the effects of Tylenol during pregnancy. But outside those convictions, Trump has never seemed to care much about clean air, clean water or providing health care to all Americans regardless of income or job status.

Millions have lost access to health care under Trump’s watch. MAHA stalwarts, like Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, are starting to defect, reportedly because of the administration’s lack of progress on food policy.

Republicans appear to have frittered away Americans’ trust on health care costs completely in the past two years. According to a survey published earlier this month, “About twice as many voters say they trust the Democrats over the Republicans on the cost of health care.” It is hard not to conclude that the Trump administration’s promise to restore trust in public health has also been a flop. A poll conducted by Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the de Beaumont Foundation published earlier this year found that “only 50 percent of U.S. adults say they trust health recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (C.D.C.), compared with 77 percent in spring 2025.”

Republicans, Democrats and independents overwhelmingly still trust their own doctors. By leading with their experience as physicians and public health champions, candidates like Andrews, Acton and El-Sayed have an opportunity to start the long process of rebuilding America’s federal public health system.

If these candidates prevail, they have the expertise and authority to actually hold Kennedy to account for many of the disastrous decisions that he has made, and continues to make. Just this week, Kennedy put forth, against the advice of the administration’s scientists, a plan to bypass the Food and Drug Administration and give Americans access to a wide array of unproven peptides.

Of all the physician candidates running, Andrews might be the most effective antidote to MAHA. When she’s out of her white coat, she looks and sounds exactly like all the anti-vaccine influencer moms I see on my feed whose support made Kennedy who he is today. A 40-something mom of three, with perfectly styled blond hair and an approachable demeanor, she seems to relish going after Kennedy. On Instagram she posts memes showing the White House’s East Wing in shambles, suggesting that this is what Kennedy has done to America’s public health system.

In her launch video, Andrews talked about how the National Institutes of Health cut funding to study childhood cancer because of Trump administration malfeasance, and that gun violence is no longer classified as a public health crisis. “I also just happen to be someone who isn’t afraid of a fight,” Andrews said.

I want to see that fight on the Senate floor.

gerrymandering-colonization-gilded-age.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 24  Words: 1547/1659
================================================================================

SUMMARY

To colonize elections, political machines needed mobile voters. Years later, as Jim Crow squelched African Americans’ voting rights in the South, Republicans political bosses in the North cooked up a scheme to put “wheels on the suffrage” by relocating Black voters to places like Indiana and Connecticut to help their party win there. Political machines gathered colonized voters wherever they could.

ARTICLE

Why Manipulate the Lines When You Can Just Move People Around?
Gerrymandering, Gilded Age-style.
By Jon Grinspan
Published 2026-10-31 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/opinion/gerrymandering-colonization-gilded-age.html

The 2026 election cycle has seen heated redistricting battles — fought through legislatures, referendums and courts — as both parties vie to craft favorable election maps. But what if American history contained another way for politicians to pick their voters? A way so audacious that it hasn’t really been tried for a century, a weapon blunter than gerrymandering, a move so blatant that it calls into question the meaning of representative democracy itself?

What if, instead of moving the map to fit the voters, politicians moved voters to fit the map?

Party bosses worked this scheme throughout the 19th century: rounding up drifters and drunkards, registering them at flophouses in swing districts and herding them to the polls on Election Day. Cunning politicos realized that by relocating just a few thousand voters, they could sway races, elect presidents, shape a nation of millions. Americans called it colonization — a fitting name in an era when political machines settled empires not overseas but in Manhattan or Sheboygan, Wisc.

After importing a crew of Mexican citizens to vote in his South Texas stronghold, the political boss Jimmy B. Wells borrowed a cattleman’s metaphor, bragging, “With my corral, I hold the balance of power.”

Political machines held that power for decades. Colonization is as striking for its staying power as its outlandishness, a wildly undemocratic scheme practiced from the 1830s into the 1900s. Many Americans just shrugged at the sneakiness of the bosses, even as good-government reformers, like The Chicago Eagle, shouted, “THERE IS NO REASON WHATEVER WHY THEY SHOULD BE TOLERATED.”

Then, after a lifetime of toleration, Americans significantly reformed voting in the early 20th century, closing the loopholes that allowed colonization to succeed. What had seemed like a permanent flaw in our democracy was killed so decisively that it sounds made up today. Perhaps there’s a lesson here, as many look beyond the 2026 midterms and see a future of endless electoral shenanigans.

Colonizing elections worked because it exploited the peculiar development of democracy in America. In the 1800s, the United States was a highly mobile nation hurtling toward modernity and also a novel experiment in popular participation. The result was both a reckless gamble with self-government and a hothouse for crooked creativity.

To colonize elections, political machines needed mobile voters. And 19-century America teemed with down-and-outers willing to move into some flophouse, “fattening” — in the words of a disgusted Buffalo observer — “on beer and bad whiskey until they have cast their votes.”

Over 32 million immigrants came to the United States between 1840 and 1920, the equivalent of shipping the entire Civil War-era populace into the country. Big cities and industrial towns filled with footloose bachelors and bachelorettes until there were as many single men in 1890 as today. Large numbers were experiencing relatively new phenomena like unemployment and homelessness. Modern industrial capitalism left many struggling laborers with one asset to barter: their votes.

And America’s unique geography created a political marketplace. Instead of developing a central metropolis — a London or a Paris — political power peppered an East Coast of medium-size cities. In 1860, 20 of the 30 largest cities in America lay within a day’s train ride, helping to swing the votes of eight separate states. Parties developed a political shell game, relocating voters from Brooklyn to Boston to Baltimore.

Even within states and cities, a dense schedule of year-round local races meant elections could be decided by importing mobile voters to a new ward or precinct.

Western states, eager to attract residents, allowed recent arrivals (and sometimes noncitizens) to vote after spending a few days in town. Rural regions proved just as willing to trade voters as big cites. Bitter politics heated it all. Kansas elections became a sudden draw before the Civil War, as thousands of pro-slavery Missourians and antislavery New Englanders flooded in to decide whether the territory would allow slavery. Home to 3,000 eligible residents, Kansas saw 6,000 votes cast in the 1855 territory elections in March.

Years later, as Jim Crow squelched African Americans’ voting rights in the South, Republicans political bosses in the North cooked up a scheme to put “wheels on the suffrage” by relocating Black voters to places like Indiana and Connecticut to help their party win there.

But colonization worked best when it was hardly noticed, exploiting the tiny margins deciding the closest elections in U.S. history. James Garfield won the popular vote for president in 1880 by 1,898 votes. Just 1,149 ballots in New York made Grover Cleveland president in 1884. A few boardinghouses in Manhattan and Philadelphia could swing the nation’s most populous states and, with them, a fifth of the nation’s electoral votes. It would be like winning California, Texas and Florida today, all for the price of beds, beer and bologna.

Filling wards with temporary voters required incredible logistical power. Suppressing the vote took bigots and shotguns, but moving the vote meant housing, feeding and registering thousands. It took, in the words of an 1869 congressional inquiry into frauds in New York City, “a systematic plan of gigantic proportions, stealthily prearranged and boldly executed.” Boss Tweed won his power by orchestrating that systematic plan. A half dozen Bowery thugs actually registered to vote at Tweed’s Lower East Side address.

Political machines gathered colonized voters wherever they could. In Chicago, they slept on saloons’ sawdust floors. In Texas, they were fed barbecue. In Detroit, Congress found a Democratic leader providing his colonists with bouts of free whiskey “five or six times a day.” Voter registries show colonizers packing 152 men into a single New York address in 1868 and 230 voters in a small Greenwich Village hotel in 1902. The striking, six-foot-tall, Irish-born Katie Hicks ran a string of boardinghouses favored by African Americans in the West Village. In the early 1900s, authorities accused Hicks of marching her boarders to vote Republican en masse, waving a giant American flag.

The result blended political campaigning, social engineering and organized crime. In Coney Island, a Democratic political machine imported out-of-work Manhattan actors and housed them in off-season beachside hotels until the 1888 presidential election, feeding them cheap seafood. Think of the arithmetic that scam required of John Y. McKane, Coney Island’s party boss: combining a pool of bored men with vacant blocks of windswept November resorts, to swing an election and manufacture political power.

Around 1900, reformers realized that those boardinghouse bosses were colonization’s weakness. Cities had gained new regulatory controls over how people lived. Hygiene codes allowed inspectors to end what the Municipal Voters’ League denounced as the practice of colonized voters “sleeping like hogs on the filthy floors” of Chicago’s saloons. Shouting “Hobo rule must go,” Illinois legislators made it illegal to lodge more than six guests in a single room. Undercover investigators busted Manhattan landlords packing flophouses. New Jersey and other states stiffened registration laws, demanding that voters provide an exhaustive list of relatives and landlords in order to register.

To kill colonization, reformers tied voting rights to permanent addresses. In doing so, they also entrenched the political power of middle-class homeowners. It fit the more settled 20th-century electorate. Yet it has made registering to vote a challenge to this day, a holdover from the forgotten fight over a long-dead electoral scheme.

High mobility and close competition made colonization possible throughout the long Gilded Age. This dirty trick helps us understand what it meant to live in a developing democracy of rootless wanderers, cheap housing and enterprising bosses who knew their wards so intimately that they could say which brothel had extra beds. Colonization’s improvisatory chutzpah turned a weakness into a strength, seeing cities packed with homeless drifters as mobile political assets.

Modern gerrymandering fits our 21st-century problems, in many cases the opposite of those that gave rise to colonization in the 1800s. Falling geographic mobility, the sorting of the parties into easily mapped blocs and the shrinking number of competitive districts make it easier to move boundaries rather than people. If colonization exploited Gilded Age disruption, contemporary redistricting relies on America’s growing inertia.

But one thing is familiar from the 19th century: the dread that our democracy is becoming so permanently gamed that it leaves voters no role. Just as we worry about this “gerrymandering doom loop” today, deep in the Gilded Age the dour editor E.L. Godkin warned that there was “little prospect of escape” from America’s political “doom.” And where contemporary Americans feel a generalized hopelessness about reform, the British scholar James Bryce pointed to a “fatalism of the multitude” corroding Americans in the 1880s, certain that their democracy was beyond fixing.

And yet that doomed American electorate managed to rally against, reform and kill off a cartoonishly undemocratic practice. It would be facile to suggest that we could borrow their specific tricks today; but history tells us that it can be done, that it has been done.

It just wasn’t done once and for all. New bosses arose, dreaming up new schemes. America’s hazy political past is rich with frauds you never imagined, as well as solutions no one saw coming. Each political maneuver charted the contours of its society. Taken together, the development of our democracy looks less like a singular revolution 250 years ago and more like an endless challenge to its citizens, demanding vigilance and a deep historical memory.

Jon Grinspan is a curator of political history at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History and the author of “The Age of Acrimony: How Americans Fought to Fix Their Democracy, 1865-1915” and “Wide Awake: The Forgotten Force That Elected Lincoln and Spurred the Civil War.”
