ARTICLE

In San Francisco’s A.I. Boom, a First Date Has Become an Interview
When there is A.I. to build, who has time for romance? Techies are going out less and expecting more on each date — including a family health history.
By Emmy Martin
Published 2026-10-31 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/technology/san-francisco-ai-boom-dating.html

Mehul Agarwal, a co-founder of the artificial intelligence start-up Koyal, has a goal. He wants to find a wife before he gets rich.

The 24-year-old says he wants to be loved before the money comes, so he never has to wonder whether a partner is attracted to him or his success. But he has strict criteria.

A potential girlfriend must be smart, Mr. Agarwal said, adding that “someone who went to Stanford or M.I.T. is great.” She must be beautiful, which he is careful to distinguish from “hot,” a term he considers shallow. She must be kind, and in possession of a personality, “which is very, very hard when in San Francisco,” he said. And finally, she has to like him back.

Mr. Agarwal moved to San Francisco a year ago, when his A.I. filmmaking company, which has raised $3.4 million, joined the start-up accelerator Y Combinator. This year, he has been on a handful of dates. On one, which took two months to schedule, Mr. Agarwal said, he and his date were both exhausted from their jobs — she worked at an A.I. start-up, too — and they were so practiced at professional small talk that the evening felt less like a date than a networking meeting.

“What I’ve told my parents is if I’m 28 and haven’t found someone, then I would love to enter in the arranged marriage circuit,” said Mr. Agarwal, who has never had a girlfriend.

San Francisco’s A.I. boom has drawn a wave of young ambitious people who are now reshaping the city’s dating life. Start-up founders and engineers are dating less because they are working more as they try to build A.I. products and establish their fortunes, many said. So when they date, they bring a high-stakes mind-set to it, which means a first coffee can feel like a final-round interview.

“You don’t need to understand if they have cancer in their family, you don’t need to understand on the first date if they really want three children,” said Sina Hartung, 29, a co-founder of the A.I. health technology company Eureka Health who became exasperated by the dating scene in San Francisco. She lived there for three years before moving to New York in August.

The intensity is showing up in the daters who screen partners against fixed criteria, in those who outsource their messages to chatbots and in the dating coaches who charge thousands of dollars a month to translate romance into the language of a start-up.

Founders “don’t want to waste time, so you only go on a date when you really feel there’s something to explore,” said Mr. Agarwal, who works long hours. Many A.I. start-up workers keep “996” schedules — 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week — a norm borrowed from China’s tech scene.

Joyce Zhang, 32, a dating coach in San Francisco who charges $5,000 a month, works exclusively with tech founders, she said. A former product manager at the payments company Stripe, she coaches clients using the tech vocabulary they already think in — their “top of funnel” (the raw pool of prospects) and their “conversion rate” of dates that actually happen.

Her clients approach dating as any other problem to be solved with money, Ms. Zhang said. Some have connected their dating-app data to spreadsheets to track their matches; others obsess over gaming the apps’ algorithms.

Clients also run their replies to dates through A.I. chatbots like ChatGPT, she said. Some share their entire dating history with ChatGPT and ask the chatbot to diagnose their patterns. In those cases, Ms. Zhang said, she spends the coaching sessions pushing the techies toward trusting their intuition. Her job, she said, is to help them overcome their “blind spots.”

Amanda Chung, 25, who works at the A.I. start-up Nectar Social, is single and dates casually. Fresh off a long relationship and wanting to keep things low-key, she said most of the men she had met in San Francisco wanted something serious “even if they aren’t ready for it yet.”

One founder she saw for a few weeks would meet only after 10 p.m. because of his work schedule. Another spent an evening quizzing her about her job and her working style, “trying to check off boxes internally,” she said.

The prospects were so uninspiring that she eventually paused her Hinge account. “I was like, oh, wow, is that really it?” Ms. Chung said.

San Francisco has long had a reputation for skewing male and nerdy in the 20-something dating pool, with many female residents popularizing the phrase, “The odds are good but the goods are odd.”

The city has about 106 men to every 100 women, versus roughly 98 men to every 100 women nationally, according to the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey. Dowell Myers, who studies population change at the University of Southern California, said the recent A.I. arrivals might not yet register in census data, which lags by about two years.

In some corners of San Francisco, young singles are getting creative with dating. On a Saturday night at Kilowatt, a bar in the Mission neighborhood, people packed together for an event called “Date My Ex,” where participants on a stage pitch someone they love in five minutes or less, with a slide deck. Attendees wore name tags and waved paper hearts on sticks whenever a pitch landed, like bidders at an auction for other people’s exes.

One presenter rated the friend he had come to pitch on a bar graph against “the average dating experience.” Another slide read: “5’11” (but his hair adds 2” so kinda 6’1”)” and “works in tech (but isn’t happy about it).”

Still another presentation was about Joe Berusch, 27, who keeps “one foot out” of the tech world. He said he was convinced the intense daters who asked about family medical history on a first date were a loud local minority. A.I. has made many of the chores of adult life so frictionless that people expect dating to work the same way, but it’s “fundamentally” different, he said.

The “Date My Ex” event was part of a “Date My Friend” series run by Annalise Wulf, 25, and two friends as a tongue-in-cheek rebuke of San Francisco’s extreme dating requirements and as an alternative to dating apps.

“People in San Francisco, they work really hard, they have crazy long hours, especially in the start-up culture,” Ms. Wulf said. “So to even go on a date with someone, if it doesn’t feel amazing, if the sparks aren’t flying right away — it just takes time to develop those things, and I don’t think a lot of people in San Francisco have the time to do that.”

Mr. Agarwal, meanwhile, is still looking for someone who meets his criteria. His most promising prospect this year did not work out because of his schedule. They had two dates before he left for three weeks to India, where his start-up does much of its business. Then he spent five days in Los Angeles. Then there was more travel.

“I need to be really sure, and I don’t know her well enough to make that kind of bet,” he said.

That gives him three and a half years to find the love of his life before he turns the search over to his parents.

ARTICLE

Margaritas Rimmed With Degreaser Burn 5 People at a North Carolina Chili’s
Three customers and two employees were burned on and around their mouths after a granulated substance was mistaken for sugar, a health official said.
By Rebecca Chao
Published 2026-10-31 23:38 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/chilis-margarita-chemical-burns-forest-city.html

Five people suffered chemical burns after drinking margaritas rimmed with a white granulated substance misidentified as sugar at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, N.C., a health official said.

The people who fell ill on Wednesday were three customers and two staff members who appeared to have been burned largely on and around their mouths, Megan Rollins, a spokeswoman at Foothills Health District, said in an interview on Saturday.

She said they sustained the injuries after contact with a degreaser, which had been left in an unlabeled container near the bar.

The district, which is responsible for food safety, immediately dispatched environmental health specialists to investigate the restaurant, Jason Masters, the public health director at Foothills Health District, said in an email.

The Forest City Police Department could not be reached on Saturday. It was unclear whether it had opened an investigation.

A representative for Chili’s said in a statement that the restaurant chain “took immediate action to support those affected and avoid further injuries.”

The chemical, which was not identified by name or brand, was brought into the Chili’s early on Oct. 26 by a contractor who had been hired to power wash the building’s exterior, Ms. Rollins said. The contractor was not identified.

That worker then handed the product to a restaurant employee, who left it by the bar. It wasn’t clear why the contractor gave the employee the product, Ms. Rollins said.

On Wednesday, another employee, who was prepping the bar before lunch service, discovered the product and placed some of it in containers at the margarita station.

“It’s almost like a little tray where they put water, lime juice,” Ms. Rollins said of the station. “And then on the other side of the tray is a place to put salt or sugar.”

(Margaritas at Chili’s can be served with salt or sugar rimmers, according to the drinks menu on the company’s website.)

When the restaurant opened, three customers who ordered margaritas reported feeling an instant burn upon consuming them and raised concerns with restaurant employees.

Two workers sampled the substance and experienced the same symptoms.

All five went immediately to local urgent care centers, which alerted emergency management operations for Rutherford County, Ms. Rollins said.

The county’s emergency management agency on Saturday declined to comment, citing “privacy and confidentiality considerations.”

The Foothills Health District immediately closed the restaurant on Wednesday, temporarily suspending its permit, Ms. Rollins said.

It is unclear how severe the burns were.

“They had pretty instantaneous symptoms,” Ms. Rollins said, “so they didn’t ingest any more than they did.”

According to the Merck Manual, caustic substances can burn any tissue they touch when swallowed, from the lips and tongue to the esophagus and stomach. Industrial products, in particular, are more concentrated than ones found in homes, according to Merck, “and thus tend to be more damaging.”

Solid substances like a granulated degreaser, however, might only stick to the lips, which may limit damage, according to Merck.

On Thursday, the Chili’s restaurant reopened after complying with safety requirements.

“The establishment was instructed to wash, rinse and sanitize any and all surfaces that may have come into contact with the unknown chemical,” Mr. Masters said in an email.

An employee at the Chili’s in Forest City declined to comment, but the company representative said in the statement that it had “thoroughly investigated the circumstances and addressed the issues specific to this location.”

ARTICLE

Voters Usually Ignore Corruption as an Issue. It Now Has Their Attention.
Voters have shrugged off accusations of corruption for years, believing all politicians are corrupt, but thanks to President Trump’s unpopularity and growing wealth, the issue is breaking through.
By David Ovalle and Emily Cochrane
Published 2026-10-31 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/corruption-midterms.html

Like many Americans, Michael Nave has a hunch that politicians of both parties enrich themselves while the working class struggles to make ends meet.

But on Wednesday, Mr. Nave, a Republican, decided the party in power has become too corrupt. He cast his vote early, in Clearwater, Fla., against every Republican on the ballot, including Representative Anna Paulina Luna, who has been depicted by her opponent as emblematic of a party rife with self-enrichment and cronyism under the leadership of President Trump.

“Trump said he would drain the swamp, and he’s become the swamp,” said Mr. Nave, 61, of Dunedin, Fla.

Allegations of corruption in Washington are nothing new in political campaigns. They are usually shrugged off by voters who figure all politicians are equally guilty, whether they be Democrats such as former Senator Bob Menendez of New Jersey or Republicans like former Representative George Santos of New York. But Democratic efforts to bolster the issue this year may be resonating amid a drumbeat of stories about Mr. Trump’s staggering increase in wealth and the billionaire and corporate elites who have supported him.

Some recent polls have shown corruption has risen to the top of issues that voters say they care about most, fueled by a withering distrust in government and a sense of opacity in Washington.

“How can you always trust what’s behind a closed door?” asked Karen Jarrett, 58, who lives in Tennessee, a quick drive from the state line with Mississippi. She added, “People’s eyes are wide open now.”

But such sentiments may go only so far amid greater worries about inflation, war and personal security.

“It didn’t click with me,” Juan Pino, 51, a cook in Florida, said of corruption. He voted straight Democratic because, he said, he always votes that way.

Democrats are certainly trying to drive home the issue by tying politicians’ self-enrichment and insider trading to the soaring cost of living. Republicans, too, including Ms. Luna, are seeking to capitalize on corruption as a campaign theme.

And for some voters, it seems to be sinking in more than ever.

“It’s more out in the open now,” said Steve Wiegard, 46, who works with a fire safety company in Olive Branch, Miss. “I think about it every day.”

The word has become a constant refrain in campaign ads from both parties, even if the definition of corruption has at times been stretched. A political action committee supporting Democrats this week launched the latest corruption-themed attack ads, including one highlighting stock trades by Representative Victoria Spartz of Indiana and her family, which the ad says accompanied “policies that make life more expensive” for voters.

A committee supporting Republicans this month launched an ad labeling Troy Jackson, the Democrat challenging Senator Susan Collins of Maine, “too corrupt” for the state because his son is a lobbyist.

Corruption now seems to include secretive nondisclosure agreements struck with data centers, the war in Iran, even the gerrymandering of Black-majority districts after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act.

“We have politicians trying to pick the voters instead of voters picking the politicians,” said Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia, Tenn., and a House candidate who saw his home drawn out of the Middle Tennessee district where he was running. “That is corrupt.”

The most recent entrant: Democratic efforts to clog Alaska’s four-person ranked-choice ballot with candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, including one challenger named Dan Sullivan.

In the Tampa Bay region of Florida, corruption has emerged as central to the race between Ms. Luna and Leela Gray, a Democrat and retired Army brigadier general. Voters in the newly redrawn district overwhelmingly supported Mr. Trump in 2024, but Democrats hope to flip the seat by tying Ms. Luna to the president and portraying her as a glamorous partygoer, currying favor with wealthy donors.

One ad for Ms. Gray called Ms. Luna “part of the problem in D.C., including the culture of corruption,” highlighting allegations in the media that she gave insider information to a Republican influencer who then placed a bet on a political prediction market.

Ms. Luna has denied the report, sent a cease-and-desist letter to her opponent’s campaign over the ad and noted a Justice Department letter that confirmed she is not under investigation. In turn, Ms. Luna has sought to portray Ms. Gray as compromised because she owns stock in Big Pharma, companies building data centers and big banks buying up single-family homes.

In an interview, Ms. Luna said she has led the fight on corruption by seeking to restrict stock trading by members of Congress. “The only reason this is a national discussion is because I forced it,” Ms. Luna said.

In interviews at early voting sites with more than two dozen voters in Ms. Luna’s district west of Tampa, most agreed corruption is a problem in both parties, but many shrugged off relentless attacks as par for the course.

James Shively, the owner of a landscaping company, said both parties were untrustworthy. He voted Republican because, he said, “Democrats are socialists.” Jonathan Castro, a human resources specialist with no party affiliation, voted for Democrats because he believes Trump’s immigration enforcement policies are too draconian.

Neither said his vote hinged on corruption.

For Jeff Davis, a Republican retiree, corruption was a bank shot in his congressional choice; he said he had voted against Ms. Luna because she supports Mr. Trump, who he believes is corrupt.

Marc Bachyrycz, a personal trainer with no party affiliation, cast his ballot for Ms. Luna because like him, she is an Air Force veteran. He also appreciated that while in office, she tried to crack down on congressional stock trading.

“No party is without fault, but at least she’s trying to do something,” Mr. Bachyrycz said.

For some voters, the issue is breaking through, even if it’s not decisive.

“I know insider trading has always gone on, but I think now it’s way worse,” said April Robinson, 52, an independent who voted along with her husband for Ms. Gray. “They are purposefully manipulating the markets.”

To others, the tried-and-true of their preferred party still holds sway. Joelle Eden, 57, a former Democrat who switched parties a decade ago, voted Republican because she believes the party prioritizes public safety and border control.

“I just want to make sure the country is safe,” Ms. Eden said.

Curt Anderson and Anastasia Economides contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

As Midterms Near, Top Law Firms That Capitulated to Trump Are on the Sidelines
None of the firms that struck deals to avoid crippling executive orders are publicly involved in the major legal efforts to check the Trump administration’s attempts to meddle in the midterm elections, a review by The New York Times shows.
By Michael S. Schmidt and Jim Rutenberg
Published 2026-10-31 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/law-firms-trump-voting.html

Whenever Norm Eisen, a leader of the legal resistance against President Trump, wanted to try to hold Mr. Trump accountable over the last decade, one of his first calls was to Brad Karp, the chairman of the white shoe law firm Paul Weiss.

Without hesitation, Mr. Karp would give Mr. Eisen free legal counsel on how to best oppose Mr. Trump, and would then deploy the firm’s vast legal muscle — at no cost — to help.

“He was one of the greatest champions of voting and civil rights — and for democracy — in the country, and to have someone like that advising you, resourcing you and fighting for you was indispensable,” Mr. Eisen said.

Now, as Mr. Eisen prepares to lead a coalition that has vowed to stop Mr. Trump if he tries to interfere in the midterm elections, Paul Weiss, one of nine firms to strike deals with the administration to avoid crippling executive orders, is largely on the sidelines, according to Mr. Eisen and a lawyer with direct knowledge of the matter.

The void left by Paul Weiss is only a sliver of the impact of the deals the nine firms made with Mr. Trump early in his second term. In exchange, they pledged to do nearly a billion dollars in free legal work to causes Mr. Trump champions, casting doubt on whether they would be willing to stand up to the president.

Measuring the consequences of the deals is difficult, but the lead-up to the midterm elections offers new clues. Few of the nine firms are publicly involved in the major legal efforts to check Mr. Trump and his administration’s attempts to meddle, a review of public documents and interviews with democracy advocates, election lawyers and voting rights litigators shows.

The absence of the firms has raised serious worries about whether the legal profession is equipped to respond to the administration, which has already begun to file litigation intended to sow confusion about the outcome of the election. But lawyers like Mr. Eisen say that they are just as prepared and point to a string of recent court victories as evidence of their prowess.

Some of the firms have scrubbed their websites of their storied histories working on voting rights cases. At one firm that made a deal with Mr. Trump, several lawyers are quietly volunteering to help voting rights causes, hoping that their bosses do not find out, according to a lawyer at one of the firms who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The chilling effect, the interviews show, has extended to several of the top 100 firms in the United States that did not cut deals with Mr. Trump. Fearing being targeted, they have also avoided politically sensitive cases, according to interviews.

So many of them — including ones that have made deals with Mr. Trump and those that have not — have declined to help one longtime civil rights group, the Advancement Project, that it has started an internal tracker to stay on top of all the firms declining to team up on cases.

“I’ve been told, ‘We don’t do civil rights work involving the administration anymore,’ and, ‘We don’t do voting rights work anymore,’’’ said John Powers, the legal director at the Advancement Project, which often litigates voting rights cases by joining with better-financed private firms.

Most recently, when the Advancement Project filed suit with the N.A.A.C.P. against aspects of the Justice Department’s election-monitoring plans this fall, it had to set out on its own without a private partner. (On Friday, Mr. Powers said that it had received a new offer of help.)

“It’s been a sea change,” Mr. Powers said.

In some cases, Mr. Powers added, partners at firms working with the Advancement Project pulled back their support, dropped out entirely or agreed only to help on the condition that they not be named publicly.

“All too often we’re having to find workarounds because we don’t have the support,” he said.

Mr. Powers would not name the firms because he was hoping the private support would return in the future, he said.

“The pendulum is going to swing,” he predicted.

Law firms have played a key role since the civil rights movement in checking the federal government, even though suing the government over voting and civil rights cases typically pays far less compared with representing corporations. But the chance to work on those issues pro bono became a persuasive recruiting tool for firms. It served as evidence that incoming associates could not only make a lot of money assisting companies and wealthy people, but also do good.

During elections in recent decades, associates and partners have volunteered to be stationed in swing states where they could quickly initiate legal challenges on Election Day or if there was a contested counting of the results. Firms have pledged to represent poll workers while also bringing complex legal challenges against states encroaching on voting rights.

Paul Weiss repeatedly promoted its role in a landmark 1965 voting rights case. Dozens of articles and news releases on its website laid out its work during the Trump era on voting rights and election law.

“We remain steadfast in our commitment, supporting recent voting rights actions in several courts nationally as counsel of record,” the firm wrote on its website on a page dedicated to its pro bono election rights work.

But some time after Paul Weiss, which donated more money to Democrats in 2024 than any other firm, struck the deal with Mr. Trump in March 2025, the page for voting rights was taken down, along with 30 other pages related to its work on the subject.

A search of the firm’s website for the words “voting” and “voting rights” returns just two results.

Paul Weiss and seven other firms did not respond to questions asking for examples of voting rights cases or other matters the firm is working on in opposing the administration. (One of the firms that made a deal with Mr. Trump — Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft — merged with another firm.)

Mr. Trump’s norm-breaking use of power during his first term, like child separation at the border, led many firms to use their pro bono hours to oppose the administration. His attempts to interfere with the 2020 election only established more fodder.

But the postures of the firms changed during Mr. Trump’s second term.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, firms deployed their resources to oppose Mr. Trump because they faced no cost for doing so, financially or politically.

But now firms see those cases as liabilities for their profits.

In their place, lawyers like Mr. Eisen have helped establish a network of lawyers across the country. It includes pro-democracy groups, legal nonprofits, public interest law firms and a few of the most high-profile firms, like WilmerHale, that fought back when Mr. Trump targeted them with executive orders.

Mr. Eisen, who leads the Democracy Defenders Fund, said that while the group of lawyers may be different, the quality of the legal work remains. He added that he had more than enough lawyers to counter Mr. Trump in court.

“We have not seen a single time in the past 20 months in which I did not have the resources,” he said. “The muscle is still there.”

Even if Paul Weiss or any of the firms that made deals with Mr. Trump wanted to help, Mr. Eisen said, he and his clients would not trust that they would zealously represent them, given the leverage Mr. Trump continues to hold.

At the same time, Mr. Eisen acknowledged, the attempts to hold Mr. Trump accountable could use Mr. Karp, his expertise and the army of lawyers he used to deploy.

“I miss Brad,” he said.

Aric Toler contributed reporting. Alain Delaquérière and Seamus Hughes contributed research.

SUMMARY

Jordan Wood, a Democrat from Lewiston, Maine, was the first person to announce a 2026 campaign challenge to Senator Susan Collins, and he made a priority of winning the endorsement of the mayor of his hometown. ARTICLE

Susan Collins Is Always Keeping Score
The long-serving senator has delivered millions of dollars to every corner of her state. But in Maine, people say, it’s best to avoid getting on her bad side.
By Michael Kruse and Lisa Lerer
Published 2026-10-31 14:29 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/susan-collins-maine-senate-election.html

Jordan Wood, a Democrat from Lewiston, Maine, was the first person to announce a 2026 campaign challenge to Senator Susan Collins, and he made a priority of winning the endorsement of the mayor of his hometown. He met with Mayor Carl Sheline, a fellow Democrat, in his office and over drinks at a local Italian restaurant. They had a series of phone calls. But ultimately Mr. Sheline declined to back him.

Ms. Collins, the longtime Republican incumbent, was not in the room, at the bar, or on the line.

But she had made her presence known.

Mr. Sheline had various reasons for withholding his support, he said in an interview. Among them, he acknowledged, were a housing project, a food distribution center, and a mill museum in Lewiston. Ms. Collins had helped with the finances for all of them.

“It’s just an environment of possible retribution,” Mr. Wood said. “It is that fear she instills.”

Over nearly 30 years, Ms. Collins, a self-styled moderate in a familiar Maine mold, has cultivated a public persona as a workhorse and a fastidious maestro of constituent services and pork-barrel disbursements, using her Washington know-how to get her constituents what they need.

But for just as long, her detractors say, she has managed to mostly mask another reality. “The gentlewoman from Maine,” as her colleagues say on the Senate floor, is a formidable power broker who can play a fierce brand of politics with a how-dare-you air. According to more than 40 interviews with Republicans and Democrats in Maine politics, former staff, colleagues and longtime observers, Ms. Collins has wielded power not so much as a Yankee Republican but as a shrewd machine politician.

“It’s almost like Tammany Hall,” said Amy Fried, a retired political scientist from the University of Maine. “You’re going to get this benefit here if you vote for me.”

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and former aide to Ms. Collins, did not disagree.

“That’s exactly what it is,” he said. “She’s openly discussing the fact that Maine is going to be set back if she’s not in that position,” he added. “It puts people in the position of very clearly understanding that voting against her is a vote against their own well-being.”

Ms. Collins’s staff stresses that she has worked to bring money back to all communities in Maine — regardless of whether they support her.

Annie Clark, a longtime aide to Ms. Collins, provided The New York Times an exhaustive list of projects, from Orono and Ogunquit to Belfast and Blue Hill, for which the senator had secured funding since 2021. The senator got $234 million for 96 projects in Cumberland and Knox counties — the only two counties she lost in 2020. In Portland, where she received just 21 percent of the vote: $51.2 million for 28 projects.

“Senator Collins has been extraordinarily effective,” said Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins. “She works tirelessly to deliver results for the state, meets with thousands of Mainers every year, and she secures billions of dollars for communities in all of Maine’s 16 counties whether they vote for her or not.”

Ms. Collins, 73, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is running for re-election this fall the way she always has — no clickbait TikTok posts or big, rah-rah rallies, but a relentless focus on stops in small towns where she has brought home federal dollars for boat landings, emergency operations centers and wastewater treatment facilities.

At her campaign events, supporters hold signs that underscore the point she is trying to make: “Thank You, Susan.”

In debates this month with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a former logger and Maine Senate president, Ms. Collins was unsubtle about the crux of the deal.

“In the past five years I’ve secured $1.5 billion for properties all over the state,” she said.

She was even more blunt in a radio interview this week, citing 672 projects that she had secured across the state, including 45 new fire stations.

“All that goes away,” she said, “if Troy were to be elected.”

‘I have a lot of power’

Her whole life has been a lesson in the accrual and use of power.

Ms. Collins was born and raised in Caribou in Aroostook County, the state’s most northern terrain. The Collinses didn’t just own and run the local lumber company and hardware store. They were politicos too.

“My parents,” Ms. Collins told The New York Times this past summer, “both served as mayor of Caribou. My father was in the State Senate, my grandfather, great-grandfather served in the state legislature.”

Her parents were supporters of William S. Cohen when he ran for Congress in 1972 and beyond, and Ms. Collins was a driver and an intern for Mr. Cohen when she was in college at St. Lawrence University in Canton, N.Y. After she graduated, she was hired as an aide and was on his staff for a dozen years, known by her colleagues and peers as a meticulous note-taker and over-preparer.

She ran for governor in 1994 when she was 41 and lost. She ran for Senate in 1996 and won. She said she would serve no more than two terms but then ran for re-election in 2002, 2008, 2014 and 2020.

Over the course of her three decades in the Senate, drafting off the renown of her cordial, consensus-building Maine forebears like Mr. Cohen and Senator George Mitchell, Ms. Collins has emphasized her image as the last of a vanishing breed. She has bucked her party, and in particular President Trump, more than enough to frustrate many Republicans — albeit not nearly enough to satisfy most Democrats.

“I’m consistently sought out by both sides for cosponsorship of bills,” she told The Times in her first year in the Senate. “I have a lot of power — I like that.”

Behind closed doors, though, she long has had a reputation as a lone wolf.

Her relationship with Olympia Snowe, the Republican who was elected to the Senate from Maine two years before Ms. Collins and served three terms, was marked by rivalries and perceived slights, according to former aides to Maine lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Publicly, they issued joint statements and often voted together. Privately, the relationship was far more fraught, as is sometimes the case when a state is represented by two senators of the same party.

“She was just hypersensitive to Olympia getting more credit than she was,” said Kurt Bardella, a former press secretary for Ms. Snowe.

“It was very machine-politicky: ‘I am owed a certain level of stature and respect,’” Mr. Bardella recalled.

Ms. Collins has a bristly relationship with Angus King, the independent junior senator from Maine, who defeated her in the governor’s race in 1994 and succeeded Ms. Snowe in 2013. While they exchange occasional text messages, the two haven’t spoken in months, according to people familiar with their communications who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. They last texted Oct. 12, according to Ms. Clark. Aides in Mr. King’s office often are instructed to let Ms. Collins get the lion’s share of the credit, they said, if that’s what it takes to get a policy initiative accomplished.

When Mr. Wood announced his candidacy for Senate, he thought he knew what he needed to know about Ms. Collins. His campaign quickly became a window into what he did not know.

Elected Democrats and political donors, Mr. Wood said, told him Ms. Collins reviewed the lists of who gives more than $1,000 to whom — and kept score.

“People told me they could not give me money because they knew she would look at the report,” he said. “Democrats.”

Ms. Clark, the spokeswoman for Ms. Collins, said the senator does not review such lists.

Ultimately, Mr. Wood’s fledgling campaign was overwhelmed by the unexpected rise of Graham Platner, whose subsequent fall precipitated Mr. Jackson’s selection as the Democratic nominee. Still, he got an eye-opening tutorial in the sway of his state’s senior senator.

Last November, when he ended his Senate campaign and switched to run instead for Maine’s Second Congressional District, Mr. Wood couldn’t help but notice the difference.

This time, Mr. Sheline, the Lewiston mayor, endorsed him right away.

‘We should be thankful’

This month, politicking her way through the annual fall fair in Fryeburg, Maine, Ms. Collins walked from a cattle auction to a livestock barn, putting up with out-of-town press asking her questions about the president while trying to steer clear of manure.

“I know you don’t like me,” she told one reporter, “but don’t make me walk through shit.”

She quickly changed the subject — to $38 million in federal aid for heating oil.

“I was delighted,” she said, “that I was successful in expediting the funding.”

That matters a lot, said Mr. Dutson, the senator’s former aide.

“Federal money is incredibly important up here,” he said. “The choice a lot of people are facing right now is: OK, well, I can listen to the noise out of Washington or what my party tells me to do — or I can support the lady who got me a new fire truck in my 500-person town.”

In the past few weeks in Maine, as Mr. Jackson has campaigned in front of large, loud crowds alongside progressive megastars such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Ms. Collins has brandished a shovel at a groundbreaking at a boat landing in Orrington and attended a grand opening of a wastewater facility in Windham.

And in the stretch run of the race, people all over the state have received targeted text messages from her campaign.

“Susan Collins delivered $33 million for Knox County …”

“Susan Collins has delivered nearly $59 million for the City of Bangor …”

“Susan Collins is delivering real results across Kennebec County — 50 projects totaling more than $109.3 million …”

Her supporters say it’s why they trust her and one of the main reasons she should be re-elected.

“What she produces is real — it’s tactile,” said Chris Gardner, the executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, who has appeared in an ad for Ms. Collins. “We should be thankful.”

Kevin Raye, a former Maine Senate president and Ms. Snowe’s former longtime chief of staff, is an anti-Trump former Republican who is now an independent — “rooting,” he said, for Democrats to take control of Congress. “But I’m in the Collins camp,” Mr. Raye said, citing her record of bipartisanship. “The thought of replacing her with a reliable partisan vote, no matter the party,” he said, “is so the wrong direction for America.”

But the calculation, her critics counter, is more complicated. Her vote to advance Mr. Trump’s big domestic policy bill before she ultimately voted against it, her initial votes against setting congressional limits to military actions in Iran followed by eventual votes to do just that — all of it costs her constituents, they say, contributing to cuts to health care and higher prices for fuel, food and more. Many remain furious about her vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, a move that ultimately led to the end of Roe v. Wade.

“She’s very good at cutting ribbons,” said Betsy Sweet, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2018 and for Senate in 2020 against Ms. Collins. “She’s also really good at cutting your health care.”

Moreover, as she works to fend off her challenger in a tough year for Republicans, Ms. Collins’s sharp political style has been apparent not just to political insiders but to voters as well.

In a recent interview with Politico, Ms. Collins was startlingly cutting about her opponent.

“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” she said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.” They did now.

“This is a Susan people haven’t seen,” said Tony Payne, the executive director of the Republican Party of Maine in the 1970s who became an independent after the rise of Mr. Trump and a longtime critic of Ms. Collins. “This is the peeling off of the veneer.”

Last week, the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the Republican Party’s candidates, aired a radio ad about Mr. Jackson with a crude jingle alluding to the relationship. After it had made the rounds, Ms. Collins told reporters she “had nothing to do with that ad,” saying it should be removed from the air.

This week, Ms. Collins’s campaign has been airing a TV ad that many in Maine considered elitist. “We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Bill Green, a well-known, retired local sportscaster, says in the ad.

“For more than 30 years, Susan Collins has carefully concealed her intrinsic arrogance,” Sam Patten wrote in a post on social media castigating the ad. (Mr. Patten, a former aide to Ms. Collins, pleaded guilty during the first Trump administration to failing to register as a foreign agent.)

“She’s very smart, and she works very hard,” Mr. Patten told The Times. “There’s an arrogance in everyone in Washington,” he added, “but she never showed it before. She’s always been careful not to.”

Ted O’Meara, a former aide to Ms. Snowe who also worked for Mr. Cohen alongside Ms. Collins and managed Eliot Cutler’s campaigns for governor in 2010 and 2014, described it as a sense of entitlement. “The sense that there’s nobody else that can do this job but me or do it as well as me,” he said.

He stopped himself.

“Is this on the record?” he asked.

It was.

“She’ll be pissed,” he said.

Kitty Bennett contributed research. Tim Balk contributed reporting from Fryeburg, Maine, and Esmé E. Deprez from Caribou and Casco, Maine.

ARTICLE

‘I Came as Donald Trump’: The President Hosts a Luxury Halloween at Mar-a-Lago
President Trump attended his jungle-themed Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago dressed as a distinctly recognizable figure.
By Tyler Pager
Published 2026-11-01 03:18 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/trump-halloween-party-scene.html

There were cheetah and zebra stripes on the walls and tables. Women wore sequined leotards and elaborate headdresses, and one couple flocked around in bright-feathered costumes of jungle birds. Then President Trump arrived.

“I came as Donald Trump,” he said, outfitted in his standard red tie and navy suit. “I didn’t have time to get — people spent a lot of time and money. Rich people. They spent nine hours getting ready. I had 10 minutes, so I came as Donald Trump.”

Such was the scene Saturday night, when hundreds gathered in the ballroom at Mar-a-Lago to celebrate Halloween with the president. The theme was the jungle, if an opulent one.

There was Alaskan king crab and a caviar bar. There were bongo drums and puppets. Attendees posted photos on social media that showed a pen at the club with a zebra and a miniature pony. Nothing too scary.

Much more frightening for Republicans is the political environment across the country. And yet even as they brace for potential losses on Tuesday, Mr. Trump, whose approval rating is near historic lows, was thrilled to be entertaining.

“Look at all my rich members,” he told reporters. “They spent all day getting ready. Look at these guys.”

He added: “These are the biggest guys on Wall Street.”

It was a striking tone, with polls showing voters souring even more on Mr. Trump’s handling of the economy. One recent one from The New York Times and Siena University found that a majority of voters blame Mr. Trump for the decline: 69 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, 65 percent disapprove of the war in Iran, and nearly 75 percent disapprove of the high price of gas and diesel.

But for Mr. Trump, Mar-a-Lago is always a stage for his brand of gilded festivity.

There was Speaker Mike Johnson and Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India, in the cordoned-off section of the ballroom. SUMMARY

You don’t need to put in hours at the gym to build a strong, stable core. Engage your core as you use your left hand to lift the dumbbell across your body to the left side. Engage your core as you drop down to a forearm plank, leading with your right hand.

ARTICLE

For a Stronger Core, You Only Need 10 Minutes
Strengthening your midsection doesn’t have to take long, but it can have serious benefits.
By Jen Murphy and Theodore Tae
Published 2026-10-31 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/well/move/strong-core-workout.html

You don’t need to put in hours at the gym to build a strong, stable core.

“When it comes to training the core, quality trumps quantity,” said Joel Sanders, director of performance at EXOS, a sports training center in Phoenix. “No one needs to do 100 crunches or feel a burn. Ten to 12 minutes of core work can do the trick.”

The core, which includes muscles along your back, the sides of your body and into your pelvis, has two main functions: to protect your spine by creating stability and to help transfer power from your lower body to your upper body. Exercises where you hold a position or do slow, controlled movements improve stability, while dynamic, full-body exercises such as rotational medicine ball slams help build power.

The core is “the epicenter of strength,” Mr. Sanders said. “All movement, from a lift to a lunge to a golf or tennis swing, is tied to the core.”

If you’re a new exerciser, you should approach your “core hygiene,” as Mr. Sanders calls it, from a 360-degree perspective — doing movements that hit the front, back and sides of your body, he said.

If you focus on good form, you don’t need to do more than six to 10 reps — or less than 30 seconds — of each exercise, he added. The reason, in part, is that your core is already getting worked by many daily activities, even sitting (with good posture). Also, since it’s made up of so many small muscles, you don’t need to train it with the same volume as the glutes or quads.

Doing too many repetitions can also lead to injuries, said Karl Erickson, a performance specialist at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minn. Because your core — and particularly the deeper parts of it — acts like a corset for the spine, helping you maintain good posture, it’s particularly important to focus on form. When those muscles are fatigued, the spine can go from steal beam to wet noodle, Mr. Sanders said.

This core workout can be performed either as a standalone routine or as a warm-up before a workout, “to preheat the oven,” he said.

Overview

Time: 10 to 12 minutes

Intensity: Medium

What You’ll Need

- A mat
- A light to medium-weight dumbbell

Dumbbell Suitcase March

Purpose: Strengthens the abdominals, side muscles and glutes, as well as the shoulders and forearms

Time: 30 seconds

Pick up a weight and hold it in one hand, by your side. Keep your spine tall and your shoulders and hips square as you march in place, bringing your knees to hip height. Repeat with your other hand. To make it more challenging, hold the weight above your head with a straight arm.

Flutter Kicks

Purpose: Strengthens the abdominals, particularly the deep core and hip flexors

Time: 30 seconds

Lie face up with your legs straight and feet flexed. Place both hands either behind your head or palms down on either side of your hips for support. Draw your belly button toward your spine and use your abdominal muscles to lift your legs. Lift your legs, ideally three to six inches off the floor, but if you struggle to do that while keeping your back flat into the floor, it’s easier to lift them higher. Now flutter your legs, lifting your left, then your right and repeat.

Hip Rainbows

Purpose: Strengthens the abdominals, side muscles and shoulder stabilizers

Time: 30 seconds

Start in a forearm plank position with your elbows under your shoulders, and your knees, hips and torso in a straight line. Squeeze your glutes and engage your abdominals. Drop your right hip toward the floor, twisting your body to the right. Imagine drawing a rainbow with your hips as you bring your left hip up and over, then drop it toward the floor. Repeat for 30 seconds.

Beast Hold

Purpose: Strengthens the abdominals, side muscles and shoulder stabilizers

Time: 30 seconds

Start in a tabletop position, with your hands below your shoulders, your knees on the floor beneath your hips and your back flat. Engage your core as you lift and hover your knees one to three inches off the ground. The lower they are, the more difficult the exercise will be. Hold for 30 seconds. Bring your knees to the ground if you need a rest.

Plank Pull-Throughs

Purpose: Strengthens the abdominals, side muscles and shoulder stabilizers, shoulders, upper back

Time: 30 seconds

Start in a high plank pose with your hands directly under your shoulders and a dumbbell placed behind your right hand. If this is too hard, put your knees on the ground. Engage your core as you use your left hand to lift the dumbbell across your body to the left side. Do not let your body twist or your hips dip. Imagine balancing a cup of hot coffee on your back as you repeat, side to side, for 30 seconds. A wider stance with your feet will provide more stability.

Short-Lever Side Plank and Leg Lift

Purpose: Strengthens the side muscles, abdominals, glutes and shoulders

Time: 30 seconds per side

Start in a modified side plank: Place your right forearm on the floor and bend your right knee at a 90-degree angle, tucking your heel behind you. Keep your hips stacked as you extend your top leg. Your foot can rest on the floor for balance and your left hand can rest on your top hip or over your belly. Raise your hips off the ground, supporting yourself on right leg. Engage your core as you lift your leg just above hip level, then lower it so the inside of your foot taps the ground. Repeat for 30 seconds, then switch sides.

Plank Walk-Ups

Purpose: Strengthens the deep abdominals, particularly the deep core, shoulder stabilizers and deep back muscles

Time: 30 seconds

Start in a high plank pose with your hands directly under your shoulders. If this is too hard, put your knees on the ground. Engage your core as you drop down to a forearm plank, leading with your right hand. Press back up to plank pose, first straightening your right arm, then your left. One the next round, drop down and press up with your left side first. Continue alternating sides. If you are in a full plank, don’t let your hips rotate or sag.

ARTICLE

What’s Behind a Recent Spike in Early Social Security Claims?
Experts point to well-publicized turmoil at the government agency last year as a potential spark.
By Paula Span
Published 2026-10-31 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/well/whats-behind-a-recent-spike-in-early-social-security-claims.html

Until recently, economic researchers were cheering an encouraging trend: Older Americans were staying in the labor force longer and waiting longer to claim their Social Security benefits, aiming to enhance their financial stability in retirement.

Not everyone, of course. Despite financial advisers’ counsel and economists’ hopes, most people still claim their benefits before reaching their designated full retirement age, though that usually means a lifetime of lower monthly payments.

Early claimers might hit an unexpected financial crunch, as Alan Turner did when he lost his job as a museum exhibit designer in 2022. “I haphazardly looked for work, but my prospects weren’t very good,” he said.

For a while Mr. Turner, 69, who lives in New Castle, Del., got by on unemployment benefits and savings, hoping to reach his full retirement age — 66 and a half — before claiming. “It was doable, but it was bleak,” he said. He took his benefits at 64, reducing his Social Security income by about $5,000 a year.

Or people might feel the need to retire earlier than planned. Nancy Mansson, a nuclear medicine technologist in West Hebron, N.Y., found last year that “I was just fried,” she said. “I had to step away,” though she was more than a year short of her full retirement age.

People can claim Social Security retirement benefits as early as 62, but they face substantially reduced payments than if they wait until full retirement age, now 67 for those born in 1960 or later.

Ms. Mansson, 66, sacrificed about $300 a month by claiming early and works at a hospital one day a week to compensate.

Still, economists had documented that Americans were both retiring later and claiming their benefits later — until last year, when “all hell broke loose,” said Alicia Munnell, former director of the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College. In an unprecedented surge, hundreds of thousands more people than usual suddenly filed for retirement benefits.

Why? Understanding what’s happening with older Americans and Social Security requires looking both backward and ahead.

For decades, workers had been retiring at increasingly younger ages; that trend reversed in the 1980s, and the change accelerated in the 1990s. Changes in the Social Security law, which Congress amended in 1983 (“The last time we did anything to Social Security,” Dr. Munnell said, pointedly) provided incentives to work longer.

Most employers shifted from defined pensions to 401(k) plans and discontinued retiree health insurance, additional reasons to stay on the job. Plus, work had become less physically demanding overall, and “health and longevity were increasing,” Dr. Munnell said.

In an analysis the center published last year, the proportion of men who were filing at 62 fell to 26 percent in 2023 from 31 percent in 2019; among women, claiming at 62 dropped to 27 percent from 34 percent. Over the same period, claiming at 67 or later rose to 26 percent from 19 percent for men and to 25 percent from 20 percent for women, a trend that persisted into 2024.

By waiting, “they have more income,” Dr. Munnell said. “They can contribute to their 401(k)s. They have higher Social Security benefits and fewer years to support themselves without income.” Waiting also increases spouses’ eventual survivor benefits. Plus, most beneficiaries pay taxes on their benefits, bolstering both the Social Security system and the federal budget in general.

Delaying until 70, the age for receiving maximum benefits, brings particular rewards. Beyond full retirement age, benefits rise by 8 percent annually.

“It’s an inflation-protected annuity the private sector can’t compete with,” said Jack Smalligan, a senior policy fellow at the Urban Institute, a nonprofit research organization. “If you’re healthy and can afford it, it’s the smartest choice.”

But in 2025, he and a colleague noticed an unusual influx of new retirement claims and sounded the alarm. From October 2024 to April 2025, they found, claims jumped by 267,000 compared with the previous year, a 13 percent surge. Typically, “the fluctuations were more in the 2 to 3 percent range,” Mr. Smalligan said.

Population growth and adjustments for a small group of public employees couldn’t explain the size of that leap. “It was really a reaction to the turmoil at Social Security during that period,” Mr. Smalligan said.

The Trump administration, with its Department of Government Efficiency, was circulating false claims of widespread fraud, slashing thousands of Social Security Administration staff members and threatening to close field offices. “A whole mixture of negative signals about Social Security were coming from the White House,” Mr. Smalligan said.

“Having people go at the government with a chain saw was not helpful,” Dr. Munnell agreed, referring to a much-publicized stunt in which the DOGE chief Elon Musk appeared onstage brandishing the tool at a conservative conference. He has called Social Security “the biggest Ponzi scheme of all time.”

Perhaps it shouldn’t have been surprising that last year so many older Americans decided they’d better grab their benefits while they could.

(Something beneficiaries may not know: Those who regret claiming at full retirement age but before age 70 can direct Social Security to suspend their benefits, then reclaim them later when the payments are higher, with adjustments for money already received. “It’s not irrevocable,” Mr. Smalligan said.)

In a 2021 study by the Boston College center, researchers showed more than 3,100 participants headlines about Social Security. One referred fairly neutrally to “a long-term financing shortfall,” while others used scarier phrases like “deplete its reserves” and “headed toward insolvency.” The accompanying short text stayed the same.

“With the headlines that were more fear-inducing, people tended to say they would claim earlier, about a year earlier,” than the control group reading the neutral headline, said Gal Wettstein, associate director of health and insurance at the center and the study co-author.

By 2025, this was no longer an academic experiment. Negative media coverage was “overwhelming,” he said. “People saw it every day.”

And now?

A year later, claiming has reverted to more normal levels. From October 2025 to April 2026, new Social Security claims fell by 235,000, about a 10 percent drop. “Almost an exact reversal,” Mr. Smalligan said. The decline “effectively canceled out the surge.”

That doesn’t mean Social Security is out of the woods. Without congressional action, it will deplete its retirement trust fund by late 2032, the latest trustees’ report said. By law, beneficiaries will still get payments if that happens, but they could be up to 22 percent lower.

And despite some rehiring at the agency, “we continue to hear reports of difficulty being able to get through on the phone or make an in-person appointment,” Mr. Smalligan said, noting that Social Security’s administrative budget has been underfunded for many years.

A representative for the Social Security Administration said that the agency has provided the best customer service in its history, helping customers however they seek assistance, by phone, online or in person. Asked about the reasons behind the spike in early benefit claims, the agency did not provide a response.

In the past, Congress has come through with 11th-hour rescues. This round, Senators Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, are preparing bipartisan legislation that, among other remedies, would lift the cap that exempts wages over $184,500 from payroll taxes. Eliminating the cap would inject $3 trillion into the system over 10 years, according to the Social Security trustees.

A “solvency plan” published by the Brookings Institution, a nonprofit research and public policy organization, calls for that, too. “Of the revenue options, that one has the broadest base of acceptance” among political leaders and the public, said Mr. Smalligan, a co-author of the report.

For now, though, “the ambiguity about Social Security is making Americans anxious and unhappy,” Dr. Munnell said.

Sam Delson, a former California state employee in Elk Grove, Calif., retired five years ago at 61. With his state pension, he figured he could afford to take Social Security benefits at 70 and he still intends to.

Most of the time. “I’m not expecting the system to fall apart, but I’m not as absolutely certain as I used to be — some doubt has crept in,” Mr. Delson said. “I’m thinking 67 wouldn’t be so bad.”

trump-arch-washington-dc.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 17  Words: 1143/1211

SUMMARY

The triumphal arch was a Roman innovation conceived to honor those of good deed who “should be lifted up,” wrote Pliny the Elder, “above the rest of mortals.” Among the first was the Arch of Titus, built around A.D. The tallest triumphal arch in the world was finished on the eve of World War II in Mexico City, the Monumento a la Revolución.

ARTICLE

The Rise and Fall of the Triumphal Arch
The history of triumphal arches is long and messy. Where does Donald Trump’s proposed edifice fit in?
By Thomas J. Campanella
Published 2026-11-01 14:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/opinion/trump-arch-washington-dc.html

The triumphal arch was a Roman innovation conceived to honor those of good deed who “should be lifted up,” wrote Pliny the Elder, “above the rest of mortals.” Only later did it become associated with victorious generals returning from battle, a symbolic city gate through which triumphators passed.

Among the first was the Arch of Titus, built around A.D. 81 to commemorate the victory of Titus and Vespasian in the siege of Jerusalem a decade earlier. Its panels depict spoils taken from the Second Temple in victory — including the curved menorah featured on the national emblem of Israel.

Much later came the Arch of Constantine, from 315, adjacent to the Colosseum on the Via Triumphalis. It was the largest Roman arch, built to honor Constantine’s victory at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge. Over the centuries, the arches of Titus and Constantine became archetypes replicated around the world for a gamut of glorious purposes. Not coincidentally, the words arch and archetype share the same Greek root: Arkhein, to rule, and arkhos, chief. Triumphal arches enact a vision of power. Sometimes that is a vision founded in reality; at others, it is aspirational, even deceptive, a gesture made to tell a false tale about a country’s place in the world. President Trump’s proposed arch is just another chapter in the long history of heroic architecture pressed into the service of ideology.

The scale and symbolism of the triumphal arch continued to evolve, often to honor the fallen rather than generals, or to trumpet the aspirations of new regimes. The copper-sheeted Narva Triumphal Arch in St. Petersburg, Russia, built in 1814 and weathered to a glorious verdigris patina, honored Russia’s defeat of Napoleon in 1812, while the Arc de Triomphe in Paris — begun earlier but finished decades later — represented the opposite side, venerating those who fought and died for France in the Napoleonic Wars and preceding revolution.

But the classical references remained. The English architect John Nash channeled Constantine for his Marble Arch, originally erected at Buckingham Palace, completed in 1833 to honor the British side in the Napoleonic Wars.

As the self-styled legatee of the Roman Empire, it was only appropriate that England looked to ancient Rome for its monuments. The Marble Arch was also a riposte aimed squarely at the Arc de Triomphe, which was styled on the Arch of Titus.

New York reconstituted both archetypical arches, too: Stanford White’s exquisite Washington Arch channeled Titus; John Russell Pope’s Theodore Roosevelt Memorial — the monumental Central Park entrance to the American Museum of Natural History — aped Constantine.

The Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Arch just outside Prospect Park, completed in 1892 and topped by Frederick MacMonnies’s soaring quadriga, brought the triumphal arch back around to honor the fallen.

So did Paul Philippe Cret’s Titus-inspired National Memorial Arch at Valley Forge National Historical Park — dedicated in 1917 “to the officers and private soldiers of the Continental Army.”

Nor were triumphal arches confined to Europe and the Americas. George Wittet’s Gateway of India, completed in 1924 on the Mumbai, then Bombay, waterfront, employed elements of 16th-century Gujarati architecture to mark George V’s arrival in December 1911 — the first time a British monarch visited the subcontinent after nearly 300 years of British presence. Ironically, it would later mark the end of British rule: Through its archway in February 1948, the very last British troops departed newly independent India. “This was where the British landed,” wrote Jan Morris, “and this is where, in the end, they left.”

Arch-bloat seems to know no bounds. The tallest triumphal arch in the world was finished on the eve of World War II in Mexico City, the Monumento a la Revolución. At 220 feet, it rises to over three times the height of the Arch of Constantine.

But its standing almost ended just three years later. In 1941, Albert Speer presented plans to his Führer for a monumental arch that would tower nearly 400 feet over Berlin. Taller than the towers of the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge in New York, it would have been twice the height of the Arc de Triomphe, which could have fit snugly within its cavernous maw. Speer’s gargantua anchored the monumental axis of Hitler’s “World Capital Germania,” the proposed rebuilding of Berlin for the Thousand-Year Reich.

Today, all that remains of the megalomanic arch is a concrete cylinder used to test the load-bearing capacity of the marshy Tempelhof site — the 13,644-ton Schwerbelastungskörper.

But megalomania will endure so long as humans have the run of the planet, and so too will outsize arches rise. In North Korea, Pyongyang’s Arch of Triumph, the second tallest in the world, was erected to commemorate Korean independence after World War II. Inaugurated on Kim Il Sung’s 70th birthday in 1982, it consists of 25,500 granite blocks, each representing a day Dear Leader had lived to that point.

Unless you count the Gateway Arch in St. Louis — a polished-steel vault that celebrates manifest destiny and nods to, rather than embraces, the tradition of triumphal arches — Americans have fallen out of the triumphal arch habit this century. That, of course, may well change if Mr. Trump has his way. Despite opposition from a panoply of architectural and preservation organizations, the United States Triumphal Arch would rise to 250 feet, surpassing the Mexican arch as the world’s tallest. That would make it well over twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial and almost 100 feet taller than the Arc de Triomphe.

One issue with the so-called Arc d’Trump is its proposed location at Memorial Circle, just over the Potomac and on axis with the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Washington is a city of vistas and sightlines; few are more sacred than this one. It was to protect this visual axis that landscape architect Gilmore D. Clarke, then-chair of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, convinced President Franklin D. Roosevelt not to build the Pentagon at Arlington Farms, where it would have obliterated the backdrop of tiered headstones and Arlington House. The War Department was furious, but had to concede. The Pentagon was built instead well out of the way. But today’s so-called War Department may have revenge of a sort: The Arc d’Trump could be the first in history designed to also serve as a military installation, an aerie for snipers and drones.

But the real issue is that of purpose. What exactly is Mr. Trump’s behemoth meant to celebrate? Our abnegation as a force for good in the world? Our bitter internal divisions? Will it be another desperate display of might by a state in decline, an India Gate on the Potomac? Will it be mostly made in China? In the end, of course, it will be a taxpayer-funded monument to the vainglory of our outer-borough emperor, Donald Trump. After all, the English word “trump” — and thus “triumphal” — is derivative of the French word “triomphe.”

Thomas J. Campanella is a professor of city planning at Cornell University.

ARTICLE

Trump Has Found the Attorney General of His Dreams
The Department of Justice is in a state of moral collapse.
By David French
Published 2026-11-01 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/opinion/trump-blanche-comey-justice.html

October was a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad month for the Department of Justice.

The worst moment happened on Oct. 5, when the department made a third attempt to prosecute James Comey, the former director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The first attempt, an indictment for lying to Congress, failed when a federal court dismissed the case because the prosecutor was appointed illegally. The second, an indictment for threatening the president by posting a photo online of a collection of seashells on a beach that were arranged to say “86 47,” is still pending.

Comey, however, has filed two motions to dismiss — one based on his free speech rights and the other claiming that the government has engaged in vindictive prosecution.

The case is absurd on its face. In a 1969 case, Watts v. United States, the Supreme Court held that a far more explicit threat — the defendant had said that he would resist the draft, but “if they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J.” — was nothing more than “political hyperbole” and protected by the First Amendment.

The third attempt is, if anything, even more specious. The Department of Justice filed what is called a criminal information (not an indictment), claiming that Comey leaked classified information that ended up in The New York Times in October 2016.

This is not the first time that the Trump administration has considered bringing this charge. Trump administration prosecutors looked into this incident in 2017 and 2019 and declined to bring charges both times.

But there’s now a new sheriff in town — Todd Blanche, the attorney general of the United States and President Trump’s former personal lawyer — and Todd Blanche does what Trump says.

To be clear, an information isn’t an indictment. It can’t actually start Comey’s case. The Fifth Amendment says, “No person shall be held to answer for a capital, or otherwise infamous crime, unless on a presentment or indictment of a grand jury.”

Instead, it’s a unilateral filing by prosecutors that has the effect of sometimes tolling (that is to say, stopping) the statute of limitations. It can only actually start a federal felony prosecution if the defendant waives his right to indictment by grand jury, which Comey has not done.

In fact, the Department of Justice admits that it filed the information for the purpose of tolling the statute of limitations. It was filed on the very day that the 10-year statute of limitations was set to expire. In effect, they’re hoping it can serve as a place holder that keeps the case alive until a grand jury finally indicts.

But there’s a problem — a big problem. While some federal criminal statutes allow the department to toll the statute of limitations with an information, this one does not. As Andrew McCarthy, a former federal prosecutor, wrote in National Review, the relevant statute requires an indictment within 10 years. It makes no reference to an information.

In other words, this legal filing is a bad joke. The lawyers who brought it should be ashamed of themselves, and they should be sanctioned by the court.

But that’s not the only legal embarrassment from the last month. On Monday, a federal judge in Manhattan ruled that the Department of Justice acted illegally in 2025 when it fired Maurene Comey, James Comey’s daughter, a highly respected prosecutor in the Southern District of New York.

On Tuesday, a federal grand jury refused to indict Cassidy Hutchinson for perjury. Hutchinson was a key witness in the House of Representatives’ investigation of the events of Jan. 6, 2021.

Hutchinson joins a long line of political opponents that Trump has tried — and failed — to indict, including Attorney General Letitia James of New York and six Democratic lawmakers who had posted a video saying that members of the military had a duty to disobey illegal orders.

It is extremely rare for federal grand juries to refuse to indict. I’ve known prosecutors who’ve gone their entire careers without seeing a “no true bill” (the technical term for the refusal to indict). Under Trump, it’s a regular occurrence.

It gets worse. Also on Tuesday, Zia Faruqui, a federal magistrate judge, eviscerated Trump administration prosecutors after they tried to add a new charge against two former F.B.I. officials charged with lying to Congress without seeking court approval.

The judge ordered the new complaint struck from the record. “It is inappropriate,” he said. “I am surprised that a complaint unsigned by a judge was filed on a docket where I am unaware of that ever happening in this court.”

“Everything you are doing is just giving me more and more concern,” he said.

I’m going to stop there, but even as I do, I feel as if I’m misleading you. I’m stopping because of space, not because that’s the end of the outrages. In case after case after case, the Department of Justice is targeting Trump opponents, making frivolous arguments and engaging in vindictive, meritless prosecutions.

I blame Trump, but I also blame Blanche. He doesn’t understand his own job.

We all know that Trump has an extreme view of executive power that renders him a virtual elected monarch. His administration’s actions extend well beyond conventional unitary executive theory, which puts a premium on presidential control over the executive branch. He treats the law as his plaything, deciding on his own whim which laws will be enforced and which ones will not.

It is true that the president is the boss of every cabinet official. He can fire them at will. But it is also true that the attorney general is different from every other member of the cabinet.

Unlike, say, Pete Hegseth, Blanche has three masters, not one. The attorney general and all the lawyers working for him also answer to the judiciary, which not only decides the cases he brings; it also governs the conduct of D.O.J. officials in court. And he also answers to the bar — rules of ethics are binding on every attorney, including government attorneys.

In addition, Trump may be Blanche’s boss, but he is not Blanche’s client. Blanche’s client is the government of the United States, including its various agencies. Blanche owes his fiduciary duty to the government (and, ultimately, the Constitution), not to the president.

In the criminal context, these additional obligations have profound meaning. In a 1935 case, Berger v. United States, the Supreme Court said, “The United States attorney is the representative not of an ordinary party to a controversy, but of a sovereignty whose obligation to govern impartially is as compelling as its obligation to govern at all, and whose interest, therefore, in a criminal prosecution is not that it shall win a case, but that justice shall be done.”

Read those words, and then ask yourself: Does that sound like Todd Blanche to you?

The attorney general is no ordinary lawyer, and neither are the attorneys who work for the Department of Justice. Trump is their boss, but the Constitution is their true master, and no president can compel them to violate ethics rules or court orders.

Last month, I wrote a newsletter urging a Democratic House and Senate (should the Democrats win control on Tuesday) to follow Senator Elissa Slotkin’s advice and hold the administration’s most malevolent actors accountable for their worst misdeeds. It’s time to resurrect impeachment. I mentioned Pete Hegseth. I should have mentioned Todd Blanche too.

His “high crime” is corrupting the Department of Justice, and only a decisive act of political hygiene can cleanse the D.O.J. of MAGA’s terrible stain.
