Dr. Hilsum became known as “the father of liquid crystals,” according to The Times of London. Dr. Hilsum held more than 70 patents.

ARTICLE

That Giant HDTV That Fits in Your Living Room? Thank Cyril Hilsum.
The man who helped develop the technology for liquid crystal displays — the screens in flat-panel televisions and laptops — has died at 101.
By Michael S. Rosenwald
Published 2026-11-01 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/technology/cyril-hilsum-dead.html

In the beginning, televisions were barely smaller than Buicks. They weighed upward of 500 pounds. Finding a spot for them in the house was a challenge.

“Since we got our television set,” a TV World reader wrote to the magazine in 1953, “we’ve had to change the arrangement of furniture in our living room, and we just can’t keep the piano.”

In the 1960s, up to their antennas in complaints about these space- and power-hungry monstrosities, electronics executives and government regulators prodded scientists to find ways to shrink them. Defense officials joined in, hoping for smaller radar screens.

At the center of this herculean effort was Cyril Hilsum, an exuberant British physicist with voluminous, untamed white hair whose striking resemblance to Albert Einstein wasn’t limited to appearance.

“People say Einstein’s I.Q. was 155 or something, and I’d guess that Cyril’s was way higher than that,” J. Cliﬀ Jones, a physicist formerly affiliated with the University of Leeds in England, said in an interview. “I’m not saying Einstein wasn’t extremely important, but Cyril was that kind of man. He was that sharp.”

At the Royal Radar Establishment, a government research center, Dr. Hilsum led the team that developed crucial materials and technology for liquid crystal displays — the screens in flat-panel televisions, laptops and smartphones.

Dr. Hilsum died on Sept. 23 at an assisted-living facility in London, his family said. He was 101, having survived into his 11th decade by avoiding fresh vegetables and subsisting largely on TV dinners, chocolate and red wine.

The son of street vendors in the gritty East End of London, Dr. Hilsum was an inventing machine. He developed semiconductors that are used in remote controls, automatic doors, burglar alarms and bar-code scanners.

His work with radar technology led to the development of Claribel, a device used to detect the location of snipers in Northern Ireland, and he was also instrumental in developing radar speed detectors, which occasionally caught him exceeding the posted limits on highways.

“He didn’t have a lot of time for theoretical physics or theoretical physicists,” his daughter Lindsey Hilsum, an author and foreign correspondent for TV news, said at his memorial service. “He was a materials scientist and an engineer. It was all about applications.”

In the late 1960s, Dr. Hilsum was working on radar for the British government when his boss inquired whether there might be something he could do about the size of electronic screens.

Radar displays and early TVs were behemoths because they used bulky cathode ray tubes (or CRTs) to beam images into thick, heavy sheets of glass. Wood cabinets housed and protected the finicky gear, turning these contraptions into unwieldy pieces of furniture.

“The CRT,” Dr. Hilsum wrote in a 2010 article for Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, “was becoming more and more exposed as a dinosaur.”

At first, he wasn’t optimistic that anything could be done, but there was a new idea emerging — using liquid crystals to form images on a screen — that intrigued him.

For one thing, the crystals would use a lower voltage than CRTs. But more important, they could fit into a thin film between two slim sheets of glass. Goodbye, tubes.

The problem: Liquid crystals were stable only at high temperatures, and they dissolved quickly. No one would want to buy a new TV every few weeks.

Dr. Hilsum assembled a team of scientists to tackle the issue. The story of what they did could fill a five-part television series, but if reduced to the length of a caption in TV Guide, it would read something like this: “Scientists create a new family of stable liquid crystals known as cyanobiphenyls.”

The implications were immense.

“The world had been trying hard to find a stable material, and suddenly we had it,” Dr. Hilsum said in a 2020 interview with the journal Archives of Information Technology.

Digital watches arrived first, followed by pocket calculators, laptops, flat-screen televisions and, eventually, smartphones.

Dr. Hilsum became known as “the father of liquid crystals,” according to The Times of London. In 1976, Queen Elizabeth II visited his lab and was photographed laughing as he tried to explain the technology to her.

“There were a lot of people involved in this technology, but Cyril pushed it in the direction it needed to go, and changed the world,” Dr. Jones said. “You can now fit a massive HDTV in your living room. That all comes down to this key invention.”

The second of three boys, Mr. Hilsum was born in London on May 17, 1925, to Benjamin and Ada (Goldstein) Hilsum, who sold flat hats, chocolate and chamois leathers at stalls in Petticoat Lane and on Portobello Road.

His childhood was spartan and hardscrabble. “There was an outside loo, I can remember that,” he said in a 2002 oral history for the British Library. “We all slept, the three boys, in what seemed an enormous bed.”

Clothes were handed down or inherited from cousins. There were no presents on holidays.

“We played in the street,” he said. “We had fights. In general, I suppose it was like most families.”

But Cyril wasn’t like most other children. At 3, he was already reading. For fun, he took his toys apart.

“I wouldn’t interfere with electricity or anything like that,” he said. “But I would take toys to pieces, whether they were mine or other people’s.”

After high school, he won a scholarship to attend University College London. “I don’t know that Mum ever took it in,” he said. “Dad was thrilled. I mean, essentially it’s what he would have wanted to do.”

He studied math and physics, graduating in 1945, and received his doctorate in physics from the University of London in 1959.

Asked in the oral history what makes a good physicist, Dr. Hilsum replied: “Curiosity, curiosity. Always, you have the kind of mind that you want to know the answer to questions. You see something and you think, ‘How does that work?’ or ‘What would make that work better?’”

He said he had no interest in theoretical physics — not even the Higgs boson particle. “It would leave me completely flat,” he said. “I want things to work.”

He married Betty Cooper, his co-star in a college production of “Pygmalion,” in 1947, and frequently bought her gadgets as gifts, which he proceeded to take apart. She died in 1987. After their daughter Karen Burt, an engineer, died in 1997, Dr. Hilsum established a scholarship in her name with the Women’s Engineering Society.

In addition to his daughter Lindsey, Dr. Hilsum is survived by his partner, Anne Dell; a grandson; and his brother Charles, who is 103.

Dr. Hilsum held more than 70 patents. He received his last when he was 97. The paperwork describes the invention as an “apparatus for, or methods of, measuring force, work, mechanical power or torque, specially adapted for specific purposes for measuring tension in flexible members, e.g. ropes, cables, wires, threads, belts or bands using electrical means using sensors inserted into the flexible member.”

In plain English, it’s an ink with sensors that can conduct electricity. One possible use is in hospital beds, to track the movement of patients and prevent bedsores. Dr. Hilsum developed the idea in his kitchen, where he set up lab equipment and worked in a white coat.

“You should always be concerned,” he once said, “with what you are doing that helps the community.”

ARTICLE

Judge Rejects Trump Officials’ Move to Challenge Alaska Senate Election
In the latest defeat for the Trump administration, the ruling dismisses a lawsuit that pre-emptively contested the results of a race that includes two candidates named Daniel Sullivan.
By Anna Griffin
Published 2026-11-01 18:31 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/alaska-senate-election-lawsuit.html

A federal judge in Alaska has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit that pre-emptively challenged the results in a U.S. Senate race featuring two candidates with the same name — a Republican incumbent and another man who could be a spoiler.

The ruling is the latest in a series of court defeats for the Trump administration, which has been seeking to intervene in state-administered elections.

On Friday, the U.S. District Court in California blocked the administration from threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the department’s directives on handling ballots.

Also on Friday, a federal appeals court panel denied a request to order California officials to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claimed had been sent to possible noncitizens.

In Alaska, the Justice Department filed its lawsuit last month at President Trump’s direction, asking the judge to block certification of the state’s U.S. Senate election results if Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses but would have won had votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, gone to the incumbent instead.

In that scenario, the suit also demands an investigation into whether voters who selected the retired teacher actually intended to vote for the senator.

Federal officials have not made clear how an investigation into anonymous ballots would be conducted.

In her Sunday ruling, Chief Judge Sharon Gleason of U.S. District Court in Alaska wrote that she did not see how the federal government’s proposed solution to any confusion would solve the problem if it even existed — or how the approach could work given the right to a secret ballot is a core principle of American democracy.

The federal government, she wrote, “offers no rebuttal to the concerns regarding preservation of the secrecy of voting and provides no explanation of how its request for ballot segregation and a court-ordered investigation by law enforcement officers into certain voters’ intent could be implemented while preserving the secrecy of the ballot.”

Kiersten Pels, a spokeswoman for the Department of Justice, said the administration plans to appeal the dismissal and noted that the judge didn’t not address “the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”

The administration’s lawsuit accuses Daniel J. Sulivan of trying to “dupe Alaska’s voters into believing that he is Senator Sullivan.” Daniel J. Sullivan has said he voted for Democrats in the last three presidential races and for Mary Peltola, the current Democratic Senate nominee on the ballot, in her 2022 and 2024 campaigns for Congress.

The suit also notes that he switched his party affiliation from Independent to Republican only when he filed to run, and that his campaign website uses the same dark blue and yellow color scheme as the incumbent’s.

A New York Times investigation revealed that a Democratic operative connected to Ms. Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee enlisted Daniel J. Sullivan to run as part of a broader effort to recruit independent and third-party candidates who might peel votes away from the incumbent.

Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has ordered a criminal investigation into the Peltola campaign even as the state elections division, overseen by his lieutenant governor, also a Republican, fought the Trump administration’s civil lawsuit.

Ms. Peltola and national Democrats have denied any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy, and they joined the civil case as additional defendants along with national Democrats, the League of Women Voters and Common Cause, a self-described nonpartisan government watchdog organization.

Daniel S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, promised in an interview with CNN Sunday to support any election results but also suggested, without offering explanation or details, that the election could be “stolen.”

In its defense in the Justice Department’s lawsuit, lawyers with the state of Alaska noted that state courts had already rejected an attempt by the state’s elections agency to take Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot and that the final ballot was designed to differentiate between the two men: It lists the senator as “Dan S. Sullivan” and notes his party affiliation and incumbency, and the other man is “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party affiliation included.

Alaska also uses ranked choice voting in state and federal general elections, meaning voters are familiar with the system. Any voter confused by the existence of two Dan Sullivans could simply rank both candidates.

Judge Gleason had already expressed skepticism of the Trump administration’s case in a ruling last month agreeing to a speedy hearing. In that order, she pointed out that the federal lawsuit came after Alaskans had already begun casting ballots for November and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the state Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.

In Sunday’s dismissal ruling, she noted that federal lawyers, in their filings, said they were not attempting to interfere in the time, place and manner of Alaskan elections — matters the U.S. Constitution leaves in the hands of states.

But, Judge Gleason said, the federal government’s proposed answers to any voter confusion were “a court order preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan.

“These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska’s election,” she wrote.

If anything, the judge added, such federal intervention amid an ongoing election would cause the precise sort of voter confusion the administration says it is trying to prevent.

Bayliss Wagner and Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

What to Know About the Florida Plane Crash That Killed 9
A small jet plummeted to the ground on Sunday, exploding into a fireball and killing everyone on board. The authorities did not immediately release information about the victims.
By Bernard Mokam, Christina Morales, Georgia Gee and David Ovalle
Published 2026-11-02 02:50 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/learjet-crash-florida-palm-beach.html

The authorities are investigating why a private jet carrying nine people plunged from the sky on Sunday afternoon, falling at a rate of 20,000 feet per minute before crashing into a roadway outside Palm Beach, Fla.

Everyone on board was killed, the authorities said. They have not released information about the victims. One of the pilots was a 20-year-old aviator named Nathalia Filgueiras, according to her mother, Camila Corteleti.

The plane, a Learjet 60, was traveling from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed in a residential area, showering the neighborhood in debris and forcing the authorities to evacuate hundreds of residents.

Here’s what we know.

What happened?

Radio traffic between the pilot and air traffic control in Miami indicated that the plane was encountering “light, clear ice that is manageable” on Sunday afternoon, as well as “moderate turbulence.”

The pilot asked if she could climb to 37,000 feet, presumably to fly above the turbulent air. But moments later, she declared “mayday” to air traffic controllers, indicating a life-threatening emergency.

The plane was “descending 20,000 feet per minute,” she screamed.

“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she added.

At a news conference on Sunday, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said that footage of the crash, captured on dashboard cameras, showed what “looked like a missile going down.”

The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board said they would be investigating. The N.T.S.B. has scheduled a news conference for Monday.

Local officials said on Sunday that they were evacuating about 600 residents in the small community of trailer homes near the impact zone, where smoldering chunks of metal ignited small fires.

No one on the ground was injured, officials said.

Ms. Filgueiras, of Boca Raton, Fla., had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and earned her pilot’s license at 17, Ms. Corteleti said. She said her daughter had worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale.

What are experts saying?

The cause of the crash was not immediately clear. Aviation safety experts were studying clues such as the plane’s rapid loss of altitude and the pilot’s mention of ice.

The pilot was indicating that the “plane was uncontrollable,” said Steven Arroyo, a retired United Airlines captain who listened to an audio recording of the pilot’s conversation with air traffic controllers.

Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general for the Transportation Department, said that ice buildup on a plane’s wings could disrupt airflow and reduce lift. That could be consistent with how the plane dropped from the sky so suddenly.

“Icing can be so severe it can overcome and stall the plane,” said Ms. Schiavo, who reviewed publicly available flight data and videos posted on social media.

“That is a plane not descending, but a plane falling,” she said.

What did witnesses see?

Esteban Ruiz, a resident of the trailer home community near the crash site, said he had been relaxing on Sunday afternoon when he heard a loud noise.

“I thought maybe it was lightning,” he said, adding that he also heard what he thought was rain pelting his roof. It was actually metal debris from the plane or its impact. Mr. Ruiz said he rushed outside and saw a chaotic scene and a crater in the ground.

Stephanie Platts, who also lived near the crash site, said she had been sitting on her patio with family members when she heard what sounded like a car crash. Ms. Platts said her mobile home caught on fire, caused by flying debris.

Neighbors tried to help her put out the flames. She said she saw human remains scattered around her.

“Everything was engulfed in flames,” Ms. Platts said, “and then after the flames, was like rain of metal.”

The last straw for Representative Haley Stevens came Saturday afternoon. By last Wednesday, Ms. Stevens said she would not be campaigning with Dr. El-Sayed. Would Ms. Stevens even be there?

ARTICLE

Inside the Abdul El-Sayed-Haley Stevens Meltdown in Michigan
The relationship shattered in part because of Israel, but also because of their sensitive egos and hurt feelings. The split had been months in the making.
By Reid J. Epstein and Tim Balk
Published 2026-11-02 01:57 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/politics/el-sayed-stevens-meltdown-michigan-democrats.html

The last straw for Representative Haley Stevens came Saturday afternoon.

She was on the cusp of appearing at a unity event with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in a summer primary and became Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee. Several powerful intermediaries had been trying to broker peace between the former rivals, who were sparring over Dr. El-Sayed’s strong criticisms of Israel.

But after Ms. Stevens issued a hostile statement Friday morning calling upon Dr. El-Sayed to condemn an ad made by a supportive PAC and make other concessions, he stepped before reporters and said what his campaign had been signaling privately: He no longer wanted Ms. Stevens to join him at a Detroit church on Sunday.

It was one thing not to be welcomed by Dr. El-Sayed’s Senate campaign. It was quite another for him to say so in public.

So Ms. Stevens on Sunday did what she had been telling everyone she would not do. She endorsed former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in a race critical to control of the Senate.

“Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, that he didn’t want me there,” Ms. Stevens said while standing next to Mr. Rogers outside a Black church in Detroit, where they had just attended the Sunday service. “I did endorse the Democratic nominee, and he chose to close this campaign by saying I wasn’t welcome. I’ve never been invited to a campaign event. That’s fine. You know, he’s busy. He’s running all around.”

Ms. Stevens’s extraordinary declaration and church appearance with Mr. Rogers were a stunning denouement of her weekslong feud with Dr. El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated her in the Michigan Senate primary in August. Throughout their evident tension this fall, she insisted she was a team player and a good Democrat who would grit her teeth and back Dr. El-Sayed while working hard for other party members on the ticket.

Their dispute is deeply personal, involving slights between two mercurial millennial politicians of sizable egos quick to take offense.

Dr. El-Sayed, supremely confident, did not wish to give an inch to a defeated rival. Ms. Stevens, still absorbing her primary loss, eventually felt scorned by his campaign’s failure to include her in events or reach out to her for her views and embarrassed to be told to stay away.

But the breach also represents a major fissure coursing through the Democratic Party about what its relationship with Israel and Jewish donors should be. Dr. El-Sayed, if he wins on Tuesday and enters the Senate in January, would be the most anti-Israel U.S. senator since the formation of the Jewish state 78 years ago.

For now, the collapse of the Stevens-El-Sayed alliance has created an embarrassing and potentially costly drama for Democrats in a race that holds Republicans’ best chance of flipping a Senate seat. Ms. Stevens faced a swift backlash on Sunday from her party, which was caught off-guard by her defection.

“It’s just really unfortunate given the stakes that this has turned into such a spectacle because of one person,” said Lonnie Scott, a veteran Michigan Democratic operative. “It is definitely not ideal that we’d be talking about Haley Stevens three days out from an election.”

This account of their split is based on interviews with more than a dozen people involved in or briefed on talks with Dr. El-Sayed’s camp and Ms. Stevens’s team, some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, as well as public remarks from Dr. El-Sayed, Ms. Stevens and Mr. Rogers.

A Unity Breakfast, and Then Nothing More

Days after Dr. El-Sayed won a bitter primary race against Ms. Stevens in August that centered on disagreements over Israel, they appeared together at a unity breakfast. Ms. Stevens gave him a hug. And that was about it.

Since then, Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign hired a handful of Ms. Stevens’s campaign staff members, but he had next to no communication with her, according to Ms. Stevens and two others with knowledge of their relationship. At times, other Democrats tried to include her in the campaign.

Mr. Wert, who is active in Democratic circles, wanted to publish an opinion essay in Ms. Stevens’s name attacking Mr. Rogers in a Jewish news outlet.

Ms. Stevens was initially receptive, according to screenshots of texts Mr. Wert provided to The New York Times.

“I really like what you wrote,” she messaged to Mr. Wert on Sept. 20.

Mr. Wert replied, “I hope I captured your voice.”

“You did,” she replied. “So nice.”

In late September, Ms. Stevens was suggesting edits to the essay over text. But something seemed to change at the end of the month.

“Pls hold for now,” she wrote on Sept. 30, without elaborating. “I love you all but cannot move forward with this right now.”

At the root of the disagreement between Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed was U.S. policy on Israel. Dr. El-Sayed has emerged as one of the Democratic Party’s leading critics of Israel. Ms. Stevens, who is not Jewish, once said “I see Israel in my dreams” at a Hanukkah service. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supported her in the primary, spent at least $30 million attacking Dr. El-Sayed during the primary and began spending more starting in October.

Ms. Stevens’s fiancé is Jewish and is an AIPAC donor. She said in an interview on Friday that she is considering converting to Judaism.

The El-Sayed campaign believed no amount of acquiescence to Ms. Stevens would be sufficient, according to one of his campaign officials. So when she began to issue demands late last month that he disavow an ally’s online ad that she viewed as antisemitic, Dr. El-Sayed at first did not budge. She became increasingly critical of him in her cable television appearances. He tried to ignore her.

By last Wednesday, Ms. Stevens said she would not be campaigning with Dr. El-Sayed. That day, her fiancé, Jason Turkish, endorsed Mr. Rogers. He said that Dr. El-Sayed would make the world less safe for Jews, and that he hoped Ms. Stevens would run for the Senate again in the future.

Representative James E. Clyburn of South Carolina, a Democratic power broker and mentor to Ms. Stevens in the House, was privately growing nervous that Ms. Stevens might pull her support from Dr. El-Sayed and back Mr. Rogers.

In the eyes of some Democrats, it was time for an intervention.

On Thursday, Representative Debbie Dingell, the dean of the Michigan Democratic House delegation, sought to make peace. She arranged for Mr. Clyburn to invite both Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed to church on Sunday. Neither Ms. Stevens nor Dr. El-Sayed could refuse. Ms. Stevens looked up to Mr. Clyburn as a leader. Dr. El-Sayed needed a big turnout from Black voters. On Thursday, Ms. Stevens said she had been asked to participate in a “souls to the polls” event and would be there.

From Signs of Peace to All-Out War

Ms. Stevens had one condition. She wanted Dr. El-Sayed to disavow an ad produced by a PAC that backed him, saying it was antisemitic because it blamed U.S. support for Israel for high grocery prices.

On Friday morning, she released a lengthy statement that abruptly reignited tensions. She said that she had learned that Dr. El-Sayed planned to condemn the ad and called on him to apologize for comments he had made about Israel, as well as to take down an ad from his campaign featuring Tucker Carlson.

She said in an interview at her home later on Friday that she had been given a promise that Dr. El-Sayed would denounce the ad. She would not say who made that promise.

Dr. El-Sayed did not directly address Ms. Stevens’s public demands on Friday. But he was clearly fed up. He released a statement saying Ms. Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”

Then came Saturday.

By the afternoon, Dr. El-Sayed was getting peppered with reporters’ questions about Ms. Stevens. He condemned the ad she objected to. But he also issued a stern warning: He did not want Ms. Stevens to appear with him on Sunday.

“I don’t want any distractions,” Dr. El-Sayed told reporters after a rally outside Detroit. He added, “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”

An aide helped Ms. Stevens craft a statement of her appreciation for his stance against the ad. It did not mention his public disinvitation. As late as Saturday evening, Ms. Stevens told allies that she was still behind Dr. El-Sayed and planned to lie low through the weekend.

‘Blindsided’

Democrats were on edge Sunday morning, with uncertainty hanging over the unity event later in the day. Would Ms. Stevens even be there? Would there be some kind of confrontation? Or maybe another peace offering?

There were positive signs the night before. Around 6 p.m. Saturday, former Gov. James Blanchard of Michigan, a Democrat, received a message from Ms. Stevens asking him to join her at the service with Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Clyburn.

And about 10 p.m., Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, spoke with Ms. Stevens and pressed her on whether she was still behind Dr. El-Sayed.

“I just want to be very clear about that: You’re supporting the whole ticket, including Abdul?” he asked her. She said yes.

Mr. Raskin went on NBC’s “Meet the Press” Sunday morning and sought to assure viewers she was still on board.

His information was out of date by the time he said it.

On Sunday morning, Ms. Stevens woke up angry about being told not to come to church. She called Mr. Rogers and asked if they could attend church together, a gesture he immediately embraced, she later explained. She told none of her friends and allies in Democratic politics about her plans.

They were all shocked to see her walk into the church with Mr. Rogers.

The two sat together in the second pew through an hourlong church service. Ms. Stevens occasionally clapped and raised her arm in praise while Mr. Rogers smiled. During the service, she posted an online video announcing she was endorsing him. “I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” she said.

When the service was over Ms. Stevens and Mr. Rogers walked outside to greet a throng of reporters.

“I woke up this morning, and I decided to go to church,” Ms. Stevens said. “I’m here with the person who I am voting for for United States Senate and that is Mike Rogers.”

Mr. Raskin said he was “totally blindsided.”

‘None of this matters’

The blowback to Ms. Stevens was swift. Her congressional staff resigned en masse. Her onetime Democratic allies coordinated on group chats with the El-Sayed campaign about how they could be helpful and asked advice about what to post on social media. The Michigan Democratic Party chairman announced Ms. Stevens was kicked out of the party now and forever. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader, who privately backed Ms. Stevens in the primary, called it “a despicable betrayal.”

“I’m disappointed, but I understand,” said Mr. Clyburn, referring to Ms. Stevens’s decision.

Dr. El-Sayed brushed it off. “None of this matters,” he told reporters after attending the church service where he and Ms. Stevens were once scheduled to appear together.

Later in the day, a poll from The New York Times and Siena University showed Dr. El-Sayed leading Mr. Rogers by 11 percentage points.

Still, Republicans were gleeful for much of the day about the defection and the messy Democratic infighting. “Wow, this is BIG!” President Trump wrote on his social media site.

Mr. Rogers, standing with Ms. Stevens after church in Detroit, declared himself “honored” to have her support and said it came as a surprise. He cited the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and suggested he was in a better position than he would have been had she won the primary.

“I’m glad I’m not running against Haley Stevens today,” Mr. Rogers said.

Then he and Ms. Stevens got into separate cars and drove away.

SUMMARY

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has done a lot of growing up in the eight years since a stunning upset catapulted her from anonymous 20-something insurgent to establishment-busting avatar of American progressivism. “She has grown,” said Representative Nydia Velázquez of New York, an early Washington mentor with whom Ms. Ocasio-Cortez remains close. ARTICLE

Ocasio-Cortez Has Evolved. She Wants the Left to Evolve, Too.
The New York congresswoman, once a bane of establishment Democrats, has tried to nudge her movement in a bigger-tent direction as she weighs her 2028 options.
By Matt Flegenheimer
Published 2026-11-01 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/politics/ocasio-cortez-dsa.html

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has done a lot of growing up in the eight years since a stunning upset catapulted her from anonymous 20-something insurgent to establishment-busting avatar of American progressivism. She is pursuing alliances across the political spectrum rather than flaming other Democrats, betting that bridge-building is a better way to expand her movement.

She would like to see the left grow up, too.

In private discussions, she has urged fellow democratic socialists to foster a “culture of welcoming” rather than of “intimidation,” mindful that even she has sometimes failed their purity-minded litmus tests on issues like the war in Gaza.

She has called for “really big carrots” to attract new allies, talking up donations to colleagues in competitive House districts who take risky progressive stances.

And as she zigzags the country campaigning for some of the most liberal new voices in politics, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has taken pains to present herself as a kind of friendly neighborhood lefty: She will preach warmly to the unconverted, she suggests, whether they like it or not.

“I’ve had people say, ‘Well, we don’t want you at our luncheon’ or ‘We don’t want you around here,’” she told voters in Portland, Maine, while sharing a stage with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate. “And I’ll say, ‘That’s fine. I’m not going to stop trying to be your friend.’”

In public and private remarks, meetings with lawmakers and appearances with midterm candidates inside and outside the socialist ranks, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, 37, has begun sketching her preferred vision for the left’s next phase. She hopes to nudge the rambunctious coalition in a bigger-tent direction that mirrors her own path in Congress and stands to benefit both its collective agenda and her own potential ambitions.

She has repeatedly emphasized that she did not grow up in “a leftist household” (or, occasionally, a “militant leftist family”) that busied itself with high-minded political theory, positioning herself as an authentic champion of the working class who scrubbed toilets in her youth with her mother.

As she weighs runs for the presidency or the Senate in two years, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez hopes to establish herself as broadly palatable to Democrats — recently joking (but maybe also not entirely) that “Woke 1 was crazy” — without sounding too much like everyone else.

“There are more working people in this country than there are billionaires,” she told supporters of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, last month inside a high school auditorium in Detroit, where students, exuberant grandparents and a man in an “ACTIVISTS NEVER RETIRE” shirt creaked in wooden seats. “There are more single moms. There are more working dads.”

The flourish registered, almost, as the founding sensibility of a campaign in waiting, one that might evoke and expand upon the nation’s two most electric political movements of the left in this century: the people-over-profits populism of Bernie Sanders and the more-unites-than-divides-us appeals of Barack Obama.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez appears to believe that her base is ready to hear both of those messages at once.

“A.O.C.’s possibility and challenge really exemplify that of the larger socialist movement,” said Daniel Denvir, a D.S.A. member who hosts a popular podcast for Jacobin, the socialist magazine. “She both needs to fire up and consolidate her support on the socialist left while also appealing to a broader array of liberal voters. And from nearly the beginning, there were people on the left who were in a hurry to condemn her as a sellout for no real reason.”

That posture has not always endeared the left to the rest of the political world. Despite breakthroughs in places like New York City and Providence, R.I., socialism is viewed negatively by roughly half of likely American voters, according to a recent poll conducted by The New York Times and Siena University, while 31 percent view it favorably.

Ahead of Tuesday’s elections, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez seems determined to demonstrate that her reach can be wider.

She has conferred with Black civil rights leaders and “Make America Healthy Again” activists. She has boosted Democrats in red states and directed money to the political operations of non-firebrands like Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor. She has toured the Deep South and upstate New York, where she pandered without apology in a Buffalo Bills sweatshirt.

And she has campaigned especially aggressively in Michigan, where the Senate race will stand as a meaningful test of how her politics might resonate in a presidential swing state.

“She has grown,” said Representative Nydia Velázquez of New York, an early Washington mentor with whom Ms. Ocasio-Cortez remains close. “D.S.A. needs to learn something from her.”

‘I Guess I’m a Democratic Socialist’

Eight and a half years ago, the D.S.A. remained a fringe actor in Democratic politics — with some 35,000 members, less than a third of the current tally — and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez betrayed little interest in becoming its public face.

While the group endorsed her, it was seen as a junior partner in her 2018 primary success. In interviews back then, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was reluctant to box herself in. She called democratic socialism “part of what I am” but “not all of what I am,” noting (presciently) that “plenty of socialists would say I’m not a socialist.”

“I don’t read a book and then decide what I am,” she told Hot 97 that July, saying that she cared more about policies like “Medicare for all” and tuition-free college than political labels. “If that makes me a socialist, then all right, well, I guess I’m a socialist. I guess I’m a democratic socialist.”

At the same time, two powerful forces with a keen interest in her rise — conservative media outlets hoping to elevate her as a far-left boogeywoman and socialist organizers eager to claim her as their own — were repeating the affiliation often enough for it to congeal into canon: A.O.C. and D.S.A., D.S.A. and A.O.C.

“I don’t think she realized that the democratic socialist label would become such an all-encompassing label that would be so attached to her,” said Bhaskar Sunkara, the president of The Nation magazine and a longtime D.S.A. member. “All the sudden she’s being asked to defend and be connected to a platform that I’m not sure she ever fully agreed with.”

Whatever the label, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez established herself quickly as one of the most left-wing members of Congress. She pushed the “Green New Deal.” She irritated Nancy Pelosi. She endorsed Mr. Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign just after his heart attack, which for a time helped revive his bid.

That election year, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez emphasized positions she has been less inclined to highlight lately.

“Defunding police means defunding police,” she said that June, amid the wide-scale backlash to George Floyd’s killing. “It does not mean budget tricks or funny math.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has not clarified if this stance was part of the “Woke 1” craziness she cited, borrowing the phrase from a New York City councilman, Chi Ossé. When asked about the “Woke 1” comments in Nevada recently, she said she was referring not to policies but to her hope for a progressive movement “that is not rooted in judgment, castigation or being closed off.”

Supporters say she has begun modeling what a more accommodating left might look like, at no small cost to her credibility with some elements of the movement.

During Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s presidency, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez mostly determined, like Mr. Sanders, that working with the White House would be better for progressives than heckling from the sidelines.

After Mr. Biden’s disastrous 2024 debate performance, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was one of the most prominent Democrats publicly arguing that he should remain on the ticket.

Perhaps her most striking turn came after Mr. Biden ended his campaign: She earned a prime convention slot, just before Hillary Clinton, to celebrate Vice President Kamala Harris.

To many within the D.S.A., Ms. Ocasio-Cortez sounded far more like a Democrat than a socialist, giving Ms. Harris political cover on a major vulnerability, the war in Gaza, with a line that continues to echo grimly in D.S.A. circles.

“She is working tirelessly to secure a cease-fire,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said of Ms. Harris, a remark that some pro-Palestinian activists continue to find offensively misleading.

By then, the national D.S.A., which is considered less pragmatic than its New York City chapter, had already loudly unendorsed Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, accusing her of “deep betrayal” and condemning her for not universally opposing funding for Israel, including its Iron Dome antimissile system, among other concerns. She has more recently sworn off sending any military aid to Israel.

To Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s defenders, maintaining credibility across the party was a requirement for an inside-outside strategy that was producing results. The Biden White House, no lefty radical’s idea of lefty radicals, had listened to their movement on issues like climate change and health care. Left-wing candidates were claiming more offices up and down the ballot, often with her help.

“My motivation is winning,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said flatly on the left-leaning podcast “The Majority Report” recently. “One thing that I don’t like to be is alone.”

‘I’m Not Asking for Freedom From Criticism’

On a private D.S.A. video call this year — a congressional re-endorsement forum during which members of the New York City chapter loaded the screen with emojis (thumbs up, thumbs down, eyeballs, Palestinian flags) as she spoke — Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had a request.

“I want to be judged as a human being and as a comrade,” she said, alluding to the prolific left-wing vitriol she had often read about herself as a doom-scrolling millennial. “I’m not asking for freedom from criticism. But I think what I am asking for is to be treated as a trusted person and friend.”

While the chapter voted overwhelmingly to re-endorse her, some who know Ms. Ocasio-Cortez see a cruel irony in how pockets of the left perceive her. She has helped elevate a new class of leaders, including Dr. El-Sayed (who is not in the D.S.A.) and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York (who is) — and has occasionally suffered by comparison, in the eyes of some in the base.

Dr. El-Sayed, a student of the new attention economy whom Politico recently nicknamed “Hurricane Abdul,” has summoned a swaggering machismo that some supporters say is simply not an option for a woman in politics.

And Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is less instinctively tethered to the socialist project than Mr. Mamdani, who immersed himself in D.S.A. organizing well before his mayoral run. (Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, it emerged in August, had not even paid her membership dues for years. She quickly rejoined.)

While Mr. Mamdani has not universally pleased the left, it has long grated on some Ocasio-Cortez allies that the new mayor seems to be given more deference from more of the base than she was ever afforded.

Polling suggests that Mr. Mamdani is more popular.

“Imagine A.O.C. meeting with Bloomberg or some of the other corporate type guys,” Ms. Velázquez said, referring to Mr. Mamdani’s sessions with business leaders like Michael R. Bloomberg, the former New York mayor. “She would have been vilified. I think there is a different standard when it comes to her.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s own outreach has often taken different forms, hinting at her ambitions for the movement’s expansion — and at the “carrots” she can dangle. She recently poured $1 million into a political account for Dr. El-Sayed after sending $300,000 to help Democrats in New York.

She has advised activists to “grow movements instead of gate-keep them,” and cautioned supporters to consider the many areas where President Trump remains more popular than the Democratic Party and “work with that reality.”

Her wider endorsement slate has spanned from Tom Perriello, a former Virginia congressman running in a right-leaning House district, to Angie Nixon, a Florida state representative who is seeking to become the state’s first Black senator.

Ms. Nixon is among several Black leaders with whom Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has cultivated or deepened relationships ahead of the midterms — and ahead of 2028, when the Democratic presidential primary might well turn, as it often has, on which candidate performs best with Black voters.

“She’s really working to make sure the North and the South are connected,” said Justin Pearson, a state representative in Tennessee running for a House seat.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, who introduced Ms. Ocasio-Cortez in August at an anniversary rally for the March on Washington, said he had found her much more accessible than some of her ideological peers.

“She’s done something that a lot of D.S.A. people have not done,” Mr. Sharpton said, “which is reach out into communities that may not necessarily be supportive.”

For years, the left could be an almost consciously lonely place, exemplified by Mr. Sanders’s proudly iconoclastic monologues about millionaires and billionaires at the Capitol.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s appearances with Mr. Sanders last year on their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour were rich with generation-bridging symbolism. But in some ways, the final days of her midterm travel have doubled as a next step: persuading audiences that there is nothing radical or doctrinaire about these beliefs.

“Good schools is not communism,” she said on Tuesday night at a “Boricuas for Angie” event with Ms. Nixon in Kissimmee, Fla. “Funded hospitals is not communism.”

A responsive government, she concluded, was neither extreme, nor outlandish, nor “out far left.”

And with that she introduced Ms. Nixon, who recently joined the D.S.A.

Benjamin Oreskes contributed reporting from New York City.

ARTICLE

Democrats Are Leading or Tied in 7 Battleground Governor’s Races, Polls Find
Strong performances underscore how a favorable political environment may be lifting up Democrats, new New York Times/Siena polls found.
By Ruth Igielnik
Published 2026-11-02 00:53 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/politics/times-siena-poll-governor.html

The governor’s races in deep-red Kansas and Texas are effectively tied, while Democrats are ahead in Iowa, Alaska, Maine, Michigan and Ohio, according to the final New York Times/Siena polls before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Amid deep frustration over the economy and an unpopular war in Iran, the results of the governor’s races are a signal of the political mood in the country.

In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott, in his bid for a fourth term, narrowly trails his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, 47 percent to 48 percent. If elected, Ms. Hinojosa would be the first Hispanic woman to serve as governor of the state.

The Democratic candidate also has a narrow edge in Kansas, a state that Mr. Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024. Cindy Holscher, a state representative and the Democratic nominee, is effectively tied with Ty Masterson, the president of the State Senate.

And in Ohio, where the governor’s race has turned deeply negative, Amy Acton, the state’s former health director, has a six-point lead over Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee, who has spent the last few weeks of the campaign running an explosive ad featuring Ms. Acton’s estranged mother.

Taken together, the polls underscore how a favorable political environment may be lifting up Democrats deep into Trump country — the polls also show advantages for Democrats in the Senate races, where they lead in five of the seven polled states and have a narrow edge in Alaska and Iowa.

Across the seven states, six of which Mr. Trump won in 2024, the president’s approval rating stands at just 38 percent. Among his own voters, only half now say they strongly approve of his job performance.

In Texas, even as Mr. Abbott is narrowly trailing, he is doing far better than Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for the Senate. Mr. Paxton, who the poll found is viewed unfavorably by more than half of Texans, trails James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, by seven points.

Other high-quality polls in recent weeks have largely found Mr. Abbott with the edge in that state.

In Kansas, the tight race marks an improvement from last month for Ms. Holscher, when she trailed Mr. Masterson by five points in a Times/Siena poll.

Ms. Holscher is now winning 10 percent of Republicans, and is ahead by 17 points among independents, perhaps buoyed by the candidacy of Adam Hamilton, a Democrat who is leading his Senate race in the state by five points.

In Ohio, 8 percent of voters remain undecided. There is some evidence that Mr. Ramaswamy’s negative focus has turned off voters. Among those who made up their minds in late October, Ms. Acton has the edge.

In the other four races, Democrats hold wide leads just days before the election.

In Alaska, which uses ranked-choice voting, Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins, the Democratic nominee, leads Bernadette Wilson, a conservative radio host, 54 percent to 46 percent.

And in Iowa, Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor, holds a eight-point lead over Zach Lahn, a Republican businessman and farmer.

The widest leads are in Maine, where the Democrat Hannah Pingree has maintained a yawning 13-point lead over Bobby Charles, and in Michigan, where Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic secretary of state, leads John James by 13 points.

SUMMARY

Democrats are ahead of Republicans in almost all of the seven battleground states that will determine which party controls the Senate, according to the final set of polls from The New York Times and Siena University before the midterm elections. The surveys found that Democrats hold sizable leads in Texas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and Kansas, which has not elected one since 1932. But the new polls found Democratic candidates ahead in five states that now have Republican senators and effectively tied in a sixth.

ARTICLE

Democrats Show Strength in Final Days of Race for the Senate, New Polls Find
Democrats are up in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Maine and Ohio, have an edge in Alaska and are effectively tied with Republicans in Iowa, new New York Times/Siena polls found.
By Shane Goldmacher and Ruth Igielnik
Published 2026-11-02 00:53 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/politics/times-siena-poll-senate.html

Democrats are ahead of Republicans in almost all of the seven battleground states that will determine which party controls the Senate, according to the final set of polls from The New York Times and Siena University before the midterm elections.

The surveys found that Democrats hold sizable leads in Texas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and Kansas, which has not elected one since 1932.

To win a Senate majority, Democrats need to defend all the seats they currently hold and flip at least four seats that are currently held by Republicans. It has been seen as an uphill battle because many of the seats they need to win are in Republican strongholds.

But the new polls found Democratic candidates ahead in five states that now have Republican senators and effectively tied in a sixth. They hold leads in Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas and a narrow edge in Alaska. They are effectively tied in Iowa.

In Michigan, the lone top Senate battleground already held by Democrats, the poll found the Democratic candidate leading by double digits. (It was conducted before a Democratic feud erupted in Michigan this weekend.) The surveys did not include North Carolina, where polls have long found the Democrat leading and Republicans have pared back their campaign spending.

Dissatisfaction with President Trump and frustration over his management of the economy are dragging down Republicans, according to the polls. Just 38 percent of likely voters approved of the president’s job performance in the seven states in the poll, a strikingly low figure given that Mr. Trump had won five of the states by double digits just two years ago.

The newfound Democratic strength was powered by growing trust in the party to handle the economy — the key motivating issue for voters this year. Democrats hold a nine-point advantage on the cost of living across the battlegrounds, and they led on this crucial measure in every single state.

If the polls are accurate and these trends hold, Democrats would win control of the Senate.

But there were some reasons for Democratic concern: There are still some undecided voters, and voters who decided only in the last month favored Republicans by a nine-point margin.

In the Senate race in Texas, James Talarico, a Democratic state legislator, held a seven-point edge over Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general, 50 percent to 43 percent among likely voters. Mr. Paxton had the worst image of any candidate included in the survey — by far.

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, the last remaining Republican senator in New England, is trailing in her re-election campaign behind Troy Jackson, a Democratic former state senator. Mr. Jackson leads 51 percent to 45 percent among likely voters.

Polls are imperfect. Six years ago, Ms. Collins had trailed in every survey before the election — and she still won re-election comfortably.

But the new polls revealed a series of flashing warning signs for Republicans — about both their candidates and the broader political environment.

In every state but Maine, the Democratic Senate candidate was viewed more favorably than the Republican candidate.

And likely voters were unhappy with the leadership of Mr. Trump across the board, and said that they believed Democrats would do a better job handling the cost of living and foreign wars and doing what is best for ordinary people.

Mr. Trump has been barnstorming Republican states in a bid to re-energize his base in the final weeks before Election Day, but the polls suggest that enthusiasm for the president is slipping even within his party. In Ohio, where 82 percent of Republicans approve of the president, the share who approve “strongly” has fallen to 51 percent, down from 63 percent in June.

And in a Times/Siena poll last week, the Senate race was tied in heavily Republican South Carolina.

One key advantage for Democratic candidates is that they are leading with independent voters in every state surveyed. That includes Iowa, where Josh Turek, a Democratic state legislator, was effectively tied with Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee.

The polls found that the Democratic resurgence was powered by a renewed strength among younger voters and Latinos, as well as the relative weakness Republicans have among the party’s base of white, working-class voters.

Mr. Trump had made gains among Latino and younger voters in 2024. But this year, his party’s Senate candidates were winning only about one-quarter of younger voters and Latino voters.

Crumbling trust in Republicans on the economy — and in Mr. Trump in particular — helps to explain how Democrats are competitive in a state like Kansas. Mr. Trump won Kansas by the widest margin of any of the seven states polled, and the state has not elected a Democratic senator for nearly a century. But diesel prices that rose after the Iran war, and the administration’s decision to drop import tariffs on foreign beef, have dismayed farmers.

Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee and the pastor of the largest church in the state, leads Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, 49 percent to 44 percent.

Mr. Hamilton also has the support of 13 percent of Republicans, including James Gerety, 52, a retired National Guardsman living in Meriden, Kan., who said that he saw Mr. Hamilton as “a lot more genuine” than Mr. Marshall.

“I had reservations at first, with him being a pastor,” said Mr. Gerety, a registered Republican who considers himself more of an independent. “I get squirrelly with religion being brought into politics. But Hamilton is trying to lower prices, to get us out of this war with Iran. He’s trying to bring inflation down.”

Mr. Marshall has also faced criticism after The New York Times reported that he sued patients for unpaid medical debt, leading to arrests in some cases.

The Times previously polled all seven states in September. The Democrats improved in six of the states in the final poll (Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas) and lost ground in only one (Alaska).

White working-class voters have been the backbone of Mr. Trump’s coalition. In 2024, he won an estimated 66 percent of white voters without college degrees, according to exit polls and Times Voter Trends. Now, in these seven states, Republicans were winning just 56 percent of these voters.

Blue-collar white voters have proved particularly hard to reach in polls, and polling error has previously been among the highest in that demographic, a large group in all seven states.

In Michigan, the lone Senate seat in the survey currently held by a Democrat, the poll showed Dr. Abdul El-Sayed ahead by a wide 11 percentage points over Mike Rogers, a Republican former congressman, who narrowly lost a Senate run in 2024.

Dr. El-Sayed, who has relished political combat in a way few other Democrats do, has performed especially well with men, a group that historically tilts Republican. He is running roughly even with the group, an improvement from September.

But in the Democratic primary, polls overestimated Dr. El-Sayed’s strength. And he has been embroiled in a bitter public feud with his primary rival, Representative Haley Stevens, who endorsed Mr. Rogers on Sunday in a rare cross-partisan embrace that has given Republicans hope. Still, Dr. El-Sayed is ahead by a wide margin on every issue in the poll, including immigration, a traditional Republican strength.

In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, leads Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, 49 percent to 44 percent in a race that has drawn half a billion dollars in spending, with Republicans spending $80 million more on ads, according to AdImpact, the ad-tracking service.

In Maine, Mr. Jackson, the Democratic challenger, has improved his image since September, though he is still seen unfavorably overall. Critically, he is running in the most Democratic state on the battleground map, and he remains much more popular than Mr. Trump.

In Texas, 49 percent of likely voters view Mr. Talarico favorably, while 39 percent view him unfavorably, giving him a 10-point-edge on favorability despite an enormous, very negative ad campaign against him funded chiefly by Elon Musk, the world’s richest person.

Mr. Paxton, Mr. Talarico’s G.O.P. opponent, has seen his image decline in recent months. Fifty-four percent of likely voters there now view him unfavorably, while only 33 percent view him favorably.

Rey Gonzales, a 62-year-old Republican living in Houston, said that he had been troubled by the allegations that led to Mr. Paxton’s impeachment and by reports that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. Mr. Gonzales, who says he voted for Mr. Trump in 2016 and 2020 but did not vote in 2024, says he plans to support Mr. Talarico purely out of dislike for Mr. Paxton.

When asked what he liked about Mr. Talarico, his answer was succinct: “Nothing.”

In Alaska, Mary Peltola, the former Democratic congresswoman challenging Senator Dan Sullivan, has faced criticism after a New York Times investigation found political operatives aligned with her recruited another candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, to run as a Republican in the race to try to pull votes away from the Republican incumbent.

The poll was mostly completed before the release of the story. Even so, Ms. Peltola was the only Democrat in this set of polls to lose ground since an earlier Times/Siena poll. The poll found her with a narrow edge over Mr. Sullivan, 48 percent to 46 percent.

Sophia June contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

As he opened his speech at a recent campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., President Trump told the story of the Willie Horton crime case that helped sink the presidential campaign of the Democrat Michael S. Dukakis in 1988. ARTICLE

Threats, Gaffes and Men’s Posteriors: Trump’s Talk Gets Wilder
A Times review of the president’s public speeches finds that he is more profane, more absolutist, longer-winded and less coherent than he was in 2016.
By Peter Baker and Dylan Freedman
Published 2026-11-01 10:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/us/politics/trump-speeches-rallies-age.html

As he opened his speech at a recent campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., President Trump told the story of the Willie Horton crime case that helped sink the presidential campaign of the Democrat Michael S. Dukakis in 1988.

And then, 30 minutes later, still speaking at the same rally to the same audience from the same lectern, Mr. Trump told the same Willie Horton story all over again, using some of the same language (and getting the facts wrong both times).

Mr. Trump, who last year became the oldest person ever inaugurated as president and turned 80 in June, has demonstrated physical stamina as he barnstorms the country in advance of midterm elections. But his performances on the road and at the White House this fall have produced many head-scratching moments that have revived questions about his age and stability.

He can be forgetful and repetitive. He is more long-winded, more profane and more absolutist than when he ran for president a decade ago. His rambling speeches seem even more garbled at times. He makes comments that leave people wondering what he is talking about or that sound like he is saying something he is not. And even for a president who has never fully observed the norms of the office, he seems more willing to say things no other president would say.

He declared that at an unfenced construction site “only a Hispanic could survive that fall.” He wants to ban immigrants from Norway “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize.” He says “I don’t give a damn” if he is seen as caring more about oil company profits than struggling workers. He mispronounces the Strait of Hormuz as the “Hormone Strait.” He has told supporters to “cheat like hell” in the Nov. 3 elections. He says military leakers “should be shot.” And then there is his baffling fixation with admiring men’s posteriors.

Even Mr. Trump seems astonished at times by what comes out of his mouth — and by how much his supporters embrace him nonetheless. “I could say the stupidest things and you’d clap. ‘Oh, I love you so,’” he marveled at a recent rally in Clarksville, Tenn. “But we don’t say the stupidest things,” he quickly added. “We say things of common sense. We say things that make sense.”

For Mr. Trump, making sense often places second to having fun at rallies, and some outrageous remarks appear aimed at generating a laugh. His allies say too much is made of comments that are really just jokes. He has always been a provocative speaker, willing to outrage for the sake of outrage. Mr. Trump defends his stream-of-consciousness rambling as a “brilliant” speaking style that he calls “the weave.”

But the weave seems to be getting weavier. An A.I.-assisted New York Times review of Mr. Trump’s comments from speeches, rallies, social media, interviews and public meetings found significant changes since he began a run for president at age 69 in 2015, although not as much of a notable shift since 2024 when a similar review was conducted. Broadly speaking, the review concluded, Mr. Trump’s public communication is more vulgar, more uninhibited and less coherent than it was a decade ago.

“He’s saying so many stupid things, even for him, so many outrageous and aggressive things,” said former Representative Francis Rooney, a Republican from Florida. “This aggressive kind of attack language, that’s something I’ve never heard from a president.”

The White House denied that Mr. Trump has lost a step. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, hailed his “sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic and historic accessibility” and dismissed concerns about his provocative comments.

“The president doesn’t care about being politically correct, he cares about making America great again,” Mr. Ingle said. “The American people love how authentic, transparent and effective the president is.”

The ‘Freaking Genius’

Measuring the effects of age can be difficult without a medical exam, although that has not stopped many physicians, political commentators and everyday Americans from drawing conclusions about Mr. Trump based on what they see on television.

The Times review from 2015 through Thursday found that the president in his second term has used 19 percent more all-or-nothing words like “always,” “never,” “everything” and “totally” at rallies than he did a decade ago and 5 percent more than in 2024, a sign of black-and-white thinking that experts say often accompanies advancing age or cognitive decline. He is cruder than he used to be, using nearly 15 swear words per 10,000 words compared with 14 two years ago and six a decade ago, a change consistent with age-related disinhibition.

The review, relying on an A.I.-assisted metric, found that he makes rambling or confusing digressions in his rallies and speeches two and a half times as often in his second term as in the 2016 campaign, although roughly the same as in 2024. His vocabulary remains about the same, as does the reading level of his speaking, which hovers between fourth and fifth grade. (The average modern president speaks at an eighth-grade level.)

Mr. Trump’s public schedule is thinner, down to 1.3 events per weekday versus 2.1 in the first term. But he is posting online an average of 21 times a day, up from 13 a day in 2016 although down from 34 a day two years ago. The night owl president has posted messages between midnight and 5 a.m. on 30 percent of his nights in his second term and has had 240 bursts of 10 or more posts an hour.

The president’s doctor has said that Mr. Trump is mentally sharp. In a three-page summary released in May, Dr. Sean P. Barbabella, the White House physician, noted that Mr. Trump had scored 30 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. “Cognitive and physical performance are excellent,” he wrote.

The Montreal assessment is a quick test to screen for Alzheimer’s disease or other cognitive impairment and includes basic questions like identifying a lion, camel and rhinoceros; drawing a clock; repeating words or numbers in order; and naming as many words as possible in one minute that start with the letter F. “Nobody can do this,” Mr. Trump insisted a couple weeks ago, adding: “But I can. You know why? Because I’m a freaking genius!”

Mr. Trump appears sensitive to the perception that he is slipping, bringing up his cognitive tests without being asked at a half-dozen recent rallies. In Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday night, he called himself “a very high-IQ person,” offered an extended description of the tests and compared his brainpower to that of former Presidents Barack Obama and Joseph R. Biden Jr.

“Don’t forget I’m the only president to pass without exception — I passed three cognitive tests,” he said. “I’m the only president that agreed to take them. And they’re hard, you know? Obama couldn’t have passed it. Biden we don’t even talk about.”

‘I Don’t Give a Damn’

While Mr. Trump has been known to nod off during White House meetings, he draws energy from crowds when he is on the road. He speaks and speaks and speaks — twice as long as in 2016, according to the Times review, for an average of 85 minutes per rally compared with 42 minutes a decade ago.

He is profoundly and proudly undisciplined. He says things that are manifestly unhelpful to him. Even as many Americans are upset about the cost of filling their gas tank, he said in Perry, Ga., the other day that high oil prices were good because the fossil fuel industry was making hundreds of billions of dollars. Even as he said it, he acknowledged it would produce bad headlines. “I don’t give a damn,” he said. “I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.”

He wanders from thought to thought, often without finishing a sentence, embedding one off-the-cuff story within another. In Pendleton, S.C., he started talking about transgender athletes, interrupted to tell a story about someone he met in Israel, referred to a poll without explaining its results and then riffed on climate change:

“You have a lot of records that are not exactly going to be shattered by women. They’re going to say, ‘Who the hell broke it?’ Or the swimmer who was a great swimmer, and then she looked to her left, she looked to her right, and she saw this massive human being next to her. You’ve seen him — her on television. And she had to compete. And my wife said, ‘Please don’t tell those stories. They’re terrible stories to tell as president. Can you imagine George Washington telling these stories?’ No, because George Washington lived in sanity. He didn’t have men playing in women’s sports. I promise you this. I didn’t know George Washington personally, but they did not have the mutilization of your children for transgender purposes. Do you think George ever had any of the things that we have to go through, Tim? I don’t think so. Abraham Lincoln — I met a young man from Israel. I said, ‘Who’s your favorite president?’ He said, ‘Abraham Lincoln.’ I said, ‘Oh.’ I said, ‘That’s nice.’ We love Abraham Lincoln. But you’re going to see something later, because they have a poll — they took a poll recently. You’re going to see it. But I also declared a national emergency on energy and terminated the Green New Scam, one of the greatest hoaxes in the history of our country.”

‘He’s All Man’

Like many people in their ninth decade, he is prone to say things that seem inappropriate. His focus on the male anatomy, for instance, has become remarkably pronounced lately.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said at a rally with Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, on Oct. 12. “I started examining his body because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass.”

Five days later, he repeated his appreciation of Mr. Husted’s backside. “I examined his ass,” Mr. Trump said at a rally in Kentucky. “I never did that with, no, I never did that with a man before.” Three days later in North Carolina, he praised Mr. Husted’s derrière again. “His ass is, it’s like a pile of muscle,” he said. In Chillicothe, he did it again: “I started by looking at his ass, and it was strong as hell.”

Mr. Husted is not the only object of Mr. Trump’s manly approval. Among the others:

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina: “As much as I can fall in love with a man, which isn’t that much, I fall in love with him, and his name happens to be Tim Scott.”

The spouse of Senator Darline Graham, the other South Carolina Republican: “He’s a good-looking husband.”

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary: “He’s got the body of a 30-year-old.”

Representative Mike Collins, Republican of Georgia: “Mike Collins is a good-looking man. And he’s all man.”

In Michigan on Sunday, Mr. Trump made a point of praising a woman’s backside for a change. “I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before — Nicki Minaj,” he told the crowd. “That’s hard to miss.”

A Quick Temper

Mr. Trump has always displayed fits of public anger in ways that other presidents have not. But he seems even more prone to pounce these days.

He snaps at reporters so often now that he barely waits for their questions before calling them “sick” and ordering, “Quiet!” When a reporter asked on Thursday if he was canceling a trip to Kansas because he was tired of traveling, Mr. Trump accosted his physical appearance. “You are disgusting! Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”

His exhortations to supporters to vote have grown more vulgar and violent as well. “If you do that,” he said in Vandalia, Ohio, “we’re going to win and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass, OK?”

He depicts himself as all-powerful. “I can do whatever I want,” he told reporters in the Oval Office recently. As if to prove it, he regularly tries to rename bodies of water after America or himself. He demanded that tech companies stop using the term artificial intelligence, preferring instead “super intelligence”; those that disobey, he wrote online, are “THE ENEMY!”

He has never been burdened with excessive self-awareness, but even so, some of his recent comments have been jarring. The man who dispenses disparaging nicknames like “Talafreako” for James Talarico and “Annie Trannie” for Dr. Annie Andrews insisted with a straight face the other day that “I don’t go around mocking people.”

Likewise, the commander in chief who recently threatened to “annihilate” Iran complained bitterly that he did not win the Nobel Peace Prize. Even so, one night last month he could not remember the name of the prize he covets. “Does anybody know the name of that peace prize?” he asked in Pendleton, then came up with another: “the Pulitzer Prize.”

When he summoned the name of the Nobel Prize last week in Port Huron, Mich., he declared that he would like to ban all immigrants from Norway, where the award committee is based, because he did not win. “I don’t want anybody from Norway,” he said. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually.”

These days, even Mr. Trump seems aware that eyes are on him, watching and waiting. “I love the weave,” he told the midterm Republican convention in Dallas in September. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom or you bring in an airplane or you bring in Air Force One. But you notice I always get right back to the same topic.”

And yet, he went on, “when someday, there’ll be a time when I do the weave is weave, weave. Someday, there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject, and then you can say he’s had it. OK? You can say then he’s had it.”

Methodology

The Times collected thousands of Mr. Trump’s speeches, interviews, social media posts and schedules using data from Roll Call’s Factba.se from 2015 through late October this year. To quantify Mr. Trump’s use of all-or-nothing language and swearwords, we measured basic word frequency statistics across Mr. Trump’s presidential terms and campaign periods. To identify confusing and rambling passages of text, we used the A.I. model Claude Opus 5.5 to score more than 6,500 passages of Mr. Trump’s speeches with detailed instructions based on our previous reporting analyzing Mr. Trump’s use of rambling and profane language. We counted a speech passage as incoherent if it scored at least a seven out of 10 with this rubric, which was informed by manual review of hundreds of passages and an evaluation to ensure a high bar of accuracy.
