SUMMARY

Once you see a snake in Bangkok, the snakiest capital in the world, you see snakes everywhere. There are also, as Pinyo Pukpinyo knows, a lot of actual snakes. Mr. Pinyo has way too many snakes.

ARTICLE

He’s the Top Snake Catcher, and Business Is Booming. There’s Just One Problem.
Bangkok’s firefighters do more snake catching than firefighting, and Pinyo Pukpinyo trains them. But he refuses to kill the snakes, and he’s running out of containers.
By Hannah Beech and Lauren DeCicca
Published 2026-11-01 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/world/asia/snake-catcher-bangkok-thailand.html

Once you see a snake in Bangkok, the snakiest capital in the world, you see snakes everywhere. Loops of electrical wire look like snakes. Gas pump hoses look like snakes. Vines, green and vibrant, look like snakes.

There are also, as Pinyo Pukpinyo knows, a lot of actual snakes. In Bangkok each year, about 30,000 snakes are caught by fire and rescue personnel. On an average half-day shift, Mr. Pinyo, the top snake catcher in Thailand’s capital, wrangles more than 20 snakes, the reptiles secreted in sewers, curled in flowerpots and toilets, enmeshed in recycling, and pressed against branches ready to snack on geckoes and tree shrews.

He catches cobras, pythons, kraits and pit vipers. Those are the scary snakes. Harmless species, at least to humans, include tree snakes, rat snakes, kukris and sunbeams.

Mr. Pinyo, 56, who joined Bangkok’s fire department at 18 only to discover that firefighters here do a lot more snake catching than firefighting, wants one thing known above all else: He does not kill the snakes he catches.

Part of it is his Buddhist faith. But mostly it’s that it’s not the snakes’ fault that we humans have spread our urban jungle into actual jungle. It’s not the snakes’ fault that Bangkok floods during the monsoons, drowning their cozy habitats and forcing them to swim past malls and condominiums.

“They deserve to return to nature,” Mr. Pinyo said. “They only bite when they’re forced to defend themselves.”

This principled ban on snake extermination has left Mr. Pinyo with a problem, one that has multiplied in the months since his Bang Khen fire station in northeastern Bangkok, now under renovation, moved to a few prefab structures squeezed under an elevated monorail.

Mr. Pinyo has way too many snakes.

He is not sure how many, but it’s more than 200. Or it could be 300. It’s definitely 70 cobras. At least. In his concrete cavern of a fire station, the sun blocked by the Skytrain’s tracks, nearly every tub, every water bottle, every sack, every plastic container that might otherwise hold shoes or bedsheets, is home to a snake, sometimes multiple snakes. Some of the pythons measure 15 feet long.

Every few months, Mr. Pinyo drives out of Bangkok and unloads a horror movie tangle of snakes in a national park or forest. Then he starts again, catching and collecting snakes until it’s time for another rural pilgrimage.

Feeding all of these snakes costs about $300 a month, money that comes out of Mr. Pinyo’s pocket. His wife and daughter do not like snakes. His father, who died this year, was so upset by all of the venomous snakes that he refused to visit Mr. Pinyo when he was hospitalized with the inevitable snakebite. But snakes, Mr. Pinyo says, chose him. It is his karma.

“My father used to say that I’m stubborn, like a cobra,” Mr. Pinyo said. “Maybe it’s true. I had to learn everything myself and stick to it because no one taught me how to catch snakes.”

Mr. Pinyo’s father, a hotel limousine driver, wanted his son to land a stable government job, and Mr. Pinyo passed the police examination. But a chronic shortage of firefighters meant he was assigned to that career instead. His starting base salary was less than $100 a month. (He now makes about $1,500.) He admits he was terrified when dispatched, without any training, to catch his first python, armed only with a stick with a hook at the end.

“I wanted to catch bad guys like in the movies, not catch snakes,” he told me.

He learned fast on the job. He studied books like “The Manual of Practical Management of Snake Bites and Animal Toxin Injury.” Along the way, he discovered that as much as he liked divining the personalities of snakes — the way a cobra mimics a human’s movement or the way a baby python practices its bite — what he really enjoyed was the reaction of humans newly relieved of snakes in their homes or offices.

“They offer me many prayers and good wishes,” Mr. Pinyo said. “It’s better than what money can buy.”

Like a doctor at a dinner party burdened with the ailments of fellow guests, Mr. Pinyo is constantly called upon for his expertise. Luckily, he is generous. I shared my snake stories. In 2019, I had put a Post-it note on the door of my home office in Bangkok, warning the boys not to bother me because I was on a call. My husband had done the same. Our younger son, then 9, rapped anyway.

“Mama,” he said, “I’m sorry, but there’s a pit viper in the dining room.”

Our son was right: There was a snake in our living room, a flash of fluorescent green. I disregarded my husband’s Post-it note, and he grabbed a bucket and pasta tongs. The snake, though, exited onto the balcony on its own.

I showed Mr. Pinyo a photograph of my husband, armed with the tongs, ready to tackle the snake. He praised my husband’s choice of tool, but said our son had been wrong. It was not a pit viper. There was no streak of red near the tail.

“Only a tree snake,” he said. “No danger.”

Last month, Mr. Pinyo and his deputy snake catchers conducted a training at a Mövenpick hotel in Bangkok, the lobby carpet plush and the garden lush. Like anywhere in Bangkok, there were snakes, and everyone, from the concierge and duty manager to spa therapist and room cleaner, needed to be prepared.

The firefighters had brought 50 live snakes with them, and believable scenarios unfolded in the underground garage. Let’s say there’s a small cobra and all you have is a small water bottle.

With differing levels of terror, the hotel workers caught small cobras in small water bottles. They caught medium-size cobras in medium-size water bottles. They simulated a situation in which a snake lurks in the shower and all there is to work with is a towel. (“Please don’t open your towel and scare the snake,” Mr. Pinyo joked.) The workers took turns as impromptu matadors, gently laying the towels on cobras with their hoods raised, ready to strike.

By the end, it felt perfectly natural to think that we could all be snake catchers. My colleague Muktita Suhartono had refused to touch a snake, but under Mr. Pinyo’s supervision, she coolly decanted a golden cobra into a plastic bottle, screwing on the lid after checking that the animal’s head was nowhere near the spout.

Still, there’s a reason there are snake professionals. Mr. Pinyo has been hospitalized four times for near deadly snakebites, the last time for two months. He insists he can’t even remember how many times he’s been bitten in total.

I mentioned that my husband was bitten by a pit viper last year. After an emergency room stay, he was on crutches for weeks. Mr. Pinyo made a sympathetic noise, but then said he never seeks medical care for something as trifling as a pit viper bite. Yet a younger colleague of his became functionally paralyzed after a cobra bite during a training not so different from the one we attended.

One day in October, Mr. Pinyo sat on a plastic stool underneath the train tracks at the makeshift fire station. Occasionally, a sack shifted ominously. A hiss or rattle emanated from a box. Then the calls came: a snake in a pile of recycling, a snake in a hollow bathroom door, a snake at a medical clinic. We pulled up to the clinic, where young people were standing on a ramp at the entrance. They scattered when Mr. Pinyo asked if this was the place with the snake under the ramp.

He pulled up the ramp to find a reticulated python twisted into a misshapen pretzel. The python went into a sack, and we drove back to the fire station, with one more snake to feed and release into the wild.

“Circle of life,” Mr. Pinyo said, his fingers forming a loose loop like a python at rest.

Muktita Suhartono contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

A little over a month ago, “American Hostage” premiered. It’s a streaming service, descended from the premium channel Epix. As a critic, I know what is worthwhile, and the streaming era has created more spaces for the worthwhile to flourish.

ARTICLE

Can You Afford to Watch TV?
The streaming era has provided viewers a lot of great things to watch. But it comes at a price.
By James Poniewozik
Published 2026-11-02 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/arts/television/streaming-tv-era-cost.html

A little over a month ago, “American Hostage” premiered. The series, about a real-life armed standoff at an Indiana mortgage office in 1977, is one of those out-of-nowhere surprises I love to discover as a TV critic. It has committed performances from Jon Hamm and Giovanni Ribisi and eerily timely things to say about the frustrations of the powerless with the powerful.

You should watch it if you can. Which you probably can’t, unless you reach into your wallet, one more time.

See, “American Hostage” is on MGM+. What is MGM+? Good question! It’s a streaming service, descended from the premium channel Epix. (What is Epix? No time for that!) More saliently, it is $7.99 a month. That is, it’s $7.99 on top of the endlessly scrolling list of subscriptions you probably already have.

(Note: With many of the plans I discuss here, there are multiple pricing options — monthly or annual, with or without ads, bundled this way and that way. You may want a calculator.)

TV critics are not traditionally in the habit of considering price when they decide what to cover. This isn’t restaurant criticism. But lately TV consumption has begun to feel like high-end dining, with no limit of upcharges and price hikes and caviar supplements sending the tab to the heavens.

This is frustrating for consumers in inflationary times. But it’s also not great for the art, or at least for the experience and conversation around it. It creates yet another division of haves, choosing from a vast menu in media’s first class, and have-nots, missing out in steerage. It turns a medium that was once universal, if frustrating, into one that is increasingly inaccessible, if often excellent. “American Hostage” is good. But is it $7.99-a-month good? Is any show?

Once, TV was free — well, save for the investment in a set and an antenna and your precious time watching ads. Everyone had access to the same air and the same shows. I was born in the rabbit-ears era of TV, and I will not romanticize it as having been better. But like so many aspects of life “improved” by technology, it was less complicated.

This changed with the popularization of cable. “The Sopranos” helped turn HBO from an occasional domestic luxury (or motel-room amenity) into a cultural must-have. Increasingly, the TV worth watching and talking about was something you had to pay for. And then pay a little more. Cable channels proliferated, and the cable bundle — smushing together the channels you watched with the many you didn’t — got fatter and fatter.

Oversqueezed media consumers wished it could be different. If only you could pick and choose which platforms you subscribed to! Somewhere on Wall Street, a finger curled on a monkey’s paw, and the streaming business was born.

Now, if you had an internet connection (another fee, unless your neighbor’s Wi-Fi password hygiene was lax), you could choose your services à la carte: Netflix, Hulu, Amazon, Peacock. Disney+, Paramount+, AMC+. YouTube TV and YouTube Premium. Dropout, for comedy. Shudder, for horror. Crunchyroll, for anime. Want to follow pro sports? You may want a second job.

I am familiar with all of these because my work requires that I be able to watch anything that runs anywhere. Someday when I retire, dismantling my monthly media commitments will resemble unwinding the assets of a bankrupt Fortune 500 corporation.

At the same time, I am writing for people who are weighing another subscription against gas and groceries. And we all exist in an economy that is increasingly built around subscriptions for damn near everything, as discussed in a recent episode of “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver.” (HBO Max, starting at $10.99/month with ads.)

Sure, $7.99 is cheaper than a matinee movie ticket where I live, let alone a Broadway show or concert. But is it worth it for you? How would I know? As a critic, I know what is worthwhile, and the streaming era has created more spaces for the worthwhile to flourish.

The best of the art form is now scattered across a lot of walled gardens whose walls get a little higher every year. At this point, the rate of announcements you receive for streaming price increases — which are outstripping inflation — rivals the texts from candidates asking for donations. (PBS, despite its funding challenges, looks like a better deal every day.)

So the medium that used to be a pop-culture lingua franca becomes a Tower of Babel. The stories you experience and the references you get are determined by the purchase decisions you’ve made. A terrific show — say, last year’s “Hal & Harper” on Mubi — can languish on an obscure service, its audience curtailed before it even premieres.

And a population already fragmented by tastes, demographics and subcultures becomes further subdivided by economics. You can go rogue and share streaming passwords. You can create a system of reminders to drop various platforms. Or you can just give up, pick a service or two, and pray the algorithm gives you something good.

What’s good this year? There’s the new “East of Eden” on Netflix ($8.99 a month with ads, $19.99 without, $26.99 in 4K). There’s my favorite new series of the year, “Widow’s Bay” on Apple TV ($14.99 a month ad-free — or “free,” I guess, if you buy qualifying Apple products every three months for eternity). There’s a great new installment of FX’s “The Lowdown,” which streams on Hulu ($12.49 with ads, or part of an array of bundles as lengthy as the instructions for a tax return).

There’s also “Cupertino,” a new legal drama about the tech industry that I enjoyed more the longer it went on — and which blessedly airs on CBS, one of those old broadcast networks whose signal still flies magically through the air and can be gathered by an antenna.

Don’t have an antenna? There are plenty of streaming services with a “live TV” feature. It’ll cost you.

How much do you pay for TV streaming services? We want to know.

We will not publish or share your contact information outside the Times newsroom, and we will not publish any part of your submission without contacting you first.

ARTICLE

Gulf Economies, Torn by War in Iran, Desperately Need a Return to Normal
States like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates that have worked to rebalance from a dependence on energy have seen growth plunge in a year of strife.
By Humza Jilani
Published 2026-11-02 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/business/iran-war-gulf-economies.html

Riyadh Air, Saudi Arabia’s aspiring luxury carrier, is busing international passengers to and from an alternate airport four and a half hours from its hub, which was damaged in strikes.

The marquee Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year.

The headquarters of the state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco was struck, as was a critical pipeline. Ships running the gantlet in the vital Strait of Hormuz are still in Iran’s cross-hairs and catching fire from missile and drone attacks. It is a particularly tense time right now, with a heightened risk of escalation of the war.

Throughout the Gulf, the war in Iran, now at the start of its ninth month, and the conflict that has erupted in Yemen are taxing the region’s ability to conduct business as normal.

This week could bring a fresh test. The energy conference ADIPEC, featuring executives and government ministers from around the world, began in Abu Dhabi on Monday. At least one prominent industry leader, Darren Woods, the chief executive of Exxon Mobil, decided not to attend because of security concerns in the region, according to a person familiar with his thinking who was not authorized to speak to the media.

The event’s organizers said in a statement that “high-level participation is very strong” but did not comment on the reasons for Mr. Woods’s withdrawal.

Economic growth across the Gulf Cooperation Council, a regional bloc of Arab states, will tumble by 5 percent this year, according to the International Monetary Fund. Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar are expected to suffer double-digit contractions, linked to their near-total dependence on the besieged Strait of Hormuz to sell their energy products to the world.

On Sunday, the Saudi government said the kingdom’s economy shrank 3.8 percent from a year earlier in the three months that ended in September. The strongest force behind the decline by far was a 20.4 percent plunge in oil activity.

It could be worse. Pipelines that allow Saudi Arabia, as well as the United Arab Emirates, to bypass the Strait of Hormuz have helped keep oil flowing, as has an extensive operation run by the U.S. military to shield vessels in the strait.

But the fighting, the longer it goes on, is imperiling the two states’ ability to recast themselves as oases of stability in a volatile region and build up economic sectors like tourism and technology.

Government budgets going forward are expected to put higher priorities on resilience projects. That means spending more money on rerouting pipelines or boosting military spending.

Traffic at Dubai International Airport, the world’s busiest hub, remains below last year’s levels, as some international carriers continue to suspend operations to the region.

“Beyond hydrocarbons, tourism, including aviation and hospitality, and real estate have been hit by the confidence shock and remain exposed to prolonged uncertainty about the possibility of re-escalation,” Aurelian Mali, vice president for Moody’s Ratings in Dubai, said in an email.

“Protracted uncertainty and permanently elevated risk perceptions could damage some countries’ non-oil economic models, built on security, safety and macroeconomic stability,” he said.

The one economy expected to expand this year is Oman, the Gulf monarchy with the longest Arabian Sea coastline and thus less dependent on the Strait of Hormuz. Growth is forecast to jump to over 4 percent this year, compared with 2.4 percent in 2025, according to the I.M.F., with Oman benefiting from higher oil prices and its ability to ship products without major disruptions.

But officials elsewhere are racing to build up their buffers to prepare for new rounds of conflict — and keep exports and investments flowing.

In the Emirates, the government, which has almost $3 trillion in sovereign assets, has vowed to bring the country’s dependence on the Strait of Hormuz to “zero,” scaling up investments in alternative ports and pipelines.

The war has even imperiled some of the region’s huge artificial intelligence ambitions, a key plank of the Gulf states’ plans to diversify away from oil. Last year, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the Emirates announced A.I.-related investment plans of $120 billion. The states have courted some of Silicon Valley’s biggest tech companies to set up data centers in their deserts.

The Emirates used the energy conference on Monday to showcase its A.I. ambitions. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, signed four agreements with Abu Dhabi-based companies, including one to deploy the company’s latest business-focused A.I. system at the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company.

But now there are also discussions to spread out the locations of planned data centers and even to build some facilities underground, safe from missiles and drones. Data centers in the Emirates and Bahrain were struck by Iranian drone swarms early in the war.

So far, major investors are still placing bets on the region’s long-term potential.

Last week, Apollo Global Management announced that it was taking a 10 percent stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset management arm of a $385 billion sovereign fund in Abu Dhabi. And Investcorp, a Bahrain-based asset manager, joined a consortium of Saudi investors to buy a local fire safety and equipment company.

The Boston-based private equity company Advent last month joined other financial entities to set up shop in Abu Dhabi.

Many analysts expect the region’s economy to snap back next year. The I.M.F.’s latest forecasts, issued last month, call for almost across-the-board growth in 2027, including 7.9 percent in Saudi Arabia and 18.8 percent in Qatar. Those predictions assume that hostilities will taper off enough to allow a return to prewar conditions in the energy sector next year. Still, the fund said the economic fallout was “highly uncertain” because of the myriad ways the war has eroded trust in the region and caused political balances to shift.

“I think the short- versus long-term question is the crux of the issue,” said Tim Callen, a former International Monetary Fund official in Saudi Arabia who is now a visiting fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington.

Rebecca F. Elliott contributed reporting from New York.

SUMMARY

So now, after 71 years, Autopia is going electric. At Disney World in Orlando, Fla., an Autopia facsimile is called Tomorrowland Speedway, and still features gas-powered engines, with no known plans to go electric. As for what’s next in Tomorrowland, Mr. Menotti said he would still be a fan, even if Autopia is all electric.

ARTICLE

After 71 Years and a Lot of Exhaust, Disneyland’s Autopia Goes Electric
The gas-powered engines in Disneyland’s Autopia ride weren’t properly certified. The little cars will be replaced by E.V.s.
By David Gelles
Published 2026-11-02 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/climate/after-71-years-and-a-lot-of-exhaust-disneylands-autopia-goes-electric.html

In 1955, Walt Disney’s vision of the cutting edge came in the form of 40 candy-colored miniature cars that allowed pint-size drivers to push a real gas pedal and steer around a track at the Anaheim theme park.

Autopia, a focal point of the Tomorrowland section of Disneyland, mirrored the real-life love affair that Americans were having with the automobile. Work would soon begin on the interstate highway system, suburbs were expanding, car sales were skyrocketing and the future felt like a shiny coupe, windows down, speeding along an open road.

But Mr. Disney’s midcentury vision of the future has run up against today’s environmental reality. Autopia, the only surviving original attraction at Tomorrowland, is in violation of California’s stringent emissions regulations.

So now, after 71 years, Autopia is going electric.

The cars currently run on 8.5 horsepower Honda four-stroke engines like those typically used to run generators or industrial pressure washers. They are loud and belch exhaust for up to 16 hours a day. The result is a microclimate of smog hovering over Tomorrowland, a section of the park that includes rides like Space Mountain and Buzz Lightyear Astro Blasters.

Sometime next year, the gasoline powered engines will be phased out and Autopia will join the age of E.V.s.

Disney arrived at this decision after the powerful California Air Resources Board issued a notice of violation against the company in 2024, stating that it had not obtained the proper emissions certification for the Autopia cars.

In a settlement between Disney and the state, the company paid $56,250 and agreed “to retire the gas-engine powered Autopia fleet” by early 2027. Disney declined multiple requests for comment, and declined to permit The Times to take photos or videos inside Disneyland for this article.

Bob Gurr, who designed the attraction for Walt Disney, said the move was overdue.

“For 26 years, I’ve been arguing, ‘When are you going to do anything to get rid of that gasoline?’” said Mr. Gurr, 94, in a phone call from his home in Los Angeles. “The dirtiest place on Earth is the Autopia attraction at Disneyland in the city of Anaheim.”

After the interview, Mr. Gurr’s representative asked to retract it, saying Disney had requested Mr. Gurr stop doing interviews about the ride he designed. Mr. Gurr did not ask for the interview to be off the record, or not to be published.

Autopia has been running more or less interrupted since Walt Disney christened the park in 1955. Different designs and sponsors, including Honda, Chevron and Richfield Oil, have come and gone. By 1971, the company said some 47,756,550 people had taken a spin on the track. At that pace, total ridership today may have now eclipsed 210 million people.

An anachronism in a world of fully immersive high-tech rides, riding Autopia is not unlike strapping a lawn mower to one’s head. It is a jerky, stinky, noisy ride.

Adriel Ceja, an Angelino who was visiting the park with his wife on a recent day, said the ride seemed outdated.

“It would be more modern and feel better for Tomorrowland if it was an electric car,” he said.

Other Disney parks have featured similar rides over the years, including gas-powered versions in Tokyo and Paris, and an electric version in Hong Kong that closed in 2016. At Disney World in Orlando, Fla., an Autopia facsimile is called Tomorrowland Speedway, and still features gas-powered engines, with no known plans to go electric.

But in California, the state with the most E.V.s on the road, Autopia is finally saying goodbye to the internal combustion engine.

Mr. Gurr said that earlier this year, executives from Disney invited him to a facility and showed him a model of the new Autopia. The track will be electrified, he said, which would obviate the need for each car to have its own battery.

“It will be electric, but not the conventional idea of a battery in a car,” Mr. Gurr said. “It’s very different.”

Mr. Gurr said he was told that Honda would continue as the sponsor, but Honda declined to discuss its plans.

“Our current sponsorship agreement with Disneyland Resort runs through early 2027,” Matt Howells, a Honda spokesman, said in an email. “Discussions regarding the future of the partnership and sponsorship of the Autopia attraction are currently ongoing.”

Like other carmakers, Honda is scaling back its E.V. sales in the United States, after Republicans in Congress ended federal subsidies designed to increase electric vehicle sales, and amid the Trump administration’s efforts to promote gas-powered cars.

Honda’s only all electric model currently on the market, the Prologue, is set to be discontinued next month, and the company has not announced a new E.V. for the U.S. market.

Like many Disney rides, Autopia has inspired legions of ardent fans. Chief among them is Peter Menotti, who first encountered the ride as a boy and was immediately transfixed.

“I don’t know how to describe it, man,” said Mr. Menotti, a 59-year-old Disney superfan who runs a 3-D printing company in Los Angeles, recalling his first ride. “It’s just this feeling as a kid that I’m empowered, I’ve got a car, I can drive, I’m growing up.”

In 2001, Mr. Menotti bought a decommissioned Autopia car and spent $65,000 refurbishing it.

A friend who worked at Disney smuggled out original schematics for the car, which allowed Mr. Menotti to create a meticulous restoration, replete with a 3-D-printed steering wheel and a suspension system that allows him to navigate speed bumps.

One crucial difference: the speed of the cars at Disneyland tops out at six miles per hour, while Mr. Menotti’s roadster can travel at up to 18 m.p.h.

Mr. Menotti keeps his Autopia car covered in a tarp in the garage of his home near the Los Angeles International Airport, taking it out for the occasional drive.

On a recent afternoon, he revved up the motor and sped through his neighborhood with a reporter in the passenger seat.

“That’s part of the magic,” he said as fumes filled the air. “It’s that gas smell that takes you back. Without that buh-buh-buh-buh-buh sound, it’s just not the same.”

As for what’s next in Tomorrowland, Mr. Menotti said he would still be a fan, even if Autopia is all electric.

“Would I like it to stay the way it is? Yes,” he said. “But they’ve got to do what they’ve got to do. I mean, we’re moving into the future.”

SUMMARY

To those who have followed President Trump closely, the finding was striking and unsurprising at the same time: His public speeches have become more profane, more absolutist, longer-winded and less coherent over the past decade. That was the central conclusion of an analysis, blending artificial intelligence and old-fashioned reporting, by my colleagues Peter Baker and Dylan Freedman. DYLAN: The first time we ran this analysis, it cost more than $1,000 in A.I. token credits, took me weeks to develop the approach and had some embarrassing mistakes.

ARTICLE

How We Reviewed 7 Million Words Uttered by Trump
Two Times journalists, blending A.I. analysis and traditional reporting, evaluated public speeches to spot trends.
By Mike Abrams, Peter Baker and Dylan Freedman
Published 2026-11-02 23:06 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/insider/trump-speeches-analysis.html

To those who have followed President Trump closely, the finding was striking and unsurprising at the same time: His public speeches have become more profane, more absolutist, longer-winded and less coherent over the past decade.

That was the central conclusion of an analysis, blending artificial intelligence and old-fashioned reporting, by my colleagues Peter Baker and Dylan Freedman. It was a follow-up to a similar study they conducted in 2024.

I asked them to explain their work and — particularly for those skeptical of A.I. — to elaborate on the methodology published with the article. These are edited excerpts from our conversation.

How and when did you first realize A.I. could help assess the president’s language?

DYLAN FREEDMAN: Two months before the 2024 presidential election, I heard Peter talk about a story assessing Trump’s rhetoric in a meeting. I approached him afterward and told him I thought A.I. might be able to help us surface anecdotes. It was my first time meeting him, and I honestly didn’t know if it would work well enough, as the technology was much more nascent.

Peter and I ended up working together over the next few weeks. He would ask if we could quantify Trump’s use of negative language, swearwords, excessively rambling passages and so on. And I would translate his queries into computer code and prompts to pull excerpts. We both ended up reading a 120-page document I prepared of excerpts from Trump’s rallies and speeches over nine years, according to a five-paragraph prompt of criteria we devised, and the best ones made it into the story.

We didn’t simply trust the A.I. analysis but treated it as a tip, so we checked every excerpt in context. And we relied on more basic statistical analyses of word frequencies to assess his range of vocabulary.

PETER BAKER: What Dylan came up with was a fresh way to try to measure what we could see or hear but can be challenging to contextualize. The idea was not to make the A.I. analysis the entirety of our reporting but to complement our reporting, to provide a useful data point and to help us draw judgments. This is the advantage of having smart, tech-savvy people like Dylan working with old Luddites like me.

How did you and your editors make the judgment call about using an analysis of speech to assess the mental fitness of another person given that we do not have medical records?

PETER: We’re naturally wary of diagnosing someone when we’re not doctors, and we’re likewise reluctant to rely heavily on doctors who have not examined him themselves. The White House physician who does examine him releases only a brief summary of his status, not original medical records. So we focus on describing what we can see and hear and measure.

The analysis that Dylan came up with gives us a metric that helps us go beyond impressions and quantify changes in speaking patterns. We want to give readers something concrete in addition to observations. But at the same time, we are cautious about drawing overly definitive conclusions, focusing instead on providing information to readers who can make their own judgments.

In your article, a White House spokesman defended the president, pointing to his “sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic and historic accessibility.” Did anyone who supports him specifically address our findings?

PETER: His supporters like to point to his fairly vigorous travel schedule of campaign rallies over the past month or so — “28 days in a row of this crap,” as Trump himself described it — as proof of his physical vitality. But when it comes to whether he is growing more erratic with age, they usually brush off the question, saying it’s just Trump being Trump.

How do you prompt a tool like Anthropic’s Claude to define, as you reported, “rambling and confusing digressions”?

DYLAN: It’s not so straightforward. First, I don’t just prompt a chatbot like you might do using the app or website. Instead, I write computer code to gather all of Trump’s speeches (from Roll Call’s Factba.se), split them into chunks of text and then feed each chunk one by one into Claude. This helps ensure the results are more comprehensive and consistent.

Second, it takes a lot of iterations to get right. My first prompt did look like asking Claude to find “rambling and confusing digressions,” but it flagged something like 60 percent of Trump’s speech as a positive hit, which is too much text to be useful.

I used the excerpts we pulled for our 2024 story as a reference and developed a prompt that was much more specific, looking at several prongs, like how much a given passage of text meanders, uses non sequiturs, displays obvious signs of confusion, reflects absurdity, or uses cruel and dehumanizing language. I ask Claude to return a score between 0 and 10 for each passage, so that we could decide what score range is useful later. I also ran tests to ensure the excerpts we had manually labeled positive hits in 2024 were also flagged positively.

What other reporting is important to include in work like this?

DYLAN: Beyond anything, this is a human story, leveraging Peter’s expertise now covering his sixth presidential administration. The A.I. analysis is extra quantitative muscle that supplements, but doesn’t replace, the essential human reporting. Peter had covered many of these speeches in person. He knew the right questions to ask. He could review the excerpts we did use and ensure they weren’t taken out of context. I like to think that the best uses of A.I. are where it’s the middle layer of a sandwich of human judgment and review.

The methodology you published mentions a manual review of hundreds of passages of Trump’s speeches. But the A.I. analysis covered 6,500 passages. How do you assess accuracy using just a portion of what was reviewed by Claude?

DYLAN: There’s no one right or established way to do an analysis like this. The field is new. But I have been in the trenches with these types of stories for a few years now and try to lean on best practices across statistics, A.I. and journalism.

I ran an evaluation using our 2024 story as reference. I iterated on my prompts with Claude until I was able to accurately flag the same passages as positive and negative hits. As in 2024, Peter and I manually reviewed hundreds of excerpts. In 2026, the amount of false negatives, or passages that were flagged but shouldn’t have been, was vanishingly small according to our own judgment. At the same time, you always have to worry about false negatives, missing things that you shouldn’t have and about confirmation bias, or using A.I. to reinforce what you assume is true.

I would not have felt comfortable publishing a sweeping statement about Trump’s frequency of rambling or confusing digressions that relied on A.I. without detailing our approach transparently in the methodology section.

How has this technology changed in the past couple of years?

DYLAN: The first time we ran this analysis, it cost more than $1,000 in A.I. token credits, took me weeks to develop the approach and had some embarrassing mistakes. For instance, in 2024 the A.I. analysis we ran flagged Trump talking about a hurricane in Asheville, N.C., as something that would never happen in a million years, or about his assassination attempts as illusions of grandeur. Both actually happened, but the A.I. model wasn’t updated to reflect those recent unlikely events. We didn’t end up using either example in the story.

This time, the approach was much more seamless. It cost less money and was more accurate. A.I. helped write some of the analysis code and generate dashboards — both of which we reviewed. I also had more experience knowing not to assume that the A.I. understands where you’re coming from. Because of that, our prompt ended up exceeding 1,000 words so that it could be as specific and clear as possible.

A.I. is not perfect; it still makes obvious mistakes and can mislead you into a false sense of affirmation. But wielded carefully, it can be a powerful search tool to sift through the more than seven million words of Trump’s speeches over the past decade.

SUMMARY

Now, the very notion of identity politics is in retreat. But identity politics are not going away. And that’s where identity politics come from.”

ARTICLE

Identity Politics Have Entered a New Phase
Since Trump’s return, discussions of diversity have gone quiet. This year’s midterms have shown that Americans could be ready for something new.
By Jia Lynn Yang
Published 2026-11-02 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/magazine/identity-politics-economy-class.html

Not so long ago, Gina Hinojosa’s campaign to be the next governor of Texas would most likely have focused on her potential to make history. If she manages to defeat Gov. Greg Abbott this week after a surprisingly competitive campaign, she would become the first Latina to lead the state. She would also be the first woman elected governor since 1990.

And yet Hinojosa scarcely utters a word on race or gender — hers or anyone else’s — and insists she wants to steer clear of “culture wars.” Instead, she has risen in the polls with a disciplined message of economic populism.

“Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people?” Hinojosa said at a recent rally. “Or is this a billionaire’s world and we just live here? That is the one fight. It is the one fight of this election. It is the fight in America. And it is the fight for Texas.”

Whether or not Hinojosa wins, her campaign signifies a strong consensus in the Democratic Party this year: Race and gender are out. Class politics are back in.

This is a strategy born of defeat. President Trump reclaimed the White House two years ago largely by promoting himself as the stronger steward of the economy. For Democrats, one of the most humiliating aspects of this loss was that the president nearly doubled his support among Black voters between 2020 and 2024, and he nearly came even with Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters. Asian Americans also shifted right, and Trump’s support among women held even.

The return of Trump was the death knell for a presumption that had dominated American life since the 2010s — that identity was a stand-in for societal progress. Now, the very notion of identity politics is in retreat.

Corporations and universities speak of diversity in whispers, if at all, for fear of attacks from the White House. In 2024, 98 percent of companies in the S&P 500 disclosed the ethnic and racial makeup of their boards. Last year, that figure fell to 66 percent.

The Trump administration is attempting to undo an entire regime of civil rights protections, arguing that it divided the country and led to discrimination against white Americans. The White House has proposed ending questions in the census that ask for race, ethnicity or sexual orientation. “Dismantling the grievance industry, the oppressor-oppressed paradigm, identity politics, and other ideas that rend the national fabric is an essential cause,” Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the conservative Heritage Foundation, wrote in City Journal.

Even as Trump has decried liberal identity politics, the result of his second term has been a de facto promotion of white identity. The government has censored mentions of slavery at historic sites while restoring the names of Confederates to Army bases. It has prioritized the entry of white Afrikaners as refugees while trying to cut legal immigration from much of Africa.

We are entering a strange interregnum on identity. While the right goes on the attack, there has been a sudden retrenchment in discussions of race and gender, with even Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York saying recently that “‘Woke 1’ was crazy.” But identity politics are not going away. In fact, they may be returning to their roots.

The Rise of Representation

Until recently, the importance of diversity seemed unassailable, at least in elite settings. Representation mattered, and counting was paramount. How many senators and Supreme Court justices are women? Did any Black, Latino or Asian Americans win Oscars this year? Does every expert panel at your A-list conference include at least one “person of color”?

This is not exactly what those who originated the term “identity politics” imagined. In 1977, a group of Black feminists called the Combahee River Collective declared in a statement that their race and gender were integral to their politics — not because they hoped to join the country’s highest achievers, but because their identity gave them a singular view of America from the bottom of its class hierarchy. Then, as now, Black women are more likely to be impoverished.

In this version of identity politics, the emphasis on race and gender would act as a corrective to an unequal society. It was all too easy for the feminist movement to focus on the interests of upper-class white women. If feminism included Black women, it would inevitably make bolder demands — a higher minimum wage or universal health care, for instance — that could improve the lives of all Americans.

“We needed to have a place of our own,” Barbara Smith, a member of the group, said in an interview from the book “How We Get Free.” “We needed to have a place where we could define our political priorities and act upon them. And that’s where identity politics come from.”

The country, however, was exhausted from years of bitterness over race and war. Cynicism about government, especially after Watergate, was running high. During the 1970s and 1980s, a new political culture from the right rose to power, in part by persuading many voters that their government was more devoted to minority groups than to them. Ronald Reagan warned of Americans who he said were bilking government programs — advancing the “welfare queen” stereotype — as conservatives laid the groundwork for cutting aid to the poor.

With any chance of resurrecting a New Deal-style program foundering, another project of the liberal left found favor: winning the right for individuals to live and work as they wished.

These goals focused on removing discrimination in workplaces and in colleges, aiming for a purer meritocracy. Women, Latinos, Black Americans, gay men and lesbians all would be welcomed into the circle of comfortable middle-class achievement. Of course, bias still existed. But compared with the 1960s, opportunities became more abundant, at least for the well-educated.

This moment marked a pivotal shift for the Democratic Party, whose base became both more diverse and more professional-class.

In the 1980s, the party also adopted a muted posture toward race. By refraining from sensitive subjects like affirmative action, Democrats hoped to win back white voters who were fleeing the party over its support for civil rights. The new strategy worked to some degree: Black leaders began winning elections in white-majority cities and states, achieving powerful milestones. In 1989, L. Douglas Wilder became the first African American to be elected governor, after winning in Virginia.

At the same time, the party retreated from championing public programs aimed at helping the poor and the working class. Instead, party leaders like Bill Clinton embraced fiscal austerity and free trade policies that tended to favor the wealthy.

Democratic support among Black Americans began to soften, according to Leah Wright Rigueur, a historian at Johns Hopkins University and author of “The Loneliness of the Black Republican.” The wealth gap between white and Black Americans stopped closing in the 1980s. Deindustrialization stripped towns across the country of well-paid union jobs.

A seminal event like Barack Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign electrified Black voters. But such moments could also obscure a deeper discontent with the party itself, Rigueur said. “We’re distracted by the symbolism, which is important,” she said. “But we ignore Black voters’ very loud complaints about the relationship with the Democratic Party.”

On the heels of Obama’s win, the 2010s marked a peak for representation politics. Every barrier suddenly seemed breakable — even the glass ceiling on the presidency. Hillary Clinton, running as the heir to Obama’s multiracial coalition, adopted the slogans “Stronger together” and “I’m with her,” unabashedly trumpeting diversity and identity.

But when white working-class voters delivered Trump to the White House, many blamed the loss on identity politics. Bernie Sanders blasted his rival for failing to address the needs of the working class. “It’s not good enough for someone to say, ‘I’m a woman! Vote for me!’” Sanders said. Mark Lilla, a Columbia University professor, wrote a widely read piece in The New York Times calling for “the end of identity liberalism.”

If anything, this sensibility was about to be supercharged.

In the aftermath of the 2020 killing of George Floyd, the Democratic Party and much of corporate America rushed to demonstrate moral urgency. Human resource offices educated their employees on race. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. fulfilled his promise to put a Black woman on the Supreme Court by nominating Ketanji Brown Jackson. Karine Jean-Pierre was the first Black female White House press secretary, and also the first openly gay person in that role.

These moments carried their own significance. But perhaps the more telling data point during Biden’s term was this: Between 2022 and 2025, the median net worth of Black households fell by 25 percent, while the fortunes of every other racial group improved.

By the time Kamala Harris hurriedly ran for president in 2024, the party was determined to avoid the mistakes of the Clinton campaign. Harris underplayed her race and gender. Still, some supporters fell into familiar formations, organizing Zoom fund-raising calls with names like “White Women: Answer the Call” and “White Dudes for Harris.”

In his second term, Trump easily notched his own “firsts,” for those who are still counting. Kash Patel is the first person who is not white to serve as F.B.I. director. Susie Wiles is the first female White House chief of staff. Usha Vance is the first Asian American second lady.

Returning to the Origin

If the influence of identity politics is indeed waning, it is quite likely because enough Americans have concluded that representation alone cannot feed the family or raise wages. Without addressing economic equality, the project became easy to dismiss as a preoccupation of the upper classes. When the public no longer trusts elites, it doesn’t tend to care what the elite class looks like.

Even as this year’s Democrats replace identity politics with economic politics, race itself is hardly receding as an issue.

Angie Nixon, a Florida Democratic candidate for the Senate, is a 42-year-old Black woman still paying off her student debt, who is running an unapologetically populist campaign focused on economics. But when Vice President JD Vance suggested that she does not “belong in America” because of her views, Nixon did not dodge the issue of race. “What’s frustrating at times is that we’re kind of used to it in the South — the disrespect, being Black people, the microaggressions, and the slights, the ‘Oh you speak so well’ or ‘You’re so articulate,’ the little slights here and there,” she said.

Nixon is the underdog in her race, but her working-class persona is resonating around the country. A recent Wall Street Journal analysis showed that Nixon had become more popular on TikTok than any of the party’s more established figures.

Figures like Nixon, win or lose, could presage a return to something closer to the original conception of identity politics — one that is focused on the working class, first and foremost, but without downplaying the often harsh realities of gender and race in America.

After all, identity politics can only fade so much when awareness of racism itself remains high. A Gallup survey last summer showed that the perception that Black Americans suffer from widespread discrimination is as high as it was six years ago. The country received an education from moments like the Floyd video that it has not forgotten. Trump’s unfettered mass deportation campaign appears to be causing a backlash from Latino voters.

And Trump himself continues to practice the oldest version of identity politics. In the final weeks of the midterms, he again called Somali immigrants “low-I.Q. people” and unleashed an extended Islamophobic rant against Abdul El-Sayed, a Senate candidate in Michigan who is Muslim.

For many reasons, we are not living in the post-racial moment that some Americans thought the Obama presidency heralded. But we seem much less invested in counting how many people in each group can push their way into the upper echelon. When millions of Americans are still waiting for someone to address their material needs, they are demanding far more than symbols.

Jia Lynn Yang is a senior Times writer and the author of “One Mighty and Irresistible Tide,” a book about American immigration in the 20th century.

SUMMARY

Like a lot of Americans, I’ve grown accustomed to Supreme Court justices speaking out much more frequently and informally than they once did. Even when the court rules that it has no power to act, as it did in the partisan gerrymandering case, it has “deleterious effects” on democracy, as Justice Kagan pointed out. ARTICLE

Justice Kagan Sounds an Alarm About the Court
Of all the Democratic appointees, if not all nine justices, Justice Kagan has a reputation as the most restrained and institutionalist. Until now.
By Jesse Wegman
Published 2026-11-02 16:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/opinion/justice-kagan-speak-truth.html

Like a lot of Americans, I’ve grown accustomed to Supreme Court justices speaking out much more frequently and informally than they once did. Yet still there was more than one moment in a public conversation Elena Kagan had at Catholic University last month when I almost couldn’t believe what I was hearing.

The justices like to say that their opinions speak for themselves. In the old days, they nurtured the mystique of their delicate yet elevated position in government, rarely if ever revealing their own feelings about the law, American politics or life in general. Anyone who wanted to know what a justice really thought, they claimed, would do best simply to read their rulings.

That is no longer true. Today’s bench is among the most voluble in the court’s history — the justices seem constantly to be writing books, giving speeches, engaging with interviewers and, increasingly, complaining about the institution they serve and (sometimes) the colleagues they serve with.

Even by that new standard, Justice Kagan’s comments, which came during an hour-plus sit-down interview at Catholic University’s law school, broke the judicial omertà, both in what she said explicitly about her conservative counterparts’ blasé attitude toward American democracy and in what she appeared to say about the dangerously compromised state of the court in 2026.

The Catholic University law professor J. Joel Alicea, who interviewed Justice Kagan, started the conversation by asking her about rulings involving partisan gerrymandering, voting rights and money in politics, all of which were decided on party-line votes with her and the other Democratic appointees in the minority.

“The court got it wrong” in each of these cases, Justice Kagan said, because of a “lack of appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions.” She pointed to the Republican-appointed majority’s evisceration of the Voting Rights Act in April, which was followed almost immediately by a mad scramble in states across the South to pass new, more partisan gerrymanders aimed at erasing Black lawmakers’ districts.

Protecting Black political participation and representation was precisely what the Voting Rights Act was enacted to do, she noted. By eliminating the last meaningful tool of that landmark law, she explained, “the court kind of said, ‘Oh, well.’” Whether that was meant in the sense of “we don’t care if Black political representation plummets” or in the sense of “it won’t plummet,” Justice Kagan concluded, “the court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works, and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should.”

This wasn’t the first time she has leveled such sweeping criticisms; you can find similar charges in her dissenting opinions in that and other democracy-related cases, in which she skewered her right-wing colleagues for misunderstanding the law and disregarding Americans’ democratic rights.

But Justice Kagan was offering this critique off the bench, in public — where the justices know their words carry a special significance, particularly before the midterms. Even more surprising, of all the Democratic appointees, if not all nine justices, Justice Kagan has a reputation as the most restrained and institutionalist.

At a judicial conference in July, Justice Kagan took pains to defend her conservative counterparts against accusations that they were acting as a rubber stamp for the Trump administration. So it was that much more remarkable to hear her admit, just a few months later, such wide-ranging frustrations with her fellow justices.

And she wasn’t done: “This court is deeply conservative, and in that way very different from the court I joined 16 years ago.” That court, she added, “was by no means liberal” — it still had a 5-4 conservative majority and had only months earlier decided Citizens United v. F.E.C., which transformed the role of money in politics (and in which Justice Kagan, then serving as President Obama’s solicitor general, had argued the losing side). Still, as recently as 2017, “nobody in America thought the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party or any one anything,” she said. “The court had a kind of legitimacy. And when the court has a kind of legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country.”

Her implication, of course, is that today’s court, dominated by a right-wing supermajority that rules consistently in favor of a longstanding conservative agenda, lacks that “kind of legitimacy” — about as serious a charge as a sitting justice can make.

Justice Kagan had one more dig, which verged on the personal. Reflecting on the role of originalism in the court’s jurisprudence, she said, “I’ve never thought originalism really works,” adding that the “cartwheels” originalists perform to reach their preferred outcomes are “almost embarrassing.” In sum, she said, “the whole project is kind of misconceived, and it’s not a very good match with the Constitution we have.”

Originalism has been the coin of the conservative judicial realm for decades and is currently ascendant at the Supreme Court; as Justice Kagan said ruefully at her own confirmation hearings, “We are all originalists.” Calling it “misconceived” and its practitioners “embarrassing” may sound relatively mild to ears accustomed to the crude invective of the Trump era, but it suggests that the interpersonal conflicts on the bench aren’t getting resolved anytime soon.

I would go so far as to infer a deeper message in Justice Kagan’s remarks: When taken together, her critiques of her colleagues — their disregard for democratic rights, their undermining of the court’s legitimacy and their “misconceived” commitment to originalism — offer a coherent case for reforming the court.

It goes something like this: The conservative majority has been arrogating outsize power to itself over the past several years, claiming the authority to decide many of the most contested questions of American legal and political life, while Congress has stood idly by. Even when the court rules that it has no power to act, as it did in the partisan gerrymandering case, it has “deleterious effects” on democracy, as Justice Kagan pointed out. (That ruling has also disproportionately benefited Republican political interests, which goes to her point about legitimacy.)

Next, pair the court’s arrogation of political power with the fact that the right-wing justices apparently consider themselves accountable to no one. As Justice Samuel Alito wrongly claimed about Congress in 2023, “No provision in the Constitution gives them the authority to regulate the Supreme Court — period.”

Finally, consider this in the broader context of judicial life tenure, a functionally impossible-to-amend Constitution and — to Justice Kagan’s point about originalism — a majority in thrall to a theory of constitutional interpretation that privileges the supposed consensus of people living more than two centuries ago over the values and wishes of those alive today.

Put it all together, and the American people have no way to push the Constitution in a more democratic direction. No way to stop six justices from deciding that protecting democratic rights like voting — “just about the most important thing that the court does,” as Justice Kagan described it at Catholic University — is no longer necessary.

The court’s profoundly antidemocratic attitude was summed up neatly by Chief Justice John Roberts, who said in a 2009 interview: “The most important thing for the public to understand is that we are not a political branch of government. They don’t elect us. If they don’t like what we’re doing, it’s more or less just too bad.”

The chief justice offered one remedy: impeachment followed by conviction in the Senate. However, as he also noted, that has never happened in American history. Impeaching even a single justice would be an enormous lift.

There is a better and easier solution, and Justice Kagan’s critiques last month point directly to it: major court reform imposed by Congress.

Structural failures demand structural repairs. Whether these repairs take the form of term limits, an expanded bench, binding ethics rules, restrictions of the court’s jurisdiction or other measures, they are the only way for the American people, through their elected representatives, to reclaim power over a court gone rogue.

Is this what Justice Kagan was saying, implicitly, in her talk at Catholic University? I can’t be certain, but I’m comfortable speculating.

In this moment of rock-bottom public confidence in the court, Justice Kagan was not unaware that she was speaking outside of the formal boundaries of court decisions, and thus challenging the public appearance of judicial comity. Indeed this may be Kagan’s restraint showing up after all: With her comments, she is ringing alarm bells about the seriousness of problems at the court.

And while the justices may have concluded that they are the final word in interpreting the Constitution, no one gave them power over how we interpret their own words.

SUMMARY

A classic work of political science, “The Presidential Character” by James David Barber, offers a crystalline summation of what the presidency requires. President Trump is dwarfed by his predecessors. Mr. Trump would seem to share with Mr. Barber, the political scientist, a high regard for showmanship in presidential role-playing.

ARTICLE

What Seven Presidents Knew — and Trump Does Not
Will Americans decide this week that character does, after all, matter?
By Howell Raines
Published 2026-11-02 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/opinion/trump-character-presidents-midterms.html

A classic work of political science, “The Presidential Character” by James David Barber, offers a crystalline summation of what the presidency requires. Presidents must be protectors of “the respectability — even religiosity — of the office,” providing citizens a sense of “reassurance,” “progress” and “idealism.” To meet this test, a subhead of Mr. Barber’s first chapter offers a maxim: “Personality shapes performance.”

Mr. Barber’s book, published in 1972, is a sweeping study of the importance of character, image, ethics, political dexterity and performative talent, from Woodrow Wilson through the collapse of Richard M. Nixon. His system of classifying presidential performance was vastly influential among my generation of national political correspondents. I am among the hundreds of journalists who had a ringside seat at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. That doesn’t allow for personal intimacy, but regular exposure to a president’s public acts, and interviews with his chosen courtiers, does allow one to take the measure of a chief executive. Presidents operate in plain sight, and they can’t hide their core traits over time.

President Trump is dwarfed by his predecessors. I can attest that even in disgrace, the private Nixon had an aura of ravaged dignity that remained presidential in scale. When I watch the current president and his toadies wreck our patriotic landmarks and essential tools of governance, I recall the lament of Riddley Walker, the eponymous hero of the 1980 Russell Hoban novel. It was a best seller among intellectuals who thought a supposedly dimwitted and warlike Ronald Reagan would usher in a dystopian future. Riddley, deprived of education and speaking a degenerated dialect, is nonetheless an acute observer of the radioactive ruins of a once great technological society. He glimpses the majesty of what has been lost, saying, “O what we ben! And what we come to!”

By ending the Cold War, Reagan taught us the limits of prediction and the indispensable asset of a calm, balanced personality and, dare one say it in this environment, a kindly nature — something sorely lacking in Mr. Trump’s offenses against good taste and common-sense management. Mr. Barber’s work can seem demonstrably dated — he died in 2004 — since the MAGA faithful, in two watershed elections, chose vengeance over idealism, retribution over healing. Yet in one respect, Mr. Barber seems morbidly prescient in defining the playbook by which three presidents of benign intent — Woodrow Wilson, Herbert Hoover and Lyndon B. Johnson — drove down their approval ratings by a “narrow insistence on a failing course of action despite abundant evidence of the failure.” How better to describe Mr. Trump’s decision to launch a so far winless conflict in Iran under the guidance of a madcap secretary of war?

The historical record will show that Mr. Trump fails to measure up, even allowing for the grandiose private failings of a Nixon or a Bill Clinton. The videotaped highlights of Mr. Trump’s cabinet meetings could be marketed for reality television as “Spoiled Trust Fund Brats of New York.” What we are witnessing on the ravaged White House grounds is a kind of low-rent yard sale devoted to race cars, wrestling and housebroken rockers. Even his presumptive heirs have demeaned themselves: JD Vance by cheapening the word “hillbilly” in a book about his ersatz Appalachian upbringing, and Marco Rubio, the intellectual star of the cabinet, by defending nutty policies on Iran, Cuba and Venezuela.

Taken as a group, Mr. Trump’s management team has defeated the political journalism rulebook. As Richard Reeves observed in New York magazine in 1974, political “journalism has its limits” in describing ineptitude. Recounting President Gerald Ford’s bumbling speech to a Republican rally in Colorado, he reported, “President Ford had nothing to say and said it badly to a friendly and respectful but slightly stunned crowd of 5,000.” He added, “It is not a question of saying the emperor has no clothes — there is a question of whether there is an emperor.”

The midterm elections will test Mr. Barber’s central maxim that character matters. The public expected commanders in chief “to personify our betterness in an inspiring way,” he wrote, to exhibit “a moral idealism” that is “the very opposite of ‘politics.’” Was this era of role model presidents ended by Mr. Trump’s monetization of the White House, and the unregulated machinations of billionaires? Mr. Barber would have argued that Mr. Trump’s excesses must surely trigger the self-correcting pendulum of the old democracy. The elections of 2026 and 2028 will tell us whether the digital tide has swept that mechanism away, along with the Washington etiquette book.

Press relations is a good place to start with Jimmy Carter, whom I covered during his Georgia governorship for The Atlanta Constitution and during his presidential campaigns for The St. Petersburg Times and The New York Times. Contrary to his soft manners, Mr. Carter had a steely core shaped at Annapolis and was calculating about using the press. He first tried seduction, as when he volunteered a scathing assessment of the corruption of Georgia’s highway director. Mr. Carter and his wife, Rosalynn, and I were in a state plane on a trip to the director’s Georgia hometown, and he spoke with such vehemence that his wife tried to hush him. He reminded her, a little snappishly, that he and I had already agreed we were off the record. He was testing my honesty and also providing useful evidence to her role as a key political adviser. From his point of view, the worst that could happen was that a harshly true assessment of a political enemy would show up in the state’s paper of record. He wanted to show that he had the steel spine required at Annapolis.

I kept my word about this off-the-record rant but soon got my own snapping-at for an article that angered him. Mr. Carter had spoken at a medical meeting outside the state, touching on health care reforms that were not popular in Georgia. I made that the news of my account, and the next day I encountered Mr. Carter at the western entrance to the Capitol. He angrily said I had ignored his main points. I responded that I was exercising my right to selectivity in what I chose to report. “Next time, be less selective,” he snorted, marching away across the rotunda.

The experiences contrast with Mr. Trump in several ways. No previous Georgia governor held such frequent news conferences for the useful civic purpose of informing voters about a feckless legislature. Looking back, I realized Mr. Carter was rehearsing for his then-secret presidential aspirations. He was schooling himself in the rhetorical precision that seems to have eroded for Mr. Trump. In the Oval Office, stately address has yielded to the stream-of-consciousness rant, often with sexist targeting. And compassion, a quality glaringly missing in Mr. Trump, came naturally to Mr. Carter. There was clearly no political gain in his decisions to focus on cervical cancer screenings and day care for special needs children, both transformative in the poor counties of rural Georgia.

Highly empathetic, Mr. Carter could sometimes seem ill at ease in casual social settings. President George H.W. Bush and President George W. Bush were his opposites in that regard. The elder Bush talked a good game of “kinder and gentler,” but he was myopic about the impact of his tightfisted social policies. I had breakfast with him and Barbara Bush in their private quarters one frigid winter morning. Bush had invited me to go fishing with him and a local anchorman on the Potomac. In clear view along Pennsylvania Avenue were homeless people, bundled against the cold. How, I wondered, could they observe this every morning at breakfast and not be moved to a programmatic response to the plight of the unhoused?

Yet a few hours later, when the fast Coast Guard cutter carrying us hit an underwater object and bent its shaft, Bush displayed a more sensitive side of his personality. As the wounded boat limped along, he went forward and reassured the enlisted helmsman that he was not to blame. Like other politicians raised in privilege, he had a relaxed social manner. When he hosted his last White House Christmas party after losing the 1992 election, he told me in the receiving line that he had read about my recent promotion at The Times from chief of the Washington bureau to editorial page editor. “Your career is going like this,” he said, raising his hand in an upward slant. “And mine is going like this,” he added, reversing the gesture to indicate a steep decline.

Such grace notes did not surface frequently with his son, who invited a joking camaraderie with reporters, saddling them with nicknames like “Pancho” that had the effect of putting them in their lesser places. When reportedly drunk, he started an argument in a Dallas restaurant with Al Hunt, The Wall Street Journal’s Washington bureau chief, over Mr. Hunt’s coverage of his father. When I was editing the editorial page, he asked me how I felt about moving from Washington to New York. “I can’t stand that place,” he said with startling candor.

My takeaway was that the elder Bush’s homespun affectations — like his preference for pork rinds and country music — were politically calculated, while W.’s preference for the crude charms of Texas was unfeigned and real. His main advisers, Karl Rove and Karen Hughes, were Lone Star enforcers who made clear to me that they detested the Northeast. They assured me their client had no interest in coming to The New York Times for the editorial board meeting that was traditional for nominees of both parties. I lobbied hard through G.O.P. intermediaries and succeeded in getting their decision reversed. Mr. Bush bounced into the meeting room full of good cheer and small talk as he shook every hand. As he grasped mine, he leaned over and said, “Thank you for setting this up,” in a tone that was somewhere between sincerity and an inside joke. At the least, the younger Bush could banter without throwing bomb-like insults.

Mr. Trump would seem to share with Mr. Barber, the political scientist, a high regard for showmanship in presidential role-playing. But Mr. Trump seems not to have studied the timing and flourishes of the master of White House theatricality. Contrast Reagan’s bravura moments with the endless filibuster of a Trumpian weave. Reagan was confident that his “Evil Empire” speech and his challenge to the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev would scorch their way into the history books. His ease and language have nothing in common with Mr. Trump’s mechanical dance steps and depth-charge insults about the stupidity and ugliness of his enemies. One difference is that Reagan had an agile sense of humor and an actor’s feel for staging.

I think of the summer of 1980, when Ronald and Nancy Reagan leased Wexford, the Blue Ridge farm that John and Jackie Kennedy established as their weekend retreat. One evening, they hosted a garden party for the traveling press corps and the crew, including flight attendants, of their campaign plane. Mrs. Reagan, in a summery dress, moved through the crowd on the muscled arm of a T-shirted network cameraman who was a California bodybuilder. Reagan was encircled by reporters who asked how he felt about the jokes about approaching his 70th birthday. Well, he said, I enjoy everything that a younger man enjoys. The winking response was an amusing parry of a question that Mr. Trump most likely would have greeted with vulgarity.

In his relaxed way, Reagan never let his ideology become a MAGA-like straitjacket. When he and Tip O’Neill were at swords’ points over Social Security in 1983, Reagan’s chief of staff, James A. Baker, arranged for secret nighttime meetings at his home, where the two sides made a deal that allowed both men to save face. Reagan, for all his conservative fervor, never feared compromise or tried to humiliate his opponents.

For decades, Hugh Sidey, Time’s veteran commentator, closely monitored the appearance of the Oval Office. He regarded its understated décor and buttery light as enduring emblems of presidential character. His book “Portraits of the President” was subtitled “Power and Personality in the Oval Office.” The chapter “Home Sweet White House” tracks the subtle adjustments in paint color, drapes and rugs that took place when the elder Bush moved out for Bill Clinton. Historic art pieces were displayed on clean, uncluttered walls. Thanks to criticism on Fox News and the book “Regime Change,” we have the image of Mr. Trump gluing clutter to those walls. He claims it is real gold, but the visual statement says Hobby Lobby.

When presidents I observed deployed humor, it was seldom a weapon of ridicule. Mr. Carter told of announcing in an Iowa barbershop that he was running for president. He recalled the barber saying, “Yeah, the boys and I were just laughing about that.” I once heard Nixon jest to a small group of reporters about his failure to burn the Watergate tapes. He, like Clinton and the sometimes befuddled Reagan, was a figure of flawed majesty. For the next two years, thoughtful citizens will have no choice but to beat on against the current of a presidency that is all flaws and no majesty.

Howell Raines is a former executive editor of The New York Times. His most recent book is “Silent Cavalry,” a Civil War history.
