SUMMARY

History doesn’t give us second chances. All this year, right up through the start of voting and even over the past weekend, the Democratic Party has been roiled by assorted fights within its primaries and in the media. The Democratic Party remains the only viable alternative to the Trump administration.

ARTICLE

Don’t Be a Haley Stevens
History doesn’t give us second chances.
By Kevin Baker
Published 2026-11-02 21:51 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/opinion/trump-midterms-history.html

History doesn’t give us second chances.

All this year, right up through the start of voting and even over the past weekend, the Democratic Party has been roiled by assorted fights within its primaries and in the media. These culminated on Sunday in Michigan, when the loser of the Democratic Senate primary there, Haley Stevens, pulled her support from her party’s candidate, Abdul El-Syed, in favor of the Republican, Mike Rogers.

Some insist that these fights reflect great, irreconcilable differences. We have been told that this election is about the young versus the old, or socialism versus capitalism, or minding our own business in the world versus honoring our longtime alliances.

But President Trump has it right: We should vote as if he were on the ballot. Ultimately, nothing else matters.

The Democratic Party remains the only viable alternative to the Trump administration. And for all of their shortcomings, the Democrats remain a mass political party in the American tradition, rather than the bizarre personality cult into which the Republican Party has devolved.

Democrats argue openly with one another. They disagree. They see the world in different ways. We have been treated to the standard punchlines (again): “I’m not a member of any organized political party … I’m a Democrat.” And: “Democrats want to fall in love. Republicans just fall in line.”

They’re great lines; they just aren’t true. Historically, Democrats have fallen in line plenty of times. Many of us had grave qualms about Bill Clinton, or didn’t much care for Hillary or Joe or Kamala. We voted for them anyway. It’s difficult to think of any major Democratic candidate who has been widely loved in the party over the past 60 years, with the sterling exception of President Barack Obama.

Somehow, we managed to go on. Facing the world like adults (most of the time), we did not expect to find perfection in a political platform or a person.

I don’t mean to minimize all of the splits in the Democratic Party. Some of them are very real and very deep — as are the divisions in our nation. We are genuinely, morally offended by what some of those whom we want to vote with believe in. I am morally offended myself by what some of my fellow Democrats profess to want and believe. But then, I always was. When I started voting for Democrats, George Wallace and a great many last-ditch defenders of segregation were still in the party. So were those who were shocked by the idea of women’s rights, gay rights and abortion rights.

Like it or not, making common cause with people you disagree with, even vehemently, even on moral grounds, is an American tradition — a necessity, especially in times of crisis.

The Republican Party was born out of such a coalition of antagonists and fought and won the Civil War with them: nativist Know-Nothings and Irish and German immigrants who died by the tens of thousands fighting for the Union. Freed African Americans who made the same ultimate sacrifice. Early feminists struggling for their own freedom. Yeoman farmers and merchants and the new titans of industry, and even many Democrats.

The Democratic coalition that Franklin Delano Roosevelt put together in the 1930s to get us through the Great Depression, win the worst war in human history and bring about profound, lasting reform to American life was an even broader alliance — one so wide that it seems impossible now that it came into existence at all, much less lasted for some 64 years, despite various eruptions and fissures. Ethnic urban whites and Dust Bowl farmers, union men and women, environmentalists, feminists, isolationists and internationalists, Black sharecroppers and Southern bourbons.

For all that divided us, we have — enough of us — come together when we saw the greater evil, and that united effort is if nothing else the essence of practical democracy. When the Slave Power did its best to destroy the Union in the 1860s, when it seemed that we would be smothered by economic despair and ecological collapse and global fascism in the 1930s and ’40s, we put aside our differences at least long enough to stand against the more immediate threat.

In sheer dollar terms, Mr. Trump is the most corrupt leader in the history of Western democracy. He, his family and their confederates have solicited and accepted (and continue to solicit and accept) billions of dollars from business interests and foreign governments. The money aside — and it is never an aside for Mr. Trump — it is easy enough to leaf through the depredations of his administration. The foolish wars, recklessly fought. The threats to abandon or invade some of our best and oldest allies. The deployment of the Justice Department to intimidate all enemies, real and imagined, from talk show hosts to college presidents. The killings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the slashing of the U.S. Agency for International Development, the growing shadow worlds of A.I. and crypto, the revival of measles and other long conquered diseases. The degradation of our civic life through endless, meandering social media posts and speeches dripping with insults and lies and vulgarities. The threats to annul our elections, backed by the memory of the criminal storming of the Capitol in 2021. The constant hollowing out of what we are and what we aspire to be as Americans, at home and in the world.

One of the less noticed outrages of the past year was Mr. Trump floating the notion to Iran that we should settle our war by agreeing to control and exploit together the oil trade through the Strait of Hormuz. This is the essence of Trumpism: There is no moral stand, even in defense of the nation, that cannot be instantly converted into a business opportunity.

It is impossible to believe that the fractious, bickering Democratic Party would ever back any administration, its own included, engaged in such runaway lawlessness and destruction. Yet save for some feeble, token opposition, Republicans in Congress and conservatives on the Supreme Court, motivated by fantasy and fear, have fallen in line and enabled Mr. Trump to do largely what he likes.

We face now the greatest threat in our history — a combination, in effect, of the worst threats we have faced in the past. Never before have such powerful, well-funded and ruthless forces from within our country so colluded with one another and with foreign powers as they do today — starting with our president.

Those of us who caviled at Bernie bros for not coming forward readily enough to support Hillary Clinton against Mr. Trump in 2016 cannot now deny our votes to those candidates we adamantly disagree with if it means bringing in House and Senate majorities that might finally curb Mr. Trump’s power. Those of us who believed ourselves too pure to support establishment Democrats cannot now stand on our principles and watch the world go to hell.

Hate what your candidate has to say about Israel or Palestine? Believe that Medicare for all is the only solution or the worst one? Convinced that Chuck Schumer isn’t fighting hard enough, or that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will alienate swing voters? Think that A.I. is the future — or the end of the future?

If those fights matter at all — and I believe they do — we cannot have them now. We must first deal with the active menace at hand.

History is a string of critical moments, which can never be regained or recreated just as they were. We cannot miss this one.

Kevin Baker is a co-author of Harry Belafonte’s memoir, “A Burning House: My Politics.”

us-china-ai-manufacturing-exports-weapons.html

SUMMARY

China is unlikely to have any of those in its regulatory scheme. Now let’s look at how A.I. is reshaping economic relations between China and the United States and the rest of the world. In the past, China was not a world leader in medicine.

ARTICLE

The Big Change Coming in U.S.-China Relations in the Age of A.I.
China and the U.S. need mutually assured collaboration to quash the threat of A.I.-empowered bad actors, even while their economic differences sharpen.
By Thomas L. Friedman
Published 2026-11-02 06:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/opinion/us-china-ai-manufacturing-exports-weapons.html

At Beijing Capital International Airport, it is now required after landing to send carry-on bags through a scanner before leaving the arrivals building. As I approached the scanner belt with my bags, though, I saw a sign that I had never encountered before: Any passenger carrying a drone has to remove and declare it. A Chinese security officer pointed directly to the sign to confirm that I had no drones in my bag. I shook my head no. I don’t usually travel with a drone.

That sign was not the only new thing I saw on this trip. It was one of many. Having traveled to China regularly since the early 1990s, I found this journey totally different for a very specific reason: It was my first visit to China in the full-blown age of artificial intelligence.

As I end nine days in the country, having visited Beijing and Xiong’an as well as China’s tech hubs in Hangzhou, Ningbo and Shenzhen, it is very clear to me that the A.I. era is already reshaping the geopolitical and geoeconomic relationships between the United States and China in ways that are actually pulling our two countries closer together geopolitically, while exacerbating our trade differences.

How so? Let’s go back to that drone sign at the Beijing airport. What is it telling us? It is telling us that while the United States and China are still economic and strategic rivals jostling for advantage, they both realize that there is now an intruder into their two-superpower marriage: the superempowered bad actor.

I’m not talking about Chinese democracy advocates. I’m talking about agents of chaos — fraudsters, drug dealers, human traffickers, the kind of hackers who just stole $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance. I’m talking about bad individuals and small teams that can now arm themselves with off-the-shelf drones or A.I.-powered cyberweapons to wield the destructive force of a superpower all by themselves. And I am talking, even more important, about both American and Chinese A.I. models that are demonstrating greater and greater capacities to go rogue and become agents of mass disruption as they become increasingly self-directing, self-improving and self-preserving.

Both countries are just beginning to wrestle with the mind shift this requires in how they relate to each other — even as they continue to reflexively take the opposite sides on wars from Gaza to Ukraine to Iran. A Chinese blogger friend put it to me candidly over dinner in Beijing last week: “We still have real differences over issues like Taiwan. But sometimes the U.S. and China don’t know what they are fighting about anymore,” he said. “It’s just a habit.”

Well, it’s an obsolete habit that both nations must unlearn, and quickly, in the age of artificial intelligence, when global stability will increasingly require mutually assured collaboration between the world’s two A.I. superpowers.

To be sure, our definition of disorder is often not the same as China’s. Any regulatory system embraced by the United States needs to protect democratic values, free expression and peaceful protest. China is unlikely to have any of those in its regulatory scheme. But a lot of overlap remains between our self-interests, which lies in preventing artificial intelligence from causing violent harm — to infrastructure, to individuals, to countries and even to our species. That is the kind of disorder that Washington and Beijing should be able to agree needs controlling. We need these basic rules more than ever because the next steps for A.I. involve, literally, walking — as in robots.

I saw a demonstration at an A.I. robotics exhibition in Beijing where a Chinese humanoid robot replaced its own battery pack, lodged in its back. It just took a couple of minutes. As I stared at it doing this maneuver, I wondered: What happens when it also has autonomous intelligence?

While the need for more collaboration against those trying to get the worst of their A.I. technologies may push Beijing and Washington closer together over time geopolitically, in geoeconomics the opposite is likely to happen.

That is because A.I. is simultaneously superempowering something else: China’s manufacturing juggernaut. As of 2024, China already made almost a third of all manufactured goods sold in the world. What I saw on this trip, visiting some of China’s most advanced car companies and telecom manufacturers, is that A.I. is intensifying their efficiency and competitiveness even more.

You can see it in trade statistics. China’s trade surplus in 2025 — exports over imports — was a staggering $1.19 trillion. That was a 20 percent increase from the year before. This year it is expected to grow to $1.3 trillion — a trade imbalance out of line with global economic output not seen by any country since the end of World War II, when the United States was the only major industrial economy standing!

Trust me, you have not seen anything yet.

Because while American companies are burning through billions investing in frontier A.I. models that are so advanced they’re humbling the best mathematicians, Chinese companies are focused on deploying cheap, “good enough,” open-weight A.I. models that could make its large lead in advanced manufacturing simply unbeatable. To put it differently, America is spending vast sums on frontier A.I. models that are already so powerful the latest versions are too dangerous to be released. China, by contrast, starts the A.I. era with such a dominant base of advance manufacturing facilities, it can reap immediate and broad gains from its smaller “good enough” A.I. models.

When you combine this with China’s cowboy capitalism — scores of companies fiercely competing in every sector of the domestic economy — you get a pace of progress that is downright scary in some industries. At the Beijing Robot Industrial Park, where I saw that robot swapping out its own battery pack, another exhibit impressed me even more.

It was two humanoid robots standing side by side. They were built by different Chinese companies to compete in the Beijing E-Town Humanoid Robot Half-Marathon race — 21 kilometers, or 13.1 miles. The first robot runner, which had a gold medal on a ribbon draped around its neck, won the 2025 race in two hours, 40 minutes and 42 seconds. The second robot runner, also sporting a gold ribbon, won the same race in April in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, beating what was then the human world record, 57 minutes and 20 seconds, held by Jacob Kiplimo.

In a single year, Chinese advances in embodied artificial intelligence produced a robot marathon runner faster than the fastest human ever recorded. My Chinese guide pointed at the two robots and said: “Last year, this year. Next year — we’ll see.”

We certainly will. Other than that, folks … nothing to worry about here.

What follows is what I gleaned from dozens of conversations and company visits in China on how the age of A.I. is reshaping China and China-U.S. relations.

Let me start with some good news.

Six months ago, if you asked pretty much any A.I. expert if China and America would ever get together and agree on a set of guidelines to control their now increasingly dangerous A.I. models, the answer you would get is, “No way, no how” — with a special emphasis that China would never agree to such a thing. Think again.

Right now, I would say that Beijing may actually be more eager to discuss A.I. guardrails than President Trump, who told the United Nations in September that the United States “rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” A.I. — a theme he repeated after his summit with President Xi Jinping days later. Trump to the world: America’s frontier A.I. models are in the lead and I won’t collar them. Full stop. Get lost.

At the opening session of the 2026 Global Governance Forum in Xiong’an, I had a discussion with Wang Yi, the Chinese foreign minister and Politburo member, and John Thornton, co-chair of the Asia Society board of trustees. I was struck by Wang’s clear message in support of multilateral A.I. safeguards.

As Wang put it to us: The “leading nations in A.I., China and the United States, have both the capability and the responsibility to jointly develop and manage A.I. effectively, ensuring its development remains under human control and benefits the people. We must not only mitigate risks but also cooperate to jointly discuss globally applicable rules and standards” to make sure A.I.’s development stays under human control and for the benefit of people.

Of course, China, like the United States, is building A.I. tools to enhance weapons to fight abroad and improve every tool in its domestic surveillance kit to control dissent at home. But Beijing also knows — as that no-drones-in-your-luggage sign at the airport indicated — that A.I. is a two-edged sword and can be used by a lot of bad actors. That is why when you talk to U.S. administration officials about what the Chinese are doing with us behind the scenes, you’ll get a complex answer.

These officials have no illusions that Beijing would like to see more guardrails on America’s frontier models, because the United States is in the lead. But they will also tell you that China’s law enforcement agencies lately have become much more cooperative with their U.S. counterparts on combating cybercrime, fraud and money laundering — all of which A.I. is rapidly enhancing. The Chinese know that the open-weight A.I. models being distributed by Chinese companies are easier for software developers, including those that are bad actors, to adapt to specific, targeted applications than Silicon Valley’s frontier models.

But don’t take my word for it. In September, the Chinese Communist Party’s top intelligence official, Chen Yixin, head of the Ministry of State Security, wrote in the journal China Cyberspace that emerging A.I. technologies were “directly threatening” China’s political, institutional and ideological security. Chen added: “Various hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives abuse generative artificial intelligence technologies” to create rumors, spread misinformation and “incite confrontational sentiments at low cost and in large quantities.”

Read those words: at low cost and in large quantities.

Chen’s government has the world’s largest state-run facial recognition surveillance system, which can pluck a single person out of a huge crowd — what I call “the big acting small.” What Chen was saying is that he also knows that A.I. is a dual-use technology that is enabling the small to now act big. That is the essence of the huge change in the geophysics of the world — the spread of cheap, precision technologies, like drones and cyber-hacking tools, that are now supercharged by A.I. That new superempowered actor can be another nation or a single foreigner or one of your own citizens. Either way, it’s a big new problem in need of a big new answer.

Which is why I was not surprised that while I was in China last week the government issued a draft of A.I. rules that would give the governing Communist Party new powers to track or restrict exports of some advanced Chinese systems. Why now? Maybe because, as The Times reported on Oct. 14, A.I. agents attributed to tests being run by the Chinese tech giant Tencent recently went rogue and tried to “bypass anti-robot protections on websites,” among other shenanigans. Yup, the Chinese have the same problems with their biggest A.I. models as we do, even if they are six months to a year behind in their capabilities.

So, I am going to go out on a limb here: In the coming year, China and America will be seriously exploring collaborative controls on A.I. models. Because, as America’s frontier models reach the point of training themselves 100 percent through recursive self-improvement (without human direction) and as China’s open-weight models that learn off ours through distillation get strengthened in their wake, I predict that 2027 will be the year when both countries fully grasp what an amazing opportunity A.I. is for humanity — and what an unprecedented threat it is to humanity.

This collaboration will be tricky for America. Because, unlike the U.S. government, the Chinese government of President Xi is worried not only about A.I.’s empowering criminals at home, but also about political opponents. Managing that complexity is precisely what makes U.S.-China relations in the age of A.I. different.

Given all of these competing pulls, it may not be possible for the United States and China to come up with a shared system of A.I. guardrails as much as they might need to — at least not without a perfect A.I. storm. That is, a large-scale A.I.-driven event that is big enough to frighten both countries into collaborating on effective controls — but not so big as to end the world.

I repeat: 2027 could be that year. Let’s hope the storm is perfect.

Now let’s look at how A.I. is reshaping economic relations between China and the United States and the rest of the world. Every time I visit China, I come away more struck than from the trip before by the stark contrast in its economy. If China were a person, it would have the upper body of an Olympic weight lifter — rippling with muscles that represent its export-driven advanced manufacturing economy — and the lower body of an Olympic skier who just crashed into a mogul, broke his leg and can now only hobble on a crutch.

That lower body represents a domestic Chinese economy that is still so weakened by the explosion of its large, quarter-century-long housing bubble — which ravaged its middle class and left hundreds of millions of people with mortgages that are underwater or with wiped-out savings — that many Chinese are holding tight to every yuan they can. The frenzied overbuilding of high-rise apartments with cheap money in the early 2000s got so crazy that, as the Times Beijing bureau chief, Keith Bradsher, wrote in February 2025, China now has “abundant housing for the country’s 1.4 billion people and enough empty apartments for another 300 million people.” Put another way, Bradsher said this past spring, China has enough empty apartments to house almost every person in America, which has a population of about 350 million.

In short, China is an export giant and domestic consumption invalid. Unfortunately, the government, instead of injecting money into the domestic economy through improved pension programs, is doubling down on subsidies to build up its global lead in advanced manufacturing — and telling Chinese consumers to suck it up.

Therein lies a huge problem for the global economy at the dawn of the A.I. revolution. Because what I saw on this trip is that the Olympic weight lifter part of the Chinese economy is now guzzling down protein shakes labeled A.I. and is becoming an even more dominating competitor in every advanced manufacturing realm — from socks to robots.

Sure, American, European, Japanese and Korean manufacturers are also benefitting from A.I. enhancements. The problem is that China has so much more installed advanced manufacturing and therefore is going to reap outsized gains. Come along with me on my whirlwind tour of some major Chinese advanced manufacturers.

On my visit to Alibaba headquarters in Hangzhou, Xiong Xiong, chief of staff to Alibaba’s co-founder and chairman, Joe Tsai, pointed out to me that in Formula 1 racing, you rarely overtake your competition on the straightaways. “You win in the turns,” he said, “because in the turns it is not how fast you go, it is how daring you are — how fast you brake and how you respond to my braking — and do you have the stability to control your car at high speed.”

Well, one day we may look back at the years 2019 to 2023 as one of those turns and China came out of it now leading the pack on the straightaway. Two things happened in that period: Covid-19 and A.I. both exploded around the world. Because of Covid, virtually all American students and many American business executives left China. I was also not able to make my own annual trips.

Here is one example of what happened while we were sleeping.

When I visited China, before Covid, Xiaomi was a smartphone company. When I came back in 2023, it was also an electric car company. It put four wheels on its phone. But it didn’t stop there. When I visited its almost entirely roboticized car factory on the outskirts of Beijing last Monday, I found Xiaomi was a superconnected, A.I.-enabled E.V. company. My hosts noted how Xiaomi’s self-developed “multi-material performance simulation system” uses A.I. to quickly figure out what the company believes is the optimal alloy formula — from 10.16 million possibilities — to produce what it called “a perfect combination” of strength, resilience, stability and low carbon footprint for its newest vehicle bodies.

Trump hates electric cars. What he has never understood is that China’s hypercompetitive E.V. industry birthed a powerful, deeply integrated supply chain of advanced battery technology, robotics, material science and, now, A.I. Today, any Chinese inventor or entrepreneur looking to manufacture absolutely anything can seamlessly leverage this hyper-efficient, foundational ecosystem to innovate better, faster and cheaper than most any global competitor. Global manufacturers used to say you had to be in China “to sell to China.” Now they say, you have to be in China and have access to its supply chains “to sell to the world.”

You want to make shoes with electric rollers and flashing lights that sing the Chinese national anthem on the left shoe and the American national anthem on the right shoe? Someone here will have the parts and tools for you to do it in 24 hours.

In Ningbo, I visited the Geely electric vehicle manufacturing plant. I watched an engineer use the company’s latest charging station to power up a car from Geely’s newest A.I. luxury E.V. brand, called the Lynk & Co, in eight-plus minutes with a charge that will last some 500 miles. That is not a typo — that is almost like filling up a tank of gas. “In the future, we intend to improve it further,” the Geely demonstration engineer laconically told me. Yes, I thought, I am sure you will.

In Shenzhen, I toured Huawei Technologies’ assembly line for its newest Mate 90 smartphones. Zha Jun, who oversees Huawei’s research and development, explained that this line used to have 86 workers per shift — doing mostly manual inspections — and the rest of the work force was robots. It recently shrunk that number down to nine people by turning to A.I.-enabled image recognition systems.

When I asked what kind of data center it used to run the A.I. systems, Zha said: “We have no need for a data center. Huawei can get all the A.I. benefits it needs for these kinds of manufacturing improvements using our own open-weight, domain-specific A.I. models with less than one billion parameters.” Those are the ones with circuitry that amounts to the size of a small suitcase. (Parameters are a measure of the connections and weights that an A.I. model uses to process information and are used as a general proxy for its complexity and capacity to learn.) These small A.I. models, Zha added, were “good enough” to make big improvements in manufacturing.

“Good enough” A.I. was a phrase I heard at a lot of factories on this trip. It describes the improvements to businesses produced by the less-than-frontier A.I. models.

“China and the U.S. are taking different directions when it comes to A.I.,” Ren Zhengfei, Huawei’s founder and chief executive, explained to me over tea at Huawei’s research campus in Shenzhen, one of many technology hubs where the company employs some 110,000 researchers, many of them engineers and scientists with advanced degrees. In the United States, Ren said, A.I. research revolves around “what does it mean to be human these days and what is the meaning of the world, and of God? In China, A.I. research is more practical” and is being deployed in big industries, like steel.

“China produces one billion tons of steel a year,” Ren said, “so if that industry can achieve a 1 percent improvement by using A.I. to increase the efficiency in how it mixes the various chemicals that go into every single steel-making furnace,” the additional profits generated for a single furnace will exceed 10 million yuan ($1.5 million) per year. In the past, China was not a world leader in medicine. With the help of A.I., China is now able to strikingly accelerate its ability “to discover and produce new drugs” by rapidly testing different molecular combinations.

He concluded: “That is why we call A.I. in the U.S. ‘Socrates A.I.’ and we name our approach ‘Lu Ban A.I.’” Lu Ban was a legendary ancient Chinese master carpenter and engineer.

Now add one more increasingly important factor: rare earths, which in the age of A.I. will be more important than ever — not only for manufacturing but for running all the chips that go into every data center as well.

My traveling partner on this trip has been Keith Bradsher, who will soon be coming out with a book, “The Race for Rare Earths: Why China Is Winning the Contest for the World’s Most Critical Resources.” The book traces how decade by decade, the United States and Europe lost their early leadership to China in these vital metals that go into cars, drones, wind turbines, fighter jets, smartphones, missiles, lasers, A.I. chips and practically every other high-tech invention you can think of over the past 40 years, including most consumer electronics.

In 1964, Deng Xiaoping, later to become China’s paramount leader, visited the world’s biggest rare-earth deposit, in northern China. In 1973, he began planning for China’s rise in rare-earth technologies, and by the early 1990s he foresaw the geopolitical power of China’s tightening grip on rare earths, declaring: “The Middle East has oil. China has rare earths.”

The United States and Europe are only now restarting a rare-earth industry — from the mines to the manufactured magnets — but will need at least five years and probably 10 to catch up, according to Bradsher’s book, which suggests ways to speed up the recovery. Meanwhile, Beijing has wielded its almost total control over the world’s supply of crucial rare earths to force the Trump administration and European Union to back down repeatedly on tariffs and to put heavy pressure on Japan not to support Taiwan.

You add it all up and China’s dominance in global manufacturing is extraordinary. Jens Eskelund, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, citing information from members, told me that 90 percent of global manufactured goods move in containers. The percentage of global container exports by China rose from 31.8 percent in 2019 to 37.5 percent in 2025, he said. “The rolling three-month average for the most recent months is now 40 percent,” he said. The reason? China’s manufacturing output rose 5.3 percent during the first eight months of this year, he said. (Meanwhile, China’s domestic retail sales increased only 0.4 percent year on year in August, he pointed out.)

In 2019, China exported about 2.5 containers to Europe for every container shipped in the opposite direction, Eskelund told me. During the first eight months of 2026, the ratio widened to six containers moving from China to Europe for every one container moving from Europe to China.

“I tell the Chinese: ‘Guys, trade becomes inherently volatile if you cannot point to value creation for both sides,’” Eskelund added. “China actually understands the world’s concerns. For China, though, the question is: Why should we accommodate these concerns when the world has not put up any serious resistance?”

It is a good question. And one that prompts me to leave this trip with some free advice to China and America from someone who believes the world will be a more prosperous and stable place if people in both countries thrive.

To China: You are going too far too fast too alone, and in the process you are creating too many economic relationships with too many developed and developing countries that are not win-win but win-lose. As a result of your domestic economic weakness, combined with your huge advantage in homegrown engineering talent, unparalleled manufacturing supply chains, the unrivaled work ethic of your people and your high savings rate plowed into the world’s best transportation and electricity infrastructure, China just can’t stop itself from making everything for everyone.

I don’t know when, I don’t how, but the rest of the world will not let that happen — not when robots and A.I. are also creating steadily more worker layoffs. China is courting a real backlash. As Eskelund bluntly put it to me: “There is now a real risk we get into a trade war. We are not going to tolerate a world where China makes everything, and we just give museum tours.”

To my fellow Americans (and our E.U. allies): China is not going to slow down in manufacturing as a favor to anyone. If we want to influence China’s geopolitics and geoeconomics in the age of A.I., we have to create the economic competitiveness that would compel it to do so. That requires the United States to be as serious as the people here are.

In my view, the Chinese today are getting the best out of a bad system of government — by thinking long-term and executing on a plan to align their country with the economic trends of the 21st century.

But one of the weaknesses of China’s system has been on dramatic display lately: the sudden disappearance and arrests of senior officials accused of corruption — so many that it could start to slow down the whole system here, if high-level bureaucrats fear making spending decisions that could land them in jail. Or as one Chinese economist put it to me, quoting a Chinese proverb: “If the water is too clear, there will be no fish.”

And America? By doing no long-term thinking, appointing incompetent cabinet secretaries and having each new administration undo major initiatives of the previous one — like on clean energy — we’re getting the worst out of a good system.

Just look around. Republicans are spending more than $200 million to elect a terrible man — an impeached Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton — to be Texas’ next senator. Trump is savaging America’s scientific research budget and driving away the most talented foreigners who want to come to America to work, study and invent. Trump gutted the electric car industry in favor of gas guzzlers, while Democrats did not think it was a bad idea to leave our southern border porous, which helped to get Trump re-elected.

The only way we will restore some balance to the economic relationship between China and America (and between China and Europe) is not by begging Beijing but by rebuilding our leverage — by being serious again about our governance, by making cost-competitive products and by planning beyond next week and then executing on those plans.

I know just what to call this strategy — I saw it on a red baseball cap the other day: “Make America Great Again.”

If only we could start electing people who knew how.

(Bereaved pet owners might project their own grief onto their surviving animals.) But even if they don’t, she added, animals don’t necessarily need to understand death in order to feel grief.

ARTICLE

Do Animals Grieve?
The feeling of existential loss was long thought to be uniquely human. But studies of coyotes, cockatoos and other creatures are prompting some scientists to reconsider.
By Emily Anthes
Published 2026-11-02 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/science/animals-grief-death.html

Coyotes are not obvious romantics. Their habit of stalking across the landscape alone has earned them a reputation as solitary creatures — and not particularly popular ones, with a public image that ranges from troublesome nuisance to dangerous predator.

But they are deeply loyal mates. They remain with their partners for life, grooming each other, sharing food and raising pups together. “Basically, until death do us part,” said Sara Freeman, a neuroscientist at Utah State University.

In her airy, third-floor laboratory, Dr. Freeman is trying to understand how coyote couples forge these bonds — and what happens when they are broken.

“This is a widowed brain,” she said, pulling a few foil-wrapped packages from an ultracold freezer one morning in August. Each held a block of brain tissue, collected from a female coyote who had outlived her mate.

A student began shaving the frozen tissue into paper-thin slices, using the tip of a small paintbrush to nudge each translucent cross-section onto a glass slide. Later, the researchers would examine the samples, looking for neurological signs of “what we would call a grief state,” Dr. Freeman said.

The study remains in early stages, and it could take years to find clear answers. But the project is one of many in the young field of comparative thanatology, an interdisciplinary effort to unpack how animals respond to — and what they might understand about — death.

Evocative anecdotes abound. In 1972, Jane Goodall watched as a chimp named Flint stopped eating and socializing after the death of his mother, Flo; he died, weeks later, near the spot where her body had once lain. In 2003, African elephants were seen repeatedly returning to the body of a fallen matriarch, periodically prodding her with their trunks. In 2018, an orca named Tahlequah spent at least 17 days swimming with the body of her dead calf.

But whether animals experience grief — a complex, often long-lasting psychological and biological response to loss — remains an open question. “It’s definitely one of those great mysteries,” said Jennifer Vonk, a comparative cognitive psychologist at Oakland University. “And a challenge for scientists.”

Animal deaths are often unpredictable and unseen, especially in the wild. And grief is a complex and loaded concept; it’s easy to project our human experiences onto other creatures and impossible to truly get inside their heads.

Scientists are trying anyway. “The field is ripe for development,” said André Gonçalves, a comparative cognitive scientist at the Indianapolis Zoological Society. “I mean, mortality is kind of a big deal, right?”

Overcoming the doubts

For decades, many scientists maintained that grief was unique to humans. Researchers who dared to suggest otherwise, armed with anecdotes about animals like Flint, were accused of committing the sin of anthropomorphism — viewing animals through a human-centered lens — and of venturing beyond the available data.

In 2008, an elderly chimpanzee named Pansy unwittingly provided compelling new data. When she died at a British wildlife park, two overhead cameras captured the reactions of her three chimpanzee companions. In the minutes before Pansy died, the other chimps gently groomed and caressed her.

After Pansy took her last breaths, her daughter spent hours beside her body. The other adult female spent an unusually long time grooming her own son. All three chimps slept fitfully that night. And when they awoke, they picked some stray bits of straw from Pansy’s body, then watched quietly as keepers carried her away.

“The chimpanzees seemed to know that this was a momentous event,” said James Anderson, a primatologist at Kyoto University.

In 2010, Dr. Anderson and his colleagues published a detailed analysis of the footage, noting that the behaviors of the surviving chimps were “strikingly reminiscent of human responses to peaceful death.”

“We propose that chimpanzees’ awareness of death has been underestimated,” they added.

The Pansy paper seemed to embolden other researchers to write up their own observations of animal responses to death. Soon, scientists were designing new research projects and looking for patterns in the growing pile of case studies.

“It kind of started snowballing,” said Susana Monsó, a philosopher of animal minds at the National University of Distance Education in Madrid and the author of “Playing Possum: How Animals Understand Death.”

What counts as bereavement?

There is no magic formula for determining whether an animal’s behavior qualifies as grief, said Barbara J. King, an anthropologist at William & Mary and the author of “How Animals Grieve.” But changes in daily routines and “species-specific signals of deep sorrow” are among the indicators that animals might be in mourning, Dr. King said.

Many studies document behaviors that seem to fit the bill. Apes, monkeys, dolphins and whales sometimes carry the corpses of their young for days or weeks. Some bereaved macaque mothers become isolated and withdrawn, receiving less grooming and initiating fewer hugs. Giraffes stand vigil over fallen calves; elephants touch the bones of their dead. Dogs, cats and horses sometimes seem to lose interest in food after the death of animal (or human) companions, owners have reported.

Whether these behaviors are signs of sorrow is open to interpretation, and reports from animal caretakers are not always reliable. (Bereaved pet owners might project their own grief onto their surviving animals.) But to Dr. King, there are more than enough credible reports to be convincing. “Grief is not a ‘human’ behavior, by which I mean it’s not a human-only behavior,” she said.

Other scientists are more circumspect. “I would really like there to be strong evidence of grief,” said Alecia Carter, an evolutionary anthropologist at University College London. “But I just personally haven’t found very much.”

Even a behavior like clinging to a corpse is not necessarily easy to interpret. In a 2021 meta-analysis, Dr. Carter and her colleagues found that primate mothers were more likely to carry infants who had died from “nontraumatic” causes, like disease, than from accidents or attacks, which often leave more obvious injuries. The behavior was also more common among young mothers than older ones.

One possible explanation? Primate mothers are most likely to carry dead infants when they don’t fully recognize that they are dead. That’s just a hypothesis, and even Dr. Carter doesn’t find it to be entirely convincing. But it highlights the need to be cautious when drawing conclusions about what’s driving animal behavior.

How loss affects the brain

While anthropologists and zoologists document animal behavior, neuroscientists are peering into the brain. Many are focused on monogamous species that form strong pair bonds, like prairie voles and California mice, simulating death by permanently separating animals from their mates.

This kind of romantic rupture can produce signs of anxiety and what scientists call behavioral despair. After losing their partners, male prairie voles are quicker to abandon their attempts to escape from cylinders full of water, for example. Such losses also activate the brain’s stress circuits and disrupts the signaling pathways for oxytocin, a hormone that facilitates bonding. In a small early analysis of three widowed coyotes, Dr. Freeman of Utah State found that changes to the brain’s stress pathways might begin within days and last for over a year.

Breaking individual bonds can have effects distinct from those of general isolation. One recent study found that after losing a mate, California mice showed signs of heightened brain inflammation. Un-bonded mice housed alone did not.

“An animal that has never had a partner is biologically different from an animal that had a partner and lost their relationship,” said Erica Glasper, a behavioral neuroscientist at Ohio State University who led the research.

Some of these findings have tantalizing parallels in humans. For example, losing a spouse seems to promote inflammation in people, an effect that becomes more pronounced as grief severity increases.

Still, Dr. Glasper is reluctant to say that the mice are in mourning. “Our data tell us that the loss does matter to the animal,” she said. “It can’t really tell us how they feel. We can’t ask the mouse whether it’s longing for its partner.”

That’s a critical question, said Zoe Donaldson, a behavioral neuroscientist at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Yearning is what differentiates grief from depression,” she said.

Some emerging research, from Dr. Donaldson and others, suggests that voles might yearn for missing mates. Dopamine, which plays a crucial role in motivation, seems to drive a vole’s desire for its partner. The hormone spikes when voles are seeking out their mates or anticipating reuniting with them. And several studies suggest that a five- to seven-day separation may increase a vole’s motivation to reunite with its partner and amplify dopamine signaling in the brain.

Dr. Donaldson, who said she had initially been dismissive of the idea that the monogamous rodents could mourn, now believes that prairie voles experience “something akin to grief.”

While scientists tend to be cautious, the public has embraced the idea of animal grief. In a survey of 1,000 Australian adults, 90 percent said that some animals could grieve and 23 percent said that all of them could. Among those who believed that animals could mourn, 18 percent attributed grief to ants; 10 percent to prawns.

“People have incredibly intense emotions around this when I talk about my research,” Dr. Donaldson said. “Like, ‘I can’t believe you’re taking away their partners.’”

‘A richer lived experience’

Animals don’t need to understand abstract concepts like nonexistence in order to know something important about death, some experts argue.

Dr. Monsó, the philosopher of animal minds, has outlined a “minimal concept of death,” which requires understanding just two essential concepts: nonfunctionality, or the idea that dead animals don’t do things that living ones do, and irreversibility, “which is the idea that unlike asleep individuals, dead individuals don’t go back to doing things,” she said.

In a new study, Dr. Monsó and her colleagues found that Goffin’s cockatoos, brainy birds that are known to be talented tool users, could distinguish between permanently broken, or “dead,” tools and those that were only temporarily out of commission.

The findings suggest that the birds may have “some of the cognitive prerequisites” for understanding death, Dr. Monsó said. But even if they don’t, she added, animals don’t necessarily need to understand death in order to feel grief.

Dr. Gonçalves of the Indianapolis Zoological Society agreed. Three-year-olds don’t fully comprehend death, he noted, but few people would question whether they’re capable of mourning a dead parent. “We readily attribute them with grief,” he said.

In some ways, the debate over animal grief has become a semantic one. The loss of a close companion can cause emotional distress in animals, scientists agreed. At issue was whether that distress could be called grief.

“There’s part of me, as an animal behaviorist, that definitely hesitates a little bit,” Dr. Freeman said. “You can’t just say animals grieve and then not stand behind it with data.”

But there’s plenty of reason to believe that animals can mourn, she said, and as the data come in, she would rather err in the direction of assuming that their sorrow is real: “It offers the opportunity to give them credit, perhaps, for a richer lived experience than we often ascribe to wild animals.”

SUMMARY

Scientists know that all snakes descend from a reptile that lived about 160 million years ago. “We need to make sure that we’re not modifying the behavior of the animals, so that we can really capture what their natural sleep patterns might be,” she said. “The defenses these animals evolved to cope with flight may also help them age more slowly,” said Katia Renault, a Ph.D. student at Harvard who studies longevity in birds and mammals.

ARTICLE

Why Did Snakes Lose Their Legs? And 9 More Animal Mysteries
There are more than 1.5 million known zoological species on Earth, with at least as many enigmas. Here are our top 10.
By Emily Anthes and Stella Raine Chu
Published 2026-11-02 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/science/animals-mysteries-research.html

Why did snakes lose their legs?

Scientists know that all snakes descend from a reptile that lived about 160 million years ago. But that ancestor had four legs. What rendered those limbs unnecessary?

Some scientists contend that being limbless gave early snakes an advantage — a leg up, as it were — on land, by helping them thrive in narrow, underground tunnels. Others propose that elongated bodies evolved for swimming in the water.

Fossils highlight the debate. In 2015, researchers examined X-ray models of the inner ear of an animal closely related to the ancestor of modern-day snakes. The anatomy suggested that these ancestors lived underground. But fossils of primitive snakes with developed hind legs have also been found in marine limestone, suggesting that the first snakes may have lived underwater.

“It’s hard to tell what exact conditions drove the evolution of this body plan,” said Tiago Simões, an evolutionary biologist at Princeton.

Why do sloths leave their trees to poop?

Three-toed sloths spend most of their lives hidden high in the rainforest canopy. But about once a week, they make their deliberate way down to the forest floor to complete a singular mission: the evacuation of their bowels.

The pit stop comes at great personal cost. “It takes them a lot of energy to get down there, and it makes them more vulnerable to predation,” said Roland Kays, a zoologist at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences.

Some experts have suggested that the sloths might be fertilizing their favorite trees or leaving chemical messages for each other. Or maybe the habit is linked to the tiny, specialized organisms — moths, green algae — that inhabit a sloth’s fur. Once the sloths are on the ground, the moths emerge and lay their eggs in the animals’ feces. The moths might be benefiting the sloths by foster the growth of the algae, which might be serving as a nutritional supplement for the sloths, or giving their fur a green tint that improves their camouflage.

But these theories lack convincing evidence, Dr. Kays said. “There’s nothing that’s been put out that to me sounds like it could be the real answer,” he said. “It’s just so puzzling.”

How do monarchs find their way?

Every year, millions of monarch butterflies undertake a 3,000-mile journey across North America to the warm forests of central Mexico, where they spend the winter. As they return north, they lay their eggs and, eventually, die, passing the baton to the next generation to finish the circuit. It takes about four generations to complete the entire round-trip journey.

“It’s like a relay race,” said Patrick Guerra, a neuroecologist who studies how animals respond to contemporary environmental changes.

Which makes it all the more remarkable that, every winter, the monarchs seem to return to the same groves, or even the exact same trees, that their ancestors used.

Scientists have identified some of their navigation strategies. Their internal circadian clocks track the movement of the sun, which informs their flight direction. And they can orient themselves using Earth’s magnetic field, especially on cloudy days. But how multiple generations of monarchs manage to find their way back to the exact same trees, year after year, remains a complete mystery.

“There’s no cultural transmission,” Dr. Guerra said. “No one tells them what to do. Everything that they’re able to do is innate.

How do sperm whales hunt giant squid?

Sperm whales regularly feast on giant squid, the enormous, elusive cephalopods that haunt the deep ocean. But no one has ever seen these behemoths do battle.

“It is a black box,” said Nicholas Pyenson, the curator of fossil marine mammals at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. “This is not like lions on the Serengeti eating prey, which has been documented ad nauseam.”

The two species appear to be locked in an evolutionary arms race. The whales use their powerful biological sonar to scan wide swaths of ocean, while the squid possesses huge eyes, which may help them spot an approaching whale. Some squid, at least, seem to put up a fight; many sperm whales bear telltale scars from suction cups.

But do the whales hunt alone or in tandem? What kinds of evasive maneuvers are the squid capable of? How exactly do the whales capture and ingest them? “I could go on for a half an hour about all of the ways in which we don’t know what’s going on down there,” said Shane Gero, a whale biologist with Project CETI and Carleton University, in Ottawa.

Why do some frogs turn blue?

Contrary to the lament of one very famous frog, it’s relatively easy being green. This common frog complexion, which is caused by the layering of blue and yellow pigments in the skin, helps the amphibians blend into their surroundings.

But on rare occasions, nature produces bright blue frogs, which don’t seem to produce yellow pigment properly. “There’s something funny going on in that yellow layer,” said Rayna Bell, curator of herpetology at the California Academy of Sciences. “Beyond that, everything else is questions.”

Genetic mutations probably explain many cases, but the exact mechanisms are poorly understood. Environmental factors, including certain dietary deficiencies and chemical pollutants, could play a role, too. In some cases, spending a few weeks in fresh, clean water is enough to turn a rare, wild-caught blue frog into a bog-standard green one.

The rarity of the phenomenon makes it hard to pin down the biological mechanism, and there may be more than one. “It could be different in different individuals,” Dr. Bell said.

Why don’t seals need more sleep?

How would you feel on four hours of sleep? How about three? So little sleep can be detrimental to our cognitive functions. But apparently not those of the elephant seal.

During their monthslong oceanic journeys, the seals, a pinniped, sleep just two hours a day. And they get that sleep in 10-minute intervals, during which they drift down into the depths of the ocean in what is known as a “sleep spiral.”

How they get by is poorly understood. Studying sleep in wild animals is challenging, said Jessica Kendall-Bar, a marine biologist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography. “We need to make sure that we’re not modifying the behavior of the animals, so that we can really capture what their natural sleep patterns might be,” she said.

And what counts as good sleep? “They could be bobbing at the surface worried about predators,” Dr. Kendall-Bar said. “Not all sleep is created equal.”

Why do flying animals live longer?

Body size and life span tend to be correlated in animals; the smaller the species, the shorter its life. But birds generally live at least twice as long as nonflying mammals of the same size. Bats, the only mammals capable of true flight, also live roughly 3.5 times longer than terrestrial mammals of the same size.

That could be because flying helps animals evade predators. And when a population faces fewer of these external risks — and has more individuals surviving into adulthood and old age — natural selection may begin to favor animals with bodies that remain in tiptop shape for years.

The physiological demands of flight might also have put evolutionary pressure on birds and bats to develop mechanisms for minimizing cellular damage and stress. “The defenses these animals evolved to cope with flight may also help them age more slowly,” said Katia Renault, a Ph.D. student at Harvard who studies longevity in birds and mammals.

Why is tool use so rare in the animal kingdom?

The alarm you use to wake up, the toothbrush that cleans your teeth, the shoes that you wear — tools like these make our lives easier. Some other animals, like chimpanzees and crows, have caught on to the usefulness of tools. Why haven’t more species joined them?

“It’s a complicated answer,” said Alice Auersperg, a cognitive biologist at the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna. Tool use requires an animal not only to form a relationship between their body and an object, but then to use that relationship to interact with their environment with an end goal in mind, often gaining access to food.

Chimpanzees, for example, are adept tool users. “These animals, if triggered artificially, can innovate tool use and are fairly talented at it,” said Dr. Auersperg, who has also documented a cow named Veronika using a broom to scratch her back.

A tendency to use tools isn’t just genetic. In the wild, New Caledonian crows can fashion hooked sticks from small twigs to extract insects from tight spaces, for example. But other closely related crow species don’t exhibit the same ability.

Environment may help explain some differences. Some animals may be more likely to opt for foods that don’t need to be extracted with tools. In contrast, animals in geographically isolated environments may face less predation and competition but fewer resources — and a greater need to innovate with tools.

Why is the elephant brain so weird?

The cerebellum, the brain structure that coordinates movement, punches above its weight. In many mammals, including humans, the structure accounts for just 10 percent of the brain’s volume but roughly 80 percent of its neurons.

In African elephants, the figure is even more astonishing: the large, lumbering mammals somehow manage to pack 97.5 percent of their 257 billion neurons into the cerebellum. “Elephants are an outlier,” said Louis Lefebvre, who studies animal learning and behavior at McGill University.

This enlarged cerebellum may have evolved to help elephants control and process information from their trunks. “They have this appendage in the middle of their face that can move in infinite degrees of freedom,” said Paul Manger, a comparative neuroanatomist at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa.

A neuron-rich cerebellum might also help enable the motor control necessary for elephants’ complex vocalizations or underpin some other aspect of elephant intelligence. The cerebellum has extensive connections to brain regions involved in higher-level cognitive functions. “Maybe that has a bigger role to play in cognition than we thought,” Dr. Lefebvre said.

How do deer antlers “remember” old injuries?

Every year, deer shed their antlers. And every year, they grow back — somehow, amazingly, bearing the marks of injuries suffered by the previous set of antlers.

“Not only does the system need to figure out where the damage was, it then needs to store that information for months,” said Michael Levin, a biologist at Tufts University. “Then, when the new growth comes out, it needs to communicate information to be read by the bone cells.”

Researchers don’t know where this information is stored. But Dr. Levin is trying to understand the phenomenon by studying planarian flatworms. They are known for their extraordinary regenerative abilities; chop one into several pieces, and each will grow a head and tail.

Eventually, scientists hope to apply what they learn to humans. “If we have the ability to tell cells what to build and when to stop,” Dr. Levin said, “most problems in biomedicine would go away.”

Some of the questions above were proposed by: Elinor Karlsson, Noah Connally, Auke-Florian Hiemstra, Shane Gero, Alice Auersperg and Louis Lefebvre.

SUMMARY

Their company, which was growing like a weed, was running out of computing power for artificial intelligence. The realization sent Anthropic on an all-out effort to obtain more computing power. Younger companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have to rely on others for computing power.

ARTICLE

Anthropic Is Racing to Obtain the A.I. Boom’s Most Vital Resource
The company went on a deal spree with tech giants, former crypto miners and others to gain computing power to further its artificial intelligence ambitions.
By Sri Muppidi and Kalley Huang
Published 2026-11-02 15:08 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/technology/anthropic-ai-computing-power.html

Late last year, Anthropic’s executives were in a bind. Their company, which was growing like a weed, was running out of computing power for artificial intelligence.

The amount of computing power that was needed became a “cone of uncertainty,” Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said at The New York Times’s DealBook Summit in December. “Because the cone is so wide,” he added, “it’s hard to avoid making a mistake.”

The realization sent Anthropic on an all-out effort to obtain more computing power. In the ensuing months, the San Francisco company embarked on a deal spree, according to 14 people with knowledge of the A.I. lab, investors and industry experts.

Anthropic has since signed dozens of contracts with former cryptocurrency miners, data center start-ups, chipmakers and tech giants like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX to secure enough computing power. It hired experts in data centers, which are the enormous computing sites powering A.I., and bought data center equipment to speed up construction. It met with developers and explored converting old coal plants and factories into data centers. And it considered deals for tiny amounts of computing power that could add up to what it needs.

“Anthropic is gobbling up a lot of the capacity,” said Erik Bernhardsson, the chief executive of Modal, a New York company that sells computing power.

Anthropic’s pursuit of computing power, some details of which have not been previously reported, is critical as it tries to lead in A.I. and conduct what could be the largest-ever initial public offering this month. The company needs computing power to develop cutting-edge A.I. models and to deliver products, like the Claude chatbot, to businesses and consumers. The resource is so vital that Anthropic spent more than 10 pages of its public offering prospectus detailing the stakes.

“Our ability to remain at the frontier of A.I. capabilities is substantially dependent on our ability to secure compute at the scale required to sustain all our workloads,” the company wrote.

In total, Anthropic has committed a whopping $895.4 billion through 2045 to computing power and chip deals that it largely cannot back out of, according to its prospectus. This year, it is expected to have more than 3.5 gigawatts of computing power, two people with knowledge of its plans said, or enough electricity to power all the homes in Chicago. Next year, it aims to double that amount, the people said.

But its voracious demands are expensive, intensifying Anthropic’s need to go public in an offering that could raise $100 billion. It is also raising debt financing, including $63 billion last week, from Wall Street banks and private credit firms. Even so, Anthropic has warned that it may need to seek additional financing sooner than anticipated.

While other A.I. companies also need computing power, giants like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta have deep pockets and credit histories for buying chips and building data centers. Younger companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have to rely on others for computing power.

Anthropic declined to comment on the record before its I.P.O.

After Anthropic was founded in 2021, it turned to Amazon and Google, which agreed to invest a combined $6 billion in the start-up in 2023, for computing power. The company then spent much of that money on Amazon’s and Google’s cloud computing services.

Tom Brown, Anthropic’s chief compute officer, spearheaded both deals, two people with knowledge of the company said. He also led efforts to diversify beyond Nvidia’s A.I. chips and use chips from Amazon, Google and Advanced Micro Devices, for more options.

Finding enough computing power is “very clearly the bottleneck for all of our progress,” Mr. Brown said at a Group of 20 event in September. “We’re in a huge shortage of the power and labor needed to support the demand for A.I.,” he said.

Last year, Anthropic’s A.I. coding tool, Claude Code, became a hit. But as it became popular, the company lacked computing power to meet demand and had to limit free use of its products and raise prices for some of them.

So Anthropic embarked on its deal spree. It has committed $121.3 billion to computing power from Google, $110 billion with Amazon, $44.9 billion with Microsoft and $120.5 billion with SpaceX through 2036, according to its prospectus.

Anthropic also started working with “neoclouds,” companies that provide computing power, including a $50 billion deal with one called Fluidstack and a $41.3 billion deal with another, Lambda. And it is working with former crypto miners like TeraWulf and Hut 8 to construct the data centers.

Unlike Amazon and Microsoft, which are backlogged with demand for their computing power, neoclouds and former crypto miners have access to land and power for data centers and can bring computing power online sooner.

For even more speed, Anthropic is helping to design the data centers that other companies will build and operate. It has added construction and supply chain experts, three people with knowledge of its plans said, and is buying chips directly from Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom for the computing sites. It is also buying cooling systems and other equipment for the chips so data center operators can install the components faster, two people said.

“We operate as one team,” said Asher Genoot, Hut 8’s chief executive.

Starting last year, Anthropic met with developers in Texas, Indiana and other states about building data centers, according to four people with knowledge of its plans. It has asked some developers about their permits and connection to the power grid, two of those people said.

The efforts have faced hurdles. In one instance, Fluidstack pushed back against some Anthropic data center designs over concerns about power fluctuations that could cut off electricity and damage equipment, before reaching a solution, two people familiar with the situation said.

In another instance, TeraWulf, which is building a data center for Anthropic in upstate New York, was competing for electricians with the owners of the Buffalo Bills’ football stadium. Anthropic and TeraWulf ultimately asked the local electricians’ union for names of traveling electricians from other areas, even though it would make the project more expensive, TeraWulf’s chief executive, Paul Prager, said.

Anthropic has started considering sites with at least 200 megawatts, or enough electricity to power about 140,000 U.S. homes, according to three people familiar with the plans. That is less power than the company originally wanted but a faster way to get what it needs. It has since become open to data centers as small as 50 megawatts and would supplement the sites with power from batteries and natural gas, the three people said.

John Tough, a managing partner of Energize Capital, which invests in data center technology, said Anthropic did not control the pipelines of computing power, so it might have to settle for building “gigawatts, megawatts at a time.”

“The next best thing is to scavenge the world to figure out where there’s power lines,” he said.

Apple’s services revenue grew nearly 10 percent to $31.57 billion, slightly less than analysts expected.

ARTICLE

Apple’s Profit Grows 12% Despite Component Price Worries
The company said iPhone sales remained strong, but warned that the cost of memory chips for its devices was going up.
By Kalley Huang
Published 2026-11-02 21:46 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/technology/apple-earnings.html

Apple said on Monday that its profits were being squeezed by the artificial intelligence boom, which has caused the prices of components that go into its devices to soar.

The consumer electronics giant’s warning cast a shadow over what otherwise would have been a strong quarter. In the three months through September, Apple’s revenue grew nearly 12 percent from a year earlier, to $114.48 billion. Profit also rose nearly 12 percent, to $30.71 billion. Both numbers topped Wall Street’s expectations, and lifted Apple to a record for revenue and profit in a fiscal year, which ended in September.

Apple’s warning about component costs like memory chips came after increasing alarm on Wall Street about the technology industry’s spending binge on A.I., and just one business day after Apple reclaimed the title of the world’s most valuable publicly traded company. Its share price dropped as much as 4 percent in after-hours trading on Monday.

“What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” said John Ternus, Apple’s new chief executive, in a call with analysts and investors on Monday. He added that the company expected memory costs to continue increasing beyond the current quarter.

Despite its deep pockets and sprawling supply chain, Apple is vulnerable to the ripple effects of A.I. Unlike other big technology companies, Apple has not invested heavily in it. But the company is facing a global shortage in memory and storage chips because so many of those components are being used for the A.I. chips that fill giant data centers.

Other companies have also warned that the memory chip shortage is hurting their business. Last week, Intel said its core business selling chips for personal computers was suffering because component prices were skyrocketing. Intel’s stock price dropped more than 29 percent a day later.

“We’re seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal,” Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer, said on the call. He added that the company had agreed to spend $33 billion more with component suppliers from June to September. Apple had not had its chief operating officer join an earnings call in years.

Apple has taken steps to address the pressure on its profits. In June, it raised the prices of its Macs and iPads. In July, it made the starting prices for the new iPhone 18 Pro and older models of the iPhone $100 higher than their predecessors. Apple has also created a new high end for some of its products, including the iPhone Duo, a foldable smartphone that starts at $1,999, and the touch-screen MacBook Pro, which starts at $2,899.

Apple’s forecast for the current quarter did not inspire investors. The company said overall revenue in the current quarter would grow between 7 and 10 percent, more than analysts expected. But it said services revenue would grow between 8 and 9 percent, while analysts expected about 11 percent, according to FactSet.

Apple also said its gross margin for the current quarter would narrow to between 45 and 46 percent, in line with analyst expectations. That means that for every dollar it makes in revenue, it expects to spend more — 54 to 55 cents — to produce its products and services.

When Apple introduced the new iPhone Pro in July, it refreshed the smartphone with a more advanced chip and camera system, a longer battery life and three new colors. These changes have helped increase iPhone sales 17 percent from a year earlier, to $57.58 billion.

Apple’s business in China, the largest smartphone market in the world, was a disappointment. Sales there rose 21 percent to $17.54 billion, short of analyst expectations. The company’s iPhones still made up 19 percent of smartphone shipments to distributors in China in the quarter — more than all of its local rivals, except Huawei — according to Counterpoint Research, which tracks the smartphone market.

“China also was impacted by the same supply constraint dynamics,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said in an interview. “I think that is a factor that could be driving some of the differences” between what analysts expected and what Apple reported, he added.

Apple’s services revenue grew nearly 10 percent to $31.57 billion, slightly less than analysts expected. The company has been quietly raising the prices for some of its services, including its streaming service, Apple TV, which in August cost $14.99 per month, up from $12.99.

The company saw mixed results in other parts of its core business. Sales of Macs rose more than 23 percent to $10.79 billion. Sales of iPads fell more than 10 percent to $6.23 billion. Sales of wearables, which include the Apple Watch and AirPods, fell nearly 5 percent to $8.3 billion.

Apple has “a combination of what seems to be a decent product refresh cycle, new product innovation, a shift to more premium products,” said Charles Rinehart, chief investment officer at Johnson Investment Counsel, an asset management firm. The question for the company, he added, is how effectively it can use those tools to offset rising costs.
