SUMMARY

Just over half of young men voted for President Trump in the last election, prompting a political debate about what propelled their move to the right. Two years ago, before and after the election, The Upshot interviewed a number of young men who supported Mr. Trump. More young men, though, have extended their disapproval of Mr. Trump to the party.

ARTICLE

We Called Back Young Men Who Voted for Trump. He’s Losing Them.
Young men no longer favor Republicans, new Times/Siena data shows. We asked them why.
By Claire Cain Miller
Published 2026-11-02 10:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/upshot/poll-young-men-midterms-trump.html

Just over half of young men voted for President Trump in the last election, prompting a political debate about what propelled their move to the right.

Now, seven in 10 men ages 18 to 29 disapprove of Mr. Trump’s job performance, according to an analysis of the final three New York Times/Siena University national polls.

Two years ago, before and after the election, The Upshot interviewed a number of young men who supported Mr. Trump. To learn what changed, we called some of them back.

All of them had complaints about Mr. Trump’s presidency, particularly about prices and the war in Iran. But while some said they’d take back their vote if they could, they weren’t necessarily supporting Democrats in the midterms.

Several said they backed their state’s Republican candidates — they didn’t blame them for Mr. Trump’s decisions, and they hadn’t been persuaded by Democrats’ pitches. Others weren’t planning to vote or hadn’t given it much thought yet.

Matthew Michels, 26, an engineer in Grand Rapids, Mich., is not planning to vote, in protest against the Trump administration, and because “I haven’t seen enough pushback against some of the stuff Trump’s been doing from establishment Republicans.”

He credited the immigration crackdown for opening more jobs in his field. But he is upset by the “careless swagger” with which he said Mr. Trump conducts foreign policy. He is “deeply disappointed” by the war in Iran. He’s worried about rising gas prices.

“If I could go back, I would not cast a vote for him again,” he said.

Ranger Irwin, 22, who works at a tire store in North Las Vegas, Nev., said he felt Mr. Trump broke his promises.

“He really said he was going to be antiwar, and we’re in war in the Middle East again,” Mr. Irwin said. “The price of everything’s gone up; gas is getting ridiculous again.”

Still, he said he’d cast the same vote again, and plans to vote for the Republican candidates for Congress and governor in Nevada: “It’s not their decisions, it’s his decisions.”

More young men, though, have extended their disapproval of Mr. Trump to the party. They favor the Democratic candidate for Congress in their district by 13 percentage points, Times/Siena polls show. Forty-eight percent identify as Democrats or lean that way, compared with 42 percent who lean Republican.

The analysis, which included nearly 500 men ages 18 to 29, is broadly consistent with other polls showing young men moving away from Mr. Trump. Still, it doesn’t mean they’ll turn out to vote, said Charlie Sabgir, director of the left-leaning Young Men Research Project: “Midterms favor the highest propensity voters, and young men are the opposite of that.”

Much was made of whether young men’s support for Mr. Trump’s macho campaign marked a cultural turning point — a generation of men under the sway of the manosphere, rejecting broadening gender roles.

But a vote for Mr. Trump was not necessarily an embrace of male dominance or a desire to turn back women’s rights, a variety of research has shown. Rather, this was a group that felt undervalued and unmoored. Young men have been telling us and researchers that the path to adulthood they were counting on — get a good job, buy a home, support a family — was no longer available to them, and Mr. Trump promised to help.

“I think a lot of people misread the results of 2024, viewing it as young men are suddenly becoming more conservative, that they’re sick of woke politics,” said Melissa Deckman, a political scientist who is chief executive of the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute. “But a fundamental issue was the economy.”

In the Times/Siena polls, 90 percent of young men said the economy was poor or only fair.

In a new survey from Third Way and the American Institute for Boys and Men, a majority of men ages 18 to 29 said long-term economic goals were out of reach — including finding a good-paying job, supporting a family, affording medical care, paying down debt, owning a home and saving for retirement.

Logan Fischer, 23, got a new job as an engineering technician in Kansas City, Mo., since we last talked with him, and he credited the Trump administration for improving job opportunities. But he still feels his “lifelong goal,” buying a house to raise a family, is unattainable.

“A lot of older people will say, ‘Go to college, get a degree, then you can find a wife, build or buy a house and live happily ever after,’” Mr. Fischer said. “It’s like, I’m making good money now, but it’s not build-a-house money, when 10 years ago it would have been.”

Malachi Bohlmann, 25, a high school teacher in Phoenix, voted for Mr. Trump in part because of the strength he thought he’d show in border control and foreign policy.

But he is unhappy with Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s tactics, and with the war with Iran.

“When I was in the service, we talked about being able to be ready to strike at any given time to defend our people at any cost,” said Mr. Bohlmann, an Air Force veteran. “I don’t like America attacking first.”

He said he would vote on Tuesday but had yet to make a final decision on the candidates.

Even as some young men move away from Mr. Trump, they still don’t necessarily see a place for them in the Democratic Party.

Although young people as a whole are moving to the left this election, young women remain much more Democratic than young men. Three-quarters of them identify as Democrats or lean that way, according to the three Times/Siena polls, 27 percentage points more than young men.

While young men “might be drawn to an economic agenda that’s more Democratic, they have questions about whether they would be welcomed and wanted in the Democratic coalition,” said Daniel Cox, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank, and author of “Generation Uncoupled: America’s New Gender Divide and the Crisis of Human Connection.”

“I think there’s still this lingering hesitancy on the left to forcefully advocate for the interests of young men,” he said.

Mr. Fischer, the engineering technician in Kansas City, echoed that idea.

“I feel like one of the Democrats’ main topics in every election is for minorities, for immigrants,” he said. “I feel like their thing is to hit this niche group and get all their votes.”

Though he’s mad about the Iran war, he still thinks voting for Mr. Trump was the right choice, in part because the alternative was Kamala Harris, and “every time I saw her she was talking about abortions.” He said he’s unlikely to vote this week.

As the two parties prepare for 2028, young men swinging right and left should not be interpreted as a desire for a centrist candidate, said Mr. Sabgir of the Young Men Research Project.

Rather, he said, what resonates with many of them is a distrust of institutions and career politicians, and a belief that the system needs to be torn down and rebuilt.

In the interviews with Trump-voting young men, many said they wanted a candidate like Bernie Sanders — who also blames the establishment for disadvantaging ordinary people.

“It’s something more like the Joe Rogan approach of being pretty economically populist and thinking free health care is cool,” Mr. Sabgir said, “but also having an aversion to the excesses of wokeness that young men often associate with the Democratic Party.”

Nate Cohn contributed reporting. Production by Rachel Buigas-Lopez.

Harvard “slow-walked the pace of production” of documents and refused to provide other materials related to applicant-level admissions decisions, the administration said in its suit.

ARTICLE

Judge Dismisses Trump Lawsuit Demanding Harvard Admissions Data
Trump administration officials had sought admissions data, including student application essays, from Harvard to see if the school was complying with a court decision banning affirmative action.
By Mark Arsenault
Published 2026-11-02 20:13 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/harvard-admissions-trump-lawsuit-dismissed.html

A federal judge on Monday granted Harvard University’s motion to dismiss a Trump administration lawsuit that sought to force the school to turn over admissions documents for a government discrimination investigation.

The administration sued Harvard in February, accusing the university of trying to stymie a federal review of the school’s admissions procedures by withholding documents that the government wanted — among them, application essays written by individual students.

Harvard “slow-walked the pace of production” of documents and refused to provide other materials related to applicant-level admissions decisions, the administration said in its suit.

A federal district judge in Boston, Myong J. Joun, wrote that the administration had not cleared procedural hurdles to justify a court order for the documents.

“The ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data,” the judge wrote in a highly technical decision.

The university, in court filings, said the administration’s document demands went too far. The school portrayed the lawsuit as “part of the Trump administration’s ongoing campaign against Harvard” to try to force it into negotiations on administration priorities. The school has said that it has complied with federal law in its admissions processes.

A Department of Justice spokeswoman, Kiersten Pels, said by email that the court had dismissed the lawsuit on narrow procedural grounds and “invited the United States to amend” its complaint. “We will do exactly that.”

“Nothing in the ruling changes the core problem: Harvard continues to refuse to provide the admissions information it is required to produce,” Ms. Pels said.

Harvard did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

The Trump administration’s pressure campaign against Harvard has lasted over a year. Since the early days of Mr. Trump’s second term, officials have taken aim at Harvard over its treatment of Jewish and Israeli students, its handling of diversity in admissions decisions and even its connections to China.

The government has tried to force Harvard into submission using a number of levers, included cutting off the school’s federal research grants and denying it the ability to host international students. Harvard successfully blocked those moves through court rulings, though appeals are pending.

The dispute over Harvard’s admissions documents began in April last year, when the Trump administration started a compliance review of the university’s undergraduate program and medical and law schools. The administration has said that it began the review to determine whether the university was following the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in a groundbreaking legal case, Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard.

In that case, the high court said that race-based affirmative action in admissions was unconstitutional, although it allowed for some limited considerations of race — for example, if students wrote about an experience of discrimination in an essay.

The Education Department asked Harvard to certify that it did “not use race as a factor in making admissions decisions” or in awarding any scholarships of financial assistance, according to the government’s complaint.

Since the Supreme Court case was decided, enrollment of Asian Americans has risen at Harvard, while the proportion of Black students in incoming classes has fallen steeply. About 43 percent of incoming freshmen this fall identified as Asian American, while Black students accounted for about 9.3 percent, roughly half their share three years ago.

To verify Harvard was within the law, the administration asked the school to turn over “all admissions data for the past five academic years, including applicant test scores (SAT/ACT), G.P.A., extracurricular activities, essays and admission outcomes, disaggregated by race and ethnicity,” the administration’s complaint said.

The government said in a filing that it had asked for anonymized documents.

Harvard argued that the administration had asked for too much, including essays from applicants that could contain medical or other deeply personal and identifying information.

The school, in a filing, called the lawsuit “a procedural case about documents that are unnecessary and vastly overbroad for the alleged purpose of confirming Harvard’s compliance with the Supreme Court’s decision.”

In his ruling, Judge Joun noted that his decision was on procedural grounds — related to whether the government had shown it had taken the proper steps in determining it could not get Harvard’s voluntary compliance. He wrote that he was not ruling on key points in the dispute raised by Harvard, such as whether the government’s requests were too broad, or whether the government was making the requests out of retaliation.

In June, Harvard asked the judge to dismiss the documents case or to stay the proceedings until a final decision had been made in another case related to information that colleges are required to provide to the government.

In that information case, filed in federal court in Boston in March, Massachusetts and other states sued the Education Department over the expanded amount of data that universities were required submit to the government.

The Trump administration opposed staying its case against Harvard, arguing that the lawsuit by the states raised unrelated legal questions.

Michael C. Bender contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Jet That Crashed in Florida Carried Texas Family and Friends on Vacation
Nine people died, including two young children and a 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras, who received her pilot’s license three years ago, when she was still a teenager.
By David Ovalle, Jacey Fortin and Shahrzad Rasekh
Published 2026-11-02 15:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/nathalia-filgueiras-florida-plane-crash-pilot.html

Among the nine people aboard a private jet that plummeted to the ground on Sunday afternoon in Florida were a 20-year-old co-pilot and a Texas family that included two young children.

Everyone on the Bahamas-bound flight, which also carried a nanny to the children and two more friends of the family, died when the Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area of Palm Beach County, Fla., leaving a smoldering crater and wreckage in the street.

The pilot was Jeff Gregory, an aviator with years of experience, according to April Honnen, his former employer. His co-pilot was Nathalia Filgueiras.

Ms. Filgueiras, of Boca Raton, Fla., had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and received her pilot’s license at 17, according to her mother, Camila Corteleti. She said her daughter had worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, and was co-pilot of Sunday’s flight.

Ms. Corteleti said her daughter had been passionate about flying since childhood, a love forged soaring the skies with her father, who is a recreational pilot. She recalled that her daughter, as a child, used to enjoy going to the Boca Raton Airport to watch planes taking off and landing, and that she announced when she was about 12 that she wanted to be a pilot.

“She loved the freedom,” Ms. Corteleti said. “It was completely different seeing the world from the top.”

According to a joint statement on Monday by the families of the people on board, the plane’s passengers included Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp and their two children, Emma and Charlie. The family lived in Austin, in a neighborhood of bungalows and live oaks west of downtown. Mr. Robinson was the founder and chief executive of several technology companies. Ms. Sharp worked in public relations and had recently opened a ceramics studio.

“They were exceptional people,” said Kevin Sims, who sold a home to the family in 2019 and saw them trick-or-treating on Halloween. “They were young, dynamic, kind, generous, warm.”

With them on the plane were Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny who “cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion,” the family statement said, and another couple, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, who were “full of joy and adventure.”

The National Transportation Safety Board is leading an investigation into the crash, with assistance from the Federal Aviation Administration.

Upper Jets, the private charter firm, is cooperating with the authorities “to ensure an objective understanding of what occurred,” Thomas Noetzel, director of operations, said in a statement on Monday.

“We are committed to supporting the families of all those who lost a loved one yesterday, and are praying for them as we grieve together,” he added.

Thomas B. Chapman, a member of the N.T.S.B. , told reporters at a Monday afternoon news conference in Florida that investigators had not yet recovered a cockpit voice recorder, and that they could not yet say whether one was on the plane.

The agency has just begun documenting the crash scene, which will take several days, said Timothy W. Monville, an investigator with the board. “The biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway,” he said.

In the moments before the plane crashed, Ms. Filgueiras radioed air traffic controllers. She said that the plane was facing rain and “light, clear ice that is manageable, and moderate turbulence,” according to archived communications with air traffic controllers in Miami.

She asked whether the plane could climb to 37,000 feet, but, soon after, she desperately declared mayday, a life-threatening emergency. Ms. Filgueiras screamed into the radio that the plane was descending at a rate of 20,000 feet per minute. “We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said.

Robert Joslin, an aviation expert and associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Florida, said in an interview that a two-person cockpit typically has a pilot flying and a pilot monitoring, or P.F. and P.M. — positions commonly described as pilot and co-pilot.

It is not uncommon for young aviators to serve as pilot monitors on small jets, he said, so that they can log flight hours and move onto bigger aircraft.

Given that Ms. Filgueiras was handling radio communications, she was almost certainly the pilot monitoring, Dr. Joslin said. Her work probably involved not only communications but also keeping a close eye on the cockpit’s many instruments and gauges, while the pilot flying would have had more physical control over the aircraft.

Jared Isaacman, the administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, wrote on social media on Monday that it was too early to speculate on what might have gone wrong.

Mr. Isaacman said that Ms. Filgueiras “was doing her job, communicating with A.T.C. right to the end in a terrifying situation.”

“She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die,” he said.

Karoun Demirjian, Madaleine Rubin and Jesus Jiménez contributed reporting. Georgia Gee contributed research.

Much will depend on Election Day turnout, especially for Republicans, who have had a financial advantage throughout the campaign. Democrats lead Republicans in six of the seven battlegrounds that will determine Senate control, according to the final set of New York Times/Siena University polls released on Sunday.

ARTICLE

Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?
We’re one day away from the midterms. Here’s the state of play.
By Patricia Mazzei and Shane Goldmacher
Published 2026-11-02 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/congress-races-midterms.html

Time for some deep breaths: The midterm elections are one day away.

Democrats appear well positioned to take control of the House. The battle for the Senate remains tight, with polls slightly favoring Democrats in a set of much closer contests that could yield surprises and go well into election night or beyond (looking at you, Alaska).

Much will depend on Election Day turnout, especially for Republicans, who have had a financial advantage throughout the campaign. They have blanketed the airwaves and called and texted their loyal voters to prod them to the polls. Money often wins in American politics.

Some fundamentals have not changed. The Senate battlegrounds are mostly in states that President Trump won in 2024. Many voters dislike or distrust the Democratic Party. The country remains deeply polarized.

Gas prices are high. The Iran war is still going. Midterms tend to hurt the president’s political party, and Trump is more unpopular than he has ever been.

Now, voters get their say.

The Battle for the Senate

Democrats lead Republicans in six of the seven battlegrounds that will determine Senate control, according to the final set of New York Times/Siena University polls released on Sunday.

Democratic candidates are ahead in Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, and have a narrow edge in Alaska, the polls found. In Iowa, the seventh battleground, the candidates are effectively tied.

Republicans currently hold all of those states except Michigan. Democrats need to keep all of their seats and flip at least four in Republican hands to win a Senate majority.

The Democrats have a chance in these typical Republican strongholds because Trump and his party have lost the public’s trust on the year’s most salient issue: the economy. Across all seven states in the polls, Democrats had a nine-percentage-point advantage on the cost of living.

Some voters remain undecided. One of the few positives in the polls for Republicans is that voters who decided in the last month favored Republicans.

Still, only in one state, Maine, was the Republican candidate (Senator Susan Collins) viewed more favorably than the Democrat (Troy Jackson).

One perennial question about polls is what if they’re wrong. But our own Nate Cohn crunched the numbers and reports, “Democrats lead by enough that they could win the Senate even if the polls underestimate Republicans by as much as they did in 2016 or 2020.”

The Race for the House

Democrats could win as many as 240 seats in the House, according to the final race ratings by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. Such a large majority seemed like a long shot at the start of the election year. It would be Democrats’ largest majority since 2009.

Getting there would require Democrats flipping 25 seats, including districts that Trump won comfortably just two years ago. Republicans have spent heavily to defend the seats they hold and compete in battleground districts.

Among the races that the Cook report shifted in Democrats’ favor, citing Republican concerns about low turnout, was the North Carolina district held by Representative Richard Hudson, the chairman of House Republicans’ campaign arm.

The Money

The last three months of the campaign saw an influx of hundreds of millions of dollars, with megadonors playing an outsize role, according to a Times analysis using data from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The top 20 megadonors have put about $2 billion into federal races throughout the campaign. That amounts to roughly 15 percent of all money spent on political ads this year. Most megadonors lean Republican.

It has been the most expensive midterm election since at least 2018, as measured by political advertising.

Inside the Not-on-the-Air Wars

The video spread quickly on X after it was posted by a local radio host. There was Senator Roger Marshall, the embattled Kansas Republican, defending his pursuit of medical debts as an obstetrician in a 60-second video that looked just like an ad.

“I never had anyone arrested,” Marshall said looking straight into the camera.

Why was this his campaign’s closing message? It turns out it wasn’t. Marshall went rogue, procuring his own film crew against his campaign leadership’s wishes. Read the full story.

One Key Metric

$11.6 billion.

That is what total political advertising is expected to be by Election Day, according to AdImpact. About $5.6 billion of that is flowing to broadcast television, a figure even higher than the $5.3 billion spent on broadcast advertising in the 2024 presidential race.

Top Talker

A dizzying back-and-forth between Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, and Representative Haley Stevens, whom he defeated in the August primary, has consumed the final days of a race that could determine Senate control. An attempt to broker a peace between the two failed spectacularly, and the final split was months in the making.

First, Stevens said she would not campaign with El-Sayed before Tuesday’s election, despite having pledged to vote for him. Her fiancé publicly endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, and campaigned with him.

Then Stevens reversed course and said she would appear with El-Sayed at a church on Sunday. But she expected him to apologize for comments he had made about Israel and to disavow what she described as an antisemitic ad from an outside group.

El-Sayed, a forceful critic of Israel, responded on Friday that Stevens seemed “intent on relitigating” the primary, which he won by less than a percentage point.

Said Stevens, “I don’t think this is a melodrama.”

On Saturday, El-Sayed said he did not want Stevens to join him after all. On Sunday, Stevens did go to church — but with Rogers. She then endorsed him. Her chief of staff and other aides resigned.

One Poll Number

62 percent.

That’s the share of Texas likely voters who said in the latest Times/Siena poll that they had already voted. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, has a 10-percentage-point lead over Ken Paxton, the Republican, with the large share of Texans who have already cast their ballot: 53 percent to 43 percent.

Quote of the Week

“When I get to heaven one day, I am just going to choke Lindsey.”

That was Senator Darline Graham, Republican of South Carolina, speaking to conservative radio hosts last Wednesday about her neck-and-neck race against Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic Senate nominee. The hosts asked Graham if she was angry at her brother, Lindsey Graham, who died in July, for “putting you in this situation.” (She laughed.)

SUMMARY

Elon Musk has given more money during the midterm elections than any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle, apart from wealthy candidates who have funded their own runs for office. The New York Times compiled its estimate of Mr. Musk’s activity by analyzing the most recent filings with the Federal Election Commission and the Internal Revenue Service, as well as the campaign finance systems of states where Mr. Musk has disclosed contributions to state political committees. The figure is almost certainly an undercount, though, because Mr. Musk has also made some dark-money donations during the 2026 cycle, as The Times has previously reported.

ARTICLE

Elon Musk Tests What Nearly Half a Billion Dollars Can Buy in the Midterms
Never before has a single ultrawealthy person who was not running for office spent this much during a single election cycle.
By Theodore Schleifer
Published 2026-11-02 10:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/elon-musk-midterm-spending.html

Elon Musk has given more money during the midterm elections than any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle, apart from wealthy candidates who have funded their own runs for office.

He has contributed a stunning amount: $474 million, or nearly half a billion dollars.

That sum, which includes disclosed donations to federal and state political groups since Jan. 1, 2025, breaks down as follows:

- About $216 million to his own super PAC, America PAC, which is spending money across the country on an extensive field operation. Last year, the group spent about $47 million on an important state judicial race in Wisconsin, which Mr. Musk’s chosen candidate lost.
- $168 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Senate Republicans. Almost all of that money effectively went to support Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee in Texas.
- $30 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing House Republicans.
- Another $44 million or so to other Republican groups or candidates at the federal level.
- Roughly $16 million to state-focused political efforts in Michigan, Texas and Wisconsin.

The New York Times compiled its estimate of Mr. Musk’s activity by analyzing the most recent filings with the Federal Election Commission and the Internal Revenue Service, as well as the campaign finance systems of states where Mr. Musk has disclosed contributions to state political committees. Some donations came from Mr. Musk’s political nonprofit group, United States of America Inc.

The figure is almost certainly an undercount, though, because Mr. Musk has also made some dark-money donations during the 2026 cycle, as The Times has previously reported. And the federal records run only through Oct. 14, which means they do not account for donations he may have made in the final three weeks of the election.

Only Michael R. Bloomberg, the billionaire former mayor of New York City, has spent more during an election cycle than Mr. Musk has during the 2026 cycle (in 2020, when he ran for president).

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest person, has a lot on the line on Tuesday. Democratic lawmakers have signaled that, if they take back control of Congress, they plan to scrutinize Mr. Musk on a variety of fronts, including his stint as the head of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, his companies’ contracts with the federal government and his role in the Russia-Ukraine war.

If Mr. Paxton wins in Texas, of course, he will have Mr. Musk to thank. Should he lose, though, Mr. Musk’s spending will have been for naught.

Together, through Mr. Musk’s direct donations or through America PAC’s disclosed spending, he has spent about $212 million to support Mr. Paxton. That figure is another undercount, though, because it does not include most of America PAC’s spending in the state. Mr. Musk also donated another $12.3 million to Texas political groups this cycle, meaning his total bill for Texas efforts is currently about $224 million.

After spending roughly $290 million in the 2024 election, Mr. Musk took on an extraordinarily powerful job in Mr. Trump’s administration. But after a few months, he showed signs of unease.

“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025. “I think I’ve done enough.”

That June, Mr. Musk, angry about Mr. Trump’s domestic policy bill, had a spectacular public fallout with the president. He even threatened to start a new political party. By the fall, though, he and Mr. Trump had largely reconciled.

This year, though quietly at first, Mr. Musk has again ramped up his political spending.

ARTICLE

The Parties Make Their Closing Arguments: ‘This Isn’t Just Red Versus Blue’
Republicans, worried about losing control of Congress, are sending dire warnings about the opposing party. Democrats are trying to keep their focus on affordability, corruption and President Trump.
By Lisa Lerer
Published 2026-11-02 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/midterm-elections.html

The tumultuous midterm campaign is barreling into its final full day, with both parties offering their closing arguments in a contest defined by economic anxiety, a backlash to the Iran war and disapproval of President Trump’s second-term agenda.

Republicans, fearing deep losses across the country, have unleashed a flurry of attacks, casting their Democratic challengers as radical, dangerous and even anti-American. In Michigan, Republicans seized on a surprising last-minute endorsement of their nominee for the Senate, former Representative Mike Rogers, by Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate Democrat who lost during the primary race.

While Democrats erupted over Ms. Stevens’s decision, the party’s candidates have tried to keep their focus on the three issues that have animated their campaigns for months: affordability, corruption and what they describe as the chaos of the Trump administration.

As Democrats campaigned at tailgate parties, town-hall meetings and church services, they have centered their final arguments on Mr. Trump and his allies, arguing that Republican incumbents were enriching themselves while ordinary Americans struggled to make ends meet.

In Houston on Saturday, James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for the Senate, railed against Ken Paxton, his Republican opponent, accusing him of being controlled by Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, who has injected more than $158 million into the race.

“We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” Mr. Talarico told hundreds of supporters. “It’s why we can’t afford the basics in this economy, because the system has been rigged by billionaires and corrupt politicians like Ken Paxton.”

Mr. Paxton, for his part, has cast Mr. Talarico, who is trying to become the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades, as a “radical” who wants to transform the state into a liberal haven.

“This isn’t just red versus blue,” Mr. Paxton said on Friday at his own event in Houston. “It’s the America our founders gave us versus something they would never recognize.”

Strategists in both parties say they believe Democrats will win control of the House, although they differ on how deep into Republican terrain the party’s victories might extend. Democrats have also grown more optimistic, though cautiously, about their chances of winning a Senate majority, even as their party must flip four Republican-held seats and keep all of its own to take control.

The Senate map of contested races has significantly expanded since the start of the year, with traditionally conservative states including Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Alaska, Ohio and even South Carolina in play. All are states that Mr. Trump won by double digits just two years ago.

Polls released on Sunday night from The New York Times and Siena University found Democratic candidates ahead in five states that now have Republican senators and effectively tied in a sixth. They hold leads in Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas and a narrow edge in Alaska. They are effectively tied in Iowa. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan, was leading by double digits in the state, the lone top Senate battleground already held by Democrats.

Republicans have all but ceded the Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia, dropping their spending in those states and shifting resources to Kansas, Michigan, Ohio and South Carolina, according to data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm.

Early voting across the country reflected the intensity of the election: More than 54 million voters had already cast ballots by Sunday afternoon, with some states that have competitive Senate races showing large increases, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.

In the final weeks, Democrats have tried to capitalize on the discontent of constituencies that tilted toward Mr. Trump in 2024, including Latinos, young men, white working-class voters and rural Americans. Polling, focus groups and interviews indicate that those voters increasingly disapprove of Mr. Trump’s handling of the economy and are skeptical that his administration can bring the cost of living under control.

“I’ve gone out there and said to Republicans, ‘Look, I understand why you voted for Trump, because he accurately identified the status quo was not working for the average person,” Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Iowa, said as he campaigned at a tailgate party at Iowa State University in Ames. “Now they’re ready for a true common-sense prairie populist that’s actually going to make their lives better.”

Republicans believe that their path to success — or, at least, staving off the worst — depends on driving their core supporters to the polls.

Despite his low approval ratings, many in the party believe that the president remains their strongest surrogate. Mr. Trump announced plans to deliver a closing midterm election message on Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump took his whirlwind rally tour to Dubuque, Iowa, and Salina, Kan., and reiterated his calls for supporters to pretend that he is on the ballot.

In Dubuque, he spoke for more than two hours, spending much of the time talking about himself — his electoral margins, his intelligence and his stamina. He defended his stewardship of the economy, pointing to stock-market growth during his presidency, blaming his predecessor for high prices and calling the focus on affordability in the midterms a “hoax.”

As he has for weeks, Mr. Trump “weaved” through his campaign pitch, oscillating between personal and nasty attacks on Democrats, commentary on his renovations of the White House and now-familiar digressions on the physiques of Republican candidates. In Iowa, he praised Representative Ashley Hinson, the party’s Senate nominee, for having lost weight.

Earlier, the president celebrated Ms. Stevens’s endorsement of Mr. Rogers, calling it “fantastic.”

“Nobody expected that, but it’s a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country,” he told reporters.

Ms. Stevens’s decision ignited a firestorm within her party, as Democratic leaders spanning the ideological spectrum condemned her move.

“A despicable betrayal,” said Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, who privately backed Ms. Stevens in the primary. “The stakes are too high,” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who endorsed Dr. El-Sayed in the primary, said as she campaigned at a bar in Queens.

For his part, Dr. El-Sayed downplayed the endorsement’s significance. “None of this matters,” he told reporters before quickly turning back to attacks on Mr. Rogers and Mr. Trump.

The focus on Mr. Trump marks a shift from 2018, when Democrats won a significant number of seats during his first term. Then, the party’s candidates largely avoided putting the president at the center of their message in the closing days of the election, instead focusing on issues where they had more popular support, like health care.

Now, many Republican and Democratic candidates are delivering closing pitches that cast their rivals as emblematic of the most unpopular parts of each party.

In Ohio, where advertising spending has exceeded half a billion dollars, Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, focused on socialism, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, accused his opponent of corruption — a charge Mr. Husted denies.

Mr. Husted has painted a picture of a state under Mr. Brown where borders are open to immigrants, sports are welcoming to transgender athletes, and language is policed to the point that Ohioans have to say “birthing person” instead of “woman.”

“It’s common sense versus crazy,” Mr. Husted said at events last week across the Buckeye State.

Mr. Brown, for his part, has depicted Mr. Husted as a tech shill beholden to special interests instead of the people of Ohio.

“Ohio doesn’t have to accept this corruption,” Mr. Brown said at rally on Thursday. “Tell them we’re going to end this war. Tell them we’re going to end these tariffs. Tell them we’re going to clean up the corruption that’s all over our federal and state governments.”

Republican candidates broadly found themselves on the defensive in the final weekend, with polls showing Democrats gaining ground in key races.

In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing an unexpectedly close re-election race, closed his campaign with a video defending his treatment of patients as an obstetrician-gynecologist. His Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton, has attacked the senator over a New York Times report that found Mr. Marshall had sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical bills, with 81 later arrested for missing court dates.

Mr. Marshall’s top advisers had urged him not to run such an ad, to avoid refocusing attention on a potential vulnerability in the final days of the race. Mr. Marshall, however, went rogue, The Times reported, arranging for his own film crew to shoot the spot and sending it to people outside the campaign. On Saturday evening, the video emerged on social media.

“I never had anyone arrested,” he says in the video. “Not once.”

In Michigan, Speaker Mike Johnson spoke at length about his distrust of the polls, expressing optimism that Republicans could defy expectations on Tuesday evening.

“I can’t find a Republican anywhere who’s responding to polls right now,” he said as he campaigned for Mr. Rogers. “I’m telling you, we are going to shock them on Tuesday.”

Reporting was contributed by Tyler Pager from Dubuque, Iowa, Emily Davies from Geneva, Ohio, Benjamin Oreskes from New York City, Reid J. Epstein from Sterling Heights, Mich., and Leah McBride Mensching from Ames, Iowa.

ARTICLE

The Future of the Senate Is Riddled With Wild Cards
The likelihood of a slim majority leaves room for several hard-to-predict scenarios that could affect the balance of power.
By Carl Hulse
Published 2026-11-02 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/senate-midterms-tie-independents-wild-cards.html

No matter which party wins on Tuesday, the Senate majority is likely to be tight.

The midterm elections could yield a narrow majority for either party or even a 50-50 tie, which could prompt a party switch that would reshuffle the balance of power. There’s a long-shot chance of a scenario that hasn’t happened in decades, in which an independent senator could refuse to align with either party and keep control up for grabs. And there is a possibility that one or more election challenges could keep seats unfilled for weeks or months, leaving the majority uncertain.

Any one of those results has the potential to change how the Senate functions and its ability to pass legislation and confirm President Trump’s nominees. And those effects would intensify if Democrats were to take control of the House, as polling has indicated they are positioned to do. That would give them the ability to send legislation to the Senate to force a confrontation with Republicans or pick veto fights with the president.

Here is a look at various possibilities and their consequences:

A slim majority would empower the middle.

Based on polls and extensive reporting, Democrats appear to be in position to gain seats in the Senate, where they now hold 47 seats and Republicans hold 53. Few strategists in either party expect the G.O.P. to expand its majority, but Democrats could increase their numbers by just one or two, leaving Republicans in charge.

The tightening of the margin would make life more difficult for Republican leaders and give added leverage to those willing to break with their party and Mr. Trump. They include Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who has been attacked repeatedly by Mr. Trump, and Susan Collins of Maine, if she survives her own re-election battle.

An even or closely divided Senate has historically put pressure on lawmakers who are considered potential party switchers to make the move and swing the majority.

Should Republicans end up with 49 seats, they would almost certainly try to persuade Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, a Democrat who has expressed frustration with the party and the Senate itself, to flip and hand them back the majority. Mr. Fetterman has said repeatedly, however, that he does not intend to switch.

A 50-50 tie would tie up Vance.

If each party winds up with 50 seats, Republicans would retain control by virtue of Vice President JD Vance’s power to break Senate ties as the presiding officer. But as with recent evenly divided Senates in 2001 and 2021, the two parties would be expected to work out a power-sharing agreement likely to include equal committee representation and equity in staff and space.

The Republican leader would still control the legislative agenda, but the opposition of a single majority senator could upend plans while both parties would have zero room for defections or member absences.

Mr. Vance, expected to be a leading Republican candidate for president in 2028, would find himself tied to the Senate because of the need to be available to break ties.

Should this outcome materialize, Democrats would likely lobby Ms. Murkowski, the Alaska Republican attacked by Mr. Trump, to cross the aisle or become an independent. It would be a tough sell, as she has powerful committee positions as a Republican.

But such switches have happened before. Jim Jeffords, then a Republican senator from Vermont, became an independent in 2001 and began caucusing with Democrats, handing them the majority.

An independent could scramble control.

At least three independent Senate candidates have declared they would not align with either party should they be elected. None is favored to win, but control of the chamber could remain up in the air if one or more of them prevailed and the chamber was otherwise split between the two parties.

The Senate’s two current independents caucus with Democrats. But three running as independents this year — Todd Achilles in Idaho, Seth Bodnar in Montana and Dan Osborn in Nebraska — say they would not support the chosen leader of either party. They say that stance would force both Republican and Democratic leaders to negotiate with them on legislation and committee assignments and give them significant leverage in a closely divided Senate.

The Senate has not faced such a situation since 1952, when Senator Wayne Morse, Republican of Oregon, declared himself an independent, later moving a folding chair into the center aisle of the Senate. He was denied committee seats and ultimately joined the Democratic Party.

Independents with no party alignment would represent uncharted territory for the modern Senate.

Election challenges could leave seats unfilled.

With so much at stake, challenges to seating apparent election winners could occur, though such disputes have been rare in the Senate in modern times.

Republicans already appear to be preparing to contest the potential election of Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in Alaska, based on reports by The New York Times that her campaign recruited a candidate whose name is similar to that of Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, to try to dilute his support and boost her candidacy. A protracted fight could leave the seat open and the balance of power in the Senate hanging.

Democrats say they have been preparing for months for such election disputes given Mr. Trump’s pledges to question election results. The president has already said Ms. Peltola, a former House member, should be removed from the ballot.

Senator Al Franken, Democrat of Minnesota, was not sworn in until more than eight months after his 2008 election, after a long recount and court battle.

The last Senate fight over seating a member was in 2009, when Democrats threatened to bar Roland Burris, Democrat of Illinois. Mr. Burris had been appointed by Rod Blagojevich, then the Illinois governor, who was under federal investigation for his handling of the Senate vacancy left by Barack Obama’s election to the presidency.

Mr. Burris was eventually allowed to serve.

ARTICLE

Trump Says a Senator Has a ‘Powerful’ Rear. Will It Help Him Win?
The president has repeatedly complimented Senator Jon Husted’s body. For better or worse, it has caught the attention of voters and raised Mr. Husted’s profile in a key midterm race.
By Emily Davies
Published 2026-11-02 19:21 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/trump-husted-body-comments.html

There it was. The most famous rear end in politics.

It was hard to see under layers of flannel and quilted vest, but that was definitely it.

The one that President Trump has called a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.” The one that, as a result, starred on “Saturday Night Live” and blew up on TikTok. The one that belongs to Senator Jon Husted, the Republican candidate in a high-stakes election in Ohio, who for a brief moment at a campaign event on Saturday night turned around onstage.

“We couldn’t see it,” said Missy Hartman, 58, a baker at a grocery store.

“I never check anyone’s butt out,” said Jeff Bair, 73, a farmer.

“It’s a middle-aged ass,” said Karen Tetrick, 52, who owns an apartment complex. “I should know, I have one.”

Here is the thing about Mr. Trump’s comments about Mr. Husted’s rear: Online and across Ohio, they have more people talking about the senator than anyone has in the two years since he was appointed to the Senate to succeed Vice President JD Vance.

Mr. Trump, who first complimented the senator’s backside at a campaign rally last month and has not stopped talking about it since, can be mocking, crass and cruel with his focus of physicality. But in this case, he took a candidate who had toiled in relative anonymity and gave him an identity that stuck.

“I’m jealous,” Mr. Vance said last week on Fox News of Mr. Husted’s rump. “The president has never said that about me.”

Mr. Husted, 59, has leaned into the newfound attention. Before his physique — or rather, a description of his physique — went viral, even some hard-core Republican voters in Ohio had hardly heard of him. Many of them thought his opponent, Sherrod Brown, a Democrat and former senator who has been a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, was still in office.

Now at least some of them know about Mr. Husted’s allegedly powerful glutes. What’s his secret? His staff members declined to share his gym routine. They also declined to let a reporter join him for a workout, citing “trade secrets.”

Mr. Trump has claimed the attention on Mr. Husted’s frame has given the senator a 12-point lift in the polls. A new New York Times and Siena University poll shows Mr. Brown, a longtime economic populist, ahead by six points.

“I know nothing about Jon Husted’s body,” said Judy Kruger, 68, a Republican. “It’s not anything to make me vote one way or another.”

Jason Vannette, 50, who on Friday joined a small group of Democratic protesters outside a rally in Toledo for Republican candidates, sized up Mr. Trump’s remarks this way: “It’s weird.”

For his part, Mr. Husted has played up the president’s commentary.

At the event on Saturday in Fairlawn, he arrived with a football in his hand and kept it with him as he took the microphone and addressed the crowd.

“During the campaign, President Trump discovered that I was a college football player,” said Mr. Husted, who played at the University of Dayton nearly 40 years ago. “He’s been talking about it.”

The senator threw the football into a room of attendees eating apple pie.

There was a reason Mr. Trump said he had been “studying” Mr. Husted’s body.

Republicans in Ohio are trying to turn the Senate race, which could decide control of the chamber, into a culture war much like the ones that delivered Mr. Trump and others on the right to power.

On one side, according to Mr. Husted: socialism, transgender athletes and a world in which Mother’s Day becomes “Birthing Person’s Day.”

On the other? In the words of the president, a former football player with “a big piece of muscle” on his backside.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said last month at a rally in Youngstown. “I started examining his body.”

He apparently would like to continue to do so aboard Air Force One. Bill Pulte, a top federal housing official, made a poster of Mr. Husted for the president to display on the plane.

So far, the focus on Mr. Husted’s buttocks appears to have mixed results in Ohio — or at least it did among the voters who convened on Sunday at a bar in Geneva to meet candidates and watch the Cleveland Browns game.

“Who cares?” said Donald Goodenow, 66, a lab tech wearing a Harley-Davidson sweatshirt, when a reporter asked him if he had heard Mr. Trump’s comments about Mr. Husted.

Mr. Goodenow said he thought Mr. Brown was in office and planned to vote for Mr. Husted because “by the looks of most of the Democratic Party, they’re out to lunch.”

Ms. Tetrick said she was considering leaving Mr. Husted’s bubble blank, despite broadly supporting Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

“Sherrod Brown, I do appreciate him over the years — he did care about the people,” said Ms. Tetrick. “Husted, I just don’t know.”

Mr. Husted was not at the bar on Sunday with the other Republican candidates who had taken a bus to mingle with voters at the sports bar.

Perhaps he was at the gym.

Mack Liederman contributed from Toledo, Ohio.

ARTICLE

Trump Delivers a Closing Midterm Message. Mostly About Landscaping.
On the eve of the election, the president held forth in great detail on columns, drain pipes and granite at the newly refilled Reflecting Pool.
By Shawn McCreesh
Published 2026-11-02 23:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/trump-reflecting-pool-midterms.html

President Trump was standing in front of the Reflecting Pool on Monday afternoon, doing a little reflecting of his own.

“For some reason,” he was saying, the Washington Monument mirrored in the newly reopened pool behind him, “the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot.”

It was the day before the election, and the president had decided to come here, a place that excites him, to talk about many of the topics that make him happiest. Trouble is, almost none of those topics have anything to do with the issues that are driving this election.

At a time when voters have made clear they’re most concerned with the high prices of gas and groceries and a new war in the Middle East, Mr. Trump used his final in-person appearance before Americans head to the polls to talk about drain pipes, top soil, limestone, fountains and his favorite kind of columns.

“The pipes now are totally renovated,” Mr. Trump said. Propped up next to him was a poster board showing an aerial view of the pool, with this caption: “Back, and more beautiful than ever!”

The “brand-new pipes,” Mr. Trump said, are “very important in terms of the algae and other things. And it’s a complete job, and we’re very proud of it.”

The Lincoln Memorial in front of him, Mr. Trump addressed a small audience seated in folding chairs. There were a few dozen National Park Service employees, reporters, White House officials and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. At one point early in his speech, Mr. Trump beckoned to a young man who bounded up onstage with a stack of large printouts under his arm.

“Great,” Mr. Trump said as he took the stack and began rifling through it. He held up one of the printouts. It was a photograph of what looked like a rusty drainpipe. Another photograph showed a dumpster filled with detritus.

“This is another example of what it looked like just at water level and below,” he explained as he waved another photograph aloft. Every so often, he would look over his shoulder to check on the body of water behind him. “It’s a massive piece of pool,” he said, sounding impressed. It looked clean, dark and choppy on this early November day.

The Reflecting Pool had been closed and fenced off since July. After a series of bungled repair jobs, it became a symbol of the Trump administration’s dysfunction.

After he finished with the pictures, the president turned to other matters of national interest. Matters including: the nature of Corinthian columns (“the most beautiful in the world”); the soul of grass generally, and Bermuda grass specifically (“like the human being, grass has a life also”); the endurance of granite (“it literally has thousands of years of life”); the renovation of a public golf course on the Potomac that he’s planning; statues; the White House ballroom; graffiti; and the new White House helipad.

“The helipad,” Mr. Trump said, “was desperately needed.”

In the history of American politics, the speech may go down as one of the more unusual closing messages on the eve of an election. But it was a pretty good crystallization of what matters to Mr. Trump as he heads into the lame duck phase of his second term — despite, or maybe because of, his depressed poll numbers and voter unhappiness over the economy, corruption and an unresolved war.

And now here he was, using his final in-person address before the election to talk more about his chryselephantine fantasies of ballrooms and arches and Corinthian columns.

“The president’s a builder,” Mr. Burgum said from the little stage on Monday. “You can’t keep him away!” Large signs that aides had duct-taped to the stage before the president’s arrival read: “RESTORING OUR CAPITAL.”

The president made some of his usual comments about the war with Iran, the U.S. economy and various culture war issues, but he did not even attempt to explain how any of the renovation projects that were the focus of the speech related to any of the issues animating the midterm elections.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks,” he said. “America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

It seemed almost as though he had run out of things to say about politics and governance, and like he simply wanted to talk about what sparks joy for him.

“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation,” Mr. Trump said, “but for that you don’t have enough time.”

A ‘Pugnacious’ Vance Leans Into Personal Attacks on the Campaign Trail
Vice President JD Vance’s sharp-edged rhetoric shows his instincts as a politician as attention is about to shift to the 2028 presidential race.

In mid-October, Vice President JD Vance came face to face with a young woman who told him that he got her vote when she cast her first ballot as a U.S. citizen. At a town hall in Michigan, she asked why he was scapegoating immigrants for the issues he had vowed to solve as vice president.

“To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that’s on me,” Mr. Vance said.

But days later, when a heckler interrupted his speech with shouts of “Release the Epstein files” and “God bless our children,” Mr. Vance claimed without evidence that the man was an illegal immigrant.

And last week, at a rally in Michigan, Mr. Vance suggested that Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim American and Democrat who is running in a tight race for the Senate, would lead an uprising similar to the unrest taking place in France.

“We have to understand what happens when our nation gives in to these kinds of people, to young men with zero attachment to its land or to its history,” Mr. Vance said of Dr. El-Sayed, who was born in the United States.

“Because what we saw in France,” he added, “the hatred, the ingratitude, the desire to destroy rather than the desire to build, that exact same cancer is what has corrupted Abdul El-Sayed writ large.”

As he has sought to rally support for G.O.P. candidates before the midterm elections, Mr. Vance has repeatedly reverted to deeply personal attacks and inflammatory rhetoric, playing a leading role in a campaign in which Republicans in tightening races have adopted xenophobic, anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric.

He fat-shamed critics, and suggested that the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas was gay and had inappropriate relationships with children. He asserted that a Black Democratic candidate in Florida did not belong in the United States because of her socialist views. He questioned the Christianity of a Kansas pastor running for Senate. And he defended a widely criticized ad featuring the estranged mother of the Democrat running for governor in Ohio, Dr. Amy Acton. Dr. Acton has not spoken to her since her mother’s husband was charged with raping Dr. Acton when she was 12.

Vice presidents have historically been called on to be rhetorical attack dogs, particularly during campaign seasons, and Mr. Vance is second-in-command to a president whose go-to defense is often aggression and insults.

But Mr. Vance’s sharp-edged rhetoric is revealing of his political instincts on the eve of the next major campaign, as attention shifts to the 2028 race for the White House and his potential candidacy to succeed President Trump.

“His political juice is still very much open to question, and Vance has put a lot of his credibility on the line in the places he visited,” said Matthew Dallek, a political historian at George Washington University. “He’s looking for ways to say to his base voters that ‘I should be the one to inherit the Trump mantle. I can go where Trump also goes, and go to depths that Trump hasn’t even visited yet.’”

In response to a request for comment, Luke Schroeder, a spokesman for Mr. Vance, said in a statement that The New York Times was “cherry-picking his comments to manufacture a politically convenient caricature.”

“The vice president’s message is simple: America belongs to those of all colors and creeds who love it, not to those who hate it,” he added. “The vice president has rightly held radical Democrats accountable for their apparent contempt for the American way of life.”

Mr. Vance has demurred when asked whether he plans to run in 2028. “My wife will tell you this: I’m a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it,” he said at a recent CBS News town hall, adding, “Anything could happen, man.”

The president has so far declined to name Mr. Vance as his heir apparent. In the closing stretch of the midterm elections, he has privately questioned why Mr. Vance has not drawn bigger crowds at the rallies he has headlined.

“He’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person, but we’ve — I don’t think we’ve ever talked about,” Mr. Trump said recently when asked whether he would endorse Mr. Vance, adding: “It’s early, very early right now. We have to get through the midterms.”

Mr. Vance is often the most disciplined messenger for the Trump administration, arguing in careful talking points that Republicans are improving the lives of everyday Americans. At several recent rallies, he promoted economic policies like tax cuts and efforts to lower health care costs, as well as the administration’s fight against fraud, which he said would help steer more jobs and resources to Americans.

At a rally in Kansas, Mr. Vance leaned into his personal story, comparing the state to his hometown in Ohio, sticking largely to an economic populist message. He acknowledged that many Americans felt squeezed by rising costs, a concern that Mr. Trump has repeatedly dismissed.

“I want to speak mostly to the undecided voters,” Mr. Vance told the crowd. “You’ll hear a lot of people say that gas prices are too high. And I understand that. It is true.”

He has demonstrated his comfort invoking his Catholic faith. At a rally in Nebraska, Mr. Vance was riling up the crowd, saying the Democratic Party “needs an ass-kicking,” just before an attendee had a medical emergency. Within minutes, he was leading the crowd in the Lord’s Prayer while she received medical attention.

Throughout the campaign, Mr. Vance also presented himself as open to bipartisanship. He has lamented that the Democratic Party had changed since the 1980s and ’90s, saying in one rally that he would “frankly love to be dealing with some reasonable Democrats in Washington, D.C.”

But he also frequently veers back toward swipes at immigrants and multiculturalism.

During a recent Fox News town hall, Mr. Vance recalled a conversation with his wife,Usha, who is the daughter of Indian immigrants, about growing frustrated when he took his son to the emergency room and observed “nine different translators for nine different languages.”

“And I’m just thinking to myself, How about if everybody spoke English, and we could hire more doctors and less translators in our country?” he said.

When asked how young Americans were expected to buy homes and start families with the high cost of living, Mr. Vance placed blame for housing prices, in part, on unauthorized immigrants.

“We allowed 20 million illegal aliens into our country to buy homes that ought, by right, go to American citizens,” he said.

Economists and real estate experts have long debunked this claim, finding that while illegal immigration has contributed to population growth, a lack of supply is the primary culprit of the housing affordability crisis.

During a swing through Texas, Mr. Vance assailed one of his favorite targets, James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, implying in a fiery speech that Mr. Talarico had an inappropriate focus on children. The vice president has repeatedly suggested that Mr. Talarico’s past statements supporting transgender children were inappropriate.

“I need you to send a message on November the 3rd that America belongs to those who love it, not those who hate it,” Mr. Vance said. “I need you to tell James Talarico that his weird obsession with trans kids is not good for the state of Texas, and I need you to send a message to every far-left activist, to everybody who expects Texas to surrender, that in five days, Texas is not surrendering a damn thing.”

He has been particularly pointed when discussing Dr. El-Sayed, who earlier this year suggested that Mr. Vance’s white grandfather would not accept his wife, Usha. The vice president has falsely accused Dr. El-Sayed of supporting Shariah law and described him as someone who “defends literal terrorism.” Mr. Vance has also seized on claims that Dr. El-Sayed made about holding dual citizenship in Egypt, which his campaign later said was an error, to argue that he is not loyal to America.

On other occasions, Mr. Vance has said that he supports a country that does not judge people by the color of their skin. At the town hall in Michigan, where he addressed antisemitism, he said he condemned “anybody who would judge another human being based on who their mother or father were, what their ethnicity was, what their religion is.”

Political observers said that the midterm campaign had showcased how Mr. Vance appears to tailor his political persona to different audiences.

“I feel like this was his opportunity to really try out and see what sticks and what doesn’t,” said Alexandra Middlewood, a professor of political science at Wichita State University.

A Republican strategist close to Mr. Vance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss his private comments, said the vice president had grown more comfortable showing his personality by leaning into humor, profanity and riffing.

Mr. Vance has credited his boisterous political style to his upbringing, largely shaped by a grandmother who passed on her love of God and colorful expletives.

In a recent interview with the vice president, the political podcaster Mark Halperin pressed him on why he had so many feuds.

“I’m probably a little pugnacious,” Mr. Vance answered, laughing. “I like to have fun with it. I also like to be honest and direct.”
