SUMMARY

Since President Trump returned to office nearly two years ago, courts have frequently ordered his administration to pause or halt aggressive actions after they drew legal challenges. But again and again, his executive branch has skirted judicial constraints through delayed, contested or incomplete compliance, all while Mr. Trump has attacked judges appointed by presidents of both parties. “The word ‘contempt’ clearly applies to what Trump and some of his people have been saying about the courts,” said Michael McConnell, a Stanford law professor and retired Republican-appointed appeals court judge.

ARTICLE

Trump Skirts Court Commands as Distrust Between Branches Spirals
Repeated compliance disputes and personal attacks on judges are straining relations between the executive branch and the judiciary.
By Charlie Savage
Published 2026-11-02 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/trump-courts-judges-orders.html

Since President Trump returned to office nearly two years ago, courts have frequently ordered his administration to pause or halt aggressive actions after they drew legal challenges. But again and again, his executive branch has skirted judicial constraints through delayed, contested or incomplete compliance, all while Mr. Trump has attacked judges appointed by presidents of both parties.

An examination of confrontations across the country shows a widening breakdown in trust between the executive branch and the federal judiciary. Judges increasingly greet Justice Department representations with skepticism. Administration officials, meanwhile, have treated courts with disdain — accusing judges of bias and seeking their removal. In an extraordinary step, the administration recently filed a misconduct complaint against nearly every active district judge in Minnesota.

The result has been a poisoning of the relations between the branches to such a degree that it is now straining the judiciary’s ability to serve as a check on executive power, as Mr. Trump approaches the second half of his term.

Some conflicts have been relatively straightforward, involving findings by courts that the executive branch failed to comply with binding orders — though typically without clear evidence that officials understood themselves to be deliberately violating judicial commands.

Others have been more complex and less clear-cut. Judges and the administration have fought over interpretations of specific judicial commands and failures by officials to live up to assurances they made to courts without explicit written orders. Sometimes, the executive branch has gotten around the courts by coming up with a new legal rationale for a policy that a judge said was not authorized by the authority officials initially cited.

Taken as a whole, the constant friction has undercut the reach of judicial authority as a check and balance on executive power and undermined the interbranch comity and trust that has traditionally helped keep the American system of government functional.

“The word ‘contempt’ clearly applies to what Trump and some of his people have been saying about the courts,” said Michael McConnell, a Stanford law professor and retired Republican-appointed appeals court judge. “The judges have become skeptical and certainly are no longer giving the Justice Department the benefit of the doubt.”

The interbranch tensions have gained urgency as election-related cases reach the courts ahead of this week’s midterms. The cases include a court order blocking Mr. Trump’s plan to bar the Postal Service from delivering certain mail ballots and multiple pending requests for judicial orders barring the administration from sending armed federal agents to polling places.

In a statement, Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said the Trump administration “has always, and will continue to follow all court orders.”

“Lower courts have engaged in an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions seeking to obstruct President Trump’s agenda that the American people elected him to enact,” she continued, “but with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, President Trump’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful.”

All modern administrations have sometimes bristled at judicial setbacks. President George W. Bush said he disagreed with a 2008 ruling about Guantánamo detainee rights but would abide by it. President Barack Obama criticized a campaign-finance decision in his 2010 State of the Union, with justices seated before him. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. in 2023 said he thought the court got the law wrong when it blocked his student-loan forgiveness program, and he vowed to try again under a different authority.

Part of what makes the second Trump administration different is the sheer volume of Mr. Trump’s confrontations with the courts. They also come as the administration has destroyed the traditional principle that the White House should play no role in directing law enforcement investigative and charging decisions in specific cases.

In some cases, skeptical judges have dismissed high-profile indictments and quashed investigative subpoenas, including at times finding that the Justice Department had improper motivations. And judges have increasingly been concluding that the department has been misrepresenting facts in civil litigation hearings and filings.

In a recent Duke Law Journal article, two University of Michigan law professors, Daniel T. Deacon and Leah M. Litman, dubbed the administration’s pattern of using evasive tactics to deflect limits imposed by the courts style as “legalistic noncompliance.” And that behavior inside courtrooms has been coupled with venomous personal rhetoric about judges out of court.

Compounding the stakes, other legal checks on Mr. Trump have weakened since his first term. The Supreme Court in 2024 declared that presidents have broad immunity for crimes committed with official powers.

Mr. Trump has installed in key executive branch legal positions loyalists who were vetted as being less likely to raise objections to his ideas than even very conservative and political appointed lawyers sometimes were in his first term, and he has forbidden dissent by government lawyers. With Republicans controlling both chambers, and with the departure of some Republicans who occasionally challenged Mr. Trump in his first term, Congress has so far rarely constrained him.

That has left the courts as a principal obstacle to parts of his agenda — and a recurring target of his wrath.

Failing to Obey Orders

Before becoming vice president, JD Vance repeatedly argued that presidents could and should ignore court orders they regarded as infringements on their rightful executive powers. Soon after taking office in early 2025, he declared on social media that “judges aren’t allowed to control the executive’s legitimate power.”

To date, however, the second Trump administration has not declared that it has intentionally violated a binding order. Instead, it has disputed the meaning of orders, challenged judges’ authority to issue them or attributed failures to comply to mistakes and overwhelmed systems.

In February, for example, a Justice Department lawyer filed a report in which she identified 52 court orders in New Jersey that the government had violated after reviewing 547 immigration actions. The violations included transferring detainees out of state despite a no-removal directive and missing deadlines to present detainees for a bond hearing. The department stressed there was no evidence that any of the failures were intentional.

Similarly, when the administration flooded Minneapolis with immigration agents for a major crackdown, Patrick J. Schiltz, a Bush appointee who was then the chief judge, found that the government had violated 210 orders in 143 immigration cases in the first two months of 2026. Low-level government lawyers told courts those failures, too, were unintentional, reflecting a system overwhelmed by the volume of arrests and litigation.

For the judges, however, the repeated failures raised a more fundamental issue: The executive branch had dispatched more than 3,000 immigration agents to the city without ensuring there would be adequate lawyerly resources to deal with the predictable surge of habeas cases.

The Justice Department responded to the criticism by attacking the judges themselves. A month ago, it filed a misconduct complaint against nearly every active federal district judge in Minnesota for publicly warning, in New York Times interviews, that the administration’s systematic failure to obey the orders during the surge had jeopardized the rule of law.

The complaint singled out Judge Schiltz, whom it accused of having “publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement.” The department this month also moved to disqualify him and another district judge from immigration-related cases.

“I not only have the right to speak out when I find the rule of law threatened — whether that be by negligence, inattention, incompetence, poor planning, or by conscious violation — I have a duty to do so,” Judge Schiltz said at a recent law school conference.

In July, Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong in the Central District of California, a Biden appointee, held an array of Trump administration officials in civil contempt for failing to comply with a discovery order to provide work messages exchanged by immigration agents on personal phones. The texts were sought by plaintiffs in a class-action lawsuit concerning the immigration crackdown in Los Angeles last year.

She imposed a $500-a-day fine, which the administration — which is contesting the contempt ruling — has been paying ever since. The payments do not come out of individual officials’ pockets, limiting their coercive effect.

Other failures have been short-lived, and followed by belated compliance after lawyers returned to court.

In September, Judge Timothy J. Kelly in the District of Columbia, a Trump appointee, blocked Mr. Trump from banning reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. Journalists from the outlets were nevertheless denied entry for hours, regaining access only after lawyers filed a notice of noncompliance.

Breaching Oral Understandings

Some of the sharpest disputes have concerned instances when judges have delivered oral directives instead of or before issuing formal written orders. Traditionally, the government routinely obeys oral commands and even expressions of judicial expectations — but the Trump administration has contested their status.

In March 2025, Mr. Trump invoked an 18th-century wartime deportation law to send planeloads of people accused of belonging to a Venezuelan gang to a notorious Salvadoran prison without an opportunity to contest their identities and removals in court.

The American Civil Liberties Union sued on their behalf, and Judge James E. Boasberg, an Obama appointee who is the chief Federal District Court judge in the District of Columbia, told the administration during a hearing that they should turn any planes around so migrants aboard could receive hearings.

He also said he would issue a formal written order so there would be no confusion and did so about an hour later. While it forbade removals from the United States, it did not mention planes already in the air.

In fact, two planes of migrants were mid-flight, and the administration did not return them, instead allowing them to fly on to El Salvador and complete the transfer. Administration lawyers later argued that “an oral directive is not enforceable as an injunction,” and that the narrower written order superseded the oral directive. Judge Boasberg rejected that argument.

A former Justice Department lawyer later told Congress that during planning for the deportations, Emil Bove III, a senior Trump appointee, had said that if a court enjoined the removals, the department “would need to consider telling the courts ‘fuck you’ and ignore any such order.” Mr. Bove, whom Mr. Trump has since appointed as an appellate judge, denied it.

Judge Boasberg sought to hold contempt proceedings and establish who made the key decisions and what they knew at the time. But an appellate panel with two Trump appointees voted 2-1 to shut them down. The full appeals court is now weighing whether to let Judge Boasberg hold his inquiry, meaning the issue remains unresolved — some 20 months later.

During the dispute, Mr. Trump attacked Judge Boasberg as a “radical Left Lunatic of a Judge, a troublemaker and agitator,” calling for his impeachment. Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., a Bush appointee, rebuked Mr. Trump, writing: “Impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreement concerning a judicial decision.”

A recent confrontation over Mr. Trump’s plans to remake a century-old public golf course in Washington followed a similar cycle of seeming understandings being breached, followed by judicial anger and accusations of bias.

A preservation group and two local golfers sued in February, arguing that the government was bypassing required reviews. Justice Department lawyers told Judge Ana Reyes, a Biden appointee, that the redesign remained conceptual and promised adequate advance notice before major work began. Relying on those assurances, she held off on an injunction.

Then, at 4:55 p.m. on Oct. 9, the Friday before a holiday weekend, the administration filed notice that it intended to clear as many as 529 trees for what it styled as “maintenance activities.” Workers began cutting the next morning, removing hundreds of trees before Judge Reyes intervened.

During a four-hour emergency hearing, she excoriated the government, saying it had lost “all of its credibility.” The Justice Department sought her recusal, citing her heated remarks as intemperate. She refused to step aside, and Mr. Trump called her a “crazed lunatic” on social media while declaring that the renovation did not need approval and that work would begin “IMMEDIATELY!”

That still-ongoing dispute — Judge Reyes on Oct. 30 ordered a formal inquiry into whether Trump administration lawyers made material misrepresentations to the court — illustrated an escalating tension. Traditionally, courts routinely have depended on Justice Department lawyers’ assurances, deferring to their factual representations, a practice known as the presumption of regularity.

But courts around the country are increasingly finding that the word of Justice Department lawyers in the second Trump administration is not reliable.

In February, for example, Judge Christine P. O’Hearn, a Biden appointee in New Jersey, required sworn affidavits from officials with firsthand knowledge about the transfer of an immigration detainee, writing that the presumption previously afforded to the executive branch “has been undeniably eroded.” She added that the court would “no longer blindly accept statements of fact” from the government.

And in May, when Judge Mary S. McElroy, a Trump appointee in Rhode Island, quashed an administration subpoena for transgender children’s medical records, she approvingly cited a similar rebuke by another judge in Oregon, who had said the Justice Department could no longer be taken at its word, given how the department had withheld and misrepresented salient information in the case.

“D.O.J. has proven unworthy of this trust at every point in this case,” Judge McElroy wrote.

But the frequency with which judges of both parties are finding the Trump Justice Department to be unworthy of trust is contributing to a downward cycle. It creates pressure on judges to issue more detailed restrictions and to demand more evidence — steps the administration may then portray as unwarranted interference.

The cycle has also been exacerbated by an administration tactic of sometimes narrowly interpreting its obligations under court orders.

That tactic was central to the case of Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, whom the government mistakenly repatriated to El Salvador last year despite an immigration judge’s order barring his removal to his home country.

After the Supreme Court directed the government to “facilitate” his return, the administration argued that it needed only to let him back in if he showed up at the border, not to seek his release from El Salvador.

A federal appeals court rejected that interpretation as “not well taken.” Writing for the court, Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, a Reagan appointee, warned that the branches were increasingly coming “too close to grinding irrevocably against one another in a conflict that promises to diminish both.”

“The respect that courts must accord the Executive must be reciprocated by the Executive’s respect for the courts,” he added. “Too often today this has not been the case, as calls for impeachment of judges for decisions the Executive disfavors and exhortations to disregard court orders sadly illustrate.”

Under such pressure, the administration eventually retrieved Mr. Abrego Garcia from El Salvador.

Exploiting Loopholes

In other cases, the administration has found ways around court action blocking its policies by pursuing the same policies using alternative legal rationales.

In early 2025, the White House ordered a broad spending freeze, prompting agencies to withhold foreign aid and domestic grants. Recipients sued, and judges blocked the White House’s directive. But Trump political appointees at agencies invoked other legal authorities to keep withholding the funds, saying they were making independent decisions rather than carrying out the blocked directives.

Such disputes are inherently ambiguous. Presidents of both parties have tried similar gambits when blocked by the courts. But the Trump administration has been particularly aggressive in pressing forward rather than acquiescing to apparent court defeats.

When the Supreme Court struck down Mr. Trump’s novel use of an emergency powers law to impose tariffs in February, he attacked the justices who voted against him as “a disgrace,” “incompetent” and an “embarrassment to their families.” Mr. Vance called the 6-3 ruling “lawlessness from the court, plain and simple.” Within hours, Mr. Trump imposed a 10 percent global tariff, citing a different legal authority, also novel. The move prompted renewed litigation over whether he could lawfully impose such import taxes.

While appeals of adverse rulings are a normal part of litigation, the second Trump administration has been unusually aggressive in appealing.

The administration has started making routine use of the Supreme Court’s once-rare emergency docket, appealing district court orders before litigation has had a chance to play out at an unprecedented rate, according to data compiled by Stephen I. Vladeck, a Georgetown University law professor.

Professor Vladeck, who is also the author of a forthcoming Harvard Law Review article documenting the confrontational dynamic between the judiciary and the executive branch under the second Trump administration, said the pattern was damaging both institutions — undermining the credibility of the Justice Department and the courts’ neutral, above-the-fray image.

Professor Vladeck said that in the long term, the tensions risked “eroding trust in our institutions, when those institutions depend in lots of ways, big and small, on the very trust that is now in jeopardy.”

SUMMARY

Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline. For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. Mr. Critch often hears from Americans who don’t realize the show is Canadian.

ARTICLE

A Canadian Sketch Show Beats American Late Night to the Punchline
The long-running comedy show “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” is having a heyday playing with the fraught relationship between President Trump and Canada.
By Shawna Richer
Published 2026-11-02 05:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/world/canada/this-hour-has-22-minutes-trump-carney.html

Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline.

Some 48 hours later, and a week before the rapper Nicki Minaj traveled on Air Force One to rally for President Trump in Michigan, “22 Minutes” imagined the MAGA darling as Ms. Zacharia’s successor.

In both cases, the creative team on the show, Canada’s version of “Saturday Night Live,” did not wait for their weekly broadcast. The polished sketches went straight to the show’s TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, attracting nearly 24 million views.

For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. But “22 Minutes” is having a renaissance buoyed by Mr. Trump — in particular his trade war, tariffs, threats and insults toward Canada. Television audiences are up, and social media viewership is growing rapidly.

“Social media has opened up our show beyond what I thought was capable,” said Stacey McGunnigle, a cast member and writer who has created and portrayed many MAGA women, most memorably Karoline Leavitt, Natalie Harp and, ever so briefly, Ms. Zacharia.

“The show’s been on a long time, and we can be the butt of the joke sometimes as far as what people think our demographic is,” she said. “But in the six seasons I’ve been here, more young people are coming up to us who love it and watch it all the time.”

The characters Ms. McGunnigle most likes to play are pro-life, pro-gun, pro-war and pro-push-up bra. “Too much makeup, no moral compass, a pathological desire to protect the patriarchy, and blonde. Terrifying!” she said.

The show, which airs Tuesday nights on the publicly funded Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, leans progressive but traffics in nonpartisan political satire — anyone in the headlines is fair game. Since Mr. Trump began his second term, the show routinely points its lens at the United States and its deteriorating relationship with Canada.

“This Hour Has 22 Minutes” is the nosy neighbor with permanently raised eyebrows.

Fans include Graydon Carter, the Canadian-born former editor of Vanity Fair and co-founder of Spy magazine.

“Canadians are feeling an uncharacteristic blush of patriotism,” he said. “And there’s nothing like friction and impending chaos to bring out the satirists.”

Ms. McGunnigle operates with fast-twitch newsroom instincts. As soon as Ms. Zacharia held her first disastrous White House briefing, she knew the show had to do something. “And that 14-minute press conference,” Ms. McGunnigle said. “I felt we weren’t going to have her for long.”

While they were shooting the piece a few days later, Ms. Zacharia was fired. Ms. McGunnigle immediately began improvising, turning a sketch about Ms. Zacharia’s disastrous first news conference into one about her last. A bonus: “Saturday Night Live” was dark that week.

“Stacey McGunnigle’s Katie Zacharia was superb,” Mr. Carter said. “But for her it was a bit like getting the coveted lead in a play that closes on opening night.”

The weekly broadcast averages 571,000 viewers, up 31 percent from 435,000 last season, with 25- to 54-year-olds the leading demographic. The “Meet Katie” sketch has more than 21.5 million views across social media, and the first Leavitt sketch more than 7.8 million.

Mark Critch, a veteran cast member and writer in his 24th season, plays Mr. Trump.

“We’re the quiet house next door, and the house on the other side of the fence, they have a lot of loud parties, and there’s always arguing in the yard,” he said. “We’re watching over the fence going, ‘Oh, my God, what’s going on?’ We get to observe, which is a good thing for comedy.”

Mr. Critch has taken his Trump to Greenland. He whipped up a “Quiet, Piggy” sketch after the president insulted a reporter with the phrase. As Mr. Trump, he fulminated over The New York Times’s exclusive interview with Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a cold open. In an attempt to rekindle Canada-U.S. relations Mr. Critch, as himself, met with Gov. Janet Mills of Maine, who implored him to ask Canadians to resume visiting her state.

“I mean God almighty,” he said, “Even with all the arguing that goes on, there’s nothing a Canadian gets excited about more than American attention.”

Drawing inspiration from the Trump administration isn’t entirely new for the show. What is more recent is the speed at which the show reacts to news. Without social media, the show, taped on Mondays, would struggle to stay timely on Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States.

“TV shows are big machines, and you don’t want to be late to the party,” Mr. Critch said. “There’s another audience that we can get to right away. When something happens in the moment, now the whole building pivots.”

Mike Allison, the executive producer and showrunner, said more people tuned in as Canadian-U.S. tensions escalated. Especially amusing has been the opportunity for interplay between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney, played by Mark McKinney, on the war in Iran, reverse psychology, and McDonald’s. But not every sketch needs a Canadian tie.

“When writers pitch Kristi Noem or Kash Patel, that’s us looking over the fence at all the crazy characters running the country,” Mr. Allison said. “But U.S. politics have become Canadian politics.”

“22 Minutes has the DNA of the knowing outsider,” Mr. Carter said.

It always has. Twenty-five years ago, “Talking to Americans” was a popular segment testing how little Americans knew about Canada. Highlights included a Columbia University professor agreeing that the government should stop putting senior citizens on ice floes to die, and Mike Huckabee, then the governor of Arkansas, congratulating Canada on preserving its national igloo.

Mr. Critch often hears from Americans who don’t realize the show is Canadian.

“They will say, ‘Oh, good, thank you. That’s what I feel.’ But then you’ll get some saying, ‘You don’t know anything! That’s our president! Shut up!’” he said. “Something I see that’s actually very Canadian is Americans saying they’re sorry. ‘I’m so sorry this is happening. I’m so sorry they’re saying these things about your country. We love Canadians.’”

SUMMARY

Iran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agrees to a set of demands, its foreign ministry said on Monday, after a week of intensified negotiations to avert a return to war. The trip to Tehran, the Iranian capital, came after multiple rounds of talks between Qatari and Iranian officials in Iran and Qatar over the past week. In his news conference on Monday, Mr. Baghaei said that the United States and Israel had attacked Iran in June 2025 shortly after Iranian officials had held negotiations with Washington.

ARTICLE

Iran Says It Would Reopen Strait of Hormuz in 2 Days as Part of U.S. Deal
Iranian officials spoke of some progress in negotiating to reopen the strait, a vital oil and gas shipping lane, even as they prepare for all-out war.
By Erika Solomon, Sanam Mahoozi, Adam Rasgon and Vivian Nereim
Published 2026-11-02 13:44 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/world/middleeast/iran-deal-strait-of-hormuz.html

Iran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agrees to a set of demands, its foreign ministry said on Monday, after a week of intensified negotiations to avert a return to war.

A Qatari delegation led by Ali Al Thawadi, a senior Qatari official, arrived in Tehran on Monday evening to meet with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to continue talks aimed at achieving an agreement between Iran and the United States, according to two diplomats briefed on the visit.

The trip to Tehran, the Iranian capital, came after multiple rounds of talks between Qatari and Iranian officials in Iran and Qatar over the past week.

Iran’s demands, which include the Trump administration’s lifting sanctions on Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets, have appeared difficult for Washington to accept.

The foreign ministry’s spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, made the comments hours after President Trump had said at a campaign rally that he might eventually decide to give Iran “the hammer” if the two sides could not reach a deal to end the war.

Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas shipping in the Persian Gulf, after U.S. and Israeli forces attacked the country in February. That move roiled energy markets, and continues to shake the global economy.

American and Israeli military officials have been drawing up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after this week’s U.S. midterm elections. Iranian leaders have warned that, if the country were attacked again, its forces would expand their range of targets, and they are now publicly considering a withdrawal from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, which prohibits the development of a nuclear weapon.

Propelled by increasingly bellicose rhetoric from both Iran and the United States, Qatari mediators have been pushing to broker a last-ditch deal between the two countries.

In recent days, Iranian officials have signaled that those negotiations have made some progress, though Mr. Baghaei stressed that they were not at a point where Iranian negotiators were prepared to hold direct talks with their U.S. counterparts.

“If Iran’s legitimate demands are accepted and implemented, it would be possible to put the entire plan into operation within two days, restore security to the Strait of Hormuz, and initiate the negotiation process,” Mr. Baghaei told reporters on Monday. “The realization of this depends entirely on Washington’s will and decision.”

The global benchmark oil price, apparently responding to potential progress in the talks, declined about 8 percent on Monday to about $104 a barrel.

Still, conditions around the Strait of Hormuz remain dangerous. More than 35 ships were attacked in October, more than in any other month since the war began.

In September, Iran proposed a phased deal to reopen the strait, in which the warring countries would take turns to make concessions, culminating in Tehran ensuring safe passage through the strait, while Washington would lift a naval blockade on Iran’s ports.

After that initial phase, Iran proposed that the two sides could begin negotiating a comprehensive peace deal that would restart talks over its nuclear enrichment program. U.S. officials rejected this proposal, saying Iran should commit to nuclear concessions earlier.

Qatari mediators have managed to revive negotiations over the past few weeks, initially accelerating the implementation of the initial phase to five days, and more recently condensing that to two days, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told the broadcaster Al Jazeera on Saturday.

Mr. Araghchi made no mention of nuclear concessions. In a televised interview on Saturday, one of the officials overseeing the talks, Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s national security adviser, said nuclear negotiations could begin only after Washington had met Iranian conditions.

Alongside the demands related to sanctions and frozen assets, Mr. Araghchi said in his interview that the U.S. would also have to recognize a deal between Oman and Iran for administering passage through the strait in the future.

At the same time, Mr. Rezaei said that a recent letter sent to him about negotiations from Vice President JD Vance had shown a changed tone toward Iran, which the Iranian official called a “good sign.”

Even as Gulf leaders pin their hopes on a diplomatic solution, they are “braced for the worst,” said Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates, at the Manama Dialogue security conference over the weekend. The stakes of the negotiations are particularly high for Gulf Arab countries, which were battered by Iranian drone and missile attacks in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes.

“The rules of logic tell us that the Iranian stand and U.S. stand are far apart,” Mr. Gargash said at the conference in Bahrain. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”

Iranian officials have repeatedly stressed that they are suspicious the talks could unravel. In his news conference on Monday, Mr. Baghaei said that the United States and Israel had attacked Iran in June 2025 shortly after Iranian officials had held negotiations with Washington.

Mr. Trump’s current stance remains ambiguous. On Sunday, he told journalists that he had had a “good talk” with President Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel over the weekend, which included a discussion of the war.

“The only reason we’re not finished with Iran is I want to be nice — I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” he told a campaign rally in Iowa later on Sunday. “But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer.”

Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Israel Turns to Next Big Question: Who Gets a Shot at Being Prime Minister?
Party leaders will make competing cases to the Israeli president for either Benjamin Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot to get the first chance to build a governing coalition.
By Aaron Boxerman
Published 2026-11-02 10:30 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/world/middleeast/israel-election-prime-minister.html

This week, Israeli party leaders will trickle into the residence of President Isaac Herzog to officially recommend their pick for Israel’s next prime minister following the inconclusive election last Tuesday.

In livestreamed meetings to begin on Wednesday, politicians from 11 parties, including those representing secular liberals, ultra-Orthodox Jews and Arab voters, will make a pitch to Mr. Herzog. He will then bestow the mandate to build a coalition on whichever candidate he deems the most viable, who will have up to six weeks to form a government.

Most party leaders are expected to back either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the longtime right-wing leader, or his main center-right rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Neither man won a clear 61-seat majority in balloting for the 120-member Parliament, most likely meaning that weeks or months of negotiations among the parties and elected lawmakers lie ahead.

Behind the scenes, politicians are weighing the path forward and wrangling for the upper hand. No one emerged from the election with a decisive victory, leaving Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Eisenkot and the rest trying to cajole and squeeze opponents and would-be allies alike.

“It’s a game of chicken,” said Nevo Cohen, a political strategist who ran the 2022 election campaign for the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Mr. Netanyahu has long exercised a tight grip over his bloc of conservative and religious parties. But some could always bolt — potentially ultra-Orthodox or more moderate right-wingers in his own Likud faction — in exchange for influence in an Eisenkot-led government, political analysts said.

Mr. Eisenkot could also look to form a government by relying on Arab parties that have long sat on the sidelines of Israeli politics, or by partnering with Mr. Netanyahu to form a unity government. Either option would be tricky because some of his allies promised on the campaign trail never to work with Mr. Netanyahu, or with Arab lawmakers to form a government.

On Monday, Avigdor Liberman, a key figure in the opposition bloc, said he would recommend Mr. Eisenkot for prime minister. But he reiterated his longstanding vow not to share power with Mr. Netanyahu or serve in a minority government with Arab parties, further complicating matters for Mr. Eisenkot.

All the parties “are checking their internal situation to see how much room they have to maneuver,” said Lior Chorev, a political strategist who worked on former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s campaign, which picked up 12 seats in Parliament last week. “They want to know how far they can go.”

After the last election in 2022, Mr. Netanyahu swept to power with a 64-seat majority, allowing him to establish the most far-right government in Israel’s history. This time, the calculations are considerably more complex. Mr. Netanyahu and his allies’ majority dropped to 53 seats in Parliament, while Mr. Eisenkot’s opposition bloc garnered 48 seats.

Surging turnout among Israel’s Arab citizens also helped deliver a historic 19 seats to the two main Arab-led parties, turning them into potential kingmakers.

An Israeli opposition official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private negotiations, said that party leaders were feeling out one another’s red lines. These leaders were also drawing up legislative plans for when Israel’s Parliament, the Knesset, is sworn in this week, the official said.

The coalition talks will be extraordinarily sensitive because they could easily collapse, sending Israel back to another round of elections, said Izhar Shay, a former centrist lawmaker. So in making deals or concessions, politicians need to be cognizant of how that might play with their voters, should they find themselves back at polling stations quicker than expected.

“The parties are negotiating — but in reality, they’re still campaigning, because this might turn into an election campaign in just a few months,” said Mr. Shay. “So they’re being cautious about what they say, because it could hurt them in elections which might be in four months, rather than four years.”

Mr. Eisenkot has at least three paths to power. He could try to pick off some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies; he could form a unity government with the prime minister he swore to oust; or he could lean on the Arab bloc — and risk splitting his base.

Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s supporters say that joining with Mr. Netanyahu — although many detest the prime minister — might make the most sense, since it would keep ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties out of power.

But Mr. Netanyahu is a famously slippery partner, and he has walked away from political agreements before when they no longer served him.

In 2020, a unity government between Mr. Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, a centrist opposition leader, collapsed after less than a year of power sharing. Under their coalition agreement, Mr. Netanyahu was supposed to yield the prime minister’s seat to Mr. Gantz, but he instead dissolved the Knesset and called new elections.

“We thought we were doing the right thing, and in the end Netanyahu cheated us,” said Mr. Shay, a lawmaker in Mr. Gantz’s party at the time.

But to form a government without Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Eisenkot would most likely have to lean on the Arab parties, in particular the relatively pragmatic Raam party, which got eight seats. The Joint List, which netted 11 seats, is unlikely to join his governing coalition, but it could block a no-confidence vote against it in the Knesset, allowing him to form a “minority government” with fewer than 61 seats.

Since last week, Mr. Netanyahu has claimed that Arab citizens were “stealing the election.” His Likud party has alleged, without providing proof, that the results were subject to widespread tampering. Election officials have repeatedly said there was no evidence of systematic interference in the vote.

Analysts say Mr. Netanyahu’s racially charged campaign aims at further discrediting any attempt by Mr. Eisenkot to engage Arab parties as partners.

“That’s the only scenario that Netanyahu is afraid of, so he’s trying to do things that will make a minority government impossible,” said Michael Koplow, an expert at the Israel Policy Forum, a research group.

An incident that surfaced Thursday gave Mr. Netanyahu an opening to cast doubt on the legitimacy of the high Arab vote.

Noam Sohlberg, the Supreme Court justice overseeing the country’s elections committee, said in a letter that he had seen intelligence indicating potential “improper influence through foreign funding” in the elections. He did not elaborate or provide evidence and said he “could not attest to the veracity of the suspicions.” He nevertheless sent a letter authorizing the head of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to investigate.

The Likud party quickly issued a statement saying that the Arab parties had “stolen the elections in Israel.” The party incorrectly cited Mr. Sohlberg’s letter to Shin Bet, falsely saying it had reported that “foreign officials have bribed voters on behalf of the Arab parties.”

Three days later, Mr. Sohlberg issued a clarification, saying that there was no reason to “doubt the votes cast by Arab citizens.” But the claim that Arab parties had tainted the elections had already become a right-wing talking point.

On Sunday, the Likud party again denounced the results of the vote, saying that a “black cloud” was hovering over the election.

Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting from Modiin, Israel.

ARTICLE

Lawyers Spar Over Trump’s Executive Privilege in Kennedy Center Case
The administration is withholding communications sought by a Democratic lawmaker who is suing over the president’s management of the arts venue.
By Julia Jacobs
Published 2026-11-03 19:41 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/arts/trump-kennedy-center-executive-privilege.html

The Justice Department and lawyers for a Democratic congresswoman suing the Kennedy Center tangled in federal court on Tuesday over whether the Trump administration can legally withhold communications related to the president’s management of the arts institution.

Mr. Trump took over as chairman of the Kennedy Center at the start of his second term, making it a centerpiece of his efforts to rid Washington’s cultural institutions of what he has described as liberal leanings. He announced in February that the center would close for two years of renovations, and he has pushed for his name to occupy a prominent place on the building, which is a memorial to President Kennedy.

Lawyers for Representative Joyce Beatty of Ohio, who is an ex officio board member at the center, have sought dozens of text messages and emails involving close aides of Mr. Trump. They have described the exchanges as critical evidence in their lawsuit seeking to halt the two-year closure of the center for a $257 million renovation project.

In recent weeks, the legal battle has diverged into a fight over whether Mr. Trump should be granted executive privilege in his Kennedy Center dealings to protect his ability to speak candidly and confidentially with aides.

The Justice Department has blocked access to communications involving aides such as Natalie Harp, a chief gatekeeper to the president, as well as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is helping Mr. Trump oversee the center. The exchanges are described in court papers as intended to reflect private deliberations by the president and his staff.

In the hearing at Federal District Court in Washington on Tuesday, Nathaniel Zelinsky, a lawyer for Ms. Beatty, argued that executive privilege did not extend to Mr. Trump’s role as chairman of the center’s board.

“That would be a recipe to basically say anything in the president’s life is subject to executive privilege,” Mr. Zelinsky said.

William Jankowski, a lawyer for the Justice Department, said the president had an official role at the Kennedy Center that was assigned by Congress and involved appointing members of the board. That provision put the arts venue in the scope of Mr. Trump’s executive duties, he argued.

Judge Christopher R. Cooper, who is overseeing the case, signaled that he may ultimately decide that some communications are protected while others are not. The key question, he said, is which “hat” Mr. Trump was wearing in the context of the specific exchange: president of the United States or chairman of the board?

If the discussion revolves around core policy or politics related to the Kennedy Center, Judge Cooper suggested that the Justice Department may have an argument that executive privilege applies. If Mr. Trump is discussing the “color of the carpets” or “the ins and outs of the HVAC system,” the judge said, “that’s a tough argument.”

By taking over the Kennedy Center, Mr. Trump has established a relationship with the institution unlike that of any other president. A builder by trade, he has weighed in regularly on the minutiae of a facility that he has called “dilapidated,” helping to secure $257 million from Congress for renovations.

The board, composed mostly of Mr. Trump’s loyalists, voted to add his name to the building’s exterior in December in recognition of that effort.

In response to the lawsuit by Ms. Beatty, Judge Cooper ordered Mr. Trump’s name removed in June and temporarily blocked the plan for a two-year closure, ruling that the board had not given it proper scrutiny.

The Justice Department has been working to persuade him to change his mind after the board voted twice more to close. The center is “in a state of limbo that we’re trying to resolve as quickly as possible,” Mr. Jankowski said.

Ms. Beatty’s suit argues that trustees have continued to ignore their responsibility to the institution, acting out of fealty to the president and using the closure to deflect from the financial and artistic decline of the institution under Mr. Trump’s leadership.

The Kennedy Center’s main building has been off limits to the public since September, in what officials have described as a temporary closure intended to protect the public from crumbling infrastructure. A smaller nearby annex has been kept open for limited programming.

SUMMARY

Ryu Murakami, a novelist, filmmaker and television host whose bracing psychological explorations of the underside of Japanese society made him one of his country’s most popular writers, died on Sept. 17 at his home in Tokyo. Mr. Murakami wrote his first novel, “Almost Transparent Blue,” while still in art school. After the success of “Almost Transparent Blue,” Mr. Murakami wrote more than 40 additional novels, as well as countless short stories, screenplays and nonfiction essays.

ARTICLE

Ryu Murakami Has Died. His Writing Explored the Dark Side of Japan.
His books about sex, drugs and social misfits amid the country’s economic boom — and subsequent bust — sold millions of copies.
By Clay Risen
Published 2026-11-03 21:48 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/books/ryu-murakami-dead.html

Ryu Murakami, a novelist, filmmaker and television host whose bracing psychological explorations of the underside of Japanese society made him one of his country’s most popular writers, died on Sept. 17 at his home in Tokyo. He was 74.

Gentosha, the publisher of many of his novels, announced his death, but did not provide a cause.

Mr. Murakami wrote his first novel, “Almost Transparent Blue,” while still in art school. Published in 1976, it depicted a side of Japan that ran counter to the strait-laced, socially conservative image promoted by the nation’s mainstream — one of aimless youth, orgies and copious amounts of drugs.

The book was a huge commercial and critical success, selling more than 1.2 million copies in its first six months and winning the esteemed Akutagawa literary prize. It established Mr. Murakami as a voice of Japan’s counterculture and a sharp-eyed analyst of the cultural and social costs of the country’s rapid postwar expansion.

“I have a feeling that during this chaotic postwar rush to tremendous economic growth, we Japanese may have lost or have sacrificed something very dear,” he told The New York Times in 1977. “And instead of sitting idly by and moaning, I believe novelists must provide active leadership in this quest.”

Mr. Murakami was not related to Haruki Murakami, another beloved Japanese author and a close contemporary. They were friends, but took very different approaches to writing: While Haruki Murakami’s densely psychological books lean heavily on dream fugues and magical realism, Ryu Murakami’s novels were grounded in blade-sharp criticism of Japanese culture and politics.

After the success of “Almost Transparent Blue,” Mr. Murakami wrote more than 40 additional novels, as well as countless short stories, screenplays and nonfiction essays. As a regular radio and TV host, he became a familiar voice and face to millions of Japanese.

He directed five films, including “Topaz” (1992), released in the United States as “Tokyo Decadence” — an unsubtle title for a movie centered on a prostitute named Ai and her encounters with Japan’s wealthiest and kinkiest.

His 1997 novel “Audition” was the basis for the 1999 movie of the same name that became a cornerstone of the so-called J-horror movement, alongside films like “Ringu” (1998) and “Ju-on: The Grudge” (2002).

The story revolves around Aoyama, a widowed TV producer who uses the pretense of auditioning actresses to find a girlfriend, eventually falling for a mysterious woman named Asami. As Aoyama slowly, terrifyingly learns the truth about her, Mr. Murakami unravels a story that revels in gory details and jump-scare shocks.

“The prose in these passages is elegiac and affecting, but it has the sharp, visceral feel of the butcher’s knife or surgeon’s scalpel,” the Scottish novelist Irvine Welsh wrote in a 2009 review of the English edition for The Guardian.

As Japan sank into the economic and social doldrums of the late 1990s, Mr. Murakami’s novels began to feel almost prophetic in their depiction of a population ready to burst in violent rage at suffocating social restrictions and the fading hope for a better tomorrow.

“Many Japanese are dissatisfied and frustrated,” he told The Financial Times in 2013. “But they are not good at expressing those feelings, so they tend to wall themselves off. And because they have this pent-up anger, they are very unstable.”

While keeping up a steady pace of fiction writing, Mr. Murakami turned his pen toward nonfiction as well, in essays, opinion pieces and books that assailed the government’s failure to adapt to the end of Japan’s decades-long economic expansion.

“The days when everything worked like a dream and everyone’s standard of living kept rising are over, and have been for a long time,” he wrote in a guest essay for The New York Times in 2009. “Now that there is no longer enough money, the Japanese public has to make some hard choices.”

Surprisingly for a novelist who cut his teeth on the counterculture, Mr. Murakami became a favorite of the establishment. He once gave a lecture on Japan’s cultural crisis to 100 executives from NEC, the electronics company, and he served as an unofficial adviser to top politicians and policymakers.

But as a novelist, he insisted, his responsibility was always to the reader, not to politics.

“I’m not trying to make the world a better place,” he told The Financial Times in 2013. “Unlike politicians, whose job is to work on the masses by making society fairer and more prosperous, the duty of the novelist is to target a single reader, one person reading alone.”

Ryunosuke Murakami was born on Feb. 19, 1952, in Sasebo, a port city on the southern island of Kyushu. His father, Shinichiro, taught art; his mother, Fujiko, taught math.

Sasebo is home to major U.S. Navy installations, and from childhood Ryū was both drawn to and repulsed by America’s influence on Japanese society.

He was a rebel from an early age: As a teenager, he played drums in a rock band, and he and some friends once barricaded themselves on the roof of their high school, resulting in a three-month suspension.

After graduating, he moved to Tokyo, where he enrolled in the sculpture program at Musashino Art University. He also began writing, and dropped out of school following the success of “Almost Transparent Blue.”

Mr. Murakami’s survivors include his wife, Tazuko Takahashi, and their son.

Despite his mainstream success, Mr. Murakami assured interviewers that his heart remained with the fringes. He liked to tell a story about getting a letter from a girl who had run away from home.

“While she was waiting for a bus, she was reading one of my novels and got encouraged by the idea that there were misfits like her out there in society,” he told Vice in 2013. “Reactions and episodes like that make me feel really very happy.”

SUMMARY

Whichever party wins, the Senate majority is likely to be narrow. A split down the middle means a Republican Senate, given the vice president’s power to break deadlocks with a vote as the chamber’s “presiding officer.” That gave them a Senate majority.

ARTICLE

It’s Election Day
And we’re looking at the fight for the Senate.
By Sam Sifton
Published 2026-11-03 11:24 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/briefing/its-election-day.html

Whichever party wins, the Senate majority is likely to be narrow. Maybe neither party will have a majority!

Carl Hulse, our chief Washington correspondent, lays out the possibilities and the consequences. There are a number of them that could change how the Senate functions during the second half of President Trump’s term in office.

A slim majority empowers senators in the middle.

Democrats have 47 seats, and they’re likely to pick up more. With a majority, Democrats would make legislation impossible for the Republican leadership, but anything close to 50 could embolden Republicans who are willing to break with Trump and the party at large.

That’s Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine (should Collins win her re-election race). A slim majority for the Republicans could also put pressure on a potential party-switcher like Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, who has quarreled with Democratic leadership but who has said that he does not intend to switch.

A 50-50 tie is bad news for JD Vance.

A split down the middle means a Republican Senate, given the vice president’s power to break deadlocks with a vote as the chamber’s “presiding officer.” But a tied Senate also leaves both parties in a situation where even a single defection could alter the outcome of a vote. And a single-member absence could make it impossible to move ahead with a bill. It would also mean that Vice President JD Vance, who is expected to be a leading Republican candidate for president in 2028, couldn’t leave Washington to campaign while the Senate is in session. He’d have to be nearby to break tie votes.

In that scenario, Democrats would likely lobby Murkowski to flip her party affiliation, though she’s unlikely to do so because she’d lose her powerful committee positions by changing sides. But it has happened before, Carl reminds. In 2001, Jim Jeffords, a Republican senator from Vermont, became an independent and started caucusing with the Democrats. That gave them a Senate majority.

Independents could scramble the picture.

There are two independents currently in the Senate: Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine. Both caucus with Democrats. But at least three more are running, and they say they wouldn’t support the leadership of either party. The idea is, their independence would give them leverage over both parties.

You have to get into the way-back machine to see the last time that happened, Carl reports:

The Senate has not faced such a situation since 1952, when Senator Wayne Morse, Republican of Oregon, declared himself an independent, later moving a folding chair into the center aisle of the Senate. He was denied committee seats and ultimately joined the Democratic Party.

This could all take a while.

Challenges to election results could mean it takes time to seat new members. For example, Republicans may contest the results of the race in Alaska, where the Democrats recruited a candidate to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent. If the seat remains open during litigation, it would leave the balance of power in the Senate in question.

For how long? In 2008, it took more than eight months for Senator Al Franken, the Minnesota Democrat, to gain his seat amid a protracted recount and court battle.

Trump Is Watching Fox News, and He Is Not Thrilled

Like millions of his fellow Americans, President Trump tuned into Fox News on Tuesday for the latest updates on the midterm elections.

He did not like what he saw.

SUMMARY

Floods have overwhelmed parts of the parched American Southwest in recent days and weeks, pouring water into critically low reservoirs. But the deluge did little to ease worries over the water crisis that required significant limits on usage across the Colorado River basin earlier this year. ARTICLE

Why Floodwaters Won’t Solve the Southwestern Water Crisis
A series of storms has added to reservoirs in the Colorado River basin, but the long-term water outlook remains bleak.
By Scott Dance
Published 2026-11-03 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/climate/floods-arizona-colorado-river-water.html

Floods have overwhelmed parts of the parched American Southwest in recent days and weeks, pouring water into critically low reservoirs.

But the deluge did little to ease worries over the water crisis that required significant limits on usage across the Colorado River basin earlier this year.

Instead, it exemplified a sort of weather whiplash that is becoming more common as the climate warms, making it harder to maintain a stable water supply for the West. Right after enduring one of its driest stretches of spring and summer on record, the Southwest is now experiencing one of its wettest autumns.

“It gives us a little bit of breathing room, but we’ve just got to see how much it snows this year,” said Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

Here’s what to know about the floods and what they mean for the Colorado basin, which supplies water to 40 million people and 5.5 million acres of farmland across parts of seven U.S. states, as well as about two dozen Native tribes and two Mexican states.

How much has the rain increased water supplies?

Water levels have risen sharply in Lake Powell, the nation’s second-largest reservoir, which straddles the Utah-Arizona border. The lake’s surface rose by nearly 16 feet from mid-September through the end of October. Lake Powell is expected to continue to rise once floods that hit parts of Colorado and Arizona last weekend flow downstream.

Along with Lake Mead, Lake Powell provides a stable water supply for the Colorado River’s populous and growing lower basin, including parts of Arizona, Nevada and California.

Both reservoirs had hit record lows in August.

Will the rainfall help reverse water shortages?

Lake Powell remains less than 26 percent full, so it would take years of rainy and snowy weather — along with continuing water use cuts — to replenish it. Even with the recent precipitation, on Sunday the lake was only at 41 percent of its average for this time of year, dating to 1963.

The Colorado’s flow has diminished by about 20 percent over the past two decades, as the Southwest has endured a stretch scientists say is its driest in 1,200 years.

Nevertheless, the wet weather could provide some medium-term benefits, Ms. Sorensen said.

The rain has saturated soils across much of the Southwest, causing more precipitation to run off rather than percolate into the ground. While that is making the floods worse, it could also mean that more of any precipitation that falls in the coming months will make it into reservoirs, Ms. Sorensen said.

It may also prevent many farmers from drawing water from the river, she said, easing the strain on reservoirs.

Does the recent wet period suggest a snowy winter could be ahead?

There is no observed link between wet fall weather and the snowy winters needed to ensure a stable year-round water supply, said Cody Moser, a senior hydrologist at the Colorado Basin River Forecast Center.

A year ago, the Southwest received similarly heavy autumn rains, but a record snow drought followed in the winter. That led to drastic water use cuts this summer in states that rely on the Colorado. Melting snowpack is responsible for roughly 80 percent of the river’s flow in a typical year.

Is the ‘super’ El Niño causing the floods?

It’s definitely contributing. The climate pattern that is strengthening in the Pacific Ocean is increasing the amount of moisture reaching the Southwest, Mr. Moser said.

El Niño is tied to unusually warm waters across the central and eastern Pacific, where it has been increasing hurricane activity. That tropical moisture is fueling storms affecting the Southwest.

The phenomenon is known for delivering heavier-than-normal winter precipitation to Southern California and, to a lesser extent, the Southwest.

What about climate change?

Climate change is also adding to the intensity of the rain, as well as the whiplash the region is experiencing between drought and floods.

As temperatures warm, the air can hold more water. That means storms can carry greater amounts of precipitation and deliver more intense rainfall than in the past.

That increased capacity to hold water vapor means the air can also suck more moisture out of the landscape. So during dry seasons, vegetation and soil can become parched more quickly — counterintuitively, exacerbating drought.

“We are seeing a higher frequency of more extreme events on both ends,” Mr. Moser said. “Unfortunately, the drier events have been outweighing the wetter events over the past 25 years.”

Recent water extremes on Lake Powell demonstrate the challenging trend.

The lake received record inflows in October of about 1.6 million acre-feet, Mr. Moser said. One acre-foot of water is enough to supply two or three households for a year.

Compare that to the 1.1 million acre-feet that flowed into the lake during a key stretch from April to July, when winter snowmelt typically refills the reservoir. That was the second-lowest inflow on record for that period.

Such extremes are becoming more common, Mr. Moser said: “They both happened in the same year.”

jet-engines-ai-data-center-generators-boneyard.html

SUMMARY

But America’s soaring demand for electricity to power data centers is bringing them back to life. And data centers, desperate for power, are snapping them up. Companies supplying power for data centers, including those working with Google, say they will use ProEnergy turbines converted from jet engines, according to regulatory filings.

ARTICLE

Old, Polluting Jet Engines Are Being Scavenged to Power Data Centers
By Hiroko Tabuchi and Gabriela Bhaskar
Published 2026-11-03 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/climate/jet-engines-ai-data-center-generators-boneyard.html

Across wide stretches of the sun-bleached Sonoran desert in Arizona, thousands of retired aircraft sit nose-to-tail in graveyards of metal known as boneyards.

Many of their engines haven’t been fired up for years. But America’s soaring demand for electricity to power data centers is bringing them back to life.

Several companies are racing to strip the engines out of old aircraft to convert them into electrical generators. And data centers, desperate for power, are snapping them up.

“They’re getting creative,” said Bill Kleyman, chief executive of Apolo, an A.I. platform and infrastructure company. “Just a few years ago, a traditional data center would have been like, ‘Are you kidding me? This is ridiculous.’”

Now, data center developers are obsessed with “speed to power,” Mr. Kleyman said. “It’s like, ‘How fast can you get me energy?’”

President Trump, aware that the rapid construction of data centers has sparked concerns over rising electricity prices, has pressed center developers to generate their own power. “It was my idea,” he told reporters in August. “Data centers now are mandated by me that they build their own electricity, so they’re not taking it from the grid."

Jet engines are a plentiful and untapped source. In January, the federal Energy Information Administration said that the engines from the 4,000 old military jets it parks at a single desert base in Tucson could create 40,000 megawatts of power. That’s more than the generation capacity of the entire state.

But repurposed aircraft turbines tend to be less efficient and more polluting than engines designed for conventional gas-burning plants. And data centers need more jet-powered generators to produce the same amount of electricity.

Elon Musk’s A.I. company, xAI, has installed eight converted turbines in Mississippi to power one of its massive data centers, according to permits with the state and satellite imagery, both reviewed by The New York Times. The generators have state permission to emit carbon monoxide at twice the rate of other turbines at the site. The permits also allow a 25 percent higher limit for pollutants known as volatile organic compounds. Both carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds pose significant health risks.

Environmentalists say that reusing older and less efficient jet engines is a step backward. Patrick Anderson, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, said electric generation — particularly for something as futuristic as A.I. — “should be getting cleaner over time, not dirtier.”

His group has challenged Mississippi’s approval of xAI’s turbines. It says the manufacturer of the jet-powered generators has provided no guarantees or documents showing they meet emissions standards for pollutants like formaldehyde. It also accuses xAI of undercounting its projected emissions.

The group, on behalf of the NAACP, also sued xAI this year for running a separate batch of gas generators without permits, and for exposing a predominantly Black community to air pollutants. More than 100,000 people live within five miles of xAI’s data-centers on the Mississippi-Tennessee border, according to 2020 census data.

The manufacturer of xAI’s jet-powered generators, Missouri-based ProEnergy, was early to the business, repurposing a General Electric turbine commonly found in Boeing aircraft. Landon Tessmer, an executive at ProEnergy, told attendees at a conference in Denver in September that demand from data centers was outpacing demand from traditional utilities.

Each turbine can produce 50 megawatts of electricity, he said, enough to power 15,000 homes. “If anybody’s ever flown on a Boeing 747,” Mr. Tessmer said, “it’s the exact same aircraft engine.”

ProEnergy doesn’t name its customers. But state permits reviewed by the Times nationwide show that some of the biggest A.I. companies plan to use its turbines. Companies supplying power for data centers, including those working with Google, say they will use ProEnergy turbines converted from jet engines, according to regulatory filings.

Neither xAI nor ProEnergy commented on the environmental concerns. Google said it has opted to wait for grid-connected power.

Chips ‘piling up’

For companies stuck on yearslong wait-lists to connect to electric grids or to acquire standard turbines, these units offer a quick fix.

In February, Elon Musk expressed frustration with the difficulty of securing enough power to realize his A.I. ambitions. Electricity, not computer chips, had become the main bottleneck to A.I. development, he said on a podcast hosted by Dwarkesh Patel, a tech writer. “The chips are going to be piling up and not be able to be turned on,” he said.

In an apparent effort to alleviate the supply crunch, Mr. Musk’s SpaceX acquired a maker of mobile gas turbines.

Last year FTAI Aviation, a New York-based jet-engine leasing and repair company, launched a division that converts retired engines from Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 aircraft to power data centers. In July, an FTAI joint venture signed a $1.5 billion agreement to supply converted turbines to a data-center developer.

FTAI’s president, David Moreno, said the company was retrofitting its Montreal facility with a production line for jet conversions. “Customers want units, now,” he said on a call with investors in April.

Boom Supersonic, a start-up company initially focused on reviving supersonic passenger travel, is now also pivoting to use its jet engines for data centers.

“It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” regardless of cost or efficiency, said Audun Martinsen, an analyst at the energy research company Rystad Energy. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said, versus waiting years for grid access.

‘Engines are the first to come off’

Pinal Airpark, about an hour’s drive from Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, is one of the world’s largest commercial aircraft reclamation facilities, storing nearly 300 aircraft on roughly 20,000 acres.

And when retired planes end up there, “the engines are the first to come off,” said Lynell Merriman, a customer service manager at Pinal, as she zipped around the planes in her minivan. Much of her job involves taking clients to inspect and purchase reusable parts like engines and electronics. In many cases, the engines are more valuable than the entire airframe, she said.

The conversion of a jet engine involves several steps.

On a plane, the engine’s job is to push lots of air out the back, propelling the aircraft.

To do that, air is sucked in by a huge fan at the front and compressed by a series of rotors. Then it is combined with jet fuel in the combustion chamber to rotate a central shaft that spins the front-facing fan, pulling in more air and starting the cycle again.

Most of the air sucked in by the fan bypasses the engine core and gets shot out the back, creating thrust.

To convert the engine, the outer shell and fan are removed. The combustion chamber is modified to burn natural gas. The central shaft is connected to a gear box and electrical generator instead of spinning a huge fan.

“They take that high-speed flow and convert it into mechanical power,” said Guillermo Paniagua-Perez, professor in mechanical engineering at Purdue University.

Unused planes end up parked at boneyards across the Southwest because the desert’s arid climate greatly reduces corrosion and weather damage, and the hard-baked soil helps support the heavy aircraft without extensive concrete paving. When Spirit ceased operations in May, nearly 100 of its aircraft were stored at Pinal.

Previously, engines from retired aircraft were sold almost exclusively back into aviation for use in other planes or for parts. But in the past year, Pinal Airpark has had “a distinct uptick in inquiries from energy developers,” said Nikki Thomas, the business development manager at Ascent Aviation Services, which runs the facility.

During a recent visit, the park was a hub of activity. Two excavators hacked away at an old airframe. Workers mounted two engines on the back of a flatbed trailer, ready to be hauled away.

Pinal is now “on the front lines of a surging demand for aircraft engine cores driven by the data center and A.I. boom,” Ms. Merriman said.

The speed at which jet engines can be quickly turned into generators “is the main consideration today,” said Professor Paniagua-Perez of Purdue. “But in a year or two, I think people will start caring more about fuel cost and efficiency,” he said. “Emissions will also become very important.”

Concerns like these, however, don’t appear to be affecting demand.

Over the past year, data centers “are gobbling them up,” said Doug Scroggins III, founder of Scroggins Aviation, a specialist company that trades used aircraft and aircraft parts.

At ProEnergy, old engines enter a depot in Houston or in Sedalia, Missouri, where they are torn apart, cleaned, inspected and tested, according to the engine’s specifications. Engineers then modify the turbines so they can run on natural gas and diesel instead of jet fuel, which is costlier. They add electric generators, as well as air cooling to take into account higher ground temperatures. ProEnergy also says it adds pollution controls and casings to reduce noise.

Scott Marchand, an aviation expert who runs the Pima Air and Space Museum, said repurposing aircraft engines isn’t new. Piston engines have been used as irrigation pumps, for example.

But the use of converted jet engines as primary sources of power for a facility as gargantuan as an A.I. data center was unprecedented, he said. He also wondered how practical it really will be. “You’re going to have to have a monstrous array of engines that are really expensive to maintain, expensive to feed and generate an awful lot of heat themselves,” he said.

Despite concerns like these, the Trump administration is encouraging rapid installation of generators of all kinds at data centers.

A few months ago, in an extraordinary court intervention, the Trump administration sided with xAI against a legal challenge by environmentalists against the company’s generators, telling a judge that citizens’ groups shouldn’t be allowed to bring environmental lawsuits. In its filing, the administration said the lawsuit threatened national security by undermining Mr. Trump’s goal of “global A.I. dominance.”

ARTICLE

For the First Time, Seneca Nation Elects a Woman as Its President
Tina Abrams had served on the Senecas’ governing council since 2001.
By Jay Root
Published 2026-11-04 01:34 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/nyregion/seneca-nation-woman-president-tina-abrams.html

Tina Abrams was elected president of the Seneca Nation of Indians on Tuesday, becoming the first woman to be chosen as chief executive in the modern history of the largest tribe in New York State.

The election of Ms. Abrams was notable not just for the barrier it broke — one that has existed since at least 1848 — but for its larger symbolic significance to the Seneca Nation, a matrilineal society where women have wielded vast political power for centuries.

It also presents an opportunity to reset the often toxic dealings the nation has had with Gov. Kathy Hochul and other New York State officials, who have sparred for years with the Senecas over gambling revenue generated by the tribe’s casinos.

“I am humbled,” Ms. Abrams said in a statement on Tuesday. “Tonight, at long last, a woman will now lead our Nation as president. This is a moment inspired by generations of strong Seneca women who came before me, and one that I hope inspires generations of Seneca women who come after me.”

Ms. Abrams, who had been an elected member of the tribe’s 16-member governing council since 2001, will be formally sworn in on Nov. 10, replacing outgoing President J.C. Seneca, officials said. The nation’s presidents must leave office when their two-year terms end but can run again in subsequent, nonconsecutive elections.

In a Facebook post from her campaign after she won the Seneca Party’s nomination in September, Ms. Abrams called for unity and said she would “move forward with communication and transparency.”

The message was widely interpreted as a reference to the previous administration’s penchant for secrecy, including in its often contentious dealings with state officials over the tribal casinos.

Politically, Ms. Abrams benefited from roots in the two main territories of the Seneca Nation — Cattaraugus, where she grew up, and Allegany, where she and her husband raised three children and have lived for 40 years. She is seen as pragmatic but media shy, and deeply experienced in Seneca government after a quarter century on the council.

She now will lead a Native nation that has long placed women at the center of its identity. Clan affiliation is passed down from mothers to their sons and daughters, and only those children born to Seneca mothers can become enrolled tribal members.

Even so, women were not allowed to participate directly in elections until relatively recently. They were barred from voting and holding public office when the Seneca Nation adopted a constitution in 1848. After gaining those rights in the mid-1960s, they have held every elected position except the presidency, according to Rebecca Bowen, the Seneca Nation’s archives manager.

Leslie Logan, an enrolled Seneca and co-host of the “Seneca Citizens Podcast,” said Ms. Abrams’s ascent to the Seneca Nation presidency “just feels like a long time coming.”

As president, Ms. Abrams will be tasked with addressing a range of issues, such as directing more resources into traditional cultural education and language instruction, dealing with substance abuse in the territories and meeting a soaring demand for housing.

But it will be her relations with Ms. Hochul that will be the biggest test of Ms. Abrams’s administration.

Lori Quigley, an enrolled Seneca and professor of leadership and policy at Niagara University, said Ms. Abrams’s background might help in that relationship.

“It’s going to be one woman from western New York negotiating with another woman from western New York,” Ms. Quigley said. “I think it will go an awful long way.”

Ms. Hochul grew up in the Buffalo suburb of Hamburg — about a half-hour drive from the Senecas’ Cattaraugus Territory — and was herself the first woman to become governor of New York, after Gov. Andrew Cuomo resigned in disgrace in 2021. She was elected to a four-year term in 2022 and was expected to be re-elected to a second term on Tuesday.

Ms. Hochul infuriated the Seneca Nation when she forced the tribe to hand over more than $500 million in disputed gambling revenues by freezing their bank accounts early in her tenure as governor. The bulk of the money was used to help build a new stadium for the billionaire owners of the Buffalo Bills.

The essential terms of the Seneca gambling compact, which gives the tribe territorial exclusivity for Las Vegas-style slot machines across a large swath of western New York in exchange for a quarter of the revenue the casinos pull in from the devices, have not been changed since 2002.

Tribal leaders say the terms of the compact are overly onerous, and have been pressing Ms. Hochul for an updated compact for three years, to no avail.

Ross John, an incoming member of the governing council who served in previous terms alongside Ms. Abrams, said the new president would be no “wallflower” but would seek to find common ground with Ms. Hochul and other interlocutors.

“She has an open mind,” Mr. John said. “Even if you have a disagreement with her, you can find your way to her door and talk to her about it.”
