ARTICLE

The American People Have Repudiated Trump
Americans showed that the power to choose their leaders belongs to them. Now they must remain vigilant until officials certify every race and the winners take office.
By The Editorial Board
Published 2026-11-04 04:46 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/democracy-midterms-trump.html

President Trump has spent the past two years trying to subvert American democracy. On Tuesday, voters stood up to him.

In the face of the president’s many attempts to manipulate the midterm elections — through extreme gerrymandering, false claims of voter fraud, efforts to block mail voting and more — tens of millions of Americans responded by turning out and rejecting the Republican Party that has enabled him. Democrats retook control of the Senate and are poised to retake the House as well. The repudiation was broad enough to overcome America’s political polarization. Republicans lost races even in traditionally deep-red places, including Kansas, Kentucky, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. They lost because many independents and even Republicans consider Mr. Trump’s second term to be a failure.

The outcome creates a crucial check on Mr. Trump’s autocratic behavior. It empowers Democrats to investigate his corruption and law breaking and pass legislation that offers an alternative to his counterproductive agenda. The country already feels changed, and it will in fact be changed in January.

The country still faces many long-term problems to which neither party has offered clear solutions. And over the next two years, while Mr. Trump remains president, Congress and judges will need to be prepared to counter further attempts by him to undermine the constitutional order.

Nonetheless, this is a day to feel pride. Aspiring authoritarians often use legislative elections to cement their power and further undermine democracy. In 2026, the American people refused to allow Mr. Trump to do so. The system has held.

In addition to voters, three groups deserve particular credit: election workers, legal advocates and judges.

Election workers did their jobs this year in the face of relentless pressure from Mr. Trump. He has long claimed that widespread fraud decides American elections, despite decades of evidence to the contrary. Election workers across party lines responded to these lies by doing their jobs as diligently as they long have, helping people cast their ballots and counting those ballots.

In many states, election officials took specific actions to stop interference from the Trump administration. Last year, the Justice Department demanded that states provide the federal government with voters’ birth dates, driver’s license information and partial Social Security numbers. Officials, including several Republicans, refused to comply.

Among the standouts were Utah’s Republican lieutenant governor, Deidre Henderson; Michigan’s Democratic secretary of state, Jocelyn Benson; and West Virginia’s Republican secretary of state, Kris Warner. Each refused to comply, each drew a lawsuit from the administration, and each won in court.

Their ability to resist the president underscores an advantage of America’s decentralized government. They could refuse because the president has no power to overrule them. The elections clause of the Constitution lets each state decide how its elections are run. This federalism proved a bulwark against Mr. Trump’s authoritarian instincts.

A second group that stood up for democracy this year were legal advocates. When Mr. Trump tried to interfere in the elections — through executive orders that sought to complicate voter registration, bar states from counting some mail and direct the Postal Service to decide which voters would receive mail ballots — advocates quickly responded by filing lawsuits.

The advocates included the Brennan Center, the American Civil Liberties Union, the League of Women Voters, Common Cause and Democratic attorneys general. Some prestigious law firms have been afraid of confronting the Trump administration’s legal abuses over the past two years, making the work of nonprofits all the more important.

The lawsuits frequently succeeded because of the third group: federal judges who insisted on following the law and upholding the Constitution despite intimidation efforts by Mr. Trump and his allies. Judges appointed by presidents from both parties, including Mr. Trump himself, blocked key parts of the executive orders concerning election rules. In 27 straight district court rulings, judges rejected the Justice Department’s demands for state voter rolls.

The Supreme Court deserves both credit and criticism. The court was wrong to issue rulings that made possible Mr. Trump’s extreme partisan gerrymandering and his administration’s efforts to create a national voter database. But the justices did act to protect Americans’ ability to cast votes this fall. In September, it upheld a lower-court ruling that barred the Postal Service from taking steps that could have restricted mail voting.

That ruling was a reminder that this court does have its red lines about elections. After the 2020 election, the justices refused to hear cases with Mr. Trump’s false claims about election fraud. The justices may need to swat down similar claims in the weeks ahead.

But the challenges ahead should not overshadow what Americans accomplished. This year, election workers, lawyers and judges defended the rules that protect the vote. And tens of millions of Americans went to the polls to exercise their most fundamental democratic right. Americans showed that the power to choose their leaders belongs to them. Now they must remain vigilant until officials certify every race and the winners take office.

ARTICLE

What a Vote for Abdul El-Sayed Means
Electing Abdul El-Sayed would contribute to the normalization of the antisemitism that his candidacy has helped to produce.
By Bret Stephens
Published 2026-11-03 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/el-sayed-rogers-michigan-senate.html

On a recent visit to Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township, Mich., I heard from someone who described the state’s U.S. Senate race this year as a choice either against antisemitism or for democracy.

What he meant was that a vote for Mike Rogers, the Republican, was also a vote for President Trump and therefore a vote against democracy. But a vote for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat, was a vote not just for a stridently anti-Israel candidate but for the normalization of antisemitism that his candidacy has helped to produce. Temple Israel is the synagogue where, in March, a Hezbollah-inspired terrorist rammed a gasoline- and fireworks-laden truck through its doors with the intention (as the attacker said in a prerecorded video) of killing “as many of them as I possibly can.”

The stakes in the race were again brought home after Representative Haley Stevens, who had been El-Sayed’s opponent in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers after a falling-out with El-Sayed, largely over his refusal to condemn what may be the most nakedly antisemitic political ad in modern U.S. political history.

The ad, which came from an El-Sayed-friendly political action committee founded by Cenk Uygur, a left-wing media personality, features a couple shopping for groceries while discussing why they can no longer afford a $7 carton of eggs: The money has already been stripped from their wallets by the federal government so that it can be sent to Israel and spent on “killing Palestinians” while also “probably” funding Israel’s universal health care.

A voice-over then asks, “Why does Mike Rogers care so much about what Israelis want, and so little about what you want?”

What’s wrong with the ad? For starters, the price of a dozen eggs has fallen by about half since Trump returned to office; a price-conscious shopper in Michigan could pick up a dozen eggs at Walmart for under $2. And while prices for groceries have undoubtedly been affected by higher energy costs because of the war with Iran, for which Israel is partly responsible, they’ve also been affected by the war in Ukraine; droughts in Brazil, China and the Midwest; and Trump’s capricious tariffs. Is Israel to blame for all that, too?

The larger problem with the ad is that it unites three of the oldest antisemitic tropes in history. First: There’s a powerful Jew out there who’s picking the pockets of the less fortunate. Second, that Jew is doing so to slaughter the innocent. Third, he’s paying a non-Jewish intermediary (who, by implication, is either a dope or a stooge) to do his bidding. To suggest the ad is only about U.S. policy toward Israel would be like arguing that an ad denouncing foreign aid to African countries while featuring the worst stereotypes about people in those countries isn’t racist. It doesn’t pass the smell test.

It would have been morally right — and a political no-brainer — for El-Sayed to forthrightly and unequivocally denounce the ad. A similar dynamic played out in early 2008, when Barack Obama’s former pastor, the Rev. Jeremiah Wright Jr., turned out to have a record of incendiary rhetoric. Obama denounced the pastor’s statements, and, after Wright kept it up, broke off relations with the man. Doing so drew a firm and effective line under the controversy, underscoring Obama’s insistence that he was no radical.

Yet the most El-Sayed has said about the ad was that it “was not made by me,” that he didn’t agree with its content but that the controversy was “not worth my time.” That’s odd: It was El-Sayed himself who called Israel “an affordability issue” while adding “we should keep our money here instead of sending it there to drop bombs on people’s schools or their hospitals.” Nor has he been shy about denouncing Israel at nearly every opportunity he gets. The ad he now says he has nothing to do with merely expresses what he plainly believes.

It’s part of a broader pattern.

His initial response to the Temple Israel attack, where only a miracle spared the over 150 children and staff inside from death or injury, was that “hurt people hurt people.” It took him five months to offer a quasi apology. (“My comments may have been misconstrued.”) He campaigned alongside the antisemitic media personality Hasan Piker (who recently compared campaigning for El-Sayed in heavily Jewish West Bloomfield Township to campaigning for a Black candidate in a “Klan K.K.K. neighborhood”) and quietly distanced himself from him because he feared it was costing him votes, according to reporting by CNN. Tucker Carlson, the right’s most prominent normalizer of antisemitism, now features in one of El-Sayed’s campaign ads.

A question for Michigan voters, especially those who lean left: If the stigmatized minority here weren’t Jewish but, say, gay or Latino or Black, would you even consider a vote for any candidate abetting, or at least tolerating, the stigmatizing?

None of this will matter at all to voters who thrill to El-Sayed’s message. Nor will it matter enough to voters willing to put their misgivings about him aside because they feel that Rogers, for his part, has failed to call out the rhetorical excesses of Republicans, and that nothing is more important than sending Trump the sternest electoral rebuke they can. Yet come January, Trump will still be president, no matter how well Democrats do in the midterms.

The real issue for voters in Michigan is what moral price is worth paying for an additional seat in the Senate. There are, after all, other winnable Senate races in other states. And a vote to further strengthen the forces of antisemitism in American politics, under any party banner or political justification, is no vote for democracy, either.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Jon Ossoff Suddenly Looks Even More Presidential
Fighting corruption, the theme in his race, could work for Democrats in 2028.
By Peter Beinart
Published 2026-11-04 01:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/jon-ossoff-georgia-senate.html

A year ago, pundits declared Georgia’s Jon Ossoff the senator most likely to lose his seat. On Tuesday, he won decisively. National Republicans had largely conceded the race months ago. The Associated Press announced his victory shortly after the polls closed.

Mr. Ossoff won so decisively, in part, because he articulated a message that connected Democrats’ fear of authoritarianism to the broader public’s fear that life is unaffordable. It’s a message that other Democratic candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, have emphasized as well. It could prove central for the party again in 2028. And it boils down to one word: corruption.

Donald Trump’s shameless self-dealing made Mr. Ossoff’s argument easier. Since returning to the White House, according to news reports, Mr. Trump has made more than $1 billion from his family’s cryptocurrency businesses alone. Americans of both parties have noticed. A Washington Post poll last month found that one-third of Republicans and independents who lean Republican now believe Mr. Trump is enriching himself in office, while a Fox News poll ranked corruption as voters’ top concern nationally.

Mr. Ossoff courted Republicans by speaking in bipartisan terms: He acknowledged that Mr. Trump didn’t invent political corruption. “Yes, the system really is rigged,” he said. “But he’s not unrigging it. He is re-rigging it for himself.”

Of course, it helped that Georgia Republicans chose a weak nominee. But Mr. Ossoff didn’t only benefit from a favorable political environment. He also spoke differently from the Democrats who challenged Mr. Trump two years ago.

Authoritarianism was a central theme of Kamala Harris’s failed presidential campaign; public graft fell further down her list of concerns. That cost her. Exit polls found that Ms. Harris won 80 percent of voters who called democracy their most important issue, while 81 percent of voters who prioritized the economy backed Mr. Trump. In Ms. Harris’s 2024 Democratic National Convention acceptance speech, she used the words “freedom,” “democracy” and “liberty” a total of 15 times. She didn’t mention “corruption” once.

By stressing corruption, in contrast, Mr. Ossoff made Mr. Trump’s assault on the rule of law tangible. He showed voters how democracy and economic distress are intertwined. On the campaign trail, he argued that “corruption is why nothing works for ordinary people. It’s why you pay a fortune for prescriptions. It’s why your insurance company gets away with denying your cancer treatment after you paid your premiums for decades.” In this way, he showed that the president wasn’t just transgressing abstract norms of good governance. He was helping the rich and powerful rip Americans off.

In that sense, Mr. Ossoff was following a path forged by other parties trying to defeat aspiring autocrats. Peter Magyar, who decisively ended Viktor Orban’s 16-year rule in Hungary this spring, gained national prominence with a 2024 viral video in which he accused Mr. Orban of turning the government into a “family-owned business.” The good-government group Democracy International reported that Mr. Magyar’s campaign “reduced complex democratic concerns into a simple proposition: ‘Corruption has a cost.’”

Similarly, in Serbia this September, student protesters angry over the long and corrupt run of President Aleksandar Vucic voted in a new era. “The focus of the protest was on corruption, government corruption,” Heather Conley, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, told PBS. “We’re seeing that issue become a real global issue.”

If Democrats retake Congress, they’ll have a chance to use congressional hearings to lay the groundwork for making corruption a key theme again in 2028. Mr. Ossoff could make it the centerpiece of a presidential campaign. Given how much power the ultrarich now wield in Washington, and how many ordinary Americans are struggling simply to get by, it won’t be hard to convince Americans that JD Vance, Marco Rubio or any of Mr. Trump’s likely Republican successors are tainted by his administration’s epic graft.

The hard part will be convincing them that Democrats — who even Mr. Ossoff concedes are viewed as corrupt themselves — can be trusted to behave differently if they regain power.

Peter Beinart is a contributing Opinion writer at The Times. He is also a professor at the Newmark School of Journalism at the City University of New York and an editor at large at Jewish Currents, and he writes The Beinart Notebook, a weekly newsletter. His latest book is “Being Jewish After the Destruction of Gaza.”

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

This Was Never About Trump
The Trump administration has profoundly misread Latin America’s political winds.
By Michael Shifter
Published 2026-11-03 06:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/lula-brazil-latin-america-trump.html

In 1965, the political economist Albert Hirschman warned that the United States and Latin America were tangled in an “orgy of misinterpretation and misunderstanding” fueled by conflicting political moods and preferences. Over two decades later, looking out over a hemisphere that was just as geopolitically messy, he reflected, “I almost wonder whether I might have stumbled on some sort of law.”

Some sort of law, indeed. After a string of presidential victories by right-leaning candidates in Latin America, Washington had, up until recently, been basking in a sense of unparalleled political alignment throughout the region. Over the summer, Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the emergence of predominantly pro-American governments across the hemisphere as an “extraordinary achievement”; in September, President Trump boasted that he was “nine for nine” in backing winning candidates. The Donroe Doctrine — Mr. Trump’s project of hemispheric hegemony — seemed to be paying off.

The triumph of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, an iconic octogenarian leftist, over Flávio Bolsonaro, heir to the Bolsonaro political dynasty and avatar of Latin America’s new right, upsets the narrative of a historic ideological reconfiguration — and reveals how profoundly the Trump administration has misread the region’s political winds. The swing to the right was never about Mr. Trump; it’s the serendipitous result of a wave of discontent with the status quo and could prove evanescent. Indeed, the grievances and aspirations that brought so many far-right governments to power could just as easily undermine their political fortunes and weaken their ties to Washington in years to come.

The region’s rightward shift reflects less of an ideological transformation than a widespread frustration with governments that have overpromised and underperformed for decades. Voters are angry about crime, economic stagnation, corruption and poor public services. Right-leaning candidates in places like Argentina, Colombia, Chile, Peru, Honduras and Bolivia have successfully capitalized on that discontent, promising to restore order, revive economic growth and challenge discredited political establishments.

To some extent, Brazil’s election complicates this picture. Mr. Lula is, after all, an incumbent who managed to overcome considerable dissatisfaction with his government to win October’s election. But Brazilians had already lived through four years of Jair Bolsonaro’s Trump-backed right-wing populism. In the presidential runoff, thanks to a campaign powered by digital grass-roots mobilization, they rejected a return to that political project under his son Flávio — who almost immediately absconded to the United States, apparently fleeing a web of criminal investigations at home.

Mr. Lula’s victory should not be interpreted as an emerging leftward swing in Brazil, or in the region, where conservatives remain a formidable political force. What the final verdict does suggest is that Latin America’s electoral volatility is driven less by ideology, or even the rejection of incumbents, than by voters’ judgments about competing political alternatives and their records in office.

For the new crop of right-wing leaders, whose ascent began with the election of Argentina’s Javier Milei in 2023, delivering on their promises has already proved a tall order. Crime and economic stagnation are complicated problems that defy quick solutions. Already, there are signs that some of the right’s new guard are floundering and losing popular support. Not even a year after taking office, Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz, Chile’s José Antonio Kast and Peru’s Keiko Fujimori all face plummeting approval ratings. Mr. Milei, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s, faces mounting political difficulties as he approaches his bid for re-election next year. The same impatient electorates that propelled him and other leaders into office could just as readily turn against them.

These right-leaning leaders hardly constitute a cohesive political movement. They differ in their convictions, governing styles and policy priorities. Just as tensions have always divided Latin America’s left-wing governments, today’s right-wing bloc is quarrelsome and fragmented. Despite their ideological affinity, for example, Mr. Kast and Mr. Milei recently clashed over longstanding territorial disputes, stirring nationalist sentiments.

True, the region is largely aligned on tougher security policies in response to mounting public concern about crime. Over the past decade, driven by a booming global drug trade, criminal organizations have amassed power and territory throughout the region, expanding from illicit activities into informal economies and laying waste to vulnerable communities. Over a dozen governments in the region now participate in the United States-led Shield of the Americas, a hemispheric initiative aimed at combating drug cartels and transnational organized crime.

But governments are being forced to think through how far to accommodate Washington’s demands for a more militarized approach to law enforcement. Concerns about policy autonomy and national sovereignty extend across the political spectrum, including to right-leaning governments in Peru, Chile and Colombia, whose political affinity with Washington does not necessarily mean subordinating their national interests to U.S. priorities. Those national interests include their relationships with China: While right-leaning governments may feel considerable political kinship with the Trump administration, most also have vital economic relationships with Beijing that transcend political orientation and that they cannot or will not sacrifice.

Meanwhile, Washington is losing the confidence of people who voted Mr. Trump’s regional allies into power. The 2026 Latinobarómetro survey — conducted after Mr. Trump’s launching of the Iran war — showed that 59 percent of Latin Americans disapprove of his handling of international affairs. The share of Latin Americans who express trust in the U.S. government has fallen to 40 percent from 62 percent in 2012, according to AmericasBarometer. (Trust in China has dipped more slightly, to 51 percent from 57 percent.)

That free fall in trust has played out as the Trump administration’s policies have grown increasingly aggressive and interventionist. Tariffs, sanctions and political pressure, together with the brutal treatment of Latin American immigrants in the United States and ongoing extrajudicial boat strikes in the Caribbean and the Pacific, have reinforced longstanding suspicions of American power — and of the advantages of being in America’s spotlight. The 2026 Latinobarómetro survey revealed that while 69 percent of Latin Americans approved of the U.S. military operation in January that removed Nicolás Maduro, only 35 percent believed it had benefited Venezuela.

Those figures, and Mr. Lula’s upset in Latin America’s most populous country — as well as the enduring popularity of Mexico’s leftist leader, Claudia Sheinbaum — belie the Trump administration’s exuberant claims about the roaring success of its Latin America policy and its reassertion of an American sphere of influence in the hemisphere. Washington has been celebrating what it sees as a historic foreign policy achievement in a region where, among voters, its reputation has suffered damage that will take years to repair. What looked on the surface like a new era of hemispheric convergence could turn out to be another chapter in a long history of missed connections.

Michael Shifter is a senior fellow at the Inter-American Dialogue, a think tank focused on the Western Hemisphere, and teaches Latin American politics at Georgetown University and George Washington University.

SUMMARY

There have been three great crises in American history: the Civil War, perhaps the defining event in our history after the Revolution itself, the Great Depression and World War II. These events tested our republic and our resolve in fundamental ways, but the center always held — elections took place, there was a peaceful transfer of power and the judiciary was still independent. As we go to the polls today in this most consequential of midterm elections, we face our country’s fourth great crisis.

ARTICLE

Ken Burns: We Face Our Nation’s Fourth Great Crisis
There’s something fundamental at stake in the midterms this year, beyond policy differences.
By Ken Burns
Published 2026-11-03 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/midterm-elections-politics-ken-burns.html

There have been three great crises in American history: the Civil War, perhaps the defining event in our history after the Revolution itself, the Great Depression and World War II. These events tested our republic and our resolve in fundamental ways, but the center always held — elections took place, there was a peaceful transfer of power and the judiciary was still independent. Our core democratic institutions remained fundamentally strong, respected by the public and our leaders alike. The guardrails of our democracy held and were even strengthened as we emerged from each.

As we go to the polls today in this most consequential of midterm elections, we face our country’s fourth great crisis. Because of misinformation, which the current administration encourages, age-old fears and conspiracies have created a sense of us versus them that is fundamentally at odds with a healthy democratic society. Elections are in doubt, the highest court seems compromised, history has been distorted, books have been banned, and dictators have been coddled while our closest allies have been ridiculed and dismissed. People are rightly concerned whether our institutions are at a breaking point.

I’ve spent the better part of the past two years crisscrossing the country, discussing the release of our PBS series on the American Revolution. No matter where I went or to whom I spoke, people asked me the same questions: What did I learn about our complicated and fragile republic over the nearly 10 years it took to make the film? Can a country as divided as ours survive? What might our founders think of us today?

I think the founders would be hugely disappointed that so many members of the legislative branch have ceded so much power to the executive branch, which has filled that vacuum with corruption and assaults on the rule of law, even undermining the fundamental right to vote. John Adams, who insisted that a republic could not function without virtuous leaders, would be appalled at the prevailing vulgarity and incompetence.

From the start, the creation of the United States was unlikely. For most of human history, people had lived under authoritarian rule, but in the 13 former British colonies clinging to the Eastern Seaboard, people (white men) would create something new: citizens.

“All experience has shown,” Thomas Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence, “that mankind are more disposed to suffer, while evils are sufferable, than to right themselves by abolishing the forms to which they are accustomed.” Maintaining a democracy would be difficult, an active exercise that would simultaneously try to honor our individual freedoms (what each of us wants) and our collective freedoms (what we need).

George Washington’s great achievement was not just winning a war against overwhelming odds, but persuading 13 new states with different economies, religious beliefs and competing interests that they were now part of something new in which old animosities would yield to an individual, as well as collective, sense of union. There would be an “us,” with no “them.”

During the Constitutional Convention in the summer of 1787, delegates understood that in the many compromises they would strike, they also had to engineer defenses against the rise of a tyrant. In a letter to James Madison, Jefferson worried that a president who lost an election might “pretend false votes” and “hold possession of the reins of government.” Alexander Hamilton was also concerned that an “unprincipled” man would “mount the hobby horse of popularity” and “throw things in confusion.” “In a government like ours,” he wrote, no one is “above the law.”

Today, nearly six years after an angry mob stormed the Capitol to overturn the results of the 2020 election, election denial is still part of the current administration’s playbook. Only four of the 13 Republican candidates in highly competitive Senate races have said that they would accept the outcome of the upcoming elections unconditionally.

It hasn’t always been that way. During Watergate, as damning evidence accumulated, members of President Richard Nixon’s own party concluded that their obligation to the Constitution was greater than their obligation to him or the G.O.P. In August 1974, Republican congressional leaders went to the White House and told Nixon that his support in Congress had collapsed. He announced his resignation the next day.

Citizens today should remember that our democracy relies on an ongoing conversation between them and the past. At Gettysburg, only a few months after the largest battle ever fought on American soil, Abraham Lincoln asked the living to dedicate themselves to “a new birth of freedom,” recognizing that every generation must renew and expand on the promises first made in Philadelphia. Dwight Eisenhower, who knew better than most the terrible cost of war, reminded us in his farewell address that only “an alert and knowledgeable citizenry” could preserve liberty and security.

I’m optimistic that the American people recognize that our democratic institutions and sense of decency can bring us together.

We have come back from crises before. We were more divided than we are today during the Revolution, the Civil War, Reconstruction and Vietnam. For 250 years, our country has prevailed in fits and starts, forging achievements, however imperfect, related to race and equality in American life.

But given our divisions, as we vote we must each ask ourselves: What kind of leadership will see us through the current crisis? Why do we continue to support leaders who are invested in deepening our divides, who tap into conspiracy theories to frighten the public, deny facts and, to quote Alexander Hamilton, “throw things into confusion,” so that they “may ‘ride the storm and direct the whirlwind’”?

Most midterm elections are seen as referendums on the policies of the president. This one is no different. But there’s something more fundamental at stake here, beyond policy differences. This election is about the people — who are empowered to check our chief executive — and the candidates running for Congress, who either have sworn an oath to the Constitution or hope to do so. Whether they are prepared to honor their oath should matter enormously to everyone who values the idea of us — the idea of America.

Ken Burns is a documentary filmmaker. His last film was a series on the American Revolution.

SUMMARY

By now, the contours of the 2026 midterm elections are pretty clear: President Trump’s approval rating has tanked, and winds are blowing in a Democratic direction. But I keep thinking about our Times Opinion focus group of Texas Trump voters who said they didn’t plan to vote for the scandal-plagued Mr. Paxton. Democrats’ path to Senate control requires picking up a couple of seats in places that voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 by double digits.

ARTICLE

Five Telltale Signs of a Democratic Blowout
The political winds are blowing in Democrats’ direction. The question is: How strong are they?
By Kristen Soltis Anderson
Published 2026-11-03 10:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/midterms-democrats-republicans-senate.html

By now, the contours of the 2026 midterm elections are pretty clear: President Trump’s approval rating has tanked, and winds are blowing in a Democratic direction. Democrats have higher voter enthusiasm, and we have the normal anti-incumbent vibes coupled with overall economic discontent. The question is: How strong are those winds? Here’s what I’ll be looking at on election night.

A Texas undervote? Over half a billion dollars has been spent in the Texas Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. (In a sign of just how wild things have gotten, a couple of weeks ago I was served anti-Talarico TV ads while watching my Florida Gators defeat the Texas Longhorns in college football … while sitting on my couch in Washington.)

It’s one of the marquee contests this year, yet I wonder about the potential undervote: That’s when voters cast ballots but don’t make a selection in a particular race. Sometimes that happens when they don’t think they know enough about the candidates to make an informed decision, though that’s almost certainly not the case here — Texas voters probably know more about Mr. Paxton and Mr. Talarico than they ever wanted to.

But I keep thinking about our Times Opinion focus group of Texas Trump voters who said they didn’t plan to vote for the scandal-plagued Mr. Paxton. Some of them found something to like in Mr. Talarico, while others found him to be out of step with their values and said they wouldn’t vote for him either. In general, Mr. Talarico’s voters like him and want to vote for him. On the other hand, many of Mr. Paxton’s voters are not exactly excited for their guy. One thing Republicans are banking on is the idea that in the end, some of them will decide Mr. Paxton is the lesser of two evils and vote for him in spite of their reservations. If our focus group participants are any indication, I wouldn’t be surprised to see a noticeable number of Texans simply leaving the Senate race blank.

The pull of partisanship. Democrats’ path to Senate control requires picking up a couple of seats in places that voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 by double digits. To do that, they’ll have to overcome a trend that has grown stronger and stronger in recent Senate elections: partisanship.

In the not-too-distant past, it wasn’t abnormal for a state to vote one way at the presidential level and another for the Senate. Montana and West Virginia would back Republicans in presidential contests but then send Jon Tester and Joe Manchin to Washington. Rhode Island, Illinois and Massachusetts gave us Republican senators in Lincoln Chafee, Mark Kirk and Scott Brown. However, the phenomenon of states voting for a party’s presidential candidate by a double-digit margin while electing a senator of the other party has largely evaporated in the Trump era, Mr. Tester and Mr. Manchin notwithstanding.

In 2024, Kansas voted for Mr. Trump by a 16-point margin. Iowa went for Mr. Trump by 13. They’re both on this year’s Democratic wish list, a list that goes into deeply red terrain, including Texas, South Carolina and (checks notes) Mississippi. For Democrats to break through in some of these deep red states, they’ll have to overcome the magnetic pull of partisanship that has characterized Senate elections in recent years.

Ohio’s upscale suburbs. In 2004, Tim Russert’s famous whiteboard said it best: Ohio, Ohio, Ohio. The state’s pivotal role in that year’s presidential election confirmed its status as the ultimate bellwether state.

In the Trump era, Ohio has turned redder at the presidential level; in 2024, Mr. Trump won it by double digits — his largest margin there ever. But the wealthy suburban Delaware County, north of Columbus, has moved in the opposite direction. In 2004, George W. Bush beat John Kerry there by a ratio of two to one. However, this highly educated and fast-growing county gave the Republican Bernie Moreno only a slim 1.5-point margin in his 2024 Senate win.

Republicans have gained among rural and blue-collar voters, even while shedding support from upscale suburbanites. If Delaware County goes blue after decades as reliable G.O.P. turf, it will illustrate the limits of that strategy.

Florida’s Ninth Congressional District. Osceola County is a perennial favorite of mine to watch on election night, and not just because I basically grew up there. It’s a heavily Latino county that went from deep blue 10 years ago to narrowly preferring Mr. Trump in 2024.

Representative Darren Soto, a Democrat, has represented the area for nearly a decade, but this year’s mid-decade redistricting in Florida has put him in a much tougher district that now includes slices of rural Central Florida and some Republican-leaning chunks of the coast brimming with conservative retirees. Whether he can hang on will probably depend on whether a blue wave, powered in part by Latino voters swinging back to Democrats, materializes.

Revenge of the youngs. For years, I’ve been sounding the alarm about Republicans’ struggles with the millennial generation. Then Gen Z came along and, by and large, appeared even further left than millennials. In 2024, my prophecies of G.O.P. generational doom were put on hold, as Mr. Trump held his losses among voters 18 to 29 to a mere 11 points and among those 30 to 44 to just four.

I suspect, though, that 2026 will reveal 2024 as more of a blip than a durable rightward trend among young adults. Though early voting data isn’t a crystal ball, analysts at VoteHub are showing a missing young Republican effect emerging. Disillusionment with the status quo has transferred from a Democratic octogenarian president to a Republican octogenarian president.

Meanwhile, Democrats have elevated a number of rising millennial stars like Mr. Talarico, Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan this midterm cycle (called the Mr. Brightside caucus by one reporter). To Republicans’ dismay, this might be the year when the selfie vote strikes back.

Kristen Soltis Anderson is the author of “The Selfie Vote: Where Millennials Are Leading America (and How Republicans Can Keep Up).”

SUMMARY

Welcome to this year’s opportunity to choose your child’s school. Next, please determine whether your child is choosing the school or the school is choosing your child. Do not rank a school you would not attend.

ARTICLE

Dear American Parent: You’re Welcome!
Hey, no one said having all this freedom was going to be easy. Or survivable.
By Jennifer L. Jennings
Published 2026-11-03 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/school-choice-education.html

Good news, American parent!

Welcome to this year’s opportunity to choose your child’s school. Depending on where you live, you may now choose neighborhood schools, magnet schools, charter schools, Christian schools, virtual schools, microschools, homeschool and schools that are neither fish nor fowl, which meet in a trampoline park.

This is educational freedom.

Let’s get started. Create an account. No, not the account you use for everything else in the school district. We are a district of many accounts. Add your child using the code issued by the school’s guidance counselor. We’re sorry! That code is invalid. Please review the instructions. Codes are case-sensitive.

You are ready to choose now.

What kind of school would be the best fit for your child: STEAM, STEM, project-based learning, International Baccalaureate, performing arts, college preparatory, early college, career and technical education or a school with a website that just says “INNOVATION”?

You know your child best. Please be sure to research the options carefully.

However, you do not know the schools best. To that end, please attend your preferred school’s Open House. Open House begins at 10 sharp on Tuesday morning. Just that one Tuesday. We understand that you have a job, but our school is a good fit for parents truly committed to their child’s education.

At Open House, please determine whether the school has engaged teachers, a healthy culture, good leadership and a 21st-century bathroom. You will have 47 minutes.

A ninth grader named Madison will be your tour guide. Please ask Madison about the comparative effectiveness of the ninth-grade mathematics teachers. Next, please determine whether your child is choosing the school or the school is choosing your child. Sometimes you choose the school. Sometimes the school chooses you. Sometimes you choose the school, the school chooses you, and then an algorithm chooses whether the two of you were correct.

For some schools, students audition. To be considered for our arts school, please design a fashion outfit inspired by a fantastical sandwich.

Some schools require an exam. Other children started preparing last year. Freedom rewards foresight.

Some schools use a lottery. Please be patient while your one precious child rattles around the metaphorical bingo cage to discover his or her educational destiny. If you must scream, scream in your heart.

Now, rank your schools. Do not rank a school you would not attend. Also, do not fail to rank a school you would attend. You may rank every program in the district. There are more than 700.

And remember, do not rank strategically. Simply include a healthy mix of reach, target and safety schools. We’ve classified the schools you want to attend as reaches. This is not strategy.

You are really getting the hang of school choice!

Are you considering a private school? Exciting news! Your state may fund your Students First Education Savings Account with $8,148. Our school’s tuition is not public, however, so we’ll let you know the balance later. You may also be asked to include a spiritual reference from your pastor and to sign a Biblical Lifestyle Policy. Our expectations extend beyond school grounds and throughout the calendar year. Consider whether inviting Aunt Linda to Thanksgiving is condoning a non-biblical lifestyle.

Remember, YOU are choosing.

After our interview, at which both parents should be present, our school will determine whether we would like to participate in your choice. If so, your choice has chosen you.

If not, please make another choice. In America, you have many school choices. Some may be full, or cost more than the school voucher. Some may have closed their application window last Thursday. Please exercise your freedom more promptly next year. Feeling overwhelmed? You are experiencing parental empowerment.

At some point, say 3:24 a.m., you may wonder why obtaining a decent education requires this much work.

That is a totally different policy question. We are discussing only school choice.

Congratulations! You have exercised your educational freedom.

We will let you know where your child is going to school in the spring.

Jennifer L. Jennings is the director of education research at the Princeton School of Public and International Affairs and the author of “The Scarcity Loop: How School Choice Reshapes the Rationing of Public Education.”

SUMMARY

If only President Trump would take the hint and resign. At another level, for a right-wing president to openly declare his admiration for another man’s “ass,” as Trump has repeatedly done over the past few weeks, suggests that we will be governed for the next two-plus years by a rebuked but powerful president with fraying internal psychological guardrails. For a right-wing Republican to lovingly describe another man’s backside as “a pile of muscle,” supposedly as a strategy to cover for his failings as president, is a bridge too far, even for Trump.

ARTICLE

‘Something Is Changing With Trump’
An already dangerously erratic president is veering deeper and deeper into what amounts to hallucination.
By Thomas B. Edsall
Published 2026-11-03 16:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/opinion/trump-backsides-language-rallies.html

I’m going to rain a bit on this Democratic day of high expectation.

Voters on Tuesday are almost certainly going to repudiate the worst president in American history, turning control of the House over to Democrats, with the Senate having at least a 50-50 chance of following suit. If only President Trump would take the hint and resign.

But he is not going anywhere.

The dismal reality is that we are stuck with this corrupt and vengeful man for another two years, two months and 17 days.

At one level, Trump’s descent is great entertainment. Cultural liberals convinced of the virtue of self-expression may rejoice in the president’s open display of his androgynous love of hard male bodies, especially their buttocks.

At another level, for a right-wing president to openly declare his admiration for another man’s “ass,” as Trump has repeatedly done over the past few weeks, suggests that we will be governed for the next two-plus years by a rebuked but powerful president with fraying internal psychological guardrails. The Joint Chiefs of Staff should consider moving the threat level to DEFCON 1.

On the campaign trail, it’s all gotten weirder and weirder. Take Trump’s musings at a rally on Oct. 12 in Youngstown, Ohio, in support of the Republican senator seeking to hold on to his seat, Jon Husted:

I’m standing over here, and I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked, and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole — and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws. And I got it. You are a great athlete. I didn’t know that ’cause he doesn’t talk about that. Congratulations. Now, they finally know.

For a politician dependent on the support of MAGA voters known for their intolerance, these flights of the imagination suggest a man losing touch with reality.

A few days later, Trump brought the matter up again in Kentucky.

A few days after that, he did it again. Speaking in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20 in favor of the Republican Senate nominee there, Michael Whatley, Trump could not get his mind off Husted’s posterior:

So, he’s over here. I’m over here, and I’m studying his body. I’ve never studied the body of a man before. It’s not my thing. Nothing wrong with it, of course. I always precede it by saying, “Nothing wrong,” but it’s never been my thing, to be honest with you. But I looked at his ass, and then I looked at his legs. I said, “His ass is, it’s like a pile of muscle.” Then I looked at his legs, and I said, “Man, his feet are big.” Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. He’s like a piece of steel. I said, “This guy’s a monster!”

Trump has not confined himself to one particular body part. At least twice he has marveled before an audience at the size of Arnold Palmer’s penis.

At an October 2024 campaign rally in Latrobe, Pa., the president told supporters:

Arnold Palmer was all man. And I say that in all due respect to women, and I love women, but this guy, this guy. This is a guy that was all man. This man was strong and tough. And I refuse to say it, but when he took showers with the other pros, they came out of there, they said, “Oh, my God, that’s unbelievable.” I had to say it. I had to say it. We have women that are highly sophisticated here, but they used to look at Arnold, this is bad, but he was really something special.

I asked a number of experts in the study of the presidency what they make of Trump’s thought processes.

“With Trump it has always been hard to tell whether his breaches of norms are the result of pathological disinhibition or an ingenuity in colonizing our attention,” Steven Pinker, a professor of psychology at Harvard, wrote in an email, adding:

He’s done it again — we’re talking about an inappropriate, offensive and downright weird affectation, loosely inspired by the latest MAGA theme (in this case, ostentatious masculinity), but manifested in a quirk that comes out of left field. Both explanations may apply: Trump may be less capable of policing his fleeting thoughts but may also be indulging what he knows is outrageous because it not only has failed to cost him in the past but has worked to his advantage in remaining the topic of conversation (and to the neglect of more consequential failings).

“Something is changing with Trump,” Dan McAdams, a professor of psychology as well as human development and social policy at Northwestern University, pointed out. “Trump seems to be losing some of his powers of self-regulation, which have never been all that strong for him anyway.”

In later adulthood, McAdams continued, “regulatory powers of cognition and speech may wane somewhat. For example, when older people tell stories about their personal experiences, they often digress in unexpected ways and engage in what researchers call ‘story asides.’”

There are some who argue that Trump’s bizarre comments on body parts he finds worthy of comment are part of a diversion strategy.

Jennifer Mercieca, a professor in the department of communication and journalism at Texas A&M, questioned whether “Trump’s (admittedly very odd) comments about people’s bodies are ‘homoerotic’ or that there is a relationship between what you characterize as ‘homoerotic’ and Trump’s mental stability or his ability to control himself.”

Instead, Mercieca wrote,

if the goal is to explain the comments, then I think we could build a credible explanation in his well-established ability to set the nation’s media agenda. We live in an attention economy where what trends is determined by what is outrageous enough to attract attention, amplification and circulation. Trump’s comments about people’s bodies (including Nicki Minaj’s) attract attention and dominate online conversation, so it’s likely that he keeps making them because they’re effective. When the nation is talking about Trump’s gross comments, what aren’t we talking about? We aren’t talking about the affordability crisis, we aren’t talking about gas prices, we aren’t talking about the war in Iran, or corruption, or many other important things. Trump has very successfully used an outrage strategy to control our public sphere throughout the last 10 years.

I disagree with Mercieca. For a right-wing Republican to lovingly describe another man’s backside as “a pile of muscle,” supposedly as a strategy to cover for his failings as president, is a bridge too far, even for Trump.

Instead of treating Trump’s strange soliloquies as a diversion strategy, Paul Elliott Johnson, a professor in the communication department at the University of Pittsburgh, argued that they are evidence that

at this point he doesn’t have any mediators or processes for handling losses. How did he handle losing the 2020 election? Denial, claiming stolen elections, getting his sycophants to launch lunatic claims in the media and in the courts, self-pitying complaining so off-putting and noxious it ensured his party’s defeat in the Georgia Senate runoffs, all leading up to Jan. 6, 2021.

Johnson warned that a political loss for Trump today is “not a contingent threat but a primal one.” He sees himself about to be “stripped naked, humiliated, violated. So I firmly expect him to lash out in a catastrophic manner.”

Trump, Johnson argued, “won’t just see an electoral defeat; he’ll see his entire existence threatened and zeroed out. Because if you’re not constantly dominating and degrading others, you’re not a Real Man (which is to say in his register, a person).”

I thought Casey Ryan Kelly, professor of rhetoric and public culture in the department of communication studies at the University of Nebraska — Lincoln, had a particularly insightful take. In an email, he wrote:

Admittedly, his recent meditations on men’s physiques seem like he has lost emotional regulation. On the other hand, Trump has always fetishized “men’s men,” telling stories about “big strong” men coming up to him with tears in their eyes to thank him. He was fond of telling stories about monstrous Border Patrol agents who could really hurt people.

Trump’s fascination with men’s — and women’s — bodies does not, however, disturb his core supporters, Kelly wrote:

It probably helps that the far right is obsessed with physical fitness, testosterone, carnivorism and traditional gender roles — so praising men for their impressive physiques is an acceptable form of homoeroticism so long as it reaffirms the gender order that is so foundational to their ideology. They would not see his comments as gay fantasies but appreciation for tough guys with tough physiques, which makes them fit for office in his mind.

Kelly’s analysis, however, provides small comfort to an electorate that sees an already dangerously erratic president veer deeper and deeper into what amounts to hallucination.

Given the prospect of deeply embarrassing and shameful defeat in the midterms, the all-too-appropriate question becomes: Will Trump’s fantasies become sadistic? If so, who will he choose as his next victims?

Matthew Tobin contributed research to this essay.

But it was not yet clear whether the tail part broke off before the plane began to plummet or during the aircraft’s plunge to the ground.

ARTICLE

Key Part of Jet in Deadly Florida Crash Found Far From Impact Site
The mechanism that controls the vertical angle of the plane was found in three pieces, including one nearly four miles away. All nine people aboard were killed.
By Karoun Demirjian and Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs
Published 2026-11-03 23:46 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/florida-plane-crash-wreckage-recovered.html

A crucial part of the private jet that crashed in Florida on Sunday was found in fragments far from where the aircraft slammed into the ground in Palm Beach County, federal investigators said on Tuesday.

The fiery crash killed all nine people aboard, and the part, a mechanism that controls the angle of the plane, was found in three pieces, including at a spot nearly four miles from the crash site.

The discovery of the part, known as the left tail elevator, was a “very important piece of evidence,” Thomas B. Chapman, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, said at a news conference on Tuesday.

But it was not yet clear whether the tail part broke off before the plane began to plummet or during the aircraft’s plunge to the ground.

Still, the recovery of the part was a bit of progress in an investigation that has been hampered by a host of complications, including the powerful storms that investigators believe were a factor in Sunday’s crash. There were severe thunderstorms in Palm Beach County on Sunday afternoon when the plane, a Learjet 60, crashed nose first on a road, erupting into a fireball that was captured in harrowing video footage.

Mr. Chapman said much of the wreckage remained in a crater, still off limits to investigators, who hope to have access by Wednesday once public works teams finish clearing the site of water and other damage caused by the crash.

The extreme force of the impact, Mr. Chapman said, meant that most of the physical evidence the N.T.S.B. team had been able to recover was in very small pieces.

“We don’t even know in most cases what we’ve found,” he said on Tuesday, adding, “Even the elements of the aircraft that are in the crater are going to be very likely in smaller pieces.”

Among the missing and potentially critical pieces of evidence is the aircraft’s cockpit voice recorder, which investigators often rely on for insights into pilots’ decision-making leading up to an accident. On Monday, N.T.S.B. officials told reporters that the plane had been outfitted with such a recorder, but that they could not confirm whether it was present on the aircraft when it crashed.

The pilots were Jeff Gregory, 55, and Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who had earned her pilot’s license at 17, her mother said. Ms. Filgueiras, who was talking to air traffic control during the plane’s descent, was certified as a commercial pilot earlier this year, according to records.

Among the passengers who were killed were Adam Robinson, a technology executive; his wife Helen Sharp, who worked in public relations; the couple’s two children, Emma and Charlie; and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny for the children.

The plane was flying from Austin, Texas, where the family lived, to the Bahamas, when it plunged from the sky, eventually reaching a rate of 22,000 feet per minute.

According to the pilots’ exchanges with air traffic controllers, they initially sought permission to fly across Florida on a course that would have led them straight through a large thunderstorm system. A controller warned them that the weather was bad in the area, and flight maps show that they subsequently changed course to fly south of the worst storms.

Several minutes later, Ms. Filgueiras reported to another controller that they were encountering turbulence she described as “moderate,” what she called “manageable” problems with icing on the plane, and precipitation. But shortly after that, the pilots appeared to lose control of the plane, prompting Ms. Filgueiras to issue a mayday call as the aircraft began to plummet to the ground.

It was not immediately clear to investigators what condition the aircraft’s radar and anti-icing systems were in leading up to the accident.

In an interview, Michael McCormick, a former director of air traffic operations at the Federal Aviation Administration who now teaches at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said the Learjet 60 has three complementary de-icing mechanisms, but stressed that they work best when activated in advance of encountering bad weather.

“Any one of them could fail and you’re in trouble,” he said.

Investigators will also be trying to determine what caused the plane’s left tail elevator to break off the airplane before impact — though Mr. Chapman cautioned that it would not likely have been able to save the aircraft from disaster, even if it had remained intact.

“The function of the elevator is to control pitch up and down,” he told reporters Tuesday. “At those speeds, I don’t know if it would have been effective, even if attached to the aircraft.”

Billy Witz contributed reporting, and Georgia Gee contributed research.

SUMMARY

Google announced Tuesday that early next year it would turn off artificial intelligence tools in its popular software for K-12 students, unless school administrators explicitly choose to make such tools available. But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search. And Google is synonymous with internet search, a crucial tool for students across the globe.

ARTICLE

Google Will Turn Off Search for Schools That Reject A.I.
Google is making it easier to restrict its A.I. tools for students. But schools that block A.I. entirely will lose student access to Google’s search engine.
By Dana Goldstein and Natasha Singer
Published 2026-11-03 14:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html

Google announced Tuesday that early next year it would turn off artificial intelligence tools in its popular software for K-12 students, unless school administrators explicitly choose to make such tools available.

Executives at the tech giant said they wanted to be responsive to educators and parents who have asked for more control in how children interact with A.I.

But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search.

A.I. features are now a standard part of Google’s commercially available search engine. “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google is by far the dominant technology player in K-12 classrooms. Google’s suite of education apps — including Gmail, Docs and an assignment platform called Classroom — is ubiquitous. Google Chromebooks, low-cost laptops, are the most widely issued student devices in U.S. schools. And Google is synonymous with internet search, a crucial tool for students across the globe.

The company’s new strategy underscores Google’s powerful role in American education. If school leaders want continued student access to search within the company’s ecosystem, they will be forced to embrace Google’s A.I.

Lina Khan, a former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said in a statement that Google was using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting its A.I. She added that multiple courts had found the tech giant liable for violating antitrust laws.

“This latest move shows it remains unchastened,” Ms. Khan said of Google’s new A.I. changes for schools. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools,” she added, “Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

In recent months, Google has been promoting its Gemini chatbot as a valuable educational tool, saying it can aid teachers in planning lessons and serve as a personalized tutor for students. A new student feature within Gemini, Guided Learning, is supposed to make it harder for students to use A.I. to cheat.

“We’re evolving our approach,” said Mr. Phillips. He promised tools that would “support the productive struggle” of learning and tamp down on students turning to A.I. for easy answers.

In August, Google turned on A.I. features as the default option inside its Classroom app for K-12 schools that had allowed students separate access to the company’s Gemini chatbot. The move upset some school leaders, who felt schools should be able to decide how and when students used Google’s A.I.

Google’s August change will now be reversed.

Parent activists have been pushing back against the use of A.I. in schools, and against screen time more generally. While A.I. chatbots can be useful tools for research and coding, they can also easily be used to cheat on school assignments and can provide false information. Research shows chatbots can also hinder critical thinking and ensnare adolescents in emotional dependency.

Last week, New York State passed a chatbot safety law that would prohibit companies from providing a variety of A.I. features for minors. And in September, the nation’s two largest school districts, in New York City and Los Angeles — both Google clients — broadly restricted student access to generative artificial intelligence on school devices.

In response to Google’s Tuesday announcement, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City wrote on social media, “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margin of Big Tech.”

Officials in the Los Angeles Unified School District have said that they were hoping students would be able to conduct Google searches with A.I. overviews turned off. The overviews are A.I.-generated summaries that appear at the top of searches. They can dissuade students from seeking out multiple sources of information.

On Monday, Google executives said that for districts that do allow A.I., there will be two options for search inside school-issued accounts, beginning in early 2027. One option will be search with A.I. overviews and A.I. chats turned on, similar to the current consumer experience. The other will be search using Guided Learning, the student feature within Google’s Gemini chatbot.

Guided Learning is intended to guide students through a topic step-by-step without providing them with answers that could short-circuit learning. It is supposed to offer an experience modeled on one-to-one tutoring.

The consumer version of Guided Learning is already available within Gemini, and can enable cheating. In a reporter’s test, it produced a detailed essay in response to an Advanced Placement history prompt.

There are greater restrictions in the school version that is currently being piloted, according to Brit Mennuti, product lead for Google Classroom. She said teachers would be able to review students’ chatbot transcripts, among other capabilities.

Richard Culatta, the chief executive of ISTE+ASCD, a nonprofit group promoting “meaningful” school technology use, applauded Google’s plan to turn off its A.I. services for students by default in K-12 schools.

Tech companies, he added, should also enable schools to turn off AI features within search engines. “Our position is that schools should be able to have search that does not have A.I.-generated results in it for students,” Mr. Culatta said. (Mr. Culatta’s group has received funding from Google and other tech companies.)

Kelly Clancy is a New York City public school parent and leader in groups calling for an A.I. moratorium in schools.

She said her seventh-grade son used Google search daily to complete assignments, such as a recent earth science project that required him to learn about lab safety.

“We have to go back to the drawing board on how we are teaching kids to research,” she said, suggesting that students could use alternatives such as physical libraries or competing search engines that allow more control over A.I.

Morgan Polikoff, an education professor at the University of Southern California, said Google’s decision could further energize the anti-tech movement percolating among parents and educators.

“This is a particularly clear example of the tech industry going out of its way to force A.I. on us all — even if we have said we don’t want it,” he said.
