ARTICLE

Flouting Consumer Law, Insurers Refuse to Pay Medical Bills for Emergency Care
A law to end surprise medical bills has generated millions of high-dollar payouts for doctors. Health plans are now fighting back by frequently withholding money.
By Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff
Published 2026-11-03 10:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/insuers-nonpayment-arbitration.html

Over the past two years, Flight for Life has airlifted car crash victims, premature babies and adults struggling to breathe to hospitals across southeastern Wisconsin.

Anthem, the major health insurer, covered dozens of those patients, but it has refused to pay $2.1 million it owes the company for their helicopter rides.

The amounts due for each emergency medical flight range from $9,382 to $62,373. Anthem has historically paid its bills, but late last year it suddenly stopped.

“It was like a faucet they just shut off,” said Flight for Life’s executive director, Leif Erickson.

The insurer’s willful nonpayment is the latest in a cascade of unintended consequences brought about by a widely supported law that was intended to protect patients from surprise medical bills.

The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for arbitrators to decide appropriate levels of reimbursement, and it has already triggered millions of disputes between medical care providers and insurers. Doctors have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning arbitration settlements that sometimes far exceeded the usual insurer rates.

Now, fed up with what they consider unfair outcomes, insurers are fighting back by refusing to pay.

The law, the No Surprises Act, was enacted with a large bipartisan majority to ensure patients never got excessive bills in situations, like emergencies, where they could not pick their doctors.

The arbitration system set up by the law was supposed to resolve billing disputes when health care providers and insurers could not agree on a price: An arbitrator reviews a proposed dollar amount from each side and decides which one is most reasonable. Insurers are required to pay that amount within 30 days, and billing patients for anything beyond that is prohibited.

Lawmakers expected the system to be used rarely and to produce reasonable payments. Instead, doctors and other health care providers have been swamping arbitrators with millions of claims, often for amounts that far exceed what is customarily paid for a service. And they have won the vast majority of their cases — sometimes receiving sums such as $440,000 for a breast reduction, $73,000 for an ankle X-ray, or $125,000 for assisting on prostate surgery.

Insurers have sued doctors and lobbied Congress to change the law, contending that the large awards and lopsided results are driving up health insurance premiums.

But with Washington moving slowly, they have adopted the strategy of simply declining to pay.

Nearly 30 percent of arbitration awards has gone unpaid since 2024, according to an analysis of 400,000 such awards provided by a major medical billing firm that The New York Times reviewed.

Anthem’s nonpayment rate was the highest by far, at 74 percent, but other large insurers, including Cigna, UnitedHealthcare and Aetna, have also declined to pay a significant portion.

The standoff has created dysfunction and lawlessness in a system that a growing number of lawmakers and administration officials say needs to be changed.

“The providers are succeeding in what feel like egregious award levels, and then the insurers are also doing some of this egregious behavior by not paying,” said Katie Keith, the director of Georgetown University’s Center for Health Policy and the Law. “But there’s not accountability on either side.”

Health plans, including Anthem, criticize HaloMD, the company that provided The Times with payment data, for using business tactics that exploit the arbitration system and result in large payouts.Only one of the major insurers the Times contacted disputed the accuracy of the data. A Cigna spokeswoman said that a significantly smaller share went unpaid in 2026 than what the Halo data showed.

Most large health insurers told The Times it is their policy not to pay awards if they believe the claim should never have qualified for the arbitration process, even when the arbitrator determined it to be eligible.

In the case of Flight for Life, Anthem says it will not pay because it believes the medevac service violated the arbitration system’s complex procedural rules, an assessment Flight for Life disputes.

Ariel Bayewitz, vice president of health economics at Elevance Health, Anthem’s parent company, said that the company “believes strongly” in paying eligible awards on time. But, he said, Anthem estimates that most claims that have moved through the arbitration system should have been found ineligible, because they either didn’t follow the rules or were for situations not covered under the consumer protection law.

“More providers are submitting ineligible cases because ineligible cases aren’t being dismissed like they should be,” he said.

Smaller health plans also have been withholding payments in cases where they think the award is unreasonable. Some even have form letters they send to doctors whose awards they won’t pay.

“The determination is not merely high; it is legally defective,” says one such letter, from the New York insurer EmblemHealth, declining to pay an award 99 times its usual rate for a breast reconstruction.

“Recently, we have observed a significant increase in very high-dollar claims, which we are actively reviewing and challenging as appropriate,” said Alex Gomez, a spokesman for the plan.

A spokeswoman for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees the arbitration system, said the law always requires insurers to pay arbitration awards.

Doctors and air ambulance companies have turned to the courts, filing hundreds of lawsuits to enforce the arbitrators’ decisions, but three federal appeals courts have ruled that the No Surprises Act does not include a right to sue.

Stephen Ware, a professor of law at the University of Kansas, said that unlike most arbitration situations, the No Surprises Act does not explain how a ruling can be enforced. One appeals court decision suggested that the government could sue to force insurers to pay. So far, the Trump administration has not exercised such power.

‘We Just Want to Get Paid’

Doctors have said that the nonpayments make it hard to manage their practices. Some who have built their businesses around the arbitration system and its high payouts, have taken on debts to stay afloat.

Dr. Jennifer Raley, a managing partner at Wake Emergency Physicians in North Carolina, said her practice had $1.2 million in outstanding awards. It won 1,032 arbitration cases in 2025, with an average award around four times what insurers typically pay.

In January, it had to take out a line of credit to make payroll.

“We just want to get paid what we need to pay the people who saw the patients,” she said. PHI, a national air ambulance company, recently closed a base in Red Bluff, Calif., a small city between Sacramento and the Oregon border.

In an interview, PHI’s chief executive, Scott McCarty, cited $16.3 million in outstanding payments from Anthem as the cause of the closure.

“The insurance companies cannot unilaterally decide to breach a federal law if they don’t like the end result,” Mr. McCarty said. “That’s essentially what they are doing.”

Anthem spokeswoman Janey Kiryluik said that the insurer was “actively trying to bring PHI Air Medical into our network,” but that the medevac company had requested unreasonably high rates. She said that, in arbitration, it typically requests $56,000 per flight.

Dr. Brian McHugh, a neurosurgeon from Long Island, N.Y., has repeatedly received letters from Anthem challenging his awards on the grounds they are too expensive. Dr. McHugh often wins arbitration awards that are 40 times higher than what Anthem typically pays, according to federal data.

He said other doctors at his practice had stopped seeing Anthem patients.

Ms. Kiryluik said the insurer does not use a financial threshold as a “basis for holding payment,” and that it no longer uses the letter Dr. McHugh received.

Anthem, like all major insurers, supported the No Surprises Act when Congress was writing the legislation during the first Trump administration. But over the last six years, the company’s executives have soured on the law’s arbitration system, saying that it encourages abusive billing. Many of the high awards have been for scheduled procedures, not the emergency care the law was written to address.

Anthem defends its nonpayment policies as intentional. In a 13-page report, it estimated that 60 percent of its cases that arbitrators had decided should never have qualified. This year, it has not paid 83 percent of arbitration claims, according to the HaloMD data, a substantial jump from previous years.

The Labor Department, which oversees large employer health plans, is investigating Anthem’s failure to pay arbitration awards, according to documents The Times obtained. Ms. Kiryluik, the Anthem spokeswoman, said the plan was cooperating with the investigation.

The 400,000 claims that HaloMD shared with The Times make up around two-thirds of the total arbitration cases it has won since 2024. The data set only includes cases for which HaloMD could reliably track payments to doctors.

Anthem and other insurers contend that HaloMD is part of the problem. They say Halo typically submits unreasonably high bids to arbitration, sometimes winning 113 times typical insurer payments. The company has also been accused of filing a high volume of ineligible claims. Five insurers have sued Halo, accusing it of fraudulent behavior. Three of them, including one from Anthem, have been dismissed in federal court, on the grounds that courts can’t review the arbitrators’ decisions.

HaloMD spokesman Patrick Velliky said that the insurers’ lawsuits were “an attempt to intimidate physicians and clinicians out of seeking fair and sustainable reimbursement.”

The law set up a series of deadlines and procedures that doctors need to follow. They limited access to the system to certain situations. Cases where the patient has a government plan, like Medicare or Medicaid, are not eligible. Nor are situations where the doctor already has a contract with the health plan.

Insurers say they sometimes see doctors winning two times for the same care — first in a state-level system to resolve medical billing disputes, and then again through federal arbitration.

“We’re not going to pay it twice,” said Josh Goldberg, executive director of heath policy at Health Care Service Corporation, which covers 27 million people through six Blue Cross affiliates. “This is just a situation where we’re a little bit between a rock and a hard place.”

The insurer is “not the final decider,” said Ms. Keith. She described Anthem’s strategy as “high-risk” because it flouts binding arbitration decisions.

But insurers expressed frustration that the system incentivizes arbitrators to find claims eligible. They get paid a flat fee for each dispute they resolve. If they rule a case is ineligible, they earn nothing.

New Movement in Congress

The No Surprises Act gives the Trump administration authority to fine health insurers $100 for each day they do not pay an arbitration award. So far, it has not issued a single penalty.

Doctors have submitted hundreds of complaints about unpaid awards to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversee the system. Those that The Times spoke with said they had rarely received a response.

“There has to be some enforcement,” said Thomas LaGreca, a partner at Callagy Law, which files claims for providers. He estimates that 27 percent of clients claims remain unpaid six months after arbitration decisions. Health plans also said that C.M.S. had failed to respond to thousands of complaints about the large number of ineligible claims.

Spokespeople for both C.M.S. and the Labor Department declined to respond to questions about why they had not issued penalties to enforce the No Surprises Act.

A Trump administration spokesman told The Times in July that “the system is being gamed” by doctors and that the government was “actively working to clean it up.” The administration has not yet announced any policy changes.

Congress has recently taken a greater interest in reform, with one Senate committee hosting round table meetings and a top House Democrat introducing new legislation.

“There are problems on both sides, and I’ll readily admit that,” Representative Greg Murphy, Republican of North Carolina, said in an interview.

But Mr. Murphy, who worked as a urologist before running for office, said he believed that the “majority of abuses” had been committed by insurers who do not pay awards. He has introduced legislation that would stiffen penalties for nonpayment.

“I ran a small business,” he said. “If I don’t have income, guess what happens to the business? It dies.”

Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, chairs the Senate Health Committee and was an architect of the No Surprises Act. He has told those involved in the process that he views fixing its problems before he leaves office in January as a legacy project.

Representative Frank Pallone Jr., Democrat of New Jersey, was also an author of the original law. He has a different idea: abolishing the complex arbitration system altogether. Last month, he introduced a bill that would resolve billing disputes by setting a flat payment for doctors at the level insurers typically pay.

Mr. Pallone has been skeptical of arbitration supporting it as part of a compromise to get the surprise billing ban passed. He said the reality was even more chaotic than he had predicted. “We have the proof with the facts that shows that this arbitration system is out of hand,” he said.

ARTICLE

Voters Prepare to Deliver a Verdict on Trump’s Second Term
Republicans are bracing for losses amid a backlash to the president’s economic leadership and the Iran war. Whether that means giving up control of the Senate is Tuesday’s biggest question.
By Reid J. Epstein
Published 2026-11-03 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/midterm-elections-trump-democrats-republicans-key-themes.html

For the last two months, President Trump has offered a consistent plea: Pretend he’s on the ballot.

The midterm elections on Tuesday will give voters an opportunity to do just that. They are set to render the first national referendum on a second-term Trump agenda characterized by far-reaching tariffs, an unpopular war with Iran and an aggressive immigration crackdown.

Republican officials are bracing for a harsh judgment and potentially significant defeats. They widely expect to lose control of the House. They have grown increasingly worried about losing the Senate, too.

Democrats have sought to define their campaigns through anger over high prices driven by tariffs and the war, focusing heavily on the idea of making life cost less. Led by Mr. Trump, Republicans have struggled to articulate an affirmative counterargument, with the president dismissing concerns about the economy and sending an often scattered message.

American politics is of course full of surprises. While Republicans have underperformed in both midterm elections of the Trump era, the president has demonstrated his ability to turn out his most loyal supporters. He has also stepped up his baseless attacks on the U.S. election system, raising fears of federal interference in the results.

Democrats need a net gain of just three House seats to win a majority. The Senate is a heavier lift: Democrats must hold all of their seats and flip at least four Republican-held ones. They are competing in states like Texas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988, and Kansas, which has not done so since 1932.

And if Democrats flip at least two Republican-held governorships, they will hold a majority of them for the first time since 2010, when a backlash to President Barack Obama fueled a Republican wave that has shaped American politics ever since.

Polls will close starting at 6 p.m. Eastern. The results that follow will shape the country for at least the next two years, and perhaps much longer. Here are six themes to watch as voting ends:

How deep into Republican territory can Democrats reach?

Look at where the competitive races were in the final days of the campaign.

Solidly red Kansas and Ohio have tossup Senate races. Democrats are seriously contending in House districts like the one in northern New York being vacated by Representative Elise Stefanik — where Mr. Trump won by 21 percentage points two years ago.

Governor’s races are tight in conservative states like Florida, Nebraska and Oklahoma, where Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, the chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, spent Monday night stumping for the party’s nominee. The last Democratic presidential candidate to win even a single county in Oklahoma was Al Gore in 2000.

Over the weekend, Republicans rushed money into Louisiana’s Senate race, which had not been considered a competitive contest before then. Both parties have also directed late money to the Senate races in Mississippi and South Carolina, states that have been out of reach for Democrats for a generation.

With Democrats widely expected to win races in at least some red House districts and threatening to flip Senate seats in deep-red states, the question is how far into Republican terrain they can prevail.

How angry are voters about Trump’s handling of the economy?

Voters care most about whether they can afford their everyday needs, and polls suggest that they are angered about the high prices brought on by tariffs and a war ordered by Mr. Trump.

The president spent the day before the election talking about his alterations to the Reflecting Pool in Washington. Over the last few weeks, some of his most memorable rally lines have been about the anatomies of Republican Senate candidates.

Mr. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to record lows. Republican candidates who have recast their political identities in his image are struggling to convince voters that they can be independent.

In many cases, Republicans have not even tried to make a case that the economy is in good shape. Instead, they have tried to change the subject.

In Michigan’s Senate race, former Representative Mike Rogers has sought to push the Muslim faith and family background of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, to the center of the campaign. In Texas, voters have seen an onslaught of Republican ads about how James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, talked about transgender rights in the past. And in Maine, Senator Susan Collins is selling voters on the idea that her seniority after four terms is best for her state.

If Democrats win the House, how big will their majority be?

We could know fairly early in the evening what kind of night it will be for the House.

In Indiana and the eastern half of Kentucky, polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern. There are tight races in Kentucky’s Sixth Congressional District, which Mr. Trump carried by 15 points in 2024, and Indiana’s Fifth District, which he won by 17 points.

Both are competitive races that will reveal some of the first clues about the rest of the electoral map. They are districts that combine rural and suburban voters and are usually safe for Republicans.

There are dozens of similar House districts across the country.

Nevada’s Second District covers Reno and the state’s rural northern half. Mr. Trump carried it by 14 points. It is not a place where Democrats typically compete. But this year, Democrats have a strong candidate, the Republican incumbent is retiring and the party’s candidate is considered weak while a potential third-party spoiler is poised to siphon conservative votes with help from Democrats.

Districts like these will determine how big of a cushion House Democrats might have when new members are seated come January.

What’s the fallout from the national redistricting fight?

Starting with Texas last summer, Republican-led states began redrawing their congressional district lines to try to secure more House seats for their party.

The new maps were based on the idea that the electorate in 2026 would look somewhat like the one that carried Mr. Trump to victory in 2024.

That does not seem to be the case.

Latino voters have turned against Mr. Trump, shifting the politics of South Texas and South Florida, where Republicans tried to lock in advantages. Rural voters are furious about the price of diesel fuel. Black voters, early voting data suggests, are turning out in huge numbers.

The result is that House districts drawn with the express intent of putting them in Republican hands instead have competitive races. In Texas, Florida, Tennessee and North Carolina, there are increasingly tight races in districts Mr. Trump would have carried by double digits had they existed in 2024.

Meantime in California, voters approved a plan aimed at delivering five House seats for Democrats, and redistricting does not seem to have placed any of the party’s seats at risk.

How all of these races go may have ramifications beyond immediate House control. Several states are weighing redrawing their congressional maps before the 2028 elections. If this year’s new maps backfire, it could temper the aggression of next year’s cartographers.

What about all the Republican money?

Elon Musk spent at least $474 million to back Republicans in the midterm elections. The next four biggest donors are also Republicans. And Mr. Trump had an unmatched war chest.

If Republicans defy expectations, it will be at least in part because of a financial advantage built long before races became tight in the campaign’s final weeks.

At the same time, Democratic officials involved in House and Senate races have lamented that they do not have the money to compete in as many districts and states as they would like.

The Texas governor’s race, for example, became a source of frustration for Latino Democrats. For weeks, they have been angry that the party did not invest more in Gina Hinojosa, a state representative who polls show is running even or close behind Gov. Greg Abbott, the three-term incumbent Republican.

House Democratic officials have privately ticked through a series of districts where they believed they had chances to win if only they had more resources available.

Will Democrats be hurt by their Senate-race dramas?

The red-state Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina are competitive in part because Democrats have nominated a generally strong slate of candidates who have mostly avoided major problems on the campaign trail.

That’s not the case for their blue-state brethren.

Maine Democrats switched out their candidate in July after the primary winner, Graham Platner, was forced out of the race after a rape allegation, which he denied.

Michigan was convulsed this weekend by a late endorsement flip, with Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to Dr. El-Sayed, defecting and backing the Republican in the race, Mr. Rogers.

And in light-blue Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has led in polling in her Senate race despite being trailed by the state’s major fraud scandal and being viewed as running one of the party’s weakest campaigns.

There’s also Alaska, where a New York Times report last week about Democratic chicanery to help Mary Peltola, the party’s nominee for Senate, by recruiting a second Dan Sullivan into the race set off a wave of Republican anger.

Polls show the Democratic nominees leading or with an edge in all four races, but some of these contests — especially in Michigan and Maine, where Ms. Collins, the incumbent Republican, is a formidable opponent — have required more resources and attention than party leaders would have preferred.

ARTICLE

Drone Boat Maker Saildrone Wins Protest Over Navy Contract
A federal judge’s ruling on the side of the small defense contractor was a rarity, as most company protests against government bidding decisions do not prevail.
By Kate Kelly
Published 2026-11-03 23:31 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/politics/drone-boat-maker-navy-protest.html

A federal judge has found that the U.S. Navy improperly barred the drone boat provider Saildrone Inc. from competing for a potentially lucrative contract, a striking victory for a small defense-technology company.

Saildrone, based in Alameda, Calif., bid earlier this year for a chance to build a new type of unmanned vessel for the Navy, taking advantage of budget dollars provided by President Trump’s sprawling domestic policy bill he signed into law last year. But after the initial phase of competition, the company was excluded from demonstrating its boat at sea, ruining its chances to be selected for the new program.

Saildrone and another similarly situated drone boat company, Blue Water Autonomy, then sued the government in the Washington-based Federal Court of Claims, alleging that the Navy’s evaluation process had been improper.

The Navy disagreed. But in an opinion dated Nov. 3, a claims court judge sided with Saildrone.

“The court finds that the Navy engaged in disparate treatment, and thus acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner in its review of Saildrone’s proposal,” Judge Philip S. Hadji wrote.

Contrastingly, the judge found that the Navy’s review — and elimination — of Blue Water Autonomy for the drone boat contract was reasonable, denying its protest.

The fierce competition for the drone boat contract was explored in a New York Times article over the summer.

In his opinion, Judge Hadji demanded that the Navy offer Saildrone a new opportunity to test its vessel for the Navy at sea — the final, and most rigorous, step of the competition after which contract decisions are made.

The judge also ordered that until the evaluation is completed, the Navy must not obligate any more than $1.5 billion for the construction of the type of drone boat Saildrone seeks to build. That cap leaves about $600 million untouched for a period.

A Navy spokeswoman did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In a statement Monday, Richard Jenkins, Saildrone’s chief executive, said that “the future of naval warfare will be fought on the water, not in a courtroom. We are eager to move beyond this litigation and return our entire focus to delivering world-leading maritime autonomy for the U.S. Navy.”

Judge Hadji’s decision marks an unusual victory for the industry, in which most company protests against government bidding decisions do not prevail. It is also a challenge for the Defense Department as it tries to streamline its sourcing and purchasing of equipment to better arm troops.

Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has sought to modernize and quicken the procurement process. Prolonged waits for contracts and funding are so customary that contractors sometimes refer to the gaps between developments — periods so long that they can go out of business before government money arrives — as “the valley of death.”

The bidding to build medium-sized unmanned surface vessels, as the competition at issue in Saildrone’s lawsuit was known, was supposed to exemplify the department’s new approach.

Drone-based defense equipment has become increasingly critical in war zones like Ukraine, and the Navy has been trying to build out a drone vessel program for years. The merits of such equipment were apparent in June, when a sea drone rescued two downed helicopter pilots from the Strait of Hormuz.

But the medium drone boat program was messy from the start, leaving some participants confused and frustrated about the Navy’s review process.

Saildrone and Blue Water each filed suit in late June, contending that their respective elimination from the sea trial phase of the competition was unjust.

Tony Mazzeo, a former Navy lawyer who represents government contractors at the Norfolk, Va.-based Woods Rogers, said Saildrone’s favorable ruling was notable because winning a fight over a government bidding process “is an uphill battle.”

Mr. Mazzeo noted that in fiscal year 2025, the Government Accountability Office, which adjudicates bid protests, sustained just 14 percent of the protests it got. The Court of Claims where Saildrone sued has a higher legal threshold, he said, indicating that a company’s chances of success there are even slimmer.

He added that the opinion was significant for technical reasons, too.

By allowing the case to go forward despite the Navy’s argument that it was the wrong legal venue for the suit, the Court of Claims, he said, “arguably expanded its jurisdiction,” and could soon be hearing more similar cases.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

ARTICLE

Convicted Murderer Caught After Weeklong Escape From Tennessee Prison
Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was found hundreds of miles away, near Kansas City, Mo., after breaching a fence last week at a correctional facility where he was serving a life sentence.
By Rebecca Chao
Published 2026-11-03 22:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/tennessee-escaped-jacob-morley-captured.html

After escaping from a Tennessee prison and spending a week on the run, a man serving a life sentence for murder was captured on Tuesday in Missouri, according to the authorities.

A trooper for the Missouri State Highway Patrol took the fugitive, Jacob Allen Morley, 28, into custody around 11:30 a.m., the agency said in a statement.

Mr. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder in 2025 for the 2022 death of a co-worker, Cody Birchfield. He was serving a life sentence at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tenn., near the southeastern Missouri Bootheel region, when he escaped.

Early on Tuesday, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation received a tip that Mr. Morley had been spotted hiding in a shed at a hunting camp near Marion, Ill., where he had also stolen a truck containing three firearms, the bureau said in a statement. The vehicle license plate was then used to track him down.

Around 9:30 a.m., officials from the bureau had located him, alerting authorities in Missouri that the getaway vehicle Mr. Morley had been traveling in had been spotted using Flock camera technology, the statement from the Missouri patrol said. It was traveling westbound on Interstate 70 near Independence, Mo., just outside Kansas City.

That vehicle, according to Sgt. Justin Ewing of the Missouri patrol, was a white Ford F-350. “It was a flatbed truck with a metal toolbox attachment, a work-style struck,” he said in an interview.

Officers from various agencies began coordinating and moving into the area to locate the truck. Officers in a helicopter from the Kansas City Police Department spotted it traveling east on Missouri Route 210 before taking Missouri Route 10, according to the statement.

After entering Carroll County, about 60 miles east of Kansas City, Mr. Morley turned onto a small county road and veered off path, where his vehicle got stuck. A highway patrol trooper then took Mr. Morley into custody. There was no confrontation and no active pursuit during the capture, according to the statement.

Mr. Morley was more than 450 miles from the Tiptonville prison when he was captured.

His escape was discovered close to midnight on Sunday, Oct. 26, and security footage later revealed that Mr. Morley had breached a fence.

The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation had placed him on its Most Wanted list, with a reward of up to $17,500 for information leading to his capture.

ARTICLE

Trump’s Immigration Dragnet Sweeps Up Ukrainian Truckers Who Fled War
At least a dozen Ukrainian truck drivers were arrested this summer, according to a representative for Ukraine. Several remain in detention.
By Jazmine Ulloa
Published 2026-11-03 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/ukraine-immigrant-trucker-cdl-weigh-stations-ice.html

The 55-year-old Ukrainian truck driver was hauling a load of cars into Oklahoma when he stopped for a routine inspection at a desolate weigh station.

The driver, Mykhailo Shekhtman, had fled Ukraine’s war with Russia, settled in Georgia under a Biden-era humanitarian program to assist Ukrainians. But on that cold February evening, Oklahoma state troopers took him into custody, believing he was unlawfully present in the United States, according to a Homeland Security arrest report. It showed he had no criminal record.

“I asked, ‘Why are you arresting me? On what grounds are you arresting me?’” he recalled in an October interview from a detention facility outside of Oklahoma City.

Mr. Shekhtman is among the more than 330,000 Ukrainians who reside in the United States through Uniting for Ukraine and Temporary Protected Status, humanitarian forms of immigration protection that allowed people escaping the war to temporarily live and work legally in the country.

But the Trump administration regards the entrance of many Ukrainians and other migrants under the Biden administration as unlawful. Some Ukrainians are now living in legal and financial limbo after the federal government suspended the Uniting for Ukraine program and is now considering whether to let the largest deportation protection program, Temporary Protected Status, expire.

For Ukrainian truck drivers, the crosscurrents have been even greater because of a massive federal and state crackdown on noncitizens holding commercial driver’s licenses. Multiagency sweeps have intensified in states such as Indiana, Oklahoma and Texas, entangling hundreds of immigrant truck drivers who have been detained during traffic stops and what used to be routine inspections at weigh stations and highway checkpoints. At least a dozen Ukrainian truckers were detained in Oklahoma and Indiana this summer, according to a representative for Ukraine.

Some Ukrainian truck drivers have been deported to countries like Turkey, where they have no ties, according to interviews with truck drivers and immigration lawyers. Others have been sent back to Ukraine, a country grinding through its fifth year of war, where residents face military enlistment, occupation and relentless Russian bombardment. The Department of Homeland Security did not disclose the total number of Ukrainian truck drivers who have been arrested or deported.

Mr. Shekhtman, who has been detained since his February arrest, is awaiting a hearing on whether he will be granted bond. Through his attorney, he provided documents showing he has repeatedly reported receiving inadequate food and medical care, describing deteriorating eyesight and kidney pain.

“I feel like I’ve been cheated,” Mr. Shekhtman said from detention. “I was invited here to be protected from the war, and so on. I hoped I’d come to a democratic country, and that everything here would be fine.”

In a statement to the The New York Times, D.H.S. confirmed Mr. Shekhtman’s arrest, saying the Border Patrol had previously arrested him after he unlawfully entered the United States on April 21, 2024, before the Biden administration released him into the country. Mr. Shekhtman and his lawyer assert that he had been granted permission to enter the United States before he arrived as part of the Uniting for Ukraine program.

The agency said Mr. Shekhtman had been evaluated by specialists for vision and bladder problems and that he “continues to be monitored and receives treatment for his acute and chronic medical conditions.”

On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced the results of the latest operation in Tulsa, Okla., standing with state enforcement officials in front of a big rig adorned with images of the American flag and a bald eagle. Over several days, officers across 15 states had stopped more than 1,000 commercial trucks, arresting about 40 immigrant drivers, including some with serious criminal charges, he said. The drivers hailed from 19 countries, including Ukraine.

“These individuals came over, and they’re putting those that are driving on the road with them in jeopardy,” Mr. Mullin said.

Defending the administration’s crackdown, he also contended that allowing unauthorized immigrants to operate commercial trucks was reckless and dangerous to public safety, saying many do not speak English.

The plight of Ukrainian immigrants has exposed deep rifts in the Republican Party and prompted clashes between immigration opponents and a coalition of evangelical groups, businesses and local lawmakers who have pressured federal lawmakers to shield Ukrainians from deportation.

Representative William R. Keating, a Democrat of Massachusetts, and Representative Brian K. Fitzpatrick, a Republican of Pennsylvania, and Marcy Kaptur, a Democrat of Ohio,have sponsored bipartisan legislation that would create permanent pathways to legal residency for Ukrainians. Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican of Alaska, sponsored another bill in her chamber this year. Both bills, however, remain stalled.

The administration announced this month that Ukrainians could retain T.P.S. for now, but the program’s future remains precarious. “They pay taxes, their children are often in honor rolls in schools, they do their share,” said Anna Move, co-founder of the Leonid Foundation, which assists Ukrainian refugees. Yet without stability, she said, many are debating whether they must now go.

Enforcement against Ukrainian truck drivers has centered on the freight arteries running through the Great Plains and the Midwest. Karl Ahlgren, a licensed chaplain and diplomat representing Ukraine in Oklahoma, and Ukrainian community leaders have tracked more than a dozen Ukrainian truck drivers swept into immigration custody in Oklahoma and Indiana alone this summer.

At least five remain detained in Oklahoma, according to Mr. Ahlgren, who has visited them at Oklahoma detention centers. “These guys are the sole breadwinners for their families,” Mr. Ahlgren said.

Tim Tipton, commissioner of public safety in Oklahoma, called the enforcement operations critical to spotting human trafficking and preventing deadly crashes.

“This is a huge public safety issue in Oklahoma when it comes to somebody driving an 80,000-pound truck who has not been trained properly, can’t read or speak English,” he said.

The federal campaign against immigrant truck drivers began in earnest in April, when President Trump issued an executive order directing transportation agencies to enforce a long-dormant regulation requiring commercial drivers to read and speak proficient English.

Since then, federal officials have stopped issuing worker visas for commercial truck drivers, revoked the accreditation of thousands of truck driving schools and issued emergency rules to prohibit commercial driver’s licenses for asylum seekers, refugees and other immigrants with temporary legal status. The efforts escalated following two fatal crashes last year involving Sikh immigrant truck drivers that killed six people, leading to criminal charges against the drivers.

The pressure on Ukrainians in the United States is unfolding as Moscow has intensified its air assault in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

Mr. Shekhtman recalled enduring constant missile strikes back in his native Vinnytsia in central Ukraine. He said goodbye to several friends and relatives who went off to fight in the war and never came back. He was a professional truck driver in Ukraine, Mr. Shekhtman said.

In April 2024, he arrived in the United States and found a home near Savannah, Ga. Once he underwent criminal background checks and obtained his work permit, he passed a state driving test, acquiring a license that allowed him to drive a small truck and trailer to haul passenger vehicles. The pathway had been well worn by other Ukrainians drawn to the industry for its substantial pay and established networks of Ukrainian and immigrant drivers.

But throughout his 2024 election campaign, Mr. Trump argued that President Biden had let in too many immigrants and that too many were exploiting temporary humanitarian programs. Since taking office, he has rolled back some of those programs and sought to restrict others.

Mr. Shekhtman said that before his arrest, he had filed an application with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to extend his U4U humanitarian parole for two more years and had received an appointment date to provide his biometric data. But, he said, he missed the appointment because he was held in detention.

ARTICLE

Anthrax Outbreak in Africa’s Oldest National Park Is Killing Hippos
The disease has killed 30 hippopotamuses in Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo since September, officials say.
By Ephrat Livni
Published 2026-11-04 00:48 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/africa/congo-anthrax-hippos-virunga-park.html

An anthrax outbreak in a park in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been killing hippopotamuses, threatening vulnerable wildlife and raising concerns about human exposure to the disease.

The outbreak at Virunga National Park — Africa’s oldest national park — has killed 30 hippopotamuses since September, when observers first started noticing suspicious carcasses, Laura Parker, who leads the park’s conservation programs, said in an email on Tuesday. The cause of the animals’ deaths, and the outbreak, has since been confirmed by laboratory analyses, she noted.

This is the second outbreak of anthrax in the park since last year, and it comes as Congo is contending with an Ebola epidemic that has killed more than 4,800 people since May and strained the country’s resources.

Doctors who have analyzed anthrax outbreaks in the region say that the disease represents a significant public health challenge, intersecting with issues like food insecurity, conflict and poverty, and disproportionately affecting rural populations with limited access to health care.

Park officials have been raising awareness among local communities to ensure people do not touch or consume meat from any affected carcasses and report any such finds to the authorities, Ms. Parker said.

“Virunga’s response is focused on surveillance, safe carcass management and reducing risks to both wildlife and people. Teams are monitoring the affected area, documenting new mortalities and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses,” she said.

Anthrax is a zoonotic disease caused by a bacterium found naturally in soil around the world. It often affects livestock and wild animals that can become infected when they breathe in, eat or drink spores in contaminated soil, plants or water. The spores can lie dormant in soil for years or decades, so outbreaks recur in areas where they are already in the environment, as in the national park.

Last year’s anthrax outbreak killed about 65 hippos in the park and affected people in the region. Human exposure to anthrax is most commonly linked to contact with infected animals, and community outreach is vital to preventing deaths or illness in people, public health experts say.

Anthrax outbreaks are linked to unusual climatic conditions, including prolonged dry periods, and a lack of rain may be to blame for the latest episodes of the disease, park officials surmise. There has been significant rainfall of late and no new cases confirmed in two weeks, so they are cautiously optimistic, but monitoring protocols continue, Ms. Parker said.

Virunga National Park is recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site for its exceptional wildlife and biodiversity. It was established in 1925. While rich in natural resources, however, the park is in one of the world’s poorest countries, one that has been plagued by decades of conflict.

On its website, the park is described as being located “in a region which has been deeply impacted by the effects of war and armed conflict for over 20 years.” Conflict and poverty are among the forces driving wildlife poaching in Congo, with hippos poached for their meat by armed groups and impoverished people, as well as for the ivory in their teeth.

The park, which had about 29,000 hippos 50 years ago, saw much of the population depleted over the years. This year, it reported about 2,700 hippos, noting that the latest figures suggested efforts to protect the vulnerable animals, including by having more rangers patrolling the park, were leading to a slow recovery.

The latest anthrax outbreak has dealt a blow to the project.

Helicopters Collide Over Everest Trail, Killing 1 and Injuring 3 Others

By Ephrat Livni
Published 2026-11-03 23:19 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/asia/helicopter-crash-everest-nepal.html

A midair collision of two helicopters near Mount Everest on Tuesday left one Indian tourist dead and a visitor from New Zealand and two pilots injured, according to Nepal’s civil aviation authority.

The helicopters collided as they were attempting to land in the Pheriche area of the Solukhumbu district of Nepal around 8 in the morning, the aviation authority said in a statement. Pheriche is a village at an altitude of about 13,900 feet along the Everest Base Camp trekking route.

Video of the accident showed that, in apparently clear weather, the propellers of a lower helicopter made contact with a second aircraft that had been flying higher nearby and swooped downward rapidly. Both helicopters fell to the ground not far apart and appeared to have been destroyed in the collision.

The crash cast a pall on the popular tourist destination during the autumn climbing season and highlighted the dangers that some locals and government officials have warned of as flights in the region have proliferated.

The Nepali authorities identified the dead tourist as Vasanth Kumar Balaramaramadu, 44, of India and the injured visitor, who was being treated at a hospital in Kathmandu, as Shailesh Kisan Patel of New Zealand. The aviation authority’s statement expressed hope for a speedy recovery for the injured, including two unnamed pilots.

In a post, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu expressed “its deepest condolences on the unfortunate demise of an Indian national” and said it was working “in close coordination with Nepali authorities for early repatriation of the mortal remains of the deceased.”

The aviation authority in Nepal said it was investigating the collision and would take any actions or corrective measures needed to address potential issues. “Preliminary reports suggest miscommunication between the pilots, as the area is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport’s air traffic control tower and pilots have to communicate with each other,” Mukesh Dangol, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, told The Kathmandu Post.

The perils of heavy helicopter traffic in the mountainous region are well known, and the Nepali government has struggled to strike a balance between the needs of a thriving tourism industry and the demand for better regulation to ensure safety and preservation of the natural environment.

In 2023, five visitors from Mexico and a Nepali pilot were killed when their helicopter crashed during a sightseeing trip over Mount Everest.

Local officials and those at the Sagarmatha National Park, home to Mount Everest, have clashed with government regulators over helicopter restrictions in recent years. In 2024, the park authorities said they would begin restricting helicopter sightseeing tours and some other flights in 2025, a rule that civil aviation regulators initially said the park had no authority to enforce.

King Charles to Give ‘Unflinching’ Speech on U.K. Role in Slave Trade

By Michael D. Shear
Published 2026-11-03 12:58 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/europe/king-charles-speech-uk-slave-trade-antigua.html

King Charles III and Prime Minister Andy Burnham are both expected to confront the legacy of Britain’s role in the slave trade in speeches at a gathering in Antigua that includes the leaders of many former British colonies.

Their planned remarks follow years of pressure from members of the Commonwealth, a voluntary organization that includes 56 nations, most of which were once part of the sprawling British Empire, for Britain to apologize and pay reparations.

Mr. Burnham wrote in an essay last week that his government was open to a structured conversation with countries affected by the trans-Atlantic slave trade, which he called “a brutal and barbaric violation.” Britain trafficked millions of slaves from Africa in the 1700s and 1800s. Mr. Burnham wrote: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”

However, he rejected calls for reparations, saying that British people should not be “held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

The king has previously said that slavery “forever stains” British history and he asserted last week that the country should directly “acknowledge the great suffering of the past.”

Buckingham Palace said the king’s 15-minute address would address Britain’s colonial connection to the trans-Atlantic slave trade with “unflinching honesty.” The king, as the country’s ceremonial head of state, is constitutionally unable to issue a formal apology unless he is directed to by the government.

Neither the king nor the prime minister is expected to deliver an apology at Tuesday’s opening meeting of the Commonwealth. Government officials said a formal apology could emerge after a “structured dialogue with Commonwealth nations.” The BBC reported that could be within the next year, perhaps when Britain holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.

“Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting as we look to reshape a new era for the Commonwealth, as well as being open to discussions about the past,” Mr. Burnham will say in his speech, according to excerpts released by his office.

The prime minister is expected to announce an effort to help Commonwealth nations restructure their debt, allowing them to pay over a longer period of time and at lower interest rates. In his essay last week, he said that he had asked Gordon Brown, a former prime minister and a long-serving chancellor of the Exchequer under Tony Blair’s premiership, to attend the meeting on Tuesday and lead the debt talks.

Mr. Burnham will also announce a task force to encourage development of critical minerals, his office said. And he will promise that Britain will invest 40 million pounds (about $53 million) over the next three years to accelerate critical infrastructure investment in the Caribbean.

King Charles will focus most of his speech Tuesday morning on opportunities for the Commonwealth nations, according to the palace.

“His majesty’s most significant contribution,” the palace said in a statement, “has been helping to connect leaders, institutions and investors — many of whom he knows personally from his many years of international diplomacy — around shared areas of interest and concern, creating the conditions in which ambitious Commonwealth-led initiatives can emerge and succeed.”

The king will mention a nature initiative intended to help protect biodiversity and increase conservation. He will talk about plans for an insurance mechanism to help countries become more climate-resilient and to deal with natural disasters. And he will endorse efforts to bring heads of governments, investors and business leaders together to increase development in small economies.

ARTICLE

Poland Beefs Up Security at Border With Russia
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there had been “disturbing movement” in Kaliningrad, a Russian region just north of Poland.
By Andrew Higgins
Published 2026-11-03 17:35 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/europe/poland-russia-kaliningrad.html

Poland has launched a “special operation” involving counterterrorism police, intelligence officers and beefed-up border security on its northern frontier with Russia, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, calling it a response to “disturbing movement” that could be preparation for “armed incursions.”

Mr. Tusk, speaking in Warsaw, said the late-night movement just across the border in Kaliningrad — a Russian region sandwiched between Poland, the Baltic Sea and Lithuania — involved unidentified people carrying flashlights, whose intentions were not clear.

He said Poland had received warnings from allied intelligence services of possible “acts of sabotage or more serious provocations on the border with the Russian Federation.” Mr. Tusk added that “more precise information,” received recently, indicated that “events could occur in the first half of November, including armed incursions” into Polish territory.

“It’s not a coincidence that this tension, provoked by the Russians, is occurring today,” Mr. Tusk said, citing “global uncertainty and confusion” over the midterm elections in the United States and a “sense of conflict and instability” in Poland because of a bitter political dispute over its constitutional court.

European governments have been frazzled in recent months by a spate of sabotage operations that officials have blamed on Russia, including a failed drone attack on a German airport. There have also been warnings, citing intelligence reports, that Russia could be planning some kind of military incursion or provocation along NATO’s eastern flank.

An airport outside of Warsaw shut down briefly on Tuesday after a bomb threat was directed at a flight from London, one of two Warsaw-bound flights that were targeted in what appeared to be hoax threats. Several other flights in Europe were also subjected to bomb threats. All landed safely, and the threats were being investigated.

Some of Mr. Tusk’s political opponents accused him of using border tensions to distract attention from an effort by government-backed judges on the Constitutional Tribunal to unseat its chief justice, a supporter of Poland’s former right-wing governing party, Law and Justice. Mr. Tusk’s government sent riot police to seal off the court on Friday.

President Karol Nawrocki, a foe of Mr. Tusk and a vocal supporter of the chief justice, barely mentioned Russia at a National Security Council meeting held on Tuesday to discuss defense issues, focusing instead on the standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal.

While stating that “the aggressor,” a reference to Russia, “must be effectively deterred” even as it “operates below the threshold of war,” Mr. Nawrocki vowed to resist changes at the court and “stop this attempt to overturn the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland.”

Kaliningrad, formerly German land that was annexed by the Soviet Union after World War II, is Russia’s westernmost territory. As the headquarters of its Baltic Fleet and a major military garrison, it has long been viewed as a potential launchpad for military action.

Poland’s previous right-wing government, facing a tough election in 2023, warned that Russian mercenary fighters were mobilizing to seal off the so-called Suwalki Gap, which stretches from Kaliningrad to Belarus between Poland and Lithuania.

Once, closing the gap would have separated the three Baltic states, all members of NATO, from the rest of the military alliance. But Finland’s entry into NATO after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that. The mercenaries that the government warned about in 2023 never appeared.

Far more likely than an armed incursion from Kaliningrad into Poland, according to analysts, are small-scale provocations and sabotage operations aimed at destabilizing Mr. Tusk’s government, which Moscow reviles because of its strong support for Ukraine and the European Union.

Disorder on the frontier, according to this theory, could help turn Polish opinion against Ukraine and boost right-wing political forces that are hostile to the European Union, Ukrainian refugees and, in some cases, military support for Kyiv. Most of the weapons and ammunition that Ukraine receives from the West pass through Polish territory.

Instability on the border could also stoke further political tumult amid rising passions over the standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal. Mr. Tusk’s opponents accused him of staging a “coup d’état” after the deployment of riot police outside the court, where five new judges appointed by Parliament had supported a move to unseat the chief justice.

The right-wing opposition insists that those judges are impostors because Mr. Nawrocki, the president, refused to preside over their swearing-in ceremonies. The president has no veto power over judicial appointments, but does have ceremonial duties, something that Mr. Nawrocki has used to try to block the new judges.

On Tuesday, Mr. Tusk tied right-wing denunciations of his actions to a campaign of similar attacks by officials and state media outlets in Moscow, apparently hoping that the deep suspicion of Russia shared by nearly all Poles would help rally public opinion behind his efforts to break the judicial deadlock.

Urging his critics not to become “useful idiots,” Mr. Tusk said: “It’s invaluable today that Polish politicians don’t intentionally or foolishly serve the interests of Russia, which relies on destabilization, disregard for international law, deeming the European Union its main enemy, and so on.”

Anatol Magdziarz contributed reporting from Warsaw.

The Iran War Is Unpopular. Trump Keeps Talking About It Anyway.
President Trump has repeatedly reminded Americans of a losing campaign issue just as voters head to the polls. Why?
By Lara Jakes
Published 2026-11-03 10:45 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/middleeast/trump-iran-war-election-strategy.html

The war in Iran is deeply unpopular with Americans. Recent polls indicate as many as two-thirds of voters disapprove of President Trump’s handling of the eight-month conflict, which has driven up prices and depleted U.S. ammunition stockpiles.

Yet in the final days of the campaign, Mr. Trump kept talking about it.

“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters on Saturday.

“The only reason we’re not finished with Iran is, I want to be nice, I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” he said at a campaign rally on Sunday.

“We had a war with Iran,” he added Monday. “We won.” Hours later, officials confirmed that the U.S. military had struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what they described as a defensive measure that was not expected to escalate.

Here are three reasons why Mr. Trump kept bringing up Iran, according to analysts.

To push Iran toward a deal

Mr. Trump, who prides himself on his deal-making, could be trying to restart talks.

“By threatening strikes, he wants to send the Iranians a message: ‘Come to the table now or else,’” said Arta Moeini, managing director of the nonpartisan Institute for Peace and Diplomacy, which advocates for military restraint.

Iran’s foreign ministry on Monday said it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agreed to several demands, including lifting U.S. economic sanctions against Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.

The Trump administration is unlikely to accept either condition. For now, Mr. Trump “is going to use the promise of diplomacy again, as he has done before,” Mr. Moeini said. “He can announce that, and maybe get better results for the election, but still later say, ‘They didn’t do what they promised to do, and so we can attack.’”

‘Tough guy’ rhetoric has worked before

Threatening rhetoric is part of Mr. Trump’s brand and has helped him build a loyal following.

“There is a very real strand of American public opinion, the Jacksonian tradition, that likes a leader who projects toughness and who is prepared to whack the bad guys,” said Andrew Payne, a research director at Chatham House, a policy institute in London.

But Mr. Payne called that approach to Iran a “misguided” political strategy. “You’ve seen the polling,” he said.

He sees Iran as a legacy issue

Yet polling will matter less for Mr. Trump going forward. Regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s elections, he will be entering his final two years in office, a period when presidents often take policy risks to secure their legacies.

“He has staked his legacy in foreign policy, to some degree, on Iran,” Mr. Payne said. “It’s more important for him to try and get some favorable resolution to that in the long term than worrying about the short-term impact at the polls.”

The Trump administration is already moving three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces to the Persian Gulf region, to be ready to strike within days.

“I do believe that he will escalate no matter what,” Mr. Moeini said. “I don’t think that’s cheap talk.”

CVS to Split off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
In a breakup planned for 2028, CVS Health intends to split off its pharmacies into a new company, while keeping together its businesses in insurance and pharmacy benefits.
By Rebecca Robbins
Published 2026-11-04 12:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/business/cvs-health-split.html

CVS Health plans to split in two, in a major unraveling of the country’s largest health care conglomerate after years of rampant expansion, the company announced on Wednesday.

Under the breakup, planned for the first half of 2028, a new spinoff company, to be called CVS Pharmacy, will house the conglomerate’s approximately 9,000 retail pharmacies, in-store clinics and a warehouse-based operation that sends prescriptions through the mail.

A second company will retain the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefit manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.

CVS Health has been under mounting scrutiny from lawmakers, regulators and others who say the company — along with its peers, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna — has grown too dominant. Critics say the conglomerates have exploited conflicts to profit from their web of businesses, driving up medical costs and stifling competition.

Within the past two years, Arkansas and Tennessee have each passed laws that aim to prevent the conglomerates from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies. In Washington and other states, lawmakers from both parties have proposed similar legislation, which the conglomerates have fiercely opposed.

CVS Health generated over $400 billion in revenue last year. That ranked seventh among U.S. public companies, according to FactSet, a financial data provider.

The Financial Times on Tuesday reported the company’s plans to split itself up.

The planned breakup would end a nearly decade-long chapter in which CVS Health reached into nearly every corner of the health care system. That era began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged. That same year, Cigna bought Express Scripts, the pharmacy benefit manager.

Since then, CVS, UnitedHealth and Cigna have increasingly touched more pieces of the machinery by which Americans receive health care. Each company now encompasses a major insurer, a giant pharmacy benefit manager and a mail-order pharmacy, along with a vast array of other businesses. Critics complain that the conglomerates use their size and leverage to steer patients toward their own pharmacies.

But for CVS, merging its businesses have not met Wall Street’s demands for growth. At the end of 2024, the company’s market value fell to its lowest level in over a decade, though it has since rebounded.

Many investors see CVS’s pharmacy benefit manager as the shining jewel of the portfolio. But prospects have dimmed for the pharmacy business, amid changing consumer habits and industry-wide challenges that have shuttered other major pharmacy chains like Rite Aid.

The New York Times Company said on Wednesday that it had added 420,000 digital-only subscribers in the third quarter, boosting its total number of paid subscribers to 13.8 million.

The results keep the company roughly on pace to meet its stated goal of 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027 across the news report as well as Wirecutter, Cooking, Games and the Athletic sports news site. The company has added about 1.46 million digital-only subscribers in the past 12 months, though it had a slower second quarter with the addition of 280,000 subscribers.

Total revenue for the third quarter was $768.5 million, an increase of 9.7 percent from the same time period last year. Adjusted operating profit was $149.6 million, up from $131.4 million in the third quarter of last year.

Adjusted operating costs were $618.9 million, an increase of 8.7 percent year over year, which the company said was due to higher compensation and benefits expenses, higher general and administrative costs, and higher marketing and promotion costs. The company had forecast an increase of 8 to 9 percent.

Revenue from digital-only subscriptions grew 14.6 percent year over year, to $421.3 million for the quarter. Digital-only average revenue per user, a metric used to measure the health of subscription businesses, was $9.93, up slightly from the same time last year.

But print subscriptions continued to fall. The Times now has 540,000 print subscribers, down from 570,000 a year earlier.

Digital advertising revenue was up 12 percent to $109.9 million. Revenue from affiliate, licensing and other categories increased 6.2 percent to $78.4 million.

Meredith Kopit Levien, the company’s chief executive, said in a statement that The Times’s “subscriber growth was powered by strong engagement and retention,” and that the company had increased its profit “while continuing to invest in growth areas like video.”

The Times had $1.26 billion in cash and marketable securities at the end of September. The company in September formally expressed interest in buying Letterboxd, a social platform for film lovers, The Times reported. (A spokeswoman declined to comment.)

For the fourth quarter, the company forecast an increase of 12 to 15 percent in digital-only subscription revenue compared with the same period a year ago, and a high-single-digit to low-double-digit increase in digital advertising revenue. It also forecast a year-over-year increase of 6 to 8 percent in adjusted operating costs in the fourth quarter.

Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX Tumble After Republicans Are Routed

After Democrats claimed sweeping victories, claiming both houses of Congress and other important state races, shares of SpaceX and Tesla, which are both run by Mr. Musk, fell sharply in premarket trading on Wednesday.

Tesla’s stock fell over 6 percent before markets opened, while SpaceX was down 5.6 percent, dropping below $135, the price it sold shares for in its blockbuster public offering in June. In recent years, Mr. Musk has antagonized Democrats, spending heavily to elect President Trump, involving himself deeply in the federal government and aligning his companies’ interests with those of the current presidential administration.

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Edward J. Markey, a Democrat in Massachusetts, posted on X on Tuesday night about potential hearings for technology executives.

Mr. Musk spent at least $474 million on the midterm election, the most money of any donor in a U.S. election cycle, apart from candidates who have funded their own runs for office. About $224 million was spent on races in Texas, particularly in support of the losing campaign of Ken Paxton for a Senate seat against James Talarico.

Both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered in Texas. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Mr. Musk moved there after declaring that California had become too liberal for his taste.

Both companies are developing extensive infrastructure in Texas, including a joint effort to build a more than $100 billion chip manufacturing plant in the state, though those efforts could now face greater scrutiny. Texas is set to have a Democratic governor after the election of Gina Hinojosa, as well as a Democratic Attorney General and Lieutenant Governor.

Mr. Musk, 55, did not immediately return a request for comment.

Mr. Musk’s midterm spending, while substantial, will have little impact on his overall wealth. As of Tuesday, he was worth $898 billion, according to Bloomberg, meaning that his political contributions amounted to a tiny sliver of his net worth.

In relative terms, it was akin to a 55-year-old with the median U.S. net worth of about $411,000 spending a little more than $217.

Mr. Musk, who avoided posting on X for most of Tuesday night as votes were being counted, returned to his social media platform in the early hours of Wednesday to joke about his political losses and his companies’ prospects.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote, referring to SpaceX’s goal to put A.I. computing clusters in orbit.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Trump Administration Moves to Oust Arbitrators as Doctor Payouts Soar
The two companies settled billing disputes between doctors and insurers, keeping patients out of the middle. One let doctors win 96 percent of the time.
By Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff
Published 2026-11-04 21:53 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/health/arbitrators-medical-bills.html

The federal government plans to end contracts with two arbitration firms that settle medical billing disputes under the No Surprises Act, a consumer protection law that has come under scrutiny for high payouts for doctors.

Congress passed the law in 2020 to protect patients from surprise bills when they saw a doctor who did not have a contract with their health plan, such as in emergencies. The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for health care providers and insurers to settle on a price and when they cannot, for arbitrators to review an offer from each side, and pick one.

When the law passed, its authors expected the system to be used rarely and decisions generally to be split between the sides. But doctors have flooded the system with millions of cases and have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning more than 85 percent of them in 2025, according to the most recent federal data. Many have received awards dozens of times higher than usual insurer rates.

One New York plastic surgery practice won $440,000 for breast reduction surgeries in arbitration, The New York Times previously reported, and a surgical assistant in New Jersey won $106,500 for assisting on lower back surgery.

The law has been a financial boon for the arbitration firms as well. The government contracts with 17 firms to handle the millions of cases that now flow through the arbitration process. The arbitrators set their own fees, earning $425 to $800 for each dispute they settle, and they have collectively earned $742 million between 2022 and 2025.

While the contractors are all supposed to follow the same rules, federal data shows that outcomes vary dramatically between the arbitrators.

Some outside experts have argued that, because the arbitrators are paid per case, they have an incentive to side with the doctors to keep them coming back to the system. Doctors appear to win their cases at similar rates when they request modest or huge payments.

Insurers, who have argued that the arbitrators frequently decide cases that should not even be eligible for the process, have declined to pay some awards.

The arbitrators’ contracts last five years, and the government is now reviewing those awarded in 2022.

Two firms, Island Peer Review Organization and Network Medical Review Company, were notified on Wednesday that the government does not plan to renew their contracts, according to a notice published that day.

The notice did not say why the companies’ applications had been denied.

An FAQ document published this summer provided possible grounds for denial, which included application paperwork errors, a lack of staff training, conflicts of interest or a failure to decide cases accurately.

In a statement, Christopher Krepich, a spokesman for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees the program, said the firms’ applications had been denied for performance reasons.

“The departments determined that these entities did not substantially comply with the standards governing their performance during their current certification terms,” he said.

Island Peer Review Organization was not immediately available for comment. It had been finding in doctors’ favor 96.5 percent of the time, the highest of any arbitration firm, according to an analysis by the health data firm Turquoise. It has handled nearly 450,000 disputes through the end of last year, according to federal data.

That work had transformed the finances of the small Long Island nonprofit firm, increasing its revenues from $68 million in 2022 to $171 million in 2025, according to public tax filings, as Stat News reported.

Network Medical Review Company has handled 363,000 cases and sided with doctors in 70.8 percent of them, according to the Turquoise analysis. It is a privately held company, so information on its finances is not publicly available.

It plans to appeal the decision, a National Medical Review Company spokeswoman said, adding that the firm “reviews claims in a comprehensive, balanced and efficient manner.”

The firms have decided cases that were highlighted in Times reporting on the arbitration system. Network Medical Review Company awarded an assistant breast surgeon $220,000 for his work on a breast reduction surgery. (Another firm awarded the primary surgeon an additional $220,000 for the case.) Island Peer Review Organization awarded an assistant surgeon $50,000 for work on a prostate surgery, 27 times the fee paid to the main surgeon in the case.

In recent weeks, the administration has announced that eight other firms have met the initial criteria to earn another five-year contract. Some of those arbitrators have similar records of lopsided and high awards to medical providers. Others are still being reviewed.

The two firms losing contracts will have 30 days to dispute the government’s decision. The process must be completed by the end of the year.

The disparate win rates and high-dollar awards have caught the attention of Congress, where interest in revising the law is growing. Representative Frank Pallone Jr., Democrat of New Jersey, introduced legislation last month proposing to abolish the arbitration system entirely.

He has also opened an investigation into the arbitration firms, sending them detailed requests for information on how they make their decisions.

The Trump administration has also signaled some interest in reforms. “The system is being gamed to get higher prices, and C.M.S. is actively working to clean it up,” Mr. Krepich, the agency spokesman, told The Times in July.

This appears to be their first action to change the arbitration system.
