ARTICLE

Appeals Court Hands Win to Mamdani in Fight Over Second-Home Tax
The court reversed a judge’s order that had said New York erred in its rollout of the tax, granting Mayor Zohran Mamdani a victory over a key piece of his agenda.
By Mihir Zaveri
Published 2026-11-04 19:43 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/nyregion/pied-a-terre-mamdani-appeal-win-home-tax.html

An appeals court on Wednesday ruled that Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration can proceed with efforts to collect a new tax on high-end second homes in New York City, handing the mayor his first major legal victory over a core piece of his progressive agenda.

Uncertainty had clouded the tax for weeks, after a Staten Island judge ruled in September that the city had mishandled the rollout and ordered it to start over. The city immediately appealed, and continued rolling out the tax as the lawsuit proceeded. The decision on Wednesday, from a panel of appellate judges in Brooklyn, reversed the judge’s ruling.

The tax still faces other legal challenges. But the ruling is a win for the mayor, whose lawyers are also defending other policies he campaigned on, including a rent freeze on rent-stabilized apartments.

Mr. Mamdani had embraced the tax as a way to make good on his campaign promise to “tax the rich,” as well as a way to help close the city’s budget gap.

The mayor said in a statement on Wednesday that he was “heartened” by the ruling.

“From Day 1, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city,” he said.

Randy Mastro, a lawyer representing the homeowners who brought the lawsuit, did not say whether he planned to appeal. But in a statement, he lamented that the tax rollout, which he called “lawless and chaotic,” would “go unremedied.” Mr. Mastro added that he believed that challenges to the constitutionality of the tax itself — the main argument in the other lawsuits, including one he brought — would ultimately prevail.

The process of introducing the tax on second homes, also known as pieds-à-terre, has been turbulent.

The tax was unveiled by Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring with Mr. Mamdani’s support, and passed in the state budget. It must be paid by people who live outside New York City most of the time while also owning a high-value home in the city.

Levied as a surcharge on property tax bills, the tax applies to condos and co-ops that are used as second homes and have a “market value” — a complicated metric determined by the city’s Finance Department — of at least $1 million. It also applies to one-, two- and three-family second homes with a “market value” of more than $5 million. (The tax does not apply if the home is being rented to someone, or if a relative of the owner lives there most of the time.)

It is expected to raise some $500 million annually for the city.

The lawsuit that led to Wednesday’s ruling did not challenge the legality of the tax. Instead, it argued that the city had sowed confusion by sending out notices to about 17,000 New Yorkers informing them that their properties might be subject to the tax, without first making sure that they were not full-time residents.

The suit also took issue with the city’s publishing an online list of nearly one million “properties that may be subject to the charge” that included the owners’ names.

The city has maintained that it acted in accordance with the law that established the tax.

The notices asked property owners to provide proof of residency, such as a driver’s license, or a copy of a lease to show that the home was being rented out. As of Oct. 28, the city had approved around 8,800 applications from homeowners who said they were primary residents and should not be taxed.

The city has said in recent days that even as that figure has grown, it remains confident that the tax will yield the anticipated $500 million in annual revenue.

In a six-page decision, the appellate court said that the homeowners who sued had not demonstrated “that any bad actors have misused the information” on the published list of properties, “or that the publication itself subjected them to any crime, harassment or defined public ridicule.”

The court also said that the mailed notices did not constitute harm, concluding that the homeowners lacked the standing to sue.

Despite the ruling, two separate pending lawsuits are seeking to overturn the tax itself. Both of those suits argue that the law establishing the tax violates provisions of the state constitution that limit how much the city can collect in real estate taxes every year. Among other claims, they also argue that the tax is discriminatory under the U.S. Constitution because it applies only to residents of states other than New York.

One of the lawsuits was brought in September by former Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, his wife, Hilary Geary Ross, and the casino mogul Steve Wynn, all of whom live in Florida but own second homes in New York City.

The other was brought by the corporation that owns an Upper East Side co-op building known as the Montclair, as well as a handful of homeowners, including some who live in Florida and in Suffolk County on Long Island. That lawsuit is backed by the Real Estate Board of New York, an influential lobbying group.

ARTICLE

In Michigan, the Gamble Paid Off
Abdul El-Sayed’s victory answers several questions.
By Lydia Polgreen
Published 2026-11-04 07:42 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/abdul-el-sayed-michigan-senate.html

The gamble paid off.

Abdul El-Sayed, a charismatic populist progressive who championed Medicare for all, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending military aid to Israel, won the Senate race in Michigan. After defeating Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman who had been an F.B.I. agent, he will become America’s first Muslim senator. His victory — three years after Oct. 7 and 25 after Sept. 11 — is historic. It is sure to fuel the debate over how Democrats should wield their newfound power in Congress and what kind of candidate they should nominate for the presidency in 2028.

It’s too soon to say how that will shake out, and I expect his margin of victory to be interpreted endlessly. But El-Sayed’s win answers several questions. Can a Muslim American win in a statewide race? Can an out-and-out progressive succeed in a swing state? Can a Democratic candidate prevail without full-throated party backing and in the face of right-wing vitriol? Yes, yes and yes. More than anything, the result is an argument for the X factor in politics, the importance of skilled, talented candidates no matter their affiliation. Whatever else he was, El-Sayed was an exceptional package.

On paper, El-Sayed seems like an ideal Democratic candidate to defend a vulnerable seat in a swing state. He has brains (a Rhodes scholarship, an Ivy League medical degree) and brawn (high school football and college lacrosse). He is deeply religious, a devoted husband and a doting father to two little girls. To a party that has struggled to attract young men, he offers sculpted biceps and a genuinely jockish affect. He is handsome and telegenic, a natural communicator who fluently expounds on complex issues without sounding professorial. He has spent his life working on one of the party’s strongest and most important issues: health care. What’s not to like?

Yet for party leaders and centrist pundits, there was ample cause for reservation. El-Sayed’s policy positions were a few clicks to the left of the mainstream — encapsulated in his slogan “Money out of politics. Money in your pocket. Medicare for all.” — even if he embraced capitalism and does not identify as a socialist. Worse yet: Democrats were defending a seat they already held, crucial territory on a Senate map tilted toward Republicans. An insurgent left had won offices in deep blue states. Yet to roll the dice on an enticing but untested candidate in a crucial swing state election seemed, to many, like too big a risk.

But El-Sayed was the subject of intense scrutiny not for his policies but for his religion and heritage as the son of Egyptian Muslim immigrants. Unsurprisingly, Republicans from President Trump — who called him a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and a “terrorist” — on down uncorked wildly racist attacks on him. Perhaps more surprising, some Democrats indulged in veiled versions of this ugly argument. “In my judgment, he does not represent the values of our party or our nation,” Jamie Metzl, a former foreign policy official in the Clinton administration, wrote on social media. Representative Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary, went a step further on Sunday and bizarrely endorsed her Republican opponent.

It is a grim fact that Islamophobia stains American politics. A poll conducted by Michigan State University last month found that more than 38 percent of respondents said that they would be somewhat or much less likely to vote for a Muslim candidate, with the much less likely ones making up most of the total. Indeed, in that poll the Democratic candidate for governor had a 12-point lead over his Republican challenger. El-Sayed’s lead there, by contrast, was less than three points — in a state with the nation’s second-largest population of Arab Americans, many of whom are Muslim. It was a discrepancy that suggested the limits of American inclusion.

And yet, he won. In this time of relentless division, El-Sayed’s victory is a reminder that politics is a business of individual men and women, with their own histories and ideas, persuading one voter after another to set aside the ways we are all different and focus on our shared dreams. It is telling that the two most successful Democratic politicians of my lifetime endorsed El-Sayed. Bill Clinton, the great triangulator, urged him to run for office after seeing him speak at his college graduation. Barack Obama, the party’s great conciliator, headlined an electric rally for him in the closing stretch. Irrespective of ideology, it’s clear that game recognizes game.

El-Sayed is evidently an elite political athlete. I can’t wait to see him spike the ball on the Senate floor.

8 Writers on How the Blue Tsunami Swept America
Every Senate win holds important lessons for Democrats.
By New York Times Opinion

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/democrats-house-senate-midterms-blue-wave.html

Lindsey Graham’s legacy is in tatters.

For the first time this century, South Carolina has elected to one seat a senator whose last name isn’t Graham.

Darline Graham, the Republican incumbent, lost her bid to win the seat that for 23 years belonged to her brother Lindsey, until his death in July. Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee, will instead head to Washington.

It’s a devastating defeat for the Republican Party, which hasn’t lost a Senate campaign in South Carolina since 1998. It’s a rebuke of President Trump, who urged Ms. Graham to run for a full six-year term after her brother’s death and visited South Carolina three separate times to galvanize voter support for her campaign.

But it also will be remembered as the race that dismantled Mr. Graham’s legacy as one of the most influential lawmakers in modern American political history — a stalwart conservative career that has endured a series of indignities in the less than four months since he died.

His sister’s campaign ran into trouble straightaway. In August, Ms. Graham struggled to answer a debate question about America’s national security interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. It wasn’t a curveball — it’s a standard foreign policy question — but she fumbled it, confessing that “national security is not my thing.” In that moment, she exposed the stark contrast between her and the lawmaker she was seeking to replace. South Carolinians know Mr. Graham as a foreign policy specialist who made frequent overseas trips and knew world leaders by their first names.

As her inexperience became ever more evident, Mr. Graham’s own achievements began to unravel in Washington. On Oct. 9, Mr. Trump announced he struck a deal to purchase diesel from Russia, effectively nullifying measures established in a bill that bore Mr. Graham’s name. And the president continues to withhold support for Ukraine while publicly pressuring the president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, to curb attacks on Russian infrastructure — two stances that Mr. Graham would find unconscionable.

Now, not only has Ms. Graham lost her brother’s seat, she also has been defeated by more than 20 percentage points in around a dozen counties. This is due in no small part to Mr. Trump’s miscalculation; there were other candidates, people who were not political novices, nor in mourning, whom he could have turned to after Mr. Graham’s death.

Wherever the blame lies, the result is the same: Ms. Graham will not carry Mr. Graham’s policy positions into the future, particularly involving support for Ukraine and on the Iran conflict, which likely Democratic majorities in the House and Senate would surely push to end. Here, again, is a dismaying twist for Mr. Graham, who was an unabashed war hawk who championed military intervention against Tehran for years.

Mr. Graham recognized early on that Mr. Trump was the future of the Republican Party. By 2018, he had shifted from an early critic to an ardent public supporter of the president. Over time, he became a frequent visitor to the White House and lent credibility to many of Mr. Trump’s foreign policy decisions.

For years, Mr. Graham was chastised by Republican and Democratic colleagues alike for holding his nose for a seat at the table — or, as he told my colleague Peter Baker over dinner in Washington, playing “the hand we’re dealt.”

On Tuesday, as many of Mr. Trump’s handpicked candidates face defeat, it appears that Mr. Graham’s choice to stay close to the president was a liability — and perhaps the true beginning of the end of the politician’s legacy.

Jon Ossoff sure looks presidential.

A year ago, pundits declared Georgia’s Jon Ossoff the senator most likely to lose his seat. On Tuesday, he won decisively. National Republicans had largely conceded the race months ago. The Associated Press announced his victory shortly after the polls closed.

Mr. Ossoff won so decisively, in part, because he articulated a message that connected Democrats’ fear of authoritarianism to the broader public’s fear that life is unaffordable. It’s a message that other Democratic candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, have emphasized as well. It could prove central for the party again in 2028. And it boils down to one word: corruption.

Donald Trump’s shameless self-dealing made Mr. Ossoff’s argument easier. Since returning to the White House, according to news reports, Mr. Trump has made more than $1 billion from his family’s cryptocurrency businesses alone. Americans of both parties have noticed. A Washington Post poll last month found that one-third of Republicans and independents who lean Republican now believe Mr. Trump is enriching himself in office, while a Fox News poll ranked corruption as voters’ top concern nationally.

Mr. Ossoff courted Republicans by speaking in bipartisan terms: He acknowledged that Mr. Trump didn’t invent political corruption. “Yes, the system really is rigged,” he said. “But he’s not unrigging it. He is re-rigging it for himself.”

Of course, it helped that Georgia Republicans chose a weak nominee. But Mr. Ossoff didn’t only benefit from a favorable political environment. He also spoke differently from the Democrats who challenged Mr. Trump two years ago.

Authoritarianism was a central theme of Kamala Harris’s failed presidential campaign; public graft fell further down her list of concerns. That cost her. Exit polls found that Ms. Harris won 80 percent of voters who called democracy their most important issue, while 81 percent of voters who prioritized the economy backed Mr. Trump. In Ms. Harris’s 2024 Democratic National Convention acceptance speech, she used the words “freedom,” “democracy” and “liberty” a total of 15 times. She didn’t mention “corruption” once.

By stressing corruption, in contrast, Mr. Ossoff made Mr. Trump’s assault on the rule of law tangible. He showed voters how democracy and economic distress are intertwined. On the campaign trail, he argued that “corruption is why nothing works for ordinary people. It’s why you pay a fortune for prescriptions. It’s why your insurance company gets away with denying your cancer treatment after you paid your premiums for decades.” In this way, he showed that the president wasn’t just transgressing abstract norms of good governance. He was helping the rich and powerful rip Americans off.

In that sense, Mr. Ossoff was following a path forged by other parties trying to defeat aspiring autocrats. Peter Magyar, who decisively ended Viktor Orban’s 16-year rule in Hungary this spring, gained national prominence with a 2024 viral video in which he accused Mr. Orban of turning the government into a “family-owned business.” The good-government group Democracy International reported that Mr. Magyar’s campaign “reduced complex democratic concerns into a simple proposition: ‘Corruption has a cost.’”

Similarly, in Serbia this September, student protesters angry over the long and corrupt run of President Aleksandar Vucic voted in a new era. “The focus of the protest was on corruption, government corruption,” Heather Conley, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, told PBS. “We’re seeing that issue become a real global issue.”

If Democrats retake Congress, they’ll have a chance to use congressional hearings to lay the groundwork for making corruption a key theme again in 2028. Mr. Ossoff could make it the centerpiece of a presidential campaign. Given how much power the ultrarich now wield in Washington, and how many ordinary Americans are struggling simply to get by, it won’t be hard to convince Americans that JD Vance, Marco Rubio or any of Mr. Trump’s likely Republican successors are tainted by his administration’s epic graft.

The hard part will be convincing them that Democrats — who even Mr. Ossoff concedes are viewed as corrupt themselves — can be trusted to behave differently if they regain power.

Read more on Michigan, South Carolina, Texas, Maine, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina.

Finally. FINALLY. Texas is blue.

When I met Gina Hinojosa in September, her race to become Texas’ first Democratic governor since Ann Richards seemed like a wildly long shot. At the time, Hinojosa told me that a fifth of the state still didn’t know her name, and she was being outspent 6 to 1. Given how often Texas has broken Democratic hearts, I asked her why we should believe that the state could really flip. Hinojosa said it was because Texas Democrats finally had a team.

When Beto O’Rourke ran for Senate in 2018, he was on his own, without a strong slate of statewide candidates. But this year, Hinojosa was running alongside James Talarico, the young, dynamic Senate candidate, and, for the first time in Texas history, Democratic candidates in every statehouse and congressional district. “We’re ready,” she said.

So was Texas. If Talarico alone won on Tuesday night, it would have been an earthquake. Texas hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. In 2024, Donald Trump won the state by nearly 14 points. But now that Talarico and Hinojosa have both won, along with other Texas Democrats up and down the ballot, it’s hard to overstate the scale of the psychological blow to Republicans. Texas, after all, has long been a dependable political anchor for Republicans, much as California is for Democrats. “Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America,” the state’s right-wing comptroller, Don Huffines, warned in a post on X last week, amid an early vote showing Democratic strength. “When the foundation breaks, it ALL falls apart.”

Huffines didn’t know how right he was. On Tuesday, the foundation of the Republican Party dropped out all over the country, leading to victories in contests Democrats barely dreamed of winning — not just Kansas and Ohio, but South Carolina. Still, that shouldn’t overshadow what brilliant races both Talarico and Hinojosa won.

Talarico waged one of the best campaigns in the country, trying to inspire cynical voters with a politics of loving thy neighbor. Both he and Hinojosa, in their different ways, promised to bring together deeply divided communities to wrest back power from predatory billionaires. Kicking off his Senate campaign in Round Rock, Texas, last year, Talarico said, “The people at the top — the Elon Musks, the Rupert Murdochs, the Mark Zuckerbergs of the world — they spend so much time and energy keeping us angry and divided because our unity is a threat to their wealth and their power.” On the trail, Hinojosa often said that the race turned on a single question: “Does Texas belong to the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and we just live here?”

The Republican campaigns had their own answer. Talarico’s opponent, Texas’ attorney general, Ken Paxton, is almost comically corrupt, and Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, spent more than $160 million trying to drag him across the finish line. Republicans ran gross A.I.-generated ads meant to demean Talarico and terrify voters. One depicted him wearing a dress and singing about trans kids. Another showed him defacing a Bible with crayons.

While Musk gave much less to Greg Abbott, he was still the governor’s single biggest donor this cycle. And part of the reason Abbott was vulnerable was because he’d enthusiastically welcomed tech companies to build data centers in the state. In Texas, Hinojosa told me that A.I. is one of the forces making people feel as if their lives are out of control, and data centers are the physical manifestation of that. They are a “demonstration of the governor doing the bidding of moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves.”

It will take some time to fully digest the lessons and consequences of the staggering rout Republicans suffered on Tuesday. But in addition to being a repudiation of Trump, it was also an overwhelming rejection of the tech barons he’s allied himself with. Talarico and Hinojosa’s campaigns were leaps of faith, premised on the conviction that Texans wanted something more than billionaire bootlicking and hatreds amplified by social media algorithms. “We have a lot more work to do if we’re going to defeat the billionaire megadonors who have taken over this country,” Talarico said back in Round Rock in September of 2025, when his underdog campaign had just begun. “But this is an incredible start.”

Read more on Michigan, South Carolina, Georgia, Texas, Maine, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina.

It was time for Susan Collins to go.

Well, whaddaya know. Looks like not even Susan Collins was buoyant enough to escape President Trump’s red undertow.

After 30 years of defying even extreme national political forces, the last Republican senator holding on in a blue state has wiped out like a drunken surfer. Her defeat in Maine drives home how national politics have trumped local concerns, even for lawmakers with strong personal brands and a deep store of good will among their electorates. Especially when that reputation was increasingly built on nostalgia and wishcasting.

A relic of the dying strain of independent, northeastern Republicanism, Ms. Collins made Democrats crazy in a way few other Republicans manage. They seethed at what they saw as her empty expressions of concern about her party’s increasing radicalism. They argued that on those occasions when she voted against her party, as with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, it was theater that didn’t make a real difference. And she kept winning, even as she accumulated baggage in the Trump era, including her vote to acquit the president in his first impeachment trial and her votes to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and, more recently, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Until now. She was dragged down by the economic pain her state has suffered at the hands of Mr. Trump’s policies, most vividly his preposterous tariff war with Canada, which hit Maine hard.

Not to dismiss the Everyman charms of the new Democratic senator-elect, Troy Jackson, but this race was never about him. He was little more than a placeholder, a late-in-the-game substitute for Graham Platner, the oyster-farming populist who thrilled progressives until his candidacy collapsed beneath a pile of scandal and regret. Digging through the rubble of the primary, party elders dusted off Mr. Jackson, a former president of the State Senate who had placed third in the primary for governor.

A former logger, Mr. Jackson had more authentic working-class cred than Mr. Platner, which did not entirely redound to his benefit. He was a little too rude and rough around the edges for some people’s taste, with all the charisma of cottage cheese. Even his campaign team didn’t like his style and kept him almost hidden for much of the race.

But he avoided major missteps, and he did well in his debates against Ms. Collins — even if his telling her to “shut up” raised questions about his abrasive manner and attitude toward women. All things considered, Mr. Jackson was solidly meh. But it turned out that meh was enough to get him over the finish line. And once in the chamber, he could easily prove himself. His time in the state legislative trenches, including leadership, should give him a bit of a head start, and it’s worth noting that an electrifying campaigner and a successful lawmaker are not necessarily the same thing.

With Ms. Collins’s departure, the Senate is losing its last Rockefeller Republican. Not that the absence is likely to be keenly felt. For all her self-congratulatory moderation, the Maine senator made increasingly little difference in the hyperpolarized chamber, something even she recognized. During one of her debates this fall, when asked for an example of a time her vote against her president and party changed the outcome, she came up empty. In the end, even her vaunted independence gave way to Mr. Trump’s heavy hand.

In the Republican Senate conference Ms. Collins is leaving behind, the conditions for cross-aisle deal making have rarely looked bleaker. The only pragmatic, independent-minded moderate left standing is Lisa Murkowski. And for all her Alaska grit, there’s not much Ms. Murkowski can do by her lonesome — unless the bipartisan spirit suddenly moves the president. Which pretty much guarantees we’re in for more partisan nastiness and dysfunction until 2028 rids us of Mr. Trump’s toxic presence and his party can, hopefully, start easing its way back toward sanity.

Read more on Michigan, South Carolina, Georgia, Texas, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina.

Sherrod Brown saw what the rest of the Democratic Party couldn’t.

Democrats haven’t always appreciated Sherrod Brown’s political instincts; after all, he lost his Senate seat from Ohio in 2024. But his election this time confirms that he knows something about winning states Republicans expect to conquer. He doesn’t talk down to the working class, he champions their interests, and he mostly sidesteps the culture wars. Those will be crucial skills if Democrats are going to have a chance at winning back the White House in 2028.

While he is reliably liberal on social issues, Brown’s focus has always been on economic concerns. He kept the faith with private sector labor unions and mostly avoided the woke language that alienated so many working-class Americans.

He’s a Yale graduate but doesn’t come off as elite. Even his forever rumpled presentation, as if he had shopped at Goodwill and worn his clothes overnight, endeared him to those suspicious of anyone too Brooks Brothers. Although he lost in 2024, he outperformed Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee, in Ohio — and making Ohio competitive for Democrats is an important feat.

Throughout the industrialized world, the broad disenchantment with politicians and elites has mostly bolstered populists from the far right — from the AfD in Germany to the National Rally in France to MAGA Republicans in the United States. But populism does not inevitably mean the ethnonationalist right.

Brown’s populism has generally been sensible, and he was way ahead of the curve in warning about what is now called the China shock — the way trade with China would devastate many manufacturing towns. Many liberals like me were free-traders, and Brown was prescient about the risks of factories closing and the trail of misery that would cause.

This election cycle, many Democratic candidates followed the populist path he blazed, veering away from pronouns and identity issues while hammering Republicans on pocketbook issues like the cost of gas and diesel. James Talarico, Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper and a number of others pursued a very grounded economic populist agenda, railing against President Trump’s economic record and castigating corruption, all while underscoring their local authenticity.

The critique of Brown in the 2026 Ohio election, other than that he was a lefty who would help advance a national Democratic agenda that many Ohio voters are suspicious of, was in part that he wasn’t populist enough. To some voters, he was a forever politician who represented the status quo that they feel has betrayed them.

It’s true that Brown, 73, has been in politics for more than half a century. He was first elected to the Ohio legislature at the age of 21 and then moved to the House of Representatives in 1992 and to the Senate in 2006. But he has managed to tilt against the establishment that he long was part of. A hot issue in Ohio this year was data centers, and Brown made his skepticism about them a central issue in his campaign, criticizing his opponent Jon Husted for previously supporting incentives to construct them.

As long as inequality persists and the economy underperforms, populism will be with us, I suspect — here and in Europe. I fear that liberals worldwide have been too quick to surrender the populist ground to charlatans on the right. And here in the United States, becoming the party of the more educated isn’t a promising path, considering that less than 40 percent of Americans over the age of 25 have a four-year college degree. Six out of 10 Americans see themselves as working class, and many are suspicious of politicians generally. (I think they have a right to be, considering how poorly politicians have served them over the past half-century.)

Democrats have made progress in this election, and it’s heartening that last month a majority of likely voters said that they once again see Democrats as the party of the working class. In the new Congress, Brown won’t be an isolated liberal populist voice, as he often was in the past; he will have others who think as he does. May the rest of the Democratic Party offer them newfound respect, for in a populist world the United States and other countries will be better off if that terrain is occupied by a vanguard of social liberals who are also sensible economic populists.

Read more on Michigan, South Carolina, Georgia, Texas, Maine, Kansas and North Carolina.

Adam Hamilton showed Democrats that centrism is still a winning strategy.

Blue Kansas? Really?! Yes.

Remarkably, Adam Hamilton’s victory over the incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall became not only possible but likely as Election Day neared, even though the last time a Democrat won a Senate election in Kansas was 1932, in Franklin Roosevelt’s Great Depression landslide.

True, Kansas has elected Democratic governors and has one now. And, yes, the collapse of President Trump’s popularity and the standing of the party that bows to him played a big role in this result.

But Mr. Hamilton would not have won without, well, Mr. Hamilton. His specific shade of blue — resolutely critical of the president and his lack of “decency” but also religious, moderate and open to all — enabled him to entice converts. It will be a tempting model in other places Democrats have long written off.

Mr. Hamilton, the pastor of the largest Methodist church in the country, conveyed a happy warrior vibe, his communication skills honed by decades in the pulpit. His comfort with Republican voters came naturally: He notes that about a third of his congregation identifies with the G.O.P., as Mr. Hamilton did at times before this election.

In Mr. Marshall, he was blessed with a weak incumbent. The New York Times reported in September that Mr. Marshall, as an obstetrician-gynecologist, had sued more than 700 patients with outstanding bills, which became the subject of a tough Hamilton ad.

These dynamics played out amid a broad farm state rebellion against Mr. Trump’s tariffs and his decision to go to war with Iran. Foreign countries’ retaliation against tariffs cut off important markets for farmers, who have been hit hard by rising diesel and fertilizer prices. The result: Democrats discovered this year that they can make inroads in political terrain long seen as hostile.

In 2018, another anti-Trump midterm election year, Democrats found they could reach across old divides by nominating military and national security veterans — particularly women such as Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey, now the governors of those states. This year, they sent a message of openness to religious voters with candidates such as Mr. Hamilton and Texas’ James Talarico. Both parried critics on the religious right by speaking about the moral demands of Christianity, particularly on behalf of the poor.

What will that mean when Mr. Hamilton enters the Senate? He will probably make common cause with senators such as Raphael Warnock, a fellow minister, and pragmatic Democrats such as Chris Coons and Tim Kaine; Mr. Hamilton mentioned these three when I spoke to him in September. He has said that tackling big issues such as the deficit and Social Security will require Republicans and Democrats to work together.

“The Gospel isn’t just about a personal faith,” he said. “It’s about the call to be in the world.”

I reached Mr. Hamilton by phone on Election Day and asked him what those words meant for the kind of senator he’d like to be.

“I realized something this morning,” he replied. “There were a few years in elementary school when I was bullied. And that has always made me want to speak up for people who are being bullied. So as a senator, I want to stand up for people who are being hurt by what’s happening in Washington on matters like immigration, health care, nutrition benefits and on our farms.”

Standing up to bullies is a calling fit for the moment. So is taking on some of the country’s big problems. His ecumenical approach might even produce results.

Read more on Michigan, South Carolina, Georgia, Texas, Maine, Ohio and North Carolina.

Roy Cooper ran a relentlessly boring campaign. It’s a winning strategy.

By the time Election Day rolled around, Roy Cooper’s victory in the Senate race in North Carolina, which flipped a seat in the chamber from Republican to Democrat, was almost a foregone conclusion, given how early he took a lead in polls, how consistently he held on to it and how increasingly hostile to Republicans the midterm climate seemed to be.

But make no mistake: This is a purple state, a dab redder than it is blue, and it hadn’t chosen a Democrat in a Senate or presidential contest since 2008, when Barack Obama came out on top here. It was anyone’s to win before Cooper kicked off his bid. And his triumph speaks to a whole lot more than good timing.

“The national environment may have spotted Cooper a few points,” Asher Hildebrand, a Duke University professor who closely tracks North Carolina politics, said. “But the rest of the margin is a story of candidate quality.”

As much as any midterm race, Cooper’s affirmed the power of the right person waging the right campaign. A former two-term governor of North Carolina who had been the state’s attorney general for four terms before that, he had near-universal name recognition, so he didn’t have to waste time or money introducing himself to voters. He had been vetted thoroughly, so there were no private scandals, personal demons or other such drama in store.

He could focus on his chosen message, which is what he did — relentlessly, unerringly, with the confidence that he didn’t need sweeping exhortations, catchy slogans or viral memes to draw attention. His unelectric rallies were billed as the Make Stuff Cost Less tour, during which he spoke in prosaic terms about quotidian anxieties: access to health insurance, the cost of groceries, utility rates. Many Democratic candidates identified affordability as voters’ key concern. Few lived, breathed and droned on about it the way Cooper did.

“Low risk.” “Workmanlike.” That’s how Hildebrand described Cooper’s campaign, and he meant those terms as high compliments. “Voters like his brand of authentic, no-nonsense competence, which is refreshingly idiosyncratic in this age of partisan flamethrowing,” he said.

Cooper’s Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, was unknown to most North Carolina voters when he became the Republican nominee in March. He had never held elected office. He had no record to run on. But he couldn’t turn that inexperience to his advantage by styling himself as a fresh-faced, untainted, anti-establishment insurgent because he’d worked for many years as a lobbyist — and was on the ballot essentially because President Trump had put him there.

That made him “the classic Trump loyalty candidate,” said Michael Bitzer, a professor of political science and history at Catawba College in Salisbury, N.C. And loyalty was liability as the race progressed and Trump’s popularity continued to sink. According to an Elon University poll several weeks before Election Day, 34 percent of North Carolina adults approved of Trump’s job performance while 57 percent disapproved. Perhaps a charismatic Republican untethered to Trump could have transcended that ill will. A phlegmatic toady like Whatley was doomed.

Especially given his uncommonly unflappable and durable rival, who said to the electorate: You know me. You trust me. I’m not here with bitter grievances and gaudy promises. I’d just like the chance to lower your electric bill.

ARTICLE

The Bell Tolls for Trumpism
Ezra Klein and Aaron Retica react to the Democratic Party’s major midterm victory.
By Ezra Klein, Rollin Hu and Jack McCordick
Published 2026-11-05 00:44 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-aaron-retica-midterm-2026.html

This is an edited transcript of “The Ezra Klein Show.” You can listen to the episode wherever you get your podcasts.

The big tent is real, and the political map is fake.

That is the lesson of the Democrats’ historic midterm, the blue tsunami that we saw on Tuesday.

Democrats won in places nobody thought they even had any chance to compete a year ago: Kansas, Texas, Iowa, South Carolina.

As I record this, it’s unclear which party is going to win Mississippi. Let me say that again: It is unclear which party is going to win a Senate seat in Mississippi. That was unimaginable three months ago.

Democrats won governorships in Ohio, Texas and Iowa. This was a win that destroyed the reality of the red-blue map people had come to believe in so firmly. And so we’re entering a new era, an era when much is unsettled.

The realignment may not be what we thought it was in 2024. The realignment may be a map that is entirely up for grabs from here on out.

Democrats didn’t do this on their own, of course. To a very large extent, President Donald Trump did it for them. And what Trump and the Democrats both did wrong was the same thing: not listening.

Trump did not listen — not to the voters, not even, at times, to himself. He was elected promising to lower costs, to end wars, to bring order to the border. Instead, he raised costs through tariffs and through new wars, and he created disorder after closing the border and sending in masked ICE agents to harass and upend settled communities.

Trump at no point pivoted. He dismissed almost everything that people were angry about, and his party paid the price.

At the same time, I think the Democrats’ central political failing for years has been an unwillingness to listen. They listened to themselves — not to the voters they needed to win over.

This time around, they course corrected. In state after state, district after district, they found people who fit: Josh Turek in Iowa. Adam Hamilton in Kansas. James Talarico in Texas. They found seminarians. They found Paralympians. They found a whole new class of candidates who could put into play a whole new set of districts.

And then in some places, like North Carolina and Georgia, they had candidates of such exceptional quality, who understood their constituents so well, that they won states that should have been purple — by 20 points for Roy Cooper, 18 points for Jon Ossoff.

So there’s a tremendous amount to learn from this election and a tremendous amount that is now possible after it.

To think through both the lessons that we’re seeing already and then how Democrats, and for that matter Republicans, are going to respond to them, I’m joined here by my revered editor, one of the most beloved characters in our podcast cinematic universe, Aaron Retica, who’s going to turn the tables and interview me.

Ezra Klein: Aaron Retica, welcome back to the show.

Aaron Retica: Thank you very much for having me. Let’s start with almost a gotcha: Do you have any idea who George McGill is?

Klein: I don’t.

Retica: George McGill is the last Democratic senator in Kansas before Adam Hamilton, who won last night. McGill last won in 1932.

I was trying to think of all the different ways of expressing what happened last night, and that’s the best I could come up with.

Klein: That’s a very good way of doing it.

Retica: So everybody looking at this election, all the different constituents of the Democratic Party — they all got something. The left won some races. The center won some races. Charismatic candidates were huge. Uncharismatic candidates also did well.

Klein: The Roy Cooper juggernaut.

Retica: Roy Cooper plus 20. This has long been the dream. Was there a breakthrough for the big-tent Democratic Party last night?

Klein: Yes, but let me hold that to the side for a minute. Donald Trump asked America to vote like he was on the ballot, and it did.

Trump, of course, had, I think, the funniest possible reaction to the election.

Retica: He really did.

Klein: In the middle of the night, he posts on Truth Social:

I wasn’t on the Ballot, and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.

And people today have been remarking how he doesn’t seem very upset by the election results, and of course not. He does not mind when Republicans lose. And in fact, Republicans often lose because he intervenes in a way that is likelier to make them lose, right?

Like bringing in Ken Paxton or ensuring Ken Paxton’s victory in the Texas Republican primary.

Retica: And Darline Graham.

Klein: Pushing for Darline Graham in South Carolina. But when Republicans lose when Trump is not on the ballot, to Trump, it shows his importance. And so he, I think, doesn’t mind this at all.

It is more evidence, to him, of his essential winnerdom. What really happened here is Donald Trump has been a terrible, catastrophic president who has betrayed the mandate he was given by voters. And as he was losing — bleeding — public support, not only never changed course but never admitted what was happening at all.

And so Trump led his party to defeat, or, certainly, created the conditions for the party to go to defeat. And then there’s a question of what Democrats did with that.

Retica: So what did they do right?

Klein: The big tent is real, and the map is fake.

Democrats ran candidates who fit their states and their districts, and I think it’s just really important to center that.

Last year, I did this big essay on the show about the need for a big-tent Democratic Party. Other people have been making this argument, too — that one of the problems that has emerged over time in American politics is that the parties have become tighter in their ideological and cultural positioning.

Retica: And geographical, which is critical.

Klein: And that has made them tighter in their geographical positioning. Because they’re not willing to run candidates who differ as much from the kind of median member of the party.

What Democrats did really well here was in the way that they acted with power.

Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer kept things very focused on affordability, on the Iran war. They didn’t get distracted by a lot of other things. And then, when they ran candidates, they ran people like James Talarico, who is leading an almost religious-left revival in Texas against Ken Paxton.

Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as you mentioned, is a Methodist megachurch pastor. Scott Colom, who’s the candidate in Mississippi, looks very much like he may win by like 100 votes or something.

Retica: Not even 100.

Klein: I mean, we’ll see where it plays out, but ——

Retica: Truly insane, though.

Klein: Both Hamilton and Colom describe themselves as pro-life Democrats.

They want to create conditions under which reproductive freedom is protected, but they ran as pro-life Democrats because of their Christian faith.

Mary Peltola — what was her slogan in Alaska? “Fish, family, freedom.”

So the Democrats did a very good job in this case of picking candidates who fit the state.

And when I say the map is fake, one of the revelations from this election is you really should not treat states as off the table.

Retica: Yeah.

Klein: People were not talking about Kansas. By the way, Adam Hamilton is not a Schumer recruiting victory. Adam Hamilton decided to run.

By the way, shout-out to my colleague at Vox and colleague here at The New York Times Sarah Kliff, whose bombshell story, bombshell investigative work, on Roger Marshall’s unbelievably brutal pursuit and persecution of people who are not able to pay his medical bills was a major, major, major part of that race. And that’s a story Sarah Kliff broke here at The New York Times.

Shout-out to Sarah.

Retica: I want to throw in a shout-out while we’re at it, and that’s Howard Dean. Because the 50-state strategy is vindicated here. This is what you’re saying.

There are two reasons. One, you might actually win some of these states. But also, there are going to be talented politicians in these places who can’t necessarily win their state but who are still worth having in your coalition.

Just being out there and not writing things off is critically important.

Klein: Yes, and doing the work to recruit the candidates and then supporting them. So I think Democrats have sort of treated Florida as not winnable. And what you saw here, Angie Nixon is only going to fall a couple of points short.

Florida is winnable if you have the right candidates in the right environment. And so you have to build that kind of party strength. You have to look for those people.

Now, there’s an interesting question here. You were saying at the beginning that everybody got some of what they wanted, and that’s at least somewhat true.

I think it’s going to be fascinating to see what lessons Democrats learn from Michigan, from Maine and from Florida, which is where they ran — in contested or contestable Senate elections — much more left-wing candidates.

Abdul El-Sayed won. It looks like he’ll win by something in the seven range as we’re taping. Maine, it’s a little harder to say because they had the whole disaster with Graham Platner. Susan Collins is actually a quite good candidate because she has a reputation for independence, not totally well deserved, from the other side. Klein: There’s no Trumpism. There was only ever Trump.

The work that various right-wing intellectuals and pseudo-intellectuals tried to do, to create this coherence around Trump’s impulses and extract from that what he was going to try to do with the tariffs — what a highly structured tariff regime, to bring manufacturing back to America, would look like. That was a failure. Donald Trump’s tariffs were insane.

Trump is an end of the neocon Middle East meddling era in foreign policy — a failure. Trump did not agree with you. That was not Trumpism.

Over and over and over and over again, there have been these efforts to say what Trumpism is, but Trump himself would not hold to any of them.

And so one reason all of this collapsed, and one reason I think the infighting of it on the right is ultimately going to be so vicious, is because you’re still going to have the people who say: Real Trumpism has never been tried. You already saw this happening ——

Retica: It was happening last night. The MAGA people were all like ——

Klein: The neocons did this to us ——

Retica: The neocons brought Iran ——

Klein: Who are the neocons? It was Trump.

Retica: Yeah.

Klein: Marco Rubio didn’t get you into Iran — it was Donald Trump himself, with Benjamin Netanyahu, who got us into Iran. That wasn’t Bill Kristol. Are you kidding me? It’s ridiculous.

JD Vance is going to presumably run for president as a human sacrifice to say: This is what Trumpism could have been.

JD Vance was not an electoral juggernaut in Ohio when he ran. He underperformed terribly, and he’s not popular now.

And so the movement is going to be to try to figure out what can come after. And that jockeying, particularly outside of the House and the Senate, is already going to begin.

And the key thing is: Trump cares about his control. He doesn’t care about his ideology. Trump wants fealty. He doesn’t want consistency or coherence. He’s not an ideas guy. He wants to keep his family out of jail ——

So I was on my way here, and I was texting with a friend of mine who’s — well, she’s a historian. And I was telling her what I was doing, and she was like: OK, but don’t — as my mother always used to say: Don’t gloat.

She has the mask of the moderate, right? When things were close, she was the most likely senator to vote against Republicans. But that’s still 15, 16, 17 percent. Most of the time, she voted with them.

And she was the chief enabler of the destruction of women’s right to choose because of the change in the court. And I’m very, very happy to see her go. [Laughs.]

Vivek Ramaswamy, in Ohio. I think Roger Marshall, in Kansas, in the way that he — the incredibly cruel interest he imposed upon his own patients, the 18 percent interest rates he had.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

‘Decency Won’: 9 Writers on the Best and Worst Moments From Trump’s Midterm Rout
What mattered most in these midterms?
By New York Times Opinion
Published 2026-11-04 10:12 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/midterms-democrats-senate-house-results.html

The Democrats have taken the House and Senate — flipping seats no one thought possible even just a few weeks ago.

On election night, Times Opinion asked nine columnists and contributors to look back on these midterms and explain what mattered most. Some said tariffs, others gas prices. But what’s clear is that the American people were angry — and ready to repudiate the president and his policies. “Decency won,” one of our columnists wrote. “In an era of grubby corruption under a president who reveled in wanton cruelty, Americans have chosen a new path.”

What mattered most

Binyamin Appelbaum Antipathy toward the president trumped everything else. But for Democrats, winning was the easy part. Memories of this election cycle will be shaped by what Democrats do with their power. And they made a mess of their recent opportunities.

Josh Barro Donald Trump promised to bring down inflation and avoid new foreign wars. Instead, he launched a war that drove energy prices up (while failing to achieve its strategic purpose) and imposed tariffs that raised the cost of living. Trump claims he kept more promises to American voters than he made. Like so many things he has said, that’s a lie, and voters punished him and his party for it.

Jamelle Bouie The thing that stands out most to me was Vivek Ramaswamy’s closing argument, an ad that hinged on attacking his opponent Amy Acton for being the victim of sexual assault. An astoundingly poor decision.

Michelle Cottle This is what happens when a political party allows itself to be hollowed out and wholly defined by one man. When the public sours on that man, the party falls right along with him.

David French The state-level changes may ultimately be as consequential as the House and Senate races. Democrats may have a chance to control the entire Texas government. We haven’t begun to consider the long-term implications of that outcome.

Jean Guerrero The president wasted billions on foreign wars and waged a brutal assault on immigrants here at home. On Tuesday, voters woke up from the delusion that Trump’s an ally of working people.

Daniel McCarthy Americans supposedly don’t vote on foreign policy, but they certainly vote on its domestic consequences. The Iran war knocked down two pillars of the Trump coalition by raising fuel prices and alienating everyone opposed to more Middle East wars.

Tressie McMillan Cottom MAGA will end one day. The election results last night suggest that it could be sooner rather than later. Texas elected a Democratic governor. Georgia elected a Black female governor. North Carolina flipped innumerable contested races blue. This repudiation of Trump’s small, racist, profoundly unserious vision of America needed to win decisively. And it did.

Lydia Polgreen To borrow from Marxist thinking: We are watching the revenge of the material. You can’t lie to people about the price of a gallon of gas or the price of a pound of ground beef or the price of a ton of fertilizer. Tariffs and the lunatic war on Iran have clobbered ordinary people while Trump and his billionaire cronies have lined their pockets.

What surprised you

Appelbaum The strength of Southern Democrats. Newly elected senators like Annie Andrews and James Talarico certainly benefited from their cartoonishly objectionable Republican opponents. But the part of the South where Democrats can’t possibly compete suddenly looks a lot smaller.

Barro In states like North Carolina and Texas, Democrats are winning races for the House and in state legislatures where they did not even expect to compete. Democrats have shown that they can win back the working-class voters they had lost. To keep them, Democrats will need to maintain a focus on affordability — including keeping energy prices down.

Bouie The thing that mattered most was the vast unpopularity of the president’s core agenda: mass deportations, trade wars, actual wars and attempted cultural transformation. The headline results of the night reflect the public’s anger with each of these.

Cottle A blue Texas?! That stuns like a snowstorm in Laredo.

French The House popular vote margin, without question. If projections are accurate, it was the biggest popular vote rebuke since the post-Watergate elections in 1974.

Guerrero Xavier Becerra will become California’s first Latino governor in more than 150 years. But in his campaign, his identity as a Latino wasn’t a major talking point. That seemed to reflect a dying confidence in Latino identity as an organizing political force.

McCarthy The Carolinas, Texas and Georgia together show that the South now offers Democrats the kind of opportunity that Trump found in the Rust Belt. This shouldn’t come as a complete surprise to anyone closely watching long-term trends, but the implications are stark. Southern states won’t stay red just because of their strong economies.

McMillan Cottom Keisha Lance Bottoms’s election surprised me. Stacey Abrams had two brutal losses in 2022 and 2018. That had tempered my hope.

Polgreen Trump, king of the vulgar spectacle, won the presidency twice, though never with an outright popular majority. But this time, decency won. The Democrats who scored major wins include a megachurch pastor and a seminarian, a pediatrician and at least one public health official. In an era of grubby corruption under a president who reveled in wanton cruelty, Americans have chosen a new path.

Most memorable moment

Appelbaum The arrival of artificial intelligence ads, which used manufactured or manipulated imagery in attempts to trick voters. Many were crude, and they didn’t have discernible impacts on the results, but the tactic is likely to become more common — and more dangerous.

Barro Lacking a strong argument about how they had governed well, Republicans leaned into name-calling: Talarico was “Talafreako.” Andrews was “Trannie Annie.” Acton was a drunk liar whose mother hates her. Republicans apparently assumed that every voter shared their contempt for Democrats. Their attacks weren’t just juvenile and unpleasant; they made Republicans look as though they had lost sight of voters’ top concerns: the cost of living and a pointless war.

Bouie For me, the most surprising outcome was the scale of the sweep in Texas. These victories might fundamentally change the trajectory of the state’s politics, and it appears to rest on deep anger among Hispanic voters. If you wanted to liken it to the fallout from California’s Proposition 187 in the 1990s, you would not be off base.

Cottle In the Rio Grande Valley, in a district Trump solidly carried in 2024, I talked with a Hispanic voter who had taken a chance on Trump two years ago because of his economic promises but now felt taken for a ride. She and her husband were voting blue this time. Clearly, they were not alone.

French When Darline Graham said, “National security is not my thing,” during a primary debate, she demonstrated a remarkable disrespect for her own voters.

Guerrero I was struck by how proudly Abdul El-Sayed campaigned on abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “Our government spends billions on an agency that operates outside of the law to terrorize our neighbors,” he said in an ad pitching himself as “the only Senate candidate for abolishing ICE.” With his win, he showed that “Abolish ICE” is not a position that alienates many voters anymore.

McCarthy The most telling moment came from someone who wasn’t even running. The day before the elections, the departing Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, said on Sirius XM that the Iran war was a “big, big drag” and warned Republicans against being the party of Big Tech and data centers.

McMillan Cottom The Democrat Angie Nixon’s Florida campaign really stuck with me. Florida is not just red; it is Trump’s political home base. Nixon ran as a democratic socialist, and while she fell short, she lost by less than 3 percentage points, with a huge financial deficit — which suggests that the Democratic brand is being remade and the whole map is in play.

Polgreen Nothing appalled me quite so much in these midterms as the brazen double standard applied to El-Sayed, who will become America’s first Muslim senator. At every turn he was faced with baseless accusations of antisemitism and made to answer for the statements of people who supported him. His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, was not held to anything close to the same standard. Indeed, his supporters engaged in gleefully Islamophobic tropes throughout the campaign. It was a painful reminder that bias against Muslims is not just tolerated but even celebrated and not just in the Republican Party.

Something small but important buried in the results

Appelbaum It was a big night for Democratic candidates who talk publicly about their faith. That’s an important development for a party that needs to find ways of connecting with a broader cross-section of the American people. In future elections, Trump won’t be on the ballot.

Barro Florida voters appear to have approved a constitutional amendment that will severely restrict property taxes in the state, which already lacks an income tax. Property tax revolts around the country are undermining a revenue stream that supports important local government services. State and local officials need to do a better job convincing voters that government is efficient and worth paying for.

Bouie This is not small, but it is important: the suburban G.O.P. collapse that turned Virginia blue and made North Carolina and Georgia competitive is extending beyond those states into South Carolina, in a trend that threatens the Republican Party’s ability to build national majorities.

Cottle I am a relentless nag about paying attention to down-ballot races, so let me take this moment to cheer the Dems’ big gains in the Texas Legislature. Well played, President Trump!

French It looks as though Scott DesJarlais might lose his race in Tennessee. He was a pre-Trump version of Trump, and it’s fitting that DesJarlais’s sun would set alongside Trump’s.

Guerrero Texas is undergoing the same shift California had in the 1990s. In response to racist, rabid immigration raids, voters are souring on Republicans. That includes Latinos, whose 2024 red shift turned out to be temporary.

McCarthy Voter ID ballot initiatives succeeded in places like North Carolina and Ohio, showing that passing a key piece of legislation Trump pressed on Senate Republicans — the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, which would expand ID requirements nationwide — could have given Republicans a desperately needed boost.

McMillan Cottom Women did not give up. That didn’t get enough attention. MAGA is a movement built on men’s grievance about women’s economic and political advancements. Democratic women ran historic races this year. The women who stood out ran on economic issues without demonizing gay, trans or poor voters.

Polgreen The culture war was a dead end in this election cycle for Republicans. Conservatives like to refer to liberal causes like transgender rights and support for Gaza as luxury beliefs, disconnected from the values and concerns of ordinary Americans. But this time around, it was Republicans who seemed out of touch. No amount of scaremongering about boys in girls’ locker rooms could motivate voters in red states where transgender people have faced draconian laws that made their lives hellish. Threats of a migrant invasion fell flat when Trump had basically sealed the border and was hunting down anyone who looked foreign in the streets of American cities. It turns out that the Trump agenda may represent the true luxury beliefs after all.

Josh Barro and Jean Guerrero are contributing Opinion writers.

Jamelle Bouie, David French, Tressie McMillan Cottom and Lydia Polgreen are Times columnists.

Michelle Cottle writes about national politics for Opinion.

Daniel McCarthy is a fellow at the Heritage Foundation, a columnist for The Spectator and the editor of Modern Age: A Conservative Review.

ARTICLE

Maine Voters Finally Saw Through Susan Collins
One of the greatest survivors in U.S. politics finally falls.
By Michelle Cottle
Published 2026-11-04 05:56 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/susan-collins-troy-jackson-senate.html

Well, whaddaya know. Looks like not even Susan Collins was buoyant enough to escape President Trump’s red undertow.

After 30 years of defying even extreme national political forces, the last Republican senator holding on in a blue state has wiped out like a drunken surfer. Her defeat in Maine drives home how national politics have trumped local concerns, even for lawmakers with strong personal brands and a deep store of good will among their electorates. Especially when that reputation was increasingly built on nostalgia and wishcasting.

A relic of the dying strain of independent, northeastern Republicanism, Ms. Collins made Democrats crazy in a way few other Republicans manage. They seethed at what they saw as her empty expressions of concern about her party’s increasing radicalism. They argued that on those occasions when she voted against her party, as with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, it was theater that didn’t make a real difference. And she kept winning, even as she accumulated baggage in the Trump era, including her vote to acquit the president in his first impeachment trial and her votes to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and, more recently, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Until now. She was dragged down by the economic pain her state has suffered at the hands of Mr. Trump’s policies, most vividly his preposterous tariff war with Canada, which hit Maine hard.

Not to dismiss the Everyman charms of the new Democratic senator-elect, Troy Jackson, but this race was never about him. He was little more than a placeholder, a late-in-the-game substitute for Graham Platner, the oyster-farming populist who thrilled progressives until his candidacy collapsed beneath a pile of scandal and regret. Digging through the rubble of the primary, party elders dusted off Mr. Jackson, a former president of the State Senate who had placed third in the primary for governor.

A former logger, Mr. Jackson had more authentic working-class cred than Mr. Platner, which did not entirely redound to his benefit. He was a little too rude and rough around the edges for some people’s taste, with all the charisma of cottage cheese. Even his campaign team didn’t like his style and kept him almost hidden for much of the race.

But he avoided major missteps, and he did well in his debates against Ms. Collins — even if his telling her to “shut up” raised questions about his abrasive manner and attitude toward women. All things considered, Mr. Jackson was solidly meh. But it turned out that meh was enough to get him over the finish line. And once in the chamber, he could easily prove himself. His time in the state legislative trenches, including leadership, should give him a bit of a head start, and it’s worth noting that an electrifying campaigner and a successful lawmaker are not necessarily the same thing.

With Ms. Collins’s departure, the Senate is losing its last Rockefeller Republican. Not that the absence is likely to be keenly felt. For all her self-congratulatory moderation, the Maine senator made increasingly little difference in the hyperpolarized chamber, something even she recognized. During one of her debates this fall, when asked for an example of a time her vote against her president and party changed the outcome, she came up empty. In the end, even her vaunted independence gave way to Mr. Trump’s heavy hand.

In the Republican Senate conference Ms. Collins is leaving behind, the conditions for cross-aisle deal making have rarely looked bleaker. The only pragmatic, independent-minded moderate left standing is Lisa Murkowski. And for all her Alaska grit, there’s not much Ms. Murkowski can do by her lonesome — unless the bipartisan spirit suddenly moves the president. Which pretty much guarantees we’re in for more partisan nastiness and dysfunction until 2028 rids us of Mr. Trump’s toxic presence and his party can, hopefully, start easing its way back toward sanity.

SUMMARY

When I met Gina Hinojosa in September, her race to become Texas’ first Democratic governor since Ann Richards seemed like a wildly long shot. Hinojosa said it was because Texas Democrats finally had a team. But now that Talarico and Hinojosa have both won, along with other Texas Democrats up and down the ballot, it’s hard to overstate the scale of the psychological blow to Republicans.

ARTICLE

This Is a Huge Psychological Blow to Republicans
For Republicans, Texas has long been a dependable political anchor. Now, it’s finally blue.
By Michelle Goldberg
Published 2026-11-04 05:40 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/talarico-hinojosa-texas-democrats.html

When I met Gina Hinojosa in September, her race to become Texas’ first Democratic governor since Ann Richards seemed like a wildly long shot. At the time, Hinojosa told me that a fifth of the state still didn’t know her name, and she was being outspent 6 to 1. Given how often Texas has broken Democratic hearts, I asked her why we should believe that the state could really flip. Hinojosa said it was because Texas Democrats finally had a team.

When Beto O’Rourke ran for Senate in 2018, he was on his own, without a strong slate of statewide candidates. But this year, Hinojosa was running alongside James Talarico, the young, dynamic Senate candidate, and, for the first time in Texas history, Democratic candidates in every statehouse and congressional district. “We’re ready,” she said.

So was Texas. If Talarico alone won on Tuesday night, it would have been an earthquake. Texas hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. In 2024, Donald Trump won the state by nearly 14 points. But now that Talarico and Hinojosa have both won, along with other Texas Democrats up and down the ballot, it’s hard to overstate the scale of the psychological blow to Republicans. Texas, after all, has long been a dependable political anchor for Republicans, much as California is for Democrats. “Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America,” the state’s right-wing comptroller, Don Huffines, warned in a post on X last week, amid an early vote showing Democratic strength. “When the foundation breaks, it ALL falls apart.”

Huffines didn’t know how right he was. On Tuesday, the foundation of the Republican Party dropped out all over the country, leading to victories in contests Democrats barely dreamed of winning — not just Kansas and Ohio, but South Carolina. Still, that shouldn’t overshadow what brilliant races both Talarico and Hinojosa won.

Talarico waged one of the best campaigns in the country, trying to inspire cynical voters with a politics of loving thy neighbor. Both he and Hinojosa, in their different ways, promised to bring together deeply divided communities to wrest back power from predatory billionaires. Kicking off his Senate campaign in Round Rock, Texas, last year, Talarico said, “The people at the top — the Elon Musks, the Rupert Murdochs, the Mark Zuckerbergs of the world — they spend so much time and energy keeping us angry and divided because our unity is a threat to their wealth and their power.” On the trail, Hinojosa often said that the race turned on a single question: “Does Texas belong to the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and we just live here?”

The Republican campaigns had their own answer. Talarico’s opponent, Texas’ attorney general, Ken Paxton, is almost comically corrupt, and Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, spent more than $160 million trying to drag him across the finish line. Republicans ran gross A.I.-generated ads meant to demean Talarico and terrify voters. One depicted him wearing a dress and singing about trans kids. Another showed him defacing a Bible with crayons.

While Musk gave much less to Greg Abbott, he was still the governor’s single biggest donor this cycle. And part of the reason Abbott was vulnerable was because he’d enthusiastically welcomed tech companies to build data centers in the state. In Texas, Hinojosa told me that A.I. is one of the forces making people feel as if their lives are out of control, and data centers are the physical manifestation of that. They are a “demonstration of the governor doing the bidding of moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves.”

It will take some time to fully digest the lessons and consequences of the staggering rout Republicans suffered on Tuesday. But in addition to being a repudiation of Trump, it was also an overwhelming rejection of the tech barons he’s allied himself with. Talarico and Hinojosa’s campaigns were leaps of faith, premised on the conviction that Texans wanted something more than billionaire bootlicking and hatreds amplified by social media algorithms. “We have a lot more work to do if we’re going to defeat the billionaire megadonors who have taken over this country,” Talarico said back in Round Rock in September of 2025, when his underdog campaign had just begun. “But this is an incredible start.”

SUMMARY

Mr. Trump cares only about developments that affect him directly. Not that Mr. Trump has ever cared much about congressional authority. Maybe with the Trump Kool-Aid drinkers.

ARTICLE

Don’t Be Fooled. This Is What Trump Wanted.
The president loves combat and chaos. He’s about to get more of it.
By Michelle Cottle
Published 2026-11-04 20:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/trump-democrats-midterms.html

Talk about a thumping. After months of struggling to overcome brutal political fundamentals, most Republicans awoke Wednesday to the fresh pain of getting kicked to the curb by the American people, along with a fat dollop of dread about what comes next.

But not President Trump. I suspect he greeted the morning with a tingle of anticipation, if not outright excitement, for what lies ahead: two years of nonstop, bare-knuckle brawling with a Democratic-controlled House and Senate. In other words, Mr. Trump’s idea of heaven.

Yes, the president is a sore loser, as Jan. 6 illuminated in blood and chaos. He got busy early in this election rigging the playing field in his team’s favor, then spent the final months of it pleading with followers to pretend he was on the ballot.

But he wasn’t really on the ballot, meaning he can now tell himself this electoral humiliation had nothing to do with him. And he has never given two flips about the fortunes of the broader G.O.P. So, in his mind, Republicans belly flopping without him probably just confirms his singular importance.

Mr. Trump cares only about developments that affect him directly. As such, he might feel a whisper of unease about his lap-dog Republicans ceding control to crusading Democrats with subpoena power and two years of pent-up rage. After all, one of his go-to campaign pitches to Republican voters this year was that, if the blue team won the midterms, Democrats would immediately revive their unfair persecution of him. Maybe even impeach him a third time!

But, deep down, a Democratic win was surely what he was rooting for all along.

Conflict is Mr. Trump’s jam. The nastier the better. For all his self-aggrandizing talk about building stuff, his true talents lie in combat and destruction. He long ago shattered the spine of the G.O.P., so humiliating its members now is a minor thrill at best. But facing off against Democratic majorities in both chambers still buzzing from their electoral win? Now that is something to live for.

Expect Mr. Trump’s relations with Congress next year to make the partisan hostilities of his first term look like a meditation retreat. The incoming chairmen of the House Judiciary and the Oversight Committees have likely been protein loading and drawing up subpoena lists for months in preparation for their coming investigations into Trump & Company. At least, I sure hope so.

Not that Mr. Trump has ever cared much about congressional authority. Which means we can look forward to rampant stonewalling of Democrats’ requests for documents and witnesses. If at least a couple of administration officials aren’t held in contempt of Congress by the end of next year, it won’t be for lack of trying.

For Mr. Trump, this pandemonium is doubtless much more fun than the thankless tedium of trying to govern. The guy has never been much for policy, unless you count whipping up fear of immigrants and imposing a tariff scheme that seems to have been drawn up on the back of a napkin. And his second-term “accomplishments” thus far have been about as popular as a root canal without sedation.

True to form, Mr. Trump has responded to his failures by whining about the public’s refusal to appreciate everything he has done for them. Pre-election, members of his administration pleaded with voters to just be a little patient, to allow more time for the positive results of the administration’s policies to manifest. Maybe buy their spoiled kids fewer toys in the meantime.

That’s all over now. Going forward, Mr. Trump can simply redirect the blame for all of his incompetence onto Democratic lawmakers. High gas prices? A disastrous war in Iran? More expensive health care coverage? Rural hospitals shuttering? Pfft. If only the radical Communist extremist Democratic majorities would let Mr. Trump work his magic, all those problems and more would have been resolved by now.

Will his blame shifting work? Maybe with the Trump Kool-Aid drinkers. But it is the natural condition of the president to be blamed for most of what goes down on his watch, and a growing portion of the electorate has grown wise to his game.

There has been some speculation about whether, saddled with divided government, Mr. Trump will make an effort to cut a few bipartisan deals. Perhaps pursue populist tax changes or reduce prescription drug costs or … you know, something.

It is indeed pleasant to imagine that the president cares enough about, if not the welfare of Americans, at least his own legacy to get serious about helping people other than his rich cronies and grifter family. I wouldn’t hold my breath. Mr. Trump has never displayed much interest in or patience for working out knotty bipartisan deals. Rather than waste time on policy negotiations, he seems more likely to sit around binge watching Fox News and noodling over how to annoy his Democratic nemeses with yet another monstrous monument to himself.

The closing years of a presidency can be a drag. Especially if, like Mr. Trump, you have done a lousy job. The electorate is tired of you. Your congressional team is increasingly focused on the future beyond you. Worse, people expect you to own the problems you once railed against, along with the failed policies you have rammed through. Where is the joy in that?

Instead, Mr. Trump can now spend his waning days in office wallowing in perpetual combat and chaos. That has always been his happy place, no matter the cost for the rest of us.
