SUMMARY

To fully account for the momentousness of the electoral reversal Republicans have just suffered, we must think back to 12 months ago, when President Trump appeared well positioned to deliver on an ambitious and still-popular agenda. At that time, Mr. Trump presided over a country at peace and an economy that was growing (if unevenly). Why, then, do polls show Mr. Trump with low approval ratings on immigration?

ARTICLE

Trump Blew It
There was nothing inevitable about this comeuppance.
By Christopher Caldwell
Published 2026-11-04 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/opinion/trump-midterms-republicans.html

To fully account for the momentousness of the electoral reversal Republicans have just suffered, we must think back to 12 months ago, when President Trump appeared well positioned to deliver on an ambitious and still-popular agenda.

At that time, Mr. Trump presided over a country at peace and an economy that was growing (if unevenly). By fair means and foul, he had defanged the “deep state” bureaucracy that during his first term had slow-walked and stymied his trade and immigration policies. He had purged the vast United States Agency for International Development, which he suspected of advancing Democratic Party priorities abroad. His Justice Department had neutralized the civil-rights crusaders who opposed his attempts to undo diversity, equity and inclusion policies. He had even made inroads into the country’s cultural elite, especially in Silicon Valley, where people spoke of a “vibe shift.”

Yes, Mr. Trump had alienated domestic adversaries and foreign allies alike. He had frightened investors with his manic tariff announcements. But he had come within a hair of winning an outright majority in the popular vote in 2024. Almost a year into his second term, his administration was, if not beloved, at least sustainably popular. In late October 2025, there were still a few polls showing his approval rating near 50 percent.

Which is to say, there was nothing inevitable about his comeuppance on Tuesday. Mr. Trump blew it. He was dealt a good hand in 2024 and 2025, but this year — through a mix of vanity, instability and foolishness — he snatched defeat from the jaws of victory.

Some policies that Mr. Trump ran on and brought about — like a tightened border — remain popular. The Center for American Progress, which favors expanded legal immigration and clear pathways to citizenship, found in a poll this past spring that hardened border security was still the migration policy that commanded the most voter support.

In his first term, Mr. Trump also largely won his yearslong argument with the establishment over how mass immigration affects the working class. Contrary to the views of pre-Trump policymakers, immigration to the United States is rarely a win-win proposition; it can help businesses, but often it does so by weakening the bargaining position of native workers. Even the Nobel Prize-winning economist Angus Deaton was convinced, writing in March 2024 that he no longer agreed with “the near consensus among economists that immigration to the U.S. was a good thing.”

Why, then, do polls show Mr. Trump with low approval ratings on immigration? Because he chose swagger over rational argument. Instead of allowing his policies to have their effect, he squandered his energy humiliating his opponents. He could have effectively made the case for raids of the sort he ordered in Minnesota: Just as there was a logic to tightening the border, there was a logic to enforcing that tightening in the cities by means of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. But this required explaining, and explaining is something Mr. Trump has always been poor at. He is almost allergic to consequentiality and often speaks in a stream of non sequiturs — perhaps because he fancies himself a master of deal-making, in which granting a connection between two facts is often a sign that one is making a concession.

Mr. Trump and administration officials repeatedly claimed that welfare fraud was rampant among Somalis in Minnesota. It was a splashy justification for raids — but hardly the sober rationale that was needed. When ill-trained officers treated the operation as an exercise in terrorizing rather than problem-solving, Mr. Trump lost the country.

Similar things happened with his attacks on D.E.I. and political correctness, where Mr. Trump initially had considerable support. After he had changed Justice Department policies, he might simply have let his project jell, until the public got used to a country without invasive enforcement of affirmative action, speech codes and new gender orthodoxies. But he couldn’t leave well enough alone. He was like a child playing with his food. He sought to impose his own codes on campus speech, leaving a regime that was qualitatively — but not structurally — different than the censorious one that had existed in the heyday of woke.

This inability to sit still proved calamitous when it came to foreign policy. Mr. Trump’s ideas were often sound: Greenland was indeed an important strategic area vulnerable to being co-opted by hostile powers; it was indeed foolish for Democrats to worry more about Russia than China; countering China’s influence on our own hemisphere was indeed a strategic priority; industrial autonomy (whether attained through tariffs or otherwise) was indeed a must.

But again, with his insistence on humiliating his interlocutors, Mr. Trump created problems where none had existed. The Canadian conservative Pierre Poilievre looked certain to become prime minister until Mr. Trump began blurting out nonsense about annexing Canada as our 51st state, securing the election for Mark Carney, one of his most determined adversaries on the international stage. Mr. Trump’s insistence on besmirching Denmark led to the deployment of non-American NATO troops to Greenland, before resulting, in September, in a security agreement that is no better than what Mr. Trump could have had merely by asking for it at the outset.

Mr. Trump’s two worst ideas were the two wars he began against Iran. His poll numbers have never returned to where they were in June 2025, before he joined Israel in a bombing campaign meant to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program. When Mr. Trump announced a cease-fire days later, he seemed to have shown an impressive ability to snap out of a delusion. But then came Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28.

That war has penetrated every crevice of the Trump administration, discrediting all of it. It has humiliated the United States not just militarily but also diplomatically. It has weakened the U.S.-Israel alliance and, as a consequence, Israel itself. And it has caused gas and diesel prices to spike, forcing Mr. Trump’s supporters to bear the brunt of inflation. Districts and states that went for Mr. Trump by large margins in 2024 shifted away from Republicans across the country.

Mr. Trump’s vanity has destroyed his second term. Part of what has made this comeuppance feel more consequential than the one he received during the midterms of 2018 is that this time around he has been empowered to let that vanity rip. Mr. Trump was able to purge the executive branch of ideological opponents and to elevate his own followers to replace them. He was aided by the Supreme Court’s June decision in Trump v. Slaughter, which upheld a more powerful conception of the presidency, greatly weakening the independence of almost all the regulatory agencies.

As far as honoring the idea of the presidency enshrined in the Constitution, the Supreme Court may well have been right to decide as it did — but it seems to have given the public pause. Henceforth, if the presidency is to be given George Washington’s prerogatives, the public is going to require of its presidents something more like George Washington’s character.

ARTICLE

Beverly Whipple Has Died. She Introduced the G-Spot to the Mainstream.
Dr. Whipple studied the female erogenous zone and, with collaborators, wrote a best seller about women’s sexuality. She was 85.
By Randi Hutter Epstein
Published 2026-11-04 23:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/science/beverly-whipple-g-spot-dead.html

Beverly Whipple, a nurse, psychologist and sex educator whose 1982 book about the G-spot encouraged a generation of women to search for their erogenous zones, died on Monday at her home in Voorhees, N.J. She was 85.

Her husband, Jim Whipple, said her death was from complications of an illness consistent with Alzheimer’s disease.

Dr. Whipple’s book “The G Spot: And Other Recent Discoveries About Human Sexuality,” which she wrote with Alice K. Ladas and John D. Perry, was a New York Times best seller. It examined the concept of female sexual pleasure, and specifically the idea of the G-spot, a sensitive area on the upper vaginal wall. The book has been translated into 19 languages and has sold more than a million copies.

Dr. Whipple’s plain language and accepting attitude about sexual tastes and orientations informed, amused and shocked global audiences.

In 1981, on “The Phil Donahue Show,” Dr. Whipple inserted her finger into a plastic replica of female genitalia, pressing on what she said was a sensitive area. “It’s not easy to find on yourself, but a partner can find it quite easily,” she said.

Spectators in the studio giggled. Dr. Whipple appeared unfazed.

Later in the show, Mr. Donahue asked an older audience member if she had ever expected to discuss this subject on television. “No, I didn’t,” the woman replied. “If my mother was alive, she’d drop dead.”

Dr. Whipple’s study of female eroticism began in the 1970s, while she was teaching nursing students and providing counseling to women in New Jersey. Several of her clients confided that they worried about occasionally urinating during intercourse. Seeking answers in the medical literature, Dr. Whipple unearthed a 1950 article by Ernst Gräfenberg, a German doctor, documenting women’s ability to ejaculate. The same article mentioned an especially sensitive area in the vagina.

Seeking to confirm his findings, Dr. Whipple, along with Dr. Perry, a sexologist and psychologist, recruited 400 women from New Jersey and Vermont for a study. At a 1980 meeting of the American Association of Sexuality Educators, Counselors and Therapists, Dr. Whipple reported that all of the volunteers seemed to have an erogenous area on their vaginal walls somewhere between “11 o’clock and 1 o’clock.” Many of the participants, she added, had released a fluid that was not urine; it was similar to male ejaculate.

A colleague suggested that she call the area the Whipple Tickle. She refused because at the time there was a fictional Mr. Whipple who featured in a popular television advertisement for Charmin toilet paper.

Instead, Dr. Whipple and Dr. Perry called it the Gräfenberg spot, after the earlier researcher. That moniker was later shortened to G-spot. (Dr. Gräfenberg wasn’t the first person to study the area; Regnier de Graaf, a 17th-century Dutch anatomist, wrote about the same vaginal erogenous zone.)

After the “The G Spot” was published, Dr. Whipple appeared on more than 300 television and radio programs, podcasts and videos, and gave more than 800 talks in the United States and abroad. She also wrote more than 100 scientific articles and book chapters. In 2013, Cosmopolitan included her on its list of “10 Sexual Revolutionaries You Should Know.”

While the book propelled her and her collaborators into the public eye, not all the reviews were positive. The Washington Post wrote that “instead of defending this astounding revelation with hard-core scientific data, they chose an inordinate number of soft-core testimonials.”

In later years, Dr. Whipple downplayed the term G-spot, opting instead to use the phrase “clitourethrovaginal complex.” Along with most experts, she no longer talked about a “spot,” but instead promoted the idea that erogenous areas may vary among women and could include the clitoris, urethra and vagina.

Beverly Hoehne was born on June 30, 1941, in Jersey City, N.J., and grew up in nearby Secaucus. Her father, Howard Hoehne, was a vice president of Bankers Trust. Her mother, Beatrice (Bodei) Hoehne, was a nurse.

Beverly attended Weehawken High School and earned a bachelor’s degree in nursing from Wagner College on Staten Island.

After she graduated, in 1962, she married Mr. Whipple. In addition to him, she is survived by two children, Allen and Susan Whipple; five grandchildren; and one great-grandchild.

Her first job after graduation was teaching nursing at West Jersey Hospital in Camden, N.J. In 1975, when administrators refused to let her include lessons on sexuality, she quit and started a sex education course at Gloucester County College (now Rowan College of South Jersey) in Sewell, N.J.

That experience piqued her interest in female sexuality. She went on to earn three degrees from Rutgers University: a master’s degree in counseling, a master’s in nursing and a doctorate in psychobiology.

Her doctoral research, under the direction of Barry Komisaruk, a psychology professor and sex researcher, investigated the neurophysiology of female orgasms, focusing on the way sexual stimulation can dull pain response. The research showed that some women with severe spinal cord injuries are capable of experiencing orgasm, demonstrating that sensations could bypass the spinal cord and travel along the vagus nerve, which runs from the genitalia to the brain.

“Her interest in being able to research sex and make it a legitimate place for scientific study legitimized pleasure as a healthy force for wellness and for research,” Nan Wise, a Rutgers University neuroscientist and sex therapist who trained under Dr. Whipple, said in an interview.

Dr. Whipple wrote several other books on female sexuality, including “Safe Encounters: How Women Can Say Yes to Pleasure and No to Unsafe Sex” (1989), written with Gina Ogden; “The Science of Orgasm” (2006), written with Dr. Komisaruk and Carlos Beyer-Flores; and “The Orgasm Answer Guide” (2009), written with Dr. Komisaruk, Dr. Beyer-Flores and Sara Nasserzadeh.

Reflecting on her career, Dr. Whipple said she never intended to make women anxious about finding their G-spots.

“When you are searching for something as a goal,” she said in a 2018 episode of the Netflix documentary series “Explained” focusing on the female orgasm, “you are going to miss a lot of pleasure on the way.”

ARTICLE

Justice Alito Will Not Retire Immediately, Despite Election Outcome
The conservative justice has told friends he does not plan to step down before the end of the court’s term, even as Democrats are set to seize the Senate in January.
By Ann E. Marimow
Published 2026-11-04 23:37 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/alito-trump-supreme-court-not-retiring.html

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats’ commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

As recently as last month, Justice Alito, a forceful conservative and reliable vote in favor of Mr. Trump’s policies, had rejected the idea that he would step down if Democrats took control of the Senate.

“I intend to stick around through this term,” he told Bloomberg News, in an interview published in early October.

But the state of the electoral map after Tuesday’s election generated speculation that he or Justice Clarence Thomas — the court’s two oldest justices — could quickly announce their retirements and give the president a brief window to push through a successor during the Senate’s lame-duck session.

Over the years, Justice Thomas has ruled out retiring, suggesting he would serve for decades more. With 35 years on the bench, if Justice Thomas were to stay through May 2028, he would set the record as the longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history.

Justice Thomas, who is 78, and Justice Alito, who is 76, did not respond to requests for comment about their plans.

Despite the public conversation, legal experts were largely agreed on Wednesday that a speedy retirement would be a potentially dicey and problematic proposition that was not guaranteed to secure a seat.

A nominee would have faced the newfound independence of departing Republican senators such as John Cornyn of Texas and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who were defeated in primaries by Trump-backed challengers, in addition to Susan Collins of Maine, a moderate who lost on Tuesday. The group may have had little appetite to help Mr. Trump ram through a nominee of his choice.

After Mr. Trump won re-election in 2024, the conservative legal analyst Ed Whelan said that he expected Justice Alito to announce his retirement the next spring and predicted that Justice Thomas would step down in 2026. The moves, he had believed, would allow Mr. Trump to replace the justices with younger jurists who might secure the court’s conservative supermajority for a generation.

Of course, an unexpected vacancy due to health concerns, for instance, could arise at any time during the remainder of Mr. Trump’s tenure. But after Tuesday’s election, in which the scale of the Democrats’ win in Congress was larger than expected, Mr. Whelan said the two conservative justices now may not be able to retire before 2033 if they want to be succeeded by a nominee with a similar judicial philosophy.

“No justice is going to announce in the next few days that he will be stepping down,” Mr. Whelan wrote, adding, “Justices don’t make snap decisions about retiring.”

Robert Luther III, a professor at Antonin Scalia Law School who helped choose Mr. Trump’s judicial nominees during his first term, agreed.

“I don’t anticipate any retirements before January, and frankly, I wouldn’t advise it,” he said.

Both justices were on the bench when Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg decided not to retire before the 2016 election, a decision many court observers consider a cautionary tale. Instead of allowing President Barack Obama to pick her successor, Justice Ginsburg died while in office in 2020, creating an opening for Mr. Trump to replace the liberal icon with a conservative, Justice Amy Coney Barrett.

But now, conservatives fret that both men may be in danger of following Justice Ginsburg’s example. If a Democrat were elected to succeed Mr. Trump as president in 2028, both Justices Alito and Thomas would be in their 80s before a Republican could regain the White House and be in position to nominate a successor. Forecasts for when the G.O.P. might regain control of the Senate are even cloudier.

At the end of the Supreme Court’s last term in June, speculation had intensified about Justice Alito’s future and whether Mr. Trump would have an opening to continue to remake a Supreme Court that already includes three of his first-term nominees.

Because of Justice Thomas’s previous statements, attention centered on Justice Alito. It reached a fever pitch on the last day of the term when NPR erroneously reported, and then retracted, his retirement.

In a series of interviews published in October, Justice Alito acknowledged that he had “thought about” retiring at the end of the term, but said he had ruled it out, thinking he could still make a “valuable contribution,” as he told CBS News.

Meanwhile, a newly empowered Democratic Congress will have other implications for the Supreme Court beyond vacancies and nominations. Democrats unhappy with rulings from the conservative bench have repeatedly called for changing the structure of the court. Recent polls show bipartisan support for enacting an enforcement mechanism for the ethics code the justices adopted in 2023, and for eliminating life tenure for justices.

Gabe Roth of Fix the Court, which advocates judicial accountability, predicted on Wednesday that House and Senate committees overseeing the courts would also revive judicial ethics investigations that were largely paused two years ago.

Justice Thomas, for one, could face renewed questions surrounding gifts he accepted, but initially did not report, from his friend Harlan Crow, a Texas billionaire and Republican donor. The justice has said he was not required to report such gifts at the time.

ARTICLE

How a Blue Wave Became a Red Wipeout
Republicans lost control of the House and Senate as voters offered a stinging rebuke to President Trump’s agenda.
By Lisa Lerer
Published 2026-11-04 08:48 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/democratic-midterms-wipeout.html

In the end, it wasn’t just a wave. It was a wipeout.

A Democrat won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time since the Herbert Hoover administration. The party picked up Senate seats in Texas, North Carolina and South Carolina. Republicans even fell short in House districts in the South where they had tried to give themselves an edge by drawing new, gerrymandered maps.

The sweeping Democratic victories on Tuesday night offered a decisive rebuke to President Trump and his aggressive, often chaotic second-term agenda.

The party seized control of both houses of Congress. Voters rejected Republicans in conservative states that supported Mr. Trump by double-digit margins just two years ago, in places that had not seen competitive elections for major seats in decades.

Even some Democrats were stunned by the extent of their wins, which included defeating Greg Abbott, the three-term Republican governor of Texas; and Susan Collins, the five-term Republican senator from Maine.

“It’s a blood bath,” said Dan Sena, who was the executive director of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee during the last Democratic wave, in 2018. “Democrats are going to be in power in places they haven’t been in power in decades.”

And so the era of one-party rule in Washington ended with a crash, as voters pushed back on high gas prices, an unpopular war in Iran and stubbornly high inflation. As Wednesday dawned, there were signs that the country was entering a new and uncertain political time, in which both parties would be forced to consider how to navigate a post-Trump political era.

While Democrats have not solved all the problems that cost them the 2024 election, their wins were a powerful sign of renewal as a new generation of rising stars captured the country’s attention.

For years, Democrats seemed to compete on a smaller and smaller map, concentrating on fewer states, blue cities and diversifying suburbs and trying to cut their losses in rural America. But Tuesday’s results showed that the last two years had turned off voters even in deep red terrain. For Republicans, the losses were a generational defeat, giving Democrats a foothold from which to build a robust political operation in places that had been long out of reach.

In Seward County, Kan., a majority-Hispanic area, the Democratic Senate candidate, Adam Hamilton, won by double digits. Just two years ago, Mr. Trump won there by 40 percentage points.

In Iowa, a largely agricultural state, Democrats won the governor’s mansion and a U.S. Senate seat and flipped three of the state’s four congressional seats.

And in South Texas, Democrats won three heavily Latino border districts that Republicans had redrawn to be more favorable to their party.

In many states, Democrats ran candidates who offered a decidedly different brand of politics from the “resistance” ethos that characterized their response to Mr. Trump’s first term.

Instead, they focused their message on the deep economic anxiety that has roiled the country, arguing that the president and his Republican allies were enriching themselves while ordinary Americans struggled. Survey after survey showed a majority of voters, and a notable share of Republicans, offering low marks to his signature policies: tariffs, immigration enforcement and the Iran war.

“When Trump first came into office, there was this churn that was constantly going on,” said Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey, whose victory last year was an early indicator of Democratic wins to come. “These candidates have not gotten sucked into the churn.”

Many cast their campaigns as above partisan politics, trying to distance themselves from the party’s beleaguered national brand to woo voters in red states.

“This win is not about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, told cheering supporters at his victory party. “It is much bigger than that. There is something broken in America.” He added, “People across the political spectrum are hungry for a different kind of politics.”

The result nationally was a big tent that encompassed Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a liberal firebrand in Michigan, and Mr. Hamilton, a Kansas pastor and former Republican who fueled his rise with appeals to conservative voters.

The breadth of the victory indicated that the party’s ideological future remained unsettled, setting the stage for the 2028 primary campaign. That race is expected to be crowded with politicians eager to ride what they see as a groundswell of support into the White House.

A big tent can leave more room for disputes underneath it. In many respects, the midterms showed that the party was still divided: between progressives and moderates, over Israel, over the best path forward.

But the results leave open a crucial question: Did the Democrats really win? Or did Republicans just lose? The answer will become clear in the coming months, as Democrat try to retain their gains and work to win the presidency.

“This is just the beginning of what is going to be a decades-long rebuilding process. The worst thing Democrats could do is think all our problems are solved,” said Lis Smith, a strategist who started a Democratic political group to promote insurgent candidates. “The problem with a good election night is it can conceal a lot of weaknesses.”

Yet it was clear Democrats had repaired some of the weaknesses that cost their party the White House just two years ago. In the final national New York Times/Siena poll before the election, Democrats held an eight-point advantage on the economy and a 15-point edge on the cost of living. Those ratings mark a significant reversal from 2024, when Mr. Trump was favored on the economy.

Republicans framed the election not as a referendum on Mr. Trump but as a choice between their “common sense” policies and a Democratic Party controlled by a socialists, communists and an un-American left flank. They attempted to cast Democrats as out of touch with the values of red states, casting them as sexual predators, supporters of Shariah law and even vegans.

Again and again, Republicans tried to shift the structural dynamics of the election in their favor. They spent an extraordinary $12 billion, enlisting the help of Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, to help fund their attacks.

In an unprecedented mid-decade redistricting, they redrew congressional lines across conservative states, tilting districts in their favor.

Those efforts fell short against the realities of American pocketbooks and a clear belief that Mr. Trump’s policies were responsible for the higher prices of housing, groceries and gas.

Concern about the cost of living cut across nearly all sectors of American life. One sign — more omnipresent than any campaign billboard — provided an inescapable reminder: the price of fuel advertised at gas pumps across the nation.

“We don’t feel enough is being done to make everyday necessities affordable,” said Sateria Peterson, 42, a business owner in Columbia, S.C. “We’re stretching every dollar just to cover the basics, with less room for emergencies or savings.”

Jalyn Washington, 21, of Dayton, Ohio, said she took out her economic frustrations on the Republicans. “Whoever Trump wanted, I voted the opposite,” she said.

In addition to traditional kitchen-table concerns about gas prices and cost of living, voters expressed a growing anxiety about issues that were entirely new: data centers and artificial intelligence.

Across the country, vulnerable Republican candidates distanced themselves from the president’s full-throated support for data centers. It wasn’t the only issue where the party’s candidates, even in traditionally red states, sought to separate themselves from Mr. Trump.

On the Iran war, tariffs and immigration enforcement, they offered disagreement from Mr. Trump’s approach.

For many, the dissent came too late.

Already some Republicans are looking toward a future in which Mr. Trump will play a less prominent role.

“I do want to fight for the soul of our party — I feel like we’re going down a bad path,” said Representative Don Bacon, a retiring lawmaker from Nebraska who plans to deliver a speech this month laying out a direction for his party.

His seat in Congress, however, will be filled by a Democrat.

These Wins Could Mint a New Generation of Democratic Stars
Voters from South Carolina to Ohio to Texas have elevated a new class of Democrats who could not be more different from one another.
By Jess Bidgood
Published 2026-11-04 07:25 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/democratic-newcomers-congress.html

The Democrats’ stunning victories across the nation on Tuesday night won’t just change the balance of power in Congress and in statehouses across the country. They will also change the Democratic Party itself.

Voters from South Carolina to Ohio to Texas have elevated a new class of potential Democratic stars who could not be more different from one another. They are ideologically diverse, including progressives intent on reshaping the party’s approach to Israel and health care and moderates who spent months persuading Republicans to join their cause. Some eschew the virality of the social media era, others are a product of it. There’s a pediatrician, a pastor, a Paralympian and a former Navy helicopter pilot.

They will also change the face of power. The nation is getting its first Black female governor as well as the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate, and the first Gen Z woman in Congress.

Meet some of the party’s new rising stars.

James Talarico — Texas

A state legislator and former middle-school teacher, James Talarico conquered hundreds of millions of dollars in Republican spending — including at least $158 million from Elon Musk — to become the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate race in more than a generation. At 37, he will be the youngest member of the Senate once he is sworn in.

Mr. Talarico rocketed to prominence last year in part because of a stunt, becoming an often-viral messenger about Texas Democrats’ effort to flee the state to block Republican gerrymandering efforts. A Christian seminary student who quotes Scripture on the campaign trail, he parlayed his fame into a Senate campaign in which he likened himself to David running against President Trump’s handpicked Goliath, Ken Paxton. “You,” he told voters across the state, “are my slingshot.”

Listen: Mr. Talarico was recently interviewed on “The Daily.”

Abdul El-Sayed — Michigan

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, 42, will be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate. He is a physician who ran local health departments in Detroit, and became the party’s nominee after a bruising and expensive primary against the much-better-funded Representative Haley Stevens. He ran an explicitly progressive campaign in a purple state, and liberal icons like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez embraced his effort to transform their party.

Dr. El-Sayed’s anti-Zionism alienated some Jewish leaders and spurred the American Israel Public Affairs Committee to pour millions into opposing him. But he told voters over the summer: “Money can’t buy you a message. Money can’t buy you the truth. Money can’t buy you the people.”

Read: How Dr. El-Sayed responded to attacks on his faith and family.

Adam Hamilton — Kansas

At the beginning of 2026, Adam Hamilton wasn’t even a Democrat. He was a registered Republican and the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country.

He is now the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the state since 1932. Mr. Hamilton, 62, campaigned openly on his faith, and worked hard to distance himself from the national party as he sought to persuade moderates in his deep red state to chose him over the unpopular incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall. His was a conciliatory pitch: “If I’m elected, as a moderate or independent-minded Democrat, I’m going to work across the aisle,” he said on the debate stage in October.

Read: How Mr. Hamilton turned deep red Kansas into a tossup.

Annie Andrews — South Carolina

Dr. Annie Andrews, a 46-year-old-pediatrician, began a long-shot campaign against the long-serving Senator Lindsey Graham back in May 2025. Her focus was on somebody who would never appear on the ballot: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Mr. Trump’s controversial secretary of health and human services. Dr. Andrews vowed to impeach Mr. Kennedy and blamed the Trump administration for a 2025 measles outbreak that sickened 1,000 children in her state.

Her campaign seemed like a little less of a long shot when Mr. Graham died suddenly in July and was replaced on the ballot by his sister, Darline Graham. Dr. Andrews portrayed Ms. Graham, accurately, as someone handpicked by Mr. Trump, and pitched herself as the change candidate.

Read: A campaign dispatch from last month.

Chris Pappas — New Hampshire

There were moments this year when Chris Pappas’s assiduously low-key political style made some in his party nervous, but he insisted it was right for his low-key state. On Tuesday night, he easily dispatched an opponent with the most famous family name in New Hampshire Republican politics, John E. Sununu. Now, Mr. Pappas is set to become the first openly gay man in the U.S. Senate.

That wasn’t a major theme of his campaign, but Mr. Pappas, 46, reflected on it in a recent interview with The New York Times. “The fact is, I’m living a reality today that I didn’t think was possible when I was growing up just a few decades ago,” he said. “My state, our country, has come a long way.”

Read our recent profile.

Josh Turek — Iowa

Josh Turek was seen in Washington as the ideal recruit in solid red Iowa: a two-time Paralympic gold medalist (in wheelchair basketball) who voted for George W. Bush. He campaigned hard against Mr. Trump’s tariffs as a “prairie populist” and attacked his opponent, Representative Ashley Hinson, over the war in Iran.

In an election where voters expressed deep economic discomfort, Mr. Turek made Ms. Hinson’s personal wealth an issue, contrasting it with his own working-class upbringing. He promised in one ad that he would not be another millionaire in the U.S. Senate. “It’s families like mine who pay the price for Trump’s health care cuts,” Mr. Turek said.

Read our profile.

Gina Hinojosa — Texas

For 12 years, Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, has had an iron grip on power in Texas, and a record fourth term seemed all but assured. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic state lawmaker nominated to challenge him, was seen as little more than a sacrificial lamb.

Then she started hammering Mr. Abbott over data centers, and he halted new permits for them. Ms. Hinojosa, who is 52, also turned a wrenching personal story — her decision, as a Catholic, to carry a high-risk pregnancy to term — into an emotional campaign ad. In another spot, she invoked something many in her party have avoided: pronouns.

“I’m Gina Hinojosa,” she said. “My pronouns are Mom, Texan and, soon to be, governor.”

Watch: Ms. Hinojosa was on a recent episode of “The Interview.

Keisha Lance Bottoms — Georgia

When she entered this race, Keisha Lance Bottoms’s first task was overcoming her own party’s doubts after crime rose — and her popularity plummeted — during her tenure as mayor of Atlanta. But she managed to break away from a crowded field in the primary and cast herself as a foil to Mr. Trump in a state where he carries heavy political baggage, blaming the president for rising fuel prices and health care costs.

Now, at 56, she will be the nation’s first Black female governor, after beating the businessman Rick Jackson, who poured more than $100 million of his own money into the campaign.

Read our profile.

Amy Acton — Ohio

Dr. Amy Acton was once her state’s chief public health officer, and she made health care a centerpiece of her campaign against Vivek Ramaswamy. Dr. Acton’s traumatic childhood also became a focus of the campaign in its final weeks, when Mr. Ramaswamy ran an ad in which her long-estranged mother — who supported the stepfather accused of raping Amy when she was a child — called her daughter a liar.

Dr. Acton, 60, called the ad “despicable” and said in an interview with CNN that she had spoken publicly about her childhood because that “it might give other people hope that you can, you know, get out of circumstances.”

Read: How that ad divided Republicans.

Rob Sand — Iowa

Long before any talk of a blue wave, long before murmurs about Democrats reclaiming control of the Senate, many saw a glimmer of hope for the party in deep red Iowa: Rob Sand.

He was the state auditor. He was popular. He was a former model (though he certainly didn’t talk about that). And he was running for the open governor’s seat, asking voters if Republican dominance had really been good for their state.

Mr. Sand, 44, made the state’s high rate of cancer a centerpiece of his campaign, and promised to be a governor for all. His campaign slogan: “Not redder or bluer, but better and truer.”

Read: Our profile from early in the campaign.

It’s much more difficult to become a star as a newcomer in the larger House . Here are a few names to know:

- Rebecca Bennett (New Jersey’s Seventh District) is a former Navy helicopter pilot and health care executive. She unseated Representative Tom Kean Jr., scion of a prominent family in the state.
- Melat Kiros (Colorado’s First District), who is 29, will become the first Gen Z woman in Congress. She ran under the Democratic Socialists of America banner.
- Bobby Pulido (Texas) is a Tejano singer with two Latin Grammy Awards. He performed for free at more than 70 quinceañeras and weddings as part of his campaign.

SUMMARY

President Trump implored voters over the course of the midterm campaign to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The electoral backlash extended even into deep red states and indicated that Mr. Trump has lost his hold over the coalition that lifted him to the White House twice. “It’s the end of Trump,” he added, “even though he’s still going to be there."

ARTICLE

Angry Voters Usher in Beginning of the End to the Trump Era
The electoral backlash extended even into deep red states and indicated that President Trump has lost his hold over the coalition that lifted him to the White House twice.
By Peter Baker
Published 2026-11-04 07:08 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/midterm-election-trump-voters.html

President Trump implored voters over the course of the midterm campaign to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” He said it not once, not twice, but 47 times this fall.

And voters did — just not the way he hoped.

The Democratic wave in the congressional elections on Tuesday amounted to a stinging rebuke of a deeply unpopular president after more than a decade in which he has dominated the national stage. More than any of his predecessors, Mr. Trump deliberately made the midterm contest a referendum on himself, only to pay the price.

The electoral backlash extended even into deep red states and indicated that Mr. Trump has lost his hold over the coalition that lifted him to the White House twice. Frustrated by high gas prices, an intractable war with Iran and allegations of flagrant profiteering by Mr. Trump and members of his circle, voters who previously took a chance on an outsider promising change either rejected his party or stayed home.

As of early Wednesday morning, the Democratic margin of victory in the overall national vote for House seats was expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest that either party has lodged in a congressional election since at least 1976, according to estimates by The New York Times. It will dwarf even the margins that the Republicans won in their two big landslide victories of modern times when they defeated congressional Democrats when Bill Clinton held the White House in 1994 and Barack Obama was president in 2010.

Thanks to redistricting, that margin may not translate into as many seats as the winners gained in those watershed years. Gerrymandered House districts leave far fewer seats available for poaching by the other party than in the past. But the overall margin of Democratic victory indicates that while the president has two more years left in office and can still wield power to great effect, Americans are signaling the beginning of the end of the Trump era.

“It’s basically a repudiation of Trump and the Republicans and what they’ve done for the last two years,” said Douglas B. Sosnik, who was White House political director for Mr. Clinton and closely tracked the races this fall. “I do think starting tomorrow, we’re in this new phase and it’s a transition phase and it will last two years. And it will be much more volatile than the last two years.”

Mr. Trump quickly tried to save face by insisting that the rout by Democrats was not really a rejection of him since he was not actually on the ballot — never mind that he told voters repeatedly to vote as if he were.

“I wasn’t on the ticket, and because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote,” he told The Times in an interview Tuesday night.

Even many Republicans would roll their eyes at that assertion, as this was a campaign that revolved so demonstrably around Mr. Trump.

It was Mr. Trump who decided to start a war with Iran that jolted energy markets and sent prices at the pump soaring. It was Mr. Trump who chose the candidates, the issues, the strategy and the message.

It was Mr. Trump who demanded complete loyalty from a party whose candidates were nervous about distancing themselves from him. And it was Mr. Trump who has shrugged off questions about the ethics of his moneymaking in office, helping propel voter concerns about corruption.

The defeat of two Senate Republican candidates that he personally selected over potentially more electable contenders in deep red states — Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina — demonstrated the consequences of his interventions. His push to throw out the normal process and redraw House districts in the middle of the decade to try to stack the deck for Republicans backfired.

Many voters told pollsters and interviewers that they felt hoodwinked by Mr. Trump, believing that he was going to bring down prices and not start new wars. They expected him to close the border, but bristled at what they saw as heavy-handed arrests of people living in the country for years. They rebelled against the tariffs that increased costs for consumers.

The way Mr. Trump spent his last day before the election proved to be a metaphor for how out of sync his political instincts were with the season. Instead of emphasizing plans to address the cost of living worries weighing on many voters, he delivered his final pre-election address at the Reflecting Pool, talking about algae and pipes. It was a vivid reminder of his obsession with pet construction projects in Washington, despite the warning signs of how it rankled voters — as if Richard M. Nixon had made his final pre-election speech in front of the Watergate complex.

Even if Trumpism may be receding, Mr. Trump has the power of the presidency for two more years and will do everything he can to remain a dominant voice for as long as he can. His allies warned against assuming that he is a spent force.

“Trump’s critics have written his political obituary before and been wrong every time,” said David McIntosh, president of the Club for Growth, a group that promotes conservative economic policies.

“The fix is Republicans getting back to our principles,” he added. “That’s how we win in 2028.”

There is, of course, a natural tendency to draw great lessons from a big midterm wave, to assume that it represents a fundamental shift in the American electorate. It certainly may. But history has seen plenty of examples when it did not last long. And it remains to be seen whether Tuesday’s results signal a broader ideological shift among voters.

The post-Watergate wave of 1974 was thought to presage a long winter in the political wilderness for Republicans, but Ronald Reagan brought the party back to the White House just six years later. The 1994 and 2010 Republican sweeps were expected to presage the end of the Clinton and Obama presidencies, but both came back to win re-election handily two years later.

Lynn Vavrek, a professor of American politics and public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the most important factor in the election was sky-high gas prices so it may not follow that the country’s political character has profoundly changed.

“It doesn’t mean the MAGA coalition is crumbling,” she said. “Does it mean the shine has come off Donald Trump a little bit? Yes. Are people less enamored of him? I think the answer to that is yes.” But she said it does not necessarily mean that Republicans are going to abandon the “identity-inflected policies” on issues like immigration and diversity that have animated the party under Mr. Trump.

This is, after all, a fundamentally altered party, one that Mr. Trump forged in his own image, empowering those who defer to him and purging those who exhibit independence. “We don’t know how the president’s going to react, but thus far we’ve only seen members of his party acquiesce to him,” said Christina M. Greer, a political science professor at Fordham University.

Joe Grogan, who served as Mr. Trump’s domestic policy adviser in his first term, said that regardless of the election results, the president has changed the political landscape by advancing issues that were not adequately addressed enough before, like pushing for better trade deals and securing greater military spending by NATO allies. The party, he said, is not moving back to what it once was.

“We’re still in Trump’s party, regardless of what happens tonight,” Mr. Grogan, now at Covington & Burling, said before the polls closed. “People who expect Trumpism to get repudiated I think are mistaken. There will be some debates that I think will be healthy for the party. But I just don’t see there being a huge wellspring for the party to go back to the one that George W. Bush led for two successful elections.”

At the same time, Democrats will debate how to interpret their victory. Their main identity this year was simply being against Mr. Trump, which was more than enough. But progressives will say that it was energy on the left that powered the success, while moderates will say it was the appeal to disaffected Republicans in states like Texas and Kansas that was crucial.

“The biggest story is non-MAGA Republicans have broken with the Republican Party,” said Rahm Emanuel, a former Democratic Chicago mayor and ambassador exploring a run for president. “The question is do we want to make this election transactional or transformational? What we do in 2027 will determine that.”

James Blanchard, who was first elected to Congress in the post-Watergate Democratic sweep of 1974 and later served as governor of Michigan, said this year’s election felt similar to that historic year. But he said that does not mean that American politics will return to the way they were before Mr. Trump. “We can never go back, unfortunately,” he said. “We’re going to have to go forward.”

“It’s the end of Trump,” he added, “even though he’s still going to be there."

SUMMARY

Six days before the election, more than two dozen of President Trump’s top strategists logged onto a private video call. To win control of the Senate, Democrats needed to hold all of their seats and flip at least four, including in states that Mr. Trump won handily in 2024. In the House, where Democrats had fallen three seats short in 2024, recruiters went hunting in districts Mr. Trump had carried by 10 points or more, betting early that the emboldened president would overreach.

ARTICLE

‘I Have Seen the Enemy, and It Is Us’: Inside Team Trump’s Historic Collapse
How an unpopular president and an unpopular war provided an opening for Democrats to make sweeping gains in the midterms.
By Shane Goldmacher, Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman
Published 2026-11-05 01:28 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/trump-midterms-losses-republicans.html

Six days before the election, more than two dozen of President Trump’s top strategists logged onto a private video call.

The mood was grim. The discussion began with talk of cyanide.

“Do you want the white pill first, or the black pill first?” asked Tony Fabrizio, the president’s chief pollster.

Tim Saler, one of the Republican Party’s top data consultants, laid out two scenarios. In the first, the $400 million MAGA Inc. super PAC was reaching the voters that it had wanted and expected to vote. “That’s the optimistic scenario,” he said.

The other was a wipeout.

“I’m getting my affairs in order,” James Blair, who left the White House to oversee the president’s midterm strategy, said to laughter, according to four people on the call. “I suggest everybody else do the same.”

For roughly 30 minutes, the call ran on gallows humor: funeral arrangements, prison food, presidential pardons, even a brief riff on fleeing the country.

“At least Bibi won. He’ll protect us,” Mr. Blair said sarcastically of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country had voted the day before. (Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc fell short of a majority, and his party soon claimed the election had been stolen.)

“Maybe we could get asylum in Israel,” Mr. Fabrizio said.

Collapse at the Polls

The scope of the Republican wreckage would become clear a week later.

Democrats stormed to a huge House majority and won control of the Senate, a remarkable feat powered by victories in Republican strongholds — Kansas, South Carolina, Texas — that few could have imagined a year ago.

This account of the Republican Party’s collapse is based on interviews with more than 70 people — among them lawmakers, political strategists, party leaders, pollsters, White House officials and congressional aides — who were directly involved in the midterm elections, many of whom were granted anonymity to describe private conversations and decisions.

The scale of the defeat was far from inevitable.

Republicans had record fund-raising, the world’s richest man, a favorable Supreme Court ruling on campaign finance and a demoralized, unpopular opposition.

In the Senate, they had a map that required Democrats to compete in states they hadn’t won in decades.

And in the House, the Trump team demolished the tradition of redrawing congressional lines only once a decade in order to carve up new districts to help the G.O.P. bolster its narrow majority.

What Republicans could not overcome was a president who lost the public’s trust on the economy and so much more. And what they had not counted on was an unpopular war in the Middle East — one that would close the Strait of Hormuz and push gas prices past $4 a gallon — that would rage all the way through the election.

And Democrats were ready, this time, to seize on the G.O.P. stumbles.

A Stark Warning on the Iran War

The slide deck that Mr. Blair had circulated over the summer to officials in the West Wing was stark.

One slide linked Republicans’ polling numbers to an Iran war timeline.

It showed how the Democratic advantage had ballooned during active hostilities, shrunk during talks over a “memorandum of understanding” and then spiked again when the cease-fire collapsed.

By the end of July, Democrats had a 10-point edge on the congressional ballot.

The “bottom line” was hard to miss. It was in highlighter yellow: Republicans could still conceivably win the House if Democrats had only a four-point edge. “But that won’t happen without an extended cease-fire, Hormuz open & gas prices falling,” the slide warned.

“A final result approaching D+10 would likely cost us the Senate.”

The results on Tuesday were even worse: Mr. Trump’s party is on track to lose the national popular congressional vote by about 13 points, according to estimates by The New York Times. It is shaping up to be the worst loss in a half-century, since the aftermath of the Watergate scandal.

Even before the polls had closed, Mr. Trump had begun to ruminate on what might have been.

“If we never went into Iran, what do you think would happen in the midterms?” the president had asked privately, according to a person who spoke to him.

An Unchecked Second Term

What made the war such a potent force is that it told a simple story for voters.

As a candidate, Mr. Trump had promised no new wars. He started a new war.

He promised lower prices. Gas prices soared and inflation rose.

The story of the G.O.P. midterm implosion was not only a story of broken promises; it was also a story of radical overreach. After Mr. Trump came back from pariah status after Jan. 6, 2021, some advisers believed he had convinced himself that the rules of politics had been suspended for him alone. That illusion was obliterated on Tuesday night.

Over nearly two years, hubris had become the governing philosophy of Mr. Trump’s second presidency.

There was a seemingly endless string of investigative pieces revealing that Mr. Trump, his family and their close associates had used the presidency to enrich themselves brazenly. Those reports began to resonate with voters; an early October poll from Fox News showed corruption as the top voter concern. (Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, said: “The President only acts in the best interest of the American people. There are no conflicts of interest.”)

In 2025, Mr. Trump began a trade war with the entire world — the pain of which was still being felt more than a year later on farms all over the suddenly competitive states of Kansas, Texas and Iowa.

Throughout it all, the president flashed indifference to the struggles of Americans that his policies had exacerbated.

Soaring gas prices? “A small price to pay,” Mr. Trump insisted.

Some members of his team grew exasperated as Mr. Trump spoke seemingly more about his new ballroom than the border, golf courses than grocery prices, interior decorations than inflation.

On the eve of the midterms, he focused his closing pitch on his refurbishment of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall, joking that he was considering renaming it for himself rather than Abraham Lincoln.

Unlike in the past, Democrats mostly ignored the daily Trump distractions and sought to connect corruption to costs. They also told a story of a government focused on elites while average people struggled — from Jeffrey Epstein’s protected associates to the president’s $2.2 billion in personal profits.

In the House, Democrats quickly and unexpectedly countered Mr. Trump’s redistricting push and pursued strong candidates deep into red territory to spread the map. In the Senate, they found a series of blue-chip recruits who put once unthinkable states into play. In the final, frenzied weeks of the campaign, Republicans were redirecting cash from the usual swing states of North Carolina and Georgia to try to shore up traditional strongholds in South Carolina and even Mississippi.

The war in Iran, said Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader and now the speaker-in-waiting, helped “supercharge” the contrast between the two parties.

Republicans had tried to frame the midterms as a choice between “common sense and crazy,” relentlessly attacking the rising democratic socialist wing of the left.

Yet Mr. Trump’s own pollster’s final survey, taken two weeks before the election, showed that while both the MAGA Republican brand and democratic socialists were unpopular with voters, MAGA carried more baggage. When Republicans who were not planning to cast ballots were asked what it would take to earn back their vote, their top two answers were ending the war and addressing inflation.

On that final call before Election Day, Mr. Trump’s advisers were both clear-eyed and cynical about the state of the race, referring at one point to a Trump ally who ran for governor of Minnesota and demanded a recount in his primary despite losing in a landslide.

“Look, it’s fine,” Mr. Blair told the group sarcastically. “I think we’ll just pull a Mike Lindell and demand a recount regardless of how many points we’re down.”

Alex Pfeiffer, a spokesman for the MAGA Inc. super PAC, said that the group’s “sober and clear-eyed view of the political environment,” led to investing in House races Republicans are leading in, in Maine, Florida, Tennessee, New York and Texas.

“The people peddling these made up quotes and false gossip not only demean and belittle the historic and generous investment by the president into the party’s midterm effort, but they also slander the hard work of the many who contributed to this effort,” he said in a statement. “They are cowards and losers.”

A White House official, who declined to speak on the record, said in response to the reporting for this article: “President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot. Candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”

The official repeated that the president, who acknowledged earlier on Wednesday that the war affected the midterms, had over and over again said Iran can’t procure a nuclear weapon.

The Anti-Recruiter

While Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, painstakingly recruited top-tier Senate candidates, Mr. Trump took a series of steps that endangered the Republican majority.

After Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa flirted with opposing Mr. Trump’s most controversial nominees and Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina voted against his signature tax-and-spending bill, Mr. Trump’s allies threatened to end their careers. Both decided to retire, creating vulnerable open seats that had been held by Republicans.

In North Carolina, Mr. Trump cleared the field for Michael Whatley, a former lobbyist and Republican National Committee chairman, who proved a lackluster candidate and lost to Roy Cooper, the state’s popular Democratic former governor.

After Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died in July, Mr. Trump supported tapping his sister, Darline, to not just replace him temporarily but also to run for a full six-year term. In doing so, he elevated an inexperienced candidate with no fund-raising base, and she went on to lose in a state that had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

But no candidate proved more costly to the party than Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Texas attorney general. Mr. Trump endorsed him over Senator John Cornyn, the Republican incumbent, ignoring a year of warnings that Mr. Paxton would put the seat in jeopardy. Republicans were ultimately forced to spend close to $300 million in Texas — money that could have gone to shore up candidates in other states. Mr. Paxton lost by 12 points.

On another recent call, the Trump team mocked the haplessness of some of the Republicans they were trying to elect.

“I have seen the enemy,” Mr. Blair told the group a week earlier. “And it is us.”

Mr. Fabrizio replied: “In many places.”

The Democrats’ Playbook

In May 2025, Mr. Schumer arrived at Wildflower Farms, an upscale resort in New York’s Hudson Valley, for a secretive retreat with donors and party officials. He desperately needed to expand the Senate map.

To win control of the Senate, Democrats needed to hold all of their seats and flip at least four, including in states that Mr. Trump won handily in 2024.

Mr. Schumer spent months wooing Mr. Cooper and took at least three trips to Ohio to coax former Senator Sherrod Brown, who had lost in 2024 but had a populist brand that matched the country’s mood.

“If you retire and we lose the majority by one vote, you won’t enjoy your retirement,” Mr. Schumer recalled telling Mr. Brown, 73.

Both ran and won.

In the House, where Democrats had fallen three seats short in 2024, recruiters went hunting in districts Mr. Trump had carried by 10 points or more, betting early that the emboldened president would overreach.

An election post-mortem by the Democratic House Majority PAC circulated in April 2025 found two factors stood out among the party’s stronger 2024 candidates: being “perceived as moderate” and focusing on the economy.

“If we wanted to compete deeper in red districts, we needed to find candidates who are not immediately off-putting,” said Mike Smith, the PAC’s president.

They set about recruiting candidates with distinctive biographies: military veterans, doctors, farmers, a smokejumper, a Tejano music star — just about anyone who didn’t scream professional politician.

Redistricting Wars

Mr. Trump, meanwhile, was trying to redraw the House battlefield itself.

In the spring of 2025, Mr. Blair, then his deputy chief of staff, brought the president a plan to redraw congressional maps mid-decade to make seats safer for Republicans. The gerrymandering push started in Texas and soon spread to other Republican-led states.

When Mr. Jeffries first heard about the Texas gambit, he turned to his advisers in disbelief and declared, “You’ve got to be fucking kidding me.” He flew to Texas to urge state legislators to take a stand, and many Democrats fled the state to slow down the legislative process.

But the Trump-inspired play went through and Republicans carved themselves out five new seats that Mr. Trump would have carried by double digits in 2024 — seemingly enough to withstand even a dip in support in the midterms.

Democrats fought back. California voters approved Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to create five new seats favoring Democrats, and Virginia voters approved a map creating another four, though the Supreme Court later struck it down.

From the start, Mr. Blair was cocksure about his redistricting plan, and he and the president dismissed Republicans who worried about the maneuver backfiring.

But by April 2026, Democrats had good reason to believe that they had neutralized the threat by redrawing districts in several blue states. Mr. Jeffries held a celebratory news conference featuring a poster with the faces of Mr. Trump and Mr. Blair and an anonymous quote that had appeared in an article about redistricting in The Times: “Maximum warfare everywhere all the time.”

When Mr. Blair saw the poster, he texted one of Mr. Jeffries’s top aides, Gideon Bragin: “Can you send a copy of this to my office?”

Instead, it remained inside House Democratic headquarters through Election Day, when a blue tidal wave washed over even many of the districts drawn to favor Republicans.

The Unforced Errors

As 2026 began, the administration’s immigration enforcement surge turned violent in Minneapolis when two protesters were shot and killed by federal agents. Both killings were captured on video.

Mr. Trump told advisers he didn’t like how the videos looked.

Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, had spent months privately trying to steer him away from the hard-line immigration approach favored by Stephen Miller, the president’s top policy adviser.

Soon after Minneapolis, Democrats’ internal polls showed the party taking the edge on immigration for the first time. What had been one of Mr. Trump’s perennial strengths was for a period his top liability, according to one of the president’s senior strategists.

Then, about five weeks after the second shooting, Mr. Trump took the country to war in Iran.

Mr. Blair at first shared his boss’s optimism that the war would be a quick success. He reassured skeptical colleagues that the conflict would not be the political disaster some feared because some Defense Department officials had assured the White House it would be resolved rapidly.

But the president’s four-to-six-week timeline stretched into months.

In public, Mr. Trump crowed about a decisive military triumph. In private, advisers briefed him on the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, spiking prices of gas and fertilizer and an alarming depletion of American weaponry.

Mr. Fabrizio’s focus groups in March, about two weeks into the conflict, showed that voters did not understand why the president had started the war. They saw a broken promise that was making life more expensive.

Former allies on the antiwar right, including Tucker Carlson and the former Georgia congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, were now in open rebellion.

Mr. Trump knew the war was draining his support, according to advisers, but for a brief moment it seemed that he had found himself a way out of the mess. By mid-June, Vice President JD Vance had negotiated a memorandum of understanding with Iran, and the Trump political team exhaled. Mr. Fabrizio’s first poll of the proposal found that voters aware of the deal favored it by 41 percentage points, and 67 percent thought it would bring down gas prices.

But G.O.P. Iran hawks, including Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, pressed Mr. Trump to keep the pressure on Tehran. The deal fell apart and the war dragged on.

‘My Money’

Mr. Trump never stopped raising money after the 2024 election, assembling a roughly $400 million war chest that he made clear to advisers he saw as “my money.”

By August, with the election less than 100 days away, Republican Senate strategists still had no clarity on where Team Trump would spend. One described being “shocked at how ill-prepared they were.”

A Trump adviser said a plan existed but could not be shared because the president had not approved it.

Some days, Mr. Trump told advisers privately: “We’ve gotta win. Anything we gotta do.” On others, he sounded as if he couldn’t care less. “It says something very nice about me that they just can’t win without me,” he told aides.

Mr. Blair and others had to make the case to the president to sign off on the spending. Mr. Trump withheld his approval until the end of the summer.

The delay was costly: Ad prices soar as elections near.

One week in mid-October on a single station in Anchorage, the Trump super PAC paid nearly four times as much money as the leading Democratic super PAC did to air roughly 70 percent fewer commercials because it had not reserved the time well in advance.

The Democratic group paid $2,700 for a commercial on the local evening news; Mr. Trump’s super PAC paid $30,000 for the same slot.

Typically, endangered lawmakers distance themselves from an unpopular president in midterm elections. Team Trump wanted to do the opposite.

“We have taken that old construct and flipped it on its head,” said Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of Mr. Trump’s 2024 campaign.

Thus, the first modern midterm convention was born, a two-day celebration of the president in Dallas in September that few members of his party had wanted.

During his convention speech, Mr. Trump rolled out a splashy new proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult — but only if Republicans won.

Almost no one knew it was coming, including his senior political advisers, the speaker and the Senate majority leader.

The idea had not even been polled before Mr. Trump said it. And when a similar proposal was tested, Mr. Trump’s team found it did little to move voters toward Republicans. Some of the president’s own advisers cringed at the giveaway, with one describing it as a naked effort to “bribe” people for their votes.

The convention did bring one piece of good news: money. On the first day, Elon Musk sent $75 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC led by allies of the Senate majority leader, John Thune of South Dakota. It was one of the largest single contributions in American history.

At the convention, Mr. Paxton made his way into the fund’s suite, where Alex Latcham, the super PAC’s executive director, made a somewhat cryptic remark to him.

“You’re going to be happy tomorrow.”

The ads were about to begin.

Mr. Musk would spend more than $450 million to aid Republicans in the midterms, much of it in Texas to try to save Mr. Paxton. The super PAC he funded spent tens of millions on ads attacking the Democratic nominee, James Talarico, for his support of transgender rights, mirroring a line of attack that the Trump team had used effectively in 2024.

In other races, the focus on transgender ads became a point of disagreement between officials at the Senate Leadership Fund and Mr. Trump’s operation, which argued that the 2026 election was fundamentally about the economy and that running ads on other topics would be less effective. Senate G.O.P. strategists saw economic messages falling flat in the current political environment in some states.

The fight to save the Senate was hampered by party leadership that could barely work together. Mr. Trump and Senate G.O.P. leaders, Mr. Thune among them, never grew close. The president endorsed Mr. Paxton over their objections. And when Trump advisers met with officials from the top Republican super PAC at Camp David in March 2026 to plan for the midterms, no one from the National Republican Senatorial Committee was invited.

The Collapse

In late August, Julie Merz, the top strategist at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, gathered her team and pulled up a slide estimating a 35 percent chance of a “blue wave.”

“It’s our job,” she recalled saying, “to hand out as many surfboards as possible.”

Committee officials made the party’s most vulnerable incumbents an unusual offer: Instead of spending millions defending them, the party would move the money into deeper red territory and poll their seats to see if they needed the resources back. Most agreed, freeing up around $10 million to expand the map.

Not long after the Republican convention in Dallas, diesel prices hit all-time highs.

In the Senate, it got so bad for the G.O.P. that by early October Republicans were ordering up polls in seemingly unthinkable states, like South Dakota and Idaho.

A month before the election, the Senate Leadership Fund pulled ads from North Carolina, ceding the state to redirect money to Kansas, then South Carolina and eventually Mississippi — a state Mr. Trump had carried by nearly 23 points two years ago.

“Battleground Mississippi,” Mr. Trump’s advisers called it mockingly on a call.

In the House, the deterioration was perhaps worse.

At one point, top officials with the Congressional Leadership Fund and Mr. Trump’s super PACs had decided to give up trying to flip Representative Henry Cuellar’s South Texas seat — only to realize that Speaker Mike Johnson was set to be in the district the day the ads were going to come off the air. They delayed the announcement for a day to spare Mr. Johnson an embarrassing episode.

Mr. Cuellar won re-election in a landslide.

In the end, the map shifted so far left that House Republicans — who polled more than 100 seats — could not keep up. It surprised even some leading Democrats.

At a September dinner, Rahm Emanuel, who ran the House Democrats’ campaign arm in the 2006 wave, asked the party’s top recruits how much Mr. Trump had won their districts by. When Zach Dembo, a military veteran and former federal prosecutor running in Kentucky’s Sixth District, said 15 points, Mr. Emanuel looked at him in disbelief.

Mr. Dembo won.

The last Sunday before Election Day, Mr. Jeffries arranged for a symbolic final stop to a battleground district.

He went to Alabama, where Republicans had redrawn Representative Shomari Figures’s district to favor their party after a Supreme Court decision weakened the Voting Rights Act. It was important to go there, Mr. Jeffries said, because “he was facing a renewed effort to subject the African American community to Jim Crow-like tactics.”

“It’s fair to say that Shomari and I both felt the weight of history given the fact that the civil rights movement led by Dr. King, Rosa Parks, and so many others began in the very place where we were ending this all important 2026 campaign,” Mr. Jeffries said.

Mr. Figures won his race on Tuesday.

On the way to the airport, Mr. Jeffries made an unpublicized stop at the Freedom Monument Sculpture Park that remembers the history of enslaved people in America.

In January, Mr. Jeffries is now set to become the first Black speaker in American history.
