ARTICLE

Trump Wrestles With New Reality: A Lame Duck With Two Years Left to Fight
After a decade at the center of American politics, President Trump is politically wounded, with diminished power. Those who know him say the next two years will be unpredictable.
By Katie Rogers
Published 2026-11-04 23:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/trump-new-role-lame-duck.html

Over the course of his life, Donald J. Trump has readily embraced many identities: A hotel developer. A reality television star. A president. A firebrand.

Now, at 80 years old, he is confronting one he would rather not: a lame duck.

In the hours after voters put a check on the expansive power he has flexed in his second term, giving Democrats control of both the House and the Senate, Mr. Trump seemed to be cycling through the stages of grief. He denied that a blue wave across the country had been his fault, or a direct result of his decision to go to war with Iran. (The vice president explicitly said otherwise.) He accepted the election results. And, as he absorbed the waning power he will have in his final two years in office, he bargained, saying he’d work with Democrats while clinging to his veto Sharpie.

“I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Mr. Trump told reporters on Wednesday, standing in front of a steel beam that was being put into place as part of his cherished White House ballroom project.

He noted that he had “the power to veto,” before turning to a topic he seemed much more eager to discuss: his renovation projects.

Whether Mr. Trump adopts a pragmatic deal-making posture remains to be seen — one ally described the president as “dazed” after the rout on Tuesday.

After his loss in the 2020 presidential race, the last major political setback Mr. Trump confronted, he retreated to Mar-a-Lago, where he nursed his anger and then planned a defiant return. Once back in the White House, Mr. Trump had no use for compromise.

After a period spent as a political pariah and criminal defendant, Mr. Trump liked to say that he had gone from hunted to hunter. In his second term, his administration has tracked down his political enemies, unleashed a violent immigration crackdown and started a war that has made life more expensive for Americans. He didn’t need Congress to do any of it.

But on Tuesday, that dynamic flipped again. Democrats are vowing to investigate government abuses, alleged corruption by the president’s associates and the heavy-handed tactics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. House lawmakers plan to scrutinize top officials involved in the administration’s immigration agenda, including the White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller; Tom Homan, Mr. Trump’s border czar; and the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, according to a person with knowledge of the discussions.

“LAWYER UP,” Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat poised to lead the House Oversight Committee, wrote on social media.

The political pressure could make for an unpredictable two years for both Mr. Trump and the country, according to people who have observed firsthand his volatile personality and his refusal to acknowledge mistakes.

“When you look at things like his ability to do executive orders and grant pardons and all of these things, he’s going to still be doing enormous damage,” said Sarah Matthews, a former White House deputy press secretary who resigned after the attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. “And it’s just going to get even more chaotic and dangerous in these next two years.”

Political rivals believe that Mr. Trump, who has asserted his dominance over the Republican Party for the better part of the last decade, will also do everything to maintain his grip on a party that he effectively reshaped in his image.

“Donald Trump needs attention like most people need oxygen,” said former Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey, a Republican who is considering another presidential run in 2028. “He can’t do without it, and he’s now going to experience for the first time in his political career being a lame duck. So what he’ll need to do is to act out even more than he normally does in order to divert you from the 2028 race.”

Mr. Trump has so far been vague about how he wants to spend the next two years, telling the podcaster and former top F.B.I. official Dan Bongino in an interview on Tuesday that he has “many, many things in the hopper.”

He did not elaborate and instead pivoted into a standard part of his stump speech: “You know, right now we have more factories and plants being built in the United States than at any time ever before, and that means the Roaring Twenties, that means every — there’s never been anything like it.” (Manufacturing has actually slowed since 2024, according to the National Association of Manufacturers.)

He suggested in interviews that he might seek to join forces with his political opponents on the debt ceiling and immigration enforcement — two thorny policy issues that have bedeviled past administrations.

And he repeatedly invoked his ability to veto legislation, implicitly underscoring how much he will be on defense in his last two years in office.

In his first public appearance after Election Day, Mr. Trump stood before reporters at the White House on Wednesday and talked not about any lessons learned, or the path forward for the Republican Party. Instead, he mused about his ballroom project and his own future, particularly the subject of impeachment.

“I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that — impeachment for no reason,” Mr. Trump said. “What, for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in history.”

He paused, turning his focus back on the ballroom construction.

“Watch the beam go up,” he said. “Now envision chandeliers all over.”

Several top aides had already been planning for what Mr. Trump could accomplish through executive power alone if Republicans lost one or both chambers of Congress. Those involved include Mr. Miller; Russell T. Vought, the White House budget director; and members of the White House legislative affairs staff, according to a White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions. The president would receive a “menu of options” soon, the person said.

A hushed conversation of what comes next for Mr. Trump’s presidency and those around him played out on Tuesday night inside the White House, where Mr. Trump gathered aides and cabinet members in the East Room for what turned into a morose watch party. As the president watched the returns and fielded phone calls, some of the people around him quietly discussed whether Mr. Trump would keep in place members of his cabinet or his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, according to two people who attended.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Administration officials and Mr. Trump’s allies said the president and his staff were girding themselves for both congressional investigations and high turnover for the remainder of his time in office.

Some expressed anxiety that there had been little guidance for staff about what to do if they got pulled into investigations, other than a briefing earlier this year advising them generally how to respond to congressional oversight.

As the political conversation turns to the next cycle, Mr. Trump indicated that he was not ready to name a political heir or back a candidate to succeed him in 2028. Asked by Martha MacCallum of Fox News late Tuesday evening whether he wanted a Republican primary to determine the 2028 presidential nominee, the president said, “I think it’s going to end up being somewhat of that.”

By Wednesday morning, Vice President JD Vance had posted a lengthy message on social media placing blame for Republican losses on the decision to go to war with Iran, an apparent effort to separate himself from Mr. Trump.

Several people close to the president say they believe that he is unlikely to endorse Mr. Vance — or anyone else — anytime soon. Mr. Trump is an entertainer above all, they say, and he will want to stay in the spotlight.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting from Washington.

After Midterm Drubbing, Trump and Republicans Start Pointing Fingers
While the president attributed sweeping losses to the fact that he was not on the ballot, others in his party dismissed his explanation and pinned blame squarely on him.
By Tim Balk, Michael Levenson and Emily Davies
Published 2026-11-04 10:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/trump-republicans-blame-midterms.html

As results came in Tuesday night showing that Republicans were taking sweeping losses in the midterm elections, President Trump quickly sought to deflect blame, declaring that the drubbing happened because he was not on the ballot.

“I wasn’t on the ticket,” Mr. Trump said in an interview with The New York Times on Tuesday night before polls had closed in parts of the country. “And because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote.”

Almost as quickly, Republicans began to point their fingers back at the president.

They said their party’s loss of control of both the House and Senate, its worst midterm showing in decades, was the direct result of a series of choices the president had made in the year leading up to the election.

They cited Mr. Trump’s tariff policies. They pointed to his decision to take the country to an unpopular war in Iran that drove up prices. And they questioned his political instincts, arguing that he had imperiled his party’s chances by supporting weak candidates and going on an unconvincing tour in the final weeks of the campaign.

“Trump has almost dared Americans to vote against him,” said Jason Roe, a Republican strategist in Michigan, adding that the president had closed the midterm campaign on a “greatest hits tour on every annoying thing that could be done to aggravate the American people.”

Mr. Roe said Mr. Trump’s analysis of the results was “ridiculous,” adding a profanity, and said the president was “the engineer of the Republican collapse.”

The recriminations opened a new and difficult chapter for Republicans, who faced defeat in states where they had decades-long winning streaks. Some Republicans defended Mr. Trump, while others urged the party to move on from him, raising questions about how much influence the president will have in his party during his final two years in office.

Representative Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican from a battleground district who did not run for re-election, dismissed Mr. Trump’s analysis of his party’s defeats as “nonsense.”

“This is all about him,” Mr. Bacon said.

The “No. 1 reason” for Republicans’ showing was the president’s unpopularity, Mr. Bacon argued, followed by the president’s decision to back what the congressman said were feeble candidates in key Senate races: Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued G.O.P. nominee in Texas, and Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, a political novice who has filled the seat of her brother, the late Senator Lindsey Graham, and then ran for a full term to replace him.

“We lost the Senate race in South Carolina for Pete’s sake,” Mr. Bacon said. “He pushed bad people forward.”

Brinker Harding, the Republican who was thumped in the Nebraska district that Mr. Bacon has represented for the last decade, said he would not comment on Mr. Trump’s assertion that Republicans lost because he wasn’t on ballot. But he offered his own list of reasons.

“Gas prices are high,” Mr. Harding said. “The tariffs have been an issue.”

Republican leaders had a muted reaction to their party’s grim night.

Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, issued a 177-word statement that celebrated what he said were Republicans’ successes during the first two years of Mr. Trump’s second term.

“Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism,” he said. He did not cite any causes for his party’s dismal showing.

The House speaker, Representative Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who saw his party swept out of House control and will lose his gavel by next year, was more forceful in his defense of the president, saying that Democrats “truly do have Trump derangement syndrome.”

But election results across the country showed that Democrats had drawn voters to their side, even in reliably Republican states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.

On Fox News, Mr. Trump said some voters simply “didn’t like the candidates.”

“Some of the candidates that I endorsed fought me,” Mr. Trump said, adding that his base voters “didn’t like that they fought me.”

In Iowa, the Trump-endorsed Senate nominee, Representative Ashley Hinson, sought to overcome the political headwinds posed by the economy by calling for an end to the Iran war and criticizing the president’s tariff policies. The Trump-endorsed Senate nominee in Michigan, former Representative Mike Rogers, took a similar approach.

Both Republicans fell. But Mr. Paxton, Mr. Trump’s choice in Texas, appeared to lose by an even wider margin after seeking little space from the president.

Dick Wadhams, a Republican consultant in Colorado, said Mr. Trump’s comments were “ironic.” Most of the candidates who lost key Senate races in conservative states, Mr. Wadhams said, were recruited by or endorsed by the president.

Voters in those states, Mr. Wadhams said, were making a statement against Mr. Trump.

“This was not a pro-Democratic vote,” Mr. Wadhams said. “This was an anti-Trump vote.”

In Ohio, supporters of Senator Jon Husted, a Republican who fell to the Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, traced the party’s losses to the president.

“We pushed the envelope too far,” Luis Gio, a 59-year-old court translator, said at the Husted watch party, pointing disapprovingly to the president’s construction projects in Washington. “The White House ballroom. I mean, why push things like that when the country needs more important things?”

And in Oklahoma City, Mayor David Holt, a Republican, wrote on social media that his party was “morally and intellectually bankrupt,” adding, “It is now time to make America good again,” a twist on Mr. Trump’s signature slogan.

He said his party’s performance was a singular failing of the president.

“I can’t think of a midterm that is more directly tied to a single person and their utter failure,” Mr. Holt, who worked in the George W. Bush administration, said in an interview. “It feels like an entire country coming together and saying: Enough.”

Craig Shirley, who was a White House aide under Ronald Reagan and has written books about him and Mr. Trump, called the midterms a “black eye for the Republican Party.”

He said he believed that Republicans would continue to rally around Mr. Trump and his policies on border security and taxes. But he said the war in Iran had clearly taken a toll on Republican candidates.

“Absent the war, the results would have been a lot different,” he said. “A lot of people like Trump, but they don’t like this damn war and what it’s done to inflation and gasoline prices and diesel prices.”

Jon Fleischman, the former executive director of California Republican Party, said that in the end the president was on the ballot, in a sense. Voters were angry about the economy under Mr. Trump and fed up with the war in Iran, Mr. Fleischman said.

“They can’t show their frustration directly to the president,” he said, “so they shared their frustration with the president’s party.”

ARTICLE

‘An Earthquake’: A Democratic Rout Stuns Texas
In a seismic shift that was once unthinkable, victories by James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa upended decades of statewide dominance in what had been the nation’s most populous conservative state.
By J. David Goodman and Lauren McGaughy
Published 2026-11-04 05:27 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/texas-talarico-hinojosa-abbott-paxton.html

Texas may never be the same.

Democrats shattered the 32-year-long Republican grip on statewide offices in what had been, until Tuesday, the nation’s most populous conservative state.

James Talarico’s victory over Ken Paxton, a scandal-scarred Republican candidate, in the U.S. Senate race was only the beginning of a series of seismic victories for Democrats on Tuesday in Texas.

Gina Hinojosa made history with her defeat of Gov. Greg Abbott, the third-term governor and political powerhouse who, just a few months ago, appeared to have a lock on winning a record fourth term. She becomes Texas's first Hispanic governor.

In one night, the state was transformed.

“Talarico is a symbol. Gina is an earthquake,” said Garry Mauro, a former Texas land commissioner who was among the last Democrats to win a statewide race, in 1994. “It’s a tsunami. The world has changed. The political maps will never be the same again.”

The decades of total Republican Party domination are over. Its hegemony had resulted in a succession of increasingly conservative leaders, from George W. Bush to Rick Perry to Greg Abbott, and increasingly conservative lawmaking, including abortion bans, Christian teaching material in public schools and expanded gun rights.

Democrats in Texas rose as national blowback against the Trump administration mounted among voters troubled by the war in Iran, an intense immigration crackdown and cost-of-living concerns. But Mr. Paxton owed much of his success to his closeness to Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott tied himself closely to Mr. Trump’s policies.

Republican leaders in the state also embraced a data center boom that was unpopular in many rural and suburban areas and pushed through a school voucher program that many saw as undercutting public schools. In 2026, some party members made the state’s swelling South Asian community a boogeyman, warning of sharia law. A candidate for a top regulatory job attacked his opponents with slurs for gay and disabled people.

“I’ve watched Republicans fumble this ball from bottom to top,” said Austin Vaughn, 31, of Fort Bend County, who said he “literally checked every blue box for the first time in my life.”

He said he used to feel at home in the Republican Party in Texas, and even worked for a state legislator. But in recent years, the party “got really out of control socially.”

He now has a daughter and did not like the state’s stringent abortion ban. And, he said, while the party used to have a good message boosting and attracting businesses, they long ago lost that plot.

“No one can afford anything anymore,” he said. “Our water and air is the dirtiest and our education is horrible.”

Also swept away Tuesday was the assumption that Texas’s political future would resemble its past. In its place, something far less certain, more contested and decidedly Democratic emerged on Tuesday.

It was, for Democrats, so unexpected and so sudden, that many were still processing the implications.

“I’m jubilant,” Rafael Anchía, a Democratic state representative from the Dallas area, said as he watched the returns at Mr. Talarico’s election night party in Austin. “This is exceeding my wildest expectations.”

Mr. Anchía said that Democrats had racked up big gains all over the state, even in formerly conservative suburbs, even in rural areas where they had not competed for years: “It’s a nuke.”

The magnitude of the Democratic wave was amplified by the remarkable spectacle of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, spending hundreds of millions of dollars in a doomed effort to preserve the state’s Republican leadership. After moving parts of his business empire to Texas, Mr. Musk poured at least $212 million into supporting Mr. Paxton, which was part of at least $224 million devoted to races in the state.

Republicans were left rattled and trying to explain not only Mr. Paxton’s spectacular loss, but how Mr. Abbott, seen as such a formidable opponent, could have been washed away as well in the national Democratic wave.

“Our party is going to have a reckoning unlike any in the history of our state,” said Matt Mackowiak, a Republican strategist who worked on Senator John Cornyn’s doomed primary campaign earlier this year against Mr. Paxton, who had been Texas’s attorney general.

As the results crystallized, Democrats believed their victory would draw more campaign money into Texas for future elections, along with greater national support. The party could seize more offices and perhaps have a shot at flipping Texas blue in a presidential election.

“You never give your enemy a beachhead; once they get it, they advance,” said Chad Wilbanks, a Republican political consultant and the former executive director of the Republican Party of Texas. “The dam is broken.”

Democratic officials said the election could also reshape state policy, ending Texas’s role as a laboratory for conservative laws nationwide. Mr. Talarico, as a U.S. senator, will not directly affect day-to-day governance in Texas. But Ms. Hinojosa will have the power to veto legislation and to appoint agency leaders.

“Texas is ready for change,” said Kendall Scudder, the chairman of the Texas Democratic Party. He said Democrats were “excited and ready to deliver on the policies that will make life more affordable” and to “root out the corruption that has plagued our politics for too long.”

President Trump crisscrossed the state, hoping he could save Mr. Paxton’s campaign in its final weeks. But his efforts at bringing Texas Republicans together against a shared Democratic enemy masked deep underlying divisions within the party.

The state’s Bush-era conservatives long opposed Mr. Paxton and his Trump-aligned wing of the party, and instead supported Mr. Cornyn in the primary. They argued that the Republican Party had drifted too far from its principles.

The two main factions of Texas Republicans have been at odds for years. Mr. Paxton often found himself at the fault line of those conflicts. His 2023 impeachment on allegations of corruption by a majority in the Texas House became a referendum on the direction of the party. His defense team argued that a faction of old-school conservatives — aligned with the Bush family and longtime Republican strategist Karl Rove — had been behind the impeachment. Republicans in the Texas Senate, overseen by Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, an ally of Mr. Paxton, acquitted him.

Even before the vote on Tuesday, Republicans in Mr. Paxton’s camp were seething at those they saw as having supported him with insufficient vigor.

Steve Toth, a Republican candidate for the U.S. House and a Paxton ally, said those close to Mr. Cornyn and the Bush family were to blame for “dirtying” Mr. Paxton with the failed impeachment and during the Republican primary campaign.

“They never got on board,” Mr. Toth said on Monday at one of Mr. Paxton’s last campaign events, in Conroe, a city outside of Houston.

Those in Mr. Cornyn’s camp remained frustrated that Mr. Paxton had challenged him at all. Mr. Cornyn had shown little vulnerability among general election voters, even as Republican activists accused him of being insufficiently supportive of President Trump. Mr. Paxton, the hard right’s choice, easily defeated him in a primary runoff despite being vastly outspent.

Before Tuesday, the closest that Republicans in Texas had come to a statewide loss in recent years was in 2018, when Beto O’Rourke, a U.S. representative from El Paso, came within three percentage points of defeating Senator Ted Cruz. In response, Republicans in the state appeared to moderate their agenda in the next legislative session, focusing less on cultural issues and more on property tax and school financing reforms.

Now, any change in direction will involve the decisions not only of Republicans. It will involve Democrats as well.

“It’s a whole new day for Texas,” said Mr. Mauro, the former land commissioner. “After I lost in ’98, I was thinking we were one cycle away from winning to the next election. It’s been a long wait.”

Sabrina Tavernise contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Countries Weigh, and Worry About, What Trump Will Do After Midterm Defeat
Commentators abroad wondered what the president’s electoral losses might mean for oil prices, the war on Iran and the end of the Trump era.
By Damien Cave
Published 2026-11-04 08:37 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/world/asia/midterms-trump-foreign-policy-world.html

For two years, the world has weathered President Trump’s domineering unilateralism, enduring up-and-down tariffs, a war with Iran, aggression in Latin America, abrupt reversals on Ukraine, and a fusillade of demands for allies including Canada, Germany and Japan.

Now, with Democrats having taken control of Congress as nearly all of Mr. Trump’s preferred Republicans fall to defeat, many countries are debating what to expect from yet another case of American political whiplash.

Some analysts suggest a new Congress might slow President Trump’s most impulsive urges. Online, there was some obvious celebration. On Weibo, China’s dominant social media platform, the hashtag “Trump suffered a complete and utter defeat” was trending as results were announced.

But because presidents have enormous leeway with foreign policy, one persistent question emerged from Asia to Europe: Will the electoral losses at home spur Mr. Trump toward even more aggressive actions around the globe?

“In response to a Democrat-controlled Congress,” said Ja-Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, “Trump could try to find distractions elsewhere, including on tariffs and the use of force.”

Countries around the world are assessing how the American elections results might affect the most pressing issues in international affairs.

War With Iran

In Asia, which is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East, the Democratic victory initially produced a wisp of optimism.

“In Southeast Asia, the main challenge has been inflationary pressure caused by the war in Iran. That’s made everything a lot more expensive,” Mr. Chong said. “Now there’s hope for some sort of reprieve.”

And yet, he and many others doubt that notion. Many countries have expressed concern that the war with Iran would continue escalating in the short-term — perhaps with Mr. Trump striking Iran again after the elections — worsening the squeeze on oil and gas supplies.

For now, the mood remains more grim than gleeful: Oil prices are expected to stay high for the foreseeable future, challenging businesses and leaving many to wonder what Mr. Trump might do next.

Tariffs

U.S. trade investigators have spent months probing more than a dozen countries accused of labor violations and overproducing everything from chemicals to cars. Now that the White House is no longer concerned about drawing attention to inflation before the elections, countries might expect a reinvigorated push to impose tariffs.

Japan, China and Vietnam are all likely targets for additional tariffs. In many countries, new levies would come on top of existing ones, lifting rates back toward where they were before the Supreme Court struck down earlier tariffs in February.

Mr. Trump still has sweeping powers over trade. Congress, however, could use its newfound leverage over the federal budget and its oversight authority to shape some of the details.

“You might see Congress pushing for more tariff carve outs and exceptions in categories that affect their constituent’s pocket books,” said Stephen Olson, a former U.S. trade negotiator and visiting fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

Generally, in Asia and elsewhere, many expect American protectionism to keep marching on, with a president seeking to leave a legacy and still determined to bend the global economy toward his views.

“People are deeply uneasy about the Trump administration’s past actions and remain anxious about the future,” said Kazuhiro Maeshima, a professor of American politics and diplomacy at Sophia University in Tokyo, discussing the mood in Japan. “While there is a hope for change, whether that change will actually materialize is unknown.”

Rivalry With China

The American elections were not expected to alter the direction of U.S.-China relations, especially regarding their on-again, off-again trade truce. Both political parties have increasingly agreed to take a tougher posture on China when it comes to economic competition and disputes over contested territory.

But on Weibo, a leading Chinese social media platform, the early results led to some initial gloating at President Trump’s expense.Xu Shaolin, a prominent commentator with nearly 4 million followers, wrote that if the losses held in both houses of Congress “this unreliable president who talks big, but is prone to making empty promises, will likely become a lame duck.”

Shi Yinhong, a professor of international relations at Renmin University in Beijing, predicted nonetheless that the Democrats’ success would mean trouble for relations between the United States and China.

Xi Jinping, China’s leader, and President Trump reached an understanding at a summit in May in favor of what China defines as “constructive, strategic stability.” But Mr. Shi predicted that this understanding would break down “because Trump suddenly becomes far from all-powerful.”

A Democratic Congress might also strengthen America’s relations with traditional United States allies, including Japan, which he said would also not be good for China.

For Taiwan, the election results could be a “potentially positive sign,” according to William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group in Taipei.

He said he thought a Democrat-led Congress might intensify its pressure on the White House to approve a long-delayed $14 billion arms package that would be a boost to Taiwan’s defenses against Chinese military threats.

U.S. Alliances and Leadership

Mr. Trump has threatened his country’s own partners and allies with everything from tariffs to bombs. And in some of the once-friendly nations that Mr. Trump has alienated, the public reaction veered toward relief or celebration of the Democratic wins on Tuesday.

Ryan Cox, a philosophy lecturer at the University of Sydney, said Wednesday that he was hoping to see the Democrats “slow down the power of Trump,” to accelerate “the end of the Trump era.”

Luka Leveque, a Japanese university student in Tokyo, said he was hoping “for greater consistency — both in the approach taken between our two nations and in the continuity of U.S. policy over time.”

And yet, with two years of the Trump administration to go, skepticism about his transactional leadership style and reliability remains deeply entrenched. In a recent poll of 34 countries published by the Rockefeller Foundation, just 39 percent of respondents said they were comfortable with the United States leading on the world stage.

As Max Yoeli, a senior research fellow at Chatham House in London, noted just before the election: “A president who has made it his business to be a shock to the system retains the capacity to deliver one.”

Even in Australia, which has fought alongside America in every major war since World War I, doubts remain. Dan Ramsay, a University of Sydney politics student, said Wednesday that it would be risky for any country to jump back into relying too heavily on the United States.

“We need to take more seriously our dependencies in a whole bunch of areas and think about how we can maintain an alliance and partnership with the U.S., while also looking elsewhere and strengthening those ties with middle powers around the world,” he said.

ARTICLE

Why Doctors in Thailand Fear KFC
In a country where superstitions are as imaginative as they are many, physicians have come to fear a jinx involving Kentucky Fried Chicken.
By Max Kim
Published 2026-11-04 10:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/world/asia/thailand-kfc-curse-doctors.html

Thanat Tantinam, a colorectal surgeon in Thailand, knows a lot of things from his medical training, like the ins and outs of the human digestive system, or bowel cancer rates. But also: Never eat Kentucky Fried Chicken at work.

Since he was a medical student, around a decade ago, the American fast food franchise has been the subject of an odd superstition among Thai doctors, many of whom believe that eating its chicken at work will lead to intolerably busy shifts.

“It’s a serious superstition in some hospitals,” said Dr. Thanat, 35. “Your colleagues might be mad if you bring KFC.”

He recently tested this theory. Between 2023 and 2024, he and several co-workers at Phatthalung Hospital in southern Thailand, his employer at the time, conducted a randomized control trial of 345 surgical shifts, comparing metrics like case load or estimated blood loss in patients from three groups of surgeons: a group that ate KFC, another that got food from a local brand named Five Star Chicken, and one that ate nothing.

The study, which was published earlier this year in the Annals of Surgery Open, a medical journal based in Philadelphia, found that eating KFC does not, in fact, lead to more work. But it also left many questions unanswered: Where did the KFC curse come from? And how had it gripped some of the most educated scientific minds in the country, including Dr. Thanat himself?

“Yes, I still believe it — maybe 80 percent out of 100,” he said. “If someone brought me KFC at work, I would keep it until past my shift.”

Such superstitions abound in Thailand, where Buddhism has blended with a mélange of other spiritual traditions like animism, Hindu rituals and Chinese astrology to create a strong affinity for the supernatural in contemporary life.

“In Thailand, superstition isn’t the opposite of modernity — it lives comfortably alongside it,” said Theeranuch Pusaksrikit, a business school professor at Chulalongkorn University who researches how superstitions affect consumerist behavior. “The same person can hold a science degree, consult an auspicious date before signing a contract and wear an amulet to work.”

‘This Is Not KFC’

No occasion is too big or too small for a sprinkle of superstition. There are the infamous black magic rituals that occasionally surface in politics, and popular customs like dressing in lucky colors corresponding to each day of the week. Last year, when a sinkhole opened up and stranded a pickup truck near Bangkok’s Vajira Hospital, Dr. Thanat’s current employer, people rushed to buy lottery tickets matching the vehicle’s license plate number.

“Each hospital has their own superstition culture,” Dr. Thanat said. He has also heard of colleagues avoiding nuts, pizza or coffee while at work, and knows of at least one hospital where bananas — otherwise regarded as a lucky food — are taboo.

But few medical superstitions have been as universal and long-running as the KFC curse, a fact that has been a point of fascination at KFC itself.

“We dug into the data, it was pretty clear,” said Suhayl Limbada, who was until recently the chief marketing officer of KFC Thailand. “There was a noticeable trend at restaurants around hospitals, there was a dip in sales.”

Two years ago, he parlayed the curse into a marketing campaign. Though riffing on cultural practices had gotten Mr. Limbada in trouble before — the fried chicken-scented incense sticks the company released for Lunar New Year were widely panned — this one was much more warmly received.

Launched on doctor’s day in November 2024, the campaign offered a kind of cleansing ritual: Chicken was sold in packaging labeled with slogans like “This is not KFC” in stores near hospitals.

Mr. Limbada has his own ideas about how the curse came to be. KFC opened in Thailand in 1984 and has since become one of the most ubiquitous fast food franchises in the country — and a trailblazer of late night delivery. It operates around 1,300 stores, far outnumbering McDonald’s, which has around 240. In even the smallest rural town, chances are there is at least a KFC.

He thinks one of these rural locations might have been the ground zero, delivering one late night to an understaffed local hospital where a hungry doctor, unaware that they were about to be hit with a sanity-shattering deluge of patients, was waiting.

Building Solidarity

The superstition has since racked up a catalog of very specific lore.

It is widely understood, for example, that it only applies to departments that cannot easily leave the hospital for meals, like surgery or emergency rooms, said Titaporn Nasaarn, a 34-year-old ER doctor at Kamalasai Hospital in northeastern Thailand.

She recalled how her colleagues once successfully co-opted the superstition for good. It was during an unusually quiet evening in the surgical intensive care unit, and some of the nurses, who wanted to work, were worried they were going to lose their upcoming shifts.

“The attending anesthesiologist performed a ritual to summon cases by ordering KFC and ordering pizza,” she said. The beds filled up. But “normally, hardly anyone dares to order it,” she added.

To everyone else, of course, KFC, with Thai spinoffs like Green Curry Chicken Rice, remains a desirable food. And at many hospitals, patients or their families occasionally treat their medical caretakers to the stuff, a gesture that invariably puts Jaruda Mamuangbon, a 42-year-old nurse at Vajira Hospital, on edge.

But she and her colleagues have noticed that the number of KFC gifts has plummeted in the last two or so years.

“We have always graciously accepted the kind gift,” Ms. Jaruda said. “But I think the patients’ families have probably picked up on the superstition from social media.”

Ms. Theeranuch, the professor, sees the widespread belief in the jinx not as a posture of anti-science, but a way for Thailand’s medical workers to keep their spirits up.

“Hospital work is intensely unpredictable, and a shared rule like ‘don’t eat KFC on shift’ may give staff a small sense of control over something inherently unpredictable,” she said. “They also build solidarity.”

Dr. Thanat has settled into a similar view. Underneath the supernatural dress of the KFC curse are, he said, more sobering earthbound realities.

It is telling that the curse has largely been confined to the country’s public hospitals, where doctors — overworked and underpaid compared with their private sector counterparts — have long called for better working conditions.

“If you work at a private hospital, you would want more patients to come,” Dr. Thanat said, adding that doctors’ compensation at private hospitals scales with greater caseloads.

“I think the KFC curse is a projection of fear,” he said. “We need a scapegoat.”

Phuriphat Dejsuphong contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

For nearly 20 years, Mrs. Li’s Chinese restaurant in Edinburgh has been both her life’s work and her cross to bear. “My mum’s Chinese restaurant is dying,” Ms. He, 29, said in a video on Instagram in April.

ARTICLE

Could a Viral Video Save Her Mom’s Chinese Restaurant?
Millions viewed Lisa He’s post about her mother’s struggling business in Edinburgh. But internet fame created its own complications — and obscured bigger questions.
By Isabella Kwai
Published 2026-11-04 09:52 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/world/europe/chinese-restaurant-edinburgh-viral-social-media.html

Sophie Li wiped the tables and swept the floors every day at China Star, even though few customers came through the door.

For nearly 20 years, Mrs. Li’s Chinese restaurant in Edinburgh has been both her life’s work and her cross to bear. In better times, business was steady enough to support her and her two daughters and help send them to universities.

But early this year, the restaurant was almost always empty. Still, Mrs. Li, approaching 70, scrimped and toiled seven days a week to keep China Star open.

“I am a person who can endure hardship better than humiliation,” she said.

Down in London, her younger daughter, Lisa He, worried about the toll on her mother’s health. She traveled up to Scotland and posted a plea on social media.

“My mum’s Chinese restaurant is dying,” Ms. He, 29, said in a video on Instagram in April. She had decided to put aside several months to try to save it.

“Follow the journey and let’s see if I can turn this around,” she said.

Within days, the post had been viewed millions of times. Influencers and sympathetic locals suddenly flocked to China Star, overwhelming the modest 13-table restaurant.

Neither Ms. He nor her mother had been ready for internet stardom. She wondered whether she had made a mistake.

“It was absolutely awful,” Ms. He said. Going viral “doesn’t help when your restaurant’s already broken.”

An Immigrant’s Ambition

Sitting in China Star’s dining room can feel like taking a trip back in time.

An aquarium filled with shy fish welcomes diners, and lucky cat figurines sit in the window. Decorations from a long-ago wedding still hang on the back wall. Dishes are washed by hand.

Mrs. Li was born Wei Li but took the name Sophie after emigrating to Edinburgh in 1993 from mainland China with her husband, a doctoral candidate at the University of Edinburgh. She liked the regal sound of her new name, and hoped to live up to it. To support the family, she worked as a dishwasher and waited tables.

But she didn’t feel at ease in her new home. She worried that Lisa and her older sister, Emma, would not assimilate. In 1997, with loans from relatives and friends, she opened a restaurant, then a decade later moved to her current location, on busy West Maitland Street, beneath a large red sign with “China Star” in gold letters.

“I felt like my standing wasn’t as high when I first came,” she said. She wanted her children “to hold their head high.”

Her chefs were from Hong Kong and southern China, and they cooked a version of Chinese food that had been shaped in postwar Britain into a cuisine of its own: salt-and-pepper stir-fries, sweet and sour chicken, fried noodles and curries. Mrs. Li eventually kept two menus: one for Chinese visitors and one for locals.

She worked 15-hour days, sleeping only a few hours per night. Mornings were for cleaning and ingredient prep. Then came lunch service. She waited tables and delivered takeout orders herself, keeping the restaurant open until midnight, even on Christmas.

Time passed. Her husband returned to China. Her daughters moved to London. Mrs. Li paid off the mortgage on China Star.

But as newer Chinese restaurants opened in Edinburgh and competition grew, the restaurant began to feel more like a burden. Foot traffic ebbed, and more of her business shifted to internet orders, whose commissions ate into their margins. Online ratings for the restaurant dropped.

Mrs. Li does not consider herself tech-savvy, so she didn’t see the customer reviews that complained about small portion sizes or bland fried rice. Arthritis was slowing her down. And she felt lonely.

“I didn’t think there was much hope,” she said. “But I had to keep going. There’s no other road to walk.”

Going Viral

In London, Ms. He, who was making a living as an actress and paralegal, kept tabs on China Star by logging into its CCTV camera. She saw how tired her mother looked. Early this year, she booked a trip home, hoping to give her a break.

“I came back out of a desperation to save my mom, rather than save the restaurant,” she said.

Ms. He has complicated feelings about restaurant life. When she was a baby, her mother brought her to work, putting her in a makeshift crib in a side room. After school, she felt guilty watching her work so hard.

“I often felt like I had to give up my social life to help out at the restaurant,” she said.

Before April, Ms. He’s social media account consisted mostly of images of her dancing or in film rehearsals.

But in this video, she turned the camera on her mother and China Star and gave her own, raw assessment of something many businesses may prefer to hide: what wasn’t working, from the uninviting facade to the outdated menu. And she invited people to follow her own journey as she tried to turn their fortunes around.

Perhaps it was Ms. He’s candor, or the video’s documentary style. Or perhaps it was the feeling, for watchers online, that they could still stave off the loss of yet another family-run business in a world of corporations and chains.

Ms. He’s comments lit up with offers of help, from improving the design to revamping the menu. Diners promised to visit. Restaurant owners encouraged them to rethink the business. “Don’t give up,” one said. “It isn’t over until it’s over.”

Ms. He posted the video on a Sunday. On Tuesday, she found herself back in the kitchen, trying to manage a situation for which they were entirely unprepared.

Food bloggers and new diners filled the restaurant in the days after that viral post. Mrs. Li, who learned of her daughter’s post only after it blew up, was shocked.

Suddenly, daughter and mother were racing up and down stairs to take orders as their two cooks, used to a scattering of orders each day, suddenly had to pump out dishes.

Tensions boiled over when one frustrated chef walked out in protest during lunch as a full house waited for meals. Overwhelmed, the mother and daughter decided to shutter the restaurant temporarily.

Food and Filial Devotion

People following China Star’s struggles online replied to Ms. He with thoughts about what the restaurant needed to survive, and she decided to act on some of the advice.

She convinced her mother to slim down the menu and add Chinese wines, hired more servers and installed an electronic system for orders. They reopened after about a week with earlier hours and they closed on Mondays.

She shared updates on Instagram, where more than 200,000 accounts are now following her.

Five months after going viral, Ms. He was still working in the dining room, taking orders and mixing drinks. On a Thursday this September, the tables were filled with people who had seen her videos, drawn as much by the story of filial devotion and small-business survival as by the food.

“Usually the second generation — they don’t want to do the restaurant work,” said Wing Cheong, a visitor from Canada. “I think she is a good daughter.”

Mrs. Li, energized, could not imagine giving up China Star, and was hopeful that her daughter would take it over one day. Revenues this summer more than tripled from the year before, and the online attention has led to sponsorships.

But Ms. He wasn’t sure.

She was struggling to balance it all — the social media posts, the long days, the physical labor. There was a leak in the storeroom; a bathroom toilet seat needed fixing.

Beneath it lay a familiar generational dilemma: She had put her own career, and her ambitions to act and dance, on hold to keep her mother’s business afloat.

In one post this summer, she asked whether going viral had made their lives better, or just busier. In her mind, maybe it was time to let China Star go, for her mother to retire and for her to go back to London.

Her video had succeeded. But it had also revealed how differently mother and daughter imagined what should come next.

“If I’m tiring myself and my mom to death every day,” she said at the restaurant, in a quiet moment before lunch, “I don’t really see that as a success.”

For now, decisions on the future would have to wait. For the first time in a long time, the restaurant had large bookings for the holidays in December, and there was plenty of work to do: folding napkins, sorting prawn crackers and washing glasses. They would be back the next day to do it all again.

ARTICLE

U.K. Supreme Court Hears Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know
The government designated the protest group as a terrorist organization last year, prompting criticism. The country’s Supreme Court is hearing a challenge to the ban on Wednesday.
By Karla Adam
Published 2026-11-04 05:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/world/europe/palestine-action-ban-uk-supreme-court.html

Britain’s decision to outlaw Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian direct-action group, as a terrorist organization has been challenged in a succession of legal hearings since it was imposed last year. Now, the country’s Supreme Court is hearing a challenge against the ban to decide its future.

The British government accused Palestine Action of orchestrating “a nationwide campaign of direct criminal action,” putting national security at risk. According to the government’s independent adviser on counterterrorism legislation, it was the first time a protest group that did not call for violence against people was proscribed under counterterrorism laws.

Here’s what to know.

What is Palestine Action?

Palestine Action was founded in 2020 as a pro-Palestinian protest group that largely focuses its efforts on demonstrations against corporate and military targets linked to the sale and export of defense equipment to Israel. The group says it does not promote violence against individuals.

It was co-founded by Huda Ammori, an advocate who had previously worked for a Palestinian rights organization, and Richard Barnard, an activist linked with other grass roots movements, including Extinction Rebellion, a global environmental group.

During legal proceedings challenging the ban, Britain’s High Court said that the group claimed to have a mailing list of some 20,000 people but that the “extent and nature” of Palestine Action’s membership and organization was “largely unexplained.” Analysts said that before it was disbanded, Palestine Action was run by a relatively small, committed group of activists.

The group’s actions have drawn international attention. President Trump criticized it after activists were accused of vandalizing one of his Scottish golf resorts by defacing the clubhouse and spraying “Gaza is not 4 sale” across a green. Mr. Trump called the demonstrators “terrorists” and said he hoped they would be “treated harshly.”

Why was the group banned?

The Terrorism Act 2000, introduced under a previous Labour prime minister, Tony Blair, allows the government to ban any group “concerned in terrorism.” It contains a broad definition of terrorism that includes damage to property, not just people, if it is carried out for ideological reasons.

The British government announced its plan to designate Palestine Action a terrorist group in June 2025, three days after some of its members damaged military planes using red paint at Britain’s largest air force base, at Brize Norton in Oxfordshire. Yvette Cooper, then the home secretary, said the group’s activities met the legal definition of terrorism because they included “serious damage to property.”

The ban was imposed in July, and the group was added to the statutory list of more than 80 banned terrorist organizations, alongside the Islamic State, Al Qaeda, and Atomwaffen Division, a white supremacist group. At the time, Palestine Action said it was “plainly preposterous” to group it with such organizations.

The ban made it a criminal offense to belong to Palestine Action, express an opinion or belief in support of the group, or wear clothing or carry items that “arouse reasonable suspicion that the individual is a member or supporter” of the group, among other actions. The maximum penalty for belonging to or expressing support for the group is 14 years in prison.

In August, the United States followed suit, designating Palestine Action as a terrorist group.

More than 4,000 people had been arrested across Britain for showing support for the group as of Nov. 1, according to Defend Our Juries, a civil liberties group. Between Sept. 11, 2001, and March 31, 2025, there were a total of 5,734 terrorism arrests in Britain.

The arrests related to Palestine Action stemmed largely from coordinated demonstrations, analysts say, where some protesters have deliberately risked detention by holding placards reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Hundreds of people were detained over the weekend outside the U.S. Embassy in London after staging such a protest.

Why has the ban faced criticism?

Some civil liberties organizations argue that using counterterrorism legislation against Palestine Action is overreach and part of a wider crackdown on protest in Britain. They contend that existing criminal laws cover property destruction, whereas proscription criminalizes anyone expressing moral support for the proscribed group, including by attending peaceful gatherings.

In July 2025, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, called the move a “disproportionate and unnecessary” expansion of counterterrorism powers and called on the British government to rescind its decision.

In written submissions to the Supreme Court, Amnesty International and Liberty argue that the proscription of Palestine Action has silenced broad segments of civil society, academics, journalists and even their own human rights organizations.

David Mead, a human rights law scholar at the University of East Anglia, said the central legal dispute turns on whether the ban is proportionate.

“The surprising thing is the U.K. state’s seeming need to use terrorism legislation on a group such as this,” Professor Mead said.

How has the ban been challenged in court?

Ms. Ammori, the co-founder, first challenged the ban in June 2025, and the case has since wound its way through the legal system. In February, the High Court ruled the ban unlawful, calling it disproportionate and an infringement on fundamental rights to free expression and assembly.

That decision was overturned in June by the Court of Appeal. Ms. Ammori appealed that ruling, sending the case to the Supreme Court for what will be the final word in British domestic courts.

Supreme Court rulings are usually issued in three to six months, but legal analysts said the court could rule sooner in this case as hundreds of people arrested and charged in relation to protests are awaiting trial.

Ms. Ammori has said that if the Supreme Court upholds the ban, she plans to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights.

Stephen Castle, Lizzie Dearden and Michael D. Shear contributed reporting.

The Best Movies on Amazon Prime Video Right Now
New films, and classics, just keep coming, but you don’t have to drill down to find the finest selections to stream. We’ll do the heavy lifting. You press play.
By Jason T. Bailey
Published 2020-09-10 05:52 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/article/best-movies-amazon-prime.html

Sign up for our Watching newsletter to get recommendations on the best films and TV shows to stream and watch, delivered to your inbox.

As Netflix pours more of its resources into original content, Amazon Prime Video is picking up the slack, adding new movies for its subscribers each month. Its catalog has grown so impressive, in fact, that it’s a bit overwhelming — and at the same time, movies that are included with a Prime subscription regularly change status, becoming available only for rental or purchase. It’s a lot to sift through, so we’ve plucked out 100 of the absolute best movies included with a Prime subscription right now, to be updated as new information is made available.

Here are our lists of the best TV shows and movies on Netflix, and the best of both on Hulu and Disney+.

‘Frankenstein’ (1931)

Horror cinema was changed forever in the year 1931, when Universal — a scrappy studio known primarily for B-movies and programmers — went all in on monster movies. Tod Browning’s adaptation of Bram Stoker’s “Dracula” (also on Prime) set the template for every vampire movie to follow (doubly so for Bela Lugosi’s title turn), and James Whale’s take on Mary Shelley’s mad scientist novel, released nine months after, further solidified the template for Universal horror: moody, slyly funny, carefully crafted and sneakily poignant, thanks in no small part to Boris Karloff’s wounded work as the monster. Our critic called it “a stirring grand-guignol type of picture.” (Universal’s similarly beloved “The Invisible Man” is also streaming on Amazon.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Damsels in Distress’ (2012)

Once upon a time, the “Barbie” mastermind Greta Gerwig was known not as the director behind a billion-dollar blockbuster, but as one of the most charismatic actresses on the indie film scene. Her talents are nicely showcased in this sharp-witted, frequently quotable comedy of manners and satire of campus life. The writer and director is Whit Stillman, who helped define smart, talky ’90s indies with his triple play of “Metropolitan,” “Barcelona” and “The Last Days of Disco”; this, his first feature in 13 years, was a welcome return to form. Gerwig is at her complicated best as Violet, who helps her friends (Megalyn Echikunwoke, Carrie MacLemore and Lio Tipton, all memorable) navigate the unfortunate men of the fictional Seven Oaks College; Adam Brody is likably squirrelly as the campus cad. (If you like female-forward comedy-dramas, stream “The Edge of Seventeen” or “Valley Girl.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Sheep Detectives’ (2026)

As our critic Alissa Wilkinson noted, a certain kind of movie has all but gone extinct: “family-friendly, PG-rated movies” that were “intended for the whole family to watch.” This gentle, charming mystery-comedy is a fine demonstration of what we’ve lost. The director Kyle Balda and the screenwriter Craig Mazin (adapting the 2005 novel “Three Bags Full” by Leonie Swann) tell the story of George (Hugh Jackman), a kind shepherd who unexpectedly turns up dead. But every night at bedtime, he read murder mysteries to his flock (voiced by a boisterous supporting cast, led by Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Bryan Cranston), who then help the seemingly clueless local constable (Nicholas Braun) solve his murder. As a premise, it sounds inane — “Babe” meets “Knives Out” — and perhaps it is. But the entire enterprise is undertaken with such good humor and quiet grace that it somehow plays. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll believe that sheep can solve crimes. (For more fun yet melancholy family entertainment, stream “The Wild Robot.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Project Hail Mary’ (2026)

When Drew Goddard last adapted a novel by Andy Weir, the resultant film, “The Martian” was an earnest crowd-pleaser, with much of the drama rooted in the human need for company and companionship. This film, based on Weir’s 2021 novel of the same name, retains some of that quality, but its tone and style is shifted considerably by the directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, whose brainy irreverence made “21 Jump Street” and “The Lego Movie” into unlikely successes. Ryan Gosling stars as a middle-school teacher who is brought in to consult on an international effort to save the sun from losing its energy; over his loud objections, he becomes a last-minute addition to a crew of astronauts. Gosling’s charisma and self-aware wit have rarely been put to better use, while Sandra Hüller proves an unlikely but effective comic foil. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ (2019)

All of Quentin Tarantino’s films are, in their own way, valentines to the movies — steeped in the tropes and traditions of the films of his youth, and the ways that they influenced his perceptions of human behavior and the world around him. But this hangout movie and western riff is his most direct love letter, and specifically to the cinema of the late-1960s in which it’s set, spending a few days in the life of Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio), a TV cowboy whose career is on the skids; his stuntman and right-hand Cliff Booth (an Oscar-winning Brad Pitt); and his neighbor Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie). A.O. Scott praised its “ambling, shaggy-dog structure and the easygoing rhythm of its scenes.” (Tarantino’s “Reservoir Dogs” and “Pulp Fiction” are also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘One Battle After Another’ (2025)

Paul Thomas Anderson’s Oscar winner (nominated for 13, winner of six) and most acclaimed picture to date was in the works for decades, first getting into the filmmaker’s head in the form of the 1990 Pynchon novel “Vineland.” Over the years, that story evolved into Anderson’s tale of Bob Ferguson (Leonardo DiCaprio, pitch perfect), a burned-out formula revolutionary whose years of paranoia are finally borne out when a twisted military man (Sean Penn) organizes the kidnapping of Bob’s daughter, Willa (Chase Infiniti). The resultant “carnivalesque epic about good and evil, violence and power, inalienable rights and the fight against injustice” is the culmination of Anderson’s screen work to date, fusing the loosey-goosey friskiness of his early features with the more disciplined aesthetics and towering performances of his middle period. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Eephus’ (2024)

On paper, a group of middle-aged men getting together to play amateur baseball may not sound like riveting cinema. But these characters are developed with such singularity and sensitivity, and played with such next-door-neighbor familiarity, that their seemingly slight hopes and dreams attain end-of-the-world gravitas. They meet at the baseball diamond in the small town of Douglas, Mass., for their weekly games, but they won’t anymore; “Eephus” dramatizes the final innings they’ll play before their Soldier’s Field is bulldozed to make way for a new public school. There are no last-minute efforts to save the field, nor is there a big game whose outcome will change anyone’s life in any particular way. Instead, this is a movie about the act of playing and watching baseball, which involves a lot of hanging out, talking trash, eating garbage food and occasionally hitting a ball. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Support the Girls’ (2018)

The writer and director Andrew Bujalski (“Funny Ha Ha,” “Computer Chess”) creates what looks like a sunny workplace comedy. But he’s up to something much slyer, a smart examination of class and gender politics in one of their most pointed playgrounds: a Hooters-style sports bar and grill, where customers leer at scantily clad waitresses while the manager, Lisa (Regina Hall), tries to keep temperatures cool (and maintain her own sanity). It’s a wise, winning comedy, with a particularly sparkling supporting turn by Haley Lu Richardson, a “White Lotus” favorite. (Hall also shines in “Girls Trip.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Shiva Baby’ (2021)

Rachel Sennott found her breakthrough role as a messy young woman who finds all of the potential land mines in her life exploding simultaneously at the shiva of a family friend in this nerve-racking comedy from the writer and director Emma Seligman. The single location and collapsed time frame give it the efficiency of a well-constructed stage play, but “Shiva Baby” is as tense as any thriller, with the strained small talk, copious side-eyes and unapologetic gossip augmented by nervous camerawork, jarring sound effects and a dissonant musical score. It’s rare for a film to balance such wildly divergent tones simultaneously — to interweave big laughs with gut-wrenching discomfort — but Seligman pulls it off. (For more smart comedy, stream “Modern Romance.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Death Becomes Her’ (1992)

A commercial disappointment upon its original release, this blend of science fiction and social satire subsequently found enough of a cult audience to spawn a Broadway musical. The film stars Meryl Streep and Goldie Hawn as old friends turned romantic rivals, whose shared quest for perpetual youth leads them to a magic potion from the mysterious Lisle von Rhuman, played by the convincingly youthful Isabella Rossellini. Turns out, immortality has its drawbacks. This was one of Streep’s first major comic roles, and she throws herself into the pratfalls and verbal jousts with abandon. Hawn, meanwhile, reconfirms why she is one of the funniest actors of her time. But the real surprise is Bruce Willis, who as the object of their affections eschews his customary smirk and swagger to turn his nebbishy doctor into an inspired comic creation. (If you love wild comedies, stream “Used Cars” and “Matinee.)” Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Collateral’ (2004)

What could have been a formulaic action flick is transformed into an unpredictable, introspective two-hander, thanks to the moody direction of Michael Mann and the thrilling performances of its leads. Go-to good guy Tom Cruise is frighteningly convincing as a businesslike contract killer, the kind of villain who never raises his voice and always gets the job done; Jamie Foxx is sympathetic as the cabdriver who becomes a combination of chauffeur and hostage. The best moments in “Collateral” are the quiet ones, in which these two characters contemplate their stations in life, and their limited options for changing them. “Mann makes thrillers the way that John Ford made westerns,” our critic wrote, “using genre as a way into meaning rather than as an escape.” (Mann’s “The Last of the Mohicans” is also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Atomic Blonde’ (2017)

Charlize Theron starred in this mash-up of a Bond-style spy thriller and a contemporary bone-smashing action movie, directed by the “John Wick” co-creator David Leitch. He carries over that franchise’s “lavishly violent, inventively choreographed fights,” including one corker using kitchen utensils and other household items (giddily if incongruently scored to George Michael’s “Father Figure”), another finding our heroine taking on an army of challengers in one seemingly unbroken take. It’s an ideal role for Theron, who channels all of her sensuality, toughness and physical grace into the role; John Goodman, Toby Jones, Eddie Marsan and James McAvoy appear in memorable supporting roles. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Rain Man’ (1988)

Dustin Hoffman won his second Oscar for his meticulously wrought performance as Raymond Babbitt, an autistic savant who meets his brother Charlie (Tom Cruise) after the death of their father. But “Rain Man” is not a heartfelt, tear-jerking family drama; it’s “a becomingly modest, decently thought-out, sometimes funny film” in which Charlie, a small-time hustler, has to drag his brother on a cross-country road trip to fight what he feels is an unfair inheritance. In retrospect, though Hoffman collected all the awards and accolades, this is Cruise’s film — he’s the character who changes between the beginning and the end — and it’s a marvelous performance, expertly revealing and exploring the psychological cracks in the gleaming golden-boy persona he spent the 1980s perfecting. (If you like ’80s tear-jerkers, you can’t go wrong with “Beaches.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Blue Valentine’ (2010)

As the married couple Cindy and Dean, Michelle Williams and Ryan Gosling are “exemplars of New Method sincerity,” according to our critic, and “able to be fully and achingly present every moment on screen together.” Their director, Derek Cianfrance, tells this story in pieces as they come together and fall apart, in timelines separated by years of hard, unsatisfying living (but shot with only a month between them, an astonishing feat of physical and psychological acting). Aching and heartfelt, the film is an often upsetting yet undeniably powerful account of how not all love stories end in “happily ever after.” Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Blow Out’ (1981)

The director Brian De Palma took an “everything but the kitchen sink” approach to the conspiracy thrillers of the 1970s with his “flashy, eclectic” and ultimately tragic 1981 masterpiece, which cheerfully cribs elements of Chappaquiddick, Watergate and the Kennedy assassinations to create the hybrid story of a movie sound man (John Travolta, excellent) who accidentally tape-records what may have been a politically motivated murder. Nancy Allen gracefully transcends the clichés of her role as a prostitute, while John Lithgow is as scary as he’s ever been — which is no small statement. (DePalma’s “Carrie” and “Carlito’s Way” are also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Dirty Rotten Scoundrels’ (1988)

The 1964 comedy “Bedtime Story” wasn’t exactly a career highlight for Marlon Brando or David Niven, so it probably shouldn’t come as a surprise that this remake from the director Frank Oz has replaced it in the popular consciousness. “Scoundrels” takes the clever premise of the original — warring con artists team up and then compete for the affections and pocketbook of a scene-stealing mark (Glenne Headly) — and gives it several delicious twists, making full use of the comic gifts of Headly, Steve Martin and Michael Caine. An “enchanted featherweight folly,” it makes the case for better remakes: Rather than tampering with the classics, why not fix good ideas that were improperly executed? (For more laugh-out-loud comedy, stream “Borat” or “Fletch.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Blackcoat’s Daughter’ (2017)

Osgood Perkins (“Longlegs”) wrote and directed this snowy and chilling jigsaw puzzle of a movie, in which two seemingly unrelated stories of young women teetering on the edge of madness merge in unexpected (and satisfying) ways. Kiernan Shipka is a revelation as a boarding school freshman seemingly abandoned during winter break by her parents and driven to the brink by her feelings of rejection and fear. Emma Roberts is appropriately enigmatic as a capricious hitchhiker, en route to the school for reasons that become increasingly (and troublingly) clear. Read the review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Cape Fear’ (1991)

Martin Scorsese took on his first remake with this iteration of the 1962 potboiler from the director J. Lee Thompson, with Robert De Niro and Nick Nolte in the roles that had been played by Robert Mitchum and Gregory Peck. But Scorsese had no interest in a conventional thriller, so he juiced up this version with his trademark moral ambiguity, transforming Peck’s square-jawed good guy into a flawed adulterer who earns De Niro’s ire by purposefully failing in his duty as defense attorney. Throw in a scenery-chewing performance by De Niro and an astonishingly assured portrayal by a young Juliette Lewis as Nolte’s daughter and you’ve got a fascinating (and violent) fusion of Thompson’s suspense and Scorsese’s sensibility. Our critic deemed it “an essential work by one of our masters.” (Scorsese’s “The Age of Innocence” is also streaming on Amazon.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Queen of Versailles’ (2012)

Perhaps the most trenchant (and entertaining) commentary on the 2008 financial crisis, this biting documentary concerns David and Jackie Siegel, an obscenely rich Florida couple who are in the process of building a comically outsized mansion when the real estate bubble bursts. The director Lauren Greenfield may very well trigger gasps and laughter about the couple’s insane consumption and their subsequent attempts to curb it. But she isn’t content to take cheap shots. She sees her subjects as both perpetrators and victims of a system of conspicuous capitalism, in which too much is somehow never enough. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Chef’ (2014)

Jon Favreau began his career with intimate, indie comedy-dramas, yet he ended up at the helm of giant productions like “Iron Man” and “The Mandalorian.” This was something of a return to his roots, with Favreau writing, directing and starring as a chef who abandons his high-profile restaurant gig to get back to basics in a food truck. The sense of art imitating life is a bit much, but this low-key effort boasts plenty of charm, a handful of laughs and enjoyable appearances by Favreau’s famous friends. (For more indie comedy-drama, stream “Trees Lounge.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Bridesmaids’ (2011)

Kristen Wiig stars in and writes (with her frequent collaborator Annie Mumolo) this comedy smash from the director Paul Feig. Wiig is Annie, an aimless baker whose lifelong pal Lillian (Maya Rudolph) is getting hitched and asks Annie to serve as maid of honor. This duty sets off an uproarious series of broad comic set pieces and thoughtful introspection; both the comedy and drama are played to the hilt by an ensemble that includes Rose Byrne, Jon Hamm, Wendi McLendon-Covey, Ellie Kemper, Chris O’Dowd and an Oscar-nominated Melissa McCarthy. (For more wild comedy, stream “Joy Ride” or “Overboard.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Something Wild’ (1986)

This thrillingly unpredictable romantic comedy and crime movie mash-up from the director Jonathan Demme (“The Silence of the Lambs”) begins as a boy-meets-girl movie with a slightly psychosexual edge, seeming to tell the story of how a wild girl (Melanie Griffith) and a straight guy (Jeff Daniels) meet in the middle. Then Ray (a sensational Ray Liotta) turns up and hijacks the entire movie, turning it into something much darker and more dangerous. Throughout, Demme keeps the focus on his colorful characters and sharp dialogue. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Silence of the Lambs’ (1991)

Few fictional characters have embedded themselves in the pop culture consciousness as firmly as Dr. Hannibal Lecter, the brilliant monster brought to bone-chilling life by an Oscar-winning Anthony Hopkins in Jonathan Demme’s 1991 adaptation of the Thomas Harris best seller. The film also won awards for Best Picture, Best Director, Best Screenplay, and Best Actress — a quintuple play only matched two other times in film history — all deserving, none perhaps more so than Jodie Foster, whose indelible portrayal of the rookie F.B.I. investigator Clarice Starling sharply combines small-town naïveté with quick-witted strength. Our critic called it “pop film making of a high order.” (Fans of smart horror will also enjoy “Let the Right One In.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Thing’ (1982)

The director John Carpenter loved the 1951 sci-fi-horror thriller “The Thing From Another World” — so much so that he had the characters in his 1978 breakthrough hit, “Halloween,” watch it on television. Four years later, he went a step further by directing this terrifying update of that snowy creature feature, which gets a considerable boost from the more realistic language, themes and gore afforded by the times, as well as the jaw-dropping advances in makeup and effects. But both versions work for the same reason: the skill with which they place their characters in the claustrophobic grip of an isolated location, and then squeeze. (Carpenter’s “They Live” is also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Long Goodbye’ (1973)

Robert Altman adapted Raymond Chandler’s late-period Philip Marlowe novel as only he could: idiosyncratically, by updating the hard-boiled story’s setting to the feel-good California of the 1970s and casting one of the era’s most of-his-time actors, Elliot Gould, in the role made famous by Humphrey Bogart. Purists resisted, and some critics scratched their heads. But Gould is brilliant, Altman’s direction is brash and confident, and this “tough, funny, hugely entertaining movie” homes in on the character’s essential, outsider nature, while ingeniously rethinking the conventions of the genre. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Raging Bull’ (1980)

Robert De Niro won his second Academy Award for his fiercely physical and psychologically punishing performance in this searing adaptation of the autobiography of the middleweight champion Jake LaMotta. The stylish boxing sequences are visceral and overwhelming, shot and cut to approximate the disorientation and violence of the sport. But the most disturbing sequences are those of LaMotta in his home, terrorizing his wife, Vickie (Cathy Moriarty, in an electrifying debut) and terrifying his brother and manager, Joey (Joe Pesci, also remarkable). It’s a relentlessly downbeat piece of work, but the force of De Niro’s performance and the energy of Martin Scorsese’s direction are hard to overstate, or to forget. Our critic called it Scorsese’s “most ambitious film as well as his finest.” Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Taking of Pelham One Two Three’ (1974)

One of the greatest of all “gritty Gotham” tales — our critic called it “a movie that really catches the mood of New York and New Yorkers” — this darkly funny, white-knuckle thriller from the director Joseph Sargent concerns four armed men who take a subway car hostage, demanding a million-dollar ransom for the lives of the passengers aboard. Robert Shaw is coolly ruthless as the leader of the gang while Walter Matthau is at his hangdog best as the cynical transit cop hot on their trail. (For more old-school action, stream “The Train” and “The Great Escape.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Inherit the Wind’ (1960)

Our critic deemed Stanley Kramer’s adaptation of Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee’s stage play (based on the notorious Scopes “monkey trial”) to be “triumphant,” its climax “one of the most brilliant and engrossing displays of acting ever witnessed on the screen.” The actors Fredric March and Spencer Tracy are in career-best form as the Bible-pounding orator and the agnostic defense attorney on opposite theological and philosophical sides of the evolution debate. Kramer cranks up the carnival atmosphere, to great effect, and pulls a rare (and entertaining) nonmusical supporting turn from Gene Kelly as an H.L. Mencken-esque newspaper reporter. (For more classic drama, stream “Bicycle Thieves” and “Wuthering Heights.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Memento’ (2000)

Christopher Nolan made his first big splash with this, his second feature film, a stylish film noir riff that tells its familiar story in an exuberantly inventive way: In order to mirror the disorientation of its protagonist, Leonard (Guy Pearce), who has lost his ability to create new memories, Nolan tells the story by ordering its scenes in reverse chronology. As Leonard pursues an investigation of his wife’s murder, revelations fold back on themselves and betrayals become clear to the audience before they’re known to him. Yet even without that narrative flourish, “Memento” would be a scorching piece of work, loaded with sharp performances, moody cinematography and a noir-inspired sense of doom. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.
