SUMMARY

Our appetite for seafood is growing. In the last 60 years, the global consumption of fish has more than doubled. One way the industry could adjust would be to farm more seafood that does not need to be fed other fish.

ARTICLE

The Dirty Secret Behind the Farmed Fish You Eat
Forced labor, rancid waste, harmful chemicals. What to know about the seafood that could end up on your plate.
By Ian Urbina
Published 2026-10-08 21:39 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/08/magazine/farm-raised-fish-aquaculture-overfishing.html

Our appetite for seafood is growing. In the last 60 years, the global consumption of fish has more than doubled. As demand has increased, so have dangerous levels of overfishing: One-third of the world’s fish stocks are currently being harvested at unsustainable levels.

Fish farming, known as aquaculture, was supposed to help solve this problem by relieving some of the pressure on the planet’s oceans.

It is now a vast and innovative industry.

Norwegian companies have built enormous, semi-submersible structures in the open ocean that can house as many as 1.5 million salmon.

In China, huge aquaculture ships are equipped with breeding cabins capable of holding 90,000 cubic meters of water.

Today, more than half of all the seafood that’s eaten comes from aquaculture rather than wild catch.

But aquaculture has a dark secret: Most of this farm-grown seafood is raised on other seafood taken from the oceans.

Think about it: Farm-raised fish have to eat something.

The most efficient way to feed them is to sweep up vast numbers of other smaller fish, which are turned into a nutrient-rich powder called fishmeal — or its liquid equivalent, fish oil.

As a result, instead of relieving the pressure of overfishing, aquaculture is making the problem worse.

Those of us who have recently eaten farm-raised seafood are participating in a developing environmental crisis.

That would be bad enough, but the so-called reduction industry driving the crisis also flouts the law and puts people in danger. The production of fishmeal often involves forced labor and has led to worker deaths and the polluting of communities around the world. It has provoked political unrest in places like India and prompted countries to accuse others of violating their territorial waters. Dangerous chemicals, including antimicrobials, fire retardants and anesthetics, are often added to fish ponds and make their way into the seafood.

Some of the most popular types of seafood consumed in the United States — salmon and shrimp — are predominantly imported from farms that use fishmeal. They end up in supermarkets throughout the country, including popular retailers such as Walmart and Kroger, and appear on the menus of hundreds of thousands of restaurants and cafeterias, including those on Capitol Hill where senators and members of Congress eat lunch.

But the problem remains mostly invisible to the American consumer, obscured by marketing campaigns that highlight the clever, eco-friendly adaptations of the aquaculture industry. To create a clearer picture of its impact on humans and the planet, we conducted the most extensive audit ever of the fishmeal supply chain.

Our reporting, which involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, mapped more than 1,400 fishmeal plants and identified more than 2,400 ships connected to fishmeal production. We visited factories and farms; we boarded ships at sea. A team of a half-dozen researchers searched company websites; social media; trade, regulatory and court records; product catalogs; and foreign press reports for visual evidence of the industry’s dangers, which we then corroborated with other independent sources.

What we found is that more than 250 seafood companies have had crimes or concerns documented within their supply chains.

In their marketing, seafood companies routinely claim that what they’re selling is ethical and sustainable. They tend to focus on the engineering marvel of the farms and ignore the crimes and costs located further upstream in their supply chains. Our goal was to reveal all of those costs in order to understand the dark underbelly of an industry that has become one of the world’s dominant food suppliers.

To get the full picture, you have to start on the ships.

The fishing fleets that supply the world’s fishmeal industry total more than 10,000 vessels.

These ships primarily target small schooling fish like anchovies, sardines and sprat that are caught specifically to be reduced into feed.

Along some coasts, they also catch larger fish that would otherwise be sold for people to eat.

Some fishmeal is made from the heads, guts and other remains after wild-caught fish have been processed for human consumption.

At any given time, many fishing vessels are operating illegally and taking measures to avoid detection by the authorities. Scientific studies have classified at least half of the species they capture as “overexploited,” or in danger of disappearing. Hundreds of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet are bottom trawlers, using weighted nets to scrape the ocean floor and devastating virtually everything in their path.

Our reporters boarded fishmeal ships from the South China Sea to the far reaches of the North Atlantic. We reviewed logbooks, interviewed workers and documented illegal practices. Hundreds of fishmeal vessels were found to be fishing in closed or protected seas, violating quotas on certain species, or fishing without licenses.

Working conditions on some ships were abysmal. Deckhands described having their passports confiscated, being forced to work 15-hour days, and being beaten by ship officers. On Chinese and Russian ships, we uncovered worker fatalities and injuries and forced labor, including cases of debt bondage and deckhands who asked to leave the ship but were forbidden. Crew on one Chinese ship off the coast of West Africa slept on deck, exposed to waves and rain, or in dangerously hot and cramped quarters filled with exhaust fumes.

Since 2019, more than a dozen people have died working in the fishmeal industry in Peru, which is the world’s largest producer, typically providing more than a fifth of the global supply. Workers on the country’s vessels have sometimes fainted from the toxic gases emitted by the hundreds of tons of decaying fish in their holds. In 2023, two men asphyxiated after they fell into the hold of a ship while unloading anchovies for Copeinca, a major fishing company operating in Peru. (CFG Investment, the company that owned Copeinca at the time, did not respond to a request for comment. The current owner, the Canadian company Cooke, said the accident was not Copeinca’s responsibility but the fault of the fishermen themselves.)

Other workers fell overboard or were fatally struck by heavy equipment. Also in 2023, a fisherman with another Peruvian company, TASA, died at sea when he was hit by a cable. A spokesman for the company said TASA “mobilized all necessary human and logistical resources” in response to the accident and provided care to those affected by the death, including psychological support for the family.

Workers are far from the only ones affected. Over the last decade, the fishmeal industry has decimated the food security and livelihoods of coastal communities.

For generations, the waters off West Africa were fished by fleets of brightly painted wooden pirogues and sustained a vibrant industry of dockworkers, traders and transporters, as well as thousands of women who smoked, dried and sold fish in local markets. But scores of fishmeal ships now plunder those waters, sending their catch to dozens of fishmeal factories in Mauritania, Senegal and Gambia.

Though new regulations have limited fishing intensity, Mauritania has been especially attractive because its waters are unusually rich in marine life, fed by a robust nutrient upwelling that the Canary Current generates along the coast. There, Chinese and Turkish ships sweep up bonga shad, sardines, and round and flat sardinella — species known as forage fish, which are toward the bottom of the food chain and are eaten by other marine life or seabirds.

They’re also eaten by humans. Such fish are critical to the food security of millions of people in West Africa; sardinella, a small fish that provides an outsize dose of vital nutrients, is among the region’s cheapest and most important sources of animal protein. Since the fishmeal industry expanded into West Africa, round sardinella stocks have fallen to their lowest level ever recorded. Today, three of those four species are classified by the United Nations as overexploited.

Much of the damage being done by the foreign fishmeal ships off West Africa, it turns out, has gone undetected. Ships turn off their transponders or falsify their bearings through “position spoofing” to avoid any meaningful monitoring by local authorities. This practice is especially common off the coast of Mauritania: From 2019 to 2025, at least 21 foreign fishing vessels operating there disguised their location, according to satellite data. Many others routinely engaged in transshipment, the banned practice of transferring fish to refrigeration ships instead of returning to port, thereby skirting local taxes, quotas and regulations for protected species. Fishing vessels can more easily evade this rule if they disappear from satellite tracking.

The Mauritanian government’s oversight of its fish stocks and the livelihoods they support has been mixed. While the World Bank in 2025 ranked Mauritania ahead of most African countries at keeping industrial vessels out of protected waters, watchdogs say the government still struggles to determine who is fishing, how much is caught and whether regulators consistently enforce the rules for vessels at sea.

In at least one instance, Mauritania’s government appeared to want to keep the problem of illegal fishing quiet. On July 22, 2025, Ali Bakar, an environmental activist in the country, shared a post to Facebook claiming that a Turkish fishmeal ship was falsifying its location while operating in the Banc d’Arguin National Park, a nature reserve along the country’s coast. “It’s very likely to be involved in an illegal hunting activity,” Bakar wrote. That same day, the police showed up at his home and arrested him.

Charged with “publishing misleading information” on the internet, he was imprisoned, his head was shaved, and he was put in a rat- and roach-infested cell with two dozen others. Unwilling to sign a letter apologizing to the coast guard and the fisheries agency, he was held for roughly two months and then released after pressure from international human rights organizations.

Much like Mauritania, Senegal appears to have little desire to prioritize its people’s interests over foreign investment. In 2024, the European Union issued a “yellow card” warning to the country for insufficient cooperation in combating illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.

The ravaging of these already overexploited fish stocks has been a major driver of migration, according to the United Nations. Thousands of Senegalese fishermen have lost their jobs, prompting many of them to use their boats to flee the country. Typically, they try to make the nearly 1,000-mile journey from Senegal to Europe’s nearest touch point, Spain’s Canary Islands.

The migration route from West Africa to the Canary Islands has claimed thousands of lives. In September 2024, a fishing boat carrying roughly 100 migrants bound for Spain capsized, killing more than two dozen people. One survivor was Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old who made it to shore by clinging to the wreckage for 10 hours. He explained to our reporters how the fishmeal industry played a role in his decision to migrate. “We’re fishermen,” he told them, “but there’s no fish left here.”

After the fish are caught, the next step in turning them into feed is to deliver them to one of the 1,400 fishmeal plants around the globe.

During our investigation, we visited plants in Peru, Gambia, India, Indonesia, Mauritania, Senegal and Thailand.

Often found along the coast, these facilities are warehouses filled with huge mounds of decaying fish that are shoveled or backhoed into giant machines that cook, press, dry and then grind them up.

Despite corporate promises that fishmeal plants would create significant numbers of jobs, most of the facilities visited by our reporters had fewer than six workers present at any given time. Their jobs consisted of bagging the meal, driving forklifts and loading sacks onto trucks and shipping containers.

The cooking and pulverizing of millions of tons of fish creates a rancid, overpowering smell that can harm tourism by scaring off beach visitors and causing restaurants to close. The odor is more than just unpleasant; it’s a health hazard. In 2021, two fishermen in Chancay, Peru, died from chemical asphyxiation while unloading a vessel at a fishmeal plant. (The company, Pesquera Caral, did not respond to a request for comment.)

The unique “fishy” smell from rotting seafood comes from a chemical called trimethylamine, or TMA, which has been found to be carcinogenic. Globally, more than 16.5 million people, including nearly two million under the age of 15, live within a mile of the industry’s 1,400 plants.

In India alone, 388,000 people, including thousands of young children, live close to such plants. As of 2022, India was producing more than 300,000 tons of fishmeal annually, at least half of which was consumed domestically, largely to feed the country’s shrimp farms. Most of the remaining fishmeal was exported, making India the world’s third largest source of the feed.

But that economic success has not prevented fishmeal production from being a source of civil unrest. In recent years, plants in India were frequently the target of protests or strikes that aimed to shut them down. Residents claimed that the odor emanating from the plants was unbearable and caused breathing problems for children, elderly people and pregnant women. Protesters have blockaded roads to stop trucks, clashed with the police and, in one instance, spurred a boycott of local elections.

Such demonstrations sometimes turn violent. On April 19, 2024, the police clashed with protesters seeking to shut down the NPM fishmeal facility and other fish processing plants in the southern state of Tamil Nadu. When residents of one village staged a sit-in protest in the streets, a group of masked men carrying knives, bottles and clubs — thought to be acting at the behest of plant owners — emerged from an S.U.V. and attacked the protesters. Villagers lobbed stones at the S.U.V. and vandalized police squad cars. (NPM did not respond to a request for comment.)

The pollution at fishmeal plants goes beyond carcinogenic odors. In November 2020, authorities discovered that four facilities in an industrial area in Goa were disposing of waste into secretly drilled boreholes on their land, contaminating groundwater and sickening livestock and locals. In 2024, sections of the Periyar River in the state of Keralam frequently turned black, and thousands of dead fish rose to the surface — a pattern that residents said was most likely caused by fishmeal and other factories dumping their waste upstream.

Fire is another hazard at these plants. Fishmeal heats up as it decomposes and can combust spontaneously when stored. Since 2018, there have been at least 20 fires or explosions at fishmeal plants or on fishmeal vessels globally. On Aug. 7, 2023, three explosions at a fishmeal plant in Chimbote, on Peru’s coast, shattered windows of neighboring houses and sent dark smoke billowing into the sky. Angry residents took to the city’s streets in protest. “Don’t murder my children,” one protester’s sign read.

Local officials said they were gathering evidence that the explosions had been harmful to residents. “It must be demonstrated whether there have been any health effects,” an official from the local environmental assessment office told a Chimbote radio station. (An executive at the company that owned the plant, Pesquera Exalmar, said the explosions had occurred strictly within its boundaries and had “no impact on the structural integrity of adjacent homes.”)

Policing the fishmeal industry has proved difficult because the countries in which the feed is produced are typically poor and therefore eager for foreign investment. In Peru, foreign companies control the industry through direct plant ownership and dominant product purchasing power. Some of the biggest players driving global expansion are Cooke in Canada, which acquired Peru’s top fishing company in 2024; Austevoll Seafood in Norway, which owns the major Peruvian producer Austral Group; and several Chinese companies, which claim the bulk of Peru’s catch quota for anchoveta, a species of anchovy. As a result, these outside companies wield undue political leverage when it comes to ignoring rules.

So where does all the fishmeal — produced at such high human and environmental costs — end up?

Mostly in China, India, Indonesia, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Norway, which have turned fish farming into an industrial enterprise.

More than a thousand farm sites dot Norway’s coastline, where companies like Mowi, which controls about a fifth of the world’s farmed salmon business, have bred fish that resist infection.

Robots use underwater lasers to kill sea lice, a parasite that feeds on salmon.

These operations have an immense impact on the world’s ecosystems. At some Norwegian fish farms, a single salmon can eat anywhere from two to more than five times its weight in wild-caught fish. Altogether, the country’s fish farms produce three times as much waste in a year as the country’s 5.6 million residents flush down their toilets, according to a recent report from the Sunstone Institute, a global data science organization. The farms’ waste, which consists of salmon feces, rotting carcasses and uneaten feed, mostly cascades to the coastal seafloor, forming a noxious sludge that smothers marine life.

No country, however, is a larger producer of farmed seafood than China. Remarkably, China has built its aquaculture industry even in its far northwest Xinjiang region, the most landlocked part of the planet. Though just a tenth of Xinjiang’s 620,000 square miles are fit for human habitation, the region now hosts roughly 1,000 fish farms. These operations, which include farms in the Taklamakan Desert, China’s largest, produce almost 200,000 tons of seafood annually: salmon, trout, crayfish, bass, carp, crab, shrimp and tilapia.

The Chinese government directed the development of inland aquaculture in response to the environmental harms from its earlier fish-farming efforts, which were concentrated along the eastern coast. Through the 1980s and 1990s, local governments converted tidal flats and estuaries into shrimp ponds and marine cages, building hatcheries, feed mills and export infrastructure. But waste runoff from fish farms became a major source of pollution, degrading critical waterways, including the Yangtze River, which supplies much of the freshwater to Shanghai, and the Pearl River Delta, which supplies Hong Kong.

To create fish farms in the Taklamakan Desert, bulldozers flattened and compacted the sand before engineers tapped shallow wells — about six feet deep — to fill artificial ponds with brackish groundwater. Technicians seeded them with microorganisms that adjust the water’s chemistry to something closer to seawater, effectively transforming desert groundwater into a marine environment.

China trumpets its success in this forbidding region — an undeniable feat. Its state media refers to the desert fish farms as the “blue miracle.” Xinjiang’s aquaculture is not merely about producing fish, a column published by the state news outlet CGTN boasted in 2025, but also about the nation’s “protein security” and sustaining harmony between people and nature. “From snow-fed rivers to desert oases,” the column said, “Xinjiang has shown that blue dreams can indeed flourish on dry land.”

The company Xinjiang Tianyun Organic Agriculture, one of China’s most celebrated success stories, produces seafood that is exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States. The government aggressively promotes the region’s products, funding media tours of its fish farms for foreign reporters and drawing visitors to what one official has called “Xinjiang’s first cold-water fish theme park,” featuring a museum and a seafood restaurant.

China’s farmed seafood exports have become a source of concern among academic researchers and watchdog organizations for their extensive use of antimicrobials and anesthetics, which are used to ward off disease and keep fish calm in their crowded pens. By 2017, according to a paper in the journal Scientific Reports, more than half of all antifungals and antibiotics used in aquaculture worldwide were dispensed at Chinese facilities. Fish farmed this way can pose a health risk to those who consume it.

The people who produce this fish in China have faced additional risks. The state has tried to use fish farming, among other industries like cotton growing and tomato farming, to assimilate the non-Han ethnic minorities that predominate in Xinjiang — an effort that has also involved forced sterilization and the suppression of religious practices and native languages. This assimilation has largely been overseen by the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, a corporate entity loosely tied to the Chinese Army. The X.P.C.C. is made up of former soldiers turned economic developers and has a notorious international reputation for its coercive tactics. (The X.P.C.C. did not respond to a request for comment.)

By the time farmed seafood reaches your plate, it bears no trace of the harms to people and the environment that were required to produce it.

More than 80 percent of the seafood eaten in the United States comes from overseas.

Since 2022, the country has been the world’s largest importer of seafood, bringing in enormous quantities of shrimp, salmon, tilapia and catfish.

Only a tiny fraction is inspected on its way into the country.

The United States imports so much seafood in large part because American aquaculture is subject to significant oversight and regulation to protect health, safety and the environment. Federal and state rules dictate where fish farms can be built and the allowable levels of water quality, waste discharge, genetic modification and antibiotic use. These operations end up paying more than their counterparts abroad for higher-quality water treatment systems and testing equipment. Across commonly farmed seafood varieties, including salmon, shrimp and tilapia, domestic brands consistently command a steep price premium over foreign ones — in some cases double the cost.

In recent decades, often in response to public pressure, the American government has started to crack down on illegally or unfairly produced foreign goods, such as diamonds, garments and coffee. But there has been little outcry to date about seafood imports or the government’s performance in policing their origins and quality.

As of now, farmed fish produced using fishmeal is everywhere, sold in big grocery stores like Walmart and Kroger and served in cafeterias — even on Capitol Hill. If in the past year or so you sat down at any of the handful of cafeterias frequented by members of Congress, their staffs, and visitors in town for a tour, there’s a decent chance you dined on farmed seafood produced using fishmeal. Some of it could even have originated in Xinjiang, despite the fact that, in 2021, Congress banned entry of any goods produced “wholly or in part” in the region, on the presumption that such products involve state-imposed forced labor. (The U.S. government has formally characterized China’s actions in Xinjiang as a form of genocide.)

But American authorities inspect only a minuscule fraction of the seafood that is imported by China to the United States. Just this summer, after the Outlaw Ocean Project testified before Congress about the illegal flow of seafood from Xinjiang into the United States, the federal government added another Chinese exporter of farmed seafood to its list of banned companies: Xinjiang Tianyun Organic Agriculture.

Producing about 40 percent of China’s farmed salmon, Tianyun ships its fish through a major Chinese processor, Dalian Rich, which has supplied the American seafood brand Aqua Star, whose products are sold by Walmart and other major outlets, like the food distribution giant Sysco. Food from Sysco goes to nearly every corner of the American marketplace — more than 400,000 businesses in the last six weeks alone — as well as public school cafeterias, federal prisons, military bases and the dining halls on Capitol Hill.

(Xinjiang Tianyun Organic Agriculture said that it strictly complies with China’s laws on labor and contracts, and that it “has never been involved in, nor will it ever participate in, any form of forced labor.” A Sysco spokeswoman said the company takes seriously its obligation and commitment to uphold all international and local laws that protect labor, human and child labor rights, as well as the environment. Dalian Rich and Aqua Star did not respond to requests for comment. Walmart confirmed that it sources seafood from Aqua Star.)

Sysco says on its website that its “reputation is built upon the highest ethical standards of business conduct and fair dealing.” But our investigation found that fishing ships that supply Copeinca, the company whose workers died by toxic fume inhalation and that produces fishmeal for shrimp sold by Sysco, were tied to at least 30 fishing violations or other concerns, including fishing in marine protected areas, exceeding catch limits, and operating without a valid permit. (Copeinca said that it had “all valid permits required under Peruvian fisheries regulations,” and that there were no “final sanctions” on some of these matters because the company was disputing or appealing them.)

The gap between marketing rhetoric and supply-chain realities is common across the industry. Since 2019, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against seafood companies in the United States. The companies paid more than $2 million in settlement fees to resolve the cases. Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with SeaChoice, a Canadian sustainable-seafood group, says that as the public exerts more pressure on the seafood industry to better police supply chains, “investors will begin to see material, not just reputational, risk, and companies will have to adjust.”

The popularity of farmed seafood, in the United States and elsewhere, is only going to grow. The United Nations predicts that almost two-thirds of seafood eaten worldwide will come from aquaculture by 2035. Most of that production is likely to rely on fishmeal.

One way the industry could adjust would be to farm more seafood that does not need to be fed other fish. Bivalves like mussels, oysters, clams and scallops grow by filtering food from the water, so they don’t require manufactured feed. And where that feed is still needed, it could be made through the more efficient processing of leftovers — wasting less of the fish caught in the wild — and alternative ingredients such as algae, insects and microbial proteins.

Otherwise, the once-glowing promise of fish farming — grow more fish, catch fewer fish — is likely to remain broken.

ARTICLE

NATO Details Plan to Shield Ukraine’s European Allies From Russia
With the Russians intensifying sabotage, arson and cyberattacks against European nations supporting Ukraine, NATO divulged a blueprint, in case of war, to deter the Kremlin.
By Marc Santora and Steven Erlanger
Published 2026-10-12 17:06 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/nato-strategy-russia-europe.html

With Russia intensifying efforts to destabilize European nations that support Ukraine, NATO’s top military commander on Monday detailed a blueprint to deter Moscow in the event of outright war, a concept he summarized as “block, blunt and break.”

The commander, Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich of the U.S. Air Force, said the alliance does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable,” despite Russian sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and disinformation aimed at rattling European resolve and severing weapons supply lines to Ukraine.

But in that environment, the general said he had made a deliberate decision to publicly disclose the core of NATO’s classified war plan — known as its “theory of victory” — to bolster confidence across 32 allied countries.

“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this,” General Grynkewich said on Monday at the Warsaw Security Forum. “We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”

Yet even as the American four-star commander stressed that NATO’s ultimate defense rests on unity, stark geopolitical contradictions echoed through the conference hall. President Trump’s decision to unilaterally ease sanctions on the Kremlin in order to purchase Russian diesel fuel highlighted a jarring disconnect between NATO’s military planning and European support for Ukraine, and the White House’s transactional diplomacy and hostility toward Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump appeared to blame Ukraine — not for the first time — for the war, and said it should “get a new president.”

By injecting hard cash directly into the Kremlin’s coffers, the administration risked undercutting years of allied economic pressure, muddying the Western coalition’s deterrence messaging and testing the very solidarity General Grynkewich was in Warsaw to project.

Even if the amounts of diesel purchases are small, the symbolism of division is large. Ukraine and Europe argue that only economic and military pressure will persuade President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to end the war he started. Mr. Trump and his envoys apparently favor enticing Mr. Putin with “deals,” instead.

The tension was evident earlier in the day when Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland warned that the defense of Ukraine and the security of NATO are inextricably tied.

“Anyone who, for any reason — treason, stupidity, or money — wants to weaken Ukraine in its defense against Russian aggression is clearly acting against their own nation, the security of their own state, and its sovereignty,” Mr. Tusk said.

Pressed afterward on whether European allies could count on Washington to defend them, General Grynkewich dismissed suggestions that the United States would waver, citing the thousands of American forces along NATO’s eastern flank, including in Poland. He also pointed to recent summit communiqués that reaffirmed the bedrock collective-defense guarantee of Article 5.

European fears of an emboldened Russia have been increasing. Michal Koudelka, the director of the Czech Security Information Service, the country’s domestic spy service, warned his Parliament on Monday that Russia could escalate “in a matter of months rather than years to a significantly riskier and more serious operation,” which could include, down the road, limited military action against a NATO state.

General Grynkewich said the new NATO doctrine draws directly on modern battlefield lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East.

Specifically, he said, the blueprint pairs precision weapons with what he described as “affordable mass” — large numbers of autonomous systems, drones, and electronic warfare assets designed to sustain a protracted war of attrition.

The “block, blunt, and break” strategy he outlined is designed to stop an invasion in its tracks without trying to conquer the enemy’s homeland.

First, he said, allied forces immediately “block” an attack at the border to prevent the enemy from seizing territory, a change in strategy since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Next, they “blunt” the offensive by hitting advancing troops from the air, sea and land to strip their momentum. Finally, if the attack continues, they “break” the enemy by targeting the supplies, communication links and command networks that keep their frontline forces fighting, weakening the aggressor to the point of collapse.

General Grynkewich stressed that NATO is not interested in taking an adversary’s land. By limiting the objective strictly to the tactical and operational neutralization of the adversary, NATO intends to deny the enemy any pretext for escalation, he said, placing the moral and strategic burden of expanding the war squarely on the aggressor.

“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt, should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”

Kremlin officials have routinely dismissed the alarms being raised across Europe.

“We have no intention to fight Europe, to engage in warfare with Europe; that is utter nonsense,” Sergey V. Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, said during a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly in September. “But Europe is preparing for war with us,” he said. “This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy.”

Adam Goldman contributed reporting from London.

ARTICLE

How a Book Editor Lives on $74,000 in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn
Mo Crist has three family goals, but financing them is a tricky proposition in an expensive city like New York.
By John Leland
Published 2026-10-12 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/12/nyregion/nyc-budgeting-affordability-crist.html

How can people possibly afford to live in one of the most expensive cities on the planet? It’s a question New Yorkers hear a lot, often delivered with a mix of awe, pity and confusion.

We surveyed hundreds of New Yorkers about how they spend, splurge and save. We found that many people — rich, poor or somewhere in between — live life as a series of small calculations that add up to one big question: What makes living in New York worth it?

Mo Crist arrived at Barnard College from a small town in western Pennsylvania with plans to become a doctor, then made one of those decisions that come with long-term ramifications.

“I thought if I can’t really hack it in the sciences, maybe I should do something that I really love, which is reading and writing,” Mx. Crist said. “And so I did my undergrad in English.”

Looking back on the career path that followed, they added, “I knew that it wasn’t going to pay the big bucks or help my life in New York to become the ‘Sex and the City’ kind of situation.”

At 30, after eight years of working in book publishing, they have a coveted editing job at Bloomsbury Publishing, a list of writers they enjoy and an apartment in a desirable neighborhood in a city that continues to delight them.

They also have student debt of $15,000, for which they are about $1,000 behind in payments.

And a salary of $74,000.

For Mx. Crist, who did not choose their career for the money, money now plays a large role in the choices they make. They and their partner, Sophie Pugh-Sellers, an assistant editor at Grove Atlantic, share an apartment in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn, where they pay $2,600 in rent. They were lucky to find it through a friend, Mx. Crist said, but it has its quirks, including slanted floors and occasional “electrical issues.”

“We want three things,” Mx. Crist said. “We want to get married, to have kids and to buy property. And it feels like in our position in the world now, it’s really only possible to do one of those things, and so we’re constantly thinking about how to change that.

“Having kids is the one that feels the most necessary or the most exciting and doable to us. But there’s so much standing in the way financially. I think that we definitely don’t want to stay in this apartment when we have kids.”

No Fast Fashion

Mx. Crist regularly scans the apartment listings online, but even the unpromising places rent for $3,000 or more. “So we both feel stuck in this apartment right now, knowing that we have such a good deal in such a good location, but also knowing that it can’t last forever,”

In the meantime, the couple have lives to live and bills to pay.

At work, Mx. Crist said, many of their peers rely on money from their parents to afford New York City on a book publishing salary. Mx. Crist uses those people as motivation, they said. “I would say that my career has been fueled in large part by resentment and competition, which is not always the healthiest.”

Mx. Crist and their partner get most of their food from the Park Slope Food Co-op, which keeps their combined grocery expenses to around $700 to $750 per month. The couple takes turns paying for restaurant meals. About once a week, the two use the app Too Good to Go, which offers end-of-the-day “surprise bags” of food from restaurants for under $10.

They still go out to dinner twice a month, which they treat as special — i.e., costly — occasions. A recent dinner at a new Indian restaurant in their neighborhood, Malvan — “absolutely amazing,” Mx. Crist said — set the couple back $200 for entrees, a shared appetizer and a drink each. “I’m actively trying to stop myself from going there more often because it was pretty expensive,” they said.

By taste and by necessity, Mx. Crist buys their clothing and furniture used. “I’m firmly against buying any fast fashion, fast furniture kind of stuff,” they said. “And so I didn’t want to go the IKEA route or Wayfair or things like that. It’s so much more exciting and interesting to have a vision for something that you want, and then go out and find it. I find as much joy in the hunt as I do in finding the object.”

The Furniture Hunt

During the Covid pandemic, Mx. Crist’s parents gave them the car they’d driven as a teenager, a hatchback now 15 years old, with 250,000 miles on it. The car made it easier to go to the Hudson Valley for vintage furniture stores or estate sales — and also to get out of the city for hikes.

After a long search Mx. Crist found a midcentury dining room table at Dobbin Street Vintage Co-op in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, for $700, then matched it with four Cesca chairs from the ’70s, designed by Marcel Breuer, which they found at an estate sale for $40 each. “That was a great deal,” they said.

A less successful deal was a $250 coffee table from an antique shop in Beacon, which seemed like a good idea at the time. “I’m pretty good at not regretting my purchases,” they said. “But that’s one that I definitely regret.”

Mx. Crist shares the car with a friend, which keeps expenses down, but repairs still run to $2,000 to $3,000 a year. They recently switched insurance carriers, which cut their shared bill to $100 a month, from $300.

Mx. Crist eschews expensive haircuts or spa treatments, and dresses in a “uniform” from thrift stores like MyUnique Thrift in the Bronx or L Train Vintage in Bushwick, Brooklyn: “Black jeans, T-shirt and some kind of overshirt, which are all thrifted,” they said.

Priced Out of Dogs and Weddings

The couple don’t take vacations, except for an annual week in Cape Cod with Ms. Pugh-Sellers’s family. They had to skip two friends’ out-of-town weddings recently because they could not afford the airfare. They would like to have a dog, but that, also, is too expensive, so they foster dogs on a short-term basis, for a rescue agency that pays for medical care and food.

Asked about splurges, Mx. Crist considered. They are not really the splurging type, they said.

“I think the biggest splurge is living in New York itself, and having access to the New York life,” they said, speaking a few weeks before turning 30. “That feels every month like a splurge.”

Turning 30 has made them think more about the future than they did in their 20s, which has meant thinking more about money, which can be an uncomfortable subject. If they lived in Pittsburgh, they acknowledged, they could do a lot more for less.

“But I don’t think I would be as happy going into 30 if I didn’t live in New York,” they said. “I’m kind of shocked almost daily at how much I love about my life and how much that is dependent on the city that I live in.”

ARTICLE

Four Hours and Three Minutes in Ithaca
On the most traumatic night in a young woman’s life, a good man could not be found.
By David French
Published 2026-10-11 11:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/opinion/cornell-jane-doe-vietnam-my-lai.html

Four hours and three minutes.

That’s the total time that elapsed between 1:42 a.m. — the apparent moment when a Cornell student put the words “free pussy” in a group Snapchat message that could be seen by dozens of members of the Cornell chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity — and 5:45 a.m. on Oct. 20, 2024, roughly the time when Jane Doe says she lost consciousness, bringing her ordeal to an end.

What happened during that time? Multiple men came into the room and — according to a lawsuit filed by Jane Doe last month and various documents disclosed in the case — at least some of the men snorted drugs off her body and had oral and vaginal sex with her, all when she was unquestionably very drunk and very high.

As dreadful as all that is, I’m also interested in what didn’t happen. No one, apparently, acted to end the encounter. Instead — as the group message indicates — men celebrated. “I fucking love chi phi,” one brother wrote. “Like you can walk in and whip it out,” he said later. “Shop still open?” asked another.

I want to be careful here and not draw a straight line from our porn-saturated culture to this dreadful incident. Sexual depravity existed long before pornography was ubiquitous, but this encounter was almost a textbook example of what porn teaches men about sex. It’s not about intimacy. It’s not a manifestation of love, much less care. Instead, sex is an entirely self-regarding and inherently exploitative act.

I’m not writing this column to adjudicate legal guilt. The facts are complicated, and it is almost always difficult to know precisely what happened when copious amounts of drugs and alcohol are involved.

Hovering over the entire case is a New York legal standard that draws a sharp distinction between voluntary and involuntary intoxication. Put simply, if you’re voluntarily intoxicated but not “physically helpless” (passed out, for example), proving incapacitation becomes extremely difficult. But if you’re involuntarily intoxicated, you are considered incapacitated — even when your level of intoxication is the same as that of the voluntarily intoxicated person.

Think of it like this: If the Cornell men forced Jane Doe to drink shots or snort ketamine, then, in the state’s eyes, she’d be incapacitated. But if she voluntarily drank and consumed ketamine to the same level of intoxication, she would not be considered incapacitated.

This makes little sense. Calling intoxication voluntary doesn’t render intoxicated people more aware or capable of making informed decisions. They’re just as vulnerable to predation as they would be if, say, they were unknowingly served spiked fruit punch.

Any man of decency should recognize that the legal distinction (assuming he is aware of it) isn’t a grant of moral permission. And any man with any degree of moral fiber who saw that message should have immediately acted to end the encounter, even if it cost him the “brotherhood” he loves.

Last week Christine Emba wrote a beautiful and compelling guest essay in our pages about the inadequacy of consent as the primary moral basis for sexual intimacy. It’s the legal base line, not a moral threshold. But what is the moral threshold?

Conservative Christians like me often respond with a pat answer: marriage. But even that’s inadequate and incomplete. Marital sex can be every bit as abusive and exploitative as an encounter in a frat house. Instead of consent, I’d suggest a different standard, one that applies not just to sex in marriage — and not just to sex alone — but to all of our human interactions.

Let’s talk about care.

In other words, we should constantly ask ourselves, “If I cared for this person, what would I do?” Even if an obviously drunk or high person is asking you for sex (though whether that happened in this case is disputed, especially as events unfolded later in the evening) — and even if you’re powerfully attracted to that person — if you truly cared for the person, would you initiate or engage in an encounter that any sentient person knows might be deeply regretted the next morning, the next day or the next week?

Is an orgasm so sacred to you that you can’t wait until sobriety to have sex?

And if you see a message like the Snapchat message at Cornell, imagine what you’d do if you actually cared for the person they’re talking about. Would you not put “STOP” in all caps in the chat and race to that room? Or do we delegate any concern or regard for people like Jane Doe to someone who might have a closer relationship to her?

It can take an immense amount of courage to actually care enough about another human being to intervene — especially if a person you don’t know needs protection from people you do know. This month, just as new details about the Cornell case seemed to be hitting the news every day, we covered the My Lai massacre during the Vietnam War in the Law of War class I teach at Lipscomb University in Nashville.

For those who don’t remember, the My Lai massacre was one of the worst episodes in American military history. American soldiers in Vietnam went on a killing spree, murdering hundreds of innocent civilians.

Obviously, the massacre was far more extreme than anything that happened at the Chi Phi house, but I bring it up for a simple reason: to introduce you to a man named Hugh Thompson.

Thompson is an American hero. He was the Army helicopter pilot who saw the massacre from the air, immediately radioed an alarm and landed his aircraft, placing it between his own brothers-in-arms and a small group of innocent civilians they were pursuing. He even ordered his crew to open fire on American soldiers if they tried to kill the people he was protecting.

He cared for innocent people he did not know and probably would never know, and he cared for them enough to risk his life and the rejection and scorn of his own brotherhood to save their lives. In the process, he also showed care for his brothers-in-arms — he stopped them from continuing to commit the most heinous of crimes.

Think about how much less courage it would have taken to act that night at Cornell. Then consider again that no one intervened. To them, “Free pussy” wasn’t an alarm bell; it was an invitation.

Details of the Cornell case emerged just as we learned more about the criminal case against Andrew Tate, one of the most celebrated influencers in the manosphere. He made his fortune (such as it is) in part through pornography, by reportedly coercing women into becoming cam girls online.

Now he’s facing charges in Britain, including rape, human trafficking and possessing extreme pornography (including images of bestiality). This man was celebrated in parts of right-wing America.

In fact, as ProPublica reported in 2025, Paul Ingrassia, a White House official (and a former lawyer for Tate and his brother), asked Department of Homeland Security officials to return Tate’s electronic devices to him when they were seized upon his entry to the country.

Chi Phi at Cornell, which was shut down in 2024 and remains barred from campus, represents the culture that Andrew Tate and countless others like him have built. We do not have to declare what happened that terrible night illegal to know that it was depraved.

Thompson and Tate sit at opposite ends of the moral spectrum. They represent the angel and devil on the shoulders of young men. One was willing to lay down his life for people he did not know. The other offers aggression without virtue, sex without love and money without meaning.

But to put things in language that many young men will understand: Hugh Thompson was strong. Andrew Tate is weak. Tate is a slave to his desires, and all his aggression is directed at those who are more vulnerable than he is.

“Courage,” C.S. Lewis wrote in one of my favorite quotes, “is not simply one of the virtues but the form of every virtue at the testing point, which means, at the point of highest reality.”

How do we know what courage is? When we see a man risk himself to care for another person, that’s courage. The legal judgment may be uncertain, but the moral verdict is already in. On the most traumatic night in a young woman’s life, a good man could not be found.

SUMMARY

While President Trump has claimed that noncitizens voted en masse and even tipped the scales in recent elections, research from partisan and nonpartisan groups alike has shown that instances of noncitizen voting are so rare that they have never been significant enough to change the outcome of an election. Investigations into noncitizen voting have historically followed a pattern. Nowhere did federal and state charges for noncitizen voting exceed 25 people in a state in a recent election, The Times found.

ARTICLE

How Claims of Widespread Noncitizen Voting Fall Apart
Investigations into noncitizen voting follow a pattern. Each inquiry ends with few, if any, prosecutions.
By Amy Schoenfeld Walker, Jeremy White and Seamus Hughes
Published 2026-10-15 23:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/15/us/politics/noncitizen-voting-data.html

While President Trump has claimed that noncitizens voted en masse and even tipped the scales in recent elections, research from partisan and nonpartisan groups alike has shown that instances of noncitizen voting are so rare that they have never been significant enough to change the outcome of an election.

Investigations into noncitizen voting have historically followed a pattern. First, state or federal election officials report that hundreds or thousands of noncitizens may be on their voter lists. After further review, the figures often shrink to dozens. Each inquiry ends with few, if any, prosecutions.

“We keep finding the same story over and over and over again, which is very, very small numbers,” said Christopher Mann, the research director at the Center for Election Innovation and Research in Washington, which tracks reports of ineligible voting.

But just how small are those numbers?

The center tracks public reports of suspected noncitizen registration and voting made by election officials and prosecutors. The New York Times reviewed those reports and examined additional court records dating back to 2020. Nowhere did federal and state charges for noncitizen voting exceed 25 people in a state in a recent election, The Times found.

Florida, Pennsylvania and Texas were among the states with the most charges for noncitizen voting in the 2024 election.

Election officials regularly check their voter lists for ineligible voters and either remove them or refer them to prosecutors. But Trump administration officials have said that the government will find more of these cases if it simply looks harder, and they have launched a robust campaign to root out voter fraud. In recent weeks, federal prosecutors have brought charges against dozens of people.

“We’re just getting started,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in late September.

The Department of Homeland Security has assigned hundreds of agents to hunt for noncitizens on state voting lists, and it has begun investigating nonprofits it says may be recruiting noncitizens to vote. Justice Department leaders have threatened state election officials with criminal charges if noncitizens cast ballots in their states.

Even so, the administration’s claims of large-scale voter fraud have not stood up to scrutiny. Election officials and experts say federal investigators have relied on matching names from voter lists to a massive federal database, when both sources may be incomplete or out of date.

People who recently became naturalized citizens, for example, can be flagged as false positives.

In one instance, D.H.S. officials told Nevada this summer that they had found nearly 16,000 noncitizens registered to vote in the state. When the agency later sent a list of 185 names, state election officials said that all were citizens.

D.H.S. also said it had found more than 2,500 noncitizen voters in Georgia. The state reviewed the list and said that no more than 150 had voted.

Prosecutions under the effort have also been scarce. A review of federal court records shows that, since 2025, the Trump administration has charged 131 people with illegally registering or voting as a noncitizen.

Most of these cases are ongoing, but 25 people have been found guilty or pleaded guilty. Two people have been acquitted, and charges were dropped or cases were dismissed for four other individuals.

The federal government has traditionally been more reliant on states to handle voter fraud. During the Biden administration, court records show, federal prosecutors charged 13 people.

Research shows that earlier convictions for noncitizen voter fraud were exceedingly rare. The Heritage Foundation identified 71 criminal convictions nationwide for noncitizen voting between 2000 and 2025.

It is possible that a larger number of noncitizens may register to vote or cast a ballot and never be prosecuted for voter fraud. State election officials sometimes remove potential noncitizens from voter lists without bringing charges against them. Prosecutors typically have to prove that people knowingly registered or voted to win a conviction.

But noncitizens often appear on voter rolls because of mistakes rather than an intention to commit fraud, researchers and voting rights advocates say.

For example, New Jersey improperly added as many as 6,600 noncitizens to its voter lists in 2023 and 2024 because of a motor vehicle department software error that registered people to vote when they applied for a driver’s license or state identification card.

State officials said that approximately 340 of those people had cast ballots, one of the larger confirmed instances of noncitizen voting, though it represents just a tiny share of the state’s voting public.

It’s also just a fraction of the number of noncitizen voters that the Department of Homeland Security claimed to have found in New Jersey — 35,152.

SUMMARY

Here’s a short poem by Emily Dickinson that doesn’t so much close or narrow the gap as somersault over it, landing us in a place where the rules of time, space and meaning have been rewritten by the sheer force of an imaginative will, reveling in language’s generative potential. And because this is a Dickinson poem, it doesn’t proceed in tidy sing-song fashion. In the first stanza of another poem written around the same time, Dickinson associates prose with confinement and punishment.

ARTICLE

This Poem Will Hit You Where You Live
Emily Dickinson makes 50 words contain endless possibilities.
By A.O. Scott
Published 2026-10-21 22:41 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/21/books/emily-dickinson-poem-i-dwell-in-possibility.html

We are all too aware of the gap between what is and what might be. On one side are the plain facts we are supposed to face, on the other the wild speculations we would rather indulge.

Here’s a short poem by Emily Dickinson that doesn’t so much close or narrow the gap as somersault over it, landing us in a place where the rules of time, space and meaning have been rewritten by the sheer force of an imaginative will, reveling in language’s generative potential.

In 50 words, Dickinson works her way through a single, elaborate metaphor.

The speaker takes on the voice of an architect, a builder — maybe even a real estate broker — as she details the features of her miraculous dwelling.

We’re given a brisk, three-stanza tour of the property. (“Stanza,” it’s worth recalling, is an Italian word for “room.”)

So much light!

You know it’s special from the moment you walk in.

Durable construction.

Plenty of privacy.

And the views!

“Gambrels” is an architectural term, referring to a sturdy, expansive roof design — the kind you might see on a barn.

But in a footnote, Dickinson offers “gables” as an alternative, for those who prefer a narrower, pointier option.

Of course this fantastic house isn’t for sale. It’s the speaker’s home, where she entertains dazzling company and goes about her work.

That work might be writing poems, something Dickinson herself always did by hand.

She copied out her poems and sewed them together into booklets known as fascicles.

(Here are those “Gambrels” and “Gables.”)

This poem is a solid piece of work. Rhymes and near rhymes are scattered throughout.

The lines have a vigorous rhythm, four beats followed by three (sometimes known as “hymnal meter” because of its ubiquity in Protestant sacred music).

And because this is a Dickinson poem, it doesn’t proceed in tidy sing-song fashion. There is syncopation and surprise, a music that is as otherworldly, and as precise, as the metaphor.

Such marvellous craft. Such pleasing carpentry.

Not that Dickinson was a stranger to prose, or to the pleasures of the literal. “They say that ‘home is where the heart is,’” she once wrote in a letter to a friend. “I think it is where the house is, and the adjacent buildings.”

Her own home — where she was born in 1830, died in 1886 and wrote most of her nearly 1,800 poems — was a solid brick Federal-style house in Amherst, Mass. It belonged to her father, a prominent lawyer and politician. During the Civil War, when this poem was bound in its fascicle, the Dickinson household included Emily, her parents and her sister. An adjacent building on the property was home to Emily’s brother; his wife, Susan Huntington Gilbert Dickinson; and their children.

Dickinson is sometimes thought of as a recluse — a devout, solitary shut-in communing with God, her genius and a handful of acquaintances, including a few well-known New England literary figures. But while it’s true that after the mid-1850s she rarely ventured far from the Dickinson homestead, she was nonetheless part of a busy social network.

She was a prolific letter writer, with many warm and familiar relationships, none more intense than the bond with Susan, her neighbor, sister-in-law and intimate lifelong friend. She wrote to Susan in both prose and verse — more than to any other correspondent, including early drafts and “letter poems” — enlisting her as critic, confidante and muse.

Let’s leave the house of prose and slip back into the poem.

If we take the first line as literally as we can, we can say it describes a conditional state of being, a place that is not a place at all.

It’s a more beautiful (and perhaps, in another meaning, a more equitable) situation than the alternative.

In the first stanza of another poem written around the same time, Dickinson associates prose with confinement and punishment.

To be shut up in prose is to be silenced. To be released from it is to find a particular kind of voice, though one that is not without constraints of its own.

The poetic house has a structure, though it doesn’t conform to prosaic building codes. The poem may be made of lines, but it isn’t linear. Its meanings radiate.

The house is full of windows and open to the sky …

… but it’s also solid and secret.

It’s the speaker’s personal domain, but she isn’t always alone in it.

And what exactly happens in this final room?

Is she writing herself a mansion of heavenly bliss? Gabling — or gambreling — her hands into a gesture of prayer? Greeting a religious vision? Enfolding her lovely visitor in an embrace?

Maybe this guest has dropped by from the humdrum place next door, to be welcomed into a private Eden built for two. A fairer home for the fairest one of all.

Anything is possible.

SUMMARY

Economists argue that, overall, life is more affordable now. But sober economic assessments don’t necessarily affect how people feel when they’re staring at the skyrocketing costs of the big items needed to achieve a middle-class life, like housing or education. This critical component of modern life has had one of the biggest cost increases.

ARTICLE

Life Feeling Too Expensive? It’s Not Just You. And It’s Not Just Inflation.
Affordability is expected to be a major issue for younger voters in the midterms. Here’s a snapshot of some reasons people are feeling pinched.
By Sabrina Tavernise, Eden Weingart, Nico Chilla, Georgia Gee and Steven Rich
Published 2026-10-22 01:09 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/21/us/inflation-prices-real-estate-child-care-affordabilty.html

Your parents may talk about how they scrimped in their 20s. But the truth is, it probably wasn’t long before they owned a house. The median age of the first-time home buyer in 1987 was 29. Today, that first-time home buyer is 40.

Economists argue that, overall, life is more affordable now. Our wages are far higher and we pay far less for many basic goods than we did 40 years ago. But sober economic assessments don’t necessarily affect how people feel when they’re staring at the skyrocketing costs of the big items needed to achieve a middle-class life, like housing or education.

How exactly have these costs changed? Let’s take a closer look.

Housing

Housing is the financial and emotional center of many people’s lives. Prices have risen rapidly.

You can find similar increases in the price of homes throughout the country.

Stratospheric real estate prices might not be surprising in a place like New York City:

Two-story family home in Brooklyn

But what about a starter home in Spokane, Wash.:

Four-bedroom house in Spokane, Wash.

Or a townhouse in Atlanta:

Attached townhouse in Atlanta

Child Care

For many families, child care is an essential expense. The modern economy is more or less built around two working parents. There again, costs have exploded.

Children’s activities have gotten more expensive too. When your parents went to the YMCA summer day camp in the 1970s and 1980s, it was cheap. Not anymore.

One week of summer day camp in Newark, Del.

Entertainment

OK, these next items are luxuries. But we included them because they make life fun, and because we remember going to a Van Halen concert in 1984 for $13.50 (about $45 in today’s dollars). In other words, middle-class people could afford them.

The Super Bowl is extreme. But what about something more basic, like camping, visiting an amusement park or skiing? A night of babysitting used to bring in enough money to cover a one-day ski pass. Not anymore.

Ski ticket in Breckenridge, Colo.

Single day pass to Disney World

Even camping in a national park, still relatively affordable, has more than doubled in price.

Camping in Yosemite at Bridalveil Creek

Education

Perhaps the single most important ingredient for a secure place in the American middle class is a college degree.

Health Care

Last but not least is health care. This critical component of modern life has had one of the biggest cost increases.

Why have prices gone up so much, well beyond the rate of inflation? Many complicated forces were behind each of these increases. With housing, for example, demand has gone up faster than supply. With child care, a labor-intensive industry, it has more to do with rising wages.

But don’t despair. The costs of some key things have gone down. Groceries, for example, used to take up a far bigger portion of our income. We also now spend far less for computers, clothes, toys and televisions than we did 40 years ago.

Mid-sized Sony television

American Girl Doll

So even if you can’t become a homeowner anytime soon, you can probably afford a much nicer TV for the place you’re renting.

midterms-pollsters-pundits-scorecard-october.html

SUMMARY

My head sees Trump’s incredibly dismal approval ratings, the strong polling for Democrats in Senate races — even in traditionally conservative places like Iowa, Kansas and Texas — and the huge Democratic lead in the House generic ballot. All that points to Democrats taking 235 to 240 House seats and winning a Senate majority. Win two of those three, and Democrats are on track to win the Senate.

ARTICLE

Opinion | The Midterms Are Next Week. Here’s Who We Think Will Win.
It’s crunch time and still looking bullish for Democrats.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-26 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/26/opinion/midterms-pollsters-pundits-scorecard-october.html

Which party will control the House and the Senate?

If the elections were held today …

My head sees Trump’s incredibly dismal approval ratings, the strong polling for Democrats in Senate races — even in traditionally conservative places like Iowa, Kansas and Texas — and the huge Democratic lead in the House generic ballot. All that points to Democrats taking 235 to 240 House seats and winning a Senate majority. But my heart says I would rather not be disappointed again. I’ll go with the heart and predict a solid Democratic win — but not an epic blowout.

A 50-50 Senate seemed a stretch earlier this year; now it’s one of the least optimistic Democratic scenarios, and the debate in the House is how big a majority Democrats will get. What’s changed for the G.O.P. is that nothing has changed. Gas prices are still high, the war and scandals continue, the president is doing nothing to help his party, and Republican spending hasn’t moved the needle. That doesn’t mean there isn’t uncertainty. Most major forecasts center on a 51- or 52-seat Democratic majority in the Senate — I come down on 52! — but my model gives any outcome between 49 and 54 seats a roughly 10 percent chance.

Nothing has slowed Democrats’ momentum heading into Election Day, which means they should easily take the House. Redistricting has emptied out the truly competitive battlegrounds that Trump won in 2024 by 10 points or less, but the Democrats’ national advantage now lets them raid the far more numerous prizes beyond that threshold. The Senate is closer to a tossup than most people think. The prospect of another red-state polling error looms — particularly in the Midwest. But even with a normal polling error, states like Alaska, Ohio and Texas are no worse than a tossup. Win two of those three, and Democrats are on track to win the Senate.

I’m taking numbers from the Silver Bulletin model “as is” for the Senate and the House. Republicans seem to be all but giving up on the House, and if something like the Times/Siena generic ballot poll is anywhere close to right (with Democrats favored by 11 percentage points), even Republican gerrymanders that were intended to produce flips might start to fail. That’s a big “if.” But if that’s the national environment we’re seeing, you’ll probably also see some surprising pickups in House districts against Republican candidates who have never faced an environment like this one.

Despite improved Democratic polling, I’m not moving my Senate forecast up, because of the base-line partisanship of the states in many of the close Senate races. It is looking like a very good year for Democrats, so a state like Ohio, at Trump plus 11.2 in 2024, seems like a safe Democratic pickup. The trio of seats around plus 13 (Alaska, Texas, Iowa) are also all in play. However, the next seat after that is Kansas, at Trump plus 16, followed by South Carolina at plus 18. Democrats are likely to top out in the Alaska-Texas-Iowa zone, winning two of those three states.

Two forces are shaping these midterms: discontent and calcification. People are frustrated with the status quo, and they blame the president and his party. But at the same time, voters know the parties want to build very different worlds — and they know which world they prefer. Under these conditions, it’s hard to entertain voting for the other side. It makes politics feel stuck, or calcified. To account for both forces, my rule was to examine the close races in each chamber and assume Democrats (1) win the competitive seats they already hold, (2) pick up close seats if they won them recently and (3) otherwise lose.

Pay attention to these numbers

Which 2024 voters will turn out in 2026?

Midterms have drastically lower turnout than presidential elections. About 159 million people voted in 2020, but only around 108 million did in 2022. So one big question every midterm is “Which party brings back more of its presidential voters?” Right now, it looks like Democrats will. Eighty-seven percent of 2024 Kamala Harris voters say they are backing Democratic candidates this fall, compared with 77 percent of Trump 2024 voters supporting Republican hopefuls, according to a recent Pew survey. If Ken Paxton in Texas or another struggling G.O.P. candidate ends up winning, I would assume that some of that 23 percent of wary Republicans ultimately showed up for their party.

How are friends and families voting?

Can we gauge how the prevailing winds are pushing less partisan voters? A personal favorite: My firm, Equis, asks voters how their close contacts are planning to vote. It gives us a sense of what they consider normal or popular. I’ll use Hispanic voters: The share reporting that their social circles were mostly supporting Trump went from 19 percent in 2016 to 30 percent in 2020 to 42 percent in 2024, per our best estimates. In our latest poll, we see a reversal, almost to the level of 2016: Just 22 percent of Hispanic voters say most of the people they interact with regularly are supporting Republicans in the midterms.

Trump’s approval rating is even worse than it looks

There’s been a lot of talk about Trump’s approval ratings, but in some ways they’re even worse when you get under the hood. According to our tracking, only about 20 percent of Americans strongly approve of Trump’s performance, while nearly 50 percent strongly disapprove. That’s hardened, vociferous opposition that would typically correlate with turning out to vote. Meanwhile, the deep devotion of Trump’s base has eroded into lukewarm support. His most fervent fans might turn out if Trump were on the ballot. But what about for Roger Marshall or Ken Paxton?

The vanishing American dream

In 1986, The Wall Street Journal asked people if they thought the American dream was still alive. That year, just 11 percent of Americans said the dream was “not really alive.” An Economist/YouGov poll repeated the question recently. In 2026, the number who think the American dream is not alive jumped to 43 percent — almost half the country thinks it’s dead. In a similar vein, in a 1984 Time magazine poll, 61 percent of the country said they had grown more optimistic about life over the past decade. Today, less than a quarter of the population feels this way. Many Americans no longer believe tomorrow will be better than today. Democrats may get the nod this November, but this is a challenge for both parties — and right now, a bigger one for Republicans.

Gas prices could climb even higher

Gas prices have driven Trump’s approval rating to historic lows and set the stage for a blue wave. The question now is if late movement in those highly visible prices will turn public sentiment even further. A sudden spike to $5 a gallon, for example, could convince a lot of Republican voters to just stay home. If you’re the incumbent party, you really don’t want the last thing a voter notices before driving to the polls to be the cost of that drive.

Swinging away from Trump

Of the Trump 2024 voters who now disapprove of the job he’s doing, 42 percent rate the cost of living their top issue. Worry about costs is stronger among Trump defectors than it is for any other swing group. The very constituencies that helped get Trump elected again — working-class Latinos and young men — are the ones feeling the affordability crisis the hardest and now swinging away from him the most. If Democrats do win control of Congress, the reason will be simple: affordability concerns exacerbated by high gas prices brought on by the war in Iran.

How confident are you in the polls?

I’m fairly confident in the polls, in part because we have another indication that Republicans are unusually vulnerable this cycle: The party’s various campaign committees are spending millions of dollars in districts and states that are normally reliably Republican. I am very confident that Democrats will win a House majority and gain Senate seats (though maybe not a majority). When it comes to specific gubernatorial and Senate races, I’m less confident. I’m thinking of female Democratic governors in Ohio, Georgia and Texas. Or in Senate races, Democrats winning seats in Iowa, Kansas and Texas, and in Georgia and North Carolina by close to double digits. I just worry all of those polls are just too blue to be true. Pollsters may not have reached enough conservative-leaning white people for the polls to be accurate.

What polls offer is perspective, not prophecy. They have taken us as far as they can, in painting the national environment, identifying voters on the move and spotting competitive seats. You look at surveys in a place like Kansas and see Trump voters hanging out in the undecided column. How those voters break, or whether they stay home, can be informed by polling, but ultimately we’re giving educated guesses. That said, I generally assume support for Democrats is overstated among white voters in red areas (and underestimated among Black voters everywhere). The current estimates could also be misreading the makeup of the electorate — for example, if more younger voters turn out than we’d normally expect in a midterm, the polls will have underrated Democrats.

Based on the polls, a good, if not great, Democratic night feels inevitable. But it is possible to read the environment right and the map wrong. Consider 2016: The national polls were not that far off the final margin in the popular vote, but they failed catastrophically in the very states that decided the election. There’s little evidence that the difficulty pollsters have had in contacting rural, working-class voters has been resolved. On the contrary, the problem seems worse this year than ever before. If there’s a recurring pattern, it’s that of overestimating Democrats in red states. And geographic sorting has made these states exactly where Senate control is decided.

Most analysts seem to have little to no confidence in the polling, but maybe they should. Polls in the past two midterms were pretty accurate and unbiased. More important, they may not be projecting anything all that remarkable. “Waves” are very normal in the midterms and almost the default outcome. You might expect a bigger-than-average wave given Trump’s approval numbers, gas prices, Iran and Epstein. I could absolutely see the polls being wrong again, especially in the Midwest, where they have overestimated Democrats in the past. But polling error can run either way; I could imagine Republican turnout collapsing, giving Democrats an even bigger rout.

I believe the polls are broadly correct, and Republicans hoping for a huge miss are fooling themselves. At the same time, I’m expecting the polls to be slightly too optimistic for Democrats, perhaps by two points, with variation by state. I’m particularly concerned about certain groups — like 2024 nonvoters and vote switchers who in 2026 are voting for a Democrat — responding to polls at high rates. This is difficult to correct as a source of error that could inflate Democratic polling margins, although reputable pollsters are aware of this and working to counter it. There are also state-specific factors that make polling difficult — in Texas, for example, reaching an accurate cross section of the Hispanic population, or in Maine, the high instances of ticket splitting.

You might look back at recent elections and believe polls have gotten worse and decide to discount them. But that’s a mistake. Polling hasn’t gotten worse — elections have just gotten closer, making it harder to identify winners even when polling is just as accurate. A high-quality poll with a three-point margin of error can typically predict a winner in a race that is determined by seven points. But that same high-quality poll will have a harder time predicting the winner if the race comes down to a point or two, as in many recent elections. The poll didn’t get worse; the race just got harder to predict. Some of these midterm races seem quite close. That’s what the polls are reporting to us, and we should believe them.

american-dream-affordability.html
Source: RenderedHtml  Paragraphs: 15  Words: 816
