ARTICLE

Live Updates: Fresh Jobs Figures to Bring Insights on U.S. Economy
The job market has been strong and unemployment steady as inflation has unsettled markets and raised costs for consumers.
By Talmon Joseph Smith, Colby Smith, Eshe Nelson, Ben Casselman, Tony Romm, Jeff Sommer, Sydney Ember, Maddie McGarvey, Gregory Schmidt, Lisa Friedman, River Akira Davis and Joe Rennison
Published 2026-10-02 09:48 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/02/business/jobs-report-economy

Latest

Here’s the latest.

The Labor Department is set to release employment numbers for September on Friday, at a time of stability in the job market and volatility elsewhere in the American economy.

U.S. employers and workers have experienced successive shocks in recent years. First, the pandemic, then inflation, then wars and tariffs that have pushed prices higher still. Throughout, however, unemployment has remained low and economic growth has been solid.

One reason for steadiness in the job market is a shift in supply: Even as hiring rates have slowed, baby boomers have retired at a notable pace and the Trump administration’s immigration restrictions have limited entrants to the work force. Yet labor force participation among midcareer workers remains strong, an indicator that there is still enough demand for workers to keep employment rates historically high.

Here’s what else to know:

The powerful yet fragile force propping up stocks and the economy.

Despite all the turmoil in the bond market, both the stock market and the broader economy appear to be reasonably strong.

I pointed out one reason for this apparent anomaly last week. Oil prices and the war in Iran have driven up interest rates sharply, often dominating the financial news and causing hardship for millions of people. But while the rates on 10-year U.S. Treasuries have hit their highest level since 2002, those rates were considered normal in the era before the financial crisis that started in late 2007.

The world has certainly changed, though. A potent but fragile force is now propping up the stock market and the economy: the artificial intelligence industry.

For a measure of how important A.I. has become for the stock market, consider that the iShares U.S. Technology ETF, an exchange-traded fund that serves as a rough proxy for A.I.-led tech stocks, returned 33.7 percent for this calendar year through Thursday. That compares with 4.1 percent for the ProShares S&P 500 Ex-Technology ETF, which strips out many, but not all, of the tech stocks of the benchmark S&P 500.

A.I.’s role in the overall U.S. economy is harder to quantify, but it is substantial.

Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, told me that A.I. accounted for a hefty chunk of the U.S. economy’s growth this year. The latest government report says real gross domestic product grew at an annual rate of 2.3 percent in the second quarter of this year. Mr. Zandi estimated that 0.6 to 0.7 percentage points — or perhaps 30 percent of the economy’s inflation-adjusted growth this year — came from the A.I. boom, directly or indirectly.

But this may be a precarious economic foundation.

Concerns about the dangers of the technology have mounted, after reports that rogue A.I. agents hadn’t merely escaped their confines but also appeared to hide their tracks.

Evan Hubinger, an Anthropic safety researcher, estimated the potential threat from A.I. in a post on X, saying he believed the chance that A.I. “could kill all humans” within the next decade was greater than 10 percent.

No wonder leaders of A.I. companies have been calling for a slowdown in the pace of development of the technology until human safety can be assured. “Guardrails” for A.I. are being widely discussed, if not always swiftly put in place.

President Trump has denounced such concerns as a “hoax.” My New York Times colleagues David E. Sanger, Jonathan Swan, Cecilia Kang and Dustin Volz have reported that the president worries that if the A.I. boom falters, the stock market could crash and a recession could quickly follow.

I have no way of knowing exactly what would happen if the A.I. momentum were to suddenly decelerate or even reverse. But I have no doubt that it would be a blow to the economy and a bigger setback for the stock market.

The Stock Market

It wouldn’t necessarily take a major new A.I. safety threat, or the imposition of new regulations or a slowdown in A.I. investment, to stop the A.I. stock market boom.

Many Wall Street strategists expect that to happen on its own, sooner or later.

In an analysis on Tuesday, for example, Capital Economics, an independent financial research service based in London, warned, “There are growing signs that the A.I. equity market boom is in its final stages.”

A.I. has driven stock prices so high that it has formed a giant market “bubble” that is likely to burst — perhaps not quite yet, but before the end of next year, the firm says. In the meantime, it says, rising bond yields and energy prices are testing the “resilience” of world stock markets.

The bursting of a market bubble is difficult to pinpoint in advance. I’m reluctant to go as far as Capital Economics has because corporate profits are remarkably high at the moment, and they are making stock market valuations look cheaper and more reasonable. That’s not the typical pattern for a late-stage market bubble.

What has been happening is this: When earnings rise faster than stock prices, the price-to-earnings ratio — a standard comparison of share prices and underlying corporate profits — drops. Stocks have fallen close to their price levels of early June, while Wall Street analysts estimate that S&P 500 earnings grew more than 29 percent in the three months through September.

If the sizzling earnings pace can be sustained — a big if — the stock market’s advance will look less like a bubble and more like a remarkable rally, one powered by A.I.

That said, as I’ve pointed out, the A.I. boom that the release of ChatGPT in 2022 initiated has already made the stock market extremely concentrated. For the first time since their inception in the 1970s, S&P 500 index funds are no longer diversified.

In May, just 10 stocks, all of them tech companies, accounted for more than 40 percent of the total market capitalization of the S&P 500. The Vanguard 500 Index Fund’s biggest holdings are Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Micron and Tesla, followed by JPMorgan Chase. All but JPMorgan are involved in developing A.I., to one degree or another (with Apple a laggard in that regard). A major blow to A.I. stocks would hurt millions of people who hold them in retirement funds.

The Economy

A sharp stock market decline would also damage the broader economy, which is being stimulated by A.I. in two principal ways, Mr. Zandi said.

First is the “wealth effect,” through which rising asset prices, like those for stocks and homes, make affluent people more likely to spend money. In February, he estimated that “for every $1 increase in net worth, consumer spending ultimately increases by 2 cents.” In 2025, he said, “the wealth effect added a full percentage point to consumer spending growth and over 0.7 percent to G.D.P. growth.”

This wealth effect — supercharged by A.I. — helps to explain how the richest 20 percent of consumers have contributed to growing consumer spending this year, even as overall consumer sentiment declines.

After a market crash, the wealth effect would reverse itself “and the economy would take a hit,” Mr. Zandi told me.

The second way that A.I. is spurring the economy is through enormous corporate spending on data centers, power supplies and infrastructure. The sums involved are staggering. Goldman Sachs estimated in August that it would amount to $1 trillion worldwide in 2026. And that’s just a start, if the A.I. industry has its way.

In a new research paper, “Financing the A.I. Buildout,” presented at the Brookings Institution late last month, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia University business professor, estimated that by 2032 total capital expenditures by A.I. companies in the United States could amount to $10.3 trillion. That number is so big that it demands some perspective, which Professor Van Nieuwerburgh provided.

He estimated that capital expenditures on A.I. could average 3.63 percent of G.D.P. each year and become the biggest infrastructure project in U.S. history — “larger, relative to the economy, than the major U.S. canal, railroad, electrification, highway and telecommunications investment booms.”

I’m not sure that all that spending will take place. Whether A.I. investment grows to that level — and generates profits high enough to justify the stupendous cost — is a $10 trillion question.

It has already intertwined with the fluctuations of the bond market. Financing these projects requires mountains of debt.

Higher bond interest rates will make A.I. projects more expensive. This, in turn, could act as a drag on the stock market and the broader economy.

Yet the A.I. boom is powering ahead, despite concerns about safety, cost, ultimate profitability — and existential questions about whether advanced A.I. might actually be a new form of consciousness. The stakes couldn’t be higher.

If A.I. penetrates the entire economy and turns out to be a truly transformative technology, it could bolster productivity and create some new jobs. But many jobs that exist now could disappear. Those without the education and skills for an A.I. world could be grievously damaged.

The short-term effects are also likely to be painful if the development of A.I. slows anytime soon.

For long-term investors, the implications are profound. Sticking with the broad stock market during the A.I. boom has paid off so far. It may continue to do so, though extraordinary risks clearly abound.

Diversifying with bonds has been unsatisfying lately. But the turmoil in the bond market has made bonds much more attractive — in comparison with stocks — than they were just a couple of years ago. The higher income provided by bonds at today’s yields makes them better buys, compared with stocks.

Short-term interest rates are rising, too. While that is painful for borrowers, it makes money-market funds and high-yield savings accounts more appealing places to stash the extra cash you may need if you are worried about potential trouble ahead.

Soaring instrument prices could stop the music at many schools.

Jeff Lipscomb, a high school orchestra director in Kanawha County, W.Va., has been doing a lot of math.

For example, he has 12 cellists but only 10 cellos. If the school district gives him a total budget of $500 to $600 for the year, but one new cello costs more than $1,000, what should Mr. Lipscomb do? What if he needs some new violins and violas, too?

“I’ve actually had to buy instruments out of my own pocket,” Mr. Lipscomb said from his classroom at South Charleston High School on the first Monday of the school year. “I just kind of have to.”

Like many music teachers, Mr. Lipscomb has become attuned to tight budgets. Lately, though, the cost of instruments has ballooned beyond his ability to make do.

Pandemic-era supply chain snarls lifted prices for goods across the board. President Trump’s global tariffs further swelled the cost of foreign-made instruments. Then in August, the Trump administration proposed additional 25 percent tariffs on trumpets, tubas and other brass instruments, citing “national security threats” under a provision it has used to impose duties on foreign metals.

The consequences have reverberated across the country. Higher instrument prices are a particular threat to lower-income districts where enrollment and budgets are shrinking.

An elementary school music teacher in Beaverton, Ore., has considered 3-D printing ukuleles because she cannot afford them. In Passaic, N.J., an arts administrator is doubling down on encouraging students to clean and care for their instruments so they last longer. The superintendent of a small district in Washington County, Pa., has taken to scouring eBay and Facebook Marketplace for used instruments.

Proponents of musical education say the tariffs are endangering school music programs and threatening to push the extracurricular activity out of reach for many families. John Mlynczak, the chief executive of the National Association of Music Merchants, a trade group, warned that higher instrument prices could lead to “empty music classrooms.”

“The camaraderie that happens in a community when everyone goes and supports the Friday night football game?” he said. “Imagine that without a marching band.”

Some instruments, such as higher-end Fender and Gibson guitars, are made in the United States. But most elementary, middle and high schools rely on less expensive beginner instruments that are largely made in China. Many school districts own or rent instruments they lend to students at no or little cost.

As Mr. Trump escalated his trade war with China last year, music teachers grew wary.

Schools were already dealing with a confluence of challenges, including the end of federal pandemic aid, budget cuts and declining enrollment. Inflation was driving up costs.

“It’s kind of like a perfect storm of all these different things happening at once that can cause a bigger mess,” said Annamarie Bollino, a seasoned public school arts administrator who sits on the executive board of the National Association for Music Education, an advocacy group.

She said she expected that the proposed tariffs on brass instruments would further push up prices.

The effective tariff rate on instruments in June was about 13 percent, said Cullen Hendrix, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. That was down from a peak of nearly 24 percent last September but more than twice as high as before Mr. Trump’s second term.

Band and orchestral instruments have been hit the hardest, he said. In the second quarter of this year, imports of instruments were down nearly 20 percent from the same period in 2024. Imports of orchestral string instruments, including violins, violas and cellos, dropped 50 percent. Brass instruments fell 43 percent.

“It’s hitting the horns, it’s hitting the strings, it’s hitting the percussion,” Mr. Hendrix said. “All of those things combined are kind of sapping the available pool of tools that we can provide these children to begin their journey.”

Carolynn Langston has been teaching music at low-income elementary schools in Oregon for two decades. Her room this year, at a school in Beaverton, has a colorful rug surrounded by a rainbow of paw prints to indicate where her students should stand. In one corner are patterned drums and other percussion instruments. She described her musical philosophy as “sing, dance, play.”

Schools like hers will feel the higher instrument prices most.

“I don’t even have a budget,” Ms. Langston said. “Zero money.”

When she wants to buy instruments — or a carpet, for that matter — she applies for grants, including from a local educational foundation. Sometimes she requests money from people directly. She considered using a 3-D printer to make plastic ukuleles. At least they would be more durable.

In May 2025, Ms. Langston asked the local foundation for $700 to replace a large bar on one of her xylophones. “It’s one note you can play — it’s very loud and very low,” she said.

By the time she went to buy the part that fall, the cost had jumped to $750. The foundation agreed to pay the extra, but the increase stung.

“Instruments are more expensive, which then squeezes even tighter on somebody like me,” she said.

Latasha Casterlow-Lalla, the supervisor of visual and performing arts for Passaic Public Schools in northern New Jersey, said many instruments had doubled or tripled in price since the pandemic. A student saxophone that used to be $420 is more than $900. Tubas are at least $9,000, and the high school band wants four. If the proposed brass tariffs go into effect, she said, buying all of them would probably take her five or six years. By then, the would-be tuba players would have graduated.

Students are hard on their instruments, and Ms. Casterlow-Lalla estimated that each one lasted 10 years at most, and often less. Anticipating that costs will continue to rise, she is pushing principals for better storage to keep instruments functioning longer. She is also emphasizing proper cleaning and care to students and parents.

She worries above all that she will not have enough instruments for all the students who want to play. If registration in school music programs falls as a result, it could create a domino effect where the district pulls funding.

“We’re going to eventually hit our rubber-meets-the-road moment,” she said.

When Mr. Lipscomb was growing up, he variously wanted to be a paleontologist, an astronaut or a computer programmer. But from the moment he graduated from high school, he dreamed of teaching music. He got a college degree, a teaching degree and a master’s degree and then a doctorate in music composition from Louisiana State University.

“I like how it sounds — I like how it makes me feel,” he said. “I’m normally an introverted person, but it’s one of the few times that I actually enjoy being around people.”

For 15 years, Mr. Lipscomb has taught orchestra classes in Kanawha County’s high schools, including Capital High School, his alma mater. The only full-time orchestra director in the district, he spends a lot of time driving from one school to the other.

His music program is small, typically around 60 students. When he has a particularly strong class, he teaches it a challenging repertoire. Otherwise, he focuses on scales and technique.

The district provides instruments for some students who cannot afford to buy or rent them, but Mr. Lipscomb’s $500-to-$600 annual budget is not enough. He spent all of the money he was allocated last year and this year on two cellos.

One student, a freshman viola player, told him shortly after the school year began that she had to drop his class because her family could not afford to rent her instrument. He said he could lend her one free of charge, but she declined.

Mr. Lipscomb worries that rising instrument prices mean the students who stay will be stuck playing old instruments. He knows that when children play on instruments that sound bad, they do not blame the instruments. They blame themselves.

But the district is in a budget crunch, in part because it is losing students. He wishes he had thought to buy more instruments earlier in his career, before prices rose so much.

“It’s tough for me to say, but you got to work with what you’ve got,” Mr. Lipscomb said. “Unfortunately a lot of these old instruments, it’s what I got.”

As mortgage rates climb, buyers are seeking loan options that come with more risk.

Mortgage rates continue to rise, compounding an affordability crunch that has squeezed many Americans’ wallets. Now, soaring rates are prompting some home buyers to roll the dice that they will fall in a few years.

The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage, the most popular home loan in the United States, rose to 7.28 percent this week, up from 7.03 percent last week and the highest since November 2023, the mortgage financing giant Freddie Mac said Thursday.

“Mortgage rates jumped to their highest level in almost three years, pushing borrowers to the sidelines,” said Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, a trade group.

Mortgage rates had fallen below 6 percent at the end of February, but began to climb after the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The war in Iran has driven up energy costs, which in turn has stoked inflation fears. In response, investors have pushed up the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which on Thursday reached its highest level since 2002.

The 10-year Treasury yield underpins a wide range of consumer and corporate borrowing, including mortgages. With the yield climbing quickly, the jump in mortgage rates this week was the biggest since October 2022.

Adjustable-rate mortgages can be significantly lower than their fixed-rate counterparts, real estate experts say, sometimes as much as a full percentage point, a difference that can potentially save home buyers thousands of dollars annually. The ARM, as the loan is known, also comes with the risk that rates will continue to climb, hurting owners when the loan resets.

ARMs are an enticing option among buyers put off by the jump in fixed-rate mortgages, Mr. Kan said.

The Mortgage Bankers Association reported a recent uptick in the share of ARM applications, to 10.3 percent of overall mortgage applications, the highest in a year.

Here’s what you need to know about adjustable-rate mortgages.

How does an adjustable-rate mortgage work?

Fixed-rate mortgages lock in one rate over the lifetime of the loan, usually 30 years. ARMs, on the other hand, offer a low “teaser” rate for a set time, typically five, seven or 10 years, after which they readjust to the market rate, often annually, for the remainder of the loan. This helps owners keep their monthly payments lower during the introductory period.

Borrowers who use ARMs are betting that mortgage rates will eventually fall, giving them the opportunity to refinance their loan at a lower rate or sell their home before the introductory period ends and the rate begins to fluctuate.

ARMs make up a small portion of the overall mortgage market, which is dominated by fixed-rate products. But now that fixed-rate mortgages have climbed above 7 percent, interest in ARMs is starting to grow, said Archana Pradhan, the principal economist at Cotality, a provider of housing market data.

The national average rate for an ARM with a five-year introductory rate that resets annually is 6.56 percent, according to Bankrate.com.

“The wider the gap between ARM rates and the fixed rates, the stronger the incentive to choose an ARM,” Ms. Pradhan said.

How safe is an ARM?

ARMs offer savings for borrowers, but they also introduce market volatility.

The loans were popular during the early 2000s housing bubble, peaking at around 36 percent of overall mortgage applications in 2005, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association. After the housing market crashed in 2008, the share of applications for ARMs plunged to about 6 percent.

Stricter underwriting standards have made ARMs safer for consumers, who are protected by limits that prevent the variable rate from jumping too high.

Still, they are not for everyone, said Nick Rocco, a mortgage loan officer in the Baltimore area. Borrowers need to have a plan for what to do after the introductory period ends regardless of where mortgage rates are. “There is no crystal ball,” he said.

Who should apply for an ARM?

Nearly 72 percent of buyers who take out an ARM have a chance within five years to refinance it into a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage that is at least 0.5 percentage points lower than their original rate, according to a report from Redfin, an online real estate marketplace.

That can translate into big savings every month for borrowers, Ms. Pradhan said. “It’s more meaningful for higher loans, because they are able to save hundreds of dollars compared to the lower amount of loans,” she said.

Mr. Rocco said he recently worked with a couple who used an ARM to finance the purchase of a $750,000 home. The buyers had experience with ARMs, he said, and knew to put 20 percent down, which lowered their introductory rate.

“They have a little more risk tolerance and they’re a little bit more comfortable knowing the fact that they can refinance out of that adjustable rate,” he said.

But Ms. Pradhan said ARMs made better sense for buyers who intended to sell after the introductory period ended.

“Refinancing may be an exit strategy, but it’s not a guarantee,” she added. “One of the risks of an ARM is the higher payment in the future.”

Trump’s threat to ban diesel exports sets off global alarms.

The Iran war has sent diesel prices soaring around the world, straining national budgets, adding costs to businesses and snarling supply chains from farms to ports.

Now President Trump is threatening to ban or restrict the export of diesel from the United States, which is the top supplier to more than a dozen countries including Mexico, Canada and much of Europe. Oil executives and world leaders are issuing increasingly dire warnings that the result could be global price spikes on everything from groceries to jet fuel.

“I think it would have a whole bunch of consequences that need to be considered,” Meg O’Neill, the chief executive of the British oil giant BP, said in an interview on Thursday.

Ms. O’Neill noted that talk of a ban comes as BP and other oil companies are focused on “getting as much through our system as we possibly can every day, trying to get every liter of gasoline or diesel to our customers.”

Often called the workhorse fuel of the global economy, diesel is made from crude oil at refineries. It powers the heavy machinery, trucks, tractors and agricultural equipment crucial to heavy industry. When diesel prices rise, so do freight charges and other transportation costs, which often cascade into higher prices for things like food at the supermarket or even gasoline at the pump — because the heavy-duty tankers that deliver gas themselves run on diesel.

The primary reason for the price jump is a lack of refining capacity caused by the war in Iran. Missile strikes have damaged refineries in the Middle East, and the disruptions in shipping in the region have made it harder to transport. In addition, Ukraine has attacked and damaged many Russian refineries. That has forced Russia, a major exporter, to hoard its supplies of diesel.

In the United States, retail diesel prices climbed last month to a record high of more than $6.50 per gallon — nearly 70 percent more than this time last year. That’s put intense pressure on Mr. Trump and Republicans to find ways to lower costs, particularly before the midterm elections in November.

The crunch touches many corners of the world.

In Europe and Britain, the price of diesel has gone up by 40 percent since mid-June. In Canada prices have surged to record highs of more than 2 Canadian dollars per liter for the last 12 weeks, up about 59 percent compared with before the war. In some places, diesel shortages and high fuel costs are leaving irrigation pumps empty, damaging rice harvests.

Analysts are warning, nearly uniformly, that if the United States held back its diesel from the global market, the result would briefly lower prices for Americans, but rapidly hurt the rest of the world. Even in the United States, many warn, a ban would soon be self-defeating.

“This would be a tremendous shock and blow,” said Robert McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group, a research and consulting firm in Washington. “The rest of the world would have no choice but to absorb a huge price increase for diesel,” he said.

Capital Economics, a research firm based in London, warned that a U.S. diesel export ban could cause a shock comparable to the natural gas crisis in Europe after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which caused gas prices to surge more than 180 percent, according to the European Central Bank.

Mr. Trump on Wednesday indicated that he is still considering a ban. “I’m thinking about it,” he said.

Ben Dietderich, a spokesman for Chris Wright, the U.S. energy secretary, said Trump administration officials “continue to work closely together as they consider a variety of options to help lower energy costs for the American people.”

A U.S. export ban on diesel would be deeply damaging in Europe, which has become increasingly dependent on American fuel since the loss of supplies from Russia.

The continent is also going into the winter with natural gas storage levels at multiyear lows, driven by the disruptions in the Middle East.

“Europe is one of the most exposed regions, if not the most exposed one, when it comes to diesel, because Europe imports a huge amount of diesel and we are entering the harsh season, the winter season,” Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, said this week ahead of a European Union energy ministers meeting in Dublin.

Europe imports about 1.5 million barrels a day, with a third coming from the United States, according to S&P Global, a market data firm. The dependency on American imports is made more difficult by a reduction in European refineries in recent years because of high operating costs and climate regulations.

“I’ve sent a very clear signal to my American counterpart and also the public, which is that it is not in the interest of anybody — not the U.S., not us — to not have as free a flow of energy as possible in these difficult times,” Dan Jorgensen, the European Union’s energy minister, said on Tuesday.

In general, analysts expect Asia to be less directly affected by a potential ban on U.S. diesel exports than other regions, including Europe. That is because Asia largely draws from regional producers, including South Korea and China, which are among the biggest in the world.

Asia is typically a net exporter of diesel and receives only a small percentage of U.S. diesel exports each year, according to Vortexa, a commodities-data firm.

The problem for Asia is that reduced diesel supply to Europe, Latin America and elsewhere will drive up prices globally, said Sushant Gupta, research director of Asia Pacific refining and oils at Wood Mackenzie, an energy consultancy.

“The world is already reeling under the pressure of diesel shortages,” Mr. Gupta said. If Europe runs low on diesel, it will bid up prices from available suppliers, he said. “Whether it is Asia or whether it’s Europe, they’re all globally connected.”

Asia is still managing to secure most of the oil it requires, but at much higher costs, which are reflected in diesel prices. Benchmarks for diesel sold in Asia have come down from a high of more than $200 a barrel in March, though at around $180 a barrel in mid-September, current levels remain twice their prewar values.

The countries most vulnerable to supply shortages and diesel price increases include Australia and many nations in Southeast Asia, which are the region’s biggest diesel importers.

In the Philippines and elsewhere, the high cost of diesel and other fuels has caused inflation to rise. The Asian Development Bank forecasts that inflation in developing Asia and the Pacific region will accelerate to 4.2 percent this year from 3 percent last year. Several governments, including Indonesia and Malaysia, have begun subsidizing energy to help lower prices, but this adds to national debt burdens.

A big unknown for global markets is how much diesel China, the world’s largest importer of oil, will export in the coming months. Immediately following the start of the war in Iran, China restricted diesel exports — a move that worsened already-high prices for diesel and other petroleum products for major importers in Asia.

But, analysts say, China has started again to restrict some of its sizable exports of refined crude products including diesel.

Right now, “China is the only country which has spare capacity to run more crude to produce diesel,” said Wood Mackenzie’s Mr. Gupta. If the United States decides to ban exports, “other major refineries can’t run more to produce more diesel to fill up that gap.”

Rick Joswick, an oil analyst for S&P Global, said the most acute pain would be felt in countries with little or no refining capacity, particularly in Latin America. Honduras, for example, gets about 40,000 barrels a day of diesel from the United States, and Panama which gets 30,000. Those aren’t enormous amounts, but neither country has a refinery.

“It would be a traumatic loss for Europe, but for those countries it would be catastrophic,” Mr. Joswick said.

U.S. bond yields hit their highest level since 2002, driving up borrowing costs.

A global sell-off in the government bond market continued on Thursday after the yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury notes reached its highest level since 2002, driving up borrowing costs for consumers and companies around the world.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield, which underpins corporate and consumer interest rates, soared as high as 5.34 percent on Thursday, its highest since 2002, before easing back to around 5.24 percent, ending the day at it highest level since 2007.

The yield on 10-year French bonds rose to 4.92 percent, also its highest since 2002. Benchmark 10-year notes in Italy and Japan also rose on Thursday, while other regions were more mixed. When bond yields rise, the price, or value, of that bond declines.

The latest moves came as oil prices remained elevated, intensifying short-term inflation pressure that is likely to keep central banks around the world from lowering interest rates soon. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, is trading above $100 a barrel, even as more oil is flowing from the Middle East than at any point since the start of the war with Iran. Brent has risen roughly 40 percent since the start of the conflict in late February.

Stocks, which are typically sensitive to rising interest rates and oil prices, eased lower in early trading before rebounding, with the S&P 500 ending the day 0.2 percent higher on Thursday, which is the start of the fourth quarter.

The S&P 500 wrapped up the third quarter with a small 2 percent gain, as A.I. companies continued to push the broader market higher. But there were also signs in the quarter that the higher yields were putting pressure on some sectors of the stock market.

Utilities, which borrow heavily in the bond market, trailed the index, falling more than 13 percent for the quarter. The Russell 2000 index of smaller companies, which also tend to be exposed to changes in borrowing costs, fell 7.2 percent in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of gains.

“The Middle East war has really turned everything around,” said Mahmood Pradhan, a nonresident fellow at Bruegel, a think tank in Brussels, and former deputy director of the European department at the International Monetary Fund. He added that central banks were back to raising interest rates, which is increasing costs for the government and leaving it even less cash to support the economy should conditions worsen.

Aside from the war with Iran, analysts and investors have attributed much of the rise in yields to a sharp increase in global growth expectations, driven by the expansion of artificial intelligence.

The build out of data centers and other A.I. infrastructure is leading investors to anticipate that the Fed may need to keep interest rates elevated to prevent the economy from overheating.

But there are also many other forces pushing yields higher, from resurgent inflationary pressure to worries about heavy public debt loads that are becoming more expensive for governments to maintain as yields and interest rates rise.

Markets are “very nervous” following long-running concerns about public debt, Mr. Pradhan said.

Though bond prices fluctuated on Thursday, the trends pushing up yields are unlikely to dissipate soon, analysts warn.

The boom in artificial intelligence-related investment in the United States is both supporting economic growth and increasing the supply of bonds in the market. The conflict in the Middle East and its disruptions to world oil supplies grind on.

Central bankers are increasingly alert to the threat that inflation could stay above their targets for too long. Last month, the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan increased rates, and traders expect them to do so again this year. The Bank of England signaled it could raise interest rates, too.

These higher borrowing costs are colliding with high government debt levels and creating difficult budget choices because of punishing debt interest payments. In Europe, attention has turned to France, which is trying to pass a budget that will slightly reduce its deficit. But the country has repeatedly struggled to do so, and the coming presidential election, set for April, has made many investors skeptical of France’s ability to improve its fiscal situation in the short term.

While yields are rising across Europe, French bonds are also underperforming. The spread between the yield on French 10-year bonds and German bonds, which are Europe’s benchmark safe asset, widened to nearly 1.3 percentage points, the most since 2012, reflecting investors’ demand for a bigger premium to hold French debt.

SUMMARY

An NBC News/Telemundo poll released on Monday found that only 27 percent of registered Latino voters approve of President Trump’s current performance. Over 60 percent of these voters said they viewed the Republican Party negatively, the highest share since the summer of 2016, when 64 percent said the same. Democrats lead among likely voters in the Senate races in Texas and Alaska, two states that consistently vote Republican, the polls found.

ARTICLE

Trump Rallies in Nebraska to Try to Lift Republican Incumbents
By Bayliss Wagner, Chris Cameron, Emily Davies, Theodore Schleifer, Shane Goldmacher, Reid J. Epstein, Matt Zdun, Tim Balk, Caroline Soler, Anna Griffin, Ruth Igielnik, Sejal Govindarao, Patricia Mazzei, Sophia June, John Yoon and J. David Goodman

Battle for the Senate

New Polling

Hispanic voters overwhelmingly disapprove of Trump.

An NBC News/Telemundo poll released on Monday found that only 27 percent of registered Latino voters approve of President Trump’s current performance.

Over 60 percent of these voters said they viewed the Republican Party negatively, the highest share since the summer of 2016, when 64 percent said the same.

The poll, conducted in late September by the Washington-area polling firms Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies, found that the Democratic Party’s image also declined among Latino voters over the same period, with the share holding negative views rising from 14 percent in 2016 to 42 percent last month. But most of that shift happened before the 2026 midterm cycle — views of the Democratic Party have remained relatively stable since then.

Views of the Republican Party, however, are 16 percentage points worse than they were in 2024.

About 60 percent of Latino voters said they would prefer Democrats to take the majority in the House of Representatives, essentially matching the share that said so in the fall of 2018. However, in a lone bright spot for Republicans, the party also gained some ground since then, with 35 percent of Latino voters now preferring a Republican-controlled Congress, up from 26 percent in 2018 — the highest level of Republican support in this series in a midterm year. Much of this movement may have come from the undecided share of Latino voters, which decreased from 14 percent in 2018 to 6 percent now.

The Democratic Party also holds sizable leads in voters’ views on which party would do a better job on nearly every issue tested, with the largest, 30 percentage points, related to health care. The only issue that the party does not hold an edge on is border security; there, Republicans and Democrats are tied.

These findings could be particularly important in Florida and Texas, where Democrats hope to pick up Senate seats and where Hispanic voters make up a large share of the electorate. Movement among Latino voters in those states could be a key factor in whether Senate control changes hands in November.

Democrats lead governor races deep in Republican territory, polls show.

One month until Election Day, voter dissatisfaction with the economy, concerns about political extremism and frustration with President Trump have Democrats within reach of flipping four Republican-held governorships, opening a wide lead in Iowa and an expanding advantage in Ohio among likely voters, according to new polls by The New York Times and Siena University.

In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican fixture in the state for decades, is now narrowly behind his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa.

The Democratic candidate also has an advantage in the race for governor of Alaska. The only place surveyed where the Republican is ahead in the campaign for the governor’s office is Kansas, now held by a retiring Democrat.

The polls also show Democrats with an advantage in the Senate in these states, with Democrats ahead in Texas and Alaska, and with the edge in Ohio, while the races in Kansas and Iowa are neck-and-neck.

While national attention has fixated on the fight for control of Congress, governorships will be important heading into a wide open presidential election in 2028. Not only will governors influence the electoral process, they will help shape the redistricting wars that are likely to spill into 2027 and beyond.

The polling results underscore how Democrats have been able to push into states that have traditionally favored Republicans, as voters have soured on Mr. Trump amid frustration over the economy, rising gas prices and a deeply unpopular war in Iran.

Still, the polls show that even as many of the Republican candidates for governor are at a disadvantage, they are outrunning the difficult political environment. Mr. Trump’s approval rating stands at just 40 percent across the five states. In four of five states surveyed, the Republican candidates for governor are doing better than the president’s approval ratings.

Democrats, meantime, are boosted by broadly well-liked candidates who are, for the most part, seen as more politically moderate than their Republican opponents.

Texas

In Texas, for example, just 28 percent of voters worried that Ms. Hinojosa was too far to the left, compared to 45 percent who were concerned Mr. Abbott was too far to the right.

Gov. Abbott was expected to have an easy path toward re-election in a state that hasn’t put a Democrat in the governor’s office since Ann Richards, who served one term before losing to George W. Bush in 1994.

Ms. Hinojosa, an Austin lawyer and former school-board president, has tried to turn the election away from national culture-war issues toward affordability, support for public schools and a backlash against the rapid construction of power- and water-hungry data centers.

Mr. Abbott retains an enormous financial advantage, but since a Times/Siena poll in June, Ms. Hinojosa has picked up support among white voters, Hispanic voters, voters younger than 45 and independent voters.

Mark Rios, a 38-year-old Republican from Dallas, said he is supporting Ms. Hinojosa because he wants a fresh pair of eyes in office. He said he supported Mr. Trump in three elections but has seen higher gasoline prices since the president took office. The economy seems to be getting worse, he said.

“There needs to be a change,” Mr. Rios said.

Ms. Hinojosa is viewed far more positively than negatively in the state, though about a third of voters said they had not heard of or did not yet have an opinion of Ms. Hinojosa. By comparison, Texans know Mr. Abbott well after 11 years as governor and another 12 as attorney general. Forty-seven percent of voters viewed him positively, and another 47 percent viewed him negatively.

“It’s baffling to hear him say, ‘Oh, I’m fighting this and this and this.’ Dude, you’ve been there more than a decade, and your party has been in charge for forever. You’re the problem,” said Jeanette Fierro, a Democrat and hospital marketing director in Odessa, Texas.

Ms. Fierro, the daughter of immigrants from northern Mexico, said she knew little about Ms. Hinojosa when the campaigns began but believes Texans, particularly Hispanic voters, will embrace her if she can find the money to compete: “The more I have learned, as a Latina and a single mom, the more I like,” Ms. Fierro said. “She’s a chingona, you know? A badass.”

Iowa

The widest Democratic lead was in Iowa, where Rob Sand, the state auditor and the only Democrat holding statewide office, holds an advantage over Republican businessman and farmer Zach Lahn to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds, a conservative Republican who is retiring after nine years in office.

Mr. Sand has built his campaign around a bipartisan persona and a promise to address government accountability and the economy. He’s benefiting from high voter appeal: more than half of Iowa’s likely voters view him positively, including more than 20 percent of Republicans.

Since June, Mr. Sand has grown his support across nearly every demographic group. He is now ahead among voters over 65, a group that typically tilts Republican.

Iowa hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since 2006.

Ohio

In Ohio, which also hasn’t voted in a Democratic governor in 20 years, a summer of bad news for the president and his party has taken a toll on the Republican candidate for governor.

The June Times/Siena poll showed billionaire pharmaceutical entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy and the Democratic former state health director, Amy Acton, neck-and-neck. Now she has an advantage, including 11 percent of Mr. Trump’s 2024 supporters who say they intend to vote for Ms. Acton. She also has a significant lead with independent voters.

Alexandria Hensley, 27, described herself as conservative and voted for Mr. Trump two years ago, but said she wants a governor who will work toward “the middle ground.”

A domestic violence worker from Cincinnati, Ms. Hensley said her concerns were less about Mr. Ramaswamy and more about the economy, the spread of data centers and politics broadly. She said social issues such as whether transgender girls should be allowed to play on girls’ teams never mattered to her as much as politicians seem to think.

”Everyone seems to focus so much on what we disagree on, when I think we all tend to agree on more basic things,” she said.

Alaska

In Alaska, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins led a crowded August primary field and has maintained that advantage over three Republicans, Bernadette Wilson, a businesswoman and conservative radio host; Dave Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor; and Treg Taylor, a former Alaska attorney general, the poll found.

A former state legislator who helped lead a bipartisan coalition in the statehouse and won repeatedly in a district carried by Mr. Trump, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins has promised his cabinet will include a balance of Democrats, Republicans and independents. All three of the Republican candidates are populist conservatives in the mold of Mr. Trump. Alaska’s current Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, is barred from re-election by term limits.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, but while Democrats have united around a single candidate, Republicans have not. Ms. Wilson urged Republicans to coalesce around one person, fearing that multiple candidates will benefit the Democrat. Mr. Bronson and Mr. Taylor declined, arguing that Republicans can use the system to their advantage as long as their potential voters don’t rank Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins.

Anita Baker, a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel in Eagle River, Alaska, who supports Ms. Wilson, said she fears her fellow conservatives won’t understand the system. “You could add a couple of expletives to how worried I am,” she said.

Ms. Baker said she fears the damage a Democratic governor could do and still supports Mr. Trump.

“He might say things that make my eyebrows go up or make me scratch my head sometimes, but the policies are there,” she said.

The Times/Siena poll, which simulated the ranked-choice voting process, showed the three Republicans collectively winning a larger percentage of initial responses but Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins with a slight lead over Ms. Wilson after three rounds. He’s trying to become the youngest governor in Alaska history at 37 and the first Democrat elected to lead the state since 1998.

Kansas

Republicans can hope for their own flip in Kansas, where outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, won tight races in 2018 and 2022 despite the state’s conservative leanings. The Times/Siena poll showed the Republican state senate president, Ty Masterson, with a four-percentage-point lead over the Democrat, fellow state lawmaker Cindy Holscher.

Chris Martsolf, a 53-year-old commercial general contractor from Wichita, Kan., said Republicans are about as disorganized as Democrats these days. But after eight years of Democratic control, the governorship needs to go back to Republicans, he said.

“If we don’t win midterms, there probably will be no more Republican Party,” he said.

Voters in Kansas were the least likely to say their state is headed in the wrong direction, and a majority of Republicans say the economy in Kansas is excellent or good.

Mr. Masterson also benefits from some crossover appeal. He has the support of 8 percent of voters who say they also plan to support the Democrat in the Senate race, the Rev. Adam Hamilton.

Right now, Republicans hold 26 of the nation’s 50 governorships, so this year’s elections could tip the balance of power in statehouses. States operate independently, and the political philosophies within either major party can vary greatly from state to state. A Democrat on the liberal West Coast is very different than one in the Midwest or Southeast.

Still, Democratic organizers believe holding a majority of governorships would give them an additional bulwark against Mr. Trump on policies that cross state lines, including immigration enforcement, House gerrymandering and the rollback of health care funding and environmental regulations.

Here are 8 takeaways from the Times/Siena polls.

The path to Democratic control of the Senate is widening as the party’s fortunes improve in five reliably Republican states, according to new polls from The New York Times and Siena University.

Underneath the hood of the polling results, which showed Democrats effectively tied in states that were once seen as long shots, and with at least an edge in states seen as tossups, there are more data points to concern Republicans as they try hold on to their Senate majority.

Even in states President Trump won by double digits in 2024, voters — including many who backed Mr. Trump — appear to be discontented with the economy and uncertain about Republicans’ handling of other issues, among them artificial intelligence and immigration.

Here are eight key findings from the polls in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas.

Voters are not sold on the economy. Especially in Alaska.

Voter agreement cuts across age, education level, gender and race. In the five states, they tend to be united on this much: their state’s economies are not in great shape.

The assessment was particularly bleak in Alaska, where nearly three-quarters of voters said the state’s economic conditions were only fair or poor.

In Iowa, Kansas and Ohio, two-thirds or more of those surveyed rendered the same judgment on their state’s economic conditions. Voters took a slightly more optimistic view in Texas, where 44 percent of voters said the economy was excellent or good, and 56 percent said it was only fair or poor.

In Texas, Talarico and Paxton are running even on immigration.

Mr. Trump had a 10-percentage-point advantage on voters’ trust to handle immigration in Times/Siena battleground polls conducted in September 2024. Republicans’ edge has shrunk to just three points in the most recent round of Senate battleground polls.

The dynamic is especially striking in Texas, where 12 percent of voters listed immigration as the top driver of their vote, more than in any other state. Voters in Texas are evenly split on who they trust more to handle the issue, the Republican Senate candidate, Ken Paxton, or the Democratic candidate, James Talarico.

Republican frustration with Trump is evident, particularly when it comes to gas prices in the Midwest.

Across the five states, Mr. Trump’s approval rating sat at just 40 percent. That included 20 percent of voters who supported him in 2024, but who now said they disapproved of his job performance.

Even as Mr. Trump’s numbers have fallen since the summer, his base has largely continued to back him.

That makes it even more striking to see half of Republicans in Iowa — and nearly half of Republicans in Ohio and Kansas — disapprove of the president’s handling of gas prices. Across all other issues, in every other state polled, Republicans did not come anywhere close to this level of disapproval.

In Ohio, Sherrod Brown has a sizable advantage on data centers.

Sherrod Brown, a Democratic former senator trying to stage a comeback in Ohio, has focused heavily on data centers in his race against Senator Jon Husted, a Republican — and it seems to be working in his favor.

Mr. Husted supported data center investments in his state while serving as its lieutenant governor from 2019 to 2025, and Democrats have cast him as the “face of data centers” in Ohio. (Mr. Husted has tried to recover on the issue by sponsoring a bill intended to protect consumers from high energy costs linked to data centers.)

Most Ohio voters say they are opposed to data center construction. And by a wide, 11-point margin, voters favor Mr. Brown over Mr. Husted to handle the issue, the largest advantage for any candidate across the states when it comes to data centers. Even 11 percent of Republicans in the state say they prefer the Democrat’s position.

Still, only 3 percent of voters in Ohio said that data centers were the most important issue driving their vote. Though small, that proportion was much higher than in any other state, where hardly any voters mentioned the issue.

Most say the Democratic Party is too far to the left …

Fifty-two percent of voters across the five states said the Democratic Party was too far to the left ideologically, in a year in which voters nominated progressives or democratic socialists in several primaries.

… but they don’t see specific Democratic candidates that way.

Voters tend to view their own members of Congress more favorably than they view Congress overall, and that trend seems to extend to Senate candidates. Only 35 percent of voters across the five states said the Democratic nominees running in their states were too far to the left.

Democrats have an edge on character.

In all five states, the Democratic Senate nominee edged the Republican nominee on the question of who had better character. In some Senate races, the gap was slim. But in Texas, the Democratic nominee, James Talarico, held a 23-point lead over the scandal-plagued Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, on the question of character.

The most-liked Democratic nominee is from Alaska.

The candidate contrast was stark in Alaska, where Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who has faced allegations of staff mistreatment, was viewed favorably by a majority of voters, including 15 percent of Republicans. By a wide margin, she was also seen as more trusted than Dan Sullivan, the Republican nominee, to act in the best interest of ordinary Alaskans.

Senate races in 5 Republican states are tilting toward Democrats, polls find.

A month before the midterm elections, Democrats have opened leads or battled their way to ties or near-ties in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats to win control of the chamber, according to new New York Times/Siena University polls.

Democrats lead among likely voters in the Senate races in Texas and Alaska, two states that consistently vote Republican, the polls found. They have an edge in Ohio, which has been tilting rightward for years. Republicans have a slim edge in Iowa, and Democrats are neck-and-neck with Republicans in Kansas, which has not voted for a Democratic senator since 1932.

President Trump’s deep unpopularity, disapproval of the Iran war and frustration over high gas prices and the cost of living are reshaping the electoral landscape, the polls found.

Taken together, the new polls suggest that the Democrats have multiple paths to retake the Senate majority, despite a challenging map that had favored Republicans going into the midterms. To win Senate control, Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats while holding on to their current seats in three battleground states, a difficult task.

But there are signs that it is increasingly possible. On Friday, a top Republican super PAC pulled its money out of the Senate race in North Carolina, signaling that the party is not optimistic about being able to defend its seat there. The super PAC, called the Senate Leadership Fund, plans to redirect resources to Kansas, where Republicans have growing concerns about holding their seat.

The polling suggests Democrats are increasingly competitive in these Republican states.

[Follow all of the latest polls heading into November’s elections.]

In Texas, James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, has opened up a six-percentage-point lead in the race against Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued attorney general and Republican nominee who has been strongly supported by Mr. Trump.

Austin Vaughn, 30, an independent voter who works for a nonprofit and lives in the Houston area, said he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but plans to support Mr. Talarico this fall.

“He’s the one actually listening and hearing that those are problems,” said Mr. Vaughn, referring to rising costs. “And the Republicans on the other side are gaslighting everyone and saying they aren’t real problems.”

In Alaska, former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, is ahead of Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by seven percentage points. The polling aligns with the results of the state’s nonpartisan primary in August, when Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan appeared on the same ballot, and she won by eight points. A majority of voters there said that they viewed Ms. Peltola favorably; the poll was conducted after allegations of poor treatment toward her staff came to light.

In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, holds a narrow three-point edge in his comeback bid against Senator Jon Husted, the Republican incumbent, with voters saying they prefer the well-known Mr. Brown over Mr. Husted on nearly every issue in the poll. Mr. Brown has an 11-point advantage over Mr. Husted on the question of who would better handle the increasingly potent political issue of data centers, the poll found.

And in Iowa and Kansas, two Midwestern states that have been hit hard by the economic effects of Mr. Trump’s policies, the races are neck-and-neck. In Iowa, Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, has a one-point edge over State Representative Josh Turek, the Democrat. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, and Senator Roger Marshall are locked in a dead heat.

The polls suggest Democrats are performing well with independent voters, who often decide elections. Across the five states, Democrats hold a 24-point advantage with the group. On issue after issue, independent voters say they trust Democrats over Republicans — including a 30-point advantage on which party does what’s best for ordinary people in their state.

In all but one of the states, Democratic candidates are seen as less ideological than their Republican counterparts. In Ohio, voters were about equally concerned that the candidates were too ideological; 37 percent said they thought Mr. Brown was too far to the left, and 36 percent said Mr. Husted was too far to the right.

It is a striking transformation in five states Mr. Trump won every time he was on the ballot. In Ohio, which he carried with 55 percent of the vote in 2024, only 38 percent now approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance, down from 44 percent in June.

Soaring gas prices, which were driven above $4 a gallon by the Iran war, have continued to hurt the president’s popularity, particularly in the Midwest. About half of Republicans in Iowa and Ohio said that they disapproved of Mr. Trump’s handling of gas prices. Across all five states, Democrats are now more trusted than Republicans to handle the cost of living — reversing the advantage Mr. Trump had on the issue in those states just two years ago.

“You used to be able to get a house — a pretty good house — for under $200,000,” said Bethany Deines, a 58-year-old Democrat in Hamilton, Ohio, who supports Mr. Brown for Senate. Homes in her area now go for more than double that, she added: “I mean, it’s just not manageable for everyday people to be able to really even afford quality housing.”

Perhaps nowhere is Democrats’ advantage more remarkable than in Texas, where Mr. Talarico has been boosted by a growing share of voters — now 60 percent — who say that he has the right kind of moral values, up from 51 percent in June.

Many establishment Republicans, including Senator John Cornyn, whom Mr. Paxton defeated in a primary, warned this year that Mr. Paxton was a flawed candidate who could put what had been seen as a safe Senate seat at risk.

The poll suggests that may have proved true, with a majority of Texas voters saying Mr. Paxton does not have good character. And 45 percent say his past scandals, including his impeachment over corruption charges and a messy divorce from his wife, make them question supporting him — or mean they will not support him at all.

But Mr. Paxton will have a big financial advantage heading into November. Republican groups recently began spending large amounts of money to prop him up, reserving about $190 million in ads supporting him for the final two months of the race.

About half of voters across the five states — 49 percent — say they want a candidate who can provide a check on the president, according to the polls. Just 27 percent say they would prefer candidates who support Mr. Trump.

Nowhere is that more apparent than Iowa, where 53 percent of likely voters, including nearly 20 percent of Mr. Trump’s own supporters, say they want a candidate who can provide a check on the president.

Brayden Blocker, an 18-year-old Republican and college student in Iowa City, said Congress should be “less extreme.”

“With the new Congress coming in, I would say that I think it should just be more moderate members that aren’t necessarily, like, just what Trump wants to do,” he said. “It’s what their constituents want to do instead.”

The divide in voter concern about parties being too ideological is particularly stark in Kansas, where voters are more likely by a 10-point margin to say that the Republican is too far to the right than to say that Mr. Hamilton, the Democrat, is too far to the left.

Senator Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent, is an obstetrician-gynecologist who filed lawsuits against hundreds of patients over outstanding bills, leading to the arrest of at least 81 patients, a New York Times investigation found. That has become an issue in the campaign.

Half of voters also say they worry that he will support Mr. Trump too much.

“You couldn’t pay me enough money to back Donald Trump or anybody that backs him,” said Alexis Price, 42, a travel adviser in Kansas City who said she does not align with either party. “I think what the Republican Party and a lot of the Republican nominees are doing is disgraceful and disgusting. And I have to vote to my conscience over any sort of party affiliation.”

Across the five polled states, Democrats hold an advantage on nearly every issue, including on the cost of living, which is the single most important issue to voters, along with the economy. Even Republicans’ edge on immigration is slipping. Republicans held just a three-point advantage on the issue across the five states.

Among the strongest measures for Democrats is that voters say that they trust them more to do what’s best for ordinary voters. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola has a eight-point advantage on that question.

Ms. Peltola is viewed very favorably by a majority of Alaskans, including 15 percent of Republicans, and has managed to grow her lead in a state that nonetheless favors Republicans continuing to hold control of the Senate.

“I see her out in the community,” said Jessica Romer, a 38-year-old Democrat in Anchorage. “And I just really like that she’s interacting with people, like getting to know them and what their needs and wants are.”

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is planning to spend $13 million in the coming week in 35 House races, according to an ad-buy plan shared with The New York Times. Live Updates: Spain Calls Early Election After Housing Crisis Roils Government
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain has faced rising challenges to his authority amid a migration crisis and several corruption scandals involving his inner circle.

Here’s the latest.

Small left-wing parties are rushing to choose their leaders ahead of the Nov. 29 election and to capitalize on protests across Spain. Podemos, a far-left party, has proposed holding joint primary elections with other smaller formations this month. Sumar, the junior party in the current governing coalition, has announced that it and other parties would relaunch as an alliance called Frente Amplio. The left’s inability to unite under a single platform could complicate Sánchez’ gambit of trying to secure a parliamentary majority through new elections.

Voters from both the left and the right have welcomed the news of a snap election.

Gonzalo Matías, a 28-year-old civil servant from Madrid, says he hopes the election will allow the left to win the majority in Parliament that it currently lacks. Matías calls Sánchez “the best asset the left has” and praises his focus on human rights and global social justice.

Chavela Quesada, an 82-year-old pensioner, says she believes the election is “the best news Spain could have received, because the country is sinking.” She calls the current government “incompetent,” adding: “Everything they have done has been wrong: immigration, the invasion of Ceuta, everything is horrible.”

Spain’s government has faced months of spiraling crises.

Corruption

Migrant surge

Housing prices

Hundreds of activists have been sleeping in tents in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol in recent days to protest the housing crisis. On Monday, a court in the capital denied a request by the regional government to clear the encampment. Organizers said they would remain in the square despite the call for early elections and stay until a national strike is held.

Analysts say Sánchez’ decision to call a snap election, after a housing bill defeat, reflects an opportunity to mobilize sluggish left-wing voters around social issues.

Pablo Simón, a political science professor at Universidad Carlos III, says Sánchez will likely campaign on the risks that a right-wing coalition could pose to social rights, including housing.

“That could mobilize some left-wing voters and narrow the gap between the right and left-wing blocs,” Simón says, but “it still makes a renewed left-wing government unlikely.”

Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the right-wing regional leader of Madrid and one of Sánchez’ most prominent political antagonists, raised doubts on Monday about the integrity of the coming election.

“I’m asking everyone not to even think about voting by mail,” Ayuso said on Monday, according to the Spanish news agency EFE. The government says the postal vote system is safe and secure.

Opinion polls in Spain have consistently shown broader support for right-wing parties in recent months. According to current projections, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’ left-wing bloc is falling well short of the numbers needed for a parliamentary majority.

But analysts are wary of counting Sánchez out. After nearly a decade of leading the country, he has built a reputation for political comebacks. In 2023, with polls showing the conservative Popular Party ahead, many expected the right to remove Sánchez from office. He ultimately secured another term by winning the support of Junts, a right-wing Catalan separatist party.

Spain’s failure to pass housing legislation last week was a defeat for the government, but it also handed Sánchez an opportunity to rally his base.

In his speech announcing the early elections, he said voters would have to choose between keeping Spain as “a bastion of social justice” or a “far-right wave that brings regression wherever it governs.”

Sánchez said it was necessary that “to secure a much larger progressive majority in Parliament — one capable of taking on the elites, achieving new social advances and continuing to transform Spain.”

Despite the political turmoil, Spain is currently one of Europe’s economic bright spots. The country’s economy is expected to grow 2.1 percent this year, which is three times the rate forecast for the wider eurozone, according to Goldman Sachs. While Sánchez has taken a tough approach to migrants illegally entering Spain from North Africa, his government’s relative openness to immigration from places like Latin America has supported economic growth. Spain’s unemployment rate is just below 10 percent, the lowest it’s been since 2008.

The immediate backdrop to Sánchez’ decision was the recent eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old pensioner. Though she was eventually allowed to return, the sight of police officers forcing open her front door last month touched a nerve in a country increasingly frustrated with high housing costs. The eviction set off protests and put intense pressure on the government, which had promised to make housing a priority, leading it to try to enact new tenant protections last week. The measures were voted down because the government lacked a majority in Parliament — underlining its inability to pass key legislation and setting the stage for early elections.

Sanchez’ decision to call an early election has added to the shakiness that has been troubling European assets in financial markets recently. On Monday, the euro dropped to about $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025 against the U.S. dollar.

The currency has been under pressure for weeks, falling more than 3 percent in the past month as investors have become increasingly wary of the political and fiscal challenges in Europe.

While much of the attention has recently been on France, where the government is struggling to control debt levels, Spain’s move to call an early election shows that the turmoil is broadening throughout the region.

Sánchez and other left-wing politicians are seeking to frame the early election around Spain’s housing crisis, after thousands of people protested in recent days against soaring rents and home prices. But the conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox party are expected to focus instead on the crisis in Ceuta, the Spanish territory in North Africa where thousands of migrants remain after surging in last summer, and on Sánchez himself, a deeply unpopular figure among right-wing voters.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said that his party was “ready” for the election and criticized the government for its handling of the crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa where tens of thousands of migrants entered in late July from neighboring Morocco.

“We’re going into an election with Ceuta invaded and with a candidate who is aligned with Morocco’s interests,” Abascal said in a TV interview on Monday, echoing a longstanding conspiracy theory on the Spanish right that Sánchez is beholden to Morocco.

Recent polls have shown a rise in support for Vox. The party has placed third with around 18 percent in recent polls, compared to its score of 12.4 percent in the previous election, in 2023.

The recent surge of tens of thousands of migrants into Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, compounded the recent pressure on Sánchez. At least 141 people died during the crossings. While most of the migrants returned quickly to Morocco, thousands stayed — creating a lingering logistical and social challenge for Sánchez’ government.

Critics said Sánchez’ migrant-friendly policies had encouraged migrants to try their luck. He allowed more than one million undocumented immigrants to apply for legal status earlier this year, to bring them into the formal labor force.

Mónica García, the health minister in Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’ government, said that the early elections would be an opportunity to “defend the right to housing against speculators,” seeking to frame the vote around the housing crisis.“The Spanish people will rise to the occasion,” she wrote on social media. García is one of five ministers from a group of left-wing parties governing alongside Sánchez’ Socialist Party. She is among the top candidates who could lead a new left-wing party, Frente Amplio, that would likely partner with the Socialists in a future coalition.

Sánchez’ inner circle has faced growing corruption charges and accusations. Those include:

• José Luis Ábalos, a former top official in Sánchez’ party, who was sentenced in June to 24 years in prison for corruption.

• Sánchez’ brother, David, who was banned from public office after being convicted of receiving a patronage job.

• Begoña Gómez, Sánchez’ wife, who is being investigated for corruption and influence peddling.

• José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, a former Socialist prime minister, who is being investigated for receiving kickbacks.

• A police raid on the Socialist Party headquarters, as officers searched for evidence of a mudslinging campaign against judges investigating Sánchez’ family.

They have all denied the accusations.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s main conservative opposition party, welcomed the decision to call an early election. “Finally, Spain will speak its mind; finally, the Spanish people will decide,” Feijóo tells a news briefing.

Feijóo says the election would offer a choice between “four more years” of the same left-wing government and an “opportunity for change.”

“Spaniards’ difficulties have piled up over the years,” Feijóo says. “The state has had more resources at its disposal than ever before, and yet housing is now out of reach, there are too few doctors and too many strikes, educational standards are declining, and immigration is out of control.”

Battle for the House

As the race in Ohio tightens, Republicans are resuming their tepid support of Max Miller.

After Representative Max Miller, the Republican from Ohio accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and young daughter, rebuffed calls from his own party to drop out of his re-election campaign, aides close to President Trump stepped in.

They advised Republicans who had demanded Mr. Miller’s resignation to quiet down and let him try to win, according to two people familiar with the conversations who were granted anonymity to speak candidly.

They also spoke and texted directly with Mr. Miller, urging him to stop talking about his family drama in public.

Their warnings have largely been heeded, forcing many Republicans to walk an awkward line between helping Mr. Miller win and staying away from his embattled campaign. The pivot from urging Mr. Miller to withdraw his candidacy reflects the importance of his seat to the Republican Party’s effort to retain control of Congress. At a time when both parties are contending with the possibility that Mr. Trump’s unpopularity, along with rising costs, will sweep Democrats to power, the G.O.P. can ill afford to lose what should have been an easy win in a conservative part of the country.

Mr. Miller is fighting to win a third term in a Cleveland-area district that Mr. Trump won in 2024 by double digits. It was considered safely Republican until this summer, when Mr. Miller’s ugly custody battle with his ex-wife — the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, another Republican from Ohio — spilled into the public square, with each portraying the other as violent, unstable and dishonest.

The dueling allegations detailed in court documents, along with wavering Republican support for Mr. Miller, have proved to be a windfall for Mr. Miller’s Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker. In the last quarter, Mr. Poindexter’s campaign raised more than $2.4 million, according to an official familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to discuss numbers not yet made public.

As the race has tightened, political committees aligned with Republican House leaders have spent more than $5 million on the race, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Mr. Trump has told his aides he feels loyalty toward Mr. Miller, who has been devoted to the president since his 2016 campaign, one of the people said. But over the weekend, when Mr. Trump traveled to Ohio for a rally designed to support down-ballot candidates in tight races, Mr. Miller was nowhere to be found and did not merit a mention from the president.

“You have to go out and vote Republican,” Mr. Trump told the crowd at the rally on Saturday. “That includes for these great people sitting right over here.”

Beside him were the state’s Republican candidates for Senate and governor — and two congressional hopefuls. Mr. Miller was invited but was unable to make it, a spokeswoman said, because “his district schedule had been set in stone for months and he didn’t want to cancel on any of his constituents.”

“It’s unfortunate that timing didn’t work out,” Abigail Angelos, the spokeswoman, said in a statement. “President Trump agreed that Rep. Miller’s time would be best spent campaigning in the district.”

Asked what Mr. Miller was doing during the rally, Ms. Angelos said he was spending time with his family.

In August, as the deadline for Mr. Miller to withdraw neared, Mr. Trump called him and urged him to consider his odds. He did not ask him to drop out or rescind his endorsement. Mr. Moreno and Senator Jon Husted, another Republican from Ohio facing his own tough re-election bid, both called Mr. Miller unfit for office and pressed him to resign.

Mr. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of throwing scalding water at her and fracturing their young daughter’s collarbone. Mr. Miller has denied the allegations and said his ex-wife and former father-in-law fabricated stories to sabotage his career.

With early voting underway in Ohio, Mr. Poindexter is seeking to remind voters in the conservative-leaning district what Republicans said about his opponent before Trump aides told them to fall in line.

Mr. Poindexter’s campaign is planning to publish a digital ad this week featuring audio of Mr. Moreno telling reporters that Mr. Miller once withheld his daughter’s favorite blue bunny toy during a custody exchange, the official said. A spokeswoman for the Ohio Democratic Party said it was planning to send out mail pieces this week featuring Republicans calling on Mr. Miller to resign.

Republicans have sought to defend the seat by depicting Mr. Poindexter as a criminal with a long rap sheet.

During his teenage years in Cleveland, he picked up a string of misdemeanor charges, including assault. A single felony charge came when he and some buddies “got in a scrap” at a local beach, he said.

Mr. Miller has acknowledged that the lack of support from the party’s leadership has hurt his chances.

“This was Republican-on-Republican violence that the Democrats are now using to bludgeon me in a general election,” he said on a conservative talk show in Ohio last week.
