Here’s the latest.

About 50 million Americans have already cast ballots in this year’s midterm elections, a surge of early voting that is outpacing the last midterm cycle in every major Senate battleground as campaigning draws to a close on Monday. In several states, the share of the early vote from registered Democrats was higher than in 2024, an encouraging sign for the party as it seeks to flip control of Congress.

Still, millions more ballots are expected to be cast on Election Day, and candidates had one final chance on Monday to deliver their closing arguments in high-stakes races all over the country. Interviews with more than 28,000 voters conducted by The New York Times and Siena University revealed consistent themes: economic anxiety, President Trump’s unpopularity and the importance of individual candidates over party affiliation.

Mr. Trump, who has been buffeted by plummeting approval ratings and worrisome polls, said he hoped voters were “ready to do the right thing” during remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. But he also seemed prepared for the possibility of defeat: “For some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” he said, “but we gave this a very strong shot.”

His appearance came just hours after his administration appealed to the Supreme Court in its latest effort to intervene in a state’s elections. In an emergency filing, the administration asked the justices to order California officials to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claims were provided to noncitizens.

Democrats, energized by positive polls in several close races, expressed hope that reclaiming control of the Senate — a goal that once seemed well out of reach — was possible. “I am hopeful that tomorrow we can celebrate,” the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine, Troy Jackson, said as he spent Monday rallying voters and canvassers in Portland, a Democratic stronghold.

For weeks, surveys have indicated that voters’ frustration with the high cost of living has turned even deeply conservative states competitive, as Mr. Trump’s popularity has deteriorated. The latest Times/Siena polls, released on Sunday night, showed Democratic Senate candidates leading their Republican rivals in seven major battleground states.

Here’s what else to know:

“Why do we live in fear? We don’t need to live in fear.” Ruba Haddad, 47, a Jordanian-American who has lived in Maine for 10 years and is concerned about the presence of ICE in the state. She is still undecided, and said she’s read negative stories about both the Republican incumbent Susan Collins and the Democratic nominee Troy Jackson.

In the Florida governor’s race, Democrats are ‘feeling like this is our moment.’

David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for Florida governor, leaped onto a church stage on Sunday and insisted over and over again, with a sense of conviction unusual for Democrats in this Republican state: “We’re going to win this race!”

He sounded more like a preacher than a politician. And, against all odds, he has started to turn some Florida Democrats into believers.

The state has not elected a Democratic governor since 1994. It has become only more Republican over the last eight years, giving the G.O.P. a wide advantage in voter registration. Mr. Jolly has been outraised and outspent by Representative Byron Donalds, his Republican rival, who has the backing of both President Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis, the state’s most popular Republican.

Yet it is Democrats who feel the wind at their backs ahead of Tuesday, at least in the governor’s race. Last week, a New York Times/Siena University poll found Mr. Donalds with only a slim lead in the unexpectedly close race.

At Mr. Jolly’s campaign rally on Sunday, Democrats took the microphone one after the other and said what few of them have dared to imagine for many election cycles now.

“Anybody feeling like this is our moment?” Mayor Eileen Higgins of Miami asked to cheers.

“I am so damn ready,” said Mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade County. “I feel for the first time in about a decade that there is real hope for change.”

Mr. Jolly, a former Republican congressman, campaigns from what he calls the “post-ideological space,” telling voters that he is trying to grow the Democratic coalition by welcoming Republicans and independents looking beyond party labels. The son of a pastor, he speaks about moral values driving public policy for the greater good.

“The new coalition that’s emerging in American politics is actually believing in the fundamental goodness of a nation that should provide opportunity to the most number of people, to build a bigger table and create better opportunity,” he said on Sunday at the Coral Gables Congregational Church.

In the audience were two of the three Democrats running for statewide cabinet positions, and one running for Congress. All were looking for a lift from Mr. Jolly’s campaign.

Some Florida Republicans have started to sound alarms about sluggish turnout.

Mr. DeSantis, the protagonist of many of Florida’s recent Republican victories, warned on Sunday that if G.O.P. lag persisted through Election Day, his party might be in trouble.

“If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened,” he said at a campaign event in West Palm Beach for James Uthmeier, the state’s Republican attorney general. “That’s just the reality.”

When he won re-election by 19 percentage points in 2022, Mr. DeSantis noted, “We had real strong enthusiasm.”

“Now, the atmospherics are different,” he added. “I mean, the reality is, gas is higher. That’s not good. Some of these Republicans that try to act like it’s no big deal, I disagree with that. That is a big deal for people.”

Even in Mr. Trump’s adopted home state, which has looked solidly red, not all Florida Republicans may be able to outrun Mr. Trump’s unpopularity and widespread voter discontent over the high cost of living. Mr. Trump has rallied in the state twice over the past 10 days.

There are also dynamics at play particular to the governor’s race.

Mr. Donalds, who would become Florida’s first Black governor, did not win some largely white, rural counties in North Florida in the August primary election. Some Republicans looked at that underperformance with concern about whether some white Republicans would be willing to vote for a Black nominee in the general election. Mr. Donalds has tried to win crossover votes from Black Democrats, but it is unclear how successful he has been. Mr. Jolly is white.

Meantime, traditional Democratic voters, including young voters and Black voters, appear to be turning out in part thanks to State Representative Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee.

Ms. Nixon, who is Black, ran a grass-roots campaign drawn from her experience as a union and community organizer that led to a shocking primary win. Democrats privately credit her efforts in the general election with bolstering Mr. Jolly’s chances, even though she may not win her own race. As a former Republican, Mr. Jolly might not have otherwise appealed to some loyal Democrats.

Mr. Jolly has leaned into his political evolution. He does not say that the G.O.P. left him; instead, he says that he spent years as an independent and then found his “political home” in the Democratic Party. When he began to explore a run for governor, he drove to meet party activists across the state. Many later backed him.

“We are a nation that is broken,” he said on Sunday, at times pounding the church lectern.

“Our leaders on the other side keep telling us that if we just stay divided, somehow life’s going to improve,” he added, “and it’s not working.”

“Politics has become a professional sport — a team you root for and you’re either on one team or the another.” Mike Massie, 52, a teacher in suburban Cincinnati who said he finds it lonely in the center. He said he leans Republican and laments the loss of being able to have civil conversations with people of all political affiliations.

Trump says he would not hesitate to issue pre-emptive pardons for Elon Musk and other allies.

President Trump said he would be willing to issue pre-emptive pardons to aides and allies, including the Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk, if Democrats win enough seats to take control of the House and Senate and carry out widespread investigations and potential prosecutions.

In an interview with The New York Post released on Monday, Mr. Trump called the supposed threats against Mr. Musk just “talk,” as the interviewer suggested that Democrats wanted to arrest the tech mogul, “seize his factories” and “nationalize SpaceX,” which the government relies on to get payloads into orbit. Democratic leaders have discussed possible investigations into Mr. Musk and his business practices, but have not called for his arrest.

“I can tell you this, if they do, we just have to protect those people,” Mr. Trump said when questioned by Miranda Devine, a Post columnist.

Ms. Devine then followed up by asking if that could be done by “pre-emptively” pardoning Mr. Musk and others.

“I would if I needed to, sure,” Mr. Trump responded, noting that he had signed an executive order granting broad clemency to more than 1,500 of his supporters who were charged after storming the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. “I would not even think about it. I’d do it. I did it for J6.”

Mr. Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last month, Senator Alex Padilla, Democrat of California, called for an investigation into Mr. Musk, after reports that Ukrainian forces had experienced restrictions in satellite internet services built by SpaceX and used for communications in the country’s war against Russia. Mr. Musk has said that Ukraine violated the system’s terms of service, and that he was later asked by Mr. Trump to restore the communications network, according to reporting by The New York Times.

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest man, with a net worth that hovers around $1 trillion, has also come under scrutiny for pouring nearly half a billion dollars into the midterm elections in support of Republican causes and candidates. In an election where voters are focused on affordability and cost-of-living concerns, Democrats have hammered Mr. Trump’s party for its relationship with wealthy donors.

In social media posts, Mr. Musk has framed Tuesday’s election in alarmist terms, claiming that Democrats would turn the country into a “permanent one-party state.” He has used similar language in past election cycles, and issued a challenge to Democrats that dared to open investigations into him or his companies.

“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” he wrote on X, the social network he owns, last month. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.”

We talked to 28,000 voters, and some clear themes emerged.

In the run-up to Election Day, people have looked to polls for indications of how the contest for control of Congress may play out. But beyond the horse race, polls this fall have sent some clear messages about what voters care about.

This year, the Times/Siena Poll made nearly four million phone calls to 1.6 million voters, completing more than 28,000 interviews. We will find out on Tuesday how accurate the polls were by our team and by other pollsters across the country, but there are issues on which voters’ opinions are consistent enough that the lead extends well beyond the margin of error. Those issues help shed light on the current political environment and the motivations behind various midterm election decisions.

It’s the economy …

Polls have consistently shown that the top issue for voters this year is the economy. Every Times/Siena poll conducted in 2026 has found voters listing it as their single biggest driver.

The economy was also a top issue in the 2024 presidential election, but in a departure from recent years, voters are placing their trust in Democrats this time. Nationally, they favor Democrats to handle the economy over Republicans by eight percentage points. The shift is a reversal from just two years ago, when Donald J. Trump was favored by six points over Kamala Harris on this issue.

Across the seven states in our final battleground poll, six of which Mr. Trump won in 2024, voters were nine percentage points more likely to say they trusted Democrats to handle the cost of living. In Kansas and Texas, both states that the president won by double digits in 2024, Democrats also held a nine-point advantage on the issue.

Trump is deeply unpopular, but he has a reliable base.

Regardless of the outcome of the elections on Tuesday, one thing is clear: Voters are frustrated with Mr. Trump. The president’s disapproval rating stands at 60 percent nationally, according to the New York Times presidential approval tracker.

Mr. Trump’s approval rating for his handling of the economy has fallen to 35 percent, a drop from 43 percent in April last year. It is down among men and women; white, Black and Hispanic voters; Democrats, independents and, to a lesser extent, Republicans.

A vast majority of Republicans, however, remain loyal supporters. More than 80 percent of Republicans in the latest Times/Siena poll said they approved of the president’s job performance. Signs of a mass Republican exodus are not there.

Democrats are not especially popular, either.

Democrats are expected to have a strong year, but polls show that the party should not take that as a positive sign for its political brand.

Only 28 percent of voters said they were satisfied with the Democratic Party in a Times/Siena poll from last month, compared with 36 percent who said the same about the Republican Party.

The dynamic can be seen most acutely in Texas, where a CNN/SSRS poll found James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, leading the Senate race by six percentage points in a state where he was more popular than the party that nominated him. He had positive favorability (44 percent favorable, 43 percent unfavorable) among likely voters, while the Democratic Party in Texas was decidedly underwater (36 percent favorable, 56 percent unfavorable).

Immigration is declining as a priority.

For the last two years, the immigration crackdown has dominated the headlines at times. But only 10 percent of voters listed immigration as the top issue motivating their vote this year, down from 15 percent in 2024, and it is mostly Republicans who cite it as an issue.

Trust on the issue has also changed hands. Voters now give Democrats a four-point advantage on trust to handle immigration, after Mr. Trump had an 11-point edge on the issue in 2024.

The individual candidates matter.

Voters’ feelings about individual candidates, not just their political parties, have been shown to matter a great deal.

In South Carolina, a recent Times/Siena poll found the race effectively tied between Senator Darline Graham and Annie Andrews in a state that Mr. Trump won by about 18 percentage points in 2024. Candidate quality has seemed to play a major role in making the race so close.

The poll found that supporters of Ms. Andrews, the Democrat, said their top reasons for backing her were related to positive views of her policies or character (and negative views of Ms. Graham). For Ms. Graham, the Republican appointed to the seat after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died this year, voters’ primary reason for backing her was to help the Republican Party. Less than half as many cited her policies.

Who is Jason Turkish, Haley Stevens’s fiancé?

Even before the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens scrambled Michigan’s U.S. Senate race on Sunday by endorsing the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, another man in her orbit had garnered increased attention: Jason Turkish, her fiancé.

Mr. Turkish said last Wednesday that he would not support the Democratic Party’s nominee for U.S. Senate, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, over his criticisms of Israel. Then, on Sunday, Ms. Stevens threw her support behind Mr. Rogers after joining him for services at a prominent Black church in Detroit, despite previous assurances to Democratic leaders that she would support her party’s ticket.

The feud between Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed — and the role that Mr. Turkish may have played in the intraparty spat — underlines how the debate over U.S. support of Israel has roiled Democratic politics.

Here’s what else we know.

Who is Jason Turkish?

Mr. Turkish, 39, is a lawyer and fund-raiser for Democratic candidates and Jewish causes. He is based in Southfield, a suburb of Detroit. He is also the president and managing partner of Nyman Turkish, a disability rights firm. He has been legally blind since birth.

What is his political background?

Mr. Turkish is a longtime political donor. A self-proclaimed “lifelong Democrat,” he and his firm have given money to multiple Democratic campaigns across the country but he has also donated to at least one Republican, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, according to federal records.

Former Gov. James Blanchard of Michigan, a close friend of Ms. Stevens’s, described Mr. Turkish as “a real political junkie” who has raised a lot of money for Democratic candidates in the state. He is also active in the state’s Jewish and pro-Israel circles and is a donor to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. He has relatives who live and were born in Israel.

How did he meet Haley Stevens?

Mr. Turkish and Ms. Stevens met after the 2022 midterm elections through a mutual friend. They bonded as they discussed her disability rights legislation, she said in interviews, and their conversations about policy evolved into a romantic relationship. They announced their engagement in August, shortly after Ms. Stevens lost the primary election to Dr. El-Sayed.

“We just fell in love,” Ms. Stevens told The Detroit News in August. “We had years of just friendship and conversation, and we have a lot of shared values and commitment to family and friends in Michigan.”

The couple vacationed in Italy and Israel after sharing the news of their engagement. Ms. Stevens has said she has met with a rabbi to discuss converting to Judaism before they get married next summer.

Why is he involved in the Senate race?

In the final week of the campaign, Mr. Turkish said he would vote for Mr. Rogers because he felt Dr. El-Sayed had not sufficiently moderated his views on Israel. Mr. Turkish attended an event for the Republican Jewish Coalition supporting Mr. Rogers shortly after endorsing him.

“I watched Haley graciously concede an election, and open her arms and her heart to Abdul on Aug. 5, the day after the primary, and I prayed that he would moderate, and he hasn’t,” he said in an interview before the event.

On Friday Mr. Turkish appeared on TMZ to explain his support for Mr. Rogers, pointing to a digital advertisement from supporters of Dr. El-Sayed that blames rising grocery prices in the United States on its support for Israel’s military campaign. He called on Dr. El-Sayed to disavow the ad and suggested that if he did not, Ms. Stevens would not support him. Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign sought to distance the candidate from the ad, saying that it was created by a left-wing political action committee, Rebellion PAC, and was “not affiliated in any way” with him or his candidacy.

On Sunday, when Ms. Stevens appeared alongside Mr. Rogers at the Perfecting Church in Detroit, Mr. Turkish was also in attendance.

“I did not want Abdul, and I didn’t want Mike Rogers either. So I left that one blank.” Julie Bolen, 56, voting early in Harrison Township, Mich., but not for Abdul El-Sayed or his Republican opponent in the state’s high-profile Senate race. She said she voted as a Republican for Donald Trump in 2024, but regrets it and is now an independent. As a cancer survivor, she said health care is a big issue for her, and that she thinks neither party has a vision of where they’re going.

“I’m very upset about the way the federal government is handling our day-to-day lives.” Jeanne Russell, 77, of Verona Island, Maine. She listed her complaints — "tax breaks for billionaires, taking away health care from the people, ICE shooting people in the streets" — as reasons she will vote for Democrats on Tuesday.

The Trump administration asks the Supreme Court to order California to set aside 20,000 ballots.

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to require that California set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claims have been provided to noncitizens.

The emergency application to the justices came after a divided federal appeals court rejected the administration’s arguments that California officials should impound the ballots for further scrutiny.

Legal experts have been skeptical of the Trump administration’s arguments in the case. Filing just one day before the midterm elections may forestall a ruling in the case — and a potential loss for the administration — until after Election Day.

The request requires the Supreme Court to consider how much power the federal government has to order states to make last-minute changes to their vote-counting procedures. Under the Constitution, states have responsibility for administering elections. The Justice Department has claimed that it is empowered by a federal law that makes it illegal for noncitizens to cast ballots.

In their emergency application, lawyers for the administration urged the justices to grant what they called a “modest remedy,” requiring California to separate ballots of “citizens and suspected noncitizens.” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote that such an order by the court “would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens.”

The legal challenge to 20,000 California ballots is part of a broader effort by the administration to argue that the elections could be marred by illegal votes by noncitizens. The effort comes as polls show Republicans could lose control of one or both chambers of Congress and as President Trump has sought to cast doubt on the validity of the vote, despite little evidence of widespread problems with illegal voting. California officials have said the voter list provided by the Trump administration is filled with errors.

The solicitor general appeared to distance the lawyers in his office, an elite division of the Justice Department that represents the federal government before the Supreme Court, from direct knowledge of whether the people on the list were actually noncitizens.

Mr. Sauer wrote that his office “has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals” who appeared to be registered to vote in California and who “in the United States’ view, are likely not U.S. citizens.”

California leaders denounced the election-eve appeal to the Supreme Court.

The state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement that the administration’s filing “reeks of desperation,” calling it “another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law.”

Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, said in a statement that he had visited voting locations throughout the county over the weekend and was pleased to see voters and elections “not distracted by the outside noise and attempts to disrupt or sow distrust.”

The administration’s emergency application was assigned to Justice Elena Kagan, who handles such petitions from that region of the country and can choose to refer the matter to the full court. It was not clear how quickly she intended to act or whether the justices would take up the application before Election Day.

One elections law expert, Richard L. Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, called the administration’s move an “emergency Hail Mary petition” that was unlikely to succeed.

As the lawsuit has wound through the lower courts, the administration has also threatened criminal charges over claims of noncitizens voting, including charging 28 people with violating federal election laws and subpoenaing county election workers in California.

The Justice Department sent the list of 20,000 names to Los Angeles County elections officials in October, claiming that those ballots should be separated because the names had been flagged through a government process as potential noncitizens. Officials have been vague about exactly how the list was prepared, and county officials have said that the list appeared to include people with addresses throughout California. Only 7,035 names on the list sent to Los Angeles were listed with addresses in Los Angeles County. Officials confirmed others were born in the United States and were citizens.

Shortly after, the Justice Department sued to stop the counting of mail-in ballots sent to people on the list until their citizenship could be verified.

On Friday, a divided three-judge panel on a federal appeals court rejected arguments by the Justice Department to segregate the contested ballots, finding that the administration had overstepped its bounds by interfering with the state’s role in setting its election rules. The panel also cited a principle repeatedly upheld by the Supreme Court that federal courts should avoid ordering changes to how ballots are counted too close to an election.

That same panel of federal judges had already rejected an appeal in the same case earlier in the week, declining to leapfrog a trial judge.

That judge, David O. Carter, then sided with California officials, writing that the federal government’s request could “wreak havoc” on state election administration and “create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike.”

Trump returns to a landmark that has come to symbolize his administration’s dysfunction.

President Trump on Monday will make his closing argument before the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a landmark whose failed repair job became a high-profile symbol of his second administration’s struggles with governing.

The Reflecting Pool has been closed and fenced off since July, after earlier repairs ended in a debacle: The pool’s new blue waterproof coating peeled up, and algae blooms turned the water bright green.

Since then, contractors have applied a new layer of waterproofing and flushed out the pool’s filtration system. Photos of the pool in recent days have shown it gradually refilling.

Mr. Trump is scheduled to speak at the pool at 2 p.m. Eastern on Monday.

On Sunday, while campaigning for Republican candidates in Iowa, the president told reporters that he wanted to return to the pool to show “how beautiful it is.”

“It’s been finished,” Mr. Trump said.

Then he again blamed vandals for the pool’s problems, even though federal prosecutors and the contractors who repaired the pool said the biggest problem was flaws in the repair work.

“It was vandalized badly,” Mr. Trump said in Iowa. “We have cameras all over the place now for the vandals.”

Fences that have surrounded the pool since July were down on Monday morning, and the pool appeared to be refilled. That entire section of the National Mall was surrounded by a much larger perimeter of fencing set up for Mr. Trump’s visit.

The Interior Department, which oversees the pool, did not respond to questions about the repair work on Monday.

The Reflecting Pool, which is more than 100 years old, is a vast shallow concrete pond that reflects the Lincoln Memorial at one end and the Washington Monument at the other. For years, it has been plagued by leaks and algae.

Mr. Trump has spent millions of dollars seeking to repair and remake Washington landmarks, as well as to build new projects including a White House ballroom and a 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Those repairs have often come at the expense of other parks around the country; the administration used at least $67 million in revenue from park entrance fees to help fund projects in Washington.

The Reflecting Pool was one of the icons he sought to fix. Mr. Trump’s administration tried to perform a rush repair job this spring, to fix the pool’s problems in time for the country’s 250th birthday celebrations.

But the repairs quickly veered off course. Instead of a shining symbol of the president’s efforts to beautify the capital, the pool became a stark reflection of dysfunction, dishonesty and the administration’s willingness to use the justice system against its perceived enemies.

The repair project began in April, when the Interior Department awarded a no-bid contract for the pool to Atlantic Industrial Coatings, a small firm in Virginia that had never won a federal contract before. The company was assigned to carry out a plan — designed in part by the general manager of Mr. Trump’s golf course in Bedminster, N.J. — to spread coating in a shade called “American flag blue” across the pool’s concrete slabs.

In all, the government paid that company close to $15 million. It also gave a no-bid contract to a company connected to one of Mr. Trump’s political donors, hiring that firm to upgrade the pool’s filtration system.

After weeks of work, the pool was refilled the first time in June. But its water quickly turned green with algae, and sections of the new blue coating began to tear and separate.

Mr. Trump blamed both problems on vandals, and federal prosecutors charged several people with crimes, saying that they tore the blue coating. But a few weeks later, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, asked the court to drop those charges, saying that a botched repair job had actually caused the damage.

Atlantic, the company that carried out the repairs, reached a similar conclusion. It informed the Interior Department that the problems were caused by “human oversight” in the application of the blue lining and a flawed design in which one layer of coating destabilized the one underneath it, according to government documents reviewed by The New York Times.

After the pool was drained a second time, Atlantic returned to fix its original work under warranty. The company said that it had shifted its approach to minimize human error and that it would avoid layering the incompatible chemicals atop one another, government documents show.

A federal judge said last month that federal prosecutors could never revive the one felony charge they had filed against the former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of pulling up a piece of the pool’s blue coating. Lawyers for Mr. Hearn have asked internal government watchdogs to investigate the case, saying senior administration officials ignored evidence of the botched renovation in a rush to satisfy Mr. Trump’s demands for criminal charges.

“I would rather pay $10 a gallon for gasoline than vote for Democrats.” Tina Chisenhall, 61, voting on Friday with her husband, David, in Butler County, Ohio. They both said they are willing to wait for the economy to get better and believe some of the angst people are feeling is being driven by unfair media narratives. “Economics take awhile to catch up, we are still paying for Biden’s policies,” Mr. Chisenhall said.

Early voting totals reveal a surge of registered Democrats in several key states.

Election Day is Tuesday, but about 50 million ballots have already been cast, with early turnout outpacing the last midterm cycle in each of the major Senate battlegrounds.

In several key states, the share of registered Democrats has increased in the early vote, which includes mail-in ballots and early in-person voting. The overall picture offers few positives for Republicans, who saw strong early in-person turnout in 2024. And the surge provides indications that it could be a high-turnout election in the realm of 2018 and 2022, which set records for midterm turnout.

But millions of voters will cast their ballots on Election Day — in recent elections, around half of the votes nationally have come that day — and the impact of the early vote will be known only after polls close. That makes it difficult to pinpoint what those early votes say about each race.

While the early vote can’t reliably predict who is going to win, the numbers through Monday morning offer clues about which subgroups are turning out, and there are a few warning signs for Republicans.

Early turnout is up, with Democrats at an advantage.

In every Senate battleground that we are tracking, the number of early ballots cast has surpassed the total number of early ballots cast in 2022. That year trailed only 2018 for total turnout in a midterm election. (Midterms typically run well below presidential elections in total voters.) In Maine, South Carolina and Texas, early turnout this year is closer to what was seen for the 2024 presidential election.

Democrats have traditionally been more likely to vote before Election Day than Republicans, so their advantage in the early vote was to be expected. Still, in several states, the partisan makeup of the electorate is even more Democratic than it was in 2024. (In Georgia, where voters do not register with a political party, The Times estimates partisanship using party primary participation.)

The increased early turnout could be a sign that overall turnout will be much higher this year. But it is unreliable to project overall turnout by extrapolating from early vote totals. Such an inference would have vastly overestimated turnout in 2024, for instance, when the share of early in-person votes surged in many competitive states.

It is possible that the higher early-vote tallies are a matter of people who would have previously voted on Election Day deciding to vote early instead.

In the South, Black early turnout is up.

In Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina — Southern states that went for Donald J. Trump in 2024 but are a focus of Democrats’ goal of flipping the Senate — Black voters make up a larger share of the advance vote than they did in recent cycles. (All three states record race on their voter files.)

Black voters in North Carolina made up 21 percent of early votes cast through Oct. 31, which was only a couple of percentage points higher than it was in 2022 and 2024. But with Black voters in these three states leaning so heavily Democratic — in 2024, Kamala Harris won between 87 and 90 percent of Black voters in each, according to Times Voter Trends — even small increases in their share of the electorate are significant.

The unanswerable question is whether a disproportionate number of Black voters chose to vote early this year rather than on Election Day, and whether Tuesday’s turnout will skew significantly toward white voters. In all three states, a majority of votes are typically cast during the early voting period, making the early vote in past years more representative than it was elsewhere.

Early voting gets younger as Election Day nears.

Older voters traditionally dominate the earliest ballots, as they tend to become politically engaged earlier in the cycle. That pattern is particularly pronounced during midterm elections, and this year is no exception.

For example, in Michigan, the median age of those who have voted so far is 67. That is roughly on par with 2022, when it was 65. (In 2024, it was 59.)

The final days and weeks of early voting, however, typically see a surge of young voters. Four weeks ago, about 11 percent of the ballots cast in Michigan came from those under the age of 45. In the past week, it was 30 percent.

Other states followed a similar trend. In general, mail ballots that are received later tend to lean Democratic. This could be relevant in states like Michigan, where in past elections, a batch of late-arriving mail ballots from Detroit grew the Democratic candidate’s vote share after Election Day.

Turnout in Texas surges in Hispanic counties.

The vast majority of Texans cast their ballots before Election Day, and early turnout in Texas this year has approached presidential levels, with ballots cast through Oct. 30 off by only 15 percent from the same point in 2024.

Given that the state is broadly seen as a tossup for the first time in decades, with a Senate race that has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars in spending, such high turnout is unsurprising. Still, the raw numbers are staggering. Nearly eight million Texans have cast their ballots thus far, rapidly approaching the total turnout of 2022 — including Election Day votes.

Turnout is highest in the most Hispanic counties. Of the eight counties running ahead of their 2024 totals, seven of them are more than 70 percent Hispanic. That could be good news for Democrats, with the most recent New York Times/Siena poll of Texas showing James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate, leading among Hispanic voters by 38 percentage points.

But high turnout among this group is not always a good sign for Democrats. In 2020 and 2024, large South Texas counties with high Hispanic populations, like Hidalgo and Starr Counties, saw record-breaking turnout paired with massive Republican gains — and Mr. Trump flipped many of them two years ago.

Latest

Here’s the latest.

Voters across the United States began heading to the polls on Tuesday, capping a divisive midterm campaign that will determine control of Congress and offer the first nationwide verdict on President Trump’s second term.

Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly urged his supporters to act as if he is on the ballot, has insisted that Republicans would win if his base turned out. Democratic campaigns have blamed the president and his signature policies for the struggles of Americans trying to make ends meet.

Republicans attempted to transform the election from a referendum on Mr. Trump into a choice between their party and Democratic opponents they cast as radical, far-left activists.

Polls show that Democrats are widely favored to win control of the House, although it is not clear how deep into Republican terrain their victories might extend. Surveys also indicate that Democrats are on track to increase their numbers in the Senate, and party leaders are cautiously optimistic about winning a majority.

But that is a tall order. Democrats would have to flip four Republican-held seats and defend all of their own to take control of the chamber.

Early voting has broken recent midterm records, with more than tens of millions of ballots already cast. Early turnout exceeded that of the last midterm cycle in each of the major Senate battlegrounds. And in several key states, the share of registered Democrats has increased in the early vote.

So has spending. This is the most expensive midterm election, as measured in political advertising, since at least 2018, according to data from AdImpact. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, contributed $474 million to Republican candidates and their allies, more than any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle.

The first polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern, but it could take days or weeks before the full results are known, particularly if many of the races are close. In 2024, it took three weeks to determine the winners in California’s closest House races.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

Here’s what you can (and can’t) do at polling sites.

In America, it is largely up to each state to decide the laws that govern elections. That means there is a jumble of rules in place around the country on Election Day, including whether voters have to present identification to cast a ballot, and even how closely you can approach a polling place with a political sign or T-shirt.

As such, it’s important to check your state government’s website to make sure you’re within the bounds of specific regulations. But here’s a broader look at what is and isn’t allowed at polling sites across the country.

Electioneering

Every state has some kind of law about political activity near polling places. And at a federal level, actual or attempted voter intimidation or coercion are criminal offenses.

Electioneering refers to any kind of overtly political activity near a polling site while voting is taking place. Most states restrict the display of signs or the handing out of campaign literature within 100 feet of a polling site.

Some states go further, and bar voters from wearing clothing or pins that bear a candidate’s name or political messaging. A handful prohibit general loitering around polling stations, and eight states prohibit the taking of exit polls as voters leave polling sites.

Providing ID

Most states require some sort of ID to vote. In the 14 that don’t, identification is instead required at the time of voter registration, and poll workers are not allowed to ask voters for identification on voting day.

Selfies

Snapping a selfie with your completed ballot is illegal in 15 states, including New York, New Jersey, Georgia, Massachusetts and Minnesota.

Arizona, Texas, Tennessee and West Virginia allow ballot selfies, but only for absentee or mail-in ballots.

While some argue that ballot selfies are a form of protected speech, critics have claimed that it can facilitate vote buying by giving people a legal way to prove they supported a specific candidate or ballot question.

Closing times

Each state decides the hour its polls close, but they all agree on one point: If you are in line to vote when that hour arrives, you will be allowed to cast a ballot.

Stepping out of that line after the polls have closed, however, is different. If you leave a voting line after polls have closed, you most likely will not be allowed to rejoin it.

Election Day could be a rainy one in some areas.

With millions of voters having cast their ballots already, experts say the weather likely won’t determine the outcome of Tuesday’s elections, even with rain in the forecast for states with competitive races, such as Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi and Florida.

But then again, it could.

Weather has always been an uncontrollable and slightly unpredictable factor in elections.

In recent decades, scientists have turned years of anecdotes into rigorous analyses of voting and weather data. Their conclusion: Yes, weather can indeed (slightly) influence turnout.

Overall, Tuesday is shaping up to be a “pretty tranquil day,” with the East Coast and West Coast looking clear and comfortable, said Jennifer Tate, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. The exceptions will be portions of the central United States and Florida.

There will be at least some risk of thunderstorms from Iowa to Texas on Tuesday, and pockets of excessive rain that could lead to minor flash flooding.

How much does the weather matter?

It depends on whom you ask, and ongoing research continues to examine the trends in weather and voter turnout.

Bad weather in one or two tight districts could affect an outcome by keeping some voters at home, Kasper M. Hansen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen and an author of a study on weather and turnout, told The New York Times in 2024.

In that study, he found that what he termed “marginal voters” — people who only occasionally turn out to vote — are more likely to opt out if Election Day arrives with consistent, miserable rain.

Thomas Fujiwara, an associate professor of economics and international affairs at Princeton University, has also found that rainfall lowers turnout, though by modest amounts. He is an author of a 2016 paper that examined the effect of rain on one election and whether it reverberated in future cycles.

On Monday, Mr. Fujiwara said he hadn’t conducted any new research on elections and weather since then. But he noted that the impact on turnout is likely smaller today than in the period he analyzed (1948 to 2012), because a larger share of the electorate now votes early or by mail.

On the other hand, Mr. Hansen, suggested that recent research suggests that bad weather continues to suppress turnout, “especially on the marginal voter (e.g., young voters).”

Mr. Hansen’s research has shown that die-hard voters aren’t likely to be deterred by the weather. Those people tend to vote early, or will stand in line in any conditions. Instead, he has found, the people most likely to avoid voting in inclement weather are those for whom voting doesn’t fit easily into a busy schedule, or those living alone — typically people ages 21 to 30.

Here’s a guide to The New York Times’s Election Day coverage.

It’s Election Day. Millions of Americans are casting ballots in an election that will determine which party controls the House and Senate during President Trump’s remaining two years in office. Later, they will be watching for results — and signs of how the electorate, both parties and the nation may be evolving.

The New York Times will be tracking the results of the races reaching their conclusion on Tuesday and offering news and insights that draw on the work of more than 400 reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers in election battlegrounds and across the country.

Here’s how to follow our election coverage:

The live blog: The main hub for The Times’s election coverage is our live blog. This is the home for real-time updates on race calls, interviews with voters, result forecasts and analysis.

When the first polls close on Tuesday evening, the full picture of outcomes will begin to emerge gradually, in pieces, possibly late into the night, depending on race margins and each state’s counting procedures. We will provide round-the-clock updates managed by our newsrooms in New York, London and Seoul.

Mobile app: All midterm elections coverage is, for a limited time, free in the Times app. Readers using the app can also sign up for race calls and news alerts. The app can be downloaded here.

Home page: The home screen of the app and our website, nytimes.com, will feature headlines from our live blog and, as polls close, visualizations of the election results and forecasts.

The Needle: Our real-time election night forecast tool will go live as results begin trickling in. The Needle estimates the likelihood of outcomes, applying a statistical model to continuously processed partial results. To understand the mechanics, read more here.

Voter trends: Late on election night, we will begin publishing a series of Times Voter Trends graphics that will break down estimates for the results of House and Senate races by age, race, education and gender in every state. The goal of is to reveal how different groups shifted from previous elections. See our findings from the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections here.

The Iran war is unpopular. Why does Trump keep talking about it?

The war in Iran is deeply unpopular with Americans. Recent polls indicate as many as two-thirds of voters disapprove of President Trump’s handling of the eight-month conflict, which has driven up prices and depleted U.S. ammunition stockpiles.

Yet in the final days of the campaign, Mr. Trump kept talking about it.

“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters on Saturday.

“The only reason we’re not finished with Iran is, I want to be nice, I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” he said at a campaign rally on Sunday.

“We had a war with Iran,” he added Monday. “We won.” Hours later, officials confirmed that the U.S. military had struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what they described as a defensive measure that was not expected to escalate.

Here are three reasons why Mr. Trump kept bringing up Iran, according to analysts.

To push Iran toward a deal

Mr. Trump, who prides himself on his deal-making, could be trying to restart talks.

“By threatening strikes, he wants to send the Iranians a message: ‘Come to the table now or else,’” said Arta Moeini, managing director of the nonpartisan Institute for Peace and Diplomacy, which advocates for military restraint.

Iran’s foreign ministry on Monday said it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agreed to several demands, including lifting U.S. economic sanctions against Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.

The Trump administration is unlikely to accept either condition. For now, Mr. Trump “is going to use the promise of diplomacy again, as he has done before,” Mr. Moeini said. “He can announce that, and maybe get better results for the election, but still later say, ‘They didn’t do what they promised to do, and so we can attack.’”

‘Tough guy’ rhetoric has worked before

Threatening rhetoric is part of Mr. Trump’s brand and has helped him build a loyal following.

“There is a very real strand of American public opinion, the Jacksonian tradition, that likes a leader who projects toughness and who is prepared to whack the bad guys,” said Andrew Payne, a research director at Chatham House, a policy institute in London.

But Mr. Payne called that approach to Iran a “misguided” political strategy. “You’ve seen the polling,” he said.

He sees Iran as a legacy issue

Yet polling will matter less for Mr. Trump going forward. Regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s elections, he will be entering his final two years in office, a period when presidents often take policy risks to secure their legacies.

“He has staked his legacy in foreign policy, to some degree, on Iran,” Mr. Payne said. “It’s more important for him to try and get some favorable resolution to that in the long term than worrying about the short-term impact at the polls.”

The Trump administration is already moving three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces to the Persian Gulf region, to be ready to strike within days.

“I do believe that he will escalate no matter what,” Mr. Moeini said. “I don’t think that’s cheap talk.”

TV viewers will have a plethora of options on Election Night.

Inflation may be a top concern for voters in Tuesday’s midterm elections — but broadcast TV is embracing it.

As recently as 2014, the Big Three networks — ABC, CBS and NBC — aired little more than an hour or two of live coverage of midterm results, barely a blip between reality shows, sitcoms and procedurals.

On Tuesday, NBC will offer its local stations 13 consecutive hours of nonstop coverage, beginning in the late afternoon and extending all the way through early Wednesday. CBS and ABC will hand over their entire prime-time coverage to election results, and will return for more coverage overnight.

Because the results span hundreds of local races, midterm nights do not always offer the same tidy on-air narrative that a presidential election promises. But with the balance of power in Congress at stake — and Democrats and Republicans alike calling the evening existential — executives are expecting significant audience interest in Tuesday’s returns.

Here is a look at how the broadcast and cable networks, as well as some of the newer digital outlets, are covering the results.

The Broadcast Networks

NBC will start coverage at 5 p.m. Eastern, and won’t stop until 6 a.m. Wednesday. (Local affiliates will have the opportunity to take the entire package, or to take breaks for their local newscasts.)

The network’s coverage will be helmed by the “Today” anchor Savannah Guthrie, the “Nightly News” anchor Tom Llamas, the “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker and the correspondent Hallie Jackson. The popular data-cruncher Steve Kornacki will return to his usual perch, ready to frantically punch at his big board. The “Kornacki Cam,” a continuous livestream of the NBC data analyst, will go live at 5:30 p.m.

CBS formally kicks off coverage at 7 p.m., led by the “Evening News” anchor Tony Dokoupil, the morning show co-hosts Gayle King and Norah O’Donnell, and the “Face the Nation” moderator Margaret Brennan. A livestreamed “Nerd Show” featuring the network’s polling experts will simultaneously air online from 5 p.m. to 2 a.m.

And ABC will kick off four consecutive hours of coverage at 7 p.m., with the “World News Tonight” anchor David Muir leading the coverage. Mr. Muir, along with a team that includes “World News Tonight” Sunday anchor Linsey Davis and “This Week” co-anchor Martha Raddatz, will be live for seven consecutive hours on ABC News Live, Hulu and Disney+.

The Cable Networks

Fox News’s coverage will be hosted by the anchors Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum, with Bill Hemmer utilizing the interactive digital map known as “The Bill Board.” An A.I. chatbot has been created on the channel’s app so users can ask specific questions about ongoing results. And Arnon Mishkin, the cello-playing pollster, will again be in charge of the network’s decision desk.

Jake Tapper and Anderson Cooper will lead CNN’s coverage, which includes John King and his usual “magic wall,” the name of his touch screen interactive map. The network said Mr. King would be outfitted with multiple magic walls for the first time, featuring additional data. On MS NOW, Rachel Maddow will lead an ensemble team including network favorites like Nicolle Wallace and Ari Melber. The anchor Ali Velshi is in charge of the “Big Board,” its digital interactive map.

Digital Livestreams

Of course, there will be hundreds of online sources for voters to consult, too. Nate Silver, the veteran election forecaster, will host a livestream with, among others, the writer Matt Yglesias. The Dispatch will host another livestream that begins at 9 p.m. Eastern. Chuck Todd and Chris Cillizza are collaborating with Decision Desk HQ, a polling and results-counting service, for livestreamed coverage. (The NewsNation cable network will also be using data from Decision Desk for its five-hour special beginning at 7 p.m.) The Free Press will also have a livestream with Mark Halperin’s video platform, “2WAY.”

Late-Night Shows

There will be, however, few late-night shows offering an on-the-fly comedic take on the results. CBS’s “Late Show” with Stephen Colbert, which regularly aired live episodes on major election nights, was canceled this year. NBC’s extensive coverage means there will be no reactions from Seth Meyers or Jimmy Fallon. “The Daily Show” has a new episode (with Ronny Chieng hosting), but it is taping in the late afternoon.

ABC’s “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” will air a new episode in its usual slot at 11:35 p.m., but it will not be live. Still, there could be some news. “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” is taping later than usual — after 9 p.m. Eastern — so it can incorporate some early results, and Mr. Kimmel’s guests will be the progressive hosts from the “Pod Save America” podcast.

How will tonight go? Here are the races that will provide early clues.

On Election Day, states where polls close and ballot counting begins early could offer the first concrete clues for how the rest of the night will go, with control of Congress on the line.

Here are some poll closures to watch in the first hours of election night. All times are Eastern.

6 p.m.: Kentucky and Indiana

President Trump won Kentucky’s Sixth Congressional District by 15 points in 2024, but its House race this year has been rated a tossup by nonpartisan election forecasters. If the Democratic candidate, Zach Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy veteran, beats the Republican, Dr. Ralph Alvarado, a physician and former state senator endorsed by Mr. Trump, it would signal Democrats’ strength overall.

In Indiana’s traditionally conservative Fifth District, Representative Victoria Spartz, a Republican, won by about 19 points in 2024 and is favored to retain the seat on Tuesday, according to forecasters. But her lead has narrowed the area, where Democrats are usually not competitive. If the winner is her Democratic challenger, State Senator J.D. Ford, it could signal broader Democratic victories.

Democrats do not usually win votes from rural white voters in either district, and if one or both Democratic candidates prevail, that “would indicate that we are winning in a way that is going to translate across the country in many similar districts,” said CJ Warnke, a spokesman for the House Majority PAC, the biggest super PAC for House Democrats.

If a Republican wins either race, it could mean that their party might mitigate its losses elsewhere.

7 p.m.: Florida

Republican state lawmakers redrew several congressional districts to favor their party. Despite that, analysts say many of these districts have close races. If Democrats win in the Seventh, Ninth, 14th, 22nd or 25th Districts, it could bode well for them elsewhere.

Republican victories in these districts could mean that the party’s redistricting efforts successfully blocked a Democratic surge during a difficult year for Republicans.

Republicans are favored to win the Senate and governor’s races in Florida, according to analysts. But Democrats have lately been hopeful about the governor’s race, where David Jolly, the Democratic nominee, is challenging Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican. If Democrats win the Senate and governor’s races, they are having a very good night.

Even if there is a victory for Mr. Donalds or the Republican incumbent in the Senate, Ashley Moody, Democrats may find that some demographic groups bear watching.

Each Hispanic and Black community in the United States is unique, but significant shifts in how the groups vote in South Florida could indicate how Democrats elsewhere, like James Talarico in the Texas Senate race, will fare. Hispanic voters, who make up about a third of the Texas electorate, are a key swing voting bloc in the state.

7 p.m.: South Carolina

South Carolina’s First District has not only been traditionally conservative-leaning, but it has also been gerrymandered by Republicans to further benefit their party. Still, the race has been rated a tossup by analysts.

If Nancy Lacore, a Democratic former Navy admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, wins the open seat over Jenny Costa Honeycutt, a Republican local councilwoman and lawyer, it would signal that a strong Democratic candidate could win in red territory elsewhere in the country. But if Ms. Honeycutt wins, it could reflect the strength of the region’s conservative base and the redrawn district lines.

The chances of a Democratic victory in the state’s Senate race are slimmer, but the lead held by Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, has narrowed throughout her campaign. If she loses to Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician running as a Democrat, that could mean that Republicans may lose their majority in the upper chamber.

7 p.m.: Virginia

Virginia’s Second District traditionally swings, and analysts said that the Democratic candidate, former Representative Elaine Luria, was favored to flip it. The result could indicate whether a strong Republican candidate like Jen Kiggans, a two-term incumbent, can survive Democratic momentum.

Mr. Trump won the neighboring First District by five points in 2024, but analysts said the House race there this year was a tossup. If Shannon Taylor, a Democratic prosecutor, defeats Representative Rob Wittman, a Republican first elected in 2007, Democrats could be in for a great night.

Voters prepare to deliver a verdict on Trump’s second term.

For the last two months, President Trump has offered a consistent plea: Pretend he’s on the ballot.

The midterm elections on Tuesday will give voters an opportunity to do just that. They are set to render the first national referendum on a second-term Trump agenda characterized by far-reaching tariffs, an unpopular war with Iran and an aggressive immigration crackdown.

Republican officials are bracing for a harsh judgment and potentially significant defeats. They widely expect to lose control of the House. They have grown increasingly worried about losing the Senate, too.

Democrats have sought to define their campaigns through anger over high prices driven by tariffs and the war, focusing heavily on the idea of making life cost less. Led by Mr. Trump, Republicans have struggled to articulate an affirmative counterargument, with the president dismissing concerns about the economy and sending an often scattered message.

American politics is of course full of surprises. While Republicans have underperformed in both midterm elections of the Trump era, the president has demonstrated his ability to turn out his most loyal supporters. He has also stepped up his baseless attacks on the U.S. election system, raising fears of federal interference in the results.

Democrats need a net gain of just three House seats to win a majority. The Senate is a heavier lift: Democrats must hold all of their seats and flip at least four Republican-held ones. They are competing in states like Texas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988, and Kansas, which has not done so since 1932.

And if Democrats flip at least two Republican-held governorships, they will hold a majority of them for the first time since 2010, when a backlash to President Barack Obama fueled a Republican wave that has shaped American politics ever since.

Polls will close starting at 6 p.m. Eastern. The results that follow will shape the country for at least the next two years, and perhaps much longer. Here are six themes to watch as voting ends:

How deep into Republican territory can Democrats reach?

Look at where the competitive races were in the final days of the campaign.

Solidly red Kansas and Ohio have tossup Senate races. Democrats are seriously contending in House districts like the one in northern New York being vacated by Representative Elise Stefanik — where Mr. Trump won by 21 percentage points two years ago.

Governor’s races are tight in conservative states like Florida, Nebraska and Oklahoma, where Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, the chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, spent Monday night stumping for the party’s nominee. The last Democratic presidential candidate to win even a single county in Oklahoma was Al Gore in 2000.

Over the weekend, Republicans rushed money into Louisiana’s Senate race, which had not been considered a competitive contest before then. Both parties have also directed late money to the Senate races in Mississippi and South Carolina, states that have been out of reach for Democrats for a generation.

With Democrats widely expected to win races in at least some red House districts and threatening to flip Senate seats in deep-red states, the question is how far into Republican terrain they can prevail.

How angry are voters about Trump’s handling of the economy?

Voters care most about whether they can afford their everyday needs, and polls suggest that they are angered about the high prices brought on by tariffs and a war ordered by Mr. Trump.

The president spent the day before the election talking about his alterations to the Reflecting Pool in Washington. Over the last few weeks, some of his most memorable rally lines have been about the anatomies of Republican Senate candidates.

Mr. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to record lows. Republican candidates who have recast their political identities in his image are struggling to convince voters that they can be independent.

In many cases, Republicans have not even tried to make a case that the economy is in good shape. Instead, they have tried to change the subject.

In Michigan’s Senate race, former Representative Mike Rogers has sought to push the Muslim faith and family background of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, to the center of the campaign. In Texas, voters have seen an onslaught of Republican ads about how James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, talked about transgender rights in the past. And in Maine, Senator Susan Collins is selling voters on the idea that her seniority after four terms is best for her state.

If Democrats win the House, how big will their majority be?

We could know fairly early in the evening what kind of night it will be for the House.

In Indiana and the eastern half of Kentucky, polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern. There are tight races in Kentucky’s Sixth Congressional District, which Mr. Trump carried by 15 points in 2024, and Indiana’s Fifth District, which he won by 17 points.

Both are competitive races that will reveal some of the first clues about the rest of the electoral map. They are districts that combine rural and suburban voters and are usually safe for Republicans.

There are dozens of similar House districts across the country.

Nevada’s Second District covers Reno and the state’s rural northern half. Mr. Trump carried it by 14 points. It is not a place where Democrats typically compete. But this year, Democrats have a strong candidate, the Republican incumbent is retiring and the party’s candidate is considered weak while a potential third-party spoiler is poised to siphon conservative votes with help from Democrats.

Districts like these will determine how big of a cushion House Democrats might have when new members are seated come January.

What’s the fallout from the national redistricting fight?

Starting with Texas last summer, Republican-led states began redrawing their congressional district lines to try to secure more House seats for their party.

The new maps were based on the idea that the electorate in 2026 would look somewhat like the one that carried Mr. Trump to victory in 2024.

That does not seem to be the case.

Latino voters have turned against Mr. Trump, shifting the politics of South Texas and South Florida, where Republicans tried to lock in advantages. Rural voters are furious about the price of diesel fuel. Black voters, early voting data suggests, are turning out in huge numbers.

The result is that House districts drawn with the express intent of putting them in Republican hands instead have competitive races. In Texas, Florida, Tennessee and North Carolina, there are increasingly tight races in districts Mr. Trump would have carried by double digits had they existed in 2024.

Meantime in California, voters approved a plan aimed at delivering five House seats for Democrats, and redistricting does not seem to have placed any of the party’s seats at risk.

How all of these races go may have ramifications beyond immediate House control. Several states are weighing redrawing their congressional maps before the 2028 elections. If this year’s new maps backfire, it could temper the aggression of next year’s cartographers.

What about all the Republican money?

Elon Musk spent at least $474 million to back Republicans in the midterm elections. The next four biggest donors are also Republicans. And Mr. Trump had an unmatched war chest.

If Republicans defy expectations, it will be at least in part because of a financial advantage built long before races became tight in the campaign’s final weeks.

At the same time, Democratic officials involved in House and Senate races have lamented that they do not have the money to compete in as many districts and states as they would like.

The Texas governor’s race, for example, became a source of frustration for Latino Democrats. For weeks, they have been angry that the party did not invest more in Gina Hinojosa, a state representative who polls show is running even or close behind Gov. Greg Abbott, the three-term incumbent Republican.

House Democratic officials have privately ticked through a series of districts where they believed they had chances to win if only they had more resources available.

Will Democrats be hurt by their Senate-race dramas?

The red-state Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina are competitive in part because Democrats have nominated a generally strong slate of candidates who have mostly avoided major problems on the campaign trail.

That’s not the case for their blue-state brethren.

Maine Democrats switched out their candidate in July after the primary winner, Graham Platner, was forced out of the race after a rape allegation, which he denied.

Michigan was convulsed this weekend by a late endorsement flip, with Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to Dr. El-Sayed, defecting and backing the Republican in the race, Mr. Rogers.

And in light-blue Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has led in polling in her Senate race despite being trailed by the state’s major fraud scandal and being viewed as running one of the party’s weakest campaigns.

There’s also Alaska, where a New York Times report last week about Democratic chicanery to help Mary Peltola, the party’s nominee for Senate, by recruiting a second Dan Sullivan into the race set off a wave of Republican anger.

Polls show the Democratic nominees leading or with an edge in all four races, but some of these contests — especially in Michigan and Maine, where Ms. Collins, the incumbent Republican, is a formidable opponent — have required more resources and attention than party leaders would have preferred.
